verses.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Mahā Pāla is the elder son of a rich man of Sāvatthī who got his children by a vow to the spirit of a great tree. He hears the Buddha teach, gives his whole estate to his younger brother, and becomes a monk. Spending the rains in a border village with sixty companions, he vows not to lie down for three months. His eyes fail, a physician's ointment does nothing, and one night his sight and his defilements go out together, and he wakes an arahant, blind. On the road home his nephew, newly ordained to make the journey safe, leaves him in the forest for a woman he hears singing as she gathers firewood, and Sakka, king of the gods, takes the end of his staff and brings him to Sāvatthī by a short way. When visiting monks find insects crushed on his walking path after rain, the Buddha says that he did not see them and meant no killing, and that his blindness came from a former life in which, as a physician, he blinded a woman who had cheated him of his fee.
bg.history:
Methodism grew quickly during the Revolution on the Delmarva Peninsula, between the Chesapeake and the Delaware. Many of its preachers would not swear the state oaths, and patriots suspected them of loyalism. Francis Asbury spent most of a year sheltered in Delaware, Joseph Hartley was jailed in Talbot County and preached to the townspeople through the bars, and Freeborn Garrettson was jailed at Cambridge in 1780, sleeping on the floor with his saddlebags for a pillow. That same year the preachers' conference declared slavery “contrary to the law of God, man, and nature” and required traveling preachers who held slaves to promise to free them. By 1783 the movement had eighty-two traveling preachers. The early conference minutes are reprinted in Nathan Bangs's history of the Methodist Episcopal Church. Mr. Wesley's definition of sin, “a voluntary transgression of a known law of God,” comes from a 1772 letter to Elizabeth Bennis.

Under a Maryland act of 1752, a master could free an enslaved person only by a deed under hand and seal, witnessed by two people, acknowledged before a justice and recorded within six months, and only if the person freed was no older than fifty and able to earn a living. The seventeen-year cicadas of Brood X, which colonists called locusts, came up across Maryland and Delaware in 1766 and again in 1783; Benjamin Banneker remembered both emergences. The Great Cypress Swamp on the Maryland–Delaware line, now the largest forest on the Peninsula, was cut for shingle timber and drained for farming, and one peat fire burned there so long that people called it the Burnt Swamp. Ointment of tutty, a crude zinc oxide salve, was mainly used for sore eyes.

sections.heading: I. The Oak
sections.text: Thomas Haddaway had eleven hundred acres on the Choptank, a brick house laid in Flemish bond with the glazed headers making a checkerboard down the gable end, a landing where the sloops took his tobacco down the bay to the London ships, and fifty-three people in the quarters who did the work. He had been married nine years and had no child. One evening in August he was riding home from swimming his horses in the river and saw at the head of Island Creek a white oak so wide that he got down and walked around it, counting his steps. Twenty-two. It stood alone in a field gone to briars, full of birds. He was not a praying man. But he stood a while in the shade of it and thought that a tree like that must have somebody in it. The next week he had the briars grubbed out and the oak fenced with split rails, and strips of red cloth tied on the low limbs. Then he stood inside the fence with his hat in his hand and said out loud, so that the men who had done the grubbing heard it and told it afterward in the quarters, If I get a child of my own I will do you honor all my life. His wife was brought to bed of a son the next spring, and they named him Levin. Three years later came another boy,

sections.heading: II. The Swamp
sections.text: He rode five years. He rode the Dorset circuit and the Kent and the Sussex, preaching every day and twice on Sundays in barns and kitchens and under trees, and slept in lofts with the hired men. They were dangerous years for a Methodist on the Peninsula. Many of the preachers would not take the state oath, and the patriots took them for Tories. Levin saw a preacher locked in the Easton jail who went on preaching through the grate to the people in the street, until the town said that if they did not let him out he would convert the whole county. Levin himself spent one night in the Cambridge jail with his saddlebags for a pillow. In 1780 the Conference in Baltimore resolved that slavery was contrary to the law of God, man, and nature, and required every traveling preacher who held slaves to promise to set them free. Levin held none. He had given them to his brother. Nothing was required of him. In May of 1782, at the Conference in Baltimore, he found Eli Truitt sitting on a bench in the yard of the preaching house with a handkerchief to his mouth, and sat down beside him. Brother Truitt. How many duties are there in this work? Two. The books and the closet. The books is the Bible an

sections.heading: III. Tutty
sections.text: By the first of December his eyes had begun to run. The water came out of them all day and all night, the way it comes out of a cracked jar, and they were red to the lids and swollen, and every morning they were gummed shut and he had to wet them open with his fingers. The peat was still smoldering in the swamp from the summer, and the cabin chimney drew badly, and there was smoke in everything. The young men saw his face and asked what was the matter. The wind cuts my eyes, brothers. Dr. Hudson said to send for him. Send, then. Hudson sent back a little pot of ointment of tutty, the grey kind that comes in a white jar, and said to lay it along the lids at night. Levin laid it on, sitting on his stool. A week later Hudson met him on the Snow Hill road. I hear the wind is at your eyes, Mr. Haddaway. That's so. Did you use the tutty? I did. And how are they? The same. Hudson frowned. One pot of tutty had never failed him. When you put it on, were you sitting up, or lying down? Levin said nothing. Hudson asked again, and a third time, and Levin sat his horse and did not say a word, and that afternoon Hudson rode out to Burnt Branch himself. The preachers were out. He went into the cab

sections.heading: IV. The Coat
sections.dateline: Burnt Branch and Talbot County · April and May, 1783
sections.text: The peace came in April. A shingle wagon brought the news back from Snow Hill, and the shingle-getters fired off every gun in the settlement, and that week the young men came to Levin together. Brother, the Conference sits in Baltimore at the end of May. We want to go up and see Brother Truitt. He had thought about it already. Between the swamp and the Choptank there were sixty miles of bad road, and thickets a man could lose himself in for a week, and men in the woods who had gone there in the war and had not come out. If he went with them they would have to lead him every step and go hungry for it. You go on ahead. And you? I'm weak, and you'd only be slow on my account. Go on. When you get to my brother, tell him I've lost my eyes, and he'll send somebody down for me. Give my love to Brother Truitt, and to all of them. They argued, and he would not hear it, and at last they asked his pardon for arguing and went. The people of Burnt Branch walked with them out to the end of the causeway, crying, and stood there until they were out of sight. They came up the Choptank road in the second week of May, and Littleton Haddaway knew them by their coats before they were through the gate.

sections.heading: V. The Lightwood Song
sections.text: They had come most of the way through the swamp by the old shingle road when they passed the camp at Bald Cypress, where Levin had preached the first autumn. Beyond the camp, off in the trees, a woman was singing as she gathered lightwood for her fire. Levin could hear the dry sticks snapping and the voice going on over them, not loud, a long sad song about a young man dying of love and a hard-hearted girl, Barbara Allen, the one everybody knows. Her voice went into the woods and came back. There is no sound on earth that goes into a young man like a woman's voice. Kemp heard it and stopped walking, and stood there, and Levin felt the end of the staff go loose in his hand. Wait here a minute, Uncle. I have some business. He went off through the trees. Levin stood in the road. The singing went on a little longer. Then it stopped, all at once, in the middle of a line, and did not start again. Levin stood with the staff and thought: I heard somebody singing just now, and it was a woman. And the boy is a long time about his business. And he knew. After a while Kemp came back through the leaves. All right, Uncle, let's be off. Kemp. Have you done wrong? Kemp said nothing. Levin asked hi

sections.heading: VI. The Short Way
sections.text: He stood long enough for the birds to come back. Then somebody was near him in the road, shuffling his feet in the leaves the way a man does who doesn't want to come on you by surprise. Who is it? A traveler, sir, going up to Talbot. Where are you bound? To Talbot too. Then let's go together. I'm slow. I'll keep you back. I'm in no hurry, the man said. And it's a good work to help a preacher on his way. Let's go together. He had a voice like anybody's. Levin thought, this is some good Methodist from up the road. All right. Take hold of the end of the staff. The man took it, and they walked. Levin knew the roads by their feel. Sand and black muck and the logs of the causeway, then the long sand ridges, then the clay. It seemed to him the ground changed under his feet faster than ground should. It was evening when he heard a gun, far off, and then drums, and church bells under the drums, and he stopped in the road. Where is that? That's Easton, sir. They're still firing for the peace. Easton. Levin stood very still. Friend, when I came down that road last fall it took us the better part of three days. I know a short way. And Levin knew then that whoever had the end of his staff was n

sections.heading: VII. The Brood
sections.text: The Conference rose in Baltimore at the end of May, and three of the young preachers coming down the Peninsula turned in at the Haddaway landing because they had heard there was a blind preacher there who had been made perfect in a swamp. They came up the creek road at evening, and a storm came up off the bay with them, and they turned back to the big house and said they would go down to the cabin in the morning. It rained hard until midnight. Then it stopped. Levin had always been a walker. In the last hours of the night he came out and walked the brick path Littleton had laid for him, from the cabin door to the fence of the oak, forty steps and forty back, until the birds started. That night, all over Talbot County, the ground opened. It had been seventeen years. The rain had softened the earth and the warm night had come after it, and out of every inch of ground under every tree the locusts came up, brown and blind and wet, by the thousands, and crawled up whatever was nearest to split their backs and come out of themselves. They came up through the cracks between the bricks of the path. They crawled across it toward the oak. Levin walked up and down on them in the dark and did

sections.heading: VIII. The Husks
sections.text: When the preachers had ridden on, Levin asked Isaac to take him out to the oak. Isaac took the end of the staff and led him in through the gate of the old fence, where the red rags still hung on the low limbs, faded to pink, and sat him down with his back against the trunk. Levin put his hands out on the bark on either side of him. It was covered with the husks. They were dry already, and light as paper, each one hooked into the bark by its little feet and split straight down the back where the thing inside had climbed out of it and gone on up into the leaves, and the leaves overhead were roaring with them. He sat a long time feeling them. Then he asked Isaac whether Hester Copper was living. She's living. She stays with her daughter, in Easton, back of the courthouse. Will you take me there tomorrow? Isaac did not answer right away. He looked at the man sitting against the oak with his white eyes and his hands full of empty shells. I'll take you, he said. What she does about it is up to her. In the morning Isaac took the tip of the staff, and they went up the Easton road together, slowly, with the noise in every tree on both sides of them, and the dry husks coming loose from the b

title: Locust Year
logline: A Choptank planter gives his estate to his brother, rides with the Methodists, and vows not to lie down all winter.

verses.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with a pure thought, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin of Sāvatthī is so stingy that people call him Adinnapubbaka, “Never Gave.” He beats out a pair of earrings for his only son himself to save a goldsmith's fee, so the boy is known as Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, “Burnished Earrings.” When the son falls ill with jaundice, the father doses him with home remedies rather than pay a physician, and when the boy is dying he lays him out on the terrace so that visitors will not see the wealth inside. The Buddha, passing on his alms round, sends out a ray of light; the boy turns, sees him, and dies with a heart full of faith, and is reborn among the gods. Later he appears to his grieving father at the cremation ground, weeping for a pair of wheels for his golden chariot, and asks for the sun and the moon. The father, shamed out of his grief, takes refuge, invites the Buddha to a meal, and asks whether anyone reaches heaven by faith alone.
bg.history:
After 1975, and above all after the boat exodus that began in 1978, refugees from Vietnam settled in Westminster and Garden Grove, and by the mid-1980s their business district was known as Little Saigon, now the largest concentration of Vietnamese people outside Vietnam. Many first-generation families ran small businesses such as nail salons and restaurants. The boat people often paid for their passage in gold, and many passed through camps like the one on Pulau Bidong in Malaysia. A 1992 study for U.S. law enforcement described home-invasion gangs that chose victims they believed ran businesses and kept their savings at home instead of in banks. Gold passed a thousand dollars an ounce for the first time in March 2008, as the financial crisis began.

About one in twelve Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders lives with chronic hepatitis B, according to the Centers for Disease Control, as many as two in three of them without knowing it, and the group accounts for more than half of all Americans with the infection. In Vietnam, as across East Asia, Pure Land devotion to the Buddha Amitābha is an important part of Buddhist practice. His eighteenth vow promises rebirth in his western paradise, Sukhāvatī, to anyone who sincerely trusts him and calls on him even ten times. The Amitābha Sūtra, or Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha, describes that land's golden sands and jewel trees and its lotuses as large as chariot wheels. The passages in the story are from F. Max Müller's translations of the two Sukhāvatīvyūha sūtras in the Sacred Books of the East (1894).

sections.heading: I. Uncle No
sections.text: Phạm Văn Lộc came out of Vietnam in 1980 on a fishing boat with fourteen taels of gold leaf sewn flat into the waistband of his trousers, paid nine of them to the boat owner, two to a guard on the beach, one to a man on Pulau Bidong for a place in the shade, and arrived in Orange County with two. He never forgot the arithmetic. In twenty-eight years he never again paid one cent for anything he could get for nothing or do with his own hands. By 2008 he owned two nail salons on Brookhurst Street and a ranch house on a side street off Bolsa, paid for in cash. He did his own taxes, his own plumbing and his own haircuts, and they looked it. He drove a 1994 Camry with a cracked dashboard. At Tết he put one-dollar bills in the red envelopes, new ones, so they would crackle. He had never given the temple so much as an orange, and the whole of Little Saigon called him Chú Không, Uncle No, because no was the answer to everything, and he did not mind it. A man named No keeps what he has. What he had, he kept mostly in a floor safe under the carpet in the bedroom closet, in gold. He did not trust banks. In Saigon he had watched the banks close and the money change overnight and the people who

sections.heading: II. Yellow
sections.text: In March of the year he turned sixteen, Bảo's eyes went yellow. It started as tiredness. He fell asleep in class. He stopped eating. Then one morning Thu looked at him across the breakfast table and put down her spoon, because the whites of his eyes were the color of old piano keys, and by the end of the week his skin had gone the same color, and his urine was dark as tea. Anh. He's sick. Take him to the doctor. A doctor means the hospital. The hospital means three thousand dollars before they say hello. We have no insurance. You want to give them the house? Then what will you do? I'll take care of it, said Lộc. Without throwing money in the street. He went to the herb shops on Bolsa, one after the other, and asked at each one what they gave for yellow eyes, as if he were asking about the weather. At each one they told him nhân trần, and gardenia, and rhubarb root, and he wrote it down. He bought the cheapest he could find and brewed it himself on the back burner in an old aluminum pot, and the whole house smelled of it, bitter, like wet hay. Bảo drank it. Bảo got worse. By the middle of April he could not get up the stairs, and then he could not get out of bed, and his belly swell

sections.heading: III. The Garage
sections.dateline: Before dawn, the last day of April
sections.text: Two streets over there was a temple in a ranch house. The lawn had been taken out and gravel put down, and in the middle of the gravel stood a white statue of Quan Âm taller than the mailbox, pouring water from a vase, and on the porch there was a rack for shoes. Three nuns lived there in gray robes with shaved heads. The neighborhood called the eldest of them, who was not old, Sư Cô Tịnh Liên. Every morning at five-thirty she walked to the bakery on Bolsa to buy bread for the others and walked back, and she went by the Phạm house both ways. That morning, the other nuns said afterward, she went out a quarter of an hour early and took the long way around, which she never did. Old Mr. Huỳnh across the street was always out in his driveway at that hour, doing his exercises, and he is the one who told it. He said the boy was lying on the cot in the open garage with his face to the wall, toward the house, where his father had put him. He said the nun came up the sidewalk in the dark with her bag of bread, and stopped at the foot of the driveway, and looked in. The boy did not see her. Then, Mr. Huỳnh said, a light came out from her. Not from a flashlight. From her. It went up the drivew

sections.heading: IV. The Wall
sections.dateline: The memorial park on Beach Boulevard · May and June
sections.text: They cremated him on a Thursday. Lộc paid for the cheapest container the funeral home would allow and argued about the price of the chapel. He took the gold studs out of his son's ears himself before they closed the lid and put them in his shirt pocket, and he did not know why he did it, and he kept them there. The urn went into a niche in the long granite wall at the memorial park on Beach Boulevard, the third row from the top, with a little brass vase and a photograph behind glass of Bảo in his school shirt, grinning, with the lumpy studs showing. Then something happened to Uncle No that nobody on the side street had expected. He began to go to the wall every day. He went before he opened the salons and again after he closed them. He stood in front of the niche in his work clothes with his hands at his sides and cried out loud, in front of anybody, the way the old women cry at funerals in the countryside, and the groundskeepers learned to leave that row for last. Bảo ơi. Con ở đâu? Bảo. Where are you? He stopped eating. He let the salons run themselves. He stood in front of the wall in the sun until the security guard came and asked him to go home. Thu bought the paper offerings

sections.heading: V. Wheels
sections.text: It was a weekday, past noon, and the memorial park was empty except for the sprinklers. Lộc stood at the wall saying what he always said. After a while he became aware that someone else was crying, not far off. A boy, at the end of the same row of niches, sixteen or so, in a school shirt, with both hands over his face, sobbing like a child. Lộc thought, I am crying because my son is dead. What is that boy crying for? He went down the row. Hey. Em. Why are you crying? You're young. You have everything. What's the matter? The boy took his hands away from his face. He looked very much like Bảo. He wore two gold studs in his ears. Lộc could not stop looking at them. I have a car, the boy said. A beautiful car. All gold. But it doesn't have any wheels. I've looked everywhere and I can't find wheels for it, and without wheels I'm going to die. Lộc wiped his face on his sleeve. Something in his chest that had been closed since April came open a crack, and what came through was the oldest thing in him, the thing that had sewn gold into its trousers and got off the boat with two taels left. That's all? Wheels? I'll get you wheels. Tell me what kind. Gold? Jade? Chrome? Silver? Tell me, and

sections.heading: VI. The Meal
sections.dateline: The house on the side street · a Sunday in July
sections.text: He went home and told Thu they were inviting the Sư Cô and the other nuns to the house to be fed. Thu sat down on the kitchen floor. Then he walked the two streets to the temple in his work clothes. He did not take off his shoes on the porch, or bow to the Buddha on the altar, or greet anyone. He found Sư Cô Tịnh Liên in the kitchen cutting tofu and stood in the doorway. Sư Cô. Come with the others and eat at my house on Sunday. I want to ask you something. She looked at him, and at his shoes, and put down the knife, and said yes. He spent more money that week than he had spent in twenty-eight years. He hired a vegetarian caterer on Bolsa and ordered everything on the list. He bought new folding tables and borrowed chairs from the salons, and a white cloth for the table where the nuns would sit, and set up an altar in the living room with Bảo's photograph and a bowl of oranges stacked in a pyramid, the most expensive oranges in the market. The whole side street came, and half of Bolsa. They came the way people come to see an accident. Some of them came because Chú Không was paying for a meal and they wanted to see it with their own eyes. Some of them came because they had heard he

sections.heading: VII. Sun and Moon
sections.text: People on the side street said afterward that the money came out of that house the way water comes out of a broken main. The temple got a new roof, and a parking lot that satisfied the city, and a van. The herb shop on Bolsa found an envelope under its door with a note in it, for the next family who cannot pay. The forty-dollar jeweler got forty dollars and did not know what for. At Tết the children on the side street opened their red envelopes and found hundred-dollar bills, so new they crackled, and ran to show their mothers. Nobody called him Chú Không after that, though for a while nobody could think what else to call him. He kept the gold studs. He did not give those away. He set them on the altar in the living room in front of Bảo's photograph, side by side on a saucer, the two lumpy yellow things he had hammered out on the vise in the garage to save forty dollars. In the mornings, when he lit the incense before he went to open the salons, the sun came in low through the front window and lay across the altar, and one of the studs, the bigger one, caught it and burned like a coal. The other one sat just outside the light, in the shadow of the incense bowl, pale and round and p

title: Uncle No
logline: A Little Saigon miser who hammered his son's earrings himself won't pay for a doctor when the boy's eyes turn yellow.

verses.text: "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.
"He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"--in those who do not harbour such thoughts hatred will cease.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Tissa is the Buddha’s older cousin, his father’s sister’s son, who becomes a monk as a fat old man and takes to sitting in the middle of the monastery hall in well-pressed robes. Visiting monks mistake him for a great elder and offer to wait on him. When a young monk learns that he has not kept a single rains retreat, which is how monks count seniority, he rebukes him and snaps his fingers. Tissa goes weeping to the Buddha, who asks whether he rose, took the visitors’ things, brought water or seats, or rubbed their feet, and then tells him to ask their pardon. He refuses. The Buddha then tells of the ascetic Devala, who lay down across a doorway, was stepped on twice by the ascetic Nārada, and cursed him: at sunrise his head should split in seven. Nārada, seeing that the curse would fall on Devala himself, kept the sun from rising until the king forced Devala to bow, and then saved him with a lump of clay and a pond.
bg.history:
The Koyukuk drains the south slope of the Brooks Range, north of the Arctic Circle. In the summer of 1898, overflow from the Klondike rush went up it by steamboat; one stampeder later remembered sixty-eight small steamers frozen in that autumn with nine hundred people aboard, most of whom walked out over the ice (the account is quoted in the National Park Service history of the region, Gaunt Beauty, Tenuous Life). The camps that lasted were far upriver at Coldfoot and Wiseman, supplied by horse-drawn scows from Bettles in summer and by a monthly dog-team mail in winter. By the early 1920s only about a hundred white miners remained, living beside Koyukon Athabascan and Kobuk Iñupiaq families, many of whom had ties to the Episcopal mission of St. John’s-in-the-Wilderness at Allakaket. The forester Robert Marshall described the district a few years later in Arctic Village. A later chapter of the same history covers the 1920s. Notch Creek, its roadhouse and its ridge are invented. In a camp under a ridge at that latitude the sun stays hidden for weeks in midwinter, and its return was the great day of the year. A newcomer, or cheechako, became a sourdough by staying through a winter.

Many of the Gaelic-speaking Presbyterians of Cape Breton came from the Highlands and Hebrides in the early nineteenth century and kept the old way of singing the metrical psalms without instruments, a precentor giving out each line and the congregation singing it back, a practice called lining out. The psalm Murdo sings is from the Scottish Psalter of 1650, the English metrical version approved by the Church of Scotland and still in use. The verse from Ephesians is given in the King James Version.

sections.heading: I. The Chair
sections.dateline: Notch Creek, Middle Fork of the Koyukuk, Alaska Territory · autumn 1922
sections.text: Murdo Morrison kept the roadhouse at Notch Creek, seventy miles north of the Arctic Circle, and the men on the creeks called him the Precentor. In the church on the North Shore of St. Ann’s Bay, in Cape Breton, where he was raised, there was no organ and no hymnbook. There were the psalms of David in Gaelic, and one man who stood under the pulpit and gave out each line for the people to sing after him. Murdo’s father had been that man, and Murdo after him for two years, until he went over the Chilkoot in the spring of ’98 with a sack of oatmeal and a borrowed sled. He had not sat under a minister since. He kept the psalms. On Sunday nights he sang one at the stove, giving out the line to nobody, and the Swedes and the Irishmen and the one Montenegrin in the room let him get on with it, the way you let a man wind his watch. He was fifty-four years old and had twenty-four winters in. In that country a man’s age was his winters. Summers did not count, because anybody can stand a summer. A man who had seen the ice come and seen it go out again was a sourdough, and a man who had not was a cheechako if he was seventy, and when two teams met on a trail too narrow to pass, the driver with

sections.heading: II. Mail Day
sections.text: The mail came once a month by dog team, relayed up from Tanana, and in January it came on the seventh, two days ahead of the sun, so that anybody who could travel was at Morrison’s already or on the way. Billy Dunne drove the upper end of the contract. He was twenty-six and had nine winters in, having come into the country at seventeen, and he was vain of them the way a boy is vain of his first moustache. Three sleds came in behind him that afternoon, in the blue dusk that passed for the middle of the day. Tom Skaggs drove the first. He had come over the pass to the Yukon in ’86, ten years before anybody heard the word Klondike, and he had thirty-six winters in, and had left the end of his nose and two fingers in the worst of them. Hans Lien had walked off a farm in Goodhue County, Minnesota, at nineteen, and had twenty-five. He carried his mother’s blue china cup in his grub box, the one with the chip, and drank from nothing else. On the third sled were Jonas and Mary, Kobuk people, baptized with those names at the mission down at Allakaket. They hunted sheep and caribou for the camp, and nobody tried to count their winters, since their grandparents had wintered on that river befo

sections.heading: III. The Flour Bin
sections.text: Murdo came in from the cache with frost on his eyebrows and the bucksaw in his hand. He found his cousin sitting on the flour bin with tears running into his collar, and four men and a woman standing along the wall. Norman. What is it? You’re crying. These people have insulted me. Where were you sitting? In the chair. By the stove. Did you see them come in? I saw them. Did you get up? I did not. Did you take their mitts from them, or their robes? No. Did you see to their dogs? Did you get them water? No. Did you bring any of them a seat? Did you look at their feet? I did not. Murdo laid the saw on the table. Norman, every one of those things was yours to do, for every one of them. A man who won’t do them has no business in that chair. The fault here is yours and nobody else’s. Ask their pardon. They insulted me, Murdo. That boy snapped his fingers in my face. I’ll not ask pardon of the like of them. Don’t be this way. The fault is yours. Ask their pardon. I will not. He’s a stubborn old man, Murdo, said Tom Skaggs from the wall. He said it without heat. He is that. And it isn’t new. We can see for ourselves what he is now, Tom said. What do you mean, it isn’t new? Sit down, the lot

sections.heading: IV. Potter’s Cabin
sections.text: The first winter, Murdo said, was the winter of the boats. In the summer of ’98 the overflow from the Klondike went up the Koyukuk in little steamboats that drew too much water, and the river dropped and then froze, and there they were. Most of them walked out over the ice before Christmas. The ones who stayed built cabins where the boats had stopped and called them cities. There was one such place, and he would not say which, up a side river in under the hills, where the sun had been gone for weeks and was owed back at noon on a day in January that every man in camp had marked on the wall. They had chosen a steamboat captain named Rask to be judge for the winter, there being no other law nearer than the Yukon. The night before the sun was due, a man came in off the hills. He had been eight months up a creek by himself and had come down for salt and matches. He was a big man, heavy, with his hair grown past his shoulders the way it will in eight months, and he was known as a hard one to share a tent with. He asked two boys at the edge of camp where a traveler could sleep. They sent him to a trader named Potter, who had a storehouse cabin, a large one, that stood empty at night. Pot

sections.heading: V. The Pool
sections.dateline: The same camp · the next day
sections.text: Noon came. The whole camp stood out on the ice in whatever it had that was clean, looking at the hill, and the sky behind the hill never so much as turned yellow. They waited an hour. Then they went in a body to Captain Rask’s cabin, eighty men, and stood in front of his door and set up a noise. Captain, the sun hasn’t come back, and you’re the judge here. Make it come up for us. Rask was a fair man. He went back over the winter in his own mind, what he had ruled and said and thought, the claims, the split of the flour, and he could find nothing crooked in it. Then he thought, there is a quarrel in this camp that I don’t know about. Has anybody come in lately? Two men last night, Captain, off the hills. They’re in Potter’s cabin. He went there with men carrying lanterns ahead of him at one o’clock in the afternoon, and found the two of them sitting against opposite walls. He took off his cap to the young one and sat down on a crate. A man can’t see to work, Rask said. He can’t see to cut his wood. I’m asking you. Why has it gone dark on us? The young man told him all of it. He cursed me, and I cursed him back. I said, let it fall on whichever of us is to blame. Then I looked to see

sections.heading: VI. The Notch
sections.text: The kitchen was quiet. The cook had come to the door with the dog ladle in his hand and stayed there. Who was the young one? said Billy Dunne. A boy off the North Shore with more temper than sense. He has kept a roadhouse since. Rask died at Nome. The big man I never learned the name of. Murdo looked at his cousin. But I knew him, Norman, when you came off the scow. I knew the way he lay down. Then he spoke to his cousin and to nobody else, though the rest of them heard it. A man who goes on telling it over to himself, they insulted me, they laid hands on me, they got the better of me, they took what was mine, that man’s quarrel never gets done. It will be with him in the ground. And the man who leaves off telling it over, his gets done. That’s the whole of it, Norman. There is a text you know as well as I do. It was written for a country where the sun goes down every night. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath — Ephesians 4:26 Up here it has been down since November. A man can keep his wrath a long while on this creek. It was a Sunday. He sang then, standing by the flour bin with his cap in his hand, the way he had stood under the pulpit on the North S

title: No Winters
logline: In an Arctic roadhouse where a man's age is his winters, a stout newcomer takes the old-timers' chair and will not get up.

verses.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a barren wife, afraid that a fertile second wife will make her a servant in her own house, chooses the second wife herself, then secretly gives her drugs that make her miscarry, twice. The third time the child lodges crosswise and the young wife dies cursing her, vowing to come back and devour her children, and the husband beats the barren wife to death. The two are reborn in the same house as a cat and a hen, and then as a leopardess and a doe, and in each life one eats the other's young and vows revenge. At last one is born a woman of Sāvatthī and the other a yakkhinī, an ogress, who comes as a friend and devours two of her babies. With the third, the mother flees into the monastery and lays the child at the Buddha's feet. The Buddha has the ogress brought in, tells them that hatred is never ended by hatred, and has the mother hand her the child. The ogress kisses it and weeps because she has never had enough to eat; the mother takes her home, tries lodging her in one place after another, and settles her outside the village, where she tells the farmers whether the year will be wet or dry and is fed by all of them.
bg.history:
In the drought of 1930, June and July were the driest Arkansas had recorded, Little Rock went seventy-one days without rain, and August temperatures reached 113 degrees. Between a third and a half of the state's crops were lost, and by November outbreaks of pellagra and typhoid were being blamed on it. When the Red Cross opened its food program in January 1931, more than 165,000 people signed up in three days. On January 3, a few hundred farmers gathered in the town of England, in Lonoke County, and demanded food for their hungry neighbors; local merchants handed it out, and the England food riot made national news.

The Assemblies of God was founded at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914, and from its first year it gave credentials to women as evangelists, though not as pastors until 1935; by the fall of 1914, 142 of its 512 credential holders were women missionaries or evangelists. Country revivals were often held under a brush arbor, poles driven into the ground with cut branches laid across the top, put up when a traveling preacher sent word ahead. Decoration Day, when families clean the graves of a country cemetery and spread a dinner on the ground, is kept on a Sunday each spring or summer throughout the Upland South, including Arkansas and southern Missouri.

sections.heading: I. Hagar
sections.text: Jesse Coffey's daddy died when Jesse was fifteen, and after that Jesse did it all himself, the plowing and the fence and the stock and the wood, on forty acres of rocky bottom and steep ridge where Cutter Branch comes into the Little Buffalo. He kept his mother too. She had the rheumatism and could not do much but sit on the porch and shell beans and watch him work. Son, let me go fetch you a wife. I don't want a wife, Mama. I want to see after you as long as you live. You're doing the field work and the house work both, and it ain't right, and I won't have it. Let me fetch you a girl. He said no, and no, and then he quit saying anything. When she put on her bonnet to go up the creek to the Villines place, where there were four grown girls, he asked her where she was going, and when she told him, he said not there, and told her about a family down at the Gap he liked better. So she went where he wanted, and came back with Ada Treat, who was eighteen and red-headed and could outwork any two men on the creek. They were married at the Gap in the fall of 1886. Ada had no children. One year. Three years. Five. You picked her yourself, his mother said at last, and she's barren as a rock.

sections.heading: II. Pennyroyal
sections.text: As soon as Lettie was in the house Ada thought: if she has a baby, it's her house. That's just how it'll be. I can't let her have one. Honey, she told Lettie, the minute you think you're carrying, you tell me first. I'll see you through it. Lettie said she would, and when it happened she did. Every evening Ada fixed her a cup of sassafras tea with her own hands, and that night she put pennyroyal in it, a good handful, steeped strong. Lettie lost the baby before the month was out. In the spring Lettie told her again, and Ada fixed the tea, and Lettie lost that one too. That summer at a quilting at the Villines place, with Ada not there, the women sat around the frame and asked Lettie about it, and she told them, and they looked at one another across the quilt. Child, you're a fool. Who do you reckon fixes your tea? That woman is afraid you'll get the upper hand. She's putting something in it. Next time you don't tell her nothing. So the third time Lettie said nothing. But in the fifth month Ada saw her bending over the washpot in the yard, and saw the shape of her. Why didn't you tell me you was carrying? You brought me down here, Lettie said, and twice you've made me lose my babies

sections.heading: III. The Cat and the Hen
sections.text: The house on Cutter Branch stood empty after that, with the door open and the old woman's rocker still on the porch. Nobody would live in it. People said things about it, the way people do. What the old women on the creek said was this. That the spring after the funerals, a yellow cat took up in the Coffey house, a thin one with a torn ear that nobody had ever seen before. And a red hen that had gone wild when the stock was sold was still laying in the loft. And the cat found the hen's nest and ate the eggs. And the hen laid again, and the cat ate them again. Three times. They said that the third time the hen stood in the loft door with her feathers all out and made a sound no hen makes, and then she went at the cat, and the cat killed her. And they said if you had been there and heard it, you would know who those two were. They said more. That a few years after, a painter came down out of the bluffs above the Little Buffalo, a she-painter, the last one anybody in Newton County ever saw, and every spring for three springs she took the fawns from one doe that came down to drink at the mouth of Cutter Branch. They said the doe stood on the gravel bar and bleated for them, three sprin

sections.heading: IV. The Cradle
sections.text: Dorcas lived wherever somebody would let her, in a smokehouse, in a corn crib, in the loft of the church house one winter till the deacons found out. She did washing and hoed corn for whoever would pay her in meal. She was dark and thin and nobody could guess how old she was. Dorcas is a Bible name. It means a deer. She and Opal had been thick as thieves since they were girls. Opal was the storekeeper's daughter, with shoes in winter, and Dorcas was nobody's, and they had sat together on the store porch with their feet hanging off and talked the way girls do. When Opal married Clell Henson in 1928 and went to live at the mouth of the hollow, where the mail road comes in off the ridge, Dorcas was the first one to walk out and see the new house. The baby came the next fall, a boy. Dorcas walked out to see it. Where's Opal at? In the back room, Clell's mother said. She just had the baby. Boy or girl? Let me look at it. She went in and bent over the cradle, close, the way women do, and nobody thought a thing about it. She stayed a while and then she went home. In the morning the baby was dead in the cradle with not a mark on him. People on the creek said what they said, that she had be

sections.heading: V. The Baptizing Hole
sections.text: Dorcas came back in the middle of August with what she had on and walked straight out to the Henson place at the mouth of the hollow. Where's Opal at? Clell's mother stood in the door. Where you won't get at her. Something's been coming in this house and killing her babies, and she's gone to her mama's to have this one. She can go where she likes, Dorcas said. She won't get away from me. And she turned around and started for the Gap, walking fast in the heat, and Clell's mother said afterward that the dog would not go out from under the porch for an hour. There was a revival on at the Gap that week, a brush arbor on the flat by the creek, cedar posts with oak boughs laid across the top for shade and split-log benches under, and lanterns hung on nails at night. The preacher was a Pentecostal girl from over in Missouri named Velma Gentry. She was nineteen years old and had been preaching since she was fourteen. She wore a plain white dress and no jewelry and no paint, and she did not holler, and she did not dance on the benches, and people came from three counties anyhow, in wagons and on foot and in a Model T or two, to sit under the arbor in the heat and listen to her. Her brother

sections.heading: VI. Bread
sections.text: Opal, Sister Velma said. Pick up your baby and give him to her. Opal looked up from the sawdust. I'm scared to. I know it. Don't be. You've got nothing to be scared of from her now. Opal picked up the baby off the sawdust and stood up in her wet slip, shaking, and held him out, and Dorcas took him. She held him a long time. She put her face down against his head and smelled of it, the way women do. She kissed him on the forehead and on both his hands. Then she gave him back to his mother, carefully, the way you hand somebody something that might spill, and stood there in front of everybody and began to cry. What are you crying for? Sister Velma said. I never had enough to eat, Dorcas said. Not one day of my life. I've always got by somehow, but I never had enough. Not once. And now I don't know how I'm going to live. Sister Velma looked at her a while. Then she turned to Opal. Take her home with you. Let her live in your house. Feed her the best you've got. If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee. — Proverbs 25:21–22 Then Ancel struck up the guitar

sections.heading: VII. Wet Year, Dry Year
sections.text: Opal took her home and made her a pallet in the loft over the front room and fed her the best they had, which that year was cornbread and sorghum and a little side meat, and buttermilk when the cow was fresh. But in September Clell started knocking corn off the cob for meal on the porch below the loft, with a stick of hickory, and every time the stick came down Dorcas sat straight up on her pallet. I can't stay up here. It sounds like it's coming down on my head. Put me somewhere else. So Opal put her in the crib by the meal grinder, and then in the springhouse, and then in the kitchen lean-to, and then in the cellar, and then in the shed by the ash hopper, and then in the little house by the mail road gate. And Dorcas would not stay in any of them. The grinder sounds like it's grinding me. The boys come and empty the slop buckets right by the door. The dogs lay up against the wall all night. The boys use that side of it for a toilet. Your mama-in-law throws the sweepings right there. And the big boys sit on the gate and tell fortunes with a broom straw and a Bible and holler. At last Clell said there was nobody living in the old Coffey house up at the head of Cutter Branch. It had

title: Dinner on the Ground
logline: In the Ozark drought, a young mother whose first two babies died flees with her third into a girl preacher's brush arbor.

verses.text: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
If a man find a prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, he may walk with him, overcoming all dangers, happy, but considerate.
If a man find no prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, let him walk alone, like a king who has left his conquered country behind,—like an elephant in the forest.
It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two monks of Kosambī, a teacher of the Dhamma and an expert in the monastic rules, fall out because one of them left his washing water standing in a vessel in the latrine. The quarrel splits their pupils, the lay supporters and, the text says, the gods up to the highest heaven. The Buddha asks them three times to make peace, tells them fables of quarrelling quails and the story of Prince Dīghāvu, who spared his father's killer, and is told to leave them to it. He walks off alone into the Protected Forest, where a great elephant who has left his own crowded herd serves him through the rains and a monkey brings him honey, picking out the insect eggs first. The lay people refuse the quarrelling monks seats and food until they repent. Ānanda comes with five hundred monks to bring the Buddha home; the elephant follows him to the edge of the village and dies of grief. The Buddha forgives the monks and closes with verse 6.
bg.history:
After the death of the financier Baron Maurice de Hirsch, his fund in New York incorporated the Jewish Agricultural and Industrial Aid Society in 1900 to help Jewish immigrants buy and keep farmland, including by issuing mortgage loans. Financed in large part by the Hirsch money, an organized effort moved Jews from the city tenements to thousands of small farms in the Neversink and Rondout valleys, especially in Sullivan County, and hundreds of them survived by taking in summer boarders. Some of the great resorts of the later Borscht Belt grew out of farms that Jewish immigrants established in the early twentieth century, in part because some established hotels advertised “No Hebrews or Consumptives.” The New York, Ontario and Western Railway carried both the boarders and the milk.

Consumptives came anyway. Around 1900 the large Loomis Sanatorium for tuberculosis patients was established at Liberty, and the mountain air drew many more to farms and cottages. The woods they came to were second growth. Through much of the nineteenth century the Catskills' hemlock stands were cut for the tannin in their bark, until the tanneries closed one after another; at Grahamsville in Sullivan County the last one shut in 1878. The rule Feivel forgets belongs to Jewish ritual handwashing: by custom, water once used to wash the hands is not to be left standing where people pass or put to any other use, but poured away at once.

sections.heading: I. The Cup
sections.dateline: Sheldrake Hill, Sullivan County, New York · autumn 1905
sections.text: Fourteen Jewish families farmed the stony side of Sheldrake Hill above Centreville Station, on land the Yankees had given up on. The Society in New York had lent them the money to buy it. They kept a few cows each and shipped the milk down to the creamery by the depot, where it went into the cans on the Ontario and Western and was in the city by morning. In summer they took boarders, garment workers and their wives who came up on the train for two weeks of air, and sometimes a young man with a cough who had been sent up from the East Side because the big hotels at Liberty advertised in the newspapers, No Hebrews or Consumptives. In winter there was nothing but cows and snow and Torah. Their prayer house had been a wagon shed. It had a stove, an ark built by a cabinetmaker from Minsk out of pine boards, and behind it a privy, and in the privy a tin basin and a two-handled washing cup, so that a man could wash his hands before he went back in to stand before God. Two learned men lived on the hill, and each of them had his following. Feivel Melnik was the melamed. He taught the boys their Hebrew in his kitchen through the winter, and on Sabbath afternoons he preached, and when he prea

sections.heading: II. The Old Man
sections.text: Reb Ezra Lifshitz had been the rav of a town of four thousand Jews in Volhynia, and now he kept six cows on the last farm at the top of the road, where the fields gave out into woods. He was seventy-one. He had buried a wife there and a daughter in Brooklyn. Both of the learned men had been his pupils. When the colony first came up to the hill it was Reb Ezra they had followed, and he still came down for the Sabbath in a long coat gone green at the seams, walking, with his stick. His grandson Leybl, who was nineteen and hauled the milk, carried word down the hill. The Rov says, be one congregation. He came back up. They say they can't. The second time the same. The third time Reb Ezra put on his coat and said, The congregation is torn. The congregation is torn, and walked down in the snow. He stood in the wagon shed with both of them in front of him and told Hirsh his wrong, which was that he had passed a sentence over a cup of water against a man he had already forgiven. He told Feivel his wrong, which was that he would not see a fault because it was Hirsh who had found it. He told them both to pray under one roof. Where they could not stand to sit together at a table, he said, le

sections.heading: III. The Road Up
sections.text: Reb Ezra lay awake in the upper farmhouse. The house was too full. Leybl had his bed in the kitchen and his cousins came up every evening to argue it out by the stove, one for Hirsh and one for Feivel, and the cows below the floor shifted and coughed all night, and nobody he spoke to listened to a word. He said to himself, I could go up where there are no people. On Friday he came down for the Sabbath and stood in one shul and then walked to the other and stood there, and said nothing in either. On Sunday before light he put his tallis and tefillin in their bag, and a loaf and a block of cheese and a tin cup in a sack, and left the cows to Leybl, and went up the road without saying goodbye to anybody. The first night he slept at the hut of an old man who burned charcoal alone in the woods above the Sheldrake Kill and had not spoken to another living soul since the fall. The old man was not a Jew and said he was nothing. They sat by his pit and watched the smoke come up out of the earth, and Reb Ezra told him, in his bad English, that he had picked a good way to live. The old man said, I didn't pick it. Nobody would have me. Reb Ezra said that was how most people picked things. The

sections.heading: IV. The Bear
sections.dateline: The hemlock hollow · January to March 1906
sections.text: What happened up there was told afterward by Amos Dibble, a Yankee who trapped mink along the Kill and had no reason to make up stories about Jews. He told it in the store at Centreville Station to anybody who would buy him a cigar, and he never changed it. There was a big black bear in those woods, an old male, that had denned every winter under the same ledge. That year, Amos said, he didn't den. Amos had seen his sign around the ledge in the fall, two other bears and a sow with cubs crowding him out of his own place, the young ones tearing open his logs and the sow eating the beechnuts he wanted. It was as if he had looked at all of it and thought, I could go off and be by myself. And he came down through the snow to the hollow where the shanty was, where the old Jew was sitting on a log in the sun with his coat around him, and stood in front of him a long time, and then lay down. After that he kept house. Amos saw it with his own eyes. The bear broke a hemlock bough off with his paw and swept the snow from the front of the shanty with it. He dragged in down wood for the fire. He carried water from the spring in the old man's bucket, holding the bail in his teeth, and set it by

sections.heading: V. Leybl
sections.text: By the time the roads opened, the whole county had heard that the old rabbi was living in the woods with a bear. A paper in Monticello printed a paragraph about it under the heading A Hebrew Hermit. Gitl Rapoport and Moishe Sacks, who kept the store and had given the land for the wagon shed, came to Leybl and said, Bring him down. We want to see him. A letter came from the Society in New York saying the same, more politely. And when the young men of the hill came home in March from their winter work in the city, they came to Leybl too. We haven't heard him since the fall. Take us up. There were nineteen of them. Leybl took them up the north road and over the ridge and down past the pond, and when he could see the smoke from the shanty he stopped and told them to wait by the water. He's been alone near three months. You don't walk in on a man like that with a crowd. He went on alone. The bear saw him first. It came out of the hollow at a run with the limb in its jaws, and Leybl stood where he was because there was nothing else to do. Let him be, said Reb Ezra from the doorway. Let him come. He's mine. The bear dropped the limb. It came and stood in front of Leybl and nosed at the sa

sections.heading: VI. The Edge of the Woods
sections.dateline: The north road · two days in March
sections.text: They had not gone fifty yards before the bear walked out ahead of them and lay down across the path. What does he want? He wants to give you something before you go, said Reb Ezra. He's done for me all winter. You don't hurt him. Turn around. So they turned around and went back to the shanty, twenty men in a shanty built for four, and slept on the floor and in the woodshed. In the morning there was food piled in front of the door: beechnuts, and frozen wild grapes, and cranberries from the bog, and apples. Apples in March, red, sound, as if they had just come off the tree. Nobody could say where the bear had found them. There was more than twenty men could eat, and they ate until they could not eat any more and filled their pockets, and Mottel Gross went home with apples in his hat. Then Reb Ezra took his stick and started down, and the bear went past all of them and lay down across the path again, in front of him. Now what? Now he wants me to stay. Reb Ezra stood and looked at the bear. I'm going down, he said to it, and I won't come back. You can't come with me where I'm going. Up here there's nothing more for you to learn from me. Get up. The bear got up. It put a paw over its f

sections.heading: VII. The Water
sections.dateline: The wagon shed · the Sabbath before Purim, 1906
sections.text: When the two learned men heard that Reb Ezra was home, they put on their good coats to go up and beg his pardon. The Society's man happened to be up from New York that week, Mr. Adler, to see about the loans, and when he heard who was coming he went to Reb Ezra. Rabbi, I'll tell you frankly. I've had those letters. If it were up to me, neither of those two would set foot in that shul again. Moishe Sacks said the same. It was his land the shul was on. They're good men, said Reb Ezra. They had a quarrel, and they didn't listen to me. Now they're coming to say so. Let them come. And Moishe Sacks was quiet. On the Sabbath Reb Ezra had a bench set for the two of them by themselves, against the back wall, and nobody sat with them or stood near them. Every farmer and every farmer's wife and every child who came in through the door looked around and asked the same thing. Where are they? And Reb Ezra pointed. There. And they said it to each other all down the benches, There they are, there, and pointed with their chins, and the boys pointed with their fingers, until Hirsh Kagan and Feivel Melnik could not lift their heads. Then the two of them got up off their bench and came and went down o

title: The Washing Cup
logline: On a Catskills dairy hill, a basin of standing water splits a Jewish farm colony, and the old rav walks into the woods.

verses.text: He who lives looking for pleasures only, his senses uncontrolled, immoderate in his food, idle, and weak, Mara (the tempter) will certainly overthrow him, as the wind throws down a weak tree.

He who lives without looking for pleasures, his senses well controlled, moderate in his food, faithful and strong, him Mara will certainly not overthrow, any more than the wind throws down a rocky mountain.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two merchant brothers, Mahā Kāḷa and Culla Kāḷa, are halted with their caravan of five hundred carts when the elder hears the Buddha teach and decides to go forth. The younger follows him into the order, privately meaning to bring him home. Mahā Kāḷa practices at night in a charnel ground, where Kāḷī, the woman who burns the dead, gives him her rules and promises to show him a fitting body. She shows him a beautiful young woman who died suddenly, and he asks to be told when the fire has taken hold. He sees the burned body and reaches awakening. When the Buddha visits the brothers' town, Culla Kāḷa's wives mock him, strip off his robes and send him back into lay life. Mahā Kāḷa's eight wives try the same thing the next day. While the monks are asking whether he can hold out, the Buddha speaks of the weak tree and the rocky mountain, and Mahā Kāḷa rises through the roof of the house and comes down at the Teacher's feet.
bg.history:
The Shakers (the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing) followed Mother Ann Lee, lived celibate and held their property in common. Brothers and sisters lived as separate orders under one roof, and their worship was a disciplined dance. Missionaries from New Lebanon, New York, came to Kentucky after the great revivals of 1801, and in 1806 converts near Harrodsburg signed a covenant that became Pleasant Hill, on the high ground above the Kentucky River palisades. By the early 1830s it had several communal families, including a gathering family for newcomers, along with a meetinghouse built in 1820 to take the shock of the dancing and a great Centre Family dwelling of limestone, begun in 1824 and finished in 1834. The Sunday meetings drew curious visitors from the surrounding country. When a married person joined, the spouse left behind sometimes fought back, in court and in print, and those quarrels were among the bitterest in the Shakers' history. The village is preserved today as Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill.

The Pleasant Hill Shakers opposed slavery in a slave state and bought the freedom of enslaved people who wished to stay among them. Over the community's history about twenty-eight Black and mixed-race Believers lived there, often, as the village's own historians note, at the margins of its social life. Kentucky drovers walked hogs, cattle and mules south across the mountains to the Carolina markets, about eight miles a day. American medical schools were short of cadavers, and grave robbing for the dissecting rooms was a real fear. Families watched new graves at night. In the summer of 1832 Asiatic cholera reached New York and spread down the river valleys, and in 1833 it killed about one Lexingtonian in fourteen.

sections.heading: I. The Drove
sections.dateline: The Harrodsburg road, Mercer County, Kentucky · November 1831
sections.text: There were three Cole brothers on the Salt River below Harrodsburg, and the county told them apart by size. Josiah, the eldest, was Big Cole. Thomas, the youngest, was Little Cole, though he stood half a head taller than Josiah and always had. Absalom, in the middle, kept the store at the crossroads, and nobody called him anything but Ab. Every fall, when the hogs had fattened on the mast, Big Cole and Little Cole bought up a drove in the Bluegrass and walked it south, down the Wilderness Road and through the Gap and over the mountains into Carolina, eight miles a day, buying corn at the stands as they went. They came home in February with money sewn into the linings of their coats and a wagon of coffee, sugar, calico and salt for Ab to sell, and the women of the three houses came out to the road to meet them. That November they had four hundred and twenty hogs, six hired drivers and a wagon of corn, and on the Saturday night they turned the drove into a woods lot by the turnpike, a mile below the Shaker village at Pleasant Hill. The hogs settled. The drivers built a fire. Little Cole took off his boots. On Sunday morning the road was full. Buggies came down from Lexington, and a c

sections.heading: II. Two Labors
sections.text: The village sat on the high ground above the Kentucky River, where the river had cut down through the limestone and left cliffs on either side, grey walls three hundred feet high with red cedars growing out of the cracks. The Believers were building a great house of that stone, quarried out of the cliffs and hauled up the hill. They had been at it seven years and it was not done. Big Cole hauled stone. Little Cole was put in the broom shop, where he talked. After a month Big Cole went to Elder Jonas in the joiner's shop. The Elder was planing a drawer front and did not stop. How many works are there here? Big Cole asked him. Two, said Elder Jonas. One is to learn the gift. The songs, the steps, the order, the testimonies of Mother. Some of them are a long time learning it. The other is to labor with yourself until you're clean. I'm too old to learn all those songs, said Big Cole. I can't keep the steps now. I'll take the other. Elder Jonas set the plane down and looked at him a while, the way he had looked at the benches. Then go sit with the dead, he said. After the retiring bell. Come in before the rising bell. I'll square it with your elders. So every night, when the family had

sections.heading: III. The Rules
sections.dateline: The burying ground · winter and spring 1832
sections.text: Sister Dorcas had laid out every sister who died at Pleasant Hill for sixteen years, and dug some of their graves. She had come over the mountains from Virginia as a girl, the property of a family who heard the Shakers preach and signed the covenant, and when that family lost its faith and went back to the world, the Society paid them her price so she could stay. She sat at the end of the sisters' rank in meeting. She ate where she was put. She kept the key to the little stone house by the burying ground where the bodies waited, and she kept the burying ground, and she had seen a man in it at night. She watched him for most of a week. He came after the retiring bell and went before the rising bell. He did not dig. He did not carry anything. He sat, and stood, and walked the rows. She could not make him out. So one night she lit the lantern in the dead-house and left it burning in the window, and took the two children from the Children's Order who were given to her charge, a boy and a girl, and waited with them behind the cedar at the corner of the fence. When the man came over the pasture and sat down, she came out with the children holding her skirt. Brother, she said. Do you stay

sections.heading: IV. The Cooling Board
sections.text: The summer came in hot and stayed. The corn curled in the fields by noon. The Trustee came back from Lexington with a newspaper and said there was cholera in New York, a hundred dying in a day, and that it was coming down the rivers. Lovina Shryock was seventeen. Her mother had brought her to the Children's Order when she was six, and her father, who grew hemp in Woodford County and did not believe in anything, had never forgiven any of them. She had a high clear voice that came over the top of the singing. She had a face that the brothers were taught not to look at and looked at anyway, across the open floor, in the dance, so that more than once a brother lost the step, and once a whole rank of them came down a half-beat late with a sound like a dropped load of lumber, and the Elder stopped the meeting. Big Cole had looked at her too. He had been a man in the world for fifty-four years. On a Thursday evening she sat down on the bench by the wash house and said she was tired, and an hour later she was dead. There was no fever and no sweating. She had not been sick a day. The doctor said it was her heart, and could not say why. Her father sent a rider. He was coming, and nobody was

sections.heading: V. A Coat and a Hat
sections.text: Late that summer Elder Jonas went out on a journey with six brothers to open the testimony in the country south of Harrodsburg, and the Cole brothers went with him, because the country was theirs. The word went ahead of them. In Little Cole's house on the Salt River, Polly and her sister Jane heard it and looked at each other across the churn. Now we'll get him back, said Polly. So they sent word to the Elder that he and his brethren were welcome to hold meeting at the Coles' and take their dinner there. Elder Jonas would not eat in a house of the world unless it was set in the Believers' order, so one brother always went on ahead to tell the family how things were to be set, since the Believers did not sit as the world sat: the brothers at one table and the sisters at another, the elders at the head, and the meal taken in silence. Big Cole, who was standing with the brothers' hats, turned to his younger brother. Tom, you go on ahead and tell them how to set the tables. Polly and Jane saw him coming down the lane in his broad hat and his drab coat with no collar on it, and they started laughing before he reached the gate. While he stood in the yard explaining, they carried the tabl

sections.heading: VI. The Roof
sections.dateline: Big Cole’s house · the next day
sections.text: In the brick house a mile down the river, Rhoda Cole heard about it before dark. Big Cole's house held eight women. There was Rhoda, who had been married to him thirty years. There was his mother, seventy-six. There were their three daughters, Sarah, Lucy and little Rhoda. There were Rhoda's widowed sisters Ellen and Prudence, who had come to live with them after the fever of 1822, and their son William's wife Martha, who stayed with them while William was off in Missouri. Ab's house up the road held four, and Little Cole's held two. People in the county did the arithmetic. Polly got hers back, said Rhoda. We'll get ours. So the next day the Elder and the brethren were invited to the brick house. But that morning a different brother went ahead to tell them how to set the tables, a quiet young man from the West Family named Brother Eli, and Rhoda's women could not think how to make sport of him, and set everything as he asked. The brothers ate at one table and the sisters at another, and the Elder sat at the head, and the meal was taken in silence. Big Cole ate cornbread and beans and drank water. When they had finished, Rhoda came and stood by the Elder's chair. Elder, she said, Jo

title: The Cooling Board
logline: A Kentucky hog drover joins the Shakers and sits nightly in their burying ground; his younger brother follows, meaning to bring him home.

verses.text: He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin, who disregards temperance and truth, is unworthy of the yellow dress.
But he who has cleansed himself from sin, is well grounded in all virtues, and regards also temperance and truth, he is indeed worthy of the yellow dress.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha’s two chief disciples visit Rājagaha, and Sāriputta preaches on the four kinds of givers: those who give, those who urge others to give, those who do neither and those who do both. A layman is moved to feed all thousand monks and canvasses the city; the food is pooled and cooked in one place. A householder adds a perfumed yellow robe worth a hundred thousand, to be sold if the food falls short and otherwise given to any monk. By a majority of four the people give it to Devadatta, who is always among them, “ever ready like a waterpot,” and not to Sāriputta, who comes and goes. Devadatta cuts it up and wears it, and people say it does not suit him. When the Buddha hears of it he tells of an elephant hunter who stole a holy man’s robe so that the elephants would kneel to him, and of the elephant king who caught him and spared him out of respect for the robe. In Pāli the verses turn on a pun between kasāva, a stain, and kāsāva, the dyed robe.
bg.history:
During and after the Bosnian war of 1992–1995, St. Louis took in more Bosnian refugees than any other American city. With later arrivals from other states the community grew to an estimated 70,000, centered on the old German neighborhood of Bevo Mill, where Bosnians opened bakeries, butcher shops, cafés and trucking firms (see Bosnian Americans). In 2014 the community gave the city a replica of the Sebilj, the wooden public fountain in Sarajevo’s old market. Utica, New York, has another large Bosnian community. The džemat, its people and its hall in this story are invented. A hafiz is someone who has memorized the Qur’an; a bula is a Bosnian woman who teaches children and leads women’s religious gatherings; a ćurak is a fur-lined cloak. In 2017 Ramadan ended with Bajram (Eid al-Fitr) on June 25, and American truckers still kept paper logs; electronic logging devices became mandatory that December.

In July 1995, after Bosnian Serb forces took the United Nations “safe area” of Srebrenica, women and children were deported by bus from the UN base at Potočari, and a column of some ten to fifteen thousand men tried to walk through the woods to Tuzla. More than eight thousand men and boys were killed in what international courts have ruled a genocide. The trial judgment in the Krstić case records that soldiers called to the men in the forest with megaphones, and that some used stolen UN equipment to make them believe the UN was present to see them treated properly. The Qur’an passages are from Marmaduke Pickthall’s translation, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930); sura 107 is the one he titles “Small Kindnesses.”

sections.heading: I. The Guests
sections.dateline: Bevo Mill, St. Louis, Missouri · Ramadan, June 2017
sections.text: For the last ten nights of Ramadan the džemat on Gravois had two guests from Bosnia. Hafiz Senad Mehić taught at a medresa in Sarajevo and carried the whole Qur’an in his head, and he had been sent for the month, the way scholars are sent every year to the congregations abroad, to lead the long night prayers and recite. With him came a young muezzin named Adem. They slept in the two rooms over the hall, which had been a furniture store, and they had one suitcase each. Nobody let them eat a meal alone. To feed a guest who is fasting is counted a great good, a sevap, and the families of Bevo had divided up the thirty evenings back in April, by twos and threes and sometimes a whole street together. Emir Selimović’s wife had the eleventh night with her sisters and cooked for two days. Emir drove a truck. A good third of the men in the džemat did. He was thirty-six and owned his own Freightliner, leased on to Fadil Kovač’s company, and ran refrigerated freight to upstate New York and back. He had come to America at sixteen, to Utica, with his mother and without his father, and to St. Louis at twenty-two because a cousin said there was work and the houses were cheap. On the twenty-fifth

sections.heading: II. The Thousand
sections.dateline: Gravois Avenue · the next two days
sections.text: Mirsad Begić had the bakery across from the windmill. He had given all his life. He had never once asked. He lay awake on it, and in the morning he went up the stairs over the hall. Efendija, tomorrow is the twenty-seventh night. Be my guest. Gladly. How many are you feeding? How many come to pray on the twenty-seventh night? With the people from Affton and the county, they tell me a thousand. Then bring the thousand. He went down Gravois with a notebook. He went into the butcher’s and the cafés and the insurance office and the place that sent money home, and he stood in the door of each and said the same thing. I have invited a thousand people to break the fast tomorrow. How many can you feed? How many can you? They told him. The butcher said two hundred and wrote down six lambs. The women of Itaska Street said a hundred, in pita, cheese and potato and meat. A widow on Morganford said ten, and it was the most she could do, and he wrote it down the same size as the lambs. The trucking men said the tea and the sugar and the dates and the water, for everyone. By evening the notebook came to a thousand and some over. Good, Mirsad said. Now nobody cooks at home. Bring it all to the hal

sections.heading: III. The Count
sections.text: There was enough. A thousand and sixty people broke the fast at tables that ran out the back door and across the parking lot, and when the last of them had eaten there were somuns left to send to the shelter on Chippewa and lamb to send home with the students. Nothing had to be sold. So after the night prayer, while the men were stacking chairs, Mirsad held up the cloak in its bag. Brothers, this was given for a purpose, and the purpose is met. Who gets it? The hafiz, somebody said, and a good many said it after him. Who else? Then Zijad the roofer spoke up from the back. The hafiz is a fine man. The hafiz comes when the cherries are ripe and goes home before the plums. Who is here in February? Who washed my father’s body? Who stood in line with my mother at Social Security for four hours? Nermin. Nermin is here on Bajram and he is here on a wet Tuesday. He’s like the sebilj on the corner. Give it to Nermin. Nermin Hadžić had no diploma from any medresa. He had a good voice and a black robe, and when the imam was away he led the prayer. He washed the dead. He recited at the seventh day and the fortieth. He knew which window at the county building and which form. There was hardly a

sections.heading: IV. Exit 31
sections.text: Emir went out at three on Thursday morning with forty thousand pounds of frozen ravioli for a warehouse in Syracuse. A traveler is excused from the fast and can make up the days in winter, when they are short. He kept it anyway. The cab was cool, and it gave him something to do with Ohio. He wrote his hours in the paper log with a ruler, as he always had. In December the government was going to put a box in every truck to do it for him. Indiana went by in the dark and Ohio in the heat. On the phone the Bosnian drivers kept one another awake the way they always did, one long conversation running from Des Moines to Jacksonville about the price of diesel and whose son was marrying whose daughter, and that day it was all the cloak. Before Columbus he had heard his own vote described to him by a man in Kentucky who did not know whose it was. He was empty by ten on Friday, and at noon he came off the Thruway at Exit 31 and parked the tractor behind the mosque that had been a Methodist church. Then he walked four blocks with a bag of Mirsad’s somuns to see his bula. Hatidža Hadžiavdić was seventy-four. In the village above the Drina where she was born she had been the bula, the woman who

sections.heading: V. The Spring
sections.text: In the time of the sultans, the bula said, there was a spring under a cliff, and beside the spring a house of dervishes. They were poor men. Each had a bowl and one cloak, a hrka, patched until you could not find the first cloth. Red deer lived in the beech woods above, a great herd of them, and they came down a certain path every morning to the meadows and went back by it at night. One day the deer saw the dervishes at the spring. From that day, going and coming, every deer that passed stopped on the path and bent its forelegs and lowered its head to the ground, as a deer does to drink, though there was no water in that place. Then it got up and went on. There was a hunter in the town who lived by killing deer and selling the hide and the antler and the meat. Deer are hard to come near. He watched them on the path, and he thought, what is it they see that makes them go down like that? He decided it was the cloak. So he waited by the spring until one of the dervishes took off his hrka to wash for prayer and laid it on a rock, and he stole it. The next morning he sat down beside the path with the cloak drawn over his head and a spear under it. The deer came down. They saw the cloak

sections.heading: VI. Raiment
sections.dateline: Utica · that evening, and St. Louis · Sunday, June 25
sections.text: He stayed to break the fast with her. The sun went down at a quarter to nine.
