They ate Mirsad’s bread and her soup at the kitchen table where he had learned his letters, and afterward she spoke about it once more and not again. Senad gave you the first half of that sura, she said. He is polite. He stops before the hard part. I am old and I will give you the rest. Ah, woe unto worshippersWho are heedless of their prayer;Who would be seen (at worship)Yet refuse small kindnesses! — Qur’an 107:4–7 Nermin does not refuse them. He sells them. Sixty dollars, you said. For a widow it is forty, I hear, he is not a monster. A kindness with a price on it is a shop. There is no sin in keeping a shop. But you don’t give a shopkeeper the kadija’s cloak. She gathered the crumbs on the oilcloth into her palm. And the cloak itself. Listen. He told us there were two kinds of clothes, and He told us which one He meant. O Children of Adam! We have revealed unto you raiment to conceal your shame, and splendid vesture, but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best. This is of the revelations of Allah, that they may remember. — Qur’an 7:26 A man who has not washed himself out, who does not hold hi

title: Four Votes
logline: After a Ramadan feast for a thousand, a Bosnian congregation votes on who should wear a judge's hundred-year-old fur-lined cloak.

verses.text: They who imagine truth in untruth, and see untruth in truth, never arrive at truth, but follow vain desires.
They who know truth in truth, and untruth in untruth, arrive at truth, and follow true desires.

bg.commentary: The word Müller renders "truth" is sāra, the pith or heartwood of a tree. In the commentary, Upatissa and Kolita, sons of the leading families of two neighboring villages and friends from birth, lose their taste for a hilltop festival and go looking for what does not die. They exhaust the teaching of the skeptic Sañjaya, wander all India questioning teachers, and agree that whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other. Upatissa meets the monk Assaji on his alms round and is won by a two-line summary: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and their ceasing. Sañjaya refuses to go with them (a great jar, he says, cannot become a dipper; let the wise go to Gotama and the many fools come to him), and half his following leaves. The Buddha names the two his chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the same day. When older monks complain of favoritism he tells what each of them once wished for: the giver of first fruits nine times, the friends who buried the poor, the three brothers whose stewards ate the monks' food and became hungry ghosts until a kinsman's gift fed and clothed them, and the two friends themselves, one of whom long ago held a canopy of flowers over a Buddha for seven days.
bg.history:
The Eleutheran Adventurers, about seventy Puritan Independents from Bermuda, were wrecked on the Devil's Backbone reef off north Eleuthera around 1648 and sheltered in what is still called Preacher's Cave; their leader went for help to Virginia in a small boat. Their descendants on Harbour Island and at Spanish Wells lived by wrecking, turtling, salt and dyewood, above all braziletto, whose red heartwood was the only part the dyers bought. After a hurricane wrecked the Spanish treasure fleet on the Florida coast in July 1715, the salvagers and raiders it drew made ungoverned Nassau their base, the so-called Republic of Pirates: by one governor's count more than a thousand pirates beside about a hundred settlers. Vessels were hove down for cleaning on the harbor beaches and on Hog Island, now Paradise Island.

George I's proclamation of pardon reached Nassau in force with Captain Vincent Pearse of HMS Phoenix in February 1718. Pearse listed 209 men who said they would take it, fewer than half of those on the island, and the pirate company split between those who came in and those, like Charles Vane, who sailed out when Governor Woodes Rogers arrived that July. The creed in the second section is given to Bartholomew Roberts in Captain Charles Johnson's General History of the Pyrates (1724). Jayne, Darrell, his yard and everyone in it are invented, and the three tales of the winter in the cave are told here as island legend, not as record. Bermuda's cedar sloops, and the free and enslaved Black shipwrights who built many of them, were the best regarded in those waters.

sections.heading: I. Braziletto
sections.dateline: Harbour Island and Spanish Wells, off Eleuthera · 1695 to 1716
sections.text: Two women at the north end of Eleuthera were brought to bed on the same day. One was a Sands, of Harbour Island, and her son was named Tobias. The other was an Albury, of Spanish Wells, two hours' sail to the westward, and her son was named Cornelius. The Sandses and the Alburys had been friends for three generations, since the night their grandfathers came in off the reef called the Devil's Backbone holding to the same spar, and when one house had a christening the other house cooked for it. Each was the first family of its settlement, which in those islands meant a house with a board floor and a sloop. The men cut braziletto. It is a crooked, thorny tree, nothing to look at, and all its worth is inside it. The dyers in London want the heart, which is as red as a cut thumb. The white sapwood round the heart gives no color and nobody will pay freight on it. So a braziletto cutter spends his days chipping sap from heart with a hatchet, and by the time the two boys were ten years old they could do it by the sound. They grew up in and out of each other's boats. Whatever there was to learn in the islands, piloting, turtling, raking salt, working a wreck, they had it sooner than other b

sections.heading: II. The Fair
sections.text: In the summer of 1715 the Spanish plate fleet went ashore in a hurricane on the coast of Florida, eleven ships with the King of Spain's silver in them, and every sloop in the Bahamas went over to fish the wrecks. The fishing turned to taking. Those who took did not go home. A year later there were a thousand of them at Nassau, where there had been a hundred settlers and no governor, and the harbor was the merriest place in the Indies. A town of old sails stood along the beach, stretched over spars. There were fiddlers and punch houses and women from Jamaica. There was a man who sang the lament of Captain Kidd, all the verses. There was a great deal of silver, and it went from hand to hand like sand. The two friends sailed over to see it, as the young men of all the out islands did. Room was made for them under the best awning, and for some days they saw the show as it was meant to be seen. When the company laughed, they laughed. When the singer came to the verse at Execution Dock, they wept with the rest. When the hat came round, they threw silver into it. Then there came an evening when the fiddles struck up and there was nothing in it for either of them. Tobias sat and looked at

sections.heading: III. Every Port
sections.text: They talked it over on the forecastle. If that was all, there was nothing to stay for. But the sea was wide, and there were a good many men on it who had the name of knowing something. They would go round and ask. They went in Jayne's ship while she served and in other bottoms when she did not. At Port Royal they sat with old men who had crossed the Isthmus behind Morgan. On the Mosquito shore they sat with a striker who could feed a hundred hands with one harpoon. They talked with a Spanish friar taken out of a prize, and with a ship's surgeon who had been to a university, and in Boston with a minister who came down to the jail to pray with men of their own trade before they were hanged. Whatever these people asked, the two friends could answer. What the two friends asked, nobody could. It was always the one question. What keeps? After a year and a half they had been everywhere a keel would take them, and they came back to Nassau and to Jayne's ship, having found nothing. Before they turned in that night Tobias said, Whichever of us comes on it first tells the other. Cornelius gave his hand on it.

sections.heading: IV. Old Rope
sections.text: While they were gone a shipwright had come down from Bermuda in a cedar sloop of his own building. His name was Jeremiah Darrell. He was an old man and a free man of color, forty years in the Bermuda yards, and it was said of him that he had once walked away from a good house and a wife and a young son, and had worked six years as no man ought to work, before he understood his trade. Now he kept a careening yard on the back of Hog Island, across the harbor from the town. He would heave down and clean a vessel for anybody and take his pay in whatever they had. Men who went over to Hog Island to see a bottom cleaned did not always come back to their ships. Five came to him first, an old hand named Cundall before the others. Then a merchant's son from Charles Town with his friends, then thirty young wreckers in a body, then three long-haired brothers named Cash who had kept a turtlers' fire on a cay in the Exumas and brought their whole camp with them. Mr. Pinder, one of the old settlers, who had a storehouse on the bay, gave the ground the yard stood on. By that winter above a hundred men worked there. At the end of February His Majesty's ship Phoenix came in with the King's proclama

sections.heading: V. The Water Butt
sections.dateline: Aboard Jayne's ship · the same day
sections.text: Jayne was on his quarterdeck. Well, he said. In all your ports, did you find the man who could tell you what keeps? We have found him, Captain. He is across the harbor. And the King's pardon lies open on the beach for any man to walk in under. You are sailing empty. There is no heart in the timber. Come over with us. You go. I cannot. Why not? I have been captain to a hundred and forty men. For me to go and be a hand in another man's yard would be the water butt going to the well for a dipper. I could not do it. Do not take it that way, Captain. Never mind. You go. I stay. Captain, with the pardon come, every man in this harbor will be crossing to him. What will you do? Tell me one thing. Which are there more of in this world, fools or wise men? Fools, Captain. Wise men are few. Then let the wise men go over to your wise carpenter, and let the fools come to me. I shall never want for a crew. Go on, the pair of you. You will be a famous man, Captain, they said, and went down the side. As they pulled for the beach the ship emptied behind them. Men dropped into the boats and men swam. Jayne stood and looked at his bare deck, and then he leaned over the rail and brought up blood, hot,

sections.heading: VI. Right Hand and Left
sections.text: Darrell was sitting on a baulk of timber in the middle of the yard, with a sloop hove down on the sand in front of him, talking to his hands and to some of the townspeople who had rowed over to listen. He saw the boats while they were still small. Here come two friends, he said. Sands and Albury. Those two will be my right hand and my left. They came up the beach with their hats off. Master, we would work under you, if you will have us. Come on, then, said Darrell. The trade is plainly taught here. Work at it until there is an end of grief. The yard always held that by dark those two were going over the hull with adze and maul like men forty years out of their time, and that nobody could say where they had got the tools. That same evening, when the hands sat down together, Darrell put Tobias on his right and Cornelius on his left, and said that these were his two mates, and what they said about the work he said. The seventy who had come over with them had the trade through and through within days. The two friends were slower. Cornelius was a week at it, and on the seventh day was nodding over the pitch kettle when the old man shook him awake and sat down beside him and took a ship

sections.heading: VII. Heart and Sap
sections.text: When he had done, the two friends stood up, and told the yard the rest: the fair, and the evening the fiddles went dead, and Jayne, and every port, and the man with the sack. Then they told what Jayne had said on his quarterdeck, about the water butt and the dipper, and about the fools. Darrell listened to the end. There was a billet of braziletto in the firewood by his foot, with the bark on, and he turned it over with his toe so that the cut end showed, the red in the middle and the white ring round it. Jayne has taken the sap for the heart, he said, and he looks at heart and calls it sap. A man who cuts that way never comes to the heart at all. He goes where his wanting takes him, and it takes him wrong. You two knew heart for heart and sap for sap. You were bred to it. So you chipped off what was nothing and kept what was something, and you have come to the heart. Your wanting was sound, and it brought you in. A good many who sat by the fires that night, hands and townspeople both, got up from them changed. Jayne slipped out by the eastern passage with his seventy before the Governor came, and he was a famous man for the better part of two years. In the morning there was a plan

title: Heart and Sap
logline: Two friends from Eleuthera sign with a pirate captain at Nassau to learn what keeps, and ask the question in every port for a year and a half.

verses.text: As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.
As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Nanda is the Buddha's half-brother, the son of his mother's sister. On the day of Nanda's consecration, house-warming and wedding, the Buddha puts his alms bowl into Nanda's hands and walks away, and Nanda, too respectful to call after him, follows with it all the way to the monastery while his bride, her hair half combed, begs him to come back soon. He is ordained against his wish. The Buddha's small son Rāhula follows too, asking for his inheritance, and is ordained, and the grieving grandfather obtains the rule that no child be ordained without his parents' leave. Nanda pines and means to leave, so the Buddha shows him a singed monkey on a burnt stump, then five hundred dove-footed nymphs in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, and guarantees him the nymphs if he will stay. The monks call him a hireling. He practises alone, becomes an arahat, and releases the Buddha from the promise. The Buddha then tells how, in an earlier life, the same Nanda was a balky donkey won over by the promise of a mate.
bg.history:
After 1617 the Virginia Company granted large tracts along the James to private groups of investors, who settled them as "hundreds" or particular plantations, each expected to bring its own people and its own minister. Mereworth Hundred and everyone in it are invented; Berkeley Hundred, founded in 1619 on the same reach of the river, is a real one. Company tenants served seven years. New arrivals died in great numbers in their first summer, and the Company and the City of London shipped out poor children taken from the London streets, beginning with a hundred in 1619. The English built in wattle and thatch, and from their first years on the river also learned from their neighbors to cover houses with bark. The Weyanock were one of the peoples of the Powhatan paramount chiefdom, with towns on both banks of the James; among the Powhatan the women built the houses and made the mats. The peace that followed the marriage of Pocahontas in 1614 ended on March 22, 1622, three months after this story closes, when Opechancanough's forces struck the plantations that had spread along the river and killed about 347 colonists. The verse is by Thomas Tusser, the East Anglian farmer-poet whose rhymed calendar of farm work went through edition after edition from 1557 and was got by heart in country households. A reed thatcher's bat, for driving the butts of the reed up even, is still called a legget.

In 1619 the Company resolved to send young women "to make wives" for the planters, hoping that men with families would stop thinking of Virginia as a place to leave. About ninety came in 1620 and fifty-seven more were sent in 1621, some of them in the Marmaduke; the Company claimed "extraordinary care and diligence in the choice of them," required that each be free to choose her husband, and asked 150 pounds of good leaf tobacco from the man she chose, to cover her passage and outfit. They are remembered as the tobacco brides. The National Park Service has more on women at Jamestown.

sections.heading: I. The Cup
sections.text: Ned Fenn was a reed thatcher, the son and grandson of reed thatchers, and at twenty-three he had the name of the best hand between Gravesend and the Medway. On the Tuesday after Easter three things came to him in one day. His uncle, old Mr. Lyle, who had raised him, made over to him the tools and the custom of the trade. He was to sleep that night for the first time under a roof of his own, a cottage of two rooms at the marsh end of Chalk, which he had built through the winter and thatched with reed of his own cutting. And at nine in the morning he married Joan Barrow, whom the whole parish called the Fair Maid of Kent, after the old princess, and nobody in the parish thought the name too much for her. His cousin came to the wedding. Thomas Lyle was the old man's only son, twelve years older than Ned, and when Ned was small he had followed Thomas about the marsh the way a dog follows a cart. Thomas had gone up to Cambridge and taken orders and buried a young wife. Now he was going out as minister to a new plantation in Virginia, and his ship lay off Gravesend that same morning, waiting on the searchers and the ebb. He came over the fields in his black coat. He ate bride-cake standi

sections.heading: II. The Portion
sections.text: Thomas Lyle had a son, Rafe, seven years old, whom the grandfather kept. The boy's nurse had dressed him that morning in his best and walked him down to the water and pointed. That is your father, in the black coat. He is going over the sea, and he has not left you so much as a spoon. Go and ask him for your portion. The boy went down the stairs and into the next boat as if it had been sent for him. He came up the ship's ladder behind Ned and took hold of his father's coat and said, It is pleasant standing by you, sir. Then he said, Father, give me my portion, and when Thomas walked aft he walked aft behind him, saying it. The sailors could not get him off the coat, and Thomas did not shake him off. Thomas looked at the boy a good while. Whatever there was to leave him in England would be spent, or would spoil him. He said to the mate, Let him stay. I will give him a portion that does not waste, and the boy was entered too. So old Mr. Lyle, who had walked down behind the rest with his stick, stood at the head of Gravesend stairs beside a girl with her hair half braided, and watched his son and his nephew and his grandson go down the river on one ebb. He was a man who seldom asked f

sections.heading: III. New Ground
sections.dateline: Mereworth Hundred, on the James · 1618 and 1619
sections.text: The hundred was some forty men and six women, a palisade, a storehouse, and a church that was a tobacco barn with a table in it, on the north bank a day's row above James City. Behind it the new ground ran back into the woods. It had been cleared the way the people of the country cleared theirs: the great trees ringed with a hatchet and left to die standing, the brush burned, and corn and tobacco hilled up among the black stumps. Across the river and above were the towns of the Weyanock, who had planted that shore longer than anyone could say. There had been four years of peace. Weyanock men came into the hundred with venison to trade, and went about looking into the English houses with the plain interest of people seeing how strangers live. In the first summer a third of the newcomers died of the fluxes and the burning fever, which the old hands called the seasoning. Ned lived. The boy Rafe lived, and carried the cup in its case behind his father to every sickbed, and was not heard to ask for his portion again. Ned was set to roofs. There was reed in plenty along the creeks, taller and coarser than Thames reed, and he cut it and carried it, and by Christmas he had roofed the store

sections.heading: IV. Wages
sections.text: It could not be kept, and Ned was no man to keep it. He went about for a week with his mouth open. Before the corn was up, every soul in Mereworth knew that the thatcher was staying for wages, that the parson had gone bail for them, and what the wages were. They did not let it lie. There were men in the hundred who had come for land, and men who had come because a justice gave them the choice, and two or three who would have said, if you pressed them, that they had come for God. Not one of them had come for five hundred barefoot maids. They called him the hireling. They called him the bought man. Good morrow, Ned, and how do your wages? It was said at the storehouse door and across the church. He was despised for it, and he knew that he was, and he could not say they were wrong. He stopped talking. He went to the work, since the work was the condition; and because nobody now would hand reed up to him, he did it alone. He began by stripping the church. He had the whole slack roof off and on the ground, and he stood and looked at it, and saw it for what it was, the work of a man who had been somewhere else. Then he crossed the river. He had watched the Weyanock men look into the Engl

sections.heading: V. The Maids
sections.text: The year before, the Company in London had sent over ninety young women to make wives for the planters, so that the men might be more settled and less ready to go home. Now it sent fifty-seven more. The first of them came in the Marmaduke before Christmas, chosen with extraordinary care, the Company wrote, and a man who wanted one must first win her consent and then pay the Company a hundred and fifty pounds of best leaf for her passage. Every man in Mereworth who had the leaf got ready to go down to James City by boat. Some of them came round by the thatcher first, for the sport. Ned had tobacco hanging. He had been paid in it for two years of roofs. Here are your wages come up the river at last, Ned, said one, and only a hundred and fifty weight the head. Will you go down with us? No, said Ned. Two years back you stood in the storehouse and said, I am sick of it, I cannot bear it. Do you say so now? No. I have no mind that way at all. Nor back to Kent either. They did not believe him. A man who had stayed for five hundred would hardly turn up his nose at one. They went to the minister in a body and told him the thatcher was a liar. Thomas heard them out. Then he walked them acros

title: Beat In the Reed
logline: A Kentish thatcher follows his cousin's communion cup from his own wedding onto a Virginia ship, and every roof he lays there leaks.

verses.text: The evil-doer mourns in this world, and he mourns in the next; he mourns in both. He mourns and suffers when he sees the evil of his own work.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Cunda makes his living for fifty-five years by killing pigs near the monastery where the Buddha lives. In famine years he trades a little rice in the villages for piglets and fattens them behind his house, and he kills them with deliberate cruelty, clubbing them and pouring boiling water down their throats. He never gives the Buddha so much as a handful of flowers or a spoonful of rice. When he falls ill, the fire of the Avīci hell rises up before him, and for seven days he crawls through his house grunting and squealing like a pig while his family keeps the doors barred and no one in the seven houses around can sleep. Monks passing by assume he is slaughtering pigs for a feast and say so to the Buddha, who tells them that Cunda has not been killing anything: his own deeds have overtaken him, he died that day, and he will suffer in the next world as he did in this one.
bg.history:
Dutch immigrants began arriving in Sioux County in northwest Iowa in 1869, and Dutch is still the most commonly reported ancestry there. The county's Reformed churches shape its life, and Sioux Center has been called the place with the most Dutch Americans in the country, though Mexican immigrants have come to do much of the hard work in town. It is also hog country. A 2020 study by the state's pork producers ranked Sioux County second in Iowa, with about 1.3 million hogs.

In April 2009 a new strain of H1N1 influenza was first identified in Mexico, and the press called it swine flu, though it passed from person to person and required no contact with pigs. China, Russia and more than a dozen other countries banned American pork. Hog farmers had already been losing money for a year as feed costs nearly doubled; the scare pushed prices down further, and economists estimated it cost the industry more than $900 million. That autumn was also one of the latest harvests in memory: as of November 8, only 34 percent of Iowa's corn had been harvested.

sections.heading: I. Fifty-Five Years
sections.text: Gerrit Brink killed his first hog in the fall of 1954, when he was eighteen, in his father's locker plant on the main street of town, where farm families rented a frozen-food locker by the year and brought in their own steer or hog to be cut and wrapped and labeled in grease pencil, and he killed his last one fifty-five years later in the machine shed behind his house on the gravel road east of Hull. In between he killed more hogs than anybody could count, though people in the county tried. When the locker closed in the seventies, because the big plants in Sioux City and Sioux Falls could do it cheaper, Gerrit put up a confinement barn on the home place and then another, and kept killing at home on the side, for anybody who wanted a hog done cheap and did not want to watch. Everybody in that part of the county had a story about how he did it. He did not stun them right. He did not care to. He drove them out of the pen with a length of steel pipe and beat them along the alley to make them run, because he said a hog that had been run bled out better and the meat came up red. He hung them by a hind leg off the hoist and stuck them while they were still kicking, and he caught the blood

sections.heading: II. Swine Flu
sections.text: That April the news came out of Mexico about the new flu. Within a week the television was calling it swine flu, and it did not matter how many times the men from the pork board and the Department of Agriculture went on the air to say you could not catch it from a hog or a pork chop. People quit buying pork. China and Russia shut their doors to it. Hog prices, which had already been under water a year because the ethanol plants had run the price of corn up and feed had nearly doubled, fell through the floor. By June there were men in that county losing twenty dollars and more on every hog they shipped. Some of them had been in hogs three generations. Some of them sat up nights at the kitchen table with a calculator and the paper from the bank. Young men who had built barns on borrowed money in 2006 called around to see if anybody would take their feeder pigs, because they could not afford the corn to finish them. Gerrit Brink took them. He drove his gooseneck from one farm to the next all that summer and took weaned pigs off men's hands for five and ten dollars a head, and some for nothing, from a few who just wanted them gone. He took them from the sons of men he had gone to grade

sections.heading: III. The Slats
sections.text: The stroke took him in the machine shed on a Thursday morning, standing over the scald tank. His son Wes found him on the concrete by the drain. The doctor in Orange City said it had not been a bad one, as strokes went, and sent him home on Saturday with pills and a walker. On Saturday night he started to see the fire. He sat up in the bed and told Alida the barn was burning. She went to the window. The barns were dark under the yard light, the way they always were. He said not that barn. He said the floor. He said he was standing on the slats and they had gone red under his feet, the whole floor of the barn red-hot, all the way out, farther than a barn went, farther than the section, for miles, and under the slats the pit was boiling. He said there was no end to it. He said he could not get off it. Alida called Wes, and Wes came over from his own place and sat up with him, and Gerrit talked about the slats until it got light. He was not raving. That was what frightened Wes. His father talked about the fire the way he talked about the price of corn, in the same flat voice, as if it were a thing anybody could see who bothered to look, and he described it exactly: how far it went, th

sections.heading: IV. Seven Nights
sections.dateline: The gravel road east of Hull · Sunday to Sunday
sections.text: It had been a cold, wet fall, and the harvest was the latest in years. That second week of November two-thirds of the corn in Iowa was still standing, and every man on that road was running his combine past midnight under the lights, trying to get it out before the snow. They would shut down at one or two in the morning and climb down out of the cab into the quiet, and hear it. Sound carries on that ground at night, with nothing between one farmstead and the next but a windbreak and the corn. That week nobody slept on the section. The Van Peurs, a half mile north, heard it through closed windows. The Hulstein boys, who had a sow unit on the next road over, went out at two in the morning with flashlights, thinking a sow had gotten loose and was down in the ditch with a broken leg. Mrs. Vander Berg, who was ninety and nearly deaf, called her daughter in Sioux Center to say something was screaming out there and would not stop. In the old Kooiker house on the corner, which the Hulsteins rented to the family of the man who ran their sow barn, Mrs. Ramírez got up and lit the candle under the picture of the Virgin of Guadalupe on her dresser and sat with it on the edge of the bed, and her

sections.heading: V. The Teacher
sections.dateline: Miss Rozeboom's kitchen · Sunday night, late
sections.text: Her kitchen had not changed since their mothers sat in it. The same oilcloth with the little blue windmills, the same clock over the sink, the same calendar from the elevator in Hull. Arend Hulstein, who had been in hogs forty years himself, sat with his hands flat on the oilcloth. Then he got it here, he said. And he's going where he gets it there too. Yes, she said. Arend looked at his hands. I've run hogs through that sale barn in Rock Valley when I didn't care what shape they were in. I've had men work for me I knew were rough on them and I let it go because they were cheap. He did not finish. Miss Rozeboom said it did not matter whether a man wore a church coat or never had one on. A man who did not watch what he was doing paid for it in this life and in the next one, and the paying was nothing but seeing, finally, what he had done. She did not say more about it than that. She opened the Bible on the table to a place she did not have to look for, the old American Standard her father had read at that table, and put her finger on the line and read it to them the way she used to read to them at the end of the day, before the bell. Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy

title: The Slats
logline: In the swine-flu autumn, Dutch Reformed farmers on an Iowa gravel road hear hogs screaming from a cruel neighbor's house every night.

verses.text: The virtuous man delights in this world, and he delights in the next; he delights in both. He delights and rejoices, when he sees the purity of his own work.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Dhammika is a lay disciple of Sāvatthī who, with his wife and fourteen children, keeps up sixteen different kinds of almsgiving. Dying, he asks the Buddha to send monks to recite the discourse on mindfulness. In the middle of it, six chariots arrive from six heavens to carry him away, and he cries “Wait! Wait!” to them. The monks think he means them, stop, and leave, and his children weep that even their father fears death. He explains, has them throw a garland of flowers, and the garland hangs in the air on the pole of the invisible chariot from the Tusita heaven, “the abode of the mothers and fathers of the Buddhas.” He dies and is reborn there, and the Buddha tells the monks that the righteous rejoice in both worlds.
bg.history:
Salvadorans began arriving in the Washington suburbs in large numbers during the civil war of 1979–1992, which killed some 75,000 people; among its worst atrocities was the Sumpul River massacre in Chalatenango in May 1980. By 2000, Langley Park, built after World War II as garden apartments around the intersection of University Boulevard and New Hampshire Avenue, had the highest proportion of Salvadoran residents of any place in the United States. Salvadoran Americans are now one of the largest Latino groups in the country. Many belong to hometown associations that raise money for roads, water systems and schools in the towns they came from, and families sending a body home have long relied on collections among coworkers and neighbors, since repatriation can cost many thousands of dollars.

After two earthquakes struck El Salvador in early 2001, the U.S. granted Salvadorans already in the country Temporary Protected Status, renewable every eighteen months. On January 8, 2018, the Department of Homeland Security announced it would end TPS for El Salvador, giving about 200,000 people until September 9, 2019 to leave or find another status. On October 3, 2018, a federal court in California blocked the terminations in Ramos v. Nielsen, and the litigation kept the program alive for years. The buses in Don Chepe’s vision are the brightly painted former school buses of Central America, often called chicken buses. The izote (Yucca gigantea), whose flowers are eaten, is El Salvador’s national flower; it cannot survive a Maryland winter, but its cousin Adam’s needle grows wild there.

sections.heading: I. The Sixteen
sections.text: José Alvarenga came up from Suchitoto in 1983 with a pair of work boots, a Bible with a cracked spine and the address of a cousin in Langley Park written on the inside of his wrist in ballpoint, in case they took his papers. They did not take his papers. He did not have any. He hung drywall for thirty-one years, and by the end he could tape a seam so the light went across it like water across a plate, and contractors in three counties asked for him by name, which was Don Chepe. Marta came two years later with the four oldest. They lived in two bedrooms in the garden apartments on Fourteenth Avenue, then in a basement off Riggs Road with a dehumidifier running day and night, then, in 1996, in a brick rambler with a carport at the dead end of a short street on the Hyattsville side, which they bought with drywall money and the money Marta made cleaning houses in Bethesda, and with a loan Don Chepe paid off eleven months early because he did not like owing. By then there were fourteen children. Seven sons and seven daughters, the oldest born in a mud-brick house in Cuscatlán with a lamp burning, the youngest at a hospital in Takoma Park with a television on the wall. People said it the

sections.heading: II. The Bed
sections.text: On the eighth of January it was on Univision. The government was ending the program for El Salvador. About two hundred thousand people, the man on the television said, had eighteen months to arrange their affairs. The last day was the ninth of September, 2019. Ana Gloria turned the television off. Nobody in the kitchen said anything. Ten of the fourteen had been born in Maryland and were citizens. The four oldest had come up with their mother as children, and two of them were on the same cards as their father, and two were somewhere in between, in a file in an office that none of them had ever seen. Don Chepe finished his coffee. Eighteen months is a long time, he said. You can make a lot of pupusas in eighteen months. In February his eyes went yellow. In March a doctor at the hospital showed him a picture of the inside of him on a screen, with a shadow on the pancreas the shape of a thumbprint, and said months, and when Iris pressed her, said not many. Don Chepe laughed out loud in the examining room, and the doctor looked at Iris, and Iris had to explain. He says good. He says he will leave before they make him. He kept the griddle going under the carport through April, sitting o

sections.heading: III. The Reading
sections.text: Hermana Chayo did not come herself. It was Thursday, and Thursday nights she had the whole twelfth floor of a law firm by herself because the other woman was out with her back. But she sent them. Eight came, as he had asked, and then four more, because word goes around, and they stood in the living room with their Bibles, and the ones who did not fit stood in the kitchen doorway. Don Rafa came, who had been a deacon in the church since it was in a basement, and drove the van, and drove Hermana Chayo home from K Street at two in the morning three nights a week because the buses stopped. Two sisters from the Tuesday circle came, and a young man named Ulises who had been out of the detention center in Virginia for six weeks, and a woman with a baby asleep on her shoulder. The fourteen were there too, most of them, and some of the grandchildren, and Marta, and Mr. Pratt standing just inside the front door with his hat in his hands. Don Chepe opened his eyes and looked at them all for a long time. Hermanos, he said. It is going to be hard for me to see you after this. I am very tired. Read me just one thing. What do you want to hear, Don Chepe? Juan catorce, he said. The one about the w

sections.heading: IV. The Izote
sections.dateline: The front walk · the same evening
sections.text: After a while Don Chepe came back to himself and looked around the room. Why are you crying? Nobody wanted to say it. Finally Morena did, because she was the youngest daughter, and the youngest daughter in that family had always been allowed. Papi, you sent for the hermanos, and they came, and they were reading what you asked for, and you told them to stop. You stopped them yourself. So we thought, even Papi. Even him, at the end. Where are the hermanos? They left. Don Rafa said it wasn’t the time for them. Don Chepe closed his eyes. Ay, Rafa, he said. Mija, I wasn’t talking to the hermanos. Then who were you talking to? He told them. The six buses along the curb with their lights on. The paint. The music. The young men hanging in the doors calling him by his name, telling him to get on, telling him to leave the cracked jar and take the gold one. They were talking over the Word, he said. I wanted to hear the end. I told them to wait. Wilfredo went to the window and looked out. The street was empty. A light was on in the Guatemalan family’s kitchen next door. Mr. Pratt had gone back across and was standing in his own driveway with the hose, watering his tomatoes in the last of the l

sections.heading: V. The Circle
sections.dateline: New Hampshire Avenue · two in the morning
sections.text: Don Rafa picked Hermana Chayo up at two, as he always did on Thursdays, at the side door of the building on K Street where the cleaners came out. She got in the van in her smock with her purse on her knees, and he drove up Sixteenth Street and across and out New Hampshire Avenue toward Maryland, past the dark embassies and then the dark churches and then the dark car lots, and for a long way he did not say anything. Did he hear the Word? she asked at last. Yes, hermana. We read him John fourteen, like he asked. But in the middle of it he called out, wait, wait, and stopped us. Then the children started crying. So we said, this isn’t the time for us, and we left. Hermana Chayo looked out the window at the orange barrels where they were tearing up the road for the new train. He wasn’t talking to you, Rafa. Don Rafa kept his hands on the wheel. Who was he talking to? To the ones who came for him. They came for him in the middle of the reading, and they were calling him to get on, and he didn’t want to miss the end. So he told them to wait. He drove a whole block before he said it. Is that true, hermana? It’s true. Don Rafa had known her twenty-six years. He had driven her home from K

sections.heading: VI. The Way Home
sections.dateline: Dulles, San Salvador, Suchitoto, Riggs Road · summer 2018
sections.text: Nelson emptied the Folgers can. For once it was for his own father, and nobody said a word against it, and it was not enough, so the people it had been for came, the ones whose sons and husbands and mothers had gone home in it over twenty years, with envelopes. A man came all the way from Manassas with four hundred dollars in twenties and would not come in the house. The coffin went out of Dulles on a Tuesday in the belly of the plane, taking up the room of twelve suitcases, and Rigoberto and Marta flew with it, upstairs, with the tickets Kevin found on the internet. Yesenia posted the video that night. By August it had been seen more than two million times. People in the comments said it was fishing line. People said it was a drone. People said it was the CGI. A man in Texas made a video of his own explaining how it was done, frame by frame, with arrows, and that one got two million too. Yesenia stopped reading the comments. Mr. Pratt, who did not have a Facebook, told anybody who asked that he had been standing right there with the hose, and that the only thing in the air on that street was flowers, and that he was seventy-one years old and had carried the mail for thirty-four of

title: The Izote
logline: In the Maryland suburbs, a dying Salvadoran drywaller whose fourteen children keep sixteen kinds of giving asks the church to read him one chapter.

verses.text: The evil-doer suffers in this world, and he suffers in the next; he suffers in both. He suffers when he thinks of the evil he has done; he suffers more when going on the evil path.

bg.commentary: The commentary gives Devadatta's whole career. He goes forth with five Sakyan princes, among them Anuruddha (whose mother once sent him an empty covered bowl to teach him the words "there isn't any," and the gods filled it), and with their barber Upāli, whom the princes have ordained first to humble their pride. Devadatta gains only lesser powers. When visitors ask after every great disciple but him, he wins over Prince Ajātasattu, appearing to him first in a frightening form; loses his powers the moment he wants to lead the order; asks the aging Buddha to hand it over; is refused and called a lickspittle. He urges Ajātasattu to kill his father the king, hires assassins who are converted instead, hurls down a rock that wounds the Buddha's foot, and sends the drunken elephant Nālāgiri, before which Ānanda stands. After the elephant the people turn on him and the king withdraws his support. He demands five stricter rules, is told that whoever wishes may keep them, leads five hundred young monks away by a vote with tickets, and imitates the Buddha's manner until Sāriputta and Moggallāna bring the monks back. He coughs up hot blood, is sick nine months, and asks to be carried to the Buddha, who says he will not see him; set down by the lotus pool at Jetavana while his bearers bathe, he sinks into the earth, taking refuge in the Buddha with his last breath. The people celebrate, and a birth story tells of a doorkeeper who wept at a cruel king's funeral for fear he would be sent back. This story continues Four Votes (1.7).
bg.history:
Refugees from the Bosnian war settled in St. Louis by the tens of thousands from the 1990s on, first in Bevo Mill and then increasingly in the suburbs of south St. Louis County, and founded coffee shops, bakeries, auto shops and trucking companies (see History of Bosnian Americans in St. Louis). Some came from beyond Bosnia, from the Bosniak region of Sandžak in Serbia and Montenegro, which takes in the high Pešter plateau. Goražde, in eastern Bosnia, was besieged from 1992 to 1995; when the convoys were cut off, food was dropped to it from the air. The džemat, its people, the Kovač company, the old Pizza Hut and the collapse at the lake are invented.

Carondelet Park, some 180 acres on the city's south side, was bought by the city in 1874 and opened the next year. Its rolling ground was shaped by caves and sinkholes in the limestone beneath it: Horseshoe Lake was made in 1913 by joining nine sinkholes, and the boathouse went up in 1918. The Qur'an tells of Korah (Qarun), one of Moses' own people, who grew proud of his wealth and was swallowed by the earth with his house (28:76–82). The scripture is from Marmaduke Pickthall's translation, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930).

sections.heading: I. The Washers
sections.dateline: Gravois Avenue, St. Louis · 2004 and after
sections.text: Ramiz-efendija Kurtović came to St. Louis in 1998 from the Pešter plateau in Sandžak, where the winter is so long that the sheep come down off the summer grass in September. For six years he mopped floors at night in a hospital on Kingshighway and on Fridays led the prayer in a rented room over a car-parts store. In 2004 the džemat bought the old furniture store on Gravois and could pay him, a little. The first thing he asked for was young men to learn the washing of the dead. He asked it from the minbar, in the plain way he said everything. At home the old men had done it. Here the old men were tired, or in the ground, or had never learned. Who is going to wash us, he said, when it is our turn? Six came, all from the same few streets, all between twenty and twenty-five. The Mujkić brothers, Kenan and Mirza, whose father had the biggest house on Itaska Street and the first Mercedes on Gravois. Samir Karić, who was studying to be a pharmacist. Emir Selimović, just down from Utica, who drove a truck for Fadil Kovač. Nermin Hadžić, who had the best voice of any young man in the džemat and had been told so since he was nine. And Haris Mehmedović, who was from Goražde. About Haris the s

sections.heading: II. The Lickspittle
sections.dateline: Bevo Mill and Oakville · autumn 2017 to spring 2018
sections.text: After the summer of the cloak, people on Gravois stood a little differently around Nermin Hadžić. Nothing was said. But when a family came into the hall now to ask for someone to wash their father, they asked for the imam, or for Bego, or for Emir if he was in town. They asked whether the hafiz was coming back for Ramadan. They asked after Haris, and after Kenan, and after the hafiz's young muezzin, whose name they had already forgotten. Nobody asked where Nermin was. He stood at the back of the hall in the tea-colored jacket with the fox collar and listened to them not ask. He thought about it in the evenings. I went in with them, he thought. I learned it faster than any of them. What do they have that I don't? He thought about who he could go to. Not the Mujkić family; Kenan was president and had a long memory. Not Fadil Kovač, who had given the money for the building and the cloak both, and who had prayed every prayer in the hall since 2004 in the same place, behind the imam on the right. But Fadil had a son. Dino Kovač was thirty-one. He had an MBA from Saint Louis University and an office at the company's yard in Oakville with a window onto forty trucks, and he knew what every

sections.heading: III. The Truck
sections.text: Ramiz-efendija lived on Holly Hills Boulevard, in a brick house across from Carondelet Park, with his daughter and her husband and three grandchildren. In May two of Dino's drivers came to see him there at nine o'clock at night. They were Šemso Hodžić and a young one called Kemal, and they had been paid five hundred dollars each by somebody to go and talk to the old man, as it had been put to them, and make him understand that he was tired. Šemso had brought a tire iron and left it in the truck. The imam opened the door himself in his slippers. He looked at the two of them a moment and said, Come in, the coffee is on, though it was not, and went and put it on. They sat in the front room for three hours. His granddaughter brought them Turkish delight on a plate. Mostly the old man asked Šemso about his mother, who was from a village near Sjenica where the imam had known a cousin, and Šemso, who had not cried since 1995, cried in the imam's front room, and Kemal looked at the carpet. On Friday both of them were in the hall, at the back, and came every Friday after, and gave the money to the džemat, and told Dino so. In June, on the last Friday of Ramadan, the imam was at the side doo

sections.heading: IV. The Clipboard
sections.dateline: Gravois and Affton · October 2018 to June 2019
sections.text: In October he asked to speak at an extraordinary meeting of the džemat, and the board, because it was the rule, let him. He had five things to put before them. Every man in the džemat should pray all five prayers in the hall and none at home. Every man should fast Mondays and Thursdays, all year. No meat should be eaten in any house but at the two Bajrams. No man or woman should wear gold. No wedding should have music. He said them in his broken voice, standing, with a sheet of paper. The imam heard him out. The Prophet fasted Mondays and Thursdays, he said. Whoever wants to, let him fast. Whoever wants to eat no meat, let him eat bread. Whoever can come to all five prayers, I'll be glad to see him. I will not make a law where God made none. Nermin turned to the hall. Brothers. Whose words are stricter, his or mine? Whoever wants to be saved, come with me. And he took a clipboard from under his arm, with a sign-up sheet on it, and walked out to the parking lot and stood there under the light with a pen on a string. Forty-three young men signed it. Most of them were under twenty-five, sons of drivers, boys who had been born in St. Louis and learned their prayers on Saturdays and had

Of the four boys who had stayed at the Pizza Hut, three went home by Christmas, and the lease ran out on the building in January, and Nermin lay in a rented room above a nail salon on Gravois Road with Hamza and the last boy, Edin, who was seventeen, to bring him water. In February he asked to see the imam. Take me to him. Hamza said no. When you were on your feet you threw bricks at him. You sent a truck at him. Now you want him? I hated him, Nermin said. I'll give you that. But he never hated me. Not this much. He held up his finger and thumb with nothing between them. Not one hair. Take me. He said it every hour, and on the third day they did it. They laid him on the mattress in the back of Hamza's minivan with the seats folded down, and drove him in along Loughborough Avenue toward Holly Hills, and Edin called ahead to his cousin on Itaska Street, who called the imam's son-in-law, who told the imam. sections.text: Ramiz-efendija went to the fence the first night, after the night prayer, alone, with a flashlight. He stood at the chain-link with the lake behind him and recited the Yasin over the hole, the whole of it, the way it is recited over the dying, and when he came home he called Kenan Mujkić and told him to take the džemat book out of the safe and write Nermin Hadžić's name in it again, where it had been struck out in 2018, as a member in good standing. Efendija. After everything? He was on his way here, the imam said. Write it. There was no washing, because there was nothing to wash. There was no grave. On Gravois it was not the same as a death. People who had not said Nermin's name in a year said it over and over now, at the bakery and at the butcher's and on the phones between the trucks, and some of them said it was God's justice and said it with satisfaction, and a girl on Facebook posted the verse about Korah, whom the earth swallowed, and four hundred people shared it. On the Friday after, the women brought trays of baklava and tulumbe to the hall and set them out after the prayer, the way you would for a wedding or a boy coming home from the army, and the men stood around the t

verses.text: The virtuous man is happy in this world, and he is happy in the next; he is happy in both. He is happy when he thinks of the good he has done; he is still more happy when going on the good path.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the great lay supporter Anāthapiṇḍika feeds two thousand monks a day in his house at Sāvatthī, but he is so much in demand to advise other donors that he cannot serve the monks himself. He appoints his eldest daughter, who reaches the first stage of awakening, marries and leaves, and then the second, who does the same. The youngest, Sumanā, reaches the second stage, does not marry, stops eating and sends for him. On her deathbed she calls him “younger brother” and dies. He goes weeping to the Buddha, sure that she died out of her mind, and is told that she spoke exactly: he had reached only the first stage, and she was his elder on the path. She has been reborn in the Tusita heaven.
bg.history:
The Moravians, or Unity of the Brethren, bought the Wachovia tract in the North Carolina piedmont in 1753 and founded Salem in 1766 as a congregation town, in which the church owned the land and regulated trades, residence and marriage. Members were grouped by age, sex and marital state into “choirs,” each with its own spiritual helper, and were buried by choir in God’s Acre under identical flat stones. Each member left a memoir, or Lebenslauf, to be read at the funeral, and regularly “spoke” with the choir helper before Communion (see the Moravian Archives’ glossary). Deaths were announced by a trombone choir, with a chorale that identified the choir of the departed. Marriages were submitted to the Lot, slips drawn by the Elders after prayer, which the Brethren took as the Saviour’s own answer; the requirement was dropped for most American members in 1818. The lovefeast, a simple shared meal of buns and coffee served during a service of song, and the Easter sunrise service in the graveyard, held at Salem since 1772, are still kept. The tavern, rebuilt in brick in 1784, was set at the edge of town to keep outsiders apart; the Rothe family and the guest table are invented. Salem is preserved today as Old Salem in Winston-Salem.

The Moravians of Wachovia held people in slavery, most of them owned by the church itself and hired out, including to the tavern. Black Moravians were baptized and received as brothers and sisters, and at first worshipped and were buried alongside white members. The Elders began seating them separately in 1789, closed God’s Acre to them in 1813, and in the 1820s set up a separate congregation, later St. Philips. Salem Academy and College has published an account of one enslaved Moravian family. John Cennick (1718–1755), who wrote the hymn, was an English evangelist who joined the Moravians in 1745. The Easter Morning Litany dates from 1749; the English text is the one printed in Philip Schaff’s Creeds of Christendom (1877).

sections.heading: I. The Guest Table
sections.text: Brother Heinrich Rothe kept the tavern at the lower end of Main Street, where the Brethren had put it on purpose, a good walk from the square, so that the wagoners and drovers and lawyers who stopped there would trouble the town as little as possible. He fed them all. In a week when the wagons were moving he fed sixty at a sitting. But that was the congregation’s business, done for the congregation’s account, and it was not what people meant when they spoke of Brother Rothe’s table. They meant the table in the back room. Any brother or sister on the road for the Saviour ate there, and the Elders had put it in his charge. Missionaries going out to the Cherokee at Springplace ate there, and ministers on the five-week road from Bethlehem, and the country preachers in from Friedberg and Hope with mud to the knee. Nobody at that table paid. In sixteen years it was hardly empty for a week together. He had a gift for it, and the gift was known. In all of Wachovia nobody held a lovefeast without asking Brother Rothe first. He knew how many buns Bethania would eat and how many it would carry home in its pockets. He knew that Friedberg wanted the coffee sweet and Bethabara wanted it strong,

sections.heading: II. The Lot
sections.text: In Salem in those years nobody married without the Lot. A brother who wished to marry said so to the Elders, or the Elders thought of it for him, and a sister’s name was proposed. Then they laid it before the Saviour. There was a bowl with three slips of paper rolled in it, one that said Yes, one that said No, and one blank, which meant the question should not have been asked. An Elder drew. If the slip said Yes the sister was asked, and might still refuse. If it said No, that was the end of it, and nobody spoke of it again, or was supposed to. In 1806 the name of Anna Rosina Rothe was proposed for a brother called to the Cherokee mission, and the Lot said Yes, and so did she. She went out to Springplace on a wagon in October with a feather bed and a box of slates. Her father put the second daughter, Maria Elisabeth, at the wall in the back room. Maria Elisabeth stood there four years. The same thing happened to her that had happened to her sister, in her own time and her own way, over a dish of stewed apples, while a deaf old preacher from Hope was telling how he had been found. In 1810 the Lot said Yes for her and a miller at Bethania, and she went to live at the mill. That left

sections.heading: III. Over the Kitchen
sections.dateline: The tavern · the second week of March 1816
sections.text: Brother Rothe was at Friedland that day, eleven miles out, in the kitchen of the meeting house, with two hundred buns on boards and a married sister weeping because the coffee had boiled. A boy came on the tavern’s mare. Sister Benigna asks for her father. He left the buns and rode. It was eleven miles, and the whole way he thought of things he had meant to say to her at some time when the house was quieter. He tried to remember when he had last sat down in the back room, and could not. He came up the back stairs with his hat still on. She lay propped on the bolster, with her hair tied back. She had got very thin. Her eyes were clear, and she was looking at the door when he came through it, as if she had known to the minute how long the mare would take. Sarah was sitting by the bed with a basin and got up to give him the chair. What is it, my dear daughter? What is it, Benigna? What are you saying, little brother? He took off his hat. He looked at Sarah, who looked at the basin. You are wandering, child. I am not wandering, little brother. She said it kindly and without hurry, as she might have told him his coat was buttoned wrong. He sat down and took her hand, which weighed nothi

sections.heading: IV. The Single Sisters’ Row
sections.text: They read her life in the church before they carried her up the hill. Every brother and sister wrote one, or had it written, an account of the road they had come, and it was read over them at the end. Benigna’s was a page and a half in her own round hand. It said she was born in the tavern in 1795 and had been a happy child. It said that in her sixteenth year, at her father’s table, the Saviour had come so near that she had not since been able to find the place where she left off and His kindness began, and that she had tried to deserve the back room. It did not mention the Lot. The last lines, on her illness and her going, were added in another hand, as was the custom. The burying ground at Salem lay along the ridge above the town, behind a row of cedars, and it was laid out by choirs. The married brethren lay in one square and the married sisters in another, the single brethren and the single sisters each in their own, and the little boys and the little girls. Within each square they lay in the order they had come, one after the next. Every stone was the same, a flat white square, set level in the grass, with the name and the two dates. No one in that ground lay beside a husband,

sections.heading: V. Sister Dorel
sections.dateline: The Single Sisters’ House · the same day
sections.text: Anna Dorothea Schumann had charge of the single sisters’ souls. That was her office, and it had a name, Pflegerin, the one who tends. She was forty-four, a short, quick woman from Lititz who had come down the Wagon Road at twenty with her loom in pieces, and she was thirteen years younger than the man who stood in her doorway holding his hat. Once in four weeks, before each Communion, every sister in the choir came to her alone and told her how it stood with her heart. Sister Dorel had heard Benigna Rothe in that way some eighty times. She had written none of it down. For the last three years she had come away from those quarter hours with the feeling that it was she who had been heard. She did not get up from the tape loom. She pointed him to the other stool. Brother Rothe. You have been weeping, and you are weeping now. What is it? Sister, my Benigna is dead. Well, and why do you weep? Is there anyone in Salem who is not going home? I know that. I have known it all my life. But she was such a modest girl, Sister, and so careful in everything. What I cannot bear is that she did not have her right mind at the end. She went out of the world talking nonsense. What did she say to you?

sections.heading: VI. Easter Morning
sections.text: On the Saturday before Easter the people of Salem went up the hill with buckets and brushes and scrubbed every stone in the burying ground, and laid flowers on each, on all of them alike. It was a cold spring and there was not much, some daffodils, the first redbud, green box. Benigna had no stone yet. Her father laid his on the raw clay. Before light on Easter morning the trombones went through the streets to wake the town. The congregation gathered in front of the church in the dark and heard it said that the Lord was risen, and answered, and then walked up the cedar avenue two and two behind the horns, some hundreds of people, into the burying ground, and stood among the stones in their choirs, facing east. It had been done so in Salem every year since the town was a clearing. The thing was timed, and the Brethren were good at timing. The sun was meant to come up over the ridge while they prayed for the ones who had gone that year. Brother Rothe stood with the married brethren. Sarah stood at the edge, by the cedars, with the other Black sisters and brethren. Three years before, the Elders had ruled that the hill was closed to her. When her time came she would lie in the strange

title: Little Brother
logline: In Moravian Salem, where the Lot decides who marries, a tavern keeper's dying youngest daughter calls him by a name he cannot understand.

verses.text: The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.

The follower of the law, even if he can recite only a small portion (of the law), but, having forsaken passion and hatred and foolishness, possesses true knowledge and serenity of mind, he, caring for nothing in this world or that to come, has indeed a share in the priesthood.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two friends from Sāvatthī go forth together. After five years, one, who has gone forth late in life, takes up the duty of meditation, goes off to the forest in rag robes and becomes an arahant with many pupils. The other takes up the duty of study, learns the Three Baskets by heart and teaches five hundred monks in eighteen communities. When the forest elder’s pupils send greetings, the scholar scoffs that the old man does not know a four-line verse, and resolves to question him. Foreseeing that this would ruin the scholar, the Buddha comes as if on his rounds and sits in the seat always kept ready for him. He asks both monks questions. The scholar answers everything about the meditative absorptions, but nothing about the paths; the elder answers every question, and the Buddha praises him four times while the gods applaud. To the scholar’s offended pupils he says their teacher is like a man who tends cows for wages, while the elder enjoys the products of the cow as his own.
bg.history:
Berlin, in the North Country, was a paper town for more than a century, and much of it still speaks New England French. Fraser Papers closed the Berlin pulp mill in 2006, and the town later took a federal prison, opened in 2012. New Hampshire’s per-capita overdose death rate was among the highest in the country in these years: 485 people died of drugs in 2016 and 487 in 2017. The state’s dairies were going under at the same time. In 2016, as drought set in and milk fell to $14.80 a hundredweight, 19 of the state’s 120 dairy farms closed. Haverhill, on the Connecticut River, is the Grafton County seat; the county offices and courthouse stand on Route 10 just north of North Haverhill. Pontook Falls, the Pike farm and every person in the story are invented.

Seneca wrote his 124 moral letters to Lucilius at the end of his life. Richard Mott Gummere’s translation of them appeared in the Loeb Classical Library, whose Latin volumes are bound in red, beginning in 1917. Stoicism has had a long modern revival: the founders of cognitive therapy traced their method back to the Stoics, and the Navy pilot James Stockdale credited Epictetus with carrying him through years as a prisoner in Hanoi. That made it a philosophy many American servicemen and veterans took up, and in the 2010s and 2020s it found a large online audience. Ray dug at the Beirut barracks, where 241 American servicemen were killed in October 1983. Kyle’s studio is in the Millyard, the brick mill buildings of the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company, which went bankrupt in 1935.

sections.heading: I. The Tuesday Table
sections.text: Chief Lise Pelletier ran the Tuesday table at the VFW post on Main Street because the men would not come to anything called a group. She had tried calling it a group. Two men came, and one of them was the minister. She had driven trucks in the Marines in the first Gulf war and come home to a town of two thousand people that had lived for a hundred years on the pulp mill in Berlin and had not yet worked out how to live without it. The mill shut in 2006. By 2012 the Pontook Falls police department was the chief, three officers and a cruiser with a quarter of a million miles on it. Mostly what they did was drive men home. She was forty-five. She had read Seneca since a lieutenant in Saudi Arabia left a paperback in a tent, and she now owned the three red volumes of the old Loeb edition, bought used in Hanover, the spines held together with packing tape. On Tuesdays at seven she read one letter aloud, slowly, the way you would read a will. Then she asked one question and said nothing else. Some nights the men talked until ten. Some nights nobody said a word. They drank their coffee and went home, and she counted that a good night too. Before anyone sat down, somebody set a chair for he

sections.heading: II. The Hired Man
sections.text: Monique’s cousin Gordon Pike had forty-four Holsteins in a tie-stall barn on the river flats below Route 10, a bad back, and nobody to milk. His children had gone to Concord and Charlotte and were not coming back. Fourteen-eighty a hundredweight, he told Ray, standing in the milk house that December with his hands under his armpits. That was the summer before last. I lost money on every can of it. Half the farms in this valley sold out. I could pay you in a room and whatever’s left. Ray sold the house in Pontook Falls for what it would bring. He took nothing much. His barn coat came out of the donation box at the post and had somebody else’s name, GAUTHIER, stitched over the pocket. He moved into the old hired man’s rooms over the milk house, two rooms and a hot plate, and at fifty-three he learned to milk. Four-thirty in the morning and four-thirty in the afternoon. Dip, strip, wipe, attach. The pipeline overhead carried the milk through glass to the tank, and you could see it go by, white, over your head. He learned each cow by her name and her temper. He learned to read a heifer’s tail and to pull a calf. He did not read anything. He was too tired to read, and it turned out he d

sections.heading: III. The Watch
sections.text: Kyle quit the prison in 2018 and moved to Manchester, to a third-floor studio in one of the old Amoskeag mill buildings on the river, brick walls and maple floors still dark with a hundred years of loom oil. He bought two good cameras and a microphone on an arm and began to talk. He was good at it. He would have told you so himself, but it was also true. He had read every one of the hundred and twenty-four letters twice, and Epictetus, and the Meditations in Greek with a dictionary propped open beside him. He could give you the three disciplines, the four passions, the difference between an impression and an assent. He could give them to a nineteen-year-old lance corporal in Jacksonville at two in the morning in words the boy could hold on to. He called the channel The Watch. He signed off every episode the same way: Stand your watch. When the pandemic closed the gyms and the bars in 2020 and young men all over the country sat alone in their rooms with their phones, they found him by the hundred thousand. By the summer of 2021 he had five hundred and twenty thousand subscribers. He had eighteen chapters that met in VFW halls, church basements and the back rooms of breweries, from B

sections.heading: IV. The Third Chair
sections.text: Ray came over for the second Muster on a Saturday in June, the first day he had taken off the farm in four and a half years. Tyler and the others were milking. He parked in the function hall lot at ten in the morning in Gauthier’s coat, though it was already warm. He found Kyle on the stage running cables and gave him the coat and his feed-store cap. Watch these. I’m going up to see the chief. He drove up to Pontook Falls in Gordon’s truck and sat in the chief’s office for half an hour. Then he went down Main Street to the post, where the old men were at the bar drinking coffee at eleven in the morning, the Korea men, the Vietnam men, the ones from his own war. He shook every hand. Then he drove back to Gorham. Kyle had the stage ready. Two chairs, the same make and the same height. He had checked. He was not going to have it said he had put Ray in a lower chair. Then, without thinking, the way you put your keys in the same pocket, he set a third chair at the end of the table, and stood looking at it, and left it. In her office that morning the chief had listened to Ray tell her, without any edge in it, that Kyle wanted to ask him some questions on the stream that afternoon. After

sections.heading: V. That’s Right
sections.text: But it was she who asked the questions, and Kyle let her, because it was her table. She asked him what is in our power and what is not. He gave it to her in Greek and then in English. She asked him the four virtues, and he gave them. She asked him the three disciplines, the passions and their kinds, the reserve clause, the view from above, what Seneca meant by a day’s accounts. He answered every one of them correctly, without a card, in good plain sentences, and the hall clapped, and in the corner of the laptop the chat ran faster than anyone could read it. Then she said, Kyle. When were you last afraid? He began to tell her what fear is. It is a judgment about a future evil, he said; the evil lies in the judgment, not in the thing. He went on in that way, well, for most of a minute. When, she said. He opened his mouth and nothing came. He was afraid at that moment and could not say so. Four hundred men watched him not say it. She turned to Ray. When were you last afraid? Tuesday, Ray said. Two in the morning. A heifer calving backwards. I thought she’d die and the calf with her. Then I got my arm in up to here. He touched his shoulder. You can’t be scared and have your arm in a co

sections.heading: VI. Other Men’s Cows
sections.text: In the front rows the chapter leaders had gone quiet in a way that was not respect. A man from the Albany chapter said it out loud, and the chat said it louder. Kyle knew all of it, every letter, every line, and the chief had not said That’s right to him once. She had said it four times to an old man in a borrowed shirt who could not name the three disciplines. What’s the trouble? the chief said into the microphone, and the man from Albany told her. She heard him out. Then she said, Ray says he’s the hired man. He’s wrong about that. Kyle’s the hired man. He’s like a fella you pay to stand at the gate and count another man’s cows through. He’ll get the number right every time, and he won’t get a glass of milk out of it. Ray milks his own. She took the first red volume out of her jacket, where it had been all along, and opened it at a page she had marked with a parking ticket, and read it the way she read on Tuesdays. For a man, however, whose progress is definite, to chase after choice extracts and to prop his weakness by the best known and the briefest sayings and to depend upon his memory, is disgraceful; it is time for him to lean on himself.
