title: The Third Chair
place: Gorham and North Haverhill, New Hampshire
logline: A police chief's Seneca table sends one friend to milk another man's cows and the other to half a million subscribers.

verses.text: Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death. Those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.
Those who are advanced in earnestness, having understood this clearly, delight in earnestness, and rejoice in the knowledge of the Ariyas (the elect).
These wise people, meditative, steady, always possessed of strong powers, attain to Nirvana, the highest happiness.

bg.commentary: The longest story in the commentary is a cycle about King Udena of Kosambī and his court. Udena is born in a tree after a monster bird carries off his pregnant mother, grows up with a hermit who gives him a lute that charms elephants, and rides home on an elephant to claim his throne. The foundling Ghosaka survives seven attempts on his life by the rich man who bought him. The orphan Sāmāvatī, named for the fence she builds around an almshouse, becomes one of Udena's three chief queens; another, Vāsuladattā, he wins while held prisoner by her father, who lured him with a wooden elephant; the third, Māgandiyā, comes to hate the Buddha after he refuses her in marriage with a scornful verse about the body. Sāmāvatī's hunchbacked maid Khujjuttarā hears the Buddha while buying flowers and teaches the queen's women. Māgandiyā hires men to revile the Buddha, frames the women with dead cocks and a snake hidden in Udena's lute, and when the arrow Udena shoots at Sāmāvatī turns back, she has their house set on fire with all of them inside. Udena punishes her and her kin with fire, plow and knife. Asked which of these women are alive and which are dead, the Buddha speaks verses 21–23.
bg.history:
Spanish New Mexico hung off the north end of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the road of some 1,590 miles from Mexico City that was used from 1598 to 1882. Governor Diego de Vargas reestablished the villa of Santa Cruz de la Cañada in 1695, and its church was built between 1733 and 1748. Trade ran south by mule train and cart to Chihuahua, and so did the wine and brandy of El Paso del Norte, hundreds of barrels of it in a good year. Down the same road, the smallpox epidemic that swept North America in those years left the Valley of Mexico in 1779 and reached El Paso and points north in 1780, killing around 5,000 Pueblo people upriver.

Genízaros were detribalized Native people, most of them captives taken or bought from Comanche, Apache, Navajo and other nations and ransomed into Spanish households, where they typically owed ten to twenty years of service and were taught the Catholic faith. By 1793 they may have made up a third of the colony's people. In 1754 Governor Vélez Cachupín gave 34 genízaro families a land grant at Abiquiú on the Chama in return for defending the frontier, and it became the archetypal genízaro settlement. On the feast of San Juan, June 24, the people of the northern valleys still keep old traditions of bathing in the streams, and the rivers and acequias are blessed.

sections.heading: I. The Red Blanket
sections.dateline: The Truchas peaks, New Mexico · the 1740s
sections.text: Don Bernardo Quintana was the richest man between the Chama and the Truchas. One morning in March his wife doña Isabel sat with him in the sun of the placita, heavy with their first child, wrapped in his red Saltillo blanket, playing with his silver ring, which she had slipped off his finger. A shadow went over the yard. Don Bernardo looked up and ran for the door, and doña Isabel, who was eight months along, could not run. The old people in the valley say it was an eagle, and some say it was something worse. It saw the red blanket and took it for meat. It came down and closed its feet on her and carried her up over the walls, over the river and the black mesa, into the mountains, and set her in the fork of a great yellow pine where it kept the bones of the lambs it took. She kept silent while it flew, knowing it would drop her, and when it settled and bent its head to her she clapped her hands and screamed, and it flew off. That night, in a storm, alone in the tree, she had her baby. He was born as the clouds broke and the morning star came out over the mountain, and she called him Lucero for the star. Below the pine lived a hermit named Anselmo. He had been a rich man in Taos, an

sections.heading: II. The Luck-Child
sections.dateline: Santa Cruz de la Cañada · the 1750s
sections.text: A woman who lived by men at the edge of the plaza had a son, and because a son was no use to her she put him in an old winnowing basket and left him on the dung heap. The dogs and the crows came and sat around him in a ring all morning, and not one of them touched him. A man going by saw the ring of dogs and took the boy home. That same day the padre told don Cosme Baca, who ran the mule trains to Chihuahua, that by the almanac a boy born in the Cañada that day would be the richest man in the valley. Don Cosme's wife was near her time. He sent his servant Juana to buy the boy, meaning to marry him to his daughter if she had one. She had a son. So don Cosme gave Juana her orders. She laid the baby across the gate of the corral at dawn, where the oxen would come out over him, and the lead ox, that always came out last, came out first that morning and stood over the child with its four feet around him while the herd went by on either side. The herdsman took him home. Juana bought him back. She laid him in the road in front of the carretas leaving for Chihuahua, and the oxen of the first cart threw off their yoke and would not go on, though the drover yoked them again and again until t

sections.heading: III. The Fence
sections.text: Ventura had a friend he had never met, don Fermín Ledesma of El Paso del Norte. For twenty years they had sent each other presents by the caravans, wine and brandy north, wool and piñones south. In the fall of 1780 the smallpox came up the river from Mexico. It went through El Paso and through every pueblo on the Rio Grande. In don Fermín's house the servants died first, and then the children, and when there were three of them left, don Fermín and his wife and their daughter Paz, they broke a hole through the back wall of the house and went out that way, and not by the door the sickness had come in, and started north to find Ventura. They came into the Cañada in January, black from sun and wind, so starved they could hardly stand, and lay down in a shed by the road. Don Fermín would not go to his friend's door looking like a beggar. They would eat a few days at the kitchen at his gate first. So Paz, who had been brought up never to go out of the house without her mother, covered her face with her rebozo and stood in line with the beggars and the widows and the children of the smallpox. How many? Three. They gave her three bowls. Her father ate all of his, and could not keep it, and

sections.heading: IV. The White Horse
sections.text: Don Ignacio Saavedra, whom they called el Bravo, ran his sheep from Bernalillo to the Puerco, and one day he asked his men whether anybody on the river was as grand as he was. Only el Lucero of the Cañada, they said, who had a guitar that called horses, and more horses than God. He meant to take him. Nobody could, they said. But el Lucero would ride a long way for a good horse. So el Bravo had a stallion built out of cottonwood and hide, white as the snow on the Truchas, with men inside it to walk it, and set it loose by the hot springs at Ojo Caliente. When el Lucero heard of it he rode out after it and played the third song, and the white horse did not stop, because it had no ears. He rode on alone after it, faster than his men could follow, and el Bravo's riders closed in from both sides. El Bravo locked him in his torreón and feasted for three days, until el Lucero sent down word that a man who takes his enemy alive must let him go or kill him, and getting drunk was neither. El Bravo came up. He would let him go, he said, for the songs. El Lucero said he would teach them to anyone who knelt to him first. El Bravo said he would sooner have him hanged. Hang me, then. You're maste

sections.heading: V. The Footprint
sections.text: In those years there was a man the valley called el Hermano. He had been born among some people out on the plains, nobody knew which, and taken as a child by the Comanches, and ransomed at the Taos fair by a family of Abiquiú who raised him to work for them for twenty years and taught him the catechism. When his years were served he went to live alone in a hut below the black mesa by the river. He belonged to no brotherhood and took no vows. People came to sit with him anyway, and some of them stayed. Every winter a band of men who lived summers in the mountains came down to the Cañada, and three rich men, Ventura and don Gaspar Gallegos and don Lázaro Tafoya, kept them until spring. One fall, coming down, they sat under a great cottonwood by the river, and the oldest thought how good a drink of water would be, and there was water. He thought of food, and there was food. Who's there? A peon in his work clothes came out of the trunk. He had worked for a family in Abiquiú that followed el Hermano, and one Holy Thursday he came in from the fields at dark, starving, and found the whole house keeping the fast. He kept it with them, though it was late, and the cramps took him, and he die

sections.heading: VI. Castile Roses
sections.text: El Lucero gave Paz eight reales a week to buy roses for the altar in her room. Her servant Chona went for them, a hunchbacked genízara who had been bought at the Taos fair as a girl. She bought them from Simón, the gardener of the three rich men, who grew the old roses of Castile along his ditch, and every week she paid him four reales and kept four. One day Simón said, No roses yet. El Hermano is eating at my house today. Stay, and you can have what's left over after. So Chona stood in Simón's doorway while el Hermano ate his bread and said his thanks. What he said was very short. She went home with eight reales' worth of roses. Did the patrón give us double this week? No, señora. Every other week I kept four reales for myself. Why not this week? Because I heard el Hermano. Paz did not call her a thief. She said, You've had a drink of something. Give me some. She had water heated and bathed Chona herself and put a new skirt on her and her own rebozo, and sat her in her own chair with her painted fan, and Chona told them everything el Hermano had said, word for word, to Paz and all her women. When she was done they said, From now on, don't take anything. Be our mother. Go every day

sections.heading: VII. The Guitar
sections.text: Clara Mondragón saw the holes and found out what they were for, and went to el Lucero. Paz and her women are cutting holes in your walls. In a few days they'll kill you. He did not believe her. The third time she told him he went and saw the holes, and said nothing, and had them filled with adobe and new windows set in all the rooms, small, and high up in the wall, so that a woman inside could see the sky and nothing else. That is why the old houses in the Cañada have their windows so high, people say. Then Clara paid the idlers of the plaza to follow el Hermano. Thief, they shouted, Comanche, dog, mule, devil, you're going to hell. His companion, a young man named Cruz who carried his water jar, said, Hermano, let's go somewhere else. Where? To Santa Fe. And if they shout at us in Santa Fe? Then to Albuquerque. And there? Cruz had no answer. Trouble that starts in one place has to be settled in that place, el Hermano said. I'm like a horse in a fight. The arrows come from every side. It's my work to stand. And he gave Cruz a line to hold on to. Take all that shall be brought upon thee: and in thy sorrow endure, and in thy humiliation keep patience. — Ecclesiasticus 2:4 Seven days,

sections.heading: VIII. The Morning Star
sections.text: Clara could think of nothing else. On a day when el Lucero had ridden out to his sheep camps on the Chama, she sent her uncle into Paz's house. He opened the storerooms, soaked rags in tallow and piñon pitch, and began to wind them around the posts of the portal and the ends of the vigas. Paz's women came out to see. The patrón wants the wood cured, he told them. Who knows why they do anything in a rich man's house. Go in, ladies, you'll get pitch on your skirts. When they had all gone into their rooms he barred the doors from outside and set fire to the rags one after another and walked away. Paz called through the walls to her women. Who knows how many times women like us have burned. In this valley, in the raids, in every country there ever was, all the way back. Watch. She did not say watch what. Chona was at Simón's that morning, and so she lived to say that from the road she could hear them through the high windows, praying, not screaming, until the roof came down. Cruz and the mountain men brought the news to el Hermano at noon. Paz's house burned with all her women in it. What will become of them? Not one of them is lost, said el Hermano. Each one of them received what was

title: Castile Roses
place: Santa Cruz de la Cañada, New Mexico
logline: In Spanish New Mexico, a jealous third wife plots against the women who watch a genízaro hermit through holes in their walls.

verses.text: If an earnest person has roused himself, if he is not forgetful, if his deeds are pure, if he acts with consideration, if he restrains himself, and lives according to law,--then his glory will increase.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, plague strikes the house of the richest man in Rājagaha. The dying parents tell their son to break through the wall and flee, and tell him where their fortune is buried. He comes back twelve years later, unrecognized, finds the treasure untouched, and leaves it in the ground, afraid he will be taken for a thief. He hires himself out to the servants to wake the workers every morning. King Bimbisāra, who can tell anyone by their voice, hears him and says it is the voice of a rich man. A palace servant woman takes her daughter and moves into his hut, wins him with good cooking, cuts the cords of his bed until it collapses, and marries him to the girl. Then she has the king order compulsory holidays, so the young man has to dig up coins, which she sends to the king. Dragged before the king, he admits his wealth; the king has it carted to the palace, honors him, and gives him his daughter. The Buddha says that such a man's glory increases.
bg.history:
In January 1760 smallpox swept Charles Town, brought in, it is believed, by soldiers returning from the campaign against the Cherokee in the northwest of the province. According to the South Carolina Historical Society, more than half the town's residents were infected and some nine hundred died, while the physician Alexander Garden inoculated more than two thousand people in two weeks. The Anglo-Cherokee War ended with the Treaty of Charlestown in December 1761, and the deerskin trade that had made merchants like the fictional Moses Valverde rich resumed. The town's new Exchange was built between 1767 and 1771.

Kahal Kadosh Beth Elohim was founded in 1749 as an Orthodox Sephardic congregation, mostly by Jews who had come from London. Its members worshipped in houses converted to synagogues until they dedicated a building on Hasell Street in 1794, and in 1764 they acquired the burial ground on Coming Street. Congregations like it across the Atlantic world were visited by emissaries from the Land of Israel, rabbis who traveled for years collecting for the poor of Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, and who preached and taught wherever they stopped. One of them, Raphael Haim Isaac Carigal of Hebron, was sent to the West Indies and the North American colonies in the early 1770s. Hakham Gabay, the parnas Mordecai Lobo and the Valverde family are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Wall
sections.text: Moses Valverde bought deerskins from the packhorse men who came down out of the Cherokee hills, and indigo from the planters on the Santee, and he sold both to London. In twenty years of it he had become one of the richest Jews between New York and the Spanish islands. He had a house on Elliott Street with a brick kitchen in the yard behind it and a fig tree against the back wall, and he kept his money in gold, in the ground, because his own father had left Lisbon in a single night with nothing but what was sewn into the lining of his coat. The smallpox came down to the town that winter with the soldiers coming home from the Cherokee war. By the middle of January nobody on Elliott Street was counting funerals anymore, and the carts went by at night. In the Valverde house it went the way the old women always said it went. First the ones who carry the water, then the ones who give the orders. Jemmy, who was eleven and fetched water from the pump on the corner, took sick first, and his mother Phibbah nursed him in the loft over the kitchen and buried him on a Monday, and on the Thursday she was lying where he had lain. Then the mistress. Then the master. David was fourteen. His father

sections.heading: II. The Woodsman
sections.text: He came back down the Broad Path in a hunting shirt and leggings, with his hair to his shoulders and a beard that had never seen a razor, and nobody in Charles Town knew him. The town had grown. There was a new Exchange at the foot of Broad Street with a cupola on top of it, and ships so thick at the wharves that the masts looked like a burnt wood. The house on Elliott Street was gone. A fire had taken that end of the street some years back, and since there was no heir anyone could find, the lot had gone into Chancery, and the lawyers had let it sit. Weeds stood in the yard as high as his chest. The fig tree had grown wild over the hole in the back wall, which nobody had ever closed. The brick kitchen stood with no roof, and its chimney stood above it, black inside. He went in by the old hole that night with a borrowed spade. The third brick from the left. He lifted the hearth bricks one by one and laid them in a row in the order he took them up, and he dug, and at two feet the spade rang on iron. The pot was just where they had left it. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth that was still sound, the gold lay as if somebody had put it there that afternoon: Portuguese joes and half-joes, Span

sections.heading: III. The Ear
sections.text: Mordecai Lobo had been parnas of the congregation more than once. He was past seventy, and his eyes had gone milky, so that he could tell light from dark and not much else. But he had been a merchant for fifty years, and a merchant learns to listen. He knew every man in Charles Town by his voice. He knew them by their coughs, by the way they set down a glass. Men said you could not lie to Mordecai Lobo across a table, because he would hear it, and men who had tried it said the same. He lay awake before dawn, as old men do. On the third morning that the new man came calling up Tradd Street, he lifted his head off the pillow. Esther. Who is that? Esther Carvajal kept his house. She was a widow from Jamaica with a daughter, and she had been in that house eight years, and there was nothing that happened in it that she did not know about before it happened. She was at the window already, building up the fire. The shamash’s new man. The one from the woods. That, said Mordecai Lobo, is the voice of a rich man. Esther said nothing. But she thought: it doesn’t matter what he says, a thing like that ought to be looked into. And when the old man was dressed and gone down, she sent the boy who

sections.heading: IV. The Rope Bed
sections.dateline: The yard behind the synagogue house
sections.text: She put Rebecca into an old calico gown with a torn hem and put on another herself, and they went out of the back of the Lobo house with one bundle between them like two women on the road. At the poor rooms behind the synagogue house she knocked and said they were going on to Savannah and wanted a place to lie down for a day or two. Mrs. Nathan said there were nine of them in two rooms and it was out of the question. But the woodsman is all alone over the woodshed. Ask him. David said no. She asked again, and he said no again. She stood in his doorway and asked a third time and a fourth, and finally said, One night only, master, just this one night, and we’re gone at first light, and set her bundle down inside the door and would not pick it up again. In the morning she was still there. When he came back from calling the minyan she said, Master, before you go to your work, give me what you would spend on your dinner, and I’ll cook it for you. Never mind that. I cook for myself. She asked him again, and again, and in the end he gave her his rice and the few coppers he had. She went to the market with them and with some of the twenty pounds besides, and when he came in that evening fr

sections.heading: V. The Feasts
sections.text: A few days later Esther sent a note round to Tradd Street. Let the parnas and the elders give out from the reading desk that this year every householder of the congregation is to keep Purim properly, to send portions to his neighbors and give to the poor, and that any householder who does not will pay a fine of forty shillings and have his name read out. The old man had it given out. Congregations had their rules in those days, and their fines, and nobody thought this one strange except that it was strict. My son, Esther said to David, the elders say every householder has to keep Purim this year or pay. What shall we do? Mother, I live on a peck of rice. What do you want me to do? My son, a man with a door of his own can borrow. The elders have to be obeyed, but a debt gets paid somehow or other. Go and find a coin or two somewhere. He was angry enough to break something. He went out that night in a black temper by the old hole in the wall behind the fig tree, and lifted the third brick and the others in their order, and dug, and took out one coin, a single half-joe, and filled it all in again and came back with the dirt still under his nails and put it in her hand. Esther sent the

sections.heading: VI. The Drays
sections.text: Two porters and the beadle came for him while he was sweeping. Which of you is the woodsman? The parnas wants you. David was frightened. He said the parnas did not know him and he had done nothing. He said a good deal more. The porters took him by the arms, and when he would not walk they took him by the arms and legs and carried him out of the yard like a sack of meal, with the broom still in his hand until he dropped it. Esther came flying down the stairs. You dogs. You’re not fit to put your hands on my son-in-law. And to David: Go along, my son. Don’t be afraid. When I see the parnas I’ll see to it that these two never carry another load for this congregation as long as they live. Then she took Rebecca by the hand and ran ahead of them all the way to Tradd Street, and went in by the back door, and took off the torn calico and put on her own good black silk and her garnets, and put Rebecca into the blue silk the old man had given her at New Year, and the two of them stood together at the door of the front room. The porters brought David in and set him on his feet. He bowed to the old man in the armchair and stood in front of him. You are the woodsman? Yes, sir. Why do you hide y

sections.heading: VII. The Hakham
sections.text: That spring there was a guest lodging in the Lobo house, a rabbi from Hebron in the Land of Israel. His name was Hakham Eliezer Gabay, and he had been two years on the road, through Leghorn and Amsterdam and London and the islands, collecting for the poor of his city, the way such men had always come round to the scattered congregations, with a letter of credentials and a box. He was a small man with a gray beard who ate very little and said less. He had come up from Jamaica in the spring and would go on to Savannah when the weather turned. The old man took David to him by the hand, the way you take a boy. Hakham, look at this one. I never saw such a man. He has a fortune in the ground and it never once went to his head. He put on rags and worked for rice in the yard and swept the floor and called us to prayer every morning in the dark, and nobody knew. I found him out by his voice. I made him own to it, I had it carried up to my house, I put him on the east bench, I gave him a wife. I never in my life saw anyone so wise. The hakham looked at David for some time. Who called the minyan this morning? I did, Hakham. And tomorrow? David had not thought about it. He thought about it now

title: Paid in Rice
logline: A bearded woodsman calls the Jews of Charles Town to prayer each dawn, and a blind old merchant hears money in his voice.

verses.text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.

bg.commentary: The commentary tells this verse's story through Culla Panthaka, the slowest of the Buddha's disciples, who could not learn four lines in four months, was turned out by his own brother, and woke to the whole teaching while rubbing a clean cloth in the sun.
bg.history:
Alabama's 1901 constitution forbade the legislature from ever authorizing a marriage between a white person and a Black person, and state law made such a marriage a crime. A couple like Eleanor and Amos had no lawful way to exist in the state; leaving was the only option, and leaving was dangerous. The U.S. Supreme Court struck down these laws nationwide in Loving v. Virginia in 1967, but the dead language stayed in Alabama's constitution until voters removed it in 2000, with about 40 percent voting to keep it. More at anti-miscegenation laws in the United States.

The road north the couple took was the road of the Great Migration, which carried some six million Black Southerners to Northern and Western cities between 1910 and 1970. In Detroit, Hastings Street ran through Black Bottom and Paradise Valley, the center of Black business and music in the city, until urban renewal and the I-375 freeway cleared it in the late 1950s and early 1960s. The grove sits on the Tombigbee, which runs south through Alabama's western Black Belt.

sections.heading: I. The Road
sections.text: The Pruett house sat on the only hill in Caddo Springs, three stories of white board and green shutter, and Harlan Pruett kept his daughter in it the way he kept the deeds in his safe. He locked her up, counted on her every night, and brought her out for church. Eleanor was nineteen that summer. Amos Reed was twenty-four. He drove the Packard, cut the grass, and hauled the ice up from the depot wrapped in croker sacks. Nobody in town would ever be able to say how it started, because nobody in town could imagine that it had, and the two people who knew never told. It went the way water goes through a levee, one grain and then another, and then there was no levee. They left in October on the night train to Birmingham with forty dollars and a cardboard suitcase. In Birmingham they did not sit together. In Memphis they did not walk together. They did not stop being afraid until somewhere north of Cairo, Illinois, and even then they never stopped all the way. Detroit took them in the way Detroit took everybody, without asking and without caring. Amos found work at a foundry on the river. Eleanor found a room above a tailor's on Hastings Street where nobody looked twice, because everybod

sections.heading: II. The Carriage House
sections.text: It was Wayland who asked first. Other boys on Hastings Street had grandmothers who came on Sundays with pound cake. Where were theirs? Eleanor said far. Wayland asked how far. Eleanor said Alabama, and Wayland, who was quick, went to the library and found it on a map, and came home and said that wasn't so far, he'd measured it with a string. Eleanor wrote her father that winter. He answered in March, two lines in his bank hand. I will not see you or that man. Send the boys. Amos said no. Amos said it for a year. Then the ladle chain at the foundry let go and a pour of iron came down where his feet had been half a second before, and took his left foot anyway, and the money ran out the way it does. In June of 1952 Eleanor pinned paper tags to two jacket lapels and put her sons on the City of New Orleans and did not cry until the train was gone. Harlan Pruett met them at the Caddo Springs depot after dark with his hat pulled low. He looked at Wayland a long time, because Wayland had his mother's eyes and the town's own color, nearly. He looked at Little a shorter time, because Little was darker, and had his father's quiet, and looked at the old man the way a dog looks at weather. The

sections.heading: III. The Grove
sections.dateline: The old Mabry place, on the Tombigbee · 1956
sections.text: Past the end of the Pruett land, where the road gave up and turned to sand, there was a pecan grove that had belonged to the Mabrys until the Mabrys died out. A man named Sutton lived there now. Some said he had taught chemistry at Tuskegee. Some said he had done eleven years at Kilby. Some said both, and that the order mattered. He was tall and grey at the temples and he moved slowly, as if he had already been everywhere he was going. Men came out to the grove to hear him, and some of them stayed. A sharecropper from Sumter County. A veteran who did not sleep. A white boy from Mobile with burn scars up both arms. A man who had been the worst drunk in Marengo County and was now nothing at all, which he said was better. They wore plain khaki. They owned what they could carry. Mornings they walked into town with tin pails and stood quiet at back doors, and took what people gave, and said thank you either way. There were fifty of them, give or take, and the town did not know what to make of them, and so mostly left them alone. That was the closest thing to a miracle anybody in Caddo Springs would admit to. Wayland was seventeen when he started going out there on Sunday afternoons. He

sections.heading: IV. The Verse
sections.text:
Little was not stupid. He could tell what was wrong with a truck by listening to it idle. He knew every bird on the river by its call and most of them by the sound of their wings. He could walk the grove in the black dark and never touch a tree. But words slid off him like rain off a tin roof. They hit, and they made a sound, and they were gone. Every man who came to the grove learned one verse first. Brother Sutton gave it to them the first week. Wayland gave it to Little. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow;
    they toil not, neither do they spin:
    And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory
    was not arrayed like one of these. — Matthew 6:28–29 Little said it at the well. He said it in the outhouse. He said it walking to town with his tin pail and walking back. He said it in his sleep; men heard him. Every morning he would have the first two lines. By noon the second line would have pushed the first one out, the way a new hen pushes an old one off the roost. By night he would have the lilies of the field and nothing else, standing there with no idea how they grew. That went on for four months. On the first Friday in August, Wayland took him out p

sections.heading: V. The Gate
sections.text: Brother Sutton was sitting on an upturned bucket by the gate, as if he had been there all night. Maybe he had. Where you headed? My brother says I'm no good for it. Your brother didn't bring you in here, Sutton said. I did. A man doesn't go home because his brother says so. Come here. He took a handkerchief out of his shirt pocket. It was white cotton, ironed, still holding the creases from the iron. He shook it out and handed it over. Sit on that step where the sun's going to hit. Rub this between your hands. And while you rub it, say: taking the dirt out. Just that. Can you hold three words? Yes sir. I can hold three words. So he sat. The sun came up over the river the color of a peach, then the color of brass. He rubbed the handkerchief between his hands and said taking the dirt out, taking the dirt out, low, under his breath, the way he had said the lily verse, except this time nothing slid off, because there was nothing to slide. His hands had been washed. He had washed them at the pump. But the sun climbed, and the heat came up out of the ground, and the handkerchief went from white to the color of dishwater to the color of a mule's flank, and it was his hands doing it, his o

sections.heading: VI. The Supper
sections.text: Dr. Coleman had strung bulbs through the chinaberry trees in his yard and set out sawhorse tables with white sheets on them, and his wife and Hattie Greer and four women from Mount Pisgah had been cooking since Thursday. Ham and greens and butter beans and sliced tomatoes and cornbread in iron skillets, and peach cobbler under dish towels against the flies. When the men were seated, the doctor brought out a basin and a pitcher, as was his custom, to pour water over Brother Sutton's hands before the meal. Sutton put his hand flat over the basin. Is there anybody left out at the grove? Wayland answered. He had the roll in his shirt pocket. No sir. Nobody. There's somebody. Wayland started to say something and didn't. Dr. Coleman looked from one of them to the other and then called for his son Marcus, who was eleven and had a red Schwinn, and told him to ride out to the Mabry place and bring back whoever he found. Marcus was gone a half hour. He came back slow, walking the bike, and he was the color of ash, and he went straight to his daddy and not to Brother Sutton. Daddy, it's full. What's full? The grove. There's men under every tree. There's men on the porch roof. There's men sitt

sections.heading: VII. The Island
sections.text: The men built a fire by the river after, because nobody was going to sleep. They kept saying it to each other. Four months he couldn't hold a verse. One breakfast with Brother Sutton and he held all of it. Sutton came down and sat on a stump and listened to them a while. He's always been slow, he said. And I've always been around. That's all it is. Somebody asked him what he meant, always, and he told them a story instead, which was his way. There was a rich man in Mobile, he said, a cotton factor, walking down Dauphin Street with his clerk, and he stepped over a dead rat in the gutter, and he said, half a joke, A sharp boy could make a living off that. A shoeshine boy on the corner heard it and did not take it for a joke. He picked up the rat by the tail and sold it to a woman down by the wharf who had a cat to feed, for one penny. With the penny he bought a jar of cane syrup, and he carried a bucket of well water and the syrup down to where the flower women came in off the boats in the heat, and gave them sweet water for nothing, and they gave him flowers. He sold the flowers. With the flower money he bought a hatchet, and cut the deadfall after a storm, and sold the firewood. He

title: Little Wayland
logline: A boy who can't hold four lines of scripture, a white handkerchief, and a pecan grove full of himself.

verses.text: Fools follow after vanity, men of evil wisdom. The wise man keeps earnestness as his best jewel.
Follow not after vanity, nor after the enjoyment of love and lust! He who is earnest and meditative, obtains ample joy.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the city of Sāvatthī keeps a seven-day Fools’ Festival, when revelers smear themselves with ash and cow-dung and stand in doorways shouting coarse abuse at everyone, kin, friends and monks alike, until people pay them a coin to go away. The Buddha’s lay followers ask him to stay at the monastery for the week, send food out to the monks, and do not leave their own houses. On the eighth day they bring him into the city with great offerings and tell him how their ears nearly burst. He answers that fools behave this way, and that the wise guard heedfulness (appamāda, attention, earnestness) as their greatest treasure, and many who hear him enter the stream.
bg.history:
Fort Lauderdale’s spring break began when the Colgate University swim team came to train there over Christmas in 1934. The 1960 novel and film Where the Boys Are, which featured the Elbo Room on the corner of Las Olas and the beach, brought the crowds, and by the early 1980s the city drew 250,000 to 350,000 students a season. Florida’s drinking age was 19 until the federal National Minimum Drinking Age Act pushed it to 21. In 1985 Mayor Robert Dressler said on Good Morning America that students were no longer welcome; the city banned open containers on the beach side of A1A and overnight beach parking, and enforcement brought more than 2,500 arrests. By 1989 about 20,000 students came.

Many of the retirees along the Florida coast had spent their working lives in New York’s garment trade and in the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union, which ran classes, a press and a Pocono resort, Unity House, for its members. Many of its Jewish dressmakers belonged to Local 22; its Italian dressmakers formed Local 89 in 1919, numbered for the year of the French Revolution and led for decades by the anti-fascist Luigi Antonini. The Maestro’s Dante is the Longfellow translation of 1867; the running souls of the slothful are on the fourth terrace of the Purgatorio, canto XVIII.

sections.heading: I. The Chair
sections.text: Every morning at a quarter to six Bella Kagan took the folding chair out of the hall closet of the Coral Arms, the aluminum one with the green and white webbing, and carried it down the stairs and across A1A and over the soft sand to the place where the sand turned hard. Then she went back for the Maestro. He was eighty-seven years old and he could still walk, if it was slow and somebody had his elbow. He wore a linen cap and a white shirt buttoned to the collar and the same grey trousers every day of the year, and he carried a cane he mostly did not lean on. His eyes had gone in the last few years. He could see light and dark and the shape of a person against a window, and that was about all. When they reached the chair he felt for its arms, turned himself around and sat, and Bella put the cane across his knees and went back up to make coffee. He stayed there an hour. He did not read, because he couldn't, and he did not sleep, and he did not pray, because he had not prayed since 1911. He listened. sections.heading: II. The Strip
sections.dateline: A1A, between Las Olas and Sunrise
sections.text: They had known about the college students when they bought the building. Everybody in Fort Lauderdale knew. Since before the war the colleges had sent their swimmers down at Christmas, and after the movie with Connie Francis in 1960 the rest of the students came after the swimmers, every year a few more, every spring, for the weeks around Easter. In the first years at the Coral Arms the residents had thought it was charming. The boys were polite. The girls wore white bathing caps. Mrs. Fishbein from 4C fed them rugelach on the steps. By 1985 there were three hundred and fifty thousand of them in a season, and the city could not count them except by the garbage. They came in March in cars with plates from Ohio and Michigan and New York and Ontario, eight to a car, and they drove up and down A1A from Las Olas to Sunrise and back again, bumper to bumper, all day and half the night, with their arms out the windows and the radios loud. They slept eight to a motel room and in their cars and on the beach. sections.heading: III. The Week
sections.text: The board met that Thursday night instead of Dante. Sol Pomerantz, who had been a cutter in Local 10 and was the president of the co-op, stood at the end of the pinochle table with a copy of the Sun-Sentinel and read out of it. The big schools from the Midwest had their break the next week, all at once. The paper said the next week would be the worst week of the season. Sol said he had talked to a man at the Chamber of Commerce and the man had said the same, and had also said, in a way Sol did not care for, that the students brought a great deal of money into the city. So what do we do? said Mrs. Fishbein. We do what we did in the shop when the boss went crazy, said Carmela. We keep our heads down until he gets tired. They decided it among themselves in twenty minutes, which for that room was a record. For seven days nobody would go out who did not have to. They would bring in groceries on the Sunday and not go out again until the Sunday after. Anybody who had a doctor's appointment would take a taxi from the back door on the side street. They would keep the blinds down on the ocean side. And the Maestro, they all agreed, would not go to the beach. Not at six in the morning, not at

sections.text: They carried his meals up the stairs on trays covered with dish towels, as they had agreed. On Sunday it was Bella's brisket. On Monday it was Carmela's escarole and beans, and Mrs. Fishbein's chicken soup at night, because Mrs. Fishbein believed that the Maestro, being thin, was always one day from death. On Tuesday Angelo Esposito's wife Philomena sent up eggplant, and Sol, who could not cook, sent up a box of rugelach from the bakery on Sunrise and a note in his cutter's square capitals that said STAY INSIDE. The Maestro ate a little of everything, and sent every plate back washed. Outside it was as the paper had said. The cars on A1A did not move at all for whole afternoons, and the students stood up through the sunroofs and on the hoods and shouted from car to car. Someone set up a loudspeaker on a hotel balcony down the block and played the same song by Bruce Springsteen over and over until a policeman went up and took it away, and then someone played it from another balcony. A police helicopter went up and down the beach. On Monday night a boy climbed the Coral Arms' palm tree and could not get down, and the fire department came. sections.heading: V. The Eighth Day
sections.text: At half past five on Sunday Bella woke and did not know why, and then she knew. It was quiet. She dressed. She did not put on a housedress. She put on her good navy blue with the white collar that she wore to Morris's grave, and her straw hat, and went down. Carmela was already in the lobby in black with a cake box tied with string. Sol was there in pressed slacks and a jacket, holding four folding chairs under each arm like a cutter carries bolts. Angelo and Philomena came down the stairs with a coffee urn between them from the card room, the big one they used for funerals. Mrs. Fishbein had a tablecloth. They kept coming down, out of the elevator and down the stairs, in their good clothes, as if somebody had sent out invitations, though nobody had. Thirty, forty of them. Women in hats. Men who had not worn ties since the last bar mitzvah. Every one of them carrying a chair. Bella went up for the Maestro. He was waiting, dressed, with his cap on and his cane across his knees. I heard, he said. They're gone. They crossed A1A all together, slowly, at the pace of the slowest, which was his. There were no cars. sections.heading: VI. The Tracks
sections.text: That year the mayor went on morning television and told the students of America that they were not welcome in Fort Lauderdale anymore, and the city commission banned open containers on the beach side of A1A and overnight parking on the beach. The police made more than two thousand arrests enforcing it. The spring after that there were fewer students, and fewer the year after, and within a few years they had mostly gone on to Daytona and Panama City and Mexico, where the drinking age was lower. The bar owners on the Strip complained to the paper. The Coral Arms did not. Jason telephoned in May. He said he was sorry about the money. He said he was going to pay it back, and Bella said to keep it and buy a book, and he laughed and said, okay, Grandma, what book, and she told him Dante, the Longfellow, and to read the part about the mountain. She did not know if he did. He did send her a postcard of the Oneonta bus station, which was a joke, and she put it on the refrigerator. The Maestro died in February, in his chair by the window, in the dark, at eighty-eight. title: Folding Chairs
logline: During the worst week of spring break, retired garment workers on A1A keep their blind Dante teacher indoors and wait out the noise.

verses.text: When the learned man drives away vanity by earnestness, he, the wise, climbing the terraced heights of wisdom, looks down upon the fools, serene he looks upon the toiling crowd, as one that stands on a mountain looks down upon them that stand upon the plain.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest. The Elder Mahā Kassapa, a great ascetic who lived in a cave and ate what he was given on his morning round, comes back from his round one day, eats, and sits down to survey with his inner sight all living beings as they are born and die, in the water, on the earth and on the mountains. The Buddha, seated far away, asks himself what Kassapa is doing, sees it, and says that the whole of the rising and falling of beings is beyond a disciple's range: a being is conceived in a womb without even its mother or father knowing, and only a Buddha can know all of it. He sends a radiant image of himself to sit face to face with Kassapa and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Bristol Bay has the largest sockeye salmon runs in the world, and until the 1950s nobody could say how many fish escaped the commercial nets to spawn. In 1951 a biologist noticed that migrating sockeye could be counted from a high bank at the outlet of Lake Aleknagik on the Wood River, because they travel in narrow bands close to each shore. W. F. Thompson of the University of Washington's Fisheries Research Institute tested counting from towers in 1953, and the Wood River towers have been counted every summer since 1956. The method is a systematic sample: an observer with a hand tally counts for a set part of each hour (ten minutes became the standard) and the count is expanded to the whole hour. Compared against weirs, it proved accurate to within a few percent. Carol Ann Woody's chapter on tower counts gives the history. Alaska became a state in 1959 and took over its fisheries from the federal government in 1960. Powered fishing boats had been illegal in Bristol Bay until 1951, so men of Evon's age had fished it under sail. The road from Dillingham to Aleknagik was built in 1959, and Moravian families had settled the lake's north shore a few years earlier.

The influenza pandemic reached Bristol Bay in the spring of 1919, months after it had burned through the rest of the country, in spite of a winter-long quarantine. It killed adults and largely spared children. When the cannery ships arrived in May they found villages with almost no grown people alive, bodies unburied and loose sled dogs among them. Cannery crews took in the orphaned children for the summer, and in the fall they were sent to the government hospital at Kanakanak, near Dillingham, which grew an orphanage to raise them. No complete count of the dead was ever made. Many Bristol Bay families today descend from those children; Alaska Public Media has an account. The Moravian Church came to southwestern Alaska in 1885 and kept a mission and school called Carmel on the Nushagak from 1886 to 1906. From the start it relied on Yup'ik lay "helpers," who led most village congregations. Evon, Anuska and the others in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. Ten Minutes
sections.dateline: The outlet of Lake Aleknagik, Bristol Bay, Alaska · July 1961
sections.text: The tower stood on the right bank where the lake let go into the Wood River. It was twenty feet of pipe scaffold guyed with cable to four spruce stumps, with a plank floor on top, a rail around the floor, and a canvas fly for the rain. Another like it stood on the far bank. The men from the university in Seattle had put up the first towers some years back, and now the state had them. Alaska had been a state for two years and had managed its own fish for one, and the new Department of Fish and Game wanted to know how many red salmon got past the nets in the bay and up into the lakes to spawn. Nobody had ever known that. The canneries knew to the case what they packed. What went by them, up the rivers, to make the fish of four and five years on, had been anybody's guess for seventy years. The way to know it was a man on a tower. The reds came up out of the bay and they did not use the middle of the river. They kept to the banks, in water a man could wade, in a band four and six and ten fish wide, one band to each side, steady as people going into church. sections.heading: II. The Small Book
sections.text: He had learned to count at Kanakanak. The sickness came into Bristol Bay in the spring of 1919, about the time the ice went out. It was the same sickness that had filled the cities the autumn before, and the country had been shut against it all winter, with no travel between the villages and no church, and it came anyway. It did a strange thing. It left the children and the very old and took the grown men and women. Evon was eleven, in a village on the Nushagak shore. His father died on a Tuesday and his mother on the Thursday, and his mother's sister and her husband in the next house, and his grandfather. By the end of that week there was no grown person in the village on his feet. He stayed four days in the house with his sister Akilina, who was three. The dogs had not been fed. They broke their chains and went in and out of the houses, and he sat in the doorway with his father's fish pew across his knees, the pole with the one steel tine, and kept them out of his. He could hear them in the other houses. He was eleven and he tried to work out how many people there had been in the village on the Sunday and how many there were now, and he did not have the figures to do it with. He

sections.heading: III. All of It
sections.dateline: The tower · the second week of July
sections.text: The run built through the first days of July. At the start he pressed the lever thirty and forty times in his ten minutes. By the sixth he was counting by tens, a press for every ten backs, and the band below him never broke. The fifty minutes began to trouble him then. He did his ten and wrote his number, and the fish kept going by. They went by all the rest of the hour with nobody's thumb on them. The state was content with that. Evon had never in his life let a fish go past him untallied, and on the night of the eighth, when his ten minutes were up, his thumb kept on. He was honest about it. He wrote the ten-minute number on the state's sheet, where it belonged. The other number, the whole hour's, he wrote in a school composition book he had bought at the store for fifteen cents. Dale came up the ladder at six that morning and found him at the rail where he had left him at six the night before. He had not sat down. After that he came at noon as well. He would finish his round, eat in whatever house it was, and come back and climb the tower in the hours that were his to sleep in. He sat on an upturned lard bucket behind Dale with the composition book on his knee. There were thing

sections.heading: IV. The Fish Rack
sections.text: Anuska was sixty-four that summer. She had buried a husband, who was a helper before Evon was, and she lived in a small house on the bluff at Kanakanak, in sight of the hospital where she had done the washing for thirty years. The Moravian people on the Dillingham side were few then and met where they could, and it was Anuska who kept their book, with the baptisms in the front and the burials in the back. She had the other book too, the cannery tally book with the red spine. It was in a pilot bread tin under her bed. People came to her. She did not preach, and it was not a thing a woman did among them then. But the ones she had washed in the tub in 1919 were grandparents now, on every river that ran into the bay, and when one of them could not get a thing straight, he found a reason to go to Dillingham. That afternoon she was at her rack behind the house, cutting reds her grandson had brought up from the beach. Her granddaughter Nettie, who was twelve, hung them as she cut. Anuska slit a fish along the back with the uluaq and opened it and scored the meat, and reached for the next, and stopped with her hand on it. What is Evon doing today? she said. Nettie did not know any Evon. Al

sections.heading: V. The Lard Bucket
sections.text: Dale was at the rail with the counter, four minutes into the three o'clock count. Evon sat behind him on his bucket with the composition book. There was a second bucket on the platform, where the day man put his lunch. Dale heard a woman's voice and turned around. An old woman was sitting on the second bucket. He had not heard the ladder, and the ladder was iron pipe and rang under a cat. She wore a kerchief and a canvas apron wet to the lap, with fish scales on it, and her hands were wet. She was looking at Evon. The day was grey, with cloud down on the hills, and there was a brightness on her that the day did not account for. It was like the shine on the river when the sun gets in under the edge of the cloud. Dale lost his count. It was the only count he lost that summer. She spoke in Yup'ik and he understood none of it. The words out of the Bible she said in English, the way she had learned them from the Moravians at Carmel, and those he understood. The rest he had from Evon later. What have you got in the book? she said. Evon held it out to her. She did not take it. She looked at the open page. How far have you got? The fish on this bank since Saturday. sections.dateline: Lake Aleknagik · to the end of the run
sections.text: Evon climbed down and went home and slept until evening. It was the first whole sleep he had had in a week. At six he came up the ladder with the composition book in his coat. He gave it to Dale and said to start the stove with it in the morning. Dale did not. He kept it forty years, through a doctorate and a career of counting fish on four rivers, and he showed it to very few people, and to each of them he told about the old woman and the bucket in the same words, leaving nothing out and adding nothing. That night Evon stood his ten minutes at the top of each hour, and he stood them differently. He set his feet. He did not let his eyes go off the panel. When the lamp on the pole came on for the short dark, he counted under it the same way. Nothing got past him in those ten minutes, up or down, and the biologist came to use Evon Nicolai's sheets as the ones he checked the other towers against. Then he wrote the number, set the counter on the rail, sat down on the bucket, and laid his hands open on his knees. He watched the fish go by for fifty minutes with nobody's thumb on them. title: The Counting Tower
logline: A Yup'ik church helper hired to count salmon ten minutes an hour decides to count every living thing that comes and goes.

verses.text: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two monks receive a meditation subject from the Buddha and go off together to a forest hermitage for the rains. One spends his evenings bringing firewood, tending the charcoal brazier and chatting with the young monks, and goes to bed when his friend comes in from walking meditation. The other warns him once (“the favor of the Buddhas may not be won by double-dealing”), gives up when he will not be told, walks in the first watch of the night, rests in the second, rises in the third, and soon reaches arahatship. When they return, the busy one tells the Buddha that his friend did nothing but sleep, and that he himself never did. The Buddha answers that he has mistaken heedlessness for heedfulness, and compares him to a worn-out hack beside a racehorse.
bg.history:
The winter of 1976–77 was one of the coldest on record in the eastern United States, and interstate pipelines could not deliver natural gas as fast as the cold burned it. Across Ohio, gas companies curtailed industrial customers and schools; the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland reported in February that schools in its district had closed widely, that General Motors had laid off nearly 26,000 workers in the Dayton area for several days, and that some 110,000 manufacturing workers had been idled. Ohio State cancelled classes on January 18 at the request of Columbia Gas and the electric company to save fuel. On February 2, two weeks after his inauguration, President Carter gave his first fireside chat, wearing a cardigan, and asked Americans to keep their thermostats at 65 degrees in the daytime and 55 at night.

Worthington was founded in 1803 by the Scioto Company, a band of settlers from Granby, Connecticut, led by James Kilbourne, who laid it out around a New England village green; by the 1970s it was a prosperous suburb on the north edge of Columbus. Drafting offices of the period still drew by hand and reproduced their sheets on the diazo or “blueline” process, developed in ammonia fumes. Miss Bevington’s school stands in for the Methodist women’s mission in Lucknow that grew into Isabella Thoburn College, founded in 1870 by the first woman missionary the Methodist Episcopal Church sent to India. Her father’s fair ran at Powell until 1937, when it moved to Delaware, where the Little Brown Jug for three-year-old pacers has been run since 1946. Charles Wesley, the hymn writer, preached “Awake, Thou That Sleepest” before the University of Oxford in 1742; it became the third of the standard sermons of Methodism.

sections.heading: I. The Parlor
sections.dateline: Worthington, Ohio · the first Sunday of 1977
sections.text: The Thursday prayer group met in the church parlor, under a framed print of John Wesley preaching from his father’s tombstone, and on the first Sunday of the new year Miss Ruth Bevington stayed after the late service to tell it goodbye until Easter. She was going to her sister’s in Bradenton, as she did every winter. She was seventy-four. She had taught arithmetic and English for thirty-eight years at the Methodist girls’ school in Lucknow, and when she came home in 1962 the church had given her a dinner and an engraved silver tray and then had not quite known what to do with her, so she had made the Thursday group herself, out of four widows and a percolator. Jerry Kessler and Walt Mohr waited by the coat rack until the widows had their boots on. They were both in their forties and both in sport coats, and they lived across the court from each other in a subdivision off Morning Street, and they worked at the same engineering firm out on the east side, and they had come to her together because it had been Jerry’s idea and Walt had not said no. sections.dateline: Pruitt & Hale, Consulting Engineers · January and February
sections.text: That was the coldest January anybody in Ohio could remember. The pipelines could not carry gas north fast as the state was burning it, and Columbia Gas cut back the factories, and then the schools, and then asked everybody else please. Ohio State called off a whole day of classes to save fuel. In Dayton the General Motors plants sent twenty-six thousand men home. In Worthington the school board talked about running Saturdays in June. The landlord at the office park put a locked plastic box over every thermostat in the building and set them all at sixty-five. Jerry had been the office manager at Pruitt & Hale for nine years. It said Administration on his door, which meant the keys, the payroll, the postage meter, the Bunn coffee maker, the softball team, the bowling league, and the big cardboard United Way thermometer in the lobby, which he colored in with a red marker every Friday. The building was one story of brown brick and smoked glass in a row of others just like it, set down in what had been a soybean field, with a retention pond out front that froze solid that winter and had three ducks standing on it most mornings like they had been told to wait. sections.heading: III. Four-Thirty
sections.text: Walt got up at half past four. He did not set an alarm. He had been a Navy man and he woke when he decided to. He went down in his socks so as not to wake Lois and took the straight chair from the end of the kitchen table and turned it toward the window over the sink, and sat. For the first weeks it was nothing but trouble. He fell asleep sitting up and woke with his chin on his chest. He planned drawings. He lettered in his head, a whole sheet of a sewage plant for the city of Marion, and when he caught himself his right hand was moving on his knee. He argued with Jerry. He argued with Jerry a good deal. He thought about his daughter in Toledo, and his knee, and money. Every time he found himself gone he came back, the way you bring a pencil back to the edge of the bar when it has wandered, without making a fuss about it, and was gone again inside a minute. The house was fifty-five degrees. He could see his breath, almost. The furnace came on under the floor with a thump and a tick and ran a while and went off. The refrigerator hummed and quit. She had come home brown from Florida. They brought her an Easter lily in foil from the church, and she put it on the radiator next to the bowl and sat down across from them with her hands in her lap. Well, she said. Did you watch? Jerry answered first. He had been thinking about how to say it all the way over. Miss Bevington, I’ll be honest with you, because I know Walt won’t mind. sections.text: Jerry woke in the dark without the alarm. The clock said four thirty-one. He lay a while listening to Barb breathe and then got up and went down the stairs in his robe and stood at the front window. The court was dark. Eleven houses in a horseshoe, their porch lights off, their station wagons nosed up to their garage doors, the wet lawns gray in the light from the one streetlamp at the mouth of the court.
