logline: In the gas-shortage winter of 1977, two Methodist friends at a suburban Ohio engineering firm are told to get up early and watch.

verses.text: By earnestness did Maghavan (Indra) rise to the lordship of the gods. People praise earnestness; thoughtlessness is always blamed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young noble named Mahāli asks the Buddha whether he has really seen Sakka, king of the gods, or only some counterfeit. The Buddha answers that he knows Sakka and what made him Sakka, explains each of his names, lists the seven vows he kept, and tells his past life. As the villager Magha he cleared a place to stand, was shoved out of it, and cleared another; then he mended the road, and thirty-two others joined him. A headman who profited from drink denounced them as thieves, and the king had them laid before an elephant, which would not trample them. Pardoned, they built a rest-house at the crossroads and shut the women out of the work, but Sudhammā got her name on its roof-pinnacle, Nandā dug a bathing pool and Cittā planted a garden. Sujātā did nothing, and was reborn as a crane. Reborn as lord of the Thirty-Three, Magha tested the crane with a fish that was not dead, brought her jewels disguised as cucumbers when she was a potter’s daughter, and at last carried her off from the house of his enemies, turning his chariot back in mid-flight so as not to crush a forest of nestlings.
bg.history:
The North American Free Trade Agreement took effect on January 1, 1994, and that December the peso collapsed; the recession of 1995 sent people north to the border for work. Laredo, Texas, and Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas, became the busiest inland port in North America. Freight does not simply drive across. A long-haul truck drops its trailer in a yard on one side, and a short-haul tractor, called a transfer, pulls it over the bridge to a yard on the other; the drivers, many of them from Nuevo Laredo, are paid by the crossing and spend much of the day in line. Until the World Trade Bridge was completed in April 2000, most trucks used a single commercial lane on the downtown bridge, and the line could run for miles. The pedimento is the Mexican customs declaration that travels with each load. The yards, the brecha, the paradero and everyone in this story are invented, and no such order by any comandante is recorded.

The catechism of the Spanish Jesuit Jerónimo de Ripalda, first printed at Burgos in 1591, was reprinted hundreds of times and carried all over Spanish America; generations of Mexican children learned their doctrine from “the Ripalda” by heart, in questions and answers. The lines here follow a Madrid printing of 1850, with its punctuation. January 2 is one of the days kept for Saint Macarius. Texas ebony, ébano, is the evergreen shade tree of the lower Rio Grande. The colorín is a coral tree, kin to the tree that stands in Sakka’s heaven in the old story, and the tronadora is the yellow trumpet-flower that grows wild on both banks. A Dina was a truck built by Mexico’s state-owned Diesel Nacional.

sections.heading: I. Saint Macario’s Day
sections.dateline: Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas · January 2, 2019, before light
sections.text: Magali Lizcano had a degree in foreign trade from Monterrey and a desk in her father’s customs agency, and on the second morning of the year she was standing in the dark at the gate of the transfer yards with a folder of pedimentos under her arm, because a driver had gone home with the wrong ones. It was cold. A norther had come down in the night. Forty or fifty men stood around an oil drum with a mesquite fire in it, on a piece of ground that was swept and level and as big as a threshing floor. At the edge of the light doña Alba had her table, her two pots and her comal. She had sold breakfast at that gate since before Magali was born: flour tortillas with egg and dried beef, with beans, with potato, and coffee boiled with cinnamon in a blue enamel pot. The men ate standing. This morning each of them, before he drank, tipped a little of his coffee onto the ground. For don Maca, one of them said. It’s his saint’s day. He doesn’t need it. Up there he has his own yard, ten thousand leagues across, and his thirty-three with him, and no line at the bridge. And a truck as long as from here to Monterrey. That one I’ve seen, doña Alba said, turning a tortilla. Nobody laughed. Magali had h

sections.heading: II. A Place to Stand
sections.text: This is what she told. He came the winter after the peso fell, from a rancho past Anáhuac, with one change of clothes. The work was transfers. A man hooked a trailer on this side, stood in line for the bridge, dropped it at a yard on the other side and came back for the next one, and he was paid by the crossing. But first he had to be given a trailer, and for that he stood at this gate in the dark with two hundred others and waited for the checker to call him. In those days the ground here was ruts. When it rained it was soup, and when it froze it was knives. The first morning, Macario scraped a place flat with the side of his boot, big enough for his two feet, and stood in it. A man came up, put a shoulder into him and took the place. Macario said nothing. He moved over and scraped another. A second man shouldered him out of that. He scraped a third. One after another they came out of the dark and pushed him off whatever he had made, and by the time the checker opened his window there was a row of flat places along the fence with a man standing in each, and Macario at the end of the row in the ruts. He looked down the row. They all seem pleased, he said to himself. If it makes the

sections.heading: III. The Dina
sections.text: There was a delegate in the yards then. He was supposed to speak for the drivers. What he did was keep a beer depot across from the gate, with a back room of slot machines, and the men who drank there were the men the checker called first. Now he looked across the road in the mornings and saw his customers standing around a fire with doña Alba’s coffee, and thirty-three of them not there at all, because they were out on the brecha with shovels. He thought: These men have got hold of the wrong work. If they would go out to the ranches for cabrito, and drink, and play the machines, I would make something off them. He sent for them. What is it you’re doing out there? Making a road to heaven, jefe. That is no work for men with families. Bring in meat from the monte, have your beer, enjoy yourselves a little. They would not. The more he pressed them, the more they would not. So he got angry, and he said to himself, I’ll finish them. He went to the Comandante. There is a gang of thieves working the brecha at night. They stop the trailers with shovels in their hands, as if they were mending the road. It was a thing that happened on other roads, and the Comandante did not look into it. Bri

sections.heading: IV. Justa’s Beam
sections.text: When they were tired of that, they talked it over. We ought to do more. What should it be? They settled on a paradero, a resting place, at the crossing where four roads came together, for anybody who came down any one of them. It would be built strong, with a roof that would stand. They sent for a master builder, don Artemio, who had put up half the churches between here and Sabinas. They also agreed among themselves that this was men’s business, and the women were to have no part in it. Now there were four women in Macario’s house: his sisters Justa, Lety and Clara, and his wife, Geni. Justa went to don Artemio by herself, with money tied in a handkerchief. Maestro, see to it that the biggest share in this building is mine. It can be done, he said. He went out into the monte and marked a mesquite for the main beam, and cut it, and laid it up to cure. When it was cured he hewed it and planed it and bored it for the pegs, and along the face of it he cut letters with a chisel: ESTE ES EL PARADERO DE JUSTA. Then he wrapped it in a tarp and left it in her yard. The walls went up. The day came to close the roof, and don Artemio took off his hat. Señores, there is one thing we forgot. Wh

sections.heading: V. The Country of the Thirty-Three
sections.text: There were people in that country already, old residents, and when they heard that new ones had come they made a welcome and brought out their best drink. Macario passed the word down his men that nobody was to touch it. The old residents drank it themselves and got drunk. Macario thought, why would I share a country with these? He made a sign, and the thirty-three took them by the heels and pitched them over the edge, and they fell headfirst into the sea at the bottom of the mountain. Even so, they had something to their credit. A town came up for them down there, and a tree with it, the yellow trumpet-flower that people here call tronadora. When that was over, the city of the Thirty-Three stood up. It is ten thousand leagues from the east gate to the west, and the same from north to south, and it has a thousand gates, and gardens, and tanks of water. In the middle of it, as the fruit of the paradero, is a house called Victory. It is seven hundred leagues high. It flies banners three hundred leagues long, gold banners on jeweled poles and jeweled banners on gold poles. From the ebony he planted, there came up a coral tree, a colorín, a hundred leagues around. From the stone bench

sections.heading: VI. Pepinos
sections.text: Macario looked over his household. Justa was there, and Lety, and Clara. Where had Geni come out? He looked, and saw her standing on one leg in the Río Bravo. He thought: The foolish girl did nothing, and now she is a bird. I will have to get her to do something, and bring her here. He put off his own looks and went down to her as somebody else. What are you doing here? Who are you, señor? Your husband, Macario. Where did you come out? In the country of the Thirty-Three. Do you know where your sisters-in-law are? No. They are there too, in my house. Would you like to see them? How would I get there? I’ll carry you. He set her on the palm of his hand and carried her up, and put her down on the shore of the lake called Lety. Then he went to the three. Would you like to see Geni? Where is she? On the shore of Lety’s lake. They went and looked. Ay, look what the señora got for all those hours at the mirror. Look at the beak on her. Look at the feet. Look at those legs. Doesn’t she look lovely? And when they had said it, they went away. Macario came back to her. Did you see them? I saw them. They laughed at me and left. Take me back. He took her back and set her in the water. Did you se

sections.heading: VII. The Seventh One
sections.text: The sky over the river had gone the color of the inside of a shell. A line of trailers was already moving on the road. So that is Macario, doña Alba said. She was scraping the comal. He took the road of not getting careless. It was the only road he had, and it got him the charge of two countries. You went to catechism? With the Ripalda. Then say me the seven that stand against the seven. Magali had not said them since she was nine. They came out in order, as if they had been stacked somewhere. Contra estos siete vicios hay siete virtudes. Contra Soberbia, Humildad.Contra Avaricia, Largueza.Contra Lujuria, Castidad.Contra Ira, Paciencia.Contra Gula, Templanza.Contra Envidia, Caridad.Contra Pereza, Diligencia. P. Qué cosa es Pereza?R. Andar con tristeza y tedio en las cosas divinas.P. Y Diligencia qué es?R. Presteza, y gozo de todo esto. — Ripalda, Catecismo de la doctrina cristiana (Madrid, 1850) The seventh one, doña Alba said. Against sloth, diligence. Everybody praises it, and everybody has a hard word for the one who lets things slide. And what is it? Quickness, and gladness in the whole business. That was him. Go on now, you’ll be late. Magali drove out by the old brecha, which

title: Caliche
logline: At a border truck-yard gate, a taco seller tells a customs broker's daughter how a transfer driver with a shovel came to run heaven.

verses.text: A Bhikshu (mendicant) who delights in earnestness, who looks with fear on thoughtlessness, moves about like fire, burning all his fetters, small or large.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk takes a meditation subject from the Buddha at Jetavana and goes off to practice it, but makes no progress. He sets out to go back and ask for a subject better suited to him. On the way he sees a forest fire and climbs a hill to watch it, and he thinks: as this fire goes on burning everything, large and small, so should I go on, burning away every fetter with the fire of knowledge. The Buddha, sitting in his chamber, knows his thought and sends an image of himself that seems to sit before the monk, radiant, and speaks the verse. The monk reaches awakening on the spot, travels through the air to the Buddha, praises him, and goes.
bg.history:
From 1972 Yellowstone let most lightning-caused fires burn as part of the natural order, and in 1988, in what became the worst drought in the park's recorded history, fires that began in June spread under that policy until it was suspended on July 15. The North Fork fire, which started accidentally on July 22, burned more than 410,000 acres by itself. On August 20, remembered as Black Saturday, the fires roughly doubled in a single day; on September 7 a fire storm reached Old Faithful; and on September 11 about a quarter inch of snow stopped their advance. In all some 793,880 acres, about 36 percent of the park, burned (National Park Service; Wikipedia).

Many lodgepole pines carry serotinous cones, sealed with resin and held on the tree for years, which open in the heat of a fire. After 1988, surveys found between 15,000 and two million seeds per acre on the burned ground, and a year later between 2,000 and 12,000 seedlings per acre (NPR). Ardis reads from John Muir's The Yosemite (1912), chapter 6, "The Forest Trees in General," where Muir describes fire in the Sierra's two-leaved pine, a variety of the same species. The people in the story are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Cone
sections.text: On the last night of training, Ardis Hollister gave each of the new seasonals one thing. She was sixty-four and had taught botany for thirty years at the college in Kearney, Nebraska, and spent twenty-six summers in the park in the gray shirt and the flat hat, and she did it every year. A girl from Ohio got a feather from a raven. A Navajo kid from Window Rock who wanted to be a geologist got a chip of obsidian. A retired dentist from Billings got a piece of elk antler that a porcupine had gnawed. Kyle Nordquist got a lodgepole cone. It was small and brown and hard as a stone, shut tight, glazed with old resin. He turned it over in his hand. It's waiting for something, Ardis said. Carry it around until you know what. Kyle was twenty-four and from Brainerd, Minnesota. He had done one year at the Lutheran seminary in St. Paul and quit in May, because for two years before that he had prayed every morning and every night and something that used to be on the other end of it was not there anymore, and he could not see standing up in a pulpit in that condition. His mother told people he was taking a year. He had taken a job talking to tourists about bison. That last night Ardis read them

sections.heading: II. Smoke
sections.text: They posted him at Madison, where the Firehole and the Gibbon come together, to give the evening program at the amphitheater and rove the campground in the day. Every morning before his shift he sat on a log by the river with the cone in his hand, the way he used to sit with a Bible open on his knee, and waited for it to tell him what it was waiting for. It did not tell him anything. It was a pinecone. He knew what it was waiting for, in the sense that he had read it on a sign. That was not what she meant, and he knew that too, and the knowing did not go anywhere. It was the same as the praying. He would sit, and the river would go by, and his mind would go off after a girl at the Old Faithful Inn, or his father's face when he told him about the seminary, or what he was going to say about bison that night, and he would bring it back to the cone, and it would go off again. It was the driest summer anyone in the park could remember. The fires had started in June, lightning fires, and by the park's policy they were allowed to burn, as they had been since the early seventies, because the forest had burned before there were rangers and would burn after. In the middle of July the policy

sections.heading: III. The Road
sections.text: His day off was a Saturday. He started north at noon in his Datsun with the cone in his shirt pocket, and by the time he was past the Gibbon Falls the wind was blowing so hard it rocked the car on its springs, and the sky over the plateau to the west had gone the color of a bruise. Later they called it Black Saturday. The fires in and around the park doubled in a single afternoon. A ranger in a yellow shirt had a sawhorse across the road at a pullout and was turning everyone back. Kyle parked. He did not turn back. He walked up a little rise of rock above the road to see. Below him the fire was coming through the lodgepoles toward the river, and it was the thing Ardis had read to them in June. It came along the ground first, low and quick and almost quiet under the roar of the wind, eating the needles and the cones and the dead twigs, every one of them, the way a hand goes along a row. When it reached the foot of a tree it climbed, and the whole tree went up at once in a column of flame twice its height, with a sound like a sheet shaken out, and then it was gone, and the next tree went, and the next. Small and large, it made no difference to it. It did not skip the twigs to get to

sections.heading: IV. Mammoth
sections.text: The seasonals tell the rest at the amphitheater, after the visitors have gone. The road north of the sawhorse was closed the rest of that day. The ranger who held it swore nobody went past him, on foot or otherwise, and Kyle's Datsun sat on the pullout for two days under a quarter inch of ash. All the same, at a little after six that evening he knocked on the door of Ardis Hollister's trailer at Mammoth, thirty miles away, with no soot on his shoes. She opened the door in her socks. She was not surprised to see him, or did not act it. She had been home all afternoon, she said, listening to the radio. He took the cone out of his pocket and held it out to her. It was open, every scale standing back from the core like a little tree. She took it and tapped it on the doorframe, and the seeds came out into her hand, four or five of them, each one with its thin brown wing. Well, she said. He did not ask for the elk. Snow fell on September 11, a quarter inch, and the fires lay down. That winter people said Yellowstone was ruined. title: The Closed Cone
logline: A seminary dropout working as a Yellowstone seasonal ranger can make nothing of the pinecone his teacher gave him, until the summer the park burns.

verses.text: A Bhikshu (mendicant) who delights in reflection, who looks with fear on thoughtlessness, cannot fall away (from his perfect state)—he is close upon Nirvana.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young man of good family from a market town near Sāvatthī becomes a monk and is known as Tissa of the Market Town. He goes for alms only in the village where his relatives live and never comes to the city, though the great donors there are giving lavishly. The monks complain that he lives entangled with his kin. Questioned by the Buddha, Tissa says he takes from them only what he needs to eat, coarse or fine, and seeks nothing more. The Buddha applauds him, says that contentment was his own habit too, and tells the birth story of the parrot king who would not leave his fig tree even when the god Sakka withered it to dust, and who asked, when offered any gift, only to see the tree in leaf again. Then he speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story. The parrot's couplet here comes from the 1897 Cambridge translation of the Jātaka; the verse the Baksha recites is the same Dhammapada verse as it stands in the Udānavarga, the collection preserved in the Tibetan canon that Kalmyk and Mongolian Buddhists inherited, in W. W. Rockhill's 1883 translation from the Tibetan.
bg.history:
The Kalmyks are a western Mongol people, Tibetan Buddhists, who have lived on the lower Volga and the Don since the seventeenth century. Some hundreds left Russia with the defeated White armies in 1920 and settled in the Balkans; in Belgrade they built a temple in 1929, one of the first Buddhist temples in Europe, and left it in 1944. Others came west during the war. On December 28–31, 1943, the Soviet government deported the entire Kalmyk population, more than 93,000 people, to Siberia and abolished their republic; a Kalmyk Autonomous Oblast was re-established by decree on January 9, 1957. The Kalmyks stranded in displaced persons camps near Munich were at first barred from the United States as Asians. In 1951 the Attorney General's office ruled them admissible, and most arrived between December 1951 and April 1952, sponsored by the Tolstoy Foundation, Church World Service and the Society of Friends.

They settled mainly in north-central Philadelphia and in Freewood Acres, on U.S. Route 9 in Howell Township, New Jersey, where their temples still stand. Fred Adelman's 1961 article "The American Kalmyks" describes the two colonies, the Philadelphia factory jobs, the New Jersey men's work in housing construction and "until the recent recession, a carpet factory," the butter tea, the fried bortsak and the budan soup, and a senior monk who was a doctor of Tibetan medicine. The recession of 1957–58 is the one in this story. Zul, the lamp festival in early winter, is the Kalmyk new year of age. Sanji, the Baksha, Mrs. Thayer and the temple on North Tenth Street are invented, and the east-end khurul is not any of the real Howell temples.

sections.heading: I. The Round
sections.dateline: Freewood Acres, Howell Township, New Jersey · September 1957
sections.text: Gelung Sanji ate once a day, before noon, and he ate it in Freewood Acres. He had done so for five years, and in that time he had not once eaten his meal anywhere else. Freewood Acres was a few streets of small houses laid out on sand among scrub pine, on both sides of U.S. 9, which was one lane each way then, with egg farms beyond in every direction. There were Russians there already. The Kalmyks came in the winter of 1951 and 1952, off the transports from the camps around Munich, after the Attorney General in Washington had been persuaded that a Mongol people who had lived three hundred years on the Volga and the Don could be let in as Europeans. Most of the ones in Freewood Acres were Astrakhan people, who had come out of Russia in the war. A few houses at the east end belonged to Don Kalmyks, the old emigration, who had left in 1920 with the White army and spent twenty-four years in Belgrade. Sanji's mother lived in one of those houses. His mother's brother had the next, and a cousin the one after that, and across the road lived a widow named Kermen who had known him since he was baptized, as she put it, because she had lived so long among Serbs that she used their word. The me

sections.heading: II. The City
sections.text: The larger part of the Don Kalmyks had settled in Philadelphia, fifty-five miles down the road, in the row houses north of Girard Avenue. There was steady work there in the needle trades and the cigar and candy factories. The principal temple was there, on the ground floor of a row house, and the old lamas lived above it. The head of them was the Baksha, Lidji, who was eighty-one, and who was an emchi, a doctor of the Tibetan medicine, which he had learned as a boy on the Don from a man who had learned it in Lhasa. People came up the stairs to him all day. He took a wrist in three fingers and listened to it with his eyes shut, for as long as another man would take to read a letter, and then he said what was wrong and went to his jars. He had brought the jars from Belgrade through the camps wrapped in his bedding. He had lost the high lama's cushion on the way, and his books of ritual, and he said that he could manage without those. He had been Sanji's teacher from the day the boy was brought to the temple school at seven. He was not a talker. In twenty-three years Sanji had heard him say perhaps four things that were not about medicine or the order of a service, and remembered all

sections.heading: III. Three Bowls
sections.text: That autumn the work went. The whole country slid into a recession, and the rug mill in Freehold cut to four days and then to three and let the newest hands go, and the newest hands were Kalmyks. The contractors stopped starting houses. The egg farmers, who had been getting poorer for three years, quit buying anything. In the east end of Freewood Acres four families of the old emigration packed and went to Philadelphia, where a cousin could speak for them at the candy factory, and their houses stood with paper over the windows. Sanji went out on the sand road every morning as before, and what was in the pots changed. There had been no budan since September. First the butter went out of the tea, and after that the nutmeg. By November his mother's tea had milk in it only because she gave him the milk and drank her own black. He saw that and said nothing, since there was nothing to say that would not shame her. He ate her bortsak, which was made now with oil saved from the last frying, and told her it was the bortsak of Belgrade. On a morning in the middle of November it was the widow Kermen who opened her door. She was seventy-four and lived alone on what a son sent from Philadelphia

sections.heading: IV. The Question
sections.dateline: North Tenth Street · the week before Zul, December 1957
sections.text: He went down on two buses with his outer robe in a paper bag, because of how people looked at it. The second bus came into the city past miles of row houses with lit windows, and stores, and a factory with its night shift going in at the gate carrying lunch pails. He looked at all of it with interest, as he would have looked at a river in flood, and he felt no wish to stay in it. The monks were all in the upper front room. The Baksha sat by the window on a kitchen chair with a blanket over his knees. He was a very small man. His hands smelled of the roots he ground. Sanji made the three prostrations and sat on the floor. They tell me, said the Baksha, that you live up there in the middle of your family. That you are in and out of your mother's house and your uncle's house all day, and that this is why you never come to us, with everything that is given here. Is it so? No, Baksha. The old man waited. I go out once in the morning, Sanji said. Somebody calls me in. Some days it is my mother and some days it is a house where I am no relation. I take from them what I can eat at that sitting. When I have had what will keep me that day, I go back and shut the door. It may be coarse or it

sections.heading: V. The Parrot
sections.dateline: A fig grove on the Ganges · long ago
sections.text: There was a grove of fig trees on the bank of the river Ganga, under the snow mountains, and so many parrots lived in it that when they rose the sky went green. Each had its tree. The king of the parrots had his, and he ate its figs, and drank from the river. A year came when the figs on his tree were finished. He ate the shoots, and when those were gone he ate the leaves and then the bark. He drank from the river and sat in his tree, and he was content. He was so entirely content that up in his heaven the seat of Khormusta, the king of the gods, grew warm under him. Khormusta looked down to see who on earth had that much merit. He saw a green bird in a bare tree. Khormusta thought he would see how deep it went, and he dried the tree. It died where it stood. It became a grey stump full of holes, and when the wind blew, the stump moaned and dust came out of the holes. The other birds had long since gone to trees with fruit on them. The parrot ate the dust. He drank from the river and sat on top of the stump in the wind and the sun, and he went nowhere. Then Khormusta took the shape of a wild goose and came down with his queen and perched on a branch nearby. Bird, he said, there are

sections.heading: VI. Zul
sections.dateline: Philadelphia and Freewood Acres · the middle of December
sections.text: They kept him for Zul, the feast of lamps, when every Kalmyk becomes a year older on the same night. The women had kneaded dough and shaped it into small boats, and in each boat they set wicks of grass stalk wound with cotton, one for each year of the person's age and one over, and filled it with melted butter. When it was dark the lamps were lit and carried up and set before the altar. There were more than a hundred of them. Mrs. Thayer's lambs had come that afternoon. She sat among the old women holding a dough lamp with sixty-eight wicks, which she had counted out herself. The Baksha was helped down the stairs. He did not go to the high seat. He stopped in front of Sanji, who was at the end of the row of monks, in his cotton robe among the brocade. He said a verse over him in Tibetan, and then in Kalmyk, slowly, so that the people behind could hear it. It is in the book of the Teacher's sayings that the Kalmyks have from the Tibetans, who have kept it a thousand years. The Bhixu who delights in purity and who looks with dread on impurity is so near nirvana that he cannot fail (to reach it). — Udānavarga 4:30, tr. W. W. Rockhill (1883) The word they have put as purity means takin

title: Salt Tea
logline: A young Kalmyk monk eats only what the refugee houses on his road can spare, while a rich patron feasts the lamas in Philadelphia.

verses.text: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
As a fish taken from his watery home and thrown on dry ground, our thought trembles all over in order to escape the dominion of Mara (the tempter).

bg.commentary: The commentary refers to the old discourse about Meghiya (Udāna 4.1), who was for a time the Buddha's attendant. Coming back from his alms round along a riverbank, Meghiya sees a lovely mango grove and asks leave to go and meditate there. The Buddha says: wait, I am alone, until another monk comes. Meghiya asks a second and a third time, and the Buddha answers that when a man speaks of striving there is nothing to say, and he should do what he thinks it is time for. Meghiya sits all day at the root of a tree and is overrun by three kinds of thought, of sensual pleasure, of ill will and of cruelty, and is astonished that he, who left home out of faith, should be so caught. In the evening he goes back and tells it. The Buddha reproves him for leaving when he was asked to stay, tells him the mind is flighty and must be kept in hand, and speaks the two verses.
bg.history:
Between 1838 and 1917 the British shipped several hundred thousand indentured laborers from north India to the sugar estates of Trinidad and British Guiana. Their descendants, the Indo-Caribbean people, kept a Hinduism centered on the Ramcharitmanas, the Ramayan that Tulsidas composed in Avadhi in the sixteenth century: yard flags on bamboo poles (jhandi), multi-night household readings called yagnas, and the open-air Ramleela plays, for which central Trinidad villages such as Felicity are known. From the 1960s on many families moved again, to New York, Toronto and South Florida, where Broward County towns like Lauderhill and Miramar have large Trinidadian and Guyanese communities and many mandirs. Pandits were by custom Brahmin men; women began to be installed as pandits in Trinidad in the 1990s, and the question is still argued. The Pandita reads from the English prose version by F. S. Growse, a British magistrate in India, first published in parts beginning in 1877; her gloss on the doha is fair to the original, where it is the mind (man) that the devotees make a fish in that lake.

The Redland is the farming district of southern Miami-Dade County, named for its pockets of red clay over limestone, and it has grown mangoes commercially for generations. The Julie, a small, flattened, richly flavored mango on a dwarf tree, is the favorite of Jamaica and Trinidad and is grown in Florida mostly by Caribbean families in their yards, since it suffers from fungus in the humid summers. Old groves in the Redland have been giving way to housing for decades. The drainage canals of South Florida are full of introduced fish, among them the South American armored catfish released from aquariums. The people, the yagna and the grove in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. Five Leaves
sections.dateline: The Redland, south Miami-Dade County, Florida · June 2019
sections.text: The Boodrams had a house and five acres off Krome Avenue, down where the county quits being city and goes to nurseries and avocado and mango, and for nine nights that June they were holding a Ramayan yagna in the yard. They had put up a rented tent with the sides rolled, and two hundred folding chairs, and a low stage with a white sheet over it and a cushion for the reader. Along the fence, nine new jhandi flags stood on bamboo poles. Every evening at six the cars came down from Broward, from Lauderhill and Miramar and Pembroke Pines, where the Trinidadians and Guyanese mostly lived, and people sat until ten hearing the Ramayan of Tulsidas sung and explained, and ate curry off paper plates afterward, and drove an hour home. The reader was Pandita Chandra Maharaj. She was sixty-six. She had been born in Felicity, in central Trinidad, where her father made the bows and arrows for the village Ramleela every year, and she had come to Florida in 1984 and worked twenty-six years doing the books for a tile importer in Hialeah. When her husband died she went back to what she had learned sitting under her father's elbow. She studied for six years, and a mandir off State Road 7 installed her

sections.heading: II. Three Times
sections.text: The Pandita was at the stove with a bundle of bamboo garden stakes from the Home Depot. The mandir's children did Ramleela every October, and every summer she made the arrows, forty of them, because there was nobody else who knew how. She took the five leaves and looked at each one and nodded. Panditaji, he said. There's a mango grove down the canal. An old one. Nobody's in there. It's the kind of place the rishis sat. I want to go and sit there today. Do my sadhana properly, the whole afternoon, till it's time. I think I need that. She turned a stake over the gas flame. Wait, she said. I alone here today. Wait till somebody else reach. Shanta Aunty's coming at five. So wait till five. He washed the leaves and set them in the brass lota around a dry coconut, and he swept the stage. At half past eleven he came back to the kitchen door. Panditaji, you have everything here. You finished what you had to do. I haven't finished anything. I don't see how I'm going to get anywhere carrying a harmonium. I'd like to go to that grove. I alone here, Kavi. Wait. He went out and wiped down two hundred chairs that did not need it. At noon he came back a third time and said it again, and this time

sections.heading: III. The Grove
sections.dateline: Under the Julie trees · the afternoon
sections.text: He chose the fourth Julie from the culvert because its roots made a seat. He folded his legs and set his back straight the way the videos said, with his hands in his lap. He shut his eyes and began to say the name of Ram with his breath. He had perhaps four minutes of it. Then, without any decision on his part, he was thinking about Reshma Singh. She sang in the youth group. At Phagwah in March she had been soaked to the skin in a white kurta, pink and green with abeer, laughing with her head back. He had looked away at the time. He did not look away now. He looked for a long while, and when he had finished with what he had actually seen, his mind supplied the rest. After Reshma there were others. He had gotten rid of certain things on his phone in January, and the phone was in the car, and it made no difference at all. He had them all by heart, and here in the place of the rishis they played for him one after another, and nothing interrupted them. He opened his eyes. He was sweating. He shut them and went back to the name. It was his cousin Darren next. Darren had the dispatcher's job at their uncle's trucking yard, the job that had been promised to Kavi in front of the whole fami

sections.heading: IV. The Bank
sections.text: It stopped in forty minutes and the sun came out and the limestone steamed. He walked back along the canal, wet through, with six Julie mangoes in the front of his shirt, because he could not think what else to bring her. Two boys had been fishing at the culvert before the storm and had gone. On the bank road, a yard from the water, lay a fish they had thrown there, a brown armored catfish, the kind from the aquarium trade that is in every canal now and that nobody wants on a hook. It was not dead. It lay on the hot white rock and bent itself double and sprang, and it came down in the same place. It did this again and again without any direction to it, and its gills worked. The water was three feet away and clear as glass. It had no way of knowing that. Kavi stood over it a long time, longer than made sense. Then he put the side of his shoe under it and flipped it into the canal. It hung in the water where it fell for a second or two, then went down into the weed. When he came into the Boodrams' yard he saw what the storm had done. The wind had got under the tent on the south side and torn four stakes out, and that whole wall of canvas was down across the chairs. The white sheet on

sections.heading: V. The Arrow
sections.text: He put the mangoes on the counter. He did not sit down. Tell me, she said. He told her. He was twenty-two and it was not easy to say to a woman of sixty-six, a pandita, what had gone through him under that tree, and he said it anyway. He told her about the girl and the others, and about Darren and his father, and about the man in the parking lot. He told her about the stone in his hand. I went there out of faith, he said. I swear I did. And that is all that came. Those three things, round and round. I don't understand it. She heard all of it without moving her face. You do a wrong thing today, she said. I not vex. But hear it. I tell you wait, I alone. Three times. And you went your way. When I ask you to stay, you must not leave me alone and go. I am not saying it for the hip. She lifted the peas and set them down again. You went because the mind say go. The mind see a pretty place and it start to jump, and you follow it out the gate like a man following a goat. Then you sit down in the pretty place and you surprise that it still jumping. Is the same mind, child. You carry it there. She pulled the bundle of bamboo toward her across the table and drew one stake out. Look down this.

sections.heading: VI. The Sixth Night
sections.text: Shanta came at five with the singers and found Kavi and the Boodram sons driving tent stakes. By six the wall was up and the sheet had been changed, and the cars were turning in off Krome Avenue. He carried the harmonium out and set it on the stage, and then the book stand and the book, and went back for her. She came across the yard on his arm, slowly, in a dry sari, and nobody watching would have known about the hip. Mrs. Boodram had come home to a wet yard and a wet reader and had started to cry, and the Pandita had told her to go and see about the pumpkin. She read that night from the first book, out of her order, and she made no remark on it. She sang the doha once in the Avadhi, to the old tune, with Shanta on the dholak, and then gave it in English out of the worn green Growse she had from her father, who had it from a schoolmaster in Chaguanas. Free from sensual passions and absorbed in devout affection to Ráma, the soul disports itself like a fish in the ambrosial lake of his beloved name. — Rámáyana of Tulsi Dás, Childhood, dohá 26, tr. F. S. Growse The Englishman put soul, she told the two hundred chairs. Tulsidas put man. The mind. He say the mind is a fish. Now a fish

title: Julie Mango
logline: A young man who carries a pandita's harmonium begs leave to go and meditate alone in an old mango grove by a canal.

verses.text: It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty, rushing wherever it listeth; a tamed mind brings happiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, sixty monks spend the rains retreat in the village of Mātika, where the headman’s mother builds them a monastery. They agree that no two of them will ever be together and that a bell will be struck only if someone falls sick. When she strikes it herself and sees them come one by one, she thinks they have quarrelled; they teach her the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body, and she attains insight before they do. Seeing that only their food is lacking, she feeds them exactly what each one wishes, and they reach the goal. Another monk hears of her and comes, wishes for one thing after another, and receives each; frightened that she knows his every thought, he flees back to the Buddha, who tells him this is the very place for him and that he need guard only one thing, his mind. He returns, attains, and looking back sees ninety-nine lives in which she, as his wife, killed him; she tells him to look further, and in the hundredth he sees that she spared him.
bg.history:
Dora’s family history follows the valley’s. Jerome, built on Cleopatra Hill above the Verde, was one of the great copper camps of the West; by 1930 about sixty percent of its people were Latino, alongside Irish, Italian and Slavic miners. The United Verde mine ran from 1876 to 1953, and when it closed the town shrank to fewer than a hundred people. Its smelter town, Clarkdale, founded by William A. Clark in 1912 on the river below, closed its smelter the same year and left a long black slag pile along the Verde.

In June 2021 a record heat wave struck the Southwest, and Phoenix hit 118°F on June 17. After two nearly rainless summers, the North American monsoon returned in force: Tucson had its wettest July on record, and floods off the 2019 Museum Fire burn scar ran through Flagstaff neighborhoods. At the same time the Delta variant filled Arizona’s hospitals. COVID patients in the state’s intensive care beds tripled over July and August, the patients were younger than in earlier waves and mostly unvaccinated, and nurses who had worked through the first winter described themselves as burned out. More on the COVID-19 pandemic in Arizona.

sections.heading: I. The Bend
sections.dateline: Verde River below Cottonwood, Arizona · June 2021
sections.text: They came up from Phoenix the week the heat broke the records down there, when it was a hundred and eighteen at the airport on a Thursday and the radio said not to touch the seat belt buckle. There were sixty of them. They came in Subarus, pickups, a Prius with a cracked windshield, and one old school bus painted the color of a cantaloupe. At the Circle K on Main Street they asked the man buying ice where a person could stay cheap for the summer, near water, where nobody would bother them. The man buying ice was Matt Matkovich. Matt ran the volunteer fire company on that stretch of the river, sat on the ditch board, and knew whose well was going dry and whose cows were on whose lease. People called him the mayor of the river road, though the river road was not a town and had never had a mayor. He looked at the bus. He said they had better talk to his mother. Dora Matkovich was seventy-five. She had been born in Jerome in 1946, up on the side of Cleopatra Hill, when the mine was still working and her father went underground every morning with his lunch in a lard can. When the mine closed in 1953 the family came down the mountain to Clarkdale, like almost everybody else, and she grew

sections.heading: II. The Bell
sections.text: In the second week of July Dora went down the bank in the late afternoon with her grandson Nico carrying a cooler. She had made a jug of agua de jamaica, red as a stoplight, and a pan of empanadas de calabaza, and two pounds of grapes from the Safeway because it seemed to her those people did not eat fruit. The park was silent. The trailers had their blinds down. The tents had their flaps tied. Nobody was in the ramada or the bathhouse or the river. Old Mr. Esquivel was fishing for carp off the gravel bar, as he had every evening for thirty years, and she asked him where they had all gone. They’re here, he said. Each one in his hole. You want them, ring the bell. They come running. So she rang it. It was louder than she remembered. The sound went down the river and came back off the bluff, and then the doors began to open. They came out of trailers, tents, cab-over campers, the cantaloupe bus, and the mesquite thickets along the bank where some of them had been sitting on folded blankets. She watched them cross the gravel toward her. It was the strangest thing. They came one at a time. Each one by his own path. Two would be coming from the same end of the park, and one would bend w

sections.heading: III. Thirty-Two
sections.text: The rains came that year like they had not come in two summers. The Weather Service counts the monsoon from the middle of June to the end of September, but for two years there had been next to nothing, and people in the valley had started to say the word as a joke. In the third week of July a wall of brown dust came up the valley from the south in the late afternoon, a mile high, and swallowed Cottonwood, and right behind it came the rain. The whole valley smelled of wet creosote and hot stone. The Verde came up brown and fast, full of sticks. Matt’s fire company pulled a man and his dog off the roof of a pickup at a low-water crossing. In Flagstaff the water came down off the burned mountain and went through people’s houses. Dora did the practice at her kitchen table at four in the morning, before the heat, with the window open on the noise of the river. She did not have to look far for any of it. Hair of the head: grey, thin at the crown, the same hair her mother had brushed out every night on the back step in Jerome with a tortoiseshell brush. Nails: ridged, yellow on the big toes. Teeth: eleven of her own and a partial plate she took out at night and put in a glass. Skin: the b

sections.heading: IV. The Garage
sections.text: The second summer of the sickness was worse in the hospitals than anyone outside them wanted to know. Over July and August the number of COVID patients in the state’s intensive care beds had gone up three times over. The new ones were younger. They came in at twenty-four and thirty-eight and forty-one, and the nurses who had been through the first winter said this one was harder, because the first time nobody had known and this time everybody could have. Graciela came down the stairwell to the fourth level at ten past seven in the morning. Two of hers had died in the night. She was forty-four and had grown up in the Apostolic church on South Seventh Avenue, where her grandmother had taught her to read out of a black Reina-Valera with a zipper on it, and she was carrying her lunch bag, which she had not opened. The sixty were waiting by her car. They were standing close together, talking quietly, which she had not seen them do before. She looked at them. You all ate, she said. They laughed, all of them at once, and then they told her about Dora. The bell. The tables under the mesquite. How she knew what each one of them wanted before they knew it themselves; how they would be sittin

sections.heading: V. What He Wanted
sections.text: Shane drove up the Black Canyon Freeway on a Friday afternoon and came over the cattle guard after dark. Dora’s son had left a key under a rock on the step of the trailer where Hollis had stayed. He opened the door and turned on the light and stood there. Nobody had been in it for two weeks. There was dust on everything, a dead moth in the sink, a smell of hot plastic. He had driven a hundred miles. He thought: I can’t clean this tonight. I wish she’d send somebody. Ten minutes later there was a knock. A tall boy of fifteen stood on the step with a broom, a bucket, and a bottle of Pine-Sol. My grandma said, said Nico, and swept the trailer out, and wiped the sink, and went away. Shane sat on the clean bed. He was thirsty. He wanted something cold and sweet, not water. When he opened the door to get air there was a jar on the step, sweating in the dark, red as a stoplight, with ice in it. In the morning he woke up thinking about rice pudding, the warm kind, with butter melting on top, which his grandmother had made in Safford when he was small. There was a covered bowl on the step. Arroz con leche, still warm, with a pat of butter going soft in the middle and cinnamon on the butter.

sections.heading: VI. Above Everything
sections.text: He waited for her by the car on the fourth level. She came out of the stairwell at ten past seven and saw him and stopped. You’re not up there. I can’t be up there. Why not? She knows everything I think. Everything. And I think garbage, Graciela. All day. You don’t know what goes on in here. He put his hand flat on his chest as if it were a door. One bad thought and she’ll run me off that place like a thief. Graciela set her lunch bag on the roof of the Corolla. That’s the place for you, she said. That’s exactly the place. I can’t. I won’t. Okay. She leaned on the car. Can you guard one thing? What thing? Just what goes on in there. Your thinking. Not her. Not what she sees or doesn’t see. Not anything else. Just that one thing. It’s hard enough by itself. It goes wherever it wants. It lands on anything. She shut her eyes for a moment, standing up. My grandma’s Bible has it. She made me say it every night before I could have the light off. Sobre toda cosa guardada guarda tu corazón; porque de él mana la vida. — Proverbios 4:23 She said it again for him in English, her own way, slowly. Of everything you’re guarding, guard your heart. Your whole life comes out of it. That’s it? That’

sections.heading: VII. The Hundredth
sections.text: Dora was at her kitchen table on the Sunday afternoon when the car came back over the cattle guard. She did not get up to look. He found a teacher, she said, to nobody, and got up and put the beans on. He took Hollis’s trailer again. He did not think about her anymore, or about what she could see. He thought about his thinking, and when it went somewhere, he went and got it and brought it back, the way you bring back a dog that has got out of the yard, without hitting it. Hair of the head. Nails. Teeth. Skin. The food came every day on the step, the right food, and he ate it and washed the bowl and set it back out. In the mornings he walked the river road alone. On the third morning there was a rattlesnake stretched across the path in the first sun, as thick as his wrist. He stood a long time. Then he found a long cottonwood stick and lifted the snake gently into the brush, and it went. In a few days he finished. He was sitting in a camp chair facing the river when it happened, and afterward he sat on there in the clear blank peace of it for a long time. The first thing he thought when he could think again was of her. She held me up. Without that woman I’d never have got here. And

title: The Dinner Bell
logline: Sixty followers of a pandemic nurse's one-minute videos spend the monsoon at a widow's empty RV park on the Verde River.

verses.text: Let the wise man guard his thoughts, for they are difficult to perceive, very artful, and they rush wherever they list: thoughts well guarded bring happiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich man's son asks a monk who comes to his house for alms how to be released from suffering. The monk tells him to give: meal tickets, fortnightly food, lodging for the rains, bowls and robes, a third of everything he has. He does it all and asks if there is anything else. He is given the five precepts, then the ten, then told to go forth, and because he does each thing in order he comes to be called Anupubba, “Gradual.” As a monk he has one teacher who drills him in the Abhidhamma and another who drills him in the monastic rule, until he decides there is “not even room for me to stretch out my hands” and that he may as well be free as a householder. He stops practicing and grows thin, jaundiced and scabbed. His teachers bring him to the Buddha, who tells him that if he can guard one thing he need not guard the rest: his own thoughts.
bg.hist_title: Las Vegas and the fighting-game scene, 2013
bg.history:
The fighting-game community grew out of arcades in the early 1990s and still runs largely on small local weeklies and volunteer organizers. Its largest gathering, the Evolution Championship Series, moved to Las Vegas in 2005. Evo 2013 took place on July 12–14 in the Bally's Event Center and the ballroom of Paris Las Vegas, with open registration and a record 3,538 competitors across nine games, among them Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition. The game runs at sixty frames a second, and serious players study “frame data,” tables of how many frames each attack takes to start, stay active and recover. Some of its combinations allowed a window of a single frame. Players speak of protecting their “mental” much as the verse speaks of guarding thoughts.

Las Vegas has so many residents from Hawaiʻi that islanders call it the ninth island, and for decades the downtown casinos have courted them. Table-game dealers work under surveillance cameras and a long list of hand procedures. Before leaving a table a dealer “clears” the hands, turning them palm up and palm down for the camera to show they are empty; the usual rotation is a twenty-minute break after an hour or so of dealing (see croupier). The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius were written in Greek as private notes, some of them on campaign. The passages here are from George Long's translation of 1862, the text of many cheap paperback editions.

sections.heading: I. The List
sections.text: Goodwin Sayre was eighteen and his father built houses. Sayre Homes had put up a good part of the northwest valley, and after the crash, when whole streets of it stood empty with the pools gone green, his father had bought the paper back cheap and waited. By 2011 there was money again. There was a house out toward Red Rock with a room over the garage, and in the room were two consoles, two of the flat monitors the tournaments used, and a hole in the drywall beside the door with a calendar hung over it. He played Street Fighter. He had played it online since he was fourteen and was good the way a boy alone in a room gets good, and every loss went through him like something swallowed wrong. He could feel it coming in the second round. Heat behind the eyes, cold hands, then a noise in his head like a room full of people talking about him. Afterward he couldn't eat. He had thought that winning more would stop it. He won more, and it got worse. Ro Mendez came to the house on Tuesdays. Ro was thirty-one and ran the Thursday weekly in the back of a card shop on Spring Mountain Road. He gave lessons for forty dollars an hour and whatever was in the refrigerator, which at the Sayres' was a

sections.heading: II. The House
sections.text: The house was a four-bedroom rental that a headset company paid for. Five players lived in it with an analyst and a manager, and the living room had been cleared down to a row of stations and a camera on a tripod. The analyst was called Ko. He had the whole game in a three-ring binder and again in a spreadsheet with eleven tabs: thirty-nine characters, and for every move of every one of them the number of sixtieths of a second it took to come out, the number it stayed out, the number it left you standing there afterward with your arm extended. Ryu's uppercut came out in three. Some combinations had to be struck inside a single sixtieth or they did not happen. Whenever Goodwin sat down beside him Ko had the binder open. Here this is correct. Here that is incorrect. You pressed a button there. You can't ever press a button there. The manager was Dana Whitlock, who had run a call center before this and ran the house off a laminated sheet on the refrigerator. Up by nine. Eight hours on the stream. Nothing to drink the night before a bracket and nothing posted for an hour after one. Wrist stretches on a timer. The sheet had a paragraph on where the heel of the hand should rest on the st

sections.heading: III. The Garage
sections.text: Dennis Kaneshiro was forty-four. He had grown up in Kalihi and come to Las Vegas at twenty, like half of Kalihi, and he dealt blackjack and pai gow on swing shift at a downtown house where the coffee shop served oxtail soup after midnight and the players at his table talked to him in pidgin. People who had been around in the early nineties said that for three years there had been no Street Fighter cabinet between San Diego and Seattle he could be beaten on. Then he married and had two daughters, and the tournaments saw him about once a year. He got off at two and was home by half past. From then until half past three he played, with his wife and the girls asleep on the other side of the wall, and then he slept until it was time to drive them to school. One hour. Players who trained ten hours a day drove out to North Las Vegas at that hour to sit beside him, and they drove home quiet. He was at the utility sink in his black-and-whites with the bow tie off, washing his hands, when Dana's car pulled in. What brings you folks? This one isn't happy in the house, Ko said. Dennis dried his hands on a shop towel. He looked at Goodwin's knuckles before he looked at his face. That true? Yes.

sections.heading: IV. Pools
sections.text: He stayed in the house. The binder was still the binder and the sheet was still on the refrigerator. He kept what he could of both and watched the one thing, and over the spring he found that most of the rest got kept without his standing over it. He ate. The skin closed over his knuckles and came in pink. Ko, who had heard all of it from beside the water heater, took to stopping a session in the middle to ask a player what he had in his head. The seventeen-year-olds started saying it to each other across the kitchen, this or that, as a joke at first. Evo that year drew more than thirty-five hundred players to the Strip. Six of them slept at his father's house. His pool was called on Friday morning, at a long table under ballroom lights with a number taped to the monitor. He won twice. His third match was against a boy from Fresno who had his sleeping bag in the Sayres' guest room. In the last round it came the way it always had, the heat and the cold hands and the room full of people. He turned and looked. They're all going to see. There it was. He let it sit where it was, and his hands did what they knew, and he lost the round by a sliver. He lost the next match to someone else a

title: Clear Hands
logline: A builder's son does everything the fighting-game scene asks of him, in order, until a team house leaves him no room to move his hands.

verses.text: Those who bridle their mind which travels far, moves about alone, is without a body, and hides in the chamber (of the heart), will be free from the bonds of Mara (the tempter).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, an elder named Saṅgharakkhita is ordained after hearing the Buddha and becomes an arahant within days. His youngest sister names her son after him, and the boy is ordained under his uncle. After a rains retreat the nephew is given two robes, one seven cubits long and one eight, and sets his heart on giving the longer one to his uncle. He sweeps the elder’s quarters, sets out water for his feet, and fans him, but the elder refuses the robe because he already has a full set. Still fanning, the nephew drifts into a daydream: he will leave the order, sell the robe, buy a she-goat, grow rich on her kids, marry, and take his wife and son in a cart to visit his uncle, and on the road his wife will drop the child under the wheels and he will strike her with his stick. His fan comes down on the elder’s head. The elder, who has seen the whole daydream, says, “You did not succeed in hitting the woman; what has an old elder done to deserve a beating?” The nephew flees, is caught by the young monks, and is brought to the Buddha, who tells him not to be troubled, because the mind travels far. Read the full commentary story. The daydream belongs to a family of tales that includes the milkmaid and her pail; see The Milkmaid and Her Pail.
bg.history:
The first patented drive-in theater opened in Camden, New Jersey, in 1933, and the form boomed after the Second World War, when thousands were built on the edges of towns across the country; Wisconsin had about eighty at its height. Most ran only in the warm months, nightly through Labor Day and on weekends after it until the cold. Until xenon bulbs replaced them, projectors used carbon arc lamps, which burned two carbon rods down in a bright, hot arc and had to be tended by hand. A feature came on reels of about twenty minutes each, run on two projectors in turn; the projectionist watched for the small cue marks in the upper right corner of the frame, the first to start the second machine and the second, about seven seconds later, to switch to it.

The Fox River valley around Appleton and Kaukauna was paper country, its mills lined along the river’s fall to Green Bay, and Wisconsin had led the country in fur farming since before the war, as it still leads in mink. Walt Kuehl’s division, the 32nd Infantry Division, the “Red Arrow,” was formed from Wisconsin and Michigan National Guard units and fought at Buna in New Guinea and on Leyte and Luzon; it logged more days in combat than any other American division in the war. Yours, Mine and Ours, with Lucille Ball and Henry Fonda, opened in April 1968 and was one of the year’s biggest hits.

sections.heading: I. The Starview
sections.text: Walt Kuehl came home from the Pacific in the fall of 1945 with the red arrow of the Thirty-second Division on his shoulder and a habit of sitting with his back to a wall. For three years he worked the wet end of a paper machine at the mill in Kaukauna and drank most of what they paid him. He was not mean about it. He was quiet, and then he was gone for a day or two, and then he was back at the machine. In the summer of 1948 Harold and Irene Voss opened a drive-in on forty acres of Harold’s father’s hayfield east of the highway. It had a screen tower of fir planks painted white, two hundred and forty speaker posts in curved rows, and a cinder-block building in the middle of the field that was a snack bar downstairs and a projection booth up. They called it the Starview. Harold ran the projectors. Irene sat in the box office at the gate and took the money. One night in August, after the second feature, when the last cars had pulled out onto the highway and Harold had shut down the arcs, Irene walked the rows with a flashlight to pick up the speakers people had dropped in the gravel. In the back row she found one car still parked with its speaker hanging in the window and a man sittin

sections.heading: II. Two Shirts
sections.dateline: Sister Bay, Door County · Labor Day 1968
sections.text: That May the man who ran the booth at the Peninsula Outdoor, north of Sister Bay, got his notice from the draft board, and Irene’s cousin Ruth Bergstrom called long distance to ask if she could borrow the boy. So Little Walt spent the summer he turned nineteen on the Door, sleeping in a cabin behind a cherry orchard and running the show for people up from Chicago and Milwaukee, who honked at everything. He picked cherries in July for the money. He swam off the town dock on his nights off. He did not miss a changeover all summer, and he thought about that more than he meant to, and wished his uncle could know it without his having to say it. On Labor Day night, after the last show of the season, Mrs. Bergstrom met him at the foot of the booth stairs with a paper sack from the store in Sturgeon Bay. In it were two wool shirts, red and black check, the heavy kind, one a medium and one a large. One for you and one for your uncle, she said. You tell him thank you for the loan of you. He drove home the next morning down 57 in his brother’s old Chevrolet with the sack on the seat beside him. Somewhere before Green Bay he decided that the large one was for his uncle. It was the better shir

sections.heading: III. The Booth
sections.dateline: The Starview · the Saturday after Labor Day
sections.text: After Labor Day the Starview ran Fridays and Saturdays only, until the frost. Little Walt got out there a little after three. Irene’s Buick was gone from beside the box office, which meant she had driven his uncle into Appleton to the Greyhound depot to pick up the film. He climbed the outside stairs to the booth. It was close and hot under the tar roof and smelled the way it always smelled, of carbon ash and machine oil and old popcorn coming up through the floor. He swept the ash and the film trimmings into the dustpan. He emptied the coffee can of carbon stubs. He washed the two port glasses with newspaper and vinegar until the white screen at the far end of the field stood in each of them clean as a sheet of paper. He set his uncle’s chair by the rewind bench. He went down to the snack bar and filled a dishpan with water from the cold tap and carried it up without spilling and stirred in a handful of Epsom salts from the box on his uncle’s shelf, because his uncle stood all night and his feet were bad. He put the paper sack with the shirt in it on the shelf above the rewind bench, where he could reach it. Then he stood at the port and watched the drive. A few blackbirds walked

sections.heading: IV. Mink
sections.dateline: The same night · the first feature
sections.text: By nine the lot was full. The picture was Yours, Mine and Ours, which had been playing all summer, a widow with eight children marrying a widower with ten, and the laughter came up out of the field in waves through two hundred little speakers, a fraction behind the picture. The arc lamps hissed in their housings. The heat of them filled the booth until the air above the machines shook. Moths came to the ports and beat at the glass, and some of them got in through the vent and went into the beam, and showed on the screen as soft gray birds the size of cows that crossed Lucille Ball’s kitchen and were gone. His uncle sat between changeovers with his feet back in his shoes and his hands on his knees, the way he sat, and Little Walt stood beside him and fanned him with the Post-Crescent. After the third reel he reached down the sack and took out the large shirt and laid it across his uncle’s knees. Mrs. Bergstrom sent this. It’s for you. I picked you the big one. His uncle unfolded it and held it up into the light from the port, and rubbed the wool between his thumb and finger. That’s a good shirt, he said. I’ve got my three. You wear it. I got it for you. I was thinking of you the who

sections.text: He ran across the lot between the rows with the picture enormous above him. Faces turned in windshields. A woman in a Rambler said Hey! He tripped on a cord and kept his feet and went on toward the back fence and the cornfield, where it was dark. The Hoffmann brothers, who worked the lot with flashlights, saw him go, and so did Duane, coming out of the snack bar with a tray of coffee, and the two Gloudemans girls behind the counter. Duane put the tray down on a car hood. They caught him at the fence. He was not hard to catch; he had stopped there with his hands on the top wire, not knowing what came next. They walked him back between the cars, one at each elbow, Carol Gloudemans behind with Duane’s flashlight, and nobody said anything, and they brought him to the box office. Irene Voss sat under the lamp with the cash drawer open, counting the night’s dollar bills into piles of twenty. She looked up at the four of them in her window. What’s this. sections.text: His uncle was standing at the port of the first machine when he came in. He did not turn around. He tipped his head toward the second machine, which was threaded and waiting with its douser down, and Little Walt went and stood at it with his hand on the switch and his eye to the port. The newspaper was on the floor where he had dropped it. The shirt lay folded on the rewind bench. He watched the upper right corner of the screen. He thought about the mink, and the thought went out a long way, to the sheds out by Medford, and he went after it and brought it back. He thought about the space between Carol Gloudemans’s teeth, and fetched that back too. He thought about the tire, and his hand, and it was a long way to go for that one, and he went and got it. Out in the field two hundred people sat in the dark in their cars and went wherever they went. A moth crossed the beam. The corner of the screen was gray and still. Then the first dot came, a small pale circle, there and gone, and he was there for it. He started the motor and counted. At seven the second dot came, and he threw the changeover, and the picture went on from the one machine to the other, and nobody out in the field knew

title: Three Shirts

verses.text: If a man's thoughts are unsteady, if he does not know the true law, if his peace of mind is troubled, his knowledge will never be perfect.
If a man's thoughts are not dissipated, if his mind is not perplexed, if he has ceased to think of good or evil, then there is no fear for him while he is watchful.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young man out looking for a lost ox stops at a monastery, is fed the monks’ leftovers, and decides to become a monk for the food. He grows fat, goes home, grows thin, and comes back, six times, until the monks call him Cittahattha, “led by his mind.” The seventh time, coming in from the fields, he sees his pregnant wife asleep with her mouth open and her clothes fallen away, and she looks to him like a corpse. He runs from the house tying his robe on as he goes, while his mother-in-law wakes her daughter to tell her he is gone for good, and the wife says he will be back in a few days. On the road, repeating that all things pass, he reaches the first stage of awakening; the monks, who say his head is “like a grindstone” from so many shavings, take him back one last time, and soon he is an arahat. When he says he has no more desire to leave, they call it a lie, and the Buddha answers with these verses. Afterward he tells how, in a past life, he himself went forth and came back six times for the sake of a blunt spade and half a pot of seed beans, until he threw them into the Ganges with his eyes shut and cried “I have conquered!”, a cry overheard by a king just home from war, who renounced his throne, followed by six more kings.
bg.history:
About 1919 the preacher known as Father Divine settled with a small group of followers in a house at 72 Macon Street in Sayville, on the south shore of Long Island. During the Depression his free banquets drew crowds by bus and car from Harlem, Newark and elsewhere, as many as three thousand at a time by 1931, colored and white at the same table. Followers lived communally under strict rules against liquor, tobacco, profanity and sex, even within marriage, and many took new spiritual names; the movement found jobs for them, often in domestic work. Neighbors complained of the noise and the traffic. Father Divine was arrested for disturbing the peace in May 1931, and on the night of November 15, after a town meeting, police and state troopers broke up a meeting at the house and arrested seventy-eight people, fifteen of them white. Forty-six pleaded guilty and paid five-dollar fines; Father Divine, by the familiar story, paid with a five-hundred-dollar bill. His trial the next spring before Judge Lewis J. Smith ended in the maximum sentence, and the judge’s sudden death four days later became a famous legend. The movement soon moved its center to Harlem as the International Peace Mission movement.

In Harlem, the block of West 133rd Street between Lenox and Seventh Avenues was lined with Prohibition speakeasies and clubs, where stride pianists played through the night. The spiritual Sister Still Water sings, “I Know That My Redeemer Lives,” was printed among the songs of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the Nashville student choir whose tours from 1871 onward first brought the spirituals to concert audiences in the North and in Europe. The text quoted here follows the 1898 London edition of J. B. T. Marsh’s The Story of the Jubilee Singers, Including Their Songs; the song appears in the earlier editions as well.

sections.heading: I. Leftovers
sections.text: Lemuel Pryor played piano in a cellar on West 133rd Street from midnight until the milk wagons, for two dollars and whatever went into the cigar box on the lid. The cellar had no name on the door. People called it the Coal Hole, because that was what it had been, and the gin came down the steps in teapots and went out to the tables in cups. Lem had a left hand that could walk a tenth all night without looking, and a right hand that got bored and wandered, and between the two of them he made enough to pay half the rent on two rooms over an undertaker on 131st Street, where he lived with his wife Ida and her mother. Ida did day work in the Bronx. Her mother, Mrs. Odessa Bynum, did nothing, and did it from a cot in the front room, where she could see the door. In August Ida's cousin Bernice, who was seventeen, went out to Sayville on the train to the man the papers called God and did not come back. She sent a postcard with a picture of the bay on it. It said she was well and happy and fed, and it was signed with a name none of them knew. Mrs. Bynum read it twice and held it out to Lem with two fingers. You go get her. You’re the only man in this house, and you sleep all day anyhow. He

sections.heading: II. The Ledger
sections.dateline: Sayville and Harlem · autumn 1930 to autumn 1931
sections.text: The kitchen women called her Sister Still Water. Nobody used whatever name she had come up from Tennessee with, and nobody asked it. There was an upright piano in the front parlor that nobody played well, and the second evening Lem sat down at it, and after that the house had a piano player. He played at the banquets. They sang Mission songs and the old songs, and he put a walking bass under all of them, and the people at the long table rose one after another to testify and sat down again shining. At the head of the table sat a small bald man in a good suit, and the platters went down the table from him, and he was God to everybody in the room. Lem never spoke to him. He watched him from the piano bench, at a distance, the way you would watch weather coming across a bay. In ten days his collar would not close. In three weeks he had let out the back seam of his only suit. Then one morning, carrying a stack of plates, he thought: what kind of a man eats at another man’s table for nothing? A man ought to be paid for his hands. He thought of the Coal Hole, and the cigar box, and of Ida turning over in the bed. He took his coat off the nail and walked to the station. That winter the Coa

sections.heading: III. The Kitchenette
sections.dateline: West 131st Street, Harlem · a Saturday in November 1931
sections.text: He came up from the Coal Hole at a quarter to seven in the morning with eighty cents in his pocket and his mind made up. He would get his good shirt and his razor and be on the eight-something out of Penn Station, and he would be at Macon Street by the noon table. He had told nobody. He never did. Downstairs, through the undertaker’s front window, he could see a man laid out on a board under a sheet, waiting for his people, with only his face showing, the mouth a little open. Lem looked at him the way you look at anything in a window and went on up. The bedroom had one window on the airshaft and the light that came down it was gray. Ida was asleep on her back. She was seven months along and she could not sleep any other way now. The quilt had slid off her onto the floor, and the strap of her slip had come down, and the slip had worked up around her middle so that the great round of her belly stood up out of it, bare. Her mouth was open. She was snoring with a catch at the end of each breath, and a wet line ran from the corner of her mouth into the pillow, and her hands lay at her sides palm up. He stood in the door with his hat in his hand. He had seen her asleep a thousand times.

sections.heading: IV. The Montauk Train
sections.dateline: Long Island Rail Road · the same morning
sections.text: He paid his fare with the eighty cents and a dollar he kept folded in his shoe. He sat by a window in a car that smelled of wet wool, with his hat on his knees, and the wheels found the rail joints and kept time on them, and under the time he heard the song. Just watch that sun, and see how it runs. He said it under his breath. He said it at Jamaica, changing trains, and on the platform, and again when the city fell away behind and the flat country opened out, brown fields with the potatoes up and gone, crows walking the furrows, a boy on a fence. Each thing the window gave him, it took away. A white church. A gas station with one pump. A woman taking in a wash with the wind trying to have it. A dog that ran beside the train and gave up. He watched them come and go, and he said the line, and every one of them went exactly the way the man downstairs had gone and Ida was going and he was going. None of it would hold still. None of it was ever going to. Somewhere past Babylon, where a creek ran down through the marsh grass, he caught a long look at the bay, flat and pewter-colored, with a few oyster boats out on it and the long low line of the beach beyond. Something in him that had b

sections.heading: V. Stand Still
sections.text: He played for the noon table and the evening table. He washed. He swept the long room under the roof. In the evenings when the house was quiet he sat on the back step and watched the light go off the bay, and that was all he did with the evenings. By Wednesday the brothers had started to look at him sideways. By Friday they had started to talk. They meant no harm by it. At the end of the evening table one of the young ones leaned down the board toward him. Brother Weathervane. Which way is the wind today? They laughed. Lem laughed with them. You’ll let us know when you’re fixing to go, said another. You’ve been here a long while this time. It’s nearly a week. I’m not going, Lem said. Not till Thursday. When I was hooked to all that, Lem said, I went. I’m not hooked to it. I don’t have anyplace to go. He said it plainly, the way he would say what key a song was in, and went back to his pie. The young men looked at each other. Later that night three of them went into the kitchen, where Sister Still Water was setting the bread to rise for the morning under clean flour sacks, and Brother Glad Tidings went with them because he kept the book. Sister. You know what Brother Weathervane is

sections.heading: VI. The Wagons
