sections.text: That Sunday the people came out from Harlem and Newark and Brooklyn and the towns around in buses and cars and on foot from the station, and there were three thousand of them in the house and on the porch and on the lawn and standing in the road, and the singing went on into the night. A few days before, the white people of Sayville had held a meeting at which they said they had nothing against colored people. They had said other things too. A little before midnight the police came, from Sayville and the towns nearby, with state troopers behind them, and men from the town who were neither. They stood at the edge of the lawn with their lights and said the meeting would disperse in fifteen minutes. The singing did not stop. In the parlor Lem kept on playing. When the fifteen minutes were up they came in. They took seventy-eight people, colored and white, out of the house and off the porch and put them in wagons and cars to go to the courthouse. Some of the women cried. Some of the young men shouted. One of the brothers who had laughed at the table that week stood on the porch steps with his fists shut and his whole face shaking. Lem closed the lid of the piano. He got up and put on h

sections.heading: VII. Seed Peas
sections.dateline: The kitchen on Macon Street · that night
sections.text: They sat in the kitchen afterward, the ones who had come back, too tired to go up. Somebody had put coffee on. The young men talked about Brother Weathervane, who had gone up to bed. They did not call him that now. They talked about him the way you talk about a man who has come through a fever. Seven times, one of them said. Seven times in the book. What kind of a hook has a man got in him, that it takes seven times to pull it out? Sister Still Water was at the board with her back to them, cutting lard into flour with two knives. That’s not much of a hook, she said. I knew a woman it took seven times for a hoe. They waited. She went on cutting. She came up from Tennessee, she said, with a hoe with the edge gone off it and a snuff can of crowder peas her mother saved, for seed. She got a little patch in a lot behind a church on Lenox Avenue, where the ground was all brickbats, and she grew her peas. Then she came out here to Father. And come the spring she thought, who’s going to plant my peas? I can’t let my peas go. So she went back and planted them. And she picked them in August, and she saved a can of them for seed, and she came back out here. And come the spring she thought abo

title: The Weathervane
logline: A Harlem stride pianist joins Father Divine's Sayville household for the food, goes home to his wife, and comes back, six times.

verses.text: Knowing that this body is (fragile) like a jar, and making this thought firm like a fortress, one should attack Mara (the tempter) with the weapon of knowledge, one should watch him when conquered, and should never rest.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred monks take a meditation subject from the Buddha and travel a hundred leagues to a village, whose people feed them and ask them to spend the three months of the rains in a nearby forest grove. The tree spirits there, unwilling to live above the monks' heads, come down with their families and sit on the ground waiting for them to leave; when the monks stay, the spirits show them headless bodies and bodiless heads, make them hear voices, and afflict them with sneezing and coughing until the monks flee back to the Buddha. He sends them back with a "weapon," the Discourse on Loving-Kindness, to be recited outside the grove before they enter. The spirits welcome them, carry their bowls, rub their hands and feet, and stand guard. Contemplating the body as fragile as a potter's jar, the monks develop insight, and the Buddha, though a hundred leagues away, appears before them sending out six-colored rays and speaks the verse; all of them reach awakening. This is the traditional origin story of the Karaniya Metta Sutta.
bg.history:
In 1975 the young teachers Joseph Goldstein, Sharon Salzberg, Jack Kornfield and Jacqueline Schwartz, who had trained in Burma, Thailand and India, bought a former Catholic novitiate in Barre, Massachusetts, for $150,000. The Insight Meditation Society opened there on February 14, 1976. The house had been the Blessed Sacrament novitiate since 1946. The old chapel became the meditation hall, stained glass of Christ stayed in the walking room, and a bowling alley stayed in the basement; early yogis remember the clanging radiators of the old oil-fired heat as the house's first mindfulness bells (IMS at 50; a profile of the founding). Its three-month retreat, modeled on the monastic rains retreat, was first held in Barre that year, with about thirty people. The practice was largely the noting method of the Burmese teacher Mahasi Sayadaw, in which the meditator silently labels each experience as it arises: rising, falling, hearing, seeing.

In Burma, belief in nats, spirits of trees, places and households, sits alongside Theravada practice, and the Metta Sutta is among the protective discourses chanted to keep peace with them. The six colors that the Buddha's body is said to have emitted are the colors of the Buddhist flag, designed in Colombo in 1885; in Burma its orange stripe is read as pink. Daw Tin Hla, her students, the Lacasses and all the events at Barre in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Living Room
sections.text: Daw Tin Hla taught on Saturday mornings in her son's apartment off Connecticut Avenue, with the sofa pushed against the wall and the air conditioner going in the window like an outboard motor. She was sixty-eight, a widow from Rangoon, and she had sat long retreats at the meditation center there in the fifties, before her husband's posting brought them to Washington and then his heart gave out and left her in it. Her son was an economist at the World Bank and was gone by seven. On the bookshelf were a small brass Buddha, a little paper flag in stripes of blue, yellow, red, white and pink, and a row of her husband's English books from the university, gone soft in the heat of two countries. Out on the balcony, eleven floors up, she kept a round clay water pot on an iron stand with a lid and a tin dipper, the way people did along the roads at home, so that anyone passing could drink. Nobody passed eleven floors up. She filled it every morning anyway. Her students that summer were four young Americans who had found her through a notice on the board at a health food store in Takoma Park. Nora Kessel catalogued books at the Library of Congress and had not been able to sleep through a nig

sections.heading: II. The Fathers' House
sections.text: They went up in Dewey's Volkswagen bus with their cushions and their sleeping bags and a cooler of Bev's granola, nine hours with the engine whining up every hill, and came into Barre in the late afternoon, a town of white houses around a long green common, with dairy farms going off on every side into the hills. They stopped at a luncheonette on the common because Ellis was hungry, and the woman behind the counter, a Mrs. Lacasse, gave them coffee and pie and looked at their cushions. Where are you kids headed? Somewhere quiet, Nora said, which was what Daw Tin Hla had told them to say. Well, you found it. When she understood they were going up the hill to the old novitiate for three months, she put down the coffee pot. The whole three months? Without talking? She thought about that. My aunt cleaned for the Fathers up there twenty years. That was a lot of house for a few priests. You stay the three months, and I'll tell you what. I'll keep my Roland out of those woods this deer season. He'll hate it. She did not charge them for the pie. The house stood at the top of a long drive in eighty acres of oak and pine and old pasture, a great old house that the Blessed Sacrament novitiate

sections.heading: III. Seeing, Seeing
sections.text: Dewey saw it first, at four in the morning, at the far end of the third-floor corridor where the night light was: a man in a long black cassock standing by the radiator with his hands folded, and above the white collar nothing at all. Dewey had seen a good many things in Quang Tri Province and did not scream. He noted it. Seeing, seeing. It did not go away when he noted it. He went back into his cell and sat on the bed until the wake-up bell with his back against the wall. Ellis saw a head. It was in the walking room in the afternoon, a young man's head, pale, with its hair combed wet, hanging in the air at the far end of the room under one of the windows of Christ, and looking at him with great patience, and nothing under it. He turned at the end of his lane as he had been taught, turning, turning, and when he came back it was still there, and when he came back the next time it was nearer. Bev heard the voices. In the night, under the floor, men's voices murmuring together in a language she did not know, and then the long rumble of a ball down the lane in the bowling alley and the crash of pins, over and over, when everyone in the house was asleep and the basement door was locked.

sections.heading: IV. The Weapon
sections.text: Daw Tin Hla opened the door in her housecoat and looked at the four of them on the mat, with their sleeping bags and their red noses, and stood aside to let them in. She did not seem surprised. She made tea. She let them tell it, all of it, the cassock and the head and the pins and the three o'clock door, and she listened with her hands in her lap the way she listened to the rain. You could not stay there? No, Nora said. We couldn't. Of course there are beings there, said Daw Tin Hla. Tree spirits. Nats. Thirty years they had that hill with only a few quiet priests. Now you come and walk under their houses all day long and sit on their doorsteps. They don't like it. Would you? She drank her tea. You must go back. We can't, said Dewey. The first time you went with nothing in your hands. This time you will take a weapon. Dewey, who had carried an M16 for thirteen months and had not touched a gun since, looked at her for a long moment. What kind of weapon? She went to the bookshelf and took down one of her husband's soft old books, a thick one in dark blue cloth, and found the page without looking for it. She said that this had happened before, a long time ago, to some monks who went

sections.heading: V. The Driveway
sections.dateline: Barre · the end of October to December
sections.text: Dewey stopped the bus at the bottom of the long drive at dusk and turned off the engine. The four of them got out and stood in the gravel in the cold, facing up the hill toward the dark woods and the lit windows of the house, and said it, the Pāli and then the English, all the way through, not very loudly. Ellis knew it best and kept the time. Their breath went up white. A car went by on the road behind them and slowed down to look and went on. When they finished, nothing happened that any of them could point to. They got back in the bus and drove up. Their sleeping bags were on their beds when they came in. None of them had carried them up. Nobody in the office knew anything about it. Then it was quiet. It is the thing everyone who sat that course remembers about the second half of it: how quiet that house became. The radiators still clanged when the burner came on, but not in the night. The bowling alley was silent. Nobody saw a head anywhere. The coughing in the hall thinned out over a week and stopped. In the kitchen at five in the morning Nora found the oatmeal pot from the night before already scoured and turned upside down on the drainboard, though she had left it to soak, a

sections.heading: VI. The Pot
sections.text: In April Bev drove up from Washington alone, with a round clay pot in a box of straw on the seat beside her. She had thrown it on the wheel on Carroll Avenue and fired it thin, the way Daw Tin Hla had told her the potters did at home. She set it on a flat stone at the bottom of the long drive, where the four of them had stood in the gravel and said the words, and filled it from the hose at the house, and put a lid on it and hung a tin dipper on its rim. She did not ask anyone's permission. People drank from it. The mailman, the oil truck driver, yogis going down to the road to stretch their legs, a boy on a bicycle, Mrs. Lacasse once, on a Sunday, out for a drive with Roland. Somebody at the house filled it every morning. Nobody could ever say who. It lasted until the first hard freeze the next November. In the morning it stood on the stone split down one side, with a fan of ice standing in the crack and the dipper still hanging from the rim, and it was cool to the touch, and it held nothing, and it was a good pot.

title: The Water Pot
logline: Four Washington meditators sent to sit three months in an old Catholic novitiate find the woods around it already occupied.

verses.text: Before long, alas! this body will lie on the earth, despised, without understanding, like a useless log.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young man of good family from Sāvatthī becomes a monk named Tissa. Sores break out over his body, growing from the size of mustard seeds to the size of large fruit, until they burst; his robes stiffen with blood and his bones begin to break apart, and his fellow monks, unable to bear it, put him out on the ground. The Buddha, who surveys the world at dawn and at dusk, sees him. He goes to the fire-hall, washes a pot and heats water, and takes hold of the end of Tissa's bed, and the monks hurry to carry it in for him. The Buddha has Tissa's robes washed and dried in the sun while he bathes him with his own hands, dresses him, and speaks this verse at his pillow. Tissa reaches awakening and dies. When the monks ask why so good a monk suffered so, the Buddha tells them that in a past life Tissa was a fowler who broke the legs and wings of his captive birds so they could not escape, and who once filled the bowl of a saint at his door with his best food and asked to reach what the saint had reached.
bg.history:
Young Filipino men came to California in large numbers in the 1920s and early 1930s, until the Tydings–McDuffie Act of 1934 all but closed the door, and they did much of the state's migrant field work. Laws against interracial marriage, and how few Filipina women had come, left most of them single for life; they are remembered as the manong generation, from the Ilocano word for elder brother. Stockton's Little Manila was their winter home, and they met violence across the state, most notoriously in the Watsonville riots of January 1930, when Fermin Tobera was shot dead in a bunkhouse. On September 7, 1965, Filipino members of the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee met at the Filipino Community Hall in Delano and voted to strike the table-grape growers the next morning, the beginning of the five-year Delano grape strike. Many of the strikers were past fifty. Growers cut off water to the labor camps and put the men out.

When the union's grape contracts expired in 1973 and growers signed with the Teamsters, the strike resumed, and in mid-August two strikers were killed in Kern County: Nagi Daifallah, a young Yemeni immigrant struck by a sheriff's deputy, and Juan de la Cruz, shot on a picket line near Arvin (Welga Digital Archive). That same season some thousand volunteers were building Agbayani Village, a fifty-nine-room retirement home for the old Filipino strikers at the union's Forty Acres outside Delano, named for Paulo Agbayani, who died of a heart attack on a picket line. It opened in 1974. Andoy's word gabà is the Visayan idea of a comeuppance that falls on wrongdoers, cruelty to animals among them, with no god needed to send it; talunan, "loser," is the sour stew made from the tough meat of a rooster that lost its fight.

sections.heading: I. The Walkout
sections.text: Celestino Abellana came from Bohol, from a town above the river where his father taught the fourth grade and owned four hundred coconut trees. That made the Abellanas people of some standing. In 1929, when Celestino was nineteen, his father sold sixty of the trees and bought him passage to San Francisco and a fountain pen, so that he could study at the university in California and come home an engineer. He got as far as the asparagus. By the spring of 1930 he was on his knees in the peat of the Delta islands west of Stockton with a long knife, cutting spears at first light, and the fountain pen was in a pawnshop on Lafayette Street. He never went home. Nobody he knew went home. For thirty-six years he followed the crops up and down the state, asparagus and lettuce and apricots and tomatoes and grapes, and by the time he was fifty-five he was what all of them were, a manong, an old bachelor in a bunkhouse with a good suit in a cardboard box under his cot, because California would not let him marry a white girl and there were hardly any Filipinas to marry. On the night of the seventh of September, 1965, he sat on a folding chair in the Filipino Community Hall in Delano with more than

sections.heading: II. The Mustard Seed
sections.text: The first one came up on his shin in March, a red point no bigger than a mustard seed. Tino scratched it and forgot it. By April there were a dozen of them, on both shins and on the backs of his hands, and the first one was the size of a monggo bean. In May they were the size of garbanzos. That spring and summer the union's grape contracts ran out, first down in the desert at Coachella and then here, and the growers signed with the Teamsters instead, and the strike began again, the whole thing, the pickets and the sheriff's deputies and the trucks coming out of the vineyards with their windows rolled up. The old men in the Garces house went out on the line in the mornings in their straw hats. Tino went with them, in long sleeves buttoned at the wrist. In June the sores on his shins were the size of Thompson seedless grapes. In July they were as big as walnuts, and the biggest, on his left ankle, was as big as a Santa Rosa plum and the same dark color. Then, one after another, they opened. After that there was no hiding them. The smell went before him into a room. His long-sleeved shirt stuck to his forearms and had to be peeled off at night, and the cotton undershirt underneath it

sections.heading: III. The Pepper Tree
sections.text: It was a hundred and six degrees in Delano on the day they moved him out. Nobody decided it, exactly. It was decided at the kitchen table over rice and dried fish, the way everything in the house was decided, with the radio on. Siso said the smell got into the rice. Pidiong said his brother in Stockton had caught something like that from a man in a bunkhouse in 1948 and lost an eye. Andoy, who was Visayan like Tino and the oldest of them after Propesor, said nothing for a long time and then said the word they had all been not saying, which was gaba. It was the old word from home for the thing that comes back on you. You waste rice, you mock an old person, you are cruel to an animal, and one day it comes back on you. Nobody has to send it. It comes by itself. He must have done something, said Andoy. A man doesn't rot like that for nothing. Propesor was at work that day, weeding a Japanese family's strawberries out by McFarland, because a man has to eat during a strike too. So the others carried Tino's cot out into the yard and set it under the pepper tree by the chicken wire, where there was shade until two in the afternoon. They gave him a gallon jug of water and a fly swatter and

sections.heading: IV. The Kaldero
sections.text: Propesor came out into the yard at first light, as he always did, and stood by the chicken wire and looked. Tino was lying half on the broken cot and half on the ground, on his side, with his cheek in the dirt and his eyes open. His shirt had dried onto him. There were ants going in a line up the cot leg and down again. Propesor stood there longer than he usually stood anywhere. He was thinking that the men in the house were not bad men. They were old and they were scared and they had nothing, and when you have nothing you are careful with it, even your own nose, even your own fear. He was thinking that Tino had no brother and no wife and no son, and that his father and his four hundred coconut trees were forty years in the ground in Bohol, and that the union had its hands full and the priest did not come out this far. He was thinking that the man had nobody now but him. He did not go to Tino. He went into the kitchen. He took down the big aluminum kaldero they cooked the rice in for nine men, and he scrubbed it out at the sink with steel wool until it shone, and filled it at the tap, and put it on the big burner and lit the gas. Then he stood by the stove with his arms folded and

sections.heading: V. The East Room
sections.text: Propesor did all of it. He went to the county office in Bakersfield for the papers. He went to the funeral home in town and argued about the price in Ilocano and English and paid it out of the coffee can where the house kept its money for the dead, because they had always buried each other and there was nobody else to do it. He went to the rectory, and the priest came, and the funeral Mass was said at the church in town, and Propesor stood at the very back by the holy water with his hat in his hands, where the men from the Garces house could see that he had come inside. They buried Tino in the cemetery at the edge of town, in his good suit, the brown one from 1931 that was too big for him now. Volunteers came from the Forty Acres, some of the long-haired kids, and stood at the grave in their work boots with mortar still on them. One of the girls had brought her notebook and did not know what to do with it and held it against her chest. In the spring of 1974 Agbayani Village was finished, and the union opened it with a big ceremony at the Forty Acres, and the old men moved in with their suitcases and their suit boxes, each man to his own room, with a bed that was not a cot and a win

sections.heading: VI. Talunan
sections.text: The men from the Garces house still ate together at one end of the long table in the new dining hall, and still argued, and still said the things they had said in the old kitchen, only now there were twenty other men to hear them. One night in the summer, after the plates had gone back, Andoy said it. Propesor. Where is he now? Who? Tino. Heaven? Purgatory? Where? Propesor turned his coffee cup a quarter turn on the table. Nowhere, he said. He finished. Andoy did not like that answer. None of them did. Siso said that was no answer. Pidiong said what kind of a thing was that to say about a man. Andoy put his two hands flat on the table. Then tell me this. He was the best of us. On the line he was the best of us. Why does a man like that rot like a dead dog under a tree? Why do his bones go? And then, at the end, why does he go so easy? I have seen men die. Nobody dies like that. He went like a man getting on a bus. Propesor did not say anything for a long time, and they thought he was not going to. Then he said: You want gaba, Andoy. I'll give you gaba. But you have to take the whole thing. In the thirties, he said, he and Tino had shared a room in Stockton over a barbershop on Lafa

title: Hot Water
logline: During the 1973 grape strike, old Filipino farmworkers carry their festering housemate out under the pepper tree, and their quietest man lights the stove.

verses.text: Whatever a hater may do to a hater, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly-directed mind will do us greater mischief.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Nanda is a wealthy herdsman who tends the cattle of the great lay patron Anāthapiṇḍika. For a long time he keeps inviting the Buddha to his home, and the Buddha waits until Nanda is ready. At last the Buddha sits down under a tree near Nanda’s place, and Nanda feeds the monks with the products of the cow for seven days. On the seventh day he hears a teaching and enters the stream. He carries the Buddha’s bowl a long way down the road, until the Buddha tells him to stop and turn back. On the way home a hunter’s arrow kills him. The monks say that if the Buddha had never come, Nanda would still be alive. The Buddha answers that wherever Nanda had gone, he could not have escaped that death, and speaks the verse about the wrongly directed mind. No one asks what Nanda had done in a past life, so the Buddha says nothing about it.
bg.history:
Hmong families began arriving in Wausau as refugees in the late 1970s, most of them families of men who had fought for the CIA against the Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese in the Laotian Civil War. After 1975 tens of thousands crossed the Mekong into Thailand. Many spent years in camps such as Ban Vinai before churches and agencies resettled them in towns like Wausau, where by 2002 Hmong residents made up about an eighth of the city. Many of the first generation worked in Marathon County’s ginseng gardens, under black shade cloth. More on the Hmong in Wisconsin.

On November 21, 2004, the second day of the gun deer season, a confrontation over a tree stand on private land near Birchwood left six white hunters dead and two wounded. The shooter, Chai Soua Vang, a Hmong hunter from St. Paul, was convicted in September 2005 and sentenced that November to life without parole; the hunters and Vang gave sharply different accounts of who fired first. The killings left deep tension between white and Hmong hunters. When the 2005 season opened, Hmong hunters reported harassment, the DNR aired safety and trespass announcements in Hmong, Spanish and English, and the township near the shooting posted signs in all three languages. Wisconsin’s nine-day gun deer season opens on the Saturday before Thanksgiving.

sections.heading: I. The Steer
sections.text: Walt Brandt milked ninety Holsteins in a tie-stall barn on County Road N, west of Marathon City, in the same barn where his father had milked forty, and he was the one farmer in the township the Hmong families called when somebody died. It started by accident. A young man named Tou Xiong drove out one April morning with a cousin and a borrowed stock trailer, looking for a steer. The farms nearer town had told him no, or named a price meant to send him home. Walt had a Holstein steer he had kept back for the freezer. He sold it for what it would have brought at the sale barn, and helped them load it, and asked what it was for. My uncle’s wife, said Tou. For the funeral. The uncle had come along. He stood by the trailer in a gray nylon windbreaker with his hands folded behind his back, a small old man with a face as brown and creased as a harness, and before they loaded the steer he walked around it twice, slowly. He ran his palm down its back. He looked at its feet and its eyes and the inside of its lip. It was how Walt’s father used to go over a cow at an auction, and Walt had never seen anybody from town look at an animal like that. He kept cattle, Tou said. In Laos, before. Cows,

sections.heading: II. Signs
sections.text: Then the thing happened up north in Sawyer County. On the second morning of the deer season in 2004, on private land near Birchwood, a party of hunters found a Hmong hunter from St. Paul sitting in one of their stands and told him to get off the property. Nobody afterward agreed about everything that was said, or who raised a rifle first. When it was over, six of the hunters were dead and two were wounded, and the man from St. Paul was arrested a few hours later, when he came back out of the woods to his camp. Walt heard it on the radio in the milkhouse. By the end of the week there was nobody in Marathon County, white or Hmong, who was not talking about it, and nobody who was talking about anything else. That winter you heard things at the co-op you had not heard said out loud before. Somebody’s brother-in-law knew a fellow up north who had found the Hmong camp and done his business in their cooking pots. Somebody had a bumper sticker. A man Walt had sat next to in church for twenty years said, standing at the feed counter, that they ought to send every one of them back where they came from, and then looked at Walt as if waiting for him to say something, and Walt paid for his mine

sections.heading: III. The Bur Oak
sections.dateline: The Brandt farm · the week before the opener
sections.text: He did not come up to the house. Walt found him on Saturday morning when the milk truck pulled out, sitting under the big bur oak at the end of the lane, on a folding canvas chair he must have brought with him, with a plastic grocery bag at his feet and his hands folded on his knees. Tou had dropped him there at daybreak on his way to the Saturday shift at the paper mill. The oak still had its leaves, brown and stiff, the way bur oaks hold them into winter, and they rattled over his head in the wind. Mr. Xiong. Why didn’t you come up? I am up, said the old man, and smiled for the first time Walt had ever seen. Carol aired out the old house and made up the bed with the good quilt. And for seven days Walt Brandt fed him. Every morning after milking he carried down a gallon of milk drawn warm from the tank before the cooler took it, a dish of cream, butter Carol had worked in the kitchen with the paddle that had been her mother’s, curds, cottage cheese, a wedge of brick cheese from the plant down the road. In the evenings Tou and Kou came out after work to look over the back forty before the opener, and the boy Pheng, Tou’s son, seventeen, who drove his great-uncle wherever he needed

sections.heading: IV. Stop Here
sections.text: They walked down the lane together a little after six in the morning, in the gray before sunrise, with the frost white on the hay stubble and the oak rattling at the bottom of the hill. Walt had already milked. He carried the old man’s grocery bag and the folded canvas chair. Down at the road Pheng’s little Honda sat with its parking lights on and its exhaust going up straight in the cold. Tou and Kou had been in the back forty since five, sitting against two trees on the far fence line in their orange coats, waiting for light. All over the county trucks were parked on the shoulders. All over the state, more than half a million people sat in the woods with rifles across their knees, watching the dark go gray. In a few minutes it would be legal to shoot. Halfway down the lane, the old man stopped and turned and took his bag and his chair. Stop here, he said. Go back to your cows. Walt had meant to walk him to the car. He had meant, honestly, to stand by the car window and say something, though he did not know what. But he stopped. He did what he was told, the way he had done everything for a week. The old man took Walt’s hand in both of his and held it, and then went on down the lan

sections.heading: V. The Wardens
sections.text: Two deputies came, and the ambulance, which was no use, and before nine o’clock three wardens from the DNR, who walked the field in a line with their heads down. They found where Walt had fallen, and they stood there a long time looking west, toward the fence line and the woods, and then north, and then west again. They took Tou’s rifle and Kou’s rifle, gently, with paper tags on the trigger guards, and sat the brothers at Carol’s kitchen table in their orange coats for four hours, one at a time, with a deputy in the doorway. They asked Pheng to tell it again and again. They asked the old man, through Pheng, where he had been standing, and he showed them. By noon it was all over the county. By the time the bars in Marathon City filled up on Saturday night there was nobody in them who did not know that Walt Brandt had been shot dead on his own land on opening morning, and that Walt Brandt had let Hmong hunt his back forty, and that two Hmong had been in his back forty with rifles when it happened. Nobody needed to say the rest. A rock came through the front window of a Hmong grocery on the east side on Sunday morning. On Sunday afternoon somebody at the gas station on Highway 29 tol

sections.heading: VI. The Hymn
sections.dateline: Marathon City · the Wednesday before Thanksgiving
sections.text: Danny Brandt got home Tuesday night, thirty hours out of Baghdad by way of Kuwait, on emergency leave, in a uniform that still had the dust of the convoy route in its seams. He hugged his mother in the doorway for a long time. He did not cry. He walked out to the hayfield in the dark by himself and stood on the place, and came back in, and took his father’s deer rifle out of the gun cabinet in the den and cleaned it at the kitchen table, all of it, every part, and put it back together and did not put it away. The funeral was at the Methodist church on Wednesday morning. The church was full and the basement was full and people stood along the walls. Carol had chosen the hymns. The last one was Walt’s father’s, and Walt’s. The old man came, with Tou and Pheng, in white shirts and dark jackets, and sat in the last pew on the left. Danny saw heads turn. He saw a woman he had known all his life get up from that pew with her husband and move to the other side. He saw the man from the feed counter look at the three of them and look away. The old man sat with his hands folded on his knees and looked at the casket. They stood for the last hymn. The organ was loud. Danny did not sing. He hel

sections.heading: VII. The Ancient Foe
sections.text: He parked across the street from the narrow frame house with the engine running for the heat and the rifle across his knees. He did not know what he had come to do. He had driven a fuel truck past a hundred houses like this one on the other side of the world with a rifle across his knees, and he had always known what he had come to do, and now he did not, and that frightened him more than anything had frightened him over there. After twenty minutes the porch light came on and the old man came down the steps in a parka and house slippers and crossed the street, and opened the passenger door of the truck, and got in, and shut the door. He looked at the rifle. Then he looked out the windshield. They sat a while. Your father told me you drive the fuel, Neng Chue Xiong said. On the roads with the bombs. He told you that. Every night. Seven nights. You were the only thing he talked about that he was afraid of. The old man was quiet. On Thursday night he sang a song to the cows. The one they sang in your church. Danny’s hands tightened on the rifle. There is a part of the song, the old man said. Your father sang it for me twice, so I could learn it. And he said it, slowly, in his careful

sections.heading: VIII. Opening Day
sections.text: Danny’s enlistment ran out in the summer, and he came home to the barn. That fall a family on the east side needed a cow for a grandmother’s funeral, and they called the Brandt farm, and Danny walked them through the dry cows with a flashlight and let them take as long as they wanted. On the Saturday before Thanksgiving, after milking, he went out the mudroom door a little before six in his orange coat. Tou and Kou and Pheng were waiting by the machine shed in theirs, stamping in the cold, and they went out together down the lane in the gray toward the back forty. The old man was sitting at the bottom of the hill under the bur oak in his folding chair, with a thermos of Carol’s coffee and a blanket on his knees and an orange stocking cap that Danny had bought him at the farm store pulled down over his ears. The leaves rattled over his head. He watched them go. Four orange shapes, crossing the frost toward the woods, bright as a fire in the stubble, so that anybody sitting out there with a rifle across his knees could see them coming a long way off.

title: Blaze Orange
logline: A Wisconsin dairyman feeds an old Hmong elder for seven days, then walks him down the lane on the opening morning of deer season.

verses.text: Not a mother, not a father will do so much, nor any other relative; a well-directed mind will do us greater service.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Soreyya, a rich man's son with a wife and two sons, drives out of his city to bathe and sees the golden-skinned elder Mahākaccāna putting on his robe at the gate. He thinks, if only he were my wife, or my wife's body had his color, and at once becomes a woman. Ashamed, she follows a caravan to the distant city of Takkasilā, paying her way with a signet ring, and the caravan men present her to a rich bachelor, whom she marries and bears two sons. Years later Soreyya's old companion arrives with five hundred carts; she sees him from her window, tells him who she is, and he arranges a meal at which she bows at the elder's feet and is forgiven. Soreyya becomes a man again, refuses his husband's plea to stay, kisses the boys, and goes forth as a monk. Asked which sons he loves more, he says at first the ones he bore; after a time alone contemplating decay and death, he says his affections are set on no one, and when the monks call this a lie the Buddha speaks the verse. The commentary frames the change as the fruit of an unwise thought and repeats its age's view that rebirth as a woman is the lesser lot; this retelling keeps the change and its cause and lets the midwife answer that view.
bg.history:
The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began in West Virginia on July 14 and reached Chicago the following week. On July 25 a crowd of about ten thousand gathered at the Halsted Street viaduct; police fired into it for half an hour, cavalry came up afterward, and some thirty people were killed in what was called the Battle of the Viaduct. The true toll was never settled, since many bodies were reportedly buried at night. The same year Chicago's Czechs, angered when a young Catholic woman, Marie Silhanek, was refused burial in Catholic ground, bought land in Jefferson Township for the Bohemian National Cemetery, a place where anyone could be buried without a priest's leave. The Czech West Side, later centered on Pilsen, was home to many freethinkers, lodges and gymnastic societies.

Many Chicago Czechs moved on to the Nebraska prairie. Wilber, on the Big Blue River in Saline County, was platted in 1873, became the county seat in 1878, and by 1882 had a Czech benevolent lodge meeting in the Masons' hall on the second Sunday of every month; it is now called the Czech capital of the United States. The book the midwife keeps is The Labyrinth of the World and the Paradise of the Heart (first version 1623) by John Amos Comenius, the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, the old Czech Protestant church that was driven underground and into exile after 1620. The quotations, and the exiles' song, come from Count Lützow's 1901 English translation, which is online.

sections.heading: I. The Ford
sections.dateline: The Des Plaines River, west of Chicago · Sunday, July 22, 1877
sections.text: Václav Soukup was the son of the richest Bohemian on the West Side, and he had a way of looking at things that his mother said he got from his father and his father said he got from the lumber business. He looked at a thing and priced it. A horse, a hat, a lot on Eighteenth Street, a stand of white pine in Michigan he had only seen on paper. His father had come over with a carpenter's box and nothing else and now owned four acres of piled lumber on the South Branch and a brick house with a cupola, and Václav had grown up there learning that everything had a number on it somewhere, even if it was written very small. He was twenty-six. He had a wife, Anna, who was pretty and quiet and the daughter of a man who owned a building and loan, and two little boys, Jeník and Vojta, four and two. He loved them the way he loved the house, without thinking about it, as things that were his. That Sunday was the hottest of the summer. There had been talk all week of the railroad men striking back East, in Baltimore and Pittsburgh, of roundhouses burning. Václav did not want to hear about it. He and his friend Tomáš Pech, who had been his friend since they were boys throwing rocks at the Irish on

sections.heading: II. The Viaduct
sections.dateline: Chicago · the last week of July
sections.text: The strike reached Chicago the next morning. The switchmen walked out of the yards, and then the men in the planing mills walked out, and then the lumber shovers along the South Branch, most of them Bohemians, put down their pikes and went into the street, because they were paid little enough when they were paid at all, and a man had to stand up sometime. By Wednesday there were crowds of ten thousand on Halsted Street. The police fired into them at the viaduct over the tracks, and the cavalry came up with sabers, and at the end of the day there were boys lying dead in the street who had only come out to look. People said that some of the dead were taken away in wagons that night and buried in a pit south of the city so nobody could count them. Nobody could say if it was true. In that week nobody could say what was true about anything. Václav's father went to the morgue three times. His mother went to every police station on the West Side with his photograph in her purse, and the sergeants looked at it and shook their heads. A lumber shover swore he had seen young Soukup at the viaduct on Wednesday, throwing stones, and seen him fall. It made a kind of sense. Tomáš said nothing aga

sections.heading: III. The Blue
sections.text: Somewhere in Iowa Matěj Kolář and his brother-in-law had a long conversation at the end of the car. She heard her name in it, or the name she had given them, which was Marie, because half the women in Bohemia were called Marie and nobody would ever ask which one. She heard Kratochvíl. She heard no wife. Josef Kratochvíl was thirty-four years old and owned the grain elevator at Wilber and a store under it on the main street and three quarter-sections of bottomland along the Big Blue, and he had no wife because the frontier did not have enough women in it to go around. Matěj Kolář had sold him oxen the spring before. When the emigrants got down at the Wilber platform with their feather beds, the old man walked straight up the street to the store and said to Josef, Pane Kratochvíl, we have brought you a jewel, and Josef came down and looked at her, at her height and her hands and her teeth, and she knew exactly what he was doing, because she had done it all her life. She had looked at Anna that way across the dance floor at the Sokol hall. She had looked at a stand of pine. He was not unkind. That was the thing she would always have to say for him, when she told it. He asked her, the

sections.heading: IV. The Window
sections.text: The town was building that year, stores and houses and a hall, and nearly every board of it came from the yards in Chicago. On a Tuesday in October a special freight came down the branch from Crete with thirty cars of lumber, and riding in the caboose was the man who had sold it, come out himself to see the country and collect his money. Marie was upstairs at the front window over the store, with Emil on her hip, and saw him get down from the caboose and stand on the platform in a good coat, looking around him at the elevator and the grain wagons and the main street with that same squint he had squinted at the Irish on DeKoven Street when he was nine years old. Tomáš Pech. He had got heavier. He had a mustache. She sent the hired girl down to the platform to say that Mrs. Kratochvíl invited the gentleman from Chicago to take coffee. He came up the outside stairs puzzled, with his hat in his hand. She had set out coffee and a plate of koláče in the parlor with the good cups, and she gave him the chair by the stove, and sat across from him with her hands in her lap, and he was very polite to her, the way he had always been polite to women. Madam, I never saw you before in my life, an

sections.heading: V. The Pardon
sections.text: Tomáš drove out to Turkey Creek himself the next morning in a hired rig and found Barbora Hájková in her brother's yard boiling sheets. He took off his hat and asked her to supper at the Kratochvíls' the following day. She looked at him with her forearms red from the kettle. You're the lumber man from Chicago. What do you want with me? Never mind what I want, madam. Come to supper. She came. Marie cooked for two days: roast goose and sauerkraut, bread dumplings, cucumbers in sour cream, a poppy-seed strudel, the plum preserves she had been saving since August. Josef put on his collar. The midwife sat at the head of the table, because Tomáš insisted on it, and ate like a woman who had been up two nights out of three for thirty years, which she had. When the plates were cleared Tomáš stood. He took Marie by the hand and brought her around the table, and she knelt down on the rag rug at the midwife's feet, in front of her husband and her boys, and put her forehead on the midwife's shoe. Paní Hájková, said Tomáš. Forgive my friend. What is this? Tomáš told her. He told it plainly, the way he would have told a man about a bad debt. Barbora Hájková sat for a long time with her big chappe

sections.heading: VI. The Buggy
sections.text: She did need one. She was past fifty and the county was filling up, Bohemians and Germans and Irish and Yankees, and there were nights in a hard winter when she went out to three births in a row and fell asleep on the horse. Václav drove her. He bought a black buggy with a lantern on a hook and learned every section line and creek crossing from Crete to the Kansas border, and when the knock came on the door on Turkey Creek at two in the morning he was hitching the mare before she had her boots on. At the houses he did not go in. That was the custom and he kept it. He sat outside in the buggy with the lantern turned low, all night sometimes, in July with the mosquitoes and in January with a buffalo robe and a hot brick, and watched the one lit window, and listened. The story had gone all over the county by the first Christmas. Bohemians are great talkers. The freethinkers at the lodge in Wilber, who did not believe in anything that could not be weighed, told it to each other over beer. People came out to Turkey Creek on Sundays to look at him. They found him in the yard mending harness and they stood at the fence and asked him straight out. Is it true? It's true. Two boys in Chicago

sections.heading: VII. The Lodge
sections.text: After that, when they came to the fence on Sundays and asked him, he said something else. Which two do you love more? I don't hold on to anybody, Václav said, and went on mending harness. It made the lodge men angry. They argued about it at the hall in Wilber on the second Sunday of the month, after the dues were paid, and some of them went out to Turkey Creek together on a Sunday in March to have it out. They found the midwife at the kitchen table shelling beans, and Václav in the yard. Paní Hájková, your driver is a liar. A year ago he said he loved the boys he bore. Now he says he loves nobody. A man can't say both. One of them is a lie. The midwife went on shelling beans. Then she wiped her hands on her apron. He isn't lying. He's changed again, that's all, and this time it didn't show. She looked at them, one after the other, farmers and a harness maker and the county treasurer's clerk, every one of whom she had either delivered or delivered the children of. I've been at nine hundred births, gentlemen, and I'll tell you a thing. A mother can do a great deal for a child. A father can do some. Uncles and grandmothers. But there's nothing any of them can do for him that he can't

title: The Midwife's Driver
logline: A rich Czech son in Chicago looks at a midwife washing in the river the way he looks at everything, and his body changes.

verses.text: Who shall overcome this earth, and the world of Yama (the lord of the departed), and the world of the gods? Who shall find out the plainly shown path of virtue, as a clever man finds out the (right) flower?
The disciple will overcome the earth, and the world of Yama, and the world of the gods. The disciple will find out the plainly shown path of virtue, as a clever man finds out the (right) flower.

bg.commentary: Five hundred monks come back to Jetavana from a journey through the countryside with the Buddha and sit in the hall talking about the ground they walked over: even and uneven, muddy, gravelly, black clay, red clay. The Buddha asks what they are discussing, tells them that this is the outer soil and that they must clear the soil within, and speaks the two verses, which turn on the double sense of "earth" and on the garland-maker who knows which flower to pick. All five hundred are said to have reached awakening as he finished. Read the full commentary story. The teacher's book is Heaven and Hell (1758) by Emanuel Swedenborg, a work "from things heard and seen" in which earth, heaven and hell answer one another by correspondence; it is quoted here in John C. Ager's translation.
bg.history:
The eruption of Tambora in April 1815 brought the Year Without a Summer to New England. Frost killed crops on the high ground in May 1816; snow fell across the region on June 6 to 8; killing frosts came again in August. The historian L. D. Stillwell estimated that Vermont lost ten to fifteen thousand people to emigration in 1816 and 1817, many of them bound for western New York and Ohio. The New England hill farms they left were notorious for stones: frost heaving lifts glacial cobbles to the surface every spring, and the miles of stone walls in Vermont were built largely from what farmers picked off their fields.

The northern route west ran up the Mohawk, out the Genesee Road through the lands of the Holland Land Company at Batavia, through Buffalo (burned by the British in December 1813), and along the lake shore into the Connecticut Western Reserve, sold by Connecticut to the Connecticut Land Company in 1796. Title west of the Cuyahoga, where this story's fictional township lies, was taken from the Wyandot, Ottawa and other nations at the Treaty of Fort Industry in 1805. Whole New England congregations often moved and settled together, laying out a new town by lot.

sections.heading: I. Stony Loam
sections.dateline: Lyme Hollow, Windsor County, Vermont · June 1816 to May 1817
sections.text: No. 1. Our own. A brown loam on a hard pan, thin on the hills, better in the hollow. Full of stones of every size from a hen's egg to a cart. The stones come up anew every spring with the frost and must be picked, and are laid in walls. No man living has seen the bottom of them. — A. Pettengill, clerk It snowed on the seventh and eighth of June. Asa Pettengill was nineteen and kept the district school, and he walked out on the morning of the eighth to see the corn, and the corn was lying flat and black in rows, and the snow lay in the furrows between, and the birds that had come north for the summer were sitting on the stone walls with their feathers puffed out, and some of them were dead in the grass. Frost again in July. Frost on the twenty-first of August that took the beans. By September the town was eating its seed. That winter the men met in the meetinghouse, which had no stove, and agreed to go. Thirty-one families. They would sell what they could and go together to a township in the Connecticut Reserve that a man from Bennington had for sale, all of it, and lay it out in lots by drawing, and build a meetinghouse first. They would take their minister if he would come. He wou

sections.heading: II. Flats
sections.dateline: The Mohawk below Little Falls, New York · June 1817
sections.text: No. 9. The German Flats. A black mould of the river, deep, without one stone in it that I could find, though Capt. Lamb walked into a field to look and was spoke to sharply in Dutch. Grass to a man's belt. Wheat very good. The Dutchmen here have been on it a hundred years and say the river gives it back every spring. That was the first time the men talked soil at night. They had been talking about it all day walking, but that night at the fire they talked about nothing else, and after that it was every night. The flats were a wonder to them. Captain Lamb held up a fist of that black ground and let it go through his fingers, and nothing stayed in his palm, not a pebble, and some of the men laughed out loud. The widow did not get down from the wagon. She sat on the tailboard with her feet hanging and her book shut on her knee, and she looked at the river.

sections.heading: III. Openings
sections.dateline: The Genesee Road, beyond Canandaigua · June 1817
sections.text: No. 14. Oak openings. A light sand or gravel, the trees standing apart like an orchard, and grass between. Easy to break, they say, and easy to lose. The Holland Company's men at Batavia say it will bear wheat. Deacon W. says sand is sand. No. 15. The same, wetter. Even and uneven. Every wagon on the Genesee Road was going the same way. They passed Vermonters and New Hampshire men and a whole congregation from Connecticut with its minister riding in front on a white mare, and every one of them was talking soil. At the taverns in the evening the men stood in the yard with their hats on the backs of their heads and argued gravel and sand and clay and muck. A man from Rutland said there was land in the Indiana country where you could push a ramrod in to the thimble. A man from Pittsfield said the Reserve was all clay and the clay held water like a pan and the water bred the fever. The deacon said there was no land on earth without a fault in it, and looked at the captain when he said it. Asa wrote it all down. In the back of the book he began a list of the things people told him, which ran to four pages and contradicted itself on every one.

sections.heading: IV. Mud
sections.dateline: The lake road, Buffalo to the Pennsylvania line · late June 1817
sections.text: No. 22. Black ash swamp. Mud. No. 23. Mud. No. 24. A red clay like the inside of a brick, then mud. Lost the Wetherbees' near ox in it to the belly. Got him out. Six days from Buffalo, which the British burnt in the war. The road along the lake was a cut through the woods with the stumps left in it, and where it was not stumps it was mud, and where it was not mud it was sand that the wheels went into to the felloes. When the deacon's ox went down in the red clay at a creek east of Erie, the men of the company hauled him out with chains, and the captain put his shoulder under the yoke with the rest, and nobody said anything about it afterward, and it seemed to Asa that the two men had been given something to talk about that was not the wall, and that neither of them would take it. It rained eleven days of the fourteen. The widow was wet through, and her book was wrapped in an oilcloth inside her dress, and she did not complain once that anybody heard. The children walked beside her wagon because she would tell them things. She told them that every bird that sang had a reason, and that the angels in heaven wove crowns of flowers for children who had died small, and that her own four

sections.heading: V. Black Clay and Red
sections.dateline: The township, on the east branch of the Black River · July 1817
sections.text: No. 31. Our own again. A stiff yellow clay under beech and maple, very heavy, with a black mould on top of it about four inches deep where the leaves have lain. In the swales a black clay that will stick a boot. On the ridge toward the river a red clay with gravel in it. Abounds in mud at present. NOT ONE STONE. He wrote the last three words in capitals and underlined them twice, and that is how they are in the book. The tract had been signed away at Fort Industry twelve years before by the Wyandot and the Ottawa and the others who had used it, and in the beech woods there were still the bark frames of hunting camps falling in, and along the river old cornhills under the grass that nobody in the company could account for. Asa wrote them down too, and did not know under what heading. They drew lots on the second Sunday, out of the deacon's hat. The deacon drew the lot on the river and the captain drew the lot beside it, and the company stood in the clearing and heard it and was still. Somebody laughed. Then the captain walked to the line between the two lots, where the surveyor's blaze was on a beech, and stood there, and then he got down on his knees and began to dig at the clay wi

sections.heading: VI. The Inner Soil
sections.dateline: Captain Lamb's cabin, the first Sabbath evening in August 1817
sections.text: No. 32. This entry is not a soil. I set it down because I was asked to. The first roof in the township was the captain's, so the company met under it. It had no floor yet. They sat on the sills and on blocks of beech and on the ground, the men on one side and the women on the other, and the children in the door, and they read the psalm and prayed, the deacon praying, since there was no minister. When the prayer was done nobody went home. It was hot and the mosquitoes were bad and outside it was raining again on the clay. The men began to talk. They talked about the yellow clay and whether it would drain if you ditched it. They talked about the black clay in the swales and whether that was where the fever came from. They talked about the red clay on the ridge and the gravel in it. They talked about the flats on the Mohawk and the openings on the Genesee and the man from Rutland and his ramrod. They talked about even land and uneven, and land that abounded in mud, and land that abounded in gravel, and Asa, who had the book open on his knee because they kept asking him what number this was and what number that, saw that they were reading the whole road back to one another from the beg

title: The Stone Crop
logline: After the summer that never came, a Vermont company walks to Ohio arguing soils, carrying an old widow and a book about heaven.

verses.text: He who knows that this body is like froth, and has learnt that it is as unsubstantial as a mirage, will break the flower-pointed arrow of Mara, and never see the king of death.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest in the collection. A monk takes a meditation subject from the Buddha and goes into the forest, strives hard, and gets nowhere. He sets out to ask for a subject that suits him better. On the road he sees a mirage and takes that as his subject; then, tired, he bathes in the river Aciravatī and sits by a waterfall watching bubbles of foam form and burst, and takes that. The Buddha, seated far away in his Perfumed Chamber, sees him and says, “It is even so,” and speaks the verse, and the monk is freed where he sits. Read the full commentary story. The same pair of images, foam and mirage, stands side by side in the Qur’an, in the two verses the schoolmaster recites.
bg.history:
The National Training Center at Fort Irwin covers about a thousand square miles of the Mojave Desert north of Barstow, California. Visiting brigades fight a resident opposing force there, and laser sensors (the MILES system) register who has been hit. During the Iraq war the Army built a dozen or so mock Iraqi towns in “the Box,” first from garden sheds, then from shipping containers, later from masonry; the Army’s own account of one such village dates from 2008. Contractors bused in Iraqi Americans, many from the San Diego area, to live in the towns during each rotation and play mayors, police, shopkeepers and mourners, alongside amputee actors fitted with simulated wounds. The 2008 documentary Full Battle Rattle was filmed in the best known of these towns, Medina Wasl. Medina Nahr and everyone in it are invented. “Notional” is the Army’s ordinary word for anything simulated in an exercise, and the observer-controllers’ handheld device for killing and resetting a soldier’s sensor harness really is called the god gun.

After the 1991 Gulf War, Shia in southern Iraq rose against Saddam Hussein’s government; the uprisings were crushed within weeks, and tens of thousands fled across the Saudi border. Saudi Arabia held them in a closed desert camp near Rafha, under guard and curfew, for more than a decade. Roughly half of those who were resettled abroad from Rafha went to the United States before the American program ended in 1997, according to the U.S. Committee for Refugees; communities grew in Dearborn, San Diego, Lincoln, Nebraska, and elsewhere. Twelver Shia commonly pray with the forehead resting on earth or a small tablet of clay from Karbala, and count remembrance on clay beads. From California the direction of Mecca is northeast, over the Arctic.

sections.heading: I. The Lane
sections.dateline: Medina Nahr, Fort Irwin, California · July 2008
sections.text: Medina Nahr means River Town, and there has never been a river within sixty miles of it. The Army built it in the Mojave Desert out of shipping containers faced with plaster the color of dust: a police station, a clinic, a hotel with no beds, a row of shops, a mosque with a plywood minaret and a loudspeaker that worked. For two weeks out of every month it had people. They came up from San Diego and El Cajon on a contractor’s bus, Iraqis nearly all of them, and each was handed a card with a name that was not his name, and a trade, and a tribe, and an opinion of the Americans. They slept in trailers behind the false fronts and were the town’s butcher and its mayor and its widows until the bus took them home. The Army had a word for all of it. The word was notional. It meant a thing that existed for the purposes of the exercise. There was notional water in the water tower and a notional sheikh in the big house, and by the end of any afternoon there were notional dead in the street, who lay where they fell until a horn blew. Specialist Hayder Jassim was a medic in an infantry company that had come out from Kansas to be taught, in three weeks, the country where he had been born. His nam

sections.heading: II. Twelve Nights
sections.text: The company went out into the desert the next morning and did not see a building for twelve days. The Box is a thousand square miles of gravel and creosote bush with brown mountains standing up out of it like the backs of animals, and a regiment lives there whose only work is to be the enemy. They came at dawn out of the sun and at dusk out of the dust. By the fourth day half the battalion had been killed twice and brought back by the god gun so it could be killed again. At night, when the aid station was quiet, Hayder walked out past the last vehicle to where nobody was. He found a flat stone. He stood and faced a little east of north, because from California the shortest way to Mecca goes up over the top of the world, and he said the night prayer as his mother said it, with his forehead on the stone, since he had no tablet of clay to put it on. Then he sat down on his heels and took out the beads. He did it the way he did everything the Army had taught him, which was hard. The first night he went around the string once and his mind went around the Box eleven times. The second night he went around five times. By the sixth night he was doing three thousand breaths between midnight

sections.heading: III. The Lake
sections.dateline: The dry lake · the thirteenth day, 1300 hours
sections.text: The order came at breakfast. The last fight of the rotation would be for Medina Nahr, and the company would go in on foot, nine kilometers across the dry lake, because the vehicles had been notionally destroyed the day before and nobody had the authority to bring a vehicle back. A dry lake is the flattest thing there is. The water that made it has been gone some thousands of years, and it left a floor of pale clay cracked into plates the size of dinner trays, level to the horizon, without a stone on it. They stepped off at noon. It was a hundred and nine degrees. Each man had six quarts of water on him and drank on the hour whether he wanted to or not. Around one o’clock the lake filled. It came in from the west, quietly, a long bright sheet of it, blue and then silver, with a clean shore. Medina Nahr rose out of the far side. The minaret stood up white, and under it a second minaret hung down into the water, and the hotel with no beds floated a little off the ground with daylight under it. There were palm trees. There are no palm trees at Medina Nahr. Well, look at that, somebody said behind him. River Town got its river. They all knew what it was. They walked toward it anyway, si

sections.heading: IV. The Wash
sections.text: In July the clouds build over those mountains every afternoon, and most afternoons that is all they do. This time they went black on the bottom, and a gray curtain came down on the high ground to the south and stood there for twenty minutes. No rain fell on the company. They smelled it, wet dust and creosote, which is the best smell in that country. Past the edge of the lake bed there was a wash to cross, a gully of sand and round stones ten meters wide that had been dry since anybody’s map was drawn. They heard it before they got there. It was running bank to bank, brown as cocoa and louder than a truck, with whole bushes going by in it. The captain looked at it. The controllers looked at it and got on their radios, and the word came down the line that the war was paused for safety, that the water was real, and that anybody who went in it would answer to the sergeant major. The company sat down along the bank in its harnesses and waited for the desert to finish. Hayder went down to the edge. A little upstream a shelf of rock ran across the wash, and the flood came over it and fell about the height of a man’s knee. He took off his gloves and his helmet. He washed his face in the br

sections.heading: V. The Tea Stall
sections.text: Four kilometers west the town was being set for its last battle. Men from the contractor were burying charges in the market. The mayor was going over his lines. A young woman from El Cajon named Nadia, who played a widow and had done it for nine rotations, was pinning her scarf in the side mirror of a notional taxi beside the tea stall, and she told the rest of this afterward to anybody who asked and several who did not. The stall was a plywood counter and an awning. The old man kept a kettle on a propane ring there and a jar of cardamom pods with the lid off, and you could smell it the length of the street. He was sitting on his crate with his hands on his knees. Nadia said he lifted his head and looked east over the roofs, toward where the sky was dark, the way you look across a road at somebody you know. Then he spoke, loudly, in the voice he must have used on four hundred boys. Hajji, she said, who are you talking to? A student, he said. He poured a glass of tea, set it on the counter, and left it there. At the wash Hayder heard it at his right shoulder. It was plain and close over the noise of the water, and it was in the Arabic of Suq al-Shuyukh. Yes, my son. That is it. Like

sections.heading: VI. Endex
sections.text: They came into the town at sundown, and it went the way those things go. There were mortar simulators and a machine gun on the hotel roof, and a second car in the market, bigger than the first. Every harness in second platoon began to scream at once. Hayder’s did not. He noticed this and put it aside, because the man with one leg was down by the fruit stall again in the same place, pumping syrup and calling for his mother. The tourniquet went on in the time it takes to say so. Hayder’s hands did it and he watched them do it. He told the man in Arabic that he had him, and then, since the man was from Lakeside and had lost the leg on a motorcycle, he told him again in English, and the man stopped screaming for a second and looked up at him with interest. Hayder marked the time on the man’s forehead with a grease pencil and went on to the next one, and the one after. He was not calm the way you are calm when you are holding something down. There was nothing to hold down. He knelt in the syrup among the screaming harnesses and it was a street and some people and what his hands knew. Sergeant First Class Dunn came through with his clipboard and stopped. He looked at Hayder’s harness, wh

title: Notional Water
logline: An Iraqi-born Army medic training in a fake Iraqi town in the Mojave takes clay prayer beads from the old refugee who plays its tea seller.

verses.text: Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.

bg.commentary: The commentary tells how King Pasenadi of Kosala, wanting the trust of the Buddha’s monks, asks the Buddha’s own clan, the proud Sākyans, for a bride. They send him the daughter of a Sākyan noble and a slave woman, and the noble pretends to eat from one dish with her. Her son Viḍūḍabha, visiting his mother’s kin at sixteen, learns the truth when a slave washes the seat he sat on with milk and water, and vows to wash it in their blood. Woven through are the stories of Pasenadi’s schoolfriends, the blind teacher Mahāli and the general Bandhula, whom Pasenadi has murdered with his thirty-two sons, and of Bandhula’s widow Mallikā, who goes on serving the monks after reading the news. When Pasenadi is deposed and dies outside a shut city gate, Viḍūḍabha marches on the Sākyans. Three times the Buddha sits in his path in the thin shade of a tree; the fourth time he does not, knowing the Sākyans once poisoned a river. The Sākyans, who will neither kill nor lie, are massacred, except some who hold up grass or reeds, and the Sākyan Mahānāma, who drowns himself rather than eat with his grandson and is carried off by a serpent king. That night ants drive the army down into a dry riverbed, and a flood carries them all to the sea.
bg.history:
In January 1915 a manifesto called the Plan of San Diego called for an uprising in South Texas and the killing of white men over sixteen. Raids began that summer and peaked in August and September, with attacks on ranches and trains and telegraph lines, and about twenty-one Americans were killed. The reprisals were far worse. Texas Rangers, local lawmen and vigilantes killed Mexican Americans and Mexicans across the border country, sometimes leaving the bodies where they fell as a warning. Estimates of the dead in the decade run from three hundred to five thousand. Mexicans called the Rangers los diablos tejanos, and the years are remembered as La Matanza, the massacre; in 1919 State Representative José Tomás Canales brought about a legislative investigation of the Rangers.

Many Tejano families on the river traced their land to the porciones that a Spanish royal commission began surveying in 1767 at Laredo, Mier, Camargo, Revilla and Reynosa. Healers like Doña Natividad were part of daily life in the region; the most famous, Don Pedrito Jaramillo, “the healer of Los Olmos Creek,” treated thousands until his death in 1907 (see curanderismo). Esperanza, Rancho Santa Rita, Arroyo Prieto and every character here are invented, and so are the massacre at Santa Rita and the flood; no Ranger company was ever lost that way. The violence they stand for was real.

sections.heading: I. The Cane
sections.text: Three boys met on the steps of the Brothers’ school in San Antonio the autumn it opened, and asked each other where they were from and who their people were, and by Christmas they were friends. Ambrose Rourke was from Tennessee by way of the war with Mexico, which had brought his father to Texas and killed him there. Tomás Leal was from Laredo. Sixto Benavides was from Laredo too, from the other end of it, and could already ride anything with hair on it. They learned their Latin and their surveying and their sums together, and when they were finished they shook hands at the stage office and went home. Ambrose Rourke went down to the river country and read law and surveyed land, and the land he surveyed had a way of becoming his, and by thirty he was the county judge at Esperanza and by forty there was nothing in that county that moved without his knowing. Tomás Leal opened a school for the sons of the good families of Laredo and worked over his books by lamplight until his eyes failed him. The families said they would not turn their teacher out for that, and they gave him the toll from the river ferry for his living, and he sat by the landing all the rest of his life in a cane chai

sections.heading: II. The Plate
sections.text: In those years Doña Natividad Romero lived in a jacal of mesquite pickets on the river road with her nephew Chencho, and the sick came to her from both sides of the river. She was a cousin of the Romeros of Rancho Santa Rita, who had held their land along the Rio Grande since the King of Spain’s surveyors set their stone in 1767, and who did not let anybody forget it. She had left that house young and never gone back to live in it. She set bones, she prayed over fevers, she knew every plant in the brush, and she said very little. The women who learned from her went out every morning, two by two, to the ranches where they were wanted. Judge Rourke watched them go by his gallery. They went to the Peñas, the Ramírezes, the Garzas, never to him. He sent word that the señoras were welcome at his table any day of the week, and for a week they came, and he served them himself, and on the eighth day he had business at the courthouse and forgot them. Nobody else in that house would set a chair for them without being told. The next day he forgot them again, and the next, and by the end of the week the only one who still came was Chencho, who sat alone at the long table and ate what was put i

sections.heading: III. The Chair
sections.text: She had a son the next year. When the Judge sent old Pruitt, his foreman, to ask his own mother what the boy ought to be called, the old lady said, She’d already won every heart in this county before the baby came. Now she’ll be his darling past all reason. But Pruitt had been deaf on one side since a cannon at Glorieta, and he rode back and told the Judge she said to call him Dalton. The Judge supposed it was a name on his mother’s side. So the boy was Dalton Rourke. When he was six his father had a little tin star made for him and called him the captain of the county, and everyone laughed, and Dalton wore it on his shirt to Mass. When he was seven he asked his mother why the other boys got ponies and saddles from their grandfathers at Christmas and nobody ever sent him anything. She told him his grandfather lived a long way off down the river and was a great man and very busy. When he was sixteen he said he was going down to Santa Rita to see his mother’s people for himself, and she said no, what would he do there, and he asked again, and again, until she said yes. She wrote ahead. I am happy here. I beg my lords to receive my son as they would any of their own. The Romeros read

sections.heading: IV. Thirty-Two Sons
sections.text: Sixto Benavides’s wife Amalia had no children for years, and in the end he told her to go back to her family in Laredo. She stopped at the jacal on her way. Where are you going? said Doña Natividad. Home, because I’ve given him no sons. That’s no reason. Go back to your husband. She went back, and Sixto said, Why are you here? and she said, Doña Natividad sent me, and he thought about it and said, Then she has some reason, and let it be. Within the year Amalia was carrying, and she had a craving. In Laredo the rich families kept a bathing tank behind a wall, fed from a spring, with a wire fence over the top of the wall and a man with a shotgun at the gate, and she wanted to go down into it and swim and drink the water. So Sixto drove her to Laredo in his buggy, in by the ferry road past the cane chair where Tomás Leal sat. The blind man heard the wheels and said to the boys around him, That’s Benavides’s buggy. There’ll be trouble for somebody today. Sixto knocked down the man at the gate, pulled down the wire with his hands, and Amalia swam and drank, and he swam too, and they drove home. The rich young men of Laredo came after them on horseback, fifty or a hundred of them, though

sections.heading: V. The Shade
sections.text: The Judge made Sixto’s nephew Lucio his chief deputy after that, and Lucio went about the county telling anyone who would listen that the Judge had killed his uncle. The Judge had no peace after Arroyo Prieto. He ate without tasting it. Running the county was no pleasure to him anymore. In the summer of 1915 there was blood on the river again. Raiders from across the river were firing on trains and cutting the telegraph wires under a plan that said every Anglo man over sixteen in Texas should die, and the Rangers came down from Austin, and men who looked Mexican began to be found dead in the brush. The Judge was eighty years old. Doña Natividad was eighty years old. He drove out to the jacal to see her one evening, and left his car and his pistol and the courthouse keys and the county ledger and the seal with Lucio at the gate, and went in alone, and they sat and talked a long time like two old people. When he came out the car was gone. Lucio had left him one horse and Cata the cook. She told him: Lucio had driven to the courthouse and handed the keys and the ledger and the seal to Dalton Rourke, and the commissioners, who knew which way the wind was blowing, had made Dalton sherif

sections.heading: VI. Zacate y Carrizo
sections.text: The Romeros had a rule older than the ranch, that a Romero did not take a human life, and they were proud of it the way they were proud of everything. But they were the best shots on that river. When they saw the dust of the company coming they put on their cartridge belts and went out among the corrals and the mesquite and opened fire. They shot the hats off the Rangers’ heads. They shot the horns off saddles and the heels off boots. They put bullets between men’s arms and their ribs, and through the brims of their hats, and past their ears close enough to burn. Dalton turned in his saddle, looking around. I was always told the Romeros didn’t kill. They’re killing my men. Sheriff, said the Ranger sergeant beside him, nobody’s dead. Count them. He had them counted. Not one man was so much as scratched. Then he gave his order. Anybody who says he’s a Romero, kill him. Anybody who’s standing with Don Mariano, leave him alone. The Romeros had run out of ways to hold the Rangers off without killing anybody, and they would not do that. And they had one rule older than the other one, which was that a Romero did not lie. So as the Rangers came through the corrals asking each man, Romero?

sections.heading: VII. The River
sections.text: He took his grandfather with him when he rode out. Don Mariano was ninety and rode straight. At noon they stopped at the river below Santa Rita and the cook got a fire going, and Dalton had a table and two chairs set up in the shade of the cane and a plate brought. I’ll eat with my grandfather, he said. Sit down, abuelo. Don Mariano had sat at one plate with Pilar’s daughter once, for the length of one lifted fork, and he had lived thirty-six years since then on the strength of never doing it again. He looked at the plate and at the river. Grandson, I’m filthy from the road. Let me wash first. Go and wash, abuelo. He thought: if I don’t sit, he’ll shoot me, and if I sit, I’ve sat. Better to go by my own hand. So he went down to the water through the cane, and took off his boots, and tied his long white hair round his ankles with the cord from his hat, and threw himself into the river. The vaqueros of that river will tell you what happened next, and so will their grandchildren.
