A water snake as long as a wagon tongue came up from the bottom of the Rio Grande where the current runs green, and took the old man up on its back, and carried him across to the Mexican side and down into th

sections.heading: VIII. The Arroyo
sections.text: They came to Arroyo Prieto after dark and made camp. It had not rained in that country in two months. The arroyo bed was a road of white sand, smooth and soft and still warm from the day, and some of the men spread their blankets down there. Others threw their saddles down on the hard ground of the banks above. Among the ones who went down into the sand were the few who had held back at Santa Rita, who had kept their rifles on their saddles and said nothing and been cursed for it. Most of the ones who had not held back lay on the banks. Then the red ants came up out of the ground. Big red harvesters, the kind whose bite feels like a coal, boiling up out of their beds wherever a man had lain down, on the banks and in the sand alike. Men leaped up all over the camp in the dark, cursing and slapping. Ants! Ants, God damn it! And they changed places. The ones in the sand climbed up onto the banks, and the ones on the banks went down into the sand, Dalton with them, and spread their blankets again, and slept. Far up the country to the north, where nobody in that camp could see it, a storm that had come in off the Gulf was standing over the hills and raining as if it would never stop. Th

title: Thin Shade
logline: A proud ranching family scrubs the chair a judge's son sat in, and an old curandera sits in the road.

verses.text: Death subdues a man who is gathering flowers, and whose mind is distracted, before he is satiated in his pleasures.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a goddess of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is up a tree in a pleasure garden, throwing down flowers to deck her husband, the god Mālābhārī (“Garland-Wearer”), when she dies out of that world like a lamp flame and is born a girl in Sāvatthī, remembering him. She grows up, marries at sixteen, bears four sons, keeps the monks’ hall, sets out water and seats, and with every offering prays to be reborn with her husband, so the monks call her Patipūjikā, “Husband-Honorer,” assuming she means the husband she has. One day she gives alms, hears the teaching, keeps the precepts, and dies that evening. In heaven no time has passed, for a hundred human years are one day and night there, and her divine husband is shaken to hear how short and careless human lives are. The next morning the monks find the hall untended and weep; the Buddha tells them she has gone back to her true husband, and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Hawaiian men, called Kanakas, worked for the Hudson’s Bay Company all over the Pacific Northwest in the first half of the nineteenth century, and many married First Nations women and stayed (Kanaka workers). Hawaiians were among the crew that came up from Fort Vancouver in 1827 to build Fort Langley on the Fraser. After the Company lost its trading monopoly in 1858 and the townsite of Derby was laid out at the old fort, a number of its Hawaiian employees crossed the river with their Kwantlen wives and took up land along a stream that came to be called Kanaka Creek, in what is now Maple Ridge. They farmed and fished; the community was always small (the 1881 census counted nineteen people of Hawaiian descent there) and lasted thirty or forty years, the last house gone by 1912 (Maple Ridge Museum). The nearest priests were the Oblates of St. Mary’s Mission upriver, founded in 1861; the chapel in the story is invented.

From the 1880s the Victoria fleet of pelagic sealing schooners, at its height over a hundred vessels, followed the northern fur seal herd from the coast up to the Bering Sea and the Pribilof Islands, carrying Indigenous hunters in canoes and mixed crews of every origin. The hunt ended with the North Pacific Fur Seal Convention of 1911.

sections.heading: I. The Tree
sections.dateline: Kanaka Creek, on the Fraser River · spring 1874
sections.text: Peter Kauwila's girl did not talk until she was nearly three, and then one evening in the kitchen she said a whole thing at once, as if she had been saving it. I was up in the tree throwing flowers down for my husband, she said, and then I was here. Her mother was a Kwantlen woman from up the river, and she was cleaning a pail of eulachon at the table, and she stopped. Peter laughed. He had been laughing at that child since the day she came, because she had come in the middle of May with the wild roses out on every bank down to the water, and he had named her Lokelani, which is a rose in the language he still dreamed in, and the Oblate father from St. Mary's had written it down as Rosalie. What tree? he said. She could not say what tree. A big one, in a garden, with flowers on it all the way up, and a great many girls in it, more than she could count, some up in the branches throwing and some down on the grass picking up what fell and fastening it on him. On the man. Her husband. He was sitting in the middle and they were dressing him in flowers. Peter had come out to Fort Vancouver on a Company ship in 1845 and had not seen Oʻahu since. He knew what she was describing, or thought

sections.heading: II. Henry's Rosie
sections.text: But she made garlands. Every child on the creek could string a lei, because their fathers were homesick and showed them how, but Rosalie strung them the way other girls breathe. Nootka rose in May and June, the little pink single ones that drop their petals if you look at them, so she picked them in bud at dawn and strung them wet. Ocean spray in July, the creamy heads that look like foam on the bank. Honeysuckle off the fences, and wild syringa. In August pearly everlasting, which dried on the stem and kept its shape all winter. In winter, when there was nothing, cedar tips and salal and the red berries of the kinnikinnick. She hung them on the posts of the porch, on the cow, on her small brothers, and when the chapel was finished at the mouth of the creek she began to hang them there. It was a plank chapel, not much bigger than a smokehouse, and they called it St. Paul’s. The Hawaiian men had built it with their Kwantlen in-laws out of cedar they split themselves, on a rise above the high-water line where the creek came into the Fraser, so that it stood looking across the river at Derby, where the old fort had been. A bell came up from New Westminster on the sternwheeler one year

sections.heading: III. The Lamp
sections.text: Father came over on the Saturday that month, a young Fleming named Father Cyriel who had been in the country two years and still blessed himself every time the boat heeled. Rosalie had been up since four. She had walked to the church in the dark with the two older boys carrying the benches between them, and swept, and filled the bucket at the creek, and set the dipper on its nail. She had hung St. Paul with pearly everlasting and the last of the fireweed. At Mass she knelt at the end of the second pew with the four boys in a row beside her, the youngest asleep against her arm, and she went up to the rail and received, and came back, and listened to the whole of the sermon, which was in an English the young priest was still building as he went along, and was about the ten virgins and their lamps. Afterward she fed him at the table behind the altar. Salmon, new potatoes, a plate of blackberries, coffee. Three families had sent food that day and she had set it all out and named each family to him as he ate, so he would know whom to thank. Then she washed the plates in the bucket and swept again where the boys had tracked in the dust, and walked home with them along the shore in the lo

sections.heading: IV. The Dipper
sections.text: Father Cyriel had stayed the night on the creek so he could say a Mass on the Monday morning for the people who had come too late on the Sunday, and he walked up to the church at seven with three or four of the men. The door was shut. Inside, the benches were stacked against the wall where the boys had left them, and the floor had the boys' tracks on it, and the bucket by the door was empty and dry, with the dipper hanging over it on its nail. He stood and looked at it. In two years he had never once come into that church and found the bucket empty. Where is Henry's? he said, the way everyone said it. One of the men had already heard. He took off his hat. Father, you won't see her. Last night, after you ate and she went home, she died. The young priest sat down on the end of a bench. He had eaten her salmon not eighteen hours before and she had told him which family had caught it. He put his face in his hands and wept the way a young man does when he has not yet buried many people he knew, and the men stood around him not knowing where to look. Two of them wept as well. The older ones did not. They stood very still, the way you stand on a schooner deck when the glass has dropped an

sections.heading: V. Rose Hips
sections.text: They buried her on the Wednesday in the ground beside the church, among the Hawaiians and their Kwantlen wives and the babies, and Father Cyriel read over her the place in Wisdom about the just man taken young. Being made perfect in a short space, he fulfilled a long time. — Wisdom 4:13 Henry came home in the middle of October. The schooner had put into Victoria on the ninth, and he had heard it on the wharf there from a man off another boat, and come up the river on the sternwheeler with his money still sewn in his coat. He walked from the landing to the church before he went to his own house, and found the bucket full inside the door and the floor swept. Kaʻai had done it every Saturday since. The old man could carry the bucket only half full now and had to rest twice on the way up from the creek, but it was done. Henry did not go into the church. He went around to the side, to the new grave, where his eldest boy Joe was kneeling in the wet grass. It was too late in the year for any flowers. title: Since Morning
logline: On the Fraser, a Hawaiian sealer's wife keeps a plank chapel, praying with every offering to get back to her husband.

verses.text: As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Kosiya is a rich man of the town of Sakkhara (“Jaggery,” raw sugar) who never gives away so much as a drop of oil. Seeing a hungry countryman eat a filled cake, he craves one, hides the craving for fear of having to share, and finally has his wife cook for him alone at the top of his seven-storied house behind bolted doors. The Buddha sends the elder Mahā Moggallāna, who stands in the air outside the window, walks, sits, and pours out smoke as the miser dares him to. The cakes swell and stick together; the miser sweats his craving away, gives up the whole basket, and is carried with his wife down his own staircase to the Jetavana monastery, where the cakes feed five hundred monks and never run out. The leftovers are thrown down by the gate at a place afterward called Fried Cake Mountain. The verse is the Buddha’s praise of Moggallāna, who won the household without harming its faith or its wealth. An attached birth story tells of the miser Illīsa, who broke seven generations of family generosity until his dead father came back wearing his face.
bg.history:
On August 7, 2019, immigration agents raided seven chicken processing plants in six central Mississippi towns, among them Morton, Forest, Carthage and Canton, and arrested 680 workers. It was the largest workplace raid in a single state in American history, and it fell on the first day of school. About three hundred people were released within a day, many of them parents of small children, some wearing GPS ankle monitors; hundreds more were sent to detention centers in Louisiana. The plants had been recruiting Latin American workers for decades, and many of those arrested were Maya from Guatemala’s western highlands, the departments of San Marcos and Huehuetenango, where Mam is spoken. With paychecks gone overnight, parish halls and mission churches became kitchens, food pantries and legal clinics for months; see reporting in The Intercept and Mississippi Catholic. Ribbon Cane, the mission, and every person in the story are invented.

In highland Maya towns the patron saint’s festival was traditionally paid for by householders who took the burden in turn, a round of offices known as the cargo system; a man who carried it fed the town and could be left in debt for years. Lay catechists and Delegates of the Word have led rural Central American congregations where priests are scarce since the 1960s, and many were killed or driven out in Guatemala in the early 1980s. Catarina’s book is the Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) of St. Francis de Sales, bishop of Geneva, long read in Spanish as the Filotea; the line about the bee is quoted from the nineteenth-century English translation in the Christian Classics Ethereal Library. A tayuyo is a Guatemalan corn cake stuffed with black beans. Kudzu blooms in Mississippi in late summer.

sections.heading: I. The Tayuyo
sections.text: Efraín Maldonado had come to Mississippi in 1996 on a bus the chicken company sent to Texas, and for four years he hung live birds by their feet on a moving line in the dark. Then he saw where the money was. The money was in everything around the chicken. He bought a van and charged eight dollars a day to ride in it. He bought a trailer and rented the beds in it by the shift. He cashed paychecks for three cents on the dollar and wired what was left to Guatemala for a fee. By 2019 he owned the old dime store on what remained of the main street in Ribbon Cane, a two-story brick building with a tienda downstairs and his family upstairs, and nine trailers on a lot behind the feed mill, and four vans, and people said he had a million dollars, and nobody had ever seen him give away a lime. He did not spend it on himself either. He wore the boots he had bought in 2004. His wife Marta cooked on a stove with two working burners. His money was like one of those stock ponds out in the pines with a cottonmouth living in it. The water is right there and nothing goes down to drink. sections.heading: II. Seven Doors
sections.text: The back storeroom was at the top of the building, under the roof, behind everything. To get there from the street a person went through the steel grille and then the glass door with the bell on it. Then there was the gate in the counter, and the stockroom door, and the door to the stairs. At the top of the stairs was the door of the apartment, and at the end of the hall the storeroom door itself, which had a hasp. That made seven. Marta went up first with the hot plate. At ten o’clock Efraín told the girls he had accounts to do and followed her, and he shut every door behind him. He turned the key in the ones that had keys and shot the bolt on the ones that had bolts. He hung the padlock in the hasp from the inside, where no hasp was ever meant to be locked from, and sat down on a case of lamp oil with his knees together. The room had one window, over the alley, two stories up, painted shut. There was a smoke detector on the ceiling with its cover hanging open. He had taken the battery out in 2011 to use in a flashlight. Marta set the comal on the hot plate and wet her hands and began to pat out the masa. Sixty miles north, off the same highway, there was a metal building that had

sections.heading: III. The Window
sections.text: Efraín looked up from the comal and there was a man standing outside the window. The window was twenty feet above the alley. There was no ledge under it and no ladder. The old man stood out there in the open air about a yard from the glass, in a clean white shirt buttoned to the neck, with his hat in his hands, and looked in with the mild face of somebody waiting to be noticed at a counter. Efraín’s heart went like a fish on a bank. He knew the old man. Everybody did. This is what I locked the doors against, he thought, and he comes to the one place there is no door. He was a man whose anger went off like salt thrown on a fire. He put his face to the glass and shouted through it. What do you think you’ll get, standing in the air? You can walk up and down out there till you wear a path, you’ll get nothing from me. Tat Lencho put his hat on, and walked up and down, the length of the building and back, over the alley and the dumpster. What do you think you’ll get by walking? You can sit down out there with your legs crossed, you’ll get nothing. The old man folded his legs under him and sat down on the air, a little stiffly, as he sat on the floor of the mission with the children. What

sections.text: Efraín took the padlock out of the hasp. He carried the cream and the cheese. Marta carried the basket in both arms with the honey jar riding on top, and Tat Lencho went ahead of them down the back stairs, which were steep and dark and smelled of onions. There were fourteen steps. Efraín had counted them every day for fifteen years. At the bottom was the door to the stockroom. The old man opened it, and the noise of five hundred people came through. They stepped out onto a concrete floor under fluorescent lights. There were folding tables end to end, and children asleep on coats along the wall, and a woman in a suit from Jackson with a laptop and a line of forty people in front of her. In the corner by the outlet a young woman in a plant sweatshirt sat on a folding chair with a cord running down to her ankle. She looked up at them as if they were on time. It’s the hour to eat, hermana, Efraín heard himself say. He had not planned to say anything. Catarina unplugged herself, wound the cord around her hand, and came to the head of the first table. People sat down wherever there was a chair, and where there was not they stood. Marta lifted the top tayuyo out of the basket. It came awa

sections.text: The next night, when the dishes were done, the people who had been there sat on the folding chairs and talked about it. Mostly they talked about Tat Lencho. Efraín Maldonado, they said. Of all people. And he never shamed him. He never asked him for a cent. He stood there with his hat in his hands, and the man still has his store and his name and his wife looking at him like a bride. He lost nothing by it. We have had preachers through here who could empty a house in a week, and the family hated God afterward. Tat Lencho was not there to hear it. He was out by the gate picking up paper plates. Catarina was in her corner with the cord in the wall. She had with her the one thing she owned that had come over the mountain, a small book with the cover gone, soft as cloth. It had been her grandfather’s. A Spanish priest had given it to him in 1975, when he was made a catechist. He had kept it buried in a lard tin through the bad years, and it still smelled a little of the lard. It was the book the bishop of Geneva wrote four hundred years ago for people who have to live in the world and work. What are you talking about? she asked. They told her. title: Seven Doors
logline: Two days after the chicken-plant raids, a Guatemalan landlord locks seven doors to eat one bean cake unseen, and an old man appears outside the window.

verses.text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a housewife of Sāvatthī keeps a naked ascetic named Pāṭhika, of the fatalist Ājīvika order, and looks after him like a son. When her neighbors praise the Buddha she asks leave to go and hear him, and Pāṭhika forbids it, so she sends her boy to invite the Buddha to her house instead. The ascetic coaches the boy to hide where the house is, meaning to eat the meal himself, but a Buddha needs no directions and comes straight to the door. Hearing her applaud the teaching, Pāṭhika bursts out of the back room, abuses them both and runs off. She is too shaken to listen, and the Buddha tells her to leave other people’s doings alone and look to her own.
bg.history:
In the autumn of 1942 the Army took some 59,000 acres of Anderson and Roane counties for the Clinton Engineer Works. More than a thousand families were living there, on farms and in hamlets such as Elza, Robertsville and Scarboro. Some came home to find the notice nailed to the door or to a tree; most were given six weeks to leave and some only two. Many of the people put off the land later took jobs inside the fence. The town built over their fields held 75,000 people by 1945. Workers who earned the least were assigned to hutments and to nearly four thousand trailers, which had no bathrooms; families used shared bathhouses and carried their water. One of the camps, Middletown, stood along the Oak Ridge Turnpike. Bathhouse Seven, its Thursday meeting, Aunt Docia and the Ledfords are invented.

At the Y-12 plant, Tennessee Eastman hired about ten thousand women, most of them just out of East Tennessee high schools, to run the calutrons that separated uranium-235. These cubicle operators were trained for three weeks and told nothing of the purpose. A manager is remembered as saying, “We can train you how to do what is needed, but cannot tell you what you are doing.” They sat on stools before tall boards and kept needles in place with lettered knobs. In a week-long production race against physicists from Berkeley, the women won; the physicists could not stop investigating every flicker of a dial. Most operators learned what they had made on August 6, 1945. The song Aunt Docia sings is an African American spiritual of unknown origin. It was recorded by the Elkins-Payne Jubilee Singers in 1923 and by a white West Virginia string band in 1927 (see the Traditional Ballad Index), and its words are given here as James Weldon Johnson and J. Rosamond Johnson printed them in The Book of American Negro Spirituals in 1925.

sections.heading: I. The Boy from Home
sections.dateline: Middletown trailer camp, Oak Ridge, Tennessee · October 1944
sections.text: Ina Ledford had a trailer in Row F of the Middletown camp, a husband on the pipe gangs at K-25, a boy of eleven, and a stool in front of a board at Y-12. Besides these she had Arvil Tallent. Arvil was twenty-three and came from Englewood, the same as the Ledfords. He had been called to preach at fifteen, in a brush arbor behind the hosiery mill, and no church had called him since. The Army would not have him on account of an eardrum. He drove nails on the hutment crews and slept in a hutment with four other men, and he ate at Ina’s table. She washed his shirts in the bathhouse tubs along with Carl’s and turned his collars when they frayed. She saved him the top of the milk and what sugar the stamps allowed. When people in the row asked was he her boy, she said he was the same as. In return he told her things. He knew who in the camp drank, and who danced on the tennis courts by the recreation hall, and which trailer had a woman in it who was nobody’s wife. He knew what the foremen let slide. He knew, he said, what they were making over the ridge, and he would lean across the oilcloth and all but say it, with a billboard up on the Turnpike telling every soul who passed to leave what

sections.heading: II. The Errand
sections.text: She was on the three-to-eleven that week. Before she left for the bus she gave Doyle his orders. Go tell Miss Docia I’d be proud to have her to dinner tomorrow. Tell her Row F, the fourteenth one down, with the lard can of marigolds on the step. Doyle went by the hutments first. He generally did. Arvil was on his cot with his shoes off. Where are you headed? Mama sent me to ask Miss Docia to dinner. Don’t go. I’ve got to. She’ll skin me. There’s a stack cake, isn’t there. And a chicken. Arvil sat up. You and me could eat all that ourselves. Don’t go. She’ll whip me, Arvil. Arvil studied about it. Go on, then. But don’t tell her the row, and don’t tell her how many down, and don’t say marigolds. Let on like you live right there by the bathhouse. And when you leave, cut out toward the Turnpike like you were going someplace else, and then come back here. Doyle did it just that way. The old woman was wringing a mop into the floor drain. She heard him out and said she would be glad to come, and she did not ask him one thing. He ran off toward the Turnpike and came back around the coal pile to the hutments. What did you do? Everything you said. You did fine. Now it’s you and me that eats

sections.heading: III. The Fourteenth One Down
sections.text: Arvil came before daylight, while Carl was on his shift and Ina was down at the bathhouse filling the water can, and he took the boy in behind the curtain where the bed was. The women of the row had been at it since Friday. Mrs. Sisk had scrubbed the linoleum with lye soap. Mrs. Hembree carried over the only stuffed chair in Row F, with a doily pinned to the back of it. There were five kinds of flowers in fruit jars: marigolds and zinnias, goldenrod, ironweed, and the small late asters that people there call farewell-summer. Three households had gone in together on the sugar. There were close to four thousand trailers in Oak Ridge that fall. The ones at Middletown stood in rows on scraped red clay, every one like the next, with a plank walk down the middle and the numbers mostly gone from the doors. Men who had lived in the camp a year walked into the wrong kitchen after dark. In October the fog came up off the creek bottom and stood in the rows until nine. Aunt Docia got down off the work bus from Oliver Springs at seven, with her badge pinned to her coat. She did not stop at the bathhouse to ask anybody. sections.text: They had trained her for three weeks in a room the girls called the Bullpen. Nobody there said what the machine was for. A man told them he could teach them what to do and could not tell them what they were doing, and after that it was all knobs and gauges. Her knobs had letters on them. When M was right and G was right, the needle stood up where it belonged. When she let it get away, the unit let go with a pop, and a blue light came on, and the floor men ran. Keep yours where it goes, the supervisor said. Don’t study on it, and don’t study the next girl’s. Ina had always studied the next girl’s. The one on her right was from Lenoir City and popped twice a shift. Ina could have told you each time, and how long the floor men took, and what the supervisor’s face did. She kept a kind of account of that whole row. That night a blue light came on two boards down, and then one on her right, and feet went by behind her stool. Her hand stayed on the knob. Her needle stood. She did not know until the shift changed at eleven whose it had been.
