logline: In a secret city's trailer camp, a calutron operator asks the bathhouse woman to dinner against the wishes of the young preacher she feeds.

verses.text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.
But, like a beautiful flower, full of colour and full of scent, are the fine and fruitful words of him who acts accordingly.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Chattapāṇi (“Umbrella-in-Hand”) is a learned layman of Sāvatthī, far advanced on the path, who eats one meal a day. Seated before the Buddha, he does not rise when King Pasenadi comes in, reasoning that to stand for a provincial king in the presence of the king of kings would honor the wrong one. The Buddha praises him and the king’s anger cools. Later the king sees him crossing the palace court with umbrella and sandals, has him called up, and asks him to teach the women of the palace; Chattapāṇi declines, saying that is work for a monk. The Buddha, who cannot go regularly to any one house, sends Ānanda. Queen Mallikā, a garland-maker’s daughter, learns and practices; Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, the Buddha’s own kinswoman, does not; and the Buddha speaks the two verses of the flower.
bg.history:
The Ethiopian community of Washington, the largest outside Africa, began with those who left after the military council called the Derg deposed Emperor Haile Selassie in September 1974. The Emperor, whose title was Neguse Negest, King of Kings, was killed in August 1975, and his remains were not found until 1992. In the 1980s the exiles gathered around Eighteenth Street in Adams Morgan, and many who had been officials, officers and landholders at home drove cabs or worked in parking garages. The city’s oldest Orthodox congregations date from those years; Debre Selam Kidist Mariam was founded in 1987. In May 1991 the Derg’s ruler fled and rebel armies entered Addis Ababa, and for a season some exiles thought they might go home to what they had lost. Dejazmach was a title of the old nobility, often borne by provincial governors. Emahoy is how a nun is addressed. Everyone in this story is invented.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays and through long seasons, among them the Fast of the Apostles after Pentecost; on a fast day nothing is eaten before three in the afternoon. Its traditional schools teach commentary on four bodies of books: the Old Testament, the New, the Fathers, and the Books of the Monks. First among the last is Mar Yishaq, the seventh-century Syriac hermit Isaac of Nineveh, whose treatises reached Ethiopia by way of Arabic. The passage here is from the opening treatise as A. J. Wensinck translated it from the Syriac in 1923; the Ethiopic wording differs. Besobila is Ethiopian sacred basil, a plain plant with a strong sweet smell, dried into the spice blends of every kitchen.

sections.heading: I. The Floor
sections.dateline: Kennedy Street NW, Washington, D.C. · June 1991, the Fast of the Apostles
sections.text: The Emahoy Wolete-Tsion lived in the basement of a brick rowhouse on Kennedy Street, in one room with a radiator and a window at the level of the grass. She had been a nun for fifty years, in a convent in Gojjam and afterward wherever the times put her. A deacon named Desta, who drove a cab at night, carried what she needed down the outside steps. On the mornings of fast days people left their shoes on those steps and sat on her floor, and she had the deacon read from the books of the monks, and then she told them in plain Amharic what had been read. The one who sat nearest was Ato Tilahun. At home he had gone through the four houses of the books under a master at Gondar, the Old Testament and the New, the Fathers and the Monks, and had come out the far end without taking so much as a deacon’s orders. He had been a clerk of a court. In Washington he sat from eleven at night until seven in the morning in the cashier’s booth of a hotel garage on K Street. He carried a long black umbrella with a crook handle in every weather, as a church scholar at home carries one against the sun, and Washington rained often enough to make an honest man of him. He kept the fasts, though it was hard t

sections.heading: II. The Lot
sections.dateline: L Street · a wet morning, the week after
sections.text: His office was a room up one flight at the back of his largest lot, with a window over the cars. He was standing at it after his coffee when he saw a black umbrella coming across the asphalt between the rows, and under it a small man in a raincoat, walking as if the lot were a churchyard. Bring me that one, he told the attendant. Tilahun came up the stairs. On the landing he closed the umbrella and stood it in the corner. He took off his shoes and set them beside it, and went in in his socks, and bowed, and stood to one side. Why have you left your umbrella and your shoes outside my door? They said to me, the Dejazmach is calling you. I put them down before I came in. Then it seems that today you have found out who I am. I have always known who the Dejazmach is. If that is so, then on Friday, when you were on the Emahoy’s floor and saw me come in, why did you not get up? Dejazmach, I was sitting where the King of Kings was being read. If I had got up for the governor of one of His districts, it is the governor I would have honored, and not Him. So I did not get up. The Dejazmach looked out at his cars for a time. Let it go, he said. They tell me you know this world and the other on

sections.heading: III. Tuesdays and Thursdays
sections.dateline: A house off Sixteenth Street · that summer
sections.text: He sent to Kennedy Street. My wife, Woizero Abebech, and my brother’s widow, Woizero Aster, say they wish to learn the books. Come to my house each week, Emahoy, and bring as many of your people as you like. The answer came back by the deacon. It is not possible for me to go regularly to any one house. Then send someone. She gave it to Desta. He was twenty-six, and had the Psalter by heart and a good deal of Mar Yishaq. On Tuesdays and Thursdays he parked his cab under the Dejazmach’s oak and read to the two women in the front room and told them what it meant. Woizero Aster came of an old house, the same house as the Emahoy, and had married into another. She kept a green ledger for the lessons and wrote in it with a fountain pen, in a hand like print. When there were guests she could give back any passage, with the deacon’s explanation after it, and the guests said they had not heard it better in Addis Ababa. She kept the front room in flowers from the supermarket, roses on long stems and carnations dyed blue, and changed them every week. A person could put his whole face in them and smell the refrigerator. Woizero Abebech was a gardener’s daughter from the Entoto road, twenty year

sections.heading: IV. The Calendar
sections.dateline: Kennedy Street · September, before the New Year
sections.text: Desta, the Emahoy said, are your two ladies learning? They are, Emahoy. Which of them learns it well? Woizero Abebech learns it well, and says it over, and it gets into what she does. But your own kinswoman does not learn it that way. She writes it. She does not say it over. I cannot find where any of it has gone. Woizero Aster had sent two dozen roses down with him that morning, in paper. They stood in the mop bucket by the door. On the wall over the radiator hung a calendar from an Ethiopian grocery, with a color picture of the falls of the Abay, the river coming over brown and white. It had hung there three years and had not wet the plaster. The Emahoy looked from the bucket to the wall. Then she began the place in Mar Yishaq, and he knew it, and said it with her. Very different is the word of practice from words of beauty. Even without experience wisdom knows how to adorn its words and to speak the truth even without having any acquaintance with it, and to express itself concerning excellence without any experience of [practical] performance. A word proceeding from practice, is a treasure to confide in. But idle wisdom is a pawn causing shame; it is as when an artist paints wat

title: Besobila
logline: The summer the Derg falls, a night cashier keeps his seat on a nun's basement floor when an exiled governor walks in.

verses.text: As many kinds of wreaths can be made from a heap of flowers, so many good things may be achieved by a mortal when once he is born.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Visākhā meets the Buddha at seven and becomes a disciple. Her father is moved by royal request to a new city, and there envoys of the rich man Migāra, looking for a bride with the five beauties, see her walk calmly through a sudden rainstorm while her friends run, and hear her explain why. Her father gives her a dowry beyond counting, the jeweled “great-creeper” ornament with its golden peacock, ten riddling admonitions, and eight sponsors to judge her if she is ever accused. In Migāra’s house she refuses to honor his naked ascetics and tells a monk at the door that her father-in-law is “eating stale food,” living on old merit. Cleared by the sponsors, she stays on condition that she may serve the Buddha; Migāra, listening from behind a curtain, is converted and calls her his mother. Late in life she leaves her ornament at the monastery, buys it back herself, and with the money builds the Eastern Monastery, and on its opening day walks round it singing. The Buddha explains her vow from ages past and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Arab immigrants, many of them from Lebanon, came to work at Ford’s River Rouge complex and settled in Dearborn’s Southend, in the shadow of the plant. Muslim Ford workers there built the American Moslem Society mosque on Vernor Highway, its first floor finished by 1937 and the rest added through the 1950s. Smaller Arab Muslim communities had grown up across the Midwest; in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, Lebanese and Syrian immigrants finished the Mother Mosque of America in 1934, considered the oldest purpose-built mosque still standing in the United States.

Palestinian refugees began arriving after the 1967 war, and the Lebanese Civil War, which began in 1975, brought a long wave of families from Lebanon. According to the Dearborn Historical Museum, volunteers founded the social-service agency ACCESS in 1971, and from the late 1970s Arab Americans moved from the Southend to the east side of Dearborn, where by the 1990s a business district had grown along Warren Avenue. The Darwish and Khalifeh families, the sheikh, and the building on the east side are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Station
sections.text: When Nawal Darwish was seven years old, an old sheikh from the south of Lebanon came through the Midwest on the train, stopping wherever there were enough Muslims to fill a front room. He had been in Michigan City and Cedar Rapids and would go on to Detroit. In Toledo the Lebanese had been waiting for him a month. Her grandfather, Hajj Mahmoud, who had started with a peddler’s pack and now owned the biggest wholesale grocery in the city, said to her that morning, This is a good day for you and a good day for me. Put on your white dress and take your cousins and go and meet him. Her uncle drove the girls to the new terminal in the Packard. He pulled up at the curb in front and they all started to climb out, and Nawal said, No, Uncle, you have to drive us around to where the trains are, and he did, as far as cars were allowed to go. Then she got out and walked the rest of the way across the platform with her cousins behind her, and stood a little to one side, and waited. When the sheikh came down the steps of the car with his cane, he looked at the girl in the white dress waiting at exactly the right distance, and smiled, and spoke to her, and nobody remembered afterward what he said

sections.heading: II. The Rain
sections.text: In the Southend lived Hajj Rida Khalifeh, who owned four markets and a Pontiac dealership on Michigan Avenue and was the richest man between the Rouge and the river, and he had a son named Hassan who had just finished at Wayne State and did not want to get married. Choose anybody you like, his mother said. A house with no children falls down. Hassan said that he would marry when they found him a girl with the five beauties, and not before. Beautiful hair, that fell to the hem of her skirt and curled up at the ends. Lips like a ripe pomegranate. Teeth like a row of pearls. Skin that needed no powder. And a youth that would stay on her, if she had ten children, as if she had had one. So his mother sent out her two sisters, who had married off half the Southend between them, with money for the bus and the train and a gold necklace in a velvet box. When you find her, put it on her. The aunts went to Toledo and Cleveland and Cedar Rapids and as far as Quincy, Massachusetts, and saw a great many lovely girls, and none of them had all five. They came home tired at the end of the summer, on the Sunday of the big Lebanese picnic on Belle Isle, and went to it, and sat down in the stone pavil

sections.heading: III. The Peacock
sections.dateline: Out past Telegraph Road · the winter of 1964
sections.text: Hajj Rida wrote that he would come to fetch the bride himself, and that Abu Jamal would come with him out of respect, and half the Southend with Abu Jamal, and could the house manage? Kamal Darwish wrote back: If ten Abu Jamals are coming, let them come. They came after Thanksgiving, two hundred people in a line of cars, and Kamal put up every one of them. It was Nawal, at seventeen, who sat at the kitchen table with a pencil and decided who would sleep in which house up and down the new street and who would carry coffee to whom, so that nobody could say afterward that they came to Nawal Darwish’s wedding and spent it parking cars. Kamal had sent for an Armenian goldsmith from downtown and told him to make his daughter a set of bridal gold such as Detroit had never seen. Then the snow came, the first big storm of that winter, and closed the roads, and Kamal told Abu Jamal, Nobody leaves this house until I say so, and kept them all until the gold was finished, which was not until February. For three months that subdivision was one long party. Everybody from Abu Jamal down to the boys who parked the cars thought he was the guest of honor. When the fuel oil ran out in the cold snap in

sections.heading: IV. Yesterday’s Bread
sections.dateline: The Khalifeh house, the Southend · spring 1965
sections.text: Hajj Rida did not ask the old sheikh to the wedding, though the sheikh was living in two rooms over the mosque on Vernor Highway, ten minutes’ walk away. Hajj Rida had his own holy man. His name was Abu Khalil, and he read coffee cups and wrote charms on paper for a price, and sat in Hajj Rida’s best chair in his undershirt with his belly over his belt, with five or six hangers-on around him who laughed when he laughed. In the spring Hajj Rida gave Abu Khalil and his friends a dinner. He had lamb cooked in the yard and rice with pine nuts in the big trays, and when they were eating he sent upstairs for his son’s wife. Tell the bride to come down and kiss the hand of the holy man. She came down glad, when she heard the words holy man. She stood in the dining room door and looked at Abu Khalil, the undershirt, the grease on his chin, the coffee cups upended on their saucers on the tablecloth, the money folded under one of them. These have no shame at all, she said, and no fear of God either. Why would you call that holy, Uncle? Why would you send for me for this? And she went back upstairs. Hajj, said Abu Khalil, that girl is bad luck. I see it in the grounds. Put her out of the hous

sections.heading: V. The Curtain
sections.text: She invited the sheikh for the following Friday, after the prayer. When Abu Khalil heard that the old sheikh was going to Hajj Rida’s house, he and his friends came and sat on the porch and on the steps all round it like a ring of crows. Nawal served the sheikh and his people with her own hands. Then she sent word to her father-in-law in the back room. Uncle, everything is ready. Come and sit with the sheikh. Hajj Rida wanted to go. Abu Khalil leaned in the window and said, Hajj, don’t you go near that man, and Hajj Rida sent word that his daughter-in-law could look after the guest by herself. When the meal was finished she sent a second time. Uncle, the sheikh is going to speak. Come and listen. Now Hajj Rida thought it would be a shame not to go, and he had wanted to hear the old man for years. All right, said Abu Khalil, if you have to listen to him, listen from behind a curtain. Don’t sit in the same room with him and don’t look him in the face. And Abu Khalil’s friends went ahead of him and strung a bedsheet across the archway between the dining room and the parlor, and Hajj Rida sat down behind it on a kitchen chair. The sheikh said, to nobody in particular, A man can sit beh

sections.heading: VI. Two Fingers
sections.text: She had ten children, five sons and five daughters, and they had children, and none of them in all those years was ever seriously sick, and none of them died young, and every family in the Southend asked Umm Rida first to their weddings and housewarmings, for the luck. People said she never got a gray hair. People said that when they saw her coming up the street with all her children and grandchildren around her they could not tell which one was Umm Rida. She was strong, too, everyone knew, though nobody could say how strong. Abu Jamal, getting old and curious, wanted to find out. On the Eid one year, when half the Southend drove down to the farms in Monroe County for the sacrifice, he had the farmer let a young bull out of the pen while Umm Rida was crossing the yard with her daughters. The bull put its head down and came for her. Her daughters screamed and some of them ran and some of them held on to her. What is this? she said. Yumma, Abu Jamal let it out to see how strong you are. She thought: if I grab him hard, I’ll kill him. So she reached out and took the bull by the ring in its nose between two fingers and pushed, gently, and it sat down on its haunches in the mud in front

sections.heading: VII. The Gold on the Stair
sections.dateline: Vernor Highway and the east side · 1980–1982
sections.text: By 1980 the families were moving out of the Southend to the east side of Dearborn, along Warren Avenue, and new families were coming every month from Lebanon, where the war had been going on for five years, with nothing but what they could carry. The old sheikh was very old. That spring there was a wedding, and after the wedding lunch the whole party walked over to the mosque on Vernor Highway for the sheikh’s talk. Umm Rida had worn the great set, the peacock and all, for her niece’s sake. At the mosque door she thought: it isn’t right to walk into the house of God dressed like this. So she took it off and wrapped it in her shawl and gave it to Sakineh, the girl who looked after her, who was the only one strong enough to carry it, and put on her everyday gold, and went in and listened. When it was over she went out the side door, and Sakineh went with her, and forgot the bundle on the bench. Abu Ali, who had kept the mosque for thirty years, always went round after a gathering to pick up what people had left behind. He found the shawl and what was in it and went to the sheikh. Umm Rida forgot her gold. Put it somewhere safe. So he hung the bundle on the newel post at the foot of t

sections.heading: VIII. The Garden on a Height
sections.dateline: East Dearborn · the end of Ramadan, 1982
sections.text: On the last night of Ramadan, when the building was finished and full of people, Umm Rida went out at sunset and walked round the outside of it, slowly, with her children and her grandchildren and the first of her great-grandchildren behind her in a long line. And as she walked she sang out loud, the way village women sing at a wedding. When will I build a house of God, plastered and painted? Now it’s done. When will I give the beds and the blankets? Now it’s done. When will I feed the hungry at the breaking of the fast? Now it’s done. In all those years nobody had ever heard Umm Rida sing. Sheikh, they said, is she all right? Has something happened to her? She’s not singing, said the old man. She’s saying thank you. She made a promise a long time ago, and it’s kept, and her heart is full. What promise? When? So he told them. How in his own village in the south, when he was a boy, the women sewed the prayer rugs for the mosque by hand, and one of them, an old widow named Hajjeh Zeinab, gave all her thread and all her needles and all her cloth, and asked for nothing for it but one thing. She knelt down on the last rug she finished and asked God to give her, one day, a granddaughter

title: Yesterday’s Bread
logline: A Toledo bride who walked through the rain marries into the Southend's richest house and tells her father-in-law what he's eating.

verses.text: The scent of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor (that of) sandal-wood, or of Tagara and Mallika flowers; but the odour of good people travels even against the wind; a good man pervades every place.
Sandal-wood or Tagara, a lotus-flower, or a Vassiki, among these sorts of perfumes, the perfume of virtue is unsurpassed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, sits one evening thinking about the three finest perfumes, those of sandalwood, of roots and of flowers. Each of them travels only with the wind. He wonders whether any scent goes against it, decides not to settle the question alone, and asks the Teacher. The Buddha answers that there is one: where a man or woman takes refuge, refrains from killing, stealing, sexual wrongdoing, lying and drink, and is open-handed, glad to give and attentive to those who ask, that person's praise is spoken in every direction by ascetics, brahmins and gods.
bg.history:
The voyage of 1492 was a commercial venture. The agreement signed that April promised Columbus a tenth of the pearls, precious stones, gold, silver and spices he might find, and his journal records him showing the islanders “specimens of cinnamon and pepper he had brought from Castile.” The steady northeast trade wind that carried the three ships west frightened their crews. The entry for 22 September reads: “This contrary wind was very necessary for me, because my people were much excited at the thought that in these seas no wind ever blew in the direction of Spain.” On 19 October, anchored off the cape he named Cabo Hermoso, Columbus wrote that he “found the smell of the trees and flowers so delicious that it seemed the pleasantest thing in the world.” The sailors' evening Salve, sung “in their way,” is in the journal too. The half-hour glass turned by the ship's boys, with a verse sung at each turn, is known from later Spanish accounts. Antón, Uclés and the box are invented.

On Christmas night the Santa María grounded off the north coast of Hispaniola with the tiller in the hands of a ship's boy. The Taíno cacique Guacanagarí sent his people in canoes to unload her, and Columbus wrote that “there was not even a needle missing” and that “they are a loving people, without covetousness.” Thirty-nine men stayed behind at La Navidad. The sentence about people who “never say no” is from Columbus's letter of February 1493, printed at Barcelona in April and, in Latin, at Rome, Basel, Paris and Antwerp within the year; the same letter boasts that the men left at the fort “are alone sufficient to destroy all that land.” The second fleet of seventeen ships found the fort burned and the garrison dead; its physician, Dr. Chanca, saw eleven bodies and heard that the Spaniards had taken women. Within two generations the Taíno of Hispaniola had been reduced to a remnant, though their descendants live in the Caribbean still. The friar is Bartolomé de las Casas. Jorge Manrique wrote his Coplas on the death of his father Rodrigo, Master of the Order of Santiago, in 1476; Longfellow's English version appeared in 1833. Quotations from the journal and letter follow the translations in The Northmen, Columbus and Cabot (1906).

sections.heading: I. The Glass
sections.dateline: The Ocean Sea, west of the Canaries · September 1492
sections.text: They had been sent for spices. It was written so in the Admiral's papers from the King and Queen, along with pearls and gold and silver, a tenth of all of it to be his if he found the way. So the ship carried, besides her biscuit and salt meat and wine and forty men, a small locked box of the things they were looking for, to hold up in front of whoever lived at the other end. The box was in the keeping of the steward, an old man named Benito whom everybody aboard called Uclés, after the town he came from. He had the stores, the water casks, the lamp oil and the firebox. He had the ship's boys too, whenever nobody else was giving them orders. Antón was one of the boys, fourteen years old, from Moguer. On his watch he kept the glass. When the sand ran out he turned it and sang the verse the boys sang at every turn, that the glass going was good and the glass coming better, and the helmsman answered him from below. Eight glasses made a watch. Between glasses he fetched for Uclés. From the day they lost sight of Hierro the wind stood behind them. It blew out of the east, a little north of east, day and night, and the ship ran before it as if she were being led. The men should have been

sections.heading: II. The Box
sections.dateline: At anchor off the Cabo Hermoso · the evening of 19 October
sections.text: They had found islands a week before, and people on them, and no spice that anyone could put a name to. At each landing the Admiral had Uclés bring out the box, and Antón carried it. Inside, in small linen bags, were sticks of cinnamon bark, a hand of ginger root, a measure of cloves and a measure of pepper. The island people smelled each bag with great courtesy and pointed south. On the nineteenth they anchored off a cape so green that the Admiral named it the Beautiful Cape and could not decide which part of it to look at first. At sundown the wind fell. Then it came back off the land, the way it will at evening, and it brought the land out with it, a smell of flowers and trees so sweet that the men stopped talking. They said the Salve in their fashion, which was no two of them together. Afterward Antón sat down with the box, which he was to air before it was locked up for the night, and opened the bags one at a time. Bark, he thought, and root, and flower, since a clove is a flower that has not opened. These are the three best smells in the world. The King and Queen have sent three ships after them. And every one of them goes down the wind and no other way. I have sat to windwar

sections.heading: III. The Reef
sections.dateline: Off the north coast of the island they named Española · Christmas night
sections.text: On the night before Christmas the sea lay like water in a bowl. The Admiral had not slept in two days, and at eleven he went below. The sailor at the tiller wanted his sleep as well. The Admiral had forbidden it the whole voyage, calm or blow, but the man gave the tiller to a boy and lay down. The boy was Antón. At midnight the current set the ship onto a bank, so gently that nobody aboard felt it. Antón felt the rudder take the ground and heard the water rushing, and he cried out. It was too late then. The master and his men took the boat and rowed for the caravel that lay half a league off. The mast was cut away to lighten her. She fell over on her side all the same, and her seams opened. By the middle of the morning Antón was sitting on the sand by himself. Nobody had beaten him yet. He supposed that was coming, or a rope, and he sat apart because no man in the company would sit by him. The king of that coast had his town a league and a half away. When he was told, he wept, and he sent every person he had and every large canoe. They went out to the wreck and came back, and went out, and in a few hours they had landed everything between her decks: the casks, the biscuit, the iron

sections.heading: IV. The Name
sections.text: Thirty-nine men were left on that shore, in a fort built out of the ship's timbers, with bread for a year. Uclés asked to be one of them. His knees would not carry him over another ocean, he said, and stores want a steward. Before the caravel sailed he untied the cinnamon bag and gave Antón one stick of the bark. There was a wind for Spain after all. It lay far to the north and had to be gone up and looked for, and it nearly drowned them in February. On the way the Admiral wrote a letter. By April the letter was printed at Barcelona. By May it had been put into Latin at Rome, and before the year was out it was printed again at Basel and Paris and Antwerp, and a man in Italy had turned it into verse. In every one of those tongues it carried a sentence that Antón could have told them himself. Of anything they have, if it be asked for, they never say no, but do rather invite the person to accept it, and show as much lovingness as though they would give their hearts. So the name of that king's people went up every wind in Christendom, to towns that had never smelled a clove. The letter said another thing a little farther down, which was how few armed men it would take to master the who

title: The Contrary Wind
logline: On the first voyage west, a ship's boy who airs the Admiral's spice box asks the old steward whether any smell travels to windward.

verses.text: Mean is the scent that comes from Tagara and sandal-wood;--the perfume of those who possess virtue rises up to the gods as the highest.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Mahā Kassapa, foremost of the Buddha’s disciples in ascetic practice, rises from seven days of meditative absorption and goes on his alms round in Rājagaha, meaning to accept food only from the poor, so that they may gain the merit of giving. Five hundred celestial nymphs wait on the road with alms; he refuses them, and when they persist he snaps his fingers and they flee. Sakka, king of the gods, then disguises himself and his wife Sujā as a decrepit old weaver and his wife spinning thread in a poor lane, and when the elder stops at their door Sakka fills his bowl with food whose fragrance fills the whole city. The elder recognizes him and rebukes him for robbing the poor of their chance. Sakka answers that no one is poorer than he, because three newly arisen gods outshine him, and asks whether his deceitful gift still earned merit. Told that it did, he circles the elder, rises into the air, and cries out three times in praise of the gift. The Buddha hears him and says that gods and humans alike love one who lives as Kassapa does.
bg.history:
Wilmington grew up around the du Pont family’s black-powder mills on the Brandywine, founded in 1802 and now the Hagley Museum. The company built its research laboratory, the Experimental Station, on the same creek; nylon, Kevlar and Tyvek came out of it. In August 2017 DuPont merged with Dow Chemical as DowDuPont, and in 2019 the combined company was split into three: Dow, Corteva and a new DuPont. After the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in April 1968, the Wilmington riot was followed by a National Guard occupation that lasted the rest of the year, reportedly the longest military occupation of an American city since the Civil War. The city’s historic Black Catholic parish is St. Joseph’s on French Street. St. Martin de Porres House, the Cosgroves, Walt, Doc and Mrs. Gaines are invented.

The Catholic Worker movement, founded by Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin in New York in 1933, runs houses of hospitality and farms where volunteers live in voluntary poverty among the people they serve; its paper, The Catholic Worker, was first sold for a penny in Union Square. Many Workers have gone to prison for nonviolent protest at weapons sites. Chicken and slippery dumplings, flat rolled dumplings cut in diamonds and cooked in the broth, is a staple of Delaware kitchens, from the poultry country downstate to church suppers in the city. Doc’s scripture is the Douay-Rheims Bible in Bishop Challoner’s revision, the English Bible of American Catholics for most of two centuries.

sections.heading: I. The Rag Bin
sections.text: Walt Hollingsworth came down out of Chateau Country in the summer of 1968, while the National Guard was still parked on the East Side with bayonets on their rifles, and walked into St. Martin de Porres House on a Tuesday morning in a suit his mother had bought him at Wanamaker’s. He was twenty-eight. His great-grandfather had made black powder on the Brandywine, and his grandfather had made money out of everything that came after the powder, and Walt had an office on the ninth floor downtown with his name on the door. He had come to drop off a check. A tall Black man in a white apron took the check, folded it, put it in the apron pocket, and handed him a ladle. That was Doc. Dr. Clement Pinder had grown up six blocks from the house, been baptized at St. Joseph’s on French Street, and gone from Howard High School to Lincoln University and a doctorate in chemistry. Since 1962 he had worked in a stone laboratory at the DuPont Experimental Station on the Brandywine, one of a handful of Black chemists in the place. He came to the house every morning at five to make the coffee before he drove to work. He could tell you what was burning three blocks away and what it had been painted with.

sections.heading: II. Five Hundred Plates
sections.dateline: The second Saturday of Lent · March 2019
sections.text: That spring the company his grandfather had worked for was being cut in three. Two years before, it had married Dow Chemical; now the lawyers were taking the marriage apart into three new companies with three new names, and the newspaper was full of who would go where. Walt did not read the newspaper. He came back from Virginia on a Friday night on the Amtrak with his seven days behind him, and on Saturday morning he put on a rag-bin coat with one toggle left and walked out the door of the house with his bowl. The bowl was white enamel with a blue rim, chipped black in three places, and it was the one thing he owned that he had chosen. He meant to go out on the East Side, street by street, the way he did the first morning after every retreat, and take whatever the poorest door he came to would give him. He did not get to the corner. It was a Saturday in Lent, and the volunteers were arriving: the girls from the Catholic schools in their plaid skirts and pink running shoes, the ladies from Greenville, two vans of college students from Newark. Word had gone around that Walt was back from his seven days, and every one of them had brought him something. They came at him down the sidewa

sections.heading: III. Chairs Caned
sections.dateline: The East Side · the same morning
sections.text: Out the Kennett Pike, in a stone house with nineteen rooms, Hollis Cosgrove had been listening. He had people at the house who told him things. He had known Walt since they were eight years old and sat two desks apart at a school in the hills where boys wore ties to breakfast. Cos was eighty. His grandfather’s name was on a wing of the hospital and a gallery at the art museum, and he was by any measure the richest man Walt had ever refused. He heard the volunteers had been sent in with their plates, and he laughed out loud at his breakfast table, and his wife Sue looked at him over her glasses. Plates, Cos said. Those children can’t feed Walt. Nobody can feed Walt. He sat a while. I can. Walt went down the East Side looking for the poorest door. He had walked those blocks every morning for fifty years. He knew which windows had plywood in them and which had curtains, who was in the hospital and who was in jail and whose daughter was sending money home from Georgia. Halfway down a block of brick rowhouses below the hill, between two that had been boarded since the eighties, he came to a narrow storefront he did not remember. The window had been washed. A sign in the window, lettered

sections.heading: IV. Slippery Dumplings
sections.text: The old man took the bowl inside to a hot plate at the back of the shop where a dented pot sat on the coil. He lifted the lid and ladled, then came back out and put the bowl in Walt’s two hands. It was chicken and slippery dumplings, the way they make it downstate, the broth gold with fat and black with pepper, the dumplings rolled thin and cut in diamonds and gone soft and slick in the pot, and the chicken pulled off the bone in long pieces. The smell went up off the bowl and out along the block. It went in at the boarded windows and the curtained ones. It went down to the train station, where people waiting for the 10:40 to Philadelphia lifted their heads from their phones, and up the hill to the courthouse, and across to the old DuPont Building, where the security guard at the desk put down his coffee. In the kitchen of the hotel on Rodney Square a cook stopped with a sauté pan in the air. At St. Martin de Porres House the line for lunch, which had been forming since eleven, went silent along its whole length, and the girls in the pink shoes came out onto the step to see what it was. On the Brandywine, people walking their dogs said afterward that the dogs had all sat down at on

sections.heading: V. The Good Odour
sections.dateline: St. Martin de Porres House · noon
sections.text: Doc was eighty-eight and still came at five to make the coffee, though now one of the young Workers drove him. At noon he was sitting on a stool by the urns with his cane between his knees, and he lifted his head and turned it toward the window before the smell had reached the room. Listen, he said. That’s Hollis Cosgrove. Up over the Brandywine, hollering. Nobody else in the kitchen heard a thing. A girl in pink running shoes, the one who had brought the egg-salad sandwich with the crusts cut off, came and stood by his stool. What’s he hollering about? He fed Walt, Doc said. He tricked him into it, and now he’s flying around the sky bragging. How did he know to feed Walt? she said. She was close to tears. We all tried. Doc laughed, a dry small laugh. Everybody wants to feed a man who eats like Walt eats. Lives on what he’s handed. Keeps nobody but himself. Quiet. Watching every minute. Honey, the angels would trade places with that man if they could. A rich man would put on rags to feed him. One just did. Then the smell came in through the window. The kitchen went still, and everybody turned toward it, the cooks and the girls and the men in the line, the way people turn toward mus

title: Slippery Dumplings
logline: An old Catholic Worker will eat only what the poorest give him, and a fading chemical heir means to be the poorest.

verses.text: Of the people who possess these virtues, who live without thoughtlessness, and who are emancipated through true knowledge, Mara, the tempter, never finds the way.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Godhika lives on the Black Rock at Isigili, near Rājagaha. A long illness makes him fall away from deep meditation six times; on the seventh, fearing for his future, he takes his own life. Māra, the tempter, comes to the Buddha in disguise and urges him to stop the monk, but only because he wants to keep Godhika inside his own realm, and the Buddha recognizes him. Afterward Māra searches every direction for Godhika's consciousness as a column of smoke and a mass of darkness, then comes as a young man with a yellow lute of vilva wood to ask where Godhika has gone. The Buddha says he has gone beyond Māra's reach, and Māra drops his lute and vanishes. Read the full commentary story (it follows Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.23 almost word for word), or about Māra. In the Buddhist tradition, Godhika's case is an exception that the texts treat with great care; neither the commentary nor this retelling holds it up as an example. Here the story's center is the searcher who cannot find him, and the old brother who stays with the sick.
bg.history:
After the Second World War, the Trappist abbey of Our Lady of Gethsemani in Kentucky filled with so many new monks, many of them veterans, that it sent out foundations across the country, among them Conyers, Georgia (1944), Huntsville, Utah (1947) and Mepkin, South Carolina (1949). The Sylamore Creek foundation in this story is invented. The details of Trappist life are drawn from accounts of the time: rising at two in the morning, silence kept with a sign language, choir monks in white and lay brothers in brown with beards, and burial in the habit without a coffin. Under the 1917 Code of Canon Law, those who deliberately took their own lives were to be denied church burial; superiors and pastors often judged that illness had taken away the person's freedom, and the current Code no longer contains the rule.

Malaria was a fact of life in Arkansas well into the twentieth century. According to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, the state reported more malaria deaths than any other through most of the 1920s and 1930s, and a federal campaign sprayed hundreds of thousands of homes with DDT between 1947 and 1953. In the Pacific, the Guadalcanal campaign left many thousands of American servicemen with malaria; relapsing vivax malaria brought many of them back to fever again and again, ten relapses being not unusual, and a drug that could clear the dormant parasite was not yet in general use. Ozark folk belief long called the fiddle the devil's instrument, and in Southern folklore the devil is a stranger you meet on the road carrying a fiddle of his own.

sections.heading: I. The Warm Rock
sections.text: The monks came over from Kentucky in April of 1946, twenty-two of them in two borrowed trucks, to a worn-out hill farm on Sylamore Creek that a widow in Little Rock had left to the Church. The abbey in Kentucky was full past bursting with men home from the war, and the abbot was sending them out wherever somebody gave him land. There was a dogtrot house on the place, and a barn with a tin roof, and a spring, and about forty acres that would grow anything but money. They put up wallboard cells four feet wide in the hayloft and slept there in their habits on straw ticks. They rose at two in the morning for the Night Office. They did not speak. Brother Isidore had been born four miles up the same creek in 1884, as Lafe Sutterfield. He had farmed, and fiddled some when he was young, and buried a wife, and in 1926 he had gone to Kentucky and asked to be let in as a lay brother, and they had let him. Twenty years he had worn the brown habit and the beard and milked other people's cows. When the abbot looked for a man who knew the Arkansas hills, Isidore was the one, and so he came home. At the new place he was the cowman, because he knew cows, and the infirmarian, because there was nobod

sections.heading: II. Chills and Fever
sections.text: The first time it came back on him was in June. Isidore found him at Vespers holding the edge of the choir stall with both hands, his teeth going like a sewing machine, and walked him across the yard to the dogtrot house, where the infirmary was two rooms and a washstand. Isidore knew the look of it. Every child on Sylamore Creek in his day had had the chills and fever, every other summer, and his own mother had kept a quinine bottle on the shelf by the salt. First the shaking, so hard the cot walked on the floor. Then the fever, a hundred and four, a hundred and five, and the boy talking to somebody named Gunny who was not there. Then the sweat, and the sheets wringing wet, and then nothing, a day or two of weakness like a wrung rag, and then it came again. The doctor from Mountain View came out in his Ford and gave atabrine, which turned Paschal's skin yellow as a squash. In two weeks he was back in choir. In three he was back on the rock. But it was not the same, and he told Isidore so, because the infirmarian could speak to the sick and the sick could answer him. Isidore was changing the bed. It goes, Brother. When the fever comes, it goes. I sit out there and it isn't there. I

sections.heading: III. The Barn
sections.text: The lay brothers milked at half past three, after their own prayers, while the choir monks were still in the Night Office. It was raining. Isidore had the lantern hung on the nail and his head in the flank of a red cow when the cows down the line all stood up at once in their stanchions and turned their heads the other way. There was a man in the barn door. Isidore had not heard a car on the road or a step in the yard. The man wore a good grey overcoat and a hat, and the rain had not touched either one, and the barn cat had gone flat to the floor under the feed box and stayed there. You're the old man that sits up with him, the man said. The Marine. Kemper. He means to die this morning. You'd better go and stop him. He won't listen to a word from me. He said it in a reasonable voice, the way a neighbor tells you your gate is open. Isidore had grown up on this creek, where people knew certain things and did not say them to outsiders, and he looked at the man's dry hat and the cows' turned heads and he knew who was standing in the door. You don't care one way or another if he lives, Isidore said. You want to know where he goes. The man smiled at him. He's not yours, Isidore said, and

sections.heading: IV. The Smoke
sections.text: Bud Treat, hauling cedar posts on the Mountain View road on the Monday, saw a smoke go up the Sylamore valley against the wind with no fire under it. He told it at the store. It was a dark smoke, he said, like a brush pile of green cedar, and it went along the bluffs low and slow, and into the mouths of the little hollows one after another, and came back out of each one, and went on. Mrs. Lackey saw it go along her fence row and over her spring box and come back. Two of the novices saw it from the woodpile on the Tuesday. It went down to the creek and along the gravel bar and turned in the water like a dog casting for a scent, and came up the slope through the burying ground and stood a while there over the new dirt, and went on up into the cedars on the bluff. Isidore was splitting kindling. The novices did not speak, but one of them caught his sleeve and pointed. He stood and watched it a long time with the hatchet in his hand. It went out along the limestone shelf at the top of the bluff where the sun lay, and turned there, this way and that, and went down into the cracks, and came up. He was allowed to speak to the novices for their instruction, and he decided this was instruct

sections.heading: V. The Fiddle
sections.text: In Easter week Isidore was setting a post where the abbey lane meets the county road, because the cows had been out. It was a fine afternoon with the redbud out along the ridges. He heard the fiddle a good while before he saw the man. He knew most of the tunes in Stone County and had played half of them, before he went to Kentucky, at dances his mother prayed against, and he did not know this one. It was quick and sweet and it went down into the low notes like water going over a lip of rock, and the cows in the near pasture all lifted their heads. Then the man came walking up the county road playing it. He was young, and handsome as a picture, in a suit the color of new butter, and the fiddle under his chin was yellow. Not varnished yellow. The wood itself was yellow all through, the bright hard yellow of hedge apple, bois d'arc, which the old people said was too hard to make anything of but fence posts and bows. He stopped across the post hole from Isidore and took the fiddle down from his chin. His face had gone sad and puzzled, like a child's that has lost something in the grass. Old man, he said. I've been all over. I've been up every hollow on this creek and down the White Riv

sections.heading: VI. The Lantern
sections.text: That evening, after Compline, the two novices who had seen the smoke came and stood by the woodpile where Isidore was sitting, and waited with their hands in their sleeves. He knew what they wanted. They wanted to know what he knew, and he did not know very much. He knew that the boy had been sick and had suffered, and that the sickness had told him lies, and that the old man had not been awake when he was needed, and would carry that. He knew who had come to the barn door, and he knew that a hundred like him could hunt this creek until the Judgment and not find what they were looking for. He said it to them as Saint Paul says it, because Saint Paul says it better. For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39 (Douay-Rheims) The younger novice was crying. Isidore let him, and after a while sent them both to bed. The government spray men came through the county that summer with their hand pumps and sprayed DDT on the inside walls of the houses,

title: The Yellow Fiddle
logline: At a new Trappist house in the Ozarks, an old lay brother nurses a young Marine whose malaria keeps coming back.

verses.text: As on a heap of rubbish cast upon the highway the lily will grow full of sweet perfume and delight, thus the disciple of the truly enlightened Buddha shines forth by his knowledge among those who are like rubbish, among the people that walk in darkness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two friends of Sāvatthī are divided by their teachers: Sirigutta follows the Buddha, and Garahadinna follows the Nigaṇṭhas, ascetics who claim to know past, present and future. Tired of being pestered, Sirigutta invites the ascetics to a meal of empty pots and tips them off rigged seats into a ditch of filth, then has them beaten. Garahadinna takes him to the king, who rules against Garahadinna. In revenge, Garahadinna invites the Buddha to a feast over a hidden pit of blazing charcoal and asks him to walk in first, alone. Lotuses as big as wheels rise from the coals, the empty pots fill with exactly what Garahadinna claimed they held, and the Buddha speaks of the lotus that grows from a rubbish heap by the road. Both friends enter the stream. That evening the Buddha tells of a past life in which he walked over a fiery pit made by Māra to feed a holy man, and a lotus rose beneath his feet.
bg.history:
Mashpee on Cape Cod was a Wampanoag community governed for generations as a plantation and district under state control. In 1833 its people, with the Pequot preacher William Apess, staged the Woodland Revolt to win back some self-government. The town’s first Baptist congregation was gathered by Blind Joe Amos, a Mashpee preacher born in 1805 and totally blind, who learned the Bible by heart from his mother’s reading and was ordained in 1830. After Massachusetts passed its 1869 act making Indians citizens, the state incorporated Mashpee as a town in May 1870, over many residents’ objections, which opened its land to sale. Amos had told the legislature’s committee, we are not ready for it now. Mashpee men went whaling out of New Bedford, cut cordwood and worked the bogs and shellfish beds. The clambake, cooked on red-hot stones under rockweed, is an old Wampanoag way of cooking.

In 1877 Spiritualists held their first camp meeting at Onset Bay in Wareham, which soon became one of the country’s leading centers of the movement. Mediums there and elsewhere claimed to carry messages from the dead, and over the 1870s it became common for them to speak through “Indian” spirit controls, invented chiefs and maidens. The Onset camp later declined amid exposures of fraudulent mediums. More on Spiritualism.

sections.heading: I. The Summerland
sections.text: Isaac Wicket and Moses Freeman had been friends since they were boys spearing eels through the ice on Wakeby Pond, and by the time they were fifty they were the two most comfortable men in Mashpee. Isaac had cranberry bog on the Santuit side and an oyster grant in Popponesset Bay. Moses had bog of his own and two hundred acres of oak and pitch pine that he cut into cordwood and sent up to Boston by the schooner load. Their houses stood a quarter mile apart on the Falmouth road, and they had been in and out of each other’s kitchens for forty years. Isaac sat under Brother Simon at the Baptist meeting. Moses had sat there too, until his boy Charlie went over the side of a New Bedford whaling bark in a gale off the Azores, in the winter of 1876, and the sea did not give him back. Brother Simon had said at the memorial that the sea does not give back, that nobody could promise Moses otherwise and nobody should. Moses never went to meeting again. In the summer of 1877 the Spiritualists had opened their great camp at Onset Bay, over the line in Wareham, with tents and a speakers’ stand and a grove full of mediums who would talk with your dead for a dollar. By the next summer some of them

sections.heading: II. Supper
sections.dateline: Isaac Wicket’s place · a Saturday in August
sections.text: Isaac’s house and his late father’s house stood side by side with a long grassy space between them, and on Thursday and Friday Isaac and his three sons and two nephews dug a trench down the length of it, waist deep. They filled it with what you would expect: the slop of the hog pen, and fish heads and eel skins from the landing, and the black muck out of the bottom of an old ditch at the bog. Over the trench they set a long trestle table, and on the near side of it, five good chairs, with their front legs on the grass and their back legs resting on a rope stretched tight between two stakes. Over the chairs they spread Isaac’s wife’s best quilts, so nobody could see what the chairs were standing on. Then he took every iron kettle and crock in both houses, scrubbed them out, and set them in a row behind the kitchen with cloths over their mouths. He smeared the outsides with chowder and dabbed them with succotash and Indian pudding, so that they looked like kettles that had been filled and stirred and slopped over. They were empty. Early Saturday morning Moses came over to make sure of things. Is there supper for them? There’s supper. Where? Here, said Isaac, and walked him along the

sections.heading: III. The Trial Justice
sections.text: Moses Freeman stood in his doorway and looked at them a long time. He had known Isaac Wicket for forty-five years and had never once in that time seen him do a cruel thing. Then he went white with anger, as white as their legs. He’s ruined me, he said. They bowed to him. They came to his house as guests and he’s beaten them with sticks. My teachers. The men who brought me my son. On Monday he drove to Barnstable and swore out a complaint for assault before the trial justice, and the justice sent a summons to Isaac Wicket. Isaac came in his meeting coat and stood with his hat in his hands. Your Honor, will you hear it before you fine me? Or fine me first? I generally hear it first, Mr. Wicket. Then hear it, and do what you think is right. And he told it all from the beginning. Moses at him on the landing and the road and the store, standing and sitting, every day. What does your blind man know. The spirits know everything, the past, the present, the future, every thought in your head. The trench, the chairs, the kettles. He did not leave out the switches. The trial justice was an old Barnstable lawyer who had sat through a good many lectures on table-rapping in his time and had beli

sections.heading: IV. The Bake
sections.text: For two weeks Moses would not speak to Isaac. He passed him on the road and looked at the trees. He went the long way around to the landing. Then he thought it over, sitting by himself at night in the front room where Chief Thunder Cloud had talked. Sulking would get him nothing. What he wanted was for Isaac Wicket and Isaac’s blind preacher to be laughed at in front of the whole town the way he had been laughed at, the way his teachers had been laughed at, crawling out of a ditch. So he went to Isaac’s gate. Isaac. Moses. Folks are saying we’ve fallen out. Kin and friends fall out, and then they get over it. Why won’t you speak to me? I don’t speak because you don’t, Isaac said. But what’s done is done. I’m not going to throw away forty years over it. And after that they stood together on the landing again and sat together on the store steps the way they always had. One day on the steps Isaac said, Moses, what do you want with spirits? What did they ever give you but a bill at the court? Come back to meeting. Hear Brother Simon. It was exactly what Moses had been waiting for. It was like being scratched where he itched. And what does your Brother Simon know? Moses, don’t talk like

sections.heading: V. The Lilies
sections.text: By noon there was a crowd. Word goes around a small town. Half of Mashpee came, and people from Cotuit and Waquoit and even from Falmouth, white and Indian and colored, in wagons and on foot. Some came because Moses Freeman always set a good table. Some came because they had heard about the ditch, and the trial justice, and they knew Moses, and they wanted to see what a man like that would do to a blind preacher. And some came because Brother Simon was going to speak at a bake, outdoors, in the summer, and they wanted to hear it. Brother Simon came up the road at noon on Lemuel’s arm, with the whole Baptist church walking behind him in their Sabbath clothes, forty or fifty of them. Moses met them at his gate. He bowed to the preacher low, the way Isaac had bowed, and while he was bowing he said to him in his heart: So you know what’s past and what’s now and what’s coming, Brother Simon. So you know what’s in a man before he knows it himself. That’s what Isaac tells me. If you know it, don’t come through this gate. There’s no dinner for you. There’s a pit of fire, and you’re going in it in front of everybody. Out loud he took the old man’s hand and said, Brother Simon, welcome. Only

sections.heading: VI. Eyes
sections.text: When the eating was done Moses came and stood in front of the preacher’s chair with his hat in his hands, the way men stood in Mashpee when they wanted the minister to return thanks. Brother Simon turned his face toward the crowd. He could not see them, but he knew where they were, the way you know where the sea is at night. A good many of you came out today to see a blind man fall in the fire, he said. You have eyes. You didn’t see what was in front of you. You didn’t see the Lord, or His mercy, or the poor folks of His church sitting here on the grass. You came to look, and you didn’t see. I’m the blind one here, and I tell you there’s not more than a handful in this yard with eyes. The ones that know Him have eyes. That’s all. And then he said it the way he said everything, by heart. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory. — 1 Samuel 2:8 The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined. — Isaiah 9:2 Some of the people in that yard said for the rest of their lives that t

sections.heading: VII. The Try-Works
sections.text: That evening a crowd of them sat on the meeting house steps in the long light, still talking about it. Did you ever see such a thing. Lilies out of a fire. Did you ever in your life. Brother Simon came up the path on Lemuel’s arm and asked what they were saying, and they told him. Well, he said, and sat down on the bottom step. It’s not the first time. And because they asked him, he told them. When he was nineteen he was on a bark out of New Bedford, in the Indian Ocean. There was an old Portuguese cook in the forecastle with the fever who had not eaten in seven days, and the boy had a pannikin of soup for him, carrying it forward. They were trying out a whale that night, boiling down the blubber in the try-pots on deck, with the fire roaring in the brick try-works under them, and the ship pitched, and one of the pots went over. In a moment the deck between him and the forecastle was a sheet of burning oil, blue and yellow, running in the scuppers. Every man on deck backed off from it. And Simon Hosea, nineteen years old, looked up, and saw a man standing in the rigging over the fire, laughing. Nobody else saw him. He said the man was well dressed. I asked him did he light it, said

title: Pond Lilies
logline: Two old friends on Cape Cod, one a Baptist and one taken with traveling mediums, trade a ruined supper for a clambake over a pit of fire.

verses.text: Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala, riding his white elephant around the city on a festival day, sees a poor man's wife at an upper window and wants her. He makes the husband his servant, finds no fault in him, and sends him a league to fetch red earth and white and blue water lilies that grow only in the country of the nāgas. The man shares his half-cooked rice with a traveler and the fish, makes over the merit to whoever lives in the pool, and a nāga king in the form of an old man brings him what he needs. The king has shut the gate early; the man hangs the flowers on it, calls the city to witness and goes to sleep at the monastery. That night the sleepless king hears four syllables, du, sa, na, so, cried by four adulterers in the Iron Caldron hell, each of whom rises to the rim once in sixty thousand years and can get out only the first sound of a verse. His chaplain reads them as an omen of the king's death and prescribes a great sacrifice of living creatures; Queen Mallikā calls him a fool and takes him to the Buddha, who finishes the four verses. The king says he has learned how long a night is, the servant how long a league is, and the Buddha joins their words. The sacrifice is called off. A story of the past tells how Mallikā, as Queen Dinnā, once saved a hundred kings by weeping and laughing over a ewe she had killed.
bg.hist_title: Richland and the Hanford tank farms, 1955
bg.history:
Richland was rebuilt by the Army in 1943 as the operators' town for the Hanford plutonium works. Until the houses began to be sold to their tenants in 1957, all of it was government property managed by the contractor, which after 1946 was General Electric. Rank decided which of the lettered “alphabet houses” a family could rent, and a burned-out bulb was replaced on requisition. Construction workers lived apart, first in the wartime camp at Hanford, whose people gave a day's wages in 1944 to buy the B-17 Day's Pay, and later in the trailer camp at North Richland. Atomic Frontier Days, with its parade and floats reading “We're Here to Stay,” ran from 1948. Black workers recruited for the wartime construction were kept out of Richland and out of Kennewick, a sundown town, and lived in East Pasco. Sennett, his household, Decker's purge and Miss Whitlow are invented; no such mass suspension took place.

The chemical plants in the 200 Areas dissolved irradiated fuel and sent the leftover liquor to underground steel-lined tanks. Waste from the REDOX plant, which started in 1952, was hot enough to boil on its own decay heat, and the S and SX tank farms in 200 West were built to take it. Engineers called the sudden steam surges in these tanks “bumping.” A later engineering review records that before May 1955 it had been seen only in tanks S-101, S-104 and SX-101, and afterward in SX-104: four tanks. Radiation monitors with hand-held ion chambers nicknamed “cutie pies” set the time a worker could spend on a job. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of about 24,100 years, so roughly eighteen percent of any quantity remains after sixty thousand. Hanford still holds about 56 million gallons of waste in 177 tanks; the first of it was turned to glass in October 2025. Newton's distinction between absolute and common time is in the Scholium that follows the Definitions of the Principia, here in Andrew Motte's English of 1729.

sections.heading: I. The White Car
sections.text: Nobody in Richland owned his house that year. The government owned the houses and the lawns and the shade trees it had planted on them, and General Electric ran the town for the government the same as it ran the plant. A man's rank on the project settled which letter of house he was let to rent. An operator got half of an A house. A chief supervisor got a D or a G. If a light bulb burned out you filled in a requisition and a man came with a bulb. The house went with the job, and the job went with the clearance, and the people who could take away all three with one telephone call were the managers. That was what it was to be a manager in that town. Russell Sennett was manager of Separations, which meant both of the 200 Areas, East and West, and every tank that was buried in them. On the Saturday of Atomic Frontier Days the parade came down George Washington Way the way it did every August: the high school band, who were called the Bombers, and the sheriff's posse, and the queen and her court, and floats with WE'RE HERE TO STAY lettered down their sides. Behind the General Electric float came a white Buick convertible lent by a dealer in Pasco. Sennett stood up in the back of it in a

sections.heading: II. Six White, Six Blue
sections.dateline: The river above town · the last Saturday in August
sections.text: He called Arlo to the back step a little before three, in the worst of a day that went to a hundred and two. Go up the river to the old pump house. It's a good three miles. There's a bank of red clay there and a backwater with water lilies in it. I want a pail of the clay and a dozen lilies, six white and six blue, on this step at six o'clock when I come up from my swim. Leave the car. I may want it. If you are not here at six you can turn in your badge. Arlo stood there. There was no red clay on that river. He had driven the length of the project, and the ground in that country was gray sand and gray cobble and sagebrush, and upriver the bluffs stood as white as flour. The Columbia came down past Richland cold and fast over stones, and nothing rooted in it. He had seen white lilies on the oxbow lakes at home. A blue one he had never seen anywhere. But the order was given, and a man on staff went. He went by the trailer first, close to running. Neva, is dinner cooked? It's on. The beans want another hour. I haven't got an hour. He had her ladle them out of the pot into a lard pail, wet as they were, with the salt pork on top and a pone of cornbread on top of that. He pushed the lid

sections.heading: III. The Gate
sections.dateline: The river houses · ten minutes to six
sections.text: Sennett had been thinking too. A man in a corner will turn up anything, he thought. If he comes back with it, I am no further on than I was. So at five he had the yardman chain the gate. The Sennetts' was the one house on that street with a fence; the government had put it up for some manager before him. He took the key off the yardman's ring himself and carried it upstairs and laid it on his dresser. Arlo came down the street at ten minutes to six by the watch on his wrist, and the gate was chained. Open it, Orrin. I can't. He had me lock up at five, and he's got the key upstairs. I'm his driver. He sent me. Open the gate. I know who you are, Arlo. I can't. Arlo stood a minute with the pail in his hand. Then he tipped the red clay out on the walk in front of the gate, all of it in one heap, and hung the lilies on the pickets, six white and six blue. It was the hour when Richland watered. Up and down the street people were out on the government grass moving their sprinklers. He turned around to them and called out, and his voice carried. All you people on this street, I want you for witnesses. It is not six o'clock. I have done what Mr. Sennett sent me to do. There is his clay and

sections.heading: IV. Four Sounds
sections.text: Sennett ate a steak that night and could not have said afterward what it was. He went to bed and did not sleep. He lay with the fan going and looked at the ceiling and thought about a window in the Desert Inn. In the morning, he thought, I will have his badge for leaving his post, and Decker can find the rest. A man from Arkansas has a cousin somewhere who signed something once. He will be off the project by Wednesday and out of the camp by Friday, and she will be in that trailer by herself with the lot rent due. Under that he thought about how wide the reservation was at night and how few roads crossed it, and he did not let himself finish the thought. He heard the clock downstairs strike twelve, and then one. A little after one he heard something else. It came from the north, from the direction of the areas, across thirty miles of sagebrush, and it came in at his window as plain as the clock. Four sounds, one after another, low. Duh. Suh. Nuh. So. Each one was a man's voice starting to say something, and each was cut off before the second word, as if the man had been pulled under. Sennett sat up with the sweat gone cold on him. Is it me? he thought. Is it Jess? Is it the plant? H

sections.heading: V. Both Areas
sections.text: Jessamine Sennett had found the lilies on Saturday evening, hung on her own gate, six white and six blue, and the red clay heaped on the walk. She asked the yardman, and the yardman, who was more afraid of her than of her husband, told her. She said nothing about it then. She carried the lilies in and floated them in the big glass bowl on the dining table, and she left the clay where it lay. On Monday the wives came to her back door, two and three at a time, with the notices. She heard them out. Then she went upstairs, where her husband sat on the side of the bed in his undershirt with the blinds down. Russell, what ails you? You look like something that's been dug up. Don't you know, Jess? A snake has got in at my ear. He told her about the four sounds, and Decker, and the lists. Decker says I'm through unless I clean house. I mean to keep what I've got. You are a fool, she said. You eat a steak and three eggs every morning of your life, and you have both the areas under you, East and West, and you have not got the sense God gave a goose. Where did you ever hear of one man saving himself by finishing another? And a hundred and forty of them? Because a man who had no idea what you

sections.heading: VI. The Watch
sections.dateline: The trailer camp, North Richland · Monday evening
sections.text: They went in her car, the little Nash, and she drove. The trailer camp had been laid out for better than two thousand trailers and was more than half empty by then, lot after lot of bare gravel, each with its board sunshade standing over nothing. Miss Whitlow's was the last lot of the last row. She was sitting on her step in what was left of the light. Under the awning, on the cot, sat Arlo Minton, who had been there since Saturday night. Sennett got out of the car and stood in the gravel. He had not slept in two nights, and he was so afraid of what he was going to be told that he could not get a word out. He took off his hat and stood to one side, holding it. It was Miss Whitlow who spoke. You've come late in the day, Mr. Sennett. He said nothing. Jessamine told it for him: the sounds after one o'clock on Saturday night, and what Decker had made of them, and the lists, and the paper on the doors. That is why I've brought him to you, she said. Is that so, Mr. Sennett? Yes, ma'am. What did you hear? He told her, as near as he could make the sounds. Duh. Suh. Nuh. So. Miss Whitlow sat a moment without saying anything. title: Stay Time
logline: A Hanford manager wants his driver's wife and sends him upriver for red clay and blue lilies. That night four sounds cross the desert.

verses.text: If a traveller does not meet with one who is his better, or his equal, let him firmly keep to his solitary journey; there is no companionship with a fool.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Mahā Kassapa, the Buddha’s great ascetic disciple, lives at the Pipphali Cave near Rājagaha with two young attendants. One does the work; the other takes the credit, telling the elder his bath is ready when the faithful pupil has left only a little water steaming in a pot. Rebuked, the false pupil goes to the elder’s lay supporter, says the elder is sick, and eats the food he is given. Rebuked again, and jealous of the fine robes the elder has passed on to the other pupil, he smashes the monastery’s vessels, burns the elder’s leaf hut, beats what will not burn with a hammer, and runs. He dies and goes to hell. When a monk from Rājagaha brings the news to the Buddha, the Buddha tells the birth story of a monkey who, scolded by a hornbill for having hands like a man and no house, tore the bird’s nest to pieces, and speaks the verse. The visiting monk enters the stream.
bg.history:
The paper mills built the towns below Katahdin. Great Northern Paper’s mills at Millinocket and East Millinocket went through bankruptcy and changes of ownership after 2003; the Millinocket mill shut in 2008 and the last mill in the region, at East Millinocket, closed in 2014, ending several hundred jobs. Millinocket has lost nearly half its 1970 population. On August 24, 2016, President Obama proclaimed the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument on 87,563 acres east of Baxter State Park, donated by the family foundation of a Burt’s Bees co-founder. Many local people and the governor bitterly opposed it, and others hoped it would bring visitors back. Its north entrance lies up Route 159, the Shin Pond road, out of Patten.

Heathenry, the modern revival of pre-Christian Germanic and Norse religion, has been practiced in the United States since the 1960s, mostly in small local groups called kindreds. Its central rites are the blót, an offering of mead to the gods sprinkled over the people, and the sumbel, rounds of toasts and boasts over the drinking horn, where words spoken are held to be binding. Its scriptures are the poems of the Poetic Edda, above all the Hávamál, the the “Sayings of the High One,”ldquo;Words of the High One,the “Sayings of the High One,”rdquo; Odin’s counsel on hospitality, friendship and good sense. Some groups have also revived oracular seiðr, drawn from the seeress in the Saga of Erik the Red: the seer sits on a high seat while songs and drumming carry the gathering in trance down the world tree toward Hel, and then answers the questions people bring.

sections.heading: I. The Water
sections.dateline: Shin Pond road, above Patten · October 2016
sections.text: Wendell Kasper had piped steam in the Millinocket mill for thirty-one years, and when the mill shut he drove north past Patten and up a logging spur off the Shin Pond road and built a cabin at the end of it, and he had lived there alone since. He was seventy-one. He ate once a day, at noon. He slept on a bed of spruce poles under two wool blankets. He hauled his water from the brook in two pails because the brook was there, and he had patched his roof so many times, with tarpaper and cedar bark and the flattened lids of coffee cans, that the kindred said it was the swallows holding it up. Every May the barn swallows came back and plastered their mud cups under the eave over his door, and nobody was allowed to knock them down. Behind the cabin, in a ring of white birches, stood the hof: a lean-to of rough hemlock boards, a flat stone in front of it, a plank table. On the old feast days eight or nine people drove in from Patten and Sherman and Island Falls, and now and then somebody from Bangor, to make blót there. They poured mead into a maple bowl and lifted it to the gods and shook it with a sprig of fir over the stone and over one another. Then they sat at the plank table and pas

sections.heading: II. The Stew
sections.text: Karen Ouellette kept forty Romney ewes on a hill farm in Stacyville and wove. She was not one of the kindred. She went to Mass in Patten when she went. But she had known Kasper since her husband ran the paper machines and Kasper kept their steam up, and since her husband died she had fed the old man his one meal every Sunday at her kitchen table, as other people in those towns did on other days. He went around to them the way the mail went around: Karen on Sundays, the Hersey family in Sherman on Wednesdays, the diner in Patten when somebody there had a birthday. Two weeks before, at the Winter Nights blót, Karen had come up the spur with a cloak she had woven him on the big loom in her parlor, a heavy grey twill as long as a bedspread, with a fringe. Kasper put it on and thanked her and wore it home. The next morning he folded it over the back of Toby’s chair. I’ve got a coat, he said. Toby gathered butternut hulls along Fish Stream and boiled the cloak in the canner until it came out the brown of strong tea, and cut it with Kasper’s tin snips, which was the only shears on the place, into a long coat and a short cape. Brody had watched him do it. That Sunday, while Kasper and Toby

sections.heading: III. The Maul
sections.text: On the Saturday after the first snow, Kasper drove down to Patten for his mail and the kerosene, and Toby went with him, and Brody stayed. He started with the horns. There were two drinking horns on pegs by the door. Kasper had made the long one himself in 1991 from a steer horn he got off a farm in Littleton, boiled and scraped and polished with ashes until you could see a candle through it, and every blót the kindred had made in twenty-five years had been drunk out of it. Brody took them down and broke them across the edge of the cookstove. He took the maple bowl from the hof, and when it would not break he split it with the axe. He swept the shelves with the axe handle, and down came the jars, sixty or seventy quarts of beans and venison and fiddleheads and blueberries, which was the old man’s winter, and the lamp chimneys and the enamel basin and the mugs. Then he poured the kerosene from the lamp can over the bunk and the books and the tarpaper and lit it, and went out back and lit the hof. sections.heading: IV. The High Seat
sections.dateline: A Grange hall in Dover-Foxcroft · February 2017
sections.text: In February the kindreds from around the state met for two days in a rented Grange hall in Dover-Foxcroft, and on the Saturday night Ronda Theriault sat the high seat. She was forty-six and a hospice aide for the county. Most weeks of the year she drove a Honda with a hundred and ninety thousand miles on it from one farmhouse to another, turning people in their beds and washing them and sitting with them, and twice a year she did this. They had built her a platform at the end of the hall out of folding tables with a kitchen chair on top, and hung blankets around it, and she sat up there in a dark blue cloak with a veil of black net over her face and a staff across her knees. Down on the floor eighty people sat in the dark on metal chairs. A man with a frame drum walked them, in their minds, down the trunk of the great tree, down through the roots and the cold and the mist to the gate of the hall of the dead, and four women sang the old calling song, and when they stopped singing the seeress was somewhere else, and anybody who had a question could come up the aisle and ask it.
