sections.heading: V. Mud
sections.text: The kindred came up the spur on three Saturdays in April when the frost went out and helped raise a new cabin on the old sills. It was smaller than the first one, twelve by sixteen, of spruce logs Toby had cut and peeled over the winter at a woodlot in Stacyville, with a shed roof of second-hand steel that a man in Island Falls took off his barn. Karen gave him a cookstove from her cellar. Somebody from Bangor sent a box of quart jars in the mail with no note. The flat stone in front of the hof was in three pieces, and Kasper set them back in the ground as close together as they would go and left the cracks between them. He did not rebuild the hof that year. He said the birches would do. Toby stayed. He wore the butternut coat every day until it was too warm, and then he hung it on a nail by the door. Kasper did not take anyone else in. A young couple from Portland wrote that spring asking whether the gothi took students, and he had Toby write back that he was too old and they should go see Ronda Theriault in Dover-Foxcroft. verses.text: “These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,” with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Ānanda is a rich man of Sāvatthī with eight hundred million in treasure, who warns his son Mūlasiri every fortnight never to think it a large sum, never to give anything away, and always to get more. He shows his son his five great stores of treasure and dies in his avarice. He is reborn in a village of outcastes who hire themselves out as a crew; from the day he is conceived the crew is paid nothing, until they search out the unlucky one and drive his mother away. The child is born misshapen, and when he is old enough his mother puts a bowl in his hand and sends him to beg. He wanders into his old house, passes through three rooms unseen, frightens his grandchildren in the fourth, and is beaten and thrown on the dust-heap. The Buddha, passing with Ānanda the Elder, tells Mūlasiri the beggar is his father, and when the son will not believe it, has the beggar point out the five buried stores. Read the full commentary story, or about the Dhammapada and its commentary. The verse the achar speaks comes from the Sutta Nipāta, an early Pali collection that Viggo Fausbøll translated in 1881.
bg.history:
Under the Khmer Rouge, from 1975 to 1979, Cambodia’s cities were emptied, banks were raided and the currency and its records were burned, and something like a fifth to a quarter of the population died. Survivors who reached the Thai border after the regime fell came through camps such as Khao-I-Dang, opened in November 1979, and many were resettled in the United States. From the mid-1980s they settled in Lowell, Massachusetts, the old mill city on the Merrimack, opening dozens of small businesses; by 2010 Lowell had the highest proportion of Cambodian residents of any city in the country. More on the Cambodian genocide and on Cambodian Americans.

Pchum Ben is a fifteen-day festival at the end of the rains retreat, in September or October, when the gates of the underworld are said to open and the dead return to their families. Cambodians honor up to seven generations of ancestors with food brought to the monks, and many throw balls of sticky rice into the temple grounds for the wandering dead. An achar is a layman, often a former monk, who serves as master of ceremonies in the temple’s rites. In Cambodia gold is still bought and sold by the chi of 3.75 grams.

sections.heading: I. The Chain
sections.text: Kong Sarin sold gold on Middlesex Street, in a narrow shop between a video store and a place that wired money to Battambang, and he was the richest Cambodian in the Lower Highlands. Everybody said so, and he never once denied it, because denying it would have meant saying a number. The gold in his cases was the old kind, the soft deep yellow that bends in the hand. Chains, mostly, and bracelets, and the thick rope necklaces that a family put on a bride and took back off her to pay for a funeral. He weighed everything on a little brass scale and priced it by the chi, which is three and three-quarters grams, and he could tell you the price of a chi in Phnom Penh that morning without looking at a paper. He had been a goldsmith's apprentice in Phnom Penh before the war. In April 1975, when the Khmer Rouge marched everybody out of the city, he had walked past the bank with his mother and seen the money blowing down the boulevard in drifts, riel notes in bundles and loose, against the curbs, in the gutters, and nobody stopping to pick them up. He told that to his son Vibol many times. Paper, he said. They made it nothing in one morning. Four years later he walked out of the fields with t

sections.heading: II. Unlucky
sections.text: That autumn a crew of Cambodian women, and a few of their husbands, cleaned offices at night out on the highway. There were about forty of them. They rode out together after supper in two vans driven by a man named Heng, who got the contracts and paid the crew in cash every other Friday, and they vacuumed and emptied wastebaskets and scrubbed toilets in the glass buildings of the software companies until four in the morning, and rode home asleep against each other's shoulders. It was not much money, but it came. In November it stopped coming. Heng said the companies were slow to pay him. In December he said after New Year. All through that winter the crew went out to the buildings every night and worked and came home with nothing, and the women at the Acre began to buy rice on credit at the market and lie awake doing sums. One of them was Nhem Chann. She was twenty-four, and the man she lived with had gone to Providence in the fall to look for work and had not come back, and by Christmas she knew she was pregnant. The crew talked about it in the vans. Heng was a cheat, everybody knew Heng was a cheat, but he had been a cheat for four years and had always paid. Something had changed

sections.heading: III. Samnang
sections.text: They operated on him in Boston, three times before he was four. They closed the gap in his lip and the roof of his mouth, and moved one eye, and made his hands into hands that could hold a spoon. But they could not make him into what he would have been, and the neighborhood saw him the way it saw him. It was strange, the women said. Chann was a good worker. People wanted to give her things. But she could not take him anywhere. When she carried him to the market, the man at the register was out of change, or the line was too long, or the thing she came for was gone from the shelf. When she took him to the wat on holy days the monks blessed him like anyone, but the women in the kitchen found the rice already gone. When she left him home with the woman across the hall and went out by herself, she came home with a job, or a bag of groceries, or a ride. The children called him Unlucky. In English, so their parents would not understand, but the parents understood. He was a quiet child. He did not cry when the other children threw things. He went to the special classes at the elementary school and learned to read slowly, and the teachers liked him, because he was careful with everything,

sections.heading: IV. The Fourth Room
sections.text: He went up one street and down the next. Some doors he knocked at did not open. At some a woman looked at his face and gave him a sticky-rice cake wrapped in banana leaf and closed the door fast, as if she had paid something off. On Westford Street a grandmother sat him down on her steps and gave him rice and fish soup in a bowl and stood watching him eat with her arms crossed, and when he was finished she took the bowl back inside and washed it twice. It was past noon when he came to a big two-family house up the hill from Middlesex Street, with a porch on each floor and a chain-link fence and a clothesline in the yard. He stopped at the gate. He knew it. He did not know how. He knew the gate stuck at the bottom and you had to lift it. He knew there would be lemongrass by the fence, gone brown now, and there was. He knew the back door would be open in the daytime because the women were cooking, and it was, and the kitchen was full of steam and women and the smell of coconut and banana leaf, a dozen of them, aunts and cousins and neighbors, making num ansorm on every surface for the dead. sections.heading: V. The Achar
sections.text: Achar Moeun had slept four hours after his shift and gotten up and put on his white shirt, which was the shirt the achar wears, and his good trousers, and walked the eight blocks from his apartment because he did not drive. His grandnephew Rith walked with him. Rith was nineteen and studying to be a nurse at the community college, and he had been walking with the old man since he was fifteen, carrying the bag with the candles and the incense and the books, and asking questions, and getting answers that were usually shorter than the questions. Moeun was seventy-one. He had been a monk for nine years as a young man in Kampong Cham and had left the robes to marry, and when the Khmer Rouge came they were killing monks and men who could read, so he had stopped being able to read. He had stopped for four years. He herded water buffalo and said yes to everything and let his face go stupid, and he lived, and his wife and his two daughters did not. Afterward, in the camp, he had begun to read again, slowly, like a man learning to walk on a leg that had been broken. He had led the chanting at the Lowell wat since 1986. sections.text: Vibol came out onto the porch in his socks. He was forty now, heavy in the face, with his father's chain around his neck. He saw the achar at the gate and the boy on the trash bags and his relatives crowding out behind him onto the porch and the steps, and the neighbors coming out onto their own porches, up and down the street, because a crowd draws a crowd and because it was Pchum Ben and everybody was home. Lok Achar, I'm sorry, come in, come in. There was a boy, a thief, the children were frightened. It's nothing. Do you know this boy? Vibol looked at him. He looked at the face. No. He is your father, said the achar. Kong Sarin. Nobody on the porch said anything. A woman behind Vibol made a small sound in her throat. Somebody laughed and stopped. Vibol went red and then white. He came down the steps in his socks onto the cold walk. Lok Achar, with respect. With great respect. My father has been dead ten years. His ashes are in my house. I have his photograph. I have taken food to the wat for him every day this week. I'm not a stupid man. He pointed at the boy, who had sat up now on the bags. That is Nhem Chann's boy from the Acre. sections.heading: VII. Bay Ben
sections.dateline: The wat · the last morning of Pchum Ben
sections.text: Before light on the fifteenth day the yard of the wat was full. It was cold, and people stood in their coats over their good clothes, the old women in white, with their breath showing, and the windows of the building lit yellow behind them, and the monks chanting inside where it was warm. Each family had brought a bowl of bay ben, the little balls of sticky rice mixed with sesame and beans, and before the sun came up they walked around the building three times in the dark and threw them out into the yard and the grass and the parking lot, a handful at a time, for the dead who had no family to feed them. The old women said that was why it was done before light, because the hungry ones are ashamed to be seen. Achar Moeun stood on the steps in his white shirt and led them. He had come straight from the hospital. There was still floor wax on his shoes. Kong Vibol walked the circle with his wife and his children. Behind him walked Nhem Chann, whom he had gone to see on the Thursday in the Acre, and had sat with in her kitchen for two hours, and had given the rent and more than the rent and a job in the shop, which she would start on Monday. title: Five Places
logline: In the season when the dead come home hungry, an unlucky boy walks into a rich man's house as if he knows it.

verses.text: The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary two thieves, close companions, go with a great crowd to the Jetavana monastery where the Buddha is teaching. They are “knot-breakers,” pickpockets who undo the knots in which people tie up their coins. One of them listens and is changed; the other finds five small coins tied in the hem of a man's garment and takes them. The next day food is cooked as usual in the thief's house and none in his friend's, and the thief and his wife jeer at the friend for being so wise that he cannot get a meal. He reflects that the man takes himself for wise only because he is a fool, goes with his family to the Buddha and tells him, and the Buddha speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Natchez-Under-the-Hill was the landing below the bluff at Natchez, known up and down the Mississippi for its gambling rooms, dance houses and boatmen; a traveler said you could see an acre of flatboats lying there at any time. In July 1835 a mob at Vicksburg, upriver, hanged five gamblers, and committees in other river towns moved against theirs. Natchez in those years was also one of the great markets of the domestic slave trade, centered on the Forks of the Road east of town. Some enslaved men in the river towns, draymen among them, were allowed to hire their own time and keep what they earned above a fixed payment to their owners. The smallest coin that passed on the lower river was the picayune, the Spanish half-real, worth six and a quarter cents. Northern masters did advertise for runaway apprentices at a derisive “six cents reward.” In February 1836 volunteers for the war in Texas were passing down the river.

The first American showboat was the Floating Theatre built at Pittsburgh in 1831 by the English actor William Chapman, who with his family of nine drifted down the Ohio and Mississippi each season, playing at the landings for fifty cents or its worth in produce, and sold the boat at New Orleans. The Fennos and their boat are invented after that pattern. As You Like It had long been played on American stages. The lines here are from Act II, scene vii, where the starving Orlando bursts in on the banished Duke's supper, and from Act V, scene i, where the clown Touchstone quotes “a saying” to a country fellow who has just told him, “Ay, sir, I have a pretty wit.”

sections.heading: I. The Trumpet
sections.text: Natchez was two towns then. The one on the bluff had the brick houses and the banks. The one under the bluff was a shelf of mud between the hill and the river, a single street called Silver Street and whatever hung off it: grog shops, dance houses, boatmen's lodgings, and at the landing an acre of flatboats tied gunwale to gunwale. A mile back of the bluff, at the Forks of the Road, the traders were selling people that winter by the hundred, and the cotton those people were bought to pick came down Silver Street on drays and went out by the same landing. Tobe Finch and Dab Harker had come down the river in the fall as hands on a flour boat out of Cincinnati. Tobe was sixteen and Dab a year older. The cholera of thirty-two had made orphans of them both, and the township had bound them out, Tobe and his small brother Pim to a tanner and Dab to a man who made rope. They had run from their indentures the same week. There was a notice out for each of them in a Cincinnati paper, offering six cents reward, which came to a quarter of a cent less than one picayune a head. They lived by their fingers. Dab was the hand and Tobe was the stall. Tobe went ahead into a crowd and stopped short, or

sections.heading: II. The Banquet
sections.dateline: Aboard the Floating Theatre · that night
sections.text: They got in by the stern while the trumpet was still going. The room was as narrow as a covered bridge. There were plank benches, and a row of tallow candles in tin reflectors across the front of a stage no bigger than a wagon bed. The benches were full of Kentucky boatmen, draymen, steamboat hands, clerks down from the bluff, men with rifles on their way to Texas, and women from the dance houses. At the back by the door, where colored people were let to stand, there were hack drivers and market women with their passes. The plan was the usual one. When the place was full and the play well along, Tobe would go up the gangway between the benches and block it, and Dab would come along behind him through the standing people, working. Tobe got as far as the middle of the gangway. On the stage an old servant had lain down in a forest that was painted on a bedsheet, saying that he could go no further, that he was dying for food. Tobe had Pim at home. He stopped to hear what became of the old man, and he never went any further up the gangway that night. What became of him was this. A duke who had been turned out of his own country was sitting down to supper in the forest with his people. T

sections.heading: III. The Cold Hearth
sections.dateline: Below Silver Street · the next day
sections.text: Five picayunes bought meal and a catfish and a twist of coffee. By noon there was a fire in front of Dab's lean-to, and Sukey had the fish in the skillet and dodgers in the ashes. There was no fire in front of the other. Tobe had been at the landing since daylight asking for work. The cotton there was rolled by men whose masters were paid for them, and nobody would give a boy a picayune to do what he already owned a man to do. A storekeeper let him sweep and then said he had not asked him to. He had walked among a hundred pockets that morning with his hands at his sides, and he could not have told anyone why, only that the thing was finished. Pim sat on the sill of the lean-to with his knees up, watching Sukey's skillet. Here he is, Dab said. Here's the scholar. He went to the play and got so wise he can't find his dinner. Don't it smell good, Solomon? said Sukey. You're so almighty wise now, how is it there's nothing cooking at your house? Dab laughed until he had to put down his cup. He was the one with fish in the skillet, and it stood to reason that he was the one with sense. Tobe looked at him across the two yards of mud. He thought: he does not know. He is as big a fool as I

sections.heading: IV. The Coat of Patches
sections.dateline: Aboard the Floating Theatre · that afternoon
sections.text: By day the theatre was a house like any other. There was washing on the roof. One of the sons was painting a bedsheet into a palace. Old Mr. Fenno, who was the Duke at night, was the cook by day, and he had the plank set up on the stage and was laying dinner on it for eleven. Mrs. Fenno sat on the edge of the stage with the clown's coat across her knees, sewing a red patch over a worn green one. It was said of her that off the stage she did not use six words in a day, and that when she did speak it was a line out of some play if she could find one to fit. Tobe stood in the gangway where he had stood the night before, holding his brother's hand, and told her. He told her that he and another had come aboard to rob her house, and what his part was to have been, and that he had not done it because he was hearing the play. He told her about the five picayunes and whose they were. He told her about the cold hearth, and what Dab and Sukey had said to him across the mud. He says I've got so wise I can't get my dinner. He thinks it, too. Mrs. Fenno bit off her thread. She looked at him a good while, and then at the small boy. Then she gave him the line, in the clown's voice, which was her o

title: Welcome to Our Table
logline: Two runaway apprentices who pick pockets under the hill at Natchez slip aboard a floating theatre; only one of them remembers to steal.

verses.text: If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Udāyī lives with the Buddha at Jetavana, and whenever the great elders leave the Dhamma Hall he goes in and sits in the preacher’s seat. Some visiting monks see him there, take him for a learned elder, and question him about the aggregates, the elements and the sense-spheres. He knows nothing about any of it. Scornful, they ask what such a monk is doing in the same monastery as the Buddha and report him. The Buddha answers with this verse: a fool can wait on the wise for a lifetime and learn the Dhamma no more than a spoon learns the taste of the curry. At the end of it the visiting monks themselves are freed. The next verse in the Dhammapada (65) completes the image: the intelligent man who sits with the wise for a moment knows the truth as the tongue knows the taste of soup.
bg.history:
Until the 1960s nearly all Chinese food in the United States was Cantonese, cooked by and for families from the Pearl River delta. After the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened the country to new arrivals, and especially after President Nixon’s visit to China in 1972, New York discovered Sichuan and Hunan cooking, with its chilies, sourness and smoked and cured meats. Many of the new cooks and owners came by way of Taiwan, where mainland soldiers and officials who had retreated with the Nationalists in 1949 had opened restaurants serving their home provinces’ food. The best known of them, the Hunanese chef Peng Chang-kuei, had cooked official banquets in Taipei and opened a restaurant on East 44th Street around 1973, and the dish he is credited with, General Tso’s chicken, became the most famous Hunan dish in America; when Peng later opened a restaurant in Hunan itself, the locals found it too sweet.

Taiwanese-run restaurants spread up and down Manhattan in the following years; one of the first of the Szechuan chains opened at Broadway and 97th Street in 1976, with Taiwanese students from Columbia driving its deliveries. Zeng Shifu’s first restaurant burned in the Changsha fire of November 1938, set by Nationalist officials so that the advancing Japanese would find nothing; more than 30,000 people died and about nine-tenths of the city’s buildings burned.

sections.heading: I. The Photograph
sections.text: The Xiang Garden had nineteen tables, a red lacquer screen to hide the kitchen door, and a porcelain Laughing Buddha beside the register with his belly rubbed pale by two years of customers on their way out. Before that it had been a luncheonette, and before that a Cuban-Chinese place that sold fried plantains with the pork fried rice, and the old counter stools were still bolted to the floor along one wall where nobody had been able to get them up. Zeng Shifu did the cooking. He was sixty-six. He had been a scullery boy in a restaurant in Changsha that burned with the rest of the city in 1938, and a cook for an infantry division all through the war, and he had crossed to Taiwan in 1949 with the division and its stoves, and for twenty years he had cooked at a restaurant off Zhongshan North Road in Taipei where the generals ate. In 1971 a cousin brought him over. He wore a sleeveless undershirt and a paper hat and cloth slippers, and he did not come out of the kitchen, ever, for anybody. Yao Delu came out of the kitchen for everybody. He was from the same county as Zeng and had been at his elbow since 1940, when the division took him on to wash pots, and when Zeng crossed the strait

sections.heading: II. The Chair
sections.dateline: The kitchen · a Monday night in November
sections.text: The three young cooks came in the back way, as cooks do, a little after ten. They worked at a new Szechuan place on Second Avenue in the Fifties, and Monday was their night off, and they had come all the way uptown on the subway to see the master of Hunan cooking. Kao was from Taichung and had cooked in Taipei. Wong was from Hong Kong and spoke Cantonese and English and not much Mandarin. Lin was nineteen and the youngest and had been in New York four months, and he had cut the photograph out of the newspaper and kept it in his wallet. Through the screen door they saw the old man in the white jacket in the bamboo chair by the back door, and Lin knew him from the picture. They came in and bowed a little, and Kao said their names and where they worked, and said they had come to learn. Yao was delighted. He sent the dishwasher for more tea. He asked them where their families were from, and told them about the burning of Changsha, which he had not seen, and about the generals in Taipei, and which of them had liked his food very salty. Kao asked about the Dong’an chicken. How did Shifu balance the five flavors in it? It was the sourness that people talked about. Balance, said Yao. Yes.

sections.heading: III. The Ladle
sections.dateline: The same kitchen · Tuesday, before the lunch rush
sections.text: Kao would not go back. Wong and Lin went back the next morning at eleven, before their own shift, and came in by the alley again, and this time the bamboo chair was empty, and an old man in an undershirt and a paper hat was standing at the big burner with his back to them, lighting it with a twist of newspaper. It went up with a roar, a ring of blue jets as wide as a dinner plate, and he set the wok on it, and while it heated he turned around and looked at them. Lin told him. He told it straight, the way it had happened, and he felt bad telling it, because the old man in the white jacket had given them tea. Wong put in a word here and there in English. They had come to learn from the master of Hunan cooking. The man in the picture could not tell them which vinegar. He could not tell them how the pork was smoked. He could not name the five flavors. He had forgotten bitter. How could a man live thirty years beside the master and not know that? Zeng listened to the end. Then he laughed, a short laugh that turned into a cough, and turned back to the wok, and poured in oil, and swirled it, and did not say anything for a while. Out front somebody was vacuuming. A delivery boy came in wit

place: Upper West Side, Manhattan, New York
logline: Three young cooks ride uptown to learn from the master of Hunan cooking and find a smiling old man in the chef's chair.

verses.text: If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the thirty young men from Pāṭheyya are among the Buddha's first followers. In the older Vinaya account they are picnicking in a grove with their wives; the one without a wife has brought a courtesan, who steals their things while they are distracted and runs. Searching for her, they meet the Buddha, who asks whether it would be better for them to seek a woman or to seek themselves. They become monks on the spot, receiving bowls and robes by miracle, and take up the thirteen ascetic practices. Long afterward they return, hear him teach on the round of rebirth that has no discoverable beginning (in the Saṃyutta, the blood they have shed as slaughtered cattle, goats and pigs is more than the water of the four great oceans), and all become arahats before they rise from their seats. When the monks marvel at how quickly they understood, the Buddha tells the Tuṇḍila birth story: thirty drunken men came with nooses to buy an old woman's pig for a feast, the pig preached to them, and they took the precepts.
bg.history:
The first band of Dominican friars reached Hispaniola in September 1510 under Pedro de Córdoba. They lived poorly from the start, in rough clothing and constant fasts, in a convent built of straw in Santo Domingo. On December 21, 1511, Antonio de Montesinos preached the Advent sermon that first publicly denounced the enslavement of the island's Taíno under the encomienda, the grant of Indigenous people's labor to colonists. The Taíno population of Hispaniola had fallen to about 60,000 by 1507 and was reported at about 32,000 in 1514. That year the cleric Bartolomé de las Casas, reading Ecclesiasticus 34 for a Pentecost sermon in Cuba, gave up his own encomienda.

On his second voyage, Columbus deliberately released domestic pigs in the West Indies so later expeditions would find food, and they went wild. In Spain the fattened household pig is killed in the winter matanza. In Galicia Saint Martin's day, November 11, is the traditional day for it, which gave Spanish the saying that every pig gets its Saint Martin. Cervantes has Don Quixote use it in 1615, in Ormsby's translation: "its Martinmas will come to it as it does to every pig." The ceiba, or silk-cotton tree, is native to the Caribbean. Its seed pods are full of the cottony fiber called kapok, and the commentary's Kappāsika grove is, in Pāli, a "cotton grove." The Bahoruco mountains, where the Taíno leader Enriquillo held out against the Spanish from 1519, are in the island's southwest.

sections.heading: I. Martinmas
sections.dateline: The Ozama River, Hispaniola · the eleventh of November, 1510
sections.text: There were thirty of them, from Trujillo and Cáceres and the villages between, sons of houses that had more name than land. They had come out in the spring fleet with their swords and their fathers' debts. In the summer the governor's men had given each of them a share of Indians, so many heads written down beside each name, and they had sent those Indians up to the streams of the Cibao to wash gold. In the autumn the gold came down to the smelting house at Concepción. When the King's fifth had been taken out, what was left went into one leather purse, because they had come out together and meant to stay together. Diego de Hinojosa wore it around his neck under his shirt. On Saint Martin's day they crossed the river from the stone city to the east bank and held a matanza under the ceibas, the way their fathers did at home. In Extremadura every house killed its pig at Martinmas. Here nobody needed to keep a pig. The pigs the Admiral had let loose on the island seventeen years before had gone wild in the forest by the thousand, and that morning the dogs had run one down in the cane brakes and held it by the ears until Alonso Golfín came up with the knife. Now it hung from a low limb

sections.heading: II. The Straw House
sections.dateline: Santo Domingo and the Pearl Coast · 1510–1515
sections.text: His name was Fray Gil. He was not a priest. He was a lay brother, which meant he cooked for the others and swept and begged in the streets of the city with a basket, and before that, he told them, he had kept pigs for the Count's people on the oak plains outside Trujillo until he was twenty-six, and then he had gone to the war at Granada, and then to the friars at Salamanca. He sat with them under the ceibas until it was dark. What he said they could not afterward agree on. Some of them said he talked about the purse, and some about their mothers, and some about the Indians in the mines, and some about nothing at all. All thirty agreed that it had been very simple, and that it had not taken long, and that at the end of it he had put the basket down and said, Come, and they had come. They left the dogs at the ford. In the morning, in the friars' straw house at the edge of the city, there were thirty white habits lying folded on the dirt floor, of good Castilian wool, though the friars had brought nothing from Spain but what they wore, and no ship had come in since August. Nobody in the house would say where they had come from. The thirty put them on. They sent their papers back to t

sections.heading: III. Martinmas Again
sections.dateline: The east bank of the Ozama · the eleventh of November, 1515
sections.text: The year before, the King's men had counted the Indians of the island again so that they could divide them again, and found hardly more than half the number of the count seven years before. In the city they were saying the island would have to be filled with Indians from somewhere else, or with Africans, or the mines would stop. On Saint Martin's day Fray Gil took the thirty across the river to the old ceibas and sat them down among the roots, in their habits, brown now and patched with every color of cloth the island had. Across the water the city was killing its pigs. They could hear it from where they sat. They could smell the singeing. He let them listen a while. Then he asked them a question, the way he had the first time. Sons. Which is more, the water in the sea between here and Sanlúcar, or the blood that has run out on the ground since the first Martinmas? Some of them had crossed that sea three times now. Nobody answered for a while. Then Diego de Hinojosa said, The blood, Brother. Yes, said Fray Gil. Count. Every house in Castile, every November, one pig, since before the Moors. Every ox and every sheep and every hen. Every man at Granada, ours and theirs. Count this isl

sections.heading: IV. Every Pig
sections.text: Afterward the friars talked about it in the house. They said it had taken Fray Gil one afternoon to give those thirty what most men did not get in fifty years of prayer, and a young friar from Burgos said that it was not just, and that it did not seem to him to follow the order of grace as he had been taught it. Fray Gil was peeling yuca at the table. He said it was not one afternoon. Then he told them a story his grandmother had told him on the oak plains, which had happened, she said, in her grandmother's time, in a village outside Trujillo. An old widow there had found two piglets in a ditch where their mother had left them, and raised them in her house like children, and called the big one Snout and the little one Little Snout. When they were fat, men came every autumn to buy them, and every autumn she said, Would you sell your own children to be eaten? One Martinmas thirty young men of the village, drunk since morning, came to her door with money and ropes. She would not sell. So they gave her wine until she would, and she said, Not the big one. Take the little one. And she filled the trough by the door and called him, which she had never done before, because she always called

sections.heading: V. The Cotton
sections.text: The purse was never found, and neither was she. Gonzalo de Chaves asked about her among the Indians for a long time, in the language he had learned on the Pearl Coast, and once a fisherman told him that there was a woman in the mountains of the Bahoruco, where the King's men did not go, who had come out of the east a long time before with a purse of gold, and had walked into a river with it and come out without it. Gonzalo did not know if that was her. He went on asking. In March, in the dry season, he crossed the Ozama alone to the east bank, and the old ceibas were bare, as the Indians had said they would be, and the pods had split. The cotton was coming down out of them over the river, slowly, in no wind at all, and settling on the brown water, and riding down it toward the sea.

title: The Silk-Cotton Trees
logline: On Saint Martin's day 1510, thirty young hidalgos chase a Taíno woman who took their gold, and meet a friar under the ceibas.

verses.text: Fools of little understanding have themselves for their greatest enemies, for they do evil deeds which must bear bitter fruits.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the leper Suppabuddha sits at the outer edge of the crowd in Räjagaha, hears the Buddha teach, and is transformed. Too humble to push through the crowd, he waits until it has gone. On the road, Sakka, lord of the gods, appears in the air and tests him, promising him limitless wealth if he will renounce the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. Suppabuddha calls him a shameless fool. He is not poor, he says, because he has the seven treasures: faith, virtue, conscience, concern, learning, giving and wisdom. Sakka reports this to the Buddha, who says that no amount of money could make the leper say it. Suppabuddha visits the Buddha, is warmly received, and on his way home is killed by a young cow. The cow is a vengeful spirit, once a courtesan murdered by four young men, who has sworn to kill all four. When the monks ask about his fate, the Buddha tells them he has been reborn among the gods, and that he was a leper because in a past life he spat on a holy man.
bg.history:
In the mid-nineteenth century Norway had more leprosy than any other country in Europe, most of it in poor fishing and farming communities on the west coast. In 1856 it set up the world’s first national leprosy register, and isolation laws followed in 1877 and 1885. In 1873 the Bergen physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified the bacterium that causes the disease. Some Norwegians who had it emigrated to the Upper Midwest, and before 1890 about fifty cases were reported in Minnesota. Most patients lived with their families or on county poor farms, in rooms of their own, with their own bedding and dishes. In 1888 Hansen himself came to Minnesota and spent several weeks in Red Wing, the Goodhue County seat, studying the immigrant cases (MNopedia).

Many of those immigrants brought the revival of Hans Nielsen Hauge with them. Hauge was a lay preacher who was jailed fourteen times under the Conventicle Act, which forbade religious meetings without a parish priest until Norway repealed it in 1842. Women preached in his movement from its earliest years. In America his followers formed the Hauge Synod, a low-church body that opened its seminary in Red Wing in 1879. The old women’s cow-spirit borrows from the huldra of Scandinavian folklore, a beautiful forest woman who hides a cow’s tail under her skirts.

sections.heading: I. The Barn Door
sections.text: Everybody in the township knew Tollef, and nobody knew his other name. The Norwegians called him Spedalske-Tollef, Leper Tollef, and the Yankees in Kenyon called him the leper, and the children called him nothing at all, because when they saw him on the road they ran. He was fifty-eight years old and lived at the county poor farm in a room by himself at the end of the woodshed, with his own bed and his own towel and his own tin plate and cup and spoon, which nobody else touched and which were washed separately in a pan of their own. The state Board of Health had sent the rules, and the poor farm kept them. It was not cruel. They brought his dinner to the door. In winter they kept his stove going. He had come over from Sunnfjord in 1866 with the sickness already in him and his name already in the leprosy register, where the King’s doctors had been writing down every leper in Norway since 1856, and he had worked as a hired man on half the farms between Kenyon and Zumbrota until his hands went. sections.dateline: The section road · the same afternoon
sections.text: When the meeting was over he wanted more than anything to go and tell her. But there was no getting through. Everybody wanted to shake her hand, and they were packed in the doorway three deep, and Tollef was not a man who could push into a crowd. People made room for him, but it was the wrong kind of room. sections.text: Synneve Lien was in her kitchen baking lefse on the stove top for the preacher’s supper, and the preacher was sitting at the table shelling peas into a bowl, because she could not stand to sit with her hands empty, when a gentleman came to the screen door. Synneve said afterward that she never heard a wagon. He stood on the step in a black coat and a gold watch chain, with his hat in his hand, and he did not come in, and he spoke past Synneve to Gjertrud Hovland as if they knew each other. He told her all of it. What he had offered and to whom and what the leper had said back. He told it the way a man tells about a horse that would not be sold. Gjertrud went on shelling peas. You could stand on air over that ditch till Judgment Day, she said. You could offer him a thousand dollars, or ten thousand, or every acre in Goodhue County with the barns on it. You will not get that man to say it. Not now. There were mosquitoes coming up off the water. He was not in a hurry. Ole Kvale had a red heifer, a yearling, with a white star on her forehead, that he had bought that spring from a man in Holden who was glad to sell her and did not say why. She had been in the pasture all day. Nobody ever found out how she got through the fence. There was a rail down afterward, at the corner by the creek, but Ole swore it had been sound in the morning. The Kvale boy found Tollef in the lane at five the next morning when he went out to bring in the cows. His face was not hurt. The boy said it looked like he was asleep in church. The heifer was standing in the creek a little way down, up to her knees in the water, drinking. sections.dateline: The poor farm burying ground · three days later
sections.text: They buried him at the poor farm, in the corner of the field where the county put its own, because the churches did not want a leper in their churchyards, and no pastor came. Gjertrud Hovland came. She had stayed on in the township when she heard. A good many people came with her who would not have crossed the road to Tollef while he lived, and stood around the grave in the wind with their hats in their hands, and some of them were ashamed and some were only curious. They stood around her in the stubble and asked her things, the way people in the barn had wanted to ask. Where is he now? said Ole Kvale, who was ashamed. That was my heifer. Where did he go? verses.text: That deed is not well done of which a man must repent, and the reward of which he receives crying and with a tearful face.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, thieves who have robbed a rich man of Sāvatthī divide their loot in a farmer's field, and one of them drops a purse of a thousand coins. At dawn the Buddha passes the field with Ānanda and says, "See, Ānanda, a poisonous snake," and Ānanda answers, "I see it, a deadly poisonous snake." The farmer goes with his goad to kill it, finds the purse, covers it with earth and goes on plowing. The owners track the thieves to the field, find the purse, beat the farmer and bring him before the king, who orders him put to death. Led away under the whip, he repeats the two sentences and nothing else, and when he is allowed to explain, the king takes him to the Buddha that evening to confirm the story. The Buddha says a wise man should not do a deed he must afterward repent, and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
In 1694 the German mystic Johannes Kelpius and some forty followers settled along Wissahickon Creek northwest of Philadelphia, believing the end of the world would come that year. When it did not, they kept a school, shared their medical knowledge and went on searching the stars. Kelpius died in 1708 and the community dwindled, though some who had joined it, among them Conrad Matthai and Christopher Witt, stayed on in the neighborhood. Bruder Elias is invented. Philadelphia County was full of Irish and German servants who had sold years of labor for their passage; Pennsylvania's 1700 law gave a servant at the end of his term two suits of clothes, one new, an axe, a grubbing hoe and a weeding hoe. The Jesuit Joseph Greaton opened St. Joseph's in Philadelphia in 1733, the one place in the English-speaking world where Mass could then be said openly. Under the province's criminal act of 1718, burglary, like conjuration and witchcraft, was punishable by death, and men awaiting the Court of Oyer and Terminer were held in the stone prison at Third and High Streets.

Benjamin Franklin began printing Poor Richard's Almanack for the year 1733 under the name of Richard Saunders, a poor stargazer, and by 1739 was printing and selling it on Market Street. Besides the calendar, the weather and the stars, each month carried proverbs and squibs, most of them borrowed from books like Thomas Fuller's Gnomologia and sharpened in the rewording; the almanac for 1739 began its year in March, as the province's calendar still did, so its sixth month was August, and that is where "If thou injurest Conscience" stands. Almanac makers were often pestered to find thieves and stray horses by the stars; Poor Richard complained of it in his preface for 1742.

sections.heading: I. The Long Glass
sections.text: Owen Phelan had been four years a servant and two years a free man, and he did not yet own anything that would not go in a handcart. He had come from the county of Waterford in the spring of 1733, bound for four years to pay his passage, and a Welsh farmer on the Ridge named Hugh Jones had bought the four years off the ship at the Philadelphia wharf. When they were served, Owen got what the law of the province said a servant should have at the end: two complete suits of apparel, one of them new, a new axe, a grubbing hoe and a weeding hoe. Hugh Jones died the same winter. His widow could not work the place and would not sell it, so she let Owen have the fourteen acres along the brow of the hill on the halves, and the yoke of red oxen with them, Buck and Bright, because nobody else could drive them. In August he was breaking the stubble ground for wheat. The Welsh on the Ridge plowed a fallow three times in a summer, and this was the third. He was in the field before the sun, because by ten o'clock the heat came up out of the ground and the oxen hung their heads and would not be talked to. From the bottom of the field he could see over the treetops into the gorge where the creek ran

sections.heading: II. Tanbark
sections.text: In the night someone had robbed Lorenz Kunkel, the tanner at the foot of the township. The run that fed his vats went under his bark house in a stone culvert, and the thieves had come up through it on their hands and knees, knocked the stones out of his cellar wall, and carried off his strongbox with everything in it. Kunkel came down at first light to see to the fire and found his cellar open to the creek. His sons Hannes and Peter went after them with Velten Hoffmann the constable. It was not hard. A man who has walked through a tanyard carries ground oak bark in the welts of his shoes for a mile, and the thieves had walked out through Kunkel's yard in the dark. The bark lay in crumbs up the lane, and the dew showed where they had crossed the meadow. It led them up the Ridge to the stump at the corner of the widow Jones's fallow, where the strongbox lay on its back with the lid broken off and the grass trampled flat around it. There the thieves' tracks went off every which way into the woods. But there was another track, fresh, that came from the plowing to the stump and back: a man in heavy shoes, one of them mended at the heel with a piece of leather that did not match. It went

sections.heading: III. The Germantown Road
sections.text: They did not put him in the cart. They tied him by the wrists to the tail of it and he walked behind in the dust. Peter Kunkel drove, and Hannes walked alongside with the whip, and whenever the cart slowed on a hill, or Owen stumbled, or whenever it occurred to him, Hannes laid the whip across Owen's back. Velten Hoffmann walked on the other side and did not stop him. It was the hottest part of the day. The road went down through the Germantown fields to the long street of stone houses with their half-doors, and people came out onto their stoops to see the Irishman who had robbed Kunkel. Owen walked behind the cart and said the old man's words. He did not have the German for them. He said them the way he had heard them, in the old man's deep voice and then in the boy's high one, as near as he could make it, like a man saying a prayer in a language he was never taught. Siehst du, Jost? Eine Schlange. Ich seh sie, Bruder. Eine giftige Schlange. When the whip came down he said them. When it did not he said them. He said them past the Mennonite meetinghouse and past the market square, where the women stopped their bargaining and turned. He did not say another word. At the market square

The creek was low and loud over the rocks. The old man's hut stood above it in the hemlocks, a room of logs with a stone chimney and a ladder up to a platform on the roof, where the long glass was lashed under a piece of oilcloth. The old man was sitting on a bench by the spring. The boy was carrying water. The Justice took off his hat. He asked his questions one at a time, the way he did at the quarter sessions, and the old man answered them the same way. Brother Elias. Did you and the boy go this morning to a place where a man was plowing? Yes, your worship. What did you see there? A purse with gold in it, by the stump of a chestnut. When you saw it, what did you say? The old man said it, word for word, and the boy put down his bucket and said his part, and they were the same words Owen had said behind the cart all the way to Germantown, in the same order, and Velten Hoffmann laughed out loud and then was ashamed of it. If this man had not named you, the Justice said, he would have hanged. He saved his neck with your words. He

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the garland-maker Sumana brings King Bimbisāra eight measures of jasmine every morning. One day he meets the Buddha entering Rājagaha in a blaze of light and, reckoning that the king can at worst kill or banish him, throws all eight handfuls over the Teacher instead. The flowers hang in the air on four sides like a pavilion and travel with him, and the whole city follows to the sound of drums, waving cloths. Sumana's wife, terrified, takes the children to the king and disowns her husband. The king, a secret disciple, feigns anger and sends her home, then joins the Buddha, who chooses to sit in the palace courtyard rather than indoors so that everyone can see what the garland-maker has done. Afterward the king gives Sumana eight of everything. Asked by Ānanda what the man's reward will be, the Buddha says he will not fall into a state of suffering for a hundred thousand aeons and will one day become a solitary Buddha; the flowers fall onto the roof of the Buddha's chamber, and that evening he speaks the verse.
bg.history:
By 1857 the harbor of New Bedford held 329 vessels worth more than twelve million dollars, and the town counted as the richest per head in North America. Its whaling fortunes built the mansions and gardens along County Street; its crews were drawn from everywhere: free and escaped African Americans, Wampanoag men from Gay Head on Martha's Vineyard and Pequots, Cape Verdeans, Pacific Islanders and Europeans. The town was an important stop on the Underground Railroad; by 1853 it had 1,008 African American residents, some 700 of them escaped from slavery, and Frederick Douglass had worked on its wharves for three years after his own escape. The Port Society dedicated the Seamen's Bethel on Johnny Cake Hill in 1832; its walls carry cenotaphs for whalemen lost at sea. Today the old waterfront is the New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park.

Herman Melville sat in the Bethel before he shipped out on the whaler Acushnet in January 1841, and ten years later opened Moby-Dick in New Bedford, with Father Mapple's sermon on Jonah preached from a pulpit shaped like a ship's bow. The book sold poorly and was out of print by the end of Melville's life. The real pulpit in 1841 was most likely a plain box; the prow now standing in the Bethel was inspired by the 1956 film of the novel and first put up in 1961. Uncle Simeon, the Sumners and Captain Hathaway are invented; Melville's own harpooneer Tashtego is a Gay Head man.

sections.heading: I. Eight Bunches
sections.text: Joseph Sumner grew flowers on a lot at the top of the town that belonged to Captain Barzillai Hathaway, and every morning of the summer, before the Captain's household was up, he cut eight bunches and carried them in a flat basket on his head to the kitchen door of the Captain's house on County Street. Roses, mostly, the red ones the town was proud of, and a few white, with honeysuckle and mignonette for the smell. The cook gave him a dollar on Saturdays. He lived in a two-room cottage on the same lot with his wife Ann and their two boys, and the Captain owned the cottage too, and the well, and very nearly the ground the boys walked on to school. The Captain was called the Commodore along the wharves, though he had never commanded anything but whaleships, because he walked down to his counting room every morning as if he were taking a squadron out. He had made three voyages as master and come home rich from the third, and he had shares now in eleven ships. Men who had sailed under him said he once kept a boatsteerer in irons in the run for fifty days off the coast of Japan, for answering back. Men who owed him money crossed the street. He had buried his wife and a son, the son lost

sections.heading: II. Union Street
sections.text: A girl shaking a rug out of a window on County Street saw it first and screamed, and then the street was full. Nobody ran away. People came out of the houses half dressed, the Irish girls from the kitchens and the masters of the houses in their dressing gowns, and they went up to him and walked all the way around him, slowly, the roses and all, as if it were the only proper thing to do, and some went round him three times, and then fell in behind. By the time he reached the top of the town there were a hundred people following him, and by the time he came back down Union Street toward the water there were a thousand. Whalemen came off the ships in the harbor in their boats. Coopers came out of the shops with their adzes in their hands. Quaker women in grey bonnets walked beside Cape Verdean sailors with gold rings in their ears, and a Gay Head boatsteerer carried a white child on his shoulders so she could see. A brass band that had been practicing for the Fourth of July came out of its hall in its shirtsleeves and fell in ahead with the brass and the big drum and played whatever they knew, and people sang whatever they knew, and everybody waved whatever they had, handkerchiefs, ha

sections.heading: III. The Commodore's Yard
sections.text: Ann was at the washtub. She looked at the basket. Where are the flowers? I gave them to Uncle Simeon. The Commodore's flowers. He can turn us off the lot, Joseph said. I know that. I thought about it in the road. I would do it again. Listen. You can hear them from here. She could hear the drum down in the town and the shouting. She did not believe a word of the rest of it. Ann Sumner had been born free in Providence and had seen what happened to people who crossed men like the Commodore. She had seen a whole family put out of a house near the docks with their bedsteads in the snow, and she had seen what became of a man the merchants agreed not to hire. She told Joseph so. She told him she had the boys to think of, if he had not. Then she dried her hands, put on her good bonnet, took a boy by each hand, and walked up County Street to the Commodore's front door, which she had never in her life gone near, and asked for the Captain. He came out into the hall himself. He was a big grey man with a face like a shut door. Captain Hathaway, my husband gave your roses away this morning to Uncle Simeon Coombs, every one of them, and came home with the basket empty. I told him what I thought.

sections.heading: IV. The Roof Walk
sections.text: He sent for Joseph Sumner at five o'clock. Joseph came to the kitchen door, as he had come every morning for six summers, and the cook sent him round to the front. When you threw my roses at him, the Commodore said, what did you say? I said to myself, sir, let the Commodore turn me off the lot. I said the most he can give me is a dollar on Saturday, and the most he can take is the same. The Commodore looked at him for a long time. You are a bigger man than I am, he said. Then he gave him eight of everything he could think of. He gave him the deed to the lot and the cottage, made out that evening by a lawyer who was fetched from his supper. He gave him eight hundred dollars. He gave him eight cords of seasoned oak and eight barrels of sperm oil, enough to light the cottage the rest of his life, and eight shares in the bark that was fitting out at his wharf, and a standing order for eight bunches every summer morning at twice the price, as long as either of them lived. Ann came back from wherever she had gone to wait and found her husband sitting on the step of a house that belonged to him, with a piece of paper in his hands, laughing. Walking home down Union Street in the long June

title: The Roof Walk
logline: A Black gardener carrying a whaling captain's morning roses up County Street meets the old Gay Head harpooneer who meets every ship.

verses.text: As long as the evil deed done does not bear fruit, the fool thinks it is like honey; but when it ripens, then the fool suffers grief.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Uppalavaṇṇā, "the one with the color of the blue lotus," is a treasurer's daughter of Sāvatthī sought by so many kings and rich men that her father, unable to answer them all, asks whether she would leave the world. She agrees as gladly as if her head had been anointed with oil. As a new nun, taking her turn to light the lamp and sweep the Uposatha hall, she makes the flame her object of meditation and reaches awakening. Later she lives alone in a forest hut. A young man, her cousin, who has desired her since before she went forth, hides in the hut and assaults her; as he leaves, the earth opens and swallows him. The Buddha speaks this verse about the fool for whom evil tastes like honey until it ripens. When others wonder whether one who is awakened still feels desire, he answers that desire does not cling to such a person, as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, and he asks King Pasenadi to build a dwelling for nuns inside the city, so that they no longer live alone in the forest. At the editor's direction, this retelling changes one thing: there is no sexual assault. In its place is a different violation of her body and her solitude. Her cousin hides a camera where she bathes and spreads the images. Everything else follows the source in order.
bg.hist_title: Northern Virginia and the Page Valley, 2008
bg.history:
Korean immigrants began building businesses in Annandale, along Little River Turnpike, in the 1990s, and the area is now often called Koreatown; Fairfax County has nearly 40,000 Korean residents. Dry cleaning was a Korean trade across the region: in 2001 the Washington Post counted about 80 percent of the area's 1,200 cleaners as Korean-owned (Capital News Service). Korea is one of the few countries where the full ordination of women survived; nuns of the Jogye Order keep some 348 precepts (Korea Times). The Sutra of Forty-two Sections is traditionally held to be the first Buddhist sutra translated into Chinese; the English here is D. T. Suzuki's, from Soyen Shaku's Sermons of a Buddhist Abbot (Chicago: Open Court, 1906). The temple, the cabin and all the people are fictional.

Most of Virginia's karst follows Interstate 81 through the Valley and Ridge, where acidic water dissolves limestone into caves and the ground above can drop without warning, usually slowly and sometimes all at once; the state's highway department has recorded about 500 sinkholes that damaged roads in thirty years (Virginia Energy). Luray Caverns, found in 1878, lies under the Page Valley. Secretly filming a person undressed where she expects privacy had been a Class 1 misdemeanor in Virginia since 1994 (§ 18.2-386.1), but spreading such images was not a crime in the state until 2014 (§ 18.2-386.2). The lotus ponds the cook remembers are at Kenilworth Park & Aquatic Gardens in northeast Washington, where the lotuses bloom in the hot months of summer.

sections.heading: I. Shirts
sections.text: Han Myeong-su had a dry cleaner in a strip of shops on Little River Turnpike, between a Korean bakery and a store that sold rice cookers and phone cards. He had come over in 1979 and pressed other men's shirts for six years before he could buy a counter of his own, and he still pressed every collar himself, because a collar was where people looked. His wife had died the winter their daughter turned twelve. After that it was the two of them and the machines. Seo-yeon worked the counter after school, and then after college, when she had a degree in accounting from George Mason and no particular wish to use it. She was quiet at the register. She had a way of looking at a stain as if it had told her something, and a coolness about her that the aunts at the bakery next door said was like water in a stone basin. Customers came back. Men came back. A deacon's son from a Presbyterian church in Centreville brought one shirt at a time, so he would have a reason to come back on Thursday. A lawyer from Tysons brought shirts that were already clean. A Marine lieutenant from Quantico brought his dress blues in March and asked whether she ever went into the city. A man who owned three beauty-supp

sections.heading: II. The Candles
sections.text: The temple was a brick ranch house and a converted horse barn on four acres off Braddock Road, with a gravel lot and a stone lantern somebody had driven down from New Jersey in the back of a van. The Dharma hall was the barn. In the winter it held the cold like a well. As a postulant she did what she was told. She washed rice and scrubbed pots and cut radishes, and she was given the hall to keep. In her week she rose at half past two, swept the floor from the altar to the door, filled the water bowl, and lit the two candles before the abbot came across the yard at three with the wooden moktak to wake the house. On the fourth morning of her second week she lit the candles and did not get up. Nothing had happened. The flame stood on its wick in the cold room the way a person stands who has nowhere else to be. It leaned when the furnace came on and straightened when it stopped. She looked at it, and went on looking, and at some point the one who was looking set itself down the way you set down a bag you have carried so long you forgot it was in your hand. She did not pick it up again. When the abbot came in with the moktak she was still kneeling there, and he looked at her face, and s

sections.heading: III. The Hermitage
sections.text: A dentist's widow in McLean left the temple a cabin and twelve acres in the Page Valley, south of Luray, between the long wall of Massanutten and the Blue Ridge. You reached it by a gravel lane that ran through Delmer Breeden's pasture. Halfway along, the lane bent around a round hollow in the grass with a sycamore growing out of the bottom of it. After rain the hollow held water. The cows went around it. That's a sink, Delmer told her the first week. He was a tall man in his sixties who kept beef cattle and drove a school bus. Whole valley's hollow underneath. Luray Caverns is just the part they charge you to see. In Korea old nuns lived alone in hermitages up the mountain, and Cheongryeon asked to live at the cabin alone. The abbot did not like it. The board did not like it. She asked a second time, and then they said yes, because she was the kind of person who did not ask a third time, and because it was a long drive and nobody else wanted to go. She sat in the front room in the morning and the evening. She grew lettuce and perilla and long green peppers in a plot behind the cabin, and fed a cat that was not hers. There was no bath in the cabin, only a kitchen sink, so a previou

sections.heading: IV. The Link
sections.text: That fall the banks were failing on the television, and men who had been laid off stopped buying suits, and the cleaners on Little River Turnpike stood around their counters at three in the afternoon with nothing to press. On a Tuesday in October a link went around. It came first in emails, with a subject line in Korean that said you should see what the temple's nun is. Then it was on a community message board where people sold used Hondas and asked for immigration lawyers. Somebody had it taken down. Somebody put it back up. It was of her, in the shed, and it is not going to be described here. Enough people did that. The cook knew before anyone told her, because of the silence when she came into the temple kitchen on Wednesday and five bosals stopped talking at once. The abbot drove to Page County himself. Cheongryeon was on her knees in the pepper plants. He stood at the end of the row and told her, badly, the way men tell such things, and she listened with dirt on her hands. When he was done she got up and asked him where it would have been. Then she walked out to the shed and stood in the doorway and looked up. The deputy who came from Luray was a young man with a crew cut who

sections.heading: V. The Sink
sections.text: Nobody knows why Jang-ho drove out to the Page Valley one night in the middle of November. To take the light fixture down himself, maybe. To say he was sorry, or to say something worse. It was raining hard, the first real rain in weeks. Cheongryeon was asleep and heard nothing. Delmer Breeden, in the farmhouse at the head of the lane, heard nothing either. In the morning Delmer's cows were bawling at the fence. He walked out in his boots. Where the sink had been there was a hole in the pasture thirty feet across, with the sycamore lying over it like a dropped match, and the white van standing on its nose in brown water at the bottom. Jang-ho was inside. The rescue squad came out from Luray, and it took them until afternoon to bring him up. Delmer said he had driven that lane at dusk with a round bale on the front of the tractor, and it was solid. He said it to the deputy and to the man from the paper and to everybody at the feed store, and he was not a man who told stories. The ground had opened under that van, he said, like a mouth. On Little River Turnpike they said the same thing, with less doubt. The earth had swallowed him. The old women at the bakery said there was an old wor

sections.heading: VI. The Leaf
sections.text: The letter from Seoul did not come. The question did not go away. It was in the way the flower committee arranged its chrysanthemums with their backs to the left side of the hall, and in the way men who had brought shirts to the counter on Little River Turnpike thirteen years before now stopped talking when her name came up. At the December board meeting the woman from the flower committee asked it again. This time she did not ask the abbot. She turned around in her folding chair toward the kitchen pass-through, where the cook was wiping the counter. Bosal-nim. You cooked for nuns thirty years. You tell us. Is she still clean? The cook came out of the kitchen with the rag in her hand. She was eighty and walked as if her feet hurt, which they did. She stood at the end of the tables for a while before she said anything. Has anyone here been to the lotus ponds in Washington? By the river. Kenilworth. A few of them had. You took the children in July, when the lotuses were up. Go after it rains, the cook said. Look at a leaf. The rain sits on it like quicksilver. Big drops. The wind comes and tips the leaf, and the water runs off, all of it, and the leaf is dry. You can touch it. Dry. S

title: Honey on the Knife
place: Centreville and the Page Valley, Virginia
logline: A Korean American nun living alone in a Shenandoah Valley cabin is betrayed by the cousin who has wanted her since childhood.

verses.text: Let a fool month after month eat his food (like an ascetic) with the tip of a blade of Kusa grass, yet he is not worth the sixteenth particle of those who have well weighed the law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a resident monk grows jealous when his lay supporter honors a visiting elder with food, a robe, a barber and a bed. He tells the visitor he would do better to eat dung, tear out his hair with a palm comb, go naked and lie on the ground, and next day throws away the meal sent after him. For this he is reborn as Jambuka, who from infancy will eat nothing but excrement and will wear nothing. The naked ascetics take him in and then put him out. He lives at a flat rock used as a latrine, standing on one leg with his mouth open, tells people he eats only wind, and once a month takes their offerings on the tip of a blade of grass. The Buddha asks him for a night’s lodging, is refused, and sleeps in a cave nearby, where the Four Great Kings, Sakka and Brahmā visit him with lights. In the morning he tells Jambuka the truth about his life and its cause, tosses him a cloth to cover himself, and teaches him. Jambuka then rises seven palm trees into the air before his admirers to show them who is the teacher.
bg.history:
In 1902 the zoologist Charles Wardell Stiles identified the American hookworm, a parasite half an inch long that enters through bare feet from ground fouled with human waste (the itch it raises was called ground itch, or dew poison) and lives in the bowel on blood. It left millions of Southerners pale, thin and slow, and some of the worst cases craved clay and dirt. From 1909 to 1914 the Rockefeller Sanitary Commission paid for a campaign through the state boards of health. Its field doctors and microscopists held free county dispensaries one day a week at schools and crossroads; people brought specimens in tins, saw the eggs for themselves through the microscope, and were given thymol in capsules with Epsom salts before and after. A visitor quoted in the Commission’s report for 1911 said of the crowds, “It looks like the days of Galilee.” Kentucky’s report for 1912 mentions a young woman among its microscopists. The questions and answers are from Stiles’s school circular Soil Pollution as Cause of Ground-Itch, Hookworm Disease (Ground-Itch Anemia), and Dirt Eating (1910), the Commission’s first publication, which children were told to take home and read to their parents.

Sand Mountain is a broad sandstone plateau in northeast Alabama, a country of small farms, bluffs and rock shelters, where churches commonly had preaching one Sunday in the month and all-day singings from the shape-note books. Alabama’s dispensaries reached Marshall County, on the Mountain, in 1912. The Commission’s report for that year counted 580 children examined there and half of them infected, and of 226 country homes inspected every one fell in the two lowest classes of its privy index. The Encyclopedia of Alabama has more on the disease in the state. Shiloh church, the table rock and all the people in the story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Visiting Preacher
sections.dateline: Sand Mountain, Alabama · the fall of 1856
sections.text: There was a man named Eli Tidmore who had a good farm on the brow and no preacher nearer than the valley, so he built a room onto his house and kept one. The preacher’s name was Harmon Self. He had the room and his washing and a place at the table three times a day, and he preached at the log church two Sundays in the month and thought himself well fixed. One evening that fall an old man came up the mountain road on foot. He was a preacher too, of what persuasion nobody afterward could say. He had a way of walking and a way of standing still that Tidmore liked the minute he saw them, and Tidmore had him in. He fed him the best there was in the house. He saw the state of the old man’s clothes and brought out a length of new jeans cloth his wife had woven. Have this made up and wear it next to you. He saw the hair down on his collar and sent a boy for the neighbor who barbered. He had his own feather bed carried up to the loft. You lie on this. Then he asked both preachers to breakfast and went to bed himself. Harmon Self had watched the whole of it from his place at the table. He had eaten at that table two years, and nobody had ever sent for a barber. That night he climbed to the l

sections.heading: II. The Table Rock
sections.text: The boy the Mountain called Jim Buck was born the next spring, in a house with plenty in it: four mules, a full smokehouse, bees. Whose house it was depends on who is telling. Some say Self’s own. Some say Self died that winter with his face to the wall, and the child came to people named Buck across the gulf who had never heard of him. From the time he could walk he would not lie in a bed and he would not eat at a table. He ate off the ground. A good many children on the Mountain ate a little clay out of the chimney, and nobody thought much about it. This one ate from the ground behind the smokehouse, where the family went, there being no such thing as a privy on Sand Mountain then, and it was not only the ground he ate. His mother and father said, He is a baby. He doesn’t know any better. He got older and it was the same. By then he would not keep a stitch on him, summer or winter, and he slept in the yard like a dog. His people said, He is not fit to live in a house. He is fit for those sanctified folks and nothing else. The sanctified band were camped that year on the brow, a dozen men who had come out from all the churches and went barefoot and bareheaded and begged their meal

sections.heading: III. The Glass
sections.dateline: Shiloh crossroads · the fourth Saturday in July, 1912
sections.text: The State Board of Health sent a dispensary up the Mountain that summer, a doctor and a microscopist in a hired hack, with a tin trunk of capsules and a stack of bulletins for the schoolchildren to carry home. The doctor was a Dr. Anders from below Montgomery. The microscopist was a Miss Lura Hyatt, twenty-three years old, whose people were from the far end of the Mountain. She had been as yellow as a gourd herself until she was sixteen. Then a doctor at Albertville gave her thymol, and after it she finished school in two years and went down to the State laboratory to learn the glass. She saw him at sunup from the hack as they came along the brow: a man on a rock, on one leg, the color of tallow. She had been that color. She knew what he ate as surely as if she had stood and watched him. She thought, If that one would carry a tin box to the table, the whole Mountain would. They set up at the schoolhouse across the road from the church. People had been told from the pulpit, and they came. They came in wagons and on mules and on foot, with the specimen in a snuff tin or a baking-powder can with the name penciled on a scrap of paper, and they stood in the yard and waited their turn an

sections.heading: IV. Three Lights
sections.text: She spread her quilt on the sand and lay down. In the fore part of the night four lights came along the foot of the bluff, one from each way, and stood at the four sides of the rockhouse, and it was light as far as the far wall of the gulf. Jim Buck saw it from his rock. What light is that? At midnight one came by itself that was brighter than the four. Who is that? Toward day there came one that lit the whole woods, so that a man could have counted the leaves. The old people had a saying about that one, that with one finger he lights one world, and with ten fingers ten. Who can that be? At daybreak he went down to her. He spoke to her civilly and stood off to one side. Who was it came to you in the fore part of the night, the four of them? Four that keep the corners of this country. What did they come for? To see was there anything I wanted. And the one at midnight? He is over those four. He sat and held the lamp for me. And the one toward day? That is the one the preachers holler to. Are you greater than them, then? They came to me. I did not go to them. He studied her. You are a wonder, girl. I have lived on this rock since before you were born, eating wind and standing up, and

sections.heading: V. Fourth Sunday
sections.text: It was the day in the month when the Mountain came with its plates. They came out of the church at noon and carried them back through the trees to the table rock, and there he was, with both feet on the ground, in a canvas coat, like any old deacon in from the field, standing beside a young woman who had a brass tube under her arm. They talked among themselves. Which of them is the greater? If it was her, he would have gone down the mountain to her. She came up the mountain to him. So it must be him. She heard it. Jim Buck, settle that for them. That is the very thing I would like best to do, he said. There are people on Sand Mountain today whose grandmothers stood there and saw it. He went up off the ground to the height of a pine tree and called down, This young woman is my teacher, and I am her scholar, and came down and bowed to her. He went up again to the height of two pines, and of three, and so on until he was seven pines high and small against the sky, and each time he said the same thing and came down. Then he sat down at her feet. Nobody there had ever seen him sit. The people said, Lord, what must she know? She was not a speaker and she did not make a speech. She said,

title: The Sedge Straw
logline: A hookworm dispensary's young microscopist asks a night's lodging of the man the Mountain feeds from a sedge straw, who claims to eat wind.

verses.text: An evil deed, like newly-drawn milk, does not turn (suddenly); smouldering, like fire covered by ashes, it follows the fool.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, coming down from Vulture’s Peak with the elder Lakkhaṇa, smiles, and will say why only in front of the Buddha: he has seen a peta, a suffering ghost, with a man’s head and a snake’s body many leagues long, burning from head to tail and from tail to head. On another day he sees a crow-ghost whose tongue is five leagues long, and it tells him its whole offense was three mouthfuls of food carried home from a meal given to monks. The Buddha confirms the snake-ghost, saying he saw it himself on the day of his awakening and kept silent out of compassion for those who would not have believed him. Then he tells its past: a farmer near Benares, whose field was trampled by the crowds going morning and evening with perfumes and garlands to a solitary awakened one in a leaf hut by the river, broke the hermit’s bowls and burned his hut while he was away on his alms round; the hermit simply went elsewhere; and when the crowd came and found the ashes, the farmer said aloud that he had done it, and they beat him to death with sticks and stones. A bad deed, the Buddha says, is like milk, which does not turn the moment it is drawn.
bg.history:
On September 24, 1625, a Dutch fleet of seventeen ships under Boudewijn Hendricksz sailed into San Juan Bay. The townspeople fled inland over the San Antonio bridge while Governor Juan de Haro, who had held office less than a month, shut himself into the Castillo San Felipe del Morro with about 330 men. The Dutch occupied the empty town and besieged the fort for weeks; Captain Andrés Botello’s militia retook the Bayamón River and supplies reached the Morro again. When Hendricksz threatened to burn the town, de Haro answered that they had courage enough and wood and stone enough to build again. From October 22 the Dutch burned more than a hundred houses, including the palace and library of the poet-bishop Bernardo de Balbuena, then were driven back to their ships and sailed on November 2, leaving one ship behind. See Battle of San Juan (1625).

In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries ginger flourished on Puerto Rico and Hispaniola, and it found a better market in England and the Low Countries than in Castile, so that much of it went to English and Dutch traders outside the Spanish fleet system (see Bethany Aram, “Caribbean ginger and Atlantic trade, 1570–1648”).
