The white-necked crow, a big red-eyed forest crow whose voice is more like a parrot’s babble than a crow’s caw, lived on Puerto Rico until it was hunted out early in the twentieth century. Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605, and copies went to the Indies with the fleet that same spring; the line Lucas remembers is quoted from John Ormsby’s 1885 translation. Gaspar, Lucas, Antón, Hermano Cristóbal, Bartolomé Pérez and the cross at the river are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Glacis
sections.text: The Dutch fleet stood out past the Morro on the second of November with every ship but one, and the next morning the governor sent a corporal and eleven men down into the town to see what was left of it. Lucas Bermejo was one of the eleven. He was eighteen and came from Triana, across the river from Seville, where his father caulked boats. He had landed in Puerto Rico in August with the new governor, Don Juan de Haro, and five weeks later he was inside the Morro with three hundred and thirty men, and the Dutch were in the town, and he had spent his first autumn in the Indies eating cassava bread that came across the bay at night in canoes and listening to cannon. The Dutchman had sent a drum to the gate twice. The second time the message was that if the fort did not surrender he would burn the town. The governor had sent back word that they had courage enough, and wood and stone enough, to build it again. The whole garrison knew the words by evening. The next day the smoke began. Now it was over. The twelve went out through the gate and down across the glacis, stepping over the Dutch trenches. Lucas had heard about Gaspar Ortiz since his first week. Gaspar was born in San Germán an

sections.heading: II. The Boats
sections.dateline: The beach below the town · that evening
sections.text: Antón's canoe lay on the sand where the town came down to the bay. It was a long dugout of ceiba with a little mast, and it had crossed the bay every night of the siege with cassava and plantains and once a pig, from the Bayamón shore to the rocks under the fort, after Captain Botello's men took back the river. Antón was past seventy. He had come from Luanda as a boy in a Portuguese ship, and he had been free for thirteen years. He kept a clay pot in the bow of the canoe with coals in it under a lid of ash, so that he could light his pipe anywhere on the water, and he was sitting by it now with his back to a beached boat. Two fishermen were mending a net. A woman was beating ash out of a blanket against a post. Gaspar sat down. Lucas stood. This morning, Lucas said, on the glacis. You told me to ask you here. Gaspar took some time with it. There was a man lying along the town, he said. His head was on the rocks under the Morro and his body went down the whole length of the town and past the bridge, I could not see how far. The head was a man's head, with a man's beard. The rest of him was a snake. And he was burning. Not the town. Him. The fire started at his head and ran down him

sections.heading: III. The Cross at the River
sections.text: In the time when Antón still belonged to a widow on the Calle de la Fortaleza, a man called Hermano Cristóbal put up a cross of two mangrove poles at the mouth of the Bayamón River, on the far side of the bay, and built a hut of palm thatch beside it. He was a lay hermit in a habit of grey sacking, with the bishop's leave. People said he had been a sugar master on Hispaniola, the man who stands over the boiling coppers and says when the syrup is ready, and that one morning in the middle of the grinding he had put down his ladle and walked out of the boiling house and kept walking. He did not preach. In four years nobody heard him say more than a few words together. He lived on what he was given, and every morning he crossed to the town in Antón's canoe and stood in doorways with a gourd until it had something in it, and at noon Antón carried him back. Antón's widow hired him out to work the canoe and took four reales a day from him, and whatever he earned over the four reales was his. In the first year after the hermit came, the crossings doubled. In the second they doubled again. Every morning and every evening the canoes went over full. Women went with jasmine and roses from thei

sections.heading: IV. The Ginger
sections.text: At sundown the canoes crossed full, Antón's and five others. People got out with their flowers and their candles and went up through the ginger, and stopped. The cross was black. The hut was a ring of ash with the shards of the water jar in it. Where has the brother gone? they said. Who did this? Bartolomé had come down to watch them find it. He was standing among them. He said it plainly, the way a man says his name to the notary. I burned it. Now you can stop walking on my ginger. Somebody said, Take him. Somebody else said, Because of him we have lost the brother. And they took him. They had in their hands what people have in their hands at a landing at evening. Paddles, and the stakes of his own fence, and stones from the river mouth. Women who had come with roses. Antón would not say how long it was. He said only that he had a paddle in his hand, and that he would say no more about his paddle, and that he had been sorry for it every day since. They left Bartolomé on the sand between his ginger and the water. His wife found him there by lantern. He died before morning. The alcalde wrote that a farmer had been killed at night by persons in a crowd, and no person was named. The w

sections.heading: V. Under the Ash
sections.text: It was dark by then. Up the slope the town was dark too, except where the ash heaps breathed. Fourteen years he has been dead, said Lucas. He did one thing. Antón knocked his pipe out on the side of the canoe. Milk, he said. You draw it from the goat in the morning and it is sweet. At noon it is sweet. You would swear by it. Then in the evening it has turned, all at once, and you never saw it turn. He put the lid of ash back over his coals with two fingers. And this. Look up there. The Dutchman lit that town twelve days ago. A child could walk across it in the daytime. It is all grey. Put your hand in it. Nobody spoke for a while. The fishermen had given up their net. Then Lucas, who could not read, said a thing he had heard read aloud the winter before in a wineshop in Triana, out of the book about the mad gentleman of La Mancha that everybody was laughing at. A rich farmer was flogging his shepherd boy, and the madman rode up and stopped it, and the farmer said the knight had no business with him, and the madman answered him. “That matters little,” replied Don Quixote; “there may be Haldudos knights; moreover, everyone is the son of his works.” — Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part I, c

title: Banked Fire
logline: The morning after the Dutch burn San Juan, an old soldier looks down the length of the smoking town and smiles.

verses.text: And when the evil deed, after it has become known, brings sorrow to the fool, then it destroys his bright lot, nay, it cleaves his head.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, coming down from Vulture’s Peak with a companion, smiles at something and will explain only in front of the Buddha: he has seen a peta, a suffering ghost, three-quarters of a league tall, whose skull is crushed again and again by sixty thousand blazing hammers. The Buddha says he saw the same being long ago and kept silent out of compassion for those who would not have believed him, and then tells its past. A lame man of Benares could flick pebbles so well that he cut leaves into the shapes of animals for children; a king hired him to flick goat dung into the mouth of a talkative chaplain, and rewarded him with four villages. A man who envied this served the cripple until he was taught the art, was warned to aim only at something “with neither mother nor father,” and killed a solitary holy man, a paccekabuddha, with a stone through the ear. The crowd beat him to death. The verse the Buddha draws from it, in the commentary’s own reading, is that whatever skill a fool acquires works only to his ruin.
bg.history:
The Homestake Mine at Lead, in the Black Hills, was bought by George Hearst and his partners in 1877 and became one of the richest gold mines in the country. Its ore was crushed in stamp mills that ran around the clock: 650 stamps by the late 1880s and 1,020 at the peak in 1916. Under superintendent Thomas Grier (1885–1914) Lead was a company town with a company store (the “Brick Store”), a free library and kindergarten paid for by Phoebe Hearst, a standard wage of $3.50 a day, and, from 1906, an eight-hour shift; in the winter of 1909–10 the company locked out its whole workforce to break the miners’ union and rehired only men who signed a non-union pledge. See Richards and Myers, “An Iron Hand in a Velvet Glove” (South Dakota History, 2008). Mr. Crane, Colonel Parmalee and everyone on the Avenue are invented.

Lead’s miners came from Cornwall, Finland, Italy, Scandinavia and the South Slav lands of Austria-Hungary and Montenegro. Gwinn Avenue was known as Slavonian Alley, remembered for its Christmas-week open houses and for wine pressed from grapes that came in by iced railroad car. Serbs and Montenegrins keep Christmas by the Julian calendar, so that Christmas Eve falls on January 6. On that morning the men of a household cut a young oak, the badnjak, greet it, and bring it in at dusk to burn on the hearth over straw; someone strikes it so the sparks fly and wishes the house as many lambs and coins as there are sparks. The Orthodox Old Testament is the Greek Septuagint, quoted here in Sir Lancelot Brenton’s English translation of 1851, in which the psalm is numbered 7:16–17.

sections.heading: I. The Oak
sections.dateline: Lead, South Dakota · Christmas Eve by the old calendar, January 6, 1917
sections.text: Two men went up the ridge above the Open Cut before daylight to cut the Christmas oak. Marko Radulović was past fifty and had been a timberman in the Homestake for twenty-six years. Luka was nineteen and had come from Grahovo in the spring. Oak does not like that altitude, but there was a draw on the south side where a few had held on, and the Montenegrins and the Serbs of Gwinn Avenue had been going there on this morning since before Luka was born. They did it properly. Marko took off his cap and wished the tree good morning and a happy Christmas Eve, and threw a handful of wheat at it, and cut on the east side so it would fall toward the sunrise. He did not let it touch the ground. Then they started down with the log on their shoulders, Marko in front. It was fourteen below. Under them the town lay in its gulch with every lamp lit, and along the hillside stood the mills, one above another, steaming from every joint. The noise came up to meet them. There were a thousand and twenty stamps in the Homestake mills that winter. A stamp is an iron shoe on the end of an iron stem, the whole thing as heavy as a saddle horse. A turning cam lifts it the length of a hand and lets it drop on

sections.heading: II. Baba Stana’s
sections.text: The Americans called Gwinn Avenue Slavonian Alley. It was Dalmatians and Likans at one end and Montenegrins at the other, Catholic and Orthodox, and in a snowstorm they shoveled each other out. Stana Vukotić had kept a boardinghouse there for thirty years. She was seventy. She had buried a husband out of the mine and raised three sons into it, and fourteen men ate at her table. On paper it was a business. In fact the house was the nearest thing to a church the Orthodox end of the Avenue had, with the nearest priest of their own a long way off by train. She had the icon and the lamp, and she had the Psalter by heart, in the old language, from a childhood of standing through services at Cetinje. Men came to her kitchen with questions they would not have taken to a priest anyway. She spoke little. When she had said a thing she did not say it again. At dusk Marko carried the oak in over the threshold, right foot first. Stana threw wheat at him and he wished the house a good evening and a happy Christmas Eve, as is done. There was straw on the floor under the table, for the stable. They laid the log on the fire and poured a little wine on it. When it had caught, they ate the fast-day su

sections.heading: III. The Cottonwood
sections.text: There was a man from Cuce named Vuko Perović who lost the use of his legs in the mine in 1885, when a set of timbers let go. The company gave him a stool. He was to sit at the foot of Mill Street, where the Deadwood road comes into town past the Brick Store, and count the wood wagons going up to the boilers. There was a big cottonwood there, the only real shade in the gulch. As a boy Vuko had kept goats on the stone above Cuce with a sling. Sitting on that stool all day he found that he could do with a thumb and a finger what he used to do with the sling. He kept a pocket of creek gravel. He could flick a pebble the size of a pea through one leaf of that cottonwood, forty feet up, and not move the leaf beside it. The children found him out. They came down from every part of town, Cornish and Finn and Italian and ours, and stood around the stool. Make a horse, Vuko. Make a bear. And he would look up into the tree for a while, and then his hand would go, tick, tick, tick, faster than a sewing machine, and bits of green would come spinning down. When he was done the children looked at the ground. The sun came through the holes he had cut and lay on the dust of the road in the shape of

sections.heading: IV. The Pupil
sections.dateline: The winter of 1889 and the summer after
sections.text: There was a young man boarding on the Avenue then, a mucker, twenty-two. I will call him Mitar. His mother is dead now and it cannot hurt her. Mitar looked at the four rents and the chair with wheels, and he thought, a cripple got all that by flicking gravel. So he went to Vuko and took off his cap. Teach me. I can’t do that, friend, said Vuko. Mitar did not argue. He went to the stove and heated water. All that winter, every night after shift, he came to Vuko’s room and washed his feet and rubbed his dead legs with brandy and bear grease from the ankle to the hip. He carried him on his back to the bathhouse on Saturdays. He did this for five months and did not ask again until spring. And Vuko thought, this boy has been a son to me. He could not go on refusing him. He taught him. Mitar was quick. By June he could put out a candle across the room. It is written somewhere else, and I did not think of it in time. He that binds up a stone in a sling, is like one that gives glory to a fool. — Proverbs 26:8 (Septuagint) You have it all now, Vuko said to him. What will you do with it? Go out and show it. Show it how? Drop a cow. Or a man. Something people will talk about. Vuko was frighte

sections.heading: V. The Gulch
sections.text: By noon the next day every kitchen in town knew he had not come. Somebody found the pail under the cottonwood with yesterday’s bread in it. So they went up. The Finns and the Cornish and the Italians went, and all of the Avenue, some two hundred people on that goat track, the women with their aprons on. He was lying on his side on the pine boughs with his hands under his cheek. There was a little blood at each ear. The women began to cry out, each in her own language, and the men took off their caps. Mitar had come up with the crowd to see what the noise was. He pushed in and looked. He had not known, you understand, that anybody would mind. He said it out loud, in a voice of plain surprise, the way you would say you recognized a horse. Why, that’s the one I met at the cottonwood. I tried my hand on him. I will not tell you all of it. It is Christmas Eve. The men had come straight off shift and had in their hands what they had. They did it there in the gulch, in front of the shelter, and it did not take long, and no one who was there has ever said which of them it was. I will say that I did not look away, and I have asked forgiveness for that every year since. The coroner came up f

sections.heading: VI. Sparks
sections.text: The oak had burned halfway through. Out past the window, down the hill, the mills went on as they always did, and for once every man at the table heard them. And Vuko? said Luka. They told him in his chair. He asked which ear. Then he asked them to wheel him to the bridge, and he emptied his pocket into the creek. He never flicked a stone again, not for any child, though they came and stood around him for a year. He signed the four rents over to the lodge for widows, and he went back to the stool, and he died on it in 1903. She was quiet a moment. I was wrong, what I said in Mr. Crane’s kitchen. A craft is not a good thing. Nor a bad one. Vuko had that craft for thirty years and it made bears for children and shut one lawyer’s mouth. Mitar had it for a day. Whatever a fool learns, he learns to his own hurt. He would have been better off with his shovel. Then she said the psalm, the two verses, in the old language first and then so the young ones could follow. He has opened a pit, and dug it up, and he shall fall into the ditch which he has made. His trouble shall return on his own head, and his unrighteousness shall come down on his own crown. — Psalm 7:16–17 (Septuagint) Nobody sp

title: A Thousand Stamps
logline: Carrying the Christmas oak down past the Homestake mills, a Montenegrin timberman stops, looks at the thousand stamps, and smiles.

verses.text: Let the fool wish for a false reputation, for precedence among the Bhikshus, for lordship in the convents, for worship among other people!

“May both the layman and he who has left the world think that this is done by me; may they be subject to me in everything which is to be done or is not to be done,” thus is the mind of the fool, and his desire and pride increase.

bg.commentary: The monk Sudhamma lived at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the mango grove that the householder Citta had given, and Citta never invited anyone without naming him. When the two chief disciples came, Citta heard Sāriputta teach, invited the visitors for the next day’s meal, and only then turned to invite Sudhamma, who was stung at being asked last and refused three times. Early next morning he went to look over the food all the same, would not sit down, and remarked that only one thing was missing: sesame cake. Citta answered with the tale of a chick hatched from a hen and a crow, which cawed when it meant to crow and crowed when it meant to caw. Sudhamma said, “This is your residence; I will depart,” refused three times to stay, and walked the thirty leagues to the Buddha, who put the blame wholly on him and sent him back to ask pardon. Citta refused it. The Buddha, knowing what was needed, let him make the long journey once more without advice, and when he came back with his pride worn down gave him a companion, warned him against thinking “this dwelling is mine, this disciple is mine,” and spoke the verses. Sudhamma asked pardon in Citta’s sight, and Citta gave it and asked his in turn; within a few days Sudhamma was an arahat. Only then did Citta set out to see the Buddha himself, which is the journey told in The Bread Truck. Here is the full commentary story; the sesame cake and the crow are given at length in the monastic code, Cullavagga I.18. More about Citta.
bg.history:
Greyhound introduced the unlimited-mileage Ameripass in 1972, and for decades it was how people without money crossed the country; in the 1980s it was sold for seven, fifteen or thirty days. A rider going west from Indianapolis went by way of St. Louis, Kansas City, Denver, Salt Lake City and Reno to Sacramento, and changed there for the bus north to Weed, the old lumber town under Mount Shasta. The McCloud River Railroad hauled logs and lumber around the mountain’s south side from 1897. Hart’s remark at the table turns on a feed-trade word: press cake, or oil cake, is the solid left when oil is pressed from linseed, soybeans, cottonseed or sesame, and it is sold as livestock feed. The sweet he later puts by the register is halvah, made of ground sesame.

Mrs. Varnum reads from Emerson’s essay “Compensation” (1841), in the same volume as the “Self-Reliance” she reads from in The Bread Truck. Lowell’s pocket book is the Tao Teh King in the 1891 translation of the Scottish missionary and Oxford professor James Legge, long out of copyright and often reprinted. Lowell Sudduth, Mr. Tibbets, the store and Alder Street are invented, as they were in the earlier story.

sections.heading: I. The Loft
sections.text: Lowell Sudduth came into the store in the spring of 1978 for a pound of lentils and stayed seven years. He had been a Methodist youth minister in Kokomo until the Sunday he found he could not get through the benediction, and after that he had painted houses. He was thirty-four, long in the leg, with a voice people liked to listen to. Hart Householder took him back to the office and played him the first tape, the woman with the cough and the kitchen clock. Lowell sat through both sides of it without shifting his feet and then asked if there was a second one. By summer he was living in the loft over the old scale room, where Hart’s father had kept the seed-corn records. Hart charged him nothing and fed him. Lowell ran the register on Saturdays, and the rest of the week he ran the sitting. Before he came it had been six or eight people going down to the pawpaw patch behind the mill whenever they thought of it. Lowell gave it hours. Wednesday night and Sunday morning there was a half hour of tape, then the cassette was turned over and there was a half hour more. Afterward he read one page aloud from a small Tao Teh King, the old Legge translation, which he carried in his coat. He built

sections.heading: II. Last
sections.dateline: The book room · a Friday in late September 1985
sections.text: The two who came through that fall were her old students, a nurse and a carpenter. They were on their way east and they had been driving since Kansas. Hart went out to the edge of town to meet their car, which he had never done for anybody. Lowell set up the folding chairs in the book room. He put one at the front, turned sideways, for himself, since somebody would have to say a few words first. Nobody asked him to say them. Hart only said, These are her people, and sat down on the floor. The nurse did most of the talking. She said they were worn out and would keep it short, and it was short. Lowell did not take in much of it. He was watching Hart. In seven years of Wednesday nights he had not seen Hart’s face do what it did in that hour. When it was over Hart got up off the floor. You’ll eat with us tomorrow before you go, he said to the two of them. Noon, here in the store. Everybody in this room. Bring whoever you came with. The nurse nodded. Forty people stood up and started in talking. Hart shook hands all the way to the back of the room, where Lowell was folding chairs and stacking them against the cookbooks. You come too, Lowell. Lowell hung a chair on the stack. He had been

sections.heading: III. The Table
sections.text: Lowell did not sleep. A little after five he heard Hart moving below him, and the cooler door, and he thought he would just go and see what was being put on for them. He came down the loft stairs with his coat buttoned. Hart had laid planks across the grain bins for the length of the store and covered them with bed sheets. There was a crock of pinto beans and a pan of cornbread the size of a door. There was brown rice with walnuts, and tabouli, and the last tomatoes sliced on a platter, and a whole wheel of cheese from the Amish in Daviess County. There were six round loaves, and apple butter, and honey in the comb, and a persimmon pudding. At the far end he had set a dishpan of pawpaws, picked up that morning out of the wet grass. Two women from the Tuesday quilters were slicing bread. A farmer from over by Stanford had come in with cider and stayed to watch. Sit down, Lowell. There’s coffee. I won’t sit. I’m on my way out. He walked down the planks and looked at all of it, taking his time, like a man going over a car he does not intend to buy. It’s a fine table, Hart. There’s only the one thing you’ve left off. What’s that? Sesame cake. Hart’s father had sold cake in that buildin

sections.heading: IV. Thirty Days
sections.dateline: Indianapolis to Weed, California, and back · October
sections.text: Greyhound sold a pass in those years called the Ameripass, good for all the riding a person could stand in seven days, or fifteen, or thirty. Lowell bought the thirty-day one at the depot in Indianapolis out of the house-painting money he kept in a coffee can. It was cheaper than two tickets, and he did not know how long he would be. He did not expect to use it up. It was three nights sitting up. St. Louis, Kansas City, Denver, Salt Lake, Reno, Sacramento, and then north to a lumber town called Weed, where the bus let him down in sight of the mountain. He spent the three nights on his account of things. There were the seven years and the shed and the Wednesdays, and who had built what, and who had said what first. By Salt Lake he had it so that nobody could have found a hole in it. He walked and thumbed the nine miles to Mount Shasta and stood in the post office until a young man with a key opened the right box. I’m from Householder’s, in Indiana. The young man looked at him, and at the grip. You’d better come on, then, he said. She had a small house on Alder Street. He knew the cough before he saw her, and then the clock. She was past seventy, in a housedress and a grey cardigan,

sections.heading: V. Remnants
sections.dateline: Alder Street, Mount Shasta · the middle of October
sections.text: She looked at him in the door. Come in and sit down, Mr. Sudduth. It was the first time she had asked him to sit. The young man, whose name was Andy, put a cup in front of him. Mr. Tibbets next door is going east to see his daughter in Dayton, she said, and he doesn’t like to ride alone. You go along with him as far as Indiana. He said he would. Now listen. A man who has sat down to be quiet has no business holding a deed to it. My shed. My Wednesday night. My machine. My Hart. Once you say mine over a thing like that, everything you sat down to be rid of comes back and puts on weight. She had a book by her on the table, an old one, the back of it mended with tape. She did not have to hunt for the place. The exclusive in fashionable life does not see that he excludes himself from enjoyment, in the attempt to appropriate it. The exclusionist in religion does not see that he shuts the door of heaven on himself, in striving to shut out others. — Emerson, “Compensation” That one is mine, she said. Andy says you carry one of your own. Read me the place about the tiptoes. He had read it aloud in the shed perhaps forty times. He took the little book out of his coat and read it to her. He

sections.heading: VI. The Chair by the Door
sections.dateline: Bloomington · the end of October, and after
sections.text: They walked in from the highway, the two of them. Hart was on the loading dock with a sack of rice on his shoulder. Lowell stopped at the foot of the steps where Hart could see him and took off his cap. Mr. Tibbets stood beside him holding the suitcase and looked the mill over with interest. Hart. You asked me last and I couldn’t stand it. I came down that morning to spoil your table, and I said the meanest thing I could find, in your father’s own building. I’m sorry for it. I’m asking you to forgive me. Hart let the sack down. That’s forgiven, Lowell. That’s gone. And I had no call to bring out that crow in front of people. If I did you wrong, you forgive me. Yes. Who’s this? Mr. Tibbets. He’s going on to Dayton. Not until he eats, said Hart. Lowell kept to what she had told him. It did not take long. The ones who sat near him that month say only that some time before the first hard frost it was finished in him, and that you could tell by the fact that there was nothing left to step on. You could ask him first or last, or forget to ask him. He read the page from the little book if somebody handed it to him. Whoever sat nearest the machine turned the tape over. Two summers later Ha

title: Sesame Cake
place: Bloomington, Indiana, and Mount Shasta, California
logline: Asked last to a supper at an Indiana natural-foods store, the man who runs its meditation group insults the host and boards a Greyhound.

verses.text: “One is the road that leads to wealth, another the road that leads to Nirvana;” if the Bhikshu, the disciple of Buddha, has learnt this, he will not yearn for honour, he will strive after separation from the world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a poor Brahmin who has hidden from the elder Sāriputta for shame at having nothing to give at last gives him a whole bowl of porridge and a small cloth, and is reborn into a family of the elder’s supporters. As a baby he drops a costly blanket at Sāriputta’s feet and is named Tissa after him. At seven he becomes a novice. The town gives him a thousand bowls and cloths in two days, and another day he leads a thousand cold monks out and collects a thousand blankets; he keeps none of it. To get away from his visiting relatives he walks twenty leagues to a forest, where a village feeds him and hears nothing from him but “May you be happy, may you be released from suffering.” In three months he is an arahat. When Sāriputta and the great disciples come to see him, the villagers are astonished, and some are offended, to hear him preach all night; the Buddha arrives to reconcile them, questions the boy on a mountain above the ocean, and lets him turn back to the forest.
bg.history:
On November 7, 1861, a Union fleet took Port Royal Sound. The planters of the South Carolina sea islands fled, and about ten thousand enslaved people stayed where they were, on land that grew the finest long-staple cotton in the world; the islands remember it as the day of the big gun-shoot. What followed is called the Port Royal Experiment: Northern teachers and superintendents, wages, schools, and the first Black regiment raised from former slaves, the First South Carolina Volunteers under Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who heard the Emancipation Proclamation read at Camp Saxton on January 1, 1863, and went down the coast by steamer later that month, one transport putting in at Union-held Fernandina on Amelia Island. The superintendents’ Letters from Port Royal record that a slave household’s allowance had been cloth for two suits a year and “a pair of blankets every few years,” and that when the Government gave up Edisto Island in 1862 a thousand of its people were quartered at St. Helena Village, where the next winter they still had “nothing.” Sandy Field, the south-end settlement, the sand hill and all the people in the story are invented.

Every plantation on St. Helena had its praise house, where the Gullah people held meeting and the ring shout, with the best singers standing at the wall to “base” the shouters. Before anyone could be a member, young or old, they had to seek: to go alone into the woods or the swamp to pray, under an older guide, until they had found what they were hunting for. Higginson wrote that “de lonesome valley” was the islanders’ word for it, and that a girl who had entered it “bound a handkerchief by a peculiar knot over her head”; the editors of Slave Songs of the United States (1867) quote a boy who could not join the shout yet because he “hain’t been on my knees in de swamp.” The three songs are given as Higginson took them down from his soldiers at Port Royal in 1862 and 1863 and printed them, in the spelling he used, in the Atlantic Monthly in 1867 and in Army Life in a Black Regiment (1870).

sections.heading: I. The Pan of Rice
sections.dateline: Sandy Field plantation, St. Helena Island, South Carolina · 1854
sections.text: There was a praise house at Sandy Field, as there was on every cotton place on the island, a board cabin at the end of the street where the people met three nights in the week. The one who led it was a man called Daddy Titus. He hoed his task like anybody. But it was known from Lands End to Coffin Point that if you were down in the valley, hunting for that thing and not finding it, Titus was the one to carry your dreams to. On Sunday evenings he went down the street from door to door with a basket, for the sick and for burying, and each cabin put in what it had, a handful of grits, an egg, a copper. At the far end lived an old man named Mingo, who had been bought onto the place in the same lot with Titus’s father and had outlived his strength. He drew half a peck and had no garden anymore. When he heard the basket coming he thought, That is my own boy at the door, and I have not got one thing to put in. He doesn’t know how poor I am. He could not look him in the face. He went round behind the chimney and stood there until Titus had gone by. The next Sunday he hid again. He told himself, The first thing I get hold of, I will give him. It was a long while coming. That winter an old w

sections.heading: II. Titus’s Name
sections.text: Ten moons after Mingo was laid down, a boy was born to Rina, wife of Bacchus the boat carpenter, who kept the best cabin on the street and stood by the praise house and by Titus through everything. The women counted on their fingers and looked at one another and let it alone. While she was carrying him a craving came on her. I want to boil rice soft, with milk and molasses, and feed it to Daddy Titus and every elder on the front bench, and not quit. And I want to tie the seeker’s knot on my head again, the way I wore it when I was a girl in the valley, and sit on the back bench with my pan, and eat what the elders leave. Her people said, That is a praying kind of craving, and they did it for her. She knotted the handkerchief over her forehead and sat on the last bench and ate what was left, and the craving went off. The old women said that knot was the sign the child would seek young. On the day they named him they washed him before light and laid him in the new blanket. At Sandy Field a pair of blankets came to a house every few years, at Christmas, out of the master’s hand, and for most houses that was the whole of their wealth. This was the new one. The child lay in it and looke

sections.heading: III. Give-It
sections.text: The island had heard. They say the little seeker is coming round today. Let us do something for him. Women on St. Helena carry everything on the head, on a cloth twisted into a ring for a pad. That morning five hundred of them twisted five hundred new cloths and set five hundred pans of victuals on them, and met him on the shell road. The next day they came into the praise-house yard and did it over. In two days he had a thousand pans and a thousand cloths, and he gave every one of them to the praise house for the old and the sick. The old people said that was the square of handkerchief coming back. They began to call him Give-It. In July the Government gave up Edisto Island, and a thousand of the Edisto people were brought over and set down at the Village with what they had on their backs. One cold morning in December the boy went through the Village and saw them sitting round lightwood fires in the yards and under the houses. Why are you all sitting at the fire? We’re cold, bubba. When it is cold a body ought to wrap up in a blanket. That keeps it off. You are a lucky child. Maybe you can come by a blanket. Where are we to get one? Well, he said, everybody that needs a blanket, c

sections.heading: IV. Twenty Leagues
sections.text: His mother’s people came to the praise house to see him, and his father’s, every day, and sat and talked. On the first of January the paper was read out at Camp Saxton and ten oxen were roasted, and after that it seemed that everybody who passed Sandy Field turned in to look at him. He thought, As long as I stay here they will come and talk to me, and whether they talk or sit quiet, I will never come through. Suppose I got something to carry from the Teacher and went in the wilderness sure enough. The one the leaders themselves called Teacher was Daddy Quaco, the well-digger. He had dug most of the wells on that end of St. Helena and a good share of the graves. He watched over all the praise houses there, and he had never been known to raise a song. He stood at the wall and based. The boy went and bowed to him and asked for something to carry. Quaco looked at him awhile. Every place you lie down, ask who lay there before you. Carry that. The boy bowed to Titus. He took his pan and his blanket. If I stop anywhere near, he thought, they will send for me. So he went a long way. In the last week of January the colored regiment went down the coast on three steamers, and one of them put

sections.heading: V. Two Sayings
sections.text: Early the next morning he went into the settlement with his pan. When the people put something in it and made their manners, he said, Be glad. Be free of trouble. He said nothing else. One man who had given could not make himself go back to his house. They all had to stand and look at him. So he was fed without any hardship. The whole street got down in front of him. If you will stay by us these three months, we will build a praise house and keep it three nights in the week, and leave off what we ought to leave off. Promise us. He saw there was help for them in it, and he promised. After that he came in every morning and only for his victuals. They bowed, and he said the two sayings, Be glad. Be free of trouble, and went back to the sand hill. He kept that up the first month and the second. In the third month he came through. When the cotton was laid by, Daddy Titus went to the Teacher. I am going down to see my seeker. Go, Titus. Titus started with his own people, and on the way he said to Bristol, who led at the next place, I am going to see Tite. I will go too, said Bristol, and brought his. Blind Cupid heard and came with his, and old Kit the barber with his, and so it went unt

sections.heading: VI. The Seeker’s Pan
sections.text: Daddy Quaco, on St. Helena, looked over the world early that day as his habit was, and the people of that settlement came into his mind. Some of them are put out with the boy, he thought, and some are pleased. The ones who hold a thing against a child like my son will come to harm by it. I had better go. If I go, they will all be at peace with him. The settlement had put up a brush arbor and cooked hominy and fish, and set out benches, and sat down to wait. The leaders came in from the sand hill at the hour for eating. They had asked the boy, Are you coming with us, or after? and he had said, When it is my time I will come. You all go ahead. Quaco put on his coat at Sandy Field and took up his pan, and between one blink and the next he was standing at the head of the line of leaders as they came into the street. There was one shout. The Teacher is come! The whole place was stirred up. They found him a seat, and the leaders, and served them. Before the meal was done the boy came in from the wilderness. The people got up and filled his pan with all respect. He took as much as he needed and carried it to Quaco and held it out. Give it here, Tite. Quaco put out his hand and took the pa

sections.heading: VII. The Sand Hill
sections.text: He walked with the boy at his side, and he asked him what the places were called that they passed, and the boy told him. Buzzard Roost. Fig Yard. The Burnt Mill. Sister Pond. The Orange Old-Field. When they came to where the boy stayed, Quaco climbed the sand hill, and the boy with him. From the top of it you see the ocean. Tite, when you stand up here and look this way and that, what do you see? The big water, Daddy. What comes to you when you look at it? That in the times I have cried over my troubles, I must have cried more water than that. More than four of that. Well said, Tite. It is so. Four oceans is the small water. What one body has cried is the big water. Why would anybody go on sleeping? He had dug for sweet water all his life, and he stood a good while looking at the salt. Where do you stay? In the dug place under this hill. What comes to you while you lie there? That there is no end to the times I have died and been laid down in this ground. Well said. It is so. There is no spot of ground where people have not lain down and died. And he told him one. There was a driver on a place I knew who could not stand to be put in the hands’ burying ground among field people. He

sections.heading: VIII. The Other Road
sections.dateline: Sandy Field praise house · the fall of 1863
sections.text: They talked about it in the praise house after meeting. It is a hard thing that child is doing. From the day he was born his people fed the elders sweet rice seven times over. When he went in the valley they fed us seven nights more. The eighth day he went out with the basket, and in two days he had a thousand pans and a thousand cloths. Another day he had a thousand blankets. There were people ready to carry him to Boston. All that came to him here, and he has left the whole of it and gone in the wilderness, and he lives on what is put in his pan. Quaco came in. What are you all sitting here talking about? They told him. Yes, he said. There is one road that goes to getting, and there is another road. A seeker that takes to the wilderness with his eye on what the wilderness will bring him has four bad doors standing open in front of him. The one that knows those two roads apart turns away from what they would heap on him, and goes off by himself, and works, and comes through. Then he gave them the song for it, said over in the same flat way. You may talk of my name as much as you please,  And carry my name abroad,But I really do believe I’m a child of God  As I walk in de heavenly

title: The Heavenly Road
logline: In the first spring of freedom on St. Helena Island, a seven-year-old seeker gives away a thousand blankets and goes where kin cannot follow.

verses.text: If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Rādha is a poor old brahmin of Sāvatthī who goes to live at the monastery, cutting grass, sweeping cells and fetching water. The monks treat him kindly but will not ordain him, and he grows thin. The Buddha, walking the grounds one evening, asks him what he is doing there, then calls the monks together and asks whether anyone remembers a good deed of his. Sāriputta remembers that in Rājagaha the man once gave him a ladleful of his own food, and agrees to ordain him. Rādha is seated in the outermost row. Sāriputta takes him everywhere and corrects him constantly, and Rādha follows every instruction without resentment and soon becomes an arahat. Asked how many such pupils he would accept, Sāriputta says as many as he could get. When the monks praise Sāriputta's gratitude, the Buddha tells the birth story of the elephant whose foot was healed by a camp of carpenters, who worked for them and then gave them his white son; the young elephant would not leave with the king until the carpenters, their wives and their children had all been paid. The Buddha then says that one who points out faults should be regarded as one who shows where treasure is buried.
bg.history:
Norfolk is home to the largest naval base in the world, and its gay bars have always been full of sailors who could be discharged for being seen there. Until a federal court ruled in a 1991 case, Virginia's liquor regulations forbade licensed bars to serve homosexuals or become their meeting places. In 1993 the country argued over whether gay people could serve at all; the compromise known as "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" was signed into law that November. In June 1991 about eighty people had marched from Old Dominion University to the gates of the base. The city's drag shows go back at least to the Cue Club of the 1970s. In drag houses an experienced performer, a drag mother, names and trains a newcomer; to "read" someone is to tell her faults to her face, exactly and with wit, and it is counted an art. The Garnet Room and its cast are invented.

Until the steward and commissaryman ratings were merged on January 1, 1975, the men who cooked for, served and kept the quarters of Navy officers belonged to a branch that was largely segregated, filled by Black and Filipino sailors. Confinement on bread and water for up to three days was a lawful punishment for junior sailors aboard ship until January 1, 2019. Whitman's two lines were first printed in 1860 and stand among the last poems of Leaves of Grass. Miss Geneva's swamp tale follows the Alīnacitta Jātaka, with a mule where the old story has an elephant.

sections.heading: I. The Chief
sections.text: The Garnet Room was on Granby Street, upstairs over a uniform shop, eleven blocks from the water. It had a bar the length of the room, a stage two feet high, a mirror ball, and a show on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights. It had been there since 1971. For most of those years the state of Virginia had held it unlawful to sell a drink to a homosexual, and a federal judge had struck that rule down only two winters before. Half the men at the bar on any night were Navy and sat with their backs to the door. Everybody knew about the cars that sometimes parked across the street while a man in them wrote down base stickers. The old man started coming in that January. He was sixty-seven years old, thin, very dark and very straight. He wore a pressed white shirt buttoned to the neck and brown shoes that had been shined that day. He drank one ginger ale, tipped a quarter, and watched the show from the end of the bar as a man watches a ship he is not on. After a week he asked the bartender whether there was a mop. Within a month he had the place. He came at four, when the door was unlocked for deliveries. He mopped the stage and the stairs and filled the ice wells, and he ran the follow spot

sections.heading: II. One Good Thing
sections.dateline: The Garnet Room · the first week of March
sections.text: The show director was Miss Geneva Starr. She was fifty-one that year and had run the cast for fourteen. She had been born in Suffolk, in the peanut country, and raised in a Holiness church where her grandmother was a mother of the congregation, and she had sung there until they put her out at sixteen. She did not lip-synch. She stood at the microphone in a plain dark gown and sang, and sailors who had come upstairs to laugh went down again not speaking. Offstage she said very little. In a house where everybody read everybody, all night, for sport, Miss Geneva had read perhaps six people in fourteen years, and each of them could give you the words. She had a habit of walking the building at the end of the night, after the last number, when the girls were still at the bar. She said she liked to see what was left when the people went out of it. On a Sunday early in March she came through the dressing room at one in the morning and found Emmett Raines on his knees picking bugle beads out of the floorboards with a table knife. Chief. What are you doing here? Squaring away, ma'am. I don't mean the beads. He got up. It took him a moment. Whatever wants doing, he said. The stage. The ice.

sections.heading: III. The Wheel Book
sections.text: She gave him the last place at the dressing table, the short end by the mop sink, where the bulb over the mirror flickered. She gave him the first number on Sundays. That was the spot nobody wanted, at nine o'clock, when the room was a third full and still sober. She gave him a name. He was to be Miss Emmaline Raines, since a lady of that age would not be anything shorter. Then she started on him. Coco Lashley was the best reader in Tidewater. Her people were Lashleys out of Harlem. A great-uncle of hers had kept the door of a building on Edgecombe Avenue for forty years, and it was said in the family that he never forgot a face or what he owed it. She had his eye. She could take a queen apart from the wig lace to the shoe in one breath and be right about every piece. She had read grown performers off that stage and out of the business. She read Emmett Raines every day for seven weeks. Chief, you walk like you are carrying a tray. Put the tray down. Nobody is waiting on their coffee. Your mouth is half a beat behind the record. The lady is singing, and you are reading her lips. That is not a cheekbone. That is a stripe. The wig is wearing you. Go back and put it on like you paid fo

sections.heading: IV. Sunday
sections.dateline: The Garnet Room · the last Sunday in April
sections.text: Nobody could say afterward which Sunday it had become a different matter. It may only have been that the room was fuller. A ship had come in. He went on at nine in a gray gown that Coco had cut down for him, long in the sleeve and high at the neck. He wore a small gray wig and one strand of glass pearls. The number was an old Dinah Washington record, a slow one. He walked to the center, and he was not carrying anything. He did not work the room or beg it. He stood and let the song come through him. He was an old woman who had seen what the song said and was past minding who knew. His mouth was on every word. Somewhere in the second verse the bar went quiet, and the bartender stopped the blender with his hand. The girls in the wings said that what struck them was that he did not want anything from the house. Every one of them wanted something out there. They wanted the dollars, or the noise, or one face at one table. He stood in the light and wanted nothing. When it was over he did not bow. The room got to its feet anyway, sailors and all, and stayed there. Miss Geneva had watched from the back, beside the doorman, a man called Tiny who filled the stair and had never been seen to hu

sections.heading: V. The White Mule
sections.dateline: The dressing room · later that night
sections.text: The cast sat late. They were pleased with him and somewhat ashamed. The talk came around, as it will, to Coco, who had carried one ladle of beans in her head for fifteen years and paid it back like that. One of them said that most people wouldn't remember their own mother that long. Another said the old man had been lucky in his teacher. The first one said the teacher had been lucky too, because Coco's mouth would have killed anybody else. Miss Geneva was unpinning her hair. That's nothing new for her, she said. She has always been that kind. Then she told them a story, which she almost never did. It was her grandfather's, who had cut timber in the Dismal Swamp. There was a gang of men, he said, that went into the swamp every fall to get out juniper. They cut the logs and hewed them square on the spot. They marked every piece with a number and floated the frames down the canal to Suffolk, to be put up as houses. One fall an old mule came limping out of the reeds on three legs and lay down by their fire. She belonged to nobody. She had a splinter of cypress knee through the frog of her hoof and the leg was swollen to the shoulder. The men cut around the splinter with a chisel. They

sections.heading: VI. The Mirror
sections.text: Over the long mirror in that dressing room there was a piece of shirt cardboard, gone brown, with four lines lettered on it in green ink. Miss Dorian had put it up, who ran the cast before Geneva. She had been a high school English teacher in Newport News until 1962, when they found out about her. She died in 1989 in the hospital on Colley Avenue, and four of the girls who had sat with her were dead since. Nobody had taken the card down, and nobody new had ever been told to read it. Miss Geneva reached up and touched the corner of it. Have you learn'd lessons only of those who admired you, and were tender with you, and stood aside for you?Have you not learn'd great lessons from those who reject you, and brace themselves against you? or who treat you with contempt, or dispute the passage with you? — Walt Whitman, “Stronger Lessons,” Leaves of Grass Dorian had her poet, she said. My grandmother had it shorter. She stood with her hand on the back of Emmett's chair and said it as she had learned it, standing up in the Holiness church in Suffolk at seven years old. As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear. — Proverbs 25:12 Children,

title: Reading Glasses
logline: A retired Navy steward of sixty-seven mops the stage of a Norfolk drag bar and asks, once, to be put in the show.

verses.text: Let him admonish, let him teach, let him forbid what is improper!—he will be beloved of the good, by the bad he will be hated.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two monks who are pupils of the Buddha's chief disciples settle with their followers at Kīṭāgiri and run the place into disrepute: they plant flowering trees and give flowers to lay families to win their favor, live off what the families give, and behave so badly that well-conducted monks can no longer stay there. The Buddha sends Sāriputta and Moggallāna, telling them to expel those who will not obey and to admonish and teach those who will, since the one who admonishes is hated by fools and loved by the wise, and speaks the verse. The two elders go. Some of the monks accept correction, some return to lay life, and some are formally suspended.
bg.history:
From 1829 Quakers from Ohio and Indiana and free Black families settled the southwestern Michigan county of Cass, above all Calvin Township, where by 1850 a quarter of the people were African American, many of them families of mixed Native ancestry as well. The county was a station on the Underground Railroad, and freedom seekers who came through on their way to Canada sometimes stayed. In August 1847 Kentucky slaveholders raided the Quaker farms and seized nine people; a crowd of white and Black neighbors stopped them at a mill in Vandalia, and a local court set the captives free along with dozens of others (the Kentucky raid). The Methodist society, its people and the Rocky Fork are invented.

Sojourner Truth, born into slavery in Ulster County, New York, dictated her life to Olive Gilbert, and the Narrative of Sojourner Truth was printed in 1850; she sold it at her meetings to support herself. Its account of an 1844 camp meeting near Northampton, Massachusetts, where she faced down a mob of young men by singing, is the passage read in Mother Ruth Ann's kitchen. In September 1857 Truth moved to Michigan, near Battle Creek, some forty-five miles from Calvin, and made Michigan her home for the rest of her life.

sections.heading: I. The Mill Branch
sections.dateline: Calvin Township, Cass County, Michigan · spring 1858
sections.text: Mother Ruth Ann Hollins had come out from Northampton County, North Carolina, in a covered wagon in the fall of 1844, with her husband and four grown children and her free papers sewn into the lining of her bonnet, and by 1858 she had outlived the husband and two of the children and was the nearest thing to a bishop the colored Methodists of Calvin Township had. She was not ordained to anything. The Discipline did not ordain women. She was a class leader, which the Discipline allowed, and she prayed and testified and exhorted whether the Discipline allowed it or not, and she had been doing all three every Sunday and Wednesday for fourteen years in a log meetinghouse on the edge of a tamarack swamp. Most of the families round about had come out the same road, from Virginia and the Carolinas, free people of color with a little Indian in most of them and a lot of Indian in some. The fugitives came later, at night, by way of the Quaker farms, and some of them stayed. She did not ask them anything when they came to meeting. She asked them their names and said them back, and that was all. Two men did most of her preaching for her, and the township called them her right hand and her left.

sections.heading: II. The Book
sections.text: It was the old ones who came to her finally, three of them, Brother and Sister Anthony and old Lige Day, who had walked in from the Rocky Fork in the rain. They did not want to make trouble for anybody. They sat at her table with their hats on their knees and told it, and she listened, and when they were done she thanked them and gave them supper and sent her grandson to hitch the wagon and drive them home. Then she sent for Silas Porter and Mose Gallion. They came in from their work, the cooper with shavings in his hair and the blacksmith with his apron still on. They had heard most of it already. They knew why they had been sent for, and they did not like it, because the two young men were theirs. You will go out to the Rocky Fork, she said, you two, Saturday week, and stay the Sunday. Talk to them. Teach them. Any that will hear you, keep them, and keep teaching them. Any that won't hear you, put them out of the class. I'll stand behind you at the quarterly meeting. Mose rubbed his face. Bass will hate me for it. He will, she said. The man that tells a fool the truth gets hated by the fool. That's how it is. The ones with any sense in them will love you for it, maybe not the sam

sections.heading: III. The Schoolhouse
sections.dateline: The Rocky Fork · the last Saturday in May
sections.text: The lilacs were in full bloom when they drove up, the whole front of the schoolhouse purple and white, and the smell of them came down the lane to meet the wagon. There was a play-party starting inside. They could hear it from the road, the clapping and somebody calling the figures, and Bass Booker's laugh over all of it. Mose Gallion got down and went and stood in the schoolhouse door. He did not say anything. He did not need to. He filled it from the sill to the lintel, and the clapping stopped, and the girls stopped going round, and the boys from the mill who had been leaning on the walls stood up off them. Silas Porter came in past him and set a chair in the middle of the floor where the play had been, and sat down on it, and took out his Testament, and waited until the room was quiet. Then he talked to them. He talked until after dark, the way he would have talked to a barrel that was leaking, a stave at a time. He did not shout. He named the widow's two dollars, and the Wilkins girl, and the cards behind the mill, and he named them in front of the mothers who had set the tables and the fathers who had paid for the preaching, so that it went round the room like a draft. Then h

title: Lilac Slips
logline: Two young Methodist exhorters plant lilacs around a mill-settlement schoolhouse, and an old class leader sends her right hand and her left.

verses.text: Do not have evil-doers for friends, do not have low people for friends: have virtuous people for friends, have for friends the best of men.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Channa is the groom who rode out with Prince Siddhattha on the night he left the palace, and who carried the horse and the ornaments home from the river. Later, as a monk, he could not forgive the two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, for standing nearer the Buddha than he did, and he abused them. Three times he was admonished; each time he was silent a moment and then went on as before. The Buddha said that Channa could not be taught while he lived, and on his deathbed told Ānanda to lay on him the “supreme penalty”: he might say what he liked, and no monk was to speak to him, exhort him or correct him. When the sentence was read Channa fell down and begged not to be ruined. He went off, did his work, and became an arahat, at which the penalty lapsed of itself.
bg.history:
William Laud became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1633. That October the King’s Declaration of Sports was reissued, to be read from every pulpit, and from 1634 Laud’s vicar-general carried a visitation through the province. Ministers who would not conform were cited before the Court of High Commission, whose warrants were served by officers called pursuivants, and a good many slipped away at night and joined the migration to New England, which carried some twenty thousand people over between 1620 and 1640. The sands of the Wash could be crossed on foot at low water with a guide; William Camden wrote that when the tide was out “a man may pass over it as on dry land, but yet not without danger.” Fen Enderby, Enderby on the Merrimack and everyone in them are invented.

A New England church of the first generation had, where it could afford them, a pastor and a teacher, and a lay ruling elder beside them, and a town without a bell was called to meeting by a drum. The synod that met at Cambridge from 1646 to 1648 wrote the churches’ practice down as the Cambridge Platform; its fourteenth chapter, on censures, is quoted here from the Boston edition of 1855. The College at Cambridge was founded in 1636 so as not, in the words of New England’s First Fruits (1643), to leave “an illiterate ministry to the churches,” and the timetable printed in that pamphlet gives the fourth day of the week to Greek, with “Etymologie and Syntax” for the first-year men. Etymology then meant the forms of the single word. The verb the boys decline, typtō, “I strike,” was the stock paradigm of the old grammars, and the Greek word for a drum does come from it. The book of poets is Ralph Winterton’s Poetae minores Graeci (Cambridge, 1635), dedicated to Laud, which includes the maxims of Theognis. The English is the prose version of the Rev. J. Banks (1856).

sections.heading: I. The Wash-Way
sections.text: Mr. Josias Markby was the squire’s second son, and for nineteen years he had held the family living of Fen Enderby, in the parts of Holland. It was a fat one. It was worth a hundred and thirty pounds a year in tithe wool and tithe geese and the rent of the glebe marsh, and it came with a brick parsonage and an orchard walled against the east wind. He had a wife and a daughter in that house who loved him. John Chaney was his man. The two of them had been born in the one week in the one parish, the squire’s boy in the hall and the groom’s boy over the stable, and Chaney had saddled for him since they were both small. In the autumn of 1634 the Archbishop’s visitors came through the fens asking which ministers wore the surplice, and which had read the King’s book of Sunday sports from the pulpit as they were ordered. Mr. Markby had done neither. He was cited, and did not go. In the second week of October a neighbor sent a boy over the dyke at dusk to say that a pursuivant of the High Commission was lying at an inn in Boston with a warrant in his coat. He left that night and told nobody in the house. He came out to the stable in his gown, with a candle, and found Chaney awake already, b

sections.heading: II. The Word by Itself
sections.text: They called the plantation Enderby, since most of them had come out of the fens together, and there was salt marsh enough at the river’s mouth to make them feel they had not come so very far. Thirty-odd families gathered a church there, with Mr. Markby for its pastor, and built a meetinghouse of sawn boards with a thatched roof and no bell. Chaney beat the drum for meeting. He beat the first drum at eight and the second at nine, every Lord’s day and every lecture day, and it was understood in the town that nobody else would be asked. On the fourth day of each week Mr. Markby read Greek in his study with such boys of the town as were meant for the College at Cambridge and the ministry after it. He had one grammar and a thick little book of the lesser Greek poets, printed at the other Cambridge the year after he went over the sands and sent out to him by a friend. Its first leaf had carried a dedication to the Archbishop. He had cut that out and lit the fire with it. The boys stood in a row and told over their paradigms. Tupto, I strike. Tupteis, thou strikest. Tuptei, he striketh. Chaney carried in the wood and then sat down beside it on the floor inside the door, mending harness, s

sections.heading: III. The Second Drum
sections.text: He took to his bed at the turn of the year, in a hard frost. Stephen Anderby, a young man of the town who had been two years at the College and come home when his father died, sat up with him at night. Near the end Anderby asked him what the church was to do about Goodman Chaney. Lay the heaviest thing on him. Cast him out, sir? No. Keep him in. Let him say whatever he will. Let no one answer him, nor reprove him, nor teach him, nor bid him good day, until he is another man. Tell Mr. Sarson I ask it. He died on the eleventh of January. They kept a fire burning on the ground a day and a night before it could be opened. Chaney walked behind the bier at the widow’s elbow, as near as a man could get. On the next Lord’s day, when the afternoon exercise was over, Mr. Sarson stayed the church. He had Anderby stand and say what he had been told, in the dead man’s words. Then he took up his copy of the Platform of discipline that the Synod at Cambridge had finished the summer before, and read from its chapter of censures the place that came nearest. While the offender remains excommunicate, the church is to refrain from all member-like communion with him in spiritual things, and also from a

title: Fourth Day
logline: A pastor's old groom, who rode with him the night he fled England, cannot forgive the two men his master now leans on.

verses.text: He who drinks in the law lives happily with a serene mind: the sage rejoices always in the law, as preached by the elect (Ariyas).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Mahā Kappina of Kukkuṭavatī sends riders out every day for news that a Buddha has appeared. When weary traders arriving from Sāvatthī tell him that the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha have appeared, he is so overcome he must hear each word four times, and rewards them with a hundred thousand coins for each. He sends his kingdom to Queen Anojā on a plate of gold and sets out with his thousand courtiers to go forth; they cross three rivers on horseback without wetting the horses' hooves, by recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, and find the Buddha waiting under a banyan, shining. Anojā rewards the traders three times as much, refuses to "take into her mouth" the glory her husband has spat out, and follows with the courtiers' wives, finding no hoofprints at the rivers. The Buddha hides the new monks until the women are steady, then sends the women to the nuns at Sāvatthī. Afterward Kappina goes about exclaiming "Oh, happiness!" and the monks suppose he misses being king; the Buddha says he has drunk the Dhamma. A past-life frame tells of a weaver's wife who housed a thousand holy men a king had turned away during a festival, and of householders, caught in the rain without friends inside a monastery, who built one of their own.
bg.history:
New Jersey has called itself the diner capital of the world since its factories built the prefabricated lunch cars of the early twentieth century, and by the late century most of its diners were owned by Greek immigrant families, many of whom had started as dishwashers and countermen. The blue-and-white Anthora coffee cup, with its Greek key and amphora and WE ARE HAPPY TO SERVE YOU, was designed in 1963 for Greek-owned coffee shops in New York. The King's family story reaches back to 1922, when Greek refugees from Asia Minor poured into Greece after the war with Turkey, ahead of the population exchange. A gerondas is an elder, often a monk of long experience, sought out for spiritual counsel.

In early September 2011, days after Hurricane Irene had flooded the Passaic valley, the remnants of Tropical Storm Lee stalled over the Northeast. On September 8 and 9 the Passaic flooded again at Little Falls, the Delaware ran at moderate flood stage, and the Susquehanna rose to a record of more than 42 feet at Wilkes-Barre, forcing the evacuation of tens of thousands along its banks, from Binghamton and Tunkhannock down to Harrisburg. The psalms the abbot quotes are from Sir Lancelot Brenton's 1844 English translation of the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, whose numbering of the Psalms is the one the Orthodox Church uses (text).

sections.heading: I. The King of Route 46
sections.text: Vasilis Kappas owned five diners on Route 46 and in the towns around it, and everyone from Paterson to Parsippany called him the King, which was also what his name meant, so he could not pretend he minded. There was the Olympia, with the columns. There was the Golden Star, and the Galaxy, which had a revolving cake case with eleven kinds of cheesecake, and the Athenian, out by the river, where the truckers ate. The fifth was the Plaza, on the highway in Clifton, stainless steel and blue glass, open twenty-four hours since 1979. That one he ran himself. The other four had managers, cousins and nephews, and every morning at six he drove from one to the next in a black Cadillac with a paper cup of coffee in the holder, blue and white with the Greek key on it and WE ARE HAPPY TO SERVE YOU, and tasted the soup. He was sixty-six. He had come from a village in the hills south of Kozani at nineteen, with a cardboard suitcase and an uncle's address in Astoria, and washed dishes, and bussed tables, and fried eggs on a flat-top for eleven years before he owned a stool of his own. He married Chrysanthi from the next village over, the daughter of a saffron grower, a small round woman with skin

sections.heading: II. Hunts Point
sections.text: It had rained for two weeks. First the hurricane at the end of August had put the Passaic over its banks at Little Falls and filled the basements of half of Paterson, and the Athenian had been closed four days with mud on the floor. Then the tail of a second storm came up from the Gulf and sat over Pennsylvania and New Jersey and rained and did not stop. On the Thursday morning the King was at the Athenian at six-thirty, standing at the end of the counter in his raincoat tasting the lentil soup, when the produce truck from Hunts Point came in three days late. Stelios drove it. He was sixty, a Cretan with a mustache like a push broom who had brought lettuce and tomatoes and lemons to the King's diners for twenty-two years. His son Manolis rode with him, and a helper named Ramón from the Bronx who carried the cases. They came in soaked to the knees and sat at the counter and put their faces in their hands. Where have you been? said the King. I've got no lemons. Pennsylvania, Stelios said. We went out Monday night to Scranton with a load for the Greeks at the Brothers' diner, and the roads closed behind us. Three nights we slept in the truck at a rest stop on 380 with the rain coming

sections.heading: III. Three Rivers
sections.dateline: Little Falls to Tunkhannock · Thursday afternoon, September 8
sections.text: They left from the Plaza lot at one o'clock in the afternoon in nineteen cars, Cadillacs and Lincolns and the dishwasher's Buick and somebody's son-in-law's minivan, with the King in front, and the rain coming down so hard the wipers could not keep it off the glass. The first river was the Passaic. Where the road came down to it at Little Falls it was over its banks again, brown and fast, carrying lawn chairs, and the police had the road shut with sawhorses and flashing lights. How deep? the King asked the officer. Over the guardrail, sir. You can't go through. Nobody's going through today. Is there another way? Not today, sir. The King sat in the Cadillac with the engine running. It was the first time in his life he had been told no and did not mind. While we sit here looking for another road, he thought, we get older, and one day we die looking. He had renounced everything for Christ. What would the water do to him? He put both hands on the wheel and said aloud, in the old words, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, and drove around the sawhorses. The officer shouted. Nineteen cars followed him through. The policeman told the story afterward to anyone who would buy hi

sections.heading: IV. The Placemat
sections.dateline: Clifton · Thursday night and Friday, September 9
sections.text: Stelios brought the placemat up the hill that night in the produce truck. He rang the bell, and Chrysanthi Kappas opened the door herself in her housecoat, and he stood in the marble foyer dripping and handed it to her. She read the map of Greece side first, then turned it over. What is this? He told her about the diner, and the coffeepot, and the three placemats. He gave you the Olympia, she said. For that. Yes, kyria. For a word. For a word. What word? There's a Geronda, Stelios said. Out past Scranton. A real one. And it took her exactly the way it had taken him. She felt it in her arms, then the back of her neck. She put her hand on the newel post and said, What did you say? three times, and Stelios said it three times, and the fourth time she said, He gave you the Olympia for that? That's nothing. That's a cheap man. My husband was always a cheap man. And she went to the desk in the hall where she kept the papers for everything, and wrote on the back of an electric bill that the building on Main Avenue in Passaic, the one with the bakery and the four apartments upstairs, belonged as of this date to Stelios Daskalakis, and his son got the shore house at Seaside Heights, and Ram

sections.heading: V. The Sycamore
sections.dateline: The Monastery of the Prophet Elias, Wyoming County, Pennsylvania · Saturday, September 10
sections.text: Father Isaak knew they were coming. He did not say how. On Saturday morning, when the radio said the Susquehanna had gone higher at Wilkes-Barre than it had ever gone and was only now beginning to fall, he went into the guesthouse and told the forty new old men with their long grey beards to go into the church, all of them, and stay there, and keep quiet. He shut the doors behind them. Why, Geronda? said the young monk who kept the gate. Because their wives are coming, he said. And if a woman who has been married forty years sees her husband come out of a door with a beard to his belly in a black riassa, the first day, she will either laugh or faint, and either way she won't hear one word I say to her. Let her hear first. Then she can see. The women had slept in their cars at the bottom of the ridge road. In the morning they came up it and parked in the mud. Father Isaak was waiting for them under the sycamore at the bottom of the hill, where the flood had come up to the roots in the night and gone down again, leaving a line of leaves and bottles. The women saw the light the men had seen, the gold in the white branches and the light of no color under them. Chrysanthi got out of her

sections.heading: VI. Ti Chará
sections.dateline: The Monastery of the Prophet Elias · winter 2011–12
sections.text: Monks are not supposed to talk much, and mostly the old men from the diners did not. They worked. They were used to working. They took over the kitchen and the monastery started eating very well for the first time in its history, and they rebuilt the guesthouse porch, and the dishwasher from the village grew tomatoes against the south wall of the church that were, for the first time, very good tomatoes. The King had been given a new name with the black, Varnavas. But everyone at the monastery went on thinking of him as the King, and he did not mind that either. He went around saying it. In the morning in the dark on his way to the church, and at the woodpile, and in the kitchen with his sleeves pushed up, and walking the ridge road in the snow in the afternoon with his hands behind his back and his beard blowing. Ti chará. Ti chará. What joy. What joy. Not loudly. To himself, the way a man hums. The younger monks talked about it. They had been there before the old men came, and some of them had given up very little to get there, a graduate fellowship, a girlfriend, a Honda Civic, and they were not sure what to make of forty retired diner men who had given up Route 46. One of them w

title: The Placemat
logline: A Greek diner king who has searched for years hears from a produce driver that an elder has come, and gives away a diner per word.

verses.text: Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.

bg.commentary: The commentary opens in a past age with a man so poor he is called Mahā Duggata, the Great Pauper. When a neighbor goes around writing down how many monks each household will feed, the pauper pledges one and is left off the list. He and his wife hire themselves out, a fisherman gives him four redfish, and Sakka, king of the gods, comes disguised as a cook. The Buddha of that age hands the poor man his own bowl; the king offers money for it and is refused; the Buddha enters the low house without bowing, and afterward jewels rain down until the family has to carry the children outside. Reborn ages later to a merchant's daughter who craves to feed the monks redfish, the child is named Paṇḍita, "the Wise," and at seven becomes a novice under Sāriputta. On his eighth day, walking to the village, he sees irrigators leading water, fletchers straightening arrows over a fire and carpenters shaping wheels, asks whether these things have minds, and turns back to master his own. Sakka sets guards, the sun and moon stand still, and the Buddha himself keeps watch at the door, delaying Sāriputta with four questions about food so that the boy reaches awakening before his meal arrives.
bg.history:
Almost half of the Black Mississippians who left the state in the first decades of the Great Migration went to Chicago, many of them straight north by train, and in the second wave, from 1940 to 1960, the city's Black population nearly tripled, from 278,000 to 813,000. Hemmed in by white neighborhoods and industrial districts, they crowded into the South Side's Black Belt, where Bronzeville grew its own businesses, churches, insurance companies and newspapers. Forty-Seventh Street was its main stem; the 3,000-seat Regal Theater stood at 4719 South Parkway, the street later renamed for Martin Luther King Jr. From the Mississippi Gulf Coast, the old Gulf and Ship Island Railroad ran from Gulfport north to Jackson, and after 1925 it belonged to the Illinois Central, the line most Mississippians rode to Chicago.

Migrants brought their churches with them, many of them small congregations meeting in rented storefronts, and some kept the old practices of the rural South, including the mourners' bench, where seekers knelt or sat until they "came through" to conversion. The summer of 1952 was the worst polio season in American history, with about 58,000 cases nationwide, and parents across the country kept their children out of public swimming pools (Oak Park River Forest Museum).

sections.heading: I. Big Poor
sections.text: The family tells it starting with Isom Pruitt, who was so poor that everybody on the Coast called him Big Poor, and he answered to it. That was the year the Moderator came down from Jackson for the District Association, with twenty preachers behind him and a choir from Hattiesburg, and the whole Black side of Pass Christian turned itself inside out to feed them. On the Sunday before, at Mount Pilgrim, the church clerk, Brother Toles, stood up after the sermon with a ledger book and a pencil, and he said that the Moderator had taught them something that morning.
