He said there is the man who gives and does not ask anybody else to give, and he will have plenty but nobody beside him. And there is the man who asks everybody else to give and gives nothing, and he will have friends but no bread. And there is the man who does neither, and he will eat what other people leave. And there is the man who gives and gets his neighbors giving too, and he will have bread and company both. Brother Toles said he meant to be that last kind of man. Then he went up and down the aisles writing down how many preachers each family would feed. Two, said the Battles, who had the oyster house and the ice hous

sections.heading: II. The Bible
sections.text: That same Saturday evening a tall man in a white jacket like a dining-car waiter came walking up the shell road to Big Poor's cabin and asked if anybody needed help. He said he could cook anything. Big Poor said they could not pay him. The man said a man feeding a preacher shouldn't have to pay for a cook, and wasn't it right to do a good thing when you saw one, and he went in and took the redfish from Hettie and sent everybody else out of the kitchen. On Sunday after preaching, Brother Toles went down the ledger column and sent each preacher off with the family that had him. Big Poor stood waiting with his hat in his hands until the churchyard was empty, and then he went up to the clerk. Brother Toles. Where's my preacher? Brother Toles put his hand over his mouth. Isom. I didn't write you down. The family says it went into Big Poor like a knife. He said, You told me to give. My wife and I worked all week for hire. I was on the bayou since daylight picking greens. Give me one preacher. And he wrung his hands and cried right there in the churchyard, a grown man, and people came back to see what it was, and when they heard, they turned on Brother Toles and asked him what kind of a c

sections.heading: III. Solomon
sections.text: Big Poor lived to be seventy-one. His son Royal took a share of the money north in 1922 and opened Pruitt & Sons Funeral Home on Forty-Seventh Street, with a Cadillac hearse and a chapel that seated a hundred, and every Baptist church on the South Side had Pruitt & Sons on the cardboard fans in its pews, with a picture of Jesus in the garden on one side and the telephone number on the other. Royal's daughter Odessa married a man who taught printing at the trade school, and the Pruitts were among the people who kept Deacon Lucius Mabry in barber chairs and kept his church in folding chairs, and had for twenty years. Big Poor died in Pass Christian in the winter of 1944. That same winter Odessa found out she was carrying a child. Her craving was not for pickles. She told her mother that she wanted, more than anything, to fry redfish for the whole church, the choicest pieces, and serve the deacons and the mothers' board with her own hands, and then put on a plain white usher's dress and sit on the last bench in the back and eat whatever they left. Her mother laughed at her and then telephoned to Gulfport, and a barrel of redfish came up on the Illinois Central packed in ice, and Odess

sections.heading: IV. Seeking
sections.text: It was the polio summer, the worst one anybody could remember, and Odessa kept Solomon out of the public pools along with every other mother on the South Side. He spent July in the barbershop, sitting on the shoeshine stand and watching Deacon Mabry cut hair. One evening at supper he put down his fork and said, Mama, I want to go seeking. I want Deacon Mabry for my spiritual father. In some of the old country churches back home, children went seeking when they were old enough to know what they were asking for. They went off by themselves to pray, in the woods or the cotton, for days, and told their dreams every evening to an old man or woman of the church they had picked for their spiritual father or mother, who listened and said, Not yet, or Keep on, until the morning the child came back with a face that showed it had come through, and the church took them in. Most of the churches in Chicago had let it go. Deacon Mabry's church had not. It met in a storefront on Forty-Seventh Street that had been a shoe store, with the old pastor's name painted on the glass, and it still kept a mourners' bench up front, a plank bench with no back. Solomon was seven. Odessa looked at her husband, a

sections.heading: V. Three Things
sections.text: On the eighth morning Deacon Mabry took the boy with him on his rounds. He did not go out with the other deacons, who had left early to visit the sick and the shut-in and would eat where they were fed. He went late. First he opened the church himself, and swept the floor where nobody had swept it, and filled the water cooler, and set the folding chairs back in their rows where the revival had knocked them every which way, because the Holiness church was right across the street and he did not mean to give them a chance to say that Baptists keep a dirty house. Then he showed Solomon how to carry a Bible properly, the deacon's big one, against the chest with both arms and not swinging by the cover, and how to walk on a street beside a grown man, and they went out. It was hot already. The L went over at Forty-Seventh like a long iron roll of thunder. In a vacant lot on Evans Avenue an old man in overalls had planted collards and okra and tomatoes in rows, the way he had planted them in Mississippi, and he was watering. He had a hose run from a basement window, and he did not spray it. He laid it down at the top of the row and let the water run, and walked beside it with a hoe, and wher

sections.heading: VI. Still
sections.text: Solomon let himself into the storefront and locked the door and sat down on the mourners' bench in the half-dark behind the painted glass, and put his hands on his knees and looked at them. Then he closed his eyes and looked at them anyway. He looked at his hair and his fingernails and his teeth and his skin, the way the Deacon had told him, and then he went further in, and began to lead his own mind down the row where he wanted it, and every time it spilled over he turned it back. This is the part people on Forty-Seventh Street still argue about. They say that a little after noon the pigeons all got up off the roof of the Regal Theater at once and flew east toward the lake and did not come back. They say that four policemen, nobody knew from what station, came and stood one on each corner of the block where the storefront was, in their summer uniforms, and turned the traffic down the side streets with their white gloves, and would not say why. They say the L stopped. It stopped up on its tracks over Forty-Seventh Street with the people still in it and did not move, and the people in the cars did not complain, and the motorman sat with his hands in his lap. They say that a tall man

sections.heading: VII. Dark
sections.text: When he had eaten, he took the plate to the little sink in the back and washed it and dried it and put it on the shelf. Then the L started. The pigeons came back over the roof of the Regal all at once in a long grey sheet. The four policemen walked off in four directions and nobody ever found out what station they were from. The tall man was not at the door. And the sun, which had been standing over the street since a little past noon, went down like a stone dropped in a well, all at once, so that the streetlights along Forty-Seventh Street came on by themselves, and in the kitchenettes up and down the block women came to the windows holding dishrags to see what had happened. Some of the church people were put out about it. They said it got dark in the middle of the day and the Pruitt boy had only just eaten his breakfast, and what kind of a thing was that. They said it to Reverend Tolliver that night before the revival service, on the sidewalk outside the storefront, and he heard them out. Yes, he said. While that boy was in there seeking, the sun stood still over this street, and the police held the corners, and somebody stood at the door. And I could not sit in my own house. I c

title: Four Redfish
logline: A seven-year-old Bronzeville seeker, heir to a family legend of silver rain, watches three tradesmen at work and turns back alone.

verses.text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is only a few lines long. The elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya was a dwarf, and novices and unawakened monks used to pull his hair and tweak his ears and nose, asking, “Uncle, you tire not of the Dispensation? You take delight in it?” He showed no resentment. The monks talked it over in the hall; the Buddha came in, asked what they were discussing, and said that those who have rid themselves of the pollutants are unmoved, like solid rock. Read the full commentary story, or the short discourse on Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya in the Udāna. The Sora Argia’s lines are Virgil’s, spoken to Dante when he slows on the mountain to hear what the shades are whispering about him.
bg.history:
Barre grew from about two thousand people in 1880 to more than ten thousand in 1910 on gray granite, most of it cut into cemetery monuments. The carvers were largely northern Italians, many of them from the marble towns around Carrara, the cradle of Italian anarchism, which was put under a state of siege after the Lunigiana revolt of January 1894. In Barre they built the Labor Hall on Granite Street in 1900, and from 1903 to 1912 the anarchist weekly Cronaca Sovversiva was published in the town. Boardinghouses were commonly kept by carvers’ widows, who gave a bed, a chair and three meals and often sold wine or grappa at the table.

Pneumatic tools came into the sheds in the 1890s, and the dust they raised from Barre granite, which is rich in silica, killed the men who breathed it. They called the disease stonecutters’ tuberculosis; it was silicosis. In 1909 a dispute over a heavy surfacing tool called the bumper led the manufacturers to lock out about four thousand men for three months, and the men went back on an agreement to limit the bumper while ventilation was designed; the owners then looked for a lighter bumper instead. Dust-removal equipment did not become standard until the late 1930s. Many carvers cut their own stones, and they stand in Hope Cemetery. Nino Vanelli, the Sora Argia and the Rennie shed are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Banker
sections.text: Nino Vanelli stood four feet high in his boots, and he had cut stone for forty-four of his fifty-eight years. He was from Torano, above Carrara, where a boy went up to the marble as soon as he could carry water. He had left in the winter of 1894, when the soldiers came into the Lunigiana and a man who was known to hold the Idea did well to be on a ship. In Barre he carved what the big-handed men could not get their chisels into: the inside of a lily, the eyelids of an angel, the ivy that goes around a name. He worked at his banker standing on a plank laid across two soap boxes, and when the plank was not there he did not work, so the first thing the apprentices learned in Alexander Rennie’s shed was where to hide it. They learned the rest quickly. At the noon whistle there was half an hour, and bread and cheese do not take a boy of seventeen half an hour. So two of them would lift him off his box by the bib of his apron and stand him on a rough die block too high to get down from. One would take him by the forelock and tip his face up to the skylight. One would pinch his nose shut with a thumb and finger gray with dust and hold it until he had to open his mouth. They flicked his ea

sections.heading: II. The Table
sections.dateline: The Sora Argia’s kitchen, North End · that night
sections.text: Eleven men boarded with Argia Tonelli, and Nino had been one of them for fifteen years. She was Carrarese herself, from the town. Her husband had carved for the Rennies until the spring of 1905, when he died of the stonecutters’ consumption in the back bedroom at forty-one. Since then she had kept the house, three meals and a bed and a nail for your coat. She also sold red wine by the glass at the kitchen table, a thing that the city of Barre both knew and did not know. Nino ate early and went up. The others sat on over the wine, and that night they got to talking about him. Did you see them today? The Bossi kid had him by the nose a full minute. I counted. And nothing. He doesn’t so much as go red. He’s used to it. Fifty years of being that size, you get used to it. Nobody gets used to it. I’d have put a point through that boy’s hand. Then he’s simple. You carve one of his lilies and tell me he’s simple. Somebody brought up the other thing, which they understood no better. Two summers back a man had come up from Albany to see the monument for his wife. He had stood in front of the finished angel with his hat off, called Nino maestro before the whole shed, and laid a five-dollar go

sections.heading: III. The Doors
sections.text: It was four below zero at the whistle, with the wind coming down off Millstone Hill. Aldo Bossi and the other boy had Nino up on the die block. Aldo had his thumb and finger on the old man’s nose and was asking him whether he still liked it, when the yard gang rolled back the big doors at the end of the shed to bring in a block on the flatcar. The wind came through the shed from one end to the other. It took the dust off every ledge and beam and banker, sixteen years of it, and for the length of a breath no man in the place could see the man beside him. Caps went. The drawings went off the wall. Aldo let go to cover his own face. When the doors were shut and it had settled, the block sat on its car where the engine had left it, eighteen tons, gray, with frost on the upper face. Nino Vanelli stood on the die block with his hands at his sides and dust in his eyebrows. He had not put a hand up. The plank, he said. Aldo got it.

title: Zio Nino
logline: In a Barre granite shed, apprentices stand a four-foot anarchist carver on a block each noon and pinch his nose shut, and he waits.

verses.text: Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a married daughter named Känä has been staying at her mother’s house. Four times her mother fries cakes for her to take back to her husband, and four times a monk on his alms round comes to the door and the mother gives the cakes away. The husband takes another wife. Känä blames the monks and abuses every one she sees, until they no longer dare walk down her street. The Buddha goes to the house and eats breakfast there. Känä hides and weeps. He asks the mother whether the monks took the cakes or were given them, and what blame then falls on them. Mother and daughter each say the monks did nothing wrong, and Känä is transformed. On his way home the Buddha passes the palace. When the king hears what has happened, he says that if the Buddha has made her rich in the wealth beyond the world, he will make her rich in this one. He adopts Känä as his eldest daughter and gives her in marriage to a great noble, and she feeds monks so generously that she cannot find enough of them. The Buddha then tells the Jätaka of a mouse squeezed by four cats, whom a stonecutter saves by hiding her in a hollow crystal. Read the full commentary story, or about the Jätaka tales. The sweet cakes in the story are close cousins of the malpua, a fried cake whose name and recipe go back to Vedic India and which Pakistani families still make for Ramadan.
bg.history:
New York’s Muslim community is old and mixed. In 1939 the Grenadian-born convert Shaikh Daoud Faisal founded the Islamic Mission of America in Brooklyn Heights, now known as the State Street Mosque. After immigration law changed in 1965, and especially in the 1980s, newcomers from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Guyana, Senegal, Egypt and elsewhere settled in the outer boroughs, in neighborhoods such as Jackson Heights. In 1983 Masjid al-Falah in Corona, Queens, opened as the city’s first purpose-built mosque (Islam in New York City).

The Tablighi Jamaat was founded in 1926 by Muhammad Ilyas Kandhlawi in the Mewat region of British India. After Partition its Pakistani center grew up at Raiwind, near Lahore, and the movement has since spread to more than 150 countries, the United States among them. It is a lay movement that keeps out of politics. Members go out in small traveling parties, or jama’ats, ideally paying their own way, carrying their bedding and staying in mosques. Each day they make a gasht through the local neighborhood, with a local guide, inviting Muslims to the evening prayer. The movement asks its members to give one night a week, one weekend a month and forty days a year to this work.

sections.heading: I. Malpure
sections.text: On the block nobody called her Zubaida. Since the day her daughter was born in Gujranwala twenty-three years before, she had been Kaneez ki Ammi, Kaneez’s mother, and when she came to America in 1975 with her husband and the girl and two suitcases tied with rope, the name came with her, the way names do. Her husband drove a cab for eleven years and died of his heart in the front seat of it on the Grand Central Parkway. She kept the two-family house off Roosevelt Avenue that he had bought with the cab money, and rented the top floor to a family from Guayaquil, and sewed shalwar kameez for half the Pakistani brides in Jackson Heights at a machine in her front window, where she could see the street. Her rule about the door came from her own mother. Nobody who knocked at it went away with empty hands. Not the Jehovah’s Witnesses, not the boys selling candy for their basketball team, not the man who came around every month for the Con Edison meter. She would give them a samosa in a paper napkin or a cup of tea or an orange from the bowl. Kaneez had been embarrassed by it all through high school. In February Ammi slipped on the ice on the front steps and broke her wrist, and Kaneez came

sections.heading: II. Four Trays
sections.text: On Wednesday she made them again. The batter, the hour, the ghee, the syrup, the rows on the tray. A second tray, her other good one, the one with the handles. The doorbell rang at half past four. It was a different jama’at, from Toronto this time, six men, staying the week, and their guide was the same young man from the neighborhood who had brought the first ones, and he looked at Ammi and at the tray in the kitchen behind her with a face that said he was very sorry and also that he had smelled it from the corner. She gave it to them. Tariq’s mother called on Thursday and talked to Ammi for half an hour in a voice Kaneez could hear from across the room. The next Monday it was four men from Chicago. The Friday after that it was a jama’at of students from Long Island, boys, with their caps on crooked, and one of them had a Walkman around his neck that he had forgotten to take off, and he put his hand over it when he saw Ammi looking. She gave each of them the whole tray. She could not help it. Each time she stood in the door and meant to say, Brothers, I’m sorry, these are for my daughter’s in-laws, and each time the smell went out past her into the street and the words did not com

sections.heading: III. Roosevelt Avenue
sections.text: After that Kaneez went a little crazy, the block said, and the block was not wrong. She cursed them in the street. Any man in a white kurta and a white cap, any party of them going by in a line on gasht, any single brother coming down the stairs from the 103rd Street station with his sleeping bag on his back, she would go to the edge of the sidewalk and let him have it in Punjabi, the kind of Punjabi her mother had never let her learn and she had learned anyway. She called them beggars and thieves. She called them crows. She said they went door to door eating other people’s weddings. She said it so loud that the Colombian women at the bus stop turned around, and the man at the fruit stand stopped weighing, and the train went over and drowned her out, and she waited till it passed and said the rest. The jama’ats got so they would not come down her street. The young man from the neighborhood who guided them on gasht would stop at the corner of Roosevelt and say, Not this block, brothers. We’ll go around, and they would go around, five or six men in white walking a long way out of their way in the July heat, and Kaneez would watch them from the front steps. Ammi said nothing. She sewe

sections.heading: IV. Bhai Yusuf
sections.dateline: The house off Roosevelt Avenue · a morning in August
sections.text: He was seventy-one years old. He had worked the A train as a conductor for twenty-nine years, from Inwood to Far Rockaway and back, and retired with a pension and a gold watch he gave to his grandson. He had taken his shahada in 1962 at the old mosque on State Street in Brooklyn, where the imam was a man from Grenada and the people praying were from Harlem and Yemen and Bengal and Trinidad, and since then he had been going out in the path of God with the jama’ats, three days a month and forty days a year, for longer than most of the brothers had been alive. He had been to Raiwind. He had been to Dewsbury and to Durban and to a mosque in a strip mall in Texas. His Urdu was terrible and he knew it, and the young men from Lahore loved him for it. They called him Bhai Yusuf, Brother Yusuf, or Chacha, uncle, and the Bangladeshi boys called him Nana. He did not say much. When he did, it was short. He rang the bell at nine in the morning and Ammi opened the door and knew him, everybody knew him, and put her hand to her chest. Then she brought him in and sat him at the kitchen table in her husband’s chair, and because there was no question of anything else she made him breakfast: parathas

sections.heading: V. Chaudhry Sahib
sections.dateline: Seventy-fourth Street, Jackson Heights · the same morning
sections.text: He walked back toward the express stop under the El, the long way, because it was a fine morning and he liked to walk, and so he went past the office of Chaudhry Sahib. Everybody knew Chaudhry Sahib. He had come in 1968 with a degree in engineering that nobody in New York would honor, and driven a cab, and bought a medallion, and then another, and now he owned forty of them and a travel agency on Seventy-fourth Street that sold more tickets to Karachi and Lahore than any other in the city, and two buildings, and a share of a sweet shop, and he paid for half of everything at the masjid and did not let anybody forget it. He was sitting in his office window doing the accounts when Bhai Yusuf went by, and he said to his nephew, Is that Bhai Yusuf? Go and tell him I’m coming out. He came out onto the sidewalk in his shirtsleeves and embraced the old man and kissed his hand. Chacha-ji. Where are you coming from so early? From the house of Kaneez’s mother, in Corona. Kaneez? The one who curses the jama’ats on Roosevelt Avenue? What were you doing there? I heard she was cursing the brothers. So I went. And? Did you stop her? She stopped, said Bhai Yusuf. She’s rich now. Richer than you. Sh

sections.heading: VI. Four Doors
sections.text: She did whatever good she liked. She hired two cooks from Lahore and kept both kitchens going from Fajr to Isha. She paid four boys from the neighborhood, students, five dollars a day each, to stand at the doors of four masjids, in Corona and Jackson Heights and Astoria and Flushing, and ask every jama’at that came through whether they had eaten, and if they had not, to bring them to her house. Five men, ten men, twenty. Brothers from Leicester and Johannesburg and Trinidad and Dhaka, sleeping bags on their backs, sitting on the floor of her living room on white sheets she had spread over the carpet, eating biryani and nihari and her mother’s malpure, and the food went out of her door and down the walk and onto the sidewalk in foil trays for anybody passing, like a river that had come up over its banks. And it was never enough. That was the thing she said to the cooks, and to Rana Sahib, and to her mother, who had moved in with them and sat at a sewing machine in the front window where she could see the street. There aren’t enough of them. I can’t find enough of them. She sent the boys out again. She called the masjid in Corona and asked when the next jama’at was coming from Toront

title: Kaneez’s Mother
logline: Four times a widow in Queens fries malpure for her daughter's in-laws, and four times the doorbell rings.

verses.text: Good people walk on whatever befall, the good do not prattle, longing for pleasure; whether touched by happiness or sorrow wise people never appear elated or depressed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha and five hundred monks spend a rainy season at Verañjā as guests of a brahmin who, “under the spell of Māra,” does not think of them for a single day. There is a famine, and the monks live on measures of steamed grain given them by horse-dealers. Mahā Moggallāna offers to turn the earth over so they can eat what lies beneath it, or to take them north to Uttarakuru, and is refused both times (in the Vinaya’s telling the Buddha asks what would become of the creatures that live in the ground). Nobody complains. At the end of the season the Buddha takes formal leave of the brahmin, who honors him at last. Back at Jetavana, where food is plentiful, five hundred hangers-on who live on the monks’ leftovers and were quiet all through the famine go shouting and wrestling on the riverbank. The Buddha tells of the donkeys who got drunk on the strained washings of the wine that war-horses had drunk and stood quiet on.
bg.history:
Matsutake, the pine mushroom, cannot be farmed. When Japan’s own woods stopped producing enough of it, exporters turned to the Pacific Northwest, and from the late 1980s a circuit of commercial pickers followed the fruiting from British Columbia down to northern California. Many were Cambodian, Lao, Hmong and Iu Mien refugees. The country around Crescent Lake and Chemult, where lodgepole pine grows on deep pumice from the eruption of Mount Mazama, became the center of the trade, with independent buyers weighing mushrooms for cash at roadside sheds every evening. The price could move by many dollars in a night, and by the mid-1990s it had been as high as six hundred dollars a pound. Raking the forest floor to get at buried buttons was the practice everyone argued about. A study begun near Diamond Lake in 1994 found that removing the litter layer and not replacing it was “strongly detrimental” to later fruiting, while careful picking did no harm. The anthropologist Anna Tsing’s The Mushroom at the End of the World describes these camps closely.

The Iu Mien are a highland people of southern China and northern Laos. Many Mien men fought on the American side in the war in Laos, and after 1975 whole villages crossed into refugee camps in Thailand and were resettled, a few years later, in California and Oregon. Tsing writes that the Mien encampments in the matsutake woods were the nearest thing their elders had found in America to a village in upland Laos. Steam-rolled barley is ordinary horse feed. The dry fall, the buyer, the packer and the Saelee crew are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Padlock
sections.text: The man who invited them was named Vern, and he bought mushrooms. The November before, down in the tanoak country near the California line, he had weighed old Mrs. Saelee’s baskets five nights running and had not found a mushroom in them with a torn veil or a knife mark. On the fifth night he came around the scale and spoke to her grandson, because the old woman had no English. Tell her next fall I’ll be up in the pine. Crescent Lake Junction, on the Cutoff road, a plywood shed with my name on it. Tell her to bring her people and camp behind me. There’s a water tank. I’ll have propane, and rice on my account at the store. I pay cash at the scale every night. Tell her it’s her crew I want. Kao told her. She looked at the man for a while, and said they would come. Fahm Koy Saelee was seventy that year. She had been born in the hills above Muang Sing, in the north of Laos, and had walked out of that country in 1975 with a grandchild tied on her back. She buried her husband in a refugee camp in the north of Thailand and came at last to Redding, California, where the summers ran to a hundred and ten degrees and there was nothing anyone could think of for her to do. In the woods it was d

sections.heading: II. A Struck Measure
sections.text: Across the Cutoff from the shed stood a pole corral, and in the first week of October a man named Hank Teal backed a stock truck up to it and let down nine horses and two mules. He packed elk hunters into the Diamond Peak country every fall, and he came early to shoe and to let the string get its wind at that height. He was past sixty and he minded his own business. He minded it for four days. He watched the smoke behind the padlocked shed and he watched what came out of the woods in the white buckets at evening, and on the fifth morning he walked across the road with a fifty-pound sack on his shoulder and an aluminum feed scoop in his hand. It’s barley. Steam-rolled. It’s clean, it’s what they get. He tipped his head back toward the corral. I can’t do a lot. I’ve got eleven head to carry through November and I bought close. I can do a scoop apiece, every day. He showed Kao what he meant by it. He drove the scoop into the sack and brought it up heaped, and drew the flat of his hand across the top so that what stood above the rim fell back. Struck measure, my granddad called that. Not heaped and not scant. He did it seventeen times into the rice pot, once for each person in the camp

sections.heading: III. The Jackets
sections.text: Rain came on the twenty-third. Snow came down to the road four days behind it, and that was the season in the pine. They had picked forty pounds between the one and the other. Vern came back with the snow. He had made more in eight weeks than in the six years before, and he drove in at dusk in a different truck to fetch his scale. He saw the tarps behind the shed. Then he saw the feed sacks, nine of them, folded square and weighted with a rock, and he stood and read the printing on the top one. She came out to him herself, with Kao beside her. She hadn’t come about the water tank or the account at the store. She came because a person does not leave a man’s place without telling him. She says we go tomorrow. She says thank you for the ground to camp on. Vern had been an actor once and had a voice that could reach the back of a house, and for a while he couldn’t find any of it. I never thought about you, he said finally. Tell her that. It isn’t that I thought of it and stayed away. I never once thought of it. Kao told her. She nodded, the way she nodded when he told her the price. He was gone three hours. He came back from La Pine with a hundred pounds of rice and two cases of chicke

sections.heading: IV. The Forks
sections.text: In the Illinois Valley it had been raining for three weeks. The mushrooms there come up under tanoak and madrone, on slopes a goat would think about, and they were lifting the wet leaves everywhere a person looked. A bucket was full by ten in the morning. That was also the fall the price went where it had never been. The junction had failed, and people said the crop in Japan had failed, and there were not enough matsutake in the world. It was told for years afterward that on one night that season number-one buttons went for six hundred dollars a pound, for about two hours, at a scale in the woods. Nothing like that came to the Illinois Valley. But Vern at the old Texaco paid more each night than he had the night before, and the crew was making in a day what a good week had made them other years. On the second Saturday the relatives drove up from Redding with a pig in the bed of a pickup, and killed it by the river, and there was food for sixty people. The boys had money too. They had learned at last to see a hump under madrone leaves, or else they walked behind the pickers and took what had been missed, and at those prices what had been missed was wages. They still ate at the old w

title: Struck Measure
logline: A Mien grandmother brings her mushroom crew to the Oregon pine for a buyer who forgets them, in a fall when nothing comes up.

verses.text: If, whether for his own sake, or for the sake of others, a man wishes neither for a son, nor for wealth, nor for lordship, and if he does not wish for his own success by unfair means, then he is good, wise, and virtuous.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a householder of Sāvatthī who lives rightly tells his wife, in the middle of a pleasant conversation, that he wants to go forth. She asks him to wait until their child is born. When the child can walk he asks again, and she asks him to wait until the child is grown. He decides that her permission makes no difference, goes forth, and reaches the goal. Later he returns and teaches his son, who goes forth and reaches it too. His wife thinks, “Both of those for whom I desired to live the household life have gone forth,” and follows them. When the monks praise him for the example he set his son, the Buddha answers that a wise person seeks success neither for his own sake nor for another’s. Read the full commentary story. The triad of the verse (son, wealth, realm) is older than Buddhism. The Brihadāranyaka Upanishad, quoted here in Max Müller’s translation (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15, 1884), names the same three desires. It also tells of the sage Yājñavalkya leaving home and of his wife Maitreyī, who refuses her share of his property with the question that stands at the head of this story.
bg.history:
The Palisades plant stands in the dunes of Covert Township, Michigan, beside Van Buren State Park, and first ran at the end of 1971. On March 28, 1979, at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania, the reactor shut itself down eight seconds into the trouble, and the core was half melted some hours later because the heat still coming off it was not carried away. One of the changes ordered afterward was the shift technical advisor, an engineer on every shift whose work was to assess, not to operate. Decay heat behaves as the shift supervisor says: about six or seven percent of full power at shutdown, about one and a half percent an hour later, under half a percent after a day. Spent fuel is kept under water for years before it can be stored in air-cooled casks. Workers leaving a plant are checked in a whole-body counter, which always finds the natural radioactive potassium present in every human body. Palisades was sold to Entergy, of New Orleans, in April 2007.

Ganges is a crossroads on the Blue Star Highway in Ganges Township, Allegan County. The Vivekananda Vedanta Society of Chicago, a branch of the Ramakrishna Order, established its retreat there in 1971. Indian engineers and their families, many of them South Indian Brahmins, came to the American Midwest in numbers after the immigration law changed in 1965. Sannyasa, the formal renunciation of household life, is by tradition the last of the four stages of a life, and whether a husband may take it without his wife’s consent has been argued over for a very long time. The Ramanathans, the shift supervisor, the old swami at Uttarkashi and Visalam Mami are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Advisor
sections.text: The job had not existed before the accident. After Three Mile Island the government decided that every nuclear control room in the country ought to have one person on shift with an engineering degree and nothing to do with his hands, somebody who would stand back from the boards when the alarms came in and think. They called him the shift technical advisor. At Palisades, on the Lake Michigan dunes below South Haven, one of the first was S. Ramanathan, thirty-three years old, late of Kumbakonam, Ann Arbor and the Bechtel Corporation, whom the operators called Ram. He was good at it. The operators were Navy men and had expected to resent him, and found they didn’t. He sat at a steel desk behind the horseshoe of panels and watched. He read the logs back three shifts before he took the watch. He never touched a switch. That was the rule of the job, and Marv Dykstra, the shift supervisor, said he had the look of a man who would have kept the rule if nobody had written it down. When he was on days he stopped on the way home at the state park beside the plant and walked down to the water, because the lake was to the west and the sun went into it. There he did what his father and his fathe

sections.heading: II. The Second Asking
sections.text: The boy was born in a snowstorm off the lake, and they named him Shankar. By the next spring he was walking. He went from the couch to the coffee table and from the coffee table to his father’s knee, and one evening in May, when he had got as far as the screen door on his own and stood slapping it with both hands, Ramanathan asked again. He is walking. He is one year old. Wait until he is a man. Let him finish school and find work. Then go, and I will pack the bag for you myself. She meant it, and he saw that she did. He saw too that after the work there would be a wedding to wait for, and after the wedding a grandchild, and that she would mean it every time. He thought, It makes no difference whether she says yes. Nobody can let another person out. That summer the company offered to put him in the license class, which was the road to shift supervisor and from there to running the place. He thanked them and said no. He paid off the house. He put the savings and the car in her name, and drove to the benefits office in Jackson and signed what there was to sign. On a Tuesday in September he stood his last back shift, read the logs over to his relief, and walked out through the gate wi

sections.heading: III. Water
sections.text: She took the job. She had a bachelor of science from Queen Mary’s College in Madras that she had never expected to use, and for twenty-three years she drew samples of the water that ran through the reactor and told the control room what was in it. She was exact. People on the back shift said you could set the boron by her. She kept the house. She kept it for the boy, who came off the school bus at ten to four. She kept it also for the man, though she would not have said that to anyone living. His steel coffee tumbler stayed on the shelf where it had always stood, and she washed it when she washed the shelf. When Shankar was four he asked where his father was, and she told him as much of the truth as a boy of four could carry, that Appa had gone to live beside the Ganges. Fifteen miles north of South Haven the Blue Star Highway runs through a crossroads with a store and a township hall, and the sign there says GANGES. Somebody liked the name a long time ago. There is a retreat among the orchards that the Vedanta swamis from Chicago have kept since 1971, and she drove up some Sundays for the talk and for the Upanishad class that old Visalam Mami gave afterward. The boy saw the sign f

sections.heading: IV. Ganges
sections.text: A letter came in June, the first in twenty-two years, in a hand she knew. The swamis in Chicago had invited a teacher from Uttarkashi to give the August classes at the retreat. He would be at Ganges three weeks. The letter asked for nothing. She did not go. She told Shankar, and left the letter on the kitchen table, and on a Saturday he drove up the Blue Star Highway and turned in past the sign. His father was sitting in a lawn chair under an apple tree with his head shaved, in an orange cloth, a smaller man than the one in the photograph. He looked up at Shankar the way the boy had once looked over the people on that lawn. Neither of them moved to touch the other. Shankar had driven up with one sentence ready, and he said it. I couldn’t talk yet. You left before I could say one thing to you. Yes, his father said. He said nothing after it. He waited for the rest, and there was a great deal of the rest, and it took most of an hour, and he did not put up a word against any of it. Afterward they sat. His father asked what he did at the plant, and Shankar told him about the rounds and the readings and the license class, and the simulator in the training building where they ran the bad

sections.heading: V. Background
sections.text: In the spring he passed the license examination. In June he gave the company his notice and gave his mother the keys to his truck. She did not ask him to wait. She had asked that of somebody once. He went the way his father had gone. She stayed one more winter. The house was paid for and the pension had vested long ago. In April the company sold the plant to a firm from Louisiana, and there was a new badge to be issued and a new benefits book to read, three hundred pages of it. She sat down with it at the kitchen table, with the steel tumbler on its shelf and the door of the boy’s room shut, and got as far as the table of contents. Both the ones I kept it for are gone, she said to Visalam Mami on the telephone that night. What am I keeping? When a person leaves a nuclear plant for good, she goes into the whole-body counter before she turns in her badge. It is a shielded booth with a detector in it, and it looks through the body for anything the work has left there. She stood in it for two minutes on her last afternoon. The technician was a young woman she had trained. You’re clean, Mrs. Ramanathan. Twenty-three years. There’s nothing in you but potassium. Potassium? Everybody’s got

title: Decay Heat
logline: An engineer hired to watch a nuclear control room and touch nothing tells his wife, over coffee, that he wants to leave the world.

verses.text: Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore (become Arhats); the other people here run up and down the shore.
But those who, when the law has been well preached to them, follow the law, will pass across the dominion of death, however difficult to overcome.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the people of one street in Sāvatthī band together, give alms in common, and resolve to spend a whole night listening to the Dhamma. They cannot do it. Some are overcome by desire and go home, some are overcome by anger, and the rest sit nodding in their places and hear nothing. When the monks talk it over the next day, the Buddha says that beings mostly live clinging to existence, and that those who reach the other shore are few.
bg.history:
Burning Man has been held since the 1990s on the playa of the Black Rock Desert in Pershing County, Nevada, the bed of the vanished Lake Lahontan. For one week a city is built there and then removed. Nothing is sold in it but ice and coffee, and gifting is one of its stated principles. In 2002 the theme was The Floating World, and 28,979 people came. The Man stood on a forty-foot lighthouse, the curved streets were named for the parts of a ship from Bowsprit back to Abyss, and the radial avenues were numbered as compass bearings from 60 to 300 degrees. The large sound camps were placed at the two ends of the arc, at 60 and 300. On the Friday, the organizers’ own account says, a brief blinding dust storm in the late afternoon turned to showers and ended in a rainbow. The orange perimeter fence, put up to catch windblown trash, marks the limit of the event.

All-night dancing came to the playa with the San Francisco rave crews of the mid-1990s, and the music they brought descends from house, which Black DJs in Chicago built in the early 1980s out of disco, soul and drum machines. A set that ends at sunrise is one of the event’s customs. William Blake wrote the four lines called “Eternity” in his notebook in the 1790s. The text here is the one John Sampson printed in the Oxford edition of 1913; the manuscript’s first line is now usually read “binds.” The block on Mizzen, the flatbed and Bernadette are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Block
sections.dateline: Black Rock City, Nevada · Friday, August 30, 2002
sections.text: That year the theme was the Floating World, and the city was laid out like a chart. The dry lake was the sea. The Man stood on a lighthouse in the middle of it, and the streets that curved around him were named for the parts of a ship from bow to stern, Bowsprit and Forecastle and Mainmast and on back to Fantail, with the last street of all called Abyss. The cross streets were compass bearings. Five camps shared the block of Mizzen between 195 and 210 degrees. There was Camp Barnacle, from Fresno. There were some nurses from Reno who ran a foot-washing station, and six kids from Santa Cruz with a trampoline, and a camp that did nothing but mend zippers. And there were two brothers from Elko who had brought a smoker and a hundred pounds of brisket and had forgotten shade. Nothing is bought or sold in that city but ice and coffee, so what a block has is what it gives away. On Friday the five camps put everything in together. There was the brothers’ brisket and the nurses’ rice, and forty pounds of peaches Dale Fenner had driven up from Fresno on ice. From two o’clock until the dust came they fed whoever walked down Mizzen, something over three hundred people, out of whatever bowl or

sections.heading: II. The Shore
sections.text: They rode out in one long string as the lamplighters were coming down the avenues, forty-one bicycles wound with glow wire, and the kid in front carried a plate of brisket and a thermos for her, wrapped in a towel. The truck sat with its tail to the fence. Four speaker stacks stood strapped to the bed, and between them a plywood table held two turntables under a red work light. There was no banner and no sign. Along the side rail of the bed somebody had painted four lines in white house paint, small, so that a person had to walk the length of the truck to read them, and in the dark nobody did. Bernadette took the plate, said thank you, baby to the kid who handed it up, and set it down by the generator. She had no microphone. In all the years she had come out, nobody had heard her say a word over those speakers. The first record was already going. It was slow, slower than anything people dance to, with a kick drum in it like something asleep and breathing, and for most of an hour it hardly changed. The ones who had come to dance stood around waiting to be told what to do. From the fence the city was a long low line of colored light. It looked the way a shore does from a boat. All al

sections.heading: III. The Fence
sections.text: At two a pickup with a plywood shark built over it came out of the dark with its own stereo going and parked forty feet off the corner of the flatbed. Dale walked over to explain. The man driving the shark explained back. It took an hour and ten minutes and one of the Rangers, and it pulled eight or nine of the block in on Dale’s side. When the shark had finally backed off and gone, Dale found that he was shaking. He had not heard a note in over an hour. The thing playing in his head was everything he ought to have said. He stood another ten minutes with his jaw set, and then he got on his bicycle and rode for the city, composing it, and the ones who had been in the argument rode with him, still talking. A man from the zipper camp stayed half an hour longer to tell whoever stood near him that it had all been better in ’98. The ones left were too tired to quarrel and too tired to go. They had been on their feet since six that morning serving brisket. One at a time they sat down on the playa where they were, in their fur coats, and pulled their hats over their eyes, and told each other they could hear it fine from there. She was playing things by then that would have had them all on

sections.heading: IV. Mizzen and 210
sections.text: The block came back together around the coffee at nine, under Barnacle’s shade, and counted. It was three out of forty-one. The lovers were pleased with themselves until about ten. Dale was still giving his speech to the shark. The sleepers swore they had heard every bit of it, and one of them could hum some. The flatbed came down Mizzen at the five miles an hour the city allows, with a tarp over the stacks. She stopped at 210 and handed down the plate and the thermos, washed. How many of you all made it? Three, Dale said. We said the whole street. He told her how it had gone and who went where. He didn’t leave himself out. That’s about what it is, she said. Every year. Don’t take it hard. She looked them over, the sunburnt ones and the hungover ones and the ones newly in love. Folks come out there with their hands full. Somebody they want. Somebody they can’t stand. A blanket. You can’t hear it holding all that. It’s the same set next year. She put the truck in gear. As it rolled by, those standing nearest could read the side rail in daylight for the first time. She had copied it, she once told the nurse, out of her mother’s old blue Oxford Blake, which says bends where the newer

title: Hands Full
logline: Forty-one neighbors on one street of a desert city vow to stand through a DJ's whole set, from sundown to sunrise.

verses.text: A wise man should leave the dark state (of ordinary life), and follow the bright state (of the Bhikshu). After going from his home to a homeless state, he should in his retirement look for enjoyment where there seemed to be no enjoyment. Leaving all pleasures behind, and calling nothing his own, the wise man should purge himself from all the troubles of the mind.

Those whose mind is well grounded in the (seven) elements of knowledge, who without clinging to anything, rejoice in freedom from attachment, whose appetites have been conquered, and who are full of light, are free (even) in this world.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the slightest in the collection. Fifty monks who have spent the three months of the rains retreat in the kingdom of Kosala come to Jetavana at the end of the season to see the Buddha. He listens to the account of their season, and then gives them three verses on the life they have taken up: out of the dark state into the bright one, from home into homelessness, delight looked for in the solitude where it is hardest to find, nothing called one's own, the mind cleaned, and freedom here and not later. Many of them reach the first stages of awakening. (The Pāli title says five hundred visiting monks; the story itself says fifty.)
bg.history:
Before the combine, the wheat of the northern plains was cut, shocked and threshed by tens of thousands of migrant men who followed the harvest north by freight train from Oklahoma to the Canadian line and were paid off when the freeze stopped the threshing rigs. In the summer of 1915 the paper of the Industrial Workers of the World reported posted harvest wages in North Dakota averaging $2.50 a day, with $3 around Minot, warned that "stickups" were working that district, and told men to send their stakes ahead by postal money order. Between jobs they lived in "jungles," camps near a water tank and a stream. Nels Anderson, who had been a hobo before he was a sociologist, set down the jungle's law in The Hobo (1923): "no one can call a vessel his except at the time he uses it," and cans are to be cleaned, dried and left "turned bottom side up so that they will not fill with rainwater and rust." Jack London's The Road (1907) describes the names cut into railroad water tanks with a date and a direction: "Water-tanks are tramp directories." Minot, founded by the Great Northern in 1886 and reached by the Soo Line in 1893, was a wide-open town in a state that had been dry since statehood. In August 1913 it jailed IWW street speakers and their supporters in a bullpen and then in the Great Northern stockyard, as Prairie Public's account of the Wobblies in Minot tells it. The jungle on the river, White City and the fifty are invented.

The World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 was built largely of staff, plaster and fiber on temporary frames, sprayed white. It closed on October 30 in the middle of a national depression. Chicago's unemployed sheltered in the empty buildings that winter; a fire on January 8, 1894 destroyed the Peristyle, and another in July took most of what was left. During the Fair, the World's Parliament of Religions met downtown, and on September 18 the young Ceylonese Buddhist Anagarika Dharmapala, dressed in white, read his paper there. Anagārika is Pāli for "homeless one," the same word the verse uses. Edwin Arnold's The Light of Asia (1879), a life of the Buddha in English verse, was one of the first books to carry that story to ordinary Western readers. The lines White City says are from Books Four and Eight.

sections.heading: I. The Tank
sections.text: There was a water tank on the Great Northern a little east of the Minot yards, and one moniker had been cut into its timbers every fall for the best part of twenty years, each cut under the last: WHITE CITY, the month and the year, and on the day he left, an arrow pointing south. A man coming in off the threshing with his season's money in his shoe could read on that tank whether White City was still holding down the jungle in the willows. If the newest date had no arrow under it, he walked down to the river before he walked into town. White City was forty-five that year and had been on the road since he was twenty-five. He shocked and pitched like anybody from July to freeze-up, on the rigs north of town. When the threshing shut down he kept the camp on the Mouse River for two weeks or three, until the river skimmed over. He hustled the wood. He kept forty-odd tin cans scoured with sand and hung bottom side up on the willow stubs so they would not fill with rain and rust: lard pails for cooking, the big square ones for boiling up clothes, tomato cans for coffee. Nobody had asked him to. But men who had come through that camp told it in other camps, as far off as the Wenatchee appl

sections.heading: II. The Season
sections.dateline: The jungle on the Mouse River · the same afternoon
sections.text: In a jungle nobody asks a man his name or where he was raised. White City asked each of them one thing, where he had been since July. Then he went on peeling potatoes into the big can and let the man say. A Dane had pitched bundles for a rig north of Berthold, daylight to dark, at three dollars, and been docked for every hour it rained. He had slept in the straw stack, because the farmer's wife would not have harvest hands in the barn with the lanterns. Two of them had been in Minot in August, when the Wobblies got up on boxes at the street corners and the town swore in fifty special police. They had been held in a bullpen outside the jail, and the fire company had turned the hose on them. When the bullpen was full, the rest were put in the stockyard pens beside the Great Northern track. They were offered their dinner if they would break rock for it. One of the two had broken the rock. He said so, and nobody in the willows said anything. A brakeman out of Williston had wanted a dollar a division or hit the grit. A man with eighty cents had hit it, at twenty miles an hour, and he rolled his sleeve to show them the arm. A stiff called Ohio Red had gone between the cars at Towner, in

sections.heading: III. The King's Boy
sections.text:
You talk like men that had a thing took off you, he said. A house. A woman, some of you. I talked that way ten years. There was a rich man's boy in India one time. A king's boy. He had three houses, one for the heat and one for the cold and one for the rains, and a wife, and a new baby. He walked out on the whole spread one night, on purpose, and went on the bum. He bummed his chuck at back doors with a bowl for the better part of fifty years, and kings came down to the road to ask him how it was done. A man wrote it up. This is the boy talking, the night he goes. He means the ground. The earth. I choose
    To tread its paths with patient, stainless feet,
    Making its dust my bed, its loneliest wastes
    My dwelling, and its meanest things my mates:
