title: White City
logline: When the freeze stops the threshing, fifty harvest hands ride into a hobo jungle to see the man who keeps its cans clean.

verses.text: There is no suffering for him who has finished his journey, and abandoned grief, who has freed himself on all sides, and thrown off all fetters.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha's jealous cousin Devadatta, with the backing of Prince Ajātasattu, rolls a rock down from Vulture's Peak; a splinter wounds the Buddha's foot. He is carried to the mango grove of the physician Jīvaka, who dresses the wound with an astringent and binds it, then goes into the city to a patient, meaning to come back and take the bandage off. He returns too late; the city gate has shut, and he spends the night afraid that the bandage, left on, is causing the Buddha great pain. Knowing his thought, the Buddha has Ānanda remove it, and the wound vanishes like bark peeling from a tree. At dawn Jīvaka asks whether he suffered, and the Buddha answers that for one who has finished the journey all suffering is gone, as it was from the night of his awakening.
bg.history:
In the spring of 1953 the Atomic Energy Commission set off eleven atmospheric tests at the Nevada Test Site in the series called Upshot-Knothole. The ninth, Harry, a 32-kiloton device on a tower, was fired before dawn on May 19, and the wind carried its fallout northeast over St. George, a town of about forty-five hundred in the cotton-and-fruit country Latter-day Saint settlers called Dixie since the cotton mission of 1861. An AEC monitor in town saw his instrument go off its scale around nine in the morning. Residents were asked by radio to stay indoors for a time and were told there was no danger; cars coming from the St. George area were checked with counters and washed at St. George, Cedar City, Mesquite and other points. Children at some schools were outside at recess while the fallout settled. The shot was later called "Dirty Harry." Earlier that spring thousands of sheep driven from Nevada winter range to lambing grounds near Cedar City sickened and died, and their owners' lawsuits against the government failed.

Rates of leukemia and other cancers among the downwinders of southern Utah, Nevada and Arizona became a long public fight. In 1990 Congress passed the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, which offered payments to people with certain illnesses and apologized on behalf of the nation. The patriarch in this story holds a real office: in each stake of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints a patriarch lays his hands on members' heads and gives each one a blessing, usually once in a lifetime, which is written down as he speaks and kept. The verse he says is the fourth of William Clayton's "All Is Well," written on the trail across Iowa in April 1846 and sung ever after as "Come, Come, Ye Saints."

sections.heading: I. The Ledge
sections.text: Orson Hale had been patriarch of the stake for fourteen years, and before that he had run cattle on the Arizona Strip for fifty, and he still walked like a man who expected to be on a horse by noon. He was eighty-two. He gave blessings three afternoons a week in an adobe house in Dr. Merrill Jarvis’s orchard on the Santa Clara bench, under fig trees and pomegranates, with his grandnephew Del at a card table in the corner taking down every word on a portable Royal. His wife had kept the record for him until she died, and Del, home from his mission in Argentina, had taken it over the week of the funeral. The house had been the doctor’s grandmother’s. The doctor had come home from the Pacific in 1945 with a Bronze Star and no use for church, and his wife had died the next spring of a cancer he had found too late, and in the summer after that Brother Hale had come out to the orchard without being asked and sat on the porch with him every evening for a month and said almost nothing. In the fall the doctor gave him a key. The house is better used, he said. Come out when you want. People drove out from town and up from Hurricane and over from Mesquite, young men going on missions and wome

sections.heading: II. Burow’s Solution
sections.dateline: The Jarvis orchard · the same evening
sections.text: The doctor had been eating supper standing at his counter. He put down the plate and turned on every light in the adobe house. The splinter had gone in at the outside of the left foot below the ankle bone and come out an inch farther along. The shoe had held most of it. The doctor cut the sock off with surgical scissors and cleaned the wound with soap and boiled water and then with Zephiran, and the old man watched him do it as if the foot belonged to somebody else and he had been asked to keep an eye on it. I can give you something, the doctor said. He had a Syrette of morphine in his bag he had carried since Okinawa and never used on anybody at home. Keep it for somebody who wants it. The doctor packed the wound and laid over it a pad of gauze soaked in Burow’s solution, which drew the swelling and closed the small vessels, and bound the whole foot in an elastic bandage to the middle of the shin. He had done it a hundred times. A wet pack like that did its work for a few hours, and then it had to come off before it dried and set and began to pull. He told Del so. He told Brother Hale so. At nine the telephone rang. It was a farmer in Toquerville, twenty-five miles up the highway,

sections.heading: III. Toquerville
sections.text: The baby was turned the wrong way. The doctor worked until two, and then until three, with the farmer’s mother at the foot of the bed, and at a quarter to five he delivered a boy, blue and furious and alive. He went out to the pump in the yard to wash. The sky over the Hurricane Cliffs was beginning to go gray. He had his sleeves rolled up and his hands under the water when the whole valley went white. It was not lightning. It had no direction. Every fence post, every leaf on the cottonwoods along the ditch, every pebble in the yard stood up sharp and shadowless for a long second, and then the light went pink and drained away to the west behind the Pine Valley Mountains, and it was dark again, and a rooster that had been asleep began to crow. The farmer came out on the porch in his stocking feet and stood beside him. That’s another one, he said. That’s the ninth this spring. You can set your clock by them. The doctor looked at his watch. It was five minutes after five. The bandage had been on the old man’s foot for eight hours. Then the farmer’s mother called him from the door, and he went in, because the young woman had begun to bleed. He was with her until the bleeding stopped an

sections.heading: IV. Cedar Bark
sections.text: Brother Hale was sitting on the porch of the adobe house in a kitchen chair with his left foot bare on a cushion, in the shade of the big fig. Del was at the card table inside the open door, typing. The bandage lay rolled on the porch boards beside the chair, dry and stiff as a stick. The doctor knelt on the boards and took the foot in his hands. Where the splinter had gone in and come out there were two thin lines, pale and closed, like the marks a hatband leaves. There was no swelling. The skin moved over the ankle bone the way it should. On the porch rail lay what had come off the wound in the night, a dark curled strip the length of his finger, and it looked like nothing so much as the bark that peels off a cedar fence post in long shreds when the post is old and the bark has finished with it. What time did you take it off? Del came to the door. Midnight. He woke me up. He said, Brother Jarvis would have had that off by now. He said, Brother Jarvis is sitting up somewhere worrying about it, so take it off. I said you told us not to. He said, You take it off. Del looked at his shoes. So I did. And that was already on it. He nodded at the rail. It came away this morning when he p

title: Cedar Bark
logline: The morning of an atomic test, a Dixie doctor is kept from getting back to unbind an old patriarch's wounded foot.

verses.text: They depart with their thoughts well-collected, they are not happy in their abode; like swans who have left their lake, they leave their house and home.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha announces at Rājagaha that he will set out on a journey in two weeks. While the other monks fire their bowls and dye their robes, Mahā Kassapa, the elder most given to austerities, washes his robes, and the others say he will never leave a city so full of his relatives and supporters; he will go no farther than a nearby cave. On the road the Buddha does send him back, because someone must stay for the city's festivals and misfortunes, and most of the city are Kassapa's people. Kassapa turns back without a word. When the monks say they were right, the Buddha tells them he went back out of obedience, not attachment: he goes among households like the moon, and long ago he had wished for exactly that. He is like a royal swan that leaves a lake and does not look back.
bg.history:
Tule Lake, on the old lake bed just south of the Oregon line, opened in May 1942 as one of the ten camps where the government held Japanese Americans removed from the West Coast. In July 1943 it became the segregation center for people judged disloyal, many for their answers to the loyalty questionnaire, along with family members who chose to come with them; it got a double fence, twenty-eight guard towers and a stockade. After a 1944 law made it possible to renounce citizenship in wartime, and the government announced that the camps would close, thousands at Tule Lake renounced, many of them under pressure from inside and outside the fence. In November 1945 the San Francisco lawyer Wayne Collins won a court order that stopped mass deportations two days before a ship was to sail, and hearings followed. On March 19, 1946, the last 406 renunciants and 43 family members went by train to the Justice Department camp at Crystal City, Texas, and the next day Tule Lake, the last of the camps, closed. Its barracks were given away and sold to the homesteaders, many of them veterans chosen by lottery, who settled the reclaimed lake bed. It is now part of Tule Lake National Monument. Collins's lawsuits took until 1968 to restore citizenship to nearly five thousand people.

What was left of the lake became the Tule Lake National Wildlife Refuge in 1928; tundra swans are common there in winter and pass through in early spring and late fall. The book the priest reads is the Hōjōki, finished in 1212 by Kamo no Chōmei, a poet who had lived through the fire, whirlwind, famine and earthquake that struck Kyoto in the 1170s and 1180s and retired to a hut ten feet square that he could take apart and carry away in two carts. The English here is the 1905 translation by Minakata Kumagusu and F. Victor Dickins. Shin Buddhist temples keep Nehan-e, the memorial of the Buddha's passing, on February 15.

sections.heading: I. The Laundry Room
sections.dateline: Tule Lake Segregation Center, Newell, California · January 1946
sections.text: The war had been over for five months, and the camp was emptying the way a lake goes down in a dry year, from the edges in. Whole blocks stood shut. The stoves were cold in barracks where families had lived for three years, and the wind came down off the Oregon line and blew the tarpaper loose and nobody nailed it back. The ones still inside the wire were the ones the government had not decided about yet: men who had answered no on the questionnaire, families who had come from other camps to stay together, young people who had signed away their citizenship in the winter of 1944 and 1945 and now wanted it back and had a lawyer from San Francisco trying to get it for them. Hearings were held. Lists were posted. Some names went on a list for a ship to Japan, and some went on a list for the Justice Department camp at Crystal City, Texas, and some were let go. Hirasaka-sensei’s name came through on the twenty-eighth of January. He had been the priest of the Buddhist church in Florin, in the strawberry country south of Sacramento, for nineteen years before the war, and of the Buddhist church in Block 4 at Tule Lake for three and a half. He was sixty-one. He had a soft voice and very litt

sections.heading: II. The Gate
sections.text: The trucks came for the crates at seven and for the people at nine. It was very cold and very clear. Out past the fences the old lake bed lay flat and white with frost to the bluff of Castle Rock, which stood up from the plain like the prow of a ship, and on top of it, small and black, the cross the first people in the camp had carried up in 1942, before Tule Lake was made the place for the disloyal. Goro walked out with the others. He carried a cloth bundle about the size of a bed pillow, which was everything he had, and his mother walked beside him as far as the administration building and then stopped, and he bowed to her, and she went back. At the gate the soldier checked their names against a sheet on a clipboard. Hirasaka-sensei waited until all the names had been checked. Then he turned around to Goro. There will be funerals, he said. There are old people here who will not see the end of this. Somebody has to say the sutra for them, and they would rather it were somebody who knew them. On the fifteenth it is Nehan-e. Somebody has to put out the flowers. When the Crystal City list goes, somebody has to be at the train. He looked past Goro at the long rows of tarpaper going ba

sections.heading: III. Swans
sections.dateline: The Southern Pacific, north along the lake · the same day
sections.text: North of the camp the railroad ran up the east side of the old lake bed toward Klamath Falls, and off to the west, a mile or two across the fields, lay the open water that was left of Tule Lake, where the refuge was. It had a skin of ice at the margins and open blue in the middle. The swans were still on it. There were hundreds of them, white on the blue, so many that from the train they looked like a long drift of snow that had not yet melted. Every winter of the camp they had come down in the fall, and every spring the people had stood at the north fence to watch them go. As the train came even with them the swans began to lift. They did not all go at once. A few at a time they ran along the water on their black feet, beating, and pulled up into the air with their necks out straight, and turned north, calling to each other in a high soft voice like people far off talking, and the others followed. They did not circle over the lake. They did not look back at the water. They had eaten there all winter, and slept there, and it had held them up, and they went. The Yamane brothers had their faces at the window. Mrs. Okada held her last geranium on her lap. Hirasaka-sensei watched the s

sections.heading: IV. Not Fastened
sections.text: Goro said the sutra at four funerals in February and March. One of them was his father’s cousin from Elk Grove. He put out the flowers for Nehan-e on the fifteenth, paper chrysanthemums the women folded from old mess-hall menus because there was nothing growing yet, and he swept the Block 4 church every morning after the coal was in, even after there was no one left to come to it but his mother and the two aunts from Rohwer. On the nineteenth of March the last renunciants went to the train for Crystal City, four hundred of them and their families, and his sister and her husband and their children with them. He carried his sister’s crate. He stood at the siding until the train had gone south out of sight, as the sensei had asked, and then he walked back. The camp closed the next day. He left with his mother and the aunts on the last trucks. He had his bundle, and the coat, which he had washed again. The next year the government began giving the barracks away. Veterans who had drawn homesteads in the old lake bed, in a lottery held at the armory in Klamath Falls the week before Christmas, came with flatbed trucks and jacks and took them in halves and thirds, a barrack to a family, an

title: Castle Rock
logline: As Tule Lake empties in 1946, a coal-crew man washes his clothes while the others pack, and the camp decides he will never leave.

verses.text: Men who have no riches, who live on recognised food, who have perceived void and unconditioned freedom (Nirvana), their path is difficult to understand, like that of birds in the air.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Belaṭṭhisīsa finds the daily almsround a bother. He walks one street for alms, eats his breakfast, walks a second street, and carries home plain boiled rice with nothing on it. He dries it and stores it, and then spends several days in meditative absorption, eating the stored rice when he needs to. The other monks are offended and report him to the Buddha, who makes the rule against monks storing food. But because the elder acted before the rule existed, and because he was content with very little, the Buddha declares him blameless and speaks the verse about those who have no stores, whose track is as hard to follow as birds in the sky. The commentary's rice becomes the old Slavic sukhari here, bread sliced and dried hard to keep. Read the full commentary story. The prayer Pavlo says is the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern Orthodox tradition, often counted on a knotted wool prayer rope.
bg.history:
From June 26 to 28, 2021, the Pacific Northwest heat wave broke Portland's all-time record three days running: 108°F, then 112°F, then 116°F. TriMet stopped MAX light rail when the overhead wires sagged, and the county opened cooling shelters, among them one at the Oregon Convention Center. Seventy-two of Oregon's confirmed heat deaths were in Multnomah County, most of them in homes without air conditioning or cooled only by fans. Portland's self-governed villages for unhoused people, like Dignity Village, govern themselves, with elected officers and rules of their own. Rose's school, the Chemawa Indian School near Salem, is the oldest continuously operating Native American boarding school in the United States.

Since the 1980s, migrating Vaux's swifts have roosted each fall in the chimney of Chapman Elementary School in Northwest Portland, often thousands a night. Swifts cannot perch, and they once roosted in large hollow trees, which logging made rare. Portland Audubon's nightly Swift Watch draws crowds of a thousand or more, who boo the hawks that hunt the birds and cheer when the last one goes in. The event was cancelled in 2020 and 2021 to discourage crowds during the pandemic, but volunteers kept counting the swifts, and in 2021 they recorded most nights between two and seven thousand from late August into early October.

sections.heading: I. The Heat
sections.text: The village had twenty-two houses, if you called them houses, and everybody did, because that was one of the rules. They were sleeping pods eight feet by ten, framed in two-by-fours and sheathed in plywood by a church youth group from Beaverton and a crew of union carpenters over two Saturdays, each with a door that locked and a window of corrugated plastic and a number painted over the door. They stood in two rows on a gravel lot between a cement terminal and the on-ramp to the Fremont Bridge, and the bridge went over them so high that on clear days its long arch was most of the sky to the east. There was a shipping container fitted out as a kitchen and another for showers, four blue toilets, a chain-link fence, a gate with a sign-in book on a clipboard, and a whiteboard by the gate with the rules written on it in marker. The rules were made at the meeting on Tuesday nights and voted on by everybody who lived there. That summer there were nineteen. Rose Jim had been chair for two years. She was sixty-eight, a Yakama woman from White Swan who had come down the river at nineteen and spent most of the next forty years on the docks at Terminal 6, lashing and unlashing containers as a

sections.heading: II. Two Streets
sections.dateline: Northwest Twenty-third and Twenty-first Avenues · July
sections.text: In July the heat broke and the village went back to its routines, and so did Pavlo, and his routines were these. At six in the morning he signed out at the gate and walked up through the industrial streets, past the scrap yards and the bus barn, and under the freeway, and into Northwest, where the old Victorian houses had been turned into shops and the shops sold soap for eleven dollars a bar. On Twenty-third Avenue there was a bakery with a back door on the alley, and at a quarter to seven every morning a young woman with flour in her eyebrows opened it and put yesterday’s bread into a bin for the food bank pickup. The first time Pavlo knocked she had looked at him the way people looked at him now, and then she had looked at his forearms, and asked him where he’d worked. After that she let him take what he wanted from the bin before the van came. She offered him croissants, and the morning buns with orange peel in them, and the scones, which were the first things people threw out. He thanked her and took two loaves of plain bread. Country bread, rye, a baguette gone hard as a broom handle. No butter in it, nothing sweet. Just bread, please. She stopped offering the pastry after a

sections.heading: III. Number Fourteen
sections.text: It was Krystal who noticed first, because she lived in thirteen and she noticed everything that happened in fourteen. She was the village secretary, thirty-one, from Klamath Falls, and she kept the minutes on a laptop with a cracked screen, and she was frightened of rats beyond what anyone thought was reasonable until she told them why, which she did once, at a meeting, and after that nobody said anything about it again. He hasn’t come out, she said to Shane. Since Thursday. I hear him. I hear him moving around and I hear him talking. Real quiet. All night. Talking to who? I don’t know. It’s not English. It was in the rules that you took your turn on security, four hours on the gate with the clipboard and the radio, and Pavlo had not missed a turn. He had traded all his turns that week ahead of time, to Duane and to a boy named Marcus, and paid them in cigarettes he didn’t smoke. That was allowed. But when Shane went and looked at the gate book he saw that Pavlo had signed in on Thursday afternoon and had not signed out, not for the morning bread, not for anything, and he hadn’t been to the kitchen for breakfast or for dinner, and nobody had seen him at the showers. The heat had fr

sections.heading: IV. The Rule
sections.text: Rose did not answer them. She finished the cigarette she was smoking, which was one of four she allowed herself a day, and put it out carefully in a coffee can, and walked down the row to number fourteen and knocked. He let her in. She sat on the only chair, which was a bucket, a different bucket, upside down, and he sat on the cot. People are worried about you. I’m sorry. I am fine. What are you doing in here? He thought about it for a while. He did not seem to be thinking of what to tell her. He seemed to be thinking of how to say it in English. Nineteen years I work in the bread room, he said. At night. Eleven to seven. Mixing, shaping, the ovens. Nobody talks. And all night I say the prayer, the one my grandmother taught me. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. All night. With the hands I shape the bread and inside I say the prayer, and it goes by itself, like the mixer. Like breathing. Nineteen years. He turned the wool cord in his fingers. Then the bakery closes. Then I am here. And every day I walk to the doors, and I knock, and I ask, and the girl is kind, and the old man is kind, and I say thank you, thank you, and the prayer goes. It stops. sections.heading: V. The Chimney
sections.text: Every September since her first one in the village, Rose had walked up through Northwest in the evenings to the school on Twenty-sixth Avenue to watch the swifts go down the chimney. The school was old red brick, and on the side of it stood a big square brick chimney that had not carried smoke in years. For as long as anyone could remember, the Vaux’s swifts had come to it in the fall on their way south, thousands of them, and spent the night inside it clinging to the bricks, and the whole city came to watch. Before the sickness, the bird people from Audubon had made it an event, every night in September, with volunteers and parking and two or three thousand people spread out on the grass slope above the playing field with blankets and pizza and children sliding down the hill on flattened cardboard boxes. In 2020 the bird people had called it off, to keep the crowds down. In 2021 they called it off again. People came anyway, a few dozen a night, and sat far apart on the slope with masks around their chins, and nobody stopped them. A volunteer with a clicker counter stood at the bottom of the hill counting the birds, because somebody had to. On a Saturday in the middle of the month

sections.heading: VI. The Shelf
sections.text: The count at the school went down after the middle of the month. Six thousand. Four thousand. A night in the last week of September with a few hundred. Rose went up on the second of October and sat on the slope a full hour and the sky over the chimney stayed empty, and the volunteer at the bottom put her clicker in her pocket and went home. On the morning of the fifth Pavlo was gone. Nobody saw him go. Duane had the gate from two to six that night and swore nobody signed out, and the book bore him out; the last line in Pavlo’s hand was from the afternoon of the fourth, when he had come back from the bakeries with the day-old bread for the shelf. The door of number fourteen was unlocked and open a few inches. The cot was folded. The floor was swept. The blanket and the duffel and the picture of the saint were gone, and the wool cord, and the good shirt off the hook, and the bread knife. Rose walked up to Twenty-third and asked the young woman with flour in her eyebrows, who said she hadn’t seen him since Monday and was he all right, and Rose said she thought so. The old Italian on Twenty-first hadn’t seen him either. Rose called the sister in Vancouver, whose number was on Pavlo’s i

title: Sukhari
logline: After the heat dome, a Ukrainian baker in a Portland tent village dries bakery bread on a shower roof and shuts himself in to pray.

verses.text: He whose appetites are stilled, who is not absorbed in enjoyment, who has perceived void and unconditioned freedom (Nirvana), his path is difficult to understand, like that of birds in the air.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Anuruddha, whose robes are worn out, goes looking for cast-off cloth on refuse heaps. A goddess named Jālinī, who had been his wife three lives before, lays three heavenly cloths on a heap ahead of him so that only the hems show, and he pulls them out, remarking what a remarkable refuse heap it is. On the sewing day the Buddha and the great disciples all take part: Mahā Kassapa sits at the foot, Sāriputta in the middle, Ānanda at the head, the monks spin thread, the Buddha threads the needle, and Mahā Moggallāna fetches what is needed and brings great rose-apples. The goddess goes through the village urging everyone to bring food; Sakka draws a circle round the place and the ground turns red as lac; and far more food is left over than the monks can eat. Some monks grumble that Anuruddha must have sent for his relatives to show how many supporters he has, and the Buddha answers that one whose defilements are gone does not talk about requisites, and that a deity brought the food.
bg.history:
Burmese settlement in Fort Wayne, Indiana, began with a small group of student exiles from the 1988 democracy uprising, sponsored by local churches; hundreds more followed, and for years the city was among the most common resettlement destinations for refugees from Burma. By 2007 a local paper counted between 2,000 and 3,000 Burmese and more than 500 Mon in the city, and six Buddhist temples had opened in a dozen years, several of them in ordinary houses on the south side, where neighbors complained about cars parked on the lawns and the city required a house temple to gravel its yard.

The Kathina ceremony, held in the month after the rains retreat, is the offering of robe cloth to the monastic community; in Burma the season coincides with the Tazaungdaing festival, when weavers compete through the night to finish robes by dawn. Monks’ robes in Burma were once dyed with jackfruit heartwood; the Osage orange of Midwestern hedgerows is a relative in the same genus of dye trees and gives a similar yellow. On the night of November 8, 2003, a total lunar eclipse was visible across the Americas in the evening, the moon turning a deep red.

sections.heading: I. Trash Day
sections.text: On Tuesdays, which was trash day on the south side, Thida Win got up at a quarter to six and walked the alleys with U Wimala before the trucks came. Her grandmother had arranged it the spring before, after a woman on Oxford Street called the police about a man in a bedsheet going through her garbage cans, and two officers had stood in the alley for twenty minutes trying to get a seventy-year-old Burmese monk to explain himself in English. Thida was sixteen and a junior at South Side, and her English was better than anyone’s at the monastery. That was the whole reason. She hated it. U Wimala did not ask for food on Tuesdays. The food came to the monastery anyway, every morning, in foil pans and Tupperware, from the eleven families who took turns. On Tuesdays he asked for cloth. He did not ask anybody. He walked down the alleys between Paulding and Pettit with a canvas bag from the public library over his shoulder, and when there was a garbage bag by a fence with something soft showing through a tear, he stopped and looked at it, and if it was cloth that somebody had thrown away he took it. Old sheets. A tablecloth with a burn in the middle. A man’s white shirt with one sleeve gone.

sections.heading: II. The Hems
sections.dateline: Behind Anthony Boulevard · the last Tuesday in October
sections.text: The fabric store on Anthony Boulevard had closed in the summer, and its dumpster was still behind it in the alley, with a second dumpster from the shoe repair beyond it. It was barely light. There was frost on the lids. A woman was standing by the first dumpster as if she were waiting for a bus. She was Burmese, and old-fashioned about it, in a dark silk longyi to her ankles and a short white jacket, with a string of jasmine flowers in her hair, which Thida had not seen on anyone since she was a child in Mae Sot, and which nobody could have bought in Indiana in October. Thida thought she must be somebody’s aunt from Chicago. The woman looked at U Wimala, and then at Thida, and smiled at Thida as if they knew each other, and Thida, embarrassed, looked down at her own sneakers. When she looked up the woman was not there. The alley was long and straight in both directions, and there was nobody in it. U Wimala had not seen her. He was at the second dumpster. He had lifted the lid and was looking at something inside, near the top, on a bed of cardboard. It was three hems. Three edges of cloth, one above another, folded back so neatly that nothing showed but the hems, each a finger wide,

sections.heading: III. The Sewing
sections.text: The Sayadaw decided it in one sentence at the meal on Sunday. The cloth would be the kathina robe for that year, and it would go to U Wimala, whose robe was worn out, and it would be sewn the way the kathina robe must be sewn, from cutting to dyeing inside a single day, on the Saturday. The Sayadaw was seventy-eight. He had been eight years in Insein prison after 1988, and he did not talk about it, except that once, when one of the boys in the Sunday school could not get a thread through a needle, the Sayadaw took it from him and threaded it in one try without his glasses and said that in Insein you learned to do it by the light from under a door. He came out to the garage on the Saturday before it was light and sat on a cushion at the side, with a cardboard box of needles and a tin of thread, and for the whole of that day every needle in the room came through his hands. Monks came from two other temples in town, and one from Indianapolis, nineteen monks in all, more than the garage had ever held. U Thuzana, who was older than anyone and kept the rules so strictly that the younger monks were afraid to hand him a cup with the wrong hand, sat at the foot of the cloth. U Pyinnya, who

sections.heading: IV. The Telephone
sections.text: Nobody on the committee had called anybody. Everybody agreed about that afterward. But starting at about seven that morning, the telephone rang in every Burmese house in Fort Wayne, and there were a great many of those houses by then, and a woman’s voice with an old Mandalay accent said: They are sewing a robe for my U Wimala. The Sayadaw is there, and all the monks from the other temples. Take mohinga. Take rice. Go before eleven. And hung up. Daw Mya Mya got the call. Thida’s English teacher’s neighbors got the call, and they were Karen and Baptist. The man who ran the Asian grocery on Calhoun got it twice. By half past ten there were cars on both sides of the street from Paulding Road to the corner, and on the gravel the city had made the monastery put down over its front lawn, and on the grass of the house next door, whose owner came out in his bathrobe, looked at it, and went back in and came out again with a crockpot of chili. The folding tables went the length of the driveway. Pots of mohinga with the fish broth still steaming, coconut noodles, biryani in hotel pans, tea-leaf salad in mixing bowls, fried gourd fritters in paper towels, sago with coconut milk, three sheet cak

sections.heading: V. Too Much
sections.text: The visiting monks were offered juice and tea in the garage after the eclipse, which monks may take in the evening, and sat on the floor under the drying robe. Thida was pouring. Two of them were talking in low voices, and she heard it, and so did the Sayadaw. It is too much. Nineteen monks, and food for three hundred. Look at the tables. Nobody brings this much for a robe. He has family in Silver Spring. He telephoned them, or they telephoned the whole town. They wanted everybody to see. Old men like to show how many people they have. The Sayadaw did not raise his voice. What are you talking about? They told him. They were not ashamed of it; they were older monks and had been at many robe offerings. The Sayadaw asked whether they really thought U Wimala had sent for all this. Yes, Sayadaw. We think so. My son Wimala does not talk like that, said the Sayadaw. A monk who is finished does not spend his breath on robes and rice. He has not asked anybody for anything since I have known him. Not even in the alley. He looked up at the robe hanging over them, the color of a yolk, not quite dry. This was not ordered. A devi brought this. You were all here. You ate it. Nobody said anything.

sections.heading: VI. Up
sections.text: They offered the robe in the morning. The laypeople passed it from hand to hand down the length of the garage, everyone touching it, and the monks gave it to U Wimala in the old formula, and he put it on. It fit as if it had grown on him. His old upper robe, the one you could read a newspaper through, he folded and gave to Thida’s grandmother, who cut it into squares that winter and put one in the wallet of every grandchild. There was still food on the tables. U Kovida and Thida drove it in the van all afternoon, foil pan after foil pan, to the Rescue Mission downtown and to the apartment complexes off Hessen Cassel Road where the newest families lived, and to the house on Oxford Street whose owner had called the police on U Wimala, who stood in her doorway holding a pan of biryani and did not know what to say. When they got back the Sayadaw was standing in the gravel with his hands behind his back, looking up. Thida heard it before she saw it, a far, rolling, rattling sound like wooden wheels on a bridge, and then she found them, very high, a long loose line of big gray birds going south over Paulding Road, hundreds, calling the whole way. Cranes, said U Kovida. The Sayadaw watche

title: Three Hems
logline: On trash-day mornings a Burmese teenager walks the alleys with an old monk who will wear only what Fort Wayne throws away.

verses.text: The gods even envy him whose senses, like horses well broken in by the driver, have been subdued, who is free from pride, and free from appetites.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Kaccāyana lives far off in Avanti but travels often to hear the Buddha, and at the great Invitation ceremony at the end of the rains the other elders always leave his seat empty for him. Sakka, king of the gods, comes with his retinue bearing perfumes and garlands, notices the empty seat and wishes the elder were there, and at once Kaccāyana is sitting in it. Sakka greets him warmly, honors him with perfumes and flowers and bows to him. Some of the monks complain that Sakka has favored one elder over the others, and the Buddha answers that those who guard the doors of their senses as Kaccāyana does are dear to gods and men alike. Kaccāyana is remembered as the disciple best at drawing out the full meaning of a short saying, and Pali tradition credits him with its first grammar.
bg.history:
Sponges had been hooked from small boats off Tarpon Springs since the 1880s. In 1905 John Cocoris brought over divers and crews from Greece who worked the beds in the heavy diving suit, and before long most of them came from the Dodecanese islands of Kalymnos, Symi and Halki, which Italy ruled from 1912 until after the Second World War. In the Mediterranean the suit had killed and paralyzed divers by the thousands; the man who helped design it advised coming up at about three feet a minute, and divers trained in breath-hold diving rarely did. The Gulf beds were shallower and kinder, but the bends still came, and in one history of the sponge divers an old diver says that the careful ones, who resist greed, can dive happily all their lives.

The town's Greeks have kept the Epiphany, or Theophany, since 1903. The sponge boats stayed in port from Christmas until that day. After the Liturgy at St. Nicholas the presiding bishop blessed the water, and people carried it home with sprigs of basil; at noon a procession went down to Spring Bayou, a white dove was released, the bishop threw a cross into the water from a barge, and young men dove for it. The boats were blessed in the afternoon and the day ended in a glendi. The congregation moved into its present domed church in 1943. The teacher's lesson is the image from Plato's Phaedrus of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, one wild and one that needs no whip; the Greek word for the driver, hēníochos, means the one who holds the reins.

sections.heading: I. The Third Pew
sections.text: Every year from Christmas until the Epiphany the sponge boats stayed in. They lay along the river two and three deep with their masts bare, painted fresh white and blue for the holy day, and the divers who had been out since spring sat in the coffeehouses on the docks with their worry beads and their backgammon boards and told one another the same stories about the bottom. Every year in those twelve days, at some hour nobody saw, Barba Nikitas came back. He had dived for forty-three years, from the islands to Benghazi to the Gulf of Mexico, and he had never once had the bends. People on the docks said it the way they said a man had never once been drunk: as a fact, and a little uneasily. He had been born on Kalymnos in 1872 and gone down in the suit for the first time at sixteen, off the coast of Africa, in water so deep the light at the bottom was the color of a bruise, and in his first season four men on his boat came up paralyzed and two of them died. In Florida the beds were shallower and the bends came less often, but they came. Men came up too fast with their bags full and lay on the deck with their legs gone dead under them, and some walked again and some never did. Barba Ni

sections.heading: II. The Basil
sections.text: The bishop came down on the train from the north the evening before, with two deacons and a protopsaltis and a young man who carried his bags and his staff, and the whole town met the train. There had been a band. There were policemen to hold the crowd back and the mayor in a gray overcoat and two men from the Florida newspapers. In the morning the church was so full that people stood in the street outside the open doors and listened to the Liturgy through them, and the smoke of the censers drifted out over their heads into the sun. After the Liturgy the bishop blessed the water in the churchyard. He stood over the great basin in his gold vestments with the deacons on either side of him and dipped the cross three times, and then he took up a thick bunch of basil from the tray they held for him and began to sprinkle the people. Vasilikós, the women called it, the royal herb. The smell of it went up green and sharp in the cold sunshine. The people pressed forward with their bottles and jars to carry the water home. He came back into the church to sprinkle the pews. He went down the aisle on the men’s side, scattering water right and left, and at the third pew he stopped. Afterward pe

sections.heading: III. The Clipping Table
sections.text: The grumbling started at the glendi and went on through the week at the coffeehouses, and by Thursday it had reached the Exchange. He bowed to him, said Captain Fotis Kambouris, who owned four boats. He was standing at Kyr Lefteris’s table with the president of the community and old Papa Dimitris’s son-in-law, who sat on the parish council. A bishop. To a diver who has not brought up a sponge since Hoover. He did not bow to Papa Dimitris, said the son-in-law, who has served this parish twenty years. He did not bow to the president, said the captain. Who met him at the train. Who paid for the band. The president said nothing, but he did not say they were wrong. Kyr Lefteris finished the sponge he was trimming and set it with the others and laid the shears down. The children were coming along the dock with their slates for the afternoon lesson, and he waited for them to come up and stand around the end of the table before he spoke. Captain, he said, how many men have you seen come up with the bends? The captain told him. It was a long number. He knew all their names. And how many times did Nikitas come up too fast? Never. The captain shrugged. Everybody knows that. He came up like a

sections.heading: IV. The Fathom
sections.text: The boats sailed on the eleventh of January. Captain Fotis’s best boat had a new diver that season, a boy from Pothia nineteen years old, the same one who had come up out of Spring Bayou with the cross in his teeth on the Epiphany and been carried through the streets on the other boys’ shoulders. On his first day on the bottom, forty miles out, the boy filled his bag in an hour and felt the tug on the line, the signal to come up. He started up hand over hand, fast, the way they all did, the way the light pulled you. Then at the first fathom he stopped, without knowing why, and hung there in the green water and breathed. He thought of an old man in a black suit with a wet bunch of basil in his lap. He came up the rest of the way a fathom at a time. On the deck the captain was standing over the air hose with his face dark, ready to swear at him, and did not. Back in town the landlady had found the basil on the windowsill of the room where Barba Nikitas had not slept, dried and tied with a bit of white thread. She hung it on a nail over the third pew on the men’s side, and it stayed there, gray and sweet, until the parish moved into the new church with the dome in 1943 and the old pew

title: The Slow Ascent
logline: An old Kalymnian sponge diver who never once came up too fast writes that he cannot come to Tarpon Springs for the Epiphany.

verses.text: Such a one who does his duty is tolerant like the earth, like Indra's bolt; he is like a lake without mud; no new births are in store for him.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Sāriputta, the Buddha's chief disciple, takes leave of the monks at the end of the rains and greets each by his personal and family name, but in the crowd he overlooks one obscure monk, and the hem of his robe brushes against him. The monk tells the Buddha that Sāriputta struck him and went off without asking pardon. Moggallāna and Ānanda, sure their elder brother will "roar a lion's roar," go from cell to cell with the keys and call the whole community together. Sāriputta does not deny the charge. He describes his own mind in nine plain similes (the earth, water, fire and wind that take clean and unclean alike, a dust-rag, an outcaste boy entering a village, a bull with its horns cut, a body felt like a carcass hung round the neck, and a body carried like a leaking pot of fat), and the earth shakes nine times. The accuser confesses; Sāriputta crouches before him with joined hands and asks his pardon in return; and the Buddha says his mind is like the earth, a threshold-post and a still pool. The similes are those of the Sīhanāda Sutta, Anguttara Nikāya 9.11.
bg.history:
Camp Upton was built in the scrub-oak barrens near Yaphank in the summer of 1917, and the first drafted men arrived in September, when the camp was far from finished; they helped build it, while engineers blasted the stumps from the drill grounds. The 77th Division organized there was made of draftees from New York City, men of some twenty-five nationalities, and it took the Statue of Liberty for its shoulder patch. Experienced Regular Army officers and noncommissioned officers were sent to the new National Army camps to train them. One company's own account, Company B, 307th Infantry (1920), describes two-story barracks with kitchen and mess hall below and bunks above, straw mattresses, and drill, drill, drill. The division paraded down Fifth Avenue on Washington's Birthday, 1918, and sailed for France that April. After the war many of the camp's buildings were taken across the bay to become the first cottages of Cherry Grove on Fire Island.

The winter of 1917–18 brought a coal famine in the eastern cities, and the Fuel Administration answered with price controls, shortened factory weeks and "heatless Mondays." Most of that coal came from the anthracite fields of eastern Pennsylvania, where tens of thousands of Carpatho-Rusyn, Slovak, Polish and Lithuanian immigrants worked, and where boys as young as eight or nine sat over the chutes as breaker boys, picking slate from the coal. St. Michael's in Shenandoah, founded in 1884, was the first Greek Catholic church in America. Its people kept Christmas by the old Julian calendar, on January 7, and began it the evening before with the meatless Holy Supper, straw under the tablecloth and a cross of honey on each forehead. Captain Halpern's Bible is the Jewish Publication Society translation, which first appeared in 1917.

sections.heading: I. The Names
sections.dateline: Camp Upton, Yaphank, Long Island · September 1917
sections.text: First Sergeant Andrew Fedorko had the names in four days. The company came down from the city on the Long Island Rail Road with tags on their coats, two hundred and fifty of them, and stood in the sand between the stumps while the carpenters were still nailing the roof on their barracks. There were bookkeepers and iceman's helpers, a pastry cook from the Hotel Astor, a Chinese laundryman's son from Mott Street, a boy who had sung in the choir at the Eldridge Street synagogue, two brothers who drove a moving van in Hell's Kitchen and fought each other every night until the Top separated them by a whole floor. Italians from Mulberry Bend and Italians from Bensonhurst who did not think of each other as the same thing. Irish from Chelsea. Swedes from Bay Ridge. Poles, Armenians, a Norwegian sailor who had jumped ship in 1912, an Albanian, three Greeks who ran a lunchroom together on Eighth Avenue and had been drafted on the same morning. The other sergeants called the roll the way you push a wheelbarrow over roots. They stopped at every third name, swore, spelled it, guessed. Fedorko did not stop. He said Kowalczyk and Esposito and Der Bedrossian and Lindqvist and Moskowitz as if he ha

sections.heading: II. Russian Christmas
sections.text: The winter came down on Long Island early and stayed. By Christmas the sand was frozen like cement and the wind off the Sound came through the board walls of the barracks as if there were no walls. In the city there was no coal. People stood in line with baby carriages to buy it by the pail. At Upton the stoves were red all night and the men slept in their overcoats anyway. Fedorko had not taken a furlough in four years. On the first of January the captain called him into the orderly room and said, Your people keep Christmas on the seventh. Yes, sir. The old calendar. Go home for it. The company, sir. Go home, Sergeant. That was a long speech, for Halpern. So on the Saturday morning before the Holy Supper, Fedorko came out of the barracks in his overcoat with a barracks bag over his shoulder, to walk to the station and take the train to the city, and the ferry over to Jersey City, and the train from there into the coal country. In his bag he had a pound of honey from the canteen for his mother, a wool scarf for his brother's girl, and a German helmet spike a sergeant in the 305th had swapped him for a pocketknife, for his nephew. He had meant to slip out. He did not get the chance.

sections.heading: III. The Keys
sections.dateline: Barracks and mess hall · eleven o'clock
sections.text: Corporal Sol Abramowitz, the company clerk, drove the Ford down to the station and found the Top on the platform with the cake under his arm, stamping his feet. He told him. The Top did not say anything. He picked up his bag and got in the Ford, and they drove back past the train coming in. By then Sergeant Pat Keogh had heard it. Keogh was the supply sergeant, a structural ironworker from Chelsea who had walked the beams of the Woolworth Building, six foot three, and he loved the Top the way a younger brother does who would never say so. He found Abramowitz in the orderly room. Abramowitz had the keys. He always had the keys. He knew where everything in the company was, every blanket and spoon and every man's next of kin, and he could tell you without looking what the Top had said to the colonel on the eleventh of October. Cassidy says the Top hit him, said Keogh. I know. The Top never hit a man in his life that didn't hit him first. I know. The captain don't know the Top like we do. Keogh put out his hand for the keys. Get everybody in the mess hall. He's going to give it to that kid with both barrels, and I want them all there when he does. So they went through the barracks, the

sections.heading: IV. Nine Things
sections.text: The Top looked at the floor a while. He did not look at Kazlauskas. Sir, he said. A man who doesn't keep his own body in his eye, he might knock against another man and go off and never know it. Never say he was sorry. That could be. He stopped. Then he went on, slowly, the way he talked on the rifle range when a man was afraid of his piece. Sir, this ground here. They dig latrines in it. They bury the garbage in it. They plant the flagpole in it and they bury the dead in it. The ground doesn't care. It doesn't say, this is clean, I like it, this is dirty, I don't. I try to be like that. Water. The wash rack. Same water washes the officers' cups and the grease trap. It doesn't mind. The stove. You put in coal, you put in letters, you put in rags with lice in them. It burns them. It doesn't ask which. The wind off the Sound. It blows on the colonel's quarters and it blows on the latrines. It doesn't pick. The kitchen rag. He nodded at the cooks. Russo wipes the captain's table with it, he wipes up what the dog did. The rag doesn't get proud. Doesn't get ashamed. I try to be like the rag. Somebody near the kitchen door made a small sound. When I was a kid, the Top said, in the breake

sections.heading: V. The Floor
sections.text: Jonas Kazlauskas stood by the officers' table. All the time the Top was talking, he felt it come up through him from his feet, the way the shudder came up through the floor. It came up into his knees and his stomach and his chest and into his face, where the ear had stopped stinging an hour ago, and when the Top said a pail with holes in it it reached the top of his head, and he went down on the floor in front of the captain's table on both knees. He never hit me, he said. Sir. He never touched me. It was his muffler. It was the end of his muffler in the wind. He didn't say my name. That's all. Everybody's but mine. I made it up. I'm a liar, sir. Put me in the guardhouse. Nobody moved. The captain looked down at him a long moment. Then he looked at the Top and said, quietly, in the voice he used for everything: Sergeant. Let him off. Before his head comes apart. And the Top came across the mess hall floor between the tables. Men moved their feet out of his way. He came to where Kazlauskas was kneeling, and he did not stand over him. He went down on his heels in front of him, the way men squat at the mouth of a mine waiting for the cage, so that their faces were on a level. He put h

sections.heading: VI. Holy Supper
sections.dateline: Shenandoah, Pennsylvania · the night of January 6
sections.text: He missed the Saturday connections at Jersey City and slept on a bench in the terminal at Jersey City and came up into the coal country on Sunday afternoon on the slow train, through Tamaqua and Mahanoy, past the black hills of culm with smoke coming out of their sides where they had been burning for years, past the breakers standing up over the patches like churches, with their windows lit. There was coal here. There was coal everywhere, in heaps along the tracks, in the yards, in the gutters. In New York people were standing in line with baby carriages, and here the children were throwing it at each other. He got off at Shenandoah after dark and walked out to the patch with his bag. The snow was grey with dust. It was the old Christmas Eve, and the first star was out, and in every company house along the row there was one candle in the window. His mother had set the table and waited and given him up and set his place anyway. That was the custom. You set a place for the ones who were not there, the dead and the far away and the stranger who might come. There was straw under the tablecloth, from the cow's shed, and a loaf on the straw and a bowl of honey and a head of garlic. There

sections.heading: VII. The Sill
sections.text: They went to France in April. Of what happened there to the company, to the Top and Keogh and Abramowitz and the Hell's Kitchen brothers and the pastry cook and the captain with the cough, some of it is written down in the regimental history and some of it is not written anywhere. Jonas Kazlauskas came home in the spring of 1919 with a piece of a German shell in his hip that the doctors said to leave where it was. He went back to cabinetmaking. He married a girl from his own church in Williamsburg and they had four children, and the first boy they named Andrew, and when people asked why, he said it was after a man he knew in the Army, and did not say any more. The war ended, and the Army sold off the camp at Yaphank, the buildings and the stoves and the bunks. Some of the barracks were knocked down and carried across the bay to Fire Island, and the boards went into the first cottages at Cherry Grove, where people from the city came for the summer to swim and be left alone. In the summer of 1938, a few weeks before the hurricane, Kazlauskas was hired to hang new doors on one of those cottages, and the old sill he took out from under the kitchen door was a length of yellow pine with

title: The Doorsill
logline: A Rusyn first sergeant who says every draftee's name right misses one, and the boy swears the sergeant struck him.

verses.text: His thought is quiet, quiet are his word and deed, when he has obtained freedom by true knowledge, when he has thus become a quiet man.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Tissa of Kosambī declines his patron's gifts because he has no novice to attend him, and the patron gives him his seven-year-old son. The boy becomes an arahat the instant the razor touches his hair, while the elder gives him the first meditation on the body. On the road, the two share a lodging for a third night, which the rule forbids if the novice lies down; so the novice sits up until morning. At dawn the elder, meaning to send him out, tosses a fan whose handle puts out the boy's eye. The boy says nothing, covers the eye, does his duties with one hand, and is scolded for offering the toothstick one-handed. When the elder learns the truth and begs pardon, the novice says that neither of them is to blame, only the round of existence. The elder tells the Buddha, who speaks the verse.
bg.history:
British and Loyalist troops held Long Island from August 1776 until 1783, with garrisons at Huntington, Oyster Bay, Setauket and elsewhere, and foraging parties took hay, cattle and lodging from the farms. Intelligence about the army in New York crossed the Island and then Long Island Sound to Connecticut by several routes. The best known is the Culper Ring, organized in 1778 by Major Benjamin Tallmadge around Setauket, whose couriers rode the fifty-odd miles from the city and whose whaleboats crossed the Sound at night. Conklin, the Ketchams, the tavern and their line are invented, as is the line's rule. The rhymed alphabet is quoted from the 1777 Boston edition of The New-England Primer, the small schoolbook from which most children in the northern colonies learned to read for more than a century; Old Mans is the old name of the harbor at Mount Sinai.

The Montaukett are the people of the east end of Long Island. By the 1770s, crowded onto a fraction of their land at Montauk, many worked as whalers, farm laborers and servants across the Island, and Montaukett and Shinnecock women were known for the baskets, brooms and oak-splint scrub brushes they made and sold from door to door. Samson Occom, a Mohegan and an ordained Presbyterian minister, lived at Montauk from 1749 to 1761 as schoolmaster and preacher and married Mary Fowler, a Montaukett woman. In the 1770s he and his brother-in-law David Fowler led the plan to move Christian families of several coastal nations to Oneida land in upper New York; the war interrupted it, and the settlement, Brothertown, was founded in 1785. Dorcas is invented, and her words are her own.

sections.heading: I. The Shears
sections.dateline: South of Huntington, Long Island · March 1779
sections.text: Nathan Conklin was a minister's son from the east end who had left college in the second year of the war, and in the third winter of the King's troops on Long Island he kept a school of eleven children in the back kitchen of Deacon Jesse Ketcham's farm, and boarded there. That was all the garrison at Huntington knew of him. He also carried letters. There were lines across the Island in those years, like the one Major Tallmadge's friends kept at Setauket, by which what was seen in New York on a Monday could be in Connecticut by the week's end, and the deacon's kitchen was a station on one of them. When the school broke up for planting, the deacon set the winter's pay on the table: four yards of tow cloth, a crock of butter, a cheese, and two shillings in hard money. I thank you, and I cannot take it, said Conklin. It is what the schoolmaster has always had in this house. I have forty miles to walk and nobody to carry so much as my shoes. A man alone on the road with a pack is stopped at every post. I have no boy. The deacon thought about it for the space of a breath. Then you shall have mine, he said, and called his son Eli in from the yard. Eli was seven years old. Conklin said a b

sections.heading: II. The Third Night
sections.text: The first night they slept in a barn in the Dix Hills, and the second in a weaver's loft at Comac. On the third evening they came to a tavern at the Branch, and a foraging party of dragoons was in it. There were eleven troopers and a sergeant, their horses filling the stable and the shed and their saddles heaped in the public room. The woman of the house had one garret left, with one bed. She would let the schoolmaster have it if his boy would do the morning work, since her own girl had run off when the horses came. Eli carried up the master's pack and the primer. He beat the bed and turned it, found a candle end, brought water, and went down to learn where the broom was kept and where the back-house stood. By the time he had done all that it was full dark, and he had found no corner for himself. The stable was horses to the door. The public room was troopers. When he came up to see whether anything more was wanted, Conklin asked, Where do you lie tonight? I have not had time to look, sir. Then stay here. I'll not have you on the stairs among them. Now the line had a rule, and Conklin had given his word to it. He knew it as he knew his own name. Where the letters are, one wakes. Tw

sections.heading: III. The Basin
sections.text: He did not sit down in the yard, and he did not go and say to anyone that his eye was put out. There was the morning work, which he had promised. He kept his left palm pressed where it was and did the work with his right. He carried down the pot. He swept out the back-house and the wash bench with the birch broom. He drew a bucket at the well, one-handed, a pull and a turn round the post and another pull. The sergeant of dragoons came out to the trough in his shirt and watched this. What have you there under your arm, boy? My letters, sir, said Eli, and held the primer out to him. The sergeant did not take it. Can you read them? Eli opened the book against his chest with his one hand and read out, Whales in the Sea, GOD's Voice obey, in the voice he would have used in the deacon's kitchen. The sergeant laughed, and asked what he had done to his face, and Eli said a stick had caught it, which was true. The sergeant said he should mind where he ran, and put his own head in the trough. Then Eli swept the garret stairs and the garret, around the master's feet, and filled the basin from the bucket and brought it for the master to wash. He brought it in his right hand, held against his h

sections.heading: IV. Old Mans
sections.dateline: The harbor called Old Mans · evening
sections.text: The woman they were going to lived behind the beach at Old Mans, in a round house of poles and mats beside a patch of beans. She was one of the Montauk people. As a girl she had gone to school at Montauk to Mr. Occom, the Mohegan minister, in the years he taught there, and had her reading from him. Her name in the towns was Dorcas. She made scrub brushes of white oak splint, and splint baskets, and brooms, and walked the north side of the Island selling them at kitchen doors, and no sentry had ever asked an old Indian woman what was in a broom. Whaleboat men from the Connecticut shore bought of her too, when they came over in the dark. Her own grandson was in a whaler out of Sag Harbor, the war permitting. She meant to go up to the Oneida country with Mr. Occom's people when the roads were open, and plant there. She saw them from a long way down the beach, the man bent under two bundles and a child. When they came up she looked first at the boy's face and moved his hand and looked under it, and put the hand back. She did not say the eye would mend. Then she asked the schoolmaster, as anyone asks a traveler, whether he was well and had come without much hardship. I am well. I have h

title: One Hand
place: Smithtown Branch, Long Island, New York
logline: On occupied Long Island a schoolmaster who carries letters for a spy line takes a deacon's seven-year-old son as his boy, and sleeps through his watch.

verses.text: The man who is free from credulity, but knows the uncreated, who has cut all ties, removed all temptations, renounced all desires, he is the greatest of men.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, thirty forest-dwelling monks come to the Buddha, and he sees that they are ready. For their sake he turns to his chief disciple and asks: Sāriputta, do you believe that faith, developed and made much of, ends in the deathless? Sāriputta answers that in this matter he does not go by faith in the Blessed One, because he has seen it for himself; those who have not seen it must go by the faith of others. The other monks mutter that he has never given up his old wrong views and will not believe even the Buddha. The Buddha defends him and speaks a verse made of five words that can each be heard as an insult, faithless, ungrateful, a housebreaker, one who has ruined his chances, an eater of what is thrown up, and each of which also means its opposite: beyond mere belief, knowing the unmade, having broken the chain, having ended the occasion for rebirth, having spat out desire. The thirty reach full awakening.
bg.history:
Maria Mitchell (1818–1889), who found a comet from a Nantucket rooftop in 1847, was professor of astronomy at Vassar College from its opening in 1865. She put her students at the telescope, refused to grade them ("You cannot mark a human mind," her successor remembered her saying), and told the class of 1876, "We are women studying together." Her sister published Maria Mitchell: Life, Letters, and Journals in 1896; both passages quoted here are from her notes of the 1870s in that book. At the Harvard College Observatory, from the 1880s, Edward Pickering hired women known as the Harvard computers to measure and classify stars on photographic plates, at wages commonly given as twenty-five to fifty cents an hour. Miss Wing, Ruth Hadlock, the committee and Harlow Academy are invented. Victory and Granby are real towns in Essex County, and Robert Ingersoll, "the Great Agnostic," died on July 21, 1899.

Algol, Beta Persei, takes its name from the Arabic ra's al-ghūl, the ogre's head. Every 2 days, 20 hours and 49 minutes it fades from about magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 and recovers, over some ten hours, and the whole of it can be followed without a telescope by comparing it with its neighbors. John Goodricke, a deaf eighteen-year-old in York, worked out the period in 1782–83 and proposed that a dark body was passing in front of the star; the spectroscope confirmed it in 1889. In November 1899 the Leonid meteors, which had stormed in 1833 and 1866, were widely predicted to do so again. They did not, and the astronomer Charles Olivier later called the failure "the worst blow ever suffered by astronomy in the eyes of the public."

sections.heading: I. The Examination
sections.dateline: Harlow Academy, Caledonia County, Vermont · December 1899
sections.text: Three weeks before the fall examination, on the word of the astronomers, the whole village of Harlow sat up to see the stars fall. The Boston papers had promised it since summer. The November meteors were due again, as in 'thirty-three and 'sixty-six, when they had come down like snow. Deacon Stiles kept his hired men up at his own expense. Mr. Peck had his text chosen. They watched three nights and counted a few dozen in the best hour, and the stars stayed where they were, and afterward the village held a low opinion of astronomy that it was at no trouble to keep from Miss Wing. Miss Lois Wing taught natural science and the higher mathematics at Harlow Academy. She was forty-four. She had studied at Vassar College under Miss Maria Mitchell, and afterward she had worked six years at the Harvard observatory, measuring stars on glass plates at twenty-five cents an hour, in a room of women who were the best eyes in the country, until her mother's last illness called her home. She had brought back a three-inch glass on a tripod, a habit of saying less than she knew, and a contempt for the marking system, which the trustees had got round by having her assistant keep the mark book. The a

sections.heading: II. The Committee
sections.dateline: The upper hall · the same afternoon
sections.text: The scholars were sent down. The committee stayed. Mr. Peck spoke first, and he was not an unkind man. He said the whole county had been made fools of in November by taking the word of astronomers, and he could have understood a little modesty from that quarter in December. Instead a girl of nineteen had been stood up before the entering class to say she did not believe her teacher. It is the father, he said. She has not given up one of his notions. She would not believe Moses, and now she will not believe you. Deacon Stiles set it out under five heads, the way he did at town meeting. The girl believed nothing she was told. She was ungrateful to the woman whose bread she ate. She was a housebreaker besides, for Dow the janitor had twice found the staple drawn on the belfry scuttle. She had thrown away her chances, since Granby wanted a teacher for the spring term and the men who would be asked about her were sitting in this room. And the worst of it, he said, was that she did not appear to want anything of anybody. Miss Wing heard him through. Gentlemen, why do you say so? I did not ask her whether she believed in her Maker. I did not ask whether she was thankful for her board. I a

sections.heading: III. The Belfry Deck
sections.text: By Miss Wing's reckoning the star would be at its least a little before midnight on the sixth. She wrote the hour on the board in the lower hall, and under it one more line of Miss Mitchell's, and nothing else. We must at least question it; we cannot accept anything as granted, beyond the first mathematical formulae. Question everything else. — Maria Mitchell, Life, Letters, and Journals She did not go up herself. She had seen it. It was eight above zero and dead clear, and the young moon was down early. They came up the belfry ladder one at a time through the scuttle, which nobody had mended, all thirty, in mufflers and their fathers' coats, and stood on the deck packed like sheep. Ruth Hadlock came last. She carried the lantern up the ladder in both hands, the way a full pail is carried, with a piece of red flannel tied over the glass. She gave each of them a card with six stars pricked on it and no names. She showed them where Algol stood, at one corner of a three-cornered figure with Alpha of Perseus and Almach in Andromeda. She showed them Epsilon and Delta farther up in Perseus, and Rho, the little star close beside Algol. Then she told them the only thing she told them that

title: The Demon Star
logline: At a Vermont academy's public examination, a teacher asks her assistant whether she believes what the class has just recited about a star.

verses.text: In a hamlet or in a forest, in the deep water or on the dry land, wherever venerable persons (Arhanta) dwell, that place is delightful.
Him I call indeed a Brahmana who in this world is above good and evil, above the bondage of both, free from grief from sin, and from impurity.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Sāriputta and five of his brothers and sisters have all become monastics, and their mother marries the youngest, Revata, at seven to keep him at home. At the wedding the kin bless the bride to live as long as her grandmother, a woman of a hundred and twenty, toothless and bent; Revata sees what his brother saw, slips away from the carriage on the pretext of relieving himself, and asks some forest monks for ordination. They do not know who “Upatissa” is until he gives his brother's monastic name, and they ordain him on his brother's standing instruction. He goes off to an acacia forest and becomes an arahant within the rains. The Buddha, after twice telling Sāriputta to wait, sets out with five hundred monks by the short road through haunted country because the elder Sīvali, the disciple to whom gifts always come, is with them, and spirits feed the whole company at every league. Revata turns the thorn forest into a monastery by psychic power. Two old monks who grumble about favoritism go back for forgotten things and find only acacia thorns, with their belongings hanging on a branch. When they and two young monks give the lay patron Visākhā opposite reports, the Buddha speaks verse 98. The commentary then tells Sīvali's past: a countryman who would not sell his honeycomb for a thousand coins but gave it to a Buddha's feast, and who in a later life, on his mother's advice, starved a besieged city by shutting its little gates.
bg.history:
New Mexico's Franciscan missions depended on supply caravans up the Camino Real from Mexico City, which by royal order left every three years and took about six months each way. The road passed through the silver country of Nueva Vizcaya, where Parral had boomed since the strike of 1631. North of El Paso del Norte the road left the Rio Grande and crossed some ninety miles of almost waterless plain, a route Juan de Oñate chose because it was shorter and easier for ox carts and livestock than the river. It came to be called the Jornada del Muerto after the bones of a German were found along it in 1670. Under canon law a betrothal could be contracted once both children were older than seven.

In the 1670s drought and famine struck the province, Spaniards and Pueblo people alike were reduced to eating hides, and Apache raids increased. The missions rested on Pueblo tribute and labor, and the friars' campaign against Pueblo religion grew harsher; in August 1680 the Pueblos rose together and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years (Pueblo Revolt). The catclaw acacia, common in southern New Mexico and Chihuahua, is also called wait-a-minute bush, because a person caught in its hooked prickles has to stop and free himself.

sections.heading: I. The Grandmother
sections.dateline: San José del Parral, Nueva Vizcaya · spring 1672
sections.text: Doña Leonor de Arteaga was the widow of a silver miner, and she had seven children, and the Church had taken six. Her eldest, Diego, who should have had the mines, gave his share to the poor in the plaza of Parral on a single morning and walked north to New Mexico in the gray habit of Saint Francis, and in New Mexico they called him Fray Diego de San Antonio and had forgotten he had ever had another name. Her three daughters were in the convent of Jesús María in Mexico City behind a grille. Her second son was a Jesuit in Durango, and her third was a Franciscan somewhere in Sonora that she could not find on a map. That left Rodrigo, who was seven. If this one goes, she told her confessor, the mines go to the Crown and my husband's name goes into the ground with him. I will tie him to the house while he is still small enough to tie. The Church allowed a betrothal from the age of seven. Doña Leonor found a girl of nine from a family with a hacienda of sheep on the Florido, and arranged the promise, and on the day of the espousals she dressed her son in black velvet with a lace collar and a little sword and a gold chain across his chest, and put him in the coach with six mules, and too

sections.heading: II. The Wagon Camp
sections.dateline: The road outside Parral · the same day
sections.text: On the way home in the coach he said he needed to make water. The coachman stopped the mules, and he got down and went behind a mesquite and came back. A little farther on he said it again, and got down, and came back. The third time his mother's cousin sighed and said that the boy had eaten too much at the espousals, and nobody watched him anymore. The fourth time he said, Go on ahead, I'll walk behind, and they went on ahead. Outside Parral, where the road came down from the hills, a train of wagons was camped for the night on its way north to New Mexico, with friars going up to the missions and a few soldiers for escort, and the mules and oxen grazing around them on what grass there was. Rodrigo walked into the firelight in his velvet and his lace and his gold chain, and knelt to the first friar he saw, and asked to be given the habit. There were thirty of them in that camp, more or less. They looked at him. Child, you are dressed like a viceroy's son. We don't know whose son you are. How can we give you the habit? Don't you know me? I'm Diego de Arteaga's brother. Who is Diego de Arteaga? Rodrigo thought. You call him Fray Diego de San Antonio. The friars looked at each other,

sections.heading: III. The Catclaw
sections.dateline: The bench above the river, south end of the Jornada · summer 1672
sections.text: The catclaw grew on a gravel bench above the river in a thicket a man could not walk through standing. Every branch was set with small hooked thorns that took your sleeve and would not let it go, so that you had to stop, and back up, and unhook yourself one thorn at a time. Wait a minute, the thorns said to anyone who came in. The soldiers had worse names for it. It was a drought year, in a run of them. Up the river the pueblos had little in their granaries, and a friar had written to Mexico that Spaniards and Indians alike were eating hides and the straps of the carts. The Apaches came down on the horse herds when they were hungry, which was always. The boy lived in the catclaw on what the bench gave him, mesquite beans and the water of the river, and said his few words, and sat. In July the rains came up out of the south in the afternoons, black clouds with the lightning walking under them, and the catclaw put out its flowers, little pale yellow spikes like cattails that smelled of honey from a hundred yards off. Before the rains were over, before the cottonwoods along the river had begun to turn, the boy had come to the end of what the old friar gave him. He did not tell anybody

sections.heading: IV. The Dead Man's Road
sections.dateline: Fray Cristóbal, north end of the Jornada · October 1672
sections.text: In October, when the rains were done, Fray Diego asked a third time, and Fray Gil said, Now we will go. They went down the river from Santa Fe with a good many friars and lay brothers, and soldiers, and settlers going south, and herds, and the wagons that were going back down to Mexico empty, more than five hundred souls all told by the time they gathered at Fray Cristóbal, where the road leaves the river. Fray Lucas, who was young and kept the old friar's papers and walked at his elbow, stood with him where the road forked. Father, there are two ways to where the boy is. One is the river way, around through the mountains. It is long, but there is water every day, and there are people. The other is the Jornada, straight across. It is ninety miles and half as long, and there is no water on it, and the Apaches watch it, and since they found the German's bones out there two years ago the soldiers say it is not a place for Christians at night. Which shall we take? Is Fray Silvestre with us? Yes, Father. If Silvestre is with us, take the Jornada. Fray Silvestre was a lay brother from Zacatecas, a big soft-voiced man who looked after the mules, and he had never in his life gone without a

sections.heading: V. The Convento
sections.dateline: The bench above the river · October and November 1672
sections.text: When they came off the Jornada at the south end and turned toward the river, the catclaw bench was a convento. That is how it is told.
