There was a church of white stone with a bell in its wall, and a cloister around a garden with a fountain running in it, and a cell for Fray Gil with a bed and a writing table and a window toward the river that smelled of something like incense, and five hundred cells for the rest of them, every one with its door and its cot, and long covered walks for the hot hours and the night, and a refectory with a table that ran the length of it. The boy stood at the gate in his cut-down habit with the cord wrapped around him three times, and knelt to Fray Gil, and then to his brother. Fray Diego picked him up off the ground and held him and could not say anything at all. They stayed a month. Every morning there were voices on the road asking for Brother Silvestre, and every morning Silvestre came back with his arms full. There were two old friars in the company, Fray Hernando and Fray Blas, who had been forty years at missions where the church was mud and the friars ate what the pueblo ate, and they did not like what they saw. They said it to each other in th

sections.heading: VI. The Widow's Table
sections.text: Doña Beatriz de Anaya was the richest widow in New Mexico, as riches went there, and she gave to the friars more than anyone. Her husband's tribute came in from three pueblos in corn and blankets, in good years and in bad, and she knew where it came from, and she gave as if she knew. Any friar passing through Santa Fe who came to her door was fed in her kitchen, and there was chocolate for him if there was chocolate in the town. Fray Hernando and Fray Blas came the first morning after they got back, with their feet still bound in rags, and sat in her kitchen and drank atole. Fathers, you went with Fray Gil to see Fray Diego's little brother? We did, señora. They tell me it is a beautiful place where the child lives. Fray Hernando put his cup down. Beautiful? Señora, it is a thicket of uña de gato on a gravel bank. You cannot walk in it. It is fit for hermits and javelinas, and not many javelinas. And he showed her his hands. That same morning, a little later, two young friars came to her door who had also been with the company. One of them was Fray Lucas. She sat them down and gave them atole and asked them the same. Señora, I can't tell you what it was like, Fray Lucas said. There

sections.heading: VII. The Honey
sections.dateline: The convento at Santa Fe · Lent 1673
sections.text: That winter, at the convento in Santa Fe, the friars talked at recreation about Fray Silvestre. Why was it that a lay brother who could barely read was never once in want, when governors went hungry? And why, Silvestre's own mother had told everyone in Zacatecas, had she labored seven days to bear him, with the child lying crosswise in her, so that the women gave her up twice? Fray Gil, who heard most things, asked what they were talking about, and they told him. He said there was a tale the old people told in the Rio Abajo, which they had from the first friars, who had it from Spain, the way such tales go. He told it to them the way the friars told exempla in a sermon, and they listened the way friars listen to a sermon at recreation, half smiling. Once, he said, a king and the council of his town fell to rivalry over which of them could give the greater feast to a holy man who had come to them with his followers. The king gave a feast, and the town gave a greater one, and the king a greater, back and forth, six times. The seventh time the town swore there would be nothing lacking from its table, and they looked it over, and saw there was cooked honey but no fresh honey in the com

title: Uña de Gato
logline: Betrothed at seven by a silver widow who has lost six children to the Church, her last son slips out of the coach on the road home.

verses.text: Forests are delightful; where the world finds no delight, there the passionless will find delight, for they look not for pleasures.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk takes a meditation subject from the Buddha and goes to sit in a run-down pleasure garden. A courtesan who has been stood up by a lover wanders in, sees him alone, and decides to unsettle him: she lets down her undergarment and puts it back on, unbinds her hair and binds it again, claps her hands and laughs, and his whole body floods with excitement. The Buddha, seated far away in his chamber at Jetavana, sees what is happening, sends forth a radiant image of himself, and speaks the verse. The monk becomes an arahant where he sits, rises into the air, and goes to give thanks at the Buddha’s feet.
bg.history:
After the Second World War the Pocono Mountains of northeastern Pennsylvania sold themselves as a honeymoon capital, and resorts competed with round beds, mirrored walls and heart-shaped tubs. Penn Hills Resort in Analomink, which began as a tavern in 1944, grew in the 1960s to more than a hundred rooms with a ski slope, golf course, ice rink and a swimming pool shaped like a wedding bell. Its co-founder died in March 2009 at 102, and within two months the resort closed, owing Monroe County over a million dollars in back taxes; workers’ final paychecks were never issued. Copper thieves, floods and vandals did the rest, and on September 4, 2017, the main building burned, the third fire in three years. Brodhead Creek runs past Analomink; in the flood of August 1955 it rose thirty feet in fifteen minutes, and thirty-seven people, mostly mothers and children, died at a camp there. The casino at Mount Pocono where Dani works, Mount Airy, opened in 2007 on the site of the old Mount Airy Lodge.

Twitter launched the live-video app Periscope on March 26, 2015, and released it for Android that May. Viewers could comment in real time and tap the screen to send little hearts floating up the side of the picture. In its first year a broadcast’s replay stayed up for twenty-four hours and then vanished; Periscope did not let broadcasts be saved permanently until May 2016. Hollis went to the Rochester School for the Deaf, founded in 1876 on St. Paul Street. Rochester, home also to the National Technical Institute for the Deaf, has been found by NTID researchers to have the largest deaf and hard-of-hearing population per capita among working-age adults of any American city studied.

sections.heading: I. The Cards
sections.text: Hollis Tate went live at half past four every morning from the floor of her kitchen on Jefferson Avenue. She propped the phone against two old phone books by the baseboard, turned on the little light over the stove and nothing else, sat down on a folded blanket with her back against the refrigerator, and closed her eyes. That was the broadcast. At six she opened them, read a few of the comments that had piled up on the left side of the screen, and went to work folding hospital sheets at a commercial laundry off Lyell Avenue. She had started the week the app came out, in March, when the whole internet was pointing its phones at things to see who would watch. The title of every broadcast was the same. SIT WITH ME. NOBODY HAS TO TALK. The first morning four people watched for a minute each. By June it was two or three hundred, from Manila and Leeds and Tulsa and a truck stop outside Gallup, and some of them stayed the whole ninety minutes. There was no sound. Hollis had been Deaf since birth and had gone to the school for the deaf on St. Paul Street from the age of four, and it had not occurred to her to talk into the thing. People wrote to ask whether their phones were broken. After

sections.heading: II. The Bell Pool
sections.text: Everybody in Stroud Township knew where nobody wanted to be. Penn Hills had been the best honeymoon resort on Route 447 once, a hundred rooms on five hundred acres, with a ski slope and a golf course and an ice rink and a tiki lounge, and heart-shaped bathtubs in every villa. It had run downhill for thirty years, and in the spring of 2009 the last of its founders died at a hundred and two, and within two months the doors were chained and it turned out the place owed the county more than a million dollars in back taxes. The last paychecks never came. Now the county had it, for the taxes, and kids went up there at night to drink and paint their names on the walls, and men came with bolt cutters for the copper. Mateo had ten vacation days and took them all at once in the slow week before peak season. He parked his Corolla at a pull-off on 447, walked up the old entrance road past a row of tall streetlights with their globes shot out, and carried in two gallons of water, a sleeping pad, a blanket and the phone, which he meant to leave off. He slept in a villa at the back with the door kicked in. The bed was round. The carpet went up the walls and over the platform where the heart-shape

sections.heading: III. The Shoot
sections.dateline: Mount Pocono and Route 447 · the ninth day
sections.text: Danielle Kostelnik served drinks at the casino in Mount Pocono, the one they built where the old Mount Airy Lodge had been. She wore the black uniform with the corset top and carried a tray of comped vodka sodas up and down the slot rows from eight at night until four in the morning, and she was good at it, and she was tired of it. She was twenty-nine. Her daughter Kayla was seven and lived weekdays with Dani’s mother in Hazleton, in the house on Alter Street, where there was a yard and a school that was not falling down. On the side, under the name Honey Kosta, Dani sold photo sets of herself online. Some months that money was more than the casino money. Now and then, when the money was good and the man seemed all right, she met one in person, and she had rules about that which she kept. This one called himself a photographer. He had written to her for three weeks from somewhere in north Jersey, polite, with a portfolio of real pictures of real ruins, grain elevators and churches and a hospital in the Catskills. He wanted what he called abandoned glamour. He wanted her in a red heart-shaped tub at Penn Hills at the golden hour, a girl in a ruin, six hundred dollars for the set, an

sections.heading: IV. The Clapping
sections.dateline: Penn Hills · a quarter to eight
sections.text: The place was worse than she remembered from the pictures people posted. Somebody had written LOVE IS DEAD in silver paint across the front of the lobby and somebody else had crossed out DEAD and written BLIND, and somebody else had crossed out BLIND. Glass crunched under her flats. She walked down past the villas with their doors hanging, looking into each one, the round beds and the shag on the walls, the heart-shaped holes where the tubs had been. There were no tubs. He would have known that, she thought, if he had ever been coming. Then she came around the end of the last building and there was the pool, the bell, green as a bottle, and a man sitting at the narrow end of it with his eyes closed. She stopped. He did not move. He was young and thin and needed a shave, in a grey hoodie with a warehouse logo on it, sitting cross-legged on the concrete lip with his hands in his lap like he was waiting for a bus that would come in a hundred years. A lawn chair stood empty beside him. She looked this way and that. There was nobody else anywhere. The light was on the tops of the pines and nowhere else. Something in her that had been stood up an hour ago came up into her mouth, light an

sections.heading: V. Senses Still
sections.text: In Rochester, Hollis Tate came home from the laundry and ate supper standing up and washed the plate, and then stood in her kitchen for a while with the plate in her hand. The young man from Pennsylvania who always wrote in lower case had not been in the comments for nine days. She had noticed on the third. She did not keep track of people, as a rule; they came and went, and that was the arrangement. But she had given him the card, and she had seen his face in his little round picture, and she had thought about him on the bus. She put the plate away. She propped the phone on the phone books and sat down on the blanket with her back against the refrigerator and went live at 7:40 in the evening, which she had never done, and closed her eyes. By the pool in Analomink, the phone on Mateo’s folded blanket lit up. It had been dead five days. He had not charged it; there was nowhere to charge it. It lay face up on the grey wool by his knee and its screen came on white and then showed the notice, the way it always had at half past four in the morning, @hollis_sits is LIVE, and then the kitchen. The stove light. The shelf with the salt and the white figure. Hollis on her blanket with her ey

sections.heading: VI. The Doorbell Light
sections.dateline: Jefferson Avenue, Rochester · the same night
sections.text: Three hundred and twelve people were watching when Hollis Tate opened her eyes at 7:52 that evening and signed into her phone, and two hundred of them did not know sign, and all of them, afterward, said they had understood it. That was the first thing people argued about. The second thing was the replay. On that app in that year a broadcast stayed up for twenty-four hours and then it was gone, and this one went the way they all went, the next evening, before anyone thought to save it properly. There were screenshots. There was a grainy recording somebody in Leeds made by pointing a second phone at the first. In it you can see her hands move. You cannot see what they say. She ended the broadcast a little after eight. She was rinsing her cup when the light by the front door began to flash, the lamp her nephew had wired to the doorbell, three long pulses across the kitchen ceiling. The young man on her porch was barefoot and thin and had not shaved in a long time. He wore a grey hoodie with a warehouse logo on it and smelled of pine and of a pool that needed cleaning. She knew his face from the little round picture. He did not say anything. He knelt on the porch boards, in front of he

title: The Bell Pool
logline: A warehouse picker sits nine days beside a ruined honeymoon resort's pool, until a woman stood up by a client finds him there.

verses.text: Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a scarred man with copper-colored teeth joins a band of thieves whose leader distrusts him on sight. When the band is captured, no one will act as executioner, and every thief refuses the offer of his life in exchange for killing his companions, until the newcomer agrees. He becomes the city’s executioner for fifty-five years. When he is dismissed in old age for bungling his work, he prepares the milk-porridge he will no longer be given, bathes, and dresses in the old clothes, flowers and perfume that came with the post. At that moment the elder Säriputta comes to his door. The man gives him the porridge; the elder tells him to eat it himself, then asks whether he killed of his own will. The king made me. Then what wrong did you do? His mind grows calm and he listens. Walking home, he is killed by a cow, and the Buddha tells the doubting monks that he has gone to a heavenly world, because one word that brings peace is worth more than a thousand.
bg.history:
French Louisiana ran on the Code Noir, which Louis XV extended to the colony in 1724. Under the code, an enslaved person who ran away for a month lost his ears and was branded with a fleur-de-lis; a second time, the hamstring was cut and the other shoulder branded; a third time meant death (the text). The colony struggled to find anyone who would carry out its sentences. In 1725 the Company of the Indies freed an enslaved man named Louis Congo and made him public executioner, with land outside New Orleans, a ration, and a fee for each flogging, hanging or breaking on the wheel. He was attacked at least twice, and the records of him stop after 1737. Jean-Baptiste, his band and the people of this story are invented.

The Ursuline nuns arrived in 1727. Their convent on Chartres Street, rebuilt between 1748 and 1753, still stands. The nuns taught the catechism to enslaved women with great success, and in 1730 they sponsored a laywomen’s confraternity whose members ranged from plantation mistresses to women of color. By the 1730s orange and citron trees were doing well in New Orleans. In 1762 France ceded Louisiana to Spain, and the first Spanish governor, Antonio de Ulloa, arrived in March 1766 without the troops to take control. After the colonists drove him out in the Rebellion of 1768, General Alejandro O’Reilly condemned its leaders to hang. According to an early history of the colony, no hangman could be found in all of Louisiana, so the five men were shot.

sections.heading: I. The Swamp
sections.dateline: The cypress back of New Orleans · spring 1738
sections.text: The old women on the Bayou Road will tell you there were five hundred of them, less one. The register of the Superior Council says nine. Both are true in their way. Nine men in the cypress back of the city, where the ground goes soft and then goes to water and then goes to something that is neither, could be five hundred when they came out at night. They took hogs from the plantations at Chapitoulas and rice from the barges and powder from wherever powder was. They had a camp on a shell mound in the swamp that nobody could find twice, and a fire that nobody ever saw, and a leader called Jupiter who had run from the Company’s plantation across the river so many times that he had stopped counting the times and the King’s law had not. The law was simple. A slave who ran for a month lost his ears and was branded on one shoulder with the lily of France. Twice, the other shoulder, and the cord behind the knee. Three times, death. There was not a man on the shell mound who had both his ears. One night in March a stranger came through the water to the edge of the firelight and stood there until they saw him. He was tall and the color of a pecan shell, and his back and arms were so crossed

sections.heading: II. The Ladder
sections.text: The habitants of Chapitoulas got tired of losing their hogs. They went into the swamp with soldiers from the garrison and dogs and a Choctaw tracker the Council paid in cloth, and on the fourth day they came out with all of them, roped neck to neck, the whole five hundred, the whole nine, Jean-Baptiste walking last. The Superior Council sat in judgment. It did not take them long. They were runaways, and most of them were runaways for the third time, and they had stolen, and two of them had fired on the King’s soldiers. The sentence was that they be hanged by the neck on the square before the church until they were dead, and their bodies exposed. Then there was a difficulty, which was that there was nobody to hang them. The colony had had a hangman. It did not have one now. The procureur general walked through the town with the warrant in his hand asking, and the soldiers looked at their boots, and the carpenters who had built the gallows said they were carpenters, and a tavernkeeper said that for a hundred livres he would do it and then, when his wife heard, said that he had been joking. Nobody in New Orleans would put his hands on the rope. It was the kind of thing that stays on a

sections.heading: III. The Four Winds
sections.text: That summer the garrison brought in a band of thieves from the south, from down the river below the English Turn, where there were deserters living with runaways in the marsh. The Council sentenced them, and again there was the difficulty, and they asked the leader and he refused, and they asked every man in the band and every man refused. Then somebody on the Council said, The other day a man hanged nine. Where is he? Someone had seen him on the Bayou Road, clearing his land. They sent a soldier, and he came, and they said, Hang these men and you will be paid, and he said, Oui, certainly, and he did it, and was paid. After that the Council made it permanent. The executioner of high justice of the colony of Louisiana would have his land and his house on it. He would have thirty livres for a hanging and forty for the wheel and ten for a flogging, and a ration from the King’s stores. And because it had always been so in France, the clothes of the men he hanged would be his. Later they brought men in from the west, from across the river and the bayous beyond it, and later from the north, from Pointe Coupée and the Natchez country, and he hanged them all. The old women on the Bayou Roa

sections.heading: IV. The Coat
sections.text: That was the spring nobody knew who the king was. Louis had given the colony away to his cousin in Spain, people said, in a treaty, years ago, the way you would give someone a horse you were tired of feeding. Nobody had believed it until the Spanish governor actually came up the river in the first week of March with a sour face and not enough soldiers to take possession of anything. The flag on the square was still French. The Council still sat. Everybody was waiting to see what would happen, and in the meantime there were three men to be hanged for robbing a ship’s purser on the levee and leaving him dead in the mud. Jean-Baptiste was past sixty by then. He did not know exactly how far past. His hands had begun to shake in the mornings, and his knees did not like ladders. The first man went well enough. The second man he turned off the ladder and the knot was wrong, and the man did not die. He hung there making a sound. Jean-Baptiste took hold of his legs to pull, the way he had done a hundred times, and his arms had no strength in them, and the man kicked him away. He took hold again. He had to climb back up the ladder in the end and do something to the rope with his hands, which

sections.heading: V. The Door
sections.text: Fanchon had been on her knees in the Ursulines’ chapel since before light. She was a free woman of color, forty-four years old, a washerwoman by trade, and a member of the congregation the nuns had started for the women of the town, where planters’ wives and laundresses and slave women knelt on the same floor and said the same rosary. She taught the catechism to the new ones off the ships on Sunday afternoons, in French and in what she had of Bambara, and she was known for not saying much and for something else that people were careful how they spoke of. When she got up from her knees that morning she stood a moment in the aisle and asked, the way she always did, Where should I go today? And the way it sometimes happened, she saw it: a table on the Bayou Road, a bowl of rice and milk with the steam coming up, a crock of butter, a man in a brown coat with orange flowers in the buttonhole. She knew whose house it was. Everybody knew whose house it was. She thought, Will he let me in? And she saw that too. So she put on her headcloth and took her basket and walked out through the town gate and down the Bayou Road between the orange trees, and knocked. When he opened the door and saw h

sections.heading: VI. The Road
sections.text: When she rose to go he walked her up the road toward the town, a little way, the way you walk a guest. He did not take her arm. He walked half a step behind her, in the Swiss soldier’s coat with the flowers in it, and people working in their gardens along the road straightened up and stared, the washerwoman from the Ursulines and the hangman, walking together in the middle of the afternoon. At the bend before the town gate he stopped and bowed to her, a real bow, the way he had seen gentlemen do on the square, and she put out her hand and he took it. It was the first hand anyone had given him in twenty-eight years that was not tied. Then he turned around and walked back toward his house. The cattle of the town grazed loose on the commons along the Bayou Road, and nobody minded them much. That afternoon there was a young red heifer standing in the road where it ran between two ditches, a pretty thing with a white star, and when Jean-Baptiste came down the road toward her she lowered her head and watched him come. Toussaint saw it from the door. He said afterward that the old man was looking up into the orange trees and did not see her. He said the heifer came at a trot, then a run,

sections.heading: VII. The Congregation
sections.dateline: The Ursuline chapel · the following Sunday
sections.text: The women of the congregation met after Vespers on Sunday as they always did, and nobody could talk about anything else. Fanchon was in his house. Fanchon ate at his table. Twenty-eight years he hanged people on that square. They took away his rice on Thursday. Friday he gave it to Fanchon, Friday he heard the catechism, Friday a cow killed him in the road. All in one day. And where is he now? said a planter’s wife, a pious woman who had lost a brother at Natchez. Tell me that. Where does a man like that go? Nobody said anything. They all looked at the oldest of them. Her name was Marguerite, and she belonged to the nuns. She had come off a ship from Senegal before the town had a church, and she had taught Fanchon her prayers thirty years before, and the Ursulines themselves asked her things. She was so old that she sat on the floor against the wall during the meetings, with her legs out straight in front of her, and nobody thought it was strange. He went where the thief went, she said. The thief on the cross asked, said the planter’s wife. He had faith. This man heard a grace after meals and a few words from a washerwoman. Forgive me, Fanchon. A few words. Twenty-eight years, some

title: Copper Teeth
logline: The colony's hangman, dismissed in his sixties, cooks the last of the King's rice and milk, and someone knocks at his door.

verses.text: Even though a Gatha (poem) be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of a Gatha is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Bāhiya Dārucīriya, “the man from abroad who wears bark,” is the only survivor of a shipwreck. He wraps himself in bark, is fed and honored as a saint at the port of Suppāraka, and comes to believe it. A former companion, one of seven monks who long ago climbed a mountain and kicked the ladder down behind them, comes from the Brahma world to tell him he is no such thing. Bāhiya goes to the Buddha in a single night and begs three times in the street to be taught. When he hears “in the seen, only the seen,” he is awakened on the spot. Sent off to find his own bowl and robe, he is killed by a cow that the commentary says was a demoness. The Buddha has his body carried out on a litter, burned, and a stūpa built over it, and names him foremost of those who understand quickly.
bg.history:
The French built Fort Michilimackinac around 1715 on the Straits of Mackinac, where Lakes Michigan and Huron meet, and it became the main depot of the fur trade in the upper Great Lakes. In 1742 the Odawa moved about twenty-five miles south to L’Arbre Croche, and the Jesuits moved their mission with them. In 1743 a new parish church of Sainte-Anne went up inside the stockade (see the Mackinac State Historic Parks timeline). In the spring of 1744 France and Britain went to war again. In the colonies this was King George’s War, and English-speaking traders on the lakes were enemies. Pieter’s people belonged to the Dutch Reformed world of the Raritan valley in New Jersey, where Theodorus Frelinghuysen had preached the new birth since the 1720s. Children there learned the 129 questions of the Heidelberg Catechism.

Cadillac founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit in 1701 as a log palisade about twelve feet high, with a bastion at each corner. Its first building was a chapel to Saint Anne. Wendat people, whom the French called Hurons, came down from Michilimackinac to settle near it. They descended from Wendat and Petun refugees scattered by the wars of 1649, and today they are the Wyandot and Wendat nations. A Jesuit mission to them was founded at Detroit in 1728. In 1742 Armand de La Richardie moved it about twenty miles downriver to Bois Blanc Island, and Pierre Potier arrived there in September 1744 after studying the Huron language. In the unrest of 1747 the mission was destroyed. It was rebuilt across from the fort at La Pointe de Montréal, which is now Windsor, Ontario. Thomas and his people are fictional, as are Pieter, the bowl and the cow.

sections.heading: I. The Plank
sections.text: Eight men went into the lake in the third week of November, and one came out. They were Albany men, Dutch and English, with a north canoe they had bought from somebody who should not have sold it and a load of stroud blankets, powder and rum they meant to carry up past the French to the Odawa towns, where the Odawa would pay in beaver for English cloth, which they liked better than anything that came up from Montreal. France and England had been at war since the spring. Everybody on the lakes knew it. The men in the canoe knew it too, but they believed the lake was too big for a war to find them in. A northwest gale found them instead, at dusk, among the islands below the Straits, and put the canoe on a shoal and broke her back, and the water took them one at a time, the way cold takes the fingers. Pieter Schenck got his arms over a length of the broken gunwale and held on. He held on through the dark and the snow squalls and a cold so great that after a while it stopped being cold and became a kind of sleep he had to keep climbing out of. He was twenty-four. He came from the Raritan valley in the Jerseys, where his people had farmed since the Dutch had the country, and he had neve

sections.heading: II. The Saint
sections.text: The Jesuit was away all that winter at L’Arbre Croche, among the Odawa, and there was nobody at the Straits to ask the man in bark any hard questions. So the fort answered them for itself. He had come out of the lake in November, when nobody comes out of the lake. He wore bark like Saint John in the wilderness. He did not speak, which meant he was under a vow, which meant he was a holy man of some order nobody at the Straits had heard of, a hermit maybe, from the far missions of the West, cast up among them for a reason. By Christmas the soldiers’ wives were calling him le saint homme, the holy man, and the voyageurs who had stayed the winter called him l’Homme d’Écorce, the Bark Man, which was easier to say. He lived in a lean-to of poles and bark against the back of the new church of Sainte-Anne, which smelled of fresh-cut cedar. People brought him things. Smoked whitefish from the Straits, which were the best whitefish in the world. Sagamité in his bowl, morning and night. Cakes of maple sugar wrapped in bark. A soldier brought him a twist of tobacco, and a girl brought him a capot, a good hooded coat cut from a blanket, and he looked at it a long time and gave it back to her. A

sections.heading: III. Dirck
sections.text: The ice went out of the Straits in the third week of April, and on the first night it moved, Pieter woke in the lean-to to a sound like cannon. It was the ice. Whole fields of it were splitting and riding up on one another and grinding east toward Lake Huron in the dark. He went out to look, through the water gate, onto the beach where he had come ashore. Dirck Hoogland was standing over the ice. He was not on it. He stood a man’s height above it, on nothing, in the blue shirt he had been wearing when the sea took him, with his hair wet and his feet bare, and he was fourteen still, and very quiet, exactly as he had been on the rock. The ice moved under him and he did not move with it. Afterward the sentry who was on the bastion that night told it in every tavern from the Straits to Montreal, and he said the same thing every time and never added to it: There was a boy standing on the air. Pieter, said Dirck. You aren’t what they say. You aren’t anywhere near it. You aren’t even on the road that goes to it. What you’re doing will take you the other way. Pieter stood on the gravel in his bark. The shame went through him like the cold had gone through him in the lake, all the way in. T

sections.heading: IV. The River Gate
sections.text: The Huron canoes were drawn up on the strand below the stockade, three of them, with bags of seed corn in them for the habitants, and a half dozen young men from the mission at Bois Blanc were walking up and down on the beach in the early sun to get the stiffness of twenty miles of paddling out of their legs. They stopped when they saw him. He came up the river road with the bark hanging off him in strips and the cedar gone, and his feet bleeding through a crust of mud and ice. Where is the old man? he said. Thomas. The oldest of them, a man about Pieter’s own age with a brass crucifix on a thong at his throat, looked at him for a while before he answered. He has gone in among the houses. He’ll be back down to the canoes at noon. And then, because the man in front of him was swaying on his feet, Where have you come from? From Michilimackinac. When did you leave Michilimackinac? Last night. The young men looked at one another. Nobody laughed. One of them had a kettle of sagamité going on a little fire on the beach, and he dipped some into a bark dish and held it out. You’ve come a long way, then, said the one with the crucifix. Sit down. Eat. Wash your feet in the river and let us g

sections.heading: V. Sainte-Anne Street
sections.dateline: Inside the stockade · the same morning
sections.text: Le Détroit was smaller than he had imagined, a square of log palisade with a bastion at each corner, the little church at one end, and four or five streets so narrow two carts could hardly pass. Rue Sainte-Anne ran along the south wall. It was mud from one end to the other, April mud, with planks laid across the worst of it, and smoke coming down into it from the public bake house, which had been firing since before light, so that the whole street smelled of bread. The old man was coming up it from the bake house with a basket on his arm. Pieter knew him at once, though he could not have said how. He was old, and not tall, and there was nothing about him that anyone would turn to look at twice. He wore a blanket capot like any habitant, and leggings, and moccasins black with mud, and a brass crucifix like the young man’s at the landing. His hair was white and cut short. He walked the way a man walks who is going somewhere ordinary and is not in a hurry to get there, and he looked at what was in front of him, the planks and the mud and the dog asleep in the door of the smithy, as if each of them was all there was. Pieter went down on his knees in the mud of the street and put his fa

sections.heading: VI. The Bread Board
sections.text: The young men at Bois Blanc talked about it for years afterward, and what they said was this. Thomas could have given the man a blanket. There were two in the canoes. He could have stood in the street and said the words the Black Robes said and made him one of them on the spot. He did not, because he knew what Pieter had done on the rock. In eight years, Pieter Schenck had never given a soul so much as a crust. Every man finds his own bread. A man who has lived that way a long time finds there is no blanket waiting for him anywhere, because he has never left one anywhere for anyone else. Thomas could not change that for him. Nobody could. So he sent him to go and find his own. Pieter went out at the east gate onto the commons, where the cattle of the fort were turned out in spring, to look for a birch to peel. He was not unhappy. He had the King’s bowl in his hand. He was looking at the commons the new way, the brown grass, the wet, a crow, and there was nobody looking. There was a cow standing by the dung heap outside the gate. She was a red heifer, alone, with a white star on her forehead, and nobody saw where she came from. She put her head down and came at him across the wet gr

sections.heading: VII. The King’s Bowl
sections.dateline: Bois Blanc Island · that night, and the summer after
sections.text: They paddled back down to the mission in the afternoon with the seed corn sold and the bread in the bottom of the canoe, and that night, after the prayers, the young men sat around the fire outside Thomas’s lodge and could not leave it alone. Where has he gone, the man in the bark? To God, said Thomas. All the way. He won’t be coming back around. An Englishman? A heretic who never had the sacraments, who lay on the Straits all winter letting people kiss his hand? Yes. But when did he get there? When he heard me. When did he hear you? This morning. In the street. Outside the bake house. The one with the brass crucifix shook his head. Grandfather, you hardly said anything to him. We were watching from the gate. You said four or five words to him, standing in the mud with a basket on your arm. The Black Robes preach for an hour. How could a man get all the way to God on four or five words? Thomas was quiet for a while. The fire settled. Out on the dark river a fish jumped, and the rings went out across the water and were gone. Don’t measure it by how long it was, he said. Some men hear a thousand words and every one of them is empty. You can preach to a man from now till the Feast of

title: The King’s Bowl
logline: A castaway in birch bark is fed all winter as a saint at the Straits, until a drowned friend appears over the ice.

verses.text: Though a man recite a hundred Gathas made up of senseless words, one word of the law is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.
If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich merchant’s daughter of Rājagaha, kept on the top floor of her father’s house, sees a young robber being whipped through the streets to his execution and refuses to eat until she has him. Her father bribes the officer to free him and execute another man in his place. The robber marries her, wants her jewels, and pretends he owes an offering to the deity of Robbers’ Cliff. At the top he tells her he means to kill her. She asks to honor him one last time, walks around him three times, embraces him and pushes him over. Unable to go home, she joins a band of women wanderers, masters a thousand philosophical views, and travels from town to town planting a rose-apple branch at the gates and challenging anyone who can answer her to trample it. At Sāvatthī the elder Sāriputta has some boys trample it. He answers all her questions, then asks her one, “What is one?” She cannot answer it, asks to be ordained, takes the name Kuṇḍalakesī (“curly hair”) and soon becomes an arahant.
bg.history:
In September 1907 a mob of about five hundred men drove the Sikh mill workers out of Bellingham. Sikhs did not come back to Whatcom County in numbers for most of a century. When they did, beginning in the 1980s, they came mostly as farmers who had first prospered across the border in British Columbia. Today nearly a hundred Sikh farmers work some five thousand acres of berries there, in a county that grows about two-thirds of the raspberries in the United States (KUOW). In 1993 Washington voters approved Initiative 593, the first true three-strikes law in the country. On August 5, 2012, a white supremacist killed six worshippers at the Sikh Temple of Wisconsin in Oak Creek while the langar was being prepared.

Oyster Dome is a rock promontory on Blanchard Mountain above Samish Bay. The trail approaches it through the forest from the Samish Overlook, a hang-gliding launch, and ends at an unfenced edge with an unforgiving drop. The scripture in the story is from the Guru Granth Sahib in Max Arthur Macauliffe’s translation, The Sikh Religion, volume 1 (1909), which renders the opening words, Ik Oankar, as “There is but one God.” In Sikh weddings the couple walks four times around the Guru Granth Sahib, and at initiation, amrit, the five Ks include kesh, uncut hair. The word Sikh means a learner or disciple. Everyone in the story is fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Window
sections.text: Mohinder Singh Gill had six hundred acres of raspberries north of Lynden, a cold storage on the Badger Road, and a house on the Guide Meridian three stories high, the tallest house between Bellingham and the Canadian line. He had come down from Abbotsford in 1986 with a used tractor and a loan from his wife’s brother, with forty acres he could barely afford, and he had paid back every dollar and bought every farm that came up for sale on his road. Two-thirds of the raspberries in America came out of that county, and a good share of them came out of his fields. He was proud of that. He said so at the gurdwara, where he gave a great deal of money, and at the Rotary, where he gave a little. His daughter Simran had the whole top floor. She was eighteen, just out of high school, and the most beautiful girl in the Punjabi families from Surrey to Mount Vernon, and her father knew it, and knew what the world was, so the top floor was where she stayed. She had gone to school in Lynden and come straight home. She went to the gurdwara with her mother and sat with the women. In the summers, when the pickers came and the cousins came and the house was full, her father’s sister Jaswinder came do

sections.heading: II. The Promise
sections.text: They were married in November at the gurdwara, under the canopy, and walked the four laavan around the Guru Granth Sahib while the ragis sang, and Raj walked ahead of her as the groom does, with the end of her scarf in his hand, and the whole Punjabi Northwest came and ate and went home talking. Mohinder Singh gave them a house on one of the farms. Simran meant to be a good wife. She meant it with everything she had. Every evening she put on her gold, the heavy wedding set her mother had given her, the necklace and the earrings and the bangles, twenty-two karat, and cooked his dinner with her own hands in it, so that he would see her in it. She did not know any other way to say it. It was the gold he looked at. Before the winter was out he was thinking about it every night. Two hundred thousand dollars of gold, maybe more, walking around his kitchen. One of these days, he thought, she would have to take it off, and he could take it to a jeweler he knew in Surrey who asked no questions, and then he could eat dinner at the casino every night for a year and never come home. But she would never take it off while she was alive. He thought about that, and then he saw how to do it. In Apr

sections.heading: III. The Dome
sections.text: Oyster Dome is a knob of rock at the top of the mountain that the trail comes up to from behind, through the trees, on the easy side. On the other side there is no easy way. The rock ends in the air. Below it the mountain falls away a thousand feet and more, cliff and talus and the tops of trees, down to the highway and the railroad and the gray flat water of Samish Bay, and beyond that the islands, Lummi and Orcas and the others, one behind the other into the haze. The sign at the trailhead says to keep back from the edge. It does not say why. Anyone who has stood there knows why. She stood on the rock in her gold with the dabba in both hands and looked out at all of it. Here. Let’s give it here. Say the ardas. He said nothing. Raj? Why aren’t you saying anything? I don’t need the prashad, he said. There wasn’t any promise. I made it up to get you up here. Then why are we here? To kill you, he said, and take your gold, and go. The fear went through her so hard that the dabba shook in her hands. Raj. My gold is yours. I’m yours. Why are you saying this? She begged him. She said don’t again and again, and every time he only said, I’m going to kill you. But what do you get by killing

sections.heading: IV. The House of Questions
sections.text: She sat down on the rock and thought it through, the way she would learn to think everything through. If she went home, they would ask, Where is Raj? If she said, I pushed him off Oyster Dome, they would say, We paid for that boy. We bought him back from Walla Walla with our money, for you, and you killed him. If she said, He was going to kill me for my gold, nobody would believe her. A girl like her. A boy like him. They would not believe her at the gurdwara, and they would not believe her at the sheriff’s office in Bellingham. Then I’m finished with home, she thought. She took off the gold. The necklace and the earrings and all the bangles, one by one, and the steel kara from her right wrist, which she had worn since she was two. She laid them on the rock beside the dabba of karah prashad and the five kinds of flowers. Then she walked down the other trail, the steep one, to Chuckanut Drive, and stood at the side of the road until a woman in a pickup stopped. In the restroom of the bus station in Mount Vernon she cut her hair off with a pair of nail scissors, all of it, close to her head, and dropped it in the trash, and got on the bus to Seattle. The sheriff found Raj at the bott

sections.heading: V. The Branch
sections.text: She called herself the Branch, online, and that was what people called her, and before long a great many people knew the name. She went from Bellingham to Eugene and out to Spokane and Boise. Before she went into any town she would find the biggest church, or the mosque, or the temple, or the chaplain’s office at the college, and set a bucket of sand by the door and stand her branch up in it, and tape a card to the bucket that said, If you can answer my questions, step on this. Then she went to find something to eat. Nobody stepped on it. When she came back the branch was always standing, and somebody had always filmed it, and by evening it was online. When a branch dried out, she cut a new one. There is vine maple all over the Northwest. Some of them argued with her. Ministers, a rabbi in Portland, a Jesuit at Gonzaga who liked her and lost anyway. She asked them her questions in front of everybody, politely, one after another, and they ran out of answers long before she ran out of questions, and the videos went around. After a while nobody argued with her. When people heard the Branch was coming, they found they had somewhere else to be that week. Pastors went to conferences. The

sections.heading: VI. The Langar Hall
sections.text: In the second week of August she came to the gurdwara in the valley at Kent. She had stayed away from gurdwaras for three years. She told herself it was not on purpose. But that August a man had walked into a gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin, on a Sunday morning, while the women were cooking the langar, and killed six people with a pistol, and every gurdwara in America had been on the news since, and she found she could not stay away from this one. She set her bucket of sand by the gate in the chain-link fence, beside the bunches of flowers people had left there for Oak Creek, and stood the vine maple up in it, and taped on her card. Then she went down the street to get coffee. A crowd of boys from the Sunday Punjabi school gathered around the bucket. They knew who she was. Everybody did. They stood around the branch with their patkas on and their hands in their pockets and dared each other, and nobody touched it. Baba Kartar Singh came out the side door of the langar hall a little after one, wiping his hands. He had eaten, and washed the big pots, and was going home to sleep. He was seventy-four. He had driven a truck for thirty-one years, Seattle to Chicago and back, Seattle to L

sections.heading: VII. Curly
sections.text: Baba Kartar Singh did not make her anything. He sent her to the women. She stayed that winter with a widow from the sangat who had a room over her garage, and she worked in the langar kitchen, and she did not argue with anyone. At Vaisakhi in April, with the other initiates, she took amrit from the Panj Pyare in the gurdwara at Kent, and put on the five things, and a new steel kara on her right wrist, and kept her hair from that day uncut. It came in curly. It had been straight all her life, down to her waist, and she had cut it off in a bus station in Mount Vernon, and now it came back in tight curls that would not stay under her chunni, and the boys from the Punjabi school, who had jumped on her branch, called her Ghungrali Bibi, Curly Bibi, and then everybody did. Some time in that first spring, nobody could ever say exactly when, the thing happened to her that she had come for. She did not talk about it. People who had known the Branch did not recognize her. She rolled roti in the langar kitchen for three hundred people on a Sunday and did not say a word all morning, and the women who worked beside her said later that it was like standing next to a window with the sun coming in

title: The Branch
logline: A berry farmer's daughter marries the copper thief her father bought out of prison, and he asks her to climb a mountain.

verses.text: One’s own self conquered is better than all other people; not even a god, a Gandharva, not Mara with Brahman could change into defeat the victory of a man who has vanquished himself, and always lives under restraint.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a brahmin wonders whether the Buddha knows only what brings gain, or what brings loss as well, and goes to Jetavana to ask him. The Buddha says he knows both and names six roads to loss: sleeping after sunrise, idleness, ferocity, long drunkenness, going on a long journey alone, and other men’s wives. The brahmin praises him as a teacher and leader of a following, and the Buddha answers that no one knows loss as well as he does. Then the Buddha asks the brahmin how he lives. By gambling, he says; sometimes he wins and sometimes the other man does. The Buddha tells him that victory over another is a small thing, and that the victory of one who conquers himself is one that no god or demon can turn into defeat.
bg.history:
Black horsemen built American racing. Thirteen of the fifteen riders in the first Kentucky Derby, in 1875, were Black, and Black jockeys won fifteen of the first twenty-eight Derbies, among them Isaac Murphy, who won three. Around the turn of the century they were driven out of the saddle by racism, by violence from white riders that went unpunished, and by the shrinking of racing under anti-gambling laws. Jimmy Winkfield, the last Black jockey to win the Derby, in 1902, left to ride in Russia and Europe. After Henry King rode in 1921, no Black jockey rode in the Derby again until 2000. Many Black horsemen stayed on as grooms, trainers and hot walkers; the Smithsonian tells the story.

In January 1937 the Ohio River flood put about seventy percent of Louisville under water and drove some 175,000 people from their homes. By early February the track at Churchill Downs, more than five miles from the river, lay under about six feet of water; the crew rebuilt the strip, and the Derby was run on schedule on May 8 (the Kentucky Derby Museum has the story). After a race or a workout a hot walker leads a horse until it has cooled, and the old practice, still remembered on the backstretch, was to let a hot horse have only a few swallows of water at a time.

sections.heading: I. The Backside
sections.text: In January the Ohio had come up out of its banks and five miles across the city, and into February it stood six feet deep on the racetrack, brown and still, with the tops of the rails showing like a fence in a pond. When it went down it left the mud. The men spent March raking it off the strip and hauling it away in wagons and putting down new dirt, and by the middle of April there was fresh paint on everything, and the Derby horses were coming in on the train, and people uptown were saying the Downs looked better than before. The backside smelled the way it always did, of liniment and wet straw and coffee from the track kitchen and the manure pile behind every barn. Before light the grooms came out of the tack rooms, where most of them slept on cots between the saddles, and the exercise boys came up from Smoketown in the dark, and the roosters some of the stables kept went off one after another down the line. By six the horses were going out to the track in the fog, and the clockers stood at the rail with their stopwatches, and the men who bet for a living stood near the clockers. Isom Tandy walked hots for Mr. Dade Collier’s stable in Barn 22. He was fifty-six years old and stood

sections.heading: II. The Question
sections.dateline: Barn 22 · a morning in the last week of April
sections.text: Mr. Carroll Ashby came down the shed row at about seven, with the fog still lying on the infield and the sun just coming red through it. He was a white man of forty or so in a camel-hair coat, with field glasses on a strap around his neck and the Racing Form folded lengthwise in his pocket. He lived at the Seelbach in the season and at Hialeah in the winter, and he was known on every backside from Saratoga to New Orleans as a man who made his living at the windows and had been making it for twenty years. Isom had a gray two-year-old on the shank, just back from a bad work, blowing hard. Lafayette Moss, who was sixteen and galloped horses for Mr. Collier, sat on an upturned bucket by the tack room door with a bridle across his knees, mending a rein. Mr. Ashby fell in beside Isom and walked with him. Morning, Isom. Morning, Mr. Ashby. They tell me you know horses. They tell me you can look at one cooling out and say if he’ll run back. Isom walked. The gray put its nose down to the bucket at the corner and took three swallows, and Isom lifted its head and walked on. Now I’ve been wondering something, Mr. Ashby said. A man who knows winners. Does he know losers too? Or does he just kno

sections.heading: III. Often Cast Down
sections.text: They went around again. The sun was clear of the fog now and the shed row was striped with it, light and shadow, light and shadow, and the gray walked through the stripes with its head lower than before. Isom looked at the field glasses and the folded Form, and at the camel-hair coat, which was a good coat and had been mended once at the cuff, very well, by somebody who knew how. How do you make your living, Mr. Ashby? You know how I make it. I bet. Who wins? Some days me, Mr. Ashby said. Some days the windows. Isom let the gray drink, and lifted its head, and walked on. Beating the other man, he said, that’s a little thing. There isn’t anything in it. You beat the windows Tuesday and the windows beat you Saturday. I won a race at Latonia once by a nose, and the man I beat went out and beat me the next day by two lengths, and the next week neither one of us had a mount. That kind of winning comes back on you. It always comes back. But a man who gets the better of what’s in himself, he said, the mean, and the lazy, and the bottle, and all of it. A man who beats that, and keeps on beating it every morning, that one stays won. Nobody can take it back off him. Not the stewards up in th

title: Watering Off
logline: The spring after the great flood, a professional horseplayer asks an old hot walker at Churchill Downs whether he knows anything about losing.

verses.text: If a man for a hundred years sacrifice month after month with a thousand, and if he but for one moment pay homage to a man whose soul is grounded (in true knowledge), better is that homage than sacrifice for a hundred years.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Sāriputta visits his uncle, a Brahmin, and asks him whether he ever does a single good deed. The uncle answers that month after month he gives a thousand coins to the naked ascetics, because his teachers have told him this is the way to the world of Brahmā. Sāriputta says that neither he nor his teachers know the way there, and takes him to the Buddha. The Buddha tells him that a hundred years of such giving would bear less fruit than a single moment of looking at his disciple with a believing heart, or one spoonful of boiled rice put in his bowl.
bg.history:
Afghan families began arriving in the East Bay as refugees after the Soviet invasion of 1979, and Fremont came to hold the best-known Afghan American community in the country; Sacramento County now has the largest. After the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021, Brazil issued humanitarian visas to several thousand Afghans, and some of them went on north overland, through the Darién Gap and Mexico, to ask for asylum at the United States border. Hundreds camped for weeks in the São Paulo airport on the way. In the days after an Afghan man shot two National Guard soldiers in Washington in November 2025, immigration lawyers reported a wave of arrests of Afghans, most of them in Northern California. In Sacramento, men who had asked for asylum at the border were telephoned at six in the morning on December 1, told to report to the federal building at once, and handcuffed as they came in; volunteers counted six arrests that day. The Associated Press, which reported this, could not confirm the reasons given in each case.

California City was laid out in the Mojave Desert in 1958 for 400,000 people who never came, and it is still a grid of paved streets with few houses, the third-largest city in California by area. Its private prison, built in 1999, reopened in late August 2025 as an immigration detention center with room for 2,560 people. By January 2026 it held more than 1,400 and was the largest in the state. Visitors there have described the three sliding gates, the invisible hand stamp, and visits through glass by wall telephone. Haji Wahid, Yusuf and Ustad Latif are invented. The lines the Ustad recites are from the second chapter of the Bustan of Sa'di of Shiraz (1257), in G. S. Davie's verse translation of 1882, where an angel says them to a pilgrim who is proud of praying at every step of the road to Mecca.

sections.heading: I. The Envelope
sections.dateline: Fremont, California · the first Friday of February 2026
sections.text: Haji Wahid sold floors. He had come to Fremont in 1984 with a wife, a sister, two rugs and a cousin's telephone number. He sold the two rugs, and then other men's rugs, and when the people who bought rugs began to want laminate he learned laminate. Now there was a showroom on Fremont Boulevard with forty feet of sample racks, a warehouse in Union City, three vans, and his name on the pens. On the first Friday of every month, after the prayer, he sat down at the desk in the back of the showroom and counted ten hundred-dollar bills into an envelope. He had done it since the spring of 2004. He wrote the month on the flap in pencil and walked the envelope two doors down to the travel agency, where the man at the rear counter wrote a line in a book and made a telephone call, and by Sunday a cousin of the mullah in his father's village above Charikar had the money in his hand. In twenty-two years the envelope had built a mosque of fired brick with a blue door. Then it had built a wall around the mosque, a well, a room for the boys to learn in, a loudspeaker, and last year four solar panels. A stonecutter had put his father's name over the door. Wahid kept a photograph of it under the gla

sections.heading: II. The Road
sections.text: They left at four in one of the vans, because Wahid would not ride eleven hours in a Corolla. Yusuf's mother came out to the driveway in her coat with a pot of qabuli wrapped in two bath towels. She set it in the back among the sample boards and stood there until they turned the corner. Over the Altamont and down into the valley the fog lay on the road as if it had been poured. Yusuf drove at fifty with the trucks. At the Westley rest area Wahid got out, washed at the tap with the cold running into his sleeves, took a carpet sample from the van, a two-foot square of gray Saxony with the price on the back, and prayed the dawn prayer on it beside the picnic tables. Yusuf prayed behind him on the concrete. After that there was light, and Yusuf talked. The teacher's name was Abdul Latif, and in Herat they called him Ustad Latif. He had taught Persian literature to boys for thirty-one years in a government high school. When the schools for girls were shut he taught girls, Sa'di and Hafez and their own grammar, in his guest room with the curtain drawn, until a neighbor warned him. He was sixty-seven. He went out through Iran. Brazil was giving visas then, so he flew to São Paulo and slep

sections.heading: III. The Glass
sections.text: It had been a prison, and it was one. There were three gates that slid. A woman behind a window took their licenses, and they waited in a room with six chairs. Then a guard gave each of them a badge and pressed a stamp on the back of each right hand that left no mark at all. They put keys, belts and Wahid's prayer beads in a gray bin and took off their shoes. The visiting room was large and nearly empty, with two vending machines at the far end. Along one side ran a row of booths with glass in them, and at each booth a chair and a telephone on the wall. At the first one a woman was holding a baby up to the glass. They brought him in on the other side. Wahid had expected a holy beggar, or else a professor. He saw a small man in the loose clothes they give them, with a clipped white beard and heavy glasses mended at the hinge, who looked at Yusuf first and laughed with pleasure, and then looked at Wahid and put his hand on his heart. There was one telephone. Yusuf took it. Ustad, this is my mother's brother, Haji Abdul Wahid of Fremont. He is building a mosque in Parwan. He has sent a thousand dollars every month for twenty-two years, and he hopes for a house in the Garden. I told hi

sections.heading: IV. The Plate
sections.text: On the way out a guard passed a violet lamp over the backs of their hands, and the stamp that had not been there showed for a second, a small green wheel. Then they were through the three gates with their shoes on. The wind was blowing. Yusuf opened the back of the van and unwrapped the pot, which was still warm in the middle. He found the two plates his mother had put in, and the spoon. Wahid took the spoon out of his hand. He was the elder. In sixty-six years nobody younger had been served in front of him. He dug down to where the rice was hot and lifted a spoonful with the carrots and raisins on it and a piece of the lamb, and put it on his nephew's plate. Then he put another. Eat, he said. You have to drive. Yusuf looked at the plate and then at him. He ate standing up, with the wind lifting a corner of the towel, and Wahid, who had not yet taken any for himself, watched him. On the first Friday of March he counted ten bills into the envelope and wrote the month on the flap, as before. A village is not hurt by a well. On the Sunday after that the van went south at four with the sample boards out and the seats bolted back in, nine people from the apartment off Fulton Avenue, and

title: Each Halting Place
logline: A Fremont flooring man who has sent a thousand dollars a month for twenty-two years rides to a desert detention center with his nephew.

verses.text: If a man for a hundred years worship Agni (fire) in the forest, and if he but for one moment pay homage to a man whose soul is grounded (in true knowledge), better is that homage than sacrifice for a hundred years.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Sāriputta asks his nephew, a young Brahmin, whether he ever does a single good deed. The nephew answers that month after month he kills one animal and tends the sacrificial fire, because his teachers say this is the way to the world of Brahmā. Sāriputta tells him that neither he nor his teachers know the way, and brings him to the Buddha, who says that a hundred years of tending the fire would not come to the worth of one moment's honor paid to his disciple.
bg.history:
Brookhaven National Laboratory was founded in 1947 in the Long Island pine barrens on the site of Camp Upton, the Army post where draftees were trained in 1917 and 1918 and inducted again in the Second World War. On November 22, 1961, ecologists there began irradiating a stand of oak and pine with gamma rays from 9,500 curies of cesium-137, raised on a pole in the middle of the woods for twenty hours of every day and lowered into a shielded hole for the other four. The experiment, led by George Woodwell, ran into the 1970s. The forest died back in rings: bare ground nearest the source, then a mat of Pennsylvania sedge, then heath shrubs, then oaks without pines, then woods that looked untouched. Pines died at exposures the oaks survived, and aphids multiplied on the stressed white oaks. Cesium-137 has a half-life of about thirty years, so a source loses roughly nine-tenths of its strength in a century. The technician's routine here, the hut, the lights and the monthly tree, is imagined around those facts.

The Laboratory had its own scientific glassblowers from its first years. Many American shops of that time were run by men trained in Lauscha and the other glass villages of Thuringia. Mr. Greiner, Stash Kozakiewicz, Gene Mroz and the children's lecture are invented. Riverhead's Polish Town grew up around St. Isidore's Church, built in 1906 by immigrants who had come to work the potato farms of eastern Long Island. Michael Faraday gave his six Christmas lectures for young people, The Chemical History of a Candle, at the Royal Institution in London in 1860, and the printed text includes the relighting of a blown-out candle through its own smoke and the breath that clouds lime-water. The first sergeant who said every recruit's name right is in The Doorsill.

sections.heading: I. The Source
sections.text: Every morning at eight Gene Mroz pressed a black button in a concrete hut in the pine woods, and a hundred yards off a canister of cesium went down a pipe into the ground. The red light over the gate went out and a green one came on. For four hours after that, people could go in. At noon he counted them out against the clipboard, counted the film badges back onto their board, walked the fence, locked the gate, and pressed the other button. The canister rose to the top of its pole and stayed there twenty hours. It stayed through the afternoon and the night, in rain, on Christmas, and it shone on the trees with a light nobody could see. It had done that every day since the twenty-second of November, 1961. You could see what the light had done. From the gate you walked in through ordinary Long Island woods, pitch pine and oak with huckleberry underneath. After a while the pines were dead and only the oaks had leaves, and the white oaks there were sticky with aphids, more aphids than anybody had ever counted on a tree. Farther in, the oaks were dead too. They stood gray, with the bark coming off in plates, and nothing was green above the knee but blueberry and huckleberry. Then the bus

sections.heading: II. Sunday
sections.dateline: Polish Town, Riverhead · the same month
sections.text: After the ten o'clock at St. Isidore's they ate at his grandmother's on Pulaski Street, eleven at the table. His Uncle Stash sat at the corner by the stove, where he had sat since before Gene was born. Stash Kozakiewicz had left school at fifteen for the potatoes. In 1942 the Army swore him in at Camp Upton, on the same sand the Laboratory stood on now. His own father had been a recruit there in 1918, and used to tell about a first sergeant from the coal country who said every man's name right the first time, Kozakiewicz included. When Stash came home from Italy he went back out to Upton and asked for work, and they gave him a broom. That was 1948. He was in the glass shop now. At the table it was understood that Gene had gone further in three months than Stash had in seventeen years, and Stash had never said a word against it. He waited until the women were clearing. Genek. You do any good out there? One thing? Sure I do. What? First of the month we take a tree. And every day I put the source down in the morning and send it back up at noon. What for? Gene had not said it aloud before, and he was pleased with how it came out. That's how you get to be one of them, Uncle. You keep th

sections.heading: III. The Glass Shop
sections.text: The shop was a long room with north windows, and gas and oxygen piped along the benches. Glass tubing stood in racks by size, like organ pipes. Mr. Greiner sat at the first bench. He came from Lauscha, in the Thuringian forest, where his father and his grandfather had blown glass. He had come to New York in 1926 and to the Laboratory in its first year, and nearly everything on the site that held a vacuum had been through his hands or through Stash's. He was sixty-three, a small man in a gray shop coat buttoned to the neck, with rose-colored spectacles pushed up on his forehead. On the bench in front of him a burner made a blue cone the length of a finger. Stash told him about it in four sentences. Mr. Greiner listened and looked at Gene. It is so? As he says? Yes, sir. So. He shut the oxygen, and the flame went soft and yellow. He shut the gas. I know your fire in the woods. It is a strong thing. You may send it up and take it down a hundred years. In a hundred years it will be a tenth so strong, and you will be dead, and it will not have made anything of you. It does not know you are there. Better you sit one minute and look at a man who is already made, and look at him the way yo

sections.heading: IV. The Candle
sections.text: Every December Mr. Greiner gave a lecture for the children of the Laboratory. Nobody had asked him to, and nobody paid him for it. He did the whole of Faraday in an hour and a half, with one candle, a bell jar, a balance, and a flask of lime-water that turned to milk when he breathed into it through a tube. Stash stood at the end of the table and handed him each thing before he reached for it, as he had every year since 1950. That year Gene carried the boxes over from the shop. He sat on the aisle steps among two hundred children, and when Mr. Greiner came to the end he said the end of the book, which he did not need the book for. Indeed, all I can say to you at the end of these lectures (for we must come to an end at one time or other) is to express a wish that you may, in your generation, be fit to compare to a candle; that you may, like it, shine as lights to those about you; that, in all your actions, you may justify the beauty of the taper by making your deeds honourable and effectual in the discharge of your duty to your fellow-men. — Lecture VI Then Stash did the last thing, the one the children waited for all year. He bent and blew the candle out, cleanly, so that a thread

title: The Ring Seal
place: Upton and Riverhead, Long Island, New York
logline: A young technician who raises a radiation source over a dying forest each noon is sent to watch his uncle work glass.

verses.text: Whatever a man sacrifice in this world as an offering or as an oblation for a whole year in order to gain merit, the whole of it is not worth a quarter (a farthing); reverence shown to the righteous is better.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Sāriputta asks a Brahmin who has been his friend whether he ever does a single good deed, and the friend answers that he offers sacrificial slaughter. It was then the custom, the commentary says, to make such sacrifices at immense expense. Sāriputta brings him to the Buddha, who asks whether he has been correctly reported and then tells him that a year of it is not worth a fourth part of what a man gains who gives alms to ordinary people with a believing heart, or who pays reverence to those who walk straight.
bg.history:
San Miguel del Vado, "Saint Michael of the Ford," was settled in 1794 on the Pecos River by genízaro, mestizo and Pecos Pueblo families, and its church was built in 1805. After 1821 it was the first New Mexican town the caravans of the Santa Fe Trail reached. The Mexican government stationed troops there against smuggling, and traders repacked their loads in the village before going on to the customhouse in Santa Fe. The last families of Pecos Pueblo, upriver, left for Jemez in 1838. The Missouri trader Josiah Gregg, who made the trip eight times in the 1830s, describes all of this in Commerce of the Prairies (1844): the guards who could be had "for a trifling douceur," the interpreters who made a business of "passing goods" and arranging the duties, the custom of splitting the legal tariff among officers, merchants and government, and the few years in which Governor Manuel Armijo charged a flat five hundred dollars on every wagon, large or small, so that traders took to the largest wagons they could find. Gregg also records that fords were marked out with stakes, and that in a New Mexican letter respect was measured by the width of the left margin, a fourth of the page for an equal and nearly half for a superior. By 1839 New Mexican merchants were sending their own wagons to Missouri.

The yearly feast of a village's patron saint, the función, was in the charge of a mayordomo who served for a year and bore its costs; in New Mexico towns such as Bernalillo a new family still becomes the mayordomos of the fiesta each year. Don Ygnacio, Tomás Padilla and tío Chano are invented, and so is the custom of uncovering in the ford. The four dichos are real. They are quoted as Aurelio M. Espinosa took them down in Santa Fe and Albuquerque and printed them in "New-Mexican Spanish Folk-Lore: Proverbs" (Journal of American Folk-Lore, 1913), where they are numbers 162, 386, 382 and 591. A proverb in New Mexico, Espinosa wrote, "is considered the final word on any subject."

sections.heading: I. The Wagons
sections.dateline: San Miguel del Vado, New Mexico · July 1839
sections.text: The Americans stopped on the east bank that summer and unloaded. The governor had tired of counting varas of calico, and he now took five hundred pesos for every wagon that came in, large or small, full or half full. So on the flat across the river from San Miguel the traders pulled the sheets off their loads and made two wagons out of three. The empty ones stood about with their tongues on the ground until somebody bought them for the iron. Don Ygnacio Baca rode across to them before the first bale was down. He had his English from a Kentucky trapper who had wintered in his father's house, and he wrote a fair hand in two languages. For twenty years he had done what the Americans called passing goods. He rode up to Santa Fe with each caravan and wrote out its manifests for the customhouse. He knew which inspector liked brandy and which had a daughter marrying, and when he was done the duties were arranged. Of what the law asked, a part went to the officers, a part stayed with the trader, and something reached the treasury. Each trader paid him a fee for this and thanked him. He had a saying for it, as he had for most things. Vale más un mal arreglo que un buen pleito. A poor arrang

sections.heading: II. The Year
sections.text: Since the last feast of San Miguel, Don Ygnacio had been mayordomo of the función. For one year the saint's day was his to pay for, and he had paid as nobody on the Pecos had paid before him. There were six dozen candles of white wax from Chihuahua, where other years had burned tallow. There was a keg and a half of powder from the Americans, for the salutes at vespers and at the Elevation. There was a cloak for the saint cut from a bolt of blue Missouri silk, and two fiddlers and a guitar hired down from Santa Fe, and the padre's fee for vespers, a sung Mass, a sermon and the procession. In the last week he had forty wethers killed and two beeves, and the women of nine households were baking in the ovens behind his house. He reckoned the year at a thousand pesos, which was the duty on two wagons. He knew what he did it for. San Miguel stood over the altar with a sword in one hand and a balance in the other, and every child in the valley knew what was weighed in that balance, and when. A man who had made his living by arrangement did well to have someone standing at the scale. Hasta para ir al cielo se necesita abogado, he said. Even to get into heaven you need an advocate.
