sections.heading: III. The Ford
sections.text: The old man was in the water to his shins, working a stake back and forth to seat it. He heard Tomás out without turning round. Then he waded to the bank and looked at the mayordomo's boots, and afterward at his face. Is it as he says? It is, tío. Then listen. You have fed this valley for a week. Keep that. A hungry man's thanks is worth having. He wiped his hands down his shirt. The rest of it, the wax and the powder and the fiddles, forty sheep killed so that people will say forty, the whole year of it, does not come to the fourth part of one thing. Take your hat off one time to a man who goes straight. Your own hat. Ygnacio knew to a finger's width what respect weighed. He wrote other men's letters for them. To an equal you left a fourth of the page blank down the left side, and to the governor you left half. He had never asked himself what you left for a man who drove stakes. What straight man? he said. On this river? The old man looked at his godson, who was looking at the water. That one wrote forty when you wrote thirty-one. He lost a friend by it, and he wrote it. You have dealt in derechos for twenty years, Ygnacio, and you have arranged every one. He used the word for the

sections.heading: IV. San Miguel
sections.text: The feast was kept, since everything was bought. The saint went out in blue silk through the corn stubble and along the ditch with his balance swinging. The powder was burned, the fiddles played until the candles were stubs, and the whole valley ate mutton for three days. The mayordomo walked behind the saint bareheaded, as everyone did. It was noticed that he carried his hat in his hand through the dancing too. The last of the Americans started home in the first week of October, and Ygnacio's four wagons went with them, back to Missouri for next year's goods. He rode down to see them over. In the middle of the ford the old man stood in the current with a stake in his hand, and on the far bank the corporal was counting. Ygnacio took off his hat in midstream and held it against his chest until his horse had climbed out on the other side. The teamsters behind him were Missouri boys who did not know the country. They saw the rich man of the place uncover in the middle of the river, and they supposed it was the custom, and one after another they took off their hats to the old man in the water and the corporal on the bank. So it became the custom. For some years every wagon that crossed

title: Another Man's Hat
place: San Miguel del Vado, New Mexico
logline: At a Santa Fe Trail ford, the rich man who arranges the customs duties spends a year paying for his saint's feast.

verses.text: He who always greets and constantly reveres the aged, four things will increase to him, viz. life, beauty, happiness, power.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two Brahmin ascetics keep their austerities for forty-eight years. One of them returns to the world, sells the merit of his practice for cattle and money, marries and has a son. When the family visits the old companion, the ascetic says "Live long!" to the father and the mother and is silent for the boy, who has seven days to live. He sends them to the Buddha, who gives the same blessing and the same silence, then tells the father to raise a pavilion at his door with a seat in the middle and eight or sixteen seats around it. Monks recite the protective texts there for seven days and nights without a break, and on the last night the Buddha comes and recites until dawn. So many gods crowd in that an ogre, who had served twelve years for the right to take the boy, is pushed back and cannot reach him. The boy is promised a hundred and twenty years and renamed Āyuvaḍḍhana, "life increased."
bg.history:
In the early 1990s Bhutan forced out more than 100,000 of its Nepali-speaking southerners, the Lhotshampa. Most of them spent the next two decades in camps in southeastern Nepal, among them Beldangi, Sanischare, Timai, Goldhap and Khudunabari. Resettlement abroad began in 2008, and by early 2017 more than 90,000 of the Bhutanese refugees had come to the United States. Several thousand settled in Akron, most of them in North Hill, an old Italian neighborhood; public radio's account of the first ten years describes the elders' isolation, the language barrier and the citizenship classes. The people, the garden and the week in the tent are invented.

Under the 1996 welfare law as amended in 1997, elderly or disabled refugees can receive Supplemental Security Income for seven years after arrival and after that only as citizens, which for people who arrived in 2008 and 2009 made the English civics test, drawn from a list of one hundred questions, a matter of rent. The four hundred parts per million in Rupa's soil report was the federal hazard level for lead in bare soil where children play. The verse the elders chant is the Mahamrityunjaya mantra, Rig Veda 7.59.12, said across the Hindu world for long life; it is given here in Ralph T. H. Griffith's translation of 1896. Boju's line is Manu 2.121 in Georg Bühler's translation of 1886. Its Sanskrit and the Pāli of Dhammapada 109 share their first line and two of their four increases, life and strength.

sections.heading: I. The Lot
sections.text: The garden was on a double lot off Dayton Street where two houses had come down, and the county land bank leased it to the neighborhood for a dollar a year. Rupa Niroula kept the lease in a binder. She was twenty-four and a program assistant with the county Extension office, which came to a county car on Tuesdays and Thursdays, a soil probe, a box of sample bags, and forty-two raised beds full of other people's grandparents. She had been born in Beldangi-II, in a bamboo hut in Sector C, and had landed in Akron at seventeen. The first thing she did with the lot was push the probe into it in ten places and mail the dirt to the lab. The ground along the back fence came back at four hundred and ten parts per million of lead, a hundred years of house paint, so nobody grew in the ground. They grew in boxes of trucked compost, and every March she tested the boxes too and filed the report behind the lease. On Wednesdays, in the tool shed, she taught the hundred questions. A refugee who was old or disabled could draw a check from Social Security for seven years from the day he landed, and after that only as a citizen, and a citizen had to be able to say in English who was the Father of Our

sections.heading: II. Forty-Eight Years
sections.text: Everybody on the Hill knew about Hari Prasad Timsina and told it one way. Two boys from one village in Chirang had gone off at fourteen behind a wandering baba, and for forty-eight years the pair of them kept the hard vows: one meal a day, no roof in the dry months, no woman, no money in the hand. They kept them in Bhutan. After 1992 they kept them under the pipal by the Shiva temple in Beldangi, and people coming back from the ration line touched their feet. In the forty-ninth year Hari Prasad watched the huts around him empty, family after family gone on the bus to the airport, and he thought, There will be nobody of mine anywhere. He walked down to Birtamod, to a sawmill owner with three daughters and bad luck. He took water in his right palm and poured the merit of forty-eight years out of his hand into the sawmill owner's. The sawmill owner gave him a lakh of rupees and a buffalo in milk. With that he cut his hair and married Dhan Maya, who was half his age. Their son was born the next year, and in 2013 the three of them flew to Akron on the same papers as everybody else. Now he was sixty-eight and the boy was five. Dhan Maya worked nights in a commercial laundry. Hari Prasad

sections.heading: III. Bed Number One
sections.text: Rupa was restringing bean poles when they came through the gate. Boju sat on her bucket by bed number one with a dishpan of seed garlic in her lap. Hari Prasad came down the wood-chip path ahead of his wife with his eyes on his own feet, and when he reached the bucket he got down in the chips. Dirghayu hos, said the old woman. Dhan Maya bowed. Dirghayu hos. They set the boy down. He bowed without being pushed. Boju looked at him for some time, and then she went back to her garlic. Hari Prasad asked her what he had asked the Baba, and she gave him the Baba's answer, down to the number. Is there no way to turn it, Boju? There might be. What way? She told him in the voice she used for how deep to set an onion. Put up a tent in front of your door. Put one seat in the middle of it and chairs around that in a ring, eight, or sixteen if you can borrow sixteen. Have the Tryambakam said in that tent seven days and seven nights, and don't let it stop once, for food or for rain or for sleep. Said like that, it might turn the thing off him. A tent I can put up. Who is going to say it? I gave mine away, and I can't pay sixteen pandits for a week. You see to the tent. I'll send my people. She lo

sections.heading: IV. The Tent
sections.text: They began on a Thursday at six in the morning, in front of the duplex on Blaine Avenue where the Timsinas had the downstairs. Om tryambakam yajamahe, sugandhim pushti-vardhanam; urvarukam iva bandhanan, mrityor mukshiya mamritat. Eight said it and eight sat quiet between them, every other chair. A quarter of an hour before a watch ended the quiet eight took it up underneath, so that for a while sixteen were saying it, and then the first eight let go and went in to eat. It never had a seam in it. The boy sat on the pirka in the middle with a box of crayons. He slept there against a bolster, and ate there, and was carried in to the toilet and back by his father, who did not sit in the ring. Hari Prasad made the tea. At night he lay on the porch boards with one arm through the railing toward the tent. Rupa came before work and after. She watched Mrs. Khatiwada, who in four years had not once got past George Washington, say the whole of it nine hundred times before noon without looking at anything. None of them looked at anything. They had it the way they had their own names. Across the street lived a Mrs. DiPaolo, who was eighty-six and had been on Blaine since Truman. The first day

sections.heading: V. The Seventh Night
sections.text: Boju had not come all week. On Wednesday at dusk she came down Blaine Avenue on her granddaughter's arm, in a white cotton sari and green rubber garden clogs, and took the chair that faced the boy. The Hill came after her. People stood in the yards on both sides and then in the street, and Mrs. DiPaolo's porch was full of strangers. Those were the living. The ones who sat in the ring that night say it was fuller than that. They say the gods came, the great ones with their names and the small ones of springs and crossroads that only one village in Chirang had ever fed. When the great ones had taken their places there was no room left on Blaine Avenue, and the small ones had to give ground, back to Cuyahoga Falls Avenue, back out North Main to the High Level Bridge and over the gorge into Cuyahoga Falls. Among the small ones, they say, was a yaksha who had served Kubera twelve years and had his wages in writing: Seven days from now you may take this boy. He had come early. He had been standing by the porch steps since Thursday with his paper in his hand. When the crowd came in he was moved back with the rest, a step, then a yard, then a mile, still holding the paper up over the heads

sections.heading: VI. Four Things
sections.text: One Wednesday in September the class never got to the hundred questions. The old people wanted to talk about the boy. Seven days he had, and now it's a hundred and twenty years, said Mrs. Khatiwada. There's a reason behind a thing like that. A life doesn't get longer of itself. Boju had come into the shed for once, out of the sun, and was sitting on a fertilizer pail by the door. What are you all on about? They told her. It isn't only the years, she said. Then she gave them a line of Sanskrit, and every head in the shed came up, because each of them had it from a grandfather. Rupa had it from hers. She had never seen it in English until she looked that night. He who habitually salutes and constantly pays reverence to the aged obtains an increase of four (things), (viz.) length of life, knowledge, fame, (and) strength. — Laws of Manu 2:121 Manu said a good deal I wouldn't repeat to a girl, Boju said. That one he had right. Four things. Rupa thought of the lab report in her binder, acidity and phosphorus and potassium and organic matter, four lines that had gone up every spring in boxes of made dirt set on poisoned ground. She kept it to herself. Eleven of the Wednesday class took th

verses.text: But he who lives a hundred years, vicious and unrestrained, a life of one day is better if a man is virtuous and reflecting.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, thirty men who became monks late in life decide they are too old for the duty of study and ask the Buddha for a subject of meditation and leave to go to a forest. He sends them first to the elder Sāriputta, who makes them take along his seven-year-old novice, Saṅkicca. The boy had been found alive on his mother's funeral pyre, his eye marked by one of the stakes used to turn the fire, and had reached the goal of the path when the razor first touched his hair. "He will not be a hindrance to you," the elder says. "You will be a hindrance to him." The monks settle near a village, keep apart from one another, and agree on a bell to be struck only for sickness. A hungry traveler whom each of them feeds from his own bowl serves them two months and leaves without asking. Five hundred robbers who have vowed a human sacrifice seize him in the forest, and to save himself he leads them to the monks and tells them to ring the bell. Each monk in order of seniority offers to die; the novice insists it is why he was sent, asks their pardon, and goes. The robber chief's sword bends on the boy's shoulder and at the second blow splits like a palm leaf. The five hundred take the robe under the novice, who goes back to comfort the old men before he leads his following to Sāriputta and the Buddha. A second episode tells of his nephew Atimuttaka, who kept his word to a band of thieves even when his parents walked into them.
bg.history:
The Shriners, founded in New York in 1872, are Freemasons in red fezzes whose members are styled Nobles and whose local chief is an Illustrious Potentate. They opened their first children's hospital at Shreveport in 1922. In 1962 they voted to take on burns, and the three burn hospitals opened at Galveston in 1966 and at Cincinnati and Boston in 1968. Until 2012 no family was ever billed. Children were, and are, driven to the hospitals by Shriners in their own time. A burned child of the 1980s wore custom elastic pressure garments most of the day for a year or more, went back each year to have tightened scars released, and often gave skin from the scalp, which heals quickly. The lines Mrs. Hauck recites are from Ben Jonson's ode on Sir Lucius Cary and Sir Henry Morison, printed in 1640, as generations of schoolchildren met them in Palgrave's Golden Treasury under the title "The Noble Nature."

Southern Illinois has been called Egypt since the 1830s. Hardin County, on the Ohio, is the least populous county in the state; it had 5,383 people in 1980, fluorspar mines at Rosiclare that were worked until the early 1990s, a piece of the Shawnee National Forest, and at Cave-in-Rock a river cave that outlaws and river pirates used in the 1790s. The Shrine temple for the region was at East St. Louis. The Egypt Shrine Club, Belt's lake, the Flatheads and every person in the story are invented, and no hospital staff are drawn from life. Bikers' toy runs to children's hospitals, which became a fixture of American autumns around 1980, are real, and the story borrows them for its ending.

sections.heading: I. The Garment Room
sections.text: There were thirty of them, and they had all come to it late. There was a circuit judge off the bench, a druggist, the man who had the Chevrolet agency in Harrisburg, an undertaker, two superintendents from the fluorspar mines at Rosiclare, a barber, and the rest farmers. Not one had been under sixty-five when he took his fez. They were the Egypt Shrine Club, out of the river counties at the bottom of Illinois, the country people have called Egypt for a hundred and fifty years, and for five years they had driven the hospital run. It was three hundred miles to the Burns Institute in Cincinnati, by the Shawneetown bridge and Louisville, with somebody's burned child asleep on the back seat of a white Ford van, and three hundred miles home. That spring a man from the temple at East St. Louis came down to their ladies' night and told them there were two kinds of work in the Shrine. There was the work of the ritual, the degree teams and the ceremonials, where a man got a long part by heart and gave it without the book. And there was the work of the hospitals. Judge Harlan Oxford was eighty-four and the oldest of them. We came to this old, he said in the car going home. There's not one of

sections.heading: II. Pike
sections.text: Mrs. Lashley was the charge nurse on the acute floor, a tall Black woman from Walnut Hills who had come with the building too. She looked at thirty old men in red fezzes filling up her corridor and asked what they wanted. They said they didn't rightly know. They had been to Mrs. Hauck about a camp, and Mrs. Hauck had sent them up. Mrs. Lashley thought about that. Is the boy going with you? What boy? Then you'd better take Pike. They all knew Pike. Half of them had been on the run that first brought him. In January of 1977 a house on Peters Creek had burned to the stones in the night with a girl of nineteen in it, who was eight months gone. In the morning the volunteers from Elizabethtown went through the ashes with pike poles, hunting what was left of her, and one of the poles went into something that cried. He was sitting up in the bedsprings as if he had been set on a shelf. Nobody has ever said how. The hook had laid open his right eye, and the pupil of it healed with a notch at the bottom, like a keyhole. The nurses in Cincinnati called him Pike, for the pole, before anybody thought to name him, and his grandmother let it stand. Old women in Hardin County said that a child the

sections.heading: III. The Lake
sections.dateline: Hardin County, Illinois · June and July
sections.text: Rosiclare was glad of them. The mines had been letting men go for ten years, and here were thirty checkbooks come to spend a summer. The lumberyard opened an hour early. The women of the four churches drew up a calendar, so that each congregation carried dinner out to the lake on its own day and none was put upon twice in a week, and for one summer the Methodists and the Church of Christ were in agreement about something. The Judge knew old men. Thirty of them set to build six cabins will build one and talk five. On the first evening he gave the rule. Every man takes his own job on his own piece of ground and stays on it. We're together at breakfast and we're together at supper. The hours between, a man keeps to himself and thinks on what Mrs. Hauck told us. Eleven of them carried nitroglycerin tablets in their shirt pockets. So Bus Hobbs took the brass locomotive bell off the club's parade float and set it on a post by the dock. It was to be struck for one cause only, a man down, and at the sound of it every one of them would come. Pike had no job. He went from one old man to the next with water in a Mason jar. He wore his tan suit under his overalls through the heat of the day, a

sections.heading: IV. The White Oak
sections.text: The Flatheads had the woods north of the lake that week, six miles off. They were a motorcycle club out of Evansville and Paducah and East St. Louis, and when every chapter rode there were five hundred of them. On the Fourth of July somebody in a pickup truck had shot Dale Sisk off his machine on Route 1, and had never been found. Dale's brother Wade was their president. On the first night of the wake Wade Sisk stood up on a picnic table, with Dale's colors nailed to a white oak behind him, and swore on them that the first man to walk in on the Flatheads in that woods, whoever he was, they would kill for Dale and burn what was left. For six days nobody came. On the seventh a prospect up in a deer stand saw a man coming along the fire road with a paper sack, and waved his arm. They let him get well in. Then they closed around him and tied his hands with a bootlace. Somebody was building up the fire. Two more were digging. Mister, said Dewey Stallings, I don't see a hog anywhere. What's the pit for? You. He did not think about two months of dinners. He thought about his neck. Lord God, don't waste it on me. I'm nobody. I eat what other men leave on the plate and I always have. You co

sections.heading: V. In Order
sections.text: They came down the paths in undershirts and suspenders, a flashlight here and there, some with the little brown bottle already in their fist, each one thinking, Who's down? They sat on the plank benches of the dining hall, which had a floor and no roof yet. Then they saw the men standing all around it in the trees. Who rang that bell? the Judge said. I did. What for? We swore to kill a man for my brother. One will do. You can pick him. The Judge turned to the benches. Boys, when brothers take a thing on, the oldest has the say. I'm eighty-four. I'll go with these men. The rest of you finish the roofs, and think on what you were told. Sit down, Harlan, said Estel Belt. What the old man owes, the next one ought to carry for him. I'm eighty-one and I've buried everybody I ever cared to. It's mine. It went down the benches that way by age, the way they sat in lodge, every one of the thirty standing up in his turn to say it should be him. They were not kin. They were not saints either. Two of them had not spoken in nine years over a line fence. And not a man of them said, You go. Then Pike got down off the end of the bench. Y'all sit down. It's me. Son, said the Judge, if they shoot eve

sections.text: They did that much. They put him by a stump at the edge of the firelight with his back to it, and he sat down on the stump. He sat the way he sat in the tub room while the dressings came off, looking at nothing in front of him, and whatever they were going to hurt was not where he was. When all was ready Wade Sisk came across with the Army Colt he had carried for eleven years and set it behind the boy's ear and pulled. The hammer fell and nothing answered. I never seated it, he thought. He worked the slide and set it there again and pulled, and the barrel let go. It opened from the muzzle back in four strips that curled over like the petals of a lily, and the charge went nowhere, and neither the man nor the boy had a mark on him. Wade Sisk looked at the thing in his hand. I've put this through an engine block, he said. It's iron. It hasn't got a brain in it, and it knew what he was. I've got eyes, and I stood right here and didn't. He threw it in the leaves and got down after it on his face. Boy. Grown men see us a mile up the road and go to shaking. Two or three of them together can't get a word out. You never so much as jumped, and your face is as bright as a new penny. Why is th

logline: Thirty old Shriners building a lake camp for burned children are told to take along a seven-year-old found alive in the ashes.

verses.text: And he who lives a hundred years, ignorant and unrestrained, a life of one day is better if a man is wise and reflecting.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Koṇḍañña is given a subject of meditation by the Buddha, goes to the forest and reaches the goal there. On his way back to tell his teacher he grows tired, leaves the road, sits down on a flat rock and enters deep absorption. That night five hundred thieves who have plundered a village come by with their loot in sacks, each sack sized to the man's strength. They stop to rest at the same rock, take the seated elder for a tree stump, set one sack on his head and pile the rest around him, and sleep. At dawn they see what he is, think him a spirit and start to run; he tells them not to be afraid. They beg his pardon, and all of them ask to go forth under him. He is called Khāṇu, “Stump,” ever after. When he brings them to the Buddha, the Buddha asks, “You have obtained pupils?” and tells the former thieves that one day lived in the wisdom they have just found is better than a hundred years of last night's foolishness.
bg.history:
Lightning north of the city began knocking out transmission lines at 8:34 on the evening of July 13, 1977, and by 9:37 the whole Con Edison system was down. Power was not fully restored until late the next night. The blackout came in a heat wave, in the middle of the city's fiscal crisis, and thirty-one neighborhoods saw looting. Bushwick was among the hardest hit. Along Broadway, under the elevated tracks that divide it from Bedford-Stuyvesant, 134 stores were looted and 45 of them burned, and some two dozen fires were still going in the morning; gates were pulled off storefronts with chains run to car bumpers. The neighborhood had been losing its work for years. The Rheingold brewery on Forrest Street, one of its last big employers, closed for good in January 1976. Kessler's Men's Shop, Mrs. Gadsden and everyone else in the story are invented.

The Bahá'í Faith has no clergy. Its teaching in America has gone on largely in living rooms, at informal evenings long called firesides. Green Acre, on the Piscataqua River at Eliot, Maine, was founded by Sarah Farmer in 1894 as a summer conference on religion; ʻAbdu'l-Bahá stayed there for a week in August 1912, and it has been a Bahá'í school since. The book Mrs. Gadsden reads from is Bahá'u'lláh's Kitáb-i-Íqán, written in Baghdad in the early 1860s, in its first English translation, The Book of Ighan, made by Ali Kuli Khan and published in New York in 1904. The line about one hour's reflection is an old Islamic tradition that Bahá'u'lláh quotes there. Later Bahá'ís have read the book in Shoghi Effendi's translation of 1931; an American believer of Mrs. Gadsden's generation could still have owned the older one.

sections.heading: I. One Hour
sections.dateline: Linden Street, Bushwick, and Eliot, Maine · spring 1977
sections.text: Conrad Mayfield had loaded trucks at the Rheingold plant on Forrest Street for four years, and in the middle of January 1976 the brewery shut for good and put him out on Broadway with everybody else. He was twenty-three then. For a year he stood under the el in front of the check-cashing place with men who had thirty years in at the same plant, and he was angry all day at nothing he could have pointed to. His mother said he came into a room like a radio somebody had left on. Mrs. Lottie Gadsden lived on the third floor at the Bushwick Avenue end of Linden Street. She had worked thirty-one years in the laundry at Wyckoff Heights Hospital, the last twenty of them beside Conrad's grandmother, and she had been a Bahá'í since 1931, when she was a young woman doing day's work in Harlem. Her faith kept no preachers, so she was not one. What she kept was Thursday night. Eight or ten people sat in her front room over tea and a plate of something, and she called it a fireside, though the building had steam heat and it was all she could do to get that. Conrad started coming for the plate. In March he signed his card. In April she kept him back after the others had gone down. You are all noise

sections.heading: II. Broadway
sections.text: It was Portsmouth to Boston and Boston to the Port Authority, and then the J train over the bridge with the windows down. A heat wave had come in and it was still in the eighties after dark. He got off at Gates Avenue a little after half past nine, and he was on the el stairs with the duffel on his shoulder when the streetlights went out. The store signs went with them, and the windows over the stores, all the way down Broadway in both directions at once. Up on the structure the train he had just left sat dead with faces at the glass. Mrs. Gadsden's building was nine blocks off. He made four of them. By ten o'clock there were cars backed up over the curbs with chains run from their bumpers to the store gates. A gate came off a furniture store across the avenue with a noise like a piano going down a stairwell. People ran bent double under mattresses. He saw a woman he knew from his mother's church with a carton of canned milk on her hip, and boys of ten with shoeboxes stacked to their chins, and men off the Rheingold loading dock, because half the avenue had been out of work as long as he had. Toward Halsey Street something was burning, and the engines stood across Broadway with the

sections.heading: III. The Stuff
sections.dateline: Kessler's window · after two in the morning
sections.text: Nelson Ortiz was nineteen, and he and the ones with him had come sixteen blocks down from an appliance and furniture place near Myrtle Avenue. There were eleven of them by the count of those who were there. By Friday Broadway had it at five hundred, and the number has not come down since. Each of them carried what his back would stand. Nelson had a nineteen-inch Zenith in its carton on one shoulder. His two cousins wore a dinette chair apiece upside down on their heads. A big slow man they called Oso held a console stereo in front of him in both arms like a calf, and the smallest, somebody's brother, nine years old, had a pillowcase full of baby shoes. They had been at it since ten. Twice they had gone flat in a doorway while a patrol car rolled down the avenue with its lights off, and now there was the fire ahead at Halsey and police on foot in front of it. That's far enough, Nelson said. Sit down in here till it clears. Inside Kessler's it was as dark as the inside of a pocket. There was no moon. The floor was wet from somewhere and gritty with glass, and by feel they found that the window platform was the one clean dry place, so that was where they stacked the stuff. The Zenith

sections.heading: IV. Half Past Five
sections.text: The light came in gray under the el. Nelson woke first and went to the window for his television, and the dummy under the hat was breathing. He watched the carton of Pampers rise the width of a finger and settle. He saw eyelashes. A man was sitting in the middle of their goods with a box on his knees and a pillowcase on his shoulder and a woman's hat on, and in three hours not one thing they had put on him had shifted. Nelson made a sound he would have denied making. The others came up behind him. The boy said muerto. Oso said no, it was one of those, and did not say one of what, and every one of them went for the door at once. Don't be scared, Conrad said. He had opened his eyes. I'm nobody. I'm a man who was praying. They stopped where they were, in the doorway. We put a TV on you, Nelson said. I see that. You didn't feel it? Conrad took the question seriously. I heard you come in. It wasn't anything to do with me. Mister, forgive us. We took you for a dummy. Conrad lifted the hat off and looked at it and laughed. After that the avenue called him Manny, for mannequin, and he answered to it for the rest of his life. Nelson did not laugh. He had been running since ten o'clock with

sections.heading: V. Pupils
sections.text: They went up Linden Street at six in the morning carrying everything, since there was nowhere to leave it. Mrs. Gadsden was seventy-two. She came to her door in a housecoat and looked past Conrad at her stairs, which were full of boys and furniture down to the second landing. Well, Conrad. You have got yourself some pupils. He told her about the window. What he had come from Maine to tell her he never did get said, and he saw he did not need to. Is that so? she asked the stairs. Yes, ma'am, Nelson said. We stacked a whole store on him and he never moved. We never saw anybody do like that. We want to know how he does it. She had them in. Nothing in her refrigerator was going to keep, so they ate all of it standing up in her front room, cold chicken and potato salad and most of a pound cake, and a half gallon of butter pecan gone soft, which went around the room with one spoon. She let them finish. Then she said the only thing she said to them that morning. You could go on a hundred years the way you went last night. Up and down in the dark with something on your back, looking over your shoulder. Plenty do, and I'm not talking only about you. One day like you had this morning is wort

title: The Window Dummy
logline: On the night of the 1977 blackout, looters stack a store's worth of goods around a figure in a stripped Broadway show window.

verses.text: And he who lives a hundred years, idle and weak, a life of one day is better if a man has attained firm strength.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young man of good family becomes a monk, grows discontented, and decides that going back to lay life would be beneath him and that death would be better than staying. When the monks catch a snake in the hall where the fire is kept and carry it out in a jar, he offers to throw it away, and tries to make it bite him, even putting his finger in its mouth. It will not, and he tells the others it was only a house snake. He is also the monastery's barber. One day he takes his second razor to a tree, leans his neck on a branch and sets the blade to his windpipe. There he reviews his conduct since his ordination, finds it as spotless as the moon's disk, is filled with joy, and attains the goal. The monks think he is lying. The Buddha tells them that one who is freed cannot take his own life, that the snake had been the man's slave three lives earlier, and that his discontent went back to a former life in which a fellow monk who coveted his bowl and robes talked him out of his vocation. Asked whether so much can happen in so short a time, he answers that it can happen between lifting a foot and setting it down. The monk was afterward called Sappadāsa, "he whose slave was a snake."
bg.history:
The Overland Limited ran between Chicago and San Francisco Bay over the North Western, the Union Pacific and the Southern Pacific. Its advertisements in 1902 promised "Buffet-Library Cars (with Barber and Bath)," an electric reading lamp in every berth, and dining cars for all meals. From 1904 the train crossed the Great Salt Lake on the Southern Pacific's Lucin Cutoff, 102 miles from Lucin to Ogden, nearly twelve of them on a wooden trestle with a station called Midlake in the middle of the water.

The Pullman Company staffed its cars with Black men, and passengers called every one of them George, after George Pullman. Pullman porters were paid too little to live on without tips, worked something like four hundred hours a month, and could be suspended on the word of a Company inspector; they did not win a union contract until 1937. The job was nonetheless among the best open to Black men, and many who held it had some college. Julian's father belongs to an older elite, the Black barbers who served white customers in Northern towns and who were losing that trade to European immigrants around 1900. Wilberforce, near Xenia, Ohio, is the oldest of the African Methodist Episcopal colleges. Philip James Bailey's Festus (1839) went through many American printings, and its line about deeds and years was copied into autograph albums for half a century; the passage is given here from a New York edition of 1872. Julian Coates, Mr. Tolbert and the wreck at Carlin are invented.

sections.heading: I. George
sections.text: Julian Coates had the barber's chair in the buffet car of the Overland Limited, and there was not a colored man in the service between Chicago and Oakland Pier who would not have changed places with him. The car rode at the head of the train. It had a baggage room, then a closet with a tin bathtub, then his own cubicle with the chair and the glass and the shelf of bottles, then the library with its leather seats, where he served whiskey and seltzer to gentlemen who were three days crossing the country. A shave was a quarter. Most of them left another quarter on the shelf. His father had been a barber too, in Xenia, Ohio, with three chairs and a white trade, and was called Mr. Coates on Detroit Street by men who called no other colored man mister. He had put Julian two years into Wilberforce to make a teacher of him. Then he died. A German took the trade, and the chairs were sold. Julian heard a Pullman man speak at the church one Sunday on seeing the whole of the country from a moving window, and he believed it, and at twenty he went on the cars with his father's razors in a roll of green baize. That was seven years back. He had seen the whole of the country three hundred times sin

sections.heading: II. The Crock
sections.text: They took coal for the kitchen range at Winnemucca before daylight. When the fourth cook went to the coal box to make up the fire for breakfast, something in it sang at him like a kettle. It took three of them to get it out. The second cook pinned it with the poker, and it struck the iron twice, and a waiter got it by the tail with a dish towel and dropped it into a two-gallon butter crock, and they put the lid on and tied the lid down. Julian came through from the buffet car after he had eaten, and met them in the passage carrying the crock between two men. What have you got? Snake. Rattler, as long as your arm. What do you mean to do with it? Pitch it off. He stood there a moment. Give it here, he said. I'll pitch it. I've got the baggage door. They were glad enough to hand it to him. He carried it forward through his own car, past the chair, and into the baggage room, and shut the door behind him, and ran the side door open a foot so that the sagebrush went by in a grey strip. He sat down on a drummer's trunk with the crock between his shoes and untied the towel and lifted the lid. It lay in the bottom in a coil. He put his hand in. He laid it on the snake's back, and the snake

sections.heading: III. The Headrest
sections.dateline: The Lucin Cutoff, Great Salt Lake · that night
sections.text: A freight was on the ground at Carlin, and they sat behind it six hours. So it was past midnight, and not the middle of the afternoon, when the Overland came down out of the desert onto the lake. Late at night, with the gentlemen in their berths, Julian cut the crew's hair. The rule book did not allow for it, and old Mr. Tolbert, who had the rear sleeper and thirty-five years on the cars, did. They came forward one at a time, porters and waiters, and sat in the chair with a towel round the neck. He worked with two razors. One he used, and the other lay open on the shelf under the glass to be taken up when the first lost its edge. That night the first held. When the last man had gone back through the train he wiped it and closed it, and reached to close the second, and stood with it in his hand. He sat down in his own chair. He let his neck back onto the headrest, where four thousand white men had laid theirs, and set the blade under his jaw at the windpipe, and looked up into the glass. The car had come out onto the trestle. There are twelve miles of it, on piles, with the lake flat on both sides and no shore to be seen, and the moon was straight overhead, so that it stood in his w

sections.heading: IV. The Step-Box
sections.dateline: Promontory Point to Ogden · toward morning
sections.text: The dining-car crew were at their own supper, with two or three of the Pullman men. Where did you get to, Coates? I was in my chair with this on my neck. He had the razor in his hand yet. I went in there to cut my throat. Then how is it you're standing up? I couldn't do it now. I couldn't do harm with an edge to anything living. I went to cut my windpipe, and I cut the other thing instead, the thing that wanted it done. They looked at one another. First it's a rattlesnake that won't bite him, the second cook said, and now this. The man is telling tales. And since there was one place on that train where such a matter was taken, they got up from the table and took it there. Mr. Tolbert sat up nights in the smoking room of the rear sleeper, under the call board, with a soap box of books beside him that passengers had left in berths since 1872. He heard the cook and then he heard Julian, and he looked at Julian for some time. He's telling you the truth, he said. A man who has come clear the way he says can't take his own life. There is nobody in him to lift the hand. You call Coates clear? Mr. Tolbert, he has been the lowest man on this train since Christmas. If he had that in him, wha

sections.heading: V. Snake
sections.text: The dining-car crew went off at Ogden and told it in the yard, and it reached Omaha ahead of the train. From that trip on he was Snake Coates on every road that carried a Pullman car. He stayed forty years in the service and answered to that, and to George, and to his own name when it was offered, and it was all one to him which. They lay an hour at Ogden for the Union Pacific engine. The sun was coming up behind the Wasatch when Mr. Tolbert walked the length of the train to the buffet car and sat down in the chair and put his neck back on the headrest. I'll have a shave, Mr. Coates, he said. Julian took the second razor off the shelf and tried it on his thumb and laid it under the old man's jaw.

title: The Second Razor
logline: The barber-porter on the Overland Limited offers to throw a rattlesnake off the train, and that night cuts the crew's hair with two razors.

verses.text: Sons are no help, nor a father, nor relations; there is no help from kinsfolk for one whom death has seized.
A wise and good man who knows the meaning of this, should quickly clear the way that leads to Nirvana.
And he who lives a hundred years, not seeing beginning and end, a life of one day is better if a man sees beginning and end.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Paṭācārā is a rich merchant’s daughter, kept on the top floor of her father’s house, who runs away with a servant on the eve of an arranged marriage. Twice, near her time, she sets out for her parents’ house to give birth. The first time her son is born by the road. The second time a storm out of season catches them. Her husband is killed by a snake while cutting brush for a shelter. At dawn a hawk carries off her newborn, and her older boy drowns in a swollen river. Then a traveler tells her that her parents and brother died in the same storm when their house fell, and points to the smoke of their pyre. She goes mad and wanders naked, pelted with dirt, until the Buddha says, “Sister, return to your right mind.” He tells her that her tears over the dead are more than the four oceans and that kin are no refuge, and she becomes a nun. Years later, washing her feet, she watches spilled water run a short way, then farther, then farther yet, and sees in it death in youth, in middle age and in old age. The Buddha appears before her and speaks verse 113. She became the nun foremost in knowledge of the Discipline.
bg.history:
By the 1920s, drainage canals and the Conners toll highway had opened the black muck south and east of Lake Okeechobee to farming. Towns like Belle Glade, Pahokee, South Bay, Canal Point and Chosen filled with Black farmworkers from Georgia, the Carolinas and the Bahamas, who picked beans and cut cane. On the night of September 16, 1928, the Okeechobee hurricane drove the lake over the low muck dike on its south shore and flooded hundreds of square miles, in places more than twenty feet deep. At least 2,500 people died, about three-quarters of them migrant farmworkers, most of them Black. The few coffins were kept for white victims. Many Black dead were burned on funeral pyres in the Glades. About 1,600 were buried in a mass grave at Port Mayaca, and 674 in a mass grave at Tamarind Avenue and 25th Street in West Palm Beach. That grave went unmarked until a state historical marker was placed in 2003 (see the Historical Society of Palm Beach County). Chosen never recovered. Between 1932 and 1938 the Army Corps of Engineers built the dike that now rings the lake.

The African Methodist Episcopal Church began licensing women as lay preachers and evangelists in 1884 and created the office of deaconess in 1888. Women could not be ordained deacons until 1948 or elders until the 1950s and 1960s (see AME women preachers). Its rulebook, like that of other Methodist churches, is called the Discipline. Ozella, Lettie Brinson and their families are fictional, and so is the camp meeting of 1919.

sections.heading: I. The Upstairs Room
sections.text: Josiah Pinder came over from Andros on a sponging schooner when he was fourteen with one shirt and a cane knife, and by the time he was fifty he was the richest colored man on the lake. He had cut cane, and picked beans on his knees in the black muck by the hamper, and saved, and bought a truck, and hauled other men to the fields in it at a dime a head, and bought another truck. Now he had three trucks and a store in Chosen with a gallery on the front and a boarding house behind it with twenty rooms, and a two-story house of Dade County pine on the canal bank, painted white, the only painted house in the quarters. He was a class leader at the African Methodist church and could recite the General Rules from the Discipline without looking, and he did, often. His daughter Ozella lived on the second floor of the white house. She had been born in it. At sixteen she was the prettiest girl on the south shore of the lake, and her father knew exactly what the south shore of the lake was. There were jook joints on every road out of Belle Glade, and men who came in for the bean season with knives in their boots and left without paying their board, and the muck was full of trouble. So he kept

sections.heading: II. The Fish Camp
sections.text: They married at the courthouse in Okeechobee, and Cleon got on at a fish house on Taylor Creek, cleaning catfish for the fish cars that went north on the railroad, and they took a shack on stilts at the edge of the camp. Ozella hauled water from the creek in a lard bucket. She washed clothes in a tub and scrubbed fish scales off Cleon’s overalls with lye, and cooked on a kerosene stove that smoked, and learned to cut wood. She had never cut wood. Her hands had never been hard. The women at the fish camp laughed at her the first month, and then stopped laughing and showed her how, and that was where she learned what it cost to live, which she had not known in the white house. She was happy. She would say so, afterward, when she could say anything. She had been happy. When the first baby was due, in the summer of 1926, she began to ask him. I want to go home to have it. There’s nobody here. A mother and a father always come around for a grandbaby. Take me home. Your daddy will kill me, said Cleon. You know he will. He’ll get his pistol out from under the counter in the store and shoot me in the road in front of everybody, and the sheriff won’t even come out for a thing like that. I c

sections.heading: III. The Storm
sections.dateline: The east shore of Lake Okeechobee · Sunday, September 16, 1928
sections.text: The wind came up on Sunday afternoon out of the northeast, and the rain came with it, and by dark there was no telling one from the other. The sky went white with lightning and stayed white, and the thunder came on top of it so close that Ozella felt it in her teeth. The sawgrass lay down flat. The lake, on their right hand, which had been gray and quiet all day, stood up and began to come over the road. Then her pains started. Cleon. It’s coming. I can’t walk. Find me something. Find me a place out of this. He had the axe from the truck. There was a spoil bank by the road where they had dug a ditch years before, and on top of the spoil bank was a clump of palmetto and myrtle, the only thing standing up out of that whole flat country. He put her down in the lee of it with the boy and went up the bank with the axe to cut fronds for a lean-to. She saw him in the lightning, up on the bank, swinging. She saw him stop. The moccasin had come up out of the roots of the palmetto to get out of the water, and it was as thick as a man’s wrist, and it struck him in the calf and then again in the hand. By the next flash he was down on his knees. He tried to come down the bank to her. He did not

sections.heading: IV. The Canal
sections.text: At first light the wind dropped. She took the new baby, who was red all over as a piece of fresh meat, and put him on her hip, and gave Josiah her finger to hold. Come on, baby. Your daddy’s gone on ahead of us. She went up the spoil bank the way he had gone. He was lying there on top of it in the gray light, swollen, purple, stiff, with the axe under him and the palmetto half cut. On account of me, she said. On account of me you died out here on the road. She said it over and over, walking. She did not stop walking. A mile on, the road went down under the water where a canal came out of the lake. The rain had filled it all night. It was over her knees where the road had been and up to her waist in the middle, and moving, brown, with sawgrass and boards and a drowned hog going by in it. She could not carry them both. She was too weak to carry one. So she sat Josiah down on the road on the near side and told him to be still, and waded across with the baby held up high, and on the far side she broke a branch off a myrtle and laid it down on the bank and laid the baby on the leaves. Then she started back for Josiah. In the water she kept turning around to look at the baby. She could n

sections.heading: V. The Smoke
sections.dateline: Above Canal Point · later in the week
sections.text: She did not know how many days she walked. She slept on the road. People went by her in trucks going north and boats going south. On the third day, or the fourth, she met a man walking north along the dike road, a colored man in a white shirt gone gray, with a sack over his shoulder, coming up out of the south shore. Mister. Where are you coming from? Chosen, sister. What’s left of it. In Chosen, in the white house on the canal, by the store, there’s a family named Pinder. Do you know them? He stopped. I know them. Don’t ask me about them, sister. Ask me about anybody else in Chosen and I’ll tell you. I don’t want to know about anybody else in Chosen. That’s the only one I want to know about. The man looked at her for a long time. He put his sack down. You didn’t leave me any way out of it, he said. You felt it rain Sunday night? Felt it. Mister, I’m the only one in the world it rained on Sunday night. I’ll tell you about it some time. Tell me about the Pinders and I won’t ask you anything else. Sunday night the water came over the dike, he said, and the wind took that white house up off its blocks and turned it over, and it came down on Josiah Pinder and his wife and their boy Eld

sections.heading: VI. Forbid Her Not
sections.text: The refugees from the lake had been brought out to West Palm Beach by truck and boat, the colored ones to the colored side of town, and on the lot beside one of the colored churches there was a tarpaulin stretched between two trees where an old woman sat on a kitchen chair every evening with the people from the muck sitting on the ground around her. Her name was Lettie Brinson. She was seventy-three. She had been born a slave in Madison County and licensed as an evangelist by the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1889, the year Ozella’s father came over from Andros, and in forty years she had preached in turpentine camps and phosphate camps and convict camps from the Georgia line to Key West, but she was past most of that now. Now she sat on the kitchen chair. She did not preach much anymore. People came and sat by her anyway, because she listened, and because when she did say something it was usually the one thing. They had been to Tamarind Avenue that week, some of them, where the trucks from the lake had brought six hundred and seventy-four colored dead and laid them in one long trench with no service said. They had come back and sat by Lettie Brinson under the tarpaulin and

sections.heading: VII. Three Pourings
sections.text: She was consecrated a deaconess of the African Methodist Episcopal Church at the annual conference in the spring of 1930, in a plain black dress with a white collar. People had stopped calling her the crazy woman by then, and most of them had stopped calling her Ozella. They called her Sister Pinder. The women at the church in West Palm said that in two years she had learned the Discipline better than any preacher in the conference, and they were not exaggerating. She knew every rule in the book and the reason behind every one, and she could tell a young woman what was right without making her feel like dirt for not knowing it, which is harder. In 1932 she asked to go back to the lake, and they let her. The Army engineers were building the big dike around the south shore by then, a long wall of rock and earth higher than a house where the little dike had been, and the bean fields had come back, and the pickers had come back, from Georgia and the Carolinas and the islands, and the jooks had come back, and the girls of sixteen, and their trouble. Sister Pinder had a room behind the church in Belle Glade. The girls came to her there. She sat with them on the back step. One evening in

title: Spilt Water
logline: A rich man's daughter runs off with his truck driver, and years later walks home along the lake as a hurricane comes in.

verses.text: Death comes and carries off that man, praised for his children and flocks, his mind distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.
And he who lives a hundred years, not seeing the immortal place, a life of one day is better if a man sees the immortal place.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Kisā Gotamī ("Gotamī the thin") is a poor girl who turns a ruined merchant's charcoal back into gold and marries his son. When her small son dies, she carries his body from house to house looking for medicine, and the Buddha sends her for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died. Years later, as a nun, she reaches awakening watching lamp flames rise and go out.
bg.history:
The influenza reached Philadelphia through the Navy Yard in September 1918. On September 28 the city went ahead with the Fourth Liberty Loan parade down Broad Street, and some 200,000 people packed the sidewalks to watch. Within days the hospitals were full. On October 3 the city closed its schools, churches and theaters. On the worst day in October more than 750 people died, and by the end of the epidemic about 12,000 Philadelphians were dead. Coffins ran out, seminarians helped dig graves, and at Holy Cross Cemetery trenches were dug by steam shovel. Families hung crepe on the door: black for an adult, white for a child, grey for the old. More on the 1918 pandemic.

Nicola's regiment, the 315th Infantry, belonged to the 79th Division, made up largely of draftees from Philadelphia and the surrounding region. In the opening days of the Meuse-Argonne offensive at the end of September, the division attacked the heights of Montfaucon and took heavy losses.

sections.heading: I. Coal
sections.text: Don Saverio Ferrante sold coal in the winter and ice in the summer out of a yard on Montrose Street, and between the two he had become the richest man from Washington Avenue to the Navy Yard. He had a brick house with a parlor nobody sat in and a piano nobody played. He kept some money in the bank on Christian Street and the rest of it under the floor of his bedroom, in a tin box, in gold, because he remembered what banks had done in Palermo. One morning in March he lifted the board and opened the box, and the gold was coal. Every piece. The double eagles were lumps of anthracite the size of walnuts. He ran to the bank in his shirtsleeves and made the teller open his deposit box, and that was coal too, and the teller stepped back from it as if it might catch. His wife's earrings, in the drawer by the bed, were two little black coals on gold wires. Then the gold wires were coal. Don Saverio went to bed and did not get up. He lay there for nine days. The doctor came and left. The priest came and left. On the tenth day Mastro Pino the barber came and sat at the foot of the bed with his hat on his knee. Saverio. Get up. Put all of it in the yard by the gate, in a pile, and sit by it li

sections.heading: II. The Wagon
sections.text: Tonino was born in the summer of 1916. He walked at eleven months and by two he was running the length of the coal yard with black on his knees, chasing the cat, and Don Saverio said he would be a runner in the Olympic Games, and Concetta, who was not called Sicca anymore, said he would be a priest, and Nicola said nothing because Nicola was in France. The sickness came in off the ships at the Navy Yard in September. On the twenty-eighth there was a parade up Broad Street to sell Liberty Bonds, two miles of brass bands and soldiers and Boy Scouts, and two hundred thousand people stood on the sidewalks shoulder to shoulder to watch it. Ten days later the city had closed the schools and the churches and the saloons and the theaters, and it did not matter. By the middle of October more than seven hundred people were dying in a single day. There were not enough coffins in Philadelphia. There were not enough gravediggers, so seminarians came down from Overbrook in their cassocks with shovels, and at Holy Cross they dug trenches with a steam shovel. On every street, doors had crepe on them. Black crepe for a grown person. Grey for an old one. White for a child. Tonino woke with the fever

sections.heading: III. The Sister
sections.text: They had pushed the school desks into the yard and filled the classrooms with cots, so that people lay coughing under blackboards with the alphabet still written along the top in perfect Palmer Method, capital and small, A to Z. Sister Benedicta was sixty-eight years old and had come from County Clare in a ship before the war with the South. She wore an apron over her habit and a gauze mask she kept pulling down so people could see her mouth. She did not tell Concetta to put the child down. She did not tell her what she already knew. She lifted the corner of the blue blanket and looked at Tonino for a long time, and put the blanket back. I know the medicine, she said. You'll have to fetch it yourself. A pinch of mustard seed. Black or white, it doesn't matter. Concetta almost laughed. Everybody in Philadelphia had mustard that month. They were making mustard plasters in every kitchen in the city, smearing it on flannel and laying it on the chests of the sick. But it has to come from a house where nobody has died, said Sister Benedicta. Nobody, ever. Not a baby, not a grandmother. Not a boarder, not a cousin back in the old country. Nobody. Like the Gospel, Concetta said. Faith like

sections.heading: IV. The Doors
sections.text: Mrs. Gallo across from the coal yard had black crepe on her door. She opened it with her sleeves pushed up and said of course, of course, and went to get the jar, and when Concetta asked, she stopped with the jar in her hand. Her husband. Tuesday. They took him on the same wagon. The Dohertys on Federal Street had two crepes on the door, black and white, one above the other. Mrs. Doherty's apron was yellow to the elbow with mustard, because she was still making plasters for the three who were still in bed. Love, you can have all the mustard in the world, she said. My Frank. My Mary Kate. She was four. On South Street, in the back of a dry goods store, the mirror was covered with a bedsheet and an old man sat on a low wooden box with his shirt torn at the collar. He had mustard seed in the crock where they made pickles. He said something in Yiddish and his granddaughter, nine years old, stood in the doorway and translated. He says his wife. He says his brother. He says you should take the seed anyway. On Lombard Street Mrs. Tucker had brought mustard seed up from South Carolina in a Mason jar, to grow greens in a tub behind the house. Lord, honey, she said, and put her hand on Tonin

sections.heading: V. The Seed
sections.text: She found the wagon on Christian Street at dusk. The lamps had not been lit, because the men who lit them were sick or dead. The young man walking beside the horse was one of the seminarians from Overbrook, his cassock tucked up into his belt, his face grey with tiredness above the rag. She stopped him with her hand on his arm. This is Antonio Ferrante, she said. He is two years and four months old. His father is Nicola Ferrante, of the 315th Infantry, in France. Will you write it down? He wrote it on a card with a pencil stub and pinned it to the blue blanket, and she kissed her son's forehead through the wool and gave him to the young man, who took him the way you take something from a person who is handing it to you, carefully, with both arms, and laid him in the wagon on the clean straw at the front, apart from the others. Then the young man made the sign of the cross over her, which he had no right to do yet, and she let him. She walked back to Ellsworth Street with her arms empty. They felt light, and strange, and they kept rising a little at her sides, as if they had forgotten. Sister Benedicta was at the sink in the teachers' room washing out basins. Did you get the seed? N

sections.heading: VI. The Lamp
sections.text: She entered the Sisters in the spring of 1919. They let widows do that then, if the widow was serious, and nobody doubted she was serious. Sister Benedicta died the next winter, in the last hard wave of the sickness, on a cot in a ward she had been running the day before. The new sisters took turns with the candles. Each night one of them went into the chapel after Compline and lit the votives in their red glasses on the iron stand, and trimmed the wicks, and sat with them for an hour so nothing would catch. It was Concetta's turn on a night in February. She lit them one from another with a taper and sat in the back pew and watched. One flame jumped up high and bright and then settled. One drowned in its own wax and went out with a thread of smoke. One leaned in a draft from under the door and righted itself. Two burned side by side, then one was gone. She watched them come up and go down, all of them, all along the rack, the way she had watched the doors on Ninth Street, and she understood that she was watching the same thing. Flames came and went. People came and went. Tonino. Nicola. Mrs. Doherty's Mary Kate. Sister Benedicta. Mrs. Tucker's James. Everybody had a flame, and the

title: The Mustard Seed
logline: In the influenza autumn, a young mother goes door to door for a seed from a house where no one has died.

verses.text: And he who lives a hundred years, not seeing the highest law, a life of one day is better if a man sees the highest law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a devout widow of Sāvatthī with seven sons and seven daughters keeps her husband's estate until her children ask why she needs it when they could support her. She divides it among them, and soon every daughter-in-law and every daughter complains that hers is the only house the old woman visits. She leaves them and is ordained as a nun, and because she has come to the life so late she resolves to meditate all night, guiding herself in the dark with a hand on the pillars and then on the trees so as not to strike her head. The Buddha, seated in his own chamber at Jetavana, sends a radiant image of himself to sit face to face with her and speaks the verse, and she is awakened.
bg.history:
The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas that had shut out most Asian immigrants, and Korean families began arriving in large numbers in the following decades. Between 1990 and 2000 Georgia had the fastest-growing Korean community in the country. In metro Atlanta, Korean grocers, restaurants and shops first clustered along Buford Highway in Doraville in the 1980s, then moved north into Gwinnett County, where Duluth now has the largest Koreatown in the Southeast.

Between 60 and 65 percent of Korean Americans identify as Christian, and there are some four thousand Korean churches in the United States. Many of those families trace their faith to the north of the peninsula, where Korean Christianity was strongest before the war; many northern Christians fled south in 1950 and after. Korean churches carried over a tradition of fervent prayer: daily prayer meetings before dawn, Friday all-night vigils, and the prayer mountain, or kidowon, a retreat where believers pray outdoors through the night, sometimes holding onto trees as a sign of their devotion.

sections.heading: I. The Store
sections.text: For thirty-four years Shin Jeong-ok pressed other people's clothes. She ran Sunrise Cleaners on Candler Road with her husband, Lee Man-sik, in a strip of stores between a check-cashing place and a barbershop, and she could look at a stain on a blouse and tell you whether it was coffee or red clay or blood, and how old it was, and whether it would come out. Man-sik worked the register and the boiler and the long conveyor of plastic bags that went round the ceiling and came back down when you pushed the button. She worked the steam press and the Singer in the back. She let out the waists of church pants and took up the hems of prom dresses, and fixed zippers for a dollar, and pinned a paper ticket to every collar with a safety pin, and she was nearly never wrong about anything that came across the counter. The women called her Miss Shin, or Mama Shin, or just Mama. Some of them had been coming since they were girls, holding their mothers' hands. Daniel, the eldest, said it. He was a pharmacist and he said things in the order a pharmacist says them, gently and in a row. Umma. Abba is gone now. What do you need the store for? You're seventy-three. You stand all day on that concrete. There's no one to watch the door. We can take care of you. Isn't that what we're for? She listened, and said nothing, and got up and brought the fruit. They said it again on Chuseok in September, and again at Samuel's daughter's first birthday, and again on the phone, one son and then another, so that she could tell they had talked about it among themselves. She said nothing each time. But at night in the house on the cul-de-sac, which was too large now and made sounds she did not remember it making, she thought about her husband in the car with the engine running, and about her own knees, and about her four sons, who were good boys, who had been good boys always, who had done their homework on a milk crate. sections.text: Daniel's house was in a subdivision in Suwanee called Ashford Glen, with a pool and tennis courts and a stone sign at the entrance with water running down it. Jeong-ok had the guest room over the garage. Her daughter-in-law Jenny had put fresh towels on the bed in a fan shape, and a bottle of water on the nightstand, as if for a hotel. The first week was good. Jeong-ok cooked. She made doenjang stew with the paste from her crock, and fried anchovies with sesame and honey, and sat with her granddaughters while they did their homework and did not understand a word of it. The second week Jenny began to open the kitchen windows when Jeong-ok cooked, and to turn on the vent fan, and once, after the fish, to walk through the downstairs with a can of air freshener that smelled like an apple that had never grown on any tree. The third week the crock went out to the garage, beside the second refrigerator and the girls' bicycles, because of the smell. On a Thursday at the end of the month Jeong-ok came down the back stairs to the laundry room for a dish towel and stopped, because Jenny was in there on the phone with her sister in Marietta, in English, folding sheets. sections.dateline: Gilmer County, in the north Georgia mountains · autumn 2014
sections.text: The prayer mountain was an old Baptist youth camp the church had bought in 1988, two hours north of the city, past the apple orchards and the roadside stands selling fried pies, up a gravel road with a cable across it and a hand-lettered sign in two languages. There was a chapel with a tin roof and a long porch on cedar posts. There was a dining hall and two dormitories and a bathhouse. Up the ridge behind the chapel, through the white pines, there were thirty little prayer rooms the size of a closet, each one with a door and a window and a cushion and a Bible and a box of tissues, and at the very top of the ridge there was a white cross twenty feet tall that had a ring of electric bulbs on it and could be seen at night from the state highway. Jeong-ok had come up on Friday nights for twenty years in the church van with the other women, to pray all night in the chapel and walk the ridge in the dark and come down at dawn with their voices gone. She had never come up alone. She had never come on a Tuesday. Choi Moksa-nim, who had founded the place and had been its pastor for twenty-six years, was eighty-four. sections.text: I came late, she thought. I came to this at seventy-four years old, when the others came at forty. I can't afford to sleep. So she began to pray through the nights. She would help Deaconess Bae with the supper dishes and put on her coat and her husband's wool hat and go out to the chapel porch while the others went to bed. She prayed on the porch first. The light over the chapel door had burned out in November and nobody had gotten up on the ladder, and her eyes were not good anymore in the dark, cataracts in both, which the doctor in Duluth had wanted to fix and which she had put off for the store and then for the funeral and then for everything else. So she walked the length of the porch with her hand on the cedar posts. Post to post. Twelve posts down and twelve posts back, her palm on each one as she came to it, praying under her breath, turning the verse in her apron pocket over in her mind the way you turn a stone over in your fingers. When the porch was not enough she went up the ridge. There were no lights on the ridge path. There had never been. sections.dateline: The bench below the cross · January 2015
sections.text: In the second week of January Pastor Choi had pneumonia, and Deaconess Bae drove him down the mountain to the hospital in Jasper, and stayed with him there. That left Mrs. Kwon and Jeong-ok alone on the mountain. It snowed a little on the Thursday and froze on the Friday, and nobody came up from the city for the all-night prayer, because the gravel road was ice. Jeong-ok went up the ridge on Friday night anyway, tree to tree, with frozen pine needles cracking under her shoes. It was very cold. Her breath went out ahead of her and she could not see it go. Near the top, below the cross, there was a wooden bench where people sat to catch their breath, and a white pine beside it, and she had her hand on that pine and her forehead against the back of her hand when she saw the light coming up the path behind her. She thought at first that it was Mrs. Kwon with a flashlight. Then she thought it was a car, because it was too wide and too soft for a flashlight, and she wondered how anybody could have gotten a car up the ridge.
