verses.text: If a man would hasten towards the good, he should keep his thought away from evil; if a man does what is good slothfully, his mind delights in evil.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a poor brahmin and his wife own a single upper garment between them, so only one can go out at a time. She goes to hear the Buddha teach by day, and he goes at night. Moved by the teaching, he wants to give the garment to the Buddha, but selfish thoughts hold him back through the first and second watches of the night. In the last watch he lays it at the Buddha’s feet and shouts three times, “I have conquered!” King Pasenadi, who is in the audience, rewards him with pairs of garments, doubling each time as the brahmin gives them all away, until the king makes him keep two pairs. He gives the brahmin two costly blankets, and the brahmin hangs one as a canopy over the Buddha’s bed and the other in his own house over the place where a monk takes his meals. Seeing this, the king gives him “the gift of fours.” When the monks marvel at how quickly the good deed was rewarded, the Buddha says that had he given in the first watch he would have received sixteens, and in the middle watch eights.
bg.history:
After grasshoppers and drought destroyed the crops of 1855, Utah went into a hungry winter. That September, Brigham Young called for a Reformation, and each ward got home missionaries who visited every family and asked searching questions about their religious lives. On October 4, Franklin D. Richards reached the city with word that two late handcart companies, the Willie and Martin companies, were still on the trail. At general conference the next morning, Young called for wagons, teams, provisions and drivers. Lucy Meserve Smith remembered that “the sisters stripped off their Peticoats stockings and every thing they could spare, right there in the Tabernacle,” as recorded by the Church Historian’s Press. The first rescue party left on October 7 with sixteen wagonloads of supplies.

The Willie company was found on the Sweetwater River, out of flour. After the climb over Rocky Ridge, thirteen people died in a single night. The Martin company, caught by a blizzard near the last crossing of the North Platte, lost fifty-six people while it waited for help at Red Bluffs. The Willie company reached Salt Lake on November 9 and the Martin company on November 30, and Young told the Saints to take the survivors into their homes. The Welsh in the valley had come mostly through the work of Dan Jones, who led more than 300 Welsh converts out of Liverpool in 1849 and oversaw the first Welsh Book of Mormon.

sections.heading: I. The Shawl
sections.text: Ifan and Gwen Pugh came to the valley in the autumn of 1849 with the Welsh, three hundred of them, who had sailed out of Liverpool singing and gone up the Mississippi in a steamboat and walked from the Missouri River to the mountains. In Merthyr Ifan had cut coal. In the valley there was no coal anybody had found yet, so he cut stone. He quarried it and hauled it and squared it for the public works, and for the foundation of the Temple when they started on it, and he was paid at the tithing office in flour and potatoes and squash and paper scrip, and he and Gwen did well enough for six years. They had an adobe house of two rooms with a dirt roof, and a clock, and a feather bed, and a Book of Mormon in Welsh that had come over in a later ship, and each of them had a good coat. Then the grasshoppers came in the summer of 1855. They came out of the ground where they had been laid the fall before and ate the wheat as it sprouted. They ate the corn. They ate the squash vines down to the roots. Women threw shawls and bedsheets over their gardens to save something, and the grasshoppers ate the shawls. Gwen would not put hers out. She sat on the step all one week in August with a broom and

sections.heading: II. Sunday
sections.text: It was conference. The word had gone around the night before that Brother Franklin Richards had come in from the States with bad news, but nobody in the Welsh houses knew what it was. Morning or afternoon? Ifan said, because they could not both go. Morning, said Gwen, and put on the shawl, and went. She came back after noon without her stockings. She sat down on the stool by the fire and held out her bare white ankles in her shoes and told him why. There were people on the plains, she said. Hundreds of them. Two companies with handcarts, from the old countries, who had started too late in the year from the Missouri, and they were somewhere out on the Platte now with winter coming, and nobody in the valley had known they were coming at all. Brother Richards had passed them on the road. President Young had stood up and said they must be brought in, and help must be sent to them now, and he wanted teams and flour and teamsters, and that the faith of anybody who sat in their seat and did nothing would be in vain. And then the sisters had started to take things off. Right there in the Tabernacle. Petticoats. Stockings. Their shawls. A woman in front of Gwen had given her shoes and walke

sections.heading: III. The Watches
sections.text: Bishop Ezra Tuttle was seventy-four years old and a shoemaker. He had come from Vermont to Kirtland and from Kirtland to Missouri and from Missouri to Nauvoo and from Nauvoo across Iowa in the mud, and he had buried his wife at Winter Quarters, and he still had the same awl. He lived alone in the back of his shop on a cot. He was not a speaker. People who had been in his ward for five years would tell you they had never heard him say more than a hundred words at a meeting, and most of those were the names of the sick. At the schoolhouse that night he stood up and read out what the President had asked for, in the President’s own words, off a paper. Then he opened his Book of Mormon and read one verse. Then he sat down. And now behold, my beloved brethren, I say unto you, do not suppose that this is all; for after ye have done all these things, if ye turn away the needy, and the naked, and visit not the sick and afflicted, and impart of your substance, if ye have, to those who stand in need—I say unto you, if ye do not any of these things, behold, your prayer is vain, and availeth you nothing, and ye are as hypocrites who do deny the faith. — Alma 34:28 Ifan sat on the back bench in

sections.heading: IV. Blankets
sections.text: Hiram Bostwick had come up the street with his flour wagons a few minutes before. He had come into the valley with the first freighting trains, and he owned the biggest store on East Temple Street and a house with glass in every window, and he was bringing twenty sacks of flour to the bishop’s yard himself, because he was a man who liked to be seen to do a thing and also liked to do it. He was standing at the gate in a buffalo coat when the shouting started. What was that? Ask him what he’s won. His clerk went over and asked. Ifan told him, in English, plainly, standing in his shirt at the fire. One shawl, between the two of them. His wife had gone to the morning meeting in it and he had come to the evening. He had sat there since nine o’clock trying to give it. He had won. Bostwick stood a while at the gate. That’s a hard thing, he said. That’s a harder thing than mine. And he sent the clerk across to his store, and the clerk came back with a pair of blankets, good white Mackinaw blankets with a black stripe, and gave them to Ifan. Ifan looked at them and laid them on the shawl at the bishop’s feet. Bostwick sent the clerk back for two pairs. Ifan laid them on the pile. Four pairs

sections.heading: V. Fours
sections.text: Bostwick came to the bishop’s shop on Tuesday evening to settle a bill for boots, and he saw the robe nailed over the cot in the back room, and knew it. Bishop, who gave you that? Brother Pugh, said the bishop. Bostwick stood looking at it for some time. Then he said that a man likes to think he is the only one in the city who believes a thing all the way down, and it does him good to find out he isn’t. And the next day there came to the Pughs’ door, from Bostwick, four oxen, and four horses, and four sacks of flour, and four hundred dollars in gold in a canvas bag, and his claim to four acres of bottom land along the Jordan with water on it. The ward talked of nothing else for a week. At the meeting on Thursday night, before the bishop came in, they were still at it on the benches. The Lord had paid Ifan Pugh before the wagons were out of sight. He had given one shawl at four in the morning and been paid in oxen by Wednesday. There it was, plain as day, cause and effect, and the Reformation was right, and the Book was right, and you only had to give. sections.heading: VI. The Stripe
sections.text: The news came back over the mountains in pieces all November, and every piece was worse. The first of the handcart companies had been found on the Sweetwater out of flour, and on the night after they climbed the ridge in a snowstorm thirteen of them had died. The second was farther back, at the Platte, and they had sat in the snow waiting for help for nine days, and every morning there were more of them who did not get up. People in the valley said the names of the places as though they were the names of people. Rocky Ridge. Devil’s Gate. Red Bluffs. The last of them came in on the last Sunday in November, in a hundred wagons, while the people were at meeting. The President dismissed the afternoon meeting and told the sisters to go home and get those people something to eat, and wash them and nurse them, and receive them as their own children. The street filled with people and wagons and the steam off the teams. Gwen went down. She had a wool coat now and a new shawl from Bostwick’s store, blue, which she did not like as well. She went along the wagons looking for her husband’s oxen, and found them, thin as rails with their hip bones up like tent poles, and Ifan walking beside them

verses.text: If a man commits a sin, let him not do it again; let him not delight in sin: pain is the outcome of evil.

bg.commentary: The commentary’s story is a few lines long. The monk Seyyasaka grows discontented with the celibate life and says so to the monk he lives with, Lāḷudāyi, who puts him up to breaking a rule of the order. It is the first of the thirteen saṅghādisesa rules, the one against masturbation, and the monastic code tells Seyyasaka’s case as the reason the rule was made. After that, every time he feels discontent he does it again. The Buddha hears, sends for him, and asks whether the report is true. Seyyasaka says that it is. The Buddha calls him a foolish man for acting so against his state, lays the observance of the rules on him, tells him that such a course leads only to suffering, and speaks the verse, whose last line says that the heaping up of wrong is painful. Read the full commentary story. This retelling keeps the shape of the story and changes the habit. Curt’s is another private one, taken up for relief on a friend’s advice, forbidden to him by his place, and repeated until it is a pile.
bg.hist_title: Pull-tabs, youth hockey and the snow, 1991
bg.history:
Minnesota legalized bingo for nonprofit groups in 1945 and pull-tabs in 1981. By 1989 charitable gambling in the state took in more than a billion dollars a year, the most in the country, and most of it was paper pull-tabs sold from booths in bars for the benefit of veterans’ posts, Lions clubs, fire relief associations and youth hockey. Each organization has a licensed gambling manager who answers for the games. The law as revised in 1990 capped a ticket at two dollars and a prize at two hundred and fifty, and required a flare to be posted for every game and the big winners to be posted as they were paid. State law now bars sellers from playing at the site where they work; the card inside the glass in this story is the Boosters’ own. The Tamarack Lounge and everyone in it are invented. Coon Rapids is a real suburb north of Minneapolis.

Youth hockey associations in Minnesota lean on these games to pay for ice time, and commonly ask each family for a set number of volunteer hours a season. Squirts are the nine- and ten-year-olds, and breezers are what Minnesotans call hockey pants. The last Tuesday of October 1991 was sixty-five degrees in the Twin Cities. Snow began on Thursday, October 31, and did not stop until Sunday. The Halloween Blizzard left 28.4 inches at the Minneapolis–St. Paul airport, still the largest single snowstorm in the cities’ records, with 8.2 inches of it on Halloween itself. Children went out in costumes over snowsuits. The hard deposit a hygienist scrapes away is calculus, which builds up in layers when plaque is left on the teeth.

sections.heading: I. The Booth
sections.dateline: Coon Rapids, Minnesota · April to September 1991
sections.text: Every hockey family owed the Boosters twenty hours a season. You could work concessions at the arena, or you could sell pull-tabs. Curt Lundeen had a boy in Squirts, and he took the booth at the Tamarack Lounge on Tuesday and Thursday nights. The booth was a plexiglass box at the end of the bar, with a stool, a cash drawer and three clear bins of tickets. A ticket cost a dollar. It was two layers of cardboard, and on the back were five perforated tabs with a row of pictures under each. Three of the right picture in a row paid something. Most rows paid nothing. A game came in a case of twenty-four hundred tickets, and the flare that came with it was taped to the glass and told you every winner in the case, two at two hundred and fifty dollars and on down. When a big one was cashed, the seller crossed it off. Anybody standing at the bar could look at a bin and at the flare and form an opinion. The man on the stool did not have to form one. He had sold the tickets and he knew the count. That was why there was an index card inside the glass, typed, at eye level. SELLERS DO NOT PLAY. It was signed M.E. M.E. was Marlys Engstrom. title: The Recall Card
logline: A hockey dad selling pull-tabs for the Boosters in a suburban bar starts playing his own box, until his dental hygienist sends for him.

verses.text: If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Kassapa comes out of seven days of meditation and looks for someone poor to receive his first meal from. He chooses a young woman who is guarding a rice field and parching rice she has gathered. She pours it into his bowl with joy and asks for a share in the truth he has seen. On her way back a snake bites her, and she dies and is reborn as a goddess in a golden mansion, with a golden vessel of golden rice hung at its door to show how she came there. Wanting to make her good fortune sure, she goes each dawn to sweep the elder’s cell and set out his water. On the third morning he sees her radiance through the keyhole and sends her away, so that no preacher may one day say a goddess waited on Kassapa. She stands weeping in the air. The Buddha hears, appears before her, says that Kassapa was right to restrain himself and that she is right to want to do good, and speaks the verse. Her name afterward is Lājā, Parched Rice.
bg.history:
On November 7, 1861, a Union fleet took the two forts guarding Port Royal Sound. The planters of the South Carolina Sea Islands fled inland, and about ten thousand enslaved people stayed where they were. The islanders called that day the Gun Shoot. What followed is known as the Port Royal Experiment: Treasury cotton agents, then Northern superintendents and teachers, with the people working the abandoned plantations for wages that often came late or in store credit. In May 1862 General Hunter’s soldiers took the able-bodied men off the plantations for a regiment without warning, and in July the Army gave up Edisto Island and carried its people to St. Helena. By that winter Sea Island men were enlisting in the First South Carolina Volunteers. The National Park Service tells the larger story. Long Pond and everyone on it are invented.

Each plantation had its praise house. The Philadelphia teacher Laura Towne, who came to St. Helena in April 1862, wrote that it was “always the cabin of the oldest person in the little village,” and in 1864 she visited an old African-born woman known as a great “spiritual mother” with “tremendous influence over her spiritual children” (Letters and Diary of Laura M. Towne). Young people who were “seeking” went out alone to pray in the woods under the guidance of such an elder. Towne also noted the small ponds of the island planted in rice, which was pounded in a mortar and winnowed in a wide coiled basket called a fanner; in the old rice country people were set to keep the ricebirds off the ripening grain. Objects last used by the dead were laid on their graves. The two songs come from this place and these years. “Not Weary Yet” was taken down in the Port Royal islands by Charles P. Ware, a superintendent on St. Helena, and printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867); “Fare Ye Well” was sung by the Sea Island soldiers of Thomas Wentworth Higginson’s regiment and printed in his Army Life in a Black Regiment (1870). Both are quoted as those books give them, and the spelling is the collectors’.

sections.heading: I. The Pond
sections.dateline: Long Pond plantation, St. Helena Island · September 1862
sections.text: The white people left Long Pond on the day of the Gun Shoot. That was the seventh of November, when the Yankee ships beat down the forts at Bay Point and Hilton Head, and the sound came across the water all morning like somebody dragging furniture over a floor upstairs. The master’s family went off toward the main in the flats with what they could carry. They called on the people to come with them, and the people went into the woods and stayed there until the boats were gone. That winter the cotton agents came, and in the spring the superintendents, young men from Massachusetts with pay books. Now the people worked the cotton for the Government at so much a task, and the pay came late, or came as paper to spend at the agent’s store. In May soldiers walked down the road and took the able men off to Hilton Head without a day’s warning. In July the transports brought the Edisto people, whose island the Government had given up, and set them ashore on St. Helena with their fowls and pigs, and Long Pond took in its share. After that came the fever months. Brother March was leader of the praise house at Long Pond. He was a lean man past sixty who had been the plantation carpenter, which m

sections.heading: II. The House
sections.text: She woke the way you wake after sleeping in the daytime, not sure where the door is. She was in a house. This is how it was told on St. Helena, and nobody who told it ever made it smaller. The house was gold all through, and it was thirty miles from the front door to the back, and no hammer or nail had gone into it. She herself had grown in it as tall as a pine. She had on a new frock that had never been on anyone else, and another over that. A thousand women stood in the hall, and every one of them knew her name. Over the door, where a person coming up the steps could not miss it, hung a fanner. It was the same wide shallow basket they fanned rice in on every street in the islands, sewn round and round from the middle. This one was gold, and it was full of rice, hulled and clean, and the rice was gold too. It hung there so that whoever came would know how she had got her house. She stood in the doorway and looked at all of it. What did I ever do to come by this? she asked herself, and knew at once. It was the skillet of rice. Then she thought: If that little brought all this, I cannot sit down now. I have this to keep. I will go and do for him, the big things and the small, and ma

sections.heading: III. The Latch-Hole
sections.text: Brother March’s house was the last on the street. He had lived in its two rooms alone since his wife died. On the first morning, when he came in from his prayers, the floor was swept. It was swept into the corners, and the sand before the door was swept too, in the long curved marks a broom leaves. His water gourd was full and stood on the shelf where he could reach it. He stood and looked. One of the boys, he thought. Three young ones were seeking under him that fall, and one of them, a boy called Scipio, was forever underfoot wanting to be of use. The second morning it was the same, floor and yard and water. He thought the same thing, and meant to speak to the boy about pride. The third morning he had not yet gone out. He was on his knees by the bed in the dark, and he heard the broom. It was going over the floor of the front room in slow strokes. He got up and put his eye to the hole in the door where the latchstring ran through. The room was full of light that was neither fire nor day. In the middle of it a shape taller than the room should have held was bending and sweeping. Who is that sweeping? It is me, sir. Affy. Your child Affy. I have no child by that name. He did not. T

sections.heading: IV. The Fanner
sections.dateline: The first house on the street
sections.text: The first house on the street was Maum Binah’s. It was the praise house, since the praise house was always the house of the oldest person on the place, and nobody at Long Pond could say how old Maum Binah was. She had fanned the street’s rice since before the driver was born. When the rice was cut and pounded they brought it to her door in the mortar, and she sat on her stool with the wide fanner on her knees and threw the rice up to the wind and caught it, and threw it up again, until there was no trash left in it. Half the street had come into the world through her two hands. Forty years back, when a carpenter’s boy called March first went out into the wilderness to seek, she was the one he came to in the mornings to tell what he had seen, and she was the one who told him when it was enough. Everybody on the street heard something that morning and took it for wind, or a marsh hen. Maum Binah knew what it was. She did not get up from her stool. People saw her on it at sunrise through her open door, with the fanner in her lap. Others, just as truthful, looked up and saw her sitting in the air above the last house on the street, face to face with the tall girl, as near as two women

title: The Fanner
logline: On a Sea Island plantation the masters have fled, a refugee girl minding ricebirds gives a praise-house elder her whole skillet of parched rice.

verses.text: Even an evil-doer sees happiness as long as his evil deed has not ripened; but when his evil deed has ripened, then does the evil-doer see evil.
Even a good man sees evil days, as long as his good deed has not ripened; but when his good deed has ripened, then does the good man see happy days.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Anāthapiṇḍika, the great lay donor who bought the Jetavana grove for the Buddha, visits the Teacher three times a day and never goes empty-handed. Merchants default on loans he made them, and a flood sweeps the family treasure buried at the riverbank into the sea, but he goes on giving, though now only rice porridge and sour gruel. The Buddha tells him that no gift given with a pure heart is coarse, and recalls that in a past life, as the brahmin Velāma, he gave an enormous gift where there was no one worthy to receive it. The spirit who lives over the householder's gate, unable to bear the goodness of the monks, finally dares to speak now that he is poor, and urges him to stop giving and mind his business. He throws her out. Homeless with her children, she is turned away by the city's guardian deity and the Four Great Kings, until Sakka, king of the gods, tells her to disguise herself as the steward, collect the debts, recover the treasure from the sea and gather ownerless wealth. She does, and asks pardon, and the householder takes her to the Buddha, who speaks these verses about deeds ripening. Read the full commentary story, or about Anāthapiṇḍika. The Japanese name for Jetavana is Gion Shōja, and so the most famous opening line in Japanese literature, the bell of Gion Shōja at the start of the Tale of the Heike, rings from the monastery Anāthapiṇḍika bought.
bg.history:
On April 1, 1946, an earthquake off the Aleutian Islands sent a tsunami across the Pacific. It struck Hilo a little after seven in the morning; many people took the first warnings for an April Fool's joke, and some went down to look at the drained bay before the larger waves came. The waves killed 159 people in the islands, 96 of them in Hilo, and at Laupāhoehoe the wave swept away schoolchildren and teachers. The bayfront and the railroad were wrecked and the Japanese neighborhood of Shinmachi was largely destroyed; it was rebuilt, and destroyed again in 1960. The disaster led to the first Pacific tsunami warning system. Most of Hawaii's Chinese families trace their roots to Zhongshan (Heungshan) in Guangdong.

Five months later, on September 1, the ILWU led about 26,000 workers out on the Hawaiian sugar strike of 1946, closing 33 of 34 plantations. Strikers fed themselves through soup kitchens, hunting and fishing parties, and committees that asked stores for donations. The settlement in November brought a raise of up to nineteen cents an hour and ended the perquisite system of company housing and services in lieu of wages. Haruo's regiment, the Japanese American 442nd, fought in the Vosges in October 1944; blinded veterans trained at Old Farms Convalescent Hospital in Avon, Connecticut from 1944 to 1947.

sections.heading: I. The Can
sections.text: Chun Kwai kept a store on Mamo Street, a block up from the bay, and for twenty years nobody who came to his counter hungry had gone out of it with empty hands. He sold rice in hundred-pound bags and salt salmon out of a barrel, shoyu by the gallon tin, kerosene, Bull Durham, dried shrimp, cotton palaka shirts for the cane fields, and crack seed in tall glass jars that the children of the Hilo side pressed their faces against on the way home from school. Behind the counter, on a nail, hung the book. Everybody knew the book. A family from Wainaku or Pāpaʻikou came in at the end of a short month and said put it on the book, Mr. Chun, and he wet his pencil and put it on the book, and some of it came back and a good deal of it never did, and he did not seem to mind. When the Army took the Japanese priests and schoolmasters and the officers of the Japanese societies away in December 1941, and their wives stood at his counter not knowing what to say, he put them on the book without a word and never once asked. People said Chun Kwai had paid for the new roof on the Chinese school out of his own pocket, and for a good many funerals, and for a boy's passage to the medical college in Honolulu

sections.heading: II. April Fool
sections.text: It was a Monday. Lin was in the store early, before school, eating a manapua out of a paper and watching Ah Fong sweep. Ah Fong was her father's cousin's son, thin and serious, who kept the book and the accounts in a clear small hand and wanted to be a bookkeeper at the bank. A boy ran past the open door shouting tidal wave, tidal wave, and Ah Fong leaned on his broom and said yeah, April fool, and went on sweeping. Then more people were running, and they were not running away from the water. They were running toward it. Lin went out to the corner in her school shoes and looked down Mamo Street to the bay, and the bay was gone. She said for the rest of her life that she could not make anybody understand what that was like. The water had pulled back past the breakwater as if somebody had pulled a cloth off a table. The bottom of Hilo Bay lay out in the morning sun, black rock and grey sand and weed, and fish were flopping on it, hundreds of them, silver, and boys were running out across the wet sand with buckets to pick them up. A sampan lay on its side. The air smelled like the inside of a shell. Ah Mah came out of the kitchen with her hair still down and took Lin by the wrist hard

sections.heading: III. The Cottage
sections.text: Haruo Kubo came home in May. He had volunteered for the 442nd in 1943, at twenty-two, with half the Nisei boys on the Hilo side, and in October 1944, in the forests of the Vosges in France, a German shell had burst in the trees over his head. He came to in a field hospital and never saw anything again. The Army sent him to a hospital in Pennsylvania and then to a school for blinded soldiers at Avon, in Connecticut, in an old boys' school with stone buildings, where he learned to shave by touch and cross a street with a cane and read with his fingers. When they were done with him they put him on a ship. A Red Cross woman met him at the pier in Hilo, and on the drive into town, very carefully, she told him. He asked her to take him to the lot. She led him by the elbow across the ruined ground of Shinmachi, between the foundation stones, and he stood where she told him the house had been and tapped the ground in front of him with his cane, and there was nothing there to tap. Kwai heard by noon. He closed the store, which he never did, and walked down to the lot, and stood beside the young man a while without saying anything, and then said, Harry. It's Chun. sections.heading: IV. The Door Lady
sections.dateline: The kitchen behind the store · late October
sections.text: This is the part Ah Mah told, and Lin told after her, and you can believe it or not. The lady in the doorway had watched the door for thirty-four years, in Heungshan and in Hilo. In all that time she had never once been able to speak to Chun Kwai. When a man is rich and strong in his own house, the door spirits keep quiet; they can only stand there. But she had not liked the blind boy from the start. The first time Haruo came down Mamo Street with his white cane and stood in the store, the corners of the print had curled up off the doorframe as though somebody had set a stove too close to it. She could not abide him, or the boys who followed him, or the people coming through her door with their hands out. There was too much good in them. It made her eyes water like smoke. Now Kwai was poor. A poor man listens, she thought. So one night late in October, when he sat alone at the kitchen table with a lamp and the book with the string around it, adding columns that would not add, she stepped down off the doorframe and stood in the air in front of him, about a foot above the floor, in her red jacket, with the baby on her arm. Who is that? said Kwai. The lady of your door, she said. I ca

sections.heading: V. The Ti Leaf
sections.text: The door lady had nowhere to go. Every house in Hilo already had whatever watched its door, and none of them would make room for her. She walked the town with the children for nights. She went to the earth god in his little house at the edge of the cemetery, and told him what she had said, and asked him to go to Chun Kwai with her and ask that she be let back in. The earth god said, You said what you had no business saying. I won't go with you. She crossed the channel to the Four Kings who stand guard in the gates of temples, one with a sword and one with a lute and one with an umbrella and one with a snake, and they said the same. At last, worn out, the children crying, she went all the way up to the Jade Emperor himself. I have nowhere to live, she told him. I walk around with these children in my hands. Get me back my door. I can't speak to him for you either, said the Jade Emperor. But I'll tell you what to do. Put on the clothes of the young man who keeps his book. Copy out on a leaf every debt that is owed him, and go around and collect it. Then go to the bottom of the bay, where the can went, and bring it up. sections.heading: VI. Gion Shōja
sections.dateline: Waiānuenue Avenue · the night of December 2
sections.text: That night Kwai woke and the kitchen was full of light. Lin, on the cot in the next room, woke too, and came and stood behind the curtain. The door lady stood in the air above the kitchen floor, shining so that you could see every board, with the baby on her arm and the two boys at her skirt. Her face was wet. Who is that? said Kwai, though he knew. The blind, foolish lady who used to watch your door, she said. Forgive what I said to you. I was a fool. I did what the Jade Emperor told me. Everything you lost is back in your storeroom. I have paid for my words. I have nowhere to live and I am very tired. Kwai sat a long time on the edge of his bed. Then he put on his trousers and his grey hat. Don't tell me, he said. Come up the hill and tell him. So they went up Waiānuenue Avenue together in the middle of the night, the storekeeper in his hat and the lady walking a foot above the road with her children, and Lin came after them barefoot in her nightgown, keeping to the dark under the trees. The town was asleep. Out on the bay the lights of a ship. The cottage was dark, but Haruo was sitting on the lanai in his undershirt, because he did not sleep much, and never had since France. He

title: Going-Home Money
logline: After the April Fool's tsunami takes his buried savings, a Chinese storekeeper keeps carrying jook up the hill to a blinded veteran.

verses.text: Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little.

bg.commentary: The commentary’s story is short. A monk leaves outdoors whatever beds and chairs of the community he has used outdoors, and rain, sun and white ants ruin them. When the other monks say he ought to put things away, he answers that it is a slight fault, not worth wasting thought or bile over, and does it again. They tell the Buddha, who sends for him and asks whether it is true, and the monk gives him the same answer. The Buddha says that no one should call a wrong deed a trifle: a jar left open in the rain is not filled by one drop, but it fills. He speaks the verse and lays down a rule that a monk who leaves a bed out in the open is at fault.
bg.history:
Brush Creek rises near West 80th Street and Lamar Avenue in Overland Park, Kansas, runs through Prairie Village and Mission Hills, and crosses into Kansas City, Missouri, at the Country Club Plaza. On September 12, 1977, two storms struck the city within one day, the first from about 1 to 6 a.m. and the second from about 8 p.m. to 2 a.m., with sunshine in between. As much as sixteen inches fell. The first rain saturated the ground and the second ran off it. The U.S. Geological Survey’s report counts twenty-five dead and notes that even people living on slopes above the flood plains had hillside runoff in their garages and basements. At 75th Street and Nall Avenue in Prairie Village, where the creek has gathered only a mile and a half of suburb, the Survey estimated a peak of 3,000 cubic feet a second, well past the hundred-year flood. Downstream the water stood five to six feet deep on the Plaza. The Corps of Engineers had warned in 1970 that the creek could reach flood stage in under an hour; the Kansas City Public Library tells the story. Highview, its board, Mr. Ordway and Kim Hadley are invented.

The National Weather Service’s Cooperative Observer Program, begun in 1890, relies on thousands of volunteers who read their instruments once a day. The standard rain gauge is an eight-inch funnel over a narrow measuring tube inside a can twenty inches tall; the tube holds two inches, and whatever overflows into the can is poured back through and measured. Rain too slight to measure is entered as a trace, written T. George Perkins Marsh was born in Woodstock, Vermont, in 1801. His Man and Nature (1864) argued, from the ruined hillsides of the Mediterranean and the cut-over ones of New England, that human beings change the earth by small acts added together, and it helped to launch the conservation movement. The words on the index card are from its last section, which Marsh headed “Nothing Small in Nature.” The Latin is spelled as he printed it.

sections.heading: I. The Furniture
sections.dateline: Highview Swim Club, Johnson County, Kansas · summer 1977
sections.text: Highview was a members’ pool on the hill off Lamar Avenue, where Overland Park runs into Prairie Village and nobody but the mailman knows which is which. Two hundred and eighty families owned it in equal shares. It had six lanes, a diving well, a baby pool, a snack window that sold frozen Snickers, and a board of seven that met on the second Tuesday in somebody’s family room. In May the board had bought thirty new chaise lounges, aluminum with yellow vinyl straps, to go with the thirty old white ones. It had voted, after discussion, to keep the two pine picnic tables a member had donated in 1969. Kim Hadley was head guard that summer. She was seventeen and would be a senior at Shawnee Mission East, and it was her third year on the stand. She was good at it. She did not twirl her whistle or talk to boys through the fence. She sat forward with her elbows on her knees and counted heads, shallow to deep and back, all day. The July before, she had gone off the stand in her sunglasses and brought a four-year-old up from the bottom of the five-foot before his mother finished turning around. sections.heading: II. The Gauge
sections.text: Mr. Ordway was president of the board that year, having missed the meeting where it was decided. He was fifty-four, a long quiet man from Vermont with a daughter on the swim team. He did hydrology for the Corps of Engineers downtown, which the guards understood to mean that he was paid to know how high creeks got. He came through the gate at seven every morning of the year, winter and summer, on his way to work. He came for the rain gauge. It stood on a post in the corner of the fence behind the pump house, a galvanized can eight inches across and twenty tall, open at the top. He was what the Weather Service called a cooperative observer. The gauge had stood in his own back yard until his maples grew out over it, and the pool had the only open sky left on the hill, so the board had let him move it. Every morning he lifted off the funnel, drew out the narrow brass tube inside, put a thin stick down it, looked at the stick, and wrote in a book. The guards told him about the furniture. Doug Petrie did it, at the gate, on a Thursday, and Mr. Ordway walked around the pump house to where Kim was hosing the deck for swim practice. Kim. Is it so, what I hear about the chaises? sections.heading: III. The Can
sections.text: The pool closed on Labor Day. Kim’s last act as head guard was to chain the furniture under the pavilion for the winter and hang the key on its nail. A week later, a little after one on Monday morning, it began to rain on Kansas City and kept on until six. The afternoon was sunny. In the evening people went out to dinner on the Plaza. Around eight it began again, on ground that could not hold another cupful, and rained until two. On Tuesday she drove over at a quarter to seven, as she had all summer. She could not have said why, except that she knew he would be there. Lamar looked like a creek bed. Gravel lay across it in bars, with a doghouse, and somebody’s mailbox still on its post. The club’s parking lot had been scoured in a fan pointing downhill. At the low corner by the baby pool the chain-link lay flat, and woven into it was a hedge of other people’s things: trash cans, a Big Wheel, a redwood planter, and lawn chairs from the yards up the street. There were eleven chairs. She counted them without meaning to. The pool was the color of coffee with milk in it. A line of silt crossed the deck and stood a hand high on the pavilion posts. title: A Trace
logline: The best lifeguard at a suburban swim club leaves sixty chaise lounges out every night, until the board president hands her his rain gauge.

verses.text: Let no man think lightly of good, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha thanks the people of Sāvatthī for a meal by describing four kinds of people: the one who gives but does not urge others, who will have wealth without a following; the one who urges but does not give, who will have a following without wealth; the one who does neither, who will live on leftovers; and the one who does both and has both. A layman who hears this invites the Buddha and all his monks for the next day and goes through the town asking each household for rice and whatever else it can spare, to be cooked in one place. A rich merchant, angry that the man has invited more than he can feed himself, gives him rice and beans pinched up in three fingers and dribbles out oil and sugar; from that day he is called Biḷālapādaka, Cat's Foot, after a tiny measure. The layman keeps the merchant's gift apart, and the merchant sends a servant to watch, who sees him put a few grains and drops into every pot with a blessing. Sure that he will be shamed by name, the merchant comes to the meal with a knife hidden in his clothes. The layman blesses all the givers alike. The merchant falls at his feet and confesses, and the Buddha says that no good deed should be called a trifle.
bg.history:
Hurricane Laura made landfall at Cameron, Louisiana, about one in the morning on August 27, 2020, as a Category 4 storm, tied for the strongest landfall in the state's record. It wrecked Lake Charles and the rice parishes to the east, brought down the transmission lines that fed the region, and left some two hundred thousand people without drinking water; power in places was out for weeks, and six weeks later Hurricane Delta came ashore twelve miles away. In Jefferson Davis Parish, Entergy described crews cutting trees off the lines and setting new poles along Highway 101. Most of the first rice crop was already cut, and growers kept their bins and dryers going on generators. The same country had been hit by Hurricane Rita in 2005. Volunteer cooks with trailers of cast-iron pots, many of them organized online, fed storm towns across the region that fall.

It was also the first year of the pandemic. On April 20, 2020, the price of American crude fell below zero for the first time, and offshore crews along the Gulf were laid off by the hitch. The prairie parishes of southwest Louisiana are Cajun and Creole, largely Catholic, and many older people still have French; petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid is an old French proverb. The Sisters of the Holy Family, a congregation of Black Catholic women founded in New Orleans in 1842, taught in Lafayette from 1913. "Little Things" was written by Julia A. Carney in Boston in 1845 and sung by schoolchildren for a century afterward; its last stanza was added in later printings. Rougeau and everyone in it are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Pot
sections.dateline: Rougeau, Jefferson Davis Parish, Louisiana · August 27 to September 2, 2020
sections.text: Laura came ashore at Cameron at one in the morning on a Thursday, and by daylight the town of Rougeau had no roof that was whole. Rougeau was eleven hundred people on Highway 90 in the rice country east of Lake Charles, with a water tower, a Catholic church, and a rice dryer whose bins could be seen for six miles. The poles were down the length of the highway. The water went off that afternoon. It was ninety-four degrees, and the power company was talking about weeks. Curtis Ledet drove a school bus for the parish and had been an usher at Sacred Heart for thirty years. He and his wife Loretta rode it out in the hall closet with her mother's rosary. When they came out there was sky over the back bedroom. He got a blue tarp on it by Friday, but a tarp will leak at a nail, and this one leaked over the kitchen, a drop about every four seconds. Loretta set her big aluminum gumbo pot under it. It did not look like anything. In the morning the pot was full to the rim, and they flushed the toilet with it and set it back. On Sunday the trucks came. There were fourteen of them, pulling trailers with black iron pots on them the size of washtubs, and propane burners, and paddles like boat oars

sections.heading: II. The Wagon
sections.text: He started at seven, with his grandson's wagon. In the wagon he had a five-gallon bucket for dry goods, an ice chest, and a spiral notebook. He went to every door in Rougeau that still had one, and where there was no door he called into the yard. Mama, Daddy, he said at each place, the way an usher talks. I asked the cooks to supper tomorrow, all of them. Give what you can spare. Rice, beans, whatever you got that'll go in a pot. We'll cook it all in one place, at the hall, and it'll be from everybody. Nobody in that town had much that week, and most of it was thawing. They gave it. Mrs. Guillory gave him four pounds of smoked sausage out of a freezer that had been dead a week and packed in ice from the relief truck. He got onions and bell pepper from one house and a sack of rice with the top rolled down from the next. He got two pounds of red beans, half a bottle of oil, and a jar of cane syrup from Abbeville. A woman who had moved over from Iberia Parish gave him three jars of pepper paste that her Lao neighbors there had taught her to put up. A man with nothing in his house but a case of water gave the water. Curtis wrote each name in the notebook and what it was. By ten the wag

sections.heading: III. The Spoon
sections.text: They cooked in the yard of the hall on the krewe's own burners, which Marcus lent and would not touch. He sat in a lawn chair with his hands on his knees, the first evening in three weeks that he had not held a paddle. Loretta Ledet had the jambalaya. There was a pot of red beans, a pot of white beans with the sausage, a rice dressing, a pot of plain rice, and a dishpan of bread pudding going into the hall oven, which ran on bottled gas. Dustin stood by the fence and watched. When the pots were all on, Curtis took the handkerchief out of his shirt pocket and untied it on the table. He counted the rice into six small heaps with the tip of a teaspoon. He went to each pot and put in its heap, six or seven grains, and into the two bean pots he put the red beans, a few to each. He had the oil in the bottle cap still. He let one drop of it fall from the spoon into every pot. The sugar cubes went into the bread pudding. At each pot he said the same thing, quietly, as he would have said a response at Mass. May Mr. Vernon get it back full. Loretta asked him what in the world he was doing. He gave, Curtis said. If I dump his in with the rest, it's only in the one pot. I want him in every pla

sections.heading: IV. The Hall
sections.text: They ate at five, when the yard was in shade. The krewe sat down at the long tables, forty-three of them, in masks pulled under their chins, looking as if they did not know what to do with their hands. The linemen sat down. The town stood and served them. Vernon Trahan stood at the back, by the fence, with his shirt out. When everyone had a plate, Curtis got up on the hall steps with the notebook. Marcus Papillion had set his telephone on its tripod and turned it around to face the steps. Mr. Papillion, Curtis said. You and your people been feeding us five days. Tonight this is from Rougeau. I went around and asked, and everybody I asked gave something. They gave what they could. Some of them gave by the sack and some gave by the pinch. He did not open the notebook. I'm not going to read no names. It's all in the pots together now, and I couldn't tell you whose is whose. May every one of them that gave get it back full. That's all. Y'all eat. He came down the steps. Vernon had his hand flat against his shirt. He stood a moment longer. He said afterward that he had come there ready to kill a man for something the man had never meant to do. sections.heading: V. Little Things
sections.text: Marcus picked the pistol up by the barrel, broke it open, and shook the shells out into his hand. He gave the shells to Vernon and the pistol to a deputy who was eating at the second table. Get up, Mr. Trahan, he said. You wrong about one thing still. You think what you gave was nothing. He helped him up by the elbow. It wasn't nothing. I ate it. It was in the jambalaya and it was in the beans. He turned a little, so that he was speaking to the tables as well, and to the telephone on its tripod, though he seemed to have forgotten it. Don't none of y'all look down on a little bit of good and say it won't ever amount to nothing, it won't ever come back around to me. My maw-maw used to tell us petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid. Little by little the bird builds her nest. Mr. Curtis told me they got a pot at his house under a leak in the roof. One drop. You wouldn't cross the room for it. In the morning they can't lift the pot. A person with sense fills up the same way, a pinch at a time. So don't call it a pinch. That was all he said. He went back to his plate. title: Three Fingers
logline: After Hurricane Laura a school bus driver asks a wrecked rice town to feed the cooks who fed it, and the dryer owner gives a pinch.

verses.text: Let a man avoid evil deeds, as a merchant, if he has few companions and carries much wealth, avoids a dangerous road; as a man who loves life avoids poison.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred thieves fail to break into the house of the merchant Mahā Dhana (“Great Wealth”). When he sets out with five hundred carts, he invites five hundred monks to travel with him and promises them food on the way. The thieves hide in a forest ahead. The merchant halts at a village at the forest’s edge, and the thieves’ scout asks a friend in the village when the merchant will leave. The friend decides to warn the merchant, because the monks are living on his bounty. The merchant resolves to turn back; the thieves move to the road behind him; warned again, he decides to go neither forward nor back and stays where he is. The monks return to the Buddha, who makes the merchant’s prudence a lesson: avoid evil as he avoids that road, and as a man who wants to live avoids poison.
bg.history:
Before steamboats, farmers and merchants of the Ohio valley floated their produce down to Natchez and New Orleans on flatboats, sold the cargo and the boat, and walked or rode home. The way home was the Natchez Trace, some five hundred miles of path through the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations to Nashville. The boatmen were called Kaintucks wherever they came from. Grindstone Ford on Bayou Pierre marked the line between the Natchez District and the Choctaw nation; a plain stand there fed travelers on mush and milk. At the Tennessee River the Chickasaw Colbert family kept the ferry. Men going north carried their season’s earnings in coin, and robbers worked the road and the river. The best known, Samuel Mason, was killed in 1803. Everyone in this story is invented.

Congress made the Trace a post road in 1800. The mail went by single riders, who carried a blanket, corn for the horse and a tin trumpet. John Swaney, who rode the route in these years, remembered that Mason often stopped him to ask the news and told him no mail carrier need fear his men, since mail was of no value to them; the reminiscence is given in Otto Rothert’s The Outlaws of Cave-in-Rock (1924). The first post office at Natchez opened in November 1799. The fable the rider tells is the old one of the fox and the sick lion, quoted here from Sir Roger L’Estrange’s English Aesop of 1692, a version much reprinted in the century that followed.

sections.heading: I. The Notice
sections.text: Mayhew Dane came down from Pittsburgh that spring with five broadhorns of flour, whiskey and bar iron. By the first week of May he had sold all of it at Natchez, and the boats too, for their lumber. What he had to show for the winter was Spanish dollars, in four small kegs with NAILS painted on the heads. Everybody under the hill knew what was in the kegs. A man can’t sell five boatloads in a town that size and keep it quiet. Twice in one week somebody tried the storehouse he had hired by the landing. The second time they brought an auger, and they had three holes through the planking before the watchman’s dog made up its mind to bark. Dane sat on the kegs the rest of that night with a horse pistol across his knees. In the morning he wrote out a notice and had it nailed up at the post office on the bluff and at two of the grog shops below. Mr. Dane of Pittsburgh starts for Nashville by the Natchez road on Monday. Any men of the upper country going home that way may travel with his wagon. They will not want for bread or meat while they are with him. There were plenty to read it. The boats came down the river every spring and none of them went back. The men who had steered them walke

sections.heading: II. The Ford
sections.text: Seventy miles north of Natchez the road came down to Bayou Pierre at a place called Grindstone Ford, and there the settled country stopped. South of the bayou were cotton fields and cabins and such law as the Territory had. North of it lay the Choctaw nation. The road from there was a horse path through cane and big timber, with days between one roof and the next. There was a stand at the ford, a log house of one room where a traveler could buy mush and milk and a place on the floor. A wagon could go no farther. Dane stopped three days to sell the wagon and the oxen and buy pack horses, and he was particular about horses. The twelve lay about the yard and ate. He had been as good as his notice. There was meal and bacon twice a day and coffee in the morning, and Leeper, who had not eaten twice a day since March, began to fill out his shirt again. The stand kept a hired man named Luke Farrow, who worked the canoe when the bayou was up and saw to the stock. On the second evening somebody hallooed from the cane on the north bank to be fetched across, and Luke knew the voice before he knew the man. It was Wiley Harkins. The two of them had poled a keelboat up the Cumberland four summers

sections.heading: III. Neither Way
sections.dateline: The same place · that week and the next
sections.text: Horses are sooner bought than sold, and Dane was still at the ford when Harkins hallooed again. Luke told him the plain truth. The Pittsburgh man had given up the path and meant to go back down to Natchez. Harkins went off with that. Inside of two days the men had come out of the cane, crossed the bayou above the ford in the night, and laid up along the Natchez road, where it ran sunk between high clay banks a few miles to the south. Dane still had not gone. Harkins came a third time, and this time he came riding up from the south like any other traveler. Luke understood from that where they were lying now. He told Dane that too. Dane sat on one of his kegs in the yard a good part of that afternoon. He looked at the bayou and the spring above it. He looked at the corn standing behind the house, and at the ford, where every man going up or down the country had to wet his feet. Three parties came through while he sat there. One wanted powder and one wanted shoes, and the stand had neither to sell. I want for nothing here, he said, to nobody. I will go neither up nor back. I will stop where I am. He went over to the twelve. There were men laid for me up the path. When I thought to tur

sections.heading: IV. The Mail
sections.dateline: Colbert’s ferry on the Tennessee · June
sections.text: The mail between Nashville and Natchez went that year by one man on one horse. He had a pair of leather bags behind the saddle, a blanket, a sack of corn, and a tin trumpet to blow when he came near a house. The rider that summer was Josiah Vance. He had carried it since the road was made a post road, and had ridden express in Pennsylvania as a boy before that. He read everything that was nailed up at either end of his route. He had read Dane’s notice in Natchez. Going north, he had passed the ford while Dane was trading for horses, and had seen the twelve in the yard. He met them again a fortnight later, coming south, at the Tennessee River, where the Colberts, who were Chickasaw, kept the ferry. The twelve were sitting on the south bank waiting for the boat. Their meal had run out in the second week and they were gaunt again. Vance led his horse off the ferry and stopped in front of them. You are Dane’s men. Where is Dane? Leeper told him all of it, the men up the path and the men down the road, and Dane sitting on his keg. He is building himself a store, Leeper said. We came on. And nobody troubled you. They looked at us. Vance let the horse drink. He was a man who had whole day

title: Grindstone Ford
logline: A Pittsburgh merchant with four kegs of Spanish dollars and twelve broke boatmen reaches the last house before the Choctaw wilderness.

verses.text: He who has no wound on his hand, may touch poison with his hand; poison does not affect one who has no wound; nor is there evil for one who does not commit evil.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich man’s daughter of Rājagaha, already a stream-enterer as a girl, looks down from the top floor of her father’s house and sees the deer hunter Kukkuṭamitta drive his cart of venison into the city. She slips out in soiled clothes with a waterpot, follows his cart and marries him, and her parents hold her funeral. She bears him seven sons. One dawn the Buddha walks to the hunter’s empty nets, leaves a footprint and sits under a bush. The hunter draws his bow and is fixed there, unable to shoot or lower it; so are his seven sons; the wife arrives and cries, “Do not kill my father,” and their hearts soften. All fifteen give up killing. The monks then ask how a stream-enterer could have handed her husband his bow and arrows for so many years, and the Buddha answers with the verse of the unwounded hand. A story of the past explains their readiness: a country rich man, outbid by a city rich man for the honor of leading the building of a shrine, gave himself, his wife, his seven sons and their wives to serve it.
bg.history:
The Bible Christian Church began in Salford, Lancashire, where members signed a pledge to eat no meat and drink no alcohol. In 1817 the Rev. William Metcalfe brought a party of them to Philadelphia. Their church in Kensington was the first vegetarian congregation in the United States, a generation before Sylvester Graham, and Metcalfe helped found the American Vegetarian Society in 1850. He appears here only by name; The congregation first met in the schoolroom Metcalfe rented behind No. 10 North Front Street and from 1823 had its own chapel on North Third Street above Girard Avenue, as the church’s centennial history records. Abel Horrocks, Hannah Schofield and Brother Royle are invented, as are the Ashmeads and the Coxes.

Market sheds ran down the middle of High Street, now Market Street, until 1859. The shed between Front and Second, nearest the ferry, was the Jersey Market, where New Jersey people sold what they brought across the river; an ordinance of 1822 had it rebuilt. Game, venison included, was sold in the city’s markets through the century. The Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey supported bog-iron furnaces, charcoal burning, cedar cutting and, from the 1830s, cranberry growing. Local tradition has long held that some Piney families descend from Hessian soldiers who deserted during the Revolution. A “levy” was the Philadelphia name for the Spanish real, worth twelve and a half cents.

sections.heading: I. The Window
sections.text: Thomas Ashmead shipped flour to the West Indies and brought back sugar, and he had built his house on High Street above Front, four stories of brick with the counting room on the ground floor. He put his daughter at the top of it. Susanna was sixteen that winter. Her room looked down on the long roof of the Jersey Market, which ran up the middle of the street from Front to Second, and a serving woman named Hannah Schofield slept across her door. Hannah was from Salford in Lancashire. She had come over in 1817 with the people who followed Mr. Metcalfe, the ones the city called Bible Christians, who signed a paper promising to eat no flesh and drink no spirits and who met on Sundays in Mr. Metcalfe’s hired schoolroom behind North Front Street. The Ashmeads were Christ Church people and did not ask what Hannah did with her Sunday afternoons, or notice that for four years she had taken the child with her. Susanna had signed the paper herself at twelve. An old weaver named Abel Horrocks, whom the children of that meeting called Father Abel, had ruled the line for her name because she could not yet write straight. At her father’s table she passed the joint along and ate the bread and the

sections.heading: II. The Ferry
sections.dateline: The Market Street slip · Sunday, before light
sections.text: Susanna laid out what she meant to take, and it was not much: two shifts, a pair of stockings, a garnet ring that had come to her from her grandmother, the pledge card. She tied them flat under an old brown gown of Hannah’s that was waiting for the rag bag. Before anyone was up she went down the back stair with the kitchen pitcher in her hand, like a girl sent to the Jersey boats for buttermilk. She stood on the slip in the cold. The wagon came down empty with the two horses blowing steam. When it went onto the boat she went on behind it, and when it came off on the Jersey side and took the road east she walked in the track of its wheels. He let it go on for a mile before he stopped the horses. I do not know you, he said. You are nobody’s girl that I ever traded with. Leave off following me. You did not call me, said Susanna. I came on my own feet. Mind your team. He drove on. He stopped twice more and told her to go back, and she stood in the road each time and waited for him to finish. The third time she looked at him directly. When good fortune walks up behind a man, he has no call to send it home. His name was Micah Cox. His grandfather had been a Hessian named Hahn who walked

sections.heading: III. The Brush Fence
sections.dateline: The Pines, on a branch of the Wading River · November 1849
sections.text: In twenty-eight years she bore him seven sons, the last two together. They grew up tall and quiet like him. She got them all married before they were twenty-one, to girls from the furnace villages and the cedar swamps, and all seven couples lived within a shout of the old house. The Coxes were the best hunters in that country. They kept better than four hundred snares on six miles of brush fence for the partridge and the rabbits, and they drove the deer with hounds to where eight guns stood waiting. Every other week from frost to March a wagon went to Philadelphia. Susanna ran the bullets. She did it at the kitchen fire with a ladle and a brass mould, and trimmed them with a knife, and counted them into the pouches. In the morning she handed down the long gun from its pegs, and the horn and the pouch after it, because he was her husband and he put his hand out. She salted and hung what was not sold. She had never once eaten of it. The girls her sons married thought that was strange for about a month, and then it was only how Mother Cox was. Abel Horrocks was eighty-four that fall and still weaving check on a hand loom in Kensington. He woke one morning in the dark with fifteen peop

sections.heading: IV. Eight Guns
sections.text: Micah came along the fence at sunup with the long gun on his arm and found four hundred snares hanging empty. In twenty-eight years that had never happened. At the last gap he found the print. Somebody is walking my fence and letting out what I catch, he said. He looked up and saw an old man sitting under the holly with his hands on his knees. Micah thumbed back the hammer and brought the gun to his shoulder. He meant to shoot. The old man let him get that far and no farther. Micah’s finger would not close and his arms would not come down. He stood with the long gun leveled and could neither fire it nor lower it. The barrel began to shake. The spit ran out of the corner of his mouth, and it felt to him as if every one of his ribs had been stove in. At the house the sons said, Father is a long time on the fence. Their mother sent them to look. They came through the pines with their guns and saw him standing fixed, and saw what he was aiming at. They took the old man for some enemy of their father’s. All seven threw up their guns, and all seven stayed just as they were. There were eight men in a row among the trees with eight guns leveled, and no sound but their breathing. Then Susan

sections.heading: V. Ratsbane
sections.dateline: The Bible Christian chapel, North Third Street, Kensington · the Sunday after
sections.text: He was back at his loom by the middle of the week. On Sunday, at the tea the congregation took together after meeting, Brother Royle asked where he had been. In the Jerseys. With a hunter named Cox. And have you got him to leave off killing? Him and his seven sons and their seven wives. They are settled in it. I do not think they will be moved. Has the man no wife of his own? He has, said Abel. She signed our paper in the Front Street room when she was twelve years old. I ruled the line for her. It went around the table then who she was, and that she was not drowned. Some of the older women wept. After that the other thing began to go around. A young man put it into words. Then she kept her pledge and ran his bullets. For twenty-eight years. She handed him the gun every morning and salted down what he brought home, and sat on the wagon and sold it. Can one of ours do that? Not one of ours ever took a life, Abel said, and she did not. Her husband put out his hand and she put into it what he asked for. I asked her. In all that time she never once wished a deer dead. The wish was his. He held up his own hand, which was calloused across the fingers from the shuttle. A man with a whole

sections.heading: VI. The Meeting House
sections.dateline: Kensington, and the Jersey Market · that winter
sections.text: Another Sunday they asked him how it could be that fifteen rough people in the pines, who had never opened a book, were so ready. He told them what Susanna had shown him on the walk out to the stage road. There was a board meeting house at a fork of two sand roads, he said. It had no preacher and had not had one in years. Its roof was sound, though, and its floor was swept, and the graves beside it were kept clear of brush. When it was built, in the grandfather’s time, there had been a question of whose name should go first on the paper as the chief man of the work. The ironmaster who owned the furnace, a Philadelphia man, put down ten dollars. Old Hahn, who burned charcoal, put down twenty. They went up against each other by tens until the ironmaster said eighty. Hahn had ninety dollars in the world. He could see that if he said ninety the ironmaster would say a hundred and never feel it. So he said, I will give the ninety, and I will give myself, and my wife, and my seven sons and their wives, to keep this house as long as we live. The neighbors said a man can always get money, but this one has given his own back. They put his name first. Afterward they told him he was free of it

title: A Whole Hand
place: Philadelphia and the New Jersey Pine Barrens
logline: A merchant's daughter who has sworn off meat follows a Pine Barrens deer hunter home from the Jersey Market and runs his bullets for twenty-eight years.

verses.text: If a man offend a harmless, pure, and innocent person, the evil falls back upon that fool, like light dust thrown up against the wind.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the hunter Koka meets a monk on his alms round in the morning and blames him when he catches nothing all day. Meeting him again in the evening, he sets his dogs on him. The monk climbs a tree, and Koka pierces the soles of his feet with an arrow point until, in his agony, the monk’s robe slips off and falls over the hunter. The dogs, thinking the monk has fallen, tear their own master apart, then run off into the forest when the monk throws a stick and they see him. The monk asks the Buddha whether he is to blame and whether he is still a monk. The Buddha tells him he is innocent, and adds a story from a past life in which the same man, as a hungry physician, told boys a snake was a mynah bird and was killed when they threw it back at him.
bg.history:
Russian fur traders, the promyshlenniki, took hold of Kodiak Island in 1784, when Grigory Shelikhov’s men killed hundreds of Sugpiaq people at the Awa’uq massacre. In 1792 the company’s manager, Alexander Baranov, moved its post to St. Paul’s Harbor, Pavlovskaya Gavan, the beginning of today’s Kodiak. The company took hostages from Alutiiq villages and sent the men out in fleets of skin kayaks to hunt sea otter. The population of the region fell sharply in these years from hunting losses, hardship and disease.

On September 24, 1794, ten monks and novices from the Valaam Monastery on Lake Ladoga reached Kodiak. Their supplies never came as promised, and they tilled their gardens with wooden tools. They reported the company’s abuses to Russia, which set them against Baranov. One of them, Juvenaly, was killed on the mainland in 1796. Another, Herman, stayed on the islands until his death in 1837 and is honored as a saint. The superstition Volkov follows comes from accounts of peasant belief in White Russia: meeting a priest on the way to work was unlucky, and a man who had to go on would wait for the priest to pass, then walk back some distance so the spirits would think he had never met him, as a 1916 newspaper account describes it.

sections.heading: I. The Road
sections.text: Stepan Volkov went out after bear on the morning after the feast of the Protection, with four dogs and a spear and a musket he did not mean to fire. The dogs had come with him from Kamchatka. They were grey and yellow, with thick ruffs and tails that curled up over their backs, and he had fed them on seal meat and nothing else for a year so that the smell of meat would mean one thing to them. Their names were Volchok and Seryi and Buyan, and the bitch was Zhuchka, and she was the worst of them. The spear was a rogatina, the short heavy bear spear of the Siberian forests, with an iron crossbar under the blade so that a bear could not run up the shaft and take the man holding it. The musket was the company's. Powder at the harbor was handed out by the measure and written against a man's share, and a man who burned powder and came back without meat owed for the powder. Volkov already owed for a great deal. He had come out from Okhotsk six years before on a half share, and the half share had become a debt, the way it did for nearly everyone. He had been on the sea otter hunts, when the company sent the island men out in their skin boats by the hundred, two to a boat, down the coast to

sections.heading: II. The Letters
sections.text: The village was eleven houses dug into the slope above the beach, with grass growing on the roofs and smoke coming out of holes in the grass, so that from the trail it looked like the hillside was smoldering. There were racks of split salmon drying along the beach, red as cut cedar, and skin boats turned over on the stones. There were very few men. The company had taken the men in the spring for the otter hunt, and they had not come back yet, and some of them would not. The children saw Savvaty coming and ran down to the waterline, where the tide had left the sand smooth and hard. He drew the letters for them with a stick, big as a man's arm, and they shouted the names after him the way he had shouted them in the parish school on the Onega when he was six. Az. Buki. Vedi. Glagol. Dobro. A girl named Matrena could do the whole line by herself and would do it whether anybody asked her or not. Then the tide came in over the letters, as it did every day, and took them, and the next day he drew them again. Akulina fed him. She was a widow, or perhaps not; her husband had gone on the hunt the year before and not come back, and nobody had told her anything. Her son was eleven and was bein

sections.heading: III. The Spruce
sections.text: Volkov's dogs found bear sign before noon along a salmon creek, where the fish were dying in the shallows with their skins gone white, and the banks were trampled and littered with heads. They found the bed where a bear had lain up in the alders, pressed flat and still smelling of him. They found where he had gone up the mountain. It began to rain. The dogs ran the track up into the rocks above the trees and lost it on the bare stone in the rain and ran back and forth on the slope crying. Zhuchka cut her foot on something and came back holding it up. By the middle of the afternoon the cloud was down on the mountain so thick Volkov could not see the dogs, only hear them. He had not fired. That was something. He walked back down through the alders soaked to the waist and through the spruce in the half dark with nothing on his shoulders and the dogs strung out behind him with their tails down. At the fork, coming up the path from the bay, there was the black mantle again. Volkov stopped. He had done everything right that morning. He had spat and stood aside and walked back across the road, and none of it had worked, and here the thing was, in front of his face a second time, the way b

sections.heading: IV. The Stick
sections.text: The dogs had been told to take the black robe, and the black robe had come down out of the tree. They did what they had been fed a year on seal meat to do. Volkov's voice came out of the cloth once, muffled, and then again, and the dogs did not know it in there under the smell of the monk and the wet wool and the blood that was already running down the trunk. Or they knew it too late. Savvaty did not open his eyes. He would hear it the rest of his life, on certain nights, in a certain wind. It went on for longer than it should have. Then it stopped, and for a while there was only the sound of the dogs, and then not even that. When he opened his eyes it was nearly dark. The dogs had come out from under the folds of the mantle and were standing in a ring around the tree in the dripping half light, looking up, panting, waiting for the rest of what they had been told to take. He broke a dead branch off the trunk beside him and threw it down among them. They looked up at the sound and saw him: the monk, in the tree, in his cassock, whole. Zhuchka saw him first. She put her ears back flat against her skull. Then the others saw him, and all four of them stood very still and looked at him,

sections.heading: V. The Basin
sections.text: Father Paisy was seventy-one years old and had been at the monastery in the lake for forty of them. He had been a carpenter there and he was a gardener here, because somebody had to make potatoes grow in this ground and nobody else could. He had a long grey beard that he tucked into his belt when he dug, and very large hands, and he did not speak much, so that people at the harbor who had known him two years could not have told you what his voice sounded like. He was sitting up by the stove reading when Savvaty came in. He looked at the boy's face, and at the boots, and at the boy's shoulders with no mantle on them, and he did not ask anything. He put down the book and got up and heated water in the kettle and poured it into a basin with a handful of sea salt, and knelt on the floor and cut the boots off with his knife, a long careful cut down each side, because they could not be pulled off. Then he put the boy's feet in the basin. The water turned dark. Savvaty told him all of it, beginning at the beginning, at the fork in the path in the morning, the spitting and the standing aside and the walking back. The letters on the beach. The old man in the smoke. The dogs. The spear. The

sections.heading: VI. The Wind
sections.text: Men went up the north trail in the morning with lanterns they did not need, and came back with the mantle folded over a pole between two of them, and under it what there was of Stepan Volkov, which was not enough to need a coffin of any size. They buried it at the edge of the graveyard behind the church. Father Paisy read the service. Savvaty stood beside him on two crutches the carpenter at the harbor had made, and held the censer, and kept it swinging. The company men stood with their caps in their hands and did not look at the monks. Afterward some of them said in the barracks that the black-robes had set the dogs on him, that everybody knew they could do things like that, that they had been writing letters against him for a year and now they had found another way. The clerk wrote in the harbor book that the promyshlennik Volkov had been killed in the forest by his own dogs, which had run off, and that the matter had been reported to the manager. The manager did not come to the burial. Nobody had expected him to. What Volkov had owed for powder was written off, along with the rest of what he owed, and his musket went back to the store. The dogs were seen all that winter on the r

title: The Mantle
logline: A fur hunter who blames a young monk for his empty day sets his Kamchatka bear dogs on him in the spruce.

verses.text: Some people are born again; evil-doers go to hell; righteous people go to heaven; those who are free from all worldly desires attain Nirvana.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Tissa has taken his meals for twelve years at the house of a jeweler, who with his wife has looked after him like a parent. One day, while the jeweler is cutting meat with the elder sitting by, King Pasenadi sends a gem to be cleaned and pierced. The jeweler takes it with bloody hands, sets it down and goes in to wash, and the household's pet heron, smelling the blood, swallows it before the elder's eyes. The jeweler asks his wife and sons, then accuses the elder. His wife pleads that in all those years she has never seen a flaw in him, and that they would do better to become slaves; the jeweler answers that all of them sold as slaves would not pay for the stone. He binds the elder's head with a rope and beats him until blood runs from his head, ears and nose. The heron comes to drink the blood, and the jeweler kills it with a kick. Only then does the elder tell him to look in the bird, saying he would have died rather than speak while it lived. The jeweler finds the gem, falls at his feet and is forgiven ("it was neither your fault nor mine"), but the elder vows never again to go under anyone's roof and to take alms only at the door, says a short verse about food cooked "little by little, house by house," and soon dies of the beating. The heron is reborn in the jeweler's wife's womb, the jeweler in hell, his wife in heaven, and the elder passes into final Nibbāna.
bg.history:
Cape Coral was begun in 1957 by two brothers from Baltimore, Leonard and Jack Rosen, whose Gulf American Land Corporation dredged the mangrove flats across the Caloosahatchee from Fort Myers into building lots; the city has more than 400 miles of canals. Since Hammond Stadium opened in Fort Myers in 1991, the Minnesota Twins have held spring training there, and every February and March brings Minnesotans south to watch. The 2011 Twins went from first place the year before to last in the American League Central, at 63 wins and 99 losses.
