The great blue heron, the largest heron in North America and up to four and a half feet tall, lives mostly on fish and is at home wherever there is fish-bearing water, however built up. The Kesslers, the Lunds, Father Leo and the street are invented.

The Baltimore Catechism, issued in 1885 after the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore, was the standard Catholic school text in the United States from then until the late 1960s, and generations of children learned its questions and answers by heart; the passage here is from No. 1, the edition for First Communion classes. In Lent, Catholics abstain from meat on Fridays, and the Stations of the Cross are prayed especially on Lenten Fridays. A subdural hematoma, bleeding between the brain and its covering after a blow, can take days to show itself, with headache and growing confusion, and is especially common in the elderly.

sections.heading: I. Twelve Years
sections.text: Father Leo Brandl came down to Cape Coral in 1999, when the Diocese of St. Cloud retired him, because his lungs could not take another January in Stearns County. He was seventy. He had been a priest forty-three years, in six parishes with steeples you could see from the next town and a hundred Schmitts and Theisens apiece. He arrived in Florida with two suitcases, a set of golf clubs he did not use, and the name of one family he knew. Roger and Mary Jo Kessler had come down from St. Cloud three years before. Roger had a jewelry store in a strip mall on Del Prado Boulevard, between a Subway and a place that did nails, and they had a ranch house with a pool cage on a canal off the Caloosahatchee, one of the four hundred miles of canals the developers had dug out of the mangroves in the fifties to sell lots to people from Ohio. Mary Jo had been in Father Leo's eighth-grade religion class in Albany in 1967. The first night he was in town she had him to supper, and he came the next night too, and after that, for twelve years, he ate his supper at their table every night of the week except Sundays, when he said the nine o'clock at the parish and ate with the pastor. He had his chair. He

sections.heading: II. The Pearl
sections.text: It was the third Friday in Lent. Roger had been out at the mouth of the river since noon and come home with six sheepshead, and Mary Jo wanted them for supper before Stations, so he was at the cleaning table at a quarter to six with his hands red to the wrists. Father Leo was in his lawn chair. Herb was at the end of the dock. The radio on the table had the scores from the afternoon; the Twins had lost again, the way they were going to lose all that year. A boat came down the canal, slow, a white center-console with two big outboards, and swung in to the dock. It was Gary Lund's son-in-law. Gary Lund owned four car dealerships on Pine Island Road and was on television every night of the week in a gold paper crown, as the Car King of Cape Coral, and he was the biggest customer the store had, and the only one Roger had ever been afraid of. The son-in-law did not get off the boat. He held out a little blue velvet bag. Gary says clean it, drill it, put it on a chain. He wants it Sunday for Cheryl. It's their fortieth. Roger knew what it was before he had it open. It was the pearl from Gary's grandmother, which he had been allowed to see once, in the store, and had not been allowed to t

sections.heading: III. Stations
sections.text: He asked again, and again. It got dark. The lights came on under the pool cages up and down the canal, and the dock light came on over the table on its timer, and the bugs began. Father Leo sat in the lawn chair and said no, Roger, I don't have it, and that was all he said. Roger was a man who had never in his life hit anybody, not his kids, not a dog. He was sixty-one years old and on blood-pressure pills and sang bass in the choir. Afterward he could not have said how it began, only that he had been talking and then he had the dock line off the cleat in his hands, and he had tied the old man to the piling by the chest with it, the way you would tie a boat, and was standing over him with the fish club from the table, the short heavy billy he used to quiet the fish. And then he was not talking. He hit him on the head. He hit him again. The blood came out of Father Leo's hair and ran down into his eyes, and then it came out of his ears, and out of his nose, and his eyes were open very wide and looked as if they were pushing out of his face, and he did not say anything at all. He went down sideways against the piling as far as the rope would let him, and lay with his cheek on the boa

sections.heading: IV. At the Door
sections.dateline: Southwest Forty-Seventh Terrace · the last week of March
sections.text: Mary Jo found Roger on the dock when she came home from Stations, sitting next to the dead heron with the pearl in his open hand. She went straight down the street to Father Leo's and banged on the door until he opened it. He had washed. There was a cut in his scalp and a bruise coming up the side of his face like weather. He said he had bumped it. He said he was fine. He would not go to the hospital for her either. The next evening at six he did not come to supper. He came down the street instead, slowly, and stood at the Kesslers' front door and rang, and when Mary Jo opened it he would not come in. She brought him a plate, and he ate a few bites of it standing on the step with the plate in his hand, and gave it back to her, and thanked her, and went on to the next house. He did that every night that week. He went down Southwest Forty-Seventh Terrace in the evening the way the mailman went down it in the morning, and rang at the doors of people he had married and buried and heard the confessions of, Minnesotans and Michiganders and a family from Puerto Rico, and stood on their welcome mats and would not come in. They thought he was getting confused. They brought him whatever was

sections.heading: V. Heaven, Purgatory, and Hell
sections.text: Roger pleaded to manslaughter in the fall and went to the state prison up at Raiford. Mary Jo drove up to see him the first Saturday of every month, five hours each way. He wrote her every week in the beginning, and then less, and the letters were mostly about the food and the noise and a man from Ohio in the next bunk. In 2017 his heart stopped in the yard. He was sixty-seven. She buried him in St. Cloud next to his parents. Kyle's girlfriend had a baby that December, a boy, and they named him Leo, and when Kyle's girlfriend went back to Fort Myers in 2013, the boy stayed with his grandmother on the canal. He was a tall, thin, silent child who ate raw shrimp out of the bait bucket when nobody was looking. From the time he could walk he went down to the end of the dock in the evenings and stood on one leg at the edge of the boards, watching the water, without moving, for as long as anyone would let him. The first time Mary Jo saw him do it she sat down on the lanai step and could not get up for a while. Look at that, she said to Kyle. Herb's back. It was a family joke after that, and she was the only one who did not quite say it as a joke. Mary Jo died in the spring of 2019, in the

title: The Cleaning Table
logline: On a Friday in Lent, a Minnesota jeweler on a Cape Coral canal sets a car dealer's natural pearl down on his fish-cleaning table.

verses.text: Not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains, is there known a spot in the whole world where a man might be freed from an evil deed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, three parties of monks travel to see the Buddha. The first, eating in a village, sees a kitchen fire catch the thatch; a burning bundle of grass floats into the air and a crow flies into it and is burned. The second is aboard a ship that stops dead in mid-ocean. The passengers cast lots for the unlucky one, and three times the lot falls on the captain’s young wife; the captain has her jewels removed and a jar of sand tied to her neck so that he need not watch her struggle, and she is thrown overboard. The third party, seven monks, is shut in a cave for seven days by a fallen rock that no one can move and that at last rolls away by itself. The Buddha explains each by an old deed: the crow was a farmer who burned a balky ox in straw; the woman had drowned her faithful dog with a pot of sand; the seven monks, as cowherd boys, had stopped up a lizard in an anthill for seven days and then let it go. Asked whether there is anywhere a person can escape a deed, he speaks the verse.
bg.history:
News of California gold reached Valparaíso in 1848, and Chileans were among the first to arrive by sea. Many were experienced miners; they brought the wooden gold pan, the batea, and the ore-crushing “Chili mill.” Chilean companies often worked claims with hired peons, which American miners resented. In San Francisco they settled at the foot of Telegraph Hill in a quarter called Chilecito, Little Chile, which a nativist gang, the Hounds, attacked in July 1849. In 1850 the new state passed the Foreign Miners’ Tax of twenty dollars a month, and many Chileans and Mexicans left the diggings. The limestone country of Calaveras County, where Chili Gulch keeps the Chileans’ name, is full of caves; one near Cave City was already being shown to visitors in 1850. The Carmen, her captain, the rancho and everyone in the story are invented.

There are no crows or ravens native to South America, so the bird was new to these men. The proverb ño Bartolo quotes is given as it stands in the anonymous Refranes de la lengua castellana printed at Barcelona in 1815. The second saying, the old formula of the public crier, closes Tirso de Molina’s El burlador de Sevilla (about 1630), where the stone guest speaks it twice. Both are quoted in the original Spanish; the English beside them is this story’s own.

sections.heading: I. The Black Bird
sections.dateline: A rancho on the road down to Stockton · August 1850
sections.text: That summer three parties of Chileans set out, each without knowing of the others, to see ño Bartolo at San Francisco. The first was five men walking down out of the southern mines. That spring the Americans had put a tax of twenty dollars a month on every foreigner who dug, and these five had paid it once and could not pay it twice. Two days above Stockton they came to a rancho where a Sonoran woman fed travelers under a ramada thatched with tule. She would not take their money. She sat them in the shade and gave them beans and tortillas, and while the meat was frying she asked for the news from the mines, and they gave her all they had. The fat caught. The flame went up the post and into the tule faster than anyone could stand. It was the hour when the wind comes up the valley, and the wind took one whole bundle of the thatch off the roof, burning, and carried it out over the yard as high as a mast. A black bird was crossing just then. They had no such bird at home. In two years none of them had found a better name for it than cuervo, out of the story of Noah. It was flying straight and low the way those birds do, going somewhere. It put its neck directly into the burning bundle.

sections.heading: II. Dead Calm
sections.dateline: The bark Carmen, eleven degrees north · June 1850
sections.text: The second party came by sea. The bark Carmen was forty days out of Valparaíso with ninety passengers and a cargo of flour when the wind left her. For nineteen days she lay in the same water. The sails hung. The pitch came up soft between the deck planks, and the water in the casks went down to a hand’s depth and was served out by the cup. Sharks lay in the shadow of the hull the whole time and did not trouble to move. By the twelfth day the passengers were saying that somebody on board was unlucky. By the nineteenth they had a hat and ninety-odd dry beans in it, all white but one. The captain was a man named Rozas, and he had his wife aboard. She was nineteen. He had married her in March and would not leave her behind. Her name was Mercedes, and she was the prettiest thing any of them had seen since the hills above the harbor went under the horizon. She put her hand in the hat with the rest, and her hand came out with the black bean. Again, the passengers said, and nobody argued. They put the bean back and shook the hat. She drew it a second time. They shook it a third time, and held it higher, and she reached up and drew it again. Then they went aft in a body and looked Captain R

sections.heading: III. Seven Sleeping Places
sections.dateline: A limestone gulch in Calaveras County · July 1850
sections.text: The third party was seven men from the valley of the Choapa, above Illapel. They had come up as peons for a patrón who had since died of fever, and they had worked their way from camp to camp with one wooden batea among them. They also were going down to San Francisco to see ño Bartolo, who was from their country. One evening they came to a camp of Sonorans in a gulch, and asked for a place to lie. The Sonorans kept a cave for people passing through. It was dry, and there was a shelf at the back with room for exactly seven men to sleep side by side. The seven thanked them and went in and slept. In the night a rock as big as a chapel came down the opposite slope. It rolled across the gulch and stopped in the mouth of the cave like a stopper in a jar. The Sonorans found it at daylight. We gave them that cave, they said. We will get them out. They sent up and down the country, and men came from seven camps. There were Chileans and Sonorans and Frenchmen, and a Kanaka sailor with a ship’s tackle, and a dozen of the same Americans who had gone round in May with the tax collector. They brought bars and mules and powder. They dug under it and it settled. They blasted it and it blackened.

sections.heading: IV. The Scale
sections.dateline: Chilecito, under Telegraph Hill · the end of August
sections.text: The Chileans lived in tents and board shanties at the foot of Telegraph Hill, and the Americans called the place Little Chile. Bartolo Araya had a tent there with a table in it. He was past seventy. He had gone down the silver mines of Atacama as a boy with a hide sack on his back, and afterward he had spent forty years alone in that desert as a cateador, looking for veins. Now he kept a scale. The storekeepers’ scales in San Francisco were known to lie, so the Chileans brought their dust to him. He weighed it for nothing, wrote the weight on a paper, and put his mark under it. He was weighing when they came in, fifteen people into a tent made for four. He finished. Then he heard the five, and the three, and the seven, in that order. He did not interrupt any of them. Rosa was the only one who wept. He turned to the five first. In Colchagua there was a man who had a young ox. It would not take the yoke. It went a little way and lay down. He beat it, and it got up and went a little way and lay down again. He was a whole day at it. At the end of the day he said, Very well, lie there as long as you like. He went and got wheat straw. He bound it around the ox from head to tail the way y

title: A Jar of Sand
logline: Three parties of Chilean forty-niners, by road, by sea and out of a sealed cave, bring what they saw to an old man who weighs gold.

verses.text: Not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains, is there known a spot in the whole world where death could not overcome (the mortal).
verses.cite: Dhammapada 128 (numbered 127 in the Project Gutenberg text)

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Sākyan noble Suppabuddha holds a grudge against the Buddha, who left Suppabuddha's daughter to go forth and later fell out with Suppabuddha's son, Devadatta. One day Suppabuddha sits drinking in the street to block the Buddha's way to a meal, and will not make way however many times he is asked. The Buddha turns back and smiles, and tells Ānanda that in seven days Suppabuddha will be swallowed by the earth at the foot of the stairway on the ground floor of his palace. Hearing this from a spy, Suppabuddha moves to the top of his seven-storied palace, has the stairway taken away and the doors barred, and sets strong men at every door with orders to turn him back. On the seventh day his state horse breaks loose below; he rises to catch it, the doors open, the stairways return, his own guards throw him down from floor to floor, and at the foot of the stairs the earth opens and takes him.
bg.history:
By the First World War, Butte sat on top of one of the richest copper deposits in the world, and most of its mines belonged to the Anaconda Company. On June 8, 1917, a fire in the Granite Mountain shaft spread through the connected tunnels of the Speculator Mine and killed 168 men, most of them suffocated; a few survived by sealing themselves behind makeshift bulkheads. To work at all, a miner needed a company-issued rustling card, which could be revoked at any time and served as a blacklist against union men. When copper prices fell after the war, the mine owners cut wages by a dollar a day, the miners struck in February 1919, and federal troops kept the city under occupation until the end of 1920. Montana's statewide prohibition took effect at the end of 1918, and Butte, which had voted against it, went on drinking out of kitchen stills.

Butte's Jewish community dated to 1875. Its merchants built some of the city's leading stores, among them Symons' department store on West Park Street, and its Reform temple, B'nai Israel, was dedicated in 1904 at Washington and Galena Streets. A few blocks east lay the Cabbage Patch, more than two hundred shanties between Mercury and Silver Streets, with no electricity or running water, where miners sometimes shared a bed in turns by shift. Underneath all of it the Hill was cut through with tunnels, and later in the century the ground over the old workings sank by as much as twelve feet across central Butte.

sections.heading: I. The Watch
sections.text: Ferdinand Kahn had come to Butte in 1881 with a peddler's pack and a pair of boots that let in water, and by 1917 he owned one of the tallest buildings in Butte. The Kahn Block stood seven stories high on West Park Street, red brick and terra cotta, with his name cut into the stone over the door and a light court in the middle that went straight up through every floor to a roof of glass, so that on a clear day a woman buying gloves on the main floor could look up through six galleries of iron railing and see the sky. Kahn's sold silk from Lyon and pianos from Chicago and men's suits that came up from the basement tailors in two days. Kahn himself kept his office on the seventh floor, and from his window he could look across the whole of the Hill, the gallows frames and the smokestacks and the ore dumps and the shacks, and he liked to say that he could see every dollar in Butte from there, and that most of them were on their way to him. He had a son, Julius, and a daughter, Sophie. In 1912 Sophie married a young doctor from Chicago named Nathan Brill, whose father had been a tinsmith in Kovno and whose mother still could not write her name. Kahn had not liked it. He had given them a

sections.heading: II. Julius
sections.text: The son came down after him. That was the part the father could least forgive. Julius Kahn was twenty-six and had been to Harvard for a year and had come home without saying why. In the spring of 1918 he walked down the hill one Sunday to see what his sister's husband was doing in the Cabbage Patch, and he stayed. He swept the floor. He boiled the instruments. He carried the bag when Matti was too sick to carry it. Through the winter of the influenza he worked beside Doc for nineteen hours a day, and the women of the Patch said he was nearly as good as Doc himself, and Julius heard them say it. He was quick, and he had ideas. A real dispensary, brick, with beds. A ward for the consumptives. His father's money. His own name over the door, since his father's name was already over enough doors. Doc listened to all of it and said no. He said it gently, the way he said everything. He said the Patch did not need a building with anybody's name on it. It needed somebody to come when it called. Julius did not take it gently. He went back up the hill in January 1919, and in February, when the company cut the wage by a dollar a day and the men walked out and the soldiers came in with bayonets

sections.heading: III. The Street
sections.dateline: North Main Street · a Friday in July, 1919
sections.text: The state had gone dry at the end of December. Butte had not noticed. There were stills in kitchens all over the Hill and in half the cellars uptown, and in the Patch a man called the King sold whiskey out of a washtub at fifty cents a pint, and nobody in the city government drank any less than before, only more quietly. Ferdinand Kahn drank on North Main Street, in the middle of the afternoon, sitting on a kitchen chair in the middle of the road. He had found out from somebody that Doc was going to supper that Friday with the Trevorrows, a Cornish family on North Main whose youngest he had pulled through the influenza, and he had his driver bring the Pierce-Arrow up the hill and stop it crossways, and he had the driver carry out a chair from the car, and he sat in it with a fruit jar of the King's whiskey on his knee and his hat tipped back and waited. Ore wagons went around him. A streetcar stopped and rang its bell and could not go around him and stopped. Men came out of the saloons that were now called soft-drink parlors and stood in the doors to watch. Doc came up the hill at half past five with Matti Lahti carrying the bag. Matti saw the chair first. Mr. Kahn, said Matti, fro

sections.heading: IV. The Seventh Floor
sections.dateline: The Kahn Block, West Park Street · the same night
sections.text: Dunphy told it to Kahn word for word in the office on the seventh floor, standing, with his hat in his hands. Kahn did not laugh. He had known that man for seven years. He had seen what that man's diagnoses were worth uptown. When that man said a superintendent had a year, the superintendent had a year, to the week. When that man said a child would live, the child lived, and when he said it would not, the mother might as well go and see the undertaker. Kahn knew all this, and so he did not laugh. He sat in his leather chair and thought about it with his fingertips together, the way he had once thought about a shipment of Irish linen that was coming by way of Panama. He didn't say seven days, he said at last. He said seven days, on the ground floor, at the foot of the stairs. Those were his words? Those were his words. Then I won't be on the ground floor, said Ferdinand Kahn. And I won't be at the foot of the stairs. And in a week that man is a liar in front of the whole town. The next morning there was a card in the windows of Kahn's that said CLOSED FOR INVENTORY. By noon the brass bed from his house on Park Street had come up in the freight elevator to the seventh floor, and his

sections.heading: V. The Dispensary
sections.text: By Sunday the whole town had it. They had it in Dublin Gulch and in Meaderville and in Finntown, in the boardinghouses and the soft-drink parlors and the cribs on Venus Alley. There were bets in the cigar stores on Main Street, three to one against Kahn, and the odds got shorter every day. The dispensary was full that night, as it was full every night. Men sat on the bench along the wall waiting to be listened to with the stethoscope, holding their caps, with the cough in them that came up out of the deep levels with the rock dust and never went back down. A Serbian woman sat on the floor with a baby with croup. An Irish widow from Corktown was there with her boy's broken arm. Two of the fourteen men from the Kahn Block were there, off shift, because they had been coming to Doc for their lungs since before February and saw no reason to stop. One of them told it. The iron straps. The stairs cut off ten feet up in the air. The elevator chained at seven. Somebody laughed. Doc did not. He was listening to the Serbian baby's chest, with his head bent down close, and when he had finished listening he wrapped the baby up again and handed it back and said what to do with the kettle and the

sections.heading: VI. The General
sections.dateline: The Kahn Block · the seventh day
sections.text: The week went by on the seventh floor. Kahn read his account books. He played the Victrola, Caruso and then Sousa and then Caruso again. He drank less of the bonded whiskey than he had meant to, and slept badly in the brass bed, and in the mornings he stood at the iron railing of the light court and looked down six floors at the main floor of his store, at the glass counters under their dust sheets and the oak staircase ending in the air, and counted the days. Sophie came once, on the Wednesday, and stood across the street on the sidewalk with the boy and looked up at the seventh floor windows. He did not go to the window. The guards played pinochle on the landings. Down below in the alley, in the stable behind the store where the last of the delivery horses were kept, his saddle horse stood in its box stall and was groomed twice a day and walked in the alley in the evening. The horse was a tall dapple grey, seventeen hands, a Kentucky saddler that Kahn had bought in Louisville in 1910 and ridden at the head of every Fourth of July parade since. It had been called Kaiser until April of 1917, when it was no longer wise to call anything in Butte by that name, and then Kahn had rename

sections.heading: VII. The Rope
sections.text: It did not close all the way. It left a hole at the foot of the grand staircase about the size of a grave, square-edged, with the cut ends of the marble showing white. The company sent engineers that evening. They lowered a lantern on a rope, a hundred feet and then two hundred, and the lantern went down past rock and old timbering and came to nothing they could see, and they pulled it up again. They said it must be an old working, a drift off some claim from the eighties that was never mapped, and that the whole Hill was hollow under Butte like a honeycomb and everybody knew it, and they wrote that down. The old men who kept a minyan in a back room on East Galena Street, who had never liked Ferdinand Kahn and had never pretended to, said that the earth had opened its mouth for Korah too, in the wilderness, and that Korah had also been a rich man, and had also had a great deal to say about who should step aside for whom. The fourteen men collected their five dollars for the seventh day and went back to the Patch. None of them would ever talk about it, except the one from the fourth floor, who said only that the door had opened and he had done what he was there to do. Doc was in the

title: The Seventh Floor
logline: In Prohibition Butte, a department-store king blocks his son-in-law's path in the street, and hears what the doctor says about it.

verses.text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.

bg.commentary: The Group of Six are the standing troublemakers of the monastic rule. In this story the younger Group of Seventeen have made a lodging ready, and the Six arrive and say, We are older; this belongs to us. The Seventeen answer, We will not give it to you; we were the first to make it ready. The Six strike them, and the Seventeen, in fear of death, scream at the top of their lungs. The Buddha hears the outcry, asks what it was, and lays down the rule against striking a blow. Then he says that a person should reflect that others tremble at the rod and fear death just as he does, and speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story. The next story in the commentary is its sequel, in which the Six raise their hands again.
bg.history:
Dormont is a borough of less than a square mile, four miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, that filled with houses when the streetcar tunnel opened the South Hills. It holds more than ten thousand people to the square mile, and a great many of its houses have no driveway. The parking chair is the custom, strongest in and around Pittsburgh, of marking a street space you have shoveled out with a kitchen or lawn chair. It has no standing in law and is generally honored anyway; photographs of it go back at least to the 1950s. In 1994, according to press accounts, the Dormont police removed the markers from some two hundred spaces after too many complaints. Nevada Avenue and everyone on it are invented.

The storm of March 12–14, 1993, left about twenty-five inches in Pittsburgh, 23.6 of them on Saturday the thirteenth, at two to three inches an hour; the downtown St. Patrick’s Day parade went ahead that day, and the Turnpike and most roads were closed. The Thanksgiving-weekend storm of 1950 left about thirty inches, and tanks were used to help clear it. William Cullen Bryant drafted “Thanatopsis” as a very young man in western Massachusetts, and it was first printed in 1817; generations of American schoolchildren learned it by heart. The lines here follow the text of his collected Poems. The poem ends by asking its hearer to go to the grave not “like the quarry-slave at night, / Scourged to his dungeon,” but as one who lies down to sleep.

sections.heading: I. The Dig
sections.text: It started to snow on Friday night, and all day Saturday it came down two and three inches an hour, with thunder in it. Downtown they held the St. Patrick’s parade anyway. By dark there were two feet on the ground in Dormont and the Turnpike was shut. Sunday came up blue and bitter, with a wind. The borough plow reached Nevada Avenue about nine and did what a plow does on a street of parked cars. It opened one lane down the middle and laid a wall against every car on the block, chest high and packed like concrete. Nevada Avenue is brick foursquares shoulder to shoulder, built in the twenties for men who rode the streetcar to work, and not one of them has a driveway. Parking is on the even side. There had been a custom about that for longer than most people on the street had been alive. You dug out your space, you stood a kitchen chair in it, and it was yours until the street was bare. Nobody had ever written it down. The houses at 1245 and 1247 had been cut into apartments, and that winter seventeen people lived in them, none over thirty-one. There were four nursing students, two boys from the Art Institute, a line cook, two brothers from Altoona who hung drywall, and a respiratory

sections.heading: II. The Porch
sections.text: Mrs. Haney lived at 1249, between them. She was eighty-one. She had come to that house as a bride in 1936, and nothing on the street was older except the sycamores. She had been at her front window since the trucks pulled up. She came out on the porch in her husband’s car coat and a pair of galoshes, with nothing on her head. What was that? She did not have a big voice. But everybody on Nevada Avenue under the age of sixty had at one time or another been sent to her door with a covered dish or a snow shovel, and they stopped. The nephew let go of the coat. The girl came up out of the snow with her mouth wide open. The young ones told her, all at once. The Leskos looked at their shovels. Stanley, said Mrs. Haney. Put it down. He put it down. Nobody raises a hand to anybody on this street. Not a hand and not a shovel. Not over a parking place, and not over anything else. Mrs. Haney, with respect. Stan Lesko was breathing hard. Four winters before he had had his chest opened at Mercy Hospital, and he had just spent twenty-seven hours in a truck. We got forty-two years here. That has to count. I was fifteen years on this street the day your father backed his truck up to that house, Sta

sections.heading: III. The Brick
sections.text: After that it was simply how Nevada Avenue was. You could chair a space you had dug, and you could not lay a hand on anybody. People who moved onto the street were told both things the first time it snowed, and as a rule it was a Lesko who told them. The next winter the complaints about chairs got so bad across the borough that the Dormont police went around and took them out of two hundred spaces. They say the officer who worked Nevada Avenue took every chair on the block but one. That was later. On the Monday morning Mrs. Haney came to her window at six, as she always did. The wind had dropped. Five kitchen chairs stood along the curb at 1245 and 1247, no two alike. In front of 1251 a pickup was nosed in behind a chair she knew from Stan Lesko’s own kitchen. And in front of her house, where the plow wall had stood as high as the porch rail when she went to bed, a space had been cut down to the brick, square at the corners, long enough for a Plymouth. The red chair stood in the middle of it. She never did find out which of them dug it. A little new snow had come in the night, and it lay on the seat.

title: The Parking Chair
logline: After the 1993 blizzard, seventeen young renters dig out a curb in a Pittsburgh streetcar suburb, and six longtime neighbors come to take it.

verses.text: All men tremble at punishment, all men love life; remember that thou art like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.

bg.commentary: The Group of Six are the troublemakers of the monastic rule, the monks whose misconduct prompts one regulation after another. In the story just before this one, they come upon lodgings that the younger Group of Seventeen have made ready, say We are older; this belongs to us, and beat them out of it, and the Buddha, hearing the screams, forbids striking. This story is the sequel. The Six strike the Seventeen again, and this time the Seventeen answer with threatening gestures, raising their hands as if to strike back. The Buddha hears the outcry, asks what it is, and forbids the threatening gesture too, saying that a monk should consider that others tremble at the rod and hold life dear just as he does, and so should neither strike nor kill.
bg.history:
The Palouse of southeastern Washington is a country of steep, rolling hills built of wind-blown silt, almost all of it plowed for wheat and legumes since the 1880s; it is now the most important lentil-growing region in the country. Above it stands Steptoe Butte, a quartzite island about a thousand feet higher than the hills around it and some twelve miles north of Colfax, from which Mount Spokane can be seen seventy miles away. Oakesdale, named for a railroad official, is a small wheat town in Whitman County with its own school. Lois Kincaid, her route, Bus 2 and all the families on it are invented.

The Westminster Shorter Catechism, completed in 1647, was written to teach children the Reformed faith in 107 questions and answers, and generations of Presbyterian children learned it by heart. In 1968 the war in Vietnam reached its worst year for Americans: the National Archives counts 16,899 U.S. military deaths with a date in that year, more than in any other. Young men registered for the draft at eighteen with their local boards, and the war came into rural living rooms every night on the television news.

sections.heading: I. The Gum
sections.text: Lois Kincaid drove the north route for the Oakesdale school, forty-four miles of gravel and two of blacktop, and she had driven it since the fall of 1961, when the district bought a second bus and nobody else applied. She was out of the yard at ten to seven. She came back at a quarter past eight with forty-one children, or forty if one of the Hoffs had an earache, and she knew every one of them by the back of the head. The bus was a 1959 Chevrolet with a Wayne body, and it had a long mirror over the windshield, a strip of glass the width of the aisle and a little more, bent so that it held the whole bus at once. In it Lois could see forty-one children and the gray ribbon of road going away behind them out the back door. It was the first thing she looked at after the road and the last thing before it. She did not need to turn around. Children thought she had an eye in the back of her head, and she let them. The hills that year were already worked down for fall seeding when school began, brown and smooth as the side of a loaf, and so steep in places that the Rademachers ran a combine that leveled itself on the slope like a man leaning into a wind. Out the left-hand windows on the nor

sections.heading: II. Bang
sections.text: It held through football. It held through the election, which the bus argued about for a week in the voices of its fathers, and through the first hard frost, when she let the engine run twenty minutes in the yard before seven so the heater would have a chance, and the heater still only warmed the first four rows. The big boys sat in the middle where it was warmer and said that was why. The little ones sat in the back in their snowsuits and bounced over the axle on the washboard and liked it. Danny wrote that they had been moving around a good deal and that he was fine. He asked whether his dad had got the winter wheat in before the rain. He asked whether she was still driving the old crate, and said to tell whoever was in the back seat now that it was the best seat on the bus, because of the bounce. Gary Rademacher would be eighteen on the ninth of December. Everybody on the bus knew it, because his mother had told everybody at church, the way you tell people about an operation. His older brother Ron was a Marine and had been at a place in the north of the country all spring that had been on the television, and had come home in October and was living in the bunkhouse and did not co

sections.heading: III. The Mailbox
sections.text: Gary registered on the tenth of December, the day after his birthday, at the board in Colfax, and his mother told everybody. He went back out for basketball after Christmas and did not make it all the way back in shape, and he sat on the bench and was the one who went in to foul. At some point in the winter he moved up a seat, and then another, until he was sitting in the second row behind Lois, where the heat was, and he talked to her, mostly about the Rademachers' combine and whether a man could get on at the elevator, and once, only once, in March, about his brother in the bunkhouse, who he said had stopped sleeping. Danny wrote that he was being moved to a desk in a base camp to draw maps, which he called the luckiest thing that had ever happened to anybody, and after that his letters were longer and had drawings in them. One was of the long mirror, from memory, with forty-one heads in it, and a little square up in the corner for the card he had heard about, with two lines in it too small to read. She kept it in the glove compartment with the rest. The card stayed where it was. Nobody hit anybody on Bus 2 that year, and nobody pointed anything at anybody. By spring it was simpl

title: Rule Two
logline: A Palouse farm wife whose son is in Vietnam drives the school bus, where six older boys want the back seat seventeen children scrubbed clean.

verses.text: He who seeking his own happiness punishes or kills beings who also long for happiness, will not find happiness after death.
He who seeking his own happiness does not punish or kill beings who also long for happiness, will find happiness after death.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha is walking into Sāvatthī for alms when he sees a company of boys beating a house snake with a stick. He asks what they are doing, and why. They say they are afraid it will bite them. He tells them that whoever strikes another to make himself happy will not find happiness, and that those who seek happiness for themselves should not strike others, and he speaks the two verses. At the end of the teaching the boys enter the stream, the first stage of awakening. Read the full commentary story; the same incident is told in the Udāna (2.3).
bg.history:
The armed citizen militias of the 1990s grew out of two standoffs with federal agents: the 1992 siege at Ruby Ridge in northern Idaho, in which Randy Weaver’s wife and son were killed, and the 1993 siege at Waco, Texas. By the mid-1990s there were militia groups in all fifty states. On April 19, 1995, the second anniversary of the fire at Waco, the Oklahoma City bombing killed 168 people, nineteen of them children, many in the day care center in the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building. The attention that followed split many groups, and on June 15, 1995, a Senate Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on the militia movement. The Camas Prairie Volunteers are invented.

The gopher snake, also called the bull snake, is Idaho’s largest snake. When threatened it flattens its head, hisses, and shakes its tail in dry leaves so that it sounds like a rattlesnake, and Idaho Fish and Game notes that many are killed for it; it has round pupils and no rattle, eats rodents including ground squirrels, and may live about fifteen years in the wild. Gopher snakes and western rattlesnakes share the hot, low canyons of west-central Idaho, where a survey of Hells Canyon in 1995–1999 found them among the commonest reptiles. The Declaration is quoted from the National Archives transcription.

sections.heading: I. The Reading
sections.dateline: Salmon River, Idaho County, Idaho · June 1995
sections.text: Every morning of the muster they ran the flag up a lodgepole on the Hollister bar at seven, and Orval Pruitt read to them. Orval was seventy-three and had been a gunner’s mate on a destroyer off Okinawa, and he read in the voice he used at the Grange for the minutes, from a pocket Constitution the size of a deck of cards that had the Declaration in the front. He never read the whole thing. He read down to the part about Safety and Happiness and closed it, and the men said amen or nothing, and the women went back to the cook tent, and the boys went back to whatever they had been doing before somebody made them stand still. There were nineteen families that year on the bar, which belonged to Dale Hollister and ran a quarter mile along the river below the town, cheatgrass and hackberry and basalt, hot by ten in the morning. They called themselves the Camas Prairie Volunteers. They met the second Tuesday at the Grange hall in Grangeville. They had started in the fall of 1992, after what happened to the Weaver family up at Ruby Ridge, which was in the same state and close enough to drive to, and they had grown after Waco. Most of them had worked in the woods or at the mills, or had catt

sections.heading: II. The Woodpile
sections.dateline: The Hollister bar · the third morning
sections.text: There were eleven boys on the bar that year between eight and fourteen, and they ran in a pack, the way boys on a river do. Cody Hollister was thirteen and in charge of them because the bar was his father’s. They had wooden rifles Dale had cut on the bandsaw, and the men let them drill at the back of the line in the mornings, and the rest of the day they were in the river or under the cook tent or up in the rocks looking for arrowheads they were not supposed to keep. Jesse Ward’s little brother found the snake. He was five, and he went to get kindling for his mother from the woodpile behind the cook tent and came back without any, white, and would not say why. Jesse went to look. Then all of them went. It lay along the bottom log in the shade, as long as Cody was tall, yellow-brown with dark blotches down its back. When the boys came close it pulled itself into a loose coil and lifted its head and made the head go wide and flat, and it hissed, a long hard breath like a tire going down, and it shook its tail in the dry hackberry leaves under the pile so that they buzzed. Rattler, Jesse said. Nobody had to say it. Cody sent Travis for the shovel. The others got sticks from the woodpi

sections.heading: III. The Medic
sections.text: Della made rounds every morning on the bar with a green tackle box full of bandages. She was forty-seven and worked nights in the emergency room at the hospital in Grangeville, and on the river she went from camp to camp after breakfast the way she went from bed to bed: blisters, sunburn, a fishhook in a thumb, a toddler with an ear, ticks. She was coming back from the river with the five-gallon jug on her shoulder when she saw the ring of boys at the woodpile and heard the shovel hit. She set the jug down. What are you doing? Killing a rattler, Cody said. He did not look at her. He was breathing hard. Why? It was going to bite somebody. It was going to bite Jesse’s little brother. Some of the others said it too, all at once. It hissed at him. It rattled. We were scared it was going to bite. Della came through the ring and knelt down in the leaves. She took the length of fence rail out of the youngest boy’s hands without asking and slid the end of it under the snake, gently, and lifted the front half of it up off the ground into the light where they could see. It did not strike. It hung over the rail with its mouth open. Look at its eye, she said. Round. A rattler’s got a slit like

sections.heading: IV. Whistle Pigs
sections.dateline: The Hollister bar · the last day
sections.text: On the last afternoon of every muster the men drove up onto the benches above the river where the ground squirrels lived and shot whistle pigs, which was what everybody in Idaho County called them, for the noise they made. It was not training. It was the fun part. The boys had always gone, and the older ones shot. That year the boys stayed down at the bar. Cody went to his father and said they would rather set up cans on the rocks by the river, and Dale Hollister looked at his son for a while and said that was fine, and asked why, and Cody did not know how to say it, so he said just because. Some of the men laughed about it in the trucks going up. Orval Pruitt did not go up that year either. He sat in a lawn chair by the river and watched the boys knock the cans off the rocks with a .22, one at a time, and set them back up, and when Jesse’s little brother wanted to go up to the rockslide to look for the snake, Orval told him it was resting and to let it be. Nobody on the bar could have said what was different about the eleven of them after that. Their mothers noticed it before their fathers did. They were quieter about some things. None of them, as far as anybody knew, ever again k

sections.heading: V. The Kink
sections.dateline: Deer Creek road above the Salmon · May 2010
sections.text: Cody Hollister went to work for Idaho Fish and Game when he was twenty-four. He was a conservation officer out of Lewiston, and a good part of his summers was snakes: rattlers in garages, rattlers under porches, gopher snakes in chicken coops, and calls from frightened people who were sure the snake in the yard was a rattler and had a hoe in their hands when he got there. He went to every one of those calls. He carried a long hook in the truck and a lidded bucket, and he always looked at the eye first, and then at the tail, and he talked to the people the whole time in a low voice. In May of 2010 he was driving the gravel road up out of the canyon above the old bar, which his father had sold, when he saw a snake lying across the road in the sun. He stopped the truck. It was a gopher snake, the biggest he had ever seen, yellow-brown with dark blotches, and a third of the way down its back from the head it had a kink in it, an old bend where the spine had healed crooked. It lay there on the warm gravel a long while, not minding him. A gopher snake might live fifteen years in the wild. He knew that. He had looked it up more than once. It could not have been the same one. He sat in the

title: Bull Snake
logline: Two months after Oklahoma City, eleven militia boys on a Salmon River bar corner a snake they are sure is a rattler.

verses.text: Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee.
If, like a shattered metal plate (gong), thou utter not, then thou hast reached Nirvana; contention is not known to thee.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, from the day the monk Kuṇḍadhāna is ordained, the form of a woman follows him everywhere. Everyone sees her except him, and villagers on his alms round give one portion “for you” and another “for our female friend.” In a former life, in the time of an earlier Buddha, he had been a deity who took a woman’s form to make one of two inseparable monks look unchaste, so that the other refused to keep the Observance Day with him; the deity confessed, the monks were reconciled but never as close, and the deity went to hell. Now the monks ask the great lay supporters Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā to expel Kuṇḍadhāna; both say the Teacher will know. The monks go to King Pasenadi, who surrounds the monk’s cell, sees the woman only when the monk stands outside, searches the room three times, decides she is an apparition, and invites the monk to eat at the palace. The jealous monks call Kuṇḍadhāna the king’s bastard; he, who has never answered anyone, calls them corrupt and unchaste. The Buddha asks both sides why they spoke: the monks spoke from what they saw, but what had he seen? He tells the old deed and bids him be silent as a gong broken at the rim. Kuṇḍadhāna becomes an arahant, flies up into the air, and takes the first meal ticket, and he is later named foremost among those who receive meal tickets.
bg.history:
By the 2000s large evangelical congregations were outgrowing their buildings and moving into vacant commercial property, strip malls and empty big-box stores among it, as the Wall Street Journal reported in 2006. Many were nondenominational megachurches, usually defined as Protestant churches with two thousand or more people in weekly attendance. Anderson, on I-85 about halfway between Atlanta and Charlotte, was called the Electric City after a hydroelectric plant on the Rocky River began sending power there in 1895, and cotton mills grew up from the 1870s in Anderson, Pelzer, Belton, Honea Path and Williamston. By 1920 Anderson County had nineteen textile mills; by the 1990s foreign competition had closed many of them, leaving the mill villages behind.

Caleb’s ring belongs to the evangelical purity movement of the 1990s. The Southern Baptist campaign True Love Waits asked teenagers to sign cards pledging abstinence until marriage; on July 29, 1994, an estimated 200,000 signed cards were staked into the lawn of the National Mall, according to NPR. Many pledgers wore a ring as a sign of the promise. By 2006, when Kayleigh’s page went up, MySpace was the most visited website in the United States.

sections.heading: I. Two Coffees
sections.text: Open Field Church bought the Walmart on the bypass in 2009, a year after the store moved two miles up the road to a Supercenter, and by 2015 three thousand people came there on a Sunday. They kept the polished concrete floor and the long fluorescent bays and the loading dock. They put the sanctuary where the groceries had been, the children’s wing in Lawn and Garden, and a coffee bar called the Grounds in the corner where the Subway used to be. Out front, above the doors, you could still see where the old letters had come down: a paler place on the block wall, in the shape of the name, that no paint quite covered. The new sign hung under it. Caleb Pruitt was hired as youth pastor in January. He had wanted to be a youth pastor since he was fourteen, and he was good at it in the quiet way, the kind who remembered the name of your dog and drove you home from Wednesday night when your mama’s car broke down. The summer he was eighteen, the two boys he loved most in the world were Josh Clary and Tanner Black. They had been in the same Sunday school class at Cane Creek First Baptist since they were four, and the two of them had signed their pledge cards the same night he did, and they were so close that the youth pastor called them the Twins, though they did not look alike at all. They prayed together before ball games. They went to See You at the Pole together every September and stood at the flagpole at the high school holding hands with their eyes shut. Every first Sunday they walked down the aisle side by side when the communion was passed, and everybody in Cane Creek knew it. Caleb was always the third one, a step behind them. That spring he made a MySpace page for a girl named Kayleigh. He never could say afterward exactly why. He would sit in his car and try to say it to himself, and it always came out sounding like something smaller than what it had been. He wanted to see if the thing between them would break. sections.text: The trouble came from inside the staff. There were nine pastors on staff at Open Field, and by June the others had stopped being kind. Trent Gaines, who led worship, said the girl had been seen getting into Caleb’s car at the Waffle House. Missy Hollifield, who ran the children’s wing, said a mother had pulled her daughter out of the youth group because of the pictures from camp. Bradley Moon, the executive pastor, who had come from a big church in Atlanta and knew how these things went, said what all of them were thinking. There was a pastor in Greenville who had been in the papers. There were pastors all over the country in the papers. If it came out that the youth pastor at Open Field went around with a teenage girl in a tank top, it would not matter what anybody said afterward. It would be all of them. It would be the church. They went first to Don Rampey, who owned the Ford dealership on Clemson Boulevard and had given the money to buy the building. They sat in his office at the dealership with the shades down. Get him off the property, Don. For all our sakes. Mr. Rampey heard them out. Then he said, Is Ruth Ann not at the church? She’s there. Well, then. She’ll know. They wen

sections.text: Lamar Gentry had been chief of police in Cane Creek for nineteen years, which meant he had three officers and a Crown Victoria and knew everybody in town and what their granddaddies had done in the mill. Caleb lived in Cane Creek, in the right-hand half of a brick duplex on Mill Street, so it was Lamar the three pastors came to, with their phones full of pictures, and laid them out on his desk one at a time. We don’t know how old she is, Bradley Moon said. That’s the thing. We think she could be a minor. The chief looked at the pictures a long time. He knew Caleb Pruitt. He had known his grandmother since before the mill shut. He had also been a policeman long enough to know that you never did know. Y’all go on home, he said. I’ll see about it. He went that night after dark, with two of his officers. He put one at the back of the duplex by the clotheslines and one at the corner of Mill Street, and he stood himself in the front yard, on the grass, facing the door, and knocked on the porch post with his flashlight. Caleb came out under the porch light in his socks. He stood on the top step, facing the chief, and the chief saw her plain as day: a girl in a white top, standing in the d

sections.text: It got around, because things do. By the first of August the whole staff knew that Lamar Gentry had gone out to Mill Street to run Caleb Pruitt off and had come home and set a place for him at his own table, and that Caleb ate there every Sunday now, pot roast and rice and gravy, and that Mary Lynn Gentry set two places for him and did not say a word about it. The staff took it hard. They had gone to the law and the law had gone over to him. Trent Gaines said it first, at the coffee machine in the staff break room, which had been the Walmart’s employee break room and still had the safety poster on the wall. How’s the chief’s boy this morning? In the staff meeting Bradley Moon made a joke about whose son Caleb really was, and what his mama had been up to, and two of them laughed. Missy Hollifield did not laugh, but she did not say anything either. It went on for a week. They said it in the hallway behind the stage and in the group text he was on. Chief’s bastard. They said he had a girl in his house and a cop in his pocket. Nobody at Open Field had ever heard Caleb Pruitt raise his voice. sections.heading: VI. The Cymbal
sections.dateline: The manager’s office · the same day
sections.text: Ruth Ann Dobbins was fifty-eight. She had started Open Field with her husband Wade in 1996 in a storefront in Belton with forty folding chairs, and when Wade died of a heart attack on the riding mower in 2010 she had kept on. She was raised Free Will Baptist in Honea Path, in a white church with a piano and no drums where the women did not preach, and her grandmother, who had been a schoolteacher, had read to her out of an American Standard Bible with a cracked black cover that she still kept on her desk. When she was nineteen, with a baby and no husband, she had danced six years at a club off I-85 near the Georgia line to keep the lights on, and she had told that from the pulpit exactly once, on the first Sunday the church met, and never again, and never needed to. She preached short. Most Sundays she let Wade’s younger brother preach and sat on the front row. What she mostly did was pray with people in this office, one at a time, for as long as it took. She heard the three of them out. Then she picked up the phone and asked Caleb to come up. He came and stood just inside the door. Destiny had brought up two coffees for him at the staff meeting, and he still had the second one in

sections.heading: VII. Number One
sections.text: He did what she told him. It was harder than the pills. Trent Gaines said chief’s boy at the coffee machine the next morning, out of habit, and Caleb felt the whole sentence come up in him, ready, the way a dog comes up off a porch, and he let it lie down again. He did it the next day and the day after that. In the group text he did not answer. In his car on the way home, when the old talk started up in his head, he let that lie down too. He thought of the little dead click of the cymbal. There was a verse in the Psalms he found on his own that month in the old American Standard, and he wrote it on an index card and kept it on the dash of his car, and read it at red lights: I said, I will take heed to my ways, That I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle, While the wicked is before me. I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; And my sorrow was stirred. — Psalm 39:1–2 And something happened, though he never would claim it. It happened slowly through September, and all at once one morning in October, at the light by the Ford dealership, with the rain coming down. title: Two Coffees
logline: At a megachurch in an old Walmart, everyone sees a teenage girl following the new youth pastor except the youth pastor.

verses.text: As a cowherd with his staff drives his cows into the stable, so do Age and Death drive the life of men.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred women of Sāvatthī keep the Observance Day and go to the monastery. The great laywoman Visākhā asks each age in turn why they keep it. The oldest want a heavenly reward, the women in middle life want release from the power of their husbands, the young wives want to conceive, and the maidens want husbands while they are still young. She brings the answers to the Buddha in order. He says that birth, old age, sickness and death are like cowherds with staves, each handing living beings on to the next, and that even so nobody wishes for an end of rebirth; rebirth is all they desire.
bg.history:
Marlow and its people are invented. The annual Fast Day was real: each spring the governor of Massachusetts proclaimed a day of public fasting, humiliation and prayer, kept with public worship and abstinence from food. Massachusetts kept the holiday until 1894. Small children, and girls above all, learned to read from a neighborhood woman in a dame school. Sylvester Judd’s History of Hadley records that girls in the valley towns “learned to read and sew of school dames,” and that Northampton did not admit girls to its town schools until 1802. The same book describes the valley farmers who stall-fed oxen through the winter and drove them to market near Boston. The cattle market there, begun in 1775, stood in the part of Cambridge called Little Cambridge, which became the town of Brighton in 1807. “Fourpence ha’penny” was the New England name for the Spanish half-real, a small silver coin that passed everywhere. “Izzard” is an old name for the letter Z.

The New England Primer taught generations of children their letters through a rhymed alphabet with a small woodcut for each couplet. The couplets in the story are from the oldest surviving edition, printed in Boston in 1727 and reprinted in Paul Leicester Ford’s The New-England Primer: A History of Its Origin and Development (1897). Ford shows that between about 1740 and 1760 the worldlier rhymes were rewritten to be more pious. In an edition of 1777, T is “Young Timothy / Learnt sin to fly,” X is “Xerxes did die, / And so must I,” and Y is “While youth do chear / Death may be near.” A woman schooled in the 1730s and her granddaughters would have known different alphabets.

sections.heading: I. The Nooning
sections.dateline: Marlow, Hampshire County, Massachusetts · Fast Day, April 1805
sections.text: The Governor’s proclamation had been read from the pulpit, and it said what it said every spring: a day of public fasting, humiliation and prayer, with servile labor and recreation laid by. In Marlow that meant two sermons with an hour between them and nothing to eat until the sun was behind West Hill. The men spent the hour by the horse block, talking low. The women went where the women of Marlow had always gone at the nooning, forty rods down the hill to the kitchen of Marm Bascom, who kept the dame school. She was seventy-eight and had not climbed to the meetinghouse in four winters. She sat at the end of the settle with her bad hip to the fire. For fifty-one years she had taken the town’s children at three years old, at fourpence ha’penny a week, and kept them until they could read a chapter and the girls could hem. The boys went on to the master. The girls went home, since Marlow had never paid a master to teach girls. So every woman in that kitchen who had been born in the town had learned her letters on that floor, first off the horn-book on its string and then out of the Primer, and any of them could have put a finger on the place at the crown of her head where Marm’s thimb

sections.heading: II. The Drove
sections.dateline: The Bay Road · the same hour
sections.text: Marm Bascom did not answer, because there was a noise in the road, and she had turned to the window. It was a drove from the river towns, sixty or seventy fat oxen bound for the market at Little Cambridge. They had stood in the stall since November eating corn and English hay. The drover ought to have lain by for the Fast, and every woman at the window knew it. A man rode ahead on a gray horse. The drover walked behind with a hickory stick, and two boys with switches walked the flanks. The cattle filled the road from bank to bank, red and brindle, and steam rose off their backs. Watch how he does it, Marm said. She had watched droves from that window for fifty years. He doesn’t strike. He holds the stick out where the near ox can see it, and the ox moves off from it, and the rest go because that one goes. Hurry a fat beast and he walks his tallow off, and the tallow is what they pay for. He’ll have them eight or nine days on the road, with hay every night, and they’ll go in at the gate as sleek as they left the stall. One of the boys was no bigger than her oldest scholars. He laid his switch against the hock of a steer that had stopped to look at the meetinghouse, and the steer wen

sections.heading: III. Izzard
sections.dateline: The kitchen · before the second bell
sections.text: Then she did what she had done with all of them when they were small. She took the Primer down from the shelf over the settle. It was her own, the one she had learned from in her mother’s kitchen, and it had lost its boards long ago and was sewn into a piece of bed ticking. Say T, she said, and rapped the arm of the settle with her thimble. The girls and the young wives had it out before they could think. Young Timothy learnt sin to fly. Under them, slower, came the widows and the oldest of the wives, saying something else. There, said Marm. You hear that. When I had kept school a few years a new book came up from Boston. Somebody had gone through the letters and mended them. He took Time out at T and put in a good boy. But he couldn’t take him off the road. She did not open the book. She said the old letters as she had learned them, and the widows said them with her. As runs the GlassMans life doth pass. Time cuts down allBoth great and small.
