title: A to Izzard
logline: On Fast Day the squire's wife asks the women of a hill town what each is fasting for, while a drove of fat oxen goes by.

verses.text: A fool does not know when he commits his evil deeds: but the wicked man burns by his own deeds, as if burnt by fire.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, coming down from Vulture’s Peak with the elder Lakkhaṇa, smiles at something he will explain only before the Buddha: a peta in the shape of a python, many leagues long, with fire running from its head to its tail and back. The Buddha says his disciples have eyes and use them, and that he saw the same being on the night of his awakening but kept silent for the sake of those who would not believe. Then he tells its past. In the time of an earlier Buddha, a generous rich man named Sumaṅgala, walking out at dawn, saw a mud-footed man hiding in a rest-house by the city gate and remarked that he must be a night prowler. The man swore to get even, and burned the rich man’s field, maimed his cattle and burned his house, seven times each; then, learning from a servant what his master loved most, he burned the Perfumed Chamber the rich man had built for the Buddha. The rich man clapped for joy at the chance to build it again. When the thief came for seven days with a knife to kill him, the rich man dedicated the merit of his gifts to the unknown arsonist; the thief fell at his feet, the rich man asked his pardon in turn for the careless word, forgave him, and would not take him into his house as a servant. The thief died with the deed unspent.
bg.history:
Maryland was founded as a refuge for English Catholics, but after the Protestant revolution of 1689 the Church of England was established and the old Catholic families were pushed out of office. A 1704 act “to prevent the growth of Popery” forbade priests to exercise their office; Queen Anne then allowed Mass to be said in the chapels of private families, and so Catholic planters built “mass rooms” and “priests’ mass-houses” onto their dwellings, served by Jesuits who traveled between them (Catholic Encyclopedia, “Archdiocese of Baltimore”, which also lists a Jesuit chapel at Port Tobacco by 1697). In 1715 the colony was returned to the Calvert family only after Charles Calvert, 5th Baron Baltimore, declared himself a Protestant; new oaths followed in 1716 and Catholics lost the vote in 1718. Maryland’s labor was by then shifting from indentured servants to enslaved Africans; see Province of Maryland.

The servant law the Assembly passed in 1715 allowed a runaway to be made to serve up to ten days for each day absent (Archives of Maryland, vol. 30, p. 284) and paid four hundred pounds of tobacco to whoever took one up (p. 288); a man servant was owed at the end of his time a hat, a suit of clothes, shoes, two hoes and an axe. Teresa of Ávila’s Life circulated in English among Catholics from the early 1600s; the passage Brother Hollis reads, her vision of the place prepared for her in hell, is quoted here from David Lewis’s translation (1870; 1904 edition). Mr. Thorogood, Kit Lowry, Brother Hollis, Father Langworth, Peter Cole, Matthew Spurling and the house at Nanjemoy are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Landing
sections.dateline: St. Thomas's, Charles County, Maryland · November 1717
sections.text: The Jesuits' house stood on the high ground where Port Tobacco River runs into the Potomac, and the path down to their landing was steep enough that a man carrying oars took it sideways. Peter Cole took it sideways every morning of his life. He was about forty. He belonged to the Jesuits, as the boat did and the cattle did, and he had rowed their priests up and down the rivers of Charles County since he was fourteen, to every house on the Neck where there was a room with an altar in it. He could find a creek mouth in the dark by the smell of it. The men who worked with him said he saw further than other people, and not only on the water. Matthew Spurling carried the other pair of oars. He was seventeen and had come out of Bristol in the spring, bound for five years to pay his passage, and the Jesuits had bought his time off the ship at Annapolis. He was a Protestant and had been told he would not be made anything else, and nobody had tried. He was still afraid of the river. It was the grey before sunrise, and the frost was on the path. Father Langworth was to be rowed down to Nanjemoy to say Mass in a house there and come back by dark. Halfway down the hill, where the trees open an

sections.heading: II. The Shop
sections.text: Brother John Hollis was a Jesuit who would never be a priest. He had come out from England in 1693 as a lay brother, which meant he took the vows and kept them and was not ordained, and he did the work. He was a joiner. He had made most of the altars on the Neck, and all of the boxes they folded into, so that a priest could close up a chapel in a minute and leave a room that looked like a parlor. He was nearly seventy. He talked less than anyone at St. Thomas's, which was saying something, and men went to his shop in the evenings with things they would not take to a priest. When the boat was in and Father Langworth had gone up to the house, Peter and Matthew came to the shop. Brother Hollis was planing a cherry board by a rushlight. Matthew asked. Peter sat on the sawhorse. When we came down this morning, Peter said, there was a great snake lying in the river. His head was at the point under the house, and his body went down the Potomac past Cedar Point, farther than I could see. Thicker than a hogshead. And he was all on fire. The fire started at his head and ran to the end of him and started at the end and ran back up, and more fire came out of his sides and fell on his back. The

sections.heading: III. Four Hundredweight
sections.text: Mr. Basil Thorogood had three thousand acres on Nanjemoy Creek, and forty people who were his, and a brick house with glazed windows that he had built in the year of the Revolution, when the Protestants took the government and his family had to give up their places in it. He had been a justice of the county then. He was not one now, and would not be again, and he did not seem to mind. He was a short, loud, happy man who could not sit still at a table. He fed everybody. On a Sunday when a priest came, forty and fifty people came up from the creeks to hear Mass at his house and stayed to dinner, Catholics and Protestants both, and the Protestants came back the next time for the dinner. Since the law of 1704 a priest could not say Mass in any public chapel in Maryland, only in the house of a private family. So the Catholic families built rooms onto their houses. Mr. Thorogood's was the best on the Neck. Brother Hollis had built it for him: a long room off the west end of the house, with its own door to the yard, a plastered ceiling, and an altar of black walnut that folded shut into a press. There was a little window over the altar of colored glass that Mr. Thorogood had sent to Londo

sections.heading: IV. Seven Times
sections.text: The man was Kit Lowry. He was not a runaway. He had served out seven years in Prince George's County as a boy and had his freedom dues, a hat and a suit of clothes, two hoes and an axe, and nothing else. He had married a woman who had also served her time, and they had two children and a cabin on rented ground at the head of the creek. He fished. He took a hog out of the woods now and then that was not his, and he had been out after one that night and had lain down in the nearest dry place, and he had been priced in his sleep like a calf. Ten days later Mr. Thorogood's tobacco house by the landing burned with the whole crop hanging in it. On the Neck they say it was seven times. Seven times he burned the tobacco, and seven times he went into the woods where Mr. Thorogood's cattle ranged and cut the hamstrings of a steer, and seven times he set fire to the house. Brother Hollis said that seven was a good number for a story, and that he himself had counted three tobacco houses, the kitchen, the dairy, the barn with the corn in it, and eleven head of cattle lying in the woods with their legs cut, which the house people had to finish with an axe. Mr. Thorogood did not know who did it.

sections.heading: V. The Octave
sections.text: Brother Hollis built it twice. It took him and two men of the house from February to Lent. The walnut was harder to find the second time and the glass came from London again at twice the price, and Mr. Thorogood paid it. At Easter the priest blessed the new room, and Mr. Thorogood kept the octave. For eight days Mass was said in the room every morning and the whole Neck ate at his house every noon: shad from the creek, and hams, and hominy, and the first greens. People camped in the yard. Protestants came too, for the dinner, and stood at the back of the mass room in their hats out of curiosity. Kit Lowry came every day. He had a butcher's knife pushed down inside his breeches against his hip. He had understood by now that nothing he could burn would touch the man, and that only one thing was left. For seven days he stood in the yard and in the back of the room, and ate at the long tables, and waited, and Mr. Thorogood was never alone for a breath. People had their hands on him from morning to night. On the eighth morning, before the priest began, Mr. Thorogood stood up in front of the altar with his hat in his hands. Father, he said, you know I have had some losses. Seven times a

sections.heading: VI. The Fire Inside
sections.dateline: The shop at St. Thomas's · November 1717
sections.text: The rushlight had burned down to the clip. Brother Hollis lit another from it. He was forgiven, said Matthew. Mr. Thorogood forgave him. The priest said a Mass for him. He was, said the brother. And he did all of that. Both things. He took down a small worn book from the shelf over the bench, the life of the holy mother Teresa that Father Langworth had brought him from England, and found the place without looking long. Teresa, who saw the place made ready for her own sins, and was let out again. If I said that the soul is continually being torn from the body, it would be nothing, for that implies the destruction of life by the hands of another but here it is the soul itself that is tearing itself in pieces. I cannot describe that inward fire or that despair, surpassing all torments and all pain. I did not see who it was that tormented me, but I felt myself on fire, and torn to pieces, as it seemed to me; and, I repeat it, this inward fire and despair are the greatest torments of all. — St. Teresa of Jesus, Life, ch. 32 Nobody is burning Kit Lowry, Brother Hollis said. Mr. Thorogood is not. God is not. Kit did not know what he was doing while he did it. He knows now. It is his own f

title: Four Hundredweight
logline: A Catholic planter who prices a sleeping stranger as a runaway loses his tobacco, his cattle and then the mass room he loves.

verses.text: He who inflicts pain on innocent and harmless persons, will soon come to one of these ten states:
He will have cruel suffering, loss, injury of the body, heavy affliction, or loss of mind,
Or a misfortune coming from the king, or a fearful accusation, or loss of relations, or destruction of treasures,
Or lightning-fire will burn his houses; and when his body is destroyed, the fool will go to hell.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Mahā Moggallāna, one of the Buddha’s two chief disciples, visits the heavens and the hells and comes back to tell people what deeds lead where, and the offerings flow to the Buddha’s community. Rival ascetics pay a thousand coins to bandits to kill him at Black Rock. Twice he escapes, once through a keyhole and once through the roof, but in the third month he stays, knowing an old deed has come due. The bandits break his bones as small as grains of rice and leave him for dead. He pulls himself together, flies to the Buddha to take leave, teaches and works wonders one last time, and returns to Black Rock to die. The killers are caught when they brawl in a tavern over who struck him first, and King Ajātasattu has them and the ascetics burned in pits and plowed under. The Buddha explains that in a past life Moggallāna, turned by his wife against his blind parents, beat them to death in a forest while pretending to be bandits.
bg.hist_title: The south coast of Puerto Rico, 1994
bg.history:
Espiritismo came to Puerto Rico in the nineteenth century through the books of the French writer Allan Kardec, and grew into many forms, from strict Kardecist centros to folk practice mixed with Catholic, African and Taíno elements. At the mesa blanca, the white table, a medium hosts a spirit so that those seated can ask it questions. Kardec’s The Spirits’ Book (1857), written as questions put to spirits and their answers, teaches that spirits are reborn many times and that the trials of one life answer to the faults of earlier ones. Celestino’s past life falls in 1898, after the United States invaded Puerto Rico, when night bands called partidas sediciosas, or tiznados, raided the haciendas and stores of Spaniards in the mountains of the interior.

Sugar had ruled the south coast for a century. The great mill at Central Aguirre, between Salinas and Guayama, ran from 1899 until it closed for good in 1993, and by then the industry had been failing for decades. In 1993 Governor Pedro Rosselló began the anti-crime campaign called Mano Dura, the hard hand. Between June 1993 and March 1999 police and the National Guard carried out about eighty raids on public housing projects, each followed by an occupation that lasted weeks, with checkpoints, helicopters and fences around the projects, as the scholar Marisol LeBrón describes in the Boston Review.

sections.heading: I. The Rock
sections.dateline: The south coast of Puerto Rico · 1994
sections.text: Celestino Vega lived by himself in a wooden house with a zinc roof on the hill above the cane, beside the black rock the barrio was named for. The rock was as big as a bus and older than anybody’s story about it. Below it the cane ran down to the sea in every direction, or what was left of the cane, because the central had closed the year before and nobody was cutting it now, and the fields were going back to guinea grass and acacia, and in the dry months they burned. He had cut cane for the central for thirty-one years. He was sixty-two. He had a machete scar across the back of his left hand and a way of standing with his weight on one hip, from all those years of bending, and he wore a white guayabera every day of his life that was not a working day. Since the central closed, every day was one of those. On Thursday nights he sat at the white table in the Centro Espiritista Luz y Verdad, down in the town, and went over. That was how people in Piedra Negra said it. He closed his eyes and put his scarred hand flat on the white cloth beside the glass of water, and his breathing changed, and he went over to where the dead are, and walked among them, and came back and told the people a

sections.heading: II. The Botánica
sections.text: There were three men in the back of Botánica Los Tres Reyes after closing, among the plaster saints and the bundles of herbs and the bottles of bath oil with names on them like Abre Camino and Vence Batalla and Dinero Rápido, and they were adding up what they had lost. Wiso Medina owned the botánica. Papo Rentas had a little centro of his own in the back of his house where the spirits charged forty dollars for a cleansing and a hundred and fifty for a work against an enemy. The third was a man from the next town who called himself Hermano Ezequiel and sold prayers by the week. Business had been bad for a year. Not everyone who sold herbs and candles on that coast was a thief; most of them were not; there was a woman with a botánica two streets over who sent half her customers up the hill to Luz y Verdad and told them to keep their money. But these three had been living on the fears of the people of that coast for a long time, and the fears had gone up the hill. It’s him, said Wiso. It’s all him. He goes over there and comes back and tells them who’s in the light and who’s in the dark and why, and they believe him. He tells them for nothing. And then they don’t need us. So what do w

sections.heading: III. The Keyhole
sections.text: They came up the hill the first time on a Tuesday night with a car jack handle and two lengths of pipe and a baseball bat, and surrounded the house, one at each corner and Chiqui at the door, and Chiqui put his shoulder to the door and broke it in. The house was empty. The bed had been slept in. The coffee pot on the stove was still warm. The windows were shut and barred from inside, as they always were, and the back door was bolted from inside, and the front door had been locked from inside with the key still in it until Chiqui broke it. Doña Lula Pabón, who lived below on the cane road and was up at that hour with her sugar, told it afterward to anybody who would listen. She had seen the light go off in his window and the boys come up around the house in the dark. And she had seen, at the front door, at the height of a man’s waist, something come out of the keyhole like a thread of smoke from a cigar, white in the moonlight, and stretch out long and thin along the porch rail, and go down the steps and away across the cane toward the town. She said it was him. Half the barrio believed her and the other half said she should check her sugar again. Celestino, when he was asked, said

sections.heading: IV. The Third Month
sections.text: In April he did not leave. He knew they were coming. Everybody in Piedra Negra knew they were coming; the boys from Las Gardenias had been spending Wiso’s money all over the south coast and talking while they spent it. Celestino went to the centro that Thursday as usual and sat at the white table and went over and came back and told what he had seen, and afterward in the doorway Doña Monse took hold of his sleeve. Celestino. Stay in town tonight. Stay at my house. He put his hand over hers on his sleeve, the scarred one. No, Doña Monse. This one I owe. I’ve known it since I was a boy. I didn’t know what for, but I knew it was owed. I can’t keep going out through the roof. She looked at him a long time with her small black eyes, and let go. He went home and made coffee, and sat on the porch in his white guayabera with the cup on the rail and the light on behind him, and watched the cane road. Doña Lula, who was up with her sugar, saw him there. She said afterward he sat very straight, the way he sat at the white table, with his hands open on his knees. They came at one in the morning. They did not have to break anything this time. He stood up when he saw them on the steps and put th

sections.heading: V. The Glass of Water
sections.dateline: Centro Espiritista Luz y Verdad · the same night
sections.text: There was a session at Luz y Verdad that night after all, a late one, because Doña Monse had not gone home. She had sat down at the head of the white table at eleven with the light off in the front room and two of the older mediums with her, and said the prayer, and waited. At half past one the door opened and Celestino came in. All three of them would swear to it as long as they lived, and two of them swore to it to the police. He was in his white guayabera. It was raining outside, the first rain in a month, and he was dry. He walked straight, without the hitch at the hip. He came up the room to the head of the table and bent and kissed Doña Monse’s hand, which he had never once done in fifty years. Doña Monse. I’m going. You’re going, Celestino? Yes. Where to? To Piedra Negra. She looked at him the way she had in the doorway, and nodded once. Then give us the session before you go, she said. Because I am not going to have another one like you to look at. He sat down in his place at the white table and put his hand flat on the cloth beside the glass of water. What happened then the two old mediums told to the police and in the centro and to their grandchildren, and they told it th

sections.heading: VI. The Cafétín
sections.text: It went all over the island. It was in the San Juan papers with a photograph of the rock. Medium beaten to death at Piedra Negra. Teniente Edgardo Rosa of the district police had been at the white table at Luz y Verdad exactly once, three years before, after his son Eddie was shot outside a club in Ponce. Celestino had gone over and come back and told him where Eddie was and why, and some of it was a thing about Eddie that the lieutenant had not known and did not want to know, and some of it was a message, in words only Eddie used. The lieutenant had never gone back. He had never forgotten it either. When he heard about Piedra Negra he put two men in plain clothes into the cafétíns along the cane road with orders to play dominoes and drink Medalla and listen. It took three weeks. The boys from Las Gardenias were in a cafétín called El Guayacán on a Friday night, spending the last of Wiso’s money, and Chiqui shoved Tato off his stool, and Tato got up off the floor with his lip bleeding. What did you hit me for? Because you’re a thief and a liar, said Chiqui. You hit the old man first and you said it was me. You don’t know who hit him first. You were behind the bat. I hit him first.

sections.heading: VII. The Debt
sections.dateline: Luz y Verdad · a Thursday in June
sections.text: The centro was full every Thursday that summer, and none of the mediums could do what he had done, and everybody knew it, and at the end of the sessions people stayed and talked. He didn’t deserve it, they said. A man like that. That death. He never hurt anybody in his life. Doña Monse was putting away the white cloth. She folded it in half, and in half again. If you look at this life only, she said, no. He didn’t deserve it. They waited. She did not often say more than that, and they did not expect her to. But she put the cloth down on the table and sat down and put her hand flat on it, the way Celestino used to, and closed her eyes. And then she told them, plainly, the way you tell what you saw at the market. A long time ago, she said, before any of them were born, in the year the Americans came, there was a young man up in the coffee mountains above Yauco who took care of his father and mother with his own two hands. They were both blind. He picked coffee on shares and worked his own little plot and came home every night and cooked for them and washed their clothes and led them out into the sun in the morning and back in at night. His parents said, Son, you are killing yourself,

title: Piedra Negra
logline: Rival spirit-sellers pay five boys a thousand dollars to kill the old medium at Piedra Negra, who visits the dead for free.

verses.text: Not nakedness, not platted hair, not dirt, not fasting, or lying on the earth, not rubbing with dust, not sitting motionless, can purify a mortal who has not overcome desires.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a householder of Sāvatthī becomes a monk after his wife dies, but first has a cell, a kitchen and a storeroom built for himself, fills the storeroom with ghee, honey and oil, and sends for his own slaves to cook for him. He keeps one set of robes for the day and another for the night. Monks looking for lodging see his robes and bedding hung out to dry and bring him before the Buddha, who asks how a man gone forth under a teaching of wanting little came to own so much. Stung, the monk throws off his outer robe in the middle of the assembly and says he will go about like that. The Buddha reminds him that once, even as a water demon, he kept his sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing for twelve years; the monk covers himself and sits down. The Buddha then tells the birth story of the three princes and the demon of the lake, who released his captives when the eldest told him that the godlike are those who have conscience and concern (hiri and ottappa), and ends with the verse on the ascetic practices that cleanse no one. Read the full commentary story. The birth story is the Devadhamma Jātaka, the sixth of the Jātaka collection. Müller's "desires" in the last clause renders a word the commentary takes as doubt.
bg.history:
The Rainbow Family of Living Light has gathered on national forest land in the first week of July every year since 1972, when the first Gathering was held at Strawberry Lake in Colorado. It has no leaders, members or fees; no money changes hands on the land; kitchens are fed from a common Supply paid for by the Magic Hat; each person brings a bowl, a cup and a spoon; and the Family's own handbook says that generators are not appropriate to a Gathering and asks everyone to walk lightly on the earth. The 1995 Gathering was held on the Tres Piedras Ranger District of the Carson National Forest, at the head of the Rio San Antonio, eighteen miles in on Forest Road 87. The Forest Service estimated more than 18,000 people. The district ranger's cleanup letter of November 3, 1995 records Bus Village and its three to four miles of new trail, the mud baths and pools on the river, the spring boxes and PVC pipe, the fifty or so people who stayed from July 7 to August 4 to restore the site, more than seven inches of rain, and the spring depressions left as wildlife water. It also records the feeling of the Hispano villages nearby, some of whose residents protested the Gathering, and their advice that the Family "needs to listen more than talk."

The Rio San Antonio runs north out of New Mexico and joins the Conejos in Colorado's San Luis Valley, where water is divided by prior appropriation: in a short year the oldest decreed ditches drink first, and a state water commissioner closes the headgates of the junior ones. The winter of 1976–77 brought one of the worst droughts in Colorado's record. Vergüenza in the Spanish of the upper Rio Grande means a sense of honor and of what is owed to other people, and a sinvergüenza is someone who has lost it. The lay brotherhood of the Penitentes has kept its moradas and its Holy Week penances in these villages since Spanish times. The passage from Joel is the old reading for Ash Wednesday; the Spanish here is from the Catholic translation of Félix Torres Amat. Lyle Hoagland, Chuy Maestas and his family, Marigold and Sonny Rich are invented, and so is the plaza on the lower San Antonio.

sections.heading: I. The Outfit
sections.dateline: Bus Village, Carson National Forest, New Mexico · the last week of June 1995
sections.text: Lyle Hoagland's wife died in October, in the hospital in Alamosa, and by Christmas he knew he could not stay in the house. He was sixty-four. He had raised malting barley and seed potatoes on three quarters outside Manassa, in the San Luis Valley of Colorado. For twelve seasons in the middle of his life he had also been the water commissioner on the Conejos, which meant that from May to September he drove the river and its ditches in a state pickup and shut the headgates of men he had known since grade school. He had been good at both trades and they had left him well off. In February he sold the ground, and the water with it, to a neighbor's son. Ardith had gone once to one of the Gatherings. That was the first one, in 1972, over the mountains at Strawberry Lake. Her sister talked her into it. She was gone five days and came home sunburned, wearing a string of clay beads, and for a month afterward she would stop in the middle of the dishes and laugh. All she ever told him about it was that nobody up there had asked her what her husband did. He found the beads in her dresser in January. In April a boy at the feed store in Antonito, with hair to his belt, told him the Family was com

sections.heading: II. The Line
sections.text: They kept coming. By the second of July the rangers were guessing fifteen thousand, with the Fourth still ahead. The good ground near the river was taken, and people arriving late went looking along the edges. Four of them came up through the firs that morning. One was a woman of forty or so called Marigold, who cooked at Kid Village. There was a couple from Arkansas with a baby in a sling. The fourth was a boy of about nineteen that people called Sonny Rich, who had been on the land nine days. He had made it his business to eat at every kitchen and to ask whoever was stirring the pot what was the main thing they had found out so far. The four of them walked out of the trees into Lyle's camp and stopped. Ernestina had washed that morning. Benny had strung a hundred feet of rope from the awning to a fir, and it was full. There were two cotton shirts on it and two flannel, the drawstring trousers and the wool ones, four sheets, six towels, both quilts, a down comforter, a bathrobe, and two sleeping bags, one for cold nights and one for colder. Past the line stood the wall tents. Through the door of one they could see the white corner of the freezer, and they could hear the generator.

sections.heading: III. The Circle
sections.text: Somebody blew a conch shell at the hour when the light went long, and the meadow filled. The kitchens carried their buckets in. People sat down in rings around the fire pit, ring outside ring, and the servers went along the rows. Musicians walked the Magic Hat around behind them. There were other people in the meadow that evening. All week families had been driving in from Tres Piedras and Vallecitos and the plazas up along the Colorado line to see it for themselves. They stood along the edge in clean shirts with their arms folded. Their people had three hundred years in that country, and the Forest Service wrote them a ticket for a pickup load of firewood without a permit. Now they were watching eighteen thousand strangers build a town in the elk pasture without asking anyone. Among them stood a small old woman in a blue headscarf with two grandchildren by the hands. She had come eighty miles round from Conejos County because her nephew was mixed up in this. She wanted to see what he did every July instead of helping with the first cutting. Her nephew was Jesús Maestas, called Chuy, who was forty-six and a plumber in Antonito. He had been born in a plaza of fourteen houses on the

sections.heading: IV. The Thing in the Lake
sections.text: It was Sonny Rich who asked. He said that where he came from, shame was the thing people came up here to get rid of, and he would like to know what Chuy's father had meant by it. Chuy thought about that for some time. He said it was a different word. He said he couldn't explain it and never had been able to, but his grandmother had a story she told when she wanted the children to have it. The drums had stopped. He told it the way she did, with his hands on his knees, and he did not hurry. There was a rico on the Chama who had two sons. Their mother died and he married again, and the second wife gave him a third. The day that boy was born the old man was so pleased that he told her she could ask him for anything. She said she would ask later. When her son was grown she asked. She wanted the ranch for him, all of it. The old man said no. My two older boys walk around this country like two fires burning, he said. I can't put them out for yours. She asked again every week. He began to be afraid of what she might do. So he called the two older sons and told them how it was. Go up into the sierra and stay there, he said. When I am dead, come down and take what is yours. They kissed his h

sections.heading: V. Ash Wednesday
sections.text: The fire had been built up. Sonny Rich was not finished. He wanted to know what did it, then. He said he had been to every kitchen. He had talked to the girl who was fasting, and the man on the rock, and the mud people, and he had half a mind to go without clothes till the Fourth himself. Go ahead, Chuy said. It's warm enough in the daytime. He turned the can of pipe cement around on the ground with his foot. I've been coming sixteen years, he said. I've seen people go the whole week with nothing on. I've seen hair that never met a comb, and that mud at the river. I've seen people who don't eat till the Fourth, and people who sleep on the rocks on purpose. That man sits on his heels up there every year from sunup to dark. Most of them are good people and I've got nothing against any of it. But I never saw it wash anybody. If a man still doesn't know what he came for, he goes home the same as he came. He's dirtier, or he's thinner. He looked at Lyle. The freezer isn't it either, Don Lyle. You could give every bit of it away tonight and you'd still be standing there in your shorts. Then he told about his father. Eliseo Maestas had been an Hermano of the morada above the plaza for fif

sections.dateline: The Rio San Antonio · July 3 to August 4
sections.text: He walked back up in the dark. In the morning he shut off the Onan, and the four of them emptied the camp, Benny and Ernestina and Lyle and the boy, who had turned up at sunrise without being asked. The food at Main Circle was vegetarian, so the beef went to a kitchen by the parking lot that fed the gate crew. The honey, butter, oil and flour went down the trail to Supply on a garden cart. The quilts went to Kid Village and the comforter to the healers. The cotton trousers and the collarless shirt went into the free bin, and were seen all that week on a tall man from Oregon. He paid Benny and Ernestina through the month and asked Benny to drive the Winnebago home and sell it. Ernestina would not leave until she had seen where her beans were going. She followed the cart down, looked into the kitchen at Lovin' Ovens, and took an apron off a nail. She made tortillas there for two days for some nine hundred people. Nobody paid her, and she talked about how those children kept a kitchen for the rest of her life. Lyle kept the wool trousers and the flannel shirt, because of the nights. He kept one sleeping bag, and a bowl, a cup and a spoon out of the Winnebago's drawer, and Ardith's bea

verses.text: He who, though dressed in fine apparel, exercises tranquillity, is quiet, subdued, restrained, chaste, and has ceased to find fault with all other beings, he indeed is a Brahmana, an ascetic (sramana), a friar (bhikshu).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi rewards his minister Santati for putting down a frontier revolt by giving him the kingdom for seven days and a dancing girl. Drunk on the seventh day and riding the state elephant in all his ornaments, Santati nods to the Buddha without getting down, and the Buddha smiles and says that Santati will come to him that very day, awaken at a four-line verse, and pass away seated in the air. Skeptics wait to catch the Buddha in a lie. That afternoon the dancer, who had fasted for a week to dance more gracefully, collapses and dies in the middle of her dance, and Santati's drunkenness vanishes “like a drop of water on a red-hot potsherd.” The Buddha tells him he has wept for her more tears than the four oceans hold, and teaches him to let the past dry up, want nothing from the future and grasp nothing now. Santati awakens, asks leave to die, and at the Buddha's request rises seven palm trees high to tell his past good deed: in a former life he went about on foot praising the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, and a king gave him a garland like a string of pearls, then a horse, a chariot and an elephant, and his body smelled of sandalwood. Then he passes away in fire, and his relics fall like jasmine flowers into a white cloth the Buddha holds out, and are enshrined at a crossroads. When the monks ask whether a man who died in finery may be called a monk or a brahmin, the Buddha says he is both.
bg.history:
King Kalākaua turned fifty on November 16, 1886, and the kingdom marked it with a two-week jubilee that ran from November 15 to 29. The police force paid tribute at ʻIolani Palace at sunrise on the birthday; rockets went up from Punchbowl; there was a firemen's parade, a regatta, a ball, a state dinner and a lūʻau. The palace had been lit by electricity that July, the first electric lights in the kingdom. The legislature appropriated $15,000 for the jubilee, and the final cost was later reported at $75,000. As at his 1883 coronation, the King had the hula performed openly on the palace grounds. It had been forbidden by law under the Christian convert Kaʻahumanu and kept out of public life for decades after, and many Christian Hawaiians and much of the foreign press still condemned it; after the coronation, two Honolulu publishers were convicted of obscenity for printing the Hawaiian words of some of the coronation hula. Kalākaua had founded the Royal Order of Kalākaua in 1874; its badge carries the word KEOLA, “eternal life,” on the reverse.

Hawaiʻi's sandalwood was cut for the China trade from 1791 until about 1840, peaking between 1815 and 1826, until no large trees were left; Hawaiians had once beaten the powdered heartwood into kapa cloth as a perfume. In 1886 the road from Honolulu to Waikīkī ran through fishponds, taro patches and rice fields worked by Chinese farmers. It was renamed Kalākaua Avenue in 1905, and the wetlands around it were drained after the Ala Wai Canal was dug in the 1920s. Seven years after the jubilee, in January 1893, Kalākaua's sister and successor, Queen Liliʻuokalani, was overthrown.

sections.heading: I. The Freedom of the Town
sections.text: In the spring of that year there was trouble in the Kona uplands, the kind that had been coming for twenty years. A ranch had let its cattle into the taro patches of a whole valley, season after season, and when the planters began to spear the cattle the ranch hired men from town who carried pistols. A house burned. A boy was shot through the arm. The sheriff in Kailua wrote to Honolulu that he could not answer for what came next, and in Honolulu somebody remembered Kimo Haʻaheo. He was forty years old and had been a cowboy on the Big Island since he was twenty, the best roper between Waimea and Kaʻū, a big man with a quiet voice and a rawhide quirt he wore looped at his wrist the way other men wore a watch chain. They swore him in as a deputy and sent him up the mountain. He was there eleven weeks. He rode into the valley alone the first day and into the ranch yard alone the second, and before he was done he had used the quirt on men from both sides, and broken one man's collarbone with the butt of it, and taken eleven pistols away from the ranch's hired men and thrown them in the sea off Keauhou. Nobody else was shot. The cattle went behind a stone wall that the ranch paid for. T

sections.heading: II. The Waikīkī Road
sections.text: Halfway between town and Waikīkī, where the road ran between the fishponds and the Chinese rice fields, there was a frame house with a grass-roofed schoolroom beside it and a coconut grove behind, and an old woman lived there whom the whole road called Kumu, the teacher. Her name was Lahela. She had been born in the old time, before the kapu fell, and she could remember the year her mother first sat down to eat with her father, and how frightened everybody was, and how nothing happened. When the missionaries came with their letters she was a girl of nine. She learned to read in a month, in the shade of a hau tree, sounding out the words in a little printed primer with her finger, and in the next forty years she taught half of the Waikīkī road to do the same. She taught them in a grass house and then in a frame one. She taught the fishermen's children and the poi-pounders' children and the children of chiefs, and grown men who had been ashamed to come in daylight, and once, for most of a winter, a sea captain from Maine who wanted to read his Hawaiian wife's letters. She went to Kawaiahaʻo on Sundays and sat at the back. She had buried a husband and two sons. She did not talk much,

sections.heading: III. Kēhau
sections.text: Kimo rode the grey horse straight into the water at Waikīkī, the way he had seen chiefs do it when he was a boy, and slid off its back in the shallows and swam out past where the waves broke, still in the silk shirt. The Kona men cheered him from the sand. He lay on his back out there for a long time, under Lēʻahi, with the cross floating on its ribbon on his chest, and let the swells lift him and set him down. Then he came in and slept on the lānai of the King's cottage until the sun was low. When he woke Kēhau was already there. She had been dancing every night of the jubilee, at the palace and then for him, and for seven days she had eaten almost nothing. Nobody had asked her to. The Puna troupe was to dance before the King at the great lūʻau, and she wanted to be light for it. She wanted to come down on the boards of the long lānai they had built for the lūʻau as softly as a leaf. She drank water and a little coconut milk, and each day she felt lighter, and each day she danced better, and her teacher in the troupe looked at her and said nothing because she had never seen the girl dance like that. The sun went down behind Waiʻanae. Somebody lit the lanterns. One of the Kona men

sections.heading: IV. Water on a Hot Stone
sections.text: He walked. He left the grey horse tied at the cottage and walked up the Waikīkī road in the dark with his Kona men behind him, on foot too, leading their horses, not one of them saying anything. Their spurs rang on the coral of the road. They were not the only ones on it. Word had gone up the road ahead of them, the way word did, and by the time they reached Kālia there were lanterns in Kumu's yard and on the road outside her fence and up among the trunks of the coconut grove. The church women were there in their good holokū. The poi man was there, and the fish woman. The men from the saloon were there too, standing back by the road with their hands in their pockets, because forty dollars is forty dollars and they wanted to see it lost or won with their own eyes. Kumu was sitting on a mat on her floor with the doors open and a lamp beside her, the way she sat to hear children read. Kimo took off his hat at the door. He came in and knelt down on the mat in front of her, a big man in a ruined silk shirt with the King's cross hanging off him, and touched his forehead to her hand. Kumu, he said. Something has happened to me. You know what it is. I came because I know you can put it out

sections.heading: V. Sandalwood
sections.dateline: The coconut grove at Kālia · the same night
sections.text: He went up slowly, the way smoke goes up when there is no wind. He went out through the open doors with his knees still bent as if he were kneeling, and up past the eaves of the schoolroom to the height of one coconut palm, and stayed there, with the lanterns shining up on the soles of his boots. Then he came down again, and set his feet on Kumu's steps, and bent and pressed his nose to hers, and breathed, the old greeting. Then he went up again. He went up past one palm, and two, and three, and the lanterns were swinging all over the yard because the people holding them were shaking, and four, and five, and six, and seven, until he was as high above the grove as seven coconut trees standing one on another. There he crossed his legs and sat, the way a man sits on a mat to talk, with the lei on his hat and the King's cross on his chest, against the stars over Lēʻahi. The saloon men took their hands out of their pockets. His voice came down as clear as if he were sitting in the yard. Listen, he said. This is what I did. When I was twelve years old and could read, I sat in that schoolroom and thought: what work is there that takes away people's trouble? And I watched the ones who went

sections.heading: VI. What to Call Him
sections.text: The deacons at Kawaiahaʻo argued about it into the new year. They argued on the steps after the morning service and in the yard after the afternoon one, under the big trees, in their black coats, and the women listened from the shade. Some of them said he was a saint, and you could see it was so, because nobody else in the history of the kingdom had gone up like that, not even the old kings. Others said he was a chief, a true one at last, the King had as much as made him one. And some said it was a scandal to call him either. He had been drunk for seven days. He had died in a silk shirt with three lei on his hat and champagne in his blood and a dancing girl's death on him, wearing the King's gold, at the height of a jubilee the opposition papers had been complaining about all month. Three years before, the printers of the coronation hula program had been hauled into court for obscenity. A man could not be a saint in a hat like that. In the end two of the old deacons walked out to Kālia to ask Kumu, because she had been there, and because she had taught both of them their letters. She was in the schoolroom. It was afternoon, and the children had gone, and she was cleaning slates wit

verses.text: Is there in this world any man so restrained by humility that he does not mind reproof, as a well-trained horse the whip?

Like a well-trained horse when touched by the whip, be ye active and lively, and by faith, by virtue, by energy, by meditation, by discernment of the law you will overcome this great pain (of reproof), perfect in knowledge and in behaviour, and never forgetful.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha's attendant Ānanda meets a poor youth in a ragged loincloth carrying a begging bowl and asks whether the monk's life would not be better. The youth asks who would ordain him; Ānanda says he will, bathes him with his own hand, and ordains him. Finding no other place for his old rag and bowl, the youth hangs them on the branch of a tree. As a monk he eats well, wears fine robes, grows fat and discontented, and goes back to the tree meaning to put his rags on again; there he scolds himself for a shameless fool, his mind grows calm, and he returns. This happens three times. When the other monks ask where he is going, he says, to my teacher. Later he stops going, and says that while he was bound he went to his teacher, but now the bond is cut. The monks report this to the Buddha as a lie, and the Buddha says that Pilotika ("Rags") has spoken the truth, and gives the verses on the good horse.
bg.history:
The Civilian Conservation Corps took unemployed, unmarried young men, usually from families on relief, and gave them food, clothing, shelter and thirty dollars a month, twenty-five of which was sent home. The camps were run by Army officers, and older "local experienced men" were hired to teach the work and look after the boys. Enrollment records sorted men as white or Black only, so no one counted the Mexican Americans who served. In western Nebraska, many of them came out of the sugar-beet country around Scottsbluff, where Great Western Sugar had opened a refinery in 1910 and Mexican families worked the fields. In the Depression many of those families left for Mexico, part of the Mexican Repatriation in which a large share of those who went were American-born children.

Fort Robinson, near Crawford in the Pine Ridge country of northwest Nebraska, was the headquarters of the Ninth Cavalry from 1887 to 1898. The regiment had been organized in New Orleans in 1866 with men from Louisiana and Kentucky, and it fought at Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill in 1898. In 1919 the fort became a quartermaster remount depot, eventually the largest in the world, where horses and mules were received, schooled and issued to the Army. From 1933 to 1935 the post also served as a CCC camp, district headquarters and hospital center.

sections.heading: I. The Pail
sections.text: Jesús Ortega was eighteen years old in the fall of 1933, the third dry year running, and he owned a shirt, a pair of pants with no seat to speak of, a beet knife, and a lard pail. The shirt his mother had sewn for him in 1931 out of two cotton sacks from the Great Western sugar factory, and if you stood behind him you could still read most of the word WESTERN across his shoulders, faded to the color of weak coffee, and a piece of the word GRANULATED down the left side. The lard pail had held lard once. Now it held whatever people put in it. His family had gone back to Mexico in the spring of 1932, on a train out of Scottsbluff with forty other families, because there was no work, and men from the relief had come around to say there would be nothing more for people like them, and that the tickets would be paid. Jesús had been born in a beet shanty outside Minatare. He had never seen Mexico. Somewhere east of North Platte, in the night, while his mother slept against the window with his little sisters across her lap, he had gotten up and walked to the end of the car and stepped off the back of the train onto the ballast and stood there in the dark and watched the red light go away. H

sections.heading: II. The Cottonwood
sections.text: Fort Robinson lay under the white bluffs at the edge of the pines, a city of red brick barracks and stables and parade ground along Soldier Creek, and in every pasture for miles, in every direction, there were horses. Since the war the Army had made it the largest remount depot in the world. Horses came in by the trainload from the ranches to be broken and schooled and shipped out to the cavalry, and mules for the pack trains and the artillery, thousands of them, bays and sorrels and blacks and greys, and at evening when they were driven in to water you could hear them coming before you saw them, like weather. The CCC company had a row of the old barracks at the end of the post. The boys planted pine seedlings on the burned slopes of the ridge and built check dams in the gullies and strung fence, and the Army officers who ran the camp ran it like the Army, with reveille at six and inspection on Saturday, and the boys complained about it, and ate. At the supply room they took his name and his measurements and gave him two of everything. Two suits of wool underwear. Two olive drab shirts and two pairs of olive drab breeches left over from the war in France, smelling of mothballs. Two

sections.heading: III. Pie
sections.dateline: The mess hall · November and December
sections.text: Breakfast was oatmeal and hotcakes and bacon and coffee with canned milk, and all you could eat of all of it. Dinner was beef and potatoes and gravy and beans and bread and butter, and stewed tomatoes, and on Sundays a pie, cut in six, and there was always somebody who did not want his. Supper was the same as dinner except when it was better. The cooks were boys from the company who had been taught by an Army cook, and their gravy was famous along the Pine Ridge. The doctor weighed every boy when he came in and again every month. By Thanksgiving Jesús had put on eighteen pounds. By Christmas he had put on twenty-six. His face filled out until he did not know it in the mirror over the washstand. The breeches from France would not button. The supply sergeant issued him the next size, and then the size after that, and wrote it down. On the first of every month the company clerk sent twenty-five dollars to Rosario Ortega in Scottsbluff, and Jesús got five dollars in his hand, and spent it at the canteen on Bull Durham and candy bars and Coca-Cola. Days, he worked with the old man. Achille Dupuy did not explain much. He handed Jesús a halter and pointed at a mule, and watched, and when

sections.heading: IV. The Branch
sections.text: He went down after supper on a night in January with the snow squeaking under his shoes. The cottonwoods were bare now, grey against the grey snow, and the shirt was still there over its branch, frozen stiff in the shape of the branch, and the pail hung from its twig with a cap of snow in it. He took the shirt down. It cracked when he bent it. He held it up in the last of the light and read WESTERN backward through the cloth, and smelled it, and it smelled like the beet fields and the jungles by the tracks and the back doors and his mother's kitchen, all of it at once, and he stood there and talked to himself out loud, the way men on the road learn to do. Sinvergüenza, he said. You shameless fool. Look at you. Two pairs of shoes, and you want to throw them in the creek. Three meals a day and pie on Sunday, and you want to go back and hold out a lard pail at the Lincoln Café. Twenty-five dollars a month to your tía, and you want to stop it. Ramón Archuleta washed you in a tub like a horse, and you want to go back to the lice. Go on, then. Put it on. Go knock on doors. Sinvergüenza. He said it until he had no more to say, and then he stood there with the shirt in his hands, and somet

sections.heading: V. The Shadow of the Whip
sections.text: He did not go down to the creek again after that. March went by, and the snow went off the ridge, and the creek ran high and brown with it, and he did not go. He went to the corral every morning with the old man, and to the fence lines, and to the mess hall, and to bed. He slept every night straight through. He did not hear the freights anymore, or if he heard them it was only a train. The boys noticed that too. One night in April in the barracks Kenny Albrecht asked him, with half the room listening. Hey, Trapos. You don't go see your teacher anymore? No. How come? She throw you over? The room laughed. Jesús did not. He was sitting on his cot oiling a harness strap across his knees, and he went on oiling it. When I was tied up, he said, I had to go to my teacher. I'm not tied up anymore. So I don't have to go. Nobody in the room knew what that meant. They decided it meant that he was a liar, or that he thought he was smart, and the next morning three of them went down to the corral before work, because the old man was the only one in the camp whose word they all took, and told him about it. They said Trapos had been sneaking off after dark all winter to see a teacher, and now he s

sections.heading: VI. The Nest
sections.text: At the end of May, on a Sunday afternoon, Jesús walked down to Soldier Creek for the first time since February, because it was warm and there was nothing to do and the cottonwoods were throwing their cotton, and the whole bottom along the creek was white with it, drifting, like snow that had forgotten which way was down. The shirt was not on the branch. The lard pail was there, hanging from its twig by its bail, rusted through at the bottom, full of nothing but light. The shirt was gone. He looked under the tree and along the bank and in the shallows, and did not find it, and he stood under the cottonwood and was surprised to find that it did not matter to him one way or the other. Then he heard the bird. It was an oriole, orange and black, scolding him from somewhere overhead, and when he looked up he saw the nest, hanging from the very end of a high thin branch over the water, a little grey pouch swinging in the wind the way orioles make them, woven out of horsehair from the remount pastures and the cotton off the trees and string and grass. And woven all through it, in and out, around and around, were threads of sugar sack, unraveled and pulled out a strand at a time over the wi

verses.text: Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; good people fashion themselves.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a poor laborer in an earlier age works three years for a rich man named Gandha, who eats his costly meals on display before the whole city, to earn one bowl of that rice; when the bowl is finally his he gives all of it to a silent holy man, who carries it off through the air and feeds five hundred, and the shamed rich man gives the laborer half his fortune. Reborn in the Buddha's time, he is the son of a woman who longed in pregnancy to feed the elder Sāriputta and all his monks and eat their leftovers. Named Sukha, “Happy,” because no one in the house suffered after he was conceived, the boy goes forth at seven. On the eighth day, walking behind Sāriputta, he sees men leading water in channels, fletchers straightening arrows and carpenters shaping wheels, and reasons that if people can master things without minds, he can master his own. He sends the elder on, asking him to bring back food of a hundred flavors, and shuts himself in the elder's cell. The gods silence the birds, guard the door and hold the sun and moon still; Sāriputta is fed by a devoted household and hurries back with a second portion; the Buddha stands at the gate and delays him with four questions about what food produces, until the boy reaches awakening. Then the boy eats, the sun moves, and the monks wonder why the day was so long.
bg.history:
The Akimel O'odham (Pima) and their ancestors farmed the middle Gila with canals for many centuries, and in the 1850s and 1860s they sold wheat to emigrants, the overland mail and the army. Upstream settlers then took the river. The Florence Canal, finished in 1889, drew off most of what was left; summer crops failed eleven times between 1892 and 1904, and the community's own history calls these the years of famine. To feed their families, men cut mesquite and sold it as stove wood: by 1905 nearly twelve thousand cords a year were going to Phoenix, and in 1901 a newspaper counted more than thirty thousand cords stacked at Sacaton Station waiting for the railroad. The Presbyterian missionary Charles Cook organized the church at Sacaton in 1889, and a larger adobe meetinghouse was built there in 1918.

The Coolidge Dam on the upper Gila, built by the Bureau of Indian Affairs for the San Carlos Irrigation Project, was meant to bring water back to Pima and non-Indian fields alike. Former President Calvin Coolidge dedicated it on March 4, 1930, before the reservoir had begun to fill; Will Rogers, looking at the grass in the dry lake bed, said that if it were his lake he would mow it. The project did not restore Pima farming. In 2004 the Gila River Indian Community won one of the largest tribal water settlements in American history. The verses Elder Simon recites are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which renders the divine name as Jehovah.

sections.heading: I. The Window
sections.dateline: Phoenix and the Gila villages · the years of famine
sections.text: The grandmothers began it the same way every time, so that the children knew where they were. In the dry years, when the settlers at Florence had taken the river into their big canal and there was nothing left in the Gila but stones and tamarisk, the men of the villages cut mesquite. They cut it along the old fields that had no water any more, and stacked it by the railroad at Sacaton Station in cords as high as a house, and hauled it to Phoenix in wagons to sell for stove wood, and the money bought flour. It was the only work there was. Some years the people ate the government's flour, which had worms in it, and the government's bacon, which was green. Boys grew up who had never seen wheat standing in a field in their own village, though their grandfathers had sold wheat to the soldiers and the stage line and the whole Territory of Arizona. Luis Manuel was one of the woodcutters. He was from Blackwater. In the winter of 1897 he hauled a load to Phoenix the week before Christmas and slept in a friend's yard on Jefferson Street to save the price of a camp, and on the Saturday night the friend said, Come, you have to see the rich man eat. There was a man in Phoenix who owned a hotel

sections.heading: II. The Longing
sections.text: His granddaughter Ruth married a man from Sacaton who farmed twenty acres of allotment land on the government ditch, and in the fall of 1921, when she knew she was carrying a child, a longing came on her that she could not explain to anybody. She wanted to feed the church. All of it. Elder Simon and the other elders and the minister and the women's society and every family that came in wagons to the Sacaton meetinghouse on a Sunday, two hundred people, more. She wanted to cook for them herself, a whole day's cooking, and serve them, and then sit down at the very end with the old women behind the cook fires and eat whatever was left in the bottoms of the pots. Her husband told her she was crazy. The flour alone would cost forty dollars. Her mother told her pregnant women got notions. But the longing would not go away, and in the end the family gave it to her, because a longing like that in a woman carrying a child is not a thing you refuse. At the Thanksgiving meeting she and her sisters and aunts cooked over six fires behind the adobe meetinghouse from four in the morning. Beef stew with chili. Tepary beans. Squash. Tortillas as big as a wagon wheel, a hundred of them, two hundred.

sections.heading: III. Water, Arrows, Wheels
sections.text: That spring Mr. Coolidge, who had been President, came out to the new concrete dam up in the canyon at San Carlos and made a speech on it, and the newspapers said the water was coming back to the Pima at last. Some of the old men went up to see it. The lake behind the dam was dry. There was grass growing in it, and they said a man from Oklahoma who made jokes on the radio had looked at it and said if it were his lake he would mow it. The old men came home and did not say much. The fields at Sacaton that June were watered from the government pumps, a little, when the pumps were running, and the wheat was thin. Happy was seven. In May he had said to his mother, I want to go live with Elder Simon. Elder Simon was seventy-four that year. He had been an elder of the Sacaton church since before there was an adobe church to be an elder of, and before that, when he was young, he had been the canal boss of his village in the last good years, the man who decided who got water and when, and walked the ditches with a shovel on his shoulder before dawn. He lived alone now in a two-room adobe near the meetinghouse, with a ramada in front and one peach tree that he watered from a bucket. His sist

sections.heading: IV. The Long Morning
sections.dateline: Elder Simon's house · the same day
sections.text: Happy let himself into the old man's house and shut the door and pulled the latch string in, and sat down on the dirt floor in the cool dark with his back against the adobe wall and his new shoes in front of him. Nobody knows what he did in there. He was seven. He said afterward only that he thought about the water, and the stick, and the wheel, and about how they could not do anything for themselves and still a man could make them go right, and that if a man could do that to a ditch and a stick and a piece of wood that did not know anything, then a person who did know something ought to be able to do it to himself. And he sat there, and did it. What other people saw, they told for years. They said that all that morning no bird made a sound anywhere near Elder Simon's yard. The grackles that always quarreled in the cottonwoods by the meetinghouse sat in the branches with their beaks shut. The roosters at the agency did not crow. A woman hanging wash said the doves came down to the ditch to drink, as they always did, and stood on the bank, and did not drink, and flew away again without a sound. Four old men from four different villages, who did not know each other well, each said af

sections.heading: V. Every Good Thing
sections.dateline: The Allen place, by the agency · noon
sections.text: Elder Simon stood in the road outside the agency with the Bible under his arm and thought: where? Every family he knew was eating government flour and pump-water squash. And then, the way you remember where you put something, he thought of the Allens. Daniel Allen had one of the few fields near Sacaton that had kept its own well, and his wife had come from Salt River, where there was still water in the canals, and her family had sent her a wagonload of things that very week. When Elder Simon came to their gate at noon, the whole family came out, and Mrs. Allen said, Elder! It's good you came today of all days, and they took his Bible and his hat and sat him in the best chair under the ramada and brought him a cup of water from the well and coffee with sugar. Then they asked him to talk to them about the Word until the food was ready, and he did, sitting in the shade with their children at his feet, until he smelled that it was time and stopped. The food came. Beef and chili. Tepary beans, the brown and the white. Tortillas off the griddle, thin as paper. Squash with green corn. Cholla buds that Mrs. Allen's mother had picked and dried in April. Watermelon from Salt River. Peaches.

sections.heading: VI. The Gate
sections.text: Juana was standing at the gate when he came. She had never stood at the gate in her life. She had one hand on the gatepost, and her blind face turned toward him on the road, and he slowed down, and stopped. Sister. Let me in. I have food for the boy. What is it you've got? He did not understand why she asked, but he answered her, because she was his elder sister and he had answered her all his life. Food. And what is food for? For when you're hungry. So you feel good. And what does feeling good do? He thought about it. It fills a person out. Puts color in them. Makes them look well. And then what? Elder Simon stood in the road with the bucket and thought about the famine years, and the green bacon, and all the children he had buried, and his own sons hauling wood to Phoenix. Then they're content, he said. Then they lie down in the shade and they're glad to be alive. Juana stood listening to something past him, behind him, in the house. Then she took her hand off the gatepost. All right, she said. Go on. Give the boy his food. The old man went up to his own door. The latch string was pulled in. He knocked, and called, and pushed, and the door gave, and Happy came out into the yard i

sections.heading: VII. Which Downhill
sections.text: The elders met at the meetinghouse that night, as they did on Wednesdays, and before they prayed they sat on the benches outside in the dark and talked about the day. Everybody had felt it. The morning that would not end, the noon that went on and on, and then the evening coming all at once, as if somebody had let go of it. The boy only just finished his dinner, one of them said. At sundown. What kind of day was that? Juana had come over on her grandson's arm, which she never did on Wednesdays, and was sitting on the end of the bench with her cane across her knees. That's what a day is like, she said, when somebody inside it is working. They waited. She did not say much, ever, and they had learned to wait. This morning that boy saw men leading water in a ditch. He saw an old man straightening arrows over the coals. He saw them putting the iron on a wheel down at the agency. And he went home and shut the door and did it to himself. She turned her face toward where her brother was sitting. Simon. You were a canal boss. Say it for them. The one in Proverbs about the water. Elder Simon said it in O'odham, and then, because the minister was there, he said it in English, the way it was i

title: The Long Day
place: Sacaton, Gila River Indian Reservation, Arizona
logline: In the dry summer after the Coolidge Dam, a seven-year-old Pima boy watches men lead water, straighten arrows and iron a wheel.

verses.text: How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning? Why do you not seek a light, ye who are surrounded by darkness?

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred young men of Sāvatthī put their wives in the care of the laywoman Visākhā. After a seven-day drinking festival the women secretly finish the leftover liquor on an outing to a pleasure garden. Visākhā rebukes them, they pretend to be sick, and their husbands beat them. At the next festival she refuses to take them out, so they ask to visit the monastery and carry jugs under their cloaks. Drunk in the hall before the Buddha, and possessed by a spirit of Māra’s host, they clap, laugh and dance. He sends out a dark ray that leaves them in blackness and so frightened that the liquor dries up in them. Then he stands on the summit of Mount Sineru and sends out a light like a thousand moons, and speaks the verse. Asked how drink began, he tells the birth story of the pot: a forester finds liquor in the fork of a tree, it ruins city after city, and a king is stopped at the last moment and has the jars broken.
bg.history:
The people in this story are invented. Fells Point was Baltimore’s shipbuilding district, and the caulking trade there was largely in the hands of Black workers, free and enslaved. Black caulkers named Richard Jones, Henry Scott and John Whittington lived in the 1840s in two small wooden houses on South Wolfe Street that still stand. Frederick Douglass, then Frederick Bailey, grew up partly on Philpot Street and worked as a caulker in the Point’s yards until he escaped in September 1838. He wrote that he earned a dollar and a half a day, and that he learned his first letters from the marks ship carpenters cut into timbers: L, S, L. F., S. A. His Narrative, published in Boston in 1845, describes the week between Christmas and New Year’s as a holiday on which slaveholders encouraged drunkenness, and calls it a fraud.

Maryland did not forbid teaching Black people to read, and Black Baltimoreans supported their own schools. But laws passed after 1831 put heavy limits on free Black people, including on meeting for worship without a white person present, and an 1841 law made a free Black person found with abolitionist writing liable to ten to twenty years in prison (see the Pathways to Freedom timeline). The Phoenix Shot Tower, finished in 1828 and a little over 234 feet high, was the tallest structure in the United States when it was built. Oakum is tarred hemp fiber, often picked from old rope, which caulkers drove into a ship’s seams with an iron and a mallet. Cherry bounce is an old cordial of sour cherries, sugar and spirits.

sections.heading: I. The Bounce
sections.dateline: Happy Alley, Fells Point, Baltimore · Christmas 1845
sections.text: When a young caulker on the Point married, he took his wife to Mother Sewell. A good many of the girls were just up from the Eastern Shore. Some were free and some were hired out by a master in Talbot or Dorchester who had never seen Baltimore, and none of them knew the town. Keziah Sewell did. She owned two houses in Happy Alley, and she washed for the captains’ wives on Thames Street and employed six women to help her do it. The husbands went off to the yards at sunup, where a good caulker made a dollar and a half a day, and they knew that whatever their wives did, they did it under her eye. By that Christmas she had some thirty of them. She took them to market and to the meeting on Strawberry Alley, and two nights a week she took them up the outside stair of a chandler’s storehouse on Wolfe Street to learn their letters. In July she also taught them to make cherry bounce. They stoned the sour cherries in her yard and put them down in stone crocks with sugar and spirits, and the crocks stood in her cellar until Christmas. That was for the men. From Christmas Eve to New Year’s the yards were shut, and the caulkers of Fells Point kept the holiday the way it was kept from there to G

sections.heading: II. One Lamp
sections.dateline: A storehouse loft on Wolfe Street · Tuesday of Christmas week, 1846
sections.text: Mr. Nace Tilghman had driven oakum into the seams of ships for forty years. He had bought himself out of it a Sunday at a time, and that took eleven years. When his hands grew too knotted to hold an iron he did not leave the trade. He rented the loft over the chandler’s. There he picked old rope apart and rolled the tarred hemp on his knee into the long soft strands the caulkers used, and the yards bought all he could spin. The loft was heaped with it to the rafters. It smelled of Stockholm tar. He kept one whale-oil lamp on a chain from the ridge beam, well clear of everything, and a bucket of sand under it, and he had one rule, which was that nobody moved the lamp. Twice a week after dark he chalked letters on the wall. He started every scholar on the same four, S and L and F and A, because those were the ones the ship carpenters cut into a timber to say where it went. Starboard, larboard, forward and aft. A woman who had carried her husband’s dinner into a yard had seen them all her life. He said there had been a boy on Philpot Street who got his first four letters that way, off the timbers in a yard, with nobody to teach him. That boy had gone North eight years back, and he had

sections.heading: III. The Crock
sections.text: Mother Sewell spoke first. That drink is a wicked thing, Mr. Tilghman. These are decent women. They sat down in front of you and couldn’t keep their own feet under them. Where did such a thing ever start? The way I had it, it started with a hunter, he said. He found a tree with a hollow in the fork. The rain stood in it, and fruit had dropped in and wild grain, and the sun had worked on that all summer. He watched the birds come and drink there. They fell off the limb and lay on the ground a while, and then they got up and flew. So he drank, and he carried some to a holy man who lived by himself in those woods, and the two of them took it to a town in gourds. That town drank until it forgot to plant. It’s gone now. They went on to the next town and that one is gone too. At last they brought it to a king. He had the cup at his mouth when a stranger came to the gate with a jar on his hip, crying it like a huckster. Buy my jar! Drink this and you’ll fall down your own stair. You’ll sleep in the road and tell what you ought to hide, and you’ll strike your mother. The king put the cup down and had every pot in the place broken. He’s the only king I ever heard of with sense. It is the sa

title: The Oakum Loft
logline: In Christmas week the caulkers' wives climb to an old man's night school with jugs under their cloaks, and he puts out the lamp.

verses.text: Look at this dressed-up lump, covered with wounds, joined together, sickly, full of many thoughts, which has no strength, no hold!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Sirimā is a celebrated courtesan of Rājagaha and the sister of the physician Jīvaka. After wronging the devout laywoman Uttarā, she comes to ask her pardon while the Buddha is eating at Uttarā's house, hears him teach that anger is overcome by kindness and evil by good, and becomes a disciple. From then on she feeds eight monks every day, lavishly. One monk praises her food and her beauty so warmly that another monk falls in love with her without ever having seen her, and contrives to be among the eight the next morning. She is ill that day and is carried out trembling to greet the monks; he goes home unable to eat, and she dies that evening. The Buddha asks King Bimbisāra not to burn her body but to leave it under guard in the charnel ground. On the fourth day, with the body swollen and crawling with maggots, the king has a drum beaten through the city and fines anyone who stays away, and at the Buddha's word offers her body for a thousand coins, then less and less, down to an eighth of a coin, then for nothing, and nobody will take her. The Buddha speaks the verse on the body, and the lovesick monk reaches the first stage of awakening.
bg.history:
In the first half of the eighteenth century, St. Augustine was a poor garrison town that could barely feed itself. The royal subsidy from Mexico, the situado, came irregularly and sometimes not for years. Carolina forces had burned the town in 1702, sparing only the Castillo de San Marcos, and English and Creek raids destroyed most of the interior Franciscan missions; their surviving Christian Native families resettled in small towns close to the city. Trade with the English was illegal but went on openly, and according to the Florida Museum one observer in 1736 counted six English merchant ships in the harbor at once.

The Franciscans' friary at the south end of town, burned in 1702, began to be rebuilt in stone in 1735; the building survives as the St. Francis Barracks. Its stone, like the Castillo's, was coquina, a rock made of shell fragments, quarried on Anastasia Island across the bay. Coquina is soft when first cut and has to dry for a year or more before it can bear weight. The town's northern edge was the Cubo Line, an earthwork of earth and palm logs with a palisade and a moat, running from the Castillo to the San Sebastián River.

sections.heading: I. Hot Lard
sections.dateline: San Agustín de la Florida · Lent 1736
sections.text: In the spring of 1736 there were six English ships in the harbor at once, which was against the King's law and everybody knew it, and the men off those ships said that the most beautiful woman between Charles Town and Havana lived in a stone house south of the plaza in San Agustín, and that her name was Gloria. She was the younger sister of Maestro Pedro Leal, the surgeon of the garrison, who had set half the broken legs in the town and closed most of its knife wounds. Their father had been a soldier and their mother a soldier's widow who took in washing, and when Gloria was fifteen she stopped taking in washing. By twenty-five she owned the stone house, and a woman named Juana who had been bought for her in Havana, and a set of pearls. An English captain had once paid her an onza of gold for a single night, sixteen pieces of eight, and told it all the way up the coast. Officers of the garrison paid her in silver when the situado came from Mexico, and in promises when it did not, which was most years. The town's wives crossed the street when they saw her coming. The town's husbands did not. That Lent she was living in the house of a merchant's son named Salgado. It was an arrangeme

sections.heading: II. Three Leagues
sections.text: Fray Bernardo was old and fat and talked, and one day in June, after he had eaten at Gloria's table, he walked three leagues up the coast road to a mission town on the inland water, where a young friar named Gil kept the church for a few dozen Christian families who had come down from Guale and the islands when the English and their Creek allies burned the old missions, before Gil was born. Fray Gil was twenty-four and from Galicia and had been in Florida less than a year. He had never been in San Agustín except to land there. He gave Fray Bernardo water from the well and a hammock under the shed, and after the evening prayer the old man lay in the hammock and talked. Where did you eat today, Father? At Gloria Leal's. Is it good there? Good? Fray Bernardo laughed in the dark. There's no telling it. White bread. Butter like in Spain. She stands in the door and fills your bowl till it runs over and then she puts in more. One bowl of hers would keep you a week up here. But I'll tell you, as good as the food is, she's better to look at. And he told it, the way old men tell things, lying in a hammock in the dark with their hands on their bellies. Her hair. Her throat. The way she stood

sections.heading: III. The Fever
sections.text: Gloria had fallen sick the afternoon before, just after Fray Bernardo left her door. It began with a headache and a pain in her back, and by night she was burning. She took off her pearls and her rings and her earrings and gave them to Juana to put away, and lay down in her room with the shutters closed. At noon Juana came in and told her that the friars were at the door, eight of them, and a young one first. Gloria could not get up. She lay with her eyes closed and gave her orders from the bed.
