Let them in. Give them seats in the cool room. Give them the broth first, and bread. When it's time for the rice, fill their bowls, and fill them right, Juana, the way I do it. Don't be stingy because I'm not there to see. So Juana and the girl from the Indian town who worked for wages brought the friars in and sat them on the benches and gave them broth and bread and then the rice with milk and cinnamon, and filled their bowls the right way. Then Juana went back to the room. Carry me out, said Gloria. I want to greet them. Señora, you can't stand. Then carry me. So they carried her, Juana under her arms and the girl at her feet, in her shift with a shawl around her, and set her on a stool

sections.heading: IV. Four Days
sections.text: The Cubo line ran from the Castillo across the neck of land to the San Sebastián River, an earth wall faced with palm logs, with a palisade along the top and a ditch in front and the slope planted thick with Spanish bayonet so that no man could climb it without leaving pieces of himself. North of it the soldiers kept the ground cleared for a musket shot, so an enemy would have nowhere to hide. That was where they laid her, on a plank bier on two trestles, in her best dress, with her hands folded and her hair combed by her brother. The first day she looked asleep. People came out through the gate and stood at a distance and looked at her and went back and said she looked asleep. The second day the color went out of her. The third day there was a smell that the sea wind took toward the town in the afternoons, and the buzzards came, black ones and red-headed ones, and sat on the palisade in a row and waited, and the two soldiers on guard threw stones at them, and the buzzards moved down a few stakes and sat again. On the fourth day she had swelled. Her face was gone. From her mouth and her nose and her eyes and her ears and the other openings of the body there came the white moving th

sections.heading: V. The Crier
sections.dateline: The cleared ground · the fourth day
sections.text: The whole town was there. The friars stood together on one side of the bier, Fray Lucas at their head. On the other side stood everybody else, each in their place, the way they stood at processions. The officers of the garrison and their wives in front, and the merchants, and Maestro Pedro with his hat in his hands. The soldiers. The women of the confraternities in their black. The free Black militiamen and their families. People from the Christian Indian towns outside the lines, who had come down because the drum said everyone. Juana, who had combed her mistress's hair every morning for eleven years. At the back, standing a little apart where the road went down to the harbor, a few English sailors who did not know what was happening and had come to see. Nobody went closer than ten paces. Many of them held cloths to their faces, and some of them held oranges cut in half. Fray Lucas looked a long time at the bier. Then he turned to the governor's adjutant. Who is this woman? The adjutant thought he had misheard. Father, it's Gloria Leal. The surgeon's sister. This is Gloria? Yes, Father. Then let her be sold, said Fray Lucas. Have your crier cry it the way he cries the goods of dead

sections.heading: VI. Coquina
sections.text: They buried her that evening in the grave she had paid for, before the altar of Our Lady in the friars' church, with the shutters open and the doors open and a great deal of incense. Juana walked behind the coffin. So did Doña Inés Salgado, in black, and Maestro Pedro, and Domingo de la Cruz, and all eight of the friars who had eaten at her table, and some of the wives who had crossed the street. Fray Lucas said the Mass himself. When it was over he stood at the edge of the open grave with the holy water and said one thing more over it, quietly, the way he said everything, so that the people near him had to lean in. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised. — Proverbs 31:30 Then they closed the grave and laid the flagstone over it. Fray Gil did not go back up the coast that summer. He asked to stay and work on the new friary, and Fray Lucas let him. Every morning before light he went across the bay in the boat to the King's Quarry on Anastasia Island with the masons and the hired men, and cut coquina out of the pit, and loaded it, and rowed it back. Coquina is soft when it first comes out of the ground, so soft it can be cut wit

title: What Shall I Cry
logline: A young friar falls in love with a famous beauty he has never seen, from one old friar's talk at supper.

verses.text: This body is wasted, full of sickness, and frail; this heap of corruption breaks to pieces, life indeed ends in death.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the nun Uttarī is a hundred and twenty years old and still goes on her alms round every day. One day, coming back with food in her bowl, she meets a monk in the street, asks whether she may give it to him, and gives him all of it. She does the same on the second day and the third, and has none left for herself. On the fourth day she meets the Buddha in a crowded place, steps back to make way, treads on the hem of her robe and falls. He tells her that her body is worn out with age and will soon break up, and speaks the verse. At the end of it she enters the stream, and many others who hear it are helped.
bg.history:
The Jesuit mission of Diego Luis de San Vitores reached Guam in 1668, and the Spanish–Chamorro Wars that followed lasted almost thirty years. War, the destruction of the canoes, forced removals from the northern islands and repeated epidemics (among them smallpox in 1699 or 1700) brought the Chamorro people near to vanishing; deaths from hunger are recorded in 1706, and a Spanish census of 1710 counted about 3,500 Chamorros alive. The survivors were gathered into six church-centered villages, Agaña (Hågatña) chief among them (Guampedia). Women who had worn little before the mission began to cover themselves at the missionaries’ urging. On Guam, lågu means north, and in its older sense, toward the sea. Flour from the seeds of the native cycad, fadang, was a traditional food on the island until the 1960s.

San Vitores founded the Colegio de San Juan de Letrán in Agaña in 1669 for Chamorro boys, who learned their letters and the doctrine there; mission reports describe the children singing the doctrine in procession, and the Corpus Christi feast of 1677 with altars, songs at each station, dances and militia volleys. The techa, the lay prayer leader, most often an elderly woman, who leads the rosaries and novenas for the dead in a high, steady chant, is thought to date from at least the Spanish period; her chanting has been compared to the mourning of the dead at ancient Chamorro funerals. The old woman, the boy and the maestro are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Rounds
sections.dateline: Agaña, on Guam · the hungry year, 1706
sections.text: Nobody in Agaña knew how old she was. She had been an old woman already when the padres came, and that was thirty-eight years ago. The padres had baptized her Isabel, but most people called her the one from lågu, because she had come down from the islands to the north, from the north and from the sea side of everything, when the soldiers brought the last of her people to Guam in the boats that were not burned. She was the last one left of all those boats. Her husband was dead, and her sons, and her sons’ sons, in the fighting and the sicknesses and the crossing. She lived with a widow from Pago in a house of wood and thatch below the church, and every morning, while it was still cool, she went on her rounds. She went to the houses where somebody was sick or somebody had died. There was always one. In the year of the spotted sickness there had been so many that she went to eleven houses in a morning, and in this year, the hungry year, they were dying again, slower, of the hunger and the sickness that comes after the hunger. She went in and knelt on the mat by whoever was lying there and led the prayers the padres had taught, the Our Father and the Hail Mary and the long ones for the

sections.heading: II. The Boy
sections.dateline: The plaza wall · the last days of May
sections.text: On the way home on the first day she met a boy from the colegio. The colegio stood beside the church on the plaza, and the boys of Agaña went there from the time they were small to learn their letters and the doctrine and to sing in the church. This one was perhaps eleven. He had the high voice that the padres put at the front of the singing, and he was so thin that his shoulders stood up under his shirt like the frame of a roof. He was sitting on the plaza wall in the shade with his knees drawn up, waiting for something or for nothing. She stopped in front of him and held out the basket. May I give you this? He looked at it, and at her. Then he said yes, and took it with both hands, the way the padres had taught the boys to take a thing that is given, and opened it. There was a cake of fadang in it and a little rice. He ate all of it there on the wall, slowly, while she stood and watched him, and then he handed her back the basket. She went home with it empty. The second day she met him in the same place, on the wall in the same shade, and asked him the same thing, and he said yes. The third day it was the same. On each of the three days she gave him all she had been given, and on

sections.heading: III. The Procession
sections.text: The fourth day was the great feast, and all of Agaña was in the plaza. They had built altars at the corners under arches of palm, and the soldiers of the garrison stood in two lines in their coats with their muskets. The bells began before the sun was over the hill. The procession came out of the church with the padres under a canopy and the Host in its gold sun, and the boys of the colegio walked ahead of it in rows, two by two, singing the doctrine, and the men with the trumpets and the shawms came behind. At each altar the whole crowd went down on its knees in the dust while a song was sung, and then got up again and moved on, and the soldiers fired a volley into the air that made the children shriek and the dogs run under the houses. Every Chamorro left on the island who could walk to Agaña seemed to be there, all of them in their Manila cloth, pressed together along the edges of the plaza in the heat. She had not gone on her rounds that morning, because of the feast. She stood near the colegio wall with the widow from Pago and watched the boys come by. She saw her boy among them, in the front row, with his mouth open in the high part of the song. She was light in the head. The

sections.heading: IV. The Leaf
sections.dateline: The house below the church · that evening
sections.text: At dusk the boy from the colegio came to the door of the house below the church. He had a cake of fadang in his hands, wrapped in a leaf, from the padres’ kitchen. He held it out to her. May I give you this? She said yes. She sat on the step and ate all of it, slowly, while he stood and watched, and when it was gone she smoothed the leaf flat on her knee and handed it back to him, and he went up the hill to the colegio in the last light, folding it smaller and smaller as he walked.

title: The Hem
logline: In Guam's hungry year, a Chamorro woman older than the mission gives the food from her prayer rounds to a thin choirboy three days running.

verses.text: Those white bones, like gourds thrown away in the autumn, what pleasure is there in looking at them?

bg.commentary: Five hundred monks take a meditation subject from the Buddha into the forest, work hard, and reach deep absorption. Sure they are finished, they come back to report it. At the gate the Buddha sends word through Ānanda that they should first go to the charnel ground, and they go without asking why. Bodies a day or two dead disgust them, but the freshly dead stir their lust, and they see that their defilements are still in them. The Buddha, without leaving his chamber, sends a radiant image of himself to speak to them face to face: is it fitting, seeing such a heap of bones, to take delight? They reach awakening where they stand, and go to pay him homage.
bg.history:
The Latter Rain revival began in February 1948 among students who had been fasting and praying at the Sharon Orphanage and Schools in North Battleford, Saskatchewan. Its first camp meeting that July drew thousands, and the movement spread fast through Pentecostal churches in Canada and the United States. Its leaders laid hands on believers with personal prophecy and taught that spiritual gifts could be passed on that way. Some taught that before the end a company of overcomers, the “manifest sons of God,” would come into the full stature of Christ, and the boldest said they would step into immortality. The Assemblies of God’s General Council condemned the “New Order of the Latter Rain” in 1949, and a good many congregations split over it.

Sheridan County lies in the far northeast corner of Montana against the Saskatchewan line, dry-land wheat country with Plentywood as its county seat and 6,674 people in 1950. Most of its farm families were Norwegian, Danish and German, and in the 1920s and 1930s it had been a center of radical farm organizing. Small towns on the plains still put calls through on manual switchboards, often in the operator’s own rooms so someone could answer day and night, and customers knew their operator by name. The town of Sundal and everyone in the story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Board
sections.text: The telephone exchange was two rooms over Hegge's Drug, up a stair so steep the lineman said it was built for goats. The front room held the board. It was oak, older than most of the town, with a hundred and twenty jacks in brass rows and a little lamp over each one, and the cords came up out of the shelf on lead weights and went back down when you let them go. The back room held a cot, a hot plate, a coffee pot and a window that looked north across the flats toward Canada, nineteen miles off, where there was nothing to see but more of the same. Thea Solum worked the board from seven at night until seven in the morning, six nights a week, and had since the fall of 1929. Her husband had gone through the ice on Medicine Lake the winter before, after a coyote, and the company needed a night girl, and she was forty-three. She was sixty-four now. The town still called her the night girl. She knew who was sick before the doctor did. When the lamp came up for the Fjeld place at two in the morning, she knew it was the baby with the croup again, and had the doctor's line ringing before Mrs. Fjeld finished saying his name. She knew when the cows were calving and when a man had come home drun

sections.heading: II. The Wagon
sections.dateline: The Big Muddy breaks · September and October 1950
sections.text: After harvest they went into the breaks south of the Big Muddy, where Gilbert's uncle kept a sheep wagon on a bench above the creek, and they fasted there twenty-one days. They took water and nothing else. They read aloud by a coal-oil lantern, Romans eight mostly, over and over. For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. The first week was hunger and quarreling, and Duane walked out twice and came back. The second week was cold, with frost on the wagon sheet in the morning and the sheep dog sleeping across the door to keep them in. In the third week something gave way. It came to each of them a little differently and they told it to each other in the dark. Leland said it was like the wagon had been lifted off the ground and set down somewhere quieter. Vern said his body had gone, he could not feel the bunk under him, only a light that came up from inside and stayed. Orrin wept for two days without being sad. They stopped being hungry. They stopped being cold. They stopped, they all agreed, wanting anything at all. Not food, not land, not girls, not the new Ford tractor in the window at Plentywood. The flesh had died in them, they

sections.heading: III. The Stair
sections.dateline: Sundal · the first week of November 1950
sections.text: They went up Main Street a little after nine, in a dry snow that blew across the street without settling, and stood at the foot of the exchange stair. Old Elmer Haaland was sitting at the bottom of it in his sheepskin, where he sat most nights with a thermos, because he was the town's night marshal and there was nothing in Sundal to marshal. He ran messages up the stair for her when the board was too busy for her to leave it, which it never was. Elmer went up. They could hear the cords drop on their weights and the little ring of the night bell, and her voice saying, Number, please, and then a long time nothing. He came back down. She says not to come up yet, he said. She says first go sit with old Torger Lund. They've got him laid out in the front room at the farm and the boy's not in from Seattle till Thursday. She says go sit up with him and come back after. None of them asked why. Orrin said to the others in the truck, She's got a reason. She always had a reason. And they drove out to the Lund place, eleven miles west on the section line, in the snow.

sections.heading: IV. Two Houses
sections.dateline: The Lund farm and the Haugen farm · November
sections.text: Torger Lund had died on Saturday at eighty-one, in his chair, and the undertaker from Plentywood had come out and done what he did, and then they had laid him on a board across two sawhorses in the cold front room, with the stove door shut and the storm windows on, to keep until his son came. It was Monday. The neighbors were taking the nights. The five sat up with him on kitchen chairs. They sang a little, low, so as not to bother Mrs. Lund upstairs. The lamp was turned down. Torger's face had gone the color of a candle and fallen in around the teeth, and his hands on his chest were yellow at the nails. The room smelled of cold and of the undertaker's fluid, and under that of something else, faint and sweet, that the cold could not quite keep down. By the second hour Duane had gone out on the step twice for air. But they were steady. They looked at the old man and felt nothing but a mild distaste, the way you feel about a dead calf in a slough, and they were glad of the nothing. In the truck at dawn Leland said it for all of them. You see? Not one thing in us that wants what that is. It's dead. And they drove back to town light as boys, to tell her. Elmer was at the foot of the st

sections.heading: V. Three O'Clock
sections.text: The clock on the shelf said three. Marit's mother had gone up. The lamp was low and the stove had burned down and the five of them sat in a row along the wall where they could not see one another's faces. Then they could see them. There was light in the room, not much, as much as comes off snow under a moon, though there was no moon that night. It came from the kitchen doorway. Thea Solum was standing there in her brown cardigan, with her reading glasses on the cord around her neck and her headset pushed down around her collar the way she wore it when she went for coffee, and the light was coming off her. She did not come into the room. She looked at the girl on the door, and the white gourds on the sills, and the five of them along the wall. Is this what you were coming up my stairs to tell me? she said. You sit here with a board of bones like this, and you're glad? Nobody answered her. Then she said two verses, the way she had said them in class for fifteen years, plain, as if she were giving a number. Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord GOD, thou knowest. — Ezekiel 37:3 Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it

sections.heading: VI. The Ticket
sections.text: Elmer Haaland told it the rest of his life, in the drugstore and at the elevator, to anyone who would stand for it. He had sat at the foot of that stair from nine at night until seven in the morning, he said, with his thermos, the way he always did, and no one had come down it but him, and no one had gone up but him, and she had not left the board. He had heard her the whole night through the door. Number, please. And at five past three, he said, which was the exact time, she had put through the vet for the Sorby heifer that was calving backward, and at half past, a long-distance call to the hospital in Williston. It was on her tickets. Anybody could see the tickets. The company kept them in a drawer. The five came up Main Street at a quarter to seven, as she was going off. Elmer stood aside. They went up the goat stair one at a time, which nobody but the lineman and the night girl ever did, and into the front room, and they knelt down on the oiled floor beside the board, all five, and put their foreheads on their hands, and stayed there. The day girl came up behind them with her lunch pail and stopped in the door. Get up, Thea said. You'll scare Doris. She took off her headset and

title: The Night Board
logline: Five young farmers come home from a revival fast sure the flesh is dead in them. The night operator sends them to the dead.

verses.text: After a stronghold has been made of the bones, it is covered with flesh and blood, and there dwell in it old age and death, pride and deceit.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Rūpanandā, "Joyous Form," the Buddha's own half-sister and the most beautiful woman in the land, becomes a nun because everyone she loves has already left home to follow her brother: his son, her betrothed husband, her mother. She does it for love of them, not out of faith, and because she has heard that the Buddha calls the body impermanent and unsatisfying, she keeps out of his sight, sure he will find fault with her beauty. When the nuns finally bring her to hear him, she hides among them. The Buddha conjures a girl of sixteen in crimson, more beautiful than Rūpanandā, fanning herself beside him. As Rūpanandā watches, the girl ages, bears a child, grows old and bent, falls sick, dies, and is torn apart by crows and dogs. Seeing that the same is coming to her own body, Rūpanandā is shaken loose; the Buddha steadies her with verses, then tells her the body is a city of bones, and she reaches awakening.
bg.history:
Logan County sits in the southern West Virginia coalfields along the Guyandotte River; it saw the Battle of Blair Mountain in 1921 and the Buffalo Creek flood in 1972. By the 2000s much of the coal there came from mountaintop removal, in which explosives take off as much as 400 feet of a summit to reach the seams beneath and the leftover rock is pushed into the hollows below as "valley fills." The method supplied about 30 percent of West Virginia's coal in 2006 and needed far fewer workers than underground mining. The same years brought the prescription-painkiller epidemic to the region; in May 2007 Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty to misleading the public about the addiction risk of OxyContin and agreed to pay $600 million.

Holiness and Pentecostal churches have deep roots in the Appalachian coalfields. Many of the more conservative ones keep what they call outward holiness: women do not cut their hair, wear dresses or skirts rather than trousers, and give up jewelry and makeup, citing among other passages 1 Peter 3, the verses on "outward adorning" that Crystal feared her brother would preach at her.

sections.heading: I. Miss Guyandotte Valley
sections.text: Crystal Hollins was the prettiest girl anybody in Logan County could remember, and in Logan County people remember. She was Miss Guyandotte Valley at eighteen, in a white gown her mother drove to Charleston to buy, and the picture of her in the sash with her hands folded and her hair down her back ran on the front of the Logan paper and stayed taped up in the window of the drive-in at Chapmanville until the sun bleached it blue. A man from a modeling agency in Columbus saw that picture and drove all the way down to give her his card, and she kept it in her wallet for nine years and never called him. Men who had known her since she was in diapers still turned around in the Walmart. Old women at the post office told her mother, That girl could have been on television, and her mother said, Well, she could have. She was the baby of the family. Darrell was the oldest, fifteen years ahead of her, and Darrell had done what the Hollinses had always meant somebody to do. He had started with one dozer and a dump truck and a man who knew powder, and by 2002 Hollins Contracting had sixty men and a shop full of equipment and did the blasting and the hauling for the strip jobs from Blair to the

sections.heading: II. The Sisters
sections.text: She sold the salon. She put her jeans and her shorts in a garbage bag and took them to the Goodwill in Logan, and bought long denim skirts and long-sleeved blouses. She washed off her makeup and did not put it back on. She stopped cutting her hair, which had never been cut much anyway, and learned from her mother how to twist it up and pin it, the way the Holiness women wear it, high on the back of the head. She took off her rings and the little gold cross she had worn since she was confirmed at the Methodist church in Chapmanville when she was twelve. The church called that outward holiness, and she kept every bit of it. What she did not give up was the mirror. Every morning she stood in front of the bathroom glass on Sycamore Fork to pin up her hair, and every morning she looked a while longer than it took. Without the makeup her face was plainer, she could see that, and she could also see that it hardly mattered. Her skin was still what it was. Her eyes were still what they were. She would turn her head to one side and the other and think, with a little guilty pleasure she never told anybody about, that they could take away the lipstick and the gold and the jeans and the salon,

sections.heading: III. The Girl in Red
sections.text: The marquee sign out by the creek road said REVIVAL AUG 12–19 BRO DARRELL HOLLINS ALL WELCOME, in red letters Caleb had put up on a stepladder. The rose of Sharon bushes along the church steps were in bloom, the pink kind with the red eye, where every flower opens in the morning and is shriveled on the ground by the next one. It was the third night of the revival and the church was full to the doors, with folding chairs down the aisle and men standing along the back wall with their hats in their hands. The windows were open and the box fans were going and it did not help. Every few minutes the windows shook in their frames, because the company that had bought Darrell's old contracts was still blasting on the strip job across the hollow, on what had been Cazy Mountain, and they blasted at four and again at seven. Crystal came in late with the sisters and sat down in the next-to-last pew, right behind Sister Opal and Sister Rhonda, whose hair was pinned up so high that between the two of them she could hardly see the pulpit. That was why she had picked them. Caleb led the singing. Travis played guitar. Then Darrell got up, and the church went quiet, and Crystal leaned a little to the

sections.heading: IV. The Fan
sections.text: Darrell began to preach. He did not preach out of First Peter. He did not preach about adorning at all. Crystal never could remember afterward what he preached about, because while he preached she was watching the girl, and the girl was changing. It went slow at first. The girl was sixteen, and then she was twenty. That was all. But Crystal felt it go through her like cold water, and she thought, she's not the same. She's not as pretty as she was a minute ago. Then the girl was holding a baby on her hip, and fanning the baby with the church fan, and her face had gone a little thick under the jaw and there were blue half-moons under her eyes. Then the baby was gone and she was forty, in a sweatshirt with a Dollar General name tag pinned to it, with a home permanent and reading glasses on a string around her neck, and she was rubbing the small of her back with one hand while she fanned with the other. Crystal sat very still in the pew. She kept thinking, now that's gone. Now that's gone too. Then the girl was old. Her hair was white and thin and her teeth were gone and her mouth had fallen in, and she was bent over nearly double, the way the old women on the creek get bent from a lif

sections.heading: V. Bones
sections.text: Then the old woman on the floor was dead. Crystal watched it happen, and then watched what came after, all of it, in the time it takes to preach a sermon. The body swelled up in the red gown until the rhinestone sash cut into it. The face went dark. What was inside started coming out of every opening there is, and there were worms in it. And then the church was not a church any more but a bank by the side of the creek road, and the buzzards came down out of the sky in long circles and landed, and the crows came, and the dogs from the trailers came up out of the hollow and pulled at it, and pulled the red gown apart, and the bones came through. Crystal looked at it, and something in her went down to the bottom and stopped. She thought: that was her, and it happened right here. She got old right here, and got sick right here, and died right here. And it is coming to me. It is coming to this body I am sitting in. It is not coming someday to somebody. It is coming to this. Then she saw it was coming to everything. To the sisters in front of her, and their high pinned hair. To her mother. To Travis with his guitar. To every face in the church, and every face in the Walmart, and the pict

sections.heading: VI. The Strip Job
sections.text: Sister Opal said, on the way out to the cars, that she had never seen anything like it, and Sister Rhonda said she had told them, didn't she tell them, now he'd really preach. Sister Faye said that was the first time anybody ever saw Darrell Hollins walk out of his own pulpit in the middle of a sermon. Sister Bernice did not say anything. She took Crystal's face in both her old hands in the gravel lot, under the one light on the pole, and looked at it a long time, and let it go. Crystal never told the sisters what she had seen by the altar rail. She told Darrell once, years later, sitting on his porch, and he nodded and said he knew, and they did not talk about it again. She did not make much of herself after that, in the church or out of it. She worked at the clinic in Logan, at the front desk, and then in the back with the old people, washing them and turning them in their beds, which she was good at and did not mind. She was the one the nurses sent for when somebody was dying and the family could not stand to be in the room. Women in the church who were scared of getting old came to her, and she sat with them at their kitchen tables and did not tell them it would be all right. S

title: Outward Adorning
logline: A coalfield beauty queen follows her whole family into the Holiness church for love, not faith, and hides from her preacher brother's sermons.

verses.text: The brilliant chariots of kings are destroyed, the body also approaches destruction, but the virtue of good people never approaches destruction,—thus do the good say to the good.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi looks down from an upper window and sees Queen Mallikā in the bath-house misbehaving with her pet dog. She tells him that the window shows everyone in the bath-house double, sends him in to prove it, and calls down that she sees him with a she-goat; he believes her. She is the greatest giver in the kingdom, the one who arranged the Gifts beyond Compare and gave the Buddha a white parasol, a couch, a stand and a footstool, but she dies remembering only the lie and is reborn in hell for seven days. Each of those days the grieving king goes to ask the Buddha where she has been reborn, and each day the Buddha makes him forget the question, so that he will not lose heart and stop giving. On the eighth day the Buddha comes alone to the palace, sits in the chariot hall, and tells him she is in the Tusita heaven. Then he asks whose the three chariots are, the grandfather’s, the father’s and the king’s own, and speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story, or about King Pasenadi. The retelling turns the dog and the she-goat into two people with those nicknames and the window into a cheap camera; the king, as in the original, never learns the truth.
bg.history:
Lowriding grew up among Mexican Americans in the Southwest after the Second World War: cars lowered, repainted in deep translucent “candy” colors over metallic bases, striped by hand, and driven slowly. Cars from before the fifties are called bombs. Pinstripers pull their lines freehand with a long-haired “sword” brush and lettering enamel, and the craft passes from one hand to the next. Cities answered the cruising scene with bans. National City, just south of San Diego, passed its ordinance in 1992, and its Highland Avenue was posted with No Cruising signs for three decades. After a campaign by the United Lowrider Coalition the city council voted unanimously to repeal the ban in April 2023. That October the governor signed Assembly Bill 436, which ended local cruising bans across California and the state rule against lowered cars, from January 1, 2024.

Chicano Park lies under the approach ramps of the San Diego–Coronado Bridge in Barrio Logan, a neighborhood cut in two by Interstate 5 in 1963 and by the bridge in 1969. Residents occupied the ground on April 22, 1970, to stop a Highway Patrol station from being built there. Painting of the bridge pillars began in 1973; some ten thousand square feet went up in a “mural marathon” in April 1978; and twenty-three murals were restored in a project that started in 2012. The park became a National Historic Landmark in 2016, and lowrider clubs show their cars there every Chicano Park Day. The Monarcas, the shops, and everyone in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Wash Bay
sections.text: Rey Pacheco had the tire and alignment shop on Highland Avenue that his father had before him, two bays and a rack, with the house behind it up a flight of outside stairs and the long garage behind that. He was sixty-one and had been president of the Monarcas Car Club for nineteen years. People in National City called him el Rey, and his name was only part of the reason. When a kid from the club got married, the cars lined up at his curb. When somebody’s mother died, the envelope went around at his shop. That was the spring the city took the NO CRUISING signs down. They had been up since 1992. For thirty-one years a man could be written up for passing the same corner of Highland twice in an evening with his car sitting low, and now the council had voted, every one of them, and a city truck came with a ladder. Rey stood on the sidewalk with half the club and watched a man in a vest unbolt the sign in front of the shop. He asked if he could have it. The man said he couldn’t do that, and then looked at the faces, and left it leaning against the pole when he drove off. Behind the second bay there was a wash bay, a concrete room with a floor drain and a hose reel, where the club cars go

sections.heading: II. Mañana
sections.dateline: Highland Avenue · that night, and the year after
sections.text: Mina Pacheco did not sleep. She was fifty-eight and had been married to him since she was twenty, and she lay on her side of the bed and went over it. He believed me because of the way he is, she thought. I used that. I did a low thing in the wash bay and then a lower one on the stairs. And I put Silvia in it, who never did anything to me but save me a plate. The first one was eleven seconds and I hardly knew I was in it. The second one I thought up. Then she thought about la Maestra, and that was worse. Consuelo Ybarra had a paint shop on Newton Avenue in Barrio Logan, in sight of the bridge. She had been striping cars for forty years. She laid her lines with a squirrel-hair brush no wider than a shoelace and a can of lettering enamel, freehand, and there was not a club from San Ysidro to Oceanside that did not have her hand on a trunk lid somewhere. She was also one of the painters who went up on the lifts under the Coronado Bridge every few years to bring the murals on the pillars back, when the sun off the bay had taken them down to chalk. She did not talk much. People said she could look at a fender and tell you who had done the bodywork under the paint and what kind of a week

sections.heading: III. The Corner of the Ceiling
sections.text: On the first of January cruising was legal again in every city in California. The Monarcas went up Highland that night forty cars long behind the old Impala, slow, with the hazards going, and Mina sat in the passenger seat and waved at the sidewalks like the queen of something. On a Tuesday in February she put her hand to the side of her head in the kitchen and said Rey, and sat down on the floor. She was two days in the hospital on Fourth Street and woke once. Rey was there. He told her everybody was asking. He told her la Maestra had sent a candle. Then, because he did not know what else a person says, he started at the beginning and told her the good she had done, the way you would read someone her own record. The bikes at Christmas, six hundred in one year. The envelopes. The quinceañera dresses. The show at Kimball Park, the building note, the white umbrella. It is told that she heard none of it. Her eyes had gone past him to the corner of the room where the wall met the ceiling tiles. There was a small dark dome up there, a sensor of some kind, and her eyes stayed on it. La cámara, she said. What camera, mi vida? There’s no camera. She did not look away from it. She died that

sections.heading: IV. Seven Days
sections.text: He drove down on the Sunday. She was in the booth laying out a roof for a pattern job, and before he had his mouth open she put a roll of eighth-inch tape in his hand. Hold that end. He held it. She walked the tape down the length of the roof and came back and gave him another. While she worked she talked, which she hardly ever did. She talked about his father, who had come to her teacher’s shop in 1979 wanting scrollwork on the Impala and had argued for an hour about the color of the line. Rey had not known that. He laughed. He was back on Highland with tape gum on his fingers before he remembered what he had gone for. Tomorrow, he said to the kitchen. On Monday she was laying gold leaf on a dash, the thin kind that lifts if you breathe on it, and he stood a yard off and took small breaths for an hour and watched her press it down with a ball of cotton. On Tuesday she took him under the bridge and had him steady a bucket on the lift while she went over the blue in a pillar forty feet up. She told him the one she was touching had been repainted in 2012, over the paint of 1978, over bare state concrete. Ten or twelve years, facing the water, she said. Then you come back up. On Wedne

sections.heading: V. The Garage
sections.text: On the eighth day she came to him. She came alone and on foot, up from the trolley at Eighth Street, a little before noon, with her striping kit on a strap over her shoulder. Rey saw her from the bay. He wiped his hands and went out and took the box from her, as you would, and started for the outside stairs to bring her up to the house, where the good chairs were. She did not follow. She had stopped at the open door of the long garage. Aquí está bien, she said. So he unfolded a chair for her there among the cars, and brought down what there was in the house: a bowl of caldo, tortillas he heated himself, and two conchas from the panadería. She ate all of it without hurry. He stood until she set the bowl down. Then he turned a bucket over and sat in front of her. Maestra. Every day I came to you I had one thing to ask, and every day I got home with it still in my pocket. I want to know where Mina is. They say you know. Tell me. Con Dios, she said. She is with God, Rey. He nodded hard, several times. Where else. If she isn’t, who is? There wasn’t another one like her. Sitting down, standing up, in the car, in the middle of the night, it was the same thing out of her mouth. Tomorrow I’

title: One Shot
logline: A lowrider club president sees his wife on the wash-bay camera, believes her story about it, and later asks a pinstriper where she is.

verses.text: A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the monk Lāḷudāyi always says the wrong thing. He recites funeral verses at festivals and verses of blessing at funerals, and he never notices. The Buddha tells the monks it is not the first time. In a past life, the Brahmin Aggidatta lost one of his two oxen. His son Somadatta was a favorite of the king and would not ask the king for an ox himself, so he coached his slow father in a charnel ground called the Fragrant Bush, with bundles of grass set up to stand for the king and his officers. The father practiced the request for a year, and then asked the king to take his other ox. Somadatta saved the moment with a quick answer, and the king, pleased, gave sixteen oxen and a village. The father was Lāḷudāyi, the king was Ānanda and the son was the Buddha himself.
bg.history:
The Grange (the Order of Patrons of Husbandry) was founded in 1867. Its ritual and its seven degrees borrow from Freemasonry, and many rural towns still have a Grange hall. Each local Grange elects officers who include a chaplain and three Graces, Ceres, Pomona and Flora. Among the chaplain's duties is the charter-draping ceremony for a member who has died. Grange membership fell by forty percent between 1992 and 2007. In 2022 the National Grange reported its first net gain in almost seven decades, some of it from young farmers and homesteaders. Rural New Hampshire also keeps its Old Home Days, which go back to the Old Home Week begun by Governor Frank W. Rollins at the turn of the twentieth century to call home the sons and daughters who had left for the West.

Devon cattle came to New England with the Pilgrims from 1623 and were long the region's working oxen. They are red, with white horns tipped black. The old dairy-and-draft line, now called the Milking Devon, is rare enough to be listed as critical. An ox is a trained steer of four years or more. The teamster walks on the left, and each animal learns its side, near or off, so that a partner is hard to replace (a New Hampshire teamster explains). Ox teams still show and pull at fairs such as the Hopkinton State Fair, held since 1915. In 1980 the Federal Reserve's fight against inflation pushed interest rates to about twenty percent, the start of the 1980s farm crisis. The common lilac, planted in dooryards and burying grounds across the state, has been New Hampshire's state flower since 1919.

sections.heading: I. The Golden Wedding
sections.dateline: Clay Hill, Merrimack County, New Hampshire · June 2022
sections.text: Lyle Corliss had been chaplain of Clay Hill Grange No. 113 since the year Nixon resigned, and nobody had ever run against him. He was eighty-four. He was still the biggest man in any room he went into, with a neck like a fencepost and hands that had been broken by oxen more times than he could tell you, though he would try. He knew the opening prayer and the closing prayer by heart, and the grace, and the long part he said when the charter was draped for a member who had died. He had been saying all of them for forty-eight years. The hall was white clapboard, built in 1896, two stories, with the suppers downstairs and the meetings upstairs. Upstairs there was an altar in the middle of the floor, and on it a big American Standard Bible that a summer family had given the Grange in 1904, its corners gone soft as felt. The Assistant Stewards opened it at the start of every meeting and closed it at the end. In the corners stood the stations of Ceres, Pomona and Flora, with a sheaf of wheat, a basket of wax apples and a jar of paper roses that had been there so long they had faded to the color of skin. Bud and Arlene Fisk had been married in that hall in 1972, under a bell made of crepe

sections.heading: II. The Charter
sections.text: Vernon Hatch died in the first week of November at ninety-three. He had joined Clay Hill Grange in 1952, and he had been Overseer, Master, Steward and Gatekeeper, and for one year, by a mistake in the balloting nobody ever cleared up, Flora. On the Tuesday after the funeral the Grange draped the charter for him. The charter hung in a black frame on the wall behind the Master's station. For thirty days after a member died it wore a drape of black crepe, and the putting on of the drape was the chaplain's work, with Ceres and the two Assistant Stewards. Ceres was a girl of nineteen from the 4-H dairy club. The Assistant Stewards were the Fisks. Lyle walked to the altar with the folded crepe over his arm and opened the Bible to the place he had marked with the receipt, and read. For, lo, the winter is past; The rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth; The time of the singing of birds is come, And the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land; — Song of Solomon 2:11–12 Outside the windows it was sleeting sideways across the parking lot. Dot Hatch was in the front row in her good coat. She put her face in her hands, and the people behind her thought she was crying, and

sections.heading: III. The Sale Barn
sections.text: Tess Morin had come to Clay Hill four years before from Hartford, with a husband and two Nubian goats, and now she had twenty-two goats and was Lecturer of the Grange, which meant she planned the programs. She had joined because a Grange hall was the only room in town big enough to teach a cheesemaking class in, and she had stayed because she liked the old people more than she had expected to. She was thirty-one. She thought the Grange might live if somebody ran it right. She and Arlene Fisk drove over to the sale barn on Wednesday afternoon to find the Master. The Master was Sumner Corliss, Lyle's son. He was fifty-seven, and on Wednesdays he sold livestock from a little booth above the ring at the auction barn on the county road: cull cows, bob calves, feeder pigs, goats, lambs, rabbits in wire cages, once a camel. They sat in the bleachers and listened to him sell a Jersey cow with a bad quarter. He did not seem to breathe. The numbers went up out of him in a long rolling chant, and somewhere in the middle of it he would drop in three plain words for one man in the third row, you know her, Walt, and Walt would raise his card. Then the gavel, and the next one. When the sale broke

sections.heading: IV. Three Bales
sections.dateline: The burying ground on Clay Hill · May 1980
sections.text: In 1980 Lyle Corliss had two Milking Devon oxen called Buck and Bright, red as a brick, with white horns tipped in black, and a hundred and ten acres of hardwood and ledge. He cut cordwood with them in the winter and twitched logs for the mill. In March they drew the sap sled through the sugarbush, and on Old Home Day they pulled the stoneboat for the children. They were nine years old. They had been in the yoke together since they were calves, Buck on the near side and Bright on the off, and they could not be worked any other way. In April Buck swallowed a piece of baling wire with his hay. The vet came out and shook his head and it took Buck four days. Bright stood at the end of the tie-up looking at the empty stall and would not eat. A trained ox was not a thing you could go buy. You could buy a pair of yearling steers and train them for three years, if you had three years, and if you had the money, and money that spring was at twenty percent at the bank in Concord. Lyle had neither. He hung the yoke on two pegs in the barn with one bow empty and worked Bright alone in a single harness, which an ox hates, and he lay awake. His boy Sumner was fifteen that year. For two summers he

sections.heading: V. The Kitchen
sections.dateline: The Gladding place, Hopkinton road · May 1981
sections.text: Sumner went over early, because Saturday was a workday for him, and took his place in the barn. Lyle came at two in his good gray shirt with a present, a quart of his own syrup from March in a glass jar with a Grange ribbon on it. He took his cap off in the dooryard. He wiped his feet. Gladding was glad to see him. He came out of the kitchen with his reading glasses pushed up on his head and took Lyle's hand in both of his. Lyle Corliss. You came all the way over the hill. Sit down, sit down. Ellen, it's the Senator's father. What can I do for you? Mrs. Gladding was at the sink. Mr. Swett was at the table with the feed bills. Sumner had come in from the barn and stood by the door to the shed, where he always stood, and he saw that they were standing exactly where he had set the bales. Lyle did not sit down. He stood in the middle of the kitchen with the cap in his hands, and said it. I had two oxen, Mr. Gladding,and worked my woodlot with the pair.But one of them is dead. I'd ask you,if you'd let me, take the other. Gladding blinked. Say that again, Lyle? Lyle said it again, exactly as before, with great care, the way he had said it to the bales three hundred times. Take the other.

sections.heading: VI. The Bean Supper
sections.text: Sumner told it on the Saturday at the bean supper, standing by the kitchen pass-through with a dish towel over his shoulder, between the beans and the pie. There were baked beans, yellow-eye and pea beans both, brown bread out of the can, coleslaw, red hot dogs and eleven pies. Lyle sat at the end of the long table under the Christmas lights the Fisks' granddaughter had never taken down, and when Sumner got to the kitchen and the words changed places, Lyle laughed louder than anybody. He had heard it told a hundred times. He liked it best of all the stories about himself. Gladding was the king of this town, as far as I knew then, Sumner said. Dad was Dad. I was the boy who did the talking. I've been doing it ever since, on Wednesdays, for two percent. Tess Morin was sitting across from Lyle. She had heard the story about the sixteen oxen before, from three different people, but never with the bales in it, and never the part about the year. So he hasn't changed, she said. No, said Sumner. He hasn't learned a thing since 1981. Not one word. He said it gently, and he looked down the table at his father, who was eating pie, and said the rest of it to him, as if they were alone in the b

title: Sixteen Oxen
place: Clay Hill (fictional), Merrimack County, New Hampshire
logline: An old Grange chaplain reads funeral scripture at weddings; his auctioneer son remembers teaching him to ask a rich man for one ox.

verses.text: Looking for the maker of this tabernacle, I shall have to run through a course of many births, so long as I do not find (him); and painful is birth again and again. But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again. All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered; the mind, approaching the Eternal (visankhara, nirvana), has attained to the extinction of all desires.

bg.commentary: These two verses are traditionally the first words the Buddha spoke after his awakening. The commentary’s account is brief. Sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he overcame Māra before sunset. In the first watch of the night he recalled his former lives. In the middle watch he gained the divine eye, which sees beings passing away and arising according to their deeds. In the last watch he worked through dependent origination forwards and backwards, and at sunrise he was awake and spoke the verses. The “builder of the house” is craving. Much later he recited the verses to his attendant Ānanda, who had asked.
bg.history:
June Tolliver, her crew and her spacewalk are invented, and the story names no real flight. The setting is real. The International Space Station circles the Earth about every ninety-two minutes, so a crew sees some sixteen sunrises a day, and a spacewalk of six or seven hours passes through several orbital nights of roughly half an hour each. Spacewalkers wear the Extravehicular Mobility Unit, whose helmet carries its own lights. The lead spacewalker is called EV1 and the astronaut in Mission Control who talks to the crew is CAPCOM. The station’s robotic arm, Canadarm2, arrived in April 2001. It can carry an astronaut in a foot restraint at its tip, and its trouble in this story is made up. Columbia was lost on February 1, 2003, and shuttles did not fly again until July 2005.

Astronauts rehearse spacewalks underwater at the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory near the Johnson Space Center, a pool 202 feet long and 40 feet deep that holds 6.2 million gallons and full-size station mockups, where safety divers attend each suited trainee. The center’s Oral History Project has recorded interviews with its people since 1996. Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., physician and professor of anatomy, published “The Chambered Nautilus” in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table in 1858. Generations of American schoolchildren learned it by heart. The nautilus adds a new chamber to its shell as it grows and seals off the old one behind it.

sections.heading: I. The Question
sections.text: Andy had been a diver at the pool for twenty-two years, and for eighteen of them he had worked June Tolliver’s classes. He set up her mockups and carried her checklists, and he hung in the water beside her students with a hand on their boots. He remembered everything she had ever said in a debrief. When two instructors disagreed about how Tolliver had taught a thing, they went and asked Andy, and he gave it back to them in her words. So when the history office wanted her on tape, she said she would talk to him and to nobody else. They sat in her kitchen with the recorder between them. She was sixty-six. On the third afternoon he took a printout from his bag. It was the loop transcript from her second spacewalk, in 2002, when the station’s arm was a year old. There’s a line here nobody has ever explained, he said. Phased elapsed time four hours fifty-one. You’d been hanging on the end of the arm for three revs. Then this. EV1 There you are. I see you. You’re all done. CAPCOM EV1, Houston. Say again? EV1 Disregard, Houston. I’ve got sunrise. Who were you talking to? She looked at the page for a while. In twenty-two years nobody had asked her.

sections.heading: II. The Hold
sections.text: She was a framing carpenter’s daughter from Coos Bay, Oregon. That morning she was two hundred and forty miles up, on her way out to the end of a new girder to drive bolts. Her boots were locked in the foot restraint at the end of the arm. Okada was flying it from inside and swinging her out over the lab, and Hendry was somewhere behind her on the truss with the cable bag. Then the arm stopped. It stopped so smoothly that it took her a second to notice. Then Okada said a word in Japanese, and Houston came on. The arm’s computer had safed itself and set the brakes. They would have to bring up the backup string from the ground, and they wanted several passes to do it carefully. Hendry asked if he should go out and get her. Houston said negative. Hendry was to press on with the cables, and EV1 was in a good config where she was. June, you’re go to hang out. There was nothing within reach of her but the arm. She had the planet under her boots and the sun on her left shoulder, and about nine minutes of daylight. The voice arrived at once. Every astronaut has it and nobody talks about it. It told her that she had no business in that seat. Thousands of people had applied the year she got

sections.heading: III. First Night
sections.dateline: The first pass through the shadow
sections.text: With the lights off she could not see her own gloves. She began to remember. It did not come the way memory usually does, in scraps. She remembered in order, and each time she was all the way inside it. She was nine and sitting on a roof deck in Coos Bay with a coffee can of sixteen-penny nails between her knees. Her name there was Junebug. She ate Fig Newtons and wanted her father to look at her. Then she was at Oregon State with a slide rule on her belt, and then she was at a desk in Renton doing wing loads. At that desk her name was Tolliver and she ate out of a machine. She wanted the corner office, and when she had it she wanted Houston. She had a husband in one of those lives. After that she was in the back seat of a T-38, and after that she was on her first flight. She had been certain every time that this one was the life. Each time she had moved in and set out her things, and then she had left without looking back at the one before. She knew what it was like. Her grandmother had kept half a nautilus shell on top of the sewing machine. It was sawn through so that you could see the rooms. When June was thirteen she won a speech ribbon reciting the poem that went with it, and

sections.heading: IV. Second Night
sections.text: She spent the daylight watching Hendry’s helmet go back and forth along the truss. Houston said the backup string was looking good and to give them one more rev. She said copy. When the shadow came over the second time she left her lights off and looked down. She was a structures engineer and she did not have a word for the way she saw that night. She could see the storms over the Congo lit from inside like paper lanterns. The squid fleets in the Gulf of Thailand were green, and the Nile was a lit stem with a flower at the end of it. She had seen all of that before on her first flight. This time she could see the people too. She did not see them as dots. She saw each one, the way you see a face across a table. They were arriving and leaving the whole time. A light came on in a window in Karachi because a child had been born under it, and a light went off in Omaha. Nobody was put anywhere. Each one went on to the next place by what they had done and what they had wanted, the way water goes downhill. She saw a man who had been cruel for sixty years go where that went, and a woman who had fed strangers go where that went. She watched it for half an hour and nobody told her what it mea

sections.heading: V. Third Night
sections.dateline: The third pass · elapsed time 4:17 to 4:51
sections.text: By the third dark her feet were cold and her mind was clear, and she did what she had been trained to do with a failure. She ran the chain. Why was she on this arm? Because she had been assigned the flight. She had the flight because she had wanted it and had worked eleven years to get it. She had wanted it because the first flight had been so sweet that the day she landed she was already hungry. And the first flight was sweet because of a July night when she was eleven, when her father pointed a hammer at the moon and said there were men walking on that, Junebug. That night had felt a certain way in her chest. The feeling came from seeing, and the seeing came from having eyes and a mind turned toward it, and that came from being born. She had been born because somebody before her had wanted something too. She could not find a place where it began. Then she ran it the other direction, the way you check a load path. If there is no wanting, the next house does not get framed. And without the next house there is nobody who has to move into it, and furnish it, and stand in the door of it afraid. She saw then that she had been wrong about one thing all her life. She had thought she was

sections.heading: VI. The Answer
sections.text: That’s who, she said. The builder. I’d been looking for him my whole life without knowing I was looking. I kept getting born into the next thing and it kept hurting. Once I’d seen him he couldn’t get a rafter to stand. Andy checked that the recorder was running. You want the rest of the poem, she said. Everybody learned it as a poem about self-improvement. Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul,As the swift seasons roll!Leave thy low-vaulted past!Let each new temple, nobler than the last,Shut thee from heaven with a dome more vast,Till thou at length art free,Leaving thine outgrown shell by life’s unresting sea! — Oliver Wendell Holmes, “The Chambered Nautilus” He has it in the last two lines. I spent forty-four years on the first five. Every one of those domes shuts you in, Andy, and it doesn’t matter how big you build it. That was mine, she said, and tipped her head back, as though the helmet were still there. And then what? Then the arm came back. Okada flew me out to the end and I drove my bolts, and we went in. It was a good EVA. The next winter Columbia was lost and nobody flew for two and a half years. By the time the line moved again she had asked the office to take he

title: Third Sunrise
place: Low Earth orbit and Clear Lake (Houston), Texas
logline: A spacewalker is left hanging on a stalled robot arm through three orbital nights, and at the third sunrise says something Houston cannot place.

verses.text: Men who have not observed proper discipline, and have not gained treasure in their youth, perish like old herons in a lake without fish.
Men who have not observed proper discipline, and have not gained treasure in their youth, lie, like broken bows, sighing after the past.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Mahā Dhana ("Great Wealth") is the son of a rich family in Bārāṇasī whose parents, thinking he would never need anything else, have him taught only singing and music; his wife, from an equally rich house, is taught only dancing. When both sets of parents die, the couple hold a double fortune. Rogues who watch the road he takes three times a day to the king's palace sit drinking and eating where he can see them, and toast him; he asks his attendant what they are drinking, is told nothing in the world compares to it, and takes a little, then more. Surrounded by hangers-on, he spends his own fortune and then his wife's, sells his fields, parks, carriages, dishes and coverlets, and finally the family house, from which the new owners put him out. In old age he and his wife live against other people's walls and he begs with a broken bowl, eating leftovers handed out by novices at a rest-house. The Buddha, seeing him there, smiles, and tells Ānanda that had Mahā Dhana applied himself in youth, middle age or old age he would have been the first, second or third richest man in the city, and had he gone forth he would have reached the paths of holiness, his wife a step behind him; instead he has lost both, like a heron in a dried-up pond.
bg.history:
At the end of the nineteenth century Hartford was a manufacturing city as well as an insurance one: the Pope Manufacturing Company made Columbia bicycles there from 1878, and owned its own steel-tubing plants in the city, before the bicycle trade gave way to the automobile. The Hartford Club, founded in 1873, has met since 1908 in its clubhouse on Prospect Street, across from the Travelers Tower, which was the tallest building in New England from its completion in 1919 until 1964 (Travelers Tower). When national Prohibition came in January 1920, Connecticut was one of only two states that had refused to ratify it; its senate voted the amendment down, enforcement in the state was thin, and liquor came ashore from the "rum row" of ships anchored off the coast (Connecticut Digital Newspaper Project). The "perfect six," a three-story apartment house with two bow fronts and six flats, was a Hartford type built in large numbers on Asylum Hill and elsewhere early in the century (Historic Buildings of Connecticut).

After the Second World War, West Hartford filled up with new houses for returning veterans and their families; its population grew by more than fifteen thousand in the two decades after 1940, and the war-workers' housing built there in 1942–43 became the subject of a long fight over who could live in it (Life in West Hartford). The psalms in the story are from the Psalter of the American Book of Common Prayer of 1928, which was essentially Miles Coverdale's sixteenth-century translation (the 1928 Psalter); choirs sang it to Anglican chant, with an asterisk marking the half-verse. The Kipling song is "Gentlemen-Rankers" from Barrack-Room Ballads (1892), sung at Harvard and Yale in the early 1900s and adapted there into the Whiffenpoof Song (Gentleman ranker).

sections.heading: I. Trebles
sections.text: Hiram Holbrook made steel tubing for bicycle frames in a brick works on Capitol Avenue, and in the spring of 1897, when every clerk in Hartford rode to the office on two wheels and the craze looked as if it would never end, he sold the works for a sum the Courant printed on its front page and never went down to Capitol Avenue again. He was forty-four. He bought eleven acres on the slope west of Prospect Avenue, with a carriage house and a stand of elms. At the bottom of the lawn there was a hollow, and his wife had it dug out into a pond, planted with white water lilies, and stocked with goldfish from a dealer in Boston. Then he and Abigail sat down in the library to decide what their son should learn. There was very little, they agreed, that the boy would need. There was money in that house for three lifetimes. He would not have to sell anything or make anything or answer to anyone. Let him have what his father had never had time for. Abigail, who came from Litchfield people and had the Litchfield sort of conscience, made one condition. On his tenth birthday Dana signed a printed card at her desk, promising, God helping him, never to touch intoxicating drink, and she put the card

sections.heading: II. Prospect Street
sections.text: Dana went down to the Hartford Club three times a day, the way his father had. At ten for the mail and the New York papers. At one for lunch. At five for the hour before dinner, when the men came over from the insurance companies and somebody always asked him to sit down at the piano. Fenn drove him in the Pierce-Arrow, down Farmington Avenue and through the city to Prospect Street, and waited at the curb with the motor ticking, across from the new Travelers Tower, which was the tallest thing in New England and which Dana had watched go up from the club window one floor at a time. In January of 1920 the country went dry. Connecticut had never agreed to it. The state senate had voted the amendment down. It came anyway, and with it came a new kind of man on the sidewalks of downtown Hartford, men who lived by their wits and had found that their wits were suddenly worth a great deal. Four of them took to waiting on the iron fence across from the club. A Kerryman named Duffy, who had worked the boats out of New London. A piano player who had lost his job at a hotel bar when there were no more hotel bars. Two others whose names changed. They watched which car came at ten, and at one, an

sections.heading: III. The Ready Tin
sections.text: It took Duffy about a month to see that it had become a habit, and after that the four of them were never far away. Then they were eight. Then there were more of them than Dana could have named, though he knew them all by their faces and always had a word for each. There was a back room on Front Street behind an Italian grocer's, and a room over a garage on Allyn Street, and later a house in the Farmington Valley with the shades down. Wherever he was, he got into the way of pulling a roll of bills out of his coat and setting it on the card table in front of him, and then another roll, and peeling them off as the evening went. Fenn, take this and get flowers for the table. Take this and get the good cigars, not those. Look at this one, he can make the dice do anything he tells them. Listen to this man play! Have you ever heard anything like that? Give him a thousand. This one can do the Charleston, look at him go. Give him two. Late, he would sit down at whatever piano there was and sing. He still had the voice. He sang the old Glee Club songs and the new ones off the records, and near the end of every night, because they asked for it, the Kipling song they used to do at Mory's, abo

sections.heading: IV. Everything
sections.text: Then he sold things. He sold the farm in Simsbury, where the shade tobacco grew under white cloth in the summers like a field of tents. He sold the cottage at Fenwick with Celia's rose garden. He sold the Pierce-Arrow and then the Packard he had bought to replace it, and let Fenn go with two weeks' wages and a gold watch, which Fenn tried to give back. He sold the Gorham silver, and the Haviland china a few pieces at a time to a dealer on Pratt Street, all of it but one cup with a gold rim and a small chip, which Celia kept back without saying so. He sold his grandmother's quilts and the down comforters and Celia's sealskin coat and the chesterfield from the library and the library, shelf by shelf. Abigail's Bible went in a box of books for a dollar, and the card went with it, still at Proverbs. The Steinway went last. Two men came with a dolly and took off the legs in the front hall and carried it out on its side like a coffin. Dana stood in the empty music room and hummed a note and listened to it come back off the bare walls. In September of 1938 the hurricane came up the river and took down the elms along the drive, nine of them, and there was no money to have them cut. They la

sections.heading: V. The Kitchen Door
sections.text: Practice let out at half past eight. The trebles came clattering down the parish house stairs with their cassocks over their arms and went straight to the kitchen, because the Auxiliary ladies gave them the pans to carry out, and it was the part of Thursday they liked best. Creamed chicken in a roasting pan. A basket of rolls under a dish towel. A coffee pot with the grounds still in it. Out in the alley, under the light over the kitchen door, there were four or five men waiting, and a woman, and the boys went down the line and spooned it into whatever was held out to them. Pails. Coffee cans. A pie tin. A china cup with a gold rim. Walter Ince came out the vestry door with his music case. He was seventy-two. He had been at St. Barnabas for fifty years that autumn and the vestry had given him a dinner and a silver salver and a pension he had not asked for. He was still thin, and he still held his head on one side. He stopped on the vestry step and looked at the alley. Kenneth Lusk, who was twelve and the head chorister and stood at the end of the front row on the Decani side, was coming back with the empty chicken pan, and he saw Mr. Ince standing in the light from the kitchen wind

sections.heading: VI. The Pond
sections.text: On the first Sunday in November, with the dimes from the week, they took the bus out Farmington Avenue. Celia had wanted to for a long time and Dana had not, and then one morning he put on his hat and said, All right. The elms were gone. Mr. Gorski had put a road up the middle of the lawn where the drive had been, and paved it, and named it Holbrook Road, and on either side of it there were eleven Cape Cod houses with dormers and picture windows and young maples staked in the front yards, and in the driveways the cars of men who had been in the Pacific and the Bulge and now sold insurance downtown. The big house had been cut up into apartments. Somebody had painted the shutters green. At the bottom of the road, where the lawn had gone down into the hollow, there was the pond. Gorski had drained it in the summer to fill it for two more lots, and had not got to the filling. The bulldozer stood at the edge with frost on its seat. The lily roots were heaped on the bank, black and fibrous, the size of a man’s arm. The bed of the pond had dried and cracked into plates like a broken platter, and in the low middle there was a skin of brown water an inch deep that had already started to fre

title: The Lily Pond
logline: A Hartford boy taught nothing but singing marries a girl taught nothing but dancing, and four men wait on a fence for his car.

verses.text: If a man hold himself dear, let him watch himself carefully; during one at least out of the three watches a wise man should be watchful.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Prince Bodhi has a palace built so fine it seems to float in the air, and then, so that no one else will ever own one like it, plans to kill or blind the master builder. His friend Sañjikāputta warns the builder, who says the work is not done, asks for seasoned timber and privacy, and secretly carves a great wooden bird; his wife sells everything for gold, and one morning after breakfast the family flies out the window past the prince's guards, to found a city in the Himālaya where the builder is known as King Wooden Vehicle. The childless prince invites the Buddha to the palace festival and lays cloths from the threshold, thinking that if the Buddha steps on them he will have a child. The Buddha refuses three times and looks at Ānanda, who has the cloths rolled up. Asked why, the Buddha tells of a husband and wife shipwrecked on an island who lived all their lives on the eggs and young of its birds and were never heedful in youth, middle age or old age; if either had kept watch in even one of those three periods, the prince would have had a child.
bg.history:
From the 1850s, when the Currituck Shooting Club was formed, wealthy Northern sportsmen built clubs and lodges along Currituck Sound and hired local Bankers as guides, while market hunters shipped barrels of canvasback, redhead and other ducks north by the week. In Kitty Hawk at the 1900 census most men fished, fifteen were surfmen in the Life-Saving Service, and a few listed themselves as hunters of wild fowl. The Wright brothers flew their 1902 glider again and again from the Kill Devil Hills that autumn and left it in their camp over the winter; they returned to fly the powered Flyer in December 1903. Ellis Tillett's fortune comes from the Northern Pacific corner and the Panic of 1901.

The Narrows light and Gull Shoal are invented, but the Lighthouse Board did appoint women keepers on the North Carolina coast and sounds, most of them wives or daughters of keepers, who stood their share of the night watches, kept the log and wore linen aprons to clean the lens (Coastal Review). By the turn of the century the plume trade had stripped the state's gull, tern and heron colonies; in March 1903 the legislature passed the Audubon Act, drafted by T. Gilbert Pearson, which gave the new Audubon Society of North Carolina wardens and the power to enforce bird and game laws. Mrs. Twiford's hymnbook is A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the Methodist Episcopal Church (New York, 1838), printed before the church divided North and South in 1844; hymn 164 is "Watch Night."

sections.heading: I. Redhead
sections.dateline: The Currituck Banks, North Carolina · summer 1902
sections.text: Ellis Tillett built his house on the marsh where nobody had ever thought to build anything, on the sound side of the Banks north of the Narrows, and when it was done it looked as if it were floating. He had it set on juniper pilings driven twenty feet into the mud, so the whole of it stood a man's height clear of the marsh grass, and at high water with the wind out of the south the sound came in under it and there was nothing beneath the house but light on water. It had three stories and a cupola. It had copper gutters, cypress shingles, a porch that went all the way around, and a dining room paneled in curled juniper that Asa Quidley had planed by hand until it shone like the inside of a shell. Ellis named it Redhead, for the duck, the one the Northern men paid the most to shoot after the canvasback. Over the front door, because his mother had wanted it there, Asa had cut a line of Scripture into a juniper board and gilded the letters: EXCEPT THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE, THEY LABOUR IN VAIN THAT BUILD IT. The Northern clubs were all up and down the sound by then, the Currituck Shooting Club, the Lighthouse Club, the Swan Island Club, a dozen more, long low houses where bankers from N

sections.heading: II. Seasoned Juniper
sections.text: Edith Tillett's brother Teddy came down for September. He was twenty-two and had just finished at Yale and did not know what to do with himself, and he was the only one of Edith's people who liked Ellis, and the only one Ellis liked. He spent his days in the skiff with Asa, fishing and learning the sound, and his evenings on the porch with Ellis and the brandy. One night late, with Edith gone up to bed, Ellis told him what was in his mind. He said it quietly and reasonably, the way he talked about money. Asa could build another house. Some Pittsburgh man would see Redhead and want one, and Asa would build it, better. Then there would be two, and nothing special about either. Ellis did not intend to let that happen. A carpenter needed his hands and his eyes. There were men in Norfolk who would see to it for a hundred dollars, a fall in the boathouse, a splash of lime. Or there was the sound. Men drowned in the sound every winter and nobody asked. Teddy laughed, waiting for the joke to finish. It did not finish. Ellis poured more brandy and talked about the price of juniper. Teddy did not sleep. In the morning before light he walked down the boardwalk to the boathouse, where Asa was

sections.heading: III. The Carpets
sections.text: The cupola was never finished, but Ellis gave his party anyway. He brought the Northern men over from the clubs in his launch, with their wives. Edith's people came down from New York in a private car. He asked the Methodist preacher from Kitty Hawk, and hired a cook from Norfolk and an orchestra of four. There was canvasback roasted twelve minutes, and diamondback terrapin, and Lynnhaven oysters by the barrel, and champagne. But the guest Ellis wanted was Mrs. Tamsey Twiford, keeper of the Narrows light. The Narrows light stood on iron legs in four feet of water a mile out in the sound, a square white cottage with a lantern on its roof, and Tamsey Twiford had kept it eleven years, since her husband Joel went through the ice coming back from Coinjock with the mail. She was fifty. The Lighthouse Board had made her keeper because there was nobody who knew the light better and because the inspector, after watching her clean the lens in her linen apron, had not been able to think of a reason not to. She had two assistants, her nephew Lige Gallop, who was nineteen, and old Mr. Baum, who was deaf, and the three of them divided every night into three watches, sunset to ten, ten to two, tw

sections.heading: IV. Gull Shoal
sections.text: She ate what was given her, a little of the canvasback and a piece of bread, and drank water. When the orchestra stopped for its supper and the guests went out on the porch to look at the sound, Ellis sat down by her at the end of the table. Aunt Tamsey. I've been yours three times over. Since before I was born. You know it. Why wouldn't you walk on my carpets? What did you put them down for, Ellis? He told her. Gideon and the fleece. That's why, she said. He looked at her. She had small hard brown hands and grey eyes, and she was the only person on the Banks he had never lied to. Then there won't be any. No. Not ever. No. Why? What did I do? She did not answer that at once. She looked out the window at the sound, at the low grey line of the marsh islands to the south, and she said, as if it were a different subject: You know Gull Shoal. He knew it.
