A low island of sand and grass in the sound, a couple of miles below the Narrows, where the terns and the black skimmers nested in May so thick you could not walk without stepping on eggs. He had gone egging there with his father every spring when he was a boy, with a basket on each arm. Later the plume buyers had come down from New Yor

sections.heading: V. One Watch
sections.text: The legislature at Raleigh passed a law that spring putting the gulls and terns and herons of North Carolina under the protection of the new Audubon Society, with wardens to enforce it, and the plume buyers stopped coming to the Banks, or came at night. Ellis Tillett bought Gull Shoal from the county outright, all forty acres of sand and grass, and paid a warden's wages out of his own pocket to Lige Gallop, who took them, and the Bankers said Ellis had got religion, or got old, or both. He went over himself in May when the terns came in. He went the first night, and the second, and most of the nights of that nesting season, in a skiff, alone, with a lantern and a blanket and a jug of water, and sat on a box at the high end of the island from ten o'clock until two. He did not sleep. He kept the lantern turned low and shaded on the water side, so the birds would not mind it and so that anybody coming in a boat from the south would see it a long way off and think better of what he was coming for. Around him in the dark the island was alive. The terns sat their eggs in the open sand by the thousand, a pale shifting sheet of them going away into the night, and every so often one would s

title: One Watch
logline: A Banks boy turned Wall Street millionaire builds a lodge that seems to float, then plots against the carpenter who could build another.

verses.text: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Upananda is a gifted preacher and a greedy monk. After preaching on being content with little, he accepts a heap of robes from monks who keep the strict practices and carries off their utensils too. With the rains retreat coming, he asks four monasteries in turn what allowance they give a monk who spends the rains there, leaves his sandals at the first, his staff at the second and his water pot at the third, and settles at the fourth, which offers four robes. When the rains are over he sends for his belongings and claims the allowance from all four. On the road with his cartload he meets two young monks who cannot agree how to share two robes and a costly blanket. They ask him to divide them; he gives each a robe and walks off with the blanket, saying it belongs to those who preach. The Buddha tells the young monks the tale of two otters and a jackal who settles their quarrel over a fish by taking the middle for himself, and rebukes Upananda: one who admonishes others should first set himself right. Read the full commentary story; its fable is the Jātaka of the jackal Dabbhapuppha (no. 400).
bg.history:
Greek immigration to the United States peaked in the years before the First World War, driven by poor land, debt and the burden of providing dowries for sisters. In the West most of the newcomers went first to the mines, the mills and the railroads: the 1910 census counted 3,448 Greeks in Oregon, more than 2,100 of them railroad workers, many on the Spokane, Portland and Seattle, built along the north bank of the Columbia. Extra gangs lived in bunk cars on sidings, worked ten-hour days and often fed themselves. Fallbridge (renamed Wishram in 1926) was the junction where the Oregon Trunk crossed the river, beside Celilo Falls, a fishing place of the river peoples for thousands of years until The Dalles Dam drowned it in 1957. In Utah some 1,200 Greeks were working the Utah Copper mine at Bingham by 1912. The heavy banded robes of Pendleton Woolen Mills, incorporated in 1909, were made first of all for Native buyers in the Northwest and were costly and prized.

Before 1921 there was no Greek bishop in America. The Church of Greece was given nominal authority over the immigrant parishes in 1908, but in practice each community was governed by its own elected board, which raised the money, built or rented a church and hired a priest, sometimes one who was passing through, and dismissed him when it chose. Portland’s Holy Trinity, the first Greek Orthodox church in the Pacific Northwest, was founded in 1907; its stone church at Seventeenth and Taggart was finished in 1910. The Archdiocese was incorporated in 1921. The Prayer of St. Ephrem, said with prostrations on the weekdays of Great Lent, is quoted here in the translation of Isabel Hapgood’s 1906 Service Book. Father Chrysanthos, the monk Gerasimos, the gang at Fallbridge and every community’s offer are invented.

sections.heading: I. Food and Covering
sections.text: Father Chrysanthos Doukas had a voice they talked about in three states. He had been trained at the Rizarios school in Athens and had served in Chicago and in Lowell, and in each place he had left the community board weeping at his sermons and furious over his accounts, and he had come west that winter with two trunks, a letter from a bishop nobody in Utah had heard of, and no community of his own. The men said he could read the Gospel so that you saw the boat rocking. The men also said, more quietly, that his hands were quick. On the Sunday before the Great Fast he preached to the Cretans of the Bingham copper camp in the hall over a coffeehouse, at the memorial for two men killed in a cave-in at the Highland Boy. These Cretans were the hard ones of the canyon. They kept the Fast the old way, without oil from Monday to Friday, and they slept six to a shack and sent everything home. Father Chrysanthos took for his text the sixth chapter of Paul to Timothy, and he leaned on it the way a man leans on a gate. But godliness with contentment is great gain: for we brought nothing into the world, for neither can we carry anything out; but having food and covering we shall be therewith con

sections.heading: II. Four Towns
sections.dateline: The Oregon Short Line · the first week of Lent
sections.text: In those years there was no bishop over the Greeks in America who could make a priest go anywhere. Every community was its own master. The men of a town got together, elected a board, rented a hall or built a church, and sent for a priest, or hired one who was passing, and paid him what they had agreed, and fired him when they felt like it. And a priest who was passing could ask what a town was offering before he unpacked. The Greeks of Pocatello met him at the depot with a delegation of four in their Sunday hats. They were shop men and section men of the Short Line, and they had no church and no priest, and they wanted a preacher for the Fast and someone to give them the Resurrection at midnight in the Odd Fellows’ hall. They had heard about the voice. They took him to the coffeehouse and gave him the chair by the stove. And what does the community give, said Father Chrysanthos, to a priest who keeps the Fast here and stays for Pascha? Sixty dollars, Father, and your board. He said he would think about it and asked the way to the hotel, and in the morning he took the westbound train, and left a pair of galoshes behind in the corner of the coffeehouse by the stove. At La Grande, wh

sections.heading: III. The Cook Car
sections.text: A hundred miles up the river the extra gang of the Spokane, Portland and Seattle was relaying steel east of Fallbridge, where the new bridge of the Oregon Trunk crossed over to the Deschutes. There were forty-one men in the gang, nearly all of them from the villages around Tripoli in Arcadia, and they lived in six bunk cars on a siding below the bluffs, with a cook car at the end and a water car behind it. They worked ten hours a day, and on Sundays too when the roadmaster said so, and in the evenings the wind came up the Gorge from the west and drove grit into everything, into the bread and the blankets and the creases of their eyelids. On still nights they could hear Celilo, the falls where the river people fished, five miles off, a sound like a crowd that never went home. The cook was a monk. His name was Gerasimos and he was past sixty. He had come out from a small house of monks on the Holy Mountain two years before with a letter from his elder, to go among the Greeks of America and beg for a new roof, because the old one let the snow onto the altar. He had gone to Chicago, and to Salt Lake, and up the canyons and along the lines, and he had seen how the men lived, six to a ca

sections.heading: IV. Bright Week
sections.text: On Holy Friday the women covered the bier of Christ with flowers from the market, and the men carried it around the block in the rain behind the candles, and the Father sang the Lamentations so that the confectioners wept into their beards. On Saturday at midnight he came out of the dark sanctuary with one candle and sang Come, receive the light, and the light went from his candle to the first hand and the next and through the whole church and out the doors into the street, where there was not room for everybody, and the bells rang, and the men shouted Christ is risen at each other and cracked red eggs, and the shoeshine boys who had come in from the camps let off pistols at the sky. It was the best Pascha anybody in Portland could remember. They said so for years. In Bright Week, while the town was still eating lamb, Father Chrysanthos sat in his rooms over the confectioner’s and wrote three letters, each in his beautiful seminary hand. To Pocatello he wrote that he had left his galoshes with them as a pledge that he was among them in spirit through the holy Fast, and that he prayed for them by name every day of it, and that the community would surely wish to send what was customa

sections.heading: V. The Division
sections.text: He got off the train in a black cassock with the sheepskin coat over his arm against the wind and the silver watch-chain of the Cretans across his front, and the whole gang was at the siding to meet him in their good clothes. The roadmaster had given them the afternoon. The monk had made koliva in the big pot, wheat and walnuts and raisins and sugar, and smoothed the top of it with the flat of a knife and laid a cross on it in almonds, and the men carried it up the path to the flat above the siding on a board. Father Chrysanthos sang the memorial at the grave in that voice, and the wind took it out over the river, and some of the men said afterward that the river people fishing at the falls must have heard it. He sang Memory eternal three times, and the gang sang it after him, and Stavros and Mitsos stood at the foot of the tie-cross with their hats in their hands and did not look at each other. The collection came to thirty-eight dollars. He blessed the koliva and took a spoonful and took the collection. Then he came down to the third car to see the young man’s things, because Stavros asked him to. Yannis’s things were on his bunk. There was a razor and a strop, a bundle of letter

sections.heading: VI. The Fox
sections.text: The cousins came to the cook car at dusk. The monk was scouring the koliva pot with sand. They told him all of it, both talking at once, and when they had told it they were not angry at each other anymore, only at the priest, and ashamed, and sick, the way you feel after you have been robbed in front of people. Gerasimos set the pot down. It is not the first time, he said. That one has been taking from your plates since before you were born. Then he sat down on a flour barrel and told them a story, the way he told the boys stories at night in the village on the Holy Mountain when they had been fighting, and the men in the car went quiet to listen. Once, he said, below the falls, there were two otters. One of them hunted along the bank in the shallows and one of them hunted out in the deep water, and between them, working together, they caught a red salmon so big that the two of them together could hardly drag it out onto the rock. And then they could not agree how to share it. The head is mine, said the one. The tail is yours. No, the head is mine, said the other. And while they were shouting, a fox came down the bank, a fine one, with a fine tail. Uncle, they said, you divide it f

sections.heading: VII. The Prayer
sections.text: The cousins did not sleep much. Toward morning Mitsos said into the dark that he would like to break that priest’s neck, and Stavros said he would hold his coat, and they lay there a while and found they did not mean it, and did not know what to do with what they did mean. Before the gang went out they came to the cook car. The monk was at the oven in the bank with the long paddle, taking out the bread. They asked him what they should do about it. They meant about the priest. Should they write to the communities, to Portland, to The Dalles, to the newspaper in New York? Should they write to Yannis’s mother and tell her where her son’s robe had gone? Gerasimos set the loaves on the board to cool. Then he told them the end of the prayer they had been saying with him on their knees every evening for seven weeks, the part they had said so many times that they had stopped hearing it. Yea, O Lord and King, grant that I may perceive my own transgressions, and judge not my brother. For blessed art thou unto ages of ages. Amen. — Prayer of St. Ephraim the Syrian Start there, he said. Then, if you still have something to teach him, you can go and teach it. They stood in the door of the cook

title: The Middle Portion
logline: A Greek preacher with a famous voice shops four railroad towns for the best Lenten fee, then stops to divide a dead man's things.

verses.text: If a man make himself as he teaches others to be, then, being himself well subdued, he may subdue (others); one’s own self is indeed difficult to subdue.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the elder Padhānika Tissa, “Tissa the Striver,” takes five hundred monks into the forest with a meditation subject they have had from the Buddha. He tells them to be heedful, lies down, and goes to sleep. When the monks come in to rest at the end of the first watch of the night he wakes, asks whether they came there to sleep, sends them out again, and goes back to bed; he does the same at the end of the middle watch. Worn out and unsettled, none of them gets anywhere. At last they decide that their teacher must be a man of tremendous energy, go to watch him, and find out. When they return, the Buddha tells them it is not the first time. Once they were students who rose to their lessons at cockcrow. Their rooster died, and the one they got in his place had been raised in a cemetery and knew nothing of hours, so that he crowed at midnight and again at noon until they wrung his neck. No mother or father raised him, their teacher said, and he lived under no teacher.
bg.history:
Shavuot marks the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and in 1993 its first day fell on Wednesday, May 26. The custom of studying through the night before, the Tikkun Leil Shavuot, comes from the Zohar and the kabbalists who followed it. A later explanation, the one Mel gives, rests on a midrash to the Song of Songs in which Israel slept late on the morning of the revelation and had to be roused. The traditional book for the night is an anthology of beginnings and endings: the first and last verses of each portion of the Torah, of the other biblical books, and of the tractates of the Mishnah. The evening service of the festival waits for full dark so that the seven weeks counted from Passover are complete. After the Second World War many of Kansas City’s Jewish families moved south and across the state line, and Overland Park, in Johnson County, Kansas, became the center of the community. Congregation Tifereth Jacob and its people are invented.

The blessing for the rooster stands first in the long row of morning blessings, and comes from the Talmud (Berakhot 60b), which appoints it for the moment a person hears the cock crow. The English is Simeon Singer’s, from the Authorised Daily Prayer Book of 1890 (text), which was reprinted in America for decades. The saying from Baba Bathra is given as Abraham Cohen put it in Ancient Jewish Proverbs (1911). In the towns of Eastern Europe the sexton who went round before dawn knocking on doors and shutters to call people to prayer was the shulklapper, the synagogue knocker. Three knocks was one of the usual counts.

sections.heading: I. The First Shift
sections.dateline: Overland Park, Kansas · Tuesday night, May 25, 1993
sections.text: Shavuot came in on a Tuesday that year, and at Congregation Tifereth Jacob the evening service could not start until it was full dark, because the forty-nine days had to be finished first. So it was half past ten before Mel Tischler stood up in the social hall with a legal pad. Mel was forty-six, a district sales manager for a business-forms company, and chairman of adult education. He coached his daughter’s softball team, and most of the congregation called him Coach, including the rabbi. The all-night study was his idea. Tifereth Jacob had not held one since it moved out from the city in 1964, and Mel had read about them in a magazine. Twenty-two people had stayed. They sat at round tables with paper cloths on them, under the fluorescent lights. There was a forty-cup urn of regular and a smaller one of decaf, two cheesecakes, and Mrs. Rosenbloom’s blintz casserole under foil. Naomi Sacks was there because her son Josh was being confirmed in the morning and the confirmation class had been told to come. She was a night nurse at a hospital on the Missouri side, and this was her night off. People, Mel said. Here’s the story. The morning God gave the Torah, our ancestors overslept. Th

sections.heading: II. The Changeovers
sections.dateline: The social hall · half past twelve to four
sections.text: At twelve-thirty a small double beep came through the door of the rabbi’s study, and a moment later Mel came out with his hair flat on one side. By then the room had found its way into the night. Dr. Mandel, a retired dentist, had been reading the last verses of Deuteronomy aloud to his table, and nobody at it was thinking about the time. Others had drifted. Four were in the kitchen eating cheesecake standing up. Three of the confirmation class were lying on the carpet in the youth lounge. People, Mel said. Did we come here to lie down? Is this what we’re doing? Up. Back to the tables. Second shift. Sinai, people. He walked them in ahead of him and stood until every chair was filled. He said a few more words about commitment. Then he said he wanted to check a source, and the study door closed behind him. It took the room half an hour to get back to where it had been. Naomi was in the Book of Ruth. She knew that hour from the floor, the one where the body asks to be let off, and she knew the only cure for it was to have something in front of you that needed doing. She had just found it again when the beep came through the door at two-thirty. This time he found people on the padded b

sections.heading: III. The Gravedigger’s Rooster
sections.text: Mr. Plotkin came across the dark lot in a suit and a hat with his tallis bag under his arm. He looked at the nine of them, and at the six chairs somebody had pushed together for Mrs. Rosenbloom, and at the cheesecake. Nu, he said. You learned? They told him all of it, the shifts and the speeches and the beep through the door. Dr. Mandel told most of it. Mr. Plotkin looked over once at the study, where a raincoat rose and fell. He sat down and put his hat on the table. By us, in Lithuania, my father was the shammes, he said. Every morning before light he went down the street with a wooden hammer and knocked on the shutters. Three knocks, so a person knew it was time to get up and come to shul. That was for the householders. The boys in the study house got up before that, in the middle of the night, to learn. For them my father didn’t knock. They kept a rooster. The rooster died. So one of the boys got another one from the gravedigger, who kept a few chickens by the cemetery wall. This one was hatched out there by himself. No hen sat on him. He never once heard an old rooster. And by a cemetery it’s quiet, one hour is the same as another hour. So he crowed when it came into his head.

title: The Gravedigger's Rooster
logline: At a suburban synagogue's first all-night Shavuot study, the chairman who organized it keeps slipping into the rabbi's study to check a source.

verses.text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich man’s daughter who has longed all her life to become a nun is finally allowed to by her husband, and goes forth among the nuns of Devadatta’s faction without knowing she is pregnant. When it shows, Devadatta orders her expelled to protect his reputation; she appeals to the Buddha, who has the laywoman Visākhā examine her behind a curtain and count the months, and the elder Upāli declares her innocent before the whole assembly. King Pasenadi hears the baby crying, takes him home to be raised by his daughters, and the boy, Kumāra Kassapa (“Prince Kassapa”), learns from playground taunts that he has a mother among the nuns and asks to be ordained. After failing to progress in the forest, he is set fifteen riddles by a visitor from the Brahma world, and attains arahatship when the Buddha answers them. Twelve years after he left the world, his mother, who has wept all that time, sees him in the street and runs to him with her milk flowing; he speaks harshly to her on purpose, and she lets go of her attachment and is freed. The Buddha then tells the birth story of the banyan deer, who offered his own life in place of a pregnant doe.
bg.history:
The International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON) was founded in New York City in July 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, and in January 1967 he opened a storefront temple on Frederick Street in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury. Its devotees chanted in the streets, held free Sunday feasts, and funded the movement by selling its books, first on sidewalks and campuses and then in airports and other public places; courts generally upheld their right to do so under the First Amendment. Its central scripture is the Bhagavad Gita, which the story quotes in the 1896 translation by Annie Besant, rather than the movement’s own.

In the 1970s, as new religious movements spread, many parents of young converts hired deprogrammers, whose methods often amounted to kidnapping and false imprisonment; the best known, Ted Patrick, was eventually convicted of felonies for it. Kunti, Kashyap, Maharaj, the grove on the Salt River and the Phoenix temple in the story are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Temple
sections.text: Margaret Ashby wanted to be a nun from the time she was seven years old, and she was raised Presbyterian, which was the first problem. She asked her mother and father at seven and at twelve and at sixteen, in different words each time, and the answer was no each time, in the same words. Her father built shopping centers. He had built half of the ones on Camelback Road, and the house in Paradise Valley had a pool shaped like a kidney and a view of the mountain from every room, and his only daughter was not going to shut herself up in a convent with a lot of Catholics or anybody else. So she married. She married Doug Pruitt, who was gentle and studying architecture at Arizona State and loved her more than she knew what to do with, and she was a good wife to him for two years in a little house in Tempe with a lemon tree in the yard. Then one evening on Mill Avenue she heard the chanting. There were six of them on the sidewalk outside the bookstore, in saris and saffron cloth, with drums and little brass cymbals, and they were singing the same eight words over and over in the hot dusk, and the people coming out of the movie house walked around them as if they were a fire hydrant. Marga

sections.heading: II. The Curtain
sections.dateline: The grove on the Salt River · August 1973
sections.text: The devotees had a farm east of the city on the Salt River, twelve acres of old orange grove that a widow in Mesa had left them, with a farmhouse and a cow barn and an irrigation ditch and a pump house under the tamarisks. Four cows lived there, and a dozen men, and a sannyasi the devotees called Maharaj. He had been born Ellis Batiste in a sugarcane parish in Louisiana in 1931. He had been a cook in the Navy, and a merchant seaman, and a short-order cook in San Francisco, where in the winter of 1967 he had walked into a storefront on Frederick Street to get out of the rain and heard an old man from India explain the Bhagavad Gita to twenty hippies. He was forty-two now. He was a big man, with a grey beard cut close and a deep voice that he rarely raised and rarely used. The devotees in the city said he did not have a head for management. The devotees at the grove said nothing, but when somebody in the movement was in real trouble, sooner or later they ended up at the grove. He listened to the women from the temple tell it on the porch of the farmhouse. He looked at Kunti for a long time. Then he asked a few things that only a man who had grown up in a house with five sisters would

sections.heading: III. Raja
sections.text: One afternoon in March Mr. Bhattacharya came out to the grove about a donation and, walking past the farmhouse to his car, heard a baby crying. What’s that? That’s Kunti’s boy, Prabhu. The one from the curtain. Mr. Bhattacharya stood on the path for a while. He had three daughters and no son, and his wife had died two years before. He went and talked to Maharaj in the cow barn. And at the end of the week he came back with his three daughters in the Mercedes and took the boy home with him to Paradise Valley, a mile from the house Kunti had grown up in, and gave him to the girls to raise. Kunti let him go. She told herself that it was Krishna’s arrangement, and that a woman who had taken vows had no business with a baby, and that he would have everything in that house that she could never give him. All of it was true. She went back to the city temple, and that summer she joined one of the women’s traveling parties that went around the country in a van selling the books, and she was gone for years. The Bhattacharyas named the boy Kashyap, after a sage, at a naming ceremony with a priest and two hundred guests and a cake from the Biltmore. Nobody ever called him that. The daughters cal

sections.heading: IV. Fifteen Questions
sections.text: Maharaj gave him a practice and he took it to India. He went to Vrindavan, where Krishna had been a cowherd boy, and lived in a room by the Yamuna for a year and a half and chanted sixty-four rounds a day and fasted on the holy days and walked the circuit of Govardhan Hill barefoot in the summer heat, and he got nowhere. He could feel himself getting nowhere. It was like pushing on a door that opened the other way. So he came home to the grove. I need something else, Maharaj. What you gave me was too big for me, or too small. Maharaj looked at him and told him to live in the pump house for a while, under the tamarisks at the back of the property where it was dark even at noon, and keep chanting, and wait. In March of 1995, in the pump house, a visitor came. What Kashyap told about it afterward, and never changed in the telling, was that he woke in the middle of the night and an old man in white was sitting on the floor by his mat, a babaji with a white beard and the clay marks of the Vaishnavas on his forehead and his nose, very thin, very old, who said he had done his chanting alone in a cave on Govardhan Hill for longer than anybody now living could remember, and had come a long

sections.heading: V. The Parking Lot
sections.text: For twelve years, from the day the Mercedes took her son out to the grove, Kunti had cried. She cried on the road in the van, between Albuquerque and Amarillo and Tulsa. She cried at the morning service with her face to the wall. She cried in parking lots and airports and on college campuses, holding out the books to strangers with tears running down her face, so that people gave her money just to make her stop, and the other women said she was the best book distributor in the movement and did not know why. She chanted her rounds, sixteen a day, twenty-three years of them, and her face was always wet. Every Christmas Mr. Bhattacharya’s eldest daughter sent her a photograph, to whatever temple she was at, and she had them in a tin box: a baby, a boy on a bicycle, a boy in a school blazer, a tall thin young man with a shaved head in saffron cloth. In June of 1996 the traveling party came back through Phoenix, and on a Thursday afternoon at four o’clock, at a hundred and fifteen degrees, Kunti was standing in the parking lot of a supermarket on Main Street in Mesa with an armful of books, when a young brahmachari in saffron cloth came across the asphalt from the other side, carrying a

sections.heading: VI. The White Buck
sections.text: The story went around the movement the way stories did, from temple to temple, and by the fall it had come back to the grove. One evening, after the class on the porch, the men were talking about it in the dark, with the swamp cooler going. Balabhadra almost finished them both, one of them said. Her and the boy. Before he was even born. And Maharaj was their shelter, both times. Maharaj came out onto the porch with a glass of water and sat down on the step. That’s not the first time, he said. Let me tell you something from home. When I was a boy in St. Mary Parish, he said, the man who owned the land we lived on loved to hunt more than anything in the world. He had his supper off venison every night of the season. And every week he called out every man on the place to drive deer for him, so nobody could get his own work done, until the men got together and said, Let’s fence a piece of the swamp and drive the deer into it, and he can shoot them there and leave us alone. So they did. They went out with sticks and pans and beat the woods for miles and drove every deer in the country into that fence. There were two white bucks in the drive. Pure white, with pink eyes.
