title: Mataji
logline: A Phoenix debutante joins the Hare Krishnas without knowing she is pregnant, and must prove her vows before the temple turns her out.

verses.text: The evil done by oneself, self-begotten, self-bred, crushes the foolish, as a diamond breaks a precious stone.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the layman Mahā Kāla (“Big Black”) keeps the observance day and sits up the whole night at the monastery listening to the teaching. Toward dawn, thieves running from a house they have robbed throw their loot down in front of him as he washes his face at the monastery pool. The owners come up, tell him he has only been acting the part of a man who listens to the Dhamma, and beat him to death, and the young monks find his body when they go out with their water pots. The Buddha grants that in this life he did nothing to earn it. Then he tells of an earlier one, in which the same man was a king’s soldier posted at a forest road, wanted a traveler’s wife, had his own jewel hidden in the traveler’s carriage and found there, and saw the man beaten to death on the word of the village headman. Read the full commentary story. A later story in the same chapter begins the same way and ends differently; this series tells it as Windmill Water.
bg.history:
On January 27, 1838, Abraham Lincoln, twenty-eight years old and the junior partner in John T. Stuart’s law office, read an address called “The Perpetuation of Our Political Institutions” to the Young Men’s Lyceum of Springfield, which met in the Baptist church. Its subject was mob law. The Sangamo Journal, the Whig weekly that Simeon Francis had edited since 1831, printed it on February 3. See Lincoln’s Lyceum address; the passages quoted here follow the text in Arthur Brooks Lapsley’s edition of the Papers and Writings (1905). A country paper of that day was set by hand and worked off on a hand press. Proofs were read aloud against the copy, the type was thrown back into the cases afterward to be used again, and the apprentices were called devils. The imposing stone is the flat slab on which pages of type are locked into their iron frame. Mr. Pell, the two apprentices, Jesse Odom, Ruggles and his store, and the killing behind the office are invented. No such death is recorded at Springfield that morning.

The Mississippi that Lincoln described was two and a half years old. Late in June 1835 a rumor went through Madison County that the enslaved people of the plantations around Beattie’s Bluff, on the Big Black River, meant to rise on the Fourth of July, led by white outlaws of the kind a new pamphlet had attached to the name of John Murrell. Self-appointed committees there and at Livingston questioned black men under the lash and hanged a number of them. They also hanged several white men, among them two “steam doctors,” itinerant botanic practitioners, from the grating of the Livingston jail window. In the same week a crowd at Vicksburg hanged five gamblers. Travelers and newcomers were the first white men suspected. The ferry, its captain of patrol, the Squire and the couple from Tennessee are invented.

sections.heading: I. Press Night
sections.text: The Journal came out on Saturdays, so Friday was press night, and on press night the office was the one lit window in that part of town. Lew Carmody was fifteen and in the second year of a five-year indenture. The other apprentice, Hod, was twelve and had been bound since October. Between them they carried the wood and the water, damped the paper, rolled the ink, washed the forms in lye and swept up after, and for this they were called devils, as boys in printing offices had been called for two hundred years. The foreman was Mr. Abner Pell. He was a Vermonter of about forty, stooped from the case, who had set type in eleven towns between Brattleboro and the Sangamon. He could read a line of type upside down and backward faster than Lew could read it off the sheet. He seldom said anything in the shop that was not about the work. There was a fourth person in the office that night, and he did not work there. Jesse Odom had come up from Mississippi a year and a half before with a wagon and two mules, and he cut and hauled stove wood for half the square. He was a big man past forty, slow to speak, who signed for his money with a mark. His first winter in town he had brought a load to th

sections.heading: II. The Well
sections.dateline: The lot behind the office · first light
sections.text: What happened at the well Lew had afterward from four or five men who were in it, and they all told it alike. Sometime past five, three men got into Ruggles’s store on the square by a back shutter. Mr. Ruggles slept over the store. He woke when a brass kettle came down off its hook, and he went down the stair in his shirt with a fowling piece that was not loaded, and the three went out the way they had come with a meal sack between them. He raised the street. By the corner there were ten or a dozen men behind the thieves: his two clerks, a smith, some teamsters who had been harnessing in the tavern yard. The thieves threw down a bolt of calico in the mud, and then a caddy of tea, and the men behind ran past both. At the next corner the three split. One of them came up the lot behind the printing office with the sack. He saw a big man bent over a bucket at the well with his face in his hands, and he slung the sack down at the man’s feet and went over the fence. The others came into the lot with one lantern. What they saw was a man straightening up from a bucket with water running off his chin, and Ruggles’s sack at his boots with the kettle half out of it. Some of them knew him. It’

sections.heading: III. What He Told
sections.text: Mr. Pell went out and looked and came back in. He washed his hands at the bucket and dried them on his apron. He was here, Mr. Pell, Lew said. He never went out but for wood. He was on that box from dark till the last sheet. He didn’t do a thing. He did nothing last night. I will swear to that in front of anybody, and so will you. Sit down, both of you. They sat down on the wood box. The whole edition was stacked on the bank with the lawyer’s address on the second page, dry enough to fold. Mr. Pell stood at the imposing stone with his back to the window. I am going to tell you what he told me at this stone between one o’clock and two. Then you will know as much as I do.

sections.heading: IV. The Big Black
sections.text: In the summer of 1835 Jesse Odom kept a ferry on the Big Black River in Madison County, on a road going north out of Livingston toward the Yazoo. He had a flat on a rope, a house with two rooms for travelers, and one man, named Harry, whom he owned, who worked the rope. At the end of June a planter’s wife up at Beattie’s Bluff believed she had heard her house servants whispering about a rising set for the Fourth of July. Within a week every beat in the county had its committee. They put the black men of the Bluff plantations to the question with the whip and hanged five of them, an old preacher among the five who had said nothing under it. At Livingston the same week they hanged two white men, steam doctors, from the grating of the jail window. The talk was that a clan of land pirates stood behind the whole of it, and that their captains were riding the roads in the character of travelers. Every stranger bound north had to come down to Odom’s landing, so the committee made him captain of patrol for his beat. No one crossed without giving an account of himself. Beyond the river the road ran four miles through cane, and for a dollar Odom or one of his patrol would ride a traveler thr

title: The Imposing Stone
logline: A Mississippi wood hauler who cannot read sits up every press night in a Springfield printing office to hear the proofs read aloud.

verses.text: He whose wickedness is very great brings himself down to that state where his enemy wishes him to be, as a creeper does with the tree which it surrounds.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the monks at Veḷuvana are talking about Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin and brother-in-law, who won the favor of Prince Ajātasattu, urged him to kill his father, King Bimbisāra (the Buddha's patron), and then plotted with him to kill the Buddha. The Buddha comes in and says this is not the first time, and tells the birth story of the antelope (Jātaka 206), in which the Bodhisatta is an antelope caught in a hunter's snare and saved by his friends the woodpecker and the tortoise; the hunter is Devadatta. He compares runaway wickedness to a māluvā creeper that wraps a sāla tree and crushes it. In other episodes of the same story, a splinter from a boulder Devadatta rolled down a hill wounded the Buddha's foot, and archers sent to kill him could not do it.
bg.history:
For thirty years, Florida's wading-bird rookeries were shot out for the millinery trade. Hunters killed egrets and herons at the nest in spring, when the breeding plumes were longest, and left the young to starve. Around 1904, according to the ornithologist Frank Chapman, plumes sold for $32 an ounce, more than the price of gold. Florida outlawed the killing of plume birds in 1901, and the American Ornithologists' Union, at the Florida Audubon Society's request, hired wardens to enforce it at $35 a month. In July 1905 the warden Guy Bradley was shot and killed near Flamingo while trying to stop a plume hunter, and in 1908 DeSoto County warden Columbus McLeod disappeared near Charlotte Harbor; his sunken boat was found but his body never was. In 1910 New York, the center of the hat trade, passed the Audubon Plumage Act, other states followed, and Congress soon banned the import of plumes. More on plume hunting.

Halfmoon Key and its people are invented. The Ten Thousand Islands are a maze of mangrove keys on Florida's southwest coast, and some of the higher ones are shell works raised by the region's Native peoples, where hammock trees like gumbo limbo grow. The Florida strangler fig usually sprouts from a bird-dropped seed in the crown of a host tree, sends roots down to the ground, and as the roots fuse around the trunk it usually kills the host and stands on its own. The state asylum at Chattahoochee, the Florida State Hospital for the Insane, opened in 1876.

sections.heading: I. The Splinter
sections.dateline: Halfmoon Key, Ten Thousand Islands, Florida · April 1910
sections.text: Halfmoon Key was an old shell heap the Indians had left, nobody knew how long ago, the highest ground for ten miles in any direction, which is to say about the height of a man on a man's shoulders. Six families lived on it in houses up on cypress blocks. They fished mullet and crabbed and cut buttonwood for charcoal and grew a little cane and tomatoes on the top of the mound, and on the north side, where the landing was, an old gumbo limbo leaned out over the water with its red bark peeling like a sunburn and a strangler fig wrapped around it from the crown to the roots. Retta Sweeting had her husband's foot in her lap on the porch with a lamp on the floor and a darning needle she had held in the flame. The men sat along the porch rail, Lige Daniels and the two Whidden boys and old Cyrus Kirk, who could not hear but liked to be where talk was. The children were supposed to be asleep and were under the house. The splinter was cypress, from the gunwale of Ez's skiff, and it had gone in under the arch of his foot an inch and a half. The bullet that sent it there had come out of the mangroves at the mouth of Plover Creek that morning while he was poling through on the falling tide, and

sections.heading: II. The Talk on the Porch
sections.text: They had been talking about Duke Sweeting for most of a year, and they talked about him again now, the whole of it from the beginning, the way people will go back over a thing that has hurt them. Duke and Ez were first cousins, raised in the same house on Pine Island after Duke's mother died, and Ez had married Duke's sister. When they were boys they had shot plumes together, every spring, in the rookeries up Lostmans River and back in the Big Cypress, when the white birds were nesting and the long feathers grew down their backs. A good day's shooting then could bring more money than a man made in a season of fishing. The buyers paid by the ounce, and in the best years the ounce of plumes was worth more than the ounce of gold. Then one spring Ez had gone back into a rookery a week after they had shot it out, by himself, nobody ever knew what for. He came out and did not talk for two days. Lige was with him in the boat afterward and said all Ez ever told him was that the young ones were still in the nests, hollering, and there was nobody to feed them, and some of them were hanging over the edge. Ez never fired another shot at a bird. When the Audubon people were hiring wardens after

sections.heading: III. The Snare
sections.text: Ez sat down on the top step and put his foot back in Retta's lap so she could wrap it, and looked out at the water a while. That's not the first time, he said. That's not the first time Duke's tried to kill me. The Whidden boys looked at each other, because they had not heard of any other time. There was a buck deer, Ez said, lived back in the pines, toward the Big Cypress, by a pond. And there was a Lord God bird in a dead cypress by the same pond, one of them big woodpeckers with the white on the wings, with her young ones. And there was an old snapping turtle that lived in the pond. They were friends, the three of them, the way things are that use the same water. A man came hunting through there and saw the buck's track at the drinking place, and he set a snare in it. Rawhide, plaited, strong as a trace chain. And that night the buck stepped in it and it took him by the leg and he hollered. The Lord God bird came down, and the snapper came up out of the water. And the bird said, You've got the jaws. You chew that rope. I'll see to the man. So the snapper went to chewing, and the bird flew off to the man's house and sat in a tree by the front door. And at daylight the man come ou

sections.heading: IV. The Fig
sections.text: In the morning he limped down to the landing to look at the skiff, and Lige and the older Whidden boy came down after him, because they had not got all they wanted out of the night before. What are you going to do about him? Ez did not answer that. He was standing under the gumbo limbo. He put his hand flat on the fig roots where they came down over the red bark, grey and smooth and thick as a man's arm, grown into each other at every place they crossed so that you could not tell where one let go and the next took hold. You could see the red of the limbo only in the gaps now, in little windows here and there, and the top of the old tree was mostly bare. A bird eats a fig somewheres, he said, and sits up in the top of a tree, and the seed comes out of him. And it sprouts up there in the crotch, in a little dirt, like nothing at all. And it lets a root down. Just a string. And the tree don't pay it any mind. Then it lets down another one, and another one, and they hit the ground, and they get thick, and they start in to holding hands. He knocked on one of the roots with his knuckle. That limbo's been standing here since before the Indians quit this mound. In about five more years the

sections.heading: V. The Trunk
sections.text: That spring the State of New York passed a law against the plume trade, and New York was where the hats were made. Other states began to follow. By the fall the buyer in Key West would not answer Cal Roberts's letters. Cal took the cigar box off the counter, and after a while the brass scale. He came out to the warden's house one evening in 1911 and stood at the foot of the steps a long time without coming up, and then he set the scale on the bottom step and went home. Retta kept it, and weighed baking powder on it. Duke had shot that whole spring, the spring of the splinter, harder than he had ever shot, and kept back the best of it to wait for the price. Nobody would trade with him on Halfmoon after the business at Plover Creek, and the young men who used to follow him found other things to do. He lived by himself after that on a key toward Lostmans, and fished a little, and came to the store less and less, and when he came he did not talk. He was forty-four years old and looked sixty. Ez sent him a mess of mullet by Lige every week or so, and every week or so Lige came back and said Duke had thrown it in the water. When Duke died, in the winter of 1916, they found the trunk in h

title: Strangler Fig
logline: On a shell-mound key in the plume-hunting years, a bird warden's wife digs a splinter from his foot while the porch talks about his cousin.

verses.text: Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is a single paragraph. Devadatta, the Buddha’s cousin, has made up his mind to break the community in two. He meets the elder Ānanda on his morning round for alms and tells him that from that day he will keep the observance day, the gathering held at each new and full moon, and carry on the community’s business apart from the Buddha and apart from the monks. Ānanda goes back and repeats it word for word. The Buddha answers with a solemn utterance, that good is easy for the good and hard for the bad, and bad is easy for the bad and hard for the noble, and then with the verse. In the older account in the monastic code, Devadatta’s occasion for leaving was a list of five stricter rules that he wanted laid on everyone. Read the full commentary story. The series tells other parts of his story in Strangler Fig and The Partition.
bg.history:
The 1986 return of Halley’s Comet was the least favorable on record, with the comet on the far side of the sun from the earth at its brightest. For the northern states the best evening views came in the first half of January, before it sank into the twilight ahead of its passage round the sun on February 9: a dim patch low in the southwest, best found with binoculars, on the moonless nights around the new moon of January 10. Light pollution kept many people from seeing it at all. The Astronomical League, the federation of American amateur clubs, ran a campaign it called Dark Skies for Comet Halley, asking towns to dim their outdoor lights on the best nights. The comet is due back in July 2061. Arvada is a suburb on the northwest side of Denver. The club, the court and everyone on it are invented.

Grinding a telescope mirror by hand, glass on glass over a weighted drum with finer and finer grit, has been a hobby in America since the 1920s, and the knife-edge test can be made with a small lamp and a razor blade. A single coarse grain carried over into a finer stage will scratch the work. During the Second World War Albert Ingalls of Scientific American organized amateur mirror makers to supply roof prisms for military instruments; about eighty of them made more than twenty-eight thousand. Spinoza earned his living grinding lenses. The words on the card are the last lines of his Ethics, in R. H. M. Elwes’s translation of 1883.

sections.heading: I. The Round
sections.text: The club had observed on the Saturday nearest the new moon every month since 1969, and since November those Saturdays had belonged to the comet. By January Halley’s was low in the southwest after supper, a smudge you could find in binoculars if somebody showed you where. In November sixty people had come out to the end of Salvia Court to be shown. In December it was three hundred, with cars parked down both sides of the street as far as the stop sign. Gary Ochoa was the club’s secretary. He was thirty-four, a letter carrier out of the Arvada post office, and he had been made secretary because he could tell you a week later what everyone had said. On Thursday he finished his route at three, kept his parka on, and started up Salvia Court with a clipboard. There were fourteen houses on the court. Mrs. Vogel’s was the last on the west side, where the pavement ended at a wire fence and the grass ran on toward the foothills. That was the direction the comet was in, and it was the only dark direction there was. The Astronomical League had been after every town in the country for a year to turn its lights down on the good nights. It called the campaign Dark Skies for Comet Halley. Gary’s p

sections.heading: II. The Garage
sections.text: Ruth Vogel was sixty-three. During the war the Army had run short of roof prisms for its gunsights, and eighty amateur telescope makers around the country had made them in cellars and garages, twenty-eight thousand prisms in all. Her father, in Dayton, was one of the eighty, and from the time she was nineteen Ruth had done his fine grinding. Afterward she ground eyeglass lenses for a wholesale house on Larimer Street until her eyes were sixty. On Tuesday and Thursday nights she taught mirror making in her garage to anyone who came. There were four oil drums filled with sand to work on, and a tester at the back made from a coffee can, a flashlight bulb and a razor blade. She was at the tester when Gary came in. A boy named Kevin, who was thirteen, was at the near drum pushing a six-inch disk of glass back and forth across another one. Gary told it the way he would have read back the minutes. Mrs. Vogel. This afternoon, after my route, I took the clipboard and went up the court to ask about the lights. And while I was going up the court asking about the lights, Del Rainey saw me. He pulled over to where I was, and he said this to me: Starting this new moon, I’m holding my own observi

sections.heading: III. The New Moon
sections.text: At a quarter past five Gary walked the court once more, without the clipboard. The sun was behind the mountains and the cars had begun to come. The Akerses’ light went off while he was still on their walk. The widow’s went off when he rang. At the house for sale he stood on Mr. Akers’s stepladder and backed the porch bulb out two turns, as the realtor had said he might. Up and down the court the windows went dim one after another as people pulled their drapes. By half past five there were thirteen dark porches and Dufresne’s yard light, blue-white on its pole, laying the shadow of his spruce the whole way across the street. The telescopes stood in a row along the wire fence with their backs to it. There were two hundred people by six and more behind them. The bright thing low in the southwest was Jupiter, and half the line took it for the comet and had to be told. Mrs. Vogel ran the six-inch with the scratched mirror, because it was the one the children could reach. At twenty to six the yard light went out. Nobody had gone to the door again. Gary saw Dufresne come down his driveway in a car coat and get on the end of the line. A girl of nine or so got up on the step stool and put h

title: Porch Lights
logline: In Halley's Comet winter, a letter carrier goes door to door on a cul-de-sac asking fourteen houses to turn off their porch lights.

verses.text: The foolish man who scorns the rule of the venerable (Arahat), of the elect (Ariya), of the virtuous, and follows false doctrine, he bears fruit to his own destruction, like the fruits of the Katthaka reed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a laywoman of Sāvatthī looks after the Elder Kāla “with the tenderness of a mother for a son.” When her neighbors come home praising the Buddha’s teaching, she asks to hear it too, and three days running Kāla talks her out of it, thinking that once she has heard the Teacher she will have no more use for him. On an Observance Day she goes anyway, telling her daughter to feed the elder. When he learns where she is, he hurries to the monastery in a jealous rage and tells the Buddha the woman is too stupid for subtle teaching and should be taught only giving and the precepts. The Buddha sees his motive, tells him he strives only to his own hurt, and speaks the verse of the reed that dies when it bears fruit. The woman attains stream-entry, and the others listening benefit too. There is no past-life story.
bg.history:
The Connecticut Asylum for the Education and Instruction of Deaf and Dumb Persons opened in Hartford on April 15, 1817, in the old Bennet’s City Hotel, with Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and the French Deaf teacher Laurent Clerc, a former pupil of the Abbé Sicard’s school in Paris. The committee’s first report lists parents’ advances of a hundred dollars for six months and regrets that its means were “altogether inadequate to the support and instruction of those pupils who are in indigent Circumstances.” Two of the first pupils came from Hebron, in Tolland County. At a public examination on May 28, 1818, before the governor and both houses of the legislature, Gallaudet read aloud an address Clerc had written. It describes Sicard’s method of following “the uninterrupted line from the known to the unknown” and counts forty-two deaf pupils in the room. In the winter of 1818–19 it became the first school of primary and secondary education to receive federal aid. Pupils brought home signs and village sign languages to Hartford, where they mixed with Clerc’s French signs, and American Sign Language emerged at the school.

On October 5, 1818, Connecticut voters ratified the state’s first written constitution by a narrow margin, 13,918 votes, just under 53 percent of those cast. It ended the established church, the “Standing Order” that the Toleration Party had campaigned against (more at Today in Connecticut History). Meetinghouses were unheated, and between the morning and afternoon services many Connecticut congregations ate and refilled their foot stoves in “noon-houses” or “Sabba-day houses,” low sheds with a chimney at one end; many meetinghouses also kept a seat near the pulpit for the hard of hearing (Alice Morse Earle, The Sabbath in Puritan New England). Two years earlier, in the year without a summer, frost in June and a ruined corn crop had sent many Connecticut families west in the “Ohio fever.”

sections.heading: I. Cow
sections.text: I am the Hale boy. Keep that in front of you while I tell this. I was not born yet when this first part happened, and when the rest of it happened I was nine years old and had no words, not one. I had pointing, and I had my mother’s face. What I tell you I put together afterward, out of what I saw, and what was written down, and what Mrs. Kingsbury wrote out for me when we were both old. Watch my hands. I will go slowly. Thankful Root. Her house stood at the south corner of the green, so near the meetinghouse that on a still Sabbath the minister came in at her kitchen window, and she was the one person in the kitchen who did not know it. A fever took her hearing in her second year. In 1810 she was forty-four. She kept the books of her husband’s hat shop in figures she had worked out for herself, could cut a coat by eye and dress a hog, and on the Sabbath she sat on the short bench under the pulpit, where the town put the hard of hearing, between two old soldiers holding their tin trumpets up at the preacher, and watched his mouth for three hours and got nothing out of it. She and Ezra had made a language between them, the way two people will who have to. A sign for flour. A sign fo

sections.heading: II. Mullein
sections.dateline: The widow’s kitchen, at the nooning · 1812–1818
sections.text: Six years. She kept his shirts and knit his stockings and set his plate at her table where she had set her sons’, and he was a son to her, near enough, and he knew it, and it was the best thing he had. On the Sabbath he took notes of the morning sermon in a little book on his knee. At the nooning, while the farm families went down to the noon-houses on the lower side of the green to thaw out and fill their foot stoves, he crossed to her kitchen and ate her cold beans and brown bread and wrote the sermon out for her. The text, the doctrine, the heads. He chose the words she had. FIRSTLY. SIN. SECONDLY. GOD SEES. THIRDLY. OBEY. GIVE. She read them and nodded. He wiped the slate with the side of his hand, and they went back up the hill for the afternoon. That was her whole religion for six years: three or four words a week and a hand wiped across them. She thought it was a short religion and a hard one, and that it was all there was of it for a woman like her. He thought so too. That is the thing to understand about him. He was not lying to her. One October he taught her the weed by the pasture wall. He drew it two ways. The first year, the flat grey rosette lying on the ground, leave

sections.heading: III. No
sections.text: Monday at supper the widow made the sign for Lydia Kingsbury, a hand drawing down a braid, which she had used since the girl was in long clothes. Then two fingers out from her own eyes, toward the Bolton road. I want to see. He took the slate off its nail. NO. THEY ARE FRENCH SIGNS. YOU WOULD NOT FOLLOW. Wednesday, at the woodpile, she asked again. He wrote with the slate against his knee. YOU ARE TOO OLD TO BEGIN. IT WILL MUDDLE WHAT YOU HAVE. Friday, at the well, the third time. He wrote, and did not look at her while she read it. THE TOWN WILL LAUGH AT YOU. Why? He told himself it was for her. Here is what was under that, where a man keeps what he does not look at. If the Kingsbury girl could talk to her, the slate would go back to the schoolhouse. His plate would be a plate on the table, and he would be a boarder. For eight years he had been the only door into that house, and he could not think what he would be if there were another. I know this because he wrote it, the next year, in a letter to Huldah from Ohio. I told you she kept everything. The widow read each slate and nodded, and he wiped it, and he thought that was the end of it.

sections.heading: IV. Tree, Green
sections.dateline: The Kingsbury noon-house · the first Sabbath in November 1818
sections.text: Frost on everything. She ate her breakfast by candle and filled her foot stove from the hearth. Before they went out she put her hand on Huldah’s cheek, and pointed at the bean pot, and the bread, and Pember’s chair. Feed him. Huldah nodded. That morning the minister preached on the new constitution, voted in by a hair in October, which ended the Standing Order and, by his account, very possibly the world. Pember wrote it in his book. At the blessing the widow went out the door with her foot stove and turned away from home, across the green and down the hill toward the noon-houses. He went to the kitchen. Huldah set out the beans and the bread and a mug of cider. Huldah wrote down for me what was said. I have it here. Where is your mother? At the Kingsburys’ noon-house, sir. She has gone to see Lyddy. He put the spoon down. Huldah said his face went the color of the coals in the stove. He said out loud, to no one, So. She has done with me, and went out across the green without his hat. Now I was there. This part is mine. She came in out of the cold and sat at the end of the bench with the foot stove under her skirts, and Lydia looked at her a long time. Lydia did not begin with Har

sections.heading: V. The Wall
sections.text: In December the widow sold Ezra’s hat blocks and his bow and the last of the felt to a hatter in Coventry, and walked out the Bolton road with the money tied in a stocking, and put it on Eli Kingsbury’s table. Nobody had taught her the duty of almsgiving. In January Lydia went back to Hartford. After that, at the nooning, the widow went down to the noon-house, and old Fuller and I and two more who had heard of it and walked over from the next town sat by the fire with her, and she gave us what she had. Flour. Cow. Tree. Green. Is. She was a slow teacher. She had a great deal of time for it. Asa Pember kept the school to the end of the term. He still ate at her table; she still set his plate; there was nothing in her that wanted to punish him. But he did not take the slate off the nail again, and she did not hand it to him. In March he went west with the Pecks, who had the Ohio fever like half the hill. I saw him go. It was very early. The wagon went out past the pasture wall, where last summer’s mullein stood along the stones in a row, grey and dry, every stalk gone to seed and dead on its feet since September, and he did not look at them. He was looking back at the corner of the g

title: The Nooning
logline: A deaf widow's only sermon is the few words her boarder writes on a slate, until a girl comes home from Hartford signing.

verses.text: By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the lay disciple Culla Kāḷa (“Little Black”) spends a whole night at the monastery listening to the teaching. As he walks home at dawn, thieves running from the people they have robbed throw their loot down in front of him. The pursuers seize him, say he played the thief by night and only pretended to be listening to the Dhamma, and beat him. Some courtesans on their way to the river bathing place tell the men he did nothing of the sort and get him released. When the monks report it, the Buddha says he was saved both by the women's intercession and by his own innocence, and speaks the verse. The story opens by pointing back to an earlier one, in which a layman named Mahā Kāḷa (“Big Black”), caught the same way, was beaten to death.
bg.history:
Borger was laid out in March 1926 after oil was struck in the Texas Panhandle, and within ninety days some 45,000 people had come to it. The Handbook of Texas records a Main Street three miles long, drinking water delivered in tank wagons until wells were drilled, and a town government run by a crime syndicate. Dixon Street was the vice district; by one account its women each paid the city marshals a weekly “fine” of eighteen dollars. Armed robbers were called hijackers. Federal agents and Texas Rangers raided the town in October 1926, the Rangers returned in force the next spring, and in 1929 the governor put Borger under martial law. Thomas Hart Benton painted it as Boomtown.

The first carbon black plant in the Panhandle was authorized in Hutchinson County in March 1926. The channel process burned natural gas against iron and collected the soot for tire rubber, and within a decade the plants around Borger were darkening the town's dust storms. The Salvation Army's members are soldiers and its clergy hold military ranks; ensign was one of them in the 1920s. Its all-night prayer meetings, outdoor services with drum and concertina, and early Sunday “knee-drill” all date from its first decades. The Army's tent in Borger is invented, as are Calvin Odom, Ensign Beale, Opal Sykes and the rest, and the killing of the man called Big Black.

sections.heading: I. The Tent
sections.dateline: Borger, Hutchinson County, Texas · a Saturday night in September 1926
sections.text: The town was six months old and had forty-five thousand people in it. Most of them lived in tents and tar-paper shacks along a Main Street three miles long, and the water came from somewhere else, in tank wagons, and was sold off the tailgate. Calvin Odom was twenty-four, off a cotton farm in Wise County, and he worked in the hot houses at the carbon plant south of town. The plant burned gas against iron in long sheet-metal sheds and scraped off what the flame left. What it left was the blackest stuff there is, finer than flour. It went into automobile tires, and into Calvin. He came off shift black to the roots of his hair and coughed black in the mornings. There had been two Odoms at the plant when he hired on, no kin to each other, so the bigger man was Big Black and Calvin was Little Black. Then in July a crew looking for a stolen truck had caught Big Black on the south road at night, alone, and by the time anyone learned he'd had no part in it he was dead. Little Black had gone forward at the Salvation Army's open-air on Main Street in June. He could not have said why that night. A woman of fifty in a blue bonnet had been playing a concertina in front of a domino hall with her

sections.heading: II. The Road
sections.dateline: The south road · Sunday, first light
sections.text: He came out of the tent when the east was the color of dishwater and started for the plant camp. A quarter mile past the last shacks the road ran by a ranch windmill. It had been there before the town, an Aermotor on a thirty-foot steel tower with a round stock tank at its foot, and the rancher had not got around to fencing it off from forty-five thousand strangers. Calvin had the windmill in sight when a Ford touring car came up the road behind him with its lamps off. It went by close enough to fan his trouser legs. Something came out of the back seat, hit the caliche in front of him and slid. It was a canvas bank sack, tied at the neck. The Ford was already over the rise. He was standing over the sack, working out whose it might be, when the truck came. There were five men on it, a drilling crew, and their driller was a man named Hoyt Larrabee whose payroll had walked out of a contractor's shack at gunpoint an hour before. They saw a man alone on the south road at daybreak, black to the eyes, with their sack between his feet. There he is, Larrabee said. Sat in the Army tent all night so he'd have it to tell, and went hijacking by morning. Calvin said he had been at prayer. It was

sections.heading: III. The Tank
sections.text: Five women were coming out along the road from town. They were from Dixon Street. Anybody would have known it, at that hour, by the kimonos under their coats. Each had a towel over her shoulder and one carried a cake of soap in a saucer. The windmill tank was the only water in Borger that nobody charged for, and daybreak on a Sunday was the only hour of the week when there were neither cattle at it nor men. They came out every Sunday. They had passed the brown tent on the way, as they had passed it going the other direction at midnight. The one in front was Opal Sykes. She was thirty-five and had been in Ranger and Burkburnett, the same as the Ensign, in a different line of work. She paid the city eighteen dollars every week for the privilege, which was more than could be said for Hoyt Larrabee. You boys go on about your business, she said. This man didn't do any such thing. Larrabee kept his knee where it was. What would you know about it? I know that tent's been singing since nine last night. I went by it at twelve and I went by it at three with a sick headache, and he was on the second bench both times with his mouth open. I know that Ford. I know who was in it. He paid Jimmie o

sections.heading: IV. The Bench
sections.text: He walked back the way he had come. The soldiers were setting the benches straight for knee-drill, and they stopped when they saw him. Some men about killed me on the south road, he said. They took me for a hijacker. Some women from Dixon Street got me off. I'd be dead, only for them. They sat him down and went for the Ensign, and told it to her as he had told it. One of them, a carpenter named Tuttle who had been saved eleven years, said it was a hard thing for a praying man to owe his life to that kind of woman, and a harder thing for the Army to have it said. Ensign Beale looked at Calvin's face a while. She had her Bible, and she did not need to open it. Brother Odom is alive this morning because those women spoke up, and because he hadn't done it. It took both. They could not have talked him free if he had been guilty, and he could not have talked himself free at all. The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. — Ezekiel 18:20 What a man does is on him, she said. What he leav

title: Windmill Water
logline: A carbon-black hand walks out of an all-night Salvation Army prayer meeting in an oil boomtown, and a payroll sack lands at his feet.

verses.text: Let no one forget his own duty for the sake of another's, however great; let a man, after he has discerned his own duty, be always attentive to his duty.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha tells his monks that he will pass away in four months. Seven hundred monks who have not yet entered the stream are shaken, and they stay at his side, whispering to one another, Friends, what are we to do? Elder Attadattha (the name means "one's own good") thinks instead that he has not yet freed himself from the pollutants, and resolves to strive for arahatship with all his might while the Teacher still lives, so he stops keeping company with the others. They bring him before the Buddha as if he had done wrong. The Buddha praises him, says that those who honor him with perfumes and garlands do not truly honor him, and that only those who practice the Dhamma do, and speaks the verse. Attadattha reaches arahatship.
bg.history:
Since 1922 the White House Jesuit Retreat has given three-day preached retreats, based on the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola, on an eighty-acre campus on the Mississippi bluffs south of St. Louis. Laymen who wanted more than one retreat a year formed the first of the monthly Manresan clubs in 1921, and parish captains still recruit the men for each weekend. The full Exercises, in four "weeks," take about thirty days, and most laypeople who make them now do so in daily life, following Ignatius's Nineteenth Annotation, rather than by withdrawing for a month as the Twentieth describes. The translation quoted here is Father Elder Mullan's of 1914, from the Spanish autograph. Its Particular Examen tells the retreatant to mark on the lines of a G a dot for each time he falls into the fault he is working on. A spiritual bouquet is a Catholic gift of prayers rather than flowers: a card listing the Masses, Communions, rosaries and other devotions offered for someone.

The Coral Court Motel was built in 1941 on Watson Road, part of Route 66, in suburban Marlborough. Its two-unit buildings of yellow glazed tile and glass block, in the streamline moderne style, each had a garage, and, as Built St. Louis puts it, the motel "became famous for illicit encounters, as the individual garage units allowed one to park the car out of sight." It was demolished in 1995. Ralston Purina, which sold its animal feeds as "Chows," took its checkerboard from the four squares, physical, mental, social and religious, that its founder William H. Danforth drew in his 1931 book I Dare You! The Jesuits of Saint Louis University and the Sisters of St. Mary opened Firmin Desloge Hospital on Grand Avenue in 1933, about a mile south of the Jesuits' College Church.

sections.heading: I. The Last Conference
sections.dateline: The White House, St. Louis County · March 1949
sections.text: Every year in the third week of Lent, Norbert Vogt packed a shaving kit and two clean shirts and drove down the river road with the men of his parish to the White House, where the Jesuits had been giving retreats to laymen since 1922. It stood on the bluffs south of the city, eighty acres of oaks and lawn above the Mississippi. For three days nobody spoke. When the bell rang the men went to the chapel and sat in rows in their good suits and listened to Father Brockmeier. He had given the White House retreats for twenty-four years. He was a big, slow German from Hermann, on the Missouri, with a farmer's hands and a voice that did not rise, and the men who came back every year could have given his conferences for him. Thursday night, what a man is made for. Friday, death and judgment. Saturday, the two standards, Christ's and the other one. Sunday, love. They called him Father Brock. They had brought their sons to him, and he had married the sons. Norbert was forty-six. He was regional sales manager for Ralston Purina in southeast Missouri and southern Illinois, the Bootheel and Little Egypt: eleven salesmen and two hundred and some dealers. He spent four nights a week in hotels in S

sections.heading: II. The Bouquet
sections.dateline: South St. Louis · April and May
sections.text: The retreat captains met on Tuesday nights in Al Huelsmann's basement among the pipe fittings, and by the end of April they knew what they were going to do. They were going to give Father Brock a spiritual bouquet. Every Catholic child in St. Louis knew what that was. You did not send flowers, or not only flowers. You sent a card, and on the card was written what you had offered up for the person: so many Masses heard, so many Communions, so many rosaries, so many Stations of the Cross, so many visits to the Blessed Sacrament, so many of the little one-line prayers the Sisters called ejaculations. Al's idea was to send the cards to every parish that sent men to the White House, forty-one parishes. The Holy Name men and the sodalities and the schoolchildren of the Notre Dame Sisters would fill them in, and the captains would add the whole thing up. Frank Dunne, a bookkeeper at Anheuser-Busch, brought home an adding machine from the brewery. The cards came back by the hundred. By the middle of May the bouquet stood at 11,206 Masses, 9,840 Communions, 41,315 rosaries, 3,077 Stations of the Cross and 312,000 ejaculations, which the schoolchildren had counted on their fingers and the Si

sections.heading: III. Number Seventeen
sections.dateline: The Coral Court, Watson Road · May
sections.text: He had his two weeks of vacation, and he asked the general sales manager for sixteen days more without pay. He said it was a family matter. Agnes said that was a lie and Norbert said it was not. He went to the Jesuit residence at the university and asked for a priest to give him the Exercises, and the Father Minister, when he had stopped looking surprised, gave him Father Gallagher, who was thirty-four and taught chemistry, and had made the thirty days twice, as every Jesuit does, and never once given them. The book said a man making the Exercises would profit more the more he separated himself from friends and acquaintances, leaving his house for another room where he could get to Mass each day and nobody he knew would get in his way. Norbert could not afford a month in a hotel downtown. So he took a room by the week at the Coral Court Motel, out on Watson Road where Watson Road was Route 66, twenty minutes from his own front door, because it was cheap and because nobody he knew would ever admit to having been inside it. Everybody in St. Louis knew what it was. The Coral Court was a long curve of low yellow buildings in the trees, two rooms to a building, each room with its own ga

sections.heading: IV. Desloge
sections.dateline: Grand Avenue · the second of June
sections.text: On Thursday afternoon Al Huelsmann and Frank Dunne drove out Watson Road in Al's plumbing truck, because they had decided that somebody had to. They walked the curve reading numbers and knocked at Number 17, and Norbert opened the door in his shirtsleeves. Al had a speech ready. He had worked on it in the truck. When he saw the room he forgot it. The bed was made as tight as a barracks bed. On the dresser stood the crucifix from Norbert's bedroom at home, propped against the mirror, and next to it an order pad and a little black book, and nothing else. There was no woman. There was no bottle. There was no sign that anybody had been in that room but a man and a chair. Norbert, Al said. He's been asking. Seventy of us on that bench, and you never came once. Not once. Norbert looked at the two of them. He did not say anything. Then he went and got his hat. Father Brock had a room high in Desloge looking east over the roofs toward the river. The Sisters had cleared out most of the flowers, but there were still lilies on the radiator and peonies in a milk bottle on the sill, and on the bed table lay the red leather album with 41,315 Rosaries on the cover in gold. He was yellow now, and

sections.heading: V. The Contemplation
sections.dateline: Route 66 and the Bootheel · June to August 1949
sections.text: On the last day, the seventh of June, Norbert got up at five and did not go to Mass right away. He sat in the chair in Number 17 with the book open to the Contemplation to Gain Love. The light came up behind the glass block, grey and then yellow, the color of the tile, and the trucks began on Route 66, one, then another, then too many to count, carrying whatever they were carrying to Joplin and Tulsa and the coast. The book told him to look at how God dwells in creatures: in the elements, giving them being, in the plants, giving them growth, in the animals, giving them feeling, in men, giving them understanding, and so in him. He looked. He saw the trucks and the yellow tile and his own two hands on his knees, and for about as long as it takes a cup of coffee to go cold there was nothing in Number 17 that had not been given to him, and nothing in it he wanted to keep. Then he said the prayer at the end of the page, the one that gives back to God a man's liberty and his memory and his intellect and all his will, and walked up Watson Road to Mass. The man at the desk took back the key. Have a good time? Yes, said Norbert. It was the first word he had said out loud in thirty days to a

title: Spiritual Bouquet
logline: While his parish heaps prayers and flowers on a dying Jesuit, a Purina feed salesman takes a motel room by the week.

verses.text: Do not follow the evil law! Do not live on in thoughtlessness! Do not follow false doctrine! Be not a friend of the world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, an elder brings a young monk to breakfast at the house of Visākhā, the Buddha’s great lay patron, where cakes and rice gruel are always being given out, and goes on to another house. Visākhā’s granddaughter, straining water for the young monk, sees her face in the water-pot and laughs; he laughs too. She calls him a “cut-head,” and he answers that she is a cut-head and so are her mother and father. She runs crying to her grandmother. Visākhā tells him the word is a mark of respect for a monk whose hair and nails and robe are cut short, but he will not be calmed, and when his elder returns and rebukes him he asks why the girl is not rebuked instead. Then the Buddha arrives, hears the story, and, seeing the young monk is ready, first asks Visākhā whether it is proper for her granddaughter to call his monks cut-heads. The young monk springs up and says only the Buddha understands. The Buddha then tells him that ridicule over the pleasures of the senses is a low thing, not to be taken up, and that one should not live with heedlessness, and speaks the verse; the young monk enters the stream.
bg.history:
Hurricane Hugo struck St. Croix on September 17–18, 1989, with gusts measured at up to 168 miles an hour. More than 90 percent of the island’s buildings were damaged and power and water service failed. Looting spread in the days after, and at the governor’s request federal troops, FBI agents and U.S. marshals were sent to the island, the first deployment of American troops in response to civil disorder since 1968. Fresh water is scarce in the Virgin Islands, and most houses and businesses on St. Croix collect rainwater from their roofs in built-in cisterns.

Rastafari arose in Jamaica in the 1930s and spread through the Caribbean and its diaspora. Rastas call their way of life “livity”; it includes the Ital diet and wearing the hair in dreadlocks, which Rastas trace to the Book of Numbers and to the hair of Samson, and see as a mark of their covenant with Jah. Rastas often call non-Rastas “baldheads,” and someone who has only just begun to grow locks is a “nubbie.” In July 2025 the government of the Virgin Islands proclaimed a Rastafari Day and issued a formal apology for decades of ridicule, profiling and persecution (St. Croix Source).

sections.heading: I. After Hugo
sections.dateline: La Grange, outside Frederiksted, St. Croix · October 1989
sections.text: A month after the storm the island still looked like something had lain down on it and rolled. Hugo had come over the island on the night of the seventeenth of September, and in the morning there were hardly any roofs. The galvanize was in the cane grass, in the mangroves, wrapped around the light poles like paper around a stick. The mahogany trees along Centerline Road stood with every leaf stripped off them and their bark peeled white on the windward side, and the flamboyants were down across the road with their roots in the air. Three days after, the troops had come, the first time soldiers had been sent into an American place for looting since anybody could remember, and now there were Humvees parked in front of the fort in Frederiksted and soldiers from somewhere cold sweating in the shade of the market. There was no power and there would be none until Christmas, people said, or Easter, or never. There was no telephone. There was what was in the cistern. Every house on St. Croix had one, a concrete tank under the floor or beside the house, filled from the gutters off the roof. In most yards now the roofs were gone and the gutters were gone and the rain that had come with the s

sections.heading: II. The Calabash
sections.text: Brother Isaac came up the hill at seven with the youth. Isaac was a carpenter, a quiet big man with grey in his beard and locks to the backs of his knees bound up in a red, gold and green crown, and since the storm he had been on one roof after another from sunup, nailing down tarp the government brought in and galvanize people found in the bush. The youth was called Dervon. He was seventeen and had come to the elders in the spring, and his locks were six months grown, little tight knots all over his head that you could see the scalp between. A nubbie, they called it. That was the word for one just starting. He was proud of every one of them. Isaac ate a bowl of porridge standing up. Then he said there was a widow down the road with the rain coming in on her bed, and he put a stool under the genip tree for the youth and told him to sit and eat and wait, and went on down the hill with his hammer through his belt. Mama Cinth was in the cookhouse. Keisha brought the water. She did it the way her grandmother had shown her, the bucket let down on the rope into the cistern and hauled up hand over hand and set on the step, and a square of old sheet tied over the mouth of a calabash bowl,

sections.heading: III. Nubbie
sections.text: Youth, she said. Don’t vex. Sit down. She don’t mean you no harm. Nubbie is no bad word. Nubbie is the youth whose locks just start to grow for the Most High. It mean you take the vow. Is the Nazarite word, Numbers six. And she said it to him, standing in the yard with her wrap on her head, because she had said it so many times by now to people who asked her why. All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow. — Numbers 6:5 Mama, I know what nubbie mean, said Dervon. I know the vow. I know is a holy thing to be. But is right for she to laugh after me and call me so? Mama Cinth looked at him and looked back at the cookhouse, where her granddaughter was crying on a crate with her face in her arms, and she could not make either one of them right. She went back and forth between them twice. She brought him another johnnycake. She brought Keisha a cup of the bush tea. Neither one would take it. Then Brother Isaac came back up the hill for his level, which he had left, and stopped in the gate. What going

sections.heading: IV. The Seat of the Scornful
sections.text: Elder Absalom came up the hill a little after eight. He was past seventy and walked with a stick of guava wood, and he had come up from Jamaica in the last years of the cane to cut it, and stayed when the cane was gone, and grown his locks white. He did not come to the yard every day. When he came, the yard went quiet, the way a yard goes quiet when the wind drops. He had his own breakfast in a pan wrapped in a cloth, a piece of roast breadfruit and a little saltfish, and he set it on the step. Greetings, Mama. What happen here? Mama Cinth told it from the beginning. The bucket, the cloth, the calabash, the face, the laugh, the word, the other word, the crying, and Isaac. The elder listened all the way through with both hands on top of his stick and looked at the youth on the stool for a long time while she talked. He saw a boy who wanted very badly for somebody to be on his side, and he saw what was behind that, and he decided. Sister, he said to Mama Cinth, quite stern. Is right for your granddaughter to laugh after my youths, because their locks small yet? Because they take the vow and it don’t show plenty? Call them nubbie for a joke in the yard? Dervon was on his feet before t

title: Cistern Water
place: Frederiksted, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands
logline: A month after Hurricane Hugo, a girl straining cistern water laughs at her own reflection, and a young Rasta laughs with her.

verses.text: Rouse thyself! do not be idle! Follow the law of virtue! The virtuous rests in bliss in this world and in the next.
Follow the law of virtue; do not follow that of sin. The virtuous rests in bliss in this world and in the next.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha makes his first visit home to Kapilavatthu. To break the pride of his kinsmen he walks up and down on a jeweled cloister in the air, and they bow to him, his father the king first. A shower falls on the gathering, and he tells them it has rained on his family before, in the life of the great giver Vessantara. They all go home, and no one invites him to eat; the king, sure his son can eat nowhere else, has food and seats made ready for twenty thousand without asking. Next morning the Buddha considers what the Buddhas before him did and goes from door to door through his father’s city with his bowl. The king hurries out, pulling his cloak straight, and asks why he is being put to shame. The Buddha answers that begging is the custom of his line, the line of the Buddhas, and speaks the two verses.
bg.history:
Palestinians in Chicago began as peddlers and shopkeepers on the South Side; by the early 1970s they owned nearly a fifth of the city’s small groceries. In the 1980s many families moved out to Burbank, Oak Lawn, Hickory Hills, Bridgeview and Palos Hills. The Mosque Foundation, begun in 1954 by immigrants from the West Bank village of Beitunia, opened its mosque in Bridgeview in 1981 on a lot between railroad tracks and a trailer park, with a prayer hall for three hundred. The Barakats, Sedlak’s Banquets and the Fontaine Bluff subdivision are invented. Ramadan in 1990 ran from late March to late April.

The night waker of Ramadan, the musaharati or musahhir, walks his quarter before dawn with a small drum to rouse people for the last meal before the fast, greeting householders by name, and is paid in food or in coins at the feast. Tradition names Bilal, the freed Abyssinian slave who was the first caller to prayer, as the first of them (see this account of the trade). Edward William Lane lived in Cairo in the 1820s and 1830s and described the waker in his Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians: the drum beaten three times, the greeting to each man of the house, the house of mourning passed by, and the women who wrapped a coin in paper and set the paper alight before dropping it from the window. The waker’s cry, the words of the dawn call and the passage from a Friday sermon are quoted here in Lane’s English, from the text of his fifth edition (1860).

sections.heading: I. Sedlak’s
sections.text: Hajj Musa Barakat came to Chicago in 1956 with one suitcase, and by 1990 he owned the banquet hall on Harlem Avenue. In between there had been a grocery on Forty-Seventh Street, then three groceries, then five, then a brick two-flat in Gage Park, and, when the stores had gone to his nephews, the hall. He bought it in 1984 from a Bohemian family and left their name on the sign, SEDLAK’S BANQUETS, because the sign was paid for and the Lions Club knew where it was. Inside he changed everything. He hung chandeliers from a hotel sale downtown and put a fountain in the lobby that ran pink on wedding nights, and he had chairs for six hundred. In the southwest suburbs people who had never learned his name called him Abu Tariq, father of Tariq. People who had known the family in Beitunia remembered that his grandfather had been mukhtar of the village under the Turks, and that a Barakat did not carry his own packages. Tariq was the eldest, born over the first store. At nineteen he went to Cairo to study at al-Azhar for two years, and he stayed nine. Letters came, and then cassettes, carried home by men who had been on the pilgrimage or at a cousin’s wedding in Amman. On the cassettes a young

sections.heading: II. The Lot
sections.dateline: The mosque on Ninety-Third Street · the twenty-seventh night
sections.text: The mosque stood between the railroad tracks and a trailer park, on the lot the first families had been able to afford, and it held three hundred. On the twenty-seventh night more than a thousand came. Rugs and bedsheets and flattened cartons were laid on the asphalt between the cars. When the night prayers were finished one of the elders asked the visitor to give the lesson. The uncles had prayed in the front row inside, where they always prayed. They came out and stood at the back of the lot beside Dawud’s Oldsmobile with their hands clasped behind them, like men who mean to listen for a few minutes to be polite. It is told a few ways. The Barakats tell it one way and the families from the other villages another, and a woman who lived then in the third trailer from the fence, who is not a Muslim, will tell it to anybody. They agree on this much. He began in the ordinary manner, standing on the ground by the door. Somewhere in the first quarter hour he started to walk while he talked, up the lot and back, and he was not on the asphalt. He was as high as the roofs of the cars and then as high as the light poles, going back and forth over the people at an easy pace with his hands be

sections.heading: III. Six Hundred Chairs
sections.text: It was past one when the lot emptied. Everyone had to be up again before four to eat ahead of the fast, and everyone went home. Each family, pulling out onto Harlem, supposed that a man whose father owned a banquet hall did not need to be asked. Ismail supposed Dawud had asked him. Dawud was still wiping his face. Abu Tariq thought, If my son does not eat at my table, where will he eat? and so he did not ask him either. He drove to the hall. He had been planning it for a week. The next night’s breaking of the fast was to be the Shaykh’s dinner, for the whole community, at his expense. Twenty lambs had been in the ovens since the evening prayer. Three hundred pounds of rice stood soaking, and the cooks were breaking dried yogurt from Jordan into the big kettles, because it was going to be mansaf and it was going to be remembered. There were sixty round tables of ten, with a pitcher and a dish of dates on each. On the low stage where the bride and groom sat at weddings he had set one table apart with the two gilt chairs, and then he had one of the gilt chairs carried away. At twenty past three he was in the kitchen with a spoon in the broth when the wall telephone rang.

sections.heading: IV. The Round
sections.text: Tariq woke on the mosque carpet a little before three. The men who were keeping the ten nights there had their trays from home, brought in by sons and grandsons. Nobody had thought to bring one for him. He sat a while and considered it. For nine years he had lived in two rooms behind al-Azhar, in the Batniyya quarter, and for nine Ramadans he had walked that quarter at night with its waker. This was an old man called Amm Sayyid, who had the round from his father, who had it from his. The first years Tariq carried the lamp for him. The last years, when the old man’s hands shook, he carried the drum. He asked himself what Amm Sayyid did when he came into the quarter on the first night, and what the wakers before him had done. They did not go first to the house of a relative. They began at the first door of the first lane and went on in order to the last, passing by only a house in mourning, and they ate what was handed out to them. He took the drum out of his bag. It was most of what was in the bag, a copper bowl no bigger than a soup dish with a skin laced over it, and a leather strap to beat it with. He borrowed the flashlight from the mosque kitchen and walked a mile south in the

sections.heading: V. The Lincoln
sections.text: The call to the hall kitchen was from Dawud. Musa. Your son is going door to door in Fontaine Bluff with a drum, like the waker of some alley in Cairo, and the Polish widow is feeding him cake. Abu Tariq went out through the lobby past the fountain. He had his camel overcoat half on over his shirtsleeves, and he was still working his arm into the second sleeve when he swung the white Lincoln onto Harlem Avenue. He drove the two miles with the coat bunched behind his shoulder. He found them on his own court. His house was the fourth on Cour Lorraine, brick, with two concrete lions at the foot of the drive, and his son was standing at the third. Abu Tariq stopped the car in the middle of the turnaround and got out and left the door open, so that the chime went on ringing. Tariq. He spoke low, in Arabic. Why are you doing this to me? I am ashamed to the ground. In this town it would not be fitting for a son of mine to go from door to door in that car, with a driver. You go on foot and take bread from their hands. Why do you put me to shame? I am not putting you to shame, Yaba. I am keeping the custom of my line. Your line. Abu Tariq looked at his own house. Is it the custom of my line

sections.heading: VI. The Drum
sections.text: The dinner was eaten that night at Sedlak’s. Six hundred chairs were not enough. Abu Tariq sent the busboys with covered trays to the trailer park by the mosque, to Mrs. Gorski, to the man Dykstra, and to the front desk of the Palos Hills police. Tariq ate at a round table by the kitchen door. Nobody sat in the gilt chair. He stayed for the feast and for Nabil’s wedding, and then he went where a teacher was wanted, to a storefront mosque in another state. He has students now who have students. He left the drum on the hall table in his father’s house. The next year Ramadan came eleven days sooner, as it does, and on its first night, at a quarter past three, the drum was heard in Fontaine Bluff. It was Abu Tariq in the camel coat, sixty-three years old, alone, starting at the Mansours’ and taking every door in order. He kept it up nine years, until his knees would not do the hill on Cour Denise. He was never any good on the drum. People handed him eggs and bread, and he ate them in the driveways. The homeowners’ association took the matter up once, under Noise, and Mrs. Gorski stood and said she had lived her whole life under church bells, and nobody moved the question. After she die

title: Better Than Sleep
logline: A banquet-hall owner sets six hundred chairs for his son the shaykh, who is out before dawn with a drum, waking the cul-de-sacs.

verses.text: Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred monks take a subject of meditation from the Buddha and go to the forest. They strive hard and get nowhere, and set out to ask him for a subject better suited to them. On the road they see a mirage and fix their minds on it. As they enter the monastery grounds it begins to rain, and standing here and there on the terraces they watch the bubbles rise and burst in the downpour and think, so does this self of ours. The Buddha, seated in his own room, sends out a radiant image of himself that seems to look into each face, and speaks the verse; they are freed where they stand.
bg.history:
President Kennedy announced on the evening of Monday, October 22, 1962, that Soviet missiles were in Cuba, and the naval quarantine took effect at ten on Wednesday morning (the Cuban Missile Crisis). South Florida, the nearest piece of the mainland, filled with fighters, troops and anti-aircraft missiles; stores were stripped of canned goods, and schools ran air raid drills. Commercial flights between Havana and Miami stopped that week. They had carried, since December 1960, more than 14,000 unaccompanied Cuban children sent ahead by their parents under the Catholic Welfare Bureau’s program later called Operation Pedro Pan. Parents left behind waited until the Freedom Flights began in December 1965. Hialeah High School opened in 1954 and took students from Miami Springs, an airline town beside the airport, until the Springs got its own school in 1964. The Weather Bureau’s gauge at Miami International, a mile south of the story’s driveway, recorded a high of 84 degrees and five hundredths of an inch of rain on October 23, the only rain of that week. Miss Rountree, her five students and their Room 114 are invented.

The Latin tag homo bulla, man is a bubble, was already an old saying when Varro used it at eighty to open his book on farming; the English is from Fairfax Harrison’s Roman Farm Management (1913), which he signed “a Virginia Farmer” while president of the Southern Railway. Lucretius wrote his poem on atoms in the first century BC to free his readers from the fear of death. The pool in the street is in Book IV, among the tricks of sight, where he also explains how things send out thin images of themselves through the air; the lines on death are Book III, 838–842, and the passage opens at line 830 with the words the class could not get across. The English is William Ellery Leonard’s verse translation of 1916, reprinted in Everyman’s Library. The same pair of images, the mirage and the bubble, stands under another story in this series, set in the Mojave in 2008.

sections.heading: I. Thirteen Lines
sections.dateline: Hialeah High School, Florida · Tuesday, October 23, 1962
sections.text: Miss Alma Rountree had taught Latin in Dade County for thirty-nine years, the last eight of them at the high school in Hialeah, where the children from Miami Springs also went, the Springs having no high school of its own yet. She was sixty-four. Her fourth-year class that fall was five. On the second Friday in October she slipped on the wet terrazzo of the breezeway and broke her hip, and by the time the President went on television she had been ten days gone, first in the hospital having a steel pin put in, then at home in the Springs, in bed, under orders not to stand before Thanksgiving. She left two things behind her in Room 114. One was in the top corner of the blackboard, where every Monday she chalked a sentence for anyone who cared to take it home. That week’s was from Varro, who wrote his book on farming at eighty, and under the Latin she had put the English in her square hand, out of a translation she liked by a Virginia railroad man. Si est homo bulla, eo magis senex. If, as the saying is, all life is but a bubble, the more fragile is that of an old man. Nobody had erased it. The substitute, Mr. Purdy, taught driver education and did not like to touch the board. The oth

sections.heading: II. Okeechobee Road
sections.text: Dale had his mother’s Rambler. They went down Palm Avenue and out along the canal on Okeechobee Road, five in a station wagon with the windows down. It was eighty-four degrees, with the sun straight on the blacktop. Ahead of them the road went under water. It lay bright and flat from the canal bank to the far curb, a quarter mile on, with the sky in it. A city bus coming toward them stood in it to the axles, and a second bus hung upside down beneath the first. Dale slowed, as he had on every hot afternoon since he got his license. The water drew back and kept its distance. The bus came up out of it dry and went by. It’s the heat, Kenny said. The air right on the road is hotter than the air over it, and the light bends coming through. That’s sky. You’re looking at a piece of the sky laid down on the road. So it is truly there, María Elena said. The sky is. The water isn’t. On the road to Varadero it is the same. She was looking out the side window, south, toward the airport. My father also slows the car. Then how do you tell which things are the water? Midge said. Nobody had anything for that. Sandra said you drove up to it. Dale drove up to it for another mile. It stayed the same q

sections.heading: III. The Swale
sections.dateline: Oriole Avenue, Miami Springs · twenty minutes to four
sections.text: Miss Rountree lived with her sister Opal in a concrete-block house with a carport and a Florida room, on a lot with a sea grape by the front walk. A cloud had come up from the Glades side while they were on the bridge. The first drops struck the roof of the Rambler as Dale set the brake, big ones, far apart. By the time they were out of the car it was coming the way it comes in that country, all at once and straight down. They ran, and they did not all run to the same place. Dale and Kenny got under the carport beside Miss Opal’s Studebaker. Sandra made the front step, under the eave. Midge was caught at the sea grape and stayed under it. María Elena stood at the corner of the carport by the jalousie door of the Florida room, with the rain going past a foot from her face. The ground there is a hand’s depth of sand over rock, and water stands on it before it goes anywhere. Inside a minute the driveway was a finger deep. In the swale along the street, the low strip of grass the county leaves for the purpose, it stood deeper, and every drop that hit raised a bubble. They were perfect. Each was a dome of glass the size of a half-dollar, with the gray sky bent around it and the sea grap

sections.heading: IV. The Count
sections.text: The Navy’s line around Cuba went into force at ten the next morning, and at ten the school had its drill. Fourth period filed out into the inside corridor and got down along the lockers with their heads on their knees and their hands laced behind their necks. Mr. Boggs, the assistant principal, came along with the clipboard, counting backs. He counted Room 114 three times, and three times he came out five short. They were there. They were sitting against the lockers between the typing class and the Spanish class with their heads up, and María Elena was saying the thirteen lines over, in English now, to see whether they still held. She says she waved at him. Mr. Boggs marked the five absent and went on down the hall. The absences were never cleared. They are on five transcripts yet: fourth period, October 24, unexcused. On Sunday it was over, or people said it was. The fighters stayed at Homestead a good while. The flights from Havana did not start again. María Elena’s mother and father came out on the airlift in March of 1966, three years and five months later, when she was a sophomore at Barry College, and she translated for them at the airport. Miss Rountree came back after Chris

title: Homo Bulla
logline: In the missile week of October 1962, five Latin students who cannot translate thirteen lines on death go to ask their teacher for Caesar.

verses.text: Come, look at this glittering world, like unto a royal chariot; the foolish are immersed in it, but the wise do not touch it.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Prince Abhaya puts down a rising on the frontier, and his father the king rewards him with the kingdom for seven days and with a celebrated dancer and singer for his court. For seven days he does not leave the palace. On the eighth he bathes at the river, sits down in his pleasure garden to watch her perform, and she is seized with cutting pains and dies as she dances. He is sure no one but the Buddha can put out his grief. The Buddha tells him there is no counting how many times she has died this way in the round of births, and no measuring the tears he has shed over her, and that only the simple sink in sorrow; then he speaks the verse of the painted chariot.
bg.history:
United States troops of the 7th Infantry Division landed on Attu, in the Aleutians, on May 11, 1943, and fought there in fog and snow until the end of the month. The Treasury’s Third War Loan drive ran from September 9 to the beginning of October that year (see Series E bonds), with quotas down to the county, and towns built rallies, parades and “weeks” around any decorated man home on leave. Ruby Wells, its hotel and station KRWN are invented; the country is that of the Humboldt River and the Southern Pacific main line around Elko, Nevada.

Small stations of the time were required to keep a program log and an operating log for the Federal Communications Commission, minute by minute, and many recorded their own broadcasts on sixteen-inch lacquer discs, called electrical transcriptions. During the war, when aluminum was a critical material, the discs were made on a glass core. Tap dancers really did perform on the air, with a microphone set at the feet. The sound effects in Studio A are the ordinary ones of the trade. A “fist” is a telegrapher’s word for the personal rhythm of an operator’s sending. The engineer’s book is Thackeray’s Vanity Fair (1848), whose narrator calls himself the manager of a puppet show at a fair; the passages are from its preface and its last paragraph, as in the Project Gutenberg text.
