title: Dead Air
logline: The program log of a Nevada radio station for the week a wounded lieutenant is king of the bond drive, and the night after.

verses.text: He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk called Sammuñjani, “Broom,” sweeps the monastery morning and afternoon without regard for the hour. Finding the elder Revata sitting in his cell, he thinks him a great idler who lives on the gifts of the faithful and will not sweep so much as one room. Revata sends him to bathe, sits him down, and tells him to sweep early, go for alms, sit and contemplate the thirty-two parts of the body and its perishing, and sweep again at evening, leaving himself some leisure. The monk keeps to this exactly and soon becomes an arahant. Then the rooms fill with rubbish. Asked why he no longer sweeps, he says he did that when he was heedless and is heedful now. The monks report that he says one thing and does another, and the Buddha answers that he has spoken the truth.
bg.history:
Conservative Friends are the small branch of American Quakers who kept the old unprogrammed worship: no pastor, no hymns, a room of benches where people sit in silence until someone is moved to speak. Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) has a handful of rural and college-town meetings and owns Scattergood Friends School, founded in 1890 in Cedar County near West Branch, a town first settled by Quakers. Older Conservative Friends still said “thee” to one another in the 1990s and numbered the days and months instead of naming them. Business is done in a meeting for worship in which nobody votes; the clerk listens for the sense of the meeting and it is written down as a minute. Plum Run Meeting and its people are invented. Isaac Penington (1616–1679) was imprisoned six times beginning in 1661, the year he published the letter Lowell quotes.

The multicolored Asian lady beetle, Harmonia axyridis, was first found in Iowa in 1994 and within a few years was coming into buildings each fall to spend the winter in the walls. In December 1998 the price of hogs collapsed, and Iowa farmers were paid less than ten cents a pound for live animals, less in real terms than their grandfathers had been paid in the Depression.

sections.heading: I. Seven O’Clock
sections.text: Gene Aldinger mowed the meetinghouse lawn at seven on Seventh Day morning, and in a wet week he mowed it again on Fourth Day. He had taught industrial arts at the consolidated high school for thirty-one years and retired in the spring of 1994 with every one of his boys’ fingers accounted for and nine and a half of his own. The half he had left in a jointer in 1971 with twenty-two sophomores watching. He had wrapped the hand in a shop towel, held it up so they could all see what a jointer does, and finished the period. He was not a Friend. Marjorie was, birthright, Plum Run on both sides, and for forty years he had driven her out the gravel on First Day and sat beside her on the third bench with his hands on his knees, a Methodist waiting for somebody to start. When she died in the spring of 1996 the meeting buried her behind the old horse sheds under a stone no higher than a boot, and Gene kept coming. He did not know where else a man would go at ten o’clock on that day of the week. What he did there was work. The meetinghouse was white frame, built in 1867, with two front doors from the time when the men went in by one and the women by the other, and there was by now no part of it

sections.heading: II. The Facing Bench
sections.dateline: A Fourth Day afternoon · Tenth Month
sections.text: Lowell Mott was eighty-four and lived in the three-room cottage across the lot, which the meeting had built for a caretaker in 1951 and which had held no caretaker since Lowell’s knees went. The meeting paid his light bill. The women of the meeting left covered dishes on his step, turn and turn about. Most days after his dinner he crossed the gravel on two canes, let himself in by the east door, sat down on the facing bench under the clock, and stayed there until the windows went gray. Gene came into the meeting room that afternoon with the push broom, and there he was as usual, hat beside him, eyes down. Gene stood in the doorway. He thought: That man eats the meeting’s casseroles and burns the meeting’s lights, and then he comes over here and sits. He has two hands. Would it kill him to run a dust rag down one bench? Lowell did not lift his head. Gene. Come here. What is it? Go down and wash up. Then come back and sit by me. Gene had used that voice on other people for thirty-one years, and he found that he obeyed it. He leaned the broom in the corner, went down to the basement sink and scrubbed to the elbows with the Lava, the way he had made twenty boys an hour do it, and came

sections.heading: III. Bill of Materials
sections.text: He did it the way he did everything, which was to the letter. He swept at seven. He went home and ate two eggs. At nine he came back and sat down on the third bench by the south window, where Marjorie had sat, and he stayed there until four with a half hour out for the sandwich in the truck. At four he swept again and went home. The first week he looked at his hands and saw only what wanted doing with them. The storm windows were not up. A stair tread was working loose. He sat on the hands, literally, until they went to sleep. Then he did what he knew how to do, and wrote up a bill of materials. He wrote it in his head, as for any project. Hair of the head. Hair of the body. Nails, teeth, skin. Meat, cords, bone, and what is inside the bone. Kidneys, heart, liver. He went down the list and back up it the way he had made boys check their stock against a cut list before they were let near a switch, and it came to thirty-two items when he had it grouped right, though he never wrote it down. None of it was rated for anything. For thirty-one years he had read out to boys what a blade guard was rated for, and a chain, and a pair of safety glasses. Nobody had stamped a number on Marjorie’

sections.heading: IV. The Sills
sections.text: By spring the meetinghouse was a sight. The orange lady beetles that had come into the state a few years before had wintered in the south wall and died on the windowsills in drifts. Boxelder bugs lay among them. The mud that came in on boots during the thaw had dried in the grain of the floor, a web ran from the clock to the stovepipe hole, and somebody found mouse sign in the cloakroom. Outside, the grass stood to the shin, and the dandelions bloomed and went to seed, which had not happened on that lot since 1994. Gene was there every day. The truck pulled in at nine. He sat on the third bench by the south window with dead beetles along the sill at his elbow, and he looked like a man with nowhere else he needed to be. Friends are slow to speak to another person’s condition, and slower when that person has been doing their work for them. It was well into Fifth Month before Arlene Stanley and two others of the property committee, which had not met in five years, stopped him on the porch. Gene, the house is full of dirt. There are bugs on every sill. Why doesn’t thee sweep it? I used to, he said. That was back when I wasn’t paying attention. I’m paying attention now. He held the door

She said that for three years this man had not sat down among them one First Day, and the meeting had let him, to its shame, because it liked the paint. Now he sat all day in a dirty house and told Friends he was paying attention. He says one thing and does another, she said, and sat. Dale Hockett was clerk that year. logline: A retired shop teacher who cannot stop sweeping a Quaker meetinghouse is told by an old man to go wash up and sit down.

verses.text: He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.

bg.commentary: Aṅgulimāla ("finger-garland") was a robber who killed travelers and wore their fingers around his neck. When he chased the Buddha, running as hard as he could, he could not catch a man who was only walking. "I have stopped, Aṅgulimāla," the Buddha told him. "You stop." He threw his weapons into a pit, became a monk, healed a woman in childbirth by an act of truth, and endured being stoned in the streets.
bg.history:
The Kansas-Missouri border had been at war with itself since the 1850s. During the Civil War, pro-Confederate bushwhackers fought Union troops and Kansas “jayhawkers” in a guerrilla war of ambush, house-burning and murder. Some of the guerrillas, notably Bloody Bill Anderson's men, took scalps. On August 21, 1863, William Quantrill's raiders sacked Lawrence, Kansas, and killed more than 150 men and boys. Four days later, General Thomas Ewing issued General Order No. 11, expelling most rural residents of Jackson, Cass and Bates counties and part of Vernon. The emptied country was burned, and for years it was called the Burnt District. The chimneys left standing were known as “Jennison's monuments,” after the jayhawker Charles Jennison.

The German Baptist Brethren, called Dunkers or Dunkards, began in Germany in 1708 and came to Pennsylvania in the 1720s. They baptized by immersing believers three times forward, held a love feast with feetwashing, refused oaths, and practiced nonresistance. In the Civil War they would not bear arms for either side, which made them suspect to both.

sections.heading: I. The Burnt District
sections.text: After Order Number Eleven there was nobody left in the border counties but chimneys. The army had emptied Jackson and Cass and Bates in the summer of 1863, every family not able to swear its loyalty before a provost marshal, and then the Kansas men and the Missouri men took turns burning what was left. What stood afterward were the chimneys, stone and brick, one to a farm, rising out of the ash and the ragweed like gravestones for houses. People called them Jennison's monuments, after the Kansas colonel who had started it. You could ride a whole day and see nothing taller than a man except chimneys. Gabriel Mantooth rode alone through that country in the fall of 1864, because by then even the bushwhackers would not ride with him. He was twenty years old. He had been the best scholar at the academy in Lone Jack, could do sums in his head faster than the master could do them on the slate, could recite whole books of Milton. He had been at Lawrence with Quantrill, at nineteen, and come home with something gone out of his face. After Lawrence the others took scalps and tied them to their bridles. Gabriel took a finger. One from every man, the right forefinger, the trigger finger, and h

sections.heading: II. The Road
sections.text: Elder Jacob Ebersole of the German Baptist Brethren walked west on the Harrisonville road in the middle of a clear afternoon with nothing in his hands. He was sixty-three years old. He wore the plain coat with the standing collar and the broad black hat, and his beard went down his chest with no mustache above it, the way the Brethren wore them, because a mustache was a soldier's vanity and the Brethren did not go to war. They did not go to law and did not take oaths. They washed one another's feet at the love feast and dunked their converts three times forward in running water, which is why the world called them Dunkards, and they did not lift a hand against any living thing. Both armies thought they were cowards. Both armies had shot some of them for it. A boy herding three cows in a burnt field ran to the fence and said, Mister, don't go that way. Beads is on that road. The Elder nodded to him and walked on. A widow at a well by a chimney said, He was by here two days ago. Mister, he'll kill you for your hat. The Elder thanked her for the water and walked on. A farmer leading a mule stopped dead in the road in front of him and took hold of his sleeve. Old man. Old man. You don't

sections.heading: III. Stand Still
sections.text: Gabriel saw him from the bluff above Big Creek. One man, walking alone, in a black hat, on the open road through the burnt country, as if it were Sunday and the road went to church. Something about it made Gabriel angrier than he had been in a long time. He checked the loads in both Navy Colts and came down off the bluff at a gallop. The old man was perhaps three hundred yards ahead. Gabriel rode hard. The bay was the best horse in western Missouri and he had stolen it from a colonel. He leaned over its neck and gave it the spurs and the road went by under them like water, and the old man was walking, not hurrying, not looking back, an old man's walk, and he was three hundred yards ahead. Gabriel rode until the bay was lathered white at the chest and blowing blood. The old man was three hundred yards ahead. He got down and ran. He ran with the carbine in one hand until his lungs tore and his mouth tasted of iron and the thong of fingers rattled against his breastbone like something trying to get out. The old man was walking. He was three hundred yards ahead. Gabriel stopped in the middle of the road with his hands on his knees and screamed it at him. Stand still, old man! Stand sti

sections.heading: IV. The Colonel
sections.text: Colonel Abner Pryce of the Missouri State Militia came in the spring with forty men and a rope. There were petitions from three counties. There were widows who had walked to Kansas City to see him. He rode into the meetinghouse yard with his pistol already out and found an old man in a plain coat sitting on a bench in the sun, mending a harness. Colonel, said the Elder, is it Shelby again? Is it the guerrillas troubling you? It's one guerrilla. It's Beads. I'm told you're hiding him. I'm not hiding anybody, said the Elder, and pointed with his awl. That's him there, splitting kindling. Colonel Pryce had been at Westport and Lone Jack and had never in his life been as frightened as he was looking at the young man by the woodpile in shirtsleeves, with his hair cut short and his beard coming in with no mustache. The pistol shook in his hand. Forty men behind him sat their horses and did not breathe. You can put that up, the Elder said. There's no need. The Colonel did not put it up. But after a while he asked, because it was the only thing he could think to ask, Who are your people? Gabriel set down the hatchet. George Mantooth and Mary Mantooth. Of Lone Jack. The Colonel was quiet fo

sections.heading: V. Born Again
sections.text: Gabriel walked to Pleasant Hill twice a week for meal and salt for the brethren. On the road back one evening in July he heard a woman screaming in a cabin built up against a standing chimney, a lean-to of new boards against old brick, and he knew without asking that she had been at it a long time. A girl of ten was sitting on the step with her hands over her ears. He stood in the road a long time. Lord, he thought, how every living thing suffers. Then he went back to the meetinghouse at a run and found the Elder. Go back to her, said the Elder. Stand at the door and say: since the day I was born, I have never knowingly taken a life. By that truth, may you be well, and your child. Gabriel stared at him. That's a lie. You know it's a lie. You were there under the cedar. Then say it right, said the Elder. Since the day you were born again. Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. — John 3:3 So he went back. The midwife from Pleasant Hill met him at the door with blood to her elbows, and maybe she knew his face and maybe she didn't, but nothing else had worked and she stood aside. He did not go in.

sections.heading: VI. Stones
sections.text: It was a boy who knew him first, in the square on court day, a boy of fourteen or so, who shouted it. Then a man. Then the square. They threw clods first, and then sticks, and then a man picked up a cobble from the edge of the street and threw that, and then everybody did. Gabriel did not run. He did not lift his arms. He walked out of Harrisonville in the middle of the road with the meal sack torn open and spilling behind him like a trail, and his scalp opened over the left ear, and blood running down into his collar, and they followed him to the edge of town throwing. He walked the eleven miles back to Big Creek. The Elder washed the cut at the pump and sewed it with a harness needle and Gabriel did not make a sound. Bear it, Gabriel, the Elder said. Bear it. You're paying a little now on a debt you'd have been a long, long time paying otherwise. I know it, said Gabriel. I know it. Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. — Galatians 6:7

sections.heading: VII. The Moon
sections.text: He lived alone after that, in a cabin on the creek, and he went out working. He did not go to the people who had not been hurt. He went to the chimneys. Families were coming back to the Burnt District by then, a few at a time, after the war. They came home to a chimney in the ragweed and nothing else, and somewhere around the second week, a young man with no mustache and a scar over his left ear would come walking up the road with an axe and a froe and a crosscut saw on his back, and start cutting logs, and not leave until there was a house around the chimney again. Some of them knew who he was. Some of them ran him off. Some of them ran him off and he came back the next morning and started again, and eventually they let him. He built eleven houses in three years around eleven chimneys. On some of them he did not let himself sleep under the roof he had made, but walked home to the creek in the dark. He died in the winter of 1870 of a fever that went through the county, in his own bed, with the Elder sitting beside him. He was twenty-six. The last thing he said was something nobody could make out, a name, or the beginning of one. At the love feast that spring the brethren talked abo

title: Stand Still
logline: A bushwhacker with a string of fingers around his neck chases an old Dunkard he can't catch.

verses.text: This world is dark, few only can see here; a few only go to heaven, like birds escaped from the net.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha tells the people of Āḷavi to practice mindfulness of death: one who has done it meets death like a man who flicks a snake away with a stick, while one who has not screams like a man caught empty-handed. Everyone goes back to their business except a weaver’s daughter of sixteen, who practices it for three years. The Buddha returns for her sake and sits in silence until she comes, though she is late because her father has asked her to fill his shuttle. He asks her where she comes from, where she is going, whether she knows, and whether she does not know. Her answers (I don’t know, I don’t know, I know, I don’t know) offend the crowd until she explains them: she does not know where she came from before birth or where she will go after death; she knows she will die, but not when. He speaks the verse and she enters the stream. Going on to her father’s workshop, she startles him awake; he jerks the loom, and its end strikes and kills her. When the grieving father comes to the Buddha, he is told he has wept more tears over the dead than there is water in the four oceans, and he becomes a monk.
bg.history:
Paterson, New Jersey, built on the water power of the Great Falls of the Passaic, was America’s Silk City. After 1900 skilled Jewish textile workers came there from Łódź and Białystok, and by 1913 close to five thousand Jewish men and women worked in its silk mills, most of them as broad-silk weavers. In the 1913 strike they walked out with Italian, German and other weavers against the three- and four-loom system; in 1917 Jewish workers founded a cooperative bakery on Tyler Street. After the First World War the silk trade collapsed, mills closed for months at a time and wages were cut by more than forty percent. In August 1924 the broad-silk weavers struck again against the spread of three and four looms to a weaver. Tuberculosis was the trade’s great killer; a labor magazine in 1924 counted it behind nearly two in five deaths among women in silk work.

Many of the Jewish weavers had been members of the Bund, the Jewish socialist party of the Russian Empire, whose members filled the tsarist prisons after 1905, among them the Tenth Pavilion of the Warsaw Citadel. In June 1906 a pogrom in Białystok killed scores of Jews. In America former Bundists built the Workmen’s Circle, a mutual-aid order that paid for burials, ran a tuberculosis sanatorium at Liberty, New York, and from 1918 opened secular Yiddish schools for children. Dvoyre Mazur’s text, from the Sayings of the Fathers, is quoted in Joseph I. Gorfinkle’s 1913 translation. The Reznik family, Dvoyre Mazur and the Paterson hall are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Snake and the Stick
sections.text: That winter the mills were dark. After the war the silk trade had fallen down a well, and in Paterson the looms stood under dust sheets for eight and nine and ten months together, and the weavers who had come from Białystok and Łódź to escape the old country’s hunger walked the cobbles of Temple Street with their hands in their pockets and their bellies talking. When a mill did take people back, it took them back at sixty cents on the dollar. Everybody said it. Sixty cents on the dollar, and be grateful. In February Rivke Shapiro died. She was twenty-four and a broad-silk weaver at one of the big mills on the river, a good one, and she had the cough two years, and the Workmen’s Circle sent her to its sanatorium in the mountains at Liberty, nine months free, and she came home looking better, and then she had it in the blood, and then she was a weight under a sheet in her mother’s front room on the hill. It was the weavers’ sickness. Everybody had somebody. The lint got into you and the damp of the weave rooms got into you, and the doctors said tuberculosis and the weavers said di shvindzukht, the wasting, and buried their girls. The Workmen’s Circle held a memorial meeting for her i

sections.heading: II. Quills
sections.dateline: The Reznik shop, Van Houten Street · 1921–1924
sections.text: Her mother was already dead. The influenza had taken her in the fall of 1918, in nine days, and Bashe and her father had lived since then in two rooms on the hill, with her mother’s sewing machine under a cloth in the corner because neither of them could stand to sell it or to use it. Hershl Reznik was a weaver the way some men are tall. He had been a weaver in Białystok, and his father before him, and his grandfather on the hand looms in the cottages before there were mills, and he had the soft clean hands of the trade and its bad back and its habit of sleeping all Saturday afternoon like a dead man. In 1922, when the mills began to call people back, he did not go back. He took the money he and his wife had put by for Bashe’s wedding and bought two old Crompton looms from a shop that was closing, and rented a corner of the top floor of a brick mill by the raceway, with power off the shaft, and set up for himself. It was done all over Paterson in those years. A man with two looms and a commission from a converter in New York could weave by himself for himself and be nobody’s four-loom slave, if he did not mind working until midnight. Hershl did not mind. He worked until midnight an

sections.heading: III. The Hall
sections.dateline: The Workmen’s Circle rooms · a Thursday in April 1924
sections.text: The notice was on the board at the cooperative bakery on Tyler Street. Comrade Dvoyre Mazur of New York would speak on Thursday evening at eight on the subject of I. L. Peretz and the Jewish worker. Bashe read it with a loaf of rye under her arm and felt her heart turn over, the way it had not turned over in three years about anything. On Thursday her father had a warp to finish. A converter wanted forty yards of a yellow crepe by Friday noon, and it was eleven yards short. He came home at six to eat and said it at the table without looking up from his soup. Bashele, I need quills tonight. The whole box. I’m out by nine o’clock. Tate, Dvoyre Mazur is speaking tonight. At eight. So go after. He looked at her. He was not a hard man; he was a tired one. I’ll be there until two in the morning if I don’t have quills. You want to go to a lecture, go, but bring me the quills first. She sat with that a minute. Then she put on her coat and went down to the shop instead of to the hall, and sat at the winding frame under the bare electric bulb, and filled a hundred quills of yellow silk as fast as she had ever done it in her life, saying it on every one, and it was after eight-thirty when she

sections.heading: IV. Four Questions
sections.text: The old woman did not get up. She spoke to her in Yiddish, quietly, the way you speak to someone across a kitchen table, but in that silence the whole room heard it. Bashe Reznik. Where do you come from? I don’t know, Dvoyre. Where are you going? I don’t know. You don’t know? I know. You know? I don’t know. The hall did not like it. A man laughed out loud. Somebody said, not quietly, that Hershl Reznik’s girl had a mouth on her, to make fun of an old revolutionary to her face. A woman in the third row said that if the girl came from the Reznik shop she should say so, she had silk all over her, everybody could see where she came from, and where she was going was back to her father, so why the riddles? Somebody else said it was the kind of thing you heard from a rebbe’s daughter, mysticism, superstition, and they had not come out on a Thursday night to hear superstition. Gurevitsh the chairman stood up to say something and the old woman put a hand on his sleeve and he sat down. Bashe. When I asked where you come from, why did you say you don’t know? You know I came from my father’s shop on Van Houten Street, Bashe said. Everybody can see. You weren’t asking that. You were asking wher

sections.heading: V. The Shuttle
sections.dateline: The mill by the raceway · near ten o’clock
sections.text: The building was dark except for the top floor, where two or three of the little shops were still running, and the stairwell shook with them. Bashe went up with the box under her arm. She was not tired. She felt as if she could have climbed the stairs to the roof and stepped off and walked across the air over the raceway and the Falls and the whole of Paterson. Her father had run out of quills. He had stopped his looms and was sitting on his box between them with his back against the post, and he was asleep. His chin was on his chest and his glasses were in his lap and his mouth was open a little, and his hand was still resting on the shipper handle of the near loom, the iron lever that throws the belt over and sets the loom running. A shuttle with an empty quill lay in the shuttle box where he had dropped it, not seated right. She did not want to wake him. She came very quietly down the aisle and set the box of quills on the breastbeam of the loom, by his hand, so it would be the first thing he saw. The breastbeam is a smooth, rounded bar of maple, polished by a thousand weavers’ aprons. The box slid. It went off the far side and hit the floor and burst, and a hundred quills of ye

sections.heading: VI. All the Rivers
sections.text: They buried her in the Workmen’s Circle ground, next to her mother, and there was a rabbi after all, because Hershl at the last minute wanted one, and the Bundists stood at the back with their hats on and did not say anything about it. Hershl tore his lapel. He sat the seven days on a low box in the two rooms on the hill with the mirror covered and the sewing machine in the corner, and people came up the Golden Stairs with food and went down again, and he did not speak. On the eighth day he got up and put on his coat and took the Erie to Jersey City and the ferry across and the elevated down to East Broadway, where somebody had told him Dvoyre Mazur had a room over a printer’s. He climbed the stairs. She opened the door and looked at him and stood aside to let him in. You filled her head with death, he said, and then death came. He said it standing in the middle of her room, with his hat on. Three years. Every night. I heard her through the wall, I thought she was praying, I thought, so let her pray, it doesn’t hurt anybody. You came for her. You said so. Everybody in Paterson heard you say so. You came twenty miles for her and she came to you and then she went back to me and I kil

logline: In Silk City, a weaver's daughter winds her father's quills for three years, repeating what an old Bundist once told a memorial meeting.

verses.text: The swans go on the path of the sun, they go through the ether by means of their miraculous power; the wise are led out of this world, when they have conquered Mara and his train.

bg.commentary: Thirty monks from a distant country came to see the Buddha at Jetavana. Ānanda, arriving to wait on him, saw them going in and decided to stay at the gate until the greetings were over. The Buddha greeted them and taught them, and all thirty became arahats, rose into the air and left. When they did not come out, Ānanda went in and asked where they were. “Gone.” “By what path?” “Through the air.” “Have they already rid themselves of the pollutants?” “Yes.” Just then a flock of geese flew over, and the Buddha said that one who has developed the bases of power goes through the sky like those, and spoke the verse. That is the whole of the full commentary story. In America the people who rose and flew away from bondage were told of long before this retelling, in the legend of the flying Africans handed down along the Georgia and Carolina coast.
bg.history:
Delaware was a slave state that never seceded, with far more free Black residents than enslaved ones, and the main overland road north from Maryland’s Eastern Shore ran up through it to Wilmington and Pennsylvania. Under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 owners and their agents could pursue people into any state. The Quaker farmer John Hunn was fined so heavily for sheltering a family that his farm near Middletown was sold at sheriff’s sale in 1848. Samuel Burris, a free Black conductor born in Kent County, was jailed and put on the auction block for the same work, and was bought and freed by an abolitionist posing as a trader. Much of the guiding was done by free Black Delawareans such as those of Star Hill, near the Quaker village of Camden. Large parties were rare but real: in October 1857 twenty-eight people, many of them children, left Dorchester County together in heavy rain.

Friends dated by number, so March was Third Month, and Delaware counties are still divided into hundreds. The bayside of Kent County is tidal salt marsh, now largely within Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge, where geese winter in great numbers and leave for the north in March; marshmen there lived by muskrat, salt hay and market gunning. St. Catharines, in what was then Canada West, was one of the chief places where people who had freed themselves settled. Abram Gibbs, the Lindleys and the thirty are invented, and no daybook records them.

sections.heading: I. Thirty
sections.dateline: Little Creek Hundred, Kent County, Delaware · Third Month 1855
sections.text: They came up out of the marsh on the fourteenth of Third Month, a little before light, thirty of them in a single line. They had left three farms below the Choptank on a Saturday night and had been five nights walking. By day they had lain up in pine woods, and once in a tobacco barn. The oldest was a woman past sixty named Sabra, who had a stick she had cut on the road. The youngest was at the breast. Eleven of the children could walk and four had to be carried. A man named Ennals had brought them across the last of it in the dark by the muskrat leads, in water to the knee, each one holding the coat of the one ahead. Abram Gibbs was standing at the edge of the hard ground when they came to it. Nobody had sent him word. He had a lantern with three sides shut. Abram was a free man and had been born one. He was fifty or near it. He owned six acres of fast land and a right to the marsh in front of it, and the marsh was his living. He took muskrat from the first frost to the middle of March and cut salt hay in summer, and through the cold months he gunned wildfowl for the Philadelphia market. He sat in a class at the African Methodist meeting and was nobody’s preacher. He did not say a

sections.heading: II. The Gate
sections.dateline: The corn house lot · the same day, toward evening
sections.text: He brought the wagon down the lane as the light was going and stopped at the gate of the lot. The corn house door stood open. He could see them inside, sitting close together on the floor, and Abram in front of them on an upturned bushel with his hat on his knee. Abram was asking them their names. He went to each one, the babies as well, and asked, and waited for it, and said it back. Amos had been raised not to break in on a thing like that. He thought he would wait until Abram had done greeting them, and speak to him then about the wagon. He looped the lines over the post and stood by the gate. After the names there was talk. He could not make it out. Abram’s voice was low and did not rise. Once all of them laughed together, quietly, thirty people at once, and he had not expected to hear that from the building. Then it was still. The mare shifted her feet. A rail called out on the marsh. He waited what he judged to be a quarter of an hour more. Then, since it was coming on dark and there were twelve miles to go, he went up to the door. Abram was sitting on the bushel alone. Thirty of Hannah Lindley’s quilts were folded and stacked against the wall with the corners squared. There

sections.heading: III. The Daybook
sections.dateline: Little Creek Hundred · Third Month to Sixth Month
sections.text: The men from Dorchester came at sunup with a constable out of Dover and two dogs. They had a paper. Joseph Lindley read it through and told them they might look where they liked. The dogs took the scent down the lane with a great noise and into the corn house. There they went once around the floor and lay down. No scent went out of it. The men walked the edge of the marsh for an hour, and one went in to his thighs and had to be hauled. At the last they looked up, as men will when there is nowhere else to look. The sky was empty. They went back to Dover. In Sixth Month a letter came for Abram Gibbs by way of Philadelphia, from St. Catharines in Canada West. Abram could read print and could not read script, and he carried it up the lane to Amos. It was written in a schoolmaster’s hand. It gave thirty names, the grown people first and then the children down to the youngest, in the order Abram had asked them. A few had signed and the rest had made their marks. It said they were all well and had found work, and that old Sabra wished him told she had the stick yet. It said they had come in on the morning of the fifteenth of March. Amos read the date over twice. That was the morning the d

title: By What Road
place: Little Creek Hundred, Kent County, Delaware
logline: Thirty people walk out of a Delaware salt marsh before dawn, and a Quaker boy waits at the gate with a hay wagon.

verses.text: If a man has transgressed one law, and speaks lies, and scoffs at another world, there is no evil he will not do.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, rival ascetics in Sāvatthī lose their alms and honor as the Buddha's following grows, and they persuade Ciñcā, a beautiful young woman of their own order, to disgrace him. For months she walks toward his monastery in the evening in a red cloak, carrying perfume and flowers, sleeps at the rivals' place, and walks back in the morning, telling anyone who asks that it is none of their business; then she says she spends her nights with him. She binds cloths around her belly, then a disk of wood, bruises herself with an ox's jawbone, and accuses him before the whole assembly of fathering her child and abandoning her. He answers that only the two of them know whether it is true. The god Sakka sends four young gods as mice to gnaw through the cords, the wind lifts her cloak, and the disk falls and cuts off her toes. The crowd spits on her and drives her out with clods and sticks, and the earth opens and she is swallowed by fire “as if wrapped in a scarlet blanket.” The Buddha tells the monks it is not the first time: in a former life, as a queen, she falsely accused a virtuous prince who had refused her, and the king threw him from a cliff; the prince was saved by a serpent king, became a hermit, and refused the throne when his father came to him, and the king threw the queen from the same cliff.
bg.history:
Haitian immigrants began arriving in Springfield, an industrial city of about 59,000, around 2017, recruited to fill jobs in factories, warehouses and food processing. By 2024 there were an estimated 12,000 to 20,000 of them, most living in the country legally under humanitarian parole or Temporary Protected Status, which the federal government extended and redesignated for Haiti in June 2024. Many Haitians who came north in those years had first spent years in Brazil or Chile after the 2010 earthquake. Every January 1, Haitian households mark independence with soup joumou, the squash soup that, in the story Haitians tell, enslaved people were forbidden to eat under French rule.

In March 2024, unfounded rumors began that Haitians were taking ducks and geese from city parks. On August 10 about a dozen members of a neo-Nazi group marched through downtown with swastika flags. In early September a secondhand Facebook post claiming Haitians were eating pets went viral; on September 9 the Republican vice-presidential nominee repeated it, and on September 10 the presidential nominee repeated it in a televised debate. City, county and police officials said there was no evidence for any of it. Beginning September 12, Springfield received dozens of emailed bomb threats that emptied City Hall, schools and other buildings. More on the Springfield pet-eating hoax.

sections.heading: I. Soup Joumou
sections.text: On New Year's morning there was snow on the cars and the fellowship hall of the Methodist church on the south side smelled of squash and beef and scotch bonnet, because Frè Dieudonné had been up since four making soup joumou in the church's two big kettles, the way every Haitian house makes it on the first of January, for independence, because, the way the old people tell it, under the French the slaves cooked that soup for their masters and were not allowed to taste it. By noon there were three hundred people in a hall built for a hundred and twenty. They stood along the walls with their coats on and their bowls in their hands. They came from the two-bedroom houses where fifteen of them lived on air mattresses waiting for work permits, and from the night shifts at the auto parts plants and the Amazon sorting center and the meatpacking plant, and from the apartments out by the highway where the landlords had doubled the rent. Some of them had been in Springfield three years and some three weeks. Many had come the long way, through Brazil or Chile, where they had gone after the earthquake and stayed ten years and learned Portuguese or Spanish and then walked north through nine count

sections.heading: II. Mirlande
sections.dateline: A storefront on East Main Street · January
sections.text: There were a dozen Haitian churches in Springfield by then, most of them in rented rooms, and two of them had been doing well. Pastè Wesner had a congregation of four hundred in a former tire store on East Main, with a sound system and a praise band and a sign in the window in Creole and English. Pastè Lucner had two hundred in a Pentecostal hall he rented on Sunday afternoons. And there was a man who called himself Pwofèt Fanfan, who prayed for people on Facebook Live every night at nine and had twelve thousand followers and a Cash App. All three of them, in the year before, had also done a good business in papers. Two hundred dollars to fill out an asylum application. A hundred and fifty for the work permit. A blessing on the envelope for twenty more. Then the people stopped coming. The tithes went down. Pastè Wesner's band had to let its drummer go. In January the three of them met in the back room of the tire store, under the fluorescent light, with the snow coming down past the window, and sat for a long time not saying what they had come to say. Then Pastè Lucner said it. He fills out the forms for free. He reads the Bible for free. Who can compete with free? Is he the only m

sections.heading: III. The Red Dress
sections.dateline: The south side · winter into summer
sections.text: She had a red dress, a long one, and a red wool coat she had bought at the Goodwill. On Sunday evenings, when the three hundred people were coming out of the fellowship hall into the parking lot with their Bibles under their arms, Mirlande would be walking in, against the crowd, in the red coat, with a bunch of grocery-store roses and a little bottle of perfume in her hand. Where are you going this time of night, Sè Mirlande? What's it to you where I'm going? She went around the side of the church toward the parsonage and did not come back. She spent those nights in Pastè Wesner's car, parked two streets over, with the engine running for the heat. And on Monday mornings a little after seven, when people were coming to the parsonage door to catch Frè Dieudonné on his way home from the plant and ask him to look at a letter before they went to work, there was Mirlande in the red coat walking the other way, down the parsonage steps. Where did you sleep last night, Sè Mirlande? What's it to you where I slept? She did it for six weeks. Frè Dieudonné was at the plant every one of those nights, hosing the kill floor, with forty men who could have said so. Nobody thought to ask them. At the

sections.heading: IV. Only You and I
sections.text: The side door of the fellowship hall was propped open with a folding chair that Sunday to let in some air, because two hundred people in a room built for a hundred and twenty make their own weather. Frè Dieudonné sat on a stool at the front with his reading glasses on and the Bible open on his knee and was talking about the widow's mite, plainly, the way he talked about everything, when Mirlande came in through the side door. She walked slowly, with one hand at the small of her back, the way women walk at nine months, and the hall went quiet around her. She came up the aisle between the folding chairs and stood in front of him. Her face was puffed. Her hands were swollen and dark. Under the red dress her belly was high and round. Great teacher, she said, loud enough for the back row. Look at all these people you have. Look how they come to hear you. Your voice is so sweet. Your mouth is so soft. She let that sit. And this is your child, and my time is any day now. And you haven't found me a midwife. You haven't found me a room. You haven't brought me so much as a bottle of oil or a can of milk. And if you won't do it yourself you could say to somebody, to Madame Hale, to the men wi

sections.heading: V. Krik? Krak!
sections.dateline: The week of the lie · September 9–15
sections.text: On Monday the other story came back. It came back bigger. The duck and the goose had turned into cats and dogs. Somebody on the internet said the Haitians in Springfield were eating people's pets, and somebody bigger said it again, and on Tuesday night a man running for president said it on television, at the debate, to the whole country. On Thursday morning somebody emailed bomb threats to City Hall and to the schools, and they emptied the buildings and sent the children home, and the Haitian children walked home past the police dogs. On Friday it happened again. That week a sign turned up in the grass of a city park, professionally lettered, PLEASE DO NOT EAT THE DUCKS, and on Friday the park workers took it down. People did not go to work. People stayed off the porch. Pastè Wesner's church had forty people that Sunday. Pastè Lucner's had eleven. Pwofèt Fanfan did not go live on Facebook at all that week, or the next, and the Cash App went quiet, and by Christmas he had moved to Indiana. The fellowship hall was full. There was a police car parked out front, which Mrs. Hale had asked for. People came in and sat close and did not say much. When it was time, Frè Dieudonné did not op

sections.heading: VI. A Saucer
sections.text: The Methodists voted in October to give the Haitians the use of the sanctuary as well as the hall, since there were thirty-one of them and three hundred of the others. Mrs. Hale made the motion. It passed thirty to one. The lines for the papers went on all that fall, and Frè Dieudonné sat at the long table in the afternoons and went to the plant at midnight, and slept in the mornings in the back room of the parsonage, where anybody who wanted to could look in the window and see him sleeping alone in his clothes with his shoes on the floor beside the bed, and some people did. Mrs. Hale said one evening that she would call the exterminator about the mice in the hall, now that there were so many people eating in there on Sundays. Frè Dieudonné asked her not to. She looked at him over her glasses for a while, and then said all right. So after the soup on Sundays, when the folding chairs had been stacked and the kettles washed and the floor mopped, he would take a little rice and beans from the bottom of the pot and put it in a saucer, and set the saucer on the linoleum by the baseboard under the edge of the stage, where the four of them had come out.
