title: Only You and I
logline: Rival pastors put a church soloist in a red coat up to ruining the Haitian layman who fills out everyone's forms for free.

verses.text: The uncharitable do not go to the world of the gods; fools only do not praise liberality; a wise man rejoices in liberality, and through it becomes blessed in the other world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala and the citizens of his capital try to outdo each other in feeding the Buddha and his monks, and the citizens keep winning. The king lies down in despair until Queen Mallikā devises gifts only a king could give: a pavilion of sāla wood, five hundred white parasols held by five hundred elephants, golden boats of perfume, noblewomen to fan and serve the monks. One monk lacks an elephant; the only one left is a rogue, and Mallikā has it stand beside Aṅgulimāla, the reformed murderer, where it drops its ears, shuts its eyes and stands motionless. These are the "Gifts beyond Compare," given once in each Buddha's lifetime, and always, the commentary notes, arranged by a woman. But of the king's two ministers, Kāla resents the waste while Juṇha rejoices, and the Buddha, out of pity for Kāla, gives only a four-line blessing. When the king learns why, he banishes Kāla, gives Juṇha the kingdom's means to give alms for seven days, and the Buddha speaks this verse.
bg.history:
Azorean immigrants brought the festas of the Holy Spirit to California in the nineteenth century. In the Azores the silver crown, topped with a dove, passes from house to house on the Sundays between Easter and Pentecost, with the rosary prayed before it each night. The devotion is traced to Queen Isabel of Portugal, who fed the poor in a famine. California festas add crowned girl queens and a free meal for everyone who comes. In Gustine, in Merced County, dairymen lead decorated calves in the procession, the animals are auctioned for the society's charity, and volunteers serve sopas of beef, cabbage and bread.

In 2022 U.S. dairy farmers saw record milk prices, averaging $25.39 per hundredweight, though high feed and labor costs ate into margins and prices fell the next year. California's youth offender parole hearings, created by SB 260 in 2014 for people whose crimes were committed before age 18, give special weight to youth and later growth; for those serving 25 years to life, the hearing comes in the twenty-fifth year. With fewer American vocations, U.S. dioceses have increasingly recruited priests from Africa, including Nigeria.

sections.heading: I. The Domingas
sections.text: Frank Mendonça milked fifty-eight hundred cows on two dairies on the west side of the county, and in the spring of 2022, for the first time in his life, milk was worth what it cost to make and then some. The checks that came from the co-op in April were the biggest anybody in Valeta had ever seen. Feed was dear and diesel was dear and the drought had the canals running at a third, but the price of a hundredweight of milk went past twenty-five dollars, and the dairymen who had held on through 2009 and 2015 and the years between drove to Mass in new trucks and did not apologize for it. That was also the first spring in three that the hall could keep the festa the old way. In 2020 there had been no festa. In 2021 the ladies had put the sopas into foam boxes and handed them out of the kitchen window to cars. So everybody wanted to give. That was the trouble, if it was trouble. Valeta was one of the last halls in California that still kept the domingas the way they kept them on Terceira, where Frank had been born and where his father had come from in 1971 with eleven cows' worth of savings and four children. From Easter to Pentecost the silver crown of the Holy Ghost, with the dove on t

sections.heading: II. São
sections.text: His wife found him there at noon. Conceição Mendonça was sixty-four and had been born in Valeta, in the house behind the hall where her father was caretaker, and in 1975 she had been the festa queen, at seventeen, in a cape of red velvet four yards long that her mother had embroidered with wheat and doves by hand. Everybody called her São. What's this, she said. Are you sick? You don't know? I don't know anything. Tell me. So he told her, lying in the recliner with his boots still on. That he was the biggest dairyman on the west side of the county and the president of the festa that year, and the hall had outgiven him every second Sunday since Easter. That there was one Sunday left, the big one, Pentecost, and he could not see how to beat two thousand people and a bullfight. That if Frank Mendonça could not outgive the hall in Valeta in the best milk year there had ever been, he did not know what he was for. São looked at him for a while. Have you ever heard, she said, of a king who lets the people beat him? Get up. I'll do the festa. She sat on the arm of the recliner and told him how, counting on her fingers. The dairy had shade cloth, the white cloth they stretched over the feed

sections.heading: III. The Bull
sections.dateline: The road to the church · Saturday, June 4
sections.text: Sixty-two queens came. The oldest was eighty-seven, the queen of 1952, in a cape of white satin gone the color of cream, with her granddaughter holding up the train. The youngest had been crowned the year before in an empty church in a mask. They came from Hilmar and Gustine and Turlock and Tulare and one from Boise, and they stood in the hall parking lot on Saturday morning in their capes, red and blue and white and gold, embroidered with doves and wheat and roses and crowns, while the dairy crew led the heifers down off the trailers. On Friday night one of the heifers had gone lame. There were sixty-one. Frank found São behind the trailers. One queen doesn't have a heifer, he said. What do I do? What do you mean? There are cattle all over that dairy. Gentle ones. Halter-broke. The rest are milk cows that never saw a crowd, and they'll go crazy. There's nothing left on the trailers but the bull. Everybody on the home dairy knew the bull. He was a Holstein two years old, black and white, a ton already, bred from the best line in the herd and kept for that. In March he had put a milker named Rigoberto through a pipe gate and into the hospital in Merced with four broken ribs. The mil

sections.heading: IV. Four Lines
sections.text: After the Mass and the crowning and the parade, the people came in under the shade cloth. Frank's crew had worked two nights stringing it. It covered the whole lot from the hall to the arena fence, white, a little translucent, and the noon light came down through the weave of it soft and even, so that it was like sitting inside a cloud. Under it were tables for fifteen hundred and the copper kettles on their stands, polished so that they threw the light back, and the smell of the sopas, which is beef and cabbage and bread and allspice and cinnamon cooked down all night, and over everything the smell of the mint. São had stripped the mint beds of half the town. A sprig of it lay on every plate. The first tables went to the milkers and their wives and children, from every dairy on the west side, and the almond pickers, and the men from the shelter, and the old people from the senior apartments who came on the church van. They sat down and looked around them, not sure. Then the queens came down the rows in their capes, the queen of 1952 on her granddaughter's arm, the queen of 1975, the queen of the empty church, sixty-two of them, carrying pitchers of broth. They bent and poured it o

sections.heading: V. The Rectory
sections.text: In the morning, in the hall kitchen, the ladies scrubbing the kettles asked Nelson Rocha, who had come to help carry, whether he had not been afraid on Saturday, walking a mile with that animal on a rope. No, Nelson said. I wasn't afraid. One of the Machado men, who was stacking chairs, said loud enough for the kitchen to hear that a man who had done twenty-five years would say anything. Nobody answered him. Nelson went on carrying. Later, when somebody told Father Ikenna about it, the priest said: He told you the truth. That man has nothing left in him to be afraid with. Frank had not slept. He had lain awake all night thinking: I gave the best gift anybody in this valley ever gave, and the priest said four lines over it, the same four lines a child says over a peanut-butter sandwich, and walked out. Father Goulart would have talked an hour. It must be that I did it wrong. It must be that I gave the wrong things, or gave them the wrong way, or that the priest is angry with me about something, because a priest always blesses a gift in proportion to the gift. Everybody knows that. At eight he drove to the rectory. Father Ikenna was in the kitchen in his shirtsleeves making tea, and

sections.heading: VI. The Octave
sections.text: Lucindo Mendonça fed Valeta for seven days. He kept the shade cloth up. He kept the kettles going. He called the ladies of the auxiliary and they came, and the milkers' wives came to help them without being asked, and on Tuesday some of the queens came back in their capes, and on Wednesday more. Every day at noon he opened the gates and fed whoever walked in, the same as on Pentecost, the poor first, and he sat at the end of the first table himself and ate with them, which in forty-three years as secretary he had never once done. People who had known him all their lives said he was changed. They could not say how. His sister-in-law said that he laughed now, at nothing, at the children, at the mint, and that he had never laughed before in his life that she could remember. Nelson Rocha carried kettles all week, and at five every morning and five every evening he went back to the calf barn and fed the calves. On Thursday the Machado man who had called him a liar came into the hall kitchen and stood next to him at the sink and dried what Nelson washed. Neither of them said anything. On Friday the dead boy's mother sat at the first table. Nelson poured her broth. Her hand shook on the s

title: The Sopas
logline: In a record milk year, the richest Azorean dairyman in Valeta keeps losing the Holy Ghost festa's giving contest to everyone else.

verses.text: Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all worlds, is the reward of the first step in holiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Kāla, the son of the great donor Anāthapiṇḍika, cares nothing for the Buddha and will not even come out to see him when he visits the house. His father, afraid for him, decides that anyone can be won with gifts, and promises him a hundred coins to keep the observance day at the monastery. Kāla goes, sleeps the night away, and the next morning refuses to eat until he is paid. Then his father offers him a thousand coins to learn a single verse from the Buddha. Each time Kāla thinks he has the verse, the Buddha lets him misunderstand it, so he stays to learn the next, and listening that way, with his whole attention, he enters the stream. The next day he walks home among the monks and is ashamed when his father sets the thousand coins in front of him in the Buddha's presence, and refuses them; the Buddha explains with this verse. Read the full commentary story, or about Anāthapiṇḍika. The hymn is Isaac Watts's “Crucifixion to the World by the Cross of Christ” (1707), whose fourth stanza Watts printed in brackets as one that could be left out.
bg.history:
Relay For Life began in May 1985 in Tacoma, Washington, when a surgeon, Gordon Klatt, walked and ran around a track for twenty-four hours to raise money for the American Cancer Society. The overnight events that grew from it have teams camping around a track, a survivors' lap, and a luminaria ceremony at sunset, with candles in decorated paper bags set around the track to honor survivors and the dead. Papillion lies just west of Offutt Air Force Base, a third of which was flooded when the Missouri River rose in March 2019.

By 2019 sneaker reselling had become a market of its own. StockX, launched in 2016 with stock-market-style price histories for each shoe, was valued at a billion dollars that June. The Travis Scott Air Jordan 1, released on May 11, 2019 at $175, sold out in hours, and resellers were soon asking more than $1,000.

sections.heading: I. The Plate Lunch
sections.text: Kawika Chun ran a plate-lunch place in a strip mall on the south side of Papillion, between a nail salon and a State Farm office, and he fed more people for nothing than anybody in Sarpy County. He had come out of the Army in 2010 with a wife from Papillion and a six-year-old son and no plan, and the plan he made was rice, macaroni salad and two scoops of whatever, the way his grandmother had made it in Hilo. He called the place Kwai's, after her father, who had kept a store on Mamo Street before the war. The airmen from Offutt found it the first month, the ones from Hawaii and Guam and Samoa and then everybody else, and after the airmen the high-school wrestlers, and after them the Methodists. On Sundays after two he fed anybody in a uniform for nothing, and anybody who looked like they needed it, and sent them home with a foil pan of whatever was left. When the Missouri came over the levees in March of 2019 and put a third of the air base under water, he cooked for nine days straight and drove the pans out to the shelters himself, and lost money every one of those days, and did not seem to notice. People asked him where he got it. He said he learned it at Fort Lewis, from a Samoa

sections.heading: II. The Track
sections.dateline: The high-school track · Saturday, June 8, all night
sections.text: Every June the American Cancer Society's Relay For Life took over the track at the high school from six on Saturday evening until six on Sunday morning. Teams pitched tents on the infield and took turns walking laps all night. It ran twenty-four hours because the people it was for did not get to stop either. Kawika ran the food tent for nothing and had for eight years: teriyaki at dinner, Spam musubi at midnight, pancakes at five. The team Kawika fed best was called Carol's Crew. It was eleven people, mostly over sixty, in purple T-shirts with a photograph of a smiling woman on the back, and it was led, if anybody led it, by a retired shop teacher named Dale Petersen. Dale was seventy-four. He had taught industrial arts at the high school for thirty-eight years. Half the men in Papillion who could cut a dado had learned it from him. He was tall and stooped, with big scarred hands and a short grey haircut. He wore the same khaki pants and the same purple shirt every Relay. He mowed his lawn on Saturdays at seven in the morning, which some of his neighbors had complained about for forty years. His wife Carol had died of ovarian cancer in the summer of 2009. Since then Dale had walked

sections.heading: III. The Garage
sections.dateline: A cul-de-sac off Lincoln Street · Sunday
sections.text: That afternoon, after Kale had slept again, his father found him on the couch. Last night at the luminaria, Kawika said, Mr. Petersen sang something. By himself, by his wife's bag. A hymn. I heard it from the tent. He took an envelope out of his shirt pocket and set it on the coffee table. That's a thousand dollars. You go to his house and learn one verse of that hymn by heart. And what it means. You say it to him and he says you've got it, it's yours. Kale looked at the envelope. A thousand dollars was the Travis Scotts. One verse. One verse. Dale's house was a split-level at the end of a cul-de-sac with the straightest lawn in Sarpy County. The garage door was up. Dale was inside at the workbench, in the same purple shirt, sanding a long board of white oak with a block and a sheet of paper, while a box fan pushed the dust out the door. Along the wall were the bones of a bench: legs, rails, a back slat with letters cut into it that Kale could not read from the driveway. Kale told him what his father wanted. Dale listened, and nodded, and went on sanding. Then he said it, plain, without singing, the way you would read off a measurement. When I survey the wondrous cross, on which th

sections.heading: IV. The Envelope
sections.text: Every year on the Monday after the Relay, Kawika opened early for Carol's Crew and fed them breakfast for nothing. Kale rode over with Dale in his truck, with the finished bench in the bed under a moving blanket, and walked into his father's place in the middle of eleven old people in purple shirts. Kawika looked up from the grill and saw his son come in among them, and something in his face went still. Kale, for his part, was praying the only prayer he had. He was praying his father would not bring up the money. Not here. Not in front of Mr. Petersen, who would know then that it had been for a thousand dollars, and the afternoon in the garage with it. But Dale knew already. Dale had known from the driveway. Kawika fed the team first. Loco moco, two eggs over the hamburger patty and the brown gravy over all of it, and fried rice, and coffee. Then he made a plate for his son and set it down in front of him at the end of the long table, and Kale ate it without a word, all of it, every grain. Lin came out of the back in her apron and sat down beside him and patted his arm, not knowing why. When the plates were cleared, Kawika came over and laid the envelope on the table in front of Ka

title: The Luminaria
logline: A plate-lunch cook who feeds half of Sarpy County pays his sneaker-reselling son to stay all night at the Relay For Life.

verses.text: He whose conquest is not conquered again, into whose conquest no one in this world enters, by what track can you lead him, the Awakened, the Omniscient, the trackless?
He whom no desire with its snares and poisons can lead astray, by what track can you lead him, the Awakened, the Omniscient, the trackless?

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin named Māgandiya refuses every suitor for his beautiful daughter as not good enough. One morning, at the place where he tends his sacred fire, he meets the Buddha and offers her to him, and runs home to fetch her. When the family returns with a crowd behind them, the Buddha has moved on, leaving a single footprint. The Brahmin's wife, who knows the lore of bodily signs, reads it as the foot of a man free of desire; her husband tells her she sees a crocodile in a drop of water. When they find him, the Buddha tells the story of his Great Renunciation: how Māra met him at the city gate and promised him a world empire in seven days, followed him for seven years, and at last sat defeated by the road, until his three daughters, Taṇhā, Aratī and Ragā (Craving, Discontent and Lust), came to tempt the Buddha in the forms of women of every age. He sends them away with these two verses. Then he tells the Brahmin that he would not touch his daughter's body even with his foot, a remark the daughter never forgives.
bg.hist_title: North Texas and the Edwards Plateau, 1998–2004
bg.history:
Frisco, north of Dallas, was the fastest-growing city in the United States from 2000 to 2009, as subdivisions spread north from Plano onto blackland prairie. It grew as a bedroom community for professionals who worked across the Dallas–Fort Worth area. Telugu Americans, from Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, came first as students, doctors and scientists, and then, from the late 1980s, in a large wave of software engineers that grew around the turn of the century. The dot-com bubble that made and unmade fortunes in those years peaked in March 2000; by October 2002 the Nasdaq had lost 78 percent of its value, and many telecommunications companies went under with it. Sarma's morning fire is the agnihotra, the Vedic offering of ghee into the fire at sunrise and sunset, which the heads of Brahmin households were once obliged to make every day. Vasundhara's grandmother practices Sāmudrika Śāstra, the old Indian lore of reading character and fate from the marks of the body.

The Katha Upanishad tells of the boy Nachiketas, who goes to the house of Death and asks what happens after dying. Death tries to buy him off with herds, gold, long life, a kingdom and beautiful women, and the boy refuses all of it. The verses here are from F. Max Müller's translation in volume 15 of the Sacred Books of the East (1884); Müller numbered the Upanishad's six sections straight through, so his “6, 14” is often cited elsewhere as 2.3.14. Kiran's ranch is on the Edwards Plateau near Rocksprings, the seat of Edwards County, named for the springs in its limestone, which calls itself the Angora goat capital of the world.

sections.heading: I. The Fire
sections.text: Gopalakrishna Sarma lit his fire every morning a few minutes before sunrise, and for six years he lit it on the back patio, until the homeowners' association sent the third letter. The first letter said open burning. The second said a neighbor has expressed concern regarding odor. The third had a fine in it, a hundred and fifty dollars, and a photograph of his own backyard taken from somebody's upstairs window. So he carried the fire to the end of the street. Past the last cul-de-sac the builder had graded the land for Phase Four, poured the streets and the sidewalks and set the fire hydrants, and then stopped to wait for the market. There were no houses yet. There were curbs that went around nothing, and street signs with names on them, Calder Court and Bandera Way, standing over black clay and Johnson grass. Every morning in the blue dark Sarma walked out there in his white dhoti and a Texas Instruments windbreaker, with a copper pot shaped like an upside-down pyramid in one hand and a tote bag from Patel Brothers in the other, and set the pot down on the bare ground where the corner lot of Calder Court would one day be. He laid the dried cakes of cow dung in it, the ones the Ind

sections.heading: II. The Footprint
sections.text: Vasundhara was at the stove boiling milk for coffee when her husband came in through the garage still in his dhoti, which he had never done, and said he had found him. Found who? The one. For Madhuri. He's standing at the end of the street. Wake her up. Madhuri had worked until midnight and came down the stairs in a T-shirt from the University of Texas with her hair over her face, and her father told her to put on the Dharmavaram silk, the mango-yellow one with the green border that she had worn for her cousin's wedding, and the gold, and to hurry. She laughed at him. Then she saw that he was serious and stopped laughing, and because she was twenty-five and curious and a little afraid of him, she went and put it on. Her mother put on a cotton sari and a cardigan over it. Sarma did not change at all. It was a quarter past seven. On that street at a quarter past seven the aunties were out in their sneakers doing their morning walk in pairs, and Reddy uncle from the corner house was in his driveway in a bathrobe picking up the Dallas Morning News, and the children were at the corner with their backpacks waiting for the bus, and every one of them saw the Sarmas go by. They saw Madhuri

sections.heading: III. The Gate
sections.text: His name was Kiran Vemuri. He had been born in Houston in 1964 to a doctor from Guntur and a mother who taught him the Telugu alphabet at the kitchen table on Saturday mornings, and his grandfather, visiting for a winter when Kiran was nine, had made him learn the story of the boy Nachiketas, who went to the house of Death and would not go home without an answer. Kiran had studied electrical engineering at UT Austin. In 1993, with a friend from school named Danny Ochoa, he had started a company in a strip of offices off Campbell Road in Richardson that made switches for fiber-optic lines, the glass threads the whole world's telephone calls were starting to go through. They called it Ninefold. By 1998 it had two hundred and forty employees and offices in three countries, and in the second week of March the bankers in New York set the date for the public offering. Seven days. He worked it out on a legal pad one night, alone on the fourth floor. On the day the shares went on sale, on paper, he would be worth more than every person he had grown up with in Houston put together. He had seen some things that winter. In January he had flown to Houston and sat with his father, who did not k

sections.heading: IV. Seven Years
sections.text: The man in the grey suit kept his word. He followed Kiran for seven years. He was at the counter of a truck stop outside Brownwood in the first summer, eating pie, and he slid a business card down the counter: a firm in Austin that wanted Kiran to run its engineering for any salary he named. He was in the parking lot of a motel in San Angelo the next winter, leaning on a white Lincoln, with a cousin from Guntur Kiran had not seen since childhood who wanted to talk about a girl. He was at a feed store in Sonora. He was on the radio. Once, outside Ozona, in the August heat, he was nothing but a cold bottle of Coca-Cola standing by itself on a fence post with the sweat running down it. Every time, he was waiting for Kiran to want something. Every time, Kiran walked on. In those years Kiran was very hard on himself. Nobody made him. He thought that was the road. He slept in a borrowed deer blind in Sutton County through one whole winter. He picked pecans, and cleared cedar for ranchers for the price of a meal, and then stopped taking the meal, and then ate one handful of rice a day, and then a handful every other day. He sat in the sun on the limestone until the skin of his face cracke

sections.heading: V. Three Sisters
sections.text: He had three daughters. Kiran told Sarma their names and what the names meant. One was called Thirst. One was called Restless. One was called Heat. They came along the highway in a white car with the windows down, and when they saw their father sitting on the guardrail they pulled onto the shoulder in a spray of gravel and got out. Daddy, what's the matter with you? Why do you look like that? He told them. Seven years, and the man under the tree, and not one thing. Oh, Daddy, they said. Don't you worry about it. We'll go get him and bring him to you. You can't. Nobody can bring that one anywhere. Daddy. We're women, they said. Leave him to us. They came down through the goats to the live oak and stood in front of him in their summer dresses. Let us take care of you, they said. We'll be yours. We'll cook for you, we'll keep house for you, we'll do whatever you say. You'll never have to want for anything. Kiran did not answer them. He did not open his eyes. They went off a little way and talked it over. Men like different things, said Thirst. Some like a young girl. Some like a woman. Some like them older. Let's give him all of it and see. So they came back. Graciela Tijerina saw the

sections.heading: VI. The Sole of the Foot
sections.dateline: The retention pond · the same morning
sections.text: Kiran was quiet for a moment. The fountain in the pond was not running. Somebody's sprinklers had come on behind them, ticking. Sarma garu, he said. When those three came to me, they looked like gold. They looked like nothing you ever saw. And I didn't want them, not for one second. He looked at Madhuri. He did not look at her unkindly. He looked at her the way the foreman had looked at the footprint. Your daughter is beautiful. Everybody here can see that. But a body is a bag. It's skin over what's in a body. Blood and bile and phlegm and what the bowels carry, all of it. If my foot were dirty and she were lying across my doorway, I would not touch her with the sole of it. Every Telugu person at that pond drew in a breath at the same time. You do not touch a person with your foot. A child learns it before it can walk. If your foot so much as brushes someone by accident on a crowded bus, you touch their arm and then your own eyes, to take it back. Two of the aunties put their hands over their mouths. One of the grandmothers visiting from India began, very quietly, to pray. Vasundhara looked at her daughter. Madhuri had gone perfectly still. Her face did not change, and that was how

sections.heading: VII. Phase Four
sections.text: Madhuri asked her mother's brother in Edison, New Jersey, to find her a husband, and he did it in five months. She married a man in Saratoga, California, who had sold a software company to a bigger one for more money than any boy her father had ever turned down, and the wedding was at a hotel in San Jose with eleven hundred guests and two priests flown in from Tirupati. Her father gave her away and wept. She never came home to Frisco again without asking her mother on the phone, first, in a voice that was very light, whether that man had been seen. She kept what he had said the way some people keep a coin from a country they will never go back to, in a drawer, and take it out and turn it over. Sarma retired the next spring. He lit his fire every morning until the end, at the end of the street, but those who walked past said he did it differently. He did it the way you rinse a cup. In 2006 the market came back and the builder came back with it, and the first slab went down for a house on the corner lot of Calder Court, right where he had kept his fire, and that week he sold the big house on the cul-de-sac. He and Vasundhara gave away most of what was in it. He fed the drawer full of

title: One Footprint
logline: A Telugu engineer who has refused every suitor for his daughter offers her to a thin stranger watching his sunrise fire.

verses.text: Even the gods envy those who are awakened and not forgetful, who are given to meditation, who are wise, and who delight in the repose of retirement (from the world).

bg.commentary: The commentary’s longest story begins at Rājagaha, where a rich man hangs a red sandalwood bowl high on bamboo poles for any arahant who can fly up and take it. The rival teachers fake an attempt; the Buddha’s disciple Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja lifts a great rock over the city and takes the bowl, and the Buddha has the bowl broken up and forbids his disciples such displays. When the rivals challenge him, he says the rule binds his disciples, not himself, and promises a miracle in four months at Sāvatthī. A gardener gives him the mango meant for the king; the seed becomes a great tree overnight; wind, sun, dust and rain rout the rivals, and one drowns himself. The Buddha declines his disciples’ offers to work wonders in his place, tells two birth stories about a bull, and performs the Twin Miracle of fire and water. Then he goes up to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three to teach his mother for three months while the crowd camps and waits, and comes down on three ladders at the gate of Saṅkassa, where Sāriputta praises him and answers a question no one else can.
bg.history:
By the 1920s Harlem was the capital of Black America, filled by the Great Migration from the South and by immigrants from the Caribbean, who by 1920 made up roughly a quarter of New York’s Black population and built their own Episcopal and Methodist congregations and mutual-aid societies. Hundreds of storefront churches operated out of empty shops and basements, and in the years before the Second World War Harlem also produced a run of flamboyant charismatic leaders, of whom Father Divine became the most famous. More on Harlem.

The numbers, or policy, made fortunes in Harlem in the 1920s. Bettors picked three digits, the winning number was taken from the published Clearing House totals, and a payoff of 600 to 1 was typical. Among the biggest bankers was Casper Holstein, born on St. Croix, who also funded Harlem Renaissance literary prizes. The rock of Mount Morris Park (now Marcus Garvey Park), a hill of Manhattan schist, still carries its cast-iron fire watchtower and bell. The Woolworth Building downtown was the tallest building in the world from 1913 to 1930.

sections.heading: I. The Bowl
sections.text: Cyril Pemberton ran the biggest policy bank north of 125th Street, and every morning from May until the first frost he swam in the Harlem River, the way he had swum off the bay in Basseterre as a boy. His driver brought him down to the water at six with a wicker hamper, and he put his watch and his diamond stickpin and his good suit in the hamper so they would not walk off while he was in the water, and the driver sat on the hamper and smoked. One morning in April a block of wood came down the river on the tide and fetched up against the hamper and stayed there. It was about the size of a coal scuttle, worn round by the water, slick with weed. Pemberton came out dripping and turned it over with his foot and had the driver scrape it with his penknife, and under the weed it was red. Mahogany, Honduras mahogany, red as a cut plum, off some lighter or some barge that had broken up in the Bronx Kills. Pemberton was not a churchman and not a heathen. He had money in four churches and a gold tooth he said was for luck, and he did not believe in luck. He stood there on the rocks in his drawers and thought. Every corner in Harlem had a holy man on it. There were bishops in storefronts and p

sections.heading: II. The Peach Tree
sections.text: Josiah Thorne had been a ship's carpenter out of Bridgetown, Barbados, forty years, on schooners and then on the big steamers of the Royal Mail, until his eyes went too far for fine work. He was past seventy. He had a room on 133rd Street and worshipped at the West Indian Episcopal church on Sundays at the back, and the rest of the week he sat on his stoop, or walked, and men came and sat on the steps below him, and some of them came back. He did not preach. He did not take collections or print cards. He talked when he was asked, briefly, and spent a good deal of time sitting very still, which the children on 133rd Street tried to imitate and could not. When the holy men heard that he had made his people split the bowl, they were glad. Now we have him, they said. His men won't break his rule, and he won't break it either. And they went up and down Lenox Avenue with a bass drum telling everybody that they had kept their powers hidden out of modesty, and that Thorne's people had made a show of themselves for a dish, and that from now on they would work wonders against nobody but Thorne himself. The district leader heard it. His name was Royall, and he gave out the turkeys at Thanksgi

sections.heading: III. The Mango
sections.dateline: St. Nicholas Avenue · the full moon of July
sections.text: That morning a Grenadian named Gant, who had a pushcart of fruit on Lenox Avenue, found one perfect mango in a crate off the banana boat from Kingston. It was a Julie mango, the kind that goes from green to gold to red at the shoulder, and it was ripe, and the smell came off it so that the flies followed his cart. He wrapped it in tissue paper and set out with it to Royall's house. Royall would give him a dollar for it, maybe two. On the way he met Mr. Thorne walking with Ernest. He stood there with the mango in his hands. A dollar or two, he thought. That will not keep me alive past Tuesday. And he held it out. Mr. Thorne looked at Ernest. Ernest took the tissue paper off and put the mango in Mr. Thorne's hands, and Mr. Thorne sat down on the stone curb of the vacant lot at the top of St. Nicholas Avenue, across from the holy men's tent. Ernest borrowed a glass from a soda fountain and squeezed the mango into it with water and a sliver of ice from the iceman's cart, and Mr. Thorne drank it. Dig a hole here, Mr. Gant, he said, and plant the seed. Gant scratched a hole in the cinders of the lot with a piece of slate and put the seed in it. Mr. Thorne poured the last of the water ove

sections.heading: IV. Not for You
sections.dateline: The top of the hill · that evening
sections.text: At dusk a path appeared in the air. It ran from the East River to the Hudson, high over 145th Street, and it shone the way the inside of an oyster shell shines, so that the people coming up the hill stopped and stood with their mouths open. By full dark there were people on every street from the river to the river, on the roofs and the fire escapes and the elevated platforms and the cliffs of St. Nicholas Park, more people than Harlem had ever held, and Mr. Thorne came out from the house where he had been resting and stood on the stoop. Mother Gertrude came to him first. She was a laundress, a widow, sixty, and some people said she had been seen walking on the surface of the reservoir in Central Park at four in the morning. Mr. Thorne, while you have a daughter like me, you don't need to trouble yourself. Let me. I will turn the whole island to water and go down in it like a cormorant and come up at Coney Island, and at Yonkers, and at Jersey City, and right here in the middle. People will say, who is that, and they'll say, that's only Gertrude the washerwoman, and what must he be. I know you can, Gertrude, he said. This basket wasn't packed for you. She stepped aside. Then they ca

sections.heading: V. Three Months
sections.dateline: Mount Morris Park · summer and autumn, 1927
sections.text: Then he was gone, the way the moon goes behind a building. They looked for him all night. He's gone to Brooklyn. He's gone home to Barbados. He was ashamed to do such a thing before so many people, and he's gone where nobody knows him. Women sat on the curbs and cried. In the morning they went to Clement, who knew, and Clement said, Ask Mr. Andrews. Mr. Andrews had been blind since a boiler burst in the engine room of a Royal Mail steamer in 1899, and he saw more than anybody. He's gone up to his mother, he said. She died having him, in Bridgetown, in the hurricane year. He never got to tell her anything. He's telling her now. Three months. He'll come down when the summer's over and the rains are done. Then we'll wait, said the crowd. And they did. They camped in Mount Morris Park, on the grass and the rock, under the fire tower, with the sky for a roof, thousands of them, all summer and into the fall. The newspapers came to look and went away again. And this was a wonder too, that there were so many and the park was never dirty. The ground took whatever they dropped. Before he went, Mr. Thorne had told Clement to answer them, and told young Inniss to feed them. So every morning In

sections.heading: VI. Three Ladders
sections.text: Seven days before the end, the crowd went to Clement. We will not go home till we see him. Tell us when. Clement went down into the ground right there in Mount Morris Park, between two rocks, and came up eight miles south at the foot of the Woolworth Building, which was then the tallest building in the world, and climbed it. He climbed the outside. All Harlem was on its roofs to watch, and they could see him from there, the way you can see a yellow thread pulled through a bead, going up the white face of it. He's past the twentieth floor. He's past the fortieth. At the top he went into the sky, and found Mr. Thorne, and asked him. Where's Gus? said Mr. Thorne. At his door on Edgecombe Avenue. Seven days, then. At Gus's door. Tell them to fast, and come as if they were coming to church in their own parish, and not to bring anything. On the seventh day, in the evening, three ladders came down out of the sky onto the sidewalk in front of Gus Lashley's building on Edgecombe Avenue, where the hill falls off toward the Harlem flats and you can see the whole valley. On the right was a ladder of gold, and the dead came down it, the ones Mr. Andrews had seen, in their best clothes. On the l

title: Three Ladders
logline: A policy banker hangs a mahogany bowl ninety feet over Lenox Avenue and dares Harlem's holy men to fly up and take it.

verses.text: Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals, difficult is the hearing of the True Law, difficult is the birth of the Awakened (the attainment of Buddhahood).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young monk in the time of an earlier Buddha, riding in a boat down the Ganges, catches hold of a leaf of an eraka plant and does not let go, and it tears off. Damaging a plant is a small breach of the monks’ rule, cleared by admitting it to another monk. He thinks it a trifle and never does. After twenty thousand years of faultless practice he lies dying, feels the leaf at his throat, finds no monk to confess to, and is reborn as Erakapatta (“Eraka-leaf”), a serpent king the size of a dugout. To learn whether a Buddha has arisen, he sets his daughter in his raised hood on the river every fortnight to sing a riddle, with herself and his wealth as the prize. For a whole age no one answers. The Buddha, seated under seven trees, teaches a young man named Uttara the answer (the king is the one who rules the six doors of the senses). When the serpent hears it he lashes the river in joy, floods both banks, lifts the swamped men out in his hood, and goes weeping to the Buddha, who gives him the verse. Eighty-four thousand listeners understand; the serpent, being an animal, cannot. Read the full commentary story, or about nāgas. The riddle and its answers in the story are rendered from the commentary’s own verses. The sutra the monk recites is the Lotus Sutra, in Hendrik Kern’s translation of 1884; the same sutra tells of a serpent king’s young daughter who hands the Buddha a jewel and is awakened on the spot.
bg.history:
Refugees from Vietnam began settling on the Mississippi coast in the late 1970s, many of them fishing families who had escaped by sea as boat people. They started in Biloxi’s oyster and shrimp houses, bought and built boats, and through the 1980s became a growing share of the fleet working out of the Back Bay and Point Cadet, alongside the older Croatian (“Slavonian”) and French fishing families whose Blessing of the Fleet, with its Shrimp King and Queen, dates from 1929. Many of the newcomers were Catholic; the Buddhists among them had no temple until a pagoda opened in a house on East Howard Avenue in December 1988. See Vietnamese in Mississippi. Cô Năm, her log, the monk and the boats are invented. The full moon of the fourth lunar month, kept as the Buddha’s birthday, fell on May 12 in 1987.

A Gulf shrimp trawler of the time towed a net from each outrigger, each net held open by a pair of wooden doors, and sampled the bottom with a small try net that had two doors of its own: six in the water. A “hang” is a snag that catches a net. In 1987 federal rules were on the way requiring a turtle excluder device in shrimp nets, an escape opening for sea turtles that Gulf shrimpers fought for years. The palm is the nipa, Nypa fruticans, in Vietnamese dừa nước, “water coconut.” The commentary’s seven trees are sirīsa, an Albizia; the mimosa of Southern yards is its cousin Albizia julibrissin, whose leaves fold shut at night.

sections.heading: I. Book Five
sections.dateline: Oak Street, Biloxi, Mississippi · Tuesday, May 12, 1987 · the fifteenth of the fourth month
sections.text: I keep the radio for the boats. It sits on the kitchen counter by the window, the VHF and next to it the sideband for the big water, and beside them a school composition book and a cup of pencils. When a boat calls I write the hour, the name of the boat, and what was said. I have done it every night since 1982, when one of ours did not come home and afterward nobody on the Point could agree what day she had last called. I said then that it would be written down. So it is written down, and this is the fifth book. Where I only heard a thing I write heard. Where I was looking at it I write saw. Most nights there is nothing to see. They call me Cô Năm. We are Catholic, from Phước Tỉnh. We went out in ’78 with nineteen in the boat and landed seventeen. My husband has the Thanh Tâm, and tonight he is off Ship Shoal on the Louisiana side, because the Sound does not open until June and the note on the boat does not wait for June. Tonight is the full moon of the fourth month, which the Buddhists keep for the birthday of their Buddha. I put that down so that anybody who reads this book will know I did not make the day fit. Everybody on the Back Bay knows what happens at the fuel dock on the

sections.heading: II. Seven Mimosas
sections.dateline: Next door · a little after four · saw
sections.text: I was taking in the wash when Út came up the street in a clean shirt. He decks on the Sao Mai. He is twenty-two and his mother’s last, and he has been making up his answer since Tết. Half the Point has heard pieces of it. The thầy did not get up. Út. Dạ, thầy. Come here. He came in at the gate and bowed and sat down on his heels on the pink. Where are you going? To the fuel dock, thầy. Where ông Bảy’s daughter sings. Do you have an answer for her? I have one. Say it. Út sang it. He has a voice. It was all a captain with his six doors on the bottom and his nets full and no bank over him. I thought it as good as any I have written down. That is no answer, the thầy said. You have the number right and the wrong doors. I will give you one. Will you carry it down there? I will, thầy. How many doors does ông Bảy put in the water? Six. Two to a net, and the two little ones on the try net. Those are his. Count your own. And he touched his eye, and his ear, and the side of his nose. He put out the tip of his tongue like a boy. He laid one hand flat on the back of the other, and last he set a finger to his forehead. Things come in at these all day and all night. The man who is master of all s

sections.heading: III. Channel Sixty-Eight
sections.dateline: The base radio · a little before six to twenty past seven · heard
sections.text: The fuel dock is four blocks from this kitchen, and I have never once gone down to it on a singing night. I have no need. The Sao Mai ties up nearest, and her captain hangs his mike out the wheelhouse window, and somebody always puts it over on the sideband for the boats outside. 5:55THANH TÂM, sideband. Ship Shoal. Forty boxes. Weather fair. He asks is the old man standing his girl up tonight. I say it is the fifteenth, what does he think. He says leave the sideband on. 6:20SAO MAI. Ông Bảy is coming round. People on the bulkhead from the ice house to the net shop, sitting with their legs over. Cars from Louisiana. 6:31STELLA MARIS, old Captain Tony, in English. Mr. Bay has got his hook down right in the channel again. Somebody tell him I draw six feet. 6:33SAO MAI. She is on the roof. 6:35The mike goes out the window. I hear water on the pilings, and then I hear her. Hò ơ. 6:38A boy from Bayou La Batre, off the HẢI ÂU. The captain with a steel hull is king, he sings, and the worms are master of the wooden one. SAO MAI: She says no. 6:44A boy from Versailles, in New Orleans East. The king is the man who owes no bank. Laughing all down the bulkhead. She says no. 6:51Two brothers fr

sections.heading: IV. One Leaf
sections.dateline: Next door · ten to eight · saw, and heard twice
sections.text: They came up Oak Street in the last of the light, with the moon rising behind them over the Point. I would say two hundred. Út was in front, and ông Bảy behind him in his white boots, and the girl. After them came the ones he had fished out, still dripping, and then the rest, ours and theirs, Buddhist and Catholic, and some of the old families’ men who had only followed the crowd. They filled the street as far as my gate. A deckhand off the Kim Hoa had a hand radio on his belt. When the old man went in at the thầy’s gate, that boy held the key down and kept it down. So everything that follows I heard two times, once through the window screen and once out of the radio on my counter. I wrote from whichever was clearer. Ông Bảy went in under the flag and under the trees. The thầy was sitting where he had sat since morning. The old man got down on the pink threads in his boots and put his forehead to the ground three times. Then he stood off to one side with his hands hanging, and he cried. He is sixty-two. I have known him eight years and I had not known he could. What is this, bác? the thầy said. He called himself con, child, as a person does before the robe, though this monk was you

sections.heading: V. The Door in the Net
sections.text: For a while there was only the key held down, and the street breathing. Bác, the thầy said. You are saying it to a monk now. Do you see it? Con sees it. Then be careful after this. That was all he did about the leaf. I am Catholic and I waited for more, and there was no more. Then he spoke to the old man, but loud enough for the street. It is hard to come by a human life. You came to this one in a river boat, bác. You know how hard. It is hard to keep one. It is hard to hear the Dharma even once. And harder than all of these is for a Buddha to come into the world. That takes work and trouble past any counting. They say the government is going to make every one of you cut a door in his nets this year, to let the turtle out. You know how big the Gulf is. You know how big that door will be. The sutra says it is like that. One turtle, one hole, and the whole sea. That is how often a person is born where the Dharma can be heard. And every one of you standing in this street has put his neck through. Then he said it as it stands in their book, where two sons say it to their father and mother. He was a young man saying it to an old one, and he did not change the words. It is most difficult

sections.heading: VI. After Dark
sections.text: The girl had a jade bangle on her wrist. It was her dead mother’s, and it came through two sets of pirates sewn in a hem. She worked it off over her hand and set it down in front of the thầy, and he took it up at once, in both hands. I do not know what that means with them. My daughter says Ngọc understood him before the old man had finished crying. Út did not ask for the girl or the boat. He said he had only carried it. She said that was the first right thing any of them had said in four years. They were married in the eleventh month. That is not in this book, but I was there. Ông Bảy would have asked for the robe again that same evening. But he is sixty-two, and three families eat off his nets, and a bank in Gulfport holds the paper on the Lá Dừa. The thầy did not tell him yes and did not tell him no. He said the trees would be there on the first and the fifteenth. The old man says now that there are five times when he can be nothing but a shrimper: the morning the season opens; when the nets come up; when he is asleep in the bunk behind the wheel; when he sits with the other captains at the fuel dock; and when he dies, which he expects to do with ice in his cuffs. title: Water Coconut
logline: A Catholic woman who logs the shrimp fleet's radio writes down the night a captain's daughter sang her riddle and a deckhand answered.

verses.text: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.
The Awakened call patience the highest penance, long-suffering the highest Nirvana; for he is not an anchorite (pravragita) who strikes others, he is not an ascetic (sramana) who insults others.
Not to blame, not to strike, to live restrained under the law, to be moderate in eating, to sleep and sit alone, and to dwell on the highest thoughts,--this is the teaching of the Awakened.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the elder Ānanda, sitting alone, reflects that the Buddha has described the six Buddhas before him in every particular (their parents, their length of life, the tree each awakened under, their following, their two chief disciples, their chief supporter) but has never said how they kept the Observance Day, the regular gathering at which the community’s rule is recited. He asks whether it was the same as now. The Buddha answers that the interval differed, once in seven years for Vipassī, six for the next two, yearly for the two after, every six months for Kassapa, and that one day’s admonition lasted the whole interval; but the words were the same for all of them, and he recites the three verses.
bg.history:
The General Rules were written by John Wesley in 1743 for the first Methodist societies, under three heads: doing no harm, doing good, and attending upon the ordinances of God. American Methodists printed them at the front of their book of Discipline, and when Richard Allen and his colleagues organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia in 1816, their first Doctrines and Discipline (1817) carried the Rules too, with a direction that the elder in charge read them “once a year in every congregation, and once a quarter in every society.” The wording quoted in the story is that of 1817. A.M.E. pastors are appointed by the bishop at each annual conference and moved from charge to charge, which is how a church of forty years comes to have had seven. The anniversary souvenir journal, with its history, its page of pastors and its paid advertisements, is a fixture of Black church life. Coppin Chapel and its people are invented.

Black Jack lies in the northern suburbs of St. Louis, among subdivisions built in the 1950s and 1960s, when the McDonnell aircraft plants nearby were hiring. Residents incorporated it as a city in 1970 and at once zoned out an interfaith group’s apartment project meant for families from the city; a federal appeals court struck the ordinance down in 1974. Black families moved into North County through the 1970s and after, many congregations followed their members out from the city, and by the 2000 census Black Jack was about seventy-one percent African American. Easton Avenue in St. Louis was renamed for Dr. Martin Luther King in 1972.

sections.heading: I. Our Shepherds
sections.dateline: Coppin Chapel A.M.E. Church, Black Jack, Missouri · September 2004
sections.text: Sister Nanette Givens had been clerk of Coppin Chapel for nineteen years, and the church said of her that if the roll book ever burned she could write it out again from the front pew back, with the birthdays. She had retired from Southwestern Bell in 1996 after thirty-one years of other people’s telephone numbers, and she still had most of them. Now the Fortieth Anniversary was five Sundays off, and the Souvenir Journal was hers. On a Thursday afternoon she sat in the church office with the proofs. Out the window was the parking lot, where under the yellow lines the trustees had painted you could still make out the white ones the Lutherans had left, slanting the other way. The Lutherans had built the place in 1961, when the subdivisions were going in for the McDonnell men, and sold it in 1979, when Coppin Chapel came out to the County behind its own members. Across Old Halls Ferry Road was a strip of stores: a beauty supply, a Chinese carry-out, and a place that did taxes in the spring and sat dark the rest of the year. The ads were in. There was the full page from the funeral home, as there was in every journal of every church north of the highway. There were half pages from the b

sections.heading: II. The Study
sections.text: Reverend Yolanda Meeks was fifty-one. She had dispatched buses for Bi-State for twenty-two years before she answered her call, and she still said a thing one time and expected it to get where it was going. The Bishop had read her name out to Coppin Chapel two conferences ago. On the shelf behind her desk, between the hymnal and the current Discipline, stood a thin brown book that had been Reverend Broadnax’s, a reprint of the first Discipline of 1817. He had penciled dates in its margin. Pastor, Sister Nan said, the six before you. Did they keep the Rules the way we keep them? Or did each one have a different way? Pastor Meeks did not reach for the book. The time was different with every one. Reverend Broadnax read the Rules to this church once in seven years. Three times in his whole pastorate. Mother Crump will tell you they lived on one reading until the next. Reverend Tate read them once in his six years, the Sunday we came into this building, and Dr. Lyles once in his six. Reverend Pettis and Reverend Coates read them every year, him at Watch Night and her on Founder’s Day. Reverend Sample read them every six months. She turned her pen end for end on the blotter. I read them e

sections.heading: III. Anniversary Sunday
sections.text: Pastor Meeks came down out of the pulpit to read them. She stood on the floor in front of the rail in her robe, with Reverend Broadnax’s brown book open on her hand, and she read them entire, and slowly. In the choir stand the children had been told to sit still and were doing what they could. Sister Nan had the clerk’s seat, second pew on the aisle, and she turned in it far enough to watch the right side of the church. Eleven were left who had been on Easton Avenue. They sat together, as they always had. Mother Ida Crump was ninety-three and had not known her own granddaughter since Easter. She sat in her white with both hands on the bar of her walker, looking at the floor. When the pastor came to the list under the first head, Mother Crump’s lips began to move, and by the third line she was half a beat in front. Fighting, quarrelling, brawling, brother going to law with brother; returning evil for evil; or railing for railing; Uncharitable or unprofitable conversation: particularly speaking evil of magistrates or of ministers. Softness, and needless self-indulgence. — The General Rules, under the first head At or of ministers somebody in the back said Well, and the church laughed

title: The Souvenir Journal
logline: A church clerk who forgets nothing finds one thing missing from her fortieth-anniversary page of seven pastors, and asks the seventh.

verses.text: There is no satisfying lusts, even by a shower of gold pieces; he who knows that lusts have a short taste and cause pain, he is wise;
Even in heavenly pleasures he finds no satisfaction, the disciple who is fully awakened delights only in the destruction of all desires.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young monk is sent away by his preceptor to learn the rules of discipline. While he is gone his father falls ill, longs to see him, and dies talking about him, leaving a hundred coins with the youngest son "to buy a bowl and robe for my son." When the monk comes home his little brother throws himself at his feet in tears. The monk refuses the money, then begins to think that it would be enough to live on as a layman, and stops reciting and meditating until he looks jaundiced. The novices notice; his teachers bring him to the Buddha, who has him fetch pebbles and count out fifty for food and drink and twenty-four each for two oxen, seed, a plow, a spade and an adze, and the hundred coins run out. Then the Buddha tells the birth story of King Mandhātā, a world-ruler who could make it rain jewels by clapping his hands, who rose to rule the heaven of the Four Great Kings and then shared the throne of Sakka in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three while thirty-six Sakkas came and went, until he resolved to kill Sakka, aged, fell into a park on earth, and died sending word of all he had ruled.
bg.history:
Lakewood began as a fashionable winter resort in the 1880s, with great hotels in the pines and the estate of George Jay Gould on Lake Carasaljo (now Georgian Court University). The hotel trade declined badly in the 1960s, the woods and cranberry bogs gave way to housing, and the retirement community of Leisure Village opened for sale in 1963 (Lakewood Township). In 1943 Rabbi Aharon Kotler, who had led the yeshiva of Kletzk before escaping Europe, opened Beth Medrash Govoha in Lakewood with about fifteen students; by his death on November 29, 1962, it had some 250, and his funeral on the Lower East Side drew some 25,000 mourners (Aharon Kotler). Its married students are counted as its kollel. The yeshiva's people in this story are invented.

Jewish poultry farms spread across central and southern New Jersey with mortgage loans and advice from the Jewish Agricultural Society; Toms River, Lakewood and Farmingdale were early centers, and at the peak in the 1950s Jewish farmers produced about three quarters of the state's eggs (JewishGen KehilaLinks). In the late 1940s and early 1950s some thousands of Holocaust survivors, most with no farming experience, took up poultry, many of them around Vineland, and by the 1960s most had been driven out by falling prices and factory-scale farms (Aish). Then prices collapsed: one Farmingdale family remembered wholesale eggs falling from about ninety cents a dozen after the war to twenty-five cents by 1962, and selling their farm in 1966 for half what they had paid (New Jersey Jewish News). A few miles north, in Freewood Acres, Kalmyk Buddhist refugees had built temples in the 1950s; their monks are the subject of an earlier story in this series, Salt Tea. Eggs are still checked by candling, holding them to a light to see the yolk, air cell and any flaw through the shell.

sections.heading: I. Yoreh De’ah
sections.text: Leib Feder had been learning in the kollel at Lakewood for three years when the mashgiach called him in after Maariv and told him to go to Brooklyn for the winter. There was a rav in Williamsburg, an old man from Hungary, who taught the laws a rabbi needs, the laws of what is kosher and what is not, salting and soaking and the lung of an ox, and he took two or three young men a season into his apartment over a fish store on Lee Avenue and drilled them until they could answer a question about a chicken in their sleep. Go, said the mashgiach. Learn it properly. Come back in Nisan with semicha. The Rosh Yeshiva had died in November. Twenty-five thousand people had stood in the streets of the Lower East Side for the funeral, and the yeshiva he had brought to the pine woods twenty years before with fifteen students had two hundred and fifty, and nobody yet knew what it would be without him. It seemed a good winter to be sent somewhere and told exactly what to do. So Leib slept on a cot in the rav’s front room under a window that smelled of carp, and learned the laws of the lung, and did not go home on Shabbos because the rav did not hold with young men running back and forth. Raizel sta

sections.heading: II. Eighteen Hundred Dollars
sections.text: He did not go back to Williamsburg. The rav sent word that he understood. Leib went back to Lakewood and to the kollel, and to the minyan three times a day to say Kaddish, and for a few weeks he learned as he always had. Then he began to do arithmetic. The farm would have to be sold. His mother could not run it and Mendy was a boy. The agent from the Society had come and walked through the coop with his hands behind his back and said what it would bring, and it was half of what Moshe Feder had paid. All up and down the county the farms were going that way, Toms River and Jackson and Howell, men who had come out of the camps or out of the sweatshops to have a piece of ground and something alive to tend, selling out for what they could get to men who built houses. In Lakewood the great hotels in the pines stood half empty in the winter season, and at the edge of town a sign had gone up for a village for retired people. And Leib thought: I could keep it. He thought it first at night. Then he thought it in the beis medrash, over the open Gemara, with his chavrusa reading aloud across the table. What was he doing here? He was twenty-four years old with a wife and a child. He lived on wh

sections.heading: III. The Grading Room
sections.dateline: The county line road, Jackson Township · May 1963
sections.text: Reb Zalman Mintz had three thousand Leghorns on twelve acres of sand at the edge of the pines, where the county line road ran toward Freewood Acres, and he brought eggs to the yeshiva kitchen every Thursday in a green panel truck. That was all most of the boys knew about him. A few knew more. Before the war, it was said, he had been one of the best heads in the yeshiva at Kletzk. He had come to this country in 1949 with nobody, from where nobody asked, and bought the farm with a loan from the Society, and lived on it alone. He would not give a shiur. He would not take an honor in shul. But he learned every night in the beis medrash from ten until two, at a table by the radiator, and more than once Leib had seen the mashgiach himself go over to that table with a sefer under his arm and stand there like a boy waiting to be called on. They found him in the basement of the farmhouse, in the grading room. It was cool and dim and smelled of lime and straw. He was sitting on a stool in front of a wooden box with a light bulb inside it and a round hole cut in the front, taking eggs one at a time out of a wire basket and holding each one up to the hole so the light came through it. The shel

sections.heading: IV. The King
sections.dateline: The grading room, the same afternoon
sections.text: The mashgiach had sat down on an upturned feed bucket. Avrohom Wolpe stood by the stairs. Nobody said anything, and after a while Reb Zalman began to talk, still candling, an egg in his fingers the whole time, and set each one down where it belonged as he went. There was a king, he said. A long time ago. He had everything a king has, and seven treasures besides, and when he shut his left hand and struck it with his right, it rained. Not water. Gold. Pearls, stones, every kind, up to the knee, like hail, over the whole country. He was a prince for a long time, and he helped his father rule for a long time, and he was king for a long time. Longer than any of us. One day he was sad. His ministers said, Majesty, what is it? He said, Look what I can do. What is this little kingdom, to a man who can do what I can do? Where is there better? They said, Majesty, there is only up. So he went up. To the first heaven, where there are four kings, one at each corner of the world. They came out to meet him with flowers and gave him their throne, and he sat there. A long time. And then he began to get yellow in the face, like our friend here. The four kings said, Majesty, what is it? He said, What

sections.heading: V. The Sand Road
sections.text: The mashgiach rode back to Lakewood with Avrohom Wolpe in the yeshiva’s car. Leib said he would walk. It was eight miles and nobody argued with him. He went north first, the wrong way, up the sand road past the last of the coops, without any reason except that he did not want to arrive yet. The pines were full of the smell of the day’s heat going out of them. At a farmhouse with a tin-roofed porch, where the road bent toward Freewood Acres and the Kalmyk people lived, a man was standing at the door. He was a monk, Leib supposed, though he had never seen one. He was bald, in a plain cotton robe the color of dried blood, and he was holding out a wooden bowl in both hands. A woman in an apron came to the screen door with a kettle and filled the bowl with something milky and steaming, and the monk lifted it in both hands and drank it standing on the step, all of it, slowly, as though there were nothing else he needed to be doing that evening or any evening. There was a brass staple across a split in the rim of the bowl. Leib could see it shine when he tipped it up. Then the monk bowed to the woman, and she bowed back, and he came down the step and went on up the road to the next house,

title: A Hundred Eggs
place: Lakewood and Jackson Township, New Jersey
logline: A young scholar in the Lakewood kollel inherits eighteen hundred dollars from a chicken farmer and stops turning the pages.

verses.text: Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees.
But that is not a safe refuge, that is not the best refuge; a man is not delivered from all pains after having gone to that refuge.
He who takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church; he who, with clear understanding, sees the four holy truths:—
Viz. pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain;—
That is the safe refuge, that is the best refuge; having gone to that refuge, a man is delivered from all pain.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the brahmin Aggidatta is chaplain to King Mahā Kosala and then to his son Pasenadi, who seats him as an equal. Knowing that the favor of kings does not last, the old man gives away his wealth in a week and goes forth, and ten thousand follow him to a place on the frontier of three countries. There he teaches that refuge in a mountain, a forest, a grove or a tree frees a person from all suffering, and has his followers carry a jar of river sand to one spot whenever a sensual thought troubles them. The heap grows great, a nāga king takes it for his own, and the people of the three countries bring offerings every month. The Buddha sends Mahā Moggallāna ahead. In a storm he asks Aggidatta for lodging, is refused, asks for the sand heap instead, and overcomes the nāga in a contest of smoke and fire; in the morning he sits on the heap under the serpent's hood. The Buddha arrives, sits on the summit, and answers Aggidatta's teaching with the verses. The followers go forth, and when the people arrive with offerings and wonder which teacher is greater, Aggidatta rises seven times into the air and declares himself the Buddha's disciple.
bg.history:
The Year 2000 problem was the fear that computers storing years in two digits would read 2000 as 1900 and fail. Some people stocked food, water and guns, bought generators and drew out cash; interest in survivalism peaked in 1999, and some preachers tied the date to the end times. The United States spent an estimated $134 billion on preparation, and when the clocks turned over the failures were few and minor. January 1, 2000, fell on a Saturday.

Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee meet at Tri-State Peak, inside Cumberland Gap National Historical Park. Just to the west, Middlesboro was founded in 1886 inside the Middlesboro crater, a meteorite impact basin about three miles wide that geologists identified in the 1960s. The Old Regular Baptists, most numerous along the Kentucky–Virginia border, have preachers who are called rather than trained and serve without pay, sing their hymns lined out and unaccompanied, and baptize in running water. Brother Brand, Shelburne Coal & Land, the hollow, Lick Fork church and all the people are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Chair
sections.text: Brother Harlan Brand had preached thirty-one years at the big Baptist church on Cumberland Avenue, and for twenty-six of them he had also been the preacher of Shelburne Coal & Land. Old Lafe Shelburne had hired him to pray. He prayed at the opening of every new mine and at the funeral of every man killed in one, and on the first Monday of every month he sat in on the board and opened it, and when the old man died in 1991 it was Brother Brand who buried him. The son kept him on. Coleman Shelburne was forty-four that year, a quiet man who had been to Vanderbilt and ate his dinner at the board table without seeming to taste it, and he did a thing his father had never done. When Brother Brand came in on the first Monday, Coleman got up from behind the desk and came around it to the door to meet him, and walked him back, and pulled out a chair for him on his own side of the desk, the same chair as his, and said, Preacher, sit here by me. He did it every month for six years. Middlesboro sits in a hole in the mountains three miles across that something made when it fell out of the sky, a long time before there was anybody to see it. Brother Brand had read that in the paper the year they f

sections.heading: II. The Sand Pile
sections.dateline: A hollow on the Virginia side, east of the Gap · 1998–1999
sections.text: A man named Elmer Collingsworth, who had been a deacon under him, owned a hundred and sixty acres of steep woods in a hollow on the Virginia side of Cumberland Mountain, east of the Gap, and from the head of the hollow you could see the knob where Kentucky and Virginia and Tennessee come to a point at a marker in the rocks. He gave it to Brother Brand by deed. There was a creek in the bottom with a bar of clean sand on every bend, and a big rock house up the slope, a shelf of sandstone overhanging a floor as dry as a church, where people had taken shelter, Brother Brand said, since there were people. The first summer there were thirty of them in tents and campers. Then the papers and the television began to say what would happen when the clocks turned over to the year 2000, how the computers that ran the power plants and the banks and the water would read the two zeros as 1900 and stop, and the people who came up the gravel road the second year came with generators in their pickup beds and their children's school records in a shoebox. Men who had been laid off by Shelburne came. Women whose husbands had left came. A boy named Tyler Ely came who had done a semester at Lincoln Memori

sections.heading: III. The Lineman
sections.text: It came on to rain at dark, a cold heavy rain out of the southwest, in drops so big they rang on the trailer roofs, and the meeting in the rock house broke up early and everybody ran for their own door. Brother Brand had a single-wide at the head of the hollow, the only thing he owned. He was sitting in it with the lamp lit, because the generator was saved now for the end, when somebody knocked and called through the door. Harlan. Nobody had called him Harlan since Ruth died. The board had called him Brother Brand, and Coleman Shelburne had called him Preacher, and the three hundred people in the hollow called him Brother. He did not get up. Who is that? It's me. What do you want? A place to lay down tonight, out of this. He opened the door. There was a big man on the step in a yellow rain slicker with the hood down and the rain running off his face, a man in his forties with a lineman's forearms and a lineman's ruined hands, and nothing in them. Behind him in the dark the creek was coming up. There's no room, said Brother Brand. There's a family in every camper on this creek. Harlan, miners bunk with miners, the man said, and church folks put up church folks. You're a preacher. I'

sections.heading: IV. The Elder
sections.text: It cleared in the night and froze. In the morning the people came out to the sand pile in their coats to see whether he was dead, and he was sitting on top of it. He was dry. The slicker was folded under him. Behind him the Old Man lay coiled in a ring on the top of the pile, all the length of him, and the snake had raised his head and the front of his body up over the man and bent it forward, and held it there, broad and still, so that it made a roof over the man's head like the roof of a porch. And around the foot of the pile, all the way around, not only on the near side, the canned goods and the jugs of water and the lamp oil and the powdered milk had been set out in rows, neat, the labels all turned out, the way a woman sets a table for a reunion. The people stood in a ring. Lord, mister, said Darnell Cox. He must have give you a terrible night. Don't you see him? said the lineman. He's right here. How did a man do that, people said to one another. How did a man do that to that snake. Nobody went home. They stood around the pile all morning in the cold, and somebody brought him coffee, and he drank it. His name, he told them, was Kenny Moberly, and he worked for the electric c

sections.heading: V. Seven Times
sections.text: In the morning the people of the hollow came out of their campers and trailers and plywood cabins dressed for church. Every one of them. Men who had not had a tie on in two years had a tie on, and women who had come up the mountain with one suitcase came out in their good dresses and stockings, and children were in their Easter clothes with their hair wet down. Nobody remembered packing any of it. Afterward nobody could say where it had come from. They stood around the sand pile in the frost, quiet and settled, three hundred of them, like people who had been members of a church sixty years and had their own pews, and the Elder sat on the top of the pile in his overcoat in the sun. It was the first Saturday of the month. About ten o'clock the cars began to come up the gravel road from three states with their offerings, the pickups from Harrogate and the station wagons from Pineville, people who had stayed home in their lit houses the night before and woke up feeling a little foolish, and had come anyway. They got out with their sacks of canned goods and their jugs of water and stopped. They saw the people of the hollow all dressed for church. They saw an old man none of them knew si

title: The Sand Pile
logline: A coal company's retired preacher leads three hundred people up a mountain to wait out Y2K, where a rattlesnake takes their penance pile.

verses.text: A supernatural person (a Buddha) is not easily found, he is not born everywhere. Wherever such a sage is born, that race prospers.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is a few lines long. The elder Ānanda, sitting alone in the afternoon, reflects that the Buddha has told the monks where well-bred elephants, horses and bullocks come from, each from a named stock or country, and has never said where well-bred people come from. He goes and asks. The Buddha answers that such people are not born everywhere, only in the Middle Country (his own homeland), and there only in a household here and there, and he gives the verse: the noble one is hard to find, and the family he is born into thrives.
bg.history:
Between 1854 and 1929 the Children’s Aid Society of New York and other charities sent some 200,000 city children west by rail to be placed in farm homes, a movement later called the orphan trains. A company would be advertised by handbill, a committee of local citizens took the names of applicants, and the children were shown on the stage of an opera house, church or skating rink. The terms Mr. Hallam recites are those printed in an Iowa newspaper notice of 1890, “Boys Wanting Homes”. Riders remembered being handled like stock, and brothers and sisters were often parted. Fenwick and its people are invented.

The cattle history is real. The Shorthorn was the first breed of cattle to have a herd book, and in the 1870s American breeders bid pedigrees of the Duchess family up to a peak of $40,600 for one cow at New York Mills in 1873; the boom ended in ruin, and the plain, thick “Scotch” cattle of Amos Cruickshank’s Sittyton herd took over the breed. Cattle descended from the Kentucky importation of 1817, the “Seventeens,” were long slighted for want of a long pedigree, as Alvin Sanders tells in Short-Horn Cattle (1900). The Percheron sire Brilliant and the Poland China hog of the Miami Valley are as Felix has them. Darwin drew on breeders throughout his work; the passages Mrs. Rusk reads are from chapter V of The Descent of Man (second edition, 1874), where he doubts that the noblest human qualities could ever have been multiplied by selection.

sections.heading: I. The Private Book
sections.dateline: Elm Lawn, east of Fenwick, Iowa · April 1896
sections.text: The heifer came a little before four, in the box stall at the south end of the cow barn, and by the time there was light to see her color she was on her feet and had found the bag. Felix rubbed her off with a grain sack and stood back. She was roan, a deep strawberry roan like her dam, level along the top, with a white switch to her tail. He watched her suck until he was sure of her. Then he went up to the house, washed to the elbows at the kitchen pump, and sat down in the office off the kitchen to write her in the book.
