Mrs. Rusk kept two. One was the American Herd Book, some forty volumes along the top shelf, which belonged to the Association in Chicago and told the world what her cattle were. The other was a canvas-backed ledger as thick as a pulpit Bible, and she called it the private book. Every animal calved at Elm Lawn since 1867 had a page in it. At the top of the page went the sire and the dam. Under them was a ruled space headed Remarks, and into it, over the years, went whatever the animal did: its weights, its calves, the price it fetched, and what she had seen with her own eyes. Slack back of the shoulder. Milks like a Jersey. Sold to Gaddis; I would not have kept her

sections.heading: II. The Opera House
sections.text: The chairs had been borrowed from the Odd Fellows and set in a row across the stage, in front of a painted drop of a lake nobody in Fenwick had ever seen. The children sat with their hands in their laps. They had been washed at the hotel and their hair was still wet. Mr. Hallam, a spare man with a carrying voice, stood at the footlights and gave the terms as he had given them in two hundred towns. Boys under twelve were to stay until eighteen and be treated in schooling, clothing and training as the family’s own. Boys of twelve to fifteen were to have board and clothes until seventeen, and school a part of every year. The Society paid the fare, and could take a child back for cause. Then the people came up the side steps, and Felix, standing at the back by the stove, saw what he remembered. A man took a boy’s upper arm between his thumb and two fingers and worked down it to the wrist. Another said Open and looked at a boy’s teeth, tipping the chin toward the window. A woman turned a girl around by the shoulders, looked at her from behind, and turned her back. They were not hard people. Most of them he knew. A woman from out by the creamery got down on her knees in her good dress to

sections.heading: III. The Lamp
sections.text: He asked her after supper, in the office, when she had the lamp lit and the private book open at the new page to see what he had put. Mrs. Rusk. The well-bred men. Where do they come from? She did not look up. Butler County, Ohio. He waited. The Miami Valley. It runs about a hundred miles, top to bottom. My father held that all the good people in the United States came out of it, and he was from there. She turned a page back and forward again. And not out of every house in it, either. I knew most of the houses. One. Two, if you count my aunt. Then she got up and took a brown book down from beside the herd books. It was Mr. Darwin’s Descent of Man, the New York printing. Tobias had bought it the winter before he died, she said, to find out how to breed a better steer. He had underlined one sentence near the end, about how a man will scan the pedigree of his horses and cattle and dogs with scrupulous care before he matches them, and take no such care over his own marriage. She did not read him that. She found a place in the middle with no mark on it, and read it under the lamp in the voice she used for sale catalogues. He who was ready to sacrifice his life, as many a savage has been

title: Sire and Dam
logline: On orphan-train day in an Iowa county seat, a herdsman who knows every pedigree but his own asks where good men come from.

verses.text: Happy is the arising of the awakened, happy is the teaching of the True Law, happy is peace in the church, happy is the devotion of those who are at peace.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred monks sitting in the hall at Jetavana argue over what the best thing in the world is. Some say the pleasure of ruling, some the pleasures of love, some the pleasure of eating rice and meat. The Buddha comes in, asks what they are talking about, and tells them that all of these belong to the round of suffering, and that the good things are the arising of a Buddha, the hearing of the Dhamma, and harmony in the Sangha. He speaks the verse, and the monks reach arahantship.
bg.history:
Occupy Wall Street began in Zuccotti Park, which the occupiers called Liberty Square, on September 17, 2011. It was governed by a General Assembly that worked by modified consensus, with speakers queued in a “stack.” Because the city required permits for amplified sound, the occupiers used the human or people’s microphone, the crowd repeating each phrase of a speaker so those farther back could hear. The park’s drum circle became a sore point with residents, and in October, Community Board 1 voted to back the occupation while asking for drumming to be limited to two hours a day. On October 28 fire marshals removed six generators and the gasoline, and the occupiers turned to bicycle-powered generators. The next day the Halloween nor’easter dropped 2.9 inches of snow on Central Park, a record for October.

Shortly after midnight on November 15, police cleared the park and arrested about two hundred people. The People’s Library, which had grown from a single cardboard box to 5,554 catalogued books, was loaded into sanitation trucks. Mayor Bloomberg said the books could be retrieved from the sanitation garage on 57th Street; the librarians recovered twenty-six boxes, of which 802 books were usable. The kitchen crew and Nadège are invented. Psalm 133 is quoted from the American Standard Version (1901).

sections.heading: I. The Two Hours
sections.text: Nadège Pierre-Louis had played the djembe in the drum circle at the west end of the park since the second week, when she came down from Flatbush on her day off from the home care agency to see what the noise was about and stayed until two in the morning. She was twenty-four. She had bought the drum on Canal Street for sixty dollars the year before and taught herself on YouTube, in her bedroom, with a towel over the skin so her grandmother could sleep. At Zuccotti there was no towel. The circle went eight and ten hours a day, and when it was going the whole park leaned toward it, and people who had never danced in their lives danced on the granite, and she would look up after an hour and find the sky had gone dark over Broadway without her noticing. The neighbors could not sleep. They went to the community board to say so, and some of them came into the park and stood in the stack at the General Assembly and waited their turn: a man from Liberty Street with a baby who would not go down, a woman who worked nights and slept days, an old man in a bathrobe under his coat. Community Board 1 voted to back the occupation and asked the drummers to keep it to two hours a day. Some of the dru

sections.heading: II. The Best Thing
sections.text: On Friday the fire department came with the police and took the generators and the gas cans, six generators and a dozen cans, for safety, they said. The media tent went dark and the kitchen went cold. The bicycles that were supposed to make the electricity were still on their way from Boston. On Saturday it snowed, in October, which almost nobody in New York had ever seen, wet heavy snow that piled on the blue tarps until they sagged and dumped it on whoever was underneath. By dark there were three inches on the granite and the park smelled of wet wool and wet cardboard. About twenty of them ended up in the kitchen that night because it was the only place with a tarp that did not leak. They sat on milk crates and food-bank boxes in their coats and the donated blankets, eating cold peanut butter on cold bread, and somebody asked the question people ask when they are too cold to sleep. What’s the best thing? In the world. Honestly. Rob Szymanski said power. He had been a corporal in Anbar and had come home to a foreclosure. He did not mean the bad kind. He meant the day they were the ones the city had to listen to, the day somebody at Brookfield or City Hall picked up the phone and a

sections.heading: III. The People’s Mic
sections.text: She set the drum down on a crate and pulled the garbage bag off it and did not play it. That’s all the same thing, she said. You get it and you want it again tomorrow. Biscuit, how many plates you hand out? Every one of them was hungry again by night. She looked at Rob. And they pick up the phone, and then what? You want them to pick it up again. Nobody said anything. Snow slid off the tarp outside with a sound like a sack dropped. You want to know the best thing I saw in this park, she said. I saw a man come in here the first week so mad he couldn’t talk, and I saw him three weeks later sitting by the library like somebody turned the lights on in him. That’s one. Two is when somebody stands up in the Assembly and says the true thing, and you hear it come back to you from all those mouths and you know it’s true. Three is the night the man in the bathrobe said he wanted to sleep, and the whole plaza put their hands up for him. That’s the best thing. Everybody together and nobody fighting. She put her palm flat on the drumhead. And four is staying in it. That’s the hard one. Then she said, in the voice they used at the Assembly, Mic check. Out of habit, twenty voices answered her. Mi

sections.heading: IV. Fifty-Seventh Street
sections.text: The police came a little after one in the morning on the fifteenth of November, with the sanitation trucks behind them. They gave people a few minutes to leave. Then they took the park apart. The tents went into the trucks, and the kitchen, and the bicycles, and the library, five thousand books, thrown into dumpsters and garbage trucks with the wet sleeping bags. About two hundred people were arrested. By morning the granite had been power-washed, and there were barricades around it. Nadège was in Flatbush that night, asleep, with the drum under her bed. She heard about it at six from her phone. The kitchen crew never got the kitchen back together. Rob went to work on the Sandy relief a year later out of a church in Sunset Park, running a warehouse of donated blankets, and the people who worked with him said he never once raised his voice. Leah finished her dissertation. Biscuit cooked at a soup kitchen in the Bronx. When any of them ran into each other, anywhere, one of them would sometimes say mic check under their breath, and the other would say it back. The city said the books had been taken to the sanitation garage on Fifty-Seventh Street and could be picked up there. The libr

title: Mic Check
logline: On the snowy night the generators are taken, twenty cold occupiers in the Zuccotti kitchen argue over the best thing in the world.

verses.text: He who pays homage to those who deserve homage, whether the awakened (Buddha) or their disciples, those who have overcome the host (of evils), and crossed the flood of sorrow, he who pays homage to such as have found deliverance and know no fear, his merit can never be measured by anybody.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha, traveling toward Bārāṇasī with a great company of monks, sits down at an old shrine near the village of Todeyya and sends Ānanda to call a brahmin who is plowing nearby. The brahmin bows to the shrine and not to the Buddha, and explains that the shrine has come down to him through the generations. The Buddha praises him. When the monks are puzzled, he tells the story of the potter Ghaṭīkāra (Majjhima Nikāya 81): supporter of the earlier Buddha Kassapa, keeper of his blind parents, a man who dug no earth and let anyone take his pots, whose roof thatch was taken for the Buddha’s hut while no rain fell into his house for three months, and who dragged his proud friend Jotipāla (the future Gotama) by the hair to meet Kassapa. Then the Buddha makes a golden double of Kassapa’s shrine appear in the air, a league high, points to his monks and says it is still more fitting to honor such people, and speaks of the three kinds of shrines and the verses. The golden shrine hangs in the air for seven days; a schism arises at that time; when it returns, a great stone shrine stands in its place.
bg.history:
Ukrainian settlement in western Canada began in 1891 and 1892 at the Edna–Star colony east of Edmonton; by the First World War more than 100,000 Ukrainians and other eastern Europeans, most of the Ukrainians from Galicia and Bukovyna, had settled a band of parkland from Manitoba to Alberta, building whitewashed plastered houses and onion-domed churches, and marking graves with wooden crosses that were later replaced in iron and concrete (Canadian Encyclopedia; Canada’s History). Priests were scarce, and lay cantors led much of the singing and reading. Because most had been Austro-Hungarian subjects, during the war some 80,000 Ukrainians and others were registered as “enemy aliens” and made to report regularly to the police, and about 8,600 were interned in camps (Ukrainian Canadian internment).

Settlers from Galicia were mostly Greek Catholic, those from Bukovyna mostly Orthodox, and disputes over clergy, bishops and church property ran through the colonies. In July 1918 disaffected Greek Catholic laymen from the three prairie provinces met in Saskatoon and formed a brotherhood to organize a Ukrainian Greek Orthodox Church; its first sobor followed that December (Ukrainian Orthodox Church of Canada; Western Development Museum). The potter Hnat’s green-and-yellow ware belongs to the Hutsul tradition of Kosiv and Pistyn in the Carpathians. The dyak quotes the chapter “Concerning the honour due to the Saints and their remains” from John of Damascus’s eighth-century Exposition of the Orthodox Faith. Pruth and Cheremosh districts and the Danylchuk chapel are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Cross
sections.text: The company from Pruth district set out on the Wednesday before the Feast of the Holy Trinity to walk the twenty-two miles to Cheremosh, where a new church with three domes was to be blessed on the Sunday. There were forty-one of them. They carried birch and poplar branches for the green feast and a banner of the Mother of God on two poles, and the old women carried their icons from home wrapped in embroidered towels, the way they had carried them across the ocean in 1898. At the front walked the dyak, Fedir Ilashchuk, who was sixty-seven and had been the nearest thing to a priest that Pruth district had for twenty years: he sang the services when no priest came, which was most Sundays, and read the Epistle and the Psalms, and buried the dead, and taught the boys the responses. Once a month he also walked into Vegreville and signed the book at the Mounted Police barracks, because he had been born a subject of the Austrian emperor, and there was a war. That June the colony was quarrelling. It had begun at the reading halls and gone on to the churches, and by summer half the families north of Vegreville did not greet the other half on the road. It was over priests and bishops and who

sections.heading: II. The Potter
sections.dateline: On the Cheremosh, in the old country · 1871
sections.text: When I was nineteen, the dyak said, I was the cleverest young man on the Cheremosh, and the most foolish. I had been to school in Vyzhnytsia for two winters. I read newspapers. I thought priests were for old women and monks were for nobody. My friend was Hnat the potter, from across the river below Pistyn. Hnat made pots and jugs and bowls, green and yellow on white, the best on that river, and he made them in a strange way. He would not dig his clay with a spade. He said he did not want to cut through anything living to get it. He took only what the river had already torn out of the bank in the spring flood, or what the moles had thrown up in the meadow, and that was all the clay he ever had, and somehow it was always enough. His father and mother were both blind, and he kept them. He did not take his pots to the fair at Kuty to sell. He set them out on a bench by the road in front of his house, and anybody who needed a pot took one, and left what they liked, a little flour, a few eggs, a coin, nothing. Every evening Hnat carried in whatever had been left and cooked it for the old people, and put out more pots. Up the hill above Hnat’s house there was a little wooden church and a

sections.heading: III. The Living Icons
sections.dateline: The Danylchuk corner · the same afternoon
sections.text: What happened next was told for fifty years in Pruth district and Cheremosh and all the districts north of Vegreville, and the people who told it did not all go to the same church, and they told it the same way. The dyak stood up and looked out over the summer fallow, and the company looked where he was looking, and Danylchuk out at the far end of his field stopped his team and looked too. Over the black field, in the white heat of the afternoon, there was a church standing in the air. It was the little wooden church on the hill above the Cheremosh, the same one, every board of it, with the potter’s shingles on the roof; but it was gold, all of it, and it was as tall as a mountain, so that the poplar bluffs at the edge of the field came only to the bottom step of it. It stood on nothing. Its domes were in the clouds, and the light came off it so that the gulls behind Danylchuk’s plow were gold too. The old women went down on their knees in the road. The dyak did not kneel. He turned his back on the gold church, and with his open hand he showed them the company itself: the old women on their knees with their icons, Marusia Sorochan who had buried four children in this ground, Petro

sections.heading: IV. Seven Days
sections.text: The gold church stood over the Danylchuk summer fallow for seven days. People came from Andrew and Whitford and Hairy Hill and Mundare, and from as far as Smoky Lake with their wagons, Catholic and Orthodox and the ones who were not sure any longer which they were, and they stood along the road allowance and in the plowed ground, and the old women sang, and somebody always had bread. An English rancher came from beyond Vegreville and said it was a mirage, that the prairie did that in the heat, lifting some town from over the horizon up into the sky, and then he stood and looked at it all afternoon with his hat in his hand like everybody else. Two Mounted Policemen rode out to see what the crowd was about and did not write anything down. That was the summer the men from all three provinces met in Saskatoon to start a church of their own, and after that the quarrel in the colony did not end for thirty years. But for those seven days it was said that nobody on the Whitford road refused anybody else a cup of water. On the seventh evening the gold church went back the way it had come, east, and was not there. In the place where it had stood, at the corner of the field by the white cross

title: Summer Fallow
logline: Walking to a church blessing in the summer the colony split, an old Orthodox cantor stops at a priest's grave cross where a farmer is plowing.

verses.text: Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!
Let us live happily then, free from ailments among the ailing! among men who are ailing let us dwell free from ailments!
Let us live happily then, free from greed among the greedy! among men who are greedy let us dwell free from greed!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Sākiyans and the Koliyans, two clans joined by generations of marriage, share a dam on the Rohiṇī River. In a dry summer their field hands quarrel over the water, trade insults about the founding of each other’s royal houses, and carry the quarrel home, until both peoples march out armed to the river. The Buddha, kin to both, sees it at dawn, travels through the air, and sits above the river. The warriors lay down their weapons. He asks the nobles what the fight is about and gets no answer, and works down the ranks to the laborers, who say it is about water. He asks what water is worth and what the lives of warriors are worth, and tells them it is not right to destroy what is priceless for what is worth almost nothing. He ends with the three verses, each beginning let us live happily.
bg.history:
In December 1835 a small faction of Cherokee leaders, the Treaty Party, signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up the Nation’s lands in the Southeast for land in the West and five million dollars. The elected government under John Ross never accepted it. Many treaty families moved west in 1837; the rest of the Nation was rounded up by the army in 1838 and marched west in detachments of about a thousand through an unusually cold winter. About 4,000 died on the Trail of Tears. One detachment was led by the Baptist minister Jesse Bushyhead, and another by the Welsh missionary Evan Jones, who had learned Cherokee and who re-founded the Baptist Mission in the new country. In June 1839 Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot, three treaty signers, were killed on the same day. Boudinot had worked with the missionary Samuel Worcester on the Cherokee Gospel of Matthew, printed at New Echota in 1829 in Sequoyah’s syllabary.

Killings and revenge killings between the parties went on for seven years. In November 1845 armed men killed the treaty man James Starr and his son Buck at their home, and at least 34 political killings are counted in 1845 and 1846 (see Tom Starr). On August 6, 1846, the parties signed a treaty at Washington declaring that “all party distinctions shall cease,” pardoning past offenses, abolishing the armed police and light horse, and promising trial by jury. Wealthier Cherokee, many of them treaty men, held Black people in slavery; in November 1842 about twenty enslaved people escaped near Webbers Falls and fled toward Mexico before a force of Cherokee and Choctaw men caught them near the Red River. Afterward the Nation passed harsher slave codes (see the 1842 slave revolt). Sycamore Branch, the Saunders and Deerinwater families and Old Bark are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Low Water
sections.text: In a wet year you could hear Sycamore Branch from the Deerinwater place, a mile below the mill, going over its stones all night like an old man telling himself a long story. By the time the corn was in tassel that summer it had stopped talking. What was left of it lay in green pools along the bed, one below another, with the minnows crowded so thick in them that a child could scoop them out with a gourd, and every morning a few more pools had gone to cracked mud and the smell of fish. Above the pools stood Absalom Ware's dam. He had built it four years before at the narrows, of oak logs and rock and brush packed with clay, and behind it the branch backed up into a long brown pond where his tub mill sat under a shake roof. People brought corn to that mill from twelve miles off, on horses and in sacks over their shoulders, and Ware took his toll, one gallon in eight, and sold the meal at Tahlequah along with the peaches from his orchard and the cotton his people picked. He was a careful man. When the dry weather came in June he shut the gate in the dam and kept it shut, and ground only on Saturdays, so the pond would hold a head of water through August. Below the dam the branch went

sections.heading: II. The Rifles
sections.dateline: Both sides of the branch · the same day and night
sections.text: By noon, at the mill house, the Deerinwater boys had come up the branch with axes to tear out the dam and had broken Ned’s arm when he tried to stop them, and had said in front of witnesses that the Wares would go the way the Starrs had gone. By noon at the Deerinwater place, Absalom Ware had set his black men on Thomas Deerinwater’s sons with shovels, and Sam had said that the Ross people should go and drink out of the river with the hogs, and that was what treaty men thought of the Nation. By evening it was older than that. It was New Echota and the wagons and the five million dollars. It was the beef contract. It was June of 1839 and who had ridden out at dawn that day and who had held the knives. It was everybody’s dead. Two years before, a quarrel over a mill dam would have gone to the district judge. In the summer of 1846 nobody in the Cherokee Nation trusted a judge who belonged to the other party. Absalom Ware sent his boy David, who was fifteen and had learned English at the mission school, riding east before dark to cousins who had gone over the line into Arkansas the winter before. Thomas Deerinwater sat in front of his cabin in the evening, smoking, and said nothing, an

sections.heading: III. The Preacher
sections.dateline: The Illinois River, below Tahlequah · before daylight
sections.text: Old Bark had a cabin on a bluff over the Illinois River, sixteen miles from Sycamore Branch by the road, and he got up in the dark every morning of his life and went down to the river to pray. He was the brother of Lucy and Sally’s mother. Among the Cherokee that made him something more than an uncle: the mother’s brother was the one who taught the children, and corrected them, and spoke for them; a father belonged to another clan. He was past seventy. Evan Jones the Welshman had baptized him in the Valley River in the old country, in the cold, in front of the whole town, and for twenty years he had preached in Cherokee in brush arbors and log meeting houses, though he could not read a word of English. He carried the Gospel of Matthew in Sequoyah’s letters, a small brown book that Samuel Worcester and Elias Boudinot had made between them and printed at New Echota in 1829. He had come west in the winter of 1838 with the Baptist detachment, Jesse Bushyhead’s, and buried his sister in Kentucky and his wife in Missouri, and preached at both graves out of that book. One of the two men who had put it into Cherokee was among the three killed in June of 1839, a treaty signer. Old Bark had

sections.heading: IV. Above the Water
sections.dateline: Ware’s dam · an hour after sunrise
sections.text: Nobody on either bank saw him come. That was the first thing all of them agreed on, afterward, when they would agree on anything. The men on the east bank had their rifles up. The men on the west bank had theirs up. Absalom Ware had just said something across the water in English, which the Deerinwater side did not understand and did not need to, and Thomas Deerinwater had lifted his hand to give the word, and then he did not give it, because there was an old man sitting in the air above the pond. He was out over the water in front of the dam, about the height of a man’s head, sitting the way an old man sits on a split-bottom chair in front of his own door, with his knees apart and his hands folded on top of his stick. He had on his black preaching coat and an old grey turban. His moccasins hung a few feet above the brown water, and the water under them reflected him, coat and stick and turban, the way it reflected the sycamores. That was how the Deerinwater side told it. On the mill side some said he had been sitting on the top log of the dam all along and they had simply not seen him. Ned, who was standing behind his master with his arm in a sling, said that he had been looking s

sections.heading: V. Let Us Live
sections.text: The old man came down out of the air then. Some said he stepped down onto the top log of the dam as if off the last rung of a ladder. Some said he was simply standing there. He leaned on his stick and took the brown book out of his coat and opened it to a place he did not need to look for, and read it out to them in Cherokee, slowly, one word at a time, the way people read Sequoyah’s letters who learned them as grown men. David Ware, who had ridden all night to fetch the Arkansas cousins and was standing at the end of the line with an empty shotgun, found the same verses years later in his schoolbook Bible in English. He wrote them down on the flyleaf with the date and the name of the branch. In English they were these: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. — Matthew 5:44–45 He shut the book on his thumb. There are men in this Nation who hate me, he said. Because I am a Ross man, and because I

sections.heading: VI. Bean Bread
sections.text: In August word came from Washington that the parties had signed a treaty there, all of them together, with the government. All party distinctions were to cease. Every man in the Nation was pardoned for what he had done to any other. The armed police were done away with, and the light horse, and from now on no Cherokee would be punished for anything except by a jury. People read it to each other in English and in Cherokee, and some cried, and some spat, and the killing slowed down that fall, and then it mostly stopped. On Sycamore Branch it had stopped already. The people who were at the dam that morning said, all the rest of their lives, that something had happened to them there that the treaty had nothing to do with. They did not agree on what it was, any more than they agreed on where exactly the old man had been sitting. Some of the Flint men went to the meeting house that fall and were baptized in the Illinois. One of the Arkansas cousins was baptized too, though he was a Methodist, and had to answer for it at home. Most of them never went near a church, and still could not afterward call a man from the other party a dog. They tried it, some of them, and found that it had gone

title: Bean Bread
logline: In the dry summer after removal, two Cherokee sisters' families face each other with rifles across a mill dam on a dying creek.

verses.text: Let us live happily then, though we call nothing our own! We shall be like the bright gods, feeding on happiness!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha sees that five hundred young women of the brahmin village of Pañcasālā are ready to understand, and goes there for alms on a festival day. Māra, the tempter, takes possession of every villager, and the Buddha leaves with his bowl as clean as when it was washed. Māra waits at the village gate, asks whether he got nothing, and urges him to go round again, meaning to have the villagers clap and jeer in his face. Just then the young women, fresh from bathing and dressed for the festival, arrive at the gate and greet him, and Māra remarks that he must be suffering from hunger. The Buddha answers that though he received nothing, he will pass the day in joy, like the gods of Streaming Light who feed on rapture, and the women enter the stream. Read the full commentary story. Esther's grandfather's saying is from the tractate Berakhot of the Babylonian Talmud, a saying of Rav about the world to come, in A. Cohen's 1921 translation.
bg.history:
Los Alamos was built in secret on a mesa above the Rio Grande in 1943 for the Manhattan Project and stayed a fenced, guarded town for twelve years after the war. Under the Atomic Energy Commission, civilian guards replaced soldiers at the gates, outsiders came in only by invitation with a pass arranged in advance, and residents famously left their doors unlocked. The gates came down on February 18, 1957, when Governor Edwin Mechem drove through first without a pass, and the main guard station was later replaced for a time by a drive-in burger stand. The postwar Western Area included six experimental Lustron houses of porcelain-enameled steel, put up in 1949 on Fairway Drive and 44th Street.

The year 1950 brought the atomic spy cases home to the Hill. Klaus Fuchs, of the wartime British mission, was arrested in England in February; the courier Harry Gold confessed in May; David Greenglass, an Army machinist who had worked at Los Alamos from 1944 to 1946, was arraigned in June; and his brother-in-law Julius Rosenberg and sister Ethel were arrested in July and August (FBI history; the Rosenbergs). Clearances were reviewed across the weapons complex. It was also the year of Hopalong Cassidy, when more than a hundred companies made some $70 million worth of his merchandise. The Halperns, their street and their hearing are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Suits
sections.text: Morris Halpern had come out to the Hill from Bayonne in the spring of 1945 with a toolbox, a wife, and a five-year-old daughter who was sick on every curve of the road up from the river. He ran a lathe. He had run one at the Standard Oil works on Constable Hook and he ran one on the mesa, in a shop behind a fence, making parts he was not told the use of and did not ask about. When the war ended the people who had come for the war began to leave, and the Halperns did not. There was work. There was a house in the Western Area with a yard of pine needles and a view of the Jemez, and a school, and the gate. Everybody on the Hill knew the gate. You showed your pass to the guard at the guardhouse on the road in, and if your mother was coming from Bayonne for Passover you went down in person and signed for her a day ahead, and the guard looked at her face and then at the paper and then at her face. Nobody locked a door. Children left their bicycles lying in the street all night. The fence kept everything out, people said, and in the evening the floodlights came on along the fence by the pond and lay out across the water, white, so that the ducks slept in light. That summer the newspapers

sections.heading: II. The Doors
sections.text: Her mother bought her a mask at the commissary, a black cat on a string, and washed a pillowcase that morning and ironed it flat on the board with the sprinkle bottle, the way she ironed everything, so that it was folded in a square on the kitchen table when Esther came home from school, smelling of the iron. You don't have to go, her mother said. It's Halloween. She put the mask in her coat pocket and did not put it on. Her mother saw that and said nothing. Her father was sitting in the front room with a lamp on in the daytime and a lathe catalogue open on his knee. He got up and walked her to the door and stood in it. Who are you supposed to be? he said. Me. It was dark by six and cold, with the smell of piñon smoke coming down from the stovepipes of the older houses. Up and down the Western Area the porch lights were on, every one, and the children were out in packs, cowboys and skeletons and hoboes with burnt-cork beards, and more Hopalong Cassidys than anyone could count, because that was the year of Hopalong Cassidy, and the commissary had sold out of the black hats by the twentieth. The Dorseys' porch light went out when Esther was halfway up the walk. She stood on the step

sections.heading: III. The Fence
sections.text: The road home went past the pond, where the floodlights were on along the fence on the far side, and at the corner where the fence came down to the road there was a man. He was leaning on the post by the little gate there, the one the guards used, in a good camel-hair coat with the collar up, and he had a red devil's mask on, the kind with the horns molded in, and he was smoking a cigarette under the chin of it. He was not a guard. The guard was in his booth a hundred yards off with the radio on. Afterward nobody on the Hill could say who the man had been. The commissary had not sold a red mask that year, only the cats and the skulls. Nobody's husband owned a camel-hair coat. Hiya, Essie, he said. Nothing, huh? She stopped. She looked at the mask a long time. Why'd you do that? she said. He laughed. He had a nice laugh, a radio laugh. Go around again, he said. Go on. Go around the whole Western Area one more time. Maybe they'll have come around. He tipped his ash. He was thinking, Esther understood, about the clapping, and about how much more of it there could be the second time, and the porch lights going out one after another down the street like a row of teeth, and he wanted to

sections.heading: IV. The Guardhouse
sections.text: The hearing was in January. Morris Halpern sat at a long table in a room in the administration building and answered the same questions as in September, and some new ones, for two days. In March they gave him his clearance back, and he went back to his lathe, and nobody on Fairway Drive ever said anything about it, then or later, which was how things were done on the Hill. Mrs. Dorsey brought over a coffee cake. Esther's desk was moved back, for the light. As for the girls, the people who told the story afterward could never quite say what had happened to them, only that it had. They were not saints. They grew up and argued with their mothers and went to dances in Santa Fe. But it was noticed that not one of them, ever after, could be got to say the word the masked children had clapped. Not as a joke. Not when their fathers said it at dinner. And it was noticed that when somebody on the Hill was having a bad time, a husband let go or a boy in trouble with the police, those were the girls who turned up at the door. They did not bring anything. They sat on the step and talked, and laughed, and went home. On the eighteenth of February, 1957, the Atomic Energy Commission took down the

title: Crowns on Their Heads
logline: On Halloween in the fenced atomic town, a machinist's daughter goes door to door while her father waits for a security hearing.

verses.text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala fights his nephew Ajātasattu, king of Magadha, near the village of Kāsi and is beaten three times. (The quarrel was over that village, which had been given as a dowry to Pasenadi's sister, Ajātasattu's mother, and which Pasenadi took back after Ajātasattu killed his father.) Coming home from the third defeat, the old king says to himself, "Since I cannot beat this milk-faced boy, what is the use of my living?" and refuses food and takes to his bed. The monks tell the Buddha, who answers that the winner breeds hatred and the beaten man lies down in pain, and speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story. Zeb Crane's charge is the one given to the Senior Warden, whose jewel is the level, at the installation of a lodge's officers, as printed in Thomas Smith Webb's Freemason's Monitor, the standard American ritual handbook since 1797, quoted here from the 1867 Cincinnati edition. The Tyler is the officer who guards the lodge door with a sword and normally stays outside it.
bg.history:
In September 1826 William Morgan of Batavia, who was preparing a book exposing Masonic ritual, was jailed at Canandaigua over a small debt, released at night into a waiting carriage, and taken to Fort Niagara, after which he vanished; he is generally believed to have been drowned in the Niagara River. A badly decomposed body that washed up on the Lake Ontario shore in October 1827 was claimed as his. The Niagara County sheriff, a Mason, was removed and served twenty-eight months for conspiracy, and several other men were convicted, but the reward for information was never claimed, and the sense that Masons were shielding Masons turned grief into a movement.

In early 1827 mass meetings across western New York resolved not to vote for Masons for any office, and evangelical churches across the Burned-over District, Presbyterian, Congregational, Methodist and Baptist, condemned members and ministers who belonged to the order. Out of this came the Anti-Masonic Party, the first American third party, which won fifteen seats in the New York Assembly that fall and nominated William Wirt for president in 1832, then faded almost everywhere by 1835. Kendrick's Mills, Concord Lodge, and everyone in the story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Sister's Meadow
sections.text: Judge Amos Thurber had been Master of Concord Lodge in Kendrick's Mills four times and first judge of the county court once, and he had built the stone house at the head of the street with money he made selling lots along the creek when the canal came through. He was sixty-one. He wore his hair in a queue still, the old way, tied with a black ribbon, and in winter he walked to the lodge room over Fenn's tavern with a lantern, though it was forty rods and he knew every board of the sidewalk. His sister Lucy had married a Pease and been given, as her portion, the island meadow in the bend below the mill, eleven acres of the best grass on the creek. When Pease died owing, the judge bought the meadow back at the sheriff's sale to keep it in the family, and he kept it. Lucy died the next winter. Her boy Lyman, who was fourteen then, went to live with the judge in the stone house, and was sent to the academy at Batavia, and read law in an office in Rochester, and came home at twenty-three with a long chin and a short temper and a way of looking at the island meadow out the judge's front window that the judge's wife noticed and did not mention. That was the year a man named Morgan was tak

sections.heading: II. Three Town Meetings
sections.text: The town meeting was held in the spring at Fenn's, in the long room downstairs, with the bar shut. The judge had been supervisor of the town for nine years running. In April of 1827 his nephew stood against him on the Anti-Masonic ticket, and the town voted with its hands up, and when they were counted Lyman Pease had won by thirty-one. The judge shook his hand in front of everybody. That night he walked up to the lodge room with his lantern, and found the door locked and Zeb Crane the Tyler sitting outside it on the bench, as he always sat, with the old sword across his knees. Nobody's come, said Zeb. In 1828 the judge stood again, because his friends said the fever would pass and because he could not imagine not standing, and he lost by seventy. It was the spring after a body had come up on the Lake Ontario shore and the Anti-Masonic papers had said it was Morgan's. Two of the judge's lodge brothers took their names off the roll in a notice in the Batavia paper. Concord Lodge stopped meeting. In the stores men who owed the judge money crossed the street. In 1829 he stood a third time, against all advice, and he made a speech, which he had never done in his life. He stood at the h

sections.heading: III. The Tyler
sections.dateline: The forge below the mill · the same week
sections.text: Zeb Crane had been Tyler of Concord Lodge since it was chartered. He was a blacksmith and a short, thick, silent man, and for thirty years his whole office had been to sit outside the door of the lodge room with a sword and keep it. He let in who was entitled and kept out who was not, and he had never once in thirty years been inside while the lodge was at work. He heard it through the door: every degree, every lecture, every installation of officers, every charge. He knew the whole of it better than the Masters who said it, people said, because he had never had to think about anything else while he listened. When the lodge stopped meeting he went on keeping the key. Some evenings he still went up and sat on the bench. Nobody knew why, and nobody asked him. It was three of the old brothers who came down to the forge to tell him about the judge, Fenn the tavern keeper and two others, and stood in the door while he worked. They told it the way men tell a thing they are ashamed of: the judge would not eat, the judge would not get up, the judge had said what is the use of me. And it was that boy, Fenn said. Lucy's boy, who he had raised. He has gone round the county saying the Masons m

sections.heading: IV. The Jewel
sections.text: The judge's wife said afterward that he lay a long while after the Tyler had gone, looking at the ceiling, and then laughed once, not unhappily, and asked what there was to eat. There was bread and there was cold mutton. He ate it sitting on the edge of the bed with his feet bare, and asked for more bread, and then he tied his queue and went down. Of the three brothers who had stood in the door of the forge, people said, none of them ever spoke again of putting anybody in the creek. Fenn opened the long room the next April for the town meeting the same as always, and set out water for both tickets, and voted, people said, for whoever he pleased and told nobody. The judge did not stand again. He deeded the island meadow to Lyman Pease that summer, as Lucy's portion, with nothing asked, and Lyman did not know what to make of it, and was suspicious of it for years. When the Anti-Masonic party went to pieces in the middle of the thirties, and Lyman Pease was beaten for the assembly by a man nobody had heard of, and sat for a week in his office in Batavia with the blinds down, it was the old judge who drove over in the gig and sat with him. Nobody knows what he said. Something about a w

title: The Level
logline: After the Morgan affair, an old Mason judge loses the town election three springs running to the nephew he raised.

verses.text: There is no fire like passion; there is no losing throw like hatred; there is no pain like this body; there is no happiness higher than rest.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the parents of a young woman of good family invite the Buddha and his monks to her wedding. The bride goes back and forth straining water for the monks and serving them, while the bridegroom stands and stares at her until desire overpowers him; he neglects the Buddha and the eighty great elders and makes up his mind to take her in his arms. The Buddha sees his thought and makes it so that he can no longer see her. Gazing instead at the Buddha, the young man hears that there is no fire like passion, no wrong like hatred, no suffering like the aggregates of body and mind, and no happiness like peace. Both bride and groom enter the stream, and the Buddha lets them see each other once more. Monks in the Buddha's tradition strain their drinking water through cloth so as not to kill small creatures in it. Read the full commentary story. The old priest's friar is St. John of the Cross (1542–1591), the Spanish Carmelite reformer and companion of Teresa of Ávila. The passage is from the sixth chapter of the first book of The Ascent of Mount Carmel, on what the desires do to the soul, in David Lewis's translation of 1864 as revised in the 1906 edition.
bg.history:
Maryland was founded as a refuge for English Catholics, but by the eighteenth century its Catholics could not vote, hold office, worship in public or keep schools, so wealthy families sent their sons across the Atlantic to the Jesuit college at St. Omer and on to Liège, as John Carroll did. Jesuits rode a circuit of private chapels from plantation headquarters such as St. Thomas Manor on the bluff above the Port Tobacco River. The suppression of the Society of Jesus in 1773 left them priests without an order; the Society was restored in the United States at St. Thomas in 1805. Carroll was consecrated the first American bishop in August 1790. The Maryland Jesuits held enslaved people on their estates, among them some of the 272 men, women and children the province sold in 1838.

In July 1790 four Discalced Carmelite nuns sailed up the Chesapeake from Norfolk: Mother Bernardina Matthews, her nieces Ann Teresa and Susanna Matthews, all Maryland-born and trained in the Low Countries, and the Englishwoman Frances Dickenson. On October 15, 1790, the feast of St. Teresa, they moved onto a farm north of Port Tobacco, the first community of Catholic nuns in the new United States. Their house too was worked by enslaved people, forty-one of them in 1820. After 1830 the community moved to Baltimore. The Edelens, the Boarmans, Phillis, and Mr. Hagan in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Linen
sections.text: The spring below the Edelen house ran clear all winter and muddy every summer, after the June rains, and in the muddy months it was full of wigglers. Phillis, who cooked for the Edelens and had cooked for them since before the war with England, strained it for the table through a square of old linen tied over the mouth of the pitcher, and when Miss Monica was a little girl she stood at Phillis's elbow on a stool and watched the wigglers caught in the cloth, kicking, and asked every time whether they would live, and every time Phillis turned the linen out over the grass by the spring so that they could go back. So when Monica Edelen was nineteen and was to be married, and the old priests were coming to the wedding, she would let nobody strain the water for them but herself. She said it was because they were holy men. Phillis thought it was because she liked to. She was marrying Raphael Boarman, the second son from up the Wicomico, a tall, handsome, restless young man who had spent a winter at Annapolis studying law and come home having studied cards and dice instead, and owing a man named Dorsey sixty pounds, and hating him. He had looked at Monica at Mass at the manor at Easter and

sections.heading: II. The Priest
sections.dateline: St. Thomas Manor, on the Port Tobacco River
sections.text: He was seventy-one. He had been born in St. Mary's County and sent over the sea as a boy, because no Catholic could keep a school in Maryland then, to the English Jesuit college at St. Omer in Flanders, and from there to Liège, and had come home a priest of the Society of Jesus and ridden the circuit of the Catholic houses for twenty years, saying Mass in parlors with the shutters closed. Then in 1773 the Pope put an end to the Society. The old priests of Maryland went on living exactly as before, in the same brick house on the bluff at St. Thomas, riding the same circuits, and only were not Jesuits any more. They had had a bishop since the summer before, the first one in the country, and Mr. Hagan said that was very well and went on riding. He was a lean man with the gout in his left knee, and he spoke so little at table that visitors thought him slow. He had one book in his saddlebag that was not a breviary: a little Spanish book, worn soft, that he had bought from a Carmelite friar in Antwerp forty years before. He read it on horseback at a walk. The summer before, four Carmelite nuns had come up the bay from Norfolk in a sloop, from their convent in Flanders, three of them Mary

sections.heading: III. The Pitcher
sections.dateline: The Edelen house · the Tuesday after Corpus Christi
sections.text: They were married in the parlor in the morning with the shutters open, which Monica's grandmother said she had not lived to see in that house until that day. Then the long tables were set out on the grass under the poplars, and the old gentlemen of the county sat down at them in their wigs, the Neales and the Brookes and the Digges and the Boarmans and the Hamersleys, and five old priests in black at the head, and a fiddler, a man named Jerry who belonged to the Brookes, played from a kitchen chair under the trees. It was the bridegroom's part to see to the old men. To carry the chairs and pour the wine and stand behind his father-in-law's chair and hear old stories about the French war. Raphael Boarman did none of it. He stood in the parlor door with his arms crossed and watched his wife. She went up and down the tables with the pitcher. She stopped beside each old priest and poured the spring water into his cup through her square of linen, slowly, and turned the linen out on the grass behind the chair, and went on to the next, in her wedding gown with her sleeves turned back. And Raphael Boarman watched her go, and come back, and go, and something got up in him that he had felt a

sections.heading: IV. The Square of Linen
sections.text: They were married fifty-one years. Raphael Boarman never threw dice again, and paid Dorsey his sixty pounds in the fall, in person, at Annapolis, and shook his hand, and came home, and Dorsey told it at every tavern on the Severn as the strangest thing that had ever happened to him. Monica kept the square of linen. When the water was muddy she still strained it herself, and when there were grandchildren she stood them on a stool at her elbow and let them watch the wigglers kick in the cloth, and turned it out on the grass. Mr. Hagan rode the circuit four more years. He died at St. Thomas in the winter of 1795 and was buried in the graveyard on the bluff, and his little Spanish book went to the nuns in the woods. They kept it until they went away to Baltimore in 1831, and took it with them. Phillis told the story in the kitchen at the Edelen place and in the quarter on Saturday nights, and at the manor at St. Thomas, where her husband Ned belonged to the priests, so that she was given leave to walk over on Saturdays to see him. She told it the same way every time. She would come to the part where the young man could not find his wife, and stop, and say that she had known a good many

title: Strained Water
logline: At a Catholic wedding on the Port Tobacco River, the bride strains spring water for the old priests while the groom watches only her.

verses.text: Hunger is the worst of diseases, the body the greatest of pains; if one knows this truly, that is Nirvana, the highest happiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the Buddha sees at dawn that a certain poor man of Āḷavī is ready to understand, and walks thirty leagues with his monks to teach him. The man means to come and listen, but that morning his ox strays, and he decides to find the ox first. The townspeople feed the monks and wait for the sermon; the Buddha says he will not speak until the man he came for returns, and sits silent. The man finds his ox late in the day, drives it back to the herd, and comes straight to the Buddha without going home to eat. The Buddha asks the steward whether any food is left and has the man seated and fed before he teaches him. The commentary notes that this is the only time on record that the Buddha asked about food. When the monks grumble about it on the road, he turns around, explains that a hungry man cannot take in the teaching, and speaks the verse. Where Müller has “the body,” the Pāli word is saṅkhārā, all things that are put together.
bg.history:
Wicca reached the United States from England in the 1960s and spread through covens whose priestesses trained their successors. Its eight seasonal festivals include Lammas, the “loaf-mass” of the first grain on the first of August. In most covens the shared food comes after the rite, and many fast beforehand. Charles Godfrey Leland’s Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches (1899), with its conjuration of the meal for the witches’ supper, was one of the texts the early Wiccans drew on; the ancient Homeric Hymn to Demeter is quoted here in H. G. Evelyn-White’s translation of 1914. The middle 1980s were the years of the Satanic panic, when television specials taught rural neighbors to be afraid of people like the Lunds. In 1986 a federal appeals court held, in Dettmer v. Landon, that Wicca is a religion under the First Amendment.

The textile and shoe mills of Lewiston were worked for a century by French Canadians who settled the tenement district called Little Canada, and who were laid off in their thousands as the mills closed after the 1950s. In the Maine woods the diesel skidder replaced horses and oxen in the 1960s, though a few teamsters went on working small lots where a machine would do damage. From 1981 the Department of Agriculture gave away its surplus dairy stocks to the poor in five-pound blocks, the “government cheese” handed out at Grange halls and firehouses. Beans baked overnight in an iron kettle buried on coals are an old Maine supper. Hartwell and its people are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Gate
sections.dateline: Hartwell, Oxford County, Maine · Saturday, August 2, 1986
sections.text: Armand Gagnon was fifty-four and owned one ox. He had been born in Little Canada in Lewiston and had gone into the mill at sixteen, and when the mill let his shift go he came up to his uncle’s place in Hartwell, forty acres of ledge and popple, and stayed. He lived in a trailer set on the old cellar. For money he twitched wood. A man with a skidder will not come out for six cords on a back lot, and will tear up the lot if he does, so the summer people and the widows hired Armand, who brought the logs out to the road one at a time on a chain behind the ox and left the ground looking as if nobody had been there. He was paid by the cord, when he was paid. He also witched wells with a forked apple stick, which cost nothing, because his mother had told him it would leave him if he took money for it. The ox was a red Durham steer named Lion, said the French way, eight years old and a little over a ton, with a white star on his forehead. Armand’s mémère had kept a story about a red cow with a star that you did not turn your back on. Lion had never stepped on so much as a chicken. The people at the old Estes farm had come from Massachusetts in 1973. Their name was Lund. Armand found their

sections.heading: II. The Field
sections.text: There were about sixty of them that year, from Portland and Norway and as far as Bangor, and the twenty-two from Providence. The Maine people ate at noon on the grass, sandwiches and switchel, and offered the same to the Providence people, most of whom said no thank you. The feast was for after. It was laid out on planks under the maples with cheesecloth over it against the wasps. Brown bread steamed in coffee cans, corn waiting in its husks, three blueberry cakes. The loaf for the altar was baked in the shape of a sheaf, as long as a child. Down by the garden was the bean hole, where Tobias Lund had buried an iron kettle of yellow-eyes on a bed of coals the night before and shoveled the dirt back over it. The woman from Providence was called Doris Almeida six days of the week. She was forty-nine and kept the books at a plant in Olneyville that made clasps and earring backs. In circle her people called her the Lady, and they were a little afraid of her. On a day when there was work to do she took water from sunrise and nothing else, and she expected the same of them. She had once sent a man home from his own initiation over a roll of Life Savers. In twelve years nobody had heard he

sections.heading: III. The Bean Hole
sections.text: He found Lion at four o’clock, two miles back, at a cellar hole on the old Whitcomb place where a Yellow Transparent still stood and dropped its apples in August. The ox was lying in the fern with his belly out like a barrel, chewing. Armand sat down beside him until his legs stopped shaking. He had been up the tote road and across the power line and around the beaver flowage twice, calling, and he had had nothing since the coffee. He ate four of the apples. They were mealy and they made it worse. He got the ox up and walked him home by voice, and turned him in with Hackett’s heifers and wired the gate chain shut with a double twist. By then it was past six. The trailer was a mile one way and the Lunds’ a mile the other. It will be over, he thought. But I can go and tell her I am sorry. I can do that much. He did not go home. He went down the road as he was, with spruce pitch on his hands and burdock up one leg. They were all still there. He saw the ring in the hayfield and the four lanterns dark, and the people sitting in the stubble, and he did not understand it. He took off his cap and stood at the edge. Madame, he said to the woman on the wall, I am sorry to be late. I had to f

sections.heading: IV. The Road
sections.text: They ate the rest of the feast by lantern. Afterward the Maine people walked the Providence people down the road to where the cars were, as far as the plank bridge, and said good night there and turned back. Her own people came on behind her in the dusk, and they were sore. Ronnie Paiva said it, not very low. Twelve years. Twelve years it’s been water from sunup and not a crumb till the circle’s open. I never once heard her ask what there was to eat. And today she holds sixty people in a field for four hours and then asks after supper, for a stranger, and feeds him off the altar before the ring is cast. The Lady stopped in the road and turned around. What are you saying back there? They told her. Yes, she said. That is what I did. I drove six hours for that man. I saw in June that he was ready, and nobody else up here was. He got up before light with nothing in the house, and he spent the whole day in the woods on that nothing, hunting the one animal that keeps him alive. If I had cast at two without him, I’d have come for nothing. If I had started in on him at half past six the way he stood there, he would have heard his own stomach and not one word of mine. So I did what I did. N

title: Loaf Mass
logline: A Wiccan priestess drives six hours to a Maine hayfield for one man, who has gone into the woods after his only ox.

verses.text: If a man becomes fat and a great eater, if he is sleepy and rolls himself about, that fool, like a hog fed on wash, is born again and again.
Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala eats rice by the bucketful and comes to the Buddha so heavy with sleep that he paces up and down rather than lie down. The Buddha warns him with a verse about the overeater who rolls about like a fattened hog, then gives him a verse on knowing the measure in food. The king cannot memorize it, so the Buddha has his nephew Sudassana learn it and recite it at every meal just as the king is about to take the last ball of rice; the king throws the ball away, and the next meal is cooked with that many fewer grains. Each time he hears the verse he gives a thousand coins in alms. He grows lean and cheerful, and returns to tell the Buddha that he can hunt again, that he has made peace with his nephew by giving him his daughter Vajirā, that a lost jewel has come back to him, and that he has taken a daughter of the Buddha’s own kin into his household. The Buddha answers that health is the greatest gain, contentment the greatest wealth, trust the best kin, and nibbāna the highest happiness.
bg.history:
In the Gilded Age a formal dinner in a rich New York house ran to a dozen courses or more, set out on a card written in French: oysters, a soup, fish, entrées, a roast, a Roman punch to clear the palate, game such as canvasback duck, terrapin, ices and sweets. The great public table of the city was Delmonico’s, then at Fifth Avenue and Twenty-sixth Street. On the night of October 29, 1884, days before the presidential election, a crowd of the city’s millionaires gave a dinner there for the Republican candidate, James G. Blaine. The next morning the New York World ran Walt McDougall’s front-page cartoon “The Royal Feast of Belshazzar Blaine and the Money Kings,” in which a laborer and his family beg for crumbs from the table; Democrats circulated the menu, and the dinner is often counted among the causes of Blaine’s narrow defeat. The Meadow Brook Club, founded on Long Island in 1881, gave the rich a polo ground and a hunt.

Women physicians were still rare and often unwelcome. The Female Medical College of Pennsylvania, founded in 1850, was the second school in the world to train women for the M.D., and many of its graduates worked in free dispensaries for poor women and children in the immigrant wards of the cities. In the Civil War, Dorothea Dix recruited some 3,000 nurses for the Union Army and asked that they be between thirty-five and fifty and plain-looking. The Ruland family, Dr. Ashdown and her dispensary, Monsieur Achille and the diamond are invented. Ecclesiasticus, the Wisdom of Jesus the son of Sirach, is one of the books of the Apocrypha, which the Episcopal Church read in its lessons and the King James translators set between the Testaments.

sections.heading: I. Breakfast
sections.text: Josiah Ruland ate breakfast at half past eight in a room panelled in walnut, under a painting of a stag at bay, and on an ordinary weekday it went like this. A dozen Blue Points on the half shell. A porterhouse steak. Two mutton chops, because the steak was never enough by itself. Four eggs, shirred. Fried potatoes, a stack of buckwheat cakes with butter and Vermont syrup, a dish of stewed kidneys if the cook had them, rolls, and a pot of coffee with a pitcher of cream. He did not think of this as a large breakfast. He thought of it as breakfast. His father had been a canal-boat captain on the Lehigh who ate cornmeal mush out of a tin plate, and Josiah Ruland had made his own money out of the anthracite, and the coal roads, and the iron, and every morning he sat down to that table like a man settling an account. He was fifty-eight that winter. He had been the best rider in his club when he was forty, and now he could not mount a horse without a block and a groom, and he had not been out with the hounds in four seasons. He wheezed on the stairs. He slept badly at night and heavily in the day, in the library, in his carriage, in the pew at Grace Church through the whole of the sermon

sections.heading: II. The Dispensary
sections.text: The dispensary was in the ground floor of a tenement east of the Bowery, two rooms and a hall, with a bench along the wall of the hall and a stove at the end of it, and it had been there for eleven years. Ruland’s wife Cornelia had given the money to open it, before she died, and Ruland went on paying the rent and the coal and the doctor’s small salary because Cornelia had asked him to, and once a quarter he went down to look at it, the way he looked at a mine. The doctor was Hester Ashdown. She was sixty-one years old, the daughter of a country rector in Connecticut, and she had taken her degree at the Female Medical College in Philadelphia in 1857, when the men students at the other colleges in that city still hissed women in the street. In the war she had been one of Miss Dix’s nurses, who had to be over thirty-five and plain, and she said she had qualified on both counts with room to spare. She had nursed the wounded from the Wilderness and from Cold Harbor in the long sheds at Fredericksburg and in the river hospitals, and she had been in the ward where they brought the officers from the Second Corps, and she had sat one night with a captain named Ruland who was asking for his

sections.heading: III. The Card
sections.text: Even when the family dined alone in that house there were nine courses, and when there was company there were thirteen or fourteen, and every dinner had its card in a silver holder by each plate, written out in French in the hand of Monsieur Achille Bréval, who had cooked for an ambassador in Paris and for Mr. Ruland for nine years and was paid, the servants said, more than the president of a bank. The card for that Monday read: oysters; a clear turtle soup; a timbale of sweetbreads; a turbot with lobster sauce; a saddle of mutton with French beans; terrapin in the Maryland style; a sorbet of Roman punch; canvasback duck with fried hominy and celery; and an iced pudding with fruits and bonbons. Ruland came down to it in a bad humour, and Adela came down in a grey silk, and Kit came down with a paper folded small in his waistcoat pocket. They went through it. They always went through it. The servants came and went. The candles burned in the silver. When the iced pudding came round, molded like a castle, and the footman set a slice of it before Ruland and he took up his spoon, Kit put down his own. Be not unsatiable in any dainty thing, nor too greedy upon meats: For excess of meats

sections.heading: IV. The Sauceboat
sections.text: Cornelia Ruland’s diamond had been lost on New Year’s night. It was a single stone the size of a hazelnut on a fine gold chain, which Ruland had bought in Paris the year the first mine paid, and which Cornelia had worn at every dinner of her married life, and which Adela wore now. On New Year’s night, at a dinner for twenty-four, the clasp had given way, and the stone had gone somewhere between the soup and the ices, and was not found. The rugs were taken up. The chairs were turned over. The detectives came from the Pinkerton office and talked to the servants one by one in the butler’s pantry. Ruland dismissed the second footman, a boy named Daly who had served Adela’s side of the table and had the misfortune to have a brother who had been in the Tombs, and Daly went out of the area door in January without a character, and Adela cried, and Ruland said that was what came of it. In April, when the turbot had been off the card for two months and Monsieur Achille had given up hoping it would come back, the butler had the fish service brought out of the pantry to be wrapped in flannel and put away in the strong room for the summer. It was a great silver set, the fish dishes and the slic

sections.heading: V. Grace Church
sections.dateline: Broadway and Long Island · June to October
sections.text: The quarrel did not end in a day. It ended a little each night, at the table, over the card. A man cannot say the same words to another man every evening for three weeks, and be obeyed, without something changing between them. Kit found he could not hate a man who put down his fork when he was asked. Ruland found that the boy he had spoken to like a clerk for six years had a voice he did not mind hearing. One evening in the library, with the cheque drying on the blotter, he said without looking up that Will’s shares had been worth twice what he had paid for them in ’65, and he had known it, and he had told himself it was a fair price for the time. Kit said nothing for a while. Then he said that he knew it too, and that he had known for eight years, and that he was tired of knowing it. In June, Ruland gave his daughter to his nephew at Grace Church, with a bishop and the choir and half of Washington Square in the pews and a crowd on Broadway outside the railings to see the dresses go in. There were people who said first cousins ought not to marry and people who said the Rulands had done it to keep the money in the family, and both kinds of people came to the wedding. Ruland walked A

sections.heading: VI. The Bench
sections.text: Ruland went down to Rivington Street the week after the election, on foot from the elevated at Grand Street, in the cold, with no one with him. The bench was full, as it was always full, and he did not walk up and down this time. He sat at the end of it, among the women, with his hat on his knee, and waited his turn like anyone, and a little girl in a red hood sat next to him and looked at his watch-chain for half an hour while he let her. When Dr. Ashdown came out and saw him she brought him back into the small room and gave him the patients’ chair and sat down at her desk. Doctor, he said, I have come to tell you I’m a happy man. I don’t believe I have been one before. She waited. He told her. He told it like a report to his directors, item by item, as if he were afraid of leaving something out. He was well. He slept. He could ride again, and had taken a wall on Long Island at fifty-eight with men half his age watching, and had not fallen off. He had quarrelled with his brother’s son for six years, and now his brother’s son had his daughter and his brother’s share, and they did not quarrel, and he had not known how much the quarrel cost him until it stopped.
