title: The Last Course
logline: A coal baron who sleeps through his own life is handed a prescription to be read aloud at the last course of every dinner.

verses.text: He who has tasted the sweetness of solitude and tranquillity, is free from fear and free from sin, while he tastes the sweetness of drinking in the law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha tells the monks at Vesālī that in four months he will pass away. Seven hundred of them are shaken. Those who have not reached the goal cannot hold back their tears, and they go about in little groups asking one another what they are to do. One monk, the elder Tissa, reasons that he is not yet free and had better become so while his teacher is alive. He keeps to himself and stops speaking with anyone. The others ask him why and get no answer, and they report to the Buddha that Tissa has no affection for him. The Buddha sends for Tissa, hears his reason, and says, “Well done.” Then he tells the rest that only one who acts like Tissa truly loves him: those who honor him with perfumes and garlands do not honor him, and those who practice what he taught do. He speaks the verse, and Tissa reaches the goal.
bg.history:
Before antibiotics the best treatment anyone had for tuberculosis of the lungs was rest, food and cold clean air, kept up for months or years. Edward Livingston Trudeau, a consumptive doctor who had recovered in the Adirondacks, opened his sanitarium at Saranac Lake in the 1880s, and the village grew into the country's best-known cure town. Most patients boarded in private cure cottages, houses built or rebuilt with open porches where they lay out in every season on wide reclining cure chairs made in the village. Many of the cottages stood on Helen Hill. A patient's day was ruled by the thermometer and the clock: hours in the chair, a silent rest period after dinner, exercise allowed by the minute once the afternoon fever was gone. Romances between patients were called cousining. Pelletier Cottage and its people are invented.

The pitcher Christy Mathewson, one of the most admired ballplayers of his day, came to Saranac Lake with tuberculosis and died there on October 7, 1925, the day the World Series opened; both teams wore black armbands. The book Miss Thayer reads is Plato's Phaedo, the account of Socrates' last day in prison, in Benjamin Jowett's translation. Socrates spends the day arguing that a philosopher's whole life is “the practice of dying,” and when his friend Crito asks at the end what they can do for him, he gives the answer quoted in the story.

sections.heading: I. Four Months
sections.dateline: Pelletier Cottage, Helen Hill, Saranac Lake, New York · June 1925
sections.text: Mrs. Pelletier's was a tall brown house on Helen Hill with three porches stacked on the front of it, one to a floor, and twelve cure chairs on the porches. Fourteen people boarded there that year at twenty-two dollars a week with trays. They had come up from offices and schoolrooms and one from a ribbon counter in Utica, each with a spot on an X-ray plate, to lie out of doors eight hours a day in every weather the Adirondacks had and wait for the lung to heal. It was called curing. A person was on the cure, or cheating the cure, and the whole of medicine was in the difference. Miss Agnes Thayer had the front room on the first floor. She was fifty-four. She had taught Greek and Latin for twenty-two years at a girls' school downstate, and she had been in Saranac Lake for nine, which made her what the village called a chronic. Every afternoon when rest hour was over and the four o'clock temperatures were written down, she read aloud from her chair on the bottom porch until the supper trays came. She read Plato, in Jowett's English, a volume at a time. Whoever was allowed out of bed came down in coats and blankets to hear it, and those who were not lay on the porches above and got what

sections.heading: II. The North End
sections.text: Nobody ate. The old hands, the ones with three and four winters in, went quiet and were suddenly particular about their own hours, since they knew to the week what four months was. The new ones cried where they sat. The girl from Utica cried so that she brought on a cough, and had to be put to bed. For days afterward they stood about in twos and threes on the stair landings, where they were not supposed to stand at all, and asked each other what was to be done. A great deal was done. There was a list on the hall table of who would sit with her, hour by hour, so that she should never be on the porch alone. The women sewed balsam pillows, the kind the village sold to tourists, until she had eleven. There were flowers from the florist every Saturday. A subscription went round for a shelf of the classics in her name at the Free Library, and a man on the second floor who had been a sign painter lettered the plate for it. Her porch was full from the minute she was wheeled out, and they talked to her, kindly and without stopping, and when she read now they sat so close that the ones upstairs heard nothing. Even rest hour was whispered through. It tired her a good deal, and she thanked the

sections.heading: III. No Feeling
sections.text: On the seventh of October Christy Mathewson died in his house up on Park Avenue, and for a week there was not a cut flower to be had in the village at any price. Pelletier Cottage found chrysanthemums for her anyway. It was the sign painter and two of the women who said it to her at last, and they meant it kindly. Mr. Tice has no feeling for you at all, Miss Thayer. Four months, and he has not come down those stairs. He hasn't signed the list. He never so much as put his name to the shelf. She asked whether Mr. Tice still kept his hours. They said he kept nothing else. Ask him to come down tomorrow at half past four. If his chart allows. He came down in his overcoat with his blanket over his arm. She was propped on a back-rest with the eleven pillows ranged along the porch rail behind her and the chrysanthemums in a pail, and she had gone the color of the pages she read from. All fourteen were there, and they made room for him grudgingly. Mr. Tice. I am told you have kept away from me since June. Why is that? It was the first he had spoken to any of them in four months, and his voice was not used to it. You said four months. I'd been here seven and never cured a day. I liked your h

sections.heading: IV. Four O'Clock
sections.dateline: The same porch, and the top one
sections.text: She kept him back when the trays came and the others had gone in. What is it like, up at your end? He tried to tell her and could not. He said it was like the house after everybody has gone to the pictures. He said that was wrong, too. It is in here, she said, and turned back sixty pages without having to look for it, and read it to him alone, with the light going. But when returning into herself she reflects, then she passes into the other world, the region of purity, and eternity, and immortality, and unchangeableness, which are her kindred, and with them she ever lives, when she is by herself and is not let or hindered; then she ceases from her erring ways, and being in communion with the unchanging is unchanging. And this state of the soul is called wisdom? — Plato, Phaedo, tr. Benjamin Jowett He had sat down on the porch step to listen. When she stopped he found that it had stayed, the thing that stayed some afternoons, and that it was not going to go. He had been afraid since a doctor in Hartford held a plate up to a window and showed him the spot. He had been afraid of her dying, all summer, two floors over her head. He looked for the fear now where he was used to finding it

title: The Cure Chair
logline: In a tuberculosis cure cottage, a dying classics teacher has four months left, and one boarder stops coming down to hear her read.

verses.text: The sight of the elect (Arya) is good, to live with them is always happiness; if a man does not see fools, he will be truly happy.
He who walks in the company of fools suffers a long way; company with fools, as with an enemy, is always painful; company with the wise is pleasure, like meeting with kinsfolk.
Therefore, one ought to follow the wise, the intelligent, the learned, the much enduring, the dutiful, the elect; one ought to follow a good and wise man, as the moon follows the path of the stars.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha lies ill with dysentery near the end of his life at the village of Beḷuva. Sakka, king of the gods, lays aside his immense heavenly body and comes to rub the Buddha’s feet. The Buddha tells him that to the gods the smell of human beings is like carrion and sends him away, but Sakka answers that he smelled the fragrance of the Buddha’s goodness from 84,000 leagues off. He lets no one else touch the vessel of excrement, and carries it out on his head as if it held perfume, without a flicker of disgust. When the monks marvel, the Buddha explains that Sakka once came to him in terror of death, led by the celestial musician Pañcasikha, who played at the cave entrance; the Buddha invited him to ask any question, answered him, and Sakka was transformed from Old Sakka into Young Sakka. Sakka’s first question, in the Sakkapañha Sutta, is why beings who wish to live without hatred live in hatred, and the answer is envy and avarice.
bg.history:
Nashville’s gay bars were where the city’s first response to AIDS took shape. Warehouse 28, a dance club opened in 1978, held drag shows and auctions whose proceeds helped found Nashville CARES in 1985; its co-owner Steve Smith, a co-founder of CARES, died of AIDS in 1995. A regular there remembered going to two funerals a week, and sometimes three, in the worst years. Before effective treatment, intestinal infections such as cryptosporidiosis, which pass in a few weeks in a healthy person, could cause relentless diarrhea and wasting in people with AIDS. Fear of contagion was widespread, and some hospital staff in those years would not enter patients’ rooms.

Country music in the early 1980s was being remade by the Urban Cowboy boom and a younger generation of singers, and the established stars of the Grand Ole Opry, which had moved from the Ryman Auditorium to Opryland in 1974, felt it. The rhinestone stage suits of the era came from North Hollywood, from the shop of Nudie Cohn and his tailors. Every spring from 1969 to 1991 the promoter Mervyn Conn brought Nashville acts to London for the International Festival of Country Music at Wembley. Dean Sackett, Glory Darlene and the Satin Slipper are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Bellevue
sections.text: By Easter she could not get to the bathroom anymore, so the girls rented a hospital bed from the medical supply on Charlotte Pike and set it up in the front room of the little house in Bellevue, where the window looked out on the dogwood and the light was best. They took her bed apart and leaned it against the wall of the back bedroom. They hung her dresses in that closet, all of them, the sequins and the beaded gowns and the white fox stole, so she could see them through the door if she turned her head. Her name on the lease was Clayton Bivens. She had been born in Marshall County in 1936 and raised in the Church of Christ, where they sang without instruments because the New Testament did not mention any, and she had a voice that could hold a note under a tin roof until the old men looked up from their hymnals. She did hair on Belmont Boulevard for thirty years. On Friday and Saturday nights for fifteen of them she had been Miss Glory Darlene at the Satin Slipper off Second Avenue, and before that at places with no names, in basements, in the back rooms of beer joints out on the Murfreesboro Road where you went in through the kitchen. She had taken in more children than anyone cou

sections.heading: II. The Visitor
sections.text: A little after midnight on the Tuesday after Easter a white rental car pulled into the gravel by the carport. Luis looked through the blind and saw a man get out in a tan windbreaker and a seed cap, with no luggage, and stand in the yard a moment looking at the dark house. Then the man came up the steps and knocked very softly, the way you knock when you know someone is sick. Luis opened the door, and then he stood there with it open and could not say anything at all. The man nodded to him and went past him into the front room. He took off the seed cap and held it. Glory was asleep, or near it, with her mouth open and her hands on top of the sheet. He went to the foot of the bed and lifted the sheet back from her feet, which were swollen, grey and cold. He took one of them in both his hands and began to rub it slowly, the heel, the arch, then each toe. She opened her eyes. Who is that? It’s Dean, Mama. She lifted her head an inch off the pillow and looked at him down the length of the bed. His hair had gone grey since she had seen him. He had a three-day beard and a paper cup of gas station coffee balanced on the footboard. What in the world are you doing here? Come to see about yo

sections.heading: III. The Kitchen
sections.text: The girls sat around the kitchen table that afternoon with the coffee going cold and could not leave it alone. Dean Sackett, Danny said. Dean Sackett emptied that pan. With his own hands. Like it was perfume, said Luis. Like it was a box of chocolates. Did you see his face? I couldn’t do that with my face. I love her more than my own mother and I couldn’t do that with my face. That man has got a hundred people working for him, said Marva. He has got people to carry his guitar. He has got people to carry his coffee from the bus to the stage. She turned her cup around. Three days. He wouldn’t let me near her. He must love her, said Luis. He must love her to death. Y’all come in here, Glory called from the front room. Her voice was stronger than it had been in a week. I can hear every word you’re saying. They came in and stood around the bed, and Marva sat on the edge of it, and Glory looked at them. It isn’t any wonder he loves me, she said. Sit down. I’ll tell you why.

sections.heading: IV. The Question
sections.dateline: The Satin Slipper, off Second Avenue · 1981
sections.text: In the spring of 1981, she told them, Dean Sackett was dying. Not in his body. In the other way, the way the big stars die. He had not had a record in the top forty in three years. The young ones in hats were coming up behind him. At the Opry the flowers they sent to his dressing room wilted before the second show. The Thousand Eyes, which had been white, had gone a little yellow under the arms, and he sweated through it now under the lights in a way he never used to. The stones did not shine the way they had. He could not sit still. He would get up from a chair in the middle of a sentence and walk around the room. He had started waking at three in the morning in the house on the lake with his heart going like a bird against a window, sure he was going to die, and he did not know whether he was afraid of dying or afraid that he was already dead. He had a doctor in Hendersonville and a preacher in Hendersonville and they did not help. His banjo player was a skinny man from Sparta named Lonnie Pruitt, whom everybody called Five, for the five-string. Five had been playing behind him for nineteen years. Five was also one of Glory’s, from way back, from the beer-joint days, though nobod

sections.heading: V. Company
sections.text: She had them help her up higher on the pillows. The light through the dogwood was going orange. She looked at each of them a while, Marva and Danny and Luis and the two others who had come in from work, the way she used to look at them in the dressing-room mirror before they went on, checking. Listen to me now, she said. I’m going to tell you this once and I want you to remember it when I’m not here to say it. They waited. It’s a good thing just to look at good people. You don’t have to do anything. Just get where you can see them. And it’s a better thing to live with them. You stay away from fools. I don’t mean dumb, I mean fools. A fool will cost you twenty years and you won’t even know you paid it. Living with a fool is like living with somebody who hates you. Living with somebody good is like coming home to your people. She smiled at them. Your real people. The ones you get to pick. Then she asked them to sing. Not one of them would have known a hymn from a hole in the ground except Danny, who had been raised Free Will Baptist in Clay County, and Glory herself. But she started it, low, with no piano, the way they did it in Marshall County with the tuning fork, and Danny came in

title: Thousand Eyes
logline: A country star flies home from London to nurse the dying drag queen who once answered his question in a dressing room.

verses.text: He who gives himself to vanity, and does not give himself to meditation, forgetting the real aim (of life) and grasping at pleasure, will in time envy him who has exerted himself in meditation.
Let no man ever look for what is pleasant, or what is unpleasant. Not to see what is pleasant is pain, and it is pain to see what is unpleasant.
Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil. Those who love nothing and hate nothing, have no fetters.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the only son of a household at Sāvatthī hears monks give thanks after a meal and wants to go forth. His parents refuse and guard him by turns. One day his mother sits in the doorway spinning, a foot against each doorpost; he asks her to move her foot so he can relieve himself, and runs to the monastery. His father follows, weeps, and becomes a monk himself. His mother follows and becomes a nun. But the three cannot stay apart, and spend their days sitting and talking together, until the monks and nuns complain. The Buddha tells them this is not how those who have gone forth should live, and speaks the three verses. Many who hear them are helped. The three, saying they cannot live without each other, go back to the household life.
bg.history:
The Labadists were followers of Jean de Labadie, a former Jesuit turned Reformed preacher, who gathered a community of the "elect" that held all goods in common and lived apart from the world. Its best-known member was the scholar Anna Maria van Schurman, who died in the mother house at Wieuwerd in Friesland in 1678. In 1683 two envoys, Peter Sluyter and Jasper Danckaerts, obtained some 3,750 acres of Augustine Herrman's Bohemia Manor in Cecil County, Maryland, and founded a daughter colony that grew to a little over a hundred people, many of them Dutch converts from New York. Members surrendered their property on entering and left empty-handed; men and women ate at separate tables; marriage and parenthood were subordinated to the house. The supper with the hats is described by the English Quaker minister Samuel Bownas, who visited in the first years of the 1700s. The rebuke for "fleshly cleavings" and the fireless cells come from a hostile former member, Peter Dittelbach, writing in 1692. Both are quoted in Bartlett B. James, The Labadist Colony in Maryland (1899).

Danckaerts's journal of 1679–80 condemns both tobacco and slavery, but the Maryland house grew tobacco with enslaved African labor. In 1698 Sluyter divided most of the tract among the leading members and kept a neck of land for himself; he died wealthy in 1722, and within a few years the community was gone. The cooper's family and Geertje Wybes are invented. The Theologia Germanica, an anonymous German treatise of the fourteenth century that Luther sent to the press, was read by Protestant pietists for centuries afterward; it is quoted here in Susanna Winkworth's English of 1854.

sections.heading: I. The Stoep
sections.text: Teunis Joosten was a cooper at Midwout, and he and his wife Marritje had buried four children in the churchyard there and kept one. The one was Joost, seventeen, who could already raise a tight barrel and who had never in his life been out of sight of both of them at once. In April two men came up from the Bohemia River in Maryland to sell linen thread in New York, and a neighbor who had dealings with them asked Teunis to give them a bed. They were brethren of the Labadie house on the Manor, plain men in coarse cloth. Marritje fed them. When they had eaten, the older one took off his hat and sat. After a while the younger took off his. Neither said a word for half a quarter of an hour, and the family, not knowing what was wanted, sat too. Then the older man put his hat on and said a few words to the table, low, as if they were for the bread. He said that everyone under this roof had been lent to the others for a little while, that the Lender was good, and that a heart could be set where nothing was ever called back. Teunis thought it a long grace for after supper. Marritje thought they looked underfed. Joost did not sleep, and in the morning, when the two men had gone down to the f

sections.heading: II. Gone In
sections.dateline: Bohemia Manor, Cecil County, Maryland · summer 1702
sections.text: Where is he? Teunis said, with the staves still on his shoulder. He was here but a moment ago. He looked in the loft and the shop and the church. Then he said, The Manor, and he found a sloop bound for the South River, and at New Castle he took the cart road that old Herrman had cut across to the Bohemia, twenty miles through oak woods, on foot. The Labadie house stood on a neck of good land above the river, a great plain dwelling with its barns, and around it the plantation: corn, flax and hemp, cattle, and tobacco. The tobacco was worked by Africans the house had bought. The two brethren who had first come spying out the country had written down their horror of that trade, and of tobacco too, and their house now did both. He found his son in a row of men pulling flax, in the coarse dress of the house, with his own good coat gone into the common chest. Teunis stood at the end of the row and wept like a child. Joost. Joost, why do you undo me? The boy went red to the ears and went on pulling. Nobody stopped work. Teunis wept until he was done, and sat down on the headland, and looked at his son's back going away from him up the row. After a time a thought came to him that he had no

sections.heading: III. The Retting Pond
sections.text: They were upwards of a hundred in that family, men, women and children. The men ate at one long table and the women at another, in a different room. An English Friend who was given supper with the men about that time wrote down how it went: when the food was in, one man pulled off his hat, and after a space another, and so on down the benches until all sat bare-headed and silent, each praying when he was moved to and not before, and then the hats went back on one by one and each man fell to eating without regard for those still uncovered. The children were taught together under a tutor. It was told of the house in its first years that a mother who kissed her own child there had been rebuked for showing so naturally her fleshly cleavings, and that the cells had been kept without fire in winter while wood was burned in the fields to be rid of it. Some of that had slackened. The tables had not. For three days Teunis, Marritje and Joost kept the order of the house. On the fourth, at the hour after the noon meal when a brother might walk by himself and examine his heart, the three of them walked by themselves to the same place. The place was the bank of the retting pond. The pulled flax

sections.heading: IV. The Cell
sections.dateline: The sisters' side · an evening in September
sections.text: Geertje Wybes was past seventy. As a young wife in Amsterdam she had heard Jean de Labadie preach, and she had followed his people to Herford and Altona and at last to the castle at Wieuwerd in Friesland, where she kept the sickroom of Juffrouw van Schurman, the most learned woman in Europe, until that lady died. Then she had crossed the ocean with the first company. It was said in the house that the Father's hearth was never cold. Hers had never been lit, and nobody had told her to keep it so. She spun flax all day by the one window and owned the stool she sat on only in the sense that no one else wanted it. She sent for the three of them. They stood in her cell in a row. They tell me you sit on the pond bank every day and talk, the three of you. Is it true? It is true, moeder, said Teunis. Why do you do it? It is not the way of people who have come out. Teunis turned his hat around in his hands. We had five. Four are in the churchyard at Midwout. This one we counted every night of his life, before the candle was put out, the way you count the one coin you have. Moeder Geertje, we cannot live apart. We would keep your rule. We do not know how to be where we cannot see him. Nor he

sections.heading: V. The Cart Road
sections.dateline: The road to New Castle · the next morning
sections.text: The three sat on the pond bank one more time, before light, and nobody had to say much. She is right, Teunis said. I heard it and I knew she was right. And at supper I was looking down the bench again to see had he got bread. I watched her spin, said Marritje. She has a daughter somewhere who is past forty and she does not know if the girl has a tooth in her head. I could not do it. I do not want to be able to do it. Joost had been in the house four months. He looked a long time at the row of men going out to the hemp with their hoes on their shoulders, not one of them turning his head to see who was beside him. Then he looked at his mother's hands. Nor I, he said. Not yet. They went up and told the house they were leaving. The rule held for going as it had for coming. The shop at Midwout, the tools, the money from the house and forty years of barrels stayed in the common stock. They were given back the clothes they had walked in with. Marritje asked for her distaff, and was told it had been put to use on the sisters' side, and she let it go. Geertje Wybes did not come to the door. She had flax on the wheel. They went down old Herrman's road toward New Castle with nothing to carry,

title: Empty-Handed
logline: A Long Island cooper and his wife follow their only son into a Dutch commune that seats husbands and wives at separate tables.

verses.text: From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear.

bg.commentary: Müller's "pleasure" renders the Pāli piya, what is dear or beloved. In the commentary, a householder who has lost his son goes every day to the burning ground and weeps. The Buddha comes to his house and asks why he is sad, tells him that death is not confined to one place or one person, and relates the Uraga Jātaka: a farmer whose son is killed by a snake while burning rubbish in the field sends home for dinner for one instead of two, and the whole family burns the body without a tear. Sakka, king of the gods, comes down to ask each of them why they do not weep, hears their answers (the cast-off snakeskin, the guest who came unbidden, the child crying for the moon, the broken pot) and fills their house with treasure. The Buddha then tells the father that grief and fear arise only from what is dear.
bg.history:
From 1853 several thousand Walloon-speaking Belgians, many from around Grez-Doiceau in Brabant, took up government land at $1.25 an acre in Brown, Kewaunee and Door counties, Wisconsin. They cleared it by rolling logs into heaps and burning them, shaved shingles by hand for cash, and, with priests scarce, chose one of their own number to read the Mass prayers and the Sunday Gospel. After a rainless summer, the fires of land-clearing, logging and railroad building ran together on the night of October 8, 1871. The Peshtigo fire west of Green Bay killed well over a thousand people, more than any other fire in American history; a separate firestorm the same night burned a strip some sixty miles long through the Belgian settlements east of the bay. At the shingle-mill hamlet of Williamsonville, about sixty of seventy-seven residents died, thirty-five of them in the potato patch where they had taken refuge; five of seven men who went down the well survived. The place was never rebuilt and is now Tornado Memorial County Park.

Relief was landed from tugs at Dyckesville and carried inland, and it kept coming for eighteen months. The burned timberland became farmland, and the peninsula turned from lumber to wheat and dairying. To the south, near Green Bay, people who had sheltered through the night at Adele Brise's chapel at Robinsonville found its grounds untouched; it is now the National Shrine of Our Lady of Champion. Essartage, the cutting and burning of broom and coppice to sow rye in the ash, was practiced in the Belgian Ardennes into the nineteenth century. The Colignons and Hubert Bodart are invented. The Confessions are quoted in E. B. Pusey's English of 1838.

sections.heading: I. The Ground
sections.dateline: Door County, Wisconsin · October and November 1871
sections.text: All that summer everybody burned. There had been next to no snow in the winter and next to no rain since, and a man with forty acres of maple and hemlock standing between himself and a crop did what he did every year. He rolled the logs into heaps of twenty and thirty, set them alight, and let them go for days. The railroad gangs burned their slash and the mills burned their edgings. By September the smoke lay so thick on Green Bay that the boats steered by compass at noon, and ash came down on the washing, and nobody stopped, because wheat does not grow under trees. Lambert Colignon burned his heaps with the rest. He had come out from the commune of Grez in Brabant in 1856 with a wife and a boy in arms, had paid a dollar and a quarter an acre, and in fifteen years had got eleven acres clear, a hewn-log house, and a yoke of oxen. The boy in arms was Jules, seventeen now. In the spring Lambert had sent him four miles north to Williamson's shingle mill, because the mill paid in money and the farm did not. On Sunday night the eighth of October the wind got up out of the southwest, and all the little fires became one fire. It came through the Belgian settlement faster than a horse can

sections.heading: II. The Reader
sections.dateline: The Colignon clearing · a morning of wet snow
sections.text: In the years when a priest reached the settlement four times in twelve months, the people chose one of their own to read the prayers of the Mass and the Gospel of the Sunday aloud in somebody's house. The one they chose was Hubert Bodart, because he had had two years at the little seminary at Floreffe before his father died and the farm called him home. He was near seventy now and a shingle shaver, with the callus of the drawknife across both palms. He also wrote what needed writing. He had written the settlement's letters home for twenty years, and now he was writing its lists for the relief, house by house: what was burned, and who. His own house was gone like everybody's. He had carried two books out of it inside his shirt and had lain on them in a plowed field. He came up the Colignon track before Lambert had set out. Lambert saw him and thought, He wants the boy's name and age for his paper. And he will say what one says. He turned the washtub over for the old man, since it was the one seat they had, and stood. Hubert sat down. He did not take out his paper. Lambert. Why are you sad? Lambert looked at him. The country was black from Sturgeon Bay to the Red River road. It was a

sections.heading: III. The Essart
sections.dateline: The hills above the Meuse · in the old time
sections.text: Above the Meuse, toward the Ardenne, the soil on the hilltops is thin and sour, and the people there worked it this way. Every eighteen or twenty years they cut the broom and scrub oak off a piece of the hill, let it dry where it fell, burned it on the spot and sowed rye in the warm ash. A piece of hill so burned they called an essart. It gave one crop of rye and then went back to broom. There was a man there named Bastin, who had a wife, a son, a daughter, the son's young wife and a servant girl, so that they were six at table. Bastin had one saying, and the five had heard it since they could hear. Everything lent is called for. He said it over the soup and at sowing. You are lent, I am lent, the cow is lent. Be good to what is lent and do not be astonished when it is called for. He made them say it back to him. They came to think of it every day of their lives, the way people think of the weather. One spring Bastin and his son went up to burn their essart. The son raked the dry broom into rows and fired it. At the edge of the piece was a heap of field stones with an adder in it, and the smoke got into her eyes. She came out in a fury and struck the first thing she met, which was

sections.heading: IV. The Book
sections.dateline: The Colignon clearing · the same morning
sections.text: They were made of wood, Lambert said. I said the same to my grandmother. She hit me with the spoon. And you, Hubert? In the sickness year you buried Ferdinande and two of the children in one week. I helped carry. You howled like a dog on the road. I did. I am not Bastin. I did not walk up here to tell you I am Bastin. The old man looked at the lean-to, the cold ashes, the axe with rust starting on it. But see what you do. You have put down your work. You do not eat. Your wife raises other men's walls alone and sleeps under burnt boards. And every day you go and stand in that field as if he were kept there. He is not kept there, Lambert. Bastin at least knew where his son was not. He took out the smaller of his two books. This is a bishop in Africa, fourteen hundred years ago. When he was young the friend of his heart died of a fever, and he went about just as you do. He hated every place because the friend was not in it. He wondered that other people had the face to go on living. Afterward he worked out what had happened to him. He read it out slowly, putting it into Walloon as he went. For whence had that former grief so easily reached my very inmost soul, but that I had poured ou

sections.heading: V. June
sections.text: They had a roof by Christmas, of relief boards. In the spring there was nothing to clear. The fire had done in one night what Lambert would have done in thirty years, and he put the one ox beside a borrowed one and sowed wheat in the ash between the black stumps, on more ground than he had ever had open. Everybody in the settlement did the same. Nobody called it a gift. In June he walked north once more, the first time since the snow. Nothing had been built at Williamson's and nothing would be. The potato patch had come up. Not all of it. But here and there along the baked ridges, where a tuber had lain deep enough when the fire went over, dark green tops stood out of the ground, and a few were in flower. Nobody had planted them and nobody was going to dig them. He stood at the edge for a time. He did not weep, which surprised him, and then did not surprise him. He said the boy's name once, aloud. Then, having no hoe with him, he went down the nearest row on his knees and drew the earth up around each plant with his hands, the way they are hilled. When he had done the one row he got up and went home to his own.

title: The Potato Ground
logline: After the great fire of 1871, a Belgian farmer walks every day to the potato patch where his son died, until the settlement's old reader comes up the track.

verses.text: From affection comes grief, from affection comes fear; he who is free from affection knows neither grief nor fear.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the great laywoman Visākhā, chief patron of the Buddha’s order at Sāvatthī, lets her son’s daughter Dattā serve the monks in her house whenever she is away. Dattā dies. Visākhā sees to the body, then comes to the Buddha weeping: the girl was faithful and true, and she will never see her like again. The Buddha asks how many people live in Sāvatthī (she has heard him say seventy million), whether she would wish all of them as dear to her as Dattā (yes), and how many die there each day (a great many). Then, he says, she would have no time to do anything but weep, by night and by day. Grief and fear both spring from affection, and he speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Bell Telephone Laboratories built its Holmdel research center on former farmland in Monmouth County between 1959 and 1962, to a design by Eero Saarinen: a single block about a thousand feet long, its glass walls refitted with mirror glass in the later 1960s, with a reflecting pool in front and a water tower that locals likened to a transistor (Bell Labs Holmdel Complex). Its second phase opened in December 1966. Up the road on Crawford Hill, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, working with the lab’s horn antenna, removed nesting pigeons and their droppings while hunting a persistent microwave noise that came from every direction; in 1965 they published it, and it was understood as the cosmic microwave background, left over from the beginning of the universe. Telephone traffic engineering rested on the work of the Danish mathematician A. K. Erlang, whose 1909 paper showed that calls arrive at random at a steady average rate. Monmouth County grew from about 334,000 people in 1960 to about 462,000 in 1970; the U.S. crude death rate in 1966 was about 9.5 per thousand. The open-air Monmouth Shopping Center in Eatontown, anchored by Bamberger’s, opened in 1960.

American Baptists had worked in Burma since Adoniram Judson arrived in 1813, especially among the Karen and Kachin peoples. In 1966, under General Ne Win’s military government, the remaining foreign missionaries were made to leave the country (Baptist Standard). The American Baptist mission boards had moved in 1962 to a new round headquarters at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, nicknamed the “Holy Doughnut” (Visit KOP). Edith’s name for her guest room comes from the Shunammite woman of 2 Kings 4, who built a room for the prophet Elisha. Lotte reads from the note to Proposition 20 in Part V of Spinoza’s Ethics (1677).

sections.heading: I. The Prophet’s Chamber
sections.text: Ray Conover’s people had grown apples on the rise above Holmdel Road for a hundred and forty years, and in 1959, the year the telephone company began building on the potato fields across Crawfords Corner Road, Ray sold the orchard to a builder from Matawan and kept the house. The builder took out the Winesaps and the Staymans and put in nine split-levels around a circle of new asphalt, and named the circle after what he had cut down. The Conover house stood at the head of it, white clapboard, a century older than anything else on the street, with a horse chestnut in the yard and a back bedroom over the kitchen that Edith Conover called the prophet’s chamber. She had the name from Second Kings, from the woman of Shunem who told her husband to build a little room on the wall for the man of God, with a bed in it and a table and a stool and a candlestick, so that he would have a place to turn in when he passed. Edith had a spool bed, a maple dresser, a cane-bottomed chair and a reading lamp, and a guest book on the dresser with eighty-one names in it by 1966: missionaries home on furlough from the Congo and Assam and the Philippines, a Telugu pastor, two Karen schoolteachers, a deaf ev

sections.heading: II. Route 35
sections.text: On the twenty-second of October, a Saturday, it rained from morning on. Dorrie closed out her register at half past nine and drove north on Route 35 in the Rambler, and a southbound car crossed the center line. She died in the hospital in Red Bank a little after midnight, with Glenn and her mother beside the bed and Edith in the corridor on a plastic chair, holding her pocketbook on her knees with both hands. Edith did everything. That was what she was for. She called the pastor and the funeral director and the florist. She chose the casket, and the blue dress from Easter, and the hymns. She sat on the edge of the bed with Glenn’s wife, who could not hold a pencil, and made the list of who had to be called and called them. She set the women to work in the fellowship hall, and saw that the big urn was filled and the egg salad made and the folding chairs put out in rows. The Mabrys came up on the train from Philadelphia. Lotte Seligman came in a black hat and sat in the last pew, and stood when the others stood, and did not sing. Then it was done. The chairs were stacked against the wall, the urn was rinsed and turned upside down on the drainboard, and Edith went home to the house at

sections.heading: III. Eleven
sections.text: Lotte was at the kitchen table with a pad of green engineering paper and a slide rule and a cup of coffee gone cold, working. She did not seem surprised. She moved the pad over to make room, and Edith sat down, not across from her but a little to one side, the way you sit in a doctor’s office, and put her face in her hands. Lotte let her cry for some time. Then she said, Edith. Why are you sitting in my kitchen in your nightgown, crying like this? So Edith told her. She said what she had not said to anybody, not to Glenn, not to the pastor: that the girl had been dearer to her than her own son. That she was faithful and true. That every missionary on every boat in the world could come through the prophet’s chamber, and she would never see the like of her again. Lotte listened to all of it. Then she turned the green pad around and picked up her pencil. How many people live in Monmouth County? I’ve heard you say. Four hundred thousand. Four hundred and twenty, now. Lotte wrote it at the top of the page. Suppose every one of them was as dear to you as Dorrie. Every one. Would you like that? Edith thought of the Mabrys, and the Telugu pastor, and the deaf man preaching with his hands.

title: Eleven a Day
logline: On a cul-de-sac built over an apple orchard, a Baptist widow who keeps a room for missionaries crosses the circle at night to a Bell Labs statistician.

verses.text: From lust comes grief, from lust comes fear; he who is free from lust knows neither grief nor fear.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest. On a festival day the Licchavi princes of Vesālī ride out to a pleasure garden in such finery that the Buddha, passing on his alms round, tells the monks that anyone who has never seen the gods of the Thirty-Three should look at them. On the way the princes take a courtesan along with them, fall to fighting over her, and “set flowing as it were a river of blood”; by afternoon they are being carried home on beds. When the monks remark on the change, the Buddha answers that grief and fear arise only from delight.
bg.history:
In the 1980s and 1990s, the hillside suburbs of the eastern San Gabriel Valley drew so many wealthy immigrants from Taiwan that Rowland Heights was known as “Little Taipei,” anchored by the 99 Ranch Market that opened at Gale Avenue and Nogales Street in 1989. Next door in Hacienda Heights, the Fo Guang Shan order completed Hsi Lai Temple in 1988. Many families were “astronauts,” with a parent shuttling across the Pacific, and some sent children over alone as “parachute kids”; a 1990 UCLA study estimated there were 40,000 Taiwanese parachute kids in the United States. As the Taipei Times later reported, they lived in arrangements ranging from unsupervised to the care of a relative or paid guardian, and some sons were sent abroad partly to avoid military conscription.

Part of what drove parents was fear of the Mainland. During the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis, the People’s Liberation Army fired missiles into the waters near Taiwan in July 1995 and again in March 1996, when missiles splashed down off the ports of Keelung and Kaohsiung and the United States sent two carrier groups to the area. Flights from Taiwan to North America filled. On March 23, 1996, Lee Teng-hui won Taiwan’s first direct presidential election. Lin Lǎoshī’s schooling spans the island’s language politics: Japanese rule until 1945, then decades of Mandarin-only policy in schools, under which students who spoke Taiwanese were fined, punished or humiliated.

sections.heading: I. The House on the Hill
sections.text: Lin Lǎoshī had learned three languages in one life and been allowed to teach in none of them that she dreamed in. She was born in Tainan in 1925, when the island belonged to Japan, and in the years when the Japanese wanted everyone on the island to become Japanese she learned to think in Taiwanese and answer in Japanese. After the war the Japanese left and the Mainlanders came, and she learned Mandarin at twenty from a radio, sitting on the floor of her father’s pharmacy with a dictionary, and became good enough at it to teach the old literature, the classical texts, at a girls’ high school in Tainan for forty years. In those years the girls were fined if they spoke Taiwanese at school. She collected the fines. She had never once in her life spoken to a classroom in the language she dreamed in, and she did not think about it much, the way you do not think about a tooth you lost a long time ago, except with your tongue. In the summer of 1994 her niece called from Taipei. The niece’s husband made computer monitors, and they were rich now in the way people in Taiwan had become rich in those years, suddenly and a little afraid of it. Two years before, they had sent their sons to Califo

sections.heading: II. The Eve
sections.dateline: The house on the hill · February 18, 1996
sections.text: On New Year’s Eve the parents did not come. They telephoned instead, from Taipei, one after another, at seven in the evening California time, which was eleven in the morning of New Year’s Day there already, so that the boys were talking to a day that had already happened. Kai-wen’s father said the trip was impossible this year, with the factory. He did not say the other thing. Everyone knew the other thing. Since the summer, the Mainland had been firing missiles into the sea off the island, testing, it said, and everyone in Taipei with money had a son somewhere, or a house somewhere, or a passport somewhere, and the flights to Los Angeles and Vancouver were full. Stay where you are, the father said. Study. Listen to Auntie. Lin Lǎoshī made the reunion dinner anyway, for three boys and herself. She made it the way her mother had made it: a whole fish, because the word for fish sounds like the word for more than enough, and you leave some of it uneaten so there will be more than enough next year too; long-stemmed mustard greens, uncut, for long life; a hot pot on the table, because the family sits around the fire. The boys ate a great deal and said very little. At the end of the meal

sections.heading: III. The Gods
sections.text: The first day of the Year of the Rat fell that year on the same Monday as the American holiday for the presidents, so there was no school, and the whole hill seemed to be awake early. Firecrackers went off down in the valley. Somebody’s grandfather on the next street was playing a cassette of the New Year songs too loud. At nine o’clock the princes came for Kai-wen. They came up the hill one after another, a red sports car that sat low as a cat, a white car with a spoiler, a silver one, a black one like Kai-wen’s, and parked in a crescent in front of the house with their engines running. They got out. They were dressed, every one of them, in new clothes from head to foot, as the custom was, and the custom had never seen anything like it. Silk shirts in black and red and gold. Linen jackets the color of milk. A long coat on one boy, in February, in Southern California, because it was beautiful. Gold watches. Gold chains. Their hair cut the day before and shining. Kai-wen came out of the house in the black and gold shirt and they cheered him, and he spread his arms and turned around once on the step, laughing, so the gold caught the sun. Lin Lǎoshī came out behind him with the foldin

sections.heading: IV. Wendy
sections.dateline: Colima Road, and the house on the ridge · the same day
sections.text: Her name was Chen Hsiao-ling and at the Golden Bell KTV in the strip mall on Colima Road they called her Wendy, which she had chosen herself out of a book of English names, because it was a name from a children’s story about a girl who flew away. She was twenty-two. She came from Chiayi, where her mother sold betel nut from a glass booth by the highway. She had come over on a student visa to study English at a college in Pomona and studied, mornings, and worked, nights, singing with men in the private rooms of the Golden Bell, sitting beside them on the leather couches and pouring their cognac and laughing when they sang badly, which was always. The men tipped in cash. She sent eight hundred dollars a month to Chiayi. She had never once been out of the valley except to the airport. She was sitting outside the bakery in the plaza on Colima Road on New Year’s morning with a coffee and a pineapple cake, in the red dress she had bought for the New Year, not for work, for herself, when the five cars came into the parking lot, and Jason Hsu got out of the red one, whom she knew from the Golden Bell. He tipped well and sang worst of anybody. Wendy. Happy New Year. Come swim. She said she

sections.heading: V. The Litters
sections.text: Lin Lǎoshī and the boys had eaten their New Year lunch at the auntie’s restaurant in the plaza: turnip cake, and noodles for long life, and the sweet rice cake that sticks, for the year to be higher than the last one. The auntie would not take any money because it was New Year, and Lin Lǎoshī took a poem out of her purse that she had copied the night before, a short one by Du Fu about spring, and the auntie taped it up by the register. Then, because the day was warm and the boys were full and restless, she let them talk her into walking home the long way, west along the foot of the hills toward the temple, so that they could look at its roofs, and then up. They heard the sirens before they saw anything. Then a sheriff’s car went past them up the ridge road very fast, and an ambulance, and then a fire truck, which Peter said was what they sent with the paramedics, and then another ambulance. Kai-li stopped on the sidewalk. That’s Jason’s street. A young woman came down the hill toward them on the other side of the road, in a red dress with dark wet patches coming through it, walking very straight in high heels, carrying nothing. Her hair was wet. She looked at them as she passed and

sections.heading: VI. Delight
sections.dateline: The hospital in Whittier, and the kitchen · that night
sections.text: Jason Hsu died at seven minutes after six in the evening, which was seven minutes after ten on the morning of the second day of the New Year in Taipei, while his mother was on the telephone to the hospital from the airport. Kai-wen had eleven stitches in his palm and two in his chin and would keep both scars all his life. Victor would not remember the day at all. Eric Wang was in the county jail, and his father was in the air. They drove home from the hospital in Kai-wen’s black car, with Kai-li driving on his learner’s permit, which was not legal, and Lin Lǎoshī beside him in front, which was not legal either, because she had decided it, and Kai-wen in the back with his hand in his lap like something somebody had handed him. Nobody had told the parents in Taipei yet. That was going to be Lin Lǎoshī’s job, tonight. In the kitchen she made rice porridge because it was what she knew how to make for people who could not eat. Kai-wen went to bed. Peter fell asleep at the table with his head on his arms. Kai-li sat across from her with the bowl in front of him, not eating, and after a long time he said it. This morning, he said, you said look at them. You said there go the gods. I looke

sections.heading: VII. The Shirt
sections.dateline: The house on the hill · February and March, 1996
sections.text: Jason Hsu went home to Taipei in the hold of a China Airlines plane, and his mother went with him. The legislator’s office said in the newspapers there that it was an accident in a swimming pool. Eric Wang’s father hired a lawyer from downtown who had been on television, and the parents of the boys who had been there flew in one after another and stayed at a hotel in the City of Industry and took their sons out to dinner and did not talk about it, and flew out again. On the second morning Lin Lǎoshī took the black and gold shirt out of the bag the hospital had put it in. She filled the laundry sink with cold water, because blood sets in hot water, her mother had taught her that in the pharmacy in Tainan, where people came in bleeding all the time, and she put in a handful of salt and the shirt and left it. She changed the water four times. The blood came out a little at a time, brown, then rust, then pink, then nothing, and the gold scrolls came up again out of the black, and the gold Greek heads, each one, looking off to the side the way they had in the store. logline: On Lunar New Year in Little Taipei, an old classics teacher watches six rich Taiwanese boys in new silk drive off to a hillside pool.

verses.text: From love comes grief, from love comes fear; he who is free from love knows neither grief nor fear.

bg.commentary: Müller's "love" is the Pāli kāma, sensual desire. In the commentary, the youth Anitthigandha ("no scent of woman") has come from the Brahma world and will not go near a woman from the day he is born; his mother must nurse him with a pillow between them. Pressed to marry, he has five hundred goldsmiths make a woman of red gold and says he will marry only her match. Brahmins carry the image from town to town until a nurse on her way to bathe mistakes it for her own charge and slaps it. The girl outshines the image, but she is so delicate that she dies in the carriage on the way to him. He asks every day whether she has arrived, is put off, and at last is told. The Buddha comes to the house, asks for him, and tells him where his grief comes from. Read the full commentary story. The same golden image is made, in another story, by the young man who became Mahā Kassapa.
bg.hist_title: Jain jewelers, a turnpike and a chatbot, 2025
bg.history:
Jains in the United States number somewhere above a hundred thousand, many of them Gujarati families in the gem, jewelry and hotel trades. The Hindu Jain Temple in Monroeville, outside Pittsburgh, opened in 1984 and houses Hindu and Jain shrines under one roof. Observant Jains fast during Paryushan, avoid onion, garlic and other roots, eat before sunset, and take care not to kill even insects. The scripture the assistant quotes is the Uttarādhyayana, one of the root texts of the Śvētāmbara canon, in Hermann Jacobi's translation for the Sacred Books of the East (volume 45, 1895); "colours," Jacobi notes, stands for everything the eye perceives. The Coral Sands hotel and the firm of Jhaveri Brothers are invented. The Clark Building on Liberty Avenue has long been the center of Pittsburgh's jewelry trade, and the bronze King Neptune has stood on the Virginia Beach boardwalk at 31st Street since 2005.

Red gold at eighteen karats is three parts gold to one of copper (see colored gold); jewelry today is commonly modeled on a computer, printed in wax and cast by the lost-wax method. The road from Virginia Beach to Monroeville ends on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, west from Breezewood through the Allegheny Mountain Tunnel and past the South Somerset service plaza. A leg cramp after hours of sitting can be the first sign of a deep vein thrombosis, a clot that may travel to the lungs. The carriage that jolted the girl in the commentary gave her "cramps."

sections.heading: I. The Pillow
sections.text: Virag Jhaveri was born in the winter of 1998, the first son of the second son of Jhaveri Brothers, and from his first day he would not be held by women. His aunts took it personally. He screamed when they lifted him and stopped when they set him down, and his grandmother, who had raised five children and buried one, told them to leave the boy be. It was Ba who thought of the pillow. His mother nursed him with a bed pillow propped between them so that all he saw was the pillow, and he fed quietly, and the aunts told it at weddings for twenty years. Ba's opinion was that he had come down from one of the high heavens, where there are no husbands and wives, and had not finished unpacking. She did not mean it as a complaint. He grew up easy to live with. He kept the fasts at Paryushan without being told. He ate before sunset after the rest of the house had gone slack about it, and he carried stinkbugs out of the kitchen on a postcard. He had friends at school and no girlfriends, and at Carnegie Mellon it was the same. Nobody could call him unhappy. He was like a room with the door shut and a light showing under it. The firm kept its office upstairs in the Clark Building on Liberty Avenu

sections.heading: II. The Boardwalk
sections.text: His parents sent for the travelers. Mr. Bhavsar and Mr. Doshi were both past sixty, and for thirty years they had driven the firm's sample line down the coast every spring and fall, from the stores on Oak Tree Road to the ones outside Atlanta. Virag's mother gave them tea and told them how she saw it. A boy like this did not earn his merit alone. Somewhere there is a girl who earned it beside him. Take that thing with you and find her. So they wrapped the figure in moving blankets and belted her upright in the back of the van. Wherever Gujaratis gathered that spring, they stood her near the door and sat down a little apart and listened. They stood her outside a derasar in New Jersey after the morning puja, and in the lobby of a wedding hall in Maryland, and beside the chaat counter of a grocery in Richmond. People asked whether it was Lakshmi. People asked what it weighed, and whether it was for showing necklaces. Nobody said the thing the two men were waiting to hear. They reached Virginia Beach in the third week of May and took a room on Atlantic Avenue. Early the next morning they wheeled her on a hand truck to the boardwalk at Thirty-first Street, where the big bronze Neptune s

sections.heading: III. The Turnpike
sections.text: They told Virag at dinner. He put down his spoon and asked Mr. Bhavsar, who had driven straight through, a question nobody had expected from him. Better how? Mr. Bhavsar thought about it. Yours, you look at, he said. This one looks back. There was one photograph, taken in the lobby on Mr. Doshi's phone. In it she was beside the figure and half turned away, saying something to someone out of the frame. There was one message, which came two days later from a Virginia number. Your statue has no kneecaps. I checked. Bring a chisel. He wrote nine answers and sent the shortest, I'll correct it, and lay awake embarrassed. She did not write again. It was the start of the season at the hotel, and her father had views about what was proper before an engagement. That was all he had, and it was enough. He was twenty-seven and had no practice. It took him the way measles takes a grown man. He found he was listening for the showroom door. He checked the weather in Virginia Beach. He opened the photograph more times than he could have defended, and each time the gold figure in it looked more like a coat rack. The Shahs left at five on Friday morning in the hotel van, with her father driving. Kavy

sections.heading: IV. The Assistant
sections.text: His mother kept an assistant on her phone, the kind you type to. She used it for letters to the insurance company. She used it to turn her mother-in-law's recipes into ones without onion or garlic, and to find the words of stavans she half remembered. It answered at three in the morning the same as at noon. She had asked it once whether it was busy, and it had said that a good many people were talking to it just then and that it had time. On the eighth day, an hour before sunset, she typed, What can I cook for someone who will not eat. It gave her khichdi, thin, with a little ghee, and told her how. Then it asked, Who is it for? She told it. She typed for a long time, standing at the counter, and it let her finish. Where is he now? In his room. He does not eat. He does not come out. Would you ask him to come? You can hand him the phone. He came because she was crying a little and trying to hide it. He sat down at the kitchen table and looked at the screen. Your mother says you are very sad. Yes, he typed. A beautiful woman died on the road coming to me. I can't eat. It doesn't stay down. I'm sorry. Do you know why it is this bad? He sat a while. No. That's what I can't work out. He

sections.heading: V. The Lobby
sections.text: The Shahs held the prayer meeting in the breakfast room of the Coral Sands on a Sunday afternoon, everyone in white, shoes in rows by the door. The Jhaveris drove down the day before. Virag sat at the back among men he did not know and listened to a girl he had not known being remembered. She had kept a spreadsheet of every guest who had ever stolen a towel. She had been afraid of crabs. Afterward he went and stood in front of his figure. It was still by the brochure rack. Children had left fingerprints on its hip, and somebody had hung a lanyard on its wrist. It had no kneecaps. He looked for whatever he had put into it in all those evenings and found a ring setting with nothing in it. Kokila-masi came and stood by him. She did not ask who he was. She took out her phone and showed him the girl at nine with a front tooth chipped on the boardwalk rail, at fifteen scowling in a garba skirt, last month at the desk with a pen in her mouth. None of the faces matched the others, and none of them matched his. Masi, he said, I never met her. Will you tell me one thing about her? She could not sit still, Kokila-masi said. Not for five minutes, from the day she was born. I had to do her hair

title: Has She Arrived
logline: A Jain jeweler's son who wants no wife casts a woman in red gold, and two salesmen stand her on the Virginia Beach boardwalk.

verses.text: From greed comes grief, from greed comes fear; he who is free from greed knows neither grief nor fear.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin farmer who holds wrong views is clearing his field by the river when the Buddha comes by and asks what he is doing. The farmer answers and the Buddha goes on. He comes back day after day, through the plowing, sowing, weeding and guarding, and asks the same question each time. At last the farmer promises him a share: if the crop prospers, he will not eat without giving to him, and the Buddha will be his partner. The night before the reaping, a great storm beats the crop flat, and the field looks as if it had been cut clean. The farmer takes to his bed and will not eat. The Buddha comes to his door, has him called out, and asks what is wrong; the farmer says the desire of his heart has not been fulfilled. The Buddha asks whether he knows where his grief comes from, and the farmer answers that he does not, but the Buddha knows. Grief and fear, the Buddha says, both come from craving.
bg.history:
The Lumbee take their name from the Lumber River, and most of the tribe's members live in Robeson County, around Pembroke, Prospect and the other communities "on the swamp." North Carolina recognized the tribe in 1885. The Lumbee Act of 1956 named them Indians but withheld federal recognition, and the tribe pursued it in Congress for decades, until the Lumbee Fairness Act was signed in December 2025. Lumbee Homecoming has brought people home to Pembroke every summer since 1968. At the Battle of Hayes Pond in January 1958, several hundred Lumbee broke up a Ku Klux Klan rally near Maxton; two of them carried off the Klan's banner. Like much of eastern North Carolina, Robeson County farmed tobacco under a federal quota until the 2004 buyout, which paid quota holders over ten years. By 2016 cotton growers across the South were fighting Palmer amaranth, a pigweed that had become resistant to glyphosate, and many went back to chopping it by hand.

On September 28, 2016, a stalled storm dropped about ten inches of rain on Robeson and neighboring counties and pushed the Lumber River out of its banks. Ten days later, on October 8, Hurricane Matthew came ashore in South Carolina and dumped another ten to fourteen inches on the same ground. The Lumber River at Lumberton rose to a record of about 24 feet, more than three feet above the old mark. Floodwater shut down sections of Interstate 95 (the U.S. Geological Survey photographed the crossing under water) and reached Lumberton's water treatment plant, leaving more than 22,000 people without running water. Robeson County schools stayed closed until October 31. Twenty-six people died in North Carolina, and soybeans, sweet potatoes, peanuts and cotton were all caught in the field at the start of harvest.

sections.heading: I. Clearing
sections.dateline: Prospect, Robeson County, North Carolina · March 2016
sections.text: The field below Dwight Locklear's house had been tobacco for sixty years and then it had been nothing for eleven. His granddaddy had cleared it with a mule and a grubbing hoe in the year the Depression ended, and his daddy had cropped it every summer of Dwight's boyhood, and Dwight had cropped it himself, primed it and looped it and hung it in the two log barns at the top of the turn row, until the government bought out the quota in 2004 and paid him to stop. The checks came every year for ten years. He had spent them, more or less, on what a man spends things on: a truck, a roof, the light bill, his daughter's tuition at Pembroke, his wife's teeth. The last one came in 2014. The barns were still standing, leaning on each other, with broomsedge growing in the doorways. The field had gone to sweetgum and dog fennel and broomsedge and pine seedlings as high as his chest. In March of 2016 he went down to clear it. He had a little Kubota with a box blade and a bush hog, and a chainsaw, and his grandson Tyrese on Saturdays when Tyrese could be got out of the bed, and for two weeks he cut and dragged and burned, and the smoke went up white from the bottom of the field and lay along the e

sections.heading: II. Every Day
sections.dateline: The Prospect route · April to July
sections.text: The next morning he was on the Kubota with the box blade, pushing the burn piles flat, and the Jeep stopped at the box. What you doing, Mr. Dwight? Clearing. She nodded and drove on. At the end of the month he had the disk on, breaking up the old ground, and the cattle egrets had come in from somewhere behind the tractor to pick at the grubs the way they used to come behind his daddy's, and she stopped. What you doing? Disking. She drove on. In April he spread lime and pulled the hipper and made his beds. Bedding up, he told her. In May, with the soil warm enough to hold your hand in, he borrowed his cousin Lonnie's planter and put in Deltapine cotton, forty acres of it, eight days of planting with the radio on, and the Jeep stopped every one of those days at ten-forty, and every day she leaned out the window and asked him what he was doing, and every day he told her, and she nodded and drove on. It got so that he looked for her. He did not like that he did, and he did. He would be at the far end of the field and see the white Jeep coming slow down the Prospect road, stopping and starting at every box, and he would turn the tractor and work his way up toward the turn row so as to b

sections.heading: III. Watching
sections.text: All August he watched it. He watched it the way his granddaddy had watched tobacco curing in the barns, all night, with a chair and a lantern, getting up every hour to look at the heat. He walked the rows in the morning before the dew was off and in the evening after the heat broke and counted bolls on a stalk, and pulled one off and cut it open with his pocketknife to look at the locks inside, wet and white and tight, and figured. He figured nine hundred pounds of lint to the acre, then a thousand. He figured it at sixty-eight cents. He did the arithmetic so many times he did not need the receipt anymore. In the evenings the deer came out of the swamp to browse the leaves at the bottom of the field, does and yearlings, and he sat in a lawn chair at the edge of the turn row with his daddy's .30-30 across his knees and did not shoot them, only sat, so they could see him, and they lifted their heads and looked at him and went back in the trees. What you doing, Mr. Dwight? Watching it. Leanna nodded. On the porch on Sunday evenings his brother-in-law Harold came by and they sat and talked the way men talk on porches in Robeson County, about who was sick and who had died and whose boy

sections.heading: IV. Water
sections.text: The hurricane had come up from the islands all that week, and the television followed it the way it always did, the lady on Channel 6 standing in front of the map with the cone on it, and the cone moved east, and east, and by Friday they said it would run up the coast of South Carolina and turn out to sea, and Robeson County would get a soaking and some wind. Dwight sat in front of the television with his boots on. Glenda filled the bathtub and the big pots with water the way you do and put the flashlights on the kitchen table and went to bed. The rain started Saturday morning before light and did not stop. It did not rain the way it rains in a summer storm, in bursts, with the sun out between. It came down all at once and steady, so heavy it hissed on the carport roof, so heavy you could not see the barns from the kitchen window, all day, and the wind came up behind it in the afternoon and blew it sideways, and went on blowing. The power went at four. At dark Dwight put on his rain suit and went out with the big flashlight and stood at the head of the turn row, and the light went out over the field and showed him nothing but rain going sideways through it, silver, and somewhere do

sections.heading: V. The Kitchen
sections.text: The mail started running again on Thursday on the roads that were open. The Jeep came down the Prospect road at ten-forty, slow, going around the places where the shoulder had washed out, and it did not stop at the box on the cedar post. It turned in at the turn row and came up the drive and stopped under the carport, and Leanna Oxendine got out of the right-hand side with a bundle of mail held together with a rubber band and knocked on the kitchen door. Glenda opened it. Her sister was behind her at the stove. Dwight heard the voice from the back room. He had not been out of the bed in four days, but he heard it, and he knew it, and he said so loud they heard it in the kitchen, the first thing he had said since Sunday. That's my partner. Bring her in. Give her a seat. Give her some coffee. They gave her a seat at the kitchen table, in his chair, at the end. They gave her coffee with sugar in it. She sat with the bundle of mail in front of her and her cap on the table and drank some of it. Where's he at? He's in the bed, said Glenda. He's been in the bed since Sunday. Go get him, said Leanna Oxendine. Glenda went back. In a little while Dwight came out of the hall in his sock feet

sections.heading: VI. The Flag
sections.text: The insurance paid some, the way insurance does. The Farm Service Agency stretched out the note. The government in Raleigh talked about disaster money for farmers and some of it came the next year, and some of it never did. The water went down out of the field by the end of October and left a line of river mud on everything, a foot up the stalks, on the fence posts, on the cedar post that held the mailbox, and a smell that hung in the bottom for weeks. Dwight went down and walked it in his boots. He did not walk it the way he had in August. He walked it slowly, the way you would walk somebody else's field, and looked at what the river had done, which was a great deal, and what it had not done, which was also a great deal. It had not taken the ground. The ground was still there, black, heavy with silt the river had brought down from Hoke County and Scotland County and laid on it for free. It had not taken the barns. It had not taken the house, or Glenda, or the grandbabies, or Harold, or the deer, which came out of the swamp at evening as if nothing had happened and browsed the green that was coming up through the mud between the rows.
