title: Low Ground
logline: A Lumbee farmer clears his grandfather's old tobacco field for cotton, and every morning the mail carrier stops to ask what he's doing.

verses.text: He who possesses virtue and intelligence, who is just, speaks the truth, and does what is his own business, him the world will hold dear.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, on a festival day, the Buddha enters Rājagaha for alms with the eighty great elders and five hundred monks, and meets five hundred youths carrying baskets of cakes out to a pleasure garden. They greet him and go on without offering a single monk a cake. The Buddha says the owner of the cakes is walking at the rear, and they will eat before they go on, and he sits down with the monks under a tree. At the sight of the elder Mahā Kassapa, walking last, the youths are filled with joy; they set down their baskets, bow to him and offer him everything. He sends them back to share it with the Buddha and the Saṅgha. They serve him, watch him eat, and give him water. The monks complain of favoritism, and the Buddha answers that a monk like Kassapa is dear to gods and humans alike, and speaks the verse; the youths are established in the first fruit of the path.
bg.history:
New Orleans’s Black benevolent societies, first organized by free Creoles of color in the early 1800s and multiplied after the Civil War, paid members’ medical and burial costs and hired brass bands for funerals and parades; their successors, the social aid and pleasure clubs, still parade their neighborhoods with a brass band and the “second line” of followers behind it (64 Parishes). A traditional brass band of the period was typically trumpets, trombones, a clarinet or saxophone, tuba, snare and bass drum, as in the Eureka Brass Band. Mr. Cass goes to Mass at St. Augustine Church in the Tremé, founded by free people of color in 1841 and said to be the oldest Black Catholic parish in the United States.

The wide neutral ground of North Claiborne Avenue, shaded by live oaks, was the promenade and picnic ground of Black New Orleans and the heart of its Carnival, where clubs, Mardi Gras Indians and Baby Dolls paraded. In 1966 officials decided, over residents’ protests, to uproot the oaks and run the elevated Interstate 10 expressway down the avenue; the trees came out in the late 1960s, and concrete columns stand where they grew (A Closer Walk; Smithsonian). Longfellow’s “The Village Blacksmith,” first published in 1840, was a schoolroom recitation piece for a century; the text here follows Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904).

sections.heading: I. The Back of the Band
sections.dateline: The Tremé, New Orleans · Mardi Gras morning, 1965
sections.text: The Fair Play Social Aid and Pleasure Club came out of its hall on St. Philip Street at nine o’clock on Mardi Gras morning, the second of March, forty men in lavender suits and straw hats with gold bands, and the Silver Leaf Brass Band behind them, and the grand marshal out in front of everybody. The grand marshal was Mr. Alcée Gaudet, who had led the Fair Play since 1951 and the rest of the year taught fifth grade at the public school on Columbus Street. He had taught half the children between Esplanade and St. Bernard to do long division and the other half to sit still while the first half did it. On parade days he wore a gold sash over one shoulder with FAIR PLAY sewn on it in purple felt, and carried a gold fan, and he did not say much, in the street or in the classroom. When he lifted the fan, the band began. When he brought it down, the band stopped. The Silver Leaf was eleven men in white shirts and black pants and black caps with the band’s name across the front: three trumpets, two trombones, a clarinet, a tenor saxophone, a tuba, a snare drum and a bass drum. Behind the bass drum, by himself, walked Mr. Casimir Joseph. Mr. Cass was eighty-one. He had played second trumpet

sections.heading: II. The Cakes
sections.text: They turned onto Claiborne under the oaks. In 1965 the neutral ground down the middle of North Claiborne Avenue was a long green mile of grass under live oaks whose limbs met over it, and on Mardi Gras the whole Seventh Ward and the Tremé came out and claimed it: ladders for the children to sit on, kitchen chairs, washtubs of ice and beer, chicken in roasting pans, men cooking on halves of oil drums. Somewhere up toward Orleans Avenue the Indians were coming out in their feathers, and you could hear the tambourines before you could see anything. From the other direction, down the sidewalk, came the children. It was the Sunday school of the Greater St. Matthew Baptist Church on Galvez Street, and two other churches with it, on their way to the place under the biggest oak where the churches had their spot every year. There were five hundred of them, people said afterward, though people say a great many things on Mardi Gras. They were carrying the cakes. Pound cakes in dishpans. Tea cakes in shoeboxes. Pralines wrapped in wax paper, in a bushel basket. A king cake from McKenzie’s on a board. The big girls carried the dishpans on their heads and the big boys carried the baskets on thei

sections.heading: III. Fair Play
sections.text: Mr. Duplessis took his piece of pound cake. He ate it. Then he said, so that the men around him could hear, that he did not call that fair play. Walked right past the grand marshal of this club. Walked past the president of this club and forty members in good standing. Walked past the whole band. Gave it all to Cass. That’s favoritism, said one of the trombones. That’s what it is, said Mr. Duplessis. Mr. Gaudet was sitting on his root with his fan across his knees and a tea cake in his hand. He finished the tea cake. Hilton, he said. A man like Cass Joseph, the Lord loves him. And everybody on this avenue with any sense loves him too. That’s who the children bring the cake to. That’s all it is. He looked over at the ring of children, who had gone quiet, the way a class goes quiet when it knows what’s coming. Every one of you stood up in my room and said it. Who remembers? Bernadette Pichon remembered, and then they all did, the way they had said it in fifth grade, all together and a little behind each other, under the oak on Claiborne Avenue with the tambourines coming down from Orleans: His brow is wet with honest sweat,He earns whate’er he can,And looks the whole world in the fac

sections.heading: IV. The Columns
sections.text: The next year the state came with saws and began taking down the oaks for the expressway. People stood on the neutral ground and watched it, and some of them cried, and it made no difference. Mr. Cass died in the spring of 1967, and the Silver Leaf played him to St. Louis Number Two with the dirge going so slow that the bass drum seemed to stop between every beat, and Mr. Gaudet walked in front in his sash with the fan held down, and five hundred people came behind who had been children, or said they had. The big oak came down in 1968. Where it stood there is a concrete column now, holding up the interstate. On Mardi Gras the families still bring their ladders and their chairs and set them up on the neutral ground between the columns, in the shade of the highway, and the trucks go over all day like weather. And somebody always brings a cake, and cuts the first piece, and stands at the edge of the sidewalk holding it out for whoever is walking last.

title: Fair Play
logline: On Mardi Gras under the Claiborne oaks, five hundred Sunday-school children carrying cakes walk past a grand marshal and his brass band.

verses.text: He in whom a desire for the Ineffable (Nirvana) has sprung up, who is satisfied in his mind, and whose thoughts are not bewildered by love, he is called urdhvamsrotas (carried upwards by the stream).

bg.commentary: An elder monk has reached the third stage of awakening, that of the non-returner, who has cut off sensual desire and will not be born into this world again. When the monks who live with him ask whether he has attained anything, he says nothing, from embarrassment: even laypeople reach that stage, and he means to speak only once he is fully awakened. He dies first, and is reborn in the Pure Abodes, from which non-returners pass on to final release. His pupils weep, not because he died but because he never answered them. The Buddha tells them their teacher had freed his heart from sensual desire, and speaks of one who has “gone upstream.”
bg.history:
In January 1924 Robert and Helen Lynd and a small team of researchers began studying Muncie as a typical American small city, through documents, old newspapers, surveys and interviews. Their book, Middletown (1929), never named the town. It found 42 churches of 28 denominations, with the Methodist church the most prestigious, and described the line between the working class and the business class as the town’s deepest division. Muncie had grown on the Indiana gas boom of the 1880s, which brought Ball Brothers and their glass fruit jars in 1888; the Ku Klux Klan, strong in the town early in the decade, held parades there in 1922 and 1924. Miss Thayer, the Keevers and everyone else in the story are invented.

John Wesley taught that a believer could be made perfect in love in this life, and Methodist preachers are still asked at ordination whether they are “going on to perfection” and expect to be made perfect in love. The nineteenth-century Holiness movement made this “entire sanctification” or “second blessing” an instantaneous experience received by faith, often at the altar of a camp meeting. Taylor University in Upland, founded by Methodists, moved there in 1893 and ended its formal tie to the Methodist church in 1922. The verses are from Richard Francis Weymouth’s New Testament in Modern Speech, first published in 1903.

sections.heading: I. The Boarder
sections.text: The Keevers took a boarder that fall for the money, the way half of Jackson Street did, and because Mrs. Keever's husband had been dead four years and the house had a front bedroom nobody slept in. The boarder was a Miss Agnes Thayer from New York. She was twenty-six and wore her hair bobbed and her skirts at the shin, and she came with the people from Columbia University who were studying the town. Nobody on Jackson Street could make out what there was to study. Muncie was Muncie. It had the Ball jar works and the Warner Gear and the wire mill and forty-some churches, and it had had gas once, when the boom was on, enough to burn flambeaux on the street corners day and night, and then the gas ran out and the jar works stayed. In the summer the Klan had paraded down Walnut Street in their robes, and a good many men from the churches had marched in it. But the people from Columbia were all over town that winter with notebooks. They sat in the back of the churches and the Rotary lunches. They went into the kitchens of the wives of men at the Ball works and the wives of men at the bank and asked them what time they got up, how often they washed, whether they had a bathtub, what they re

sections.heading: II. The Question
sections.text: Paul Keever came home from Taylor University for Christmas, and he brought his roommate, Harold Tull, from up by Fort Wayne, whose people could not have him that year. Taylor was a holiness college up in Upland, an hour north, Methodist in everything but the deed, and the old holiness was still strong there. The boys had been to the meetings that fall. They had gone to the altar, both of them, and come away believing they had been sanctified wholly, that the second blessing had been given and the root of sin taken out of them. They talked about it at supper, Paul with his ears red and Harold steadily, and Mrs. Keever said that was very nice and passed the potatoes. On Christmas afternoon, while she did the dishes and Miss Thayer dried, the boys went back to the old man's room and asked him. It was a fair question among Methodists. It had been put to him once, in public, when he was a young man standing before the bishop to be taken into full connection, in the words Mr. Wesley had written: Are you going on to perfection? Do you expect to be made perfect in love in this life? He had said yes and yes. Now his grandson stood in front of him with a Taylor pennant on the wall behind him

sections.heading: III. Upstream
sections.text: He took cold in the middle of January, walking. The river was open in the middle and shelved with ice along the banks, and he went out anyway, as far as the bridge, and came back with his face grey. Dr. Bowles came twice. It went into his chest the first week of February, and on the night of the eleventh, with Mrs. Keever on one side of the bed and Miss Thayer on the other, because Miss Thayer had been sitting up with him nights and would not let anyone else take her turn, he died. He did not say anything at the end. He looked at the window and breathed out and that was all. They buried him from High Street. The church was full of old people from the country who had driven in on the frozen roads in Model T's and in a few buggies, and men from the Ball works who had been married by him, and the district superintendent preached, and the choir sang O for a heart to praise my God. Paul and Harold came down on the train. They sat in the front pew with Mrs. Keever and wept through the whole of it, and that night, in the kitchen, they were weeping still. Mrs. Keever told them to stop it. He was eighty-one, she said. He was ready. Everybody knew it was coming. We know that, Paul said. That

sections.heading: IV. The Card
sections.text: Miss Thayer had been standing in the door of the front room. She came in and sat down at the table with them. She had a white card in her hand, a five-by-eight from the study, ruled, with the old man's name at the top in her small upright hand. She laid it in front of Paul and put her finger on a line near the bottom. There's a question I ask every woman I sit with, she said. I've asked it of a hundred and some women in this town. If you had more money, what would you buy? I asked him too, the last night in November. It wasn't on his schedule. I just asked. Paul looked. Every woman in Muncie had answered it, she said, and she could tell him what they had said without looking, because they had all said the same things. A car, if they had none. A better car, if they had one. A bathroom. A washing machine. A radio. A house on the north side. Shoes for the children. Not one of them had said nothing. On his card, after the question, she had written one word and underlined it. Nothing. He thought about it a long time, she said. He said he was trying to be fair to me. Then he said he couldn't think of a thing. She took the card back. You asked him if he had it, she said. I'm not a Methodi

sections.heading: V. The Tickets
sections.text: Miss Thayer went back to New York in the summer, when the study was done. She sent Mrs. Keever a Christmas card for several years from an address on Morningside Heights, and then the cards stopped. The book came out in 1929. Paul looked in it for his grandfather, and he was not in it, and Paul thought that was about right. The White Owl box came to Paul. Inside were the class tickets, sixty years of them, small as playing cards, each with the quarter and the year and a verse printed on it, and the name of the class leader in ink. The oldest was for the first quarter of 1864, and the newest was for the last year anyone on his circuits still gave them out. Under them, at the bottom of the box, folded once, was the paper of his ordination questions, with no mark on it anywhere to show what he thought. The ice went out of the White River the third week in March. Paul came down from Upland on a Saturday and walked out along the bank in the morning, upstream, the way the old man had gone every day, against the water. Big plates of it came down past him, grey, turning slowly, knocking against the piers of the Walnut Street bridge and going on under. He went as far as the bridge. Then, bec

title: White River
logline: The winter the sociologists came to Middletown, two holiness students ask an old Methodist preacher whether he has been made perfect.

verses.text: Kinsmen, friends, and lovers salute a man who has been long away, and returns safe from afar.
In like manner his good works receive him who has done good, and has gone from this world to the other;—as kinsmen receive a friend on his return.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Nandiya is a devout young man of Bārāṇasī whose parents want him to marry his cousin Revatī, who does not believe and never gives alms. His mother sets her a test: get the house ready for the monks, prepare their seats, take their bowls, strain their water and wash up after them. Revatī does it and they marry. She becomes devout, bears two sons and runs the household when his parents die. Nandiya, now rich, feeds the monks, the poor and travelers at his door, and gives the order a four-chambered hall at Isipatana. As he pours the water of donation into the Buddha's right hand, a jeweled mansion rises for him in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. The elder Moggallāna sees it on a visit there, and the heavenly women in it beg him to tell Nandiya to come. When Moggallāna asks whether such rewards come while a man still lives, the Buddha answers that he has seen it himself, and compares the welcome of the good in the next world to kinsmen running out to meet one who comes home from far away. The commentary to the Vimānavatthu adds that after Nandiya died, Revatī stopped the alms, abused the monks and was cast alive into hell.
bg.history:
Holmes County and the counties around it hold one of the largest Amish settlements in the world, about 39,000 people in 2025. Old Order Amish worship every other Sunday in a member's home or barn, on benches carried from house to house in a bench wagon. The host family spends a week scrubbing walls and windows and serves a plain noon meal of bread, peanut butter spread, pickles and red beets (how a house gets ready for church). They sing from the Ausbund, first printed in 1564. Bishops, ministers and deacons are nominated by the members and then chosen by lot, by drawing hymnbooks until one turns up a hidden slip with a Bible verse. They have no formal training, they serve without pay, normally for life, and support themselves at their own work. Baptism is required before marriage, and only baptized members can be shunned, so a young person who leaves before joining church is not put out. In Holmes County most weddings fall on Thursdays, and they were once clustered in the winter months (Holmes County wedding customs). For trips a buggy cannot make, the Amish hire drivers by the mile, and those drivers spend much of their lives waiting in vans (a driver's account).

Pinecraft, a neighborhood of small cottages in Sarasota, took its name in 1925–26 from a tourist camp. It became the winter village of Amish and Mennonites from across North America, with the Mennonite Tourist Church on Bahia Vista Street, bought in 1946, as its landmark. The Pioneer Trails line of Millersburg, Ohio, runs buses down from Holmes County and the other northern settlements. In the busy months a crowd of a hundred or so gathers in the church lot across from the little post office to watch each bus come in, and the welcomes are over in about fifteen minutes (when the bus comes in). In the park the old men play shuffleboard by sign-up list, and adult tricycles take the place of buggies (Pioneer Trails to Pinecraft).

sections.heading: I. Church at Our House
sections.dateline: Walnut Creek Township, Holmes County, Ohio · spring 1993
sections.text: Noah Troyer was the kind of young man the old women pointed out to their daughters. He joined church at nineteen without being told twice. He sang the slow hymns from the Ausbund in a voice that held the long notes as steady as a level. When church was at somebody else's house he went over the night before to help unload the bench wagon, and when it was at his father's he scrubbed the shop floor himself so the men's horses would have a clean place to stand in the rain. His mother was Fannie Troyer, and across the township road lived her cousin's family, the Hershbergers, and their daughter Rebecca. Both mothers had settled long ago, over a quilt frame, that Noah and Rebecca would make a pair. Noah did not want her. Rebecca was twenty-two and had not joined church. She worked at a tourist restaurant in Berlin, carrying plates of broasted chicken to people from Cleveland, and she kept her tips in a coffee can and did not tell her father how much was in it. When the deacon came by with the alms list she was always upstairs. When a peddler or a man walking to Florida knocked at the Hershbergers' back door, it was never Rebecca who gave him bread. She was quick and good-looking and she

sections.heading: II. The Pallet Shop
sections.text: She kept the promise. In a few years nobody remembered that she had once been the girl upstairs when the deacon came. She was the first one there when a barn burned and the first one home from a funeral to start the coffee. She bore two boys, Eli and Mose, and she nursed Noah's father through his last two years when his lungs went, and carried his mother's meals up the stairs until his mother died too. Then she was mistress of the Troyer place, and Noah was a rich man. Old Eli Troyer had started with a sawmill. Noah built it into a pallet shop that ran two shifts, then a shop that made porch furniture for the tourist stores along Route 39, and then, because the Amish of Holmes County were building faster than they could find carpenters, a crew that put up pole barns from Wooster to Coshocton. He did not have a telephone in the house, but there was one in a shanty at the end of the lane that rang all day. He gave. He gave to the alms fund until the deacon told him to stop because people would talk. And he put a long table in the break room at the shop, with an urn of coffee and a slow cooker, and he told anyone who asked that it was for the drivers. The drivers were the English peop

sections.heading: III. The Driver
sections.text: Sadie Mast had grown up Amish on Township Road 606 and left at eighteen, the year before she would have joined church, and because she had never been baptized she had never been put out. She could still go to her mother's for Sunday dinner. She still talked to her passengers in Deitsch, which made the old ones easy with her and the young ones careful. She had been driving for twenty-two years in a white fifteen-passenger Ford with a hundred and ninety thousand miles on it, and she had driven most of Walnut Creek Township to most of its funerals. She was fifty-four. She did not talk much. She listened to the radio low, gospel or the farm report, and switched it off when the old people prayed. In January of 2016 Noah hired her to drive him and Rebecca down to Pinecraft for two weeks, because his back had gone out and he could not sit for twenty hours on the bus. Somewhere in Georgia, after dark, with Rebecca asleep on the back bench, he moved up to the seat behind Sadie and they talked. He asked her about Pinecraft, because she had been driving people down there for years. She told him what she had seen. The little white cottages on Kauffman and Graber and Yoder streets, rented a yea

sections.heading: IV. Four Rooms
sections.text: He bought a lot on Schrock Street with a tired cinderblock bungalow on it and had his own crew drive down in two vans and take it to the slab. On the slab they built a cottage with four bedrooms opening off a long screened porch, so four couples could have their own doors, and a kitchen big enough for all of them, and a shed for the tricycles. He had beds made in his own shop, oak, with rope springs for the old ones who said modern springs hurt their backs. He had rockers made for the porch. Then he went to the bishop's council and gave the whole thing to the ministers of the Walnut Creek districts and their wives, to be used in turn, every winter, for as long as there were ministers. The Amish do not dedicate buildings. There was no ceremony. Sadie drove the first four couples down herself in January, Abe Weaver among them, in his Sunday coat, and she was there when Noah walked them through it. The old bishop stood on the porch and looked at the four doors for a long time and could not say anything. His wife sat down in a rocker and wept and laughed at herself for weeping. Noah wanted to show them the water. The well man had put in a new line from the street that week, and an outs

sections.heading: V. What Mose Saw
sections.dateline: Sarasota Memorial Hospital and the road north · February 2018
sections.text: Mose Raber was one of the two ministers in Noah's district, a lean, quiet harness-maker of seventy-three who had been to Pinecraft once before in his life. He was in the cottage on Schrock Street with his wife the next winter when his heart stopped on the shuffleboard court. A retired fireman from Indiana, a Mennonite, worked on him on the concrete until the ambulance came. At the hospital they said his heart had not beaten for six minutes. He came back on the second day and lay in the bed with the tubes in his arms, and when his wife had gone down to the cafeteria he told the night nurse, a Haitian woman who listened to him as if he were telling her the weather, where he had been. He had been standing outside a house. It was white and so large he could not see where it ended in any direction, larger than all of Holmes County, and it went up until he could not see the top, and every board of it shone like the inside of a shell. There were flowers in the air in front of the door, pink and red, as if somebody had thrown a double handful of them up in the air and they had forgot to come down. At every window there were women in white, more than he could count, in white capes and white

sections.heading: VI. Rebecca
sections.text: Noah Troyer died in October of 2021 on the floor of his own pallet shop, at fifty-six, between one board and the next. They buried him on a Saturday in the Troyer graveyard on the hill behind the house, and there were a hundred and forty vans in the hayfield. The drivers ate standing up at his table in the break room, which was still set, because nobody had thought to tell Rebecca not to. She told them after that. In November she unplugged the slow cooker and took it to the house and had the table carried out to the scrap pile behind the shop. When a driver came in out of the rain in December looking for coffee she told him the shop was a business. She told the deacon the alms would be what the Ordnung asked and not a dollar over. When it came the Troyers' turn for church that spring, she sent word to the bishop that it would have to be at somebody else's house, she was not running a hotel for preachers. And she went to the bishop's council with an English lawyer from Millersburg about getting back the cottage on Schrock Street, which was hers, she said, by rights, and her sons'. Her sons were grown and married and lived down the road and did not know what to do with her. Nobody di

sections.heading: VII. The Bus
sections.text: Sadie drove three of the couples down again that winter, as she had every winter since the first. The cottage on Schrock Street had held a hundred and four ministers and their wives by then. Mose Raber's wife kept the count in the back of the guest book. The beds had not squeaked once. The rockers had worn two pale arcs in the porch boards. The fourth couple came by bus. In the fall the lot had fallen on Eli Troyer, Noah's older son, who was twenty-eight and ran the pallet shop and had two babies, and who had stood up white in the face in the Raber barn when the bishop opened the hymnbook in front of him and found the slip of paper. He had never been to Florida. His mother lay in the front room at home with her eyes on the corner of the ceiling, and his brother's wife was sitting with her, and he had not wanted to go. The bishop had told him to go. On the Wednesday Sadie walked over to the Tourist Church lot at three o'clock. A boy on a red tricycle came tearing back from Bahia Vista standing up on the pedals. It's here! The old men laid their cues across the shuffleboard courts. A hundred people came out into the sun. The bus turned in across from the post office and sighed down o

title: Everlasting Cottages
place: Walnut Creek Township, Holmes County, Ohio
logline: A rich Amish pallet maker builds a winter cottage in Florida for his unpaid ministers, and an old harness-maker sees what rose with it.

verses.text: Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage! No sufferings befall the man who is not attached to name and form, and who calls nothing his own.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Anuruddha comes home to Kapilavatthu, and everyone in the family goes out to greet him except his sister Rohinī, who is ashamed of a skin eruption. He sends for her and tells her to sell her jewels and build a two-storied assembly hall; while the kinsfolk build it, she sweeps the lower floor and sets out seats and water, and as she sweeps her skin clears. When she gives a meal for the Buddha in the finished hall, he summons her and tells her the eruption came from anger: in a past life, as a jealous queen, she put the powder of a stinging bean in a dancing girl’s bed and clothes and threw it on her body “as if in fun.” As she hears the verse her body turns the color of gold. Reborn among the gods at the meeting point of four domains, she is quarreled over by four young gods, who put the case to Sakka, their king; he wants her for himself, and they give way. Read the full commentary story. The bean is Mucuna pruriens, the velvet bean or cowhage, whose pod hairs are still used in itching powder.
bg.history:
Colorado Springs was laid out in 1871 at the foot of Pikes Peak, and so many English settlers came that it was called “Little London”; after the gold strikes at Cripple Creek in the 1890s it filled up with mining money, and by 1895 it had four mining exchanges and 275 mining brokers. Manitou Springs, just up the canyon, was founded in 1872 as a health resort around its mineral springs. In 1903 and 1904 the district was torn by the Colorado Labor Wars. On June 6, 1904, a dynamite blast under the platform of the Independence depot killed thirteen non-union miners; in the days after, the mine owners’ association and the militia rounded up union men into bullpens and deported more than two hundred of them by train across the state line.

Christian Science was founded in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy, whose Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875) teaches that sickness is rooted in mental error; it names “hatred, envy, dishonesty, fear, and so forth” among the things that “make a man sick.” Each church has two Readers, who read paired passages from the Bible and Science and Health on Sundays, and members give testimonies of healing at Wednesday evening meetings. When the extension of The Mother Church in Boston was dedicated in June 1906, a Boston paper noted that no Christian Science church had ever been dedicated “with any part of the expense of its construction remaining unprovided for.” The Manitou church, the Wellers, Mrs. Oakes and Tom Rainey are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Veil
sections.text: Frank Weller came home to the Springs in the middle of June, eight days after the depot at Independence was blown up. The whole district was still full of it. Thirteen men going on night shift at the Findley had been killed on the platform by a charge of dynamite under the boards, and in the days after it the mine owners and the militia had cleared every union man they could find out of the camp, and put them in bullpens, and loaded them onto trains and dumped them across the state line. On the porches of the North End people talked about nothing else. The word that came up most was hang. Frank had been gone four years. He had gone east to be a mining engineer and come back a Christian Scientist, which his father, who owned a third of a good mine above Victor, took about as well as he would have taken a cave-in. He had been taught in a class in Boston and had practiced for two years in Denver, and he came down on the noon train with a party of eleven Scientists from the Denver churches who wanted to see the Peak, and the whole family went down to the Antlers to meet him. His father went, and his stepmother, and two uncles, and their wives, and a crowd of cousins. Everyone went but

sections.heading: II. The Lower Room
sections.text: They built it on a lot below Ruxton Avenue, where Ruxton Creek comes down out of the canyon talking to itself over the stones. Frank drew it on butcher paper at the kitchen table. Two stories. Below, a Sunday school room and a reading room, with a stove and a row of windows on the creek side. Above, the auditorium, with the two Readers’ desks and seats for a hundred and twenty. As soon as they put the boards down overhead, he told his sister, you take your place below. Sweep it. Every day. Set out the chairs for the Wednesday meeting, and keep the water pitchers full. Frank, there’ll be carpenters walking around on top of me. There will. On the first evening, after the uncles had gone, she found Frank alone on the porch and stood in front of him with her arms folded. You think it’s in my mind. Don’t you. That I’ve imagined it. I didn’t say that. Look at it, then. And she pulled up the veil. He looked, for a long time, the way a doctor looks, without flinching and without pity, and she hated him for it, and then, for some reason, she did not. It’s real enough, he said. Get some sleep. George is bringing the wagon at seven. The diamonds went to a jeweler on Sixteenth Street in Denver

sections.heading: III. The Teacher
sections.text: They dedicated it on the second Sunday in January, in a snow that came down soft and steady out of the canyon all morning, and afterward Rowena gave a dinner for the teacher and the members at her father’s house in the North End. The teacher was Mrs. Harriet Oakes, of Denver. She was the one who had taught Frank, and half the practitioners in Colorado; she held a class every autumn in a parlor on Capitol Hill, and people came to it from as far as Cheyenne and Santa Fe. She was a widow of fifty from western Kansas, broad and plain, in a black wool dress that had been good once. She had been a country schoolteacher for twenty years before she was a Scientist. She did not talk much. When she did, people noticed that she did not raise her voice even in a full room, and that the room got quiet to hear her. Rowena did not sit down to the dinner. She had planned it for a month, and cooked half of it herself with the hired girl: a clear soup, and a roast of beef, and creamed oysters brought up in a tub of ice from Denver, and Saratoga potatoes, and hot rolls, and a jellied salad, and three kinds of pie and a coconut cake. She saw it onto the table and went back into the kitchen and stayed

sections.heading: IV. Cowhage
sections.text: Rowena did know it. She had not thought about it in seven years, which is not the same as having forgotten. The Christmas she was fifteen, Miss Antoinette Fry’s Academy of the Dance had put on a pageant at the Opera House, with a tableau of the seasons, and Rowena was to be Winter, in white tarlatan with silver spangles, and she had practiced the solo for two months. Then in the last week Miss Fry gave it to Lottie Kehoe. Lottie was a year younger. Her father worked the night shift at the Strong mine and her mother took in sewing, and she had come to the Academy free because Miss Fry said she had never seen feet like that on a child. She danced the way water runs. When Lottie danced, nobody looked at anybody else. There was a boy at the high school whose people had wintered in Florida, and he had come back with a paper of what they called cow-itch down there, and sold pinches of it to the other boys for a dime to put down girls’ collars. It was cowhage, the hairs off the pod of a bean that grows in the South, fine as pollen and gold-colored, though Rowena did not know the name then. She paid him a quarter for the whole paper. She shook it into the folds of Lottie’s costume where it

sections.heading: V. The Four Corners
sections.text: Now the Weller house stood on a corner lot on Wood Avenue, and on the other three corners of that crossing stood three other houses, and in each of the four houses, counting the Wellers’ own, where the stepmother’s nephew was boarding, there lived an unmarried young man. Every one of them had known Rowena Weller all her life. Not one of them had looked at her twice since she was sixteen. That spring every one of them looked at her, and went on looking, and by May the four of them were not speaking. She grew up on my side of the street, said the first. She grew up across from me, said the second, I could see her window. She grew up in my aunt’s house, said the third. She’s our corner’s, said the fourth, who had no argument and knew it. It got as far as a fistfight on the Antlers lawn, and then the four of them agreed, since no one of them would give way to another, to put it before somebody they would all abide by. They chose Tom Rainey, who was thirty-four and had come down from the Cripple Creek district in 1899 with more money than any of them could imagine, from a mine he had found himself with a pick, and who had a stone house on Cascade Avenue and was known to be fair. bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha has just allowed his monks to build lodgings outside the monastery walls. A monk of Āḷavī picks a tree and starts to cut it down. The spirit who lives in the tree comes out with her infant on her hip and begs him to spare her home; he says he will not find another tree like it. Hoping the sight of the child will stop him, she sets the child on a branch, but the axe is already swinging and it cuts off the child's arm. She raises both hands to strike the monk dead, then thinks better of it for three reasons and goes weeping to the Buddha, who praises her, speaks the verse, gives her a tree near his own chamber that no one afterward can shake, and makes it a rule that monks must not injure trees and plants.
bg.history:
Jains have lived in the United States and Canada in numbers since the 1960s; see Jainism in the United States. The temple of the Jain Society of Metropolitan Chicago stands in Bartlett, Illinois. Non-violence toward every living thing, plants included, is the center of Jain practice, and many observant Jains avoid root vegetables because pulling them kills the whole plant. In the eight days of Paryushana, which in 2020 ran from August 15 to August 22 for most Śvetāmbara Jains, families fast and sit the evening rite of repentance. On the last day, Samvatsari, each person asks forgiveness of everyone they know with the words micchami dukkadam. With temples closed by the pandemic that year, the rites were held by video call. The dialogue of Kesi and Gautama is the twenty-third lecture of the Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, quoted here from Hermann Jacobi's translation in the Sacred Books of the East (1895). The line about a plant falling sick is from his translation of the Ācārāṅga Sūtra (1884).

Minecraft reported 126 million monthly players in May 2020, and in that lockdown spring many families used it as a place to meet. On a private Realm the owner sets the difficulty, and Peaceful removes monsters and hunger. A dark oak grows only from four saplings planted in a square. Playgrounds across Ontario were closed by emergency order that spring.

sections.heading: I. Peaceful
sections.text: Kanchanben Vora was seventy-four the spring the derasar in Bartlett locked its doors, and in eleven years she had hardly missed a morning there. Now she did her samayik in the bedroom over the garage, forty-eight minutes by the sand timer, facing a calendar picture of Shatrunjay. After that there was the whole day. Her granddaughter Riya put the game on the iPad in the second week of March. It was so Ba could see the cousins. The family was in eleven houses in three countries and nobody could go to anybody. Riya made the world on Ba's own account, which made Ba its owner, and that suited everyone, since Ba was the one person all the branches of the family would obey. They named the world Vadi, the orchard. Ba learned to walk in it in two days and to look up in four. She wanted every setting read out to her. At Difficulty she stopped Riya. What is Peaceful? No monsters. Nobody gets hungry. It's kind of the baby setting, Ba. That one. Nothing is hunted in my house. She had other rules. Nobody killed the cows or the chickens. Nobody dug up a carrot or a potato where she could see it. The cousins called this Jain mode, laughed about it for a week, and came anyway, forty of them by May,

sections.heading: II. Outside the Wall
sections.dateline: The Realm · August, the third night of Paryushan
sections.text: Kunal was fifteen, the grandson of Ba's sister, in Edison, New Jersey. He had drawn his house on graph paper before he placed a block of it: a long hall with a dark roof, the first big thing anyone had planned beyond the gate. He had counted the logs. The dark oak forest was most of an hour's walk to the north. One dark oak stood a minute from the wall. He came to it with an iron axe a little after nine, Eastern time, and started at the root. Hetal was upstairs in it with Aarav. In the kitchen in Brampton the boy sat beside her at the table with the old tablet, up too late, as he had been all summer. She typed fast. Kunal please don't. This is our house. I can't go wandering around with him looking for somewhere else to live. There's no other tree like this one, bhabhi, he typed back. I'll be quick. He did not stop. He had his headphones on and his thumb down on the button, the way you hold it for a trunk that size, and the axe rose and fell without his deciding each stroke. If he sees the child he will stop, Hetal thought. She said it aloud in the kitchen. Go stand on the low branch, beta, where Kunal bhaiya can see you. Aarav walked out along the branch and stood over his cousin'

sections.heading: III. Both Hands
sections.text: Hetal had been given operator rights in April, to fix things for Ba. There was one line she could type that would drop Kunal dead where he stood and spill everything he carried on the grass. She typed it with her right thumb and did not send it. Her phone was in her left hand, open to Vora Parivar, sixty-three members. She had four lines written there about Kunal, who had been told, who had seen a child and kept swinging. She had one more about his mother, who had said a thing at Hetal's wedding that Hetal had carried for six years. Both thumbs were up. Under the table Aarav had stopped screaming and was only breathing loudly. Three thoughts came to her, one behind the other, and she remembered afterward that they came in order. He was a decent boy. He sat his pratikraman on a screen beside his grandmother every evening that week, and what she did to him tonight she would carry herself for a long time. Then she thought of the other mothers in that group. If she set the price of a tree at a boy's name in front of sixty-three people, every auntie would know the price by morning, and it would be paid again on other children. And the place had an owner. This was Ba's house. She put the

sections.heading: IV. The Bridle
sections.text: Ba had finished the evening pratikraman and was sitting with her mala. She propped the iPad against the steel dabba on the dresser. For the first minute all she could see was a ceiling in Brampton, and all she could hear was crying. She waited. Hetal told her all of it: the four saplings in March, the axe, the branch, the arm. She said what she had written with each hand, read both aloud, and told the three things she had thought. She had sent nothing. Shabash, beta, Ba said. Shabash. Then she told her about Kesi and Gautama, two monks of two lineages who met in a park outside Shravasti, where the elder asked the younger one riddle after another. She told it in Gujarati, as her own mother had told it during the rains. In the old English translation that Riya later found for the cousins, the part she told runs like this. 'The unruly, dreadful, bad horse, on which you sit, runs about, Gautama! how comes it to pass that it does not run off with you?' 'I govern it well in its course by the bridle of knowledge; it does not go astray with me, it keeps to the right path.' — Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23:55–56 It was up and running tonight, Ba said. Most of us only sit behind and hold the reins

sections.heading: V. The Tree by Itself
sections.text: They moved that night, the chest and both beds. For two days Aarav would not hold the tablet. On the third he sat in his mother's lap and let her walk him to the window of the new house, which looked into Ba's garden, where Ba in her blue shirt was putting in wheat. The morning after the call, when her samayik was done, Ba wrote a rule on a sign at the gate, with one finger, and it took her some time. Nobody cuts a tree that someone lives in. Nobody cuts any tree or growing thing without need, and whoever cuts, plants. The older cousins brought it to her on the family call. Ba, they're blocks. Then who was crying? she said. Riya had started looking things up by then, and in another volume of the same old translation she found a man and a plant set side by side, a line the cousins took to quoting at one another over every sapling: as this falls sick when cut, so that falls sick when cut. The birch became a game of its own. Everybody tried it. Kunal's older brother came with a diamond axe and operator rights he had talked Riya into, and the cracks spread across the white bark as they should, and then closed. The log stayed. Two uncles tried, one of whom writes software for a bank. Ri

title: Four Saplings
logline: A Jain grandmother keeps the game world on Peaceful, until a cousin takes an axe to the tree a mother and child live in.

verses.text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Puṇṇa is a poor laborer in Rājagaha who chooses to plow on a city holiday. He gives the Elder Sāriputta a tooth-stick and strained water, and his wife gives the elder the rice she was bringing to her husband. The plowed field turns to gold. When the king's men gather it as the king's property it turns back to earth, and it turns to gold again once they call it Puṇṇa's. Made a rich man, Puṇṇa is pressed into marrying his daughter Uttarā to the son of an unbelieving family, where she can neither give alms nor hear the teaching. Her father sends money to hire the courtesan Sirimā as her husband's companion for a fortnight, so that Uttarā can feed the Buddha and his monks until the end of the rains. When the husband laughs at Uttarā sweating in the kitchen, Sirimā throws boiling oil on her head. Uttarā holds no anger, and the oil feels cool. She pulls her servants off Sirimā and tends her wounds, and Sirimā begs forgiveness before the Buddha, who praises Uttarā with the verse above.
bg.history:
Chinese gold-seekers, most of them from Guangdong, began reaching the Feather River in 1849, and for decades they worked claims that others had abandoned as played out. The state taxed them for it. The Foreign Miners' Tax began at twenty dollars a month in 1850 and was reset at three dollars in 1852. By 1853 it was four dollars, collected monthly, and in practice it fell mainly on the Chinese. In People v. Hall (1854) the California Supreme Court ruled that Chinese witnesses could not testify against a white man. The town first called Ophir City was renamed Oroville in 1854 and grew up as the head of navigation on the Feather River. Its brick Chinese Temple, finished in 1863 after two earlier buildings burned, served the largest Chinese community north of Sacramento. It still stands, with its altars, its processional shrines and its teak bridal sedan chair.

On March 3, 1875, President Grant signed the Page Act, which barred Asian women brought for prostitution. In practice it shut out nearly all Chinese women. Each woman had to be examined by the American consul in Hong Kong, then by the harbor master, then again on arrival in San Francisco, where officials compared her face to her photograph and judged her answers, her feet and her bearing. In 1882 only 136 of 39,579 Chinese arrivals were women. That year Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, and the bachelor communities of the gold country slowly grew old and dwindled.

sections.heading: I. The Furrow
sections.text: Lau Ping worked for the merchant Fong Yat-sun, who kept the biggest store in Chinatown and a fan-tan house behind it, and who owned four mules, a wagon, two ditches and a strip of river bottom below the town where his men grew bok choy and winter melon to sell to the miners up the canyons. Lau Ping hauled for him, dug for him, plowed for him, and was paid a dollar a day when there was work and nothing when there was not. His wife cooked in the Fong kitchen. His daughter, Ah Lin, who was sixteen and had been born in a tent on the river at Bidwell Bar, swept the Fong floors and carried the Fong wash down to the water. All three of them slept in a lean-to against the back wall of the store, the last place in Chinatown before the willows. On the last night of the old year the whole street went up in firecrackers. Red paper hung on every door, and the smell of powder and roast pork lay over the town so thick the white people from up the hill came down to the edge of it to look. The merchants shut their counters for a week. The miners came in from Cherokee Flat and Morris Ravine in clean blue cotton and gambled away the winter. In the morning old Fong stood in the door of the store with

sections.heading: II. The Umbrella
sections.dateline: The company hall · the same week
sections.text: He sat down in the field with the clod in his hand and thought about what happens on this river to a Chinese man with gold. He had paid the Foreign Miners' Tax at Bidwell Bar for nine years, three dollars a month and then four, every month, to a collector with a pistol and a receipt book, and he had seen what the collectors did when a man said he had paid already. He had seen claims jumped, and cabins burned, and a man from his own village tied by his queue to a hitching rail. He had seen a judge in Marysville send a Chinese witness home because a Chinese witness could not speak against a white man. You could not hide a field. You could not spend it either. So he filled his wife's rice basket with gold dirt, put a cloth over it, and carried it up through the New Year crowds to the company hall beside the temple, where Old Ma, the president of the company, sat in a carved chair with a teacup and settled the quarrels of four thousand men. What is it? said Old Ma. Uncle, all the ground I plowed this morning has turned to gold. You should send carts and bring it here, before somebody else does. Who are you? Lau Ping. I work for Fong Yat-sun. And what did you do this morning? Lau Ping t

sections.heading: III. The Match
sections.text: Old Fong came across the street in the spring with his hat in his hand. That was the year after the Congress in Washington passed the law about Chinese women. In Hong Kong now every woman who wanted to sail had to stand in front of the American consul with her photograph and answer him about her father, her husband, her feet, her character, and the way she walked across the room, and then answer the harbor master, and then answer again on the dock in San Francisco, where they held the photograph up beside her face. Most of them did not come. Wives who had been sent for in letters stayed in the villages. Fong's son Wing had been promised a girl from Toishan since he was eleven years old, and she was not coming. In all of Butte County there were perhaps a dozen Chinese girls who were not owned by somebody, and one of them was Ah Lin. I won't give her, said Lau Ping. Ping. Don't be this way. All those years you lived against my wall. Now you're rich and you have the umbrella. Give her to my son. Lau Ping said nothing more to Fong, but he said to his wife that night: That house laughs at the temple. There's a fan-tan table in the back and the boy has never burned a stick of incense in

sections.heading: IV. The Bargain
sections.text: From the day she went across the street she did not see the inside of the temple. She was not allowed to burn incense or carry rice to the Old Teacher's door or sit at the edge of the room where he talked. Fong's wife kept the household money and gave her none. Wing kept his evenings at the fan-tan table and his afternoons in bed. When she asked to go across the street on the first and fifteenth, the days everybody went, her mother-in-law said the girl had married into a house of business, not a house of beggars, and that the shaved heads could feed themselves. Two months and a half went by like that. One evening in the seventh month she asked the old woman who did her hair: How much of the summer is left? Half a month, Young Mistress. Then it's the Ghost Festival. So she sent a message across the street by the boy who carried the water. Why did you put me in this prison? It would have been better to brand me on the face and sell me on the upper street like a girl off the ship than to give me to a house like this one. Since the day I came here I have not once seen the Teacher or given one bowl of rice to anyone. Lau Ping read it standing in the door of his brick house and said, My

sections.dateline: The Fong kitchen · the fourteenth day of the seventh month
sections.text: For two weeks the Old Teacher and the temple men came every noon and ate in the Fong front room, and the Fong women stayed out of it, and Wing stayed upstairs. Ah Lin was in the kitchen from before light. It was a long brick room at the back of the house with two iron woks set in a clay stove the length of one wall, and a chopping table, and a door open onto the yard because the heat of the valley at the end of summer came up out of the ground and lay on the town like a lid. She cooked rice and rice and rice. She steamed buns. She sent the boy for winter melon, bean curd, dried mushrooms off the ship from San Francisco. For the last day, the eve of the festival, she had the women making sesame balls, the round ones you fry slowly in a full wok of peanut oil until they swell up hollow and gold, a hundred and more, for the Teacher's men and for the hungry dead who would be fed at the river the next night. That afternoon Wing stood at his window upstairs looking down across the yard into the kitchen door. Tomorrow's their festival, he thought. What is that fool doing? He saw her going back and forth between the stove and the table in an old blue jacket with the sleeves tied back, her

sections.heading: VI. The Lanterns
sections.dateline: The fifteenth day of the seventh month · the Ghost Festival
sections.text: Chin Gam went down to Marysville that night on the late stage and did not sleep. In the morning she came back up the valley road in her carriage with two wagons behind it, and in the wagons were the women of her house and of every house on the alley behind First Street, the singing girls and the ones who were not singing girls, the ones who had paid off their paper and the ones who were still four years from it, forty-one of them, in the best clothes they had. They had roast duck and soy-sauce chicken and steamed white cakes and a whole roast pig on a board, and nobody in Oroville had ever seen anything like it come up the road, and half the town walked alongside the wagons to the Fong door to see what it was. When they got to the front room the Old Teacher and his men were already sitting down with their bowls, and the women stood along the wall with the dishes in their hands and did not dare to come forward and put anything in a single bowl. Ah Lin went down the wall and took the dishes from them one at a time and carried them to the table and served everything out herself. When the meal was finished, Chin Gam and the forty-one women came and knelt on the floor in front of the Ol

title: The Red Umbrella
logline: A Cantonese laborer's plowed field turns to gold, and his daughter hires Marysville's most famous singing girl to buy herself a fortnight.

verses.text: Speak the truth, do not yield to anger; give, if thou art asked for little; by these three steps thou wilt go near the gods.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, the disciple known for his powers, travels to a heaven and stops at the doors of the shining mansions there. He asks each deity how such glory was earned, and each is ashamed to say, because it was so little. One only told the truth. One, a slave in a former life under a master who would strike off a head with whatever was in his hand, kept back her anger. Others gave a stalk of sugarcane, a persimmon, a cucumber, a berry, a handful of radishes, a handful of nimb fruit. Moggallāna asks the Buddha whether such small things can win heaven, and the Buddha answers, "Why ask me? Didn't they tell you?" and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
The lower Brazos, Caney Creek and Oyster Creek were called the sugar bowl of Texas, and before the war Brazoria County made most of the state's sugar on plantations worked by enslaved people. In 1860 the county held 5,110 enslaved people, 2,027 white residents and six free Black residents. Sugar fell away after emancipation and came back, by 1871, on the labor of leased convicts; several of the old plantations later became state prison farms. In 1870 the county's voters helped elect George T. Ruby, a Black former Freedmen's Bureau teacher from Galveston, to the Texas Senate. See the Handbook of Texas on Brazoria County.

The Ninth Census took June 1, 1870 as its day and was gathered by assistant marshals going door to door. It was the first census to list every resident by name; in 1850 and 1860 enslaved people had been counted without names under their owners. The instructions to assistant marshals asked them to approach everyone "in a conciliatory manner," to read the entries back, and to describe anyone who had died since census day "as if living." Under the act of 1850 they were paid two cents for each living person and two cents for each dead one. The appointments went to Republicans, and in the South many of the assistant marshals were Black men; the census superintendent, Francis A. Walker, later judged that the count had missed several hundred thousand Black Southerners.

sections.heading: I. The Portfolio
sections.text: Moses Gallion was born with a veil over his face, and his mother said that was why he could find things. When he was six he walked straight out into the canebrake below the Ransom quarter and came back leading a two-year-old girl everybody else had been calling for since noon. When he was eleven he told the overseer where the strayed mules were, and they were there. Later he found a drowned man in Caney Creek that three boats had dragged for, and after that the people on the creek stopped asking him to find things and started being a little careful around him, the way you are careful around a well. He was twenty-six in the summer of 1870. He could read and write, which he had learned in a Bureau school in a church at Brazoria from a Massachusetts woman who kept a switch on her desk and never once used it. He had a good hand. That was why, in June, a man from the marshal's office came down the river and swore him in on the courthouse steps as an assistant marshal of the United States, and gave him a leather portfolio of blank schedules and a printed sheet of instructions, and told him he would be paid by the name, two cents for every living person and two cents for every dead one. H

sections.heading: II. Dwelling Number
sections.text: It was late in August, and he was nearly done. He had come down the west side of the creek since morning and had one more quarter to do before dark, and he crossed at a place he knew, below the old Ransom sugar house, where the bank was low and there was a gravel bar. The mule went into the water to its knees, and to its belly, and then it was climbing out on a bank he did not know. There was a lane going up from the water between two rows of chinaberry trees. At the end of it were houses. He counted eleven. They were white, with galleries all across the front, and glass in the windows, and green shutters, and every one of them stood in a yard swept clean in the pattern of a broom. He had been up and down Caney Creek his whole life and there was no lane there and there were no houses like that anywhere in the county, not even the Ransoms' before the war. The mule did not seem to mind. He let it walk. At the first gate there was a stalk of ribbon cane in full tassel standing in the air by itself, a foot off the ground, with nothing holding it, the silver plumes stirring a little the way they do in October. A man stood on the gallery. He was tall and very black and he was dressed bet

sections.heading: III. The Sugar Maker
sections.dateline: The Ransom quarter · the next evening
sections.text: Absalom Pleasant had been the sugar maker on the Ransom place for twenty-two grinding seasons. He was the one who stood at the last kettle of the train with the ladle in the steam and the whole quarter waiting behind him, and said when. Two hundred hogsheads a year depended on him knowing the moment the boiling syrup would strike and turn to sugar, and he knew it by the sound, people said, a change in the boil no one else could hear. There had been no sugar made on Caney Creek since the war. When Moses had come to him in June, Mr. Pleasant had given his name and his age, seventy, and when Moses asked his trade he had said sugar maker, and Moses had written it down, though there was nothing in the column for a man who was renting four acres of cotton on shares from his old owner's son. The instructions said that if a man could not tell intelligibly what he was, find out what he does. Mr. Pleasant had told him intelligibly. Moses found him on his step at sundown with a pan of field peas in his lap, shelling. He sat down on the ground in front of him. He did not say good evening. He told him the whole thing, the lane, the chinaberry trees, the cane standing in the air, the eleven hous

sections.heading: IV. Family Number
sections.text: He told it at the brush arbor on the second Sunday in September, because Mr. Pleasant told him to, and he read the names off the page. There were people under the arbor who had known every one of them. The girl who gave the dewberries had a sister there, who had not heard her name said out loud in nine years and put her apron over her face. Afterward people stood around under the trees and did not go home, and talked low, about small things, a dipper of water, a biscuit, a lie they had not told, a blow they had not given back, the way people talk about money they had forgotten they had put away. An old man named Ned Cotton said he had given a stalk of cane once to a preacher on the river road, before the war, and was he the one, and nobody knew. Moses sent his portfolio up to the marshal at the end of the month, every schedule filled and signed and sworn. He kept back one sheet. He was paid by the name, and he was not paid for those. By the grinding season of 1871 the kettles on Caney Creek were going again, with convicts leased from the state penitentiary to feed the fires, and the men at the furnace doors were wearing chains. title: As If Living
logline: A freedman taking the 1870 census, the first to write his people by name, crosses Caney Creek to eleven houses that were never there.

verses.text: The sages who injure nobody, and who always control their body, they will go to the unchangeable place (Nirvana), where, if they have gone, they will suffer no more.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, an old Brahmin of Sāketa meets the Buddha at the city gate, falls at his feet, takes hold of his ankles, and calls him “dear son,” scolding him for staying away so long; the Brahmin's wife does the same and tells their children to greet their brother. The Buddha says he never takes all his meals in one house, so the couple ask him to send them everyone who invites him, and they carry the food to every invitation. When the monks wonder why the Buddha lets them call him son, he says the two had been his parents, uncle and aunt, and grandparents for fifteen hundred lives each, and speaks of love that arises from living together in the past or from kindness in the present, “like a water-lily on the water.” At the end of the rains the couple die together and are carried out on one bier. Mourners console the Buddha for his parents; he does not correct them, and teaches on the shortness of life. Asked where the couple have gone, he says they have gone where there is no grief.
bg.history:
Pheasants are not native to the Dakotas. The first successful release in South Dakota was made in 1908, when three sportsmen let three pairs go north of Redfield, and the first official season, on October 30, 1919, was a single day in Spink County. Redfield, the county seat, calls itself the Pheasant Capital of the World. The 2002 season opened on October 19 with a bag limit of three roosters; 145,696 people hunted, slightly more than half of them from out of state (state figures). That summer was a drought summer across the state, and the price of hay became a political fight (Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis).

The year-long Rotary Youth Exchange began in 1958. Students usually stay about ten months, live with several host families in turn, may not drink, drive, date or use drugs, and wear a blazer covered in traded pins. Rotary clubs recite the Four-Way Test, written by Herbert J. Taylor in the 1930s. At Thai Buddhist funerals, mourners perform kruat nam, pouring water slowly from one vessel into another so the dead may share in the merit; the verse on impermanence the boy says is the stanza traditionally chanted at Buddhist funerals, here in Rhys Davids's version from Buddhist Suttas (1881). “In the Sweet By and By” was written by S. Fillmore Bennett and Joseph P. Webster and published in Chicago in 1868.

sections.heading: I. The Shoulder
sections.dateline: Ostrander, Spink County, South Dakota · September 2002
sections.text: Merle Fossum was eighty-four the year of the drought, and he still drove himself to town every morning for the mail and the markets and coffee at the Bluebird, in a white Ford pickup with the Pioneer sign half worn off the door. That September the pastures along the highway had gone the color of a paper sack. Hay was a hundred dollars a ton when you could find it, and the state agriculture secretary had said in public that the men asking it were greedy, and the men at the Bluebird talked about that and about nothing else. Gary Fossum, who farmed the home place on Turtle Creek now, had sold half the cows in August. The exchange student had been in town three weeks. The Rotary brought one most years. This one was from Thailand, from a city called Phitsanulok, sixteen years old and slight, with a navy blazer he wore to school on Fridays with pins all down both lapels: the Thai flag, the Rotary wheel, a Twins cap, and a little enamel pheasant somebody had given him the first day. His name was Siriwat. He told people to call him Ton. Ron Hagen, who sold insurance and was Rotary president that year and the boy's first host father, called him Tom, and went on calling him Tom until June. E

sections.heading: II. Hot Dish
sections.text: Dorothy wanted him at her table every night. You eat here, she said. Your dad can pick you up after school. He explained it to her as well as he could. A Rotary student lived with three families in the year, a few months each, and ate where he was asked: with the members, with the churches, with the football coach, with anybody who wanted to know about Thailand. That was what he was there for. I can't eat always in one house, he said. In Rotary, I go around. Dorothy thought about that with her hand flat on the oilcloth. Then whoever asks you, you tell them to call me. So it went all fall. When Cheryl Hagen had the Lutheran pastor and his wife over to meet the boy, the phone rang at three and it was Dorothy, and at a quarter to six Merle's pickup was in the drive with a roaster on the seat wrapped in a bath towel. When the Kjellsens had him out to the farm, Dorothy brought the supper. sections.heading: III. The Four-Way Test
sections.text: Rotary met Tuesdays at noon at the Legion hall, twenty-two members, hot beef sandwiches and mashed potatoes and a slice of bar. They said the Pledge, and then they said the Four-Way Test together off the banner on the wall, the way they had every Tuesday since most of them could remember. Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? Will it build goodwill and better friendships? Will it be beneficial to all concerned? Then happy dollars, and then the program. The program that day was the exchange student. He had a borrowed laptop and the school's projector and forty pictures. His mother and father in front of their house in Phitsanulok, his father an engineer for the provincial electric company, his mother a high-school teacher of English. His little sister in her school uniform. A rice field. A market on the river. The big temple with its gold Buddha, and himself at twelve in front of it, shaved and robed, squinting in the sun. When he was done Ron Hagen asked if there were questions, and Duane Bauer from the elevator, who was a plain man and had been the boy's second host father since December, asked the one the whole town had. sections.heading: IV. Seed Corn
sections.text: In March the boy moved to his third family, the parsonage behind the Methodist church, where the pastor was a woman named Karen Lindahl with two little boys and a husband who taught science at the school. The rule held. Whoever had him to supper, Dorothy brought the supper. Pastor Karen said that between Advent and Easter she had eaten more of Dorothy Fossum's cooking than she had of her own. In April Merle told Gary which quarter to put the beans on and which to leave for corn, and then he gave Gary his tools, all of them, the good socket set and the welder and the anvil that had been his father's. He gave his chore coat to the Bauer boy, who had been wanting one. Dorothy gave her Haviland dishes to the granddaughters, eight place settings each, and the quilts to Janice. She went to the parsonage one afternoon and sat with Pastor Karen at the kitchen table and told her which hymn she wanted, and which scripture, and that it was all written down on a card in the drawer under the phone. It's like they're packing for a trip, Janice said to her brothers on the phone. She said it as a nurse. She meant it was a sign. But nothing showed. They were well. Their color was good. They sat in

sections.heading: V. The Basement
sections.dateline: The Methodist church · the last week of May
sections.text: The church was full and so was the basement, where they had set up speakers, and people stood along the walls of both. Gary put the boy in the front pew between Janice and Rick, and nobody said anything about it. Pastor Karen read the scripture from the card in the drawer, and then they sang the hymn Dorothy had written down, which was an old one, older than the church, and which most of the people there had sung at a funeral before and knew without the book. We shall sing on that beautiful shorethe melodious songs of the blest;and our spirits shall sorrow no more—not a sigh for the blessing of rest. — S. Fillmore Bennett, “In the Sweet By and By” (1868) Afterward, when they had come back down from the hill, there was lunch in the basement. title: Hot Dish
logline: In a drought fall, an old farm couple kneel on the highway shoulder and greet a Thai Rotary exchange student as their long-lost son.

verses.text: Those who are ever watchful, who study day and night, and who strive after Nirvana, their passions will come to an end.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Puṇṇā is a slave woman in the house of a rich man of Rājagaha who is made to pound rice late into the night. Stepping outside to cool off, she sees monks walking up the mountain by a light that the elder Dabba Mallaputta, steward of lodgings, makes shine from his finger, and she supposes one of them must be sick or snakebitten. At dawn she bakes a coarse cake of rice-flour scrapings on the coals and offers it to the Buddha on the road, sure he will throw it to a dog. Instead he has Ānanda spread a robe, sits down, and eats it, while the gods squeeze heavenly nectar into it. He tells her that she stays awake because she suffers, and his monks stay awake because they watch, and speaks this verse; she is established in the first stage of awakening on the spot. When the monks marvel that he ate such poor food, he tells a birth story of a thoroughbred colt raised by an old woman on rice-water and scraps, which refuses that food once it is recognized and goes on to run over water and stand on its master's palm.
bg.history:
Daly City, on the foggy ridge just south of San Francisco, has the highest concentration of Filipinos of any midsized city in North America; a third of its residents were Filipino in the 2020 census, and it is known as the “Pinoy Capital.” Its Westlake tract inspired Malvina Reynolds' 1962 song “Little Boxes.” Many Filipino Americans work in health care: nearly a fifth of Filipina Americans have worked as registered nurses, and during the COVID-19 pandemic Filipinos, about 4 percent of the nation's registered nurses, made up nearly a third of nurse deaths, according to a 2020 report by National Nurses United. Many others, documented and not, work as caregivers in small residential homes for the elderly. “Tago nang tago” (“hiding and hiding”) is the common Filipino term for an immigrant without papers.

Simbang Gabi, the nine-day novena of Masses from December 16 to 24, began in the Spanish Philippines in the seventeenth century as a dawn Mass for farmers who had to be in the fields by sunrise; the parol, the star lantern, first lit the way to church in the dark. After Mass people eat bibingka in the churchyard: a cake of galapong, rice soaked overnight and ground on a millstone, baked in a clay pot lined with banana leaf with coals below and above. Puring's hometown, Calasiao in Pangasinan, is famous for its own rice cake, puto Calasiao. The Gospel Lola Charing recites, Mark 13:33–37, was read at Mass on the First Sunday of Advent in 2023, December 3. It is quoted here in the Douay-Rheims version as revised by Bishop Challoner.

sections.heading: I. The Grinding
sections.text: The house was pink stucco with a garage underneath, like every other house on the street, and six old people lived in it who could not live anywhere else. Mr. Rolando Bautista owned it. He owned four of them, two in Daly City and two in South San Francisco, and a black Lexus, and a house in the hills above Westlake with a view of the ocean on the days when there was no fog, and people called him Boy Bautista the way they had called him that in Batangas, though he was sixty-three. Purificación Dagdag took care of the six old people in the pink house. She was fifty-one. She had come in 2009 on a tourist visa to see a cousin and stayed when it ran out, and she had been tago nang tago ever since, hiding and hiding, which meant she could not go home. She had not gone home when her mother died in 2021, in the second year of the sickness, and had watched the funeral in Calasiao on a phone propped against the toaster. She sent money every two weeks to a daughter who was twenty-four now and a son who was twenty-one and whose faces she knew better from the screen than from memory. Everyone called her Puring. sections.heading: II. The Stairs
sections.text: Daly City in December is fog and wind off the ocean, and the wind came straight up the street from the Pacific and went through her wet shirt like water. She stood in it with her arms out from her sides. It was the best she had felt all night. Behind the houses on her side of the street the hill went up steep, too steep to build on, with ice plant on it and a few cypresses bent over sideways by eighty years of wind. A concrete stairway went up the hill from the end of the street, a hundred and forty steps, to the parking lot of Holy Child at the top. On the upper side of the parking lot, apart from the church, there was a small chapel with a glass door, and in the chapel there was a gold monstrance on the altar with the Host in it, and somebody was always there. Somebody had been there every hour of every day and night since 1994, kneeling or sitting, keeping watch, one hour each. They called it perpetual adoration. Puring had never been in it. She had never had an hour. The lamps along the stairs had been broken since the storms the winter before, when a cypress came down across them. But there were lights on the stairs now. She counted seven. They were going up, slowly, one behin

sections.heading: III. The Cake
sections.text: Junior came for the galapong at four-thirty in his mother's Sienna with the engine running and loaded the stockpots into the back without saying anything, and Puring stood in the driveway in her slippers and watched the taillights go up the hill. There was some left. There always was, at the bottom of the coolers, the broken grains and the cloudy water, and in the bottom of the blender jar a coarse paste, gritty, the part that had not ground fine. Tita Baby did not want it. Tita Baby did not use anything that was not perfect, because people paid six dollars a cake. Puring scraped it all together in a bowl with her fingers. There was not much, a cupful. She did not have an egg to spare or any sugar she could account for, so she put in nothing, only a pinch of salt and a spoon of baking powder from the cupboard. In the garage Tita Baby kept bags of charcoal for the churchyard, and Puring took eight briquettes, which she would replace, and lit them in a coffee can on the back step with a sheet of the Filipino newspaper they gave away free at the grocery.
