sections.heading: IV. The Bench
sections.text: The dawn Mass had let out. People were coming down the hundred and forty steps in the half dark in their good coats, with plates of Tita Baby's bibingka held out in front of them and steam coming off the plates, and at the bottom of the stairs, where there was a bus bench under a streetlight, Puring saw Lola Charing. Everybody in that part of Daly City knew Lola Charing. She was eighty-six. She had come from the Philippines in 1969 on a nurses' exchange visa with twenty other girls from the same school in Manila and had worked nights in a hospital in San Francisco for forty-one years. Nights, always, by choice: she said the night was when people were most afraid and there were fewer people there to see it. She had buried a husband and outlived two of her own girls from that school who died in the sickness, still nursing at seventy, and she still did not sleep at night. She kept the three o'clock hour in the chapel every day of the week, and had for years, and then went home and slept until noon. She was very small and wore a red wool coat and walked with a cane she mostly did not use. Her grandnephew Jun-jun walked with her, a big young man in hospital scrubs under a fleece, who wa

sections.dateline: The parish hall of Holy Child
sections.text: In the parish hall the ladies of the Couples for Christ and the Legion of Mary had heard all about it before Lola Charing got through the door. Someone had seen from the top of the stairs. Lola Charing had sat on a bus bench on Mission Street and eaten a burnt thing that Boy Bautista's TNT caregiver had cooked in a coffee can, when there were two hundred of Tita Baby's bibingka on the tables and a whole lechon with the skin still crackling. Kawawa naman si Lola, they were saying, poor Lola, at the coffee urn. To eat that. She's too kind. At her age. Lola Charing heard it. She sat down at the end of a long table and Jun-jun brought her a cup of salabat, the ginger tea, and she asked the ladies what they were talking about, though she knew. They told her, a little embarrassed. It's not the first time, Lola said. That I've eaten her rice. They waited. I was born in Calasiao, she said. Did you know that? Same as Puring. In 1937. My mother had no milk, and there was no money for milk, and an old woman next door who had nothing at all fed me am from a spoon. Rice water, from the top of the pot. That is what I was raised on. sections.heading: VI. The Watch
sections.text: Puring went on working in the pink house. Nothing about it changed. She ground the rice for Tita Baby every night of the novena, nine nights, and carried the sheets down the hill every morning, and slept behind the curtain in the garage with the monitor by her head. But on the night of the twenty-fourth, at three o'clock in the morning, with the galapong poured and the blender cooling in the sink and the six old people asleep down the hall, she went out and sat on the back step in her jacket. Mr. Haggerty was asleep in his pajamas. Mrs. Lim had not called since one. Mrs. Ocampo had stopped crying in her sleep three nights before, and nobody knew why. Up the hill the lights were going up the stairs, and in front of them the small white one, steady. The chapel door opened and closed at the top. She did not have an hour in Mang Dado's book. She could not leave the house. She sat on her step with her hands in her lap and listened to the house breathing behind her, six old people asleep, and kept the hour from there. title: Rice Water
logline: An undocumented caregiver grinds rice all night for a rich man's Christmas stall and sees lights climbing the stairs to the chapel.

verses.text: This is an old saying, O Atula, this is not only of to-day: ‘They blame him who sits silent, they blame him who speaks much, they also blame him who says little; there is no one on earth who is not blamed.’
There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.

But he whom those who discriminate praise continually day after day, as without blemish, wise, rich in knowledge and virtue, who would dare to blame him, like a coin made of gold from the Gambu river? Even the gods praise him, he is praised even by Brahman.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the lay follower Atula takes his five hundred companions to hear the Dhamma. Elder Revata, a solitary who delights in seclusion “as a lion delights in solitude,” says nothing, and Atula leaves angry. Elder Sāriputta expounds the Abhidhamma at great length, and Atula finds it too abstruse. Elder Ānanda teaches briefly and simply, and Atula is angry at him too. At last he goes to the Buddha, who tells him that people have always blamed the silent, the talkative and the moderate, that even kings, the earth, the sun and moon and the Buddha himself are blamed by some and praised by others, and that only the praise of the wise, who examine a person day after day, counts. All five hundred enter the stream.
bg.history:
Metro Detroit holds the largest community of Chaldean and Assyrian Americans in the country, around 150,000 people. Most Chaldean families trace their roots to villages on the Nineveh plain such as Tel Keppe, which the Islamic State captured in August 2014 and Iraqi forces retook in January 2017. Over the decades many families moved from Detroit’s Seven Mile “Chaldean Town” to suburbs such as Sterling Heights, Warren, Troy and West Bloomfield, and Chaldean grocers came to run a large share of the region’s party stores. The Chaldean Catholic Church keeps the East Syriac rite; the cathedral of its Detroit eparchy is in Southfield. In 1994 Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Dinkha IV of the Assyrian Church of the East signed a Common Christological Declaration, closing a dispute over the natures of Christ that went back to the fifth century. Three weeks before Lent, East and West Syriac churches keep the three-day Fast of the Ninevites (Ba’utha).

The monk’s home is near Alqosh, below the cliff monastery of Rabban Hormizd, founded about 640 and honeycombed with hermits’ cells cut into the rock; in 1859 a new monastery, Our Lady of the Seeds, was built on the plain about a mile away. Suhaila’s scripture is the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible of her church, in the English of James Murdock, who in 1851 published the first English translation of the New Testament made from it. Her father’s touchstone is the goldsmith’s old test: gold drawn across the dark stone leaves a streak whose color shows its purity.

sections.heading: I. The Monk
sections.dateline: Sterling Heights, Michigan · the Ninevite fast, January 2023
sections.text: Fadi Atallah sold Jeeps at a dealership on Van Dyke in Warren, and on Sunday nights, and sometimes on Wednesdays, he went live on his phone and talked about God. He called it Faith with Fadi. He had started it during the lockdown in 2020, when the churches were closed and he was living in his parents' basement with nothing to do, and for two years forty people watched it, most of them aunts. He talked about the saints. He talked about the martyrs of the Nineveh plain, and about his grandmother, who had left Telkaif in 1977 with her gold sewn into the hem of her dress, and about the Detroit Lions, whom he considered a test of faith. He was thirty-one, handsome in a heavy-eyebrowed way, and he had the dealership voice, warm and fast, the voice that tells you there is never going to be a better time than now. That January his cousin's wedding put him on the map. Somebody's video of Fadi leading the line dance at a banquet hall on Van Dyke, a hundred and forty people holding pinkies, went around the internet and came back again, and when it came back it had brought him nine thousand followers. Most of them were Chaldean, from Sterling Heights and El Cajon and Sydney and Toronto and Amm

sections.heading: II. The Doctor
sections.dateline: The parish hall · the second night
sections.text: On the second night he went to Father Raad. Everybody also knew Father Raad. He had a doctorate from the Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome and had written a book, in English, with footnotes, about the Christology of the Church of the East. On the Tuesday of the Ba'utha he was giving a lecture in the parish hall for the young adults, and the folding chairs were set out in rows, and Fadi sat in the front with his phone on a little tripod on his knee. Five hundred and forty people were watching when Father Raad began. Fadi wants the one thing, said Father Raad, smiling, when he saw the phone. So I'll give you the one thing. But to understand the one thing you must understand three words. The three words were in Syriac. One was kyana, which meant nature, and one was parsopa, which meant something like person, and the third was qnoma, which Father Raad said could not really be translated at all, though he would spend some time explaining why. He explained how the Church of the East had said for fifteen centuries that in Christ there were two natures and two qnome in one parsopa, and how the Greeks and the Latins had said two natures in one hypostasis, and how everybody had called ev

sections.heading: III. The Young Father
sections.dateline: The church on Seventeen Mile · Wednesday
sections.text: On the third day, after the liturgy that ends the fast, Fadi caught Father Danny in the sacristy taking off his vestments. Father Danny was twenty-nine and had been born at Providence Hospital in Southfield and had played point guard at De La Salle. He was the one the kids liked. He said Mass fast and his homilies were short and he was, everyone agreed, the future. Fadi told him about the monk and about Father Raad. Father Danny laughed and said Rabban was a saint and Father Raad was a genius, and Fadi said that was very nice, but he had five hundred people, and they had come for something, and they had gotten a man who wouldn't talk and a man who wouldn't stop. Okay, said Father Danny. Put it on. Fadi went live. Four hundred and eighty people were watching. Father Danny pulled his alb off over his head and folded it over his arm and looked straight into the phone. Here's the whole thing. God loves you. Jonah didn't want to go to Nineveh because he knew God would forgive them, and God forgave them. So fast when it's time to fast. Forgive somebody this week, somebody specific. Call your mom. That's it. That's the Ba'utha. God bless. It took forty seconds. Then he went to hang up the

sections.heading: IV. The Store
sections.dateline: Royal Star Market, Dequindre Road, Warren
sections.text: Suhaila Kassab was not really his aunt. She was his mother's first cousin, which in Sterling Heights is the same thing. She ran the Royal Star Market on Dequindre, the road that divides Macomb County from Oakland, a party store with a lottery machine and a beer cave and a deli counter and a wall of hot sauces she said were the best selection north of Eight Mile. She had run it alone since her husband Wadie died in April of 2020, in the first wave, in the ICU at Beaumont, while she stood in the parking lot with her phone and the nurse held the other phone to his ear. She was fifty-six. She opened the store at seven in the morning and closed it at midnight, and in between she knew everyone who came through the door, and their mothers, and what they owed her, and she told them. There was still a plexiglass shield on the counter from the pandemic, taped at the corners, with a slot at the bottom for money. Suhaila had never taken it down. She said it kept the flu off her and the lottery players' breath, and anyway Wadie had put it up. Fadi came in stamping snow. She looked at him over the plexiglass. You didn't eat. The fast's over. I know the fast is over. I didn't ask if the fast was

sections.heading: V. The Stone
sections.text: She reached under the counter, below the lottery machine, and brought out a small black stone, flat and smooth, a touchstone the size of a bar of hotel soap, and set it on the counter on her side of the plexiglass, where the phone could see it. Fadi had seen it all his life and never asked about it. It sat next to the register, under a rubber mat, with the rolls of quarters. My father's, said Suhaila. From the shop. Her father, Yousif, had been a goldsmith in Baghdad for forty years, she said, and his father before him, and in all that time he had never once asked a customer whether a piece was gold. People would come in to sell a bracelet and swear on their mothers it was twenty-one karat, and he would smile and say, of course, of course, and take out the stone. She slid her wedding ring off her finger and drew it across the stone, firmly, once. It left a short bright streak, like a struck match. You don't ask the man. You ask the stone. And the stone doesn't care who is the man. And my father, she said, tested his own gold. Every piece, before he sold it, even the pieces he made with his own hands that morning. Every day. Forty years. Because one day, he said, you will get tired,

sections.heading: VI. Five Hundred
sections.dateline: Warren and the world · after midnight
sections.text: Fadi did not notice the phone until she had locked the door behind the last customer and turned off the beer cave lights. It was still live, propped against the hot sauces. It had been live for fifty-one minutes. In the corner it said that four hundred and ninety-six people were watching. It was the number it had said when she began. He picked it up. He scrolled back through the comments, and then he scrolled again, because he did not understand what he was looking at. There were no comments. From the moment Suhaila had held her phone up to the plexiglass, nobody had typed anything at all. Not amen, not lol, not boring, not a single heart. For fifty-one minutes, four hundred and ninety-six people in Sterling Heights and El Cajon and Sydney and Toronto and Amman and the other places, people who had left the monk and left Father Raad and complained about Father Danny, had watched a woman in an apron sell lottery tickets and talk about a stone, and none of them had said a word, and none of them had gone. title: The Touchstone
logline: During the Ninevite fast, a Chaldean car salesman livestreams three teachers to five hundred viewers and is angry at all of them.

verses.text: Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body! Leave the sins of the body, and with thy body practise virtue!
Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue! Leave the sins of the tongue, and practise virtue with thy tongue!
Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind! Leave the sins of the mind, and practise virtue with thy mind!
The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is a few lines long. The monks of the Group of Six, whose misbehaviour is the occasion for a great many of the monastic rules, put on wooden shoes, take a staff in each hand and tramp up and down on a flat rock. The Buddha hears the clatter and asks Ānanda what it is; told, he lays down that a monk should control his deeds, his words and his thoughts, and speaks the four verses.
bg.history:
Beverwijck, the fur-trading village beside Fort Orange on the upper Hudson, is now Albany, New York. On December 10, 1659, its court, “having heard diverse complaints from the burghers of this place against the practice of playing golf along the streets, which causes great damage to the windows of the houses and also exposes people to the danger of being injured,” forbade the game in the streets under a penalty of twenty-five guilders a person (Fort Orange Court Minutes, tr. Charles Gehring). The game was kolf, played with a weighted stick and a ball; the ordinance is often cited as the first mention of golf in America. The six boys, the glazier and his window are invented.

The Reformed church was the only public worship the colony allowed, and Lutherans, of whom the upper Hudson had a good many, were refused a preacher of their own through the 1650s. Reformed children learned the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) by heart, and its fifty-two Lord’s Days were preached through at the Sunday afternoon service. The answer quoted is from the old English version long used by the Reformed Church in America.

sections.heading: I. The Six
sections.dateline: Beverwijck, New Netherland · Sunday, the seventh of December 1659
sections.text: There were six of them, and the village had stopped using their names. Wouter the baker’s son was fifteen and the tallest. Teunis was fifteen too, and Claes and Jochem were fourteen, and Gerrit, and Dirck, who was thirteen and did what the others did. If a sleigh was found on a roof, or a hog with a brewer’s hat tied on, people said the six and went on with their work. The river had been shut for two weeks. The last yacht had gone down to the Manhatans, the traders’ rooms were empty of beaver, and there was nothing to do until spring but cut wood and go to church. That Sunday afternoon the domine was preaching the catechism sermon in the blockhouse church where the two streets crossed. The six were not at it. They had their klompen on, with straw in them, and each one had his kolf in his two hands, a stick of ash as long as his leg with a lead-weighted foot, and they were going up and down the Jonkerstraat after a ball. The street had frozen in its ruts as hard as a hearthstone. Twelve wooden shoes on it made a noise like a mill. Meester Harmen the glazier sat at his bench by the front window with his hands in his lap. He was past seventy and came from Holstein, and he was a Luther

sections.heading: II. Three Sounds
sections.text: The game was to drive the ball from the church to the bridge over the kill in the fewest strokes. Wouter had it. He was a stroke up on Teunis and had been all afternoon, and he swung for the bridge, and Teunis stepped across him and took the ball off the toe of his stick. Wouter did not think. The kolf was already in his hands. He brought it round low and laid the weighted foot of it across Teunis’s shin, above the shoe, and it made a sound like an axe going into green wood. Teunis went down on one knee on the ice. Then he said it, loud enough for the Jonkerstraat. He called Wouter a thief, and a thief’s son, whose father sold loaves two ounces light and had been before the court for it. That last part was true, and everyone on the street knew it. Wouter did not answer him. He stood over the ball with his face gone white and still, and looked at Teunis, and went on looking. Then he hit the ball as hard as he had ever hit anything. He did not look where. It went through the glazier’s front casement, two feet from the old man’s head. The six stood where they were. Running was no use; there was nowhere in Beverwijck to run to. The door opened and Meester Harmen came out in his leather

sections.heading: III. Twenty-Five Guilders
sections.dateline: Fort Orange · Wednesday, the tenth of December
sections.text: On Wednesday the court sat in the fort. The burghers had been complaining for a month, and the glazier’s casement was only the last of it. The commissary and the magistrates had it written into the book and read out in the street: that the playing of kolf along the streets did great damage to the windows of the houses and put people in danger of being hurt, and that it was forbidden to all persons from that day, under penalty of twenty-five guilders for each one found doing it. Twenty-five guilders was more than six kolven and twelve klompen would fetch, with the six boys thrown in. That was how it always went with the six. Each thing they did turned into a rule for everybody. The court could do nothing about the rest of it. The magistrates had no ordinance for a boy’s face. Wouter came to the glazier’s door on Thursday morning by himself, without his stick. He did not say why he had come, and Meester Harmen did not ask him. The casement lay flat on the bench with the broken diamond cut out of it. The old man had a new one ready, scored and snapped from the last sheet in the crate. Wash your hands. Hold it there, by the edges. Do not press, and do not let go. Wouter held it. The gl

title: The New Pane
logline: Six boys in wooden shoes play kolf down a frozen Dutch street during the catechism sermon, past an old glazier's window.

verses.text: Thou art now like a sear leaf, the messengers of death (Yama) have come near to thee; thou standest at the door of thy departure, and thou hast no provision for thy journey.
Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise! When thy impurities are blown away, and thou art free from guilt, thou wilt enter into the heavenly world of the elect (Ariya).
Thy life has come to an end, thou art come near to death (Yama), there is no resting-place for thee on the road, and thou hast no provision for thy journey.
Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise! When thy impurities are blown away, and thou art free from guilt, thou wilt not enter again into birth and decay.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a cow-killer of Sāvatthī will not eat his rice without meat. When a friend carries off his supper, he cuts the tongue out of a living ox, and as he eats it his own tongue splits and falls into the dish; he crawls about his yard bellowing like an ox until he dies. His terrified son flees to Takkasilā, is apprenticed to a goldsmith, marries the master’s daughter and lives out his life without a single good work. His sons, who have become followers of the Buddha, bring him home in his old age and give alms in his name two days running, and each day the Buddha thanks the old man with two verses, telling him he is a withered leaf with no provisions for the journey and must make himself an island.
bg.history:
Springfield was founded in 1636 by the Puritan fur trader William Pynchon as Agawam Plantation, on land bought from the Agawam people. The Pynchons traded furs, grain and salt pork; pork packed in hogsheads went down the Connecticut River and, in time, as far as the West Indies. In 1675, during King Philip’s War, most of the town was burned. The colony’s first law code, the Massachusetts Body of Liberties of 1641, included the clause Elias Cole broke, often called the first animal-protection law in America. The psalms in the story are quoted from the Bay Psalm Book, printed at Cambridge in 1640, the first book printed in British North America, in its own spelling (with the long s modernized); eleven copies of that first edition survive.

In Boston, goldsmiths made the gold mourning rings that families gave out at funerals, decorated with skeletons, coffins and winged death’s heads in the memento mori tradition: remember that you must die. Return Cole arrives the year before the Salem witch trials and lives through the Great Snow of 1717. The awakening that reaches his sons began in Jonathan Edwards’s Northampton congregation in 1734 and spread to some twenty-five towns of western Massachusetts and central Connecticut before it waned in 1737, a forerunner of the First Great Awakening. The new precinct on the Chicopee, its minister and the Cole family are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Flesh
sections.text: Elias Cole killed beasts for fifty-five years. He came up the river at fifteen in the year the town was planted, when it was still called Agawam and there were still Indian cornfields on the meadows, and somebody put a knife in his hand that first winter and he never set it down. He killed for the families who could not bring themselves to do it and for the ones who could not spare the day. He killed the fat oxen and the barren cows in November, and hogs by the hundred, for the salt barrels that went down the river on the flatboats to Hartford, and from Hartford to Boston and the sugar islands, where they fed men he would never see. He was paid in wheat, in wampum when there was wampum, in shillings when there were shillings, and always in the best piece of whatever he had killed, which he carried home himself under his arm. He ate it with his wife and his son at his own board and sold the rest. He would not eat without flesh. Samp, hasty pudding, rye-and-Indian bread, pease, the sallet greens his wife grew by the door: none of it would go past his teeth unless there was meat on the trencher beside it. The town said Elias Cole would starve to death in a cornfield. The meetinghouse

sections.heading: II. The Ring
sections.text: It is ninety miles by the Bay Path and Return walked it in five days. He slept in barns and once in a hollow log. He ate what women gave him at back doors, and when they asked whose boy he was he said he was going to his uncle in Boston, and he had no uncle in Boston. He did not open his mouth for anything else. Boston smelled of tar and fish and the sea, and it had more people in it than he had known were in the world. He went up and down the streets near the Town House for a week, sleeping under a wharf, and on the seventh day he stood in front of a goldsmith’s window watching a man inside work the bellows at a little furnace, and the man came out and asked him what he wanted. The goldsmith was Isaac Lowde. He needed a boy. He asked if Return could read, and Return took the psalm book out of his shirt and read him the first psalm that came, and Lowde nodded and asked whose boy he was, and Return said nothing at all. Well, said Lowde, a boy who can’t be made to talk is a boy who won’t tell the customers what’s in the strongbox. And he bound him for seven years. The next summer they hanged people at Salem for things a great deal less than what Return had seen, and he heard the men

sections.heading: III. Forty Years
sections.text: Return Cole kept a shop of his own for nearly forty years. He had three sons and two daughters and he named the girls Mercy and Hannah. He made porringers and spoons and tankards and the clasps for Bibles and the buckles for shoes, but mostly he made rings, because he was the best in the town at rings and everyone knew it. He did not keep count. Hannah once tried to reckon it from the books and stopped somewhere above three thousand. Three thousand little skulls. Three thousand times he cut MEMENTO MORI round a gold hoop with a graver no bigger than a darning needle, and never once in all those years did he read the words. He was civil to everybody and spoke to nobody. He went to meeting because the law still said he must, and sat on the back bench with his hat on his knees. He never owned the covenant. He never gave the minister anything beyond his rate. When Hannah asked him why not, he said the minister had a salary, and went back to his bench. His children learned the catechism at their mother’s knee and recited it to him on Sunday evenings, and he listened with his eyes on the fire. When they asked about their grandfather he said He was a butcher. He died. When they asked how,

sections.heading: IV. The First Day
sections.dateline: The new precinct on the Chicopee · January 1737
sections.text: He was sixty-two years old. He had walked down that road at seventeen and he was carried up it at sixty-two in a sleigh under a bearskin, and it took four days, and he did not say anything the whole way except about the cold. His sons had talked something else over by the fire. Their father had never in his life done one thing for God that he was not made to do by law. He was old. Soon he would go where they could not follow him, and he would go with nothing. They could not give him a heart. But they could do what was in their power, which was to keep a feast in his name, as people do for the poor, and let him have whatever good there was in it. So they asked the minister to dine at Isaac’s house on the Thursday, and the deacons, and every soul in the precinct who could get there through the snow. The minister was a young man named Jonas Thorne. He was twenty-six, Harvard College, and he had been ordained in the new meetinghouse only in October, when the frame was barely closed in. He was thin, and he had a cough that winter that people worried over. He was not a great preacher. He read his sermons in a light voice with his eyes down. But in the year he had been on the Chicopee he

sections.heading: V. The Second Day
sections.dateline: Isaac Cole’s house · the next day
sections.text: The sons did not ask him what had happened. That night they asked Mr. Thorne to come again the next day, and he came, through new snow, with his cough worse. There was not so much to eat the second day, because they had eaten most of it the first, and it did not matter. This time the brothers said it plainly, before the meal and after it: this is for our father, Mr. Thorne. Not for us. For him only. So when they had eaten, the minister turned again on the bench to the old man. Mr. Cole. You are very far along in years. You are come almost to the door. Between here and there, there is no inn on the road, no house to put up at, no place to stop and get your breath. And you have nothing in your bag. He was quiet a while. You know how they take the dross off silver. You know it better than I do. Blow it off. Blow it off again. Quickly, while there’s fire. Get up on the high ground, Mr. Cole, and there’s a place where the water doesn’t come. Then he reached for the old man’s psalm book, which had been left on the shelf since the day before, and held it shut on his knee. He had sat up with it half the night, his landlady said afterward. He said the words from memory, in the old book’s ow

title: Neat’s Tongue
logline: A Puritan butcher’s son flees a judgment, spends forty years engraving death’s heads on Boston mourning rings, and is fetched home by his sons.

verses.text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.

bg.commentary: In the commentary a brahmin of Sāvatthī stands each morning at the place outside the city where the bhikkhus put on their robes before going in for alms. He sees a robe drag through dewy grass, and the next day clears the grass with a mattock. He sees a robe trail in the dust, and spreads sand. On a hot morning he sees them sweat, and puts up a pavilion; on a wet one he sees their robes rained on, and builds a hall. At the feast for its completion he takes the Buddha’s bowl and tells him the whole thing from the beginning, and the Buddha answers that a wise man removes his own stains just so, little by little and moment by moment, as a smith does with silver.
bg.history:
Cranston lies just south and west of Providence, and by the 1960s much of it was streets of postwar houses. The morning Providence Journal and its afternoon sister, the Evening Bulletin, were carried house to house by boys, as papers were all over the country: a district man dropped wired bundles at a corner before dawn, and the carriers folded them, bagged them and rode their routes before school. Mr. Tefft’s trade was mechanical drawing by hand, and a checker was the senior draftsman who went over every sheet before it left the room. His employer, the machine-tool and measuring-instrument maker Brown & Sharpe, left its old Providence works for North Kingstown in 1964. Larkspur Road, Wheelock Avenue and the people on them are invented. Coffee milk is what Rhode Island children drink.

The Gorham Manufacturing Company made silver in Providence from 1831, and from 1890 in a great works in the Elmwood neighborhood, not far from Cranston. Its Chantilly flatware pattern dates from 1895. Women there worked in the case room, among other departments, sewing the linings of presentation cases and the flannel bags that kept silver from the air. The evangelist Billy Sunday held some seventy meetings in a wooden tabernacle in Providence in September and October 1918, until the city closed public gatherings on account of the influenza. “Brighten the Corner Where You Are,” with words by Ina Duley Ogdon and music by Charles H. Gabriel, was published in 1913 and became the theme song of his campaigns under his song leader Homer Rodeheaver.

sections.heading: I. Grass
sections.text: Norman Tefft had been a checker in the drafting room at Brown & Sharpe for twenty-six of his thirty-eight years there. Other men drew the parts and he went over their sheets with a red pencil. He retired in 1964, when the company moved down to North Kingstown, and his wife died the winter after. Since then he had kept the house on the corner of Larkspur Road and Wheelock Avenue the way he had kept other men’s drawings. The lawn was edged with a spade along a stretched string. Beyond his lot line, in the point where the two streets met, lay a wedge of ground that belonged to the electric company. A streetlight stood on it. At five every morning a green station wagon stopped under the light and a man put out seven bundles of the Providence Journal, and by ten past there were seven boys kneeling around them. Mr. Tefft knew the boys by their faults. They left bundle wire. They cut across his corner. In 1965 he had telephoned the paper about them four times, and once he had stood over a boy named Dennis until every rubber band was picked up out of his pachysandra. He had not slept past half past four since Eleanor died. One morning in the first week of June he was standing at the kitche

sections.heading: II. Sand
sections.text: With the grass off, the ground showed for what it was. Under the streetlight, where the bundles had landed every morning for years, there was no turf at all. There was a bare place the size of a dining table, gray, and fine as flour in dry weather. He stood at the window. The boys knelt in it and folded, three folds and a tuck, and stood the folded papers on end against their knees. A bag set down sent up a little smoke of dust. The tall boy slapped at the seat of his dungarees. A front page lay face down a moment and came up with the print of the ground on it. Sand, said Mr. Tefft. He had most of a yard of washed mason’s sand behind the garage, left from the patio he had laid in 1961. He wheeled four barrows of it across before noon and spread it two inches deep with the back of a rake, and tamped it, and struck it off level with a length of two-by-four.

sections.heading: III. Shade, and Then a Roof
sections.text: In the second week of July the nights stopped cooling. At half past five one morning the sun was already over the maples across Wheelock Avenue and the thermometer on his garage stood at eighty-one. The boys had their shirts off and tied around their waists. The sweat ran down their arms as they folded, and the newsprint came off black on their forearms and went from there onto the papers. That afternoon he set four cedar posts in the sand, eight feet on centers, and stretched over them the canvas fly from the tent he and Eleanor had taken to Maine each August until her knees gave out. The fly served for six weeks. Then, on a morning late in August, it rained out of the northeast, the kind of rain that travels sideways. He watched seven boys crowd toward the middle of a square of dry sand that grew smaller as he looked. The bundles on the windward side took the water through their wrappers. The small one, whose name he had learned was Stevie, put his own body between the rain and his bag. Mr. Tefft went down cellar, where his drawing board had stood under a sheet since 1964. He took off the sheet and taped down a clean piece of vellum. He drew the thing at an inch and a half to the

sections.heading: IV. The Cookout
sections.text: When the last screw was in he thought there ought to be something to mark it. He asked the boys for Saturday noon, all seven, and he asked the man with the station wagon. The man’s name was Earl Aldrich. He was the district man for the Journal on that side of Cranston. He was fifty-eight and had put out bundles in the dark for twenty-two years, and the boys minded him without his ever raising his voice. They said that he never forgot a route or what a boy was owed, down to the penny. Mr. Tefft cooked frankfurters on the patio and carried them across in a roasting pan. There was coffee milk in the two-gallon picnic jug, and a sheet cake from the bakery in Garden City, and Eleanor’s potato salad made from the card in her handwriting. He sat Mr. Aldrich on the upper bench and the boys where they liked, some inside and some out on the sand. Because it was an occasion he had brought out the silver chest. He had not opened it since the funeral. Every fork in it had gone the color of a stovepipe. When they had eaten he took Mr. Aldrich’s paper plate from him and stood there holding it. I want to tell you how this came about, he said. He told it from the beginning and left nothing out, the

sections.heading: V. A Piece a Night
sections.text: That night after supper Mr. Tefft spread a newspaper on the kitchen table. There were seventy-two pieces in the chest, a service for twelve in the Chantilly pattern, given in 1929 by Eleanor’s people. He took out the fork with the white spot on its handle and did the whole of it with the pink paste and a soft rag, down between the tines. He rinsed it and dried it and laid it back in its slot among the black ones. Then he turned off the light. He did one the next night, and one the night after that. A few days before Thanksgiving he had been once around the chest. He lifted out the first fork to look at it, and there was a yellow cast coming in the bowl of the tines. He was not surprised. He set it on the newspaper and reached for the rag. By then it was full dark at five. He stood at the window in his bathrobe with the night’s piece drying on a dish towel behind him. The green wagon stopped under the streetlight. Seven bundles went onto the lower bench one after another, and the wagon pulled away. Then the boys came in on their bicycles out of four streets, and dropped the bicycles on the sand, and stood at the two benches under the roof with their elbows at the right height, foldi

title: The Drop Corner
logline: A retired draftsman who used to phone in complaints about the paperboys on his corner sees a canvas bag drag through wet grass.

verses.text: As the impurity which springs from the iron, when it springs from it, destroys it; thus do a transgressor’s own works lead him to the evil path.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the monk Tissa receives a length of coarse cloth and gives it to his sister, who secretly cuts it up, beats it to fiber, spins it fine and has it woven into finer, longer cloth. He refuses it until she tells him what she has done. Robe-makers sew it while she feeds them, and he folds the finished robe on the rack, meaning to wear it the next day, but dies in the night of indigestion and is reborn as a louse in the robe. When the monks, since no one nursed him, move to divide it, the louse runs up and down screaming that they are plundering his property. The Buddha has the robe set aside for seven days; the louse dies and is reborn in the Tusita heaven, and on the eighth day the monks divide it. Had they taken it while he still clung to it, the Buddha explains, he would have died hating them and gone to hell; craving eats the one it arises in, as rust eats the iron it comes from.
bg.history:
Iron ore was found near Negaunee in 1844, and the Jackson Mine there opened the Lake Superior iron country. By the 1920s the ground under the old town had been worked for generations, and roughly half of Negaunee was eventually abandoned for fear of cave-ins. In August 1928, the Mining Journal reported that the Cleveland-Cliffs Iron Company had bought most of the homes in the East End and was offering settlements; the city was asked to vacate and close several of its streets, and houses and churches, among them Immanuel and Bethany Lutheran, were moved north to new lots. Two years earlier, in November 1926, the Barnes-Hecker mine four miles west of Ishpeming had caved in and flooded, killing 51 men.

Finns came to the Upper Peninsula by the tens of thousands from the 1870s on, and many of the single men lived in boarding houses with a sauna in the yard. The Finns were divided between church people and “reds,” socialists and union men; the Finnish socialist paper Työmies, which had broken with its Lutheran backers, played a major role in the Copper Country strike of 1913–14 in the Keweenaw, to the north. Sarka is the coarse woolen homespun of the Finnish countryside. The verse comes from Richard Francis Weymouth’s New Testament in Modern Speech, first published in 1903.

sections.heading: I. The Sarka
sections.text: Toivo Rautio’s mother sent him eight yards of sarka from Ostrobothnia, folded in brown paper and tied with string and smelling, when he opened it on his bunk, of the shed where she kept the loom. It was the coarse gray homespun that farmers wore in the old country to the fields and to church and to their graves. It was as stiff as a horse blanket. He was twenty-three and had been four years in Michigan, tramming ore cars underground on the night shift, and he had not had a new coat since the one he came over in. On Sunday he took it over to his sister in Ishpeming, three miles west. Hilja was married to a timberman and had two children and a loom that took up half the front room, a big four-post loom that her husband had built her out of maple, on which she wove rag rugs for the company store at a dollar and a quarter apiece. She unfolded the sarka on the kitchen table and rubbed it between her fingers and looked at her brother, who was the youngest of seven and the only one of them besides herself who had come over, and she thought: this is not good enough for him. She did not say so. She said, Leave it with me a while. When he had gone back to Negaunee she took the shears to it.

sections.heading: II. The Coat
sections.dateline: Mrs. Lehto’s boarding house, the East End · August
sections.text: Mrs. Lehto kept fourteen men in a long frame house on the East End of Negaunee, two to a room and some of them three, the day shift sleeping in the beds the night shift had just got out of. There was a sauna in the yard that she heated on Saturdays, with an iron kettle built into the stove for the wash water. The Finns called a house like hers a poikatalo, a boys’ house, though some of the boys were fifty. The tailors cut the coat on her kitchen table, after supper, with the oilcloth rolled back. They made it the way coats were made for Sunday in Vaasa, long, with a high notch and three buttons, and they argued about the shoulders for two nights. Hilja came over from Ishpeming every evening that week, her husband driving her in the Ford when he was on days. She brought coffee and a braid of pulla with cardamom in it, and once a pan of rice pudding, and she fed the tailors and the boarders who sat around the kitchen watching, and on the last night, when the coat was done, she brought a whole cake with lingonberries on it and set out a dollar each for Kalle and Jussi on top of what Toivo owed them. Toivo put the coat on. The men stood back. He went to the piece of mirror over the was

sections.heading: III. The Seam
sections.dateline: The East End · the end of August
sections.text: They buried him from the Finnish church with the boarders for pallbearers, and when it was over and the boarders had come back to the house Hilja came with them and went down on her knees on Mrs. Lehto’s kitchen floor, among the boots, and held on to Kalle Niemi’s ankles and wept, and rolled her head against the floor, and could not be got up for a long time. Mrs. Lehto put a pillow under her. The men stood around with their caps in their hands and looked at the stove. Afterward, when Hilja’s husband had taken her home, the boarders sat around the table with the coffee, and the question of the coat came up, because it was hanging on the nail in the next room and every one of them had been thinking about it. There was a custom in the boarding houses about a dead man’s clothes. If somebody had sat up with him at the end, the clothes were his. If nobody had, they belonged to the house, and the men drew lots. Nobody had sat up with Toivo. Hilja had said, on the way to the cemetery, that the boys should have it; he would want it worn. So the coat was the house’s. Only first, because it was the custom also, it would go in the sauna kettle on Saturday and be boiled, as every dead man’s cl

sections.heading: IV. The Moving
sections.dateline: From the East End to Pine Street · the first week of September
sections.text: The ground under the East End had been mined for eighty years, and it was going. There were cracks in the backyards you could put your arm in. The Cleveland-Cliffs Iron Company had bought the houses one after another all summer, and in August it asked the city to close the streets, and now the houses were going, the ones that could be moved, up the hill to new lots on the north side of town. Two of the Lutheran churches were going, one of them parsonage and all. Mrs. Lehto had sold to the company in July, and the movers had her house on the list for the first week in September. So the seven days were the days of the moving, and the boarders packed. They packed the beds and the stove and the washstand and the piece of mirror and Mrs. Lehto’s dishes in barrels of straw, and the coat hung on its nail. The movers came on the fourth day with timbers and jacks and a team of horses and a capstan, and they jacked the house up off its stone foundation and set it on cribbing and then on rollers, and it went up the hill a few yards an hour, creaking, with the horses walking round and round the capstan and the cable singing, and men running from the back of the house to the front with the roll

sections.heading: V. The Spike
sections.text: In the morning Matti went in and took the coat down off the nail and brought it out to the kitchen and laid it across the table. Now, he said. Boil it, draw for it, do what you want. They boiled it. It came out of the kettle a little smaller and none the worse, and they hung it to dry on the line in the new yard, and that evening they drew for it with burnt matches, and Arvo Salo, who was seventeen and had been in the country since June, drew the short one, and put it on, and it fit him. Then they asked Matti. They sat around Mrs. Lehto’s table in the new kitchen, which was the same kitchen a quarter mile north and slightly crooked, so that the coffee in the cups did not sit level, and they asked him why seven days, and why the eighth. Matti looked at his hands. Toivo was in the coat, he said. You heard him. He went to sleep looking at it and he woke up in the seam. If you had boiled it the first day, he’d have gone out of the world cursing every one of you for a thief, and a man who goes out cursing goes down. So I let him run out his time. He’s gone up now. Now you can have it. Nobody laughed. Arvo, who was wearing it, sat very still. Matti got up and went out the back door and c

title: Seven Days on the Nail
logline: A young Finnish miner's sister unweaves his coarse homespun and makes him a fine coat, as the ground under their town gives way.

verses.text: The taint of prayers is non-repetition; the taint of houses, non-repair; the taint of the body is sloth; the taint of a watchman, thoughtlessness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the lay disciples of Sāvatthī go home from the monastery praising the elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and the monk Lāḷudāyi, jealous, tells them they should hear him. They invite him to teach. He sits in the preacher's seat waving a painted fan and cannot find a word; he says he will chant instead and let someone else teach, then that he will chant at night, then at dawn. Four times they seat him, and four times he gets down. At last the crowd picks up clods and sticks, and he runs and falls into a cesspool. The Buddha says it is not the first time, and tells the birth story of a boar who challenged a lion, rolled for seven days in the ascetics' dung heap, and was told by the disgusted lion, "I give you the victory." Lāḷudāyi, the Buddha says, learned a fragment of the teaching and never repeated it.
bg.hist_title: A fleet boat off the Marianas, 1944
bg.history:
The Balao-class fleet submarines, built at the Portsmouth Navy Yard in Kittery, Maine, and at other yards, carried about ten officers and seventy enlisted men and could go to four hundred feet. Every enlisted man had to qualify in submarines, learning each system of the boat well enough to operate it and explain it, before he could wear the dolphins. Waste from the heads went to sanitary tanks that were blown overboard with compressed air; a man who opened the wrong valve while a tank was under pressure got it back. Between patrols, crews rested at Waikiki's Royal Hawaiian Hotel, which the military used as a rest and recreation center for the whole war. The Articles for the Government of the Navy, known as Rocks and Shoals, were by their own terms to be hung up in a public part of every ship and read to the ship's company once a month.

Japan seized Guam on December 10, 1941, days after Pearl Harbor, and held it for two and a half years, eventually moving most of the Chamorro population into camps such as Manenggon. Twelve Chamorro men serving as Navy mess attendants had died aboard the battleships at Pearl Harbor; others served through the war without word from home. After weeks of bombardment, American forces landed on July 21, 1944, still kept on Guam as Liberation Day; see also Guampedia on the Chamorro mess attendants of 1941.

sections.heading: I. School of the Boat
sections.dateline: On patrol, west of the Marianas · June 1944
sections.text: There were nineteen men aboard who had not qualified, and every night after the evening meal, when the tables in the crew's mess had been wiped down and the coffee made again, one of the two chiefs would sit at the end of the forward table and teach them the boat. Chief Fessenden, the chief of the boat, took the hull systems: trim and drain, high-pressure air, the vents and the floods, the ballast and the negative tank. He drew them on the back of a mess tray with a grease pencil, wiped it with his sleeve, and drew them again, faster. Chief Mullan, the senior electrician, took the batteries and the motors and everything with a wire in it, and he did it without drawing at all, with his eyes shut, walking them through the boat in their minds from the forward torpedo room to the after one, valve by valve, so that a nineteen-year-old from Akron who had never seen the sea before March could close his eyes in his bunk afterward and go aft in the dark and put his hand on the right wheel. Nobody slept through either of them. The nonquals carried their qualification notebooks around the boat like missals. When they went up to the conning tower or back to the maneuvering room to get a signat

sections.heading: II. Four Times
sections.dateline: The crew's mess · the same night, and the next morning
sections.text: They had chicken that night out of a can, and Jell-O, and the cooks put out a fresh pot of coffee for the occasion. More men came than usually came for Fessenden, because word had gone around. They sat on the benches and stood in the doorway to the galley, and somebody gave Corliss the seat at the end of the forward table and a clean tray and the grease pencil. It was over ninety degrees in the mess, as it always was after a day submerged, and Corliss had brought his fan. He had won it at the rest camp at the Royal Hawaiian, a palm-leaf fan painted with a hula girl and a sunset, and he fanned himself with it now, slowly, back and forth, and looked at the clean tray. He had learned the trim system once, all of it, in the week before his board. He remembered that there was a trim pump. He remembered that there was a manifold. He remembered the feeling of knowing it, which was a good feeling, and he could not find anything else. He fanned himself. The men waited. Tell you what, he said. I'll draw it. Szabo, you talk it. You learn better saying it yourself. And he got up from the seat and handed Szabo the pencil, and Szabo, who had had it from Fessenden two nights before, stood at the

sections.heading: III. The After Head
sections.text: He went aft fast, through the crew's berthing, with twenty men behind him and potatoes knocking on the lockers, and he ducked into the after head and dogged the door, and sat down hard, and, because he had been holding it since the midwatch and because it was the first thing in two days that he did not have to explain, he finished his business and reached for the valve. There was a sign hung on the valve. The motor machinist had hung it there twenty minutes earlier, when he started blowing the sanitary tank overboard with high-pressure air, the way it was done every couple of days. Corliss had helped write the sign. He knew the order of the valves on that head as well as he knew anything aboard; he had known it once. He did not read it. The sound it made was heard as far forward as the control room. When he came out, a while afterward, he had the hula fan in his hand still, and the men in the passageway parted and pressed themselves back against the bunks to let him by, all of them, without a word, the way water parts around a hull. He went forward to the washroom. He was in there a long time. The smell went through the whole after battery and the ventilation took it into the crew'

sections.heading: IV. The Lion and the Pig
sections.text: The officers' steward was a Chamorro from Hagåtña named Vicente Taitano. He was forty-one. He had been in the Navy since 1923, as a mess attendant and then a steward, because that was what the Navy had let a man from Guam be, and he had a wife and three daughters on Guam whom he had not heard from since the Japanese came ashore in December of 1941. He made the coffee in the wardroom and ironed the captain's khakis and kept the wardroom silver, which nobody used, as bright as if somebody would. He spoke English carefully and not much. The captain sometimes asked him things that had nothing to do with coffee. He came through the crew's mess in the middle of the afternoon with a tray of cups to wash and found a dozen men around the forward table going over the whole thing again. He set the tray down. What are you all talking about? They told him: Corliss, the seat, the four times, the potatoes, the head. They were laughing again by then. Corliss was in his rack with the curtain drawn. Taitano nodded. That's not the first time for him, he said. He sat down on the end of the bench and dried his hands on the towel over his shoulder, and told them a story the friars told in the school at

sections.heading: V. Muster
sections.dateline: The first of July, and after
sections.text: On the first of the month the executive officer read the Articles for the Government of the Navy to the ship's company in the crew's mess, in two sittings so the watch could hear them, as the Articles themselves required, once a month. Everybody called them Rocks and Shoals. Most of the men could have said the long part by heart, and some of them said it along with him under their breath, the way you say a prayer you have heard a hundred times in church. Corliss stood against the bulkhead at the back with his arms folded. He had been given the after head to keep for the rest of the patrol, and it was the cleanest place on the boat. place: A fleet submarine on patrol west of the Marianas
logline: On a 1944 war patrol, a qualified torpedoman boasts he can teach the boat better than the chiefs, and the nonquals take him up on it.

verses.text: Bad conduct is the taint of woman, greediness the taint of a benefactor; tainted are all evil ways in this world and in the next.
But there is a taint worse than all taints,—ignorance is the greatest taint. O mendicants! throw off that taint, and become taintless!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a young man of good family marries a woman who is unfaithful from the day of the wedding, and he is so ashamed that he stops showing his face, even to the Buddha. When the Buddha asks where he has been, he tells him everything. The Buddha says he gave the same counsel in a former life, and at the young man's request tells the birth story: a famous teacher whose pupil came to him with the same grief was told that women are like rivers, highways, taverns, assembly halls and wells, open to all, and that the wise are not angry at them. The pupil let it go, and the wife, hearing that the teacher knew what she was, gave up her ways; and so did the wife in the present. Then the Buddha speaks of stains: bad conduct, stinginess, every wicked act, and worst of all, ignorance. Read the full commentary story and the birth story. Mr. Prys reads from Robert Burton's The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621, enlarged through 1676), which has a long section on the cure of jealousy; the text is quoted from the Project Gutenberg edition.
bg.history:
From about 1713 New Providence was the base of the so-called Republic of Pirates. On July 24, 1718, Woodes Rogers arrived as royal governor with warships and the King's pardon for pirates who surrendered, and most of the two hundred or so former pirates on the island took it. Rogers rebuilt the decayed fort, declaring martial law to make the inhabitants work on it; nearly a hundred of the people he brought died of fever while the old residents were spared. In December 1718 the pardoned pirate Benjamin Hornigold brought in ten men who had gone back to piracy, and eight of them were hanged at Nassau. A Spanish fleet came off the island in February 1720 and withdrew. Navigation in these years was done with the log, the traverse board and the backstaff or Davis quadrant, used with the observer's back to the sun, lining the shadow of a vane up with the horizon.

On the night of August 22, 1720, John Rackham and a few others who had taken the pardon stole the sloop William from Nassau harbor; among them were Anne Bonny and Mary Read, whom Rogers named in his proclamation of September 5. The tale that Bonny had left a husband on the island comes from Captain Charles Johnson's General History of the Pyrates (1724), a lively and unreliable book. Mr. Prys's young man in Port Royal belongs to the years before the earthquake of June 7, 1692, which sank much of that town into the harbor.

sections.heading: I. The School
sections.text: Mr. Prys kept his school of navigation in a palmetto house at the east end of the town, below the ridge, where the ground was too stony for anyone to want it. He had been a sea artist forty years. He was Welsh, from Carmarthen, and very old, and he had sailed as master's mate and master out of Bristol and Kingston and Boston, and in the year 1697 a pirate had taken his ship off Hispaniola and kept him eight months because a pirate who cannot find the way home is only a man in a boat. He did not talk about those months. He had come to New Providence afterward, by what road nobody knew, and stayed. When the Governor came in the summer of 1718 with his men-of-war and the King's pardon, there were two hundred and more men on the island who had been on the account, and most of them took it, and then sat about the town with nothing to do. Some of them had money and drank it. Some went turtling, or raked salt, or went out to the wrecks on the banks. A few of them, the ones who could add, came to the palmetto house in the evenings and paid Mr. Prys a piece of eight a month to learn what he knew, because a man who could keep a reckoning could get a mate's berth on any honest sloop in the In

sections.heading: II. The Town
sections.text: Nassau in that year was a few hundred men and not many women. There was a fort going up on the point that nobody wanted to work at, so the Governor had declared martial law to make them, and there was fever among the people he had brought, who died of it while the old islanders went on as if it were weather. There were taverns made of ship's planks and sailcloth all along the beach. There was always a fiddle somewhere. The gallows from the December hanging had been taken down, but people still pointed at the place. Nat Cole went to the Exumas raking salt in May, and to the banks after turtle in June, and was gone three weeks each time. Before the month was out the whole waterfront knew that his wife had not been sitting in the dark while he was away. She had been at the dancing at the sign of the Ship, and at the other places, and she had not always gone home alone. It was the kind of town where everyone knew everything by morning, and said so. He heard it the day he landed, from three men, before his feet were dry. He went home and sat in the doorway and looked at her. She looked back at him. She did not deny it. She did not explain it either, though there were things she could ha

sections.heading: III. The Backstaff
sections.dateline: The school below the ridge · August 1719
sections.text: After eleven days it came round to the first of the month, and the first of the month was when he paid the old man his piece of eight. He could not bring himself not to pay a debt. He went up after dark, by the back way along the ridge so nobody would see him, and put the coin on the table, and sat down on the bench in his old place without looking at anybody. There were four other men there, working a traverse. Mr. Prys finished showing them, and sent them home early. Then he sat down across the table, with the lamp between them. Mr. Cole. Where have you been? You have not let yourself be seen. Nat told him all of it, staring at the sand box. The salt, the turtles, the Ship. The three men on the beach. His wife in the doorway, not denying it. The old man listened. Then he said, I said all this once before, to a young man of mine. In Port Royal, in Jamaica, before the town went into the sea. His wife was the same, and he came to me the same, and sat where you are sitting. He had your way of sitting. His name was Cole as well. Nat looked up. His father had been in Jamaica as a young man; it was where the money came from that bought the sugar house in Bristol. His father had never ta

sections.heading: IV. The Fig Tree
sections.text: It was Mrs. Thompson who told her daughter, because Mrs. Thompson's sister did the old man's washing, and nothing on New Providence went unsaid for long. She told her that Nat Cole had sat in Mr. Prys's school until midnight, and that the old Welshman knew all about her, and had read to Nat out of his great book, and that whatever it was, Nat had come down from the ridge looking like a man who had been told something. Susannah had not cared what the waterfront said. The waterfront said everything about everyone and had since she was a child. But the old man had come to her wedding in his blue coat and drunk his one glass and gone home, and when she was nine and had fever, before anyone on the island had heard of a governor, he had walked up the hill every evening for a week with a lime and a little sugar in a paper and sat by the door saying the names of the stars to her until she slept. She had not known he would know. She had thought of him as somebody whose eyes were always on the sky. She sat under her mother's fig tree for the rest of that day with her hands in her lap, and the next day she did not go down to the beach, nor the day after. Nat came up the hill at the end of the

sections.heading: V. The Harbor at Night
sections.text: Mr. Prys died in the spring of 1720, after the Spanish came off the harbor in February with a fleet and went away again. He was buried on the ridge above his school, and his men carried him up, eleven of them, all mates and masters now on one coast or another, and Nat Cole took the backstaff, which the old man had said he should have. The folio went to the Governor's secretary, who said he would send it to England, and did not. On a night in late August, Nat and Susannah were sitting on their step after dark with the door open behind them for the air. There was a little wind off the land. Down in the harbor something was moving without lights: a sloop warping out quietly from the anchorage past the fort, men at her sweeps, no sound but the oars in the water and once a woman's voice laughing, out on the dark, and then a hand put over it. In the morning the whole waterfront knew that a sloop called the William had been stolen out of the harbor by a crowd of men who had taken the King's pardon and were tired of it, and that two of the crowd were women, one of them somebody else's wife, who had gone with them in men's clothes, and the Governor was going to proclaim them all. title: The Backstaff
logline: A pardoned pirate who keeps his share buried hides from Nassau's waterfront when his young wife goes dancing without him.

verses.text: Life is easy to live for a man who is without shame, a crow hero, a mischief-maker, an insulting, bold, and wretched fellow.
But life is hard to live for a modest man, who always looks for what is pure, who is disinterested, quiet, spotless, and intelligent.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Culla Sāri, a monk who lived with the elder Sāriputta, gave medical treatment to a lay household and was paid with a portion of choice food. That kind of livelihood was against the rules the Buddha had laid down for monks. On his way back he met an elder on the road and offered him some: nowhere else would he get food like this, and from now on, whenever Culla Sāri was paid like this, he would bring him some. The elder heard him out and walked on without a word. When the monks told the Buddha, he said that a man without shame, bold as a crow, lives easily, and a man with a sense of shame lives hard.
bg.history:
The first Japanese contract laborers reached Hawaii on February 8, 1885. Most of those who followed came from Hiroshima, Yamaguchi and Kumamoto, to work in the sugar fields. Okinawans began arriving in January 1900, and by 1908 more than 8,500 lived in the islands. Other Japanese looked down on them, called them pig-eaters, and mocked the hajichi tattoos on the women's hands. The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1907–08 ended new emigration of Japanese laborers. When Japanese workers struck on Oahu the next year, their pay was eighteen dollars a month, well below what Portuguese and Puerto Rican workers earned.

Most of the emigrants were Jōdo Shinshū Buddhists. The first Hongwanji temple in the islands was dedicated in 1889, and Bishop Yemyo Imamura led the Honpa Hongwanji Mission from 1900 to 1932. Its ministers traveled the camps on foot and on horseback, held funerals, wrote letters home for the workers, and settled disputes. Some plantations helped pay for the temples. On Kauai the Līhuʻe Hongwanji began in 1901 with support from the Lihue Plantation Company. Shin Buddhism rejects charms, spells and prayers for worldly benefit. The words Jisaburō recites come from the Tannishō, a late thirteenth-century record of Shinran's sayings. The common myna was brought to Hawaii from India in the 1860s to eat armyworms and cutworms in the cane, and people complained of it for its noise and its nerve. The Hawaiian name, pihaʻekelo, means "full of voice."

sections.heading: I. Moxa
sections.text: The temple in Camp Seven stood at the end of the Japanese row, past the bathhouse and the store, on posts high enough that the dogs slept under it. It was board and batten with a tin roof. The plantation had paid for the lumber, the manager having been told in Honolulu that a camp with a temple had fewer fights on payday. Inside, behind a low rail, hung a scroll of Amida Buddha standing on a lotus, and below him two brass vases and a candle stand that the women of the camp polished on Saturdays with ash from the bathhouse fire. Nishiyama Ryōun had come out from Kyoto in the spring of 1907 to take charge of it. He was twenty-six. He had a good voice for the sutras and a quick laugh, and he could write a letter home for a man in a hand that made the man’s mother proud of him. And he had one thing more, which the camp found out in his first month. His father was a village doctor in Aki, in the Hiroshima country, and the son had rolled moxa and ground powders in his father’s back room since before he could write his own name. Most of the camp was from Hiroshima and Yamaguchi, from the old Shin villages where every house had its altar and a man who had never read a book could say whole

sections.heading: II. The Ditch Road
sections.text: He had a memorial service that afternoon at Camp Nine, across the gulch, and he took the box with him to eat on the way. The road ran along the top of the ditch bank. On one side was the water, brown and quick, going down to the fields in its plank flume. On the other was cane taller than a man on horseback. At the place where a footbridge crossed the flume, an old woman sat on the planks in the shade of the cane, eating her lunch. Her name was Higa Ushi. She was from Okinawa, from a village near Nago, and she was the oldest woman in the hoeing gang. The Hiroshima women called her Obaa, grandmother, because they did not know her name. In their worse moods they called the Okinawans in the gang pig-eaters, not always out of her hearing. The backs of her hands were tattooed in dark blue, little crosses and dots and bars, from the knuckles to the wrist, the way the women of her island had been marked for centuries. Her husband had died the second year. She had stayed. She sent money home to a grandson in Nago and kept a hoe whose blade had been filed down to a crescent. She had a lunch tin on her knees, and in it two boiled sweet potatoes and a pinch of salt. Nishiyama sat down on the

sections.heading: III. The Gate
sections.text: The women told Mukai Jisaburō. They had not decided to. They meant to tell nobody. But Mrs. Ōta saw him that evening outside the store with his lantern and his shovel, going up to the night water, and she found she had stopped him and was telling it, and Mrs. Hamada was nodding beside her. Jisaburō was sixty-three. He had come out from Aki in 1885, the first year the emigrant ships came, and he had never gone home. He was the night man on the Number Four ditch. All night he walked the lines with a lantern, opening one gate and closing another so that the water went down every furrow in its turn and none of the cane went dry, and at every gate he lifted he said the Name under his breath. He was the head of the temple board because nobody would have it otherwise. Some people in the camp called him a myōkōnin, one of the wondrous good people, behind his back. He would have been ashamed to hear it. He spoke very little. He listened to the women. He thanked them. Then he set his lantern on the store step and walked down to the temple instead of up to the ditch. logline: On a Kauai sugar plantation, a young Buddhist priest paid in choice food for forbidden cures offers a share to an old Okinawan weeder.

verses.text: He who destroys life, who speaks untruth, who in this world takes what is not given him, who goes to another man's wife;
And the man who gives himself to drinking intoxicating liquors, he, even in this world, digs up his own root.
O man, know this, that the unrestrained are in a bad state; take care that greediness and vice do not bring thee to grief for a long time!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a group of lay followers at Jetavana each keep one of the five precepts: one abstains from killing, another from lying, and so on. They fall into a dispute, each insisting that his own precept is the hard one, and take the question to the Buddha. He does not rank them, and says that every precept is hard to keep. The verses follow, naming all five wrongs together. Some texts number the disciples at five hundred; the translator notes that the story itself calls for five.
bg.history:
Columbia was founded in 1967 by the developer James Rouse as a planned town between Baltimore and Washington, meant to be free of racial, religious and class segregation. It was built as a set of villages, and its streets were named from poems and novels. Sohap Lane in Oakland Mills, for example, comes from a Carl Sandburg poem. Congregations shared buildings instead of building their own. The Wilde Lake Interfaith Center opened in 1971 for a Catholic parish, a Black Baptist church, a Methodist–Presbyterian church and a Lutheran congregation, and the Catholics took down their crucifix and Stations of the Cross whenever the room was needed for Rosh Hashanah.

The Iranian Revolution set off the 1979 oil crisis, with gas lines, panic buying, and riots in Levittown, Pennsylvania. Maryland put drivers on odd-even days. Its executive order, effective June 21, 1979, explained that "Zero is an even number." On July 15 President Carter gave his televised "crisis of confidence" address. The year before, federal grand juries had begun investigating fraud and bribery at the General Services Administration, including bribes on repair contracts for federal buildings in Washington. Bernie's bookmark is in Lincoln's address of February 22, 1842 to the Springfield branch of the Washingtonians, a temperance movement begun by reformed drinkers.

sections.heading: I. The Back Rows
sections.text: The van left the lot behind the Oakland Mills village center at ten minutes to seven, and it did not wait. Everybody knew that. Bernie Ostrowski had driven it since the winter of the first gas lines, in 1974, a fifteen-passenger Dodge the color of a Concord grape, and in five and a half years he had left behind two of his own supervisors at the General Accounting Office, a woman in a wedding dress on her way to the courthouse, and once, by about forty seconds, his wife. The riders paid him by the month. He kept the van in his driveway on Sohap Lane, washed it on Saturdays, and drove it down Route 29 and Colesville Road and Sixteenth Street every working day, and he almost never said anything, because he was driving. There were eleven riders that June. Most of them slept or read the Post. The five in the back two rows talked, all the way down and all the way back, and over the years each of the five had come to know one thing about the other four, which was the thing each of them did not do. Walt Haney did not kill anything. He was thirty-three and worked for the Fish and Wildlife Service in the Interior building, where he spent half the year adding up ducks. Every winter he flew lo

sections.heading: II. Odd and Even
sections.text: By the middle of June there were lines at every station in Maryland, and the governor had put the state on odd and even. If your license plate ended in an odd number you bought gas on odd days, and if it ended in an even number, on even days. Carol had brought the executive order to the van in her purse to read them a line from it, because the state had thought it necessary to put in writing that zero is an even number. The lines ran out of the stations and down the shoulders of the roads. Up in Levittown, Pennsylvania, people had thrown bottles at the police and set two cars on fire, chanting for gas. The van’s plate was even, and Bernie bought his gas before daylight on even days and came home with the tank full, and on odd days the van went by the lines with its riders looking out at them. On a Sunday night in the middle of July the President went on television and told the country it was having a crisis of confidence. On Monday morning the radio in the van played pieces of the speech over again, until Bernie turned it off. One afternoon that week, going home, the van came to a stop on Colesville Road behind a line for a Sunoco station that had backed out of the lot and into the

sections.heading: III. The Driver
sections.text: Bernie did not turn around. He was watching the car in front, a Pinto with a dog in the back window, which had moved up about a length. They’re all hard, he said. That’s no answer, said Carol. That’s what you say to children. He started the engine and moved the van up a length behind the Pinto and turned it off again. There was a book on the dashboard, a library copy of Lincoln’s speeches with a GAO routing slip in it for a marker. He read at red lights. Everyone in the van knew that, and nobody had ever asked him what. He reached the book back over the seat without looking and Leon took it. Where the slip is, said Bernie. Read them that. Leon looked at the page a while first, the way he would look over a Scripture before he read it out on a Sunday. It was a speech Lincoln had made in Springfield in 1842, to a society of reformed drunkards. In my judgment, such of us as have never fallen victims, have been spared more from the absence of appetite, than from any mental or moral superiority over those who have. — Abraham Lincoln, Address to the Springfield Washingtonian Temperance Society, 1842 I never took a drink, said Bernie.
