logline: Stuck in a gas line on Colesville Road, five suburban commuters argue over whose one kept promise is the hardest.

verses.text: The world gives according to their faith or according to their pleasure: if a man frets about the food and the drink given to others, he will find no rest either by day or by night.
He in whom that feeling is destroyed, and taken out with the very root, finds rest by day and by night.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the young monk Tissa finds fault with every gift the great lay supporters give the monks. Cold food is too cold and hot food is too hot. A small gift is stingy, and a large one is waste. Meanwhile he boasts that his own kinsfolk keep open house for monks from all four quarters. The monks send young monks to his village to ask, and the villagers tell them that no son of a good family ever went forth from there, only a gatekeeper's son who left traveling with some carpenters. The Buddha says Tissa was a braggart in a past life too, and tells the birth story of Kaṭāhaka. Kaṭāhaka was a slave who learned to write by carrying his young master's tablets. He forged a letter under his master's seal and married a merchant's daughter on the frontier, and there he scorned everything as provincial. When his master came, Kaṭāhaka waited on him and begged not to be exposed. The master kept the secret, but he taught the young wife a verse to say whenever her husband found fault with his food. The verses on giving follow.
bg.history:
When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes with the Edict of Fontainebleau in 1685, after years of dragonnades that quartered soldiers on Protestant households, at least two hundred thousand Huguenots fled France. In 1700 and 1701 several hundred of them sailed from London to Virginia on five ships. They had been promised land on the Nansemond River. Governor Francis Nicholson and the Council settled them instead at Manakin Town, on ground the Monacan had left, about twenty miles above the falls of the James. The first sloop carrying their goods sank at Jamestown, sickness ran through the camps, and for seven years the new King William Parish was excused from levies, owing only a ripe ear of Indian corn if one was demanded.

The colony kept them alive on charity. Nicholson issued a brief commending the "poor distress'd Christian brethren" to all charitable persons, and subscribers gave pork, wheat, tobacco and corn, twenty barrels of it from the Governor himself. Planters sent beeves and corn, and in February 1701 the refugees began drawing one bushel of Indian meal a head each month from William Byrd's mill at Falling Creek. Their leaders quarreled bitterly with the minister Benjamin de Joux over goods and accounts. That May, Byrd rode up to see them and reported that, though very poor, "they seem very cheerful," and "all they seem to desire is y't they might have Bread enough." These documents are printed in R. A. Brock's Documents, Chiefly Unpublished, Relating to the Huguenot Emigration to Virginia (1886). Abraham Chabanne's book is Calvin's Institution, which Calvin himself put into French in 1541.

sections.heading: I. The Meal
sections.dateline: Manakin Town, on the James River, Virginia · December 1700
sections.text: They had been promised land on the Nansemond River, near the sea, and they had been put down instead on the old Monacan town, twenty-odd miles above the falls of the James, at the last edge of the English plantations. Beyond them there was nothing but woods, and somewhere in the woods the Monacan, who had gone away from these fields and might or might not come back. The sloop that carried most of their goods up from Jamestown had gone down in the river with their blankets in it. By December there were more than a hundred French in the huts on the old fields, and at one time or another most of them had been sick. They lived on gifts. The Governor had sent a brief through the colony commending the poor distressed French Protestants to all charitable persons, and the parishes had answered, some generously and some not. Colonel Byrd’s mill at Falling Creek ground Indian corn for them and sent it up the river road in sacks. A captain below the falls sent beeves, and corn from a widow’s mill. A planter in Henrico sent a cask of salt pork with his name burned into the head. Twenty barrels of corn came from the Governor himself. Some weeks the sacks did not come at all, because there was n

sections.heading: II. The Carpenters
sections.text: It was the young men who began to wonder about him, and two of them, Isaac Faure and a boy named Jean Sabatier, went to the elders about it. He says his father kept a table for all the preachers in Poitou, said Isaac. He says it every week. Has anybody here ever heard of such a house at Niort? Nobody had. They were from everywhere, from Languedoc and Dauphiné and the Saintonge, from the Vivarais and from Paris; there were Swiss among them, and Flemings, and a few Germans. Nobody was from Niort. So the elders asked Daniel himself, at the storehouse table, as if in passing, where his people were. At Niort, he said. Behind the market hall. Anyone there would show you the house. And how did you come out of France? With some others. On foot to Geneva. He looked at the ledger in front of Chabanne. It was a hard road. I don’t speak of it. There was a family of joiners who had come over on the same ship as Daniel, the Vidal brothers, from Saint-Jean-d’Angély, and they had not come up to the old fields at all. They had gone to work for wages on a plantation below the falls, building a tobacco house for an English planter, because a joiner could get paid in Virginia and nobody was paying any

sections.heading: III. The Steward
sections.text: The old man was sitting on a sack by the storehouse fire with his ledger on his knees. He had heard all of it already, because he had been sitting at the table the whole time with his back to them and his pen in his hand. It isn’t the first time, he said. He has done this before? Not this boy. The same boy. He shut the ledger. I have known that boy in three houses and on one ship. He is always clever, and he always reads well, and he always finds the soup too hot. I knew him first in La Rochelle, when I was younger than you, Isaac. Do you want to hear about him? They did. They pulled the sacks around. Somebody put another stick on the fire. And the old steward told it to them the way he told the household book, in order, leaving nothing out.

sections.heading: IV. The Letter
sections.dateline: La Rochelle and the Saintonge, in the old days
sections.text: There was a merchant in La Rochelle, he said, before the siege was forgotten and before the Revocation, a shipowner of the Religion named Monsieur Élie Bonnaud, and I was a boy in his kitchen. On the same day his wife gave birth to a son, a servant of the house gave birth to one too. The servant called hers Valentin. The two boys grew up in the same house, the one upstairs and the other down. When the young master was sent to his letters, Valentin carried his satchel and his slate to the master’s house and back, and sat on the stair outside the room while the young master was taught. He learned to write on the stair, by listening, with a stick in the dust. He learned it better than the young master did. In the end Monsieur Bonnaud took him into the counting house to copy letters, and then made him his own secretary, because he had the best hand in La Rochelle, and because he was handsome and well spoken, and the merchants liked to deal with him. And Valentin thought to himself, said Chabanne: I will not always be kept at this. One blot, one wrong word, and I’ll be beaten or put out in the street, and fed on what servants are fed. Monsieur has a friend, a salt merchant at Marennes,

sections.heading: V. Daily Bread
sections.dateline: The same night, and the first of February
sections.text: The young men were quiet a while. So he is Valentin, said Isaac. And we are to say so? At prayers? Before everyone? No, said Chabanne. Monsieur Bonnaud didn’t. Nobody is to say anything to him. It’s not his father’s lodge that is the trouble with him. Plenty of good men have been porters. He opened his ledger again on his knees, and from inside the back board he took a little book, very worn, with a brass clasp. It was the Institution of Master Calvin, in French, the one book he had carried out of the gate in Poitou. He did not need to look for the place. Listen. Master Calvin is speaking of the bread we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer. Of what it is to be given anything at all. He read it in French, and slowly. When we ask God to give us, the meaning is, that the thing asked is simply and freely the gift of God, whatever be the quarter from which it comes to us, even when it seems to have been specially prepared by our own art and industry, and procured by our hands, since it is to his blessing alone that all our labours owe their success. — Calvin, Institutes III.xx.44, tr. Henry Beveridge (1845) Whatever the quarter, said the old man. Colonel Byrd’s mill. The widow’s mill. That pla

title: A Peck a Head
logline: Fed on charity above the falls of the James, a young Huguenot reader finds fault with every sack of Indian meal.

verses.text: There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five lay followers sit down to hear the Buddha teach. One falls asleep, one digs at the ground with his finger, one shakes a tree, and one gazes at the sky; only one listens. When Ānanda asks why, the Buddha tells him that for five hundred lives the first was a snake that slept in its coils, the second an earthworm, the third a monkey, the fourth an astrologer, and the fifth a brahmin who recited the Vedas, so each still does what he has always done. The Dhamma is hard to hear, he says, because of passion, hatred and delusion. The fire at the end of an age burns only in its season, but there is no season when the fire of passion does not burn. The listener enters the stream.
bg.history:
The Thomas Fire started on the evening of December 4, 2017, north of Santa Paula, and under unusually strong and long-lasting Santa Ana winds it ran twelve miles to Ventura in a few hours. It reached Black Mountain above Ojai, the whole valley was put under evacuation orders, and the town’s water system stopped working for a time when the fire damaged its pumps. By the time it was contained on January 12, 2018, it had burned 281,893 acres, then the largest wildfire in modern California history, and its column had made its own weather. The first measurable rain fell on January 8; the next morning debris flows came down out of the burn scar onto Montecito and killed at least 21 people. Evacuees from Ventura and the Ojai Valley sheltered in the Mineral Building at the Ventura County Fairgrounds. Captain Ochoa, the five men and their houses are invented.

Ojai has drawn seekers for a century. The Theosophical colony of Krotona moved there from Hollywood in 1926, and theosophists later built the Taormina cottages beside it as a retirement community. Jiddu Krishnamurti settled in the valley in 1922 and died there in 1986. The town is known for its organic citrus, especially the small Ojai Pixie tangerine, and for the “pink moment” when the setting sun lights the Topatopa Mountains. Mr. Penrose’s book is The Voice of the Silence, which Helena Blavatsky published in 1889 as a translation of verses she said she had learned by heart. Its first fragment describes three Halls the disciple must cross, and warns against the fires of lust and the light of Mara, the Ensnarer.

sections.heading: I. The Gate
sections.dateline: The East End of the Ojai Valley · Wednesday, December 6, 2017
sections.text: The whole valley was under evacuation orders by Wednesday afternoon, and five men were standing at the bottom of a ranch road off Highway 150 to watch the fire come. It had started Monday night north of Santa Paula, a few miles over the hill, and the Santa Ana wind had taken it twelve miles to the sea in a few hours and burned the hillsides above Ventura. Now it had turned and come up the valley behind Black Mountain, and the mountains around Ojai that the town loved for going pink at sunset were black along the ridges and orange in the folds. The sun was a red coin. Ash came down like a slow gray snow on the windshields and the tangerine leaves. The hydrants in town had gone dry the day before when the fire got into the pumps. Captain Maricela Ochoa pulled her engine off the highway at the ranch gate because she had seen the five of them standing there and she knew every one of them by name. She was fifty-one. She had grown up in Santa Paula, where her father had picked lemons for forty years, and she had been in the fire service for twenty-six of hers. She spread the map on the warm hood of the engine. Her probationary firefighter, a boy from Camarillo named Noah, stood beside he

sections.heading: II. Five Hundred Times
sections.text: Noah waited until they were back on the highway. Cap. That was the best one I’ve heard you do. It was like a thunderstorm. And they stood there. One of them was asleep. One of them was playing in the dirt. You don’t know those men? No, ma’am. She drove for a while. The ash came down on the windshield and the wipers smeared it. I’ve been up Lionel Strand’s road four times since 1990, she said. Two fires and two times his smoke alarm went off. Every time, he was asleep. He paid a woman on Ojai Avenue a hundred and fifty dollars to read his past lives, and she told him he’d been a snake five hundred times in a row, curled up on a warm rock, asleep. He tells it at parties. He thinks it’s funny. She looked at Noah. I think she earned her money. Gil Haskins, she said, has been digging in that dirt since he was born. Ask him what he was before, he’ll tell you. A worm. Five hundred times. He says it like it’s a compliment, and maybe it is. But he can’t hear you with his hands in the ground. Kessler. You saw him with the tree. That one never stands still. Teo did his chart for him, and Teo told him he’d been a monkey for five hundred lives. Kessler had it printed on a T-shirt. And Teo? Teo

sections.heading: III. The Night
sections.text: The wind came over the ridge after midnight, the way she had said. Lionel Strand went back up his canyon and sat down in his living room in front of the big window to watch the fire, and fell asleep. At three in the morning Captain Ochoa’s crew, going up the canyon road against orders with the cab full of smoke, found him in his chair with the window glowing orange in front of him and carried him out to the engine, still mostly asleep. The house burned an hour later. He said afterward that he had dreamed of a warm rock. Gil Haskins stayed in his orchard all night with a shovel, digging a firebreak around his trees in ground too hard to dig. The embers went over him and the break and into the windbreak of eucalyptus. He lost eleven of his twenty acres. In the morning he was still digging. Brent Kessler drove back and forth on Highway 150 until four in the morning, from one roadblock to the other, unable to stay anywhere, calling everyone he knew. His listings burned. His own house did not. Teo Lindqvist stood on the roof of his building on Ojai Avenue and watched the column over the mountains until it collapsed in on itself before dawn and threw a wind down the valley that rattled e

sections.heading: IV. The Mineral Building
sections.text: Arthur Penrose spent the night on a Red Cross cot in the Mineral Building at the fairgrounds in Ventura, between a family from Casitas Springs with three children and a man who had brought only his cat. The ocean was a block away. You could hear it under the sound of the generators. He did not sleep. He sat on the edge of the cot in his good overcoat with his hands folded, and he said the book over to himself, the way he had said it every night since 1952, when a woman at a lecture in Pasadena had given him a copy and told him to learn it by heart. He knew every word of it. He had always known every word of it. He had taken down eight million words in courtrooms and he had never once misheard one. Somewhere around the second fragment, at a passage he had said perhaps twenty thousand times, he heard it. If thou would’st cross the first Hall safely, let not thy mind mistake the fires of lust that burn therein for the Sunlight of life. — H. P. Blavatsky, The Voice of the Silence (1889), Fragment I He heard it in a woman’s voice, flat and plain, the voice of somebody leaning on the hood of a fire engine with ash coming down on her shoulders. It was not a book. It was a report of what w

sections.heading: V. The Mud
sections.text: The first real rain of the season came on the eighth of January, and it fell all night on the black hills. Captain Ochoa was on Highway 150 before dawn on the ninth with a pickup and a shovel, watching the culverts below the burn, because she had said she would. Over the mountain in Montecito the hills came down in the dark onto houses where people were asleep, and twenty-one of them died. On the East End the creeks ran thick as wet cement for two days, carrying burned oak limbs, boulders the size of cars, somebody’s mailbox. They filled the culverts to the brim. Mr. Penrose came out on the second day in his overcoat with an umbrella, and stood beside her on the shoulder of the highway, and they watched the creek go by. He did not say anything about the book. He asked about her father. She told him about the lemons. Below them in the rain a black orchard stood in rows, eleven acres of it, every tree burned to the trunk. At the far end Gil Haskins was already out with his shovel in the mud, turning over the wet ground under the first dead tree, looking for worms.

title: Fire Year
logline: A fire captain from Santa Paula briefs five Ojai men at a ranch gate while the Thomas Fire comes over the ridge.

verses.text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour’s faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.

bg.commentary: The Buddha, traveling in the country of the Aṅguttaras, sees that six people in the town of Bhaddiya are ready to understand him: the rich man Meṇḍaka (“Ram”), his wife Candapadumā (“Moon-Lotus”), their son Dhanañjaya, his wife Sumanā, their small granddaughter Visākhā, and the servant Puṇṇa. The commentary then stops to explain the name. Behind Meṇḍaka’s house, golden rams as big as horses butt back to back, and whatever he needs comes out of a ram’s mouth when a ball of five-colored thread is removed. Two former lives account for them. In one he was a nephew whose uncle would not let him share in building a Buddha’s chamber, so he built an elephant stable opposite it, with a preaching seat resting on golden rams. In the other he was warned of a famine three years off and stored grain in 1,250 granaries, in pits, and even in the plaster of his walls. When all of it was gone, the five who remained on the place each gave their share of the last pound of rice to a solitary Buddha just risen from a week’s trance, and each made a wish. His was that his swept granaries would fill when he looked up. His wife’s was a pot that never emptied. The son asked for a purse that stayed full, and the daughter-in-law for a basket of seed. The servant asked for seven furrows from one plow, and to keep the same master. The washed pot was found full that evening. Reborn together, the five test their powers and feed the country. When Meṇḍaka sets out to meet the Buddha, teachers of other sects tell him that he, who believes deeds have results, is going to a man who denies it. He goes anyway, and afterward repeats what they said; the verse is the Buddha’s reply. Read the full commentary story. The granddaughter grew up to be Visākhā, the Buddha’s chief laywoman.
bg.hist_title: Ochiltree County, the Dust Bowl, and the harvest run
bg.history:
Ochiltree County lies on the flat top edge of the Texas Panhandle. Stock farming gave way to wheat there after 1900, and by 1930 the county had almost 210,000 acres in it; the Santa Fe reached the new town of Perryton in 1919. The summer of 1931 brought the southern plains a record crop into a collapsed market. Wheat sold for about a quarter a bushel, less than it cost to raise, the elevators filled, and grain was piled on the ground. Then the rain stopped. In the Dust Bowl years that followed, the government bought and destroyed starving cattle, families ate cornbread and beans, and by 1940 the county’s wheat acreage had fallen by two thirds. The worst single storm came on Black Sunday, April 14, 1935. It had been a clear day. In the afternoon a wall of dust rolled south across the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles behind flocks of fleeing birds, and turned the day to night. Fortune, the Ramseys, Mr. Krause and the man from the mesa are invented.

Custom harvesters, or cutters, own their combines and follow the ripening wheat north each year, starting in Texas in May and working through Oklahoma, Kansas and the Dakotas toward Canada, cutting for the same farms season after season. The trade grew up during the Second World War and has passed down in families since. Many of the hands now are seasonal workers from abroad, a good number of them from South Africa. Checking a combine’s loss is real practice, taught by every state extension service: stop the machine, lay a one-foot square on the ground behind it, and count. About twenty kernels of wheat to the square foot means a bushel an acre left in the field. Forty-two, the domino game of Texas, is played with partners and tricks, and a player who fails to follow suit has reneged. The Ensz crew is invented.

sections.heading: I. The Cutters
sections.text: The Ensz crew came up out of Oklahoma on a Sunday night with four combines on trailers, two grain carts, six trucks and a cook camper. They had started cutting below Vernon in May and would finish at the Canadian line in September. Nolan Ensz had bossed the outfit since he was twenty-four, the year his father died in the cab. He was thirty-one now and from Inman, Kansas. He had nine hands, and five of them were South African farm boys on summer papers. At supper in Shattuck he had told the crew there were six people north of the Canadian River he meant to see on this trip. He named them. They were R.L. Ramsey and his wife Lily, their son Win and his wife Jessie, a granddaughter called Vi who was seven, and the hired man, Fuller. He had never met any of them. He put the campers in the row of Chinese elms on the east side of Fortune, where cutters had always stopped. By Monday noon R.L. Ramsey knew he was there.

sections.heading: II. The Rams
sections.dateline: The Ramsey place · the same week
sections.text: Now, as to the name. It was Ramsey before there was anything behind the house, and people say the one came looking for the other. Behind the house are eight acres of bare caliche inside a pipe fence. In it are rams made of gold. They are the size of horses, and some run to the size of a good bull. They go at each other back to back all day and all night, and they have the ground torn up like a feedlot. Two men from Maine walked around among them one summer and came out without much to say. Each ram carries a ball of yarn in its mouth, wound of five colors. When something is wanted on the place, somebody goes out and takes the ball from the mouth of one ram. Then whatever was wanted comes out after it. It may be butter or cooking oil, honey or sorghum, work shirts or quilts, or gold in bars or in coin. It comes until there is enough for everybody from the Rio Grande to the Canadian line, and when the ball is put back it stops. Vi is not allowed in the pen. She has a peacock that follows her as far as the gate and waits. How a family comes by a thing like that is two stories, an old one and a hard one.

sections.heading: III. The Horse Shed
sections.text: The first R.L. Ramsey came into that country as a young man. He had an uncle of the same name who was already there. In 1904 the uncle undertook to build the first meeting house on that flat. The nephew went to him and asked to go in on it. I would rather not share it, the uncle said. I’ll build it by myself. So the nephew built across the wagon road from it. A preacher in that day came horseback forty miles, and what the nephew built was a shed for the preacher’s horse. He hauled cedar from the breaks for the posts. He turned every post and worked every rafter, and people came from Lipscomb County to look at a horse shed. Under the roof, for the hot months, he made a preaching stand, and on the stand a chair. Under the four legs of the chair he carved four rams lying down. He put two more under the footboard and six on posts in a ring around it. When it was done he held a meeting that ran four months. He fed everybody who came, and on the last day he gave each preacher a suit of clothes, down to the boys who led the singing. That was the old story. The shed went in the fire of 1919, and the family kept one ram for a doorstop.

sections.heading: IV. The Wheat in the Walls
sections.text: The hard one begins in July of 1931. That was the biggest wheat crop the plains had ever cut. It brought a quarter a bushel at the elevator in Perryton when the elevator would take it at all, and there were piles of it on the ground along the Santa Fe siding. R.L. Ramsey, the nephew’s son, was going in to the bank one morning. On the street he met old Krause, who kept the government rain gauge and read the sky for anybody who asked. Are you studying the weather, Mr. Krause? I am. What else have I got to do? How is the country going to fare? There’s a bad time coming. What kind? It will quit raining, and people will go hungry. When? Three years. R.L. went home and sowed every acre he had. He took what money he had and bought wheat with it, at a quarter and then at twenty cents, from men who thought he had lost his mind and were glad to see him coming. He built granaries of board and tin until there were a hundred and twenty-five of them on the section, in rows like a town. When they were full he filled barrels and lard cans and washtubs. When those were full he dug a pit, lined it with roofing tin, filled it and covered it over. There was wheat left even then. He had it mixed into a

sections.heading: V. The Same Five
sections.text: There has been an R.L. Ramsey on that ground ever since, with a wife called Lily, a son called Win who marries a Jessie, and a Fuller for a hired man. The family has a photograph from 1936 that visitors take for last year’s Christmas card. Nobody in Fortune argues about it. The rams were first seen behind the house in 1978, the week the present R.L. brought home Lily Mooney from Canadian. Some years on he decided to find out what he had. He had the hundred and twenty-five bins swept, steel ones now. He washed his head at the yard hydrant, sat down in the door of the first bin and looked up. Red winter wheat came down out of a clear sky and filled the bin behind him. He did the same at each door. Now you all try yours, he said. Lily put on her good dress. She boiled one quart of rice and sat down with it at the cattle guard in a lawn chair, with a gold spoon. Anybody hungry, come on. They came with bowls and buckets and ice chests. She dipped all day, and the pot was as full at dark as at sunup. People who stood close saw a moon in the palm of her right hand and a lily in the palm of her left, and when she slipped her shoes off they saw the same on her feet. The women of that family

sections.heading: VI. The Count
sections.text: On Wednesday R.L. Ramsey drove in to see the Kansas boy. He stopped at the co-op first. The domino table was going in the back, as it had every morning since he could remember, and among the eight men at it there were two deacons and an elder. Where are you headed, R.L.? Out to see Ensz. Nobody played for a moment. You, of all people, said Harlan Teel. You believe a man reaps what he sows. You’ve got a hundred and twenty-five bins out there that say so. What do you want with him? He never sowed an acre in his life. He goes up and down this country telling his hands that nobody reaps what they sow. I had it from a man in Follett. He stood in a field of another man’s wheat and said it right out. He’s a boy, another said. He thinks because it all runs through his machine it’s all one to him. R.L. heard them out and went on. Ensz was cutting a half section north of town. He stopped the machine and put R.L. in the buddy seat, and they made a round. Then he climbed down and walked him along the combine from front to back, as he did with every new hand. He showed him the reel and the sickle and the feeder house. He showed him the rotor, the concaves, the sieves and the fan, the clean grai

title: Seven Furrows
logline: A Panhandle family down to one pound of meal on Black Sunday; ninety years on, their heir goes to hear a young wheat cutter.

verses.text: If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow, and he is far from the destruction of passions.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest. A monk whose name means “Fault-Finder” goes about remarking on the others: this one puts on his under-robe so, that one his upper robe so. The monks report him to the Buddha. The Buddha first makes a distinction. One who keeps strictly to his duty and admonishes others to do the same is no fault-finder. But one who looks for flaws because he is minded to find them, and goes about talking of them, reaches none of the higher attainments; what the tradition calls the āsavas, the inflowing pollutants, only increase in him. Then he speaks the verse.
bg.history:
On the night of October 25–26, 1997, heavy wet snow fell on eastern Nebraska while the trees were still in full leaf. Lincoln measured 13.2 inches, double its previous record for the whole month of October. Limbs came down all night across the city; at the height of the storm more than 30,000 of Lincoln's 105,000 homes were without power, public schools and the university closed, and the last customers were not reconnected until November 3. Larkspur Circle, its association and its people are invented. The rule Mr. Larson brought to the meeting is real: under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 the Federal Communications Commission barred homeowner associations from prohibiting satellite dishes a meter or less across, effective that October. A cracked heat exchanger in a gas furnace can let combustion gases, including carbon monoxide, into the air a house breathes, and a serviceman who finds one shuts the furnace off and tags it.

Martin Luther wrote both of his catechisms in 1529, the Small Catechism for households and children and the Large Catechism for pastors and teachers. Generations of American Lutheran confirmands learned the Small Catechism's explanations by heart, each beginning “What does this mean?” The wording Kyle recites is the English text of 1912, long used among Midwestern Lutherans. The longer passage is from the Large Catechism in the translation of F. Bente and W. H. T. Dau (1921). Luther goes on, a few lines later, to except those whose office it is to look: a judge, a parent, a pastor, or “a physician who is sometimes compelled to examine and handle the patient.”

sections.heading: I. The Clipboard
sections.text: Larkspur Circle was nine houses around a bulb of concrete, split-entries and two-stories put up in 1978, and every front yard had a silver maple or a green ash that had gone in as a whip tied to a stake and now stood higher than the roof. The Larkspur Hills Homeowners Association had covenants, twenty-two pages of them, on file with the Lancaster County Register of Deeds. Since 1994 it had also had a Compliance Committee, which was Gordon Ulmer. He was fifty-six and an internal auditor for one of the insurance companies downtown. Saturday mornings he walked the circle and the two streets that fed it with a clipboard, and he was never wrong. People found that the hard part. Article VI said trash containers were to be stored out of view from the street, and you could see the Novaks' can beside their garage. Article IX allowed one basketball goal to a lot, on a permanent black pole, and the Hansens had the kind on wheels. Fences were to be stained cedar tone. The Sorensens' was nearer redwood, and Gordon carried a paint chip to hold against it. He noted how a man edged his walk, and which way the Beckers' boat sat on its trailer, and that Denny Kratky mowed with his shirt off. In 1996

sections.heading: II. Rifle Shots
sections.text: It rained all that Friday and Saturday. Sometime Saturday evening, while the Kansas game was on the radio from Lawrence, the rain went over to snow. It was thirty-three degrees and the leaves were still on the trees. By midnight the power was out, and people on the circle stood at their front windows in the dark and listened. A limb would let go with a crack like a deer rifle, and then came the long tearing and the thump. Then another would go, two yards over. It kept on until daylight. By Sunday noon there were thirteen inches on the ground, twice the most Lincoln had ever had in an October, and not a whole tree was left on Larkspur Circle. The Beckers' ash lay across their Suburban. The lights stayed off eight days out there. School was called off, and people managed. Denny Kratky had a generator from his deer camp. Marv went down the circle basement by basement with a flashlight in his teeth and wired a cord and plug onto every furnace, so that each could run an hour off Denny's machine, by turns, around the clock. Orange cords lay across three lawns and the common sidewalk. Marv would take nothing for it, and while he was down there he looked each furnace over, since that was h

sections.heading: III. What Does This Mean
sections.text: The Novaks had the generator from seven to eight. Marv was on his knees at their furnace with the access panel off, and Kyle Novak, who was thirteen, sat on the basement stairs in his coat with a flashlight and his confirmation folder, because the basement was where the heat would be. Carol came down with her yellow sheet. Denny Kratky and Paul Becker came down behind her with theirs, and the three of them stood at Marv's back and all talked at once. Gordon had done this. Gordon had said that. In the middle of a disaster, Marv. Underwear. Marv heard them out and went on with what he was doing. When they had run down he spoke without turning around. Kyle. What have you got for memory work? The Eighth. Stand up and say it. Kyle had sat under Marv in the seventh grade and knew there was no use arguing. He stood up on the stairs and said it to the furnace. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor. What does this mean? We should fear and love God that we may not deceitfully belie, betray, slander, nor defame our neighbor, but defend him, speak well of him, and put the best construction on everything. — Luther's Small Catechism Pastor give you the long one too?
