sections.heading: IV. The Mirror
sections.text: The lights came back on the third. Gordon's clean-and-check fell on the first Thursday of November, as it had for eleven years, and he saw no reason to move it. His own silver maple had split to the ground the first night and still lay across his front walk. He had been busy. On the basement stairs he mentioned that it had been six nights with the van, and Marv said he knew, he had read it. Gordon stayed down to watch. He liked to see a thing done in order, and Marv did it in order: the burners out and brushed, the flue, the filter, each reading written on the ticket as he took it. You write it all down, Gordon said. From him that was praise. I write it down so whoever comes next year knows where to look. I don't know another reason to. Marv went into the heat exchanger last, with the flashlight and the little round mirror on its wand. He was in there some time. Then he backed out and held the mirror and the light up to Gordon. Look for yourself. Left side, second cell, up top. Get the light under it. Gordon got down on one knee on his own basement floor. It took him a while to find the angle. Then it was there in the glass, a dark line as long as a finger with rust along both lips

title: Best Construction
logline: After the October snow breaks every tree on a Lincoln cul-de-sac, the compliance chairman writes eleven notices, and every one is correct.

verses.text: There is no path through the air, a man is not a Samana by outward acts. The world delights in vanity, the Tathagatas (the Buddhas) are free from vanity.
There is no path through the air, a man is not a Samana by outward acts. No creatures are eternal; but the awakened (Buddha) are never shaken.

bg.commentary: The commentary sets this story at the Buddha’s deathbed in the sal grove at Kusinārā, drawing on the account of his last days in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. Long ago, it says, the wanderer Subhadda’s younger brother gave alms of the first fruits of a crop nine times while Subhadda refused, giving only at the very end; so Subhadda came to the Buddha only at the very end too. He had put three doubts to the old teachers but never to the Buddha, whom he thought of as a youngster. Hearing that the Buddha was dying, he came to ask them. Ānanda tried to turn him away, but the Buddha told Ānanda to let him in, and Subhadda sat at the foot of the bed and asked: is there a path through the air, is there a true ascetic outside the teaching, are conditioned things constant? The Buddha answered with these two verses.
bg.history:
The Blue Mountain runs about 150 miles across eastern Pennsylvania from the Delaware Water Gap, continuing in New Jersey as Kittatinny Mountain, and the Schuylkill River cuts through it just north of Hamburg. Each fall thousands of hawks, eagles and falcons migrate along it, broad-winged hawks peaking in September and red-tails later, and the stretch now protected as Hawk Mountain Sanctuary was for generations a popular place to shoot them, for sport or to protect poultry, until Rosalie Edge leased the land in 1934 and hired wardens to keep the gunners away. The broad-winged hawks travel in great soaring flocks called kettles. The farm families below the ridge were Pennsylvania Dutch, most of them Lutheran or Reformed “church people,” who often shared one union church between the two congregations.

By 1905 gliding was a small international hobby. Otto Lilienthal made over 2,000 glides in Germany before a crash killed him in August 1896, and that summer Octave Chanute and his helpers tested gliders in the dunes of Lake Michigan, among them the strut-and-wire biplane the Wright brothers later called the “double-decker.” Wilbur Wright described their own glider trials to the Western Society of Engineers in Chicago in September 1901, and the Smithsonian reprinted the address in its annual report for 1902. Its Secretary, Samuel Pierpont Langley, had argued in The Internal Work of the Wind (1893) that the wind is never uniform, and that a soaring bird might be sustained by its constant pulsations; his own engine-driven Aerodrome fell into the Potomac twice in the autumn of 1903. Irvin Moyer, Elias and the Pulpit’s township are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Cabinet
sections.text: Elias Dreibelbis kept school at the Eck for forty-three years, and in all that time no scholar of his told him anything he did not already know. He taught three generations of the township to cipher, to read the English reader and the German Testament, and to stand up when the director came in. He caned the fathers, and later he caned their sons. When he gave up the school in 1894 the directors presented him with a clock, and he went home to his stone house under the mountain and to his birds. There were four hundred and twelve of them, in glass-fronted cases along three walls of the front room. He had shot and skinned and mounted every one himself, with arsenic soap and tow and glass eyes that came from Philadelphia by the gross. The hawks were the pride of it. He had sixty-one, from the little sharp-shins no bigger than a pigeon up to a golden eagle with its wings half open over the parlor door, and nearly all of them had come off the rock the township called the Pulpit, on the crest of the Blue Mountain, where every fall the hawks came down the ridge out of the northeast. On a good day they came one behind the other from breakfast to supper, so low along the face of the mountain

sections.heading: II. The First of Everything
sections.text: He had built the first pair from a drawing in a Chicago engineering journal: two wings of bleached muslin, one above the other, on frames of spruce from the lumberyard at Hamburg, braced with piano wire and varnished till they rang when you flicked them. He hung between them by his armpits, ran down the high pasture into the wind, and was lifted. The first summer he went forty feet and broke two ribs, his own and the machine’s. The second summer he went across the whole pasture and over the rail fence at the bottom, and the Reformed pastor preached on the tower of Babel, and the Lutheran pastor, who had a son, did not. Men drove out from Kempton on Sunday afternoons to sit on the fence and watch him, the way they would have watched a man try to ride a bull. Then there was the day in October of 1904 that Jonas Dreibelbis told about for the rest of his life. The wind had come around northwest in the night, cold, the kind of wind the old men called hawk weather, and Jonas was up in the high pasture with the Moyers’ hired boy when Irvin ran off the top of it. He did not come down. He went out over the chestnuts along the face of the mountain, the way the hawks went, and the wind coming

sections.heading: III. The Curtain
sections.text: In the third week the doctor found blood. He told Sallie at the kitchen table that it would be days, and he told the postmaster at Kempton the same thing in fewer words, and by evening it was all through the township. Elias heard it at the post office and walked home and sat down in the front room among the cases. The glass eyes looked at him. He thought: I asked a professor, and a newspaper, and the Government of the United States. I never asked him because I had kept him in at recess. If he dies before I ask him I will be sorry for the rest of my life, which is not going to be long either. He took a clean sheet of paper and wrote the three questions out again, in the same words he had used in 1891, and folded it in his breast pocket, and put on his coat. The wind had come around in the night. It was cold for September, the sky scrubbed blue, and as he crossed the stubble toward the Moyer place he saw them going over the ridge already, broad-wings, high up and many, turning in great slow kettles over the gap and then sliding off southwest one after the other as if somebody were pouring them. Sallie Moyer met him at the kitchen door. She was a big plain woman a little older than he

sections.heading: IV. Three Questions
sections.text: Irvin lay with his hands outside the quilt. The fever had taken the flesh off him, and his hair was cut short for it, so that he looked about fifteen, about the age he had been when he left the Eck. The window was open on the mountain. He did not seem to be in any pain, or if he was it was somewhere a long way off, and his face was quiet the way a pond is quiet in the morning before anything has landed on it. You have a paper, he said. Elias unfolded it and read the first question as he had written it fourteen years before, in the voice he had used for dictation. Whether there is a fixed road or path in the air, which the birds of prey keep to in their passage. He looked up. They come by the Pulpit every year. The same rock. There must be a road. Irvin turned his head on the pillow toward the window. A broad-wing was coming along the face of the mountain, low, below the crest, its wings held flat and still. There goes one. Watch where he goes. They watched it slide past the window frame and out of sight down the ridge. Now show me where he went. Elias looked at the air over the chestnuts. It was blue and empty and exactly like the rest of the sky. There’s no track, Irvin said. Ther

sections.heading: V. The Pulpit
sections.text: Irvin Moyer died two nights later, toward morning, with Sallie asleep in the chair, so that nobody heard him go. They buried him from the union church on the Saturday, and the Reformed pastor and the Lutheran pastor both spoke, which had not happened since the Civil War. Jonas carried. Elias stood at the back with his hat in his hands and did not sing. The wind that day was out of the south and soft, and nothing came down the ridge at all. It came around northwest again on the third of October. Elias was seventy-six years old. It took him the whole of the morning to climb the mountain by the old charcoal road, resting on stumps, and he went up for the first time in fifty-one autumns with nothing in his hands. When he came out onto the Pulpit at noon the wind was pouring up the north face so hard that it lifted the skirts of his coat and held them out behind him, and the hawks were coming. They came down the ridge out of the northeast, red-tails mostly by then, one, and then nothing, and then three. He stood on the rock where he had stood with a gun for half a century and watched them come. One came along the face below the crest at the height of his own head, so close that he could

title: Hawk Weather
place: Below the Blue Mountain, Berks County, Pennsylvania
logline: A retired schoolmaster who has shot and mounted sixty-one hawks goes at last to put three questions to the pupil who flies.

verses.text: A man is not just if he carries a matter by violence; no, he who distinguishes both right and wrong, who is learned and leads others, not by violence, but by law and equity, and who is guarded by the law and intelligent, he is called just.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest. Bhikkhus coming back through Sāvatthī from their almsround are caught by rain and shelter in a hall of justice, where they watch the ministers take bribes and strip lawful owners of their property. They tell the Buddha, who answers that a man who settles a case in haste (the Pāli sahasā means both rashly and by force) does not stand by the Dhamma; the one who weighs both sides and leads others without haste, by what is right, is its guardian.
bg.history:
Until 1964 the lowest courts in Illinois were those of justices of the peace and police magistrates: elected, usually not lawyers, usually holding another job, and paid by the fees of the cases brought before them. Theirs were not courts of record, so an appeal meant a whole new trial in a higher court. Critics said for decades that a judge who lives on fees leans toward the party who brings him business. A new judicial article that would have folded these courts into the circuit courts went to the voters on November 4, 1958; it drew about 64 percent of the votes cast on the question and still failed to meet the constitutional threshold. A second version passed in 1962 and took effect on January 1, 1964. The Illinois courts tell the story here. Pruett, Kinney County, Squire Dace and his Tuesday docket are invented; the Eighth Judicial Circuit that Lincoln rode as a lawyer in the 1840s and 1850s was real. The year is that of the 1958 recession, when layoffs in the Midwest’s factories left many families behind on installment contracts.

The Great Books Foundation was set up in Chicago in 1947 by Robert Maynard Hutchins and Mortimer Adler, and through the 1950s its discussion groups met every other week in public libraries across the country. Lay leaders were trained to ask questions and keep their own opinions out of it. The first-year course of that decade opened with the Declaration of Independence and went on to Plato’s Apology and Crito. The passages here are from Benjamin Jowett’s translation. The harvest supper is at a church of the Evangelical United Brethren, a denomination that existed from 1946 until it merged into the United Methodist Church in 1968. Miss Coyle’s machine is the stenotype, which prints a few letters per stroke on a narrow folding tape.

sections.heading: I. The Supper
sections.dateline: Pruett, Kinney County, Illinois · a Tuesday in October 1958
sections.text: Harold Stites kept the books at the Farmers Grain elevator and had kept them fourteen years without an erasure the auditor could find. His wife had signed the two of them up for Great Books at the library in September. She came to the first meeting, on the Declaration of Independence, and said on the way home that she had not known people could talk for two hours about the word self-evident. After that Harold went alone. The group met every other Tuesday at half past seven in the basement room of the Carnegie library, under the steam pipes. There were eleven of them, and each had the set of nine paper-covered books in a cardboard case that came down from the Foundation in Chicago. The second reading was Plato, the Apology. Harold had read it twice at the scale-house desk between trucks. It was bean harvest and the trucks came steadily, and he kept his place with a blank grain ticket. The E.U.B. church on North Chestnut gave its harvest supper that same Tuesday, chicken and noodles over mashed potatoes, a dollar a plate and nothing said if you did not have the dollar. Five of the Great Books people ate there together at the end of a long table. There was Harold. There was Mrs. Radem

sections.heading: II. The Squire’s Room
sections.dateline: The courthouse, ground floor · the same evening
sections.text: The voices came from the end of the east hall. The circuit court sat upstairs, in daylight, under a pressed-tin ceiling, and the county liked to say that Lincoln had tried cases on that ground when the Eighth Circuit came through. The room downstairs was one the supervisors rented for eight dollars a month to Orrin Dace, justice of the peace for Pruett Township. He had been elected three times. By day he kept a notary and collection office over the dime store. On Tuesday nights he held court, and people called him Squire. Two benches for the public stood along the back wall with nobody on them. The five sat down to wait out the rain. Mrs. Rademacher shook her scarf. Donna Lutz opened her Plato. The Squire sat at an oak table with his docket book and a brass inkwell he had no use for, since he wrote with a ballpoint. At a smaller table sat Vern Tolle, who worked for Burkett’s Furniture and Appliance, with a stack of contracts and a stack of file cards. Down the side wall, on folding chairs, sat fourteen or fifteen people in work clothes and church clothes. Each of them held the paper the constable had brought to the door. Burkett against Doyle Capps, the Squire said. A man stood up.

sections.heading: III. The Second Reading
sections.dateline: The Carnegie library, basement room · eight o’clock
sections.text: Miss Verna Coyle had started without them. She was the official reporter of the circuit court and had been for twenty-two years, under three judges. She led the Great Books the way the Foundation trained its leaders to. The leader asks questions. She does not answer them, and she does not say what she thinks. People who had known Verna Coyle since grade school said the training could not have cost her much effort. She looked at the five wet coats and then at the clock, and asked the only question she asked that night that was not about Plato. Where have you been? They told her, all five at once, and then Harold alone, from his ticket. She listened the way she listened upstairs, except that her hands lay still. When he was through she asked three things. How long did each one take? A minute and a half. Two. Did the Squire ask any of them what they had to say? He asked was it right. Then he stopped them. Did anybody take it down? Nobody had. A justice’s court was not a court of record. There was the docket book, with the name and the judgment and the costs, and that was all there would ever be of Doyle Capps and his August payment. Miss Coyle opened her paper Plato. Mr. Stites, will

sections.heading: IV. The Tape
sections.dateline: The Squire’s room · the Tuesday following, and after
sections.text: The next Tuesday was not a Great Books night. Harold went to the courthouse anyway. Walt Ihnen was on the back bench ahead of him, and Mrs. Rademacher, and Donna Lutz with her mother. At seven Miss Coyle came down the east hall carrying her Stenotype in its case. She stood the tripod beside the radiator, where she could see the Squire’s mouth and the folding chairs both. She fed in a fresh pack of paper and sat down with her fingers on the keys. The Squire looked at her for some time. Verna. This is not a court of record. No, she said. Who is paying you? Nobody. He could not think of a statute against it, and the room was public. Burkett against Emery, he said. The machine made its small sound, hardly more than a knuckle on a table, and the paper moved up one line. It moved up a line for everything. It moved when Vern Tolle read his card and when the Squire said That right? and when Mr. Emery said he was behind. When Mr. Emery stopped, it stopped, and the whole room could hear it waiting. The Squire heard it. Go on, he said. If you have something to say, say it. Emery said the freezer had quit in July with half a hog in it and the store never sent anybody, and that was when he quit

title: Not of Record
logline: Five members of a library Great Books group duck out of the rain into a justice of the peace's Tuesday night court.

verses.text: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.

bg.commentary: The Group of Six (Chabbaggiyā) are the troublemaking monks of the Buddhist monastic code, blamed for the misconduct behind many of its rules. In this short commentary story they go from monastery to monastery and village to village making trouble in the refectories, boasting that they alone are intelligent and wise. One morning, after breakfast in a village, some young monks and novices come back and report that the Six grabbed them from behind and poured sweepings over their heads. The monks tell the Buddha, who says that he does not call a man wise because he talks much, only one who is patient, free from hatred and free from fear.
bg.history:
Hip hop began in the West and South Bronx in the early 1970s, at parties and outdoor jams where DJs, among them the Jamaican-born DJ Kool Herc, brought the island’s sound system culture north and extended the drum breaks of funk records on two turntables. Outdoor jams often ran on power drawn from the base of a lamppost. MCs, at first the DJ’s helpers, began rhyming over the breaks, and crews toured the borough’s schoolyards, parks and community centers. In September 1979 Sugar Hill Records released the Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight”, often called the first commercial rap single, recorded by a group from New Jersey; part of its lyrics had been borrowed from the notebook of the Bronx MC Grandmaster Caz.

Mr. Lindo’s sayings come from Jamaica Negro Proverbs and Sayings, collected by Izett Anderson and Frank Cundall and published by the Institute of Jamaica in 1910. The book glosses “Hollow gourd mek mos’ noise” as the old saw about empty vessels, and “Patient man ride jackass” as meaning that a patient man will put up with a great deal, or will more slowly attain his end. The Longwood neighborhood around Fox and Kelly Streets was among the hardest hit by the fires and abandonment that emptied much of the South Bronx in the 1970s.

sections.heading: I. Sweepings
sections.dateline: Westchester Avenue, the Bronx · a Saturday in October 1979
sections.text: The Saturday after a jam, Winston Brissett and Hector Colón always ate breakfast at the bakery under the el on Westchester Avenue, because Winston’s aunt worked the counter and gave them the patties that had split in the oven for a dime apiece. They were fourteen and fifteen. They had been on the mic the night before for the first time in front of more than a hundred people, at the end of the night, when most of the older heads had gone home. Little Winnie and Kid Hex. They had worked out their routine on the roof of Hector’s building all summer, trading lines back and forth over a beat Hector kept on a garbage can lid, and the night before it had gone the way it went on the roof, which almost never happened. They sat at the counter with coco bread and a beef patty each and went over it line by line, the way you go over a ball game. Six young men came in out of the rain without shutting the door. Everybody under the el knew who they were. They called themselves the Mighty Six, from Kelly Street, and they went from jam to jam all over the Bronx, the schoolyards and the parks and the P.A.L. gyms, and wherever they went they took the mic. They did not ask for it. They walked up to the

sections.heading: II. The Boiler Room
sections.text: Mr. Fitzroy Lindo was the super of a six-story building on Fox Street, one of the few on that block that still had all its windows. He had come up from Kingston in 1967. In Kingston, people said, he had run a sound in Jones Town that played against the big ones and was never once outplayed, and you could still hear a little of it in the way he lifted a needle. Here he fixed boilers and changed fuses and kept the hallways swept, and on Saturday nights in good weather his son Delroy carried the speaker boxes up the basement steps and out to the schoolyard, and Mr. Lindo plugged his amplifier into the bottom of a lamppost and played. He did not talk on the mic. Delroy did, a little, and the boys who came around, and lately half the young men in Longwood who could put two lines together. Mr. Lindo stood behind the turntables with a felt hat on and chose records. He chose them the way a man picks fruit, slowly, turning each one in his hands, and then he dropped the needle exactly where the drums came in, and the whole schoolyard went up at once like birds. The speaker boxes lived in the boiler room. That was where the boys went. They had washed their hair at Hector’s. It did not matter.

sections.heading: III. The Lamppost
sections.dateline: The schoolyard on Fox Street · the next Saturday night
sections.text: It was the last warm night of the year and three hundred people came. Delroy ran the cable across the sidewalk to the lamppost and taped it down, and the boxes stood at the end of the schoolyard against the fence, two bass bins as tall as Winston, and the amplifier warmed up with its little red light, and Mr. Lindo laid out his crates on a folding table under the streetlamp, where the light was orange and fell on everything the same. Winston and Hector were on the mic early, when the crowd was still thin. Then the older MCs from Longwood had it, and then Delroy, and the yard filled up and the noise of it rose off the asphalt like heat. The Mighty Six came in through the gate on the Fox Street side a little after eleven, in a line, and the crowd opened in front of them because it knew them. Raheem walked straight to the table and took the mic out of the hand of the boy who had it. He talked. He was good. He talked about himself, and the Six, and Kelly Street, and about the Jersey record and the men who made it, and about every fool holding a mic from Mott Haven to Fordham Road, and about little Jamaican boys who ought to be home in bed, and his voice went up and down the yard over t

sections.heading: IV. Tuesday
sections.text: Raheem did not come Tuesday. He never came. The Mighty Six went on taking mics at other jams for a while, and then, the way crews do, there were four of them, and then nobody could say. But a boy named Tito, who was the youngest of them and had held Hector by the collar at the bakery, came down the basement steps on Fox Street on Tuesday evening with his hands in his pockets. He stood by the boxes and did not say anything, and Mr. Lindo did not say anything, and after a while Delroy handed him the end of a cable to coil. The felt hat was on a nail over the bench, next to the gourd. Mr. Lindo had not brushed it. There was still a little grit in the crease of the crown. Winston and Hector worked on their routine all that winter on Hector’s roof, in coats, with the garbage can lid. It got shorter. They started leaving holes in it, places where neither of them said anything and Hector just hit the lid, once, and let it ring, and you could hear the el go by on Westchester Avenue, and then the next line came. In the spring they tried it at the schoolyard. When they got to the first hole and stopped, the whole yard leaned in toward them, waiting, and Winston stood there in the orange ligh

title: Hollow Gourd
logline: Six MCs from Kelly Street take every mic in the Bronx, and a Jamaican super who never touches the mic keeps the record going.

verses.text: A man is not a supporter of the law because he talks much; even if a man has learnt little, but sees the law bodily, he is a supporter of the law, a man who never neglects the law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Ekudāna lives alone in a forest grove and knows only one verse, an “exalted utterance” about the heedful sage who has no grief. On Observance Days he sounds the call to hear the Dhamma himself and recites it, and the deities of the grove shout their applause with a noise like the earth splitting open. Two learned monks who know the whole canon come with five hundred followers each; he welcomes them gladly and asks them to teach. One recites and one expounds, and the grove stays silent. Then the old elder takes the fan, sits in the preacher’s seat, and says his one verse, and the deities roar. The offended monks complain to the Buddha that the deities play favorites, and the Buddha answers that one is a bearer of the Dhamma by seeing it, not by saying much.
bg.history:
German Lutheran immigrants filled the country around Fort Wayne in the nineteenth century. A Fort Wayne pastor began training men for their ministry in the 1840s, and the seminary formally organized there in 1846 was handed over to the new Missouri Synod soon after its founding in 1847; Concordia Theological Seminary moved to St. Louis in 1861 and later to Springfield, Illinois, and came back to Fort Wayne in 1976. Rural Lutheran congregations across the Midwest kept up annual mission festivals, outdoor services in a farmer’s grove with plank benches, a guest preacher, a potluck and a pop stand. Many Lutheran pastors still end the sermon with Philippians 4:7, a blessing called the votum. A stroke that takes away most speech can leave behind words a person has said or sung thousands of times; the Max Planck Society notes that people with aphasia can often still produce song lyrics and formulaic phrases.

The summer of 1988 brought drought and heat across the Corn Belt. In Indiana, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, statewide rainfall was nearly eight inches below normal by the end of September, groundwater fell to record lows in many wells, and crop yields ran from half to about four-fifths of the year before.

sections.heading: I. The Grove
sections.text: Ewald Kruse was eighty-one the summer it did not rain. He had farmed the ground on the creek east of Fort Wayne since 1931, and since Lorraine died he had lived alone in the farmhouse while his son Norbert farmed it, and at the back of the farm, where the creek bent, stood the grove. It was oaks on the high side and cottonwoods along the water, with eleven rows of plank benches set on cinder blocks under the oaks and a wooden pulpit at the front that Ewald’s father had built in 1912. Every September for seventy-six years St. Paul’s Lutheran had held its Missionfest there: preaching in the morning and preaching in the afternoon, a guest pastor for each, and in between a dinner on long tables with the pop stand run by the youth. Three years before, Ewald had a stroke in the machine shed. When he came home from the hospital he could walk with a cane and use his right hand a little, and he could not talk. Julie Bleeke, the speech therapist from the hospital in Fort Wayne, came out twice a week for three years with her flash cards and her picture books. She got him to ja and nein, which came back in German, and to the name of his granddaughter, Kristin. That was nearly all. The one whol

sections.heading: II. The Two Preachers
sections.dateline: Missionfest · the second Sunday in September
sections.text: That year the Missionfest committee aimed high, and both guests said yes. For the morning there was Dr. Harold Brandt from the seminary in Fort Wayne, who taught Old Testament and read Hebrew the way other men read the News-Sentinel, and who had written a commentary on Isaiah that pastors kept on the shelf behind their desks. He brought most of his seminarians in a borrowed school bus. For the afternoon there was Pastor Gene Rademacher of Trinity on the south side of the city, the biggest Lutheran congregation in Fort Wayne, whose sermons went out on the radio every Sunday morning, a big warm man with a voice you could hear at the back of a barn. Two charter buses of his people came out behind him, and a line of cars. Between the two preachers there were more people in the grove than anybody at St. Paul’s could remember, eight or nine hundred, in folding chairs set out behind the benches and on lawn chairs they had brought from home. It was ninety-four degrees by ten in the morning. The corn on both sides of the road stood up white and burned, half of it not worth the combine, and the creek was down to a string of pools. There was no wind. In the grove the cottonwood leaves hung st

sections.heading: III. The Fan
sections.text: Dr. Brandt preached for fifty minutes in the morning on Isaiah 55, as the rain cometh down, which in that summer made people look up. He went through it in the Hebrew, a word at a time, and opened it the way you open a seed catalog, and the seminarians wrote in their notebooks on their knees. It was a very good sermon. At the end of it he lifted his hand and said, And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus, and said Amen. The grove was silent. Eight hundred people sat with their cardboard fans going. The cottonwood leaves hung on their stems. At dinner there was fried chicken and noodles and sliced tomatoes, all that the gardens had made in a dry year, and nine kinds of Jell-O salad on a separate table, and sugar cream pie. In the afternoon Pastor Rademacher preached on the Great Commission for forty-five minutes. He told about a mission school in New Guinea, and a woman in Papua who had walked four days to be baptized, and by the end people at the back of the grove were wiping their eyes. It was a very good sermon too. He lifted his hand and said the votum, in the same English, and the Amen. Nothing. A sparrow on th

sections.heading: IV. The Pie Table
sections.text: Afterward, at the tables, Trinity’s people did not know what to make of it, and some of them were sore. Their pastor had preached his heart out. The professor had preached for fifty minutes out of the Hebrew. And an old farmer said one sentence, in German, that every one of them had heard their own pastor say ten thousand times, and the trees went off like the sectional. One man from the radio committee said those trees played favorites. Another said, laughing a little, that they were Missouri Synod trees and only understood German. People laughed at that, though not all of them. Dr. Brandt did not laugh. He went looking for somebody who could tell him, and Norbert said to ask Julie, who knew his father better than any of them now; she had come out to the house twice a week for three years, and she had come today on her own time. Julie Bleeke was thirty-four and had grown up on a hog farm near Hoagland and still kept her hair the way she had at her confirmation. She was standing at the pie table cutting sugar cream pie into eighths with a cake server. I understand he can’t say anything else, the professor said. Hardly a thing, she said. Ja and nein. His granddaughter’s name. That’s

title: The Votum
logline: In the drought summer, an old Lutheran farmer who can say only one sentence since his stroke hosts two famous preachers at the Missionfest.

verses.text: A man is not an elder because his head is grey; his age may be ripe, but he is called `Old-in-vain.'
He in whom there is truth, virtue, love, restraint, moderation, he who is free from impurity and is wise, he is called an elder.

bg.commentary: Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya (“Bhaddiya the Dwarf”) was a monk so small and young-looking that people took him for a novice, though he was an elder and fully awakened. In this commentary story he leaves after attending on the Buddha just as thirty monks from the forest arrive. The Buddha asks whether they saw an elder go out; they say they saw only a novice, and a very small one. The Buddha tells them he does not call a man an elder because he is old and sits in an elder’s seat, only one who understands the truths and harms no one, and the thirty monks are awakened as they listen.
bg.history:
Detroit techno was made in the mid-1980s by young Black musicians, most famously three high-school friends from suburban Belleville, who recorded in their basements on drum machines and synthesizers and released records on small local labels. By the late 1980s the music had found a larger audience in Britain and Europe than at home, and a second wave of Detroit artists followed in the early 1990s, many of them pressing their records in small runs with plain labels and little or no information about who made them. After the Berlin Wall fell, techno became the sound of the city’s new clubs in empty buildings; Tresor, opened in March 1991 in the vaults of a former department store on Leipziger Strasse, released records by Detroit artists on its own label.

Mr. Fuller’s plant, the Dodge Main assembly plant in Hamtramck, closed in 1980. His book is Sir James Redhouse’s 1881 translation of the first book of Rumi’s Mesnevi, which includes a selection of anecdotes about Rumi from Shams al-Dīn Aflākī’s fourteenth-century Manāqib al-ʿĀrifīn, the “Acts of the Adepts.”

sections.heading: I. The Door
sections.text: The bus from Metro Airport let them off in front of a storefront with a hand-painted sign, FULLER’S RECORDS & BOOKS, and a steel grate rolled halfway up. There were thirty of them. Most were from Berlin, a few from Frankfurt and Rotterdam, two from Osaka who had met the others at the airport by accident and been adopted. They worked in record shops and clubs. They had saved since the summer. For two years they had been playing records made in this city in cellars under a city that had been cut in half, and they had come to see where the records came from, the way people go to see a river’s source. What most of them wanted to see was one man. His records had no names on them. They came in plain white sleeves with a stamped label, and in the smooth ring of the run-out groove, where the needle goes when the music is done, someone had scratched by hand a small circle with a dot in it. That was all. In Berlin they called him the Old Man. Nobody could remember who had started it. It was what the records sounded like: patient, unhurried, as if whoever made them had already heard everything and was not in any hurry to tell you about it. Somebody had heard he was one of the first, from back

sections.heading: II. The Beard
sections.dateline: The back of the store · the same afternoon
sections.text: He came out from behind the counter and went to the shelves on the left wall, and ran a finger along them without looking, and took down a fat old book with a cracked spine and the gilt gone off its lettering. He did not open it right away. He stood with it in his hands, looking at the thirty of them, and at their good boots and their careful clothes and the bags they had carried four thousand miles to put records in. Rumi, he said. The poet. You know him? Some of them did. This is an Englishman’s book from a hundred years ago. In the back are stories about Rumi that his people told after he was dead. One day he met a Christian monk in the road. A monk with a big beard. And Rumi asked him which one was older, him or his beard. He found the page with his thumb, the way you find a place you have found many times, and read it to them through the half-glasses, slowly, in the voice of a man reading a lease aloud to somebody who cannot. The monk replied: “I am twenty years older than my beard. It came forth that number of years later.” Jelāl answered him: “Then I pity thee. Thy young beard has attained to maturity, whereas thou hast remained immature, as thou wast. …” — Eflākī, Acts of t

sections.heading: III. The Windows
sections.dateline: A warehouse loft near the Detroit River · that night until morning
sections.text: It was the fourth floor of a building that had made something once, stoves or cigar boxes, nobody there knew, with a freight elevator that did not work and a stairway that smelled of rain. The east wall was all windows, tall factory windows with a hundred small panes, some of them broken and taped. Below them, beyond the railroad tracks, was the river, black, and across the river the lights of Windsor, which was another country. There were maybe two hundred people. The thirty came in together, and stood together for the first hour, and then did not. He was at the far end on a plywood platform behind two turntables and a mixer on a door laid across sawhorses. The table was made for a taller man. Under his feet, so that he could reach, was a plastic milk crate turned upside down, with a dairy’s name stenciled on the side, and he stood on it all night and did not once look down to find it. He did not talk on a microphone. He did not raise his hands. He stood with his cap off now, and his round face lit from below by the little lamp on the mixer, and he looked like a boy at a science fair. When he took a record out of its white sleeve he held it by the edges and looked at the grooves b

title: The Milk Crate
logline: Thirty Berlin techno pilgrims come to a Grand River record-and-book shop to meet the Old Man, and a small boy holds the door.

verses.text: An envious greedy, dishonest man does not become respectable by means of much talking only, or by the beauty of his complexion.
He in whom all this is destroyed, and taken out with the very root, he, when freed from hatred and wise, is called respectable.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, some senior monks at Jetavana notice the young monks and novices dyeing robes and doing other services for their own preceptors. The elders, who are skilled with words and expert in the letter of the teaching, get no such attention, and they ask the Buddha to rule that young monks, wherever they have learned the Dhamma, must not rehearse it until they have trained under them, so that their own gain and honor will grow. The Buddha sees that the rule would be proper in itself but that they want it for their own gain, and tells them he does not count them accomplished for their talk: only one in whom envy and the rest have been cut out at the root is truly accomplished.
bg.history:
Douglas Aircraft built its DC-8, its first jet airliner, at a new factory at Long Beach Airport. The first one rolled out on April 9, 1958, first flew on May 30, 1958, and entered service with Delta and United on September 18, 1959. Before computers, every part of an airplane was drawn by hand, in pencil on vellum, in drafting rooms that held hundreds of boards; the work went from layout to detail to checker, whose initials on the drawing meant it could be released. Lettering in a standard single-stroke Gothic hand was a point of pride, and the trade itself all but disappeared once computer-aided drafting arrived.

Next door, the tract city of Lakewood went up between 1950 and 1953, 17,500 houses in under three years, sold to veterans with no money down on thirty-year loans. Lakewood incorporated in 1954. Dichondra, a low creeping plant with small round leaves, was a fashionable lawn in Southern California through the 1950s, and Bermuda grass, which the locals called devil grass, invaded it by underground runners that had to be dug out entire or would come back.

sections.heading: I. The Board Cover
sections.dateline: Engineering, the Long Beach plant · October 1959
sections.text: The drafting room was on the second floor and ran the length of a city block, two hundred boards in rows under the fluorescent tubes, every board with a drafting machine clamped to the top edge and a man on a stool in front of it, and here and there a woman. It was quiet the way a library is quiet, which is to say there was a sound under everything, two hundred pencils going and the tick of the machines' protractor heads locking and unlocking, and the hiss of the air conditioning that had been put in for the vellum and not for the people. The airplane they had drawn had gone into service with United and Delta in September. Now the changes were coming back, the way they always did, in stacks. Lloyd Ambrose had the second board from the window in the wing group. He had come out from Wichita in 1941 when Douglas was hiring anybody who could hold a pencil, and he had been a layout man since the war, and his lettering was the best in the building. People said that, and he had heard them say it. Single-stroke Gothic, upper case, an eighth of an inch high, every letter leaning exactly nowhere, every O a true O, every R with its leg kicked out at the same angle as every other R. He did it

sections.heading: II. Lunch in the Buick
sections.dateline: The parking lot · the following week
sections.text: Nobody ate in the cafeteria who could help it. Most of Engineering ate in their cars with the windows down and the radio on, in the big lot by the airport fence, and watched the airplanes. Lloyd and Russ ate in Russ's Buick, which had the better radio. It's not that I want my pencils sharpened, Lloyd said. Lord, no. It's the standard. You look at what's coming out of that training school. Half of them can't letter. They can't make a numeral eight. They come up here and they attach themselves to whoever's nice to them, and they learn whatever that person happens to do. Irene's a good checker. Nobody says she isn't. But her hand is a mess, and every one of those kids is going to letter like her in five years. Russ unwrapped a sandwich. What we ought to have, he said, is a rule. Nobody puts a line on a released drawing until he's done six weeks of lettering with one of the senior layout men. No matter where he trained. The way they used to do it at Santa Monica before the war. The way they used to do it everywhere. It'd be good for the airplane. It would, Lloyd said. He was already seeing it. He saw the memo, with his name on it and Russ's. He saw a Group Leader rating, which neither

sections.heading: III. The Chief's Desk
sections.text: Harlan Voss had a grey steel desk at the end of the room, out in the open with everybody else, where he could see the whole wing group without seeming to look. He was from Red Oak, Iowa. He had been a structures man before he was a section chief and he still did the stress checks on the hard ones himself, at home, at night. He was an elder at a Presbyterian church in Long Beach and he had never been heard to raise his voice or tell a joke. When you talked to him he looked at you the whole time with his hands folded on the blotter, and it was hard to keep talking. Lloyd talked well. He had written it out at home and practiced it in the bathroom mirror and he did not need the paper. He talked about the standard. He talked about the training school. He said that a drawing was a public document and might be in a file somewhere for forty years and that somebody they would never meet would have to read it. He did not mention Irene Kostka. He did not mention a Group Leader rating. Russ stood behind him and nodded at the right places. It took about four minutes, and when he was done he knew it had been good. Voss sat a while. That's a sound idea, he said. It's the way I was taught. A man o

sections.heading: IV. The Runner
sections.text: Lloyd lived on Hayter Avenue in Lakewood, in a two-bedroom stucco house that had cost him nine thousand dollars in 1951 with nothing down, on a street of eighty houses that had all been built in about a week. He had put in dichondra in front, like everybody, because it stayed green and flat and you hardly had to mow it, and it looked from the street like a green felt tabletop. He was proud of it. The only trouble with it was the devil grass. Devil grass was what everybody in Lakewood called Bermuda grass. It came over from the vacant lots and the neighbors and the strip by the curb, and it threw out runners under the dichondra, flat, like wire, and sent up blades every few inches along them, coarse and grey-green and ugly. Lloyd had been pulling it for eight years. He pulled it every Saturday morning, along with the rest of the street. You took hold of the blades and pulled, and they broke off at the runner, and the lawn looked clean, and in a week it was back. Everybody knew that. Nobody on Hayter Avenue had ever done anything else. He was on his knees on a folded bath mat at seven in the morning, with the coffee going cold on the step. He had not slept well. He kept hearing it, t

title: Devil Grass
logline: In the Douglas drafting room the year the DC-8 entered service, two senior draftsmen with beautiful lettering ask the chief for a new rule.

verses.text: Not by tonsure does an undisciplined man who speaks falsehood become a Samana; can a man be a Samana who is still held captive by desire and greediness?
He who always quiets the evil, whether small or large, he is called a Samana (a quiet man), because he has quieted all evil.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk named Hatthaka wins his arguments with other sects by a trick. Whenever he is losing, he names a time and place to continue the debate, goes there early, and tells the people gathered that his opponents are too afraid to come, which he calls an admission of defeat. The Buddha hears of it and sends for him. When Hatthaka admits it is true, the Buddha tells him that a shaven head does not make a man a monk if he lies and is driven by desire and greed. He is a monk who has quieted wrongdoing of every kind, small and great.
bg.history:
Hays is the seat of Ellis County in western Kansas and home to Fort Hays State University. Volga Germans, German-speaking Catholics from Russia, began settling the county in 1876, and their villages of Victoria, Schoenchen, Munjor and Pfeifer still give the county its character. At Victoria the parishioners built the church of St. Fidelis, the "Cathedral of the Plains," finished in 1911. Every member of the parish twelve or older was asked to give $45 and to haul six wagonloads of Fencepost limestone and four of sand each year until it was built.

In the years around 2010 a wave of public atheism sometimes called the New Atheism reached small campuses through student groups, books and YouTube channels, where filmed debates with believers drew large audiences. The Out Campaign, endorsed by Richard Dawkins, gave atheists a scarlet letter A to wear on pins and shirts. Many in the movement took The Age of Reason (1794–1807), Thomas Paine's attack on revealed religion, as a founding text. Its first part opens with Paine's own creed, in which he says he believes in one God and declares that "my own mind is my own church."

sections.heading: I. The Pin
sections.text: Travis Dreher shaved his head every Sunday morning, at the hour his mother was at Mass in Victoria, and he wore a red letter A on a pin on his jacket, the scarlet A that atheists had started wearing a few years before so they could find each other. He was twenty-one and a junior in political science. He had grown up in the shadow of St. Fidelis, the big twin-towered church out on the plain at Victoria that his great-great-grandfather had helped build, hauling limestone in a wagon the way every man in the parish had to, and he had quit believing at fifteen, all at once, the way some people get saved. Now he ran the Fort Hays Freethinkers, nine members on a good night, in a seminar room on the second floor of the student union, and he ran a YouTube channel called Prairie Reason, which had four thousand subscribers. He was a good talker. He had read everything. He would stand at the tables outside the union with his phone propped on a stack of books, filming, and take on anybody: the Baptist preacher who came up from Great Bend twice a semester with a sign, the Mormon elders in their white shirts, the Newman Center kids. He won most of the time. When he won, he posted it. When he lost

sections.heading: II. The Format
sections.dateline: The student union, second floor · October and November
sections.text: After that it was what he did. He lost a long argument in October to one of the Mormon elders, a boy from Idaho who had read more Hume than he had. He lost one in November to an old Lutheran pastor from Ellis who had come to the table only to buy a raffle ticket. Each time Travis said the same easy thing. This deserves a real format. Each time he named a day, a time and the room upstairs. Each time he went live early, talked to the empty chairs, and cut the clip. ELDER GHOSTS DEBATE. PASTOR WON'T SHOW. The comments loved them. Subscribers went past six thousand. A man in Phoenix sent him a fifty-dollar tip with a note that said keep exposing them. The Freethinkers loved it too, most of them. They had grown up in Ellis, Russell and Rooks Counties, in towns with a church on every corner and nobody to say any of this out loud to. Travis said it out loud for them, with his shaved head and his red pin. When he came into the Tuesday meeting after a clip went up, they clapped. Not all of them. Mariah Leiker, who kept the club's money in a cash box, said one night that it was funny how none of them ever showed. Travis said that was the point. Mariah did not say anything else. But she had b

sections.heading: III. Mrs. Haas
sections.dateline: Twenty-second Street, Hays · a Saturday in December
sections.text: The oldest member of the Fort Hays Freethinkers was Lorene Haas, who was seventy-nine and not a student. She came to every Tuesday meeting in a quilted coat with her cane hooked over the back of her chair, and mostly she listened. She had been a preacher's wife for thirty-one years, in Holiness churches in Russell, Osborne and Smith Counties. She had played the piano for every service, taught the women's Bible study, and buried a daughter. Then one winter, the year after her husband died, she sat down at her kitchen table with the Bible she had taught from all her life and read it straight through, Genesis to Revelation, like a book, in nineteen days. When she closed it she did not believe any of it anymore. She said so out loud, to her sister, her son and her pastor, and lost most of her friends in Russell County. That had been twenty-two years ago. She said it was the most honest thing she had ever done and she would do it again. Mariah Leiker went to see her on a Friday. On Saturday morning Lorene called Travis on the phone and asked him to come by the house. She lived in a small brick house on Twenty-second Street with a wheelchair ramp her son had built. She let him in and sat

sections.heading: IV. Seven O'Clock
sections.text: He took the three clips down that night. It cost him about four hundred subscribers, and the man in Phoenix wrote to ask what had happened to him. He did not answer. He wrote to Annie Pfannenstiel instead, and to the elder from Idaho, who had gone home, and to the Lutheran pastor at Ellis, and told each of them what he had done, in so many words. Then he asked Annie whether she would still have the debate. They had it on the third Thursday in January, at seven, in the seminar room on the second floor. Twenty-two people came, which was more than had ever come to anything the Freethinkers did, and Lorene Haas sat in the front row with her cane hooked on her chair. Travis did not go live early. He sat at the front of the room with the camera off and his hands on the table and watched the clock on the wall, and nobody in the room said anything. He had let his hair start to grow out over Christmas, a dark fuzz, and he had left the pin on his dresser. At 7:01 the door opened and Annie Pfannenstiel came in, out of breath from the parking lot, and said she was sorry, the lot behind the union was full. He lost, narrowly. He knew it, and so did the room. He posted all of it, an hour and fort

title: Seven O'Clock
logline: A shaved-headed campus atheist with a YouTube channel wins every debate in Ellis County, one way or another.

verses.text: A man is not a mendicant (Bhikshu) simply because he asks others for alms; he who adopts the whole law is a Bhikshu, not he who only begs.
He who is above good and evil, who is chaste, who with knowledge passes through the world, he indeed is called a Bhikshu.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin who has gone forth in another sect and lives by begging reasons that since the Buddha calls his own alms-gathering disciples bhikkhus (the word means one who asks for alms), he ought to be called a bhikkhu too, and goes and says so. The Buddha answers that he does not call a man a bhikkhu merely because he receives alms or keeps the outward forms, and speaks the two verses. That is the whole story.
bg.history:
John Law's Company of the West, chartered in 1717, was obliged to people Louisiana and could not find volunteers. An ordinance proclaimed in Paris on November 10, 1718, allowed vagabonds to be arrested and transported, and police squads nicknamed the bandouliers du Mississippi swept up beggars, deserters, smugglers and people whose families or enemies wanted them gone; they were marched to the ports in chains. The abuses were notorious, and a royal decree of May 9, 1720, ended the forced shipments. Many of those landed on the Gulf Coast died of hunger and disease. New Orleans, founded in 1718, became the colony's capital in 1722, the year a September hurricane leveled most of it. The Historic New Orleans Collection tells the story in "The Vagabond City."

In 1722 lower Louisiana was assigned to the Capuchins of the province of Champagne, a reformed branch of the Franciscans who by rule live on alms. Their superior, Father Raphaël, arrived in 1723 and reported that he could hardly find a room for his friars and that fewer than thirty people came to Sunday Mass; the brick-and-timber parish church was begun in 1725 (see the Catholic Encyclopedia on New Orleans). False pilgrims with cockle shells were an old and recognized class of Paris beggar. Jacquot and Frère Zacharie are invented, and whether the Louisiana Capuchins sent a brother out with the sack, as their houses in France did, is not recorded. Francis's "brother fly" and his rules of pilgrims are in St. Bonaventure's life of the saint, which every Franciscan knew; it is quoted in E. Gurney Salter's English of 1904.

sections.heading: I. The Shells
sections.text: He was called Jacquot la Coquille. A woman who may have been his mother set him on a church porch near the Halles when he was six, with his arm bound up in a rag to look withered, and at twelve he was taken into the trade proper. Begging in Paris had its ranks and its masters, like the drapers. There were the ones who chewed soap and fell down foaming, and the ones with a paper saying their house had burned, and the ones who went as pilgrims of Saint James, with cockle shells sewn on hat and cape and a staff with a gourd, and a tale of the long road home from Compostela. Jacquot was a pilgrim. He had the shells, the staff, a cape that was more patch than cape, and a beard to his breastbone. He had never been south of the Orléans gate. In twenty years he had not done one day's work, and he said so with some pride. He lived on what was given, he said, like the birds of the air and the friars. Then the Company wanted people for the Mississippi. In November of 1718 it was cried in Paris that vagabonds might be taken up and sent, and that winter the archers the streets called the bandouliers of the Mississippi went through the city, paid, it was said, by the head. They lifted Jacquot of

sections.heading: II. The Sack
sections.text: They were set ashore on the sand at Biloxi, where there was nothing, and a good many did not get up from it. Jacquot got up. He reached the new town on the river in time for the September storm of 1722, which blew down most of what was standing, and he stayed, having nowhere to go that was not farther. By the summer of 1724 it was a town of straight streets ruled through mud, huts of cypress posts, a levee and a guardhouse. And he found that a beggar there had no one to beg from. There were soldiers who had not been paid, clerks of the Company, men and women shipped out as he had been, and Africans who were not let to own even themselves. A man with shells on his hat got a laugh the first day and after that nothing. He lived on the levee off what fell from the boats. The Capuchins had come the year before, friars of the province of Champagne in brown habits with long pointed hoods, corded and sandaled and bearded. Their superior had hardly been able to find a room to put them in, and fewer than thirty people came to his Sunday Mass. The Company was bound to keep them and paid when it remembered. With them was an old lay brother, Frère Zacharie, who had carried the alms sack for his

sections.heading: III. The Hat
sections.dateline: New Orleans · the fever months and after
sections.text: He wore it as a joke at first. He answered to it with a bow and held out his hand. It brought him no more than the shells had. In the fever months the hospital filled. One morning Jacquot saw the old brother coming out of the shed backward, bent double, hauling a dead soldier by the armpits because there was nobody for the feet. Jacquot looked up and down the levee. Then he went over and took the feet. Nobody had asked him and nobody thanked him. The next morning he was there before the brother was, and after the burying he carried the water. Nobody saw him cut the shells off. Some children found seven cockles in the mud below the levee and played at pilgrims with them for a week. He never again asked any man to call him anything. He slept under the eave of the hospital shed, which was not his, and ate what the brother's sack brought, after the sick had eaten. It is said that when a new father came out from France and asked who the bearded man digging in the cemetery was, a child told him, That is Brother Fly, and that Frère Zacharie, who did not often correct anyone, said, Leave off the fly. Jacquot wore the same hat to the end of his life. It had seven pale places on the felt, ea

title: Brother Fly
logline: A Paris beggar shipped to Louisiana in chains tells an old Capuchin with an alms sack that they are in the same trade.

verses.text: A man is not a Muni because he observes silence (mona, i.e. mauna), if he is foolish and ignorant; but the wise who, taking the balance, chooses the good and avoids evil, he is a Muni, and is a Muni thereby; he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, wanderers of other sects thank their hosts after every meal with blessings and with warnings about mud and thorns on the roads, while the Buddha's monks get up from the table and leave without a word. The householders take offense. The Buddha tells the monks to give thanks and to sit beside their hosts and talk pleasantly with them, and the householders respond by giving more than before. The other sects then complain that the monks talk too much and that they themselves are the true sages, the silent ones. The Buddha answers that people keep quiet out of ignorance, out of timidity, or out of a stinginess that will not share what it knows, and that a sage (muni) is one who weighs and puts aside what is harmful. The Pāli plays on mona, silence, and muni, sage.
bg.history:
The Japantown of the Western Addition held more than five thousand people before the war. In 1942 its families were removed, most of them by way of the Tanforan racetrack to the Topaz camp in the Utah desert, and many who came back in 1945 found their stored belongings gone. In the late 1950s the city’s Redevelopment Agency began clearing the forty-four blocks of its Western Addition project A-1, widening Geary into an expressway and displacing about four thousand people, Japanese American and Black, by the middle of the 1960s. The Pine Street temple, its people and Mr. Dunmore are invented.

These were also the years when Americans raised on paperbacks about Zen started looking for somewhere to sit. Alan Watts’s essay “Beat Zen, Square Zen, and Zen” appeared in 1958. In May 1959 the Sōtō priest Shunryū Suzuki arrived to serve the Japanese American congregation of Sokoji, then housed in a former synagogue on Bush Street, and the early-morning sitting he opened to anyone became the San Francisco Zen Center. The two groups in such temples, the families who had built them and the newcomers who came to meditate, did not always know what to make of each other. Takuan is made much as Mrs. Oka describes it. The quotations are from James Legge’s nineteenth-century translations of the Tao Te Ching and the Analects.

sections.heading: I. The Saturday People
sections.text: The temple on Pine Street was two flats of a wooden house with the wall between the front rooms taken out. Reverend Kuwahara had died in the fall of 1957, and headquarters in Japan had been promising a new priest ever since. Until one came, his widow unlocked the door. Kuwahara Tome was seventy-one. Everyone called her Okusan, the lady of the house. She had come from Fukui in 1914 to marry a man she knew from a photograph, and she had kept his temple through one earthquake scare, one Depression, and three years in the Utah desert, and she saw no reason to stop for a funeral. Fumi Hamada kept the temple's books and did Okusan's English for her. Fumi was forty-three, born on Buchanan Street, a bookkeeper at a dry-goods store on Post. She was in the basement kitchen most Saturdays and every Sunday with Mrs. Oka and Mrs. Tani and the two Nakagawa sisters, and so she saw both kinds of Americans that came in those years. The first kind came on Saturday night. Mr. Lyman Dunmore rented the social hall for ten dollars a month to lecture on what he called the Zen way. He was fifty, a big soft man in a Japanese farmer's jacket, and he taught evenings at an academy out in Pacific Heights. Twen

sections.heading: II. Sit Beside
sections.text: Fumi told Walt Kessler. She had not planned to. He was holding the street door for her one Sunday with his eyes lowered like a man in a hospital corridor, and she heard herself say, You know they think you don't like the food. He looked up. He had a long, plain, worried face. We thought we weren't supposed to talk. Who told you that? He thought about it. Nobody, he said. The next morning after the bell, all of them stayed behind in the front room, and Walt asked Okusan, and Fumi put it into Japanese. Okusan listened with her hands folded on her apron. She did not smile, but she rarely did. After eating, say gochisōsama, she said. It means, it was a feast. Then don't run away. Sit beside. Mrs. Oka makes the takuan. Ask her how long. That was the whole instruction. Fumi wrote the word on the back of an offering envelope so they could practice it. The first Sunday was hard to watch. Eight Americans said gochisōsama in eight different ways and then sat down on the benches next to the women, holding their knees. The seaman asked Mrs. Tani if she had lived in San Francisco long. Mrs. Tani said forty-four years. Walt asked Mrs. Oka how long for the takuan, and Mrs. Oka, who had not been a

sections.heading: III. The Stone
sections.text: It got back to Mr. Dunmore. The Saturday suppers had not got any worse, but there was no salmon in them, and one of his own circle, a tall girl with a braid, had mentioned the Sunday breakfasts in his hearing. He said it at the table, to his own people, loud enough for the kitchen. We follow the wordless teaching. We are the ones who understand silence. Upstairs they have made a coffee hour of it. They sit forty minutes and then gossip with the cooks about radishes. He had a brown library book with him, one of a long set, and he opened it at a slip of paper and read. He who knows (the Tâo) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it. Fumi, in the kitchen doorway with a dish towel, put it into Japanese for Okusan as well as she could. She was angry and it came out short. Okusan was at the pickle barrel in the corner, seeing to the last of the year's takuan. She listened to the end. Then she lifted the stone off the lid. It was a flat gray stone the size of a loaf, and it had come back from Topaz in 1945 in the bottom of a suitcase, because everything she had stored in 1942 was gone when she got home, the old stone with it.
