title: The Pickle Stone
logline: In a small Zen temple, the kitchen women feed two kinds of Americans: one talks too much, and one never says thank you.

verses.text: A man is not an elect (Ariya) because he injures living creatures; because he has pity on all living creatures, therefore is a man called Ariya.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a fisherman whose name is Ariya, “Noble,” is fishing with hook and line near the north gate of Sāvatthī when the Buddha and his monks pass by. He throws down his pole and stands still. The Buddha stops nearby and asks Sāriputta and the other elders their names one by one, and the fisherman thinks, he will ask me too. The Buddha does ask, and when the fisherman answers “Ariya,” the Buddha says that those who take life are not called noble, and that the noble are those who harm no living thing. At the end of the verse the fisherman enters the stream. The word ariya, noble, is the same one used for the Buddha’s Four Noble Truths.
bg.history:
Between 1941 and 1943 nearly 400,000 people, Black and white, moved to Detroit from the South to work in the war plants. Housing was desperately short and tension ran high. In February 1942 white residents fought to keep Black defense workers out of the Sojourner Truth housing project, and in June 1943 some 25,000 white workers walked out at Packard when three Black men were promoted to the assembly line. By the end of the decade about a quarter of the workers at Ford’s River Rouge complex, which built aircraft engines and other war goods, were Black. Meat had been rationed by red points since March 1943, as the National Park Service’s account of home-front meat rationing describes.

On Sunday, June 20, 1943, fights between Black and white youths broke out on Belle Isle, and that evening they spread onto the crowded bridge, renamed for Douglas MacArthur the year before, as more than 100,000 people tried to leave the island. False rumors raced through the city overnight: in Paradise Valley, that whites had thrown a Black mother and her baby off the bridge; in white neighborhoods, that Black men had attacked a white woman. White mobs beat Black riders pulled off Woodward Avenue streetcars, and police poured into Paradise Valley. By the time federal troops arrived on the night of June 21, thirty-four people were dead, twenty-five of them Black, seventeen of those killed by police. Edwin Arnold’s translation of the Gita, The Song Celestial, was the first version Gandhi ever read, as a student in England, and Thoreau’s reflections on giving up fishing appear in the chapter “Higher Laws” of Walden (1854).

sections.heading: I. Big Boy
sections.text: His mother named him Noble because she wanted the white folks in Lowndes County to have to say it. She told him so when he was small. They will call you boy till you are ninety, she said, but every time they want you they will have to say Noble first, and it will cost them something in their mouths. It did not work out that way. In Alabama they called him boy. In Detroit, where he came up in 1937 on the Dixie Highway with nine dollars and a cardboard suitcase, they called him Big Boy. He was six foot three and weighed two hundred and twenty pounds, and he had boxed for two years out of the Brewster Center, where Joe Louis had trained, and had won eleven fights and lost two, and in the last one, in Toledo, he had hit a man named Sweeney so hard that Sweeney went to the hospital and never walked right again. Noble quit after that. He went to work in the foundry at Ford’s Rouge plant in Dearborn, pouring iron, where most of the colored men at the Rouge worked because it was the hottest and dirtiest work in the place. The foreman on his line called him Big Boy. The men on the line called him Big Boy, or Tate. At the Rouge, nobody called him Noble. The foundry was like working inside a

sections.heading: II. Names
sections.text: That Sunday was the hottest of the year so far, and it seemed like all of Detroit had come out to the island to get out of the heat. Colored and white, war workers, sailors from the armory, families with baskets, kids in the canals up to their knees. The ball fields were full. The beach was full. The grass under every tree was covered with blankets, and along the shore below the willows there was a fisherman every twenty feet. Noble had his line out and a dozen perch on the stringer by two o’clock. He had taken his shirt off and folded it on the rocks. His knuckles were still scarred white from the ring and from Hastings Street, and the sun was on his shoulders, and he was as easy as he ever got. Then he saw them coming down the path along the shore. It was an old woman in a black straw hat and a gray dress buttoned to the throat, walking slow with a cane, and behind her in a line two by two came eleven colored children in their Sunday clothes, holding hands, not one of them running, not one of them hollering. Noble had never in his life seen eleven children that quiet on a hot day. Every so often the old woman stopped and pointed with her cane at something, a heron in the shallows

sections.heading: III. The Bridge
sections.text: The trouble had been going on all afternoon in little pieces, on the far side of the island and by the casino and the ball fields, colored boys and white boys, a shove, a fistfight, somebody’s girl, somebody’s blanket, things people said. Noble had heard it the way you hear thunder off over Canada. Toward evening it was not little pieces anymore. A hundred thousand people were trying to get off the island at the same time, and there was only the one bridge, the long bridge they had just renamed for General MacArthur, half a mile of it, and by the time Noble got to the foot of it with his shirt back on, it was packed rail to rail with people and cars, and there were fights breaking out on it in the middle of the crowd, and sailors in white were wading in from the island end. He found Miss Pruitt and her children at the foot of the bridge, against the stone railing. She was standing in front of them with her cane, very straight, and the children were holding hands in a knot behind her, and James Earl Sims was crying without making any sound at all. He did not ask her. He picked up James Earl Sims and set him on his shoulders, and picked up the Coleman girl, who was the next smallest,

sections.heading: IV. Hastings Street
sections.text: The story came down Hastings Street a little before midnight, from the bars and the clubs, from mouth to mouth up the stoops and through the open windows of the flats where nobody could sleep for the heat: that white men had thrown a colored woman and her baby off the Belle Isle bridge into the river. It was not true. Nobody knew that yet. Across town, in the white neighborhoods, a different story was going around just as fast, about a white woman on the same bridge, and that was not true either. But on Hastings Street that night there was not a man who did not believe it, because there was not a man who could not believe it. Every one of them had come up from somewhere it could have happened. By one o’clock there were men in the street with bricks and bottles and pieces of pipe. Windows were going on the white-owned stores along Hastings. Somebody had set a fire. Three men came up the stairs to the second floor and knocked on Noble’s door. He knew them all. One was from his line at the Rouge. Come on, Big Boy, they said. They threw a baby in the river. Come on. We need you. You know what you can do. He did know. That was the thing. He stood in the doorway in his undershirt with th

sections.heading: V. Monday
sections.text: Before dawn on Monday white mobs were on Woodward Avenue, a few blocks west, pulling colored men off the streetcars on their way to the early shift and beating them in the street, and turning over colored people’s cars. By the middle of the morning they had come east, into the Valley, and the police came in after them in squad cars and on foot, with riot guns, and it was the colored people the police were shooting. Noble had not gone to work. Nobody on Hastings Street had gone to work. A little after noon, from the stoop, he saw a boy he knew come running out of an alley across the street with something in his arms, a carton of cigarettes, or nothing, Noble never found out. It was the Pettaway boy’s older brother, Leon, fifteen. A patrolman at the corner fired twice. Leon went down on the sidewalk with his leg turned under him and lay there calling for his mother. Noble went across the street. The patrolman swung the riot gun around at him, a big colored man coming at a run, and for a moment it was all going to end right there on Hastings Street with Noble Tate face down on the sidewalk, the way it ended that week for seventeen colored men in Detroit. Noble stopped in the middle of

sections.heading: VI. Walden
sections.text: Her name was Augusta Pruitt. She had taught school for forty-one years in Macon, Georgia, and had come north in 1940 to live with her niece over a barbershop on Hastings Street, and she did not go to church, which the church women on Hastings Street could not forgive her. She spent her Sundays instead taking whatever children she could collect on the streetcar to Belle Isle, to look at things. She called it nature study. She did not charge. Leon Pettaway’s little brother Willie was one of hers, and that was how she found out where Noble lived. Willie told her the whole thing on the streetcar going out to the island the next Sunday, the policeman and the riot gun and the big man in the middle of Hastings Street with his hands out, and she listened all the way across the bridge without saying anything, and then she pointed out a kingfisher. She came to see Noble one evening in July, when the bruise on his cheek had gone yellow. She climbed the two flights with her cane and sat at the kitchen table and drank a glass of Lurline’s iced tea, and talked with Lurline about Macon, and did not say much to Noble at all. When she was getting up to go he asked her the one thing. Miss Pruitt. Th

title: The Stringer
logline: On a hot Sunday on Belle Isle, a foundryman fishing for perch waits for an old schoolteacher to ask his name.

verses.text: Not only by discipline and vows, not only by much learning, not by entering into a trance, not by sleeping alone, do I earn the happiness of release which no worldling can know. Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a company of monks at Jetavana tell themselves that because they keep the precepts and the ascetic practices, are deeply learned, live in remote places and have mastered the meditative absorptions, they could become arahants any day they wished; some who have already reached the stage of non-return think the same. They come and sit before the Buddha, who asks whether they have finished their work. When they tell him what they have attained, he warns that no monk should think there is little suffering left until the taints are actually destroyed, and speaks these verses; at the end of the teaching all of them become arahants.
bg.history:
Longs Peak, the highest summit in what is now Rocky Mountain National Park, was first climbed on August 23, 1868, by a party with John Wesley Powell and the Denver editor William Byers. Isabella Bird described her own ascent, in the autumn of 1873, in A Lady’s Life in the Rocky Mountains. The usual way up passes through the Boulder Field and a gap in the ridge called the Keyhole, then crosses exposed ledges and climbs steep slabs to a broad, flat summit, and its afternoon thunderstorms are still the mountain’s best-known danger. In September 1884 Carrie Welton of Waterbury, Connecticut, reached the summit late in the day with her guide; a storm caught them on the descent, and she died of exposure a short distance below the Keyhole. Edward Whymper wrote the closing words of Scrambles Amongst the Alps with the first ascent of the Matterhorn in mind: in July 1865 his party of seven reached the top, and on the way down a slip pulled four of them to their deaths.

The Turners were German gymnastic societies, many founded in America by refugees of the failed revolutions of 1848–49, and the clubs served as gymnasiums and as social, political and cultural centers for German immigrants; many Turners fought for the Union, some of them in Turner regiments such as the 17th Missouri, the “Western Turner Rifles.” Denver’s Turnverein was founded in 1865. The six climbers and their Turnlehrer are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Pledge
sections.text: There were six of them that year in the mountain section of the Denver Turnverein, and by the first of July there was nothing left that they had not done to get ready. They had taken the pledge in May, standing in a row under the gaslights of the Turnhalle with their hands up: six weeks before the mountain, no lager and no tobacco. For a Turner this was not a small thing. Gustav Brenner’s father made beer for a living, and Gustav went home every evening through the smell of the malt house and drank water at supper while his brothers watched him. They had walked to Golden and back on Sundays with forty pounds of sand in their packs. They had climbed the rope to the rafters hand over hand until their palms split, and done it again the next night on the splits. Dr. Fritz Haller had bought an aneroid barometer in a leather case from an instrument maker on Larimer Street and read everything there was to read about the peak: the Hayden survey, the English lady’s letters, every paragraph the Rocky Mountain News had printed since the first party went up in 1868. Karl Ostertag had spent the whole of the past winter alone as watchman at a shut-down mine above timberline on the Divide, five m

sections.heading: II. Timberline
sections.text: They went up from Longmont by wagon and from the ranch at the foot of the trail on foot, with a mule to carry the blankets and the coffee and a wooden crate that Ruf had packed himself in Denver and would not let anybody else lift. They made camp in the last of the trees, where the spruce stood twisted and knee-high and flagged all on one side by the wind, and above them the mountain went up out of the dwarf willow into the Boulder Field and on up past it, a great square grey head with the snow lying in its seams, so close and so big in the evening light that Willi Lenz said it looked like it was leaning over to see what they had brought. Ruf opened the crate by the fire. In the straw were six brown bottles of Denver lager, sweating from the walk. He carried them one at a time to a snowbank in the lee of a boulder fifty yards from camp, where a drift had lasted the summer in the shade, and pushed them into it neck-down in a row, and covered them over, and came back and sat down. After supper the six of them came over to his side of the fire and sat down on the ground in front of him. Somebody had decided they should. They sat the way they sat on the floor of the Turnhalle when he t

sections.heading: III. The Notch
sections.text: They went at three in the morning by lantern, up through the dwarf willow and the frost, and came into the Boulder Field as the sky went grey, a mile of broken granite heaped as if a city had fallen down there, every block of it rimed white. At sunrise they were at the notch, a hole in the ridge like a keyhole with the whole western world blowing through it, and on the other side the ledges went out across the face of the mountain with nothing under them for a thousand feet. Theo went first. Nobody talked. They went across the ledges and up the long gully of loose rock beyond them, where every stone they touched went clattering away below them for a long time while they listened, and then out onto the steep slabs of the last pitch, on their hands and their feet together, and then there was no more up. The top of Longs Peak is as flat as a parade ground and nearly as large, a field of granite blocks in the sky. It was nine o’clock. They shouted. They shook hands. Willi built a little pile of stones and put his name on a card in a tobacco tin under it. Dr. Haller took the aneroid out of its case and read it three times and wrote the figures in his book and said that the Hayden survey

sections.heading: IV. The Snowbank
sections.text: Ruf had kept the fire going since noon. He had been watching the mountain since three in the morning with Haller’s spare field glass, and when the storm covered it he had gone on watching the cloud. They came down out of the Boulder Field in the last of the light, soaked to the skin, one behind the other, Theo first and Gustav last, and walked into the circle of the fire, and Ruf stood up and counted them with his finger the way he counted boys back in from a run along the Platte. Six. He did not say anything. One by one they sat down on the ground by the fire with their knees up, not because anyone told them to, and held their hands out to it, and none of them said the word top, or done, or any word at all. When the last of them was sitting down Ruf picked up the lantern and walked out to the boulder in the dark. They heard him kicking at the drift. He came back with the bottles in the crook of his arm like kindling, six of them, frosted white from neck to heel, and stood them in a row on the flat rock by the fire, and the snow slid off them in the heat and ran down the brown glass, and the firelight came through.

title: Six Bottles
logline: Six Denver Turners who have trained all summer tell their old gymnastics master that Longs Peak is as good as climbed.

verses.text: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see.
This is the way, there is no other that leads to the purifying of intelligence. Go on this way! Everything else is the deceit of Mara (the tempter).
If you go on this way, you will make an end of pain! The way was preached by me, when I had understood the removal of the thorns (in the flesh).
You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha comes back to Sāvatthī from a journey through the country and finds five hundred monks in the assembly hall talking about the roads they have walked: the road to this village is smooth, to that one rough, this one is covered with pebbles, that one has none. He asks what they are discussing, tells them that such roads are no concern of a monk, who should give himself to the Noble Path, and speaks these verses on the Noble Eightfold Path, which opens the Path chapter of the Dhammapada. At the end of the teaching all five hundred become arahants.
bg.history:
The “safety” bicycle, with two wheels of equal size and pneumatic tires, set off a bicycle boom in the 1890s that put millions of Americans, women among them, on wheels; the League of American Wheelmen, which reached 103,000 members in 1898, led the Good Roads movement, and its state divisions published road books for cyclists. Before the safety, racing was done on high-wheelers, and a few women raced professionally in multi-day indoor contests; the Canadian Louise Armaindo held a record of 843 miles in one such race in 1886. Evanston, on the lake just north of Chicago, was founded by Methodists, dry by law from 1858, and grew as a railroad commuter suburb around Northwestern University and the Garrett Biblical Institute, and the lakeshore Sheridan Road, named in 1889, was being laid out through the North Shore in those years.

Evanston was also the home of Frances E. Willard, president of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union, who at fifty-three learned to ride a bicycle she named Gladys and described it in A Wheel Within a Wheel: How I Learned to Ride the Bicycle (Fleming H. Revell, 1895). She took lessons from a young Evanston schoolteacher and in a riding gallery in Chicago, and learned the rest in England with trainers who held the machine until she could tell them, “Let go, but stand by.” Madame Lacasse, Mrs. Crane and the Davis Street Wheel Club are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Five Hundred
sections.text: That was the summer everybody in Evanston got on a wheel. The professors at the University rode, and the students, and the young ministers from the Biblical Institute rode in their black coats with their trousers clipped at the ankle. The Methodist ladies rode, in divided skirts their mothers would not have let in the house. Men who went in to the city on the Northwestern every morning came home at six and changed and were out again by seven, ringing their bells along Chicago Avenue under the elms, and the whole long town by the lake smelled of rubber cement and machine oil and cut grass, and every porch had a bicycle leaning on it, and every stable that had lost its horse had a bicycle in the stall. Most of them had learned from Madame. She had taken the old roller rink on Sherman Avenue in the spring of 1893 and painted Riding Academy over the door, and she kept a ledger of her pupils, name and date and the number of lessons it had taken, in a column as straight as a fence. By the end of June 1895 the ledger had five hundred names in it. Her own name was Odile Lacasse. She came from a parish on the river below Montreal, and in the eighties, when the wheels were high and only acro

sections.heading: II. The Fountain
sections.text: She came home on the first Monday in September, riding in from the north at sundown, brown as a farmhand, with the dust of four counties on her shoes, and she got off at the fountain because there was a crowd at it and she knew every face in the crowd. They were talking about the road to Lake Forest. Tuthill had the book open on his knee. Mrs. Bascom, who was the club’s secretary and the head of the Temperance Union in the Second Ward, had come back from it that afternoon and said it was a disgrace, that the stretch through Highland Park was nothing but pebbles the size of hens’ eggs, and that a lady could not enjoy herself for one minute on it, and Tuthill had written pebbles, H. P. in the margin and underlined it, and Dr. Pruyn was saying that he had been over it in July and it was not as bad as all that. Madame stood holding her wheel and listened to them for a while. Nobody had seen her yet. Then somebody did, and they all got up and shook her hand, and somebody gave her the place on the rim of the fountain, and she sat down. What were you all talking about, she said, when I came? They told her. The road to Lake Forest. The pebbles in Highland Park. The sand at Gross Point, the

sections.heading: III. The Nail
sections.dateline: North of Evanston · the next Saturday
sections.text: Twenty-six of them went. They rode out in a line in the cool of the morning, Madame at the head where Tuthill usually rode, and Tuthill behind her, with the road book in his coat. North of town the macadam gave out and the road turned to sand, deep and yellow and loose, the kind of road the book said you walked, and at the edge of it the line slowed and bunched up and people began putting a foot down. Madame did not stop. She called back over her shoulder, not loudly, Look up. Look at the steeple. Not at the road. The steeple, and they looked up at the spire of the church at Gross Point a mile off across the fields, and pushed. The wheels squirmed and wandered and somehow went on, with the sand hissing under the tires. Mrs. Bascom said afterward that it was like riding through sugar, and that she had not once thought about the sand until she was on the far side of it. On the far side Tuthill’s back tire went down with a sigh. They all got off and stood around it. Madame laid the wheel on its side in the grass and ran her thumb around the tire until she found it, and pulled it out and held it up for them to see: a horseshoe nail, bent, black, an inch and a half long. Every farm road

sections.heading: IV. Let Go
sections.text: Mrs. Abigail Crane was sixty-six years old, the widow of a professor at the Biblical Institute, and she was the only member of the Davis Street Wheel Club who could not ride. She had joined in June because her daughters were in it. All summer one of the men from the club had come by her house in the evenings to run beside her on the sidewalk with a hand on the back of her saddle, and she would pedal very straight to the corner, talking the whole time, and at the corner she would say, You have me, Mr. Tuthill? and Mr. Tuthill would say, I have you, Mrs. Crane, and the moment he let go she would feel it, and stop, and put her foot down. On the last evening of September Madame came instead. She held the saddle and ran, with her hitch, and Mrs. Crane pedaled and talked. She talked about her late husband, who had been against bicycles on principle. She talked about her daughters, and about Miss Willard, whom she had known when Miss Willard was a girl, and about the book, which she had read twice, and about the line in it that everybody in Evanston was saying that fall. “Let go, but stand by”—this is the golden rule for parent and pastor, teacher and friend; the only rule that at once re

title: The Road Book
logline: An Evanston wheel club talks of nothing but roads all summer, until the former racer who taught them to ride comes home.

verses.text: ‘All created things perish,’ he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred monks take a meditation subject from the Buddha into the forest and strive with all their might, but cannot reach arahantship, so they come back to ask for a subject better suited to them. The Buddha considers, and sees that in the time of the previous Buddha, Kassapa, these same monks had spent twenty thousand years meditating on impermanence. So he gives them a single verse on impermanence, and at the end of it they are all established in arahantship. Read the full commentary story, or about impermanence in Buddhist teaching. The verse Bhante chants, Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, is said in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta to have been spoken at the Buddha’s death and is still chanted at Theravada funerals. Both English renderings in the story come from T. W. Rhys Davids’s introduction to Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East 11, 1881), where he describes a funeral in Ceylon: the white cloth held between the monks and the coffin, and water poured into a cup until it overflows.
bg.history:
The Kentucky State Penitentiary, the “Castle on the Cumberland,” was built of limestone blocks by Italian stonemasons and opened in 1890; it is the state’s oldest prison and its maximum-security institution. When Lake Barkley was impounded behind Barkley Dam in 1966, the towns of Eddyville and Kuttawa were moved to new sites, and what was left by the water became Old Eddyville and Old Kuttawa. Each fall the Corps of Engineers draws the lake down to winter pool, and old roads, foundations and pavement come up out of the water.

The Cumberland River begins where its Poor, Clover and Martins forks meet at Baxter in Harlan County, flows west through Nashville, and returns to Kentucky through Lake Barkley on its way to the Ohio. In November and December 2000, while the story takes place, the presidential election hung on the Florida recount.

sections.heading: I. The Castle
sections.dateline: Kentucky State Penitentiary, Old Eddyville · November 2000
sections.text: The penitentiary stands on the bank of the Cumberland where it widens into Lake Barkley, a fortress of yellow-gray limestone with towers at the corners and battlements along the top, put up in the 1880s by Italian stonemasons out of rock quarried down the river. The men call it the Castle. When the Corps of Engineers dammed the river in the 1960s and raised the water, they moved the whole town of Eddyville up the road onto higher ground, the courthouse and the churches and the stores and every house that would go on a truck, and what would not go on a truck went under the lake. The prison stayed where it was. It was the one thing in Old Eddyville that nobody thought of moving. On the second Saturday of every month, a Sri Lankan monk named Bhante Piyaratana drove up from Nashville to meet with the Buddhists. There were four of them that year. They met in a side room off the chapel, with a steel table pushed against the wall and plastic chairs in a circle, and a correctional officer named Darla Mize sitting by the door, as one always had to, with her radio turned down low. Bhante was sixty-eight. He had come from a village outside Kandy in 1989 to look after a small temple in a brick

sections.heading: II. The Count
sections.dateline: The side room off the chapel
sections.text: Bhante did not answer him. He closed his eyes and sat with his hands folded in his lap, for so long that Anthony looked at Curtis and Curtis shrugged, and Officer Mize looked up from her radio. The furnace came on somewhere in the walls. It was about four minutes. Then Bhante opened his eyes and asked them a question that did not seem to have anything to do with it. How long have you been here? None of them had to think. That is a thing about men who are doing life. Lonnie said, Ten thousand one hundred and twenty-nine days. Raymond said, Fifty-eight hundred and forty. Curtis said, Thirty-five hundred and ten. Anthony said, Seven hundred and twelve. Bhante looked at Officer Mize. She had been at the Castle nineteen years and had never once said anything in the Buddhist meeting, and she did not intend to, and she heard herself say, I don’t count mine that way. I count what’s left. Two thousand and forty, till I can draw my pension. The men laughed. She did not mind. Bhante took a request slip out of his book bag and the stub of a pencil and added up the four numbers, slowly, carrying with his lips moving, and turned the slip around on the table so they could see it. It said 20,191.

sections.heading: III. Eleven O’Clock
sections.text: The televisions in the dayroom had been on Florida for four days, men in suits holding ballots up to the light, a recount, and then another count of the recount. Lonnie went past without looking. At a quarter to eleven he put the X on the eleventh of November with the pencil and sat down on the bunk with his back to the wall and his hands on his knees. He did not try to watch the breath at the tip of his nose. He watched it go. It came in, and he let it come in, and when it went out he put an X on it. It was gone. The next one came. X. A man two cells down was shouting at somebody about a radio. X. It was gone, and another shout came, and that was gone. The pipes knocked. Gone. The officer’s keys came down the tier for the count and passed his door and went on, and the sound of them got smaller and stopped. His knee hurt. X. It hurt again, a new hurt, and that one went too. He had been counting days for twenty-seven years without once noticing what he was looking at, and now he was looking at it, and it was everything. Nothing stayed. Not one thing in the cellhouse stayed, not the light on the ceiling, not the voices, not the smell of the floor wax, not Lonnie. Then the bar in Evar

sections.heading: IV. Winter Pool
sections.dateline: The side room, and the road home · December
sections.text: In December Lonnie asked Bhante if there was a thing the monks did for the dead, besides the verse. He said the man’s name. He had not said it out loud since his trial. Bhante took the two Styrofoam cups out of his book bag and set one on the steel table and filled the other at the water fountain in the hall, with Officer Mize’s permission. He held the full cup over the empty one and said that at home, at the grave, they pour water from one vessel into another until it fills and runs over, for the dead, so that what is given here reaches them there. He began to pour, slowly, and chanted while he poured, and the water rose in the lower cup and reached the brim and ran over onto the table and down the steel leg to the floor tiles, and he went on pouring until the upper cup was empty. Then he said the English, which was in the same old book, just after the other. As water poured on mountain topsMust soon descend, and reach the plain;So surely what is given hereWill reach and bless the spirits there! — Buddhist Suttas, Introduction Lonnie looked at the water on the floor for a while. That river out there, he said, starts on Clover Fork. Three forks come together at Baxter, below Harlan

title: Twenty Thousand Days
logline: Four lifers in the Castle on the Cumberland tell their monthly Sri Lankan monk that a year of meditation hasn't worked.

verses.text: `All created things are grief and pain,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is very short, and it is the middle one of three alike. Five hundred monks receive a meditation subject from the Buddha, strive in the forest with all their strength, and do not reach awakening, so they come back to ask for a subject better suited to them. The Buddha sees that in the time of an earlier Buddha, Kassapa, these same monks spent twenty thousand years contemplating suffering, so he gives them a single verse on that characteristic: everything conditioned, because it is oppressed, is suffering. At the end of it all five hundred are awakened, and everyone else who has gathered there benefits too. The ancient-buddhist-texts page for this story currently repeats the text of its twin, 20.2, word for word except for the verse; read the full commentary story, or about dukkha, the characteristic of suffering.
bg.history:
The Homestead Steel Works on the Monongahela, site of the 1892 lockout and battle with Pinkerton agents, employed some 15,000 people at its peak during the Second World War and closed in 1986. A shopping center, the Waterfront, opened on part of the site in 1999. Twelve brick smokestacks from the soaking pits of the 45-inch mill were left standing there, about 130 feet tall, at the edge of a movie-theater parking lot. Up the hill in Munhall, the Carnegie Library of Homestead, opened in 1898, still has its music hall and an athletic club with an indoor pool.

Mindfulness-based stress reduction began in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center as an eight-week class for patients sent by their doctors for chronic pain and stress: guided body scans, sitting and walking meditation, gentle yoga, a first-night exercise with a single raisin, and calendars of pleasant and unpleasant events. In the 2000s it became the subject of many randomized trials, often with a wait-list control group that received the course afterward. The study in this story is invented, but its shape follows real ones, among them a University of Pittsburgh pilot trial begun in 2004 that taught an eight-week program in weekly 90-minute sessions to 37 adults aged 65 and older with chronic low back pain, recruited partly through newspaper ads (trial record; University Times report).

sections.heading: I. The Ad
sections.text: Dottie found it in the Sunday paper between the obituaries and a coupon for Lenten fish sticks, and she read it to him across the kitchen table the way she read him the obituaries, slowly, in case he knew somebody. Do you have pain in your low back nearly every day? Are you sixty-five or older? Researchers at the university are looking for volunteers for a study of an eight-week program. There was a number. There was a little drawing of a man holding the small of his back, and Joe Pavlik said the man in the drawing looked like he had never lifted anything heavier than a briefcase in his life. It's free, Dottie said. They give you a gift card. Joe had run a soaking-pit crane at the Homestead Works for twenty-three years. The ingots came over from the open hearth still dark on the outside and molten in the middle, and they stood in the pits under the lids until the heat had gone all the way through them evenly, and then Joe's crane came over and the tongs went down into the glare and lifted them out, white, one at a time, and laid them on the buggy for the forty-five-inch mill. His back went in 1979 when a tong slipped and the whole cab bucked under him like a truck hitting a curb. H

sections.heading: II. The Raisin
sections.dateline: Upstairs at the Carnegie library · the first Tuesday in March
sections.text: The class met in a room upstairs at the Carnegie library on the hill, which Mr. Carnegie had built for the workingmen of Homestead six years after his company brought the Pinkertons up the river against them. The room smelled faintly of chlorine from the pool. There were eighteen of them on folding chairs in a circle, and a stack of blue foam mats against the wall that most of them looked at with suspicion. The teacher was a short woman with gray hair cut like a boy's and a man's steel watch, and Joe knew her before she said her name. Rose Kuhar. She had hired into the mill in the fall of 1977, one of the women the company had started taking on, and they had put her on the labor gang in the forty-five-inch mill shoveling scale out from under the rolls. The men had given her the business for a year and a half. Joe had not been one of the worst of them. He had not been one of the ones who stopped it, either. She went around the circle and had them each say their name and where it hurt. A retired schoolteacher from West Homestead named Helen Sabol. Gary Rusnak, who had a piece of a Chinese mortar round still in his hip from 1968 and had driven a beer truck for thirty years on top of i

sections.heading: III. The Calendars
sections.text: So Joe did it. He lay on the den carpet every morning after the coffee, with a bed pillow under his knees, and Rose's voice came out of Dottie's kitchen boom box and took him on a tour of himself. The toes of the left foot. The sole of the foot. The heel where it touched the floor. She went so slowly up the left leg that by the time she got to his knee he had planned out the whole week's errands, and some mornings he fell asleep somewhere around the pelvis and woke to her saying, kindly, that the scan was coming to an end now. Dottie stepped over him on her way to the sewing machine. When Rose got to the low back, he would breathe into it the way she said to, and wait for it to let go. It did not let go. Nobody had said it would. Rose had said, the first night, that they were not trying to get anywhere. But a man does not lie on his floor forty-five minutes a day for nothing, and Joe, who had never once in twenty-three years left a pit lid open or set an ingot down crooked, did it every morning, six out of seven, and checked the box on the sheet. The second week Rose gave them a calendar, a sheet with seven rows for one pleasant thing each day. What was the event. Were you aware of

sections.dateline: Upstairs at the Carnegie library · the last Tuesday in April
sections.text: The eighth class was the last one. The girl from the university, whose name was Megan and who was writing a dissertation, was coming at eight o'clock with the forms. Before she came Gary Rusnak cleared his throat and said what all of them had been saying in the parking lot. Rose, with respect. I been lying on that floor eight weeks. I did every one. My hip's the same as when I walked in here. Helen's the same. We're all the same. He looked around the circle and they nodded. We gave it a fair shake. Maybe this thing works for those people up in Massachusetts. Is there something else? Something more for people like us? Rose did not answer him right away. She looked around the circle at them one at a time, the way she had looked at Joe the first night, and later every one of them said the same thing, that she seemed to be looking at something a long way behind them. The engineer said it was like being looked at by somebody reading an old drawing. Then she asked each of them what they had done for work. They told her. Thirty-four years at the Westinghouse in East Pittsburgh. Twenty-nine years of nights on a ward at Braddock General, lifting people. A coal patch in Fayette County, then

Joe drove him, because Earl's eyes were bad after dark, and sat in the car with the window down and listened to the swimmers. The study came out the next year. On the whole the class had done somewhat better than the waiting list, the paper said, at managing their days, though the pain itself did not change much on either side. Dottie read it to him from the paper across the kitchen table, slowly, in case he knew somebody. Up the hill the library was dark, and down past the stacks the Monongahela went by with a single string of barges on it, pushed by a towboat with one lit window. His back was a six.
