title: Twelve Stacks
logline: Eighteen retired Mon Valley workers lie on a library floor for eight weeks in a back-pain study, and their pain does not budge.

verses.text: `All forms are unreal,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.

bg.commentary: This is the third of three nearly identical commentary stories. Five hundred monks receive a meditation subject from the Buddha, strive hard in the forest without reaching awakening, and come back to ask for a subject better suited to them. Seeing that in the time of the earlier Buddha Kassapa they had spent twenty thousand years contemplating non-self, he tells them that the aggregates are not under our control and are without self, and speaks this verse; at its end all of them are awakened, and those gathered there benefit as well.
bg.history:
On Good Friday, April 20, 1962, Walter Pahnke, a Harvard graduate student working under Timothy Leary and the Harvard Psilocybin Project, ran what became known as the Marsh Chapel Experiment, or the Good Friday Experiment. Twenty Protestant divinity students from the Boston area, divided into small groups with leaders, took capsules in a double-blind design: half received psilocybin, half a large dose of niacin, chosen because its flushing and tingling would make some of them think they had the drug. They then sat in a chapel in the basement of Boston University's Marsh Chapel while the Good Friday service led upstairs by its dean, Howard Thurman, was carried down to them by loudspeaker. Almost all of the psilocybin group reported profound religious experiences. One subject grew acutely anxious, left the chapel and went out along Commonwealth Avenue, and had to be brought back and sedated, a detail Pahnke's published account left out.

A follow-up a quarter century later by Rick Doblin found that most of the psilocybin subjects still counted the day among the high points of their spiritual lives, while most of the control group could remember few details of the service; Doblin also criticized the study's methods (MAPS archive of the study and follow-up). The mourner's bench, or altar, at the front of a camp-meeting tabernacle was central to the Holiness movement, which taught a second work of grace, entire sanctification, after conversion. All characters in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Bench
sections.dateline: Pratt County, Kansas · the summers of 1947 to 1956
sections.text: The Holiness camp meeting came every August to a grove of cottonwoods south of town, where there was a board tabernacle with a sawdust floor and open sides and, across the front of it below the pulpit, a long plank bench worn so smooth by knees and elbows that it shone like a gunstock. That was the mourner's bench. Vernon Albaugh's grandmother said twenty thousand souls had prayed through at that bench since the first camp in 1898, and she had been one of them, in 1911, in a white shirtwaist, and she had felt the old man die in her like a fire going out of a stove. That was what you went forward for. The first time was to be saved, and Vern was saved at seven, easily, on a hot night with the moths batting around the gas lamps, and cried, and was glad. The second time was for the second blessing, entire sanctification, the death of self. You knelt at the bench and gave up the old man, the carnal nature, the I that wanted its own way, and you prayed until it died and the Holy Ghost came in and took its place. Grandma Albaugh said you would know. Her favorite hymn was Not I, but Christ, and she sang it at the stove and at the clothesline and once, in Vern's hearing, in the outhouse. V

sections.heading: II. Four and Two
sections.text: There were twenty of them, divinity students from around the city, who had signed up for a doctoral study a Harvard man was running on religious experience. They were divided into groups of four, and each four had two leaders. There would be a capsule. Half of the twenty would get a drug that came from a Mexican mushroom and half would get something else, and nobody, not the students and not the leaders, would know who had what. Then they would all go down to the small chapel in the basement of Marsh Chapel, on Commonwealth Avenue, and attend the Good Friday service being held upstairs by the dean of the chapel, which would come down to them over a loudspeaker. Vern's four were himself and Hal Dunning, his roommate, a Congregationalist from Bangor who had signed up because Vern had, and two others he knew a little. One of their two leaders was a Harvard graduate student with a crew cut who was very kind and said almost nothing all day. The other was Mas Kitano. Mas Kitano was thirty-four and a Methodist minister working on a degree at the School of Theology, and he was older than any of them in a way that had little to do with his age. He had been fourteen in the camp at Heart Moun

sections.heading: III. The Pew
sections.dateline: The basement chapel · the first hour
sections.text: Hal went first. Twenty minutes in, his face began to redden from the collar up as if he were standing too near a stove, and he rubbed his neck and his forearms and looked at Vern with his eyes very wide and whispered, It's starting. His ears went crimson. He said everything was hot. Vern felt nothing at all and was ashamed of how much he envied him. The service had begun upstairs. Through the grille of the loudspeaker came the organ, enormous and thinned at the same time, like music heard through a floor, and then a deep slow voice reading, and they could not always make out the words. Vern sat in the second pew with his hands on the back of the pew in front of him and did as he had been told. He prayed. He followed the service. He prayed harder. He was a good student. He had been a good student at the mourner's bench too. Some time later he noticed that the grain of the oak under his hands was moving. It ran along the pew back in long brown lines, and the lines were flowing very slowly, like water in a ditch, and when he took his eyes off them they went on flowing in the corner of his sight. He thought, quite calmly, So it's this one, and then the calm went out of him all at once.

sections.heading: IV. No Longer I
sections.dateline: The basement chapel · the second hour
sections.text: Mas Kitano came and knelt on the floor in front of him, in the space between the pews, so that his face was a little below Vern's. He did not take Vern's hands off the pew. He looked at him for a long time, longer than he had looked at the second meeting, and Vern had the feeling, which he kept for the rest of his life and could never put better than this, that Mas was looking past him down a very long row of people kneeling at a very long bench, all the way back, and every one of them was him. You've been at this a long time, Mas said. Since I was nine. Longer than that. Mas was quiet a moment. Vern. None of it is yours to hold. Not the old man. Not the new one. Not the being afraid. You can't keep it and you can't kill it. It was never yours. Then he said the verse. He said it plainly, the way you'd read a road sign to someone who had lost his glasses, from a little brown American Standard he had carried since the camp and did not need to open. I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me: and that life which I now live in the flesh I live in faith, the faith which is in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me. — Gal

sections.heading: V. Commonwealth Avenue
sections.text: They came up out of the basement late in the afternoon into the ordinary light of Commonwealth Avenue, the four of them and their two leaders, and stood on the steps of the chapel while the traffic went by. The student who had walked out was back inside, sitting with a doctor. A girl in a raincoat went past with a bag of groceries and looked at them as if they were a little drunk, which they were, in a way, and Hal laughed and said good afternoon to her, and she said it back. Mas Kitano shook each of their hands and said he would see them on Monday for the questionnaires. Vern asked him which he had gotten, the drug or the other. Mas said he did not know. He said he had stopped wanting to know, at about the same time Vern had. Vern stood on the steps and looked at his hands. Across each palm were two deep red lines where the edge of the pew back had pressed into them all through the first hour, sharp as if they had been ruled there. He watched them. They were already going, the way the flush had gone out of Hal's face, filling in pink from the edges, softening, and he did not do anything about it. He stood on the steps with his hands open in front of him in the April light and let

title: The Mourner's Bench
logline: A Kansas Holiness boy who never could pray the self to death takes a capsule in a chapel basement on Good Friday.

verses.text: He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise, who, though young and strong, is full of sloth, whose will and thought are weak, that lazy and idle man will never find the way to knowledge.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred young men of Sāvatthī are ordained, take a meditation subject from the Buddha and go into the forest. One gives up at once; the rest become arahants. On their way back a lay follower feeds them and invites them to a meal the next morning. The Buddha welcomes the returning monks warmly and says nothing to the one who quit, who resolves to become an arahant that very night so that the Buddha will speak to him. He walks up and down all night, falls asleep on his feet, trips over a stone seat at the end of the walkway and breaks his thigh, and the others spend the rest of the night tending him and miss the meal. The Buddha says the same monk once did this to them before, and tells the birth story of the Varuṇa tree (Jātaka 71): a lazy pupil sleeps through the wood-gathering, hurts his eye climbing a living tree he took for dead, and throws green wood on top of the others’ bundles, so that the next morning the maid cannot light the fire for their early gruel and they miss a feast in the village.
bg.history:
The camp meeting came out of the Great Revival on the southern frontier. James McGready’s meeting at Gasper River in Logan County, Kentucky, in July 1800 is usually counted the first, and the Methodist John McGee held the first known Tennessee camp meeting that August at Drake’s Creek in Sumner County, as the Tennessee Encyclopedia recounts. The next August, at Cane Ridge in Bourbon County, Kentucky, somewhere between ten and thirty thousand people gathered. Families came by wagon and camped for several days, usually four, in late summer; at Cane Ridge Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist preachers all took part, and observers wrote of people falling, shouting and jerking under the preaching. Methodists would go on holding camp meetings for decades after others gave them up.

The hymn Brother Oakes says is the morning hymn of Thomas Ken (1637–1711), the English bishop who wrote it for the scholars of Winchester College; its last verse is the doxology still sung everywhere as “Praise God, from whom all blessings flow.” The text here follows The Otterbein Hymnal (1890). An infare was the feast given at the groom’s family’s house after a wedding, an old custom of the upland South.

sections.heading: I. Across the Creek
sections.text: Brother Josiah Oakes had come over the mountains from Botetourt County, Virginia, with an anvil in the bed of his wagon, and he had shod horses on Bledsoe’s Creek for twenty years and preached on Sundays for nothing. He was sixty-eight that summer. He had a voice that had been ruined by smoke and did not carry, so at the meetings he let the younger men do the hollering from the stand, and he kept a tin horn instead, a long one, made by his own hands, which he blew to call the camp to preaching and to wake it at daylight. People said you could hear it at Gallatin. People said that about a good many things. The meeting at Station Camp Creek that year ran four days, the second week of August, in a beech flat cleared out of the cane, with a stand of poles and boards at one end and split-log seats in rows on the ground before it. Families came forty miles in wagons and pitched by the creek. At night they built fires on platforms of logs packed with earth, so the trees overhead stood lit from beneath like the pillars of a house, and the preaching and the singing and the crying went on until two or three in the morning. On the first evening Brother Oakes gathered the young men who had com

sections.heading: II. Coming Through
sections.dateline: Station Camp Creek · the third evening
sections.text: On the third evening, at about sundown, the singing started on the far side of the creek. It came out of the woods a long way off and got nearer, and the people at the stand stopped what they were doing and turned, and the forty came out of the trees and down to the water. They had not eaten in three days. Their shirts were torn by the cane and they had leaves in their hair, and they were singing a hymn that most of them could not have told you the words of the week before, and they came over the stepping stones singing it, and up through the camp to the stand. Brother Oakes came down off the stand to meet them. He did not say anything at first. He went to each one, all down the line, and took him by both arms and looked into his face, and said his name, and the name of his verse, and then he held each one against his chest a moment, the way you would hold a son come back from the Indian country, and let him go and went on to the next. It took a long time. Nobody at the stand minded. Women were crying. A man from the Presbyterian side began to pray out loud and then stopped, because there was no call for it. Absalom stood at the edge of the crowd by the seats. Brother Oakes came do

sections.heading: III. The Night
sections.text: Absalom lay in the wagon bed and could not sleep. Out there among the fires the forty were lying down where they could, wrapped in blankets, some of them still singing low. The old man had looked at every one of them and had not looked at him. He had held every one of them, and not him. Then I’ll come through tonight, he thought. Tonight. And in the morning I’ll go up to him, and he’ll have to say my name. He got out of the wagon. He did not go back over the creek, because it was dark and the creek was a long way and it seemed to him that it was not the woods that mattered. He walked the meeting ground instead. He walked up between the rows of seats to the stand and back down to the fires and up again, saying his verse over, and then saying everything he could think of, and asking, and then demanding, and then asking again. The exhorters gave out at two o’clock. The last of the singing stopped. The fires on the platforms burned down to beds of coals. He kept walking. Toward morning he was so tired that he did not know which part of the ground he was on. He was walking with his eyes shut. He was asleep and walking. At the head of the rows, before the stand, the end of a split-log se

sections.heading: IV. The Infare
sections.text: Brother Oakes came over and looked at the rails and the leg and the face of the boy, and knelt and put his hand on the boy’s forehead, which was wet and cold. Then he looked around at the forty, and at the sun. You boys didn’t get to Hedge’s. No, sir. They told him how it had happened. He was quiet a while. Then he said, Well, that’s twice. They waited, and he sat down on the end of the seat that had broken the boy’s leg, as if it were any seat, and told them. Eight winters back, when I kept the school on Bledsoe’s Creek, I had a good many of you in it. You remember. In January I sent you all up the hollow for wood, and you went and cut and corded it like men, every one, but this one. This one found a big poplar that looked dead to him, and he thought, that’ll be dry, I’ll lie down and take my rest, and when they’re done I’ll climb up and break off what I need in a minute. And he spread his coat in the leaves and lay down and went to sleep and snored so you could hear him over the axes. You found him on your way home, he said to the forty, and you kicked him awake, I heard about it, and you went on and left him. And he jumped up and went up that poplar half asleep, and it wasn’t de

sections.heading: V. Daylight
sections.dateline: Station Camp Creek · the morning after
sections.text: They kept Absalom on the ground one more night, in the wagon bed on a tick of cane leaves, because he could not be moved yet over the roads. The meeting broke up around him. The families struck their camps and went off home in their wagons, and the forty went off with them, every one stopping at the wagon to say something to him, and the fires on the platforms went out and were not built up again. In the night he did not sleep much, because of the leg. He lay and looked up through the beeches and said his verse over, the one the old man had given him on the first evening, which he had hardly looked at in four days. He did not say anything else. He just stayed with it. Before light he heard the old man come out of his tent, the only tent left standing on the ground, and cough, and walk down toward the stand in the dark. Absalom raised himself on his elbows in the wagon bed. Over the creek there was no color yet. Then there was a little, a gray, behind the trunks of the beeches on the far side, and then a little yellow, and he was watching it come. When the horn blew, for nobody but the two of them and the horses, he was already awake.

title: The Tin Horn
logline: At a Tennessee camp meeting, forty young men come out of the woods converted, and the one who went back to his wagon the first night means to catch up before morning.

verses.text: Watching his speech, well restrained in mind, let a man never commit any wrong with his body! Let a man but keep these three roads of action clear, and he will achieve the way which is taught by the wise.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, coming down from Vulture’s Peak with the elder Lakkhaṇa, smiles, and explains only before the Buddha: he has seen a peta with a man’s body and a pig’s head, with a tail growing out of its mouth and maggots oozing from the tail. The Buddha confirms it, having seen the same being long before and kept silent for the sake of those who would not believe. In the time of an earlier Buddha, he says, two elders, one a year senior to the other, lived together in a village monastery like brothers, the younger carrying the elder’s bowl and robe. A gifted visiting preacher, whom they took round all their alms villages, wanted the monastery for himself; over three evenings he hinted at something too grave to say, then told each elder that the other had warned him against him. The elders were shattered like struck pots, quarreled over the bowl and robe, and left by the east and west doors, telling the preacher to stay. The villagers who were wise said the preacher must have driven them off. For a hundred years neither elder could recite or meditate; then both came to the same monastery in the far west and were given the same room, wept, asked each other whether either had ever done wrong in thought, word or deed, saw the slander, and were reconciled. They went back and drove the preacher out with a snap of the fingers, and he, who had meditated twenty thousand years, could not bear one rebuke, fled and died.
bg.history:
Under the Lighthouse Board (1852–1910) keepers were federal employees of the Treasury, appointed with a good deal of political influence until they were brought under civil service in 1896. Lamps burned kerosene from 1877; from 1884 keepers wore a navy-blue uniform with a K on the collar for the keeper and numbers for his assistants. From 1876 the Board sent isolated stations traveling libraries of about fifty books in a wooden case, exchanged every few months by the tenders. Keepers at stations in the path of the spring and fall bird migrations picked up the birds that struck the lantern at night, and some kept records of them for naturalists.

Tillamook Rock Light, lit in 1881 on a basalt rock off Tillamook Head, Oregon, was known as Terrible Tilly; keepers and supplies went on and off by derrick and breeches buoy, and four keepers lived in the dwelling built onto the tower. Maine people had gone to the Northwest since the 1850s, when the lumbermen of East Machias founded the mill town of Port Gamble on Puget Sound and recruited workers from home. Franklin’s list of thirteen virtues is quoted from his Autobiography (ed. Frank Woodworth Pine, 1916). Gull Ledge, Ragged Harbor, and everyone in the story are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Stair
sections.dateline: Gull Ledge Light, outer Penobscot Bay, Maine · September 1904
sections.text: At sunrise the keeper on watch put out the lamp, and the keeper coming on went up and helped him hang the linen curtains around the lens so the sun would not get into the glass and set the lantern afire, and then the two of them came down together. That was the rule at Gull Ledge, and it had been the rule longer than anybody now on the ledge had been there. Ora Dyer came down first that morning, and Charlie Hupper behind him. Ora was first assistant, forty-four, an island man from Ragged Harbor who had fished until his back went. Charlie was nineteen and second assistant, which meant he did what the other two told him and shoveled coal for the fog whistle. There was a window halfway down the iron stair that looked out over the west end of the ledge where the weed was, at low water. Ora stopped at it. He looked out a long minute, and Charlie, on the step above, saw the side of his face change. He smiled. It was not a thing Ora did much. Charlie leaned to see past him and saw the ledge and the weed and the tide going out. What is it? Not now, said Ora. Ask me at supper, in front of Mr. Ames.

sections.heading: II. Supper
sections.text: Josiah Ames had been head keeper at Gull Ledge since the fall before. He was a Ragged Harbor man too, sixty years old, a widower. He talked about as much as a gull post. What he did, besides keep the light, was birds. He had a book in which he wrote down every bird he saw on the ledge, the day and the hour and the wind, and every bird that came against the lantern at night and was picked up dead on the gallery in the morning, and once a year he sent a copy of it to a man at Washington who wrote him back a letter of thanks. The Lighthouse Board's library box came out on the tender every few months with fifty books in it, and when it came Ames took out whatever had to do with birds first and the Bible last, and generally read both. When the plates were cleared, Charlie asked. There was a man on the west end of the ledge, Ora said, standing on the weed at low water. He had on a keeper's coat, the dress coat, with the buttons. He had a man's body and a man's hands. And he had the head of a hog. And out of the hog's mouth there came a tail, like a hog's tail only long, down to his knees, and maggots coming out the end of it and dropping off into the weed. That's what he was. I never saw

sections.heading: III. Two Keepers
sections.text: Ansel Pote and Warren Crockett came onto Gull Ledge together in the spring of 1866, both of them out of the army. Ansel was keeper and Warren was his assistant, and they kept that light for twenty years. Ansel was one year older. In twenty years nobody on the islands heard either one say a hard word to the other. They lit the lamp together and put it out together. They wound the fog bell machinery in turns through every thick night, two hours on and two off, and wrote up the log in the same hand, near enough, so that the inspector once asked which of them had kept it. They had their Sundays. When the weather let them, one kept the light and the other rowed in to Ragged Harbor for meeting, and the next Sunday the other went. Both of them were bachelors. People said they were like a pair of oxen that had been yoked so long neither one knew which side he was on. In 1884 the Board put the keepers into uniform: a double-breasted coat of navy blue with gilt buttons and a K on the collar for keeper, and a cap with a little lighthouse on the front. Ansel wore his on Sundays and when the inspector came. Warren carried it. From the first week that was how it was. When Ansel went in to meetin

sections.heading: IV. The Third Keeper
sections.text: In the spring of 1886 the Board put a steam fog whistle on Gull Ledge in place of the bell, and a steam whistle wants a man to tend the boiler, so a second assistant was appointed. His name was Lyman Sprowl. He came out on the tender in May with a sea chest and a hymnbook. He was thirty-five and he could preach. He had been a Methodist exhorter in Waldo County, not ordained, and the first Sunday on the ledge, with all three of them there because of the weather, Ansel asked him to read them a chapter and say something on it. He read them the prodigal son and talked about it for half an hour, and when he was done the two old men sat a while without getting up. They told each other afterward that they had got a minister out of the Board, and it was more than they had expected out of the Board. That summer they took him in to the islands. Ragged Harbor had a meetinghouse and no minister, and Heron Island had no meetinghouse at all, and the Greens had nothing but a schoolhouse. Wherever the two keepers went they were known, and wherever they took Lyman the people asked him to speak, and after he spoke they asked him back. In July and August the three of them made the round of all the ha

sections.heading: V. The Islands
sections.text: The next Saturday Lyman came in to Ragged Harbor alone, and people asked him where the keepers were. Don't ask me, Lyman said. They had a falling out and both of them went off the ledge. I did everything I could to keep them. I couldn't. Some people said nothing. Others said, We have known those two twenty years and never saw so much as a cross look between them. If they were scared off that ledge, it was this one that scared them. They said it in their kitchens and not to his face, and the fall after, the Board made Lyman Sprowl keeper of Gull Ledge Light. Ansel went east, Down East, to a light at the mouth of the Machias. Warren went west, all the way, and kept lights in Oregon. Neither one of them married. Neither one of them was any good afterward, the way they told it later. They could not keep a clean log. They lost their place in a chapter. Ansel would sit up in the watch room thinking, how could he say that of me, the day he saw that man come on the ledge. Three thousand miles away Warren sat up thinking, how could Ansel say that of me. Seventeen years went by like that.

sections.heading: VI. Tillamook
sections.text: Ansel's sister's girl had married a man in the mills at Port Gamble on Puget Sound, where the East Machias people went, and when she was widowed she wrote for him. He got into the district out there. In March of 1903 he was ordered to Tillamook Rock. Tillamook Rock is a lump of black basalt a mile off Tillamook Head, with the light and the keepers' dwelling built all in one on top of it, and the sea goes over it in winter. There is no harbor and no beach. A man goes on and off it in a breeches buoy, swung up from the tender on the derrick line with his legs hanging, and his chest comes after him. Ansel was sixty-two. He came up out of the sea in the canvas breeches with his eyes shut, and the head keeper unbuckled him and took him in and showed him where he would sleep. There was one room for the assistants. There was a man sitting on the other bunk with his boots off. Ansel sat down on the empty bunk and could not stop crying. Warren had known him the moment he came through the door. He sat with his hands on his knees and his eyes full and thought, shall I say anything or shall I not. Then he thought, that is no way to think. He got up in his stocking feet and went and stood in fr

sections.heading: VII. The Slip
sections.text: They came across the continent on the cars, and from Rockland out on the mail boat, and from Ragged Harbor a man rowed them to the ledge. Lyman saw the boat coming from the gallery. He was fifty-two. He had kept Gull Ledge seventeen years and he had kept it well, and he still preached around the islands, and the islands still went to hear him, some of them. He came down to the west slip to meet the boat. He knew them both before they were close. He waded out to his knees and took hold of the bow, and when they stood up he reached to take Ansel's bag and Warren's, the way a younger keeper does. Ansel snapped his fingers in his face. Then Warren did. Don't you touch it, said Ansel. You are not fit to keep this light. That was all either of them said. It was not much. Lyman Sprowl had preached in every meetinghouse on the bay for seventeen years and been talked about by the whole coast and never once minded it, and he could not stand that one sentence. He let go of the boat. He walked up the slip and across the ledge and down the east landing, and he took the station dory and rowed out of the lee of the ledge into a southeast chop with the afternoon coming on, toward nowhere at all th

sections.heading: VIII. The Library Box
sections.text: The fog whistle had started while Ames was telling it. It went every forty seconds, and the dishes in the rack answered it. One sentence, said Charlie. He did all that and they said one sentence to him. He did all that with sentences, said Ames. He got up and went to the library box under the window, which had come out on the tender in July, and took out a book he had been reading in the afternoons. It was Franklin's life, written by himself. He had marked a page with a primary feather from a yellow-shafted woodpecker. In it Franklin set down the virtues he meant to practice, one to a page, and kept a little book in which he made a black spot against each one every day he failed it. Ames read three of them out under the lamp. 2. Silence. Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation. 7. Sincerity. Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly; and, if you speak, speak accordingly. 8. Justice. Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your duty. — Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography The mouth, and what's back of it, and the hands, Ames said. Keep them clean and you can stand to be looked at. He put the feather back in at the p

title: The Dress Coat
logline: Two keepers who have shared a Maine ledge light for twenty years take a gifted new assistant around the island harbors to preach.

verses.text: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Poṭhila knows all three baskets of the teaching by heart and recites them to five hundred monks, but has never practiced. The Buddha begins to greet him every day as “Empty Poṭhila”: come, Empty Poṭhila; sit, Empty Poṭhila; Empty Poṭhila has gone. Stung, Poṭhila leaves at dawn in the company of the least of his students, who do not notice who he is, and travels a hundred and twenty leagues to a forest hermitage of thirty monks who have all reached the goal. He asks the eldest to be his refuge, and is sent to the next, and the next, down to a seven-year-old novice sitting at his sewing. The boy agrees to teach him if he will obey, and tells him to walk into a pond in his costly robes; he does. Then the boy tells him how to catch a lizard that has gone into an anthill with six holes: stop five, and watch the one it went in by. So with the six doors of the senses. As Poṭhila sits, the Buddha, far away, sends a radiant image of himself to speak the verse.
bg.hist_title: Chicago and the hills past Mount Hamilton, 1893–1903
bg.history:
The World’s Parliament of Religions met in Chicago from September 11 to 27, 1893, alongside the Columbian Exposition, in the building that is now the Art Institute. Its best-remembered speaker was the young Bengali monk Vivekananda, who stayed on in America to lecture. His lectures in New York in the winter of 1895–96 became Raja Yoga, published in July 1896: an account of the eight limbs of practice with a free translation of the Yoga Sutras of Patañjali. Its chapter on pratyahara, the “gathering towards” or withdrawal of the senses, tells the beginner to sit and let the mind run on, and watch it. The Swami, Edwin Pottle and the Chicago circle are fictional.

In 1900 Vivekananda’s brother disciple Turiyananda took a dozen or so American students to a gift of 160 acres in the San Antonio Valley, some eighteen miles southeast of Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton. They lived in tents, hauled their own water and meditated. The place, the Shanti Ashrama, is still a retreat. Mrs. Lusk’s ranch is loosely modeled on it. The hills there are full of California ground squirrels, whose colonies dig burrow systems with many entrances, which other animals use as refuges, and of western fence lizards, which every California child knows as blue-bellies.

sections.heading: I. Empty Mr. Pottle
sections.text: Edwin Pottle had the whole Bhagavad Gita by heart in Sanskrit, seven hundred verses, and if you named a chapter and a number he would give you the verse, and then give it to you again in Telang’s English and again in Arnold’s, and tell you where each of them had gone wrong. He was forty-six years old and unmarried, an instructor in Sanskrit at the University on the Midway, and the author of The Yoga Aphorisms of Patañjali, Rendered into English, with a Running Commentary, which had been printed in Boston in 1899 and was going into a second edition. On Sunday afternoons he lectured in a hall on Michigan Avenue, and five hundred people paid a quarter to hear him. On weeknights he had eighteen parlor classes, from Prairie Avenue to Evanston, where women in shirtwaists and a few patient husbands sat in a ring of dining chairs while he took them through the eight limbs of the practice in order: restraint, observance, posture, breath, withdrawal, holding, meditation, absorption. He explained the breath very well. He drew the nostrils on a slate. He had never done it. The Swami had come to Chicago for the Parliament of Religions in 1893, as the companion of an older monk who afterward wen

sections.heading: II. The Day Coach
sections.dateline: Westbound out of the Wells Street depot · March
sections.text: He took the morning train west in the day coach, because a man going to learn something ought not to go by Pullman. The car was cold and smelled of oranges and wet wool. A man across the aisle in a brown derby nodded to him at Clinton, Iowa, and offered him a newspaper at Cedar Rapids, and somewhere on the flat white country past Council Bluffs Pottle understood that it was Mr. Hapgood. Mr. Hapgood had been in the Thursday class at a house in Kenwood for three winters. He sold gloves at Field’s. He was the slowest student Pottle had. He had never once got the eight limbs in the right order, and when he tried to say pratyāhāra it came out as something like a sneeze, and the ladies of the Thursday class were kind to him in the way that is not kind. He did not know Pottle at all. He had only ever seen him standing up, behind a little lectern, with a pointer. They rode together for three days. Mr. Hapgood was going to his married sister in Oakland, for his chest. He talked about gloves, the weights of kid and the weights of chamois, and about the Platte River, which he had expected to be bigger. On the second night, somewhere in Wyoming, with the lamps turned down, he said that he went

sections.heading: III. Down the Line
sections.text: Mrs. Harriet Lusk had been the Swami’s first student in Chicago. When her husband died, and the money from the Board of Trade came to her, she bought a hundred and sixty acres in the hills past the observatory, and in the spring of 1900 eleven of the Swami’s people came out with her to live on it. They lived in tents and in one board cabin. They had dug their own well and cut their own wood, and twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, they sat. The Swami came out for one summer to start them and then went back to his rooms over the harness shop, and they kept on without him. They did not write many letters. Pottle had thought of them, when he thought of them at all, as the ones who had left the lectures. He walked in from the stage road with his valise. Mrs. Lusk was sitting in the shade of a live oak shelling peas into a dishpan. She was sixty-eight. She looked up and knew him at once. Mrs. Lusk, he said. I’ve come to be taught. Mr. Pottle. She put down the pod in her hand. We read your Patañjali aloud by the lamp, all last winter. It is we who ought to be taught by you. Please don’t, he said. Please. Teach me. She looked at him a while longer. She looked at his collar and his good shoe

sections.heading: IV. The Tank
sections.text: The stock pond lay below the corral in a fold of the hill, brown water with a skin of gold on it from the low sun, the mud of the bank stamped all over with the hooves of a neighbor’s cattle. Pottle had on a grey worsted suit made for him by a tailor on State Street, a waistcoat, a celluloid collar, and his father’s gold watch on a chain across the front. He did not take anything off. He did not stop at the edge to think about it, which was the first thing in his life, he said afterward, that he had not stopped to think about. He walked down through the mud and into the water and kept walking until it was over his belt, and over his watch, and up to his chest, and so cold that it took his breath out of him in one piece. Up on the slope everyone had stopped what they were doing. Captain Ames stood with the maul. Mr. Brandt had flour to his elbows. Mrs. Lusk had come out from under the oak with the dishpan still on her hip. Come out now, Tessie called. He came out. The water ran out of his cuffs and his trouser legs and his pockets, and his good shoes were two lumps of mud. He climbed the slope and stood in front of the cabin step, dripping on the boards, and waited. Tessie looked hi

sections.heading: V. Six Holes
sections.text: The knoll was round and bare on top, with wild oats on its shoulders and a single blue oak, and the ground squirrels had worked it over for longer than anyone had lived there. Pottle found six holes close together where the earth was loose and pale. He carried a stone to each of five and set it over the mouth. He sat down by the sixth with his legs crossed in the way he had drawn on so many slates, and his knees told him at once what they thought of it. The first thing that happened was the Gita. It started up in his head by itself, the first chapter, the two armies drawn up on the field, and ran on verse after verse without being asked. Then it was the Sunday lecture he had not given, on the five sheaths, beautifully organized. Then it was the second edition, a misprint on page forty, a letter he ought to write to the printer. Then it was Mr. Hapgood. Then it was his father, and the watch, which had stopped at seven minutes past six. Then it was a sentence about the mind as a drunken monkey, which he had always delivered well, and which he now watched going by like a man watching a parade he had once been in. He did not chase any of it. He sat by the one hole and let it run, the w

title: The Blue-Belly
place: Chicago and the hills past Mount Hamilton, California
logline: A Chicago Sanskrit scholar whom his swami greets as "empty Mr. Pottle" goes west to a ranch of meditators to be taught.

verses.text: Cut down the whole forest (of lust), not a tree only! Danger comes out of the forest (of lust). When you have cut down both the forest (of lust) and its undergrowth, then, Bhikshus, you will be rid of the forest and free!
So long as the love of man towards women, even the smallest, is not destroyed, so long is his mind in bondage, as the calf that drinks milk is to its mother.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a company of rich old householders of Sāvatthī, friends who did good works together, hear the Buddha and decide that they are too old to stay in the world. They become monks, but they are too old to learn the teachings by heart, so they build a hut of leaves at the edge of the monastery and live there together, and on their almsround they eat at their own wives’ and sons’ houses, above all at the house of one monk’s former wife, Madhurapācikā, the “sweet cook,” who feeds them all from her store of sauces and curries. When she dies, the old monks fall on one another’s necks and weep. The other monks come running, and the Buddha tells them that the old men did the same in a former life, as crows who tried to bail out the sea to get back a drowned friend. That past-life story is the Kāka Jātaka (Jātaka 146), quoted here in Robert Chalmers’s translation (1895). The closing verses are from the Theragāthā, the verses of the early monks, in C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s Psalms of the Brethren (1913).
bg.history:
After 1975, tens of thousands of refugees from Laos crossed the Mekong into camps in Thailand, many of them men of the old Royal Lao Government and army, and thousands of officials were sent to the new government’s re-education camps, which it called seminars, many of them in Houaphan province. Many who resettled in the United States came to south Louisiana through Catholic diocese sponsorship, and found work peeling shrimp and crawfish, shucking oysters, picking peppers for the Tabasco factory, and in the oil boom. Ban Mai is fictional, but it is modeled on Lane Xang Village between Lafayette and New Iberia, where, as historian Davorn Sisavath describes, Lao families bought land in 1986, laid out streets named for Lao cities, and built a temple in 1987. The oil price collapse of 1986, part of the 1980s oil glut, gave Louisiana the highest unemployment rate in the nation that year.

Elderly Lao men often ordain as monks late in life, and in Lao and Thai temples the monks walk an almsround at dawn while laypeople kneel to place sticky rice in their bowls. In the fall harvest, south Louisiana cane growers burn the cut fields to clear the leafy trash, and the ash drifts over the towns. Vetiver, the Pali usīra, has long been grown in Louisiana, and New Orleans families folded its dried roots in with their stored linens.

sections.heading: I. The Committee
sections.text: There were five of them, and in the Lao families between Lafayette and New Iberia they were called the Committee, though they had never been elected to anything. They were old men. They had been somebodies on the other side of the Mekong. Khamsing had bought and sold rice in Savannakhet and owned two trucks. Bounlieng had been a district officer under the King and had spent four years after 1975 in a seminar camp in Houaphan, which was what the new government called the places where it sent men like him, and had come out with no teeth on one side. Phoumy had been a captain. Thongdy had taught school. Sengdao had owned a pharmacy in Pakse and still could not walk past one in Lafayette without going in to read the labels. They had swum the river or been rowed across it at night, and waited in the camp at Nong Khai for one year or three, and been sent by the Catholic diocese to a place none of them had heard of, where the land was as flat as the land around Vientiane and the water was the color of tea and the summers were the same, and the first thing every one of them said, getting off the bus in New Iberia in the wet heat, was that it was like home. Then they went to work. They peel

sections.heading: II. The Robes
sections.dateline: The temple at the end of Pakse Street · July 1987
sections.text: The new hall was finished in the summer of 1987, cinder block with a steep tin roof that the men of the village had cut and bent by hand to sweep up at the corners the way the roofs did at home, and it was painted gold at the eaves. On the first day of the rains retreat the whole village came, the women in their silk skirts with the sticky rice in baskets, the men in their good shirts with a silk sash across them, and Achan Khamphan gave the sermon. He talked about old age. He did not talk long. He said that a man is born and works and marries and has children and builds a house and builds a temple, and all of it is good, and then he is old, and the house and the children and the temple go on without him, as they should. He said there are two kinds of old men. One kind holds on harder every year to what is leaving him. The other kind puts it down while he can still choose to. He said that was all. The five of them talked about it on Mae Wan’s porch that night. Khamsing said it first. We are old men. What are we doing? We bought the land. The temple is up. Our sons have jobs. What are we waiting for, to die in a recliner in front of the Thai videos? Mae Wan, who was bringing out the

sections.heading: III. The Porch
sections.text: Every morning at six the monks walked out of the temple gate barefoot in a line, oldest in ordination first, with their bowls in front of them under their robes, down Pakse Street and up Vientiane and back along Luang Prabang, and the women knelt at the edge of their yards on mats with the rice baskets and put a ball of sticky rice in each bowl as it passed, and something wrapped in a banana leaf or a twist of plastic, and bowed, and the monks did not thank them, because it was the giver who was being done a favor. The five old men walked at the end of the line, because they were the youngest monks, and the oldest. And the thing everybody noticed, though nobody said it out loud for a long time, was that they walked slower and slower as they came down Pakse Street, and slower still in front of their own houses. Phoumy’s daughter-in-law put fried fish in his bowl that she put in nobody else’s. Thongdy’s wife cried every morning when he passed and he looked at the ground. And at Mae Wan’s gate the line simply came apart, and the old men stopped. Monks eat once a day, in the morning, and must finish before noon, and they may eat where they are invited. Mae Wan invited them. So the youn

sections.heading: IV. The Hut
sections.text: She had the sweet sickness. The Lao called it that, and the doctors in New Iberia called it diabetes, and she had had it for years and paid it no attention, because she felt fine and because she made a great deal of jeow bong. In September of 1988 her feet began to swell. She went to the hospital in New Iberia and came home and went back again. Her kidneys were going. In the second week of October, during the cane harvest, she lay down for a rest in the afternoon in the room at the back of the house and did not get up. The village did what you do. The monks went to the funeral home in Lafayette and sat in a row along the wall of the chapel while the people of the village came through, and a white cotton thread ran from her coffin to the monks’ hands, and the young monks chanted the verses for the dead, and the five old men moved their lips. Khamsing did not touch her. He could not. He sat with the thread in his fingers and looked at the coffin and did not look away from it. They came home after dark. They walked back to the temple from the van and went into their hut, and the door shut, and for a few minutes it was quiet. Then the whole village heard it. It came out of the hut at t

sections.heading: V. The Crows
sections.text: The young monks went back to the hall. They sat in the lamplight under the gold Buddha and talked about it in low voices, all of them at once: how it looked, how it would look, what the families would say, what the temple in Texas would say if it heard. A monk weeping for his wife like a husband. The other four weeping for their dinners. Achan Khamphan came in from his room and sat down. What are you all talking about? They told him. He listened to all of it. Then he was quiet a while, and the young monks waited, and outside the hut had gone quieter too, and you could hear the old men through the wall of cane, not howling now, only talking to each other in their hoarse voices, and once Bounlieng blowing his nose. This is not the first time they have done this, Achan Khamphan said. They did the same thing before. Long ago, when they were crows. And he told them the story the way the old monks used to tell it in the forest temples, in the evenings, with the lamps lit. Once there was a crow and his wife, he said, and a whole company of crows who were their friends, and they lived by the sea. One day some people came down to the shore to make an offering to the serpents who live under

sections.heading: VI. The Cane
sections.dateline: The edge of the cane · October
sections.text: The next morning they were burning the cane. The farmer who owned the land behind the temple had cut the field the week before with the big harvesters, and the stalks lay in long rows on the ground the way the machines left them, and before daylight his men went down the rows with drip torches and set the leaves on fire, as they did every fall all over the parish, to burn off the trash. By the time the monks came back from the almsround the whole field was a low wall of flame moving slowly away from the temple with the wind, and the smoke stood up off it brown and white, and the ash came down all over Ban Mai in black flakes as light as paper, on the cars and the laundry and the gold roof of the hall, and on the shaved heads of the old monks sitting in the door of their hut. They had not gone on the almsround. They had not eaten. Achan Khamphan had sat with them in the hut until very late, and nobody knew what he had said to them, and in the morning he came back and sat down on the ground in front of the door, and the young monks came and stood behind him, and some of the village came too, because they had heard the night before and wanted to see. Across the road, in the Cajun farm

title: Sweet Root
logline: Five old Lao refugees who built a temple in the Louisiana cane become monks, and still eat every morning on one woman's porch.

verses.text: Cut out the love of self, like an autumn lotus, with thy hand! Cherish the road of peace. Nirvana has been shown by Sugata (Buddha).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a handsome young goldsmith’s son goes forth under the Buddha’s chief disciple Sāriputta, who gives him the meditation on the impurity of the body, since passion is strong in the young. The young monk cannot even fix his mind on it. Sāriputta teaches it to him three times, with reasons and similes, and finally brings him to the Buddha, who says that knowing another’s inclinations belongs only to Buddhas. Seeing that the youth has been born into goldsmiths’ families for five hundred lives, the Buddha makes a golden lotus as big as a cartwheel, dripping water, and tells him to set it in a heap of sand at the edge of the monastery and repeat “Red! Red!” The monk’s mind settles through the four absorptions. Then the Buddha makes the flower wither and turn black, and the monk sees impermanence. Watching boys break lotuses from a pool and pile them on the bank, where they wilt at the tips, he sees it more clearly. A radiant image of the Buddha brushes his face and speaks the verse, and he is freed.
bg.history:
By 1920 the U Street corridor was the center of Black Washington, called “Black Broadway,” its theaters, churches, shops and offices lettered in the gold leaf that sign painters laid on the back of the glass, a craft related to the old art of verre églomisé. After Martin Luther King Jr. was killed on April 4, 1968, crowds gathered at Fourteenth and U, and four days of rioting and fire followed; about 6,000 troops were sent into the city, 13 people died and more than 6,100 were arrested (see the 1968 Washington riots). The corridor did not recover for decades. In May 1971 two congressmen came back from Vietnam reporting that some 15 percent of American servicemen there were addicted to heroin; that June the White House created a new federal drug office, and enlisted men were tested before they flew home (NPR’s account of what happened to them afterward).

Kenilworth Aquatic Gardens, on the east bank of the Anacostia in Northeast Washington, began as a Civil War veteran’s water-lily ponds in the 1880s and became a national park site in 1938. Its lotuses, including the yellow American lotus, peak in July. Recovery houses like the fictional Kenilworth House drew on the therapeutic community, a model of shared living, shared responsibility and plain talk that took hold in American psychiatry and prisons in the 1960s. “Lead, Kindly Light” was written by John Henry Newman in 1833 and became one of the best-loved hymns in English (its history). The Pettaways, Kenilworth House, Odessa Bright and Bernard Hollins are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Five Hundred Windows
sections.text: Augustus Pettaway lettered his first window in 1919, for a barber on U Street who paid him four dollars and a free shave every Saturday for a year. He lettered his last one in the spring of 1968. In between, by the count in the black ledger he kept in a cigar box under the counter of his shop on Ninth Street, he did five hundred and eleven windows in gold leaf between Seventh Street and Fourteenth, and some on Georgia Avenue, and a few out in Northeast. Barbershops and beauty parlors. Funeral homes. Pharmacies, insurance companies, a bank, two theaters, a dozen lawyers, a great many churches. When people said Black Broadway, the gold on the glass up and down U Street was a good part of what they meant, and most of it was his. It was done on the inside of the glass, backward. That was the first thing his grandson Calvin learned, at five, standing on an apple crate in a doorway with a book of leaf in his hand. You laid out the letters in reverse on a paper pattern and taped it to the street side, and then you went inside and worked the letters from behind, so that from the sidewalk they read true. sections.heading: II. The Tape
sections.text: The house was a big tired frame house on a street of tired frame houses east of the Anacostia, a few blocks from Kenilworth Avenue. It had a porch with a swing on it and a back yard that ran down to a chain-link fence and a weedy lot, and eleven men lived in it, and a few women in the house next door, and none of them was allowed to leave for ninety days. It was not a hospital and not a jail and not a church. It was a house where people who had been on heroin lived together and told each other the truth until they could stand it. There were several like it in the city that year. This one belonged to Miss Odessa Bright, who owned the house outright and had started it in 1969 with her pension from thirty years of cleaning government offices at night, and who had not had a drink since the spring of 1946. She could have spent those years on her own porch, people said, and been entitled to them. She said she would keep the door open until the last one came through it, and she did not say who the last one was. Calvin came in April, with a paper bag of clothes and a court letter. The man who took him in at the door was Bernard Hollins. Bernard was thirty-eight and ran the house day to day

sections.heading: III. Miss Odessa
sections.dateline: The kitchen · a morning in July
sections.text: She was seventy-four. She was small and dark and straight-backed and wore a man’s grey cardigan in all weathers, and her hair under a hairnet was white as cotton. She sat at the kitchen table in the mornings with a cup of coffee and a newspaper she did not read, and anybody in the house could come and sit across from her, and most of them did, sooner or later. She did not counsel. She did not run groups. She listened. People said she knew what was in a person the way you know what is in a jar by holding it up to the window, and nobody in the house, not even Bernard, knew how she did it. Bernard had said it to Calvin the first week. I can see where a man is fixing to run. Miss Odessa can see what he’s made of. That’s hers. Don’t ask me. Bernard told her the whole thing standing up, with his hands in his pockets: the tape, and three times through it, and the boy sliding off it, and three months nearly gone. Miss Odessa looked at Calvin over her coffee for a long time. Who are your people, baby? He told her. He told her about his grandfather and the ledger and the shop on Ninth Street, the gelatin in the thermos, the squirrel-hair tip drawn across his cheek, the leaf that jumps up to

sections.heading: IV. The Lotus
sections.dateline: The back fence · the same morning
sections.text: Miss Odessa got up from the table and went out the back door onto the porch and was gone about a minute. When she came back in she was carrying a lotus. The cook, a big quiet woman named Mrs. Tolliver who had been at the stove the whole time, said afterward that it was as big across as a hubcap, on a stalk as long as a broom handle, and that it was dripping. Water ran off the leaves and the stalk onto the linoleum as if it had just come up out of a pond, and there was no pond nearer than the aquatic gardens a mile away, and Miss Odessa had not been gone long enough to walk to the end of the yard. That was one thing. The other thing was that it was gold. Not yellow, the way the wild lotuses in the gardens are yellow. Gold. Mrs. Tolliver had seen gold. She had a gold tooth and her mother’s gold locket and she knew gold when she saw it, and she said that flower was gold all the way through, petals and pod and stalk, and threw the light off it onto the kitchen ceiling the way a window does in the late afternoon. Miss Odessa put it in Calvin’s hands. It was heavy. It was cool. It was the color of the leaf in his grandfather’s book when you first fold back the tissue, and his hands, whic

sections.heading: V. The Pond
sections.text: Mrs. Tolliver said that sometime after three o’clock Miss Odessa, who was sitting at the kitchen table with her coffee gone cold, looked out the window over the sink at the boy by the fence for a while and said, not to anybody, That’s far as he goes by himself. That’s enough now. Down by the fence Calvin felt it before he saw it. The light changed. He looked, and the lotus was black. It had not wilted. It had burned. The great gold petals had curled in on themselves and gone black and brittle at the edges, the stalk had sagged in the sand, and the whole flower looked like something that had been through a fire and come out the other side. It looked like the three curls of leaf stuck to the shard in the window of the pharmacy on Fourteenth Street. It looked exactly like that. He sat and looked at it, and he thought: Gold did that. Gold, that doesn’t want anything. That doesn’t need a fix, that doesn’t need a woman or a dollar or a window with its name on it. Gold did that. And I want everything. Then it went through him like the fire went up U Street. All of it, the windows and the ledger and his grandfather in his coffin on Georgia Avenue and the boy from Detroit and the vial and h

sections.heading: VI. Lead Thou Me On
sections.text: Something brushed his face. It was warm, like the light that comes off a window across the street when the sun gets low and finds it. He put up his hand and turned to see where it was coming from. Miss Odessa was standing on the dike a few yards off, in her grey cardigan and her hairnet, with the pond and the lotuses behind her and the light coming off her the way it comes off gold leaf when it has been burnished right. Mrs. Tolliver said afterward that Miss Odessa did not leave the kitchen table that afternoon, not once, from breakfast until she got up to set the table for supper, and Mrs. Tolliver would put her hand on the Bible to it. Bernard said he did not know anything about it and was not going to say. Calvin said she was there. He said he got up on his feet and put his hands together in front of him without knowing he was doing it, the way people do in church, and she smiled at him the way she smiled at people across the kitchen table, and she sang him a verse of a hymn, in an old woman’s cracked voice that was not loud, that he had heard in his grandmother’s church at Nineteenth Street when he was a boy and had not thought about since. I was not ever thus, nor prayed that

title: Gold Leaf
logline: A Vietnam veteran from a family of U Street gold-leaf sign painters can't make his recovery counselor's method work.

verses.text: ‘Here I shall dwell in the rain, here in winter and summer,’ thus the fool meditates, and does not think of his death.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the merchant Mahā Dhana ("Great Wealth") brings five hundred carts of safflower-red cloth to Sāvatthī and is stopped at the river by seven days of flood, while the city keeps holiday and nobody buys. He decides to stay the whole year, through rains, winter and summer, until his cloth is sold. The Buddha, passing on his alms round, smiles, and tells Ānanda that the man has seven days to live. Ānanda goes to the carts and tells him. The merchant feeds the Buddha and the monks for seven days, hears the verse, walks a little way with the Teacher, turns back with a pain in his head, lies down and dies. Read the full commentary story. The two verses Ānanda hears before he goes, on making an effort today because no one knows whether death comes tomorrow, are from the Bhaddekaratta Sutta.
bg.history:
The Rainbow Family of Living Light has met on National Forest land every July 1 to 7 since 1972. It has no leaders and no fees. Inside a Gathering almost no money changes hands: kitchens feed everyone, a "Magic Hat" is passed for supplies bought in town, and luxuries are bartered at a trade circle. Kid Village is the camp for families, CALM is the volunteer medical camp, and the outside world is called Babylon. On the morning of the Fourth the Gathering keeps silence and prays for peace; around noon the silence ends in a long Om, and a parade of children comes in from Kid Village. The 2023 Gathering was the first in the White Mountain National Forest, at the south end of the Kilkenny loop off Bog Dam Road, near Berlin and Gorham. It was a rainy summer, and attendance, at something over 1,700, was smaller than usual. The washed-out culvert, the people and the kitchen cook here are invented; Tea Time is a real Rainbow kitchen. The 2024 Gathering was held in northern California.

Dead & Company's Final Tour played Fenway Park on June 24 and 25, 2023, Boulder on July 1 to 3, the Gorge on July 7 and 8, and closed in San Francisco on July 14 to 16. The parking-lot market that follows the band is called Shakedown Street, after the Grateful Dead song. Madder root, fixed with alum, has dyed cloth red since antiquity. The quatrains are from Edward FitzGerald's first edition of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (1859).

sections.heading: I. The Culvert
sections.dateline: Bog Dam Road, White Mountain National Forest, New Hampshire · June 26, 2023
sections.text: Big Rich had five hundred shirts in the van, counted, in eleven totes. He dyed nothing but red. He did it in a forty-gallon kettle behind his house outside Athens, Ohio, with madder root and alum, and he tied every shirt in the same tight spiral, so that on any Shakedown Street in the country people could say, Those are Big Rich's reds, from forty feet. He had sold on the lot since the spring tour of 1990. He was sixty-one years old, six foot four, and he had never in his life missed a show to go camping. That summer Dead & Company were out on what they called the Final Tour. Rich had worked both nights at Fenway, and the lot had been fat. The plan was to drive west and be set up in Boulder by the first of July, then the Gorge, then the last three nights in San Francisco, where he meant to sell every shirt he had and think about what came after. But a kid buying a shirt at Fenway told him the Rainbow Gathering was in New Hampshire this year, three hours north, the first one ever in the White Mountains. Rich thought he could sell a hundred shirts to hippies in the parking area in two days and still make Colorado. He drove through the night and came up Bog Dam Road at first light on

sections.heading: II. The Bucket
sections.text: On Sunday morning a Forest Service crew came with a backhoe and a length of plastic pipe and filled the trench in an hour. Rich stood at his bumper and looked at the open road. It was twenty-nine hours to Boulder, and the shows there had started the night before. He talked to himself when he was alone. Most people do who drive for a living. Well, I've come a long way, he said. If I turn around now I'm just late for everything. So I'll stay right here. I'll stay through the rain and work cleanup with these people till August, and they'll know me by then. I'll winter where they winter, in Florida, at Ocala. Next summer I'll come in early with my own kitchen, wherever they go, and sell in the towns along the way. A year. I'll move it all in a year. He liked it better the more of it he said. He began taking shirts off the line and wringing them out. Two boys were coming down the spur toward the brook with a bucket. The big one was about nineteen, in a wool hat. The small one was seven and was called Early. He had been born at the Gathering in Vermont in 2016, in a tent at Kid Village, three weeks before anybody was ready. People in the Family held that a child born on the land was a li

sections.heading: III. Seven Days
sections.text: Rich had a camp stove going on his tailgate. He saw a wet kid with an empty cup and did what lot people do. He filled the cup with coffee and made him a peanut butter sandwich and did not ask what he wanted. How long are you staying? Nando said, when he had eaten half. Rich told him the whole plan. He told it well. That's a good plan, Nando said. Listen. It's hard to see it coming, for anybody. You should keep an eye out. For what? My brother says you've got a week. Who's your brother? Nando pointed with the sandwich. Down at the brook a very small boy was holding a bucket in the current with both hands, leaning back against the pull of it. Rich laughed. Then he stopped. He looked at the boy and the bucket for some time. He had been on the road thirty-three years and had heard every kind of talk, and he knew when a thing was not talk. He sat down on the tailgate. A week, he said. Saturday, said Nando. I'm sorry, man. Rich sat there until the coffee was cold. Then he got up and asked where the children ate. He drove out over the new culvert that afternoon, down to the Walmart in Gorham, and spent the Fenway money. It was twenty-three hundred dollars in a bank bag. He bought oats, ri

sections.heading: IV. The Bowl
sections.text: The Gathering ends on the seventh, and on the eighth people walk out. That Saturday the rain held off. Early's mother had a shift in Brattleboro on Monday, and their packs were by the trail. After breakfast Rich took Early's bowl from him and washed it. He did it carefully and dried it on his own shirt and gave it back. Then he sat down on a log, because he found he wanted to hear whatever there was. Early stood in front of him holding the bowl. You said you'd live here when it rains and when it snows and when it's hot. I did say that. Don't say that. You don't get to pick that. You can say, I'm here. I'm here, said Rich. Yeah, said Early. Kid Village kept a milk crate of books under the kitchen tarp, swollen with damp. Early could not read much yet. He went to the crate and took out a small one with no cover, opened it, and gave it to his brother with his thumb on the page. He had done this before. Nando had stopped being surprised at where the thumb was. Nando read it out, standing, the way he would have read the directions on a box. Think, in this batter’d CaravanseraiWhose Doorways are alternate Night and Day,How Sultan after Sultan with his PompAbode his Hour or two, and went

sections.heading: V. The Trail Out
sections.text: He carried Early's pack for him up the trail as far as the first bend, where somebody had nailed a board to a spruce that said WE LOVE YOU. There he gave the pack back. Early put his arms through the straps and went on after his mother and Nando. He did not make anything of it. Rich walked back down. At the kitchen he told Mama Jo he had something going on in his head, a kind of pressure, and that he thought he would lie down a while. He went out to the spur and lay down in the back of the van on the empty totes with the doors open. The medics from CALM found him there before dark. He had his boots off and set side by side on the bumper. The cleanup crew stayed three weeks, as it always does, filling latrines and breaking up fire rings and raking the trails back into the woods. They took his line down last. The next July the Family gathered in California. At Kid Village there were red spirals all over the meadow, on children from thirty states, and the shirts were a year closer to fitting.

title: Madder Red
place: Kilkenny, White Mountain National Forest, New Hampshire
logline: A Dead-lot tie-dye vendor with five hundred red shirts is stranded at a rainy Rainbow Gathering, where nobody uses money.

verses.text: Death comes and carries off that man, praised for his children and flocks, his mind distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.

bg.commentary: The commentary tells the story of Kisā Gotamī twice. The long telling belongs to verse 114. This second, short one returns to the moment she comes back empty-handed. Her child had died, she would not believe it, and she went about looking for a cure until someone sent her to the Buddha, who asked for a pinch of mustard seed from a house where no one had died. “In the entire village the dead are more in number than the living,” she reports. He answers that she was wrong to imagine she alone had lost a child, that death sweeps all beings away like a torrent with their longings unfulfilled, and he speaks verse 287. Read the full commentary story, or about Kisā Gotamī. The series told the long version as The Mustard Seed; the girl called Sicca in that story is the Sister in this one.
bg.history:
Levittown was built by Levitt & Sons between 1952 and 1958 on 5,750 acres of Bucks County spinach and broccoli farms, beside the new Fairless Works of U.S. Steel. The first family moved into a house on Stonybrook Drive on June 23, 1952. When building stopped there were more than 17,000 houses in six models, set on concrete slabs with radiant heat in the floor, along curving streets whose names share the first letter of their neighborhood. Veterans could buy with almost nothing down. Buyers came from Philadelphia row-house neighborhoods, from the declining anthracite towns and from the steel valleys of western Pennsylvania. Early rules forbade fences and Sunday wash lines. Levitt refused to sell to Black families, and when William and Daisy Myers bought a house in Levittown in 1957 they met weeks of mob harassment. The Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia has more.

The results of the Salk polio vaccine trial were announced on April 12, 1955, and the first shots went to young schoolchildren that spring, so the summer of 1955 was among the last in which American parents feared the disease as they had for decades. In August two storms crossed the region five days apart. The second, Hurricane Diane, caused the worst floods then on record in eastern Pennsylvania; Brodhead Creek in the Poconos overran a summer camp and killed 37 people, most of them children. The neighbors’ dead are drawn from real events: the Donora smog of October 1948, which killed twenty people in a steel town near Pittsburgh, and the bombing of Coventry on the night of November 14, 1940. The Marinos, their neighbors, Sparrow Lane and the clinic on Ellsworth Street are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Jar
sections.text: Her grandmother told it every October, when the mustard greens came in at the Ninth Street market, and she told it the same way every time, sitting on the top step with a colander of beans in her lap. There was a girl below Washington Avenue so thin the whole neighborhood called her Sicca, the stick. Some people said she had once picked coal out of a rich man’s yard and it had turned to gold in her hands, but Nonna Gallo did not vouch for that part. She had been there for the other part. In the fall of the influenza Sicca’s little boy died in her lap, and Sicca would not have it. She put him on her hip in his blue blanket and walked the neighborhood asking for medicine, and a nun at the school on Ellsworth Street, where they had made a hospital, told her the medicine was mustard seed. A pinch of it, from a house where nobody had ever died. She came to me, Nonna Gallo said. Your grandfather was four days dead. I had the black crepe on the door and she walked right past it. I went and got the jar. I had the jar in my hand, Rosalia, like this, and then she asked me. Has anybody died in this house. Rosalie was seven. She sat one step down and asked what she asked every year. Did she fi

sections.heading: II. Sparrow Lane
sections.text: The house on Sparrow Lane was nine weeks old when Eddie Marino carried her over the sill of it. It smelled of paint and cut pine. It had three bedrooms on one floor, a kitchen with a General Electric range and a Bendix washer already standing in it, a carport, and a picture window that looked out on a square of raked dirt where Mr. Levitt’s men had sown grass and staked one sapling the thickness of her thumb. There was no cellar. The heat ran in copper pipes through the floor itself, so that in January the boy would lie down flat on the kitchen tiles like a cat. Eddie had been in the Navy, and a veteran could have the house for a hundred dollars down. He worked the open hearth at the new Fairless Works on the river, four to midnight most weeks, and came home with his eyebrows singed and slept until ten. The year before, all of it had been spinach and broccoli. There were seventeen thousand houses going up on those fields, forty a day when the weather held, and there were six kinds, and on Sparrow Lane they were all one kind. The streets curved so that nobody could drive fast. Every street in Stonybrook began with an S. You could not put up a fence, and you could not hang wash on a

sections.heading: III. The Glass
sections.text: That was the spring of Davy Crockett, and Mickey had the cap. Every boy on Sparrow Lane had the cap, a ring of fur with a striped tail down the back, a dollar and change at the five-and-ten, and he wore his to the table and to the bathtub and to bed. It was also the spring of the Salk shots. They lined the first and second graders up in the school gymnasium before the term let out, and the mothers on Sparrow Lane stood in the hall and cried, because it was over; another summer or two and nobody would have to keep a child out of the pool again. Mickey was four. The four-year-olds were to have theirs next. The first storm came through on a Friday in the middle of August and rained itself out by Saturday noon. The lane was full of puddles. She let him out in them in his cap and his bathing trunks, and stood at the picture window with a cup of coffee and watched him stamp. On Sunday he had a headache and would not eat. On Monday morning he could not bring his chin down to his chest, and when she gave him milk it came back out through his nose. The doctor came to the house and looked at him for less than a minute and went to the telephone in the hall. They took him to the contagious hos

sections.heading: IV. The Pocketbook
sections.dateline: Ellsworth Street, South Philadelphia · Saturday morning
sections.text: She took the Plymouth and drove to the city with both hands on the wheel. The radio said the Delaware was out of its banks from Easton down and still rising, and that a creek in the Poconos had come up over a summer camp in the dark, and they did not have the count yet. She turned it off. The clinic was where it had always been, in the ground floor of the old school, with the same green paint to the height of a child’s shoulder. There were mothers on the bench with babies. Sister Antonia was at the scale. She was fifty-nine years old and looked like a clothes prop in a veil, and she weighed a baby and wrote the number on a card and gave the baby back before she looked up. You’re a Gallo, she said. From across from the coal yard. Rosalie. I’m a Marino now. We’re up in Levittown. The Sister took her into the room behind, where there was a low table and some small chairs left from when it was a school. She sat down on one with her knees up and waited. Rosalie stayed on her feet. She told it fast. The puddles, the milk, the glass, the tanks, the doctor with his mask down. She said they were saying her son was dead, and that she had not been let in to see for herself, and that she knew

sections.heading: V. The Doors
sections.text: She did not go into her own house. She left the Plymouth in the carport and took the tin measuring cup from the nail by the kitchen door, since a woman at your door with a cup in her hand needs no explaining, and went next door. Peg Novak came to the screen with a dish towel on her shoulder. Her face changed when she saw who it was. Everybody on the lane knew; the ambulance had seen to that. Peg, have you got any dry mustard? Just a little. A spoonful. Honey. Sure I do. Come in. Sit down, for God’s sake. I have to ask you something first. Has anybody died in your house? Peg laughed, once, out of fright. In this house? It’s the same as yours. They finished it the week before we came. She went and got the mustard, a red and yellow can, and stood in the kitchen doorway turning it over in her hand. She and Stan had come down from Nanticoke when the collieries started closing. My father, she said. A roof fall, in thirty-eight. They brought him home on a door. My sister’s little girl, with the diphtheria. I don’t know what made me think of them. She put two spoonfuls in the cup. That isn’t here, though. That’s all up home. At the Lerners’ there was a little brass case on the doorpost and

sections.heading: VI. The Lamps
sections.text: By seven the light had gone long and yellow. Somebody’s sprinkler was going on a lawn that could not have needed it, after two storms, ticking around and around. She stood in the middle of Sparrow Lane where it bent, with the cup in one hand and four cans of mustard in her arm, and the lamps began to come on. Every house had one. It was the same lamp, or near enough, on the same table, in the middle of the same window, and they came on one after another down the curve of the lane as the women went to them. She had looked at those lamps for three years and seen a new street full of young people. She saw the street now. There was a miner laid on a door in the Novaks’ living room. There were forty-one people from a town near Lublin at the Lerners’ card table. An old man from Donora sat on the Kovaches’ davenport trying to get his breath, and two women from Coventry stood in a kitchen, and a boy who had lived two days was in the house on the bend, and eleven soldiers were in the house where the man had gone back to sleep. They had come up in the moving vans with the lamps and the bedsteads. They had come over on the ships. In every one of those windows the dead outnumbered the living,
