sections.text: They buried him from St. Paul’s on Christian Street, where she had been baptized, and took him out to Holy Cross, where the Gallos had a plot. Half of Sparrow Lane drove down for it in a line of cars with their headlights on. Beyond the Gallo stone there was a long piece of ground with grass on it and no stones at all, and she saw Sister Antonia, who had come out on the trolley, stand at the edge of that ground for a minute by herself before she came over to the grave. Afterward Rosalie left Eddie with her sisters and walked to Ellsworth Street in her black dress. The clinic was closed for the afternoon. The Sister was in the back room washing bottles, and she dried her hands and sat down on one of the small chairs, and this time Rosalie sat too, knees up, across the low table. Did you get the seed? No, Sister. I got mustard. I have nine cans of mustard on my drainboard. She found she could almost laugh, and then could not. The houses are three years old, and in every one of them the dead are more than the living. They brought them along. I never knew it. I lived on that street three years and I never knew who was in those houses. You thought it was only you, said Sister Antonia. E

title: Dry Mustard
logline: A young mother on a three-year-old street goes door to door with a measuring cup, sure nobody has died in houses so new.

verses.text: Sons are no help, nor a father, nor relations; there is no help from kinsfolk for one whom death has seized.
A wise and good man who knows the meaning of this, should quickly clear the way that leads to Nirvana.

bg.commentary: The commentary tells the life of Paṭācārā at length under verse 113: a rich man’s daughter who ran off with a servant and then lost her husband to a snake, one son to a hawk, the other to a river, and her parents and brother under a fallen house, all within a few days. She went mad and wandered naked, driven off with clods, until the Buddha told her to come back to her right mind. This second, short entry returns to what he said next. Seeing that her grief had eased, he told her that neither sons nor kin can be a shelter for anyone at death, and that the wise therefore lose no time in clearing their own path. She and many who were listening were changed by it. Read the full commentary story, or about Paṭācārā. The series told the long version as Spilt Water, set in another storm on another shore.
bg.history:
A good many of the West Africans enslaved on the Georgia and Carolina sea islands were Muslims, often Fula people from Futa Jallon in what is now Guinea. The best documented is Bilali Mohammed, head driver on Thomas Spalding’s plantation on Sapelo Island, who left a thirteen-page Arabic manuscript on belief, ablution and prayer. In the 1930s his great-grandchildren told interviewers for Drums and Shadows that he and his wife prayed on a mat at sunrise, noon and sunset with a long string of beads, and that a grandmother who “come by Bahamas” made flat cakes of pounded rice and honey called saraka on the same day each year and put one in every child’s hands. The descendants of these communities are the Gullah Geechee people.

Tidewater rice was grown in diked fields flooded and drained through wooden gates called trunks, and worked by the task. Infants were minded in a children’s house by an old woman and young nurse girls. Children could be sold away from their mothers, and often were when an estate was settled. On the night of September 14, 1824, a major hurricane came ashore near Darien and St. Simons Island at harvest. The eye passed over Darien around midnight, the sea swept across the islands, and well over a hundred people drowned, many of them enslaved; the surviving reports are collected by plantation. Tarbert, the Island and everyone on them are fictional. The Fula words spoken on the step are left unquoted, and the Qur’an is given in Marmaduke Pickthall’s English of 1930.

sections.heading: I. The Driver’s Daughter
sections.dateline: Tarbert plantation, on the Altamaha, McIntosh County, Georgia · 1817–1823
sections.text: Tenah was five the year the driver’s daughter came across from the Island in a stolen canoe, and it was the first thing in her life she remembered whole. The Island was the cotton place, out past the marsh where the river met the salt. The same family owned it that owned Tarbert, and everybody at Tarbert knew about the driver there. He was a Fula man named Samba who had come by way of the Bahamas, tall, with a red cap. He prayed on a mat three times a day with his face to the east, and ran two hundred hands for old Mr. McAllan with nothing but his voice. He lived in a tabby house with a plank floor and a sleeping loft, the only loft in any quarter on that coast, and he kept his daughters up in it. He meant them for men of his own faith. There were some. There were more on Sapelo, under the old driver there, and Samba had promised his girl Medina to a boatman of that place, a man who could say his prayers. Medina wanted Cato, who was a ditcher at Tarbert and could say no prayers at all. She had seen him twice, when the flats went over with seed rice. She took a canoe in the dark of the moon and came nine miles through the creeks on the flood tide, and she was sitting on the landing

sections.heading: II. The Pencil
sections.text: The children’s house stood at the high end of the street, on the shell bluff. All the children too small to work stayed there in the day under Maum Kadi, and four or five nurse girls helped her, and three times between sunup and dark each girl took her baby on her hip and walked out along the banks to wherever its mother was hoeing, so it could be fed. Maum Kadi was older than anybody. She had been a grown girl when they took her, on a road in a country she called Futa, where her father had kept a school and taught boys to write on boards. She kept a white cloth over her head and a long string of beads in her bosom. She prayed when Samba prayed, sunrise and noon and sunset, on a square of rice sacking behind the house. On one day in the year she soaked rice overnight and beat it to paste with honey and patted it into flat cakes, and she called the children in a row and put a cake in each one’s two hands and said a word over it, and they said Ameen because she had taught them to, and ate. She did not talk much. Women brought her their trouble on the step in the evening anyhow, since she would hear all of it and usually say one thing. The old master died that winter in Savannah. In A

sections.heading: III. The Water
sections.text: The rice was cut. It lay in the fields on its own stubble to dry, a whole year of it, and another two days would have seen it tied and stacked. All that Tuesday afternoon the sky was the color of a pot bottom, and the wind blew steadily out of the northeast with rain in it. The old people did not like the look of the tide, which came up at the ebb when it should have been going down. At dark the driver sent everybody into the rice barn on the bluff, the one building at Tarbert with a second floor, and the overseer went up the river road on his mule and was not seen until Thursday. By the time a person could have walked to the lower trunk and back, it was blowing harder than Tenah had known wind could blow. It made a noise like surf on a bar. The river came up over the banks and over the fields and took the cut rice off the stubble all at once, like a cloth pulled from a table. Then it came up the bluff. It came into the street and through the cabins, and the cabins began to go. There were a hundred and sixty people in the loft of the rice barn in the dark. Tenah lay against her mother with the floor shaking under her. Maum Kadi sat by the ladder hole with five babies in her lap and

sections.heading: IV. The Landing
sections.text: On Thursday a boat came up from the Island for meal. The boatman was an old man called Ishmael who had carried Medina’s two messages across, years before, and carried back nothing. She was at the landing before he had his line fast. Uncle. You come from the Island. I come from where it was. The tabby house by the cotton barn. The driver’s house. He busied himself with the line. Daughter, don’t ask me about that house. Ask me about any other house on the Island, and I’ll tell you. I don’t care about any other house. Tenah was on the bluff with the other nurse girls, and she saw the old man stand up straight in his boat and take off his hat. The sea came over the Island six feet deep, he said. Samba put every soul on the place up in the cotton house before dark and counted them in. Then he went back for your mother. She would not leave the house without something of hers. Your brother Hamadi went after the two of them. The wave took the east wall and the loft came down on all three. We dug them out Wednesday. We put them in the sand together with their faces the way he would have wanted. He pointed down the river, where a brown smoke stood over the marsh. That’s the cattle. Four hund

sections.heading: V. The Step
sections.text: The children’s house had stood. It was on the highest of the shell, and the water had only come to its sill. Half the street was sleeping in it and under it, and in the evening they sat about the step, for there was nowhere else to sit. Maum Kadi had finished her sunset prayer and come around to the front with her beads in her hand. She saw Medina a long way off, coming along the bank against the red sky with a crowd of children behind her. Tenah was in that crowd. She had mud in both hands. The people at the step stood up. Maum, don’t let her in here among the babies. She’s gone in her head. Somebody turn her. Let her come, said Maum Kadi. Move out of her road. They moved. Medina came up the shell path saying it, one the hawk took, one the water took, and stopped at the foot of the step, because the step was in front of her and there was an old woman on it. Maum Kadi spoke to her. It was only a few words, and Tenah did not understand them. Nobody there did, except the one they were said to. They were in the language of Futa, which Samba had spoken in the tabby house and nowhere else, and which Medina had not heard in seven years. The ones who were at the step that evening told abo

sections.heading: VI. The Day of the Cakes
sections.text: Medina went to the field on Monday with the rest and shoveled mud back into the breaks. She did her task. At night she slept in the children’s house. She cried when she had to, quietly, and Maum Kadi let her, and waited. It was better than three weeks. The day for the cakes came round, and there was no honey on the place and little enough rice, but the old woman had put by a gourd of each on the rafters, and they had ridden out the water there. She soaked the rice overnight. In the morning Medina took the pestle from her without being asked and beat it, with the stroke the women of the street had taught her, and the children held out their hands in a row and said their word. That evening the two of them sat on the step. Tenah was inside the door with a baby asleep on her, and other women were about, mending. You are lighter, Maum Kadi said. A little. Then you can hear me. I would not say it to you before. She had her beads in her lap, and she did not look at Medina but out at the fields. Your father could not keep you. He built a loft to keep you in, and he could not. You could not keep your sons. You tied one to your back with a good knot. Cato could not keep himself. This is not

sections.heading: VII. The Gourd
sections.text: Before sunup the next morning Tenah was sent to the well with the piggin and the dipping gourd. She carried them around behind the children’s house. The square of rice sacking was laid out on the shell, and beside it now there was a second. Pour for her, said Maum Kadi. Medina held out her hands. Tenah poured from the gourd. The water ran over the two hands and off the fingers onto the shell and was gone into it. Maum Kadi said to do it again, and she poured again, and a third time. Then the mouth, three times. Then the face. Then the right arm to the elbow and the left. The old woman said the order of it, and Medina did it, slowly, like someone learning to beat rice. The light was coming up gray over the broken fields, and every time the water ran off into the shell Tenah watched where it went. Then the two women stood on their sacking with their faces to the place where the sun would rise, toward the marsh and the Island and the salt water, and Tenah took the empty gourd back to the house, since the babies would be waking. Medina kept the children’s house after Maum Kadi, for twenty-two years. She never left a child alone with its trouble and never told one a thing that was not s

title: The Children's House
logline: After the hurricane of 1824, a nurse girl on a Georgia rice plantation throws mud at a bereaved woman the whole quarter wants gone.

verses.text: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the city of Vesālī suffers three dangers at once: famine, the non-human beings drawn by the unburied dead, and disease. Its people find no fault in their ruler and send two envoys to King Bimbisāra, who tells them to ask the Buddha themselves. The Buddha agrees. Bimbisāra smooths five leagues of road, strews it knee-deep with flowers, holds two white parasols over the Buddha, and wades into the Ganges to his neck to launch his boat; the Licchavi princes on the far bank double every honor. When the Buddha sets foot in their country a great rain washes the corpses into the river. Ānanda walks the city walls through the three watches of the night reciting the Ratana Sutta and flinging water from the Buddha’s bowl; the drops fall like silver on the sick, who rise, and the spirits break through the walls to flee. On the way back the Nāgas of the river cover it with lotuses and offer jeweled boats, the gods raise parasols to the highest heaven, and the Buddha makes a Buddha appear in every boat. Afterward, when the monks marvel, he says the honors came from one small deed: long ago, as the Brahmin Saṅkha, he traveled to find his son, who had gone away to study, become a solitary Buddha and died, and he cleared the grass from the son’s shrine, spread sand, sprinkled water, scattered wildflowers, and raised his robe as a banner and his parasol over the mound.
bg.history:
On the night of October 1–2, 1893, a small, intense hurricane came ashore at Chênière Caminada, a French-speaking fishing village of about 1,500 people west of Grand Isle that sent oysters, shrimp and crabs to New Orleans. The Weather Bureau had not known the storm existed. The surge put the village under six feet of water within minutes; 779 people died there, and only four of its 450 houses were left standing. The storm killed about 2,000 people in all and remains the deadliest in Louisiana’s history. Survivors moved up Bayou Lafourche, “the longest Main Street in the world,” to Golden Meadow, Leeville and Côte Blanche (now Cut Off), and some to Westwego; below Golden Meadow the bayou was the only road (Louisiana Folklife). Filipino sailors who had left Spanish ships had been settling the marshes since the eighteenth century and dried shrimp for export on platform villages like Manila Village in Barataria Bay. The sickness, the lights in the marsh and every person in this story are the story’s own.

A traiteur or traiteuse treats with Catholic prayer and the laying on of hands, takes no payment, must be asked, and passes the secret prayers on to someone of the opposite sex; many say the treatment cannot cross water. The yellow fever epidemic of 1878 killed roughly 5,000 people in New Orleans; steamboats were tied up, and the fever lasted until the cold weather of late October. Longfellow’s Evangeline (1847), the tale of an Acadian girl who searches all her life for her lost Gabriel and finds him dying in a fever hospital, did more than any other book to shape how Acadians and Cajuns were seen and saw themselves. On Toussaint, All Saints’ Day, Louisiana families still clean and whitewash their tombs and bring chrysanthemums.

sections.heading: I. Three Dangers
sections.text: Before the storm there were fifteen hundred people on the Chênière and four hundred and fifty houses, and on a Sunday you could hear the church bell from Grand Isle across the pass. The men tonged oysters and dragged seines for shrimp and sailed the catch up through Barataria to the lugger landing across from New Orleans. The women kept gardens of okra and mirliton behind the houses, and there were orange trees and a little cane, and live oaks along the ridge so old that the ridge had its name from them. People came down from the bayou to marry there and stayed. The storm came in the night of the first of October with no warning anyone had heard. The water rose six feet in a few minutes and then rose two more. All night the church bell rang by itself in the wind, and the people in the water turned toward the sound of it. In the morning four houses were standing. Seven hundred and seventy-nine people were dead. That was the count they gave the newspapers later, and the people who were left said it was short. Sixty-two had lived through the night under what was left of a single roof. Others had held onto doors and pieces of gallery and drifted, and some of them came back. The dead we

sections.heading: II. The Judge’s Road
sections.dateline: Below Thibodaux · the middle of October
sections.text: Judge Arceneaux had been judge of the district so long that nobody remembered he had been anything else. He was eighty. His wife was dying in the front bedroom of the house below Thibodaux, slowly, with the window open toward the bayou, and Tante Zélie had been sitting with her since the cane began to turn color, because he had asked, and because she had promised. He received the two men from the Chênière on his gallery and heard them out. He took the shrimp and the cup and the altar cloth and laid them on the swing. Then he said, You don’t need me to ask her. You know how it’s done. Ask her yourselves. So Ulysse and Ovide went around the side of the house to the back gallery, where she was sitting on a cane-bottomed chair shelling field peas into her apron, and they took their hats off, and Ulysse asked. He told her the count. He told her about the lights. She was a small woman, past seventy, in a black dress and a sunbonnet. She went on shelling for a while. Then she put the peas in the pan. Bon, she said. That was the whole of it. Afterward people would ask Ulysse what else she had said, and he would say she had said bon, and they would not believe him. The judge would not hear

sections.heading: III. Down the Bayou
sections.text: Below Lockport there was no road at all, only the bayou, with the houses along both banks facing it like people along a street, and the word had gone down ahead of her faster than the luggers could row. The people of the lower bayou had decided among themselves that they would do twice what the judge had done. The houses on both banks were hung with whatever cloth was left after the storm. Men stood in the shallows holding up four umbrellas over the place where she would pass, and when she passed they waded out and walked alongside in the water. Where the storm had filled the channel with drift, cypress logs and roof timbers and the carcasses of cattle, the men of Leeville and the men from the Chênière who could still pull had gone out in the days before and dragged it all clear for three leagues, so that the bayou she came down was as clean as a swept floor. At every landing someone had a pot on, and they fed the crew twice what the judge had fed them, and they would not let Placide pay for so much as a cup of coffee. Where the bayou opened into the marsh and the oaks of the Chênière ridge stood up grey against the sky, broken off, half of them, like teeth, the men of the Chênière

sections.heading: IV. Placide’s Round
sections.dateline: The Chênière · the first night, and seven days
sections.text: That evening a relief steamer from New Orleans came into Caminada Bay with all her lamps lit. She carried flour and doctors and barrels of lime, and the light of her came across the water like a town arriving. Out in the marsh the little fires went out, most of them, one after another, the way lamps go out in a house when people go to bed. Tante Zélie stood at the head of the path that went up the ridge, where the gate of the graveyard had been, and called Placide to her. A traiteuse gives her prayers across, a woman to a man and a man to a woman, and they are never written down. She had been going to give them to Placide someday. She gave them to him there, in the dark, in the smell of wet ground and lime, with her mouth close to his ear, and nobody else heard them, and they are not written here. Then she took the white enamel bowl she carried in her bag, the one she used for everything, and dipped it full from the rain barrel at the Rigaud house, and put it in his two hands. Go around, she said. All the way. Three times. Placide went around the Chênière three times that night, in the three watches, from dark to the first grey, along the ridge and down through the ruin of the hous

sections.heading: V. The Manila Men
sections.dateline: Barataria and the bayou · the end of October
sections.text: The people of the Chênière took her back to the mouth of the bayou with twice the honor they had given her coming, which was everything they had, and more than they had. But the Manila men were waiting. They were the shrimp people of the bay, from the islands on the far side of the world, men who had come off Spanish ships two and three generations back and lived on platforms of cypress built out over the water, where they boiled and dried their shrimp in the sun and sent it to China. Some of them had Chinese partners and some had Cajun wives. Their platforms stood on pilings, and the storm had gone under the one in the bay where they lived and left most of it standing. They had heard about the parlor chair and the stars. They said to each other in their own language, and then in Spanish to the Cajuns, that the people of the land had honored her and they did not see why the people of the water should not. So they came out from Barataria with every boat they had. They had painted the luggers. They had hung them with colored cloth and paper lanterns and the flags of three countries. They had brought, from somewhere up the freshwater bayous, so much water hyacinth in bloom that when t

sections.heading: VI. Toussaint
sections.dateline: A sugarhouse below Thibodaux · the night of November 1
sections.text: The grinding went day and night that time of year. In the sugarhouse on the plantation next to the judge’s the kettles boiled from dark to dark, and the men who skimmed them and fed the furnaces and the women who brought them supper stayed up talking in the heat, and the smell of the cane juice cooking lay on the whole bayou like a blanket. Tante Zélie came over most nights to treat burns. On the night of the first of November, Toussaint, she came over late, from the graveyard, where the whole bayou had been all day whitewashing the tombs and setting out chrysanthemums, and sat down on a bench by the door to wait in case anyone burned himself. They were talking about her. They had been talking about nothing else for a week. The road white with shell, fifteen miles. The judge to his neck in the bayou, twice, at eighty. The rain. The tin stars. The Manila boats, the hyacinths, the birds, a hundred boats and she in every one. There was never anything like it on this bayou, said one of the kettle men. Not for a bishop. Not for the governor. It’s the gift she has, said a woman. The power. Tante Zélie said, What are you all talking about? They told her. It wasn’t any power of mine, she s

title: Toussaint
place: Bayou Lafourche and Chênière Caminada, Louisiana
logline: After the October storm of 1893, the survivors of the Chênière send up the bayou for an old traiteuse who will not treat across water.

verses.text: He who, by causing pain to others, wishes to obtain pleasure for himself, he, entangled in the bonds of hatred, will never be free from hatred.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a fisherman finds turtle eggs on a riverbank, has them cooked at a house, and gives one to a girl there, who afterward will eat nothing else. Her mother takes an egg from a hen’s nest for her, and then the girl takes them herself. The hen conceives a grudge. The two are reborn as a cat and a hen, then as a leopardess and a doe, and in five hundred lives each devours the other’s young. At last one is an ogress (yakkhinī) who, in the guise of a dear friend, twice eats a young wife’s newborn. The third time the wife bears her child at her parents’ house while the ogress is away on her turn at drawing water. On the way home the couple bathe in the monastery pool; the wife sees the ogress coming, runs into the monastery, and lays the child at the Buddha’s feet. A spirit at the gate holds the ogress back until the Buddha sends Ānanda to bring her in, saying, “Let her come; make no noise.” He tells them that hatred is never ended by hatred, and the feud is over. Read the full commentary story. The second half is also told, with a different beginning, as the story of the ogress Kāḷī, which this series retells in Dinner on the Ground. On yakkhas and yakkhinīs.
bg.history:
The twenty miles of barrier island between Melbourne Beach and Wabasso are the most important nesting ground of the loggerhead sea turtle in the Western Hemisphere, and the Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge was established there in 1991, named for the University of Florida zoologist who had died four years earlier. A female comes ashore several times in a season, about two weeks apart, digs an egg chamber with her hind flippers, lays around a hundred eggs, covers them, and leaves; she then stays away for two or three years. Raccoons are the chief robbers of nests on that coast. The tears are real: glands behind the eyes shed the salt she takes in with seawater. Beginning with Brevard County in the mid-1980s, Florida’s coastal governments required beachfront lights to be shaded or put out during nesting season, since lights turn hatchlings away from the sea. Guided night walks run under state permit in June and July, about twenty people at a time, with red lights only.

Settlers along the Indian River dug turtle eggs every summer; a state law of 1907 protected nesting turtles on the beach, and later law protected the eggs. The railroad reached Melbourne in 1893. HRS was Florida’s Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, which ran the state’s child-abuse hotline and its foster care until it was broken up in the late 1990s. The Landing, the Yates and Corbett families, Verna Platt and turtle K 4417 are invented.

sections.heading: I. One Egg
sections.text: Josiah Yates fished mullet out of the Landing, on the river side of the barrier island below Melbourne Beach, where the land is so narrow that a man standing in his boat on the Indian River can hear the surf behind him. In June the loggerheads came up the ocean beach every night. Anybody who wanted eggs had only to walk the tide line at daybreak until he crossed a track as wide as a wagon’s coming up out of the sea, follow it to the dune, and push a stick into the sand until it went in easy. One morning that June Josiah dug a lard bucket full, a hundred and some. His wife was at Titusville with her sister, so he carried the bucket next door to the Corbetts, and Mrs. Corbett boiled them for him. A turtle egg is round and has a skin like wet kid leather. It dents under the thumb and stays dented, and however long it boils the white will not set. You tear a corner with your teeth, shake in salt and pepper, and squeeze. Josiah ate two dozen at the Corbett table. He gave one to the Corbett girl, Lottie, who was six and had been standing at his elbow the whole time. After that one egg she would eat nothing else. She let grits go cold. She would not touch fish, and she held cornbread in h

sections.heading: II. Turn About
sections.text: The Corbetts tell the next part and the Yateses tell the part after it, and a person has to sit on both porches to get the whole. The Corbetts say that the week the dominicker died, a gray kitten turned up under the Yates house that nobody had given them. It grew into a rangy cat with a flat head. The year Mrs. Corbett finally got a flock of her own, that cat came through the fence and cleaned out her best hen’s nest three times, and the fourth time it took the hen. They say you could look in that cat’s face and tell who she was. The Yateses say that is foolishness. Then they say that around the year of the Armistice a Yates boy raised a doe fawn on a bottle, and she grew up and went wild only as far as the back fence, and dropped a fawn of her own in the wax myrtles. A panther swam the river from the Malabar scrub, the last one anybody saw on the island, and killed the doe and the fawn in one night and was gone by morning. A panther does not swim a mile of salt water for no reason, the Yateses say, and the Corbetts always did have a way of getting what they wanted done by something else. That is what gets told. What happened is plainer and runs the same direction. In 1926 somebody

sections.heading: III. The Bait Store Phone
sections.text: Renee Yates and Jolene Corbett were the first of the two names to be friends since their great-great-grandmothers borrowed sugar. Jolene was four years older, and she had driven Renee to the high school in Melbourne every day for two years in her daddy’s truck. People at the Landing took it for a sign that the thing had finally worn out. Renee married Travis Hamm in 1986 and they set a single-wide on the Yates lot. The first boy came the next fall. Jolene was over the day they brought him home. Where’s Renee at? Back bedroom, Travis’s mother said. They just got in with the baby. Boy or girl? Let me see him. She held him a good while. She looked at him, and she looked at the space heater, and at Travis’s cans on the counter, and at a place on Renee’s arm. Then she kissed Renee and drove to her daddy’s bait store. She picked up the pay phone by the ice machine, dialed the eight-hundred number that hung on a poster in every clinic in Florida, and told the state abuse line a number of things about the Hamm trailer. Some of them were so. Travis did drink. A woman from HRS came out with a deputy on the nineteenth day and carried the boy to a foster home in Cocoa. A year later a judge end

sections.heading: IV. Five Rules
sections.text: Verna Platt was seventy-one. She had taught fifth grade for thirty-four years, with a Yates or a Corbett in the room most of them, and she had learned early not to seat them together. Four nights a week in June and July she led the turtle society’s walk, by state permit, from the county dune crossover north of the inlet. She took twenty people at a time. Mostly they were retired couples from Indialantic and Satellite Beach, and that night there was also a family from Ohio. She gave them her five rules in the parking lot at dusk, as she had once given out the rules for the lunch line. No flashlights. No flash on your cameras. No noise. Nobody touches her. And nobody takes one thing off this beach, not a shell. The county had been making the oceanfront houses darken their windows in summer since the middle eighties. That year the government had begun buying up the dunes for a refuge, to be named for the turtle man at Gainesville. Roy Sumlin, who kept the lot for the county, stood at the head of the crossover on walk nights and saw that nobody followed the group up the beach. A college boy named Curtis scouted ahead with a red-lensed light. A little before nine he came back up the san

sections.heading: V. The Egg Chamber
sections.text: The turtle had come out of the water at ten to nine and hauled herself to the foot of the dune. With her front flippers she had thrown out a pit as long as she was. Then she had dug the chamber with the hind ones alone, one cupped flipper and then the other, a foot and a half straight down into the damp sand, a hole she would never see. The twenty knelt in a half ring behind her, where she could not see them either. Verna lay on her stomach and held the red light down into it. Then nothing happened. The turtle laid her chin on the sand and breathed. Ten minutes went by, and twenty. Verna had watched better than four hundred loggerheads on that beach, and she had never seen one finish her chamber and then lie over it empty. The people who were there say she was waiting. Renee came into the red light at a dead run. She dropped on her knees and laid the baby down on the sand, between Verna Platt and the turtle’s shoulder. Take him. I’m giving him to you. Don’t let her get him. Nobody could say afterward who she had said it to. Verna thought it was to her. The woman from Ohio was sure it was to the turtle. Back at the crossover Roy Sumlin saw a woman coming at him across the lot. Somet

sections.heading: VI. The Tag
sections.text: On Monday Jolene drove to the HRS office and asked for the file by the name on it. She sat four hours with a caseworker and went down it line by line, saying which of the things she had told them were so and which she had made. It took nine months and two hearings. The second boy came home in the spring of 1992, three years old, to people he did not know. The first had been adopted, and the judge would not open it. Renee carried that the rest of her life. So did Jolene. The two of them were not friends again. They were something else, which neither family had a word for, and Caleb grew up in and out of both houses. Jolene took Verna Platt’s five rules as though they had been said to her in particular. People at the Landing will tell you she kept them on the road and in the store the same as on the sand. She walked the dawn nest count for the society for twenty-two summers with a clipboard and a bundle of stakes. The nest by the crossover hatched at the end of August on a night when nobody was watching. Jolene found it in the morning. There was a dent in the sand the size of a dinner plate, and from it the tracks of a hundred-odd hatchlings, each no wider than two fingers, fanned do

title: The Egg Chamber
logline: Ninety-five years after a bucket of turtle eggs, a mother runs down a dark Florida beach with her third baby toward a red light.

verses.text: What ought to be done is neglected, what ought not to be done is done; the desires of unruly, thoughtless people are always increasing.

But they whose whole watchfulness is always directed to their body, who do not follow what ought not to be done, and who steadfastly do what ought to be done, the desires of such watchful and wise people will come to an end.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest in the collection. The monks of Bhaddiya took to ornamenting their footwear, making or having made sandals of grass, of thatch, of reeds, of palm leaves, of bulrush and of wool, and neglected their instruction, their questions and their training in conduct, meditation and wisdom. Other monks were offended and told the Buddha, who laid down rules about sandals and rebuked them: “You came here for one purpose, but have devoted yourselves to another.” He spoke the two verses, the second about mindfulness of the body, and the monks of Bhaddiya reached the end of the path as he finished. The story quotes the Vinaya’s chapter on footwear (Mahāvagga 5).
bg.history:
Major League clubs sign Latin American teenagers as young as sixteen and house them at academies in the Dominican Republic, where they train, take English and other classes, and play in the Dominican Summer League. The Twins and Phillies opened a shared $18 million academy at Boca Chica in January 2017, with three fields, batting cages, classrooms and dormitory space for each club (MLB.com). Many players have come from San Pedro de Macorís and the sugar bateyes around it. Until the end of 2018, Major League uniform rules required that at least 51 percent of each shoe’s exterior be the club’s designated color; after a spring of warnings to players over their cleats, the league and the players’ union loosened the rule for 2019 (MLB.com). That same year the free-to-play Fortnite Battle Royale, which makes its money selling purely cosmetic outfits and dances, was at the height of its first craze.

The Phillies won the first World Series in their history in 1980, beating the Kansas City Royals in six games (1980 World Series). Game 6 was played on October 21 before 65,838 people at Veterans Stadium, whose field was AstroTurf, and in the top of the ninth the city put police on the field, some on horses and some with dogs, to keep the crowd from storming it at the end.

sections.heading: I. Paint
sections.dateline: The Phillies academy, Boca Chica, Dominican Republic · June 2018
sections.text: The academy sat on forty-five acres of flat ground a few kilometers in from the sea, behind a wall with the two clubs’ names on the gate, the Phillies on one side of the compound and the Twins on the other. Each club had three fields, covered cages, a weight room, a video room, three classrooms with whiteboards, and a dormitory where seventy-some boys slept two and three to a room under air conditioning that most of them had never had at home. The youngest were sixteen. They had signed the summer before, on the second of July, when the international signing period opened, and some of them had received more money on that one day than their fathers had earned in their lives, and most of it was already gone, to a house for the mother, a motorbike for the brother, a debt in the colmado, and the cut that went to the buscón who had trained them since they were twelve and fed them and owned a piece of them still. It began with Yandel Ozuna’s cleats. Yandel was a shortstop from Baní, seventeen, with hands so quiet the coaches stopped talking when he took ground balls. He came back from a Sunday at home with a pair of game spikes that a man in Bayona had painted for him with leather paint o

sections.heading: II. The Older Ones
sections.text: Not everyone thought it was funny. Rainier Coss was a catcher from Maracay, nineteen, in his third summer at the academy, which meant he was running out of summers, and he had a pair of black spikes with the club logo worn off the toes from dragging them in the dirt. Junior Peralta was a pitcher from Monte Plata who had come back from elbow surgery and spent a year doing nothing but bands and towel drills in front of a mirror, and the scar on the inside of his arm was still pink. They did not say anything at first. Then one night in the lounge somebody held up Rainier’s cleats by the laces and asked who had died, and everybody laughed, and Rainier took them back and went out and sat on the steps in the dark. In the morning he and Junior went to Don Teo.

sections.heading: III. The Rule
sections.dateline: The agility field · the next morning, before six
sections.text: Teodoro Peguero was fifty-eight and had been the academy’s field coordinator for nine years. He was a small, dark man with a gray mustache and a belly, and he walked with his feet a little turned out, the way infielders do who have spent their lives getting ready to go either way. He did not shout. He did not use the whistle around his neck. In nine years most of the boys had heard him say perhaps a hundred words, and the ones who later reached Allentown or Philadelphia could repeat most of them. He had been born on a sugar batey outside San Pedro de Macorís, where the cane cutters lived in barracks between the fields and the company owned the water. He had learned to play barefoot, on a lot of packed red dirt beside the rail line where the cane carts ran, with a glove cut and folded out of a milk carton and a ball made of a sock wound with tape. He did not own a pair of shoes until the club that signed him in 1977 gave him a pair of spikes, and he said later that he had not liked them, because he could no longer feel where he was. He had played eleven years in the minor leagues, in towns whose names he could still recite in order. In September of 1980, when he was twenty, he was c

sections.heading: IV. Barefoot
sections.text: Then he sat down on the wet grass and unlaced his own shoes, a pair of old gray running shoes with the heels broken down, and took off his socks and stuffed them in the shoes, and stood up barefoot. His feet were wide and pale on the bottom and the toes were crooked from fifty years of being stepped on. Take them off. They looked at each other. Then they sat down in a row in the grass and took them off, the flags and the flames and the palm tree and Altagracia in gold, and the Crocs with the charms, and set them side by side behind them, and stood up. The grass was cold. Someone laughed, once, and stopped. Don Teo walked them out to the skin of the infield, where the dirt had been dragged smooth the evening before and not yet touched. He set himself at shortstop, knees bent, weight on the balls of his feet. Right foot. Left foot. Feel the ground take you. Now the ball is here. He showed them, without a ball. A small step with the right foot to the side, the left coming through, the glove hand down and out in front, the throwing hand closing over it, the right foot crossing behind to set, and the throw, which went nowhere, which went to first base in the air. Then again, very slowly

title: Fifty-One Percent
logline: Teenage Phillies prospects paint flags and their mothers' names on their spikes, until an old coordinator who learned the game barefoot calls them out.

verses.text: A true Brahmana goes scatheless, though he have killed father and mother, and two valiant kings, though he has destroyed a kingdom with all its subjects.
A true Brahmana goes scatheless, though he have killed father and mother, and two holy kings, and an eminent man besides.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is a few lines long. The Buddha is sitting in his day-quarters at Jetavana with some visiting monks when the elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya, “Bhaddiya the Dwarf,” walks past. The Buddha says that there goes a monk who has killed his mother and father and goes on free of pain. The visitors look at one another in doubt and ask what he means, and he answers with the verse. The commentary reads it as a riddle: mother and father are craving and conceit, the two kings are the views that the self lasts forever and that it is annihilated at death, and the kingdom with its followers is the passion for the twelve spheres of sense. The second verse, told the same way, puts a tiger fifth, which the commentary takes as the five hindrances, the fifth of them doubt. The visitors become arahats. Elsewhere the canon names Lakuṇṭaka, small and mocked for it, as foremost among monks with a sweet voice. Read the full commentary story, or about Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya and the five hindrances. Hata Sensei’s lines are a saying of the Chinese master Linji (Rinzai in Japanese), from the first series of D. T. Suzuki’s Essays in Zen Buddhism.
bg.history:
In 1923 Lucy Morgan, a teacher at the Appalachian School in the Mitchell County village of Penland, began teaching weaving to local women, and by 1929 the work had become the Penland School of Handicrafts, with classes in pottery among the first. After 1962 its second director, Bill Brown, turned it toward working artists with a resident program and longer courses, and studio potters, glassblowers and other craftspeople settled in the surrounding counties of Mitchell and Yancey. Many of the potters fire with wood. An anagama is a single sloping tunnel with the firebox at its low end and the chimney at its high one; it is stoked around the clock for days, and the wood ash that settles on the pots melts into glaze, heaviest near the fire and lightest at the back. Its line runs to medieval Japan, to kiln towns such as Shigaraki.

The same mountain counties grew burley tobacco on thousands of small allotments, cut whole in the field and air-cured for one to two months in open barns. Federal quotas had governed the crop since 1938. On October 22, 2004, the Fair and Equitable Tobacco Reform Act became law, ending the quotas and paying their holders a buyout; about $4 billion of it went to North Carolina, and most small burley growers in the mountains took it and quit. Five days later the Boston Red Sox finished a four-game sweep of St. Louis to win the 2004 World Series, their first championship since 1918.

sections.heading: I. The Kiln
sections.dateline: Laurel Branch, Yancey County, North Carolina · October 2004
sections.text: Morio Hata had come to the mountains in the summer of 1972 to teach a three-week workshop at the craft school over at Penland, and at the end of the three weeks he did not go back to Kyoto. He was the third son of a kiln family in Shigaraki, which meant there was no kiln for him at home, and he had been a Soto priest since he was nineteen, which meant he could sit anywhere. In 1975 he bought forty acres at the head of Laurel Branch from a widow named Edney who was glad to be done with them: a frame house, a springhouse, a quarter-acre burley allotment he rented back to her nephew, and a tobacco barn on the slope that he swept out and put a floor in and made into a zendo. The cracks between the boards were left as they were. In winter you sat in your coat and the wind came through in stripes. In 1983, with the help of eleven students and a mason from Spruce Pine, he dug a kiln into the hill behind the barn. It was twenty-six feet long and shaped like a loaf of bread, with a firebox at the low end and a chimney at the high one, and it lay along the slope the way a dog lies on a step. By the autumn of 2004 it had been fired forty-one times. People came from all over the country to put

sections.heading: II. Father and Mother
sections.text: By the fifth day the kiln had a voice of its own. It drew air in at the firebox with a long low sound like somebody breathing through a cold, and each time you stoked it, a split of pine laid in through the mouth, it went quiet, and black smoke rolled out the top of the chimney, and then the smoke cleared and the roar came back a little higher. The front cones had gone over in the night. The spy holes were too bright to look into without welding glasses, and when you did look, the pots inside had lost their shapes and become places where the light was a little thicker. The four from Atlanta had their shift from noon to six. They stoked when Hata Sensei raised a finger. In between they sat with him on a row of buckets and cinder blocks out of the heat and ate the rice balls Ben brought up from the house at two. The pine came from a sawmill on the Cane River, slab wood with the bark still on it, and their hands were black with pitch to the wrist. Across the branch the Edney nephew's barn was hung to the rafters with burley, turned the color of saddle leather, the last crop on the allotment. Congress had passed the buyout, and everybody on the creek was waiting for the President to si

sections.heading: III. The Painter
sections.text: The Ray boys from the sawmill came up the branch in their father's truck on the last night with a final load of slab. Cody was nineteen and Dwayne was seventeen, and their father had put in for the buyout on his quota and was talking about selling the mill too and going to work at the hospital in Spruce Pine, and Cody had a cousin in Charlotte who said he could get him on with a drywall crew, and nobody in the family could decide anything. They unloaded the slab, and then because the kiln was the only light on Laurel Branch at that hour and there was a roar coming out of it like a jet, they stayed. Hata Sensei was on his bucket. He had been up most of two nights. Flame was coming out of the top of the chimney now, three feet of it, the color of the inside of a peach, and in its light the boys could see the burley hanging in the Edney barn across the branch, and the moths. Ben came out of the dark with the side-stoking rods and went along the kiln wall, pulling a brick from each port, feeding a handful of thin pine in and putting the brick back. The heat off the ports made the air above him swim. He did it the way he did everything, without hurry and without stopping. Hata Sensei lo

sections.heading: IV. The Back
sections.text: On the morning they unbricked the door it was cold enough that the heat coming out of the kiln stood up in a column in the air, and the Edney nephew came across the branch to watch, and so did the Rays. By then the President had signed the buyout. The Red Sox had won the World Series the night before for the first time since 1918, and Ben, who had been raised in Barre on Red Sox radio, had gone to bed at nine as usual and found out at breakfast, and said, Well, good. The front of the kiln came out first. Some of it was very fine. A bottle near the firebox came out with a green ash glaze running in long beads down one side and a black glossy shoulder where the coals had lain, and the woman from Asheville who had made it held it in both hands and could not say anything. Some of it was ruined. A bowl had slumped. Two pots had fallen against each other and fused into one thing, which Hata Sensei looked at a long time and then set aside for himself. Marcy's jar came out of the second row with a gray-green crust on its shoulder like lichen on a fencepost and a long scar on its foot where the wad had torn away, and she looked at it, and then she put it down on the board with the others an

title: Ash Glaze
place: Laurel Branch (fictional), Yancey County, North Carolina
logline: During a six-day wood firing in the Blue Ridge, an old Zen potter says the small man who loads the back of the kiln killed his parents.

verses.text: The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha.
The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on the law.
The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on the church.
The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on their body.
The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their mind day and night always delights in compassion.
The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their mind day and night always delights in meditation.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two boys of Rājagaha play ball. One calls out praise of the Buddha as he throws and always wins; the other, whose family follows another teacher, copies him until the recollection becomes his own. One evening the second boy's father, a wagon driver hauling firewood, stops near a charnel ground outside the city; the oxen wander through the gate, the father follows, and the gate is shut behind him. The boy sleeps alone under the wagon. Two spirits find him. One means to eat him and drags him by the feet, but when the boy cries out homage to the Buddha it falls back in terror. The other stands guard, and together, ashamed, they bring him food in the king's golden dish, care for him "as would a mother and a father," and cut letters into the dish that only the king can read. In the morning the boy is arrested as a thief and says only that his parents came in the night. The king takes the boy and his parents to the Buddha and asks whether recollection of the Buddha is the only protection; the Buddha answers with six verses naming six recollections, and all three later reach awakening.
bg.history:
Arabic-speaking immigrants from Ottoman Syria, most of them from the villages of Mount Lebanon and the Bekaa, began arriving in the United States in numbers in the 1880s, and many started out as peddlers, carrying cases of notions, lace and religious goods from farm to farm. In North Dakota the peddlers came first and sent word home about free land; in the early 1900s more than 350 Syrians took up homesteads in the state, Christians and Muslims both. A peddler there needed a county license under the state's 1895 peddling act: twenty dollars a year on foot, thirty-five with one horse, fifty with two, with up to thirty days in the county jail for peddling without one, and incorporated towns kept the right to license peddlers on top of that. Fuel on the treeless western prairie was lignite, which lay exposed in coulee banks; some landowners simply opened the seam and let neighbors dig their own for a dollar a wagonload.

Orthodox Syrians on the plains rarely saw a priest. Raphael Hawaweeny, consecrated in New York in 1904 as the first Orthodox bishop consecrated in North America, spent years traveling by train and on foot to scattered Arabic-speaking communities and established some thirty parishes; between his visits, laymen led the prayers. Matins (Orthros) in the Orthodox Church begins with the Six Psalms, read before daylight while the church stands still. The psalms quoted in the story are in the Coverdale translation as printed in the English Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church published in 1906 by Isabel Hapgood. The Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, in September, is kept in Syria and Lebanon with bonfires on the hilltops, recalling the chain of fires said to have carried the news of the Cross's finding from Jerusalem to Constantinople.

sections.heading: I. The Can on the Post
sections.text: There were eleven Syrian claims on the flats north of the Little Muddy that summer, nine sod houses and two of lumber, strung out a half mile apart along the section lines like beads somebody had dropped and not picked up. The men had come out on the Great Northern as peddlers, with their cases on their backs, and had seen all that land lying open and free for anybody who would file on it and live on it five years. They wrote home to the villages above Zahleh, and the cousins came. By 1907 there were wives on the flats, and babies born in sod houses, and a cemetery with two Syrian graves in it at the corner of the Saba claim, marked with crosses cut from packing-case boards. The boys of the colony played ball against the side of the Saba barn. There were not enough of them to make up nine, so they played a game of their own. Somebody set a tomato can on a fence post forty paces off, and you threw at it, and if you knocked it off you threw again, and the one who knocked it off most times before dark was the winner. The ball had been wound by Mikhail Saba's mother out of an old wool sock around a rubber ball, sewn over with harness thread, and it went where you sent it. Mikhail Saba

sections.heading: II. The Coal Bank
sections.text: Assaad Malouf had gone up in the world. He had a team now, two bay geldings he called Hamdan and Zayd, and a spring wagon with a box built on behind the seat that opened out like a cupboard, and in the cupboard there were drawers: needles and pins, thread on wooden spools, buttons on cards, shoelaces, suspenders, combs, mirrors, a drawer of lace that the women of the colony had made over the winter, a drawer of little olive-wood crosses and rosaries from Jerusalem that he sold to the Catholics and laughed at in Arabic as soon as he was out of the yard. He had a county license for a single horse, which cost thirty-five dollars a year, and drove two, and dared anybody to count. Every fall he took Faris out with him for a week on the circuit, west and north among the Norwegian farms, to learn the trade. Faris learned to stand in a farm kitchen and open the drawers one at a time, slowly, so the lace came last. He learned to say Good morning, Missus and very fine and for you, special. He learned that the Norwegian women would buy anything if you let them look long enough, and that they would give you coffee whether you wanted it or not, and a piece of lefse, and sometimes, when the man

sections.heading: III. Under the Wagon
sections.dateline: The Lutheran cemetery outside Lindahl · that night
sections.text: It was a cattle drive that did it. A rancher from up on the Missouri breaks was bringing a hundred head of steers in to the stockyards by the depot to load for St. Paul in the morning, and they came along the road in the dusk with two men riding behind them, and the geldings lifted their heads out of the nosebags and watched them pass. Then Zayd, who had always been the fool of the two, went after them, hobbles and all, in a kind of rocking hop, and Hamdan went after Zayd, and the two of them were carried away down the road into Lindahl in the dust and bawling, like two pieces of wood in a flood. Assaad swore by everything Faris had ever heard him swear by and went after them on foot. Stay with the wagon, he shouted back. Stay with the coal. Nobody touches it. Faris stayed with the wagon. What happened in town he heard afterward. His father found the geldings without much trouble, in the corral behind the livery barn, where the steers had been turned in to wait for the cars. But the liveryman said they had eaten his hay and wanted fifty cents, and Assaad had spent his last money on the coal, and he took a card of lace out of his coat and said, For your wife, very fine, for you, spe

sections.heading: IV. The Tray
sections.dateline: Lindahl · the Feast of the Cross
sections.text: The Haddad women had set out the feast the night before, as they did every year, on the big tray on the table in the back room of the store, so that it would be ready for the morning: the kibbeh in its pan, the stuffed cabbage, the bread, the olives from the barrel that came out from New York, the white cheese, the honey cakes, everything under a clean cloth. In the morning the cloth was lying folded on the table and the tray was gone with everything on it. Elias Haddad’s wife screamed. Then Haddad’s clerk ran for the marshal, and the marshal, who had already had one Syrian in his lockup that night, said he knew where to look for Syrian thieves. They went through the stockyards and the livery and the section house and the depot. Then they went out the cemetery road. They brought Faris back walking between the marshal and the clerk, the clerk carrying the tray in both arms against his chest like a shield. Half of Lindahl followed them up the street, and the whole of the colony was waiting in front of the store in their feast clothes. Latifeh Malouf came running out through the door with flour on her arms and stopped when she saw who it was. At the same moment, from the other end of

sections.heading: V. Six
sections.dateline: The back room of the Haddad store
sections.text: Imm Jirjis had come in for the Feast on the Saba wagon, as she did every year, and she was sitting in the back room by the stove with a cup of coffee, where it was warm, because she was old and the cold got into her now. She had walked for twenty years with that case on her back, from Duluth to Havre, through the Red River Valley in the mosquitoes and the Montana high line in the snow, sleeping in haystacks and barns and on the kitchen floors of women who could not say her name. Her husband had died of a fever in a boarding house in St. Paul the first year. Her son, the Jirjis she was mother of, nobody in the colony had ever seen; he had died in the old country before she came, or had not, nobody knew, and nobody asked. She did not peddle anymore. She lived in a claim shack on the Saba quarter and did the Sabas’ mending, and when anybody on the flats was in trouble they went and sat with her, and came away feeling as though they had been to church. Haddad brought them in to her, the three Maloufs, and set the tray on the table in front of her, and the whole colony came crowding into the doorway behind. He told her all of it. The ball and the tomato can, which Hanna Saba told him; t

sections.heading: VI. Matins
sections.text: Assaad went to Haddad’s feast that day, and ate the lamb, and told the story of Abu Zayd afterward to the children in the long rhymed lines until they fell asleep on the floor. He kept telling it all his life. But that winter, on the Sundays when the colony met in Hanna Saba’s front room to say the prayers with no priest, he came, and stood at the back with his hat in his hands, and on the third Sunday, when Hanna got to the six psalms and his voice gave out with a cold, Assaad Malouf, who said priests ate the first lamb and the last, read them in his place, in the dark before the lamp was lit, from memory, because he had heard them every morning of his boyhood in the village and had never once forgotten a word. He took out a second license that spring, for two horses, fifty dollars. Latifeh asked him why, when nobody had ever counted. He said he had counted. Imm Jirjis died in the hard winter of 1911, in the claim shack, with the stove going. Latifeh had been sitting with her. In the spring Latifeh took the old case down from its nail, and filled it, and put it on her back, and walked the county with it for eleven years, and the farm wives who could not say her name said afterward

title: The Brass Tray
logline: A Syrian peddler's son, left alone under a coal wagon by a prairie graveyard, wakes beside the richest man's stolen brass tray.

verses.text: It is hard to leave the world (to become a friar), it is hard to enjoy the world; hard is the monastery, painful are the houses; painful it is to dwell with equals (to share everything in common) and the itinerant mendicant is beset with pain. Therefore let no man be an itinerant mendicant and he will not be beset with pain.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Vajjian prince gives up his turn to rule and becomes a monk in a forest grove near Vesālī. On the full-moon night of Kattika the whole city is hung with banners and keeps festival until morning, and the monk, walking his cloister under the moon in his plain robe, hears the drums and lutes and thinks he looks like a log thrown away in the forest. Who, he asks, is worse off than we are? The spirit who lives in the grove answers him in verse: many envy you, as those in hell envy those bound for heaven. The next day he goes to the Buddha, who names the five kinds of suffering in this verse: the going forth is hard, delight in it is hard, the household life is hard, living with the uncongenial is hard, and the traveler through the round of births is beset by suffering; so do not be a traveler. Hearing it, the monk is freed. Read the full commentary story. The same exchange with the forest spirit is told in the Saṁyutta Nikāya (SN 9.9). The mother’s poem is Emily Dickinson’s “I’m Nobody! Who are you?”, quoted as it was printed in Poems, Second Series in 1891.
bg.history:
Cheyenne Frontier Days began in 1897 as a one-day cowboy roundup and calls itself “the Daddy of ’em All.” It runs ten days around the last full week of July, with rodeo every afternoon, a concert in the arena every night, a carnival midway, parades, and three free pancake breakfasts put on by the Kiwanis that feed some 40,000 people a year. It is run by committees of more than 2,500 volunteers from the town. In 2018 it ran from July 20 to 29; the last night show was on Saturday, July 28, and the midway stayed open until midnight. The moon had been full the night before, during a total lunar eclipse that could not be seen from North America.

Farm Sanctuary, founded in 1986 and calling itself America’s first shelter for farmed animals, rescues cattle, pigs, goats and poultry and keeps them for the rest of their lives, and it promotes veganism, which refuses meat, milk and eggs alike; smaller farm-animal sanctuaries on the same pattern, some of them run by one or two people, have since been started across the country. In ranching country the ordinary way is otherwise. A 4-H member raises a market steer for most of a year and sells it at auction at the county fair, and the sale is meant to teach where meat comes from.

sections.heading: I. Forty Acres
sections.text: When Dale Lerwick died in the spring of 2012 the ranch was supposed to go to Cass. Everybody in Laramie County knew it. Her brother Wade had been gone to the Bakken since the boom started and said he was never coming back to look at the back end of a cow, and her cousin Travis had his own place on Horse Creek and his own note at the bank. Cass had grown up in the calving shed. She had shown a steer at the county fair every August from nine to eighteen and had cried in the sale barn every time and sold him anyway, the way you were supposed to. She could rope. Her father had left the brand to her in his will by name, a bar over an L, which in that country was as close as a man came to crowning somebody. She had also quit eating meat at nineteen, her second year at the university in Laramie, and quit milk and eggs two years after that. Nobody in the family had taken it seriously. Her father said it was a thing girls did in college, and when it lasted he said it was a thing she did, and he never once said anything about it at the table. When he was dying he asked her what she would do with the place, and she told him, and he looked at the ceiling of the hospital room for a long time an

sections.heading: II. The Last Saturday
sections.dateline: The forty acres · July 28, 2018, after midnight
sections.text: Frontier Days ran ten days at the end of July, and on the last Saturday night the whole town was out. Cheyenne had been hung with flags since the cattle drive two Sundays back. There had been four parades and three free pancake breakfasts, where the Kiwanis fed forty thousand people off griddles the size of a pickup bed. There had been rodeo every afternoon, and every afternoon the north wind had brought her the announcer's voice from Frontier Park in pieces, the names of cowboys and the names of their hometowns, so that she could hear a man from Texas and a man from Alberta go by on the air without hearing what had happened to them. Travis was on the rodeo committee and had been in a white straw hat and a pressed shirt for nine days. Her sister-in-law had a new one for every night. The Saturday night show let out a little after eleven. She could hear the end of it from her step, the bass more than the song, and then the crowd, and then the whole grandstand walking to its trucks. The midway ran until midnight, and above the lights of the town she could see the top of the Ferris wheel turning, and then it stopped. After that there were the bars downtown and the campers out at the pa

sections.heading: III. Dr. Kopp
sections.text: Ardith Kopp had been a large-animal vet in southeast Wyoming since 1966, when she was the only woman in her class at Colorado State and men in three counties would not let her touch a cow. She was seventy-six now and still went out, though she had given up pregnancy-checking in the winter of 2015 and said her shoulder was glad of it. She had married a rancher on the Chugwater who died young and left her eight hundred head and a note at the bank, and she had run the place for nine years and then sold it and lived alone since, in a stone house on the Chugwater road with a heeler and a shelf of journals. She had floated the teeth of every horse Cass ever owned. She had put down Cass's father's old cows one at a time as they went, out on the forty acres, and never once asked Cass what she thought she was doing. Cass drove up on Sunday afternoon, the last day, when the whole county was at the final round of the rodeo. Dr. Kopp was on her porch with iced tea. Cass told her the whole thing, the music and the post in the creek and what she had said out loud. She told her about the voice too. She had thought on the drive up that she would leave that part out, and then she did not. Dr. Kopp

sections.heading: IV. The Float
sections.text: On Monday the carnival trucks went north up the interstate past the forty acres from six in the morning on, flatbeds with the Ferris wheel folded down on them in sections and the cars of the Zipper chained on in a row. Cass was out at the stock tank in the coveralls with the hose. She looked up at them once. The steers came down to drink while the tank filled. There was a float valve that clipped on the rim, a brass arm and a copper ball, that her father had bought when she was a child, and in six years she had never once let it do its job; she always stood at the tank with the hose and shut the hydrant off by hand when the water was high enough. That morning she clipped the float on and walked away to feed the goats. When she came back the tank was full to the brim and still. The ball had come up with the water and shut it off by itself, and the steers were drinking it down, and as they drank the ball sank a little and the water came in again under it, just as much as they had taken, and no more.

title: The Night Show
logline: On the last night of Frontier Days, a rancher's daughter who gave the ranch away walks her animal sanctuary's fence alone, listening to the town.

verses.text: Whatever place a faithful, virtuous, celebrated, and wealthy man chooses, there he is respected.

bg.commentary: Citta was a rich householder of Macchikāsaṇḍa. He fed a monk whose bearing pleased him, listened to him, and understood; he gave his own wild-mango grove to the monks, and the earth shook when he did. Later the two chief disciples came to see him, and from a short talk given by Sāriputta, who was tired from the road, he reached the third stage of awakening. Having come so far without ever seeing the Buddha, he loaded five hundred carts with sesame, rice, ghee, sugar and cloth and invited anyone who wished to come along at his expense. For the month of the journey the gods fed the whole company at every league. When he bowed at the Buddha’s feet, flowers rained knee-deep. For a month more he could give away only what others kept bringing him, and at last he asked for a place to unload his carts and started home with them empty, whereupon people filled them with jewels. Ānanda asked whether all this honor came because Citta had been visiting the Buddha. The Buddha said it would have been the same wherever he went, spoke the verse, and told of Citta’s past life as a hunter who fed a meditating monk in the rain. The commentary gives the story in full at verses 73–74, with Citta’s quarrel with the monk Sudhamma, and repeats its ending at the full commentary story for this verse. More about Citta.
bg.history:
The Harmonic Convergence of August 16 and 17, 1987, was a worldwide synchronized meditation, and the newspapers covered it for weeks. Its organizers, reading a turning point into the Mesoamerican calendars, asked for 144,000 people to gather at “power centers” at sunrise, and Mount Shasta in northern California was among the chief of them. The mountain had been holy ground to American seekers for a long time. Guy Ballard said he met the master Saint Germain on its slopes, and the “I AM” Activity he founded with his wife claimed up to a million followers by 1938; its pageant has been held at Mount Shasta every August since 1950. Much New Age teaching in the 1970s and 1980s traveled by mail-order cassette and through the bulletin boards of natural-foods stores. Behind it stood the older current of New Thought, for which Emerson’s essay “Self-Reliance” (1841) was close to scripture.

On the evening of June 10, 1987, an earthquake of magnitude 5.1 centered near Olney, Illinois, was felt in some seventeen states, the largest in that region since 1968. The pawpaw is the largest fruit native to North America, a relative of the tropical custard apples that tastes something like mango and banana; it grows in shady patches along creek bottoms across southern Indiana and ripens at the end of September. Bloomington had communes in the hills around it and a food co-op from the 1970s. Hart Householder, his store, Mrs. Varnum and Alder Street are invented, and no one reported flowers.

sections.heading: I. Side One
sections.text: Hart Householder had the natural foods store on the west side of Bloomington, in the long tin building that had been his father’s feed mill. He had started with one barrel of brown rice in 1971 and by the middle eighties he was selling bulk grain and beans to six counties, with a room of books on one side and a bulletin board by the door that people drove in from Nashville and Spencer to read. He was fifty-two. He gave credit and did not write it down. If a commune out past Needmore had a bad winter, a truck came up their lane, and nobody had to ask whose it was. People who had never been inside the store knew his name. In the fall of 1977 a thin man came in off the highway with a pack. He did not ask for anything. He stood by the peanut grinder with his eyes down and waited to be in nobody’s way, and there was something in how he stood that Hart liked. Hart took him in back and gave him lunch. Before he left, the man set a cassette on the table. It had a white label, typed: SITTING, NO. 1. MOUNT SHASTA, CALIF. No name was on it. Hart played it that night on the machine in the office. It was a woman, not young, with a dry little cough she had not bothered to cut out. Behind her a k

sections.heading: II. The Patch
sections.text: Behind the feed mill four acres ran down to a creek, and the bottom of it was pawpaws, a whole grove, growing in their own shade the way they do. People had been going down there to sit for years. In June of 1987 Hart had a lawyer draw a paper giving the four acres to a little board, to be kept open to anybody from any direction who wanted to sit down and be quiet, with a shed for rain. He signed it on a card table in the patch on a Wednesday evening, with the board standing around him and the lawyer swatting mosquitoes. Well, Hart said, capping the pen, that’s planted. The ground shook. The card table walked a foot to the left. Every leaf in the grove shivered with no wind, and up in the store a row of honey jars went off the shelf one after another. It was twelve minutes before seven. Radios said afterward that it was an earthquake under Olney, Illinois, the biggest in those parts in nineteen years, and that it was felt in seventeen states. The people who had been standing in the pawpaw patch heard that and nodded and kept their own opinion. That night Hart sat in the office with the shoebox. I learned the first thing from her and never saw her, he thought. I learned the second t

sections.heading: III. The Bread Truck
sections.text: He owned a step van that had delivered bread around Monroe County through the sixties. You could still read the bakery’s name under the white paint when the sun was low. He loaded it himself. Twenty sacks of short-grain brown rice at fifty pounds, sesame seed and tahini in tins, ghee by the case, raw sugar. He put in drawstring trousers in all sizes and thirty quilts from the Tuesday women. It was for her, and for whoever was around her. Forty-three people went. There was a church bus bought at auction and five cars behind the bread truck. There were Unity ladies in sun hats, and two graduate students in religion, and a man who had laid track for the Monon, and a massage therapist with twin boys. There was a quiet veteran who drove the bus. Hart had laid in food for all of them for the whole road, in coolers, in the bus. They never opened a cooler. Outside St. Louis, at the first rest area, a family was standing by a picnic table with supper for fifty already set out, and said they had just had a feeling. At Unity Village the cafeteria would not take a dollar. In Kansas a Mennonite couple flagged the bus down from the shoulder with their trunk open. It went on like that. Boulder, L

sections.heading: IV. Alder Street
sections.text: Esther Varnum was seventy-four. Her mother had taken her into the I AM classes in Los Angeles in the thirties, when half the city seemed to be in them. She had come north with the believers and walked in the first pageants. Somewhere in the fifties she stopped going, without a quarrel, and stayed on in a small house on Alder Street with a clock in the kitchen. She had never told anyone to buy a tape. A young man named Andy copied them for her in the garage and took the mail to the box. On the Thursday she said to him, Andy. Saturday, about when the shadows get long, the man from Indiana will pull in here with a bread truck. Will anything happen? He had been with her four years and had learned to ask. Something will. What? Flowers. A good many. You may want to move your car. Andy told one person. The town that week was full to the gutters with people who had come for the mountain, sleeping in vans and on the school lawn, and by Saturday afternoon a few hundred of them had found Alder Street and stood along both sides of it with their arms full of things they had brought in case. The television crews were all up the mountain road, waiting for Sunday’s sunrise. The bread truck came ar

sections.heading: V. The Garage
sections.text: On Sunday the forty-three went up the mountain in the dark with everybody else and stood in a meadow and hummed the sun up. Mrs. Varnum did not go. It comes down this street too, she said, and sat at her kitchen table with the door open. Hart stayed a month. He had meant to cook for her. He had meant to set up his pots in her yard and feed her out of his own sacks, with her neighbors and anyone who came by. But each morning there was food on the porch before he was up. There were plums and squash and bread still warm, eggs in a bowl with a cloth over them, a salmon once. It came from the people in the vans and from the mill families, and from the pageant ladies in their pale dresses, who had not spoken to her in thirty years. More came to him than to her. Strangers put things into his hands in the street. He cooked every day for sixty and seventy, and he never had to break the seal on a sack of his own. On the fourteenth of September he stood in her kitchen with his cap in his hands. Mrs. Varnum. I loaded that truck in Indiana to give you something. I was two weeks getting here, and I have been here a month, and I have not been able to give you one grain of it. Everything I’ve hand

sections.heading: VI. Terre Haute
sections.dateline: Mount Shasta, and Bloomington · the end of September
sections.text: Andy was sweeping petals out of the gutter. There were still petals. He came in and stood by the kitchen table. Can I ask you something? He was two weeks coming and they fed him the whole way. He was a month here and couldn’t spend a dime. He left empty and they filled him up in the street. Was that because he was coming to see you? I mean with the mountain, and the weekend it was. Would any of it have happened if he had been going somewhere else? He has a sister in Terre Haute, Mrs. Varnum said. If he had driven that truck to see her it would have gone just the same. It has nothing to do with me, and less than nothing to do with that weekend. A person who has kept faith for fifty years, and kept his word, and has something to give and is known for it, will be met like that wherever he sets his foot down. Hand me that. It was the one book she had brought with her out of her mother’s house, from before the classes. She did not have to hunt for the place. Welcome evermore to gods and men is the self-helping man. For him all doors are flung wide; him all tongues greet, all honors crown, all eyes follow with desire. Our love goes out to him and embraces him because he did not need it.

title: The Bread Truck
