place: Bloomington, Indiana, to Mount Shasta, California
logline: An Indiana health-food grocer loads a bread truck with rice and drives to Mount Shasta to meet a voice he knows only from cassettes.

verses.text: Good people shine from afar, like the snowy mountains; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and his boyhood friend Ugga, who studied with the same teacher, promise each other their children in marriage. Years later Ugga visits Sāvatthī, is served so well by Anāthapiṇḍika’s daughter Cullā Subhaddā that he asks for her for his son, and takes her far away to his own city, where his household honors naked ascetics. Out of modesty she refuses to pay them reverence; her father-in-law orders her out, but the eight sponsors her father sent with her find her blameless. Her mother-in-law asks what her own teachers are like, and Subhaddā describes monks unmoved by gain and loss, fame and blame, praise and censure, pleasure and pain. Asked to bring them, she climbs to the top of the house and throws eight handfuls of jasmine into the air toward the Buddha, a hundred and twenty leagues away; the flowers form a canopy over him as he teaches, and he tells Anāthapiṇḍika that he is already invited. The next day the Buddha and five hundred monks travel through the air in gabled halls to Ugga’s city, and the household is converted.
bg.history:
When the copper and tin mines of Cornwall declined in the nineteenth century, Cornish miners carried their hard-rock skills, their pasties and their Methodism to mining camps across America. Grass Valley, in the Sierra foothills, was one of their strongholds, with the North Star, Empire and Idaho-Maryland gold mines, and it still keeps a Cornish Christmas and St. Piran’s Day. More on Cornish Americans. Methodism ran on local preachers, laymen accredited to lead worship and preach while keeping their own trades. The Revised Version of the Bible, the first official revision of the King James text, appeared in 1881 (New Testament) and 1885 (Old Testament).

Silver from Leadville made Denver rich in the 1880s, and the money built mansions on Capitol Hill and the Brown Palace Hotel, which opened on August 12, 1892. Spiritualism had a following there too: in 1876 the Rocky Mountain News reported séances in a West Denver home with a curtained spirit cabinet and materialized “forms” (Colorado Newsline). In the Denver Depression of 1893 silver fell from 83 to 62 cents an ounce, banks collapsed and many lost their savings.

sections.heading: I. The Promise
sections.dateline: Camborne, Cornwall, and Grass Valley, California · 1852–1891
sections.text: John Trevenna and Dick Uglow went down the same mine at Camborne the same week, at eleven years old, and learned their letters together at the same Sunday school in the same Wesleyan chapel, from an old tinner who had taught half the parish to read off the backs of hymnbooks. They were closer than brothers. One Sunday walking home over the downs, at fourteen, they shook hands on a thing they had heard men say in the count house. When we're grown and married, and have sons and daughters, if one of us asks the other for his daughter for his son, the other one shall give her. Then the mines in Cornwall failed, the way they did in those years, and the two of them went where the Cornish went. John went to California, to the gold quartz at Grass Valley, where they said a mine was a hole in the ground with a Cornishman at the bottom of it. Dick went to Colorado. In forty years John rose to be a mine captain, the best-paid man underground in Nevada County, with a white house on the hill above Mill Street. Dick found silver at Leadville and became something nobody in Camborne had a word for, and built a house of red sandstone on Capitol Hill in Denver with a tower on the corner and a ballro

sections.heading: II. The Gifts
sections.text: They were married in the Methodist chapel in October. John Trevenna gave his daughter away the way men in Camborne talked about for years afterward, when the news reached them: a wagon of linen and plate and furniture, a piano, a set of china from Stoke with her initials on it, a gold brooch from a jeweler in San Francisco made in the shape of a peacock with a tail of seed pearls, a buggy and a pair of matched bays, and a deed to a block of shares. He gave a dinner to every man on his shift and every woman in the chapel, and to Uncle Jabez and all the preachers on the circuit, and sent a purse to the miners' hospital. People said it was as if he were showing the world what she had coming to her. The night before she left, he sat with her in the front room and gave her his advice. She remembered it all her life and tried to write it down once and found it did not sound like much on paper. Don't carry out of the house what goes on in it, and don't carry into it what goes on in the street. Lend to them as pays back. Don't lend to them as don't. But to some you'll give whether they pay or no, and you'll know which. Sit easy at table and eat easy and sleep easy, and don't let them see y

sections.heading: III. The Dark Room
sections.text: What Dick Uglow kept in his parlor of a Sunday was mediums. He had come to it after his first wife died, the way a good many rich men did then. Now there were half a dozen of them who came to the house on Sundays and holidays and sat at his table and were paid. There was a Madame Vesper, who went into the cabinet, and a Professor Clary, who tied her in, and a pale young man who played the parlor organ in the dark, and others. On Thanksgiving and Christmas and New Year's they held a great circle in the ballroom at the top of the house, with the gas turned down to nothing and every guest holding the hands of the guests on either side, and out of Madame Vesper's black-curtained cabinet came the spirits in their muslin, glimmering, and walked among the circle and touched the sitters on the face. Dick Uglow believed his first wife came. He wept when she did. Tell Harry's wife to come up, he sent word on Thanksgiving. Tell her to come and pay her respects to our friends. Tamsin would not go. She could not look at them, she told her husband. She had seen Madame Vesper laughing in the back hall with her stockings rolled down and the muslin over her arm, and the professor with his hand on h

sections.heading: IV. Such Are My Preachers
sections.dateline: The small parlor · the same morning
sections.text: Tamsin put her sewing down. They're men that work, mostly, she said. Miners. A blacksmith. A man who keeps a store. They work all week and walk to chapel on Sunday and preach, and nobody pays them. They're quiet men. They're quiet when they walk and quiet when they stand. They look down when they pass you in the road, and they don't say much, and what they say you remember. What they do is decent, and what they say is gentle, and what they think, as near as I can tell, is clean. You'd not find a stain on Uncle Jabez if you turned him inside out. That's what my preachers are like. Most folks are up when they're paid and down when they're not. My preachers aren't paid, so they're neither. When the mine shut down at Rough and Ready and there were no wages for a year, Uncle Jabez was the same on Sunday as he'd been when we were all eating meat. Most folks are proud when they're well spoken of and sore when they're not. They called Uncle Jabez a fool in the Union, in print, for something he said about the saloons. He read it out at class meeting, the whole piece, and laughed, and went on to the next thing. Most folks are glad when they're praised and sick when they're blamed. My preache

sections.heading: V. Eight Handfuls
sections.text: She waited until the syringa bloomed. It grew along the carriage drive below the tower, the old-fashioned white mock orange that smells like a sweeter jasmine, and in the second week of June it came out all at once, so that the whole of Capitol Hill smelled of it in the evenings. She told the cook to lay in for a dinner of a hundred and to have it ready from the next noon on. Then in the long light of the evening she cut the syringa, armfuls of it, and carried it up the narrow stairs to the top of the tower, where there was a little railed walk around the roof. From there you could see the whole of the Front Range, west across the city and the plains, with the snow still on it in June, white and pink in the last of the sun, a hundred miles of it from Pikes Peak to Longs. And beyond it, she knew, more mountains, and the desert, and the Sierra, and Grass Valley. She faced west. She knelt on the tin roof, which was still warm from the day, and said the things she had been taught to say, and thought about Uncle Jabez for a long time, about his breathing and his hands and the way he stood at the front of the chapel waiting for people to finish coughing before he began. Then she stood up

sections.heading: VI. Five Hundred Roofs
sections.dateline: Over the mountains · the next morning
sections.text: Uncle Jabez chose five hundred men. He chose them by walking up Mill Street before sunup and down Main and out along the roads to the mines, stopping to get his breath, and putting his hand on a shoulder here and there. Men who had been sober the longest. Men who had never shorted a partner on a contract. Men who had sat up with the dying in the boarding houses and paid for the burying out of their own pay and never said whose. A good many of them were not Methodists. One was a Chinese cook from Boston Ravine who had been coming to class meeting in the back for two years without a word. One was Irish. Uncle Jabez did not seem to think it mattered. And they went through the air. That is how it is told in Grass Valley, and in Denver, and in Camborne, where it got to eventually by letter. Five hundred little houses with peaked roofs, like the cabins on the hills above the mines, one man in each, rose up off the flat at the foot of Mill Street at first light and went east together, over the Sierra and the snow, over the desert of Nevada and the salt and the Wasatch, over the Green River and the Laramie plains and the high peaks, and came down the long slope of the Front Range in the af

sections.heading: VII. The Snow
sections.text: The next summer silver broke. The price went from eighty-three cents an ounce to sixty-two, and the mines at Leadville shut down and the smelters went cold, and the banks in Denver failed one after another, and men who had owned whole streets were selling their carriages in the newspaper. Dick Uglow lost the most of it. Not all; he had John Trevenna's mine in Grass Valley, which was gold. But the most. They let the house on Capitol Hill go in 1895 and moved into a smaller one on Pearl Street, without a tower, with a little yard. Will Angove came there to supper every Sunday. Harry went to work for a mining company as a clerk. Grace kept house herself, with one girl. People who had known Dick Uglow in his silver days came to see how he was taking it. They were curious. They went away puzzled. He was the same, they said. He was easy. He was the same as he'd been before. He sat in his little yard in the evening in his shirtsleeves with his granddaughter on his knee and looked at the mountains, and when they asked him how he could bear it, he said that he had a daughter-in-law who had told him once what a man ought to be like, and he had been trying it for a year, and he found he liked

title: Eight Handfuls
place: Grass Valley, California, and Denver, Colorado
logline: A Cornish mine captain's daughter marries into Denver silver money and will not sit in her father-in-law's dark séance room.

verses.text: He alone who, without ceasing, practises the duty of sitting alone and sleeping alone, he, subduing himself, will rejoice in the destruction of all desires alone, as if living in a forest.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is among the shortest in the collection. An elder known to the whole fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen sat alone, walked alone and stood alone, and was called Ekavihārī, “the one who dwells alone.” The monks told the Buddha about his way of life, and the Buddha, instead of correcting him, exclaimed “Well done! Well done!” and praised the solitary life in this verse. After that, many people wished to live alone.
bg.history:
Basques had been in Buffalo, at the foot of the Big Horn Mountains, since at least 1902, and the town became one of the centers of Basque life in the Mountain West. A local radio station, KBBS, broadcast a weekly Basque-language program from 1956 to 2000. After the Second World War a shortage of herders led Congress to pass special “sheepherder laws,” and from 1950 to the mid-1970s the sheepmen’s Western Range Association brought several thousand Basques, mostly from Spain, to the West on three-year contracts. Herding was among the loneliest jobs in the country: a man spent the summer alone in the mountains with a band of sheep, a dog or two and a horse, supplied once a week by a camp tender. In town, the Basque boardinghouse was the herders’ home, and its keeper often served as their interpreter, postmaster and adviser. As wages rose in the Basque Country, the flow stopped, and by the mid-1970s fewer than a hundred Basque herders remained in the American West.

Across the West, herders left their marks on the bark of aspen groves: names, dates and hometowns, crosses, boats from fishing villages, women, the political slogan Gora Euskadi (“Long live the Basque Country”), and verses of longing for home. About 25,000 of these arborglyphs have been documented, and they are disappearing as the trees die. The Hotel Mendi, its people and the Lindgren outfit are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The End of the Table
sections.text: At the Hotel Mendi on Main Street the herders ate at one long table, family style, the bowls going hand to hand down both sides: garbanzos with chorizo, oxtail stew, lamb, of course, always lamb, a pot of red beans, bread, wine in pitchers whether you asked for it or not. In winter, when the sheep were down on the lower range along the Powder River and the men came into town by turns, there might be thirty at that table on a Saturday night, talking across each other in Basque and Spanish and the bad English of the contract, laughing, singing after the coffee. Fermín Arozena sat at the far end. Always the far end, where the table met the wall, and always with one empty chair between himself and the next man. He passed the bowls when they came to him. He answered when he was asked something, in a few words, politely. He did not sing. When he had eaten he carried his own plate to the kitchen, which nobody else did, and thanked the cook, and went up to his room, which was the single room at the end of the hall over the alley, the one with the narrow bed that the others didn’t want. In the morning he was gone before light. Joxe Etxeberri, who ran the bar downstairs and slept badly, woul

sections.heading: II. The Mountain
sections.text: In June they trailed the bands up out of the sagebrush onto the national forest, eight days of dust and bells and dogs, and then every herder was alone. That was the work. A man, a band of sheep, two dogs, a horse, a canvas tent or a wagon, a hundred square miles of mountain. The camp tender came up once a week, with the pickup as far as the road went and then with a packhorse. He brought flour, coffee, beans, canned milk and the mail, and he moved camp when the grass was eaten down. For the rest of the week the herder spoke to the dogs. Men did not do well with it. Everybody knew stories. A man from Bizkaia who had started answering the sheep in their own voice. A man who had walked down off the mountain one August without his band and was found in the stockyards in Billings with no shoes. Herders carved the aspens at the edges of the meadows: their names, the dates, the names of their villages, crosses, boats, hearts, women, verses about home and the girl and the mother who waited there. When you rode through an old grove you could read twenty years of loneliness on the white bark like the walls of a jail. Txomin Laka was the camp tender for the Lindgren bands that summer. He had

sections.heading: III. The Kitchen
sections.text: Gracieuse Irigaray, who owned the Hotel Mendi, was seventy-two. She had come over from a village above Baigorri in 1912 to marry a herder she had met twice. She had cooked in a sheep camp in the Big Horns for three summers herself, in a wagon, before he saved enough to buy the hotel, and she had run it alone since he died in 1949. She had fed perhaps two thousand herders at that long table. She had read their letters to them when they couldn’t and written their answers. She kept their money in the safe. She sat with them in the hospital, and she buried some of them. They called her Ama, every one of them, and she let them. The sheep came down at the end of September. By the second week of October the bands were on the winter range, and the men were coming through town, and they all, one way or another, ended up in her kitchen saying the same thing. Txomin told her first, standing by the stove with his hat in his hands. The empty chair. The clean bark. The man sitting at the edge of the trees until dark, not doing anything. Then the cook told her about the plate he carried to the kitchen, and the room nobody wanted. Joxe from the bar told her about the creek before light. Two of the

sections.heading: IV. The Edge of the Trees
sections.dateline: Buffalo and the Big Horns · 1965 and after
sections.text: Txomin told the others, and they told each other at the long table, in the bar, and in the sheep camps the next summer. It went around the way things went around among the Basques of that country, which is to say everywhere at once and slowly. Ama had said ondo. Ama had read the little book. Nobody could say afterward that anything much changed. But that next summer on the mountain there were herders who did not go down to Buffalo for the Fourth. There were men who sat at the tops of their meadows in the evening with their hats on their knees and did not take out their knives. Txomin noticed that some of the young ones he had worried about the summer before talked less fast when he came. Two of them asked him for the bands farthest out. One of them, a boy from Bizkaia who had carved his girlfriend’s name in fourteen trees the year before, carved nothing at all. Fermín signed on for a second contract, and then a third. He never married. When the Basque herders were mostly gone, in the seventies, when the young men stayed home in the factories of Navarre and Bizkaia and the outfits started bringing herders up from Peru instead, he stayed on in Wyoming and herded for the Lindgren gran

title: Clean Bark
logline: The herders and the camp tender worry about a Basque herder in the Big Horns who sits alone at the edge of the aspens.

verses.text: He who says what is not, goes to hell; he also who, having done a thing, says I have not done it. After death both are equal, they are men with evil deeds in the next world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, rival ascetics who have lost their followers and their gifts to the Buddha persuade a beautiful wandering nun, Sundarī, to ruin his name. Every evening she walks toward his monastery with garlands and perfumes, telling people she spends her nights with him, and every morning she walks back the same way. After some days the rivals pay men to kill her and throw her body on the heap of withered garlands near the Buddha's chamber, then report her missing to the king, lead the search, carry her body through the city, and cry out that the monks have murdered her to hide their teacher's sin. The whole city turns on the monks. The Buddha tells them only to answer with a verse about liars and deniers. The king's men find the killers quarrelling drunk over their pay, and the king makes the rivals go through the city proclaiming their own guilt and the Buddha's innocence. The same tale is told in the Udāna and the Jātaka.
bg.history:
Boley opened for settlement in 1903 on the allotment of Abigail Barnett, daughter of a Creek Freedman, and was incorporated in 1905. By 1911, the Oklahoma Historical Society records, it had more than four thousand people, two banks, three cotton gins, an electric plant, an ice plant and two colleges, and Booker T. Washington had visited and praised it; its Masonic Temple, finished around 1912, was said to be the tallest building between Okmulgee and Oklahoma City. The Freedmen of the Creek Nation, descendants of people the Creeks had enslaved, had been made Creek citizens by treaty and were allotted land on the Dawes Rolls. In 1908 Congress lifted all restrictions on the sale of Freedman land, adults' and minors' alike, and put minors' land under the county probate courts, where guardians could be appointed to manage it. The discovery of the Cushing oil field in 1912 made such land, and the papers that controlled it, far more valuable.

Oklahoma entered the Union dry in 1907, and home-brewed choc beer was sold on the quiet for decades. Boley was also a town that lived with fear. In May 1911 a crowd of white men took Laura Nelson and her son from the county jail at Okemah and hanged them from a bridge over the North Canadian River; hundreds came out to look, and the town photographer made pictures. Historians have read the photographs as a warning meant for Boley, and rumors that Boley men would retaliate set Okemah's men guarding Main Street. More on the lynching of Laura and L. D. Nelson.

sections.heading: I. The Porch
sections.text: Isaac Grayson read papers for nothing. That was the whole of it, at first. He had hung out his shingle on Main Street in the fall of 1911, a narrow frame office between the barbershop and the Farmers' Gin, with a back room where he slept on a cot. He was twenty-seven. His grandmother had been owned by a Creek family on the Arkansas River before the war, and after the war she was a Creek citizen with a Creek name, and when the Dawes men came with their books, Isaac and every one of his brothers and sisters had been enrolled as Creek Freedmen and allotted a hundred and sixty acres apiece. He had sold forty of his own to go to school. He had read law in a white lawyer's office in Muskogee, sweeping it out in the mornings, and passed the bar on the second try, and come home. He did not talk much. People said he talked in the courtroom like a Baptist preacher and everywhere else like a man who was paying for every word by the pound. In the evenings, when the heat let go a little, he carried his lamp and a kitchen chair out onto the porch of the office and sat there, and anybody who had a paper could bring it. A lease. A deed. A guardian's report from the county court. A letter from a ma

sections.heading: II. The Land Men
sections.dateline: Pettiford's Real Estate & Loan, Main Street · August
sections.text: Cyrus Pettiford had done very well indeed. He was a notary public and an agent for two lease companies in Okmulgee and a broker of farm loans, and he had sat in the front pew of the Baptist church for six years, and the county judge at Okemah had made him guardian of the allotments of eleven minor children, whose rents he collected and whose reports he filed, and nobody had ever in six years read one of those reports out loud. His partner was Lyle Ransom, who wrote letters for people who could not write, and read them their letters back for a dime, and had a way of reading a letter from a lease company so that it said what Pettiford needed it to say. They were not having a good summer. Since spring Pettiford had not closed one lease worth closing. Widows who had signed whatever he put in front of them for six years were coming into his office, sitting down, folding their hands, and saying, I believe I'll take that home and study on it. Which meant they would take it to the porch. Two of his wards' mothers had gone to the county court about the rents. Lyle Ransom had not read a letter for anybody since June. Men who used to tip their hats to Pettiford in the street now said Evening

sections.heading: III. The Flowers
sections.text: Every evening after that, when the lamp went out on the porch and the last of the line was walking home, Ora Lee Waters came down Main Street the other way, toward the gin, in her Sunday dress. She carried a fruit jar of zinnias from her mother's yard, and a bottle of bay rum from the drugstore, and a paper sack of oranges from the depot, and she walked slow, past the barbershop where the men sat out on the bench, past the pool hall, past the women on the porches. Where you going this late, Ora Lee? Going to sit up with the lawyer, she said. I sit up with him most every night. She went around behind the gin in the dark and through the cotton wagons and out the other side to Lyle Ransom's sister's house, and slept there. In the morning she came back up Main Street the same way, slow, with her hair half down, and when the women at the pump asked her where she had been all night she yawned and said, Where you think? I been with Lawyer Grayson. He don't let a girl get much sleep. And she laughed her laugh that you could hear across the street. Every morning Isaac Grayson found a jar of zinnias on his front step, or a bottle of bay rum, or oranges, and did not know where they came from,

sections.heading: IV. The Heap
sections.text: On Monday morning Cyrus Pettiford walked into the town marshal's office with his hat in his hand and his face drawn down long, and Lyle Ransom behind him. Marshal, Ora Lee Waters ain't come home. Her mother's out of her mind. Since Saturday night. Who'd she go with? Pettiford looked at the floor like a man who does not want to say a thing. Marshal, you know where she's been going nights. The whole town knows. What happened to her there, I couldn't say. The marshal was a big quiet man named Hollis Lee who had been a sergeant in the Tenth Cavalry and did not like Pettiford and did not like Grayson much either, because he did not like lawyers. He looked at Pettiford a while. Then go look, he said. They went to look. They took a dozen men with them, men from Pettiford's church and Ransom's lodge, and they went straight down Main Street to the gin, and around behind it, and Pettiford stood back with his hands folded while the others poked at the heap with cotton hooks, and it was Ransom who called out. She was lying in the zinnias. Somebody had hit her once on the side of the head and thrown her up on the heap like a sack, and she had rolled a little way down the slope of dead flowers,

sections.heading: V. What Shall Be Said
sections.text: By dark the whole town had it. By the next day the whole county. Pettiford's people went from porch to porch, and to the barbershop, and the gins, and the two colleges, and out into the bottoms on horseback, saying it. See what they did. See what the lawyer's people did. The ones who believed it said it to the ones who didn't, and after a while the ones who didn't stopped saying anything. It fell on the people who had stood in the line. Not on Isaac. On them. A widow who had taken her lease to the porch had a cup of coffee thrown on her in the bank. A young man who had been read his own guardian's report out loud, and had gone to the county court about it, was knocked down outside the pool hall by two of Pettiford's lodge brothers and kicked. Old Aunt Sukey Grant, who had been born in the Creek Nation in 1838 and could not read one word, was spat at on the board sidewalk by a girl of fourteen. Children chanted it in the schoolyard. The people from the line stopped going to the post office. They stopped going to church. On the Wednesday night seven or eight of them came to the back door of the office, because they did not dare come to the front any more, and stood in the back room a

sections.heading: VI. Choc Beer
sections.dateline: The bottoms below Boley · Saturday night
sections.text: The marshal had not been idle. On the Tuesday he had sent for his deputy, a young man named Elias Moore who had been raised in the bottoms and knew every still and choc joint between Boley and the Canadian, and told him, Go find out if anybody else did this. Oklahoma had been dry since statehood. That did not stop anybody. Down in the river bottoms below town there was a woman named Mattie who brewed choc beer in a washtub out of barley and hops and anything else that would work, the beer people called Choctaw beer from the old Territory days, and sold it out of her kitchen on Saturday nights by the dipper, and the oil field men came over from the Cushing field on payday because in Boley nobody looked twice at a colored man with money. Two of them were there that Saturday. They had been there the Saturday before, too, and had been spending free. Elias Moore sat in the corner of Mattie's kitchen with a dipper he did not drink from and listened to them get drunk. It took till midnight. Then the bigger one wanted the other one to pay for the round, and the other one said he had paid for the last three, and the bigger one said something about who had done the work, and the other one st

sections.heading: VII. The Temple Steps
sections.text: The two men told it all in the marshal's office before daylight on Sunday. The forty dollars apiece. Who paid it. The pick handle. The heap. They had not even known her name. On Monday morning Hollis Lee walked down Main Street with Elias Moore beside him and a shotgun under his arm and went into Pettiford's Real Estate & Loan and came out with Cyrus Pettiford, and then went three doors down and came out with Lyle Ransom, and walked them both up the middle of the street to the steps of the Masonic Temple, where the girl had lain under the sheet all week until her mother took her home to Castle to bury her. By then the whole town was following. He did not take them to Okemah. Not yet. He stood them on the Temple steps in front of everybody in Boley, and the mayor came out of the bank and stood beside him, and the marshal said, not loud, the way a sergeant says a thing he is only going to say once: You carried her up this street and told them who did it. Now you tell them. Pettiford looked at the crowd. He was a man who had talked his way out of a great many things. He opened his mouth, and the first thing that came out of the crowd at him, before he could say a word, was an old woma

title: The Deed Reading
logline: In an all-Black Oklahoma town, a young lawyer reads land papers aloud for free, and the land men he is costing go looking for a girl.

verses.text: Many men whose shoulders are covered with the yellow gown are ill-conditioned and unrestrained; such evil-doers by their evil deeds go to hell.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Mahā Moggallāna, known for his psychic powers, is coming down from Vulture’s Peak with the elder Lakkhaṇa when he sees hungry ghosts (petas) in the form of skeletons, and smiles. Lakkhaṇa asks why. This is not the time, Moggallāna says; ask me in the presence of the Teacher. Before the Buddha he tells what he saw: a monk flying through the air with his body on fire, and five companions behind him, their bowls, robes and girdles all burning. The Buddha explains that these were monks who had gone forth under an earlier Buddha, Kassapa, and had not lived by what they took on, and he speaks the verse to the monks sitting before him; many of them reach the first stage of awakening. The Pāli verse speaks of those with the ochre robe “around the neck.” Read the full commentary story. Nora’s sentence is from Nathaniel Hawthorne’s “Young Goodman Brown”, first published in 1835 and collected in Mosses from an Old Manse (1846); the story ends with Brown living out his life in suspicion of everyone he knows.
bg.history:
In January 2002 the Boston Globe’s Spotlight team began publishing its investigation of how the Archdiocese of Boston had handled priests who abused children, beginning with John Geoghan, who was accused of abusing more than 130 children and had been moved from parish to parish. The coverage ran all year. It led to criminal prosecutions, hundreds of civil suits and, in 2003, a Pulitzer Prize for Public Service; in 2011 the archdiocese published a list of 159 priests credibly accused. See the sexual abuse scandal in the Boston archdiocese.

In early December the archdiocese released thousands of pages of personnel files under court order. On December 9, fifty-eight Boston priests signed a letter asking Cardinal Bernard Law to resign, and on Friday, December 13, he resigned, as America reported. Two days later came the third Sunday of Advent, called Gaudete or Rose Sunday, when the priest may wear rose instead of violet. The Mission Church, the Redemptorists’ basilica on Parker Hill in Mission Hill, was dedicated in 1878. St. Ita’s and its people are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Father Rafferty
sections.text: For thirty-five years Frank Dineen drew a priest. The strip was called Father Rafferty, four panels a week, and it ran in diocesan papers from Boston to Sacramento between 1959 and 1994. Father Rafferty was a curate in a city parish with a bad knee and a worse car. He lost at checkers to the altar boys. He hid from the pastor in the confessional to eat his lunch. He had a round face and a cowlick, and Frank drew around his head, whenever he was doing something kind, five or six short pen lines, the way you draw a lamp to show that it is lit. Readers wrote in about the lines. Nuns cut the strip out and pinned it to bulletin boards. Frank drew it at a slant-top table in the attic of a three-decker on Ashmont Street, and for the first eleven years the model for Father Rafferty's face was whichever curate was newest at St. Ita's down the hill. He retired the strip when his hand began to shake, and after his wife died he kept on drawing for himself, people on the Red Line, his neighbors, the gulls at Malibu Beach. He had a way of seeing a face. His wife used to say he could look at a man across a wake and tell you what the man's mother had looked like. In January of 2002 the Globe began

sections.heading: II. Parker Hill
sections.text: On the Saturday after the cardinal resigned they buried Frank's old friend Tom Grealish from the Mission Church on Tremont Street, the big gray basilica with the two spires on the side of Parker Hill. Kevin concelebrated. Afterward, because it was a dry cold afternoon and Frank wanted the air, the two of them walked down through the streets below the hill toward the Orange Line, Kevin in his black overcoat and collar, Frank in his good hat. People looked at the collar. One man on a stoop said something, and Kevin nodded to him as if he had said good afternoon. It was nearly dark. The sun had gone down behind the hill and the sky over the city was green going to blue. They had come to the corner of Tremont and were waiting for the light when Frank stopped talking. Kevin looked at him and then looked where he was looking, up over the roofs, and saw nothing. A plane coming into Logan. The first stars. Frank was smiling. It was not a big smile. It was the smile Kevin had seen on him at the drafting table when a face finally came right, a small private one, at one side of the mouth. Uncle Frank. What is it? Not here, said Frank. Ask me at Nora's. Ask me in front of Nora. He did not say

sections.heading: III. The Sacristy
sections.text: The next morning was the third Sunday of Advent, Gaudete Sunday, when the purple of the season lets up for a day and the priest wears rose. Nora Healy had the rose vestments out on the long counter in the sacristy at seven, the chasuble on its padded hanger, the stole, the alb pressed the night before, the amice folded square, the cincture coiled in a flat white spiral like a rope on the deck of a boat. She was eighty. She had ironed for every priest in that house for fifty-one years, and three women from the altar guild who were not much younger were with her, folding purificators at the table under the window. Frank came in with Kevin at a quarter past seven and sat on the radiator in his coat. Kevin started to vest. He put the amice on his shoulders and tied the strings, and then he stopped. Ask him, said Nora, without turning around. She had been watching them since they came in. Yesterday on Tremont Street, Kevin said. He smiled at something. Up over the roofs. I asked him what it was and he said to ask him in front of you. The women at the table had stopped folding. Frank took off his hat. Six priests, he said. Going over the city at about the height of the steeple, toward th

sections.heading: IV. Rose
sections.text: Frank stayed on the radiator through the eight o'clock. He could see a slice of the sanctuary through the sacristy door, Kevin at the altar in rose, which on a young man in that light looks almost white, the color of the inside of a shell. Mrs. Coughlin's grandson was not there. The church was a third full, which in December of 2002 was a good Sunday. There was a pad of Mass cards by the sacristy phone. Frank took one, and the ballpoint pen on its chain, and turned the card over and drew Kevin from where he sat, in profile, lifting the host at the consecration, the chasuble falling from his raised arms, the cowlick standing up at the back. It took him about a minute. His hand did not shake. When he was done he looked at it a long time. Then he left it on the counter by the rose stole's empty hanger, face up, for Nora, with no lines around the head.

title: Rose Sunday
place: Mission Hill and Dorchester, Boston, Massachusetts
logline: The weekend Boston's cardinal resigns, an old cartoonist who drew a kindly priest for thirty-five years sees something over Mission Hill and smiles.

verses.text: Better it would be to swallow a heated iron ball, like flaring fire, than that a bad unrestrained fellow should live on the charity of the land.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, which takes the story from the monastic rule, a group of monks who are friends spend the rainy season on the banks of the Vaggumudā river in a year of famine, when the crops have turned to straw. They talk over how to get fed. Some propose working for the householders, others carrying their messages. They settle on praising one another to the householders as men of high spiritual attainment. The people, delighted, give them food they do not eat themselves or give to their own parents, children and workers. When the rains end and the monks of the region gather before the Buddha, the rest are gaunt and these are sleek. He asks how they fared, though he knows; they tell him; he asks whether the claims were true, rebukes them, and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
The farm crisis of the 1980s was the worst time on the land since the Depression. The average value of an acre of Minnesota farmland fell from $1,165 in 1982 to $700 in 1987, while the debts taken on against the higher figure stayed. The state began a Farm Advocate program in 1984 and required lenders to offer mediation before foreclosure in 1986; more than 600 Minnesota farmers still filed for bankruptcy in 1987. Corn that fall brought well under two dollars a bushel. It was also the year the television ministries of Jim Bakker and Oral Roberts were in the news for months. The Harvest Workers, Vang and the Skog church are invented; Swift County and Benson are real.

The 1987 World Series ran from October 17 to October 25, and the home team won every game. Game Six, on Saturday the twenty-fourth, started at three in the afternoon Central time, the last Series game played by day. The Twins trailed 5–2, and Kent Hrbek's grand slam in the sixth inning put it away, 11–5. They won the seventh game the next night. Herb Carneal and John Gordon called the games on WCCO radio, which reaches most of the Upper Midwest, and the Homer Hanky was new that October.

sections.heading: I. The Placement
sections.text: The corn was good that year, and it did not matter. It was knee-high well before the Fourth and the color of a pool table, and a bushel of it was worth about a dollar and a half. Land that had brought eleven hundred dollars an acre five years before brought seven hundred if it brought anything. There were men in the county with ten thousand bushels in the bin and a wife who drove to the food shelf in Benson on Thursdays, in the next town over's car if she could borrow it, so the neighbors would not know the plates. Reuben Lindquist had cried farm sales in six counties for forty years. Everybody called him Colonel, as they called every auctioneer. In the spring of 1984 he sold out the son of a man he had sold out in 1934, put his cane and his hat in the closet, and never took a sale bill again. He was seventy-six now, a widower with eighty acres rented out, and what he did was run the Harvest Workers. It was a small thing and it was his own. Winters, twenty or so young people sat in the old creamery at Vang and he took them through the Bible a book at a time. Summers he put them out in twos and fours with country congregations that had lost their pastor or could not pay one, from th

sections.heading: II. Three Ways
sections.dateline: The Skog parsonage · the second week
sections.text: The parsonage had been empty two years. The congregation stocked its kitchen the first Sunday, and what they stocked it with told the four of them everything: a sack of macaroni, a block of the government cheese, two jars of beans, a dozen eggs, and a note saying somebody would bring milk. By the second week it was gone, and they sat down at the kitchen table to talk about the summer the way you would talk about a long drive on a quarter tank. We could work for them, Curt said. Walk beans. Chop silage in September. A man feeds his help. You don't have to break your back, said Lori. Half these places the woman's working nights at the turkey plant and the old folks can't drive. We run their errands. Take Grandma to the clinic, carry word between the places. They'd keep us for that. Todd let them both finish. He was the one who could talk. There's no call for either. Think what they're hungry for out here. All we have to do is speak well of each other. He laid it out. When Curt was out of the room, the rest would let it be known that Curt had the gift of healing, that there was a woman in Montevideo with her goiter gone. Lori got a word of knowledge; she knew what was wrong in a house

sections.heading: III. The Tables
sections.text: It went through the township in ten days. People had watched the television preachers come apart that spring, the one in Carolina with his secretary and the one in Tulsa who said God would call him home if the money did not come in. Here were four clean young people who asked for nothing, each one too modest to speak of his own gift, so that you had to hear of it from the others. Nothing so good had come to Skog before, people said, and they said it to one another in the church basement with real gladness. And they fed them. Marlys Thorson took the last white package marked ROAST out of the chest freezer, from the steer they had butchered in 1985, and set it in the sink to thaw. Her own three ate buttered noodles at the counter that week and were told to go outside while company was at the table. Old Arne Dahl opened his wife's pears, with 1983 on the lid in her hand, which he had not been able to open since the funeral. The Schmiesings had Curt pray over a boy's ears and sent him home with a pie, a quart of pickled beets and four dollars in an envelope. Nobody's hired man got a second plate that summer, and nobody's mother in the nursing home got her Sunday chicken brought in. It

sections.heading: IV. Game Six
sections.dateline: The Lindquist place, south of Vang · Saturday, October 24
sections.text: The Workers came in to the Colonel's yard that Saturday, as they did every fall, by ones and twos in borrowed cars. Most of them looked like the country they had come out of. The pair from Appleton had walked beans in July and forked silage in September, and the cords stood out in their necks. A girl who had been alone at Louriston had gone a whole size down in her dress, and her hands were split at the knuckles. They had eaten what their houses ate. The four from Skog got out of Todd's Citation sleek as seals. The Colonel was in the machine shed with the big door open and the barn radio turned up across the yard so he could hear it. The game had started at three, the only one of the Series played in the afternoon. He was selling his old pickup and wanted the hitch ball off it first, and the nut had rusted solid to the shank. So he had the drawbar in the vise and the torch on it. He greeted each of them as they came in without turning the flame aside. You kept well? You got by up there? Got fed without trouble? We kept well, Todd said. We got by fine. We had no trouble at all. He had known since August. He had stood in every one of those yards and he still drank coffee in most of t

title: The Hitch Ball
logline: In the farm crisis, four Bible-school friends find a way to eat well among families who cannot, with the Series on a barn radio.

verses.text: Four things does a wreckless man gain who covets his neighbour’s wife,—a bad reputation, an uncomfortable bed, thirdly, punishment, and lastly, hell.

There is bad reputation, and the evil way (to hell), there is the short pleasure of the frightened in the arms of the frightened, and the king imposes heavy punishment; therefore let no man think of his neighbour’s wife.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Khema, a rich man’s son and nephew of the great donor Anāthapiṇḍika, is so handsome that women who see him cannot help themselves, and he runs after other men’s wives. Three times the king’s men arrest him at night, and three times the king, ashamed before the boy’s father, lets him go without a word. When the father hears, he takes his son to the Buddha and makes him tell the whole story, and the Buddha answers with these verses; Khema is stirred to conscience and enters the stream. The commentary explains his beauty by a past life: as a champion wrestler in the time of an earlier Buddha, he planted two colored banners on a golden shrine and wished that every woman who saw him, except his kinswomen, would fall in love with him.
bg.history:
In the summer of 2009 a Stryker brigade from Fort Lewis deployed to Kandahar province in the war in Afghanistan and took heavy losses in the Arghandab valley that autumn. On February 1, 2010, Fort Lewis and McChord Air Force Base merged into Joint Base Lewis–McChord, the Army’s main installation west of the Rockies, beside Lakewood and Tacoma. Deaths are reported to families in person by a uniformed casualty notification team. Adultery that brought discredit on the service was a crime under Article 134 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice; since 2019 the offense has been called extramarital sexual conduct. Soldiers have long sung about “Jody,” the civilian who stays home with your girl, in the marching chants called jody calls.

Samoan Americans have served in the U.S. armed forces in large numbers since the Second World War, and the Seattle–Tacoma area has one of the larger Samoan communities on the mainland; the first Samoan Christian Congregational church in Washington was founded in southeast Seattle in 1964. Washington’s high school wrestling championships, Mat Classic, are held each February in the Tacoma Dome. The Reverend Elisaia reads Proverbs from the Samoan Bible translated by the London Missionary Society, and then from the English Revised Version of 1885.

sections.heading: I. The Rear Detachment
sections.text: Everyone in Lakewood who knew the Aumua family knew that the youngest son was too good-looking, and said so, the way you might say a house was too close to the river. Iosefa Aumua was twenty-two. He had his mother's eyes, long-lashed and slow, and his father's shoulders, and a smile that he did not seem to know he was using. When he was small the aunties at church passed him from lap to lap and pinched his cheeks until he cried. When he was fifteen the girls from three high schools came to his wrestling meets and sat together in the bleachers in a row and did not watch the other matches. At seventeen he won the state title at his weight at Mat Classic in the Tacoma Dome, pinned a boy from Yakima in the third period, and when the referee raised his arm the noise from the Samoan side of the stands was so loud that people on the other mats stopped to look. His father was Tavita Aumua, Command Sergeant Major, retired. Thirty years in the Army, three wars, a Bronze Star from Mosul he never spoke of, and on the Samoan side of Lakewood he held the family's chiefly title and was called Leaupepe, and on the other side everybody from the post commander's driver to the Korean grocer on South

sections.heading: II. The First Time
sections.text: The military police found him at two in the morning in the second week of August, coming over the back fence of a duplex in the family housing, with his shoes in his hand. A neighbor had called it in as a prowler. Two MPs came with flashlights and put him against their car and asked him what he was doing, and he told them the truth, more or less, because he could not think of anything else, and one of them laughed and the other did not. They took him to the station. In the morning, because he was a soldier, they called his unit, and his unit sent the rear detachment commander, a tired major named Ochoa who had three hundred families to look after and a list on his office wall of the brigade's wounded and dead that grew every week. Major Ochoa had been a lieutenant in Mosul in 2004, and the platoon sergeant beside him there had been a staff sergeant named Tavita Aumua, who had kept him alive at least twice and taught him most of what he knew about being an officer. He read the blotter. He looked through the glass at Sefa, sitting on the bench in the hallway in yesterday's T-shirt with his shoes still in his hand, and he saw the Sergeant Major's face in the boy's face, and he felt so

sections.heading: III. The Knock
sections.dateline: An apartment off Gravelly Lake Drive · September
sections.text: It happened again. The second woman's husband was a specialist in the scouts, and she lived in an apartment complex outside the gate, off Gravelly Lake Drive, with a view of the parking lot and a picture of him in his uniform on the television. She was twenty years old. She had come out from Ohio to marry him a month before he deployed, and she did not know anyone in Washington, and it rained. At six-thirty on a Sunday morning in September, somebody knocked on her door. Sefa woke at the sound and saw her face. She was sitting straight up in the bed, with the sheet held against her, absolutely still, and her face had gone the color of the wall. Every wife at Fort Lewis knew about the knock. The Army did not tell you on the telephone. When your husband was killed the Army sent two soldiers in dress greens to your door, an officer and a chaplain, and they stood on your step until you opened it, and you knew before they said a word. They came between six in the morning and ten at night. Every woman in that apartment complex had at some point looked out a window at a car pulling into the lot and stopped breathing until it parked in front of somebody else's door. That autumn the brigade'

sections.heading: IV. The Third Time
sections.text: The third time it was a Samoan woman, and that was the end of it, because there are no secrets on the Samoan side of Lakewood. Her husband was a sergeant in the same brigade, from a family in Carson that knew the Aumuas, and her mother-in-law sang in the same church choir as Sefa's mother. The MPs caught him in the parking lot of her building at four in the morning, sitting in his truck with the engine off, waiting for her neighbor's lights to go out. There was nothing on the blotter but a man in a truck. Major Ochoa let him go a third time, and said nothing a third time, and went home and told his wife he did not know what he was going to do. But by the next Sunday the women of the church knew. By Sunday night the men knew, and by Monday morning Sefa's uncle Pita knew, because Pita knew everything that happened among the Samoans of Pierce County, sooner or later, across his kitchen table. Pita was the Sergeant Major's older brother. He had never been in the Army. He had worked thirty years on the docks at the Port of Tacoma, and since he retired he had done one thing, which was feed people. Every Sunday after church his house on the Hilltop filled up with whoever was hungry, young

sections.heading: V. The Faifeau
sections.dateline: The parsonage, South Tacoma · that evening
sections.text: The Reverend Elisaia Tuilagi had come to Seattle from Apia in 1964, the year the first Samoan Congregational church in Washington was started in the south end of Seattle, and he had been the pastor of the Samoan church in Tacoma for thirty-one years. He was seventy-nine. He had baptized Sefa, and Sefa's older brothers and sisters, and he had married the Sergeant Major's daughters and buried the Sergeant Major's mother. He was a heavy, slow, silent man with a white crew cut and enormous hands, and on Sundays he preached in Samoan for an hour and the children slept against their mothers and the old people wept, and on weekdays he hardly spoke at all. His wife let them in. The parsonage smelled of fried bananas and of the rain. The Reverend Elisaia was sitting in an armchair in the front room, under a framed picture of the church in Apia where he had been ordained, with his Bible on his knee, and he did not get up. The Sergeant Major sat down on the couch. Sefa remained standing, because nobody told him to sit. Faifeau, said his father, my son has something to tell you. And then, to Sefa, in the voice that had once carried across parade grounds: All of it. So Sefa told the old man all

sections.heading: VI. The Ribbons
sections.dateline: The church on South Tacoma Way · November
sections.text: He went to Major Ochoa the next morning, by himself, and asked to make a statement. The major looked at him for a long moment, then got out the form. Sefa took an Article 15 that winter and a reduction in rank, and a letter in his file that followed him the rest of his time in the Army, and he did not complain about any of it. In January he wrote three letters, and the Reverend Elisaia read them and told him to burn two of them, and he did, and mailed the third, to the husband in Carson's family, who did not answer. Some debts are not paid. He knew that now. He went to the chapel on post every Thursday that the memorials went on, and stood at the very back, by the door, in uniform, and left before the end, so as not to be seen. The women stopped looking at him. Or perhaps they looked at him the same as before, and he did not notice, because he no longer looked back. His mother said that his face had changed; that it was the same face, and that she could not explain it. Uncle Pita said it was simpler than that. He said the boy had finally put down a fork and gone to wash the dishes. On the Sunday before Thanksgiving, after the service, the Reverend Elisaia called Sefa over to the fr

title: Two Ribbons
logline: While his brigade fights in Kandahar, a retired sergeant major's handsome son stays behind and becomes the Jody of the cadences.

verses.text: As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell.
An act carelessly performed, a broken vow, and hesitating obedience to discipline, all this brings no great reward.
If anything is to be done, let a man do it, let him attack it vigorously! A careless pilgrim only scatters the dust of his passions more widely.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk thoughtlessly breaks off a single blade of grass, and, troubled in conscience, asks another monk what happens to a monk who does that. The other tells him nothing happens; he has only to confess it and he is free; and to show him, he seizes a clump of grass with both hands and pulls it up. The monks report it to the Buddha, who rebukes him soundly and speaks the three verses on grass wrongly grasped, the lax deed and the careless wanderer. The stubborn monk afterward becomes steady in restraint and reaches awakening. Read the full commentary story, or about the Vinaya, the monastic discipline, whose list of rules for monks says that "the damaging of a living plant is to be confessed" (the Bhikkhu Pāṭimokkha, tr. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu).
bg.history:
Peachtree City, south of Atlanta in Fayette County, was chartered in 1959 as a planned community of villages, among them Aberdeen, Braelinn, Glenloch and Kedron, each with its own shops, schools and recreation. Miles of paved paths connect the neighborhoods, churches and schools, and residents drive golf carts on them as an ordinary way of getting around. On June 20, 2006, the 217th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), meeting in Birmingham, voted 298 to 221 to adopt an authoritative interpretation, drawn from the 1729 Adopting Act, under which a candidate for ordination may declare a "scruple" and the ordaining body decides whether it departs from essentials of the church's standards (Presbyterian News Service, via Worldwide Faith News). The church, the course and the people in the story are invented.

Under the Rules of Golf in force in 2006, a player who improved the lie of the ball by bending or breaking anything growing was penalized two strokes in stroke play (USGA, Rule 13); golf is unusual among sports in expecting players to call penalties on themselves. A ball may be declared unplayable anywhere except in a water hazard, at a cost of one stroke. Pampas grass, an ornamental from South America planted widely in Southern yards and developments in the late twentieth century, has leaves with fine saw-toothed edges that cut skin easily (LawnLove).

sections.heading: I. The Seventh Hole
sections.text: Monday was the day off, and on Mondays the two associate pastors of Aberdeen Presbyterian Church played eighteen at Line Creek, the public course on the south side of town, with a 7:10 tee time that Brad Tolleson had held every week for six years and would not give up for funerals. They drove over on the cart path from their houses, past the Kroger and the middle school and the long fingers of Lake Peachtree, in Brad’s cart, which had a church parking sticker on the windshield and a cup holder he had installed himself that would hold a Chick-fil-A sweet tea in the large size. Gene Wofford and Ron Kiser, both elders, made up the foursome. Gene had been a mechanic for Delta for thirty-one years and still looked up at every plane. Scott Lindahl was the associate for pastoral care. He was thirty-nine and kind and nearly always somewhere else in his head, usually a hospital room. Brad was the associate for discipleship, which meant the youth and the men’s breakfast and the mission trip to Honduras. He was forty-six and had sold corporate travel accounts for Delta before seminary and could still close anything. People in the congregation said that Scott was the one you wanted when your m

sections.heading: II. The Grill Room
sections.dateline: Line Creek clubhouse · the same morning
sections.text: The Monday ladies’ nine had finished early and were in the grill room at the round table by the window, under the television, eating chicken salad. Dot Huckaby was at the end of the table. She was seventy-six. She had been an operating-room nurse at Piedmont Hospital in Atlanta for forty-one years, scrub and then circulating and then in charge of the whole floor, and when she retired to Peachtree City she had joined Aberdeen Presbyterian and become a ruling elder, and then the chair of the personnel committee, which was the committee to which both associate pastors answered. She drove a green cart with a Braves magnet on the back. She kept a first-aid kit under the seat of it that would have done credit to a small hospital. Gene came in ahead of the others and went straight to her. Dot, you’re not going to believe what your preachers just did. She did not ask. She went out to her cart and came back with the kit and a bottle of water, and sat Brad down on a chair at the next table, and unwrapped the towels, and looked at his hands for a long time without saying anything, turning them over in hers. Then she washed them, one at a time, with the water, over a stack of paper napkins, wh

sections.heading: III. Monday
sections.text: Brad did not play for three Mondays. He preached on the second Sunday of October with both hands taped, and held them up at the start of the sermon and told the congregation exactly how it had happened, every word he had said on the seventh hole, and then preached on something else entirely, and the youth group talked about it for a month. Something changed in him after that, though nobody at Aberdeen Presbyterian could have said exactly when. He started returning phone calls the same day. He stopped telling the story about the mission trip to Honduras in which he was the hero. The youth noticed that when he said he would be somewhere, he was there, early. When the personnel committee did his review in the spring, Dot Huckaby wrote one line in the comments box, in her square nurse’s hand, and nobody else on the committee ever saw what it said. On the fourth Monday of October he was back on the first tee at 7:10, with new pink lines across both palms where the cuts had closed, and a rule book in his back pocket, the little USGA one that nobody ever carries. The dew was still on the fairways. Every ball that rolled through it left a dark line behind it, curving where the ground curve

title: Two Strokes
logline: On their Monday off, two associate pastors of a suburban Presbyterian church argue on the seventh hole about a single blade of grass.

verses.text: An evil deed is better left undone, for a man repents of it afterwards; a good deed is better done, for having done it, one does not repent.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is one of the shortest in the collection. A woman of Sāvatthi learns that her husband has lain with a servant of the house. She binds the servant hand and foot, cuts off her nose and ears, shuts her in a hidden room, and then, to cover what she has done, takes her husband to the monastery to hear the teaching. Relatives come visiting, open the door and release the servant, who walks to the monastery and tells the Buddha what happened in front of the whole assembly. He says that no one should do even a small wrong thinking that others will not know, since a hidden deed still burns afterward, and speaks the verse. Husband and wife are changed by it, free the servant on the spot, and she becomes a follower.
bg.history:
Slavery in New York ended slowly. A law of 1799 freed no one then living; it declared children born to enslaved mothers after July 4 of that year free, but bound them to serve the mother’s master until twenty-five if female and twenty-eight if male, and required each birth to be reported to the town clerk. A second law in 1817 set July 4, 1827, as the day everyone born before 1799 would go free. Until then a master could manumit by a written paper, with the town’s overseers of the poor certifying that the person was under fifty and able to support herself; the wording in the story follows surviving certificates. More on slavery in New York. Ulster County’s farm country was among the last strongholds. Its slaveholders were largely “that class of people called Low Dutch,” in the words of Sojourner Truth, who was born there about 1797, grew up speaking only Dutch, slept as a child in a slaveholder’s cellar, and walked away from her last master in 1826. Pinkster, the Dutch Whitsuntide, was the great holiday of enslaved New Yorkers in the Hudson Valley, several days free of work. In 1826 it fell on May 14.

The voorlezer was the lay reader of a Dutch Reformed congregation, usually also its schoolmaster and often the keeper of the village records; when no minister was present he read the scripture and led the psalms. The title was fading by 1800 and Dutch preaching with it (New Paltz, nearby, went over wholly to English in 1817), though the language lingered in Hudson Valley kitchens for generations. The Dutch readings in the story, the church at the Steenkill and all its people are invented. The earmarks are not: New York towns kept registers of the cuts by which each farmer knew his sheep and hogs, entered in just such words as “a crop on the left ear and a slit in the same.” The scripture is the Dutch States Bible (Statenvertaling) of 1637, with the King James Version beneath it.

sections.heading: I. The Mark Book
sections.text: Meester Wessel Brink had been voorlezer of the stone church at the Steenkill for forty-one years. He had kept the school beside it for most of those, and for thirty he had kept the town’s books as well, because he wrote the clearest hand between Hurley and the mountains. One of the books was the mark book. Every farmer on the flats turned his sheep onto the commons and his hogs into the oak woods, and a man knew his own in the fall by the cut of their ears, and the cut was the Meester’s to write down. Petrus Oosterhoudt, a halfpenny under each ear. Widow Roosa, a swallow fork in the right. Jacobus Krom, his mark: a crop off the left ear and a slit in the right. Recorded this 2d day of April 1798. For the first pages he had drawn a small sheep’s head beside each entry, with the ears done carefully. After that the town grew and he left off drawing. He was seventy-nine now. The consistory called him the clerk, and the town had voted in a younger man for its books, and the dominie rode over from Rochester three Sundays in five and preached in English. But on the Sundays between, the old people still came, and the Meester stood at his desk under the pulpit and read them a chapter out of

sections.heading: II. The Cellar Stairs
sections.text: Jacobus began coming down the cellar stairs after New Year, when his wife was asleep. Dina slept on a straw tick by the cellar hearth. There was no door between her and the stairs and nobody within call. Nobody had ever asked Dina whether she was willing about anything, and Jacobus did not begin then. He did not think of himself as a hard man. He brought her a paper of brown sugar once from Kingston, and a ribbon, which she put in the fire. By April Trijntje knew. There was the fourth stair, which spoke. There was tallow on the cuff of his nightshirt, and they burned no tallow upstairs. One night she got up after him and stood at the head of the stairs in the dark with her hand on the wall, and listened as long as she could stand to, and went back to bed and lay with her eyes open until the window turned grey. She said nothing to him. She had been angry with Jacobus Krom for twenty-six years over smaller matters, and she knew the size of that anger and what it could not move. This was something else, and it wanted a place to go. It went down the stairs. She watched Dina carry the milk. She watched her bend to the fire. She watched the canal men at the door with their hats in their

sections.heading: III. Pinkster
sections.text: Jacobus came home after midnight and went straight up. In the morning there was no fire in the cellar and no milk on the table. She is gone, Trijntje said. Her bed was not slept in. To the canal, I expect. They have been at the door all spring. Jacobus stood with one boot on. Something went across his face, and she saw that part of it was relief, and hated him freshly for it. With ten months left, he said. It makes no sense. When did that kind ever make sense? And then, with her back to him, taking her black silk out of the kas: Kom, man. It is Pinkster. Let us go and hear the Meester read. He stared at her. It was an off Sunday, with no dominie. She had not sat through the Dutch reading in ten years. She said the old man’s voice put her to sleep and the psalms ran so slow you could knit a stocking between the lines. It is Pinkster, she said again. People will look for us. That was the whole of her reason, and she had found it in the night. Whatever was discovered, and whenever, the entire church should be able to say where Trijntje Krom was on Pinkster morning. She was in her pew with her psalm book, among them, where she belonged. Kees drove. It was a soft bright day. Along the w

sections.heading: IV. The Visit
sections.dateline: The Krom farm · the same morning
sections.text: Petrus Oosterhoudt was Trijntje’s brother, and his wife Lena had fried olykoeks on Saturday, a whole crock of them, and said it was a shame to eat them alone on a holiday with a sister three miles off. They drove over from Hurley after an early breakfast, meaning to surprise her. They found the door on the latch, the way every door on the flats was, and nobody at home. Gone to church, said Petrus. On an off Sunday. My sister. Lena went down to the cellar kitchen to blow up the fire for coffee. The hearth was cold. She was on her knees with the bellows when she heard it, a slow knocking, like a shutter loose in a small wind, except that there was no wind. It came from behind the vinegar barrel. It took the two of them to roll the barrel. Petrus opened the plank door and the light went in. Lena had known Dina since the week she was born. She had held her at Bet’s burying. She did not know her now for the space of a breath. Then she did, and she made a sound and got down on the bricks and began to pick at the knots, and Petrus cut them with his clasp knife, and they brought her out to the hearth. Petrus was a farmer. He looked once at the ears and knew what he was looking at, the way

sections.heading: V. The Aisle
sections.text: The Meester had finished the chapter and was finding the psalm when the door opened at the back and the light came up the aisle. She did not take the gallery stair. She came up the middle of the church, past the pews with the names on the doors, as far as the open place under the pulpit where they set the table on communion Sundays, and there she turned around. The men were on her right hand and the women on her left. The elders and deacons sat in their bench along the wall. Over all of them was the gallery, where old Kees had got to his feet. The ones who had followed her stood in the door. So that she had the whole of that country in front of her, as it was sorted. She undid the towel. It stuck, and she pulled it free. Nobody in the stone church made any sound at all. She spoke in Dutch, and not loudly. The old people said afterward that they had heard every word in the last pew. I am Dina. I was born of Bet in Jacobus Krom’s cellar and I owe him ten months. This winter the baas came down the stairs to me at night. I did not ask him to. Yesterday the juffrouw tied my hands with her yarn and did this with the lamb knife, and put me in the root cellar behind the vinegar. Then she c

sections.heading: VI. Whole Ears
sections.text: She did not go to the canal. She went that night to Lena Oosterhoudt’s at Hurley, in the wagon, with the crock of olykoeks between her feet, and stayed until the cuts closed, and after that she worked for wages. She had four York shillings a week and her board from a widow at Stone Ridge, and she could leave on any day she chose, and she tried it once, to see, and came back on the Monday. In September she stood up in the stone church at the communion season and was received on her confession, and the Meester wrote her into the church book. He asked what second name he should put. She had never had one. She said Bet’s. So he wrote it the old way, as a child is written after a father: Dina Bets, a free woman. It was the third time he had written her down. On the off Sundays that winter, after the reading, when the old people had gone home, she stayed. He taught her letters out of the States Bible. He began with her own name and went on from there, a line a week, his finger under the words, saying very little. She sat in the gallery no longer. She sat on the front bench on the women’s side, with her cap pushed back off her ears, and no one ever asked her to pull it down. When the Mees

title: The Ear-Mark
logline: In the last year of New York slavery, a Dutch farm wife does a thing in secret on Pinkster eve and goes to church.

verses.text: Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself. Not a moment should escape, for they who allow the right moment to pass, suffer pain when they are in hell.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a company of monks spends the rains retreat in a village on the frontier. The first month is pleasant. In the second, bandits raid the village and carry some of its people off, and from then on the villagers are so busy strengthening their town that they have no time to look after their guests, who pass the rest of the retreat in discomfort. Afterward the monks go back to the Buddha at Jetavana and tell him how hard it was. He tells them not to be troubled, since a comfortable lodging is hard to find at any time, and that a monk should guard himself as those villagers guarded their town, inside and out, and not let the moment pass. Hearing the verse, the monks are moved to urgency and reach awakening. Read the full commentary story, or about the rains retreat (vassa). The widow’s book is Blaise Pascal’s Pensées, quoted here in the English translation by W. F. Trotter (1910).
bg.history:
In 1805 Detroit was a town of a few hundred people, most of them French-speaking, packed into a few acres of log and frame houses inside a timber stockade on the river, with the old British-built Fort Lernoult on the rise behind. A town ordinance of 1802 required every household to sweep its chimneys and to keep a barrel of water, buckets and a ladder. On the morning of June 11, 1805, a fire began in or near the stable of a baker named John Harvey (the story that he knocked out his pipe there has never been proved), and by afternoon the whole town was gone except the fort and a warehouse. No one died. Michigan Territory’s new governor, William Hull, arrived on July 1 and wrote that every house was crowded and that he needed more than a week to find a place to stay. Judge Augustus Woodward laid out a new town of wide radiating avenues. See the Great Fire of 1805 and the Detroit Historical Society’s account.

The pastor of Ste. Anne’s, the Sulpician Gabriel Richard, had opened an academy for young ladies in 1804 to train teachers for the schools he planned; after the fire he sent canoes up and down the river with food and blankets for the burned-out families. His words in the ashes, Speramus meliora; resurget cineribus (“We hope for better things; it will rise from the ashes”), became the city’s motto. Forty miles south, French families from Detroit had settled the River Raisin from 1785 on long narrow “ribbon farms” running back from the water; in 1806 the militia there built a stockade with a blockhouse. See Frenchtown at River Raisin National Battlefield Park.

sections.heading: I. The Town Inside the Pickets
sections.text: The four of them came up from the River Raisin at the end of April in a trader’s bateau with forty bushels of seed wheat and a crate of hens, and the curé of Detroit, who had asked the curé at the Raisin for girls who could read, looked them over on the landing and nodded. They were Marie-Louise Couture, who was seventeen and the oldest; Archange Duval, who was sixteen and laughed at everything; Thérèse Bourdeau, who was sixteen and laughed at nothing; and Félicité Jacob, who was fifteen, and whose mother had cried on the bank as if the bateau were going to France. All four had learned their letters at the same kitchen table on the river road below the Raisin, from the widow Laforêt, who had been to the Ursulines at Quebec when she was a girl, before the English came. Now they were to learn how to teach other children their letters, at the curé’s academy for young ladies, and come home in the fall and do it. Detroit was the largest place any of them had seen. It sat on its bank inside a fence of cedar pickets taller than a man, with gates that were shut at night, and inside the pickets the houses stood so close along the little streets that a woman on one gallery could hand a cup o

sections.heading: II. The Eleventh of June
sections.text: It started a little after nine in the morning, in a stable. The girls were at their copybooks. Marie-Louise smelled it first and thought it was somebody’s bread. By the time they reached the street the stable was gone and the barn beside it was going, and the wind was up off the river, a dry hot June wind, and it took the burning hay out of the barn in pieces the size of a hand and laid them on the shingles of the houses all down the street, one roof and then the next and then the next, the way you lay out plates. The men made a line from the river with buckets. The girls got into it. Marie-Louise stood between a Scotch merchant in a good coat and an old Panis woman who belonged to somebody, and passed the full buckets up and the empty ones down until her palms bled, and every bucket went up the line and was thrown at a roof and was nothing. Behind her somebody had pulled the Beaugrands’ ladder down from the back wall and was carrying it toward the fire, and then had dropped it in the street and was running, and the ladder lay there and caught. They went out the gate with what they could carry. Madame Beaugrand had the baby and the clock. Félicité had the feather tick. Archange, wh

sections.heading: III. The Rest of the Summer
sections.dateline: The côte above the ruins · June to August
sections.text: Within a week every farmhouse for a league up the river was full. The Beaugrands went into the house of a cousin above the town, eleven people in two rooms, and the four girls from the Raisin went into the cousin’s hayloft. Nobody had time for them. That was all it was. Nobody was unkind. The men were in the woods all day cutting new pickets and squaring logs, or in the ashes all day pulling out nails and hinges and the iron of stoves, or arguing at the top of their voices about whose lot had been where, because the stakes had burned. The women were cooking for twice as many people with half as many pots. At the beginning of July the new governor arrived with the judges and could not find a bed for a week, and after that there were surveyors in the ashes with chains, laying out streets that went every which way, wide as fields, and the men stopped cutting pickets to stand and shout at the surveyors. The academy did not meet. The room behind the church was not there. The girls carried water. They minded the cousin’s children and the Beaugrands’ children together, which was nine children. They ate when the others had eaten, cold galette and whatever was left, and some nights nothing

sections.heading: IV. The Widow’s Kitchen
sections.dateline: The River Raisin · the end of August
sections.text: They went down the river with the same trader who had brought them up, past the islands and the Wyandot town at Brownstown, and out along the low shore of Lake Erie where the marsh went on for miles with nothing in it but red-winged blackbirds, and turned in at the mouth of the Raisin, which wound back and forth so much that a man could walk across a bend in the time it took a boat to go round. They walked the last of it on the river road, under the orchards, with their bundles.
