The widow Laforêt was in her kitchen, where she always was, at the end of a ribbon of land so narrow that her house took up most of the river end of it. She was seventy and small and brown as a walnut. She was sitting by her hearth in the summer evening with no fire in it but a few coals under the ash, smoking her short clay pipe, and she did not get up. Well, she said. Sit. Did it go well with you? Was it pleasant? They sat on the bench along the wall where they had sat with their slates when they were eight years old, and it all came out of them at once, the four of them talking over each other. The first month, the white bread, the strawberries, the pear trees, the copybooks. And then the fire. And then

title: Pipe Ash
logline: Four girls from the River Raisin go up to Detroit to learn to teach, and the town inside its pickets burns.

verses.text: They who are ashamed of what they ought not to be ashamed of, and are not ashamed of what they ought to be ashamed of, such men, embracing false doctrines enter the evil path.
They who fear when they ought not to fear, and fear not when they ought to fear, such men, embracing false doctrines, enter the evil path.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, some monks see a group of Nigaṇṭhas, the Jain ascetics, who wear a small covering in front, and decide they must be more modest than the ascetics who go entirely naked. The Nigaṇṭhas overhear and correct them: the covering is not for modesty at all. Even dust is alive, they say, and the cloth keeps living things from falling into their alms bowls. A long argument follows. When the monks report it, the Buddha says that those who feel shame where there is nothing shameful, and none where there is, and who fear what is not to be feared and do not fear what is, are on a bad road; and many of the Nigaṇṭhas go forth after hearing him. Read the full commentary story, or about Jainism and its care for the smallest forms of life. The widow’s books are Robert Hooke’s Micrographia (1665), whose great plate of the louse astonished its readers, and the Royal Society’s Philosophical Transactions, which in 1684 printed in English an abstract of Antonie van Leeuwenhoek’s letter describing the “Animals in the scurf of the Teeth.” Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes were single beads of glass mounted in small brass plates; in English, simple magnifiers of this kind were often called flea-glasses.
bg.history:
Smallpox reached Boston on the Seahorse from Barbados on April 22, 1721. Before the epidemic ended the next February, about 5,800 of the town’s roughly 10,600 people had caught it and 844 had died, with October the worst month. Cotton Mather had learned of inoculation years earlier from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man in his household, and from reports from Constantinople; on June 26 Dr. Zabdiel Boylston inoculated his own six-year-old son and two enslaved members of his household, all of whom survived. Most of the town’s physicians, led by William Douglass, and James Franklin’s new New-England Courant attacked the practice. Crowds forced inoculated people out to the quarantine house on Spectacle Island, and in November someone threw a homemade bomb into the room in Mather’s house where his inoculated nephew was recovering; it failed to explode. About two percent of the inoculated died, against roughly fifteen percent of those who caught the disease naturally. See the 1721 Boston smallpox outbreak and Onesimus.

Boston’s French Protestant church had been gathered by Huguenot refugees in the 1680s, after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685 and outlawed Protestant worship in France. Many of the refugees came, like the Pelletreau sisters, by way of London. See the Huguenots.

sections.heading: I. The Sign of the Quadrant
sections.text: Silas Crane had made quadrants and compasses and spectacles at the sign of the gilt quadrant in Ann Street for twenty-six years, and when he died of a quinsy in the winter of 1719 his widow took down nothing but his hat from its peg. She kept the shop. She kept his two apprentices, whose indentures had four years and six years to run, and she kept the trade, because she had been grinding his lenses for him since the year they married, and anybody on the Long Wharf who had bought a pair of Crane spectacles since 1700 had been looking through her work. Mistress Crane was fifty-eight, tall, with large red hands from the tripoli and the water. She said very little. When a ship’s master came in with a compass whose card stuck, she took it from him, and opened it, and fixed it, and told him the price, and that was the conversation. The apprentices, Josiah Pratt and Eben Mayhew, who were sixteen and fourteen, had decided she did not like them, and then decided she did not like anybody, and then, after a year, had stopped deciding anything about her and simply watched her hands. On the shelf behind the counter, in a case lined with green baize, she kept her husband’s flea-glass. It was a b

sections.heading: II. The French Ladies
sections.text: By September the town was emptying of anybody who had somewhere to go,. The General Court had gone to Cambridge. In the evenings men stood about at the head of the Long Wharf and argued about Boylston, and once a crowd went to a house in Middle Street where a man was lying sick of the inoculation and stood outside throwing stones and calling him a murderer until the constable came, and Josiah and Eben were in the crowd, at the back, and threw two stones each. They told nobody at the shop. Mistress Crane did not ask where they had been. It was on Middle Street, a week after, that they met the Pelletreau sisters. Everybody knew the three Mesdemoiselles Pelletreau, who had come from La Rochelle by way of London as girls, after the King of France took away the Protestants’ churches, and who kept a school for young ladies in two rooms over a chandler’s, French and needlework and the use of the globes. They went to the French church. They were small, upright, and old. And now, in the middle of the pox, they went about the town with fine linen tied over their mouths and noses, like the ladies in pictures of Turkey, and the eldest carried a little covered cup when she went to buy milk, wit

sections.heading: III. The Glass
sections.text: Mistress Crane was at the wheel, grinding, when they told her. She did not stop until they had finished. Then she wiped her hands, and took the flea-glass down from the shelf, and took a clean goose quill from the jar. Open your mouth, she said to Josiah. She scraped between two of his back teeth with the point of the quill and took off a little white stuff, like wetted flour. She mixed it on a slip of glass with a drop from the rain jar and touched the pin to it and gave him the brass plate and turned him to the window. He looked for a long time. Then he gave it to Eben, and Eben looked, and put the glass down on the counter very carefully, as if it might go off. It was alive. The little white stuff from between his teeth was a whole town. There were long ones that shot through the water like pickerel. There were round ones that spun like tops. There were small ones beyond counting that swarmed and turned among each other like gnats over a pond in the evening. Mistress Crane took down the odd volume of the Transactions and opened it to a page she had marked with a strip of leather, and put her red finger on a line, and Josiah read it out. The number of these Animals in the scurf o

sections.heading: IV. Going Forth
sections.dateline: Ann Street and Middle Street · October and after
sections.text: In October more than four hundred people died in Boston, the worst month, and on the twenty-sixth, the day of Thanksgiving, every meeting in the town held one sermon only, at eleven in the morning, so as not to crowd the people twice. Mistress Crane went. The boys went with her and sat by the door. Josiah went to the cooper’s yard the next day, and stood about among the staves until Peter Coffee looked up, and asked him how his mother had done it, with the thorn. Peter Coffee told him, while he drove a hoop. Then he showed Josiah how you set the hoop driver so it doesn’t slip, which Josiah had not asked. In November, in the middle of the night, somebody threw a lighted grenado through the window of Mr. Mather’s house, where his nephew was lying sick of the inoculation, with a note tied to it, and it did not go off. All the town talked about the note. Eben, who would have laughed in the summer, did not laugh. He said only that whoever had done it was not afraid of the right thing, and Josiah knew where he had got it. The Pelletreau sisters came to the shop the week after the grenado. They had heard, as everybody heard everything, about the quill and the vinegar. The eldest asked whe

title: The Flea-Glass
logline: In the smallpox summer, two apprentices praise three old Frenchwomen for covering their mouths, and learn whose sake the linen is for.

verses.text: They who forbid when there is nothing to be forbidden, and forbid not when there is something to be forbidden, such men, embracing false doctrines, enter the evil path.
They who know what is forbidden as forbidden, and what is not forbidden as not forbidden, such men, embracing the true doctrine, enter the good path.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, parents who follow other teachers see their children playing with the children of the Buddha’s lay followers. They forbid them to greet the monks or enter the monastery and make them swear to it. One hot day the children are playing outside the monastery gate and grow thirsty, and they send in the one boy who is allowed to go, to bring water out. The Buddha has him drink and then call the others in for theirs, and when they have all drunk he teaches them something suited to their age. The children tell their parents everything, and the parents weep that their sons have gone over to a false faith. Sensible neighbors talk them round, and the parents bring the children to the monastery themselves, with all their relations. The Buddha speaks the two verses about seeing fault where there is none.
bg.history:
The Soka Gakkai, a Japanese lay movement in the tradition of the thirteenth-century priest Nichiren, reached the United States largely through Japanese women who had married American servicemen. Under the name Nichiren Shoshu of America it grew quickly in the 1960s and 1970s, and a large share of its American members were Black or Latino. Its practice is the chanting of Nam-myoho-renge-kyo, the title of the Lotus Sutra, morning and evening before a scroll called the Gohonzon, together with neighborhood meetings in members’ homes. In those years it also recruited hard, on street corners and among strangers, which is the thing Dorothy Pettiford saw on Howard Street. Raymond Purnell, Mount Hebron Baptist and the families of the block are invented.

The Baltimore municipal strike of 1974 began with the city’s trash collectors at the start of July and lasted two weeks. Garbage piled up in the alleys in the July heat, piles were set alight at night, and for several days much of the police force walked out as well. The white marble steps of the city’s rowhouses, scrubbed by hand every week, were a point of pride in Sandtown as everywhere else in Baltimore.

sections.heading: I. The Bible on the Table
sections.text: Raymond Purnell had been baptized at Mount Hebron Baptist at the age of nine, in the same pool and on the same Sunday as Earl Pettiford, and for that reason the Pettifords took it harder than anybody when he came home from the Army with a new religion. He was thirty now. He drove a city bus on the split shift and lived alone at 1614 in the house his mother had left him. Twice a day, at six in the morning and again when he got in at night, the block could hear him through the front window. He said the same six syllables over and over, fast, in a strong flat voice, and then a long rattle of something that was not English, and every so often he struck a bell. He had got it at Fort Meade in 1968, after Vietnam. His first sergeant's wife was a Japanese lady from Yokohama, and she asked every soldier who came to the house whether he was happy, and waited for a true answer, and then drove him to a meeting. Raymond had gone to be polite. On Tuesday nights now there were fifteen or twenty people in his front room, and they called him the district chief. The Pettifords had no quarrel with his manners. He scrubbed his marble steps on Saturday like everyone else and spoke to every person he pa

sections.heading: II. Water
sections.text: The first of July the men who picked up the city's trash went out on strike, and inside of a week the alleys of West Baltimore were head high in it. People set the piles on fire at night. Children who had always played out back were told to stay on the front street, where there was no shade. The second Tuesday of the strike it was past ninety by noon. Eight children were playing stepball against the Boones' front steps, and by two o'clock nobody was running for the ball. The corner store was shut. The city had capped the hydrant. The Pettifords and the Boones were at work and their doors were locked until five, and the Goins children's grandmother was asleep in front of her fan and had told them what would happen to the one who woke her. Mr. Purnell's front door stood open behind its screen. He was home between shifts. Kevin, Tyrone said. You can go in there. Go ask him for some water and bring it out to us. Kevin went up the steps and in. He was gone a few minutes. He came back out with his chin wet and nothing in his hands. He said drink mine first, and I did. He said tell the rest of you come get your own. He said he's not sending his good glasses down those marble steps with a

sections.heading: III. Church Clothes
sections.text: Sheila told it at supper. She told all of it, the glasses and the cup of water for the scroll and the bell and the three rules, and then she put her hands together over her plate and said the six syllables to show how it went. Dorothy Pettiford set down the serving spoon and wept. She wept as she had not done since her own mother's funeral. Earl went out and stood on his front steps with his arms folded and looked at 1614 until it was dark. Down the block Mrs. Boone could be heard through two walls. My babies. In front of an idol. With their hands on the Book not three weeks ago. Mother Lucille Hazzard came across the street at eight o'clock with Mr. Deems the barber behind her. She was eighty-one, a deaconess of Mount Hebron, and she had taught the nine-year-olds' Sunday school class for forty years, Earl and Dorothy and Raymond Purnell among them. She took the kitchen chair that was offered and waited for Dorothy to finish. I went in that house in 1970 to pray the devil out of it, she said. I stayed for coffee. I have been watching that boy four years since, looking for the wrong in it, and I am a patient woman. Who drove Mr. Tubbs to the kidney machine three days a week till he

title: Jelly Glasses
logline: During the garbage strike, eight thirsty children sworn never to enter the chanting man's house send one boy in for water.

verses.text: Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured.
They lead a tamed elephant to battle, the king mounts a tamed elephant; the tamed is the best among men, he who silently endures abuse.
Mules are good, if tamed, and noble Sindhu horses, and elephants with large tusks; but he who tames himself is better still.

bg.commentary: Māgandiyā, whose father once offered her to the Buddha and heard her body called a thing of filth, becomes a queen and never forgives him. She bribes townspeople and slaves to follow him through the streets with the ten terms of abuse: thief, fool, ox, ass, beast of hell, with no hope of heaven. Ānanda begs him to go to another city. And if they abuse us there? Then another. The Buddha answers that trouble should be settled where it arises, and compares himself to an elephant in battle that bears the arrows from all four quarters. By the end of his teaching the people who had been paid to revile him have entered the stream. Read the full commentary story; the grudge begins in commentary 2.1.
bg.history:
In early September 1654 twenty-three Jews from Dutch Brazil, four men, six women and thirteen children by one count, landed at New Amsterdam on the bark Sainte Catherine, after the Portuguese retook Recife. The master, Jacques de la Motthe, sued them for their passage, and the court held their goods against the debt. Director-General Peter Stuyvesant wrote to the West India Company asking to expel them, citing their “customary usury and deceitful trading with the Christians.” On April 26, 1655 the directors refused, pointing to the Jews’ losses in Brazil and their capital in the Company, and let them stay so long as their poor did not burden the deacons. They could not worship in public or buy a house; in February 1656 they were granted a burial ground. Their congregation, Shearith Israel, is the oldest in the United States.

Most of the Company’s enslaved workers in New Amsterdam came from West Central Africa and were Catholic and Portuguese-speaking, with names like Anthony, Manuel or Gracia “van Angola”; in 1644 eleven of the longest-held men were given half-freedom and land north of the town. Hansken, the elephant Rembrandt drew in Amsterdam in 1637, toured the fairs of Europe for eighteen years, waving a flag, firing a pistol and picking coins out of pockets, and died in Florence in November 1655. The story of Hillel and the man who bet four hundred zuzim he could make him angry is told in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a; the version quoted is from Hebraic Literature, edited by Maurice H. Harris and first published in 1901. Valverde, Margriet Claes, Domingo and the rest are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Bark
sections.text: They came in on the Sainte Catherine at the beginning of September, twenty-three of them, four men and six women and thirteen children, out of Recife by way of the Spanish and the sea. The Portuguese had taken Recife back in January, and the Jews of Recife had been given three months to sell what they could and go. Most went home to Amsterdam. This boatload had been blown off its course, robbed by Spaniards as the story went, and picked up at Cape San Antonio by a French master named de la Motthe, who agreed to carry them to New Netherland for two thousand five hundred guilders, which they did not have. He sued them in the burgomasters' court within the week. The court held their beds and chests and kettles against the debt and gave them forty-eight hours to pay. In the third week of September the Director-General, Stuyvesant, wrote home to the West India Company that he had told them to go, on account of their customary usury and deceitful trading with the Christians, and because they were poor and would be a charge on the deacons all winter. They did not go. There was nowhere to go before spring, and the ice. The oldest of them was Elias Valverde, who was seventy. He had been bor

sections.heading: II. The Tapster's Widow
sections.text: There was a woman on the Strand who knew him. Her name was Margriet Claes, and she kept the tap-house by the Company's warehouse, where the sailors drank, and she had done well by it. She had been born in Recife too, the daughter of a Company sugar factor, and when she was sixteen and very handsome her father had gone to Elias Valverde, whose elder son was then twenty, and offered her. The boy could be baptized, the factor said. There would be a good dowry. A man of sense did not let a thing like that go by for a few old prayers. Valverde had answered him in front of the whole counting-house. The words got round Recife by evening, in Dutch and Portuguese both, and the girl heard them from her maid. He had said that his son was not to be had for a font and a pretty face, and that a face was skin over a skull, the same as his own, and would be a skull again soon enough. She married a ship's mate instead, and buried him, and came north. Now Elias Valverde had come in on a French bark with his bed sold out from under him, a beggar in her town. She did not do anything herself. She put stuivers into the hands of the boys who swept out the tap-house, and of sailors who owed her for their

sections.heading: III. The Heerestraat
sections.text: He walked every morning from the Brugh Straat up the Heerestraat toward the land gate and back, because he had walked every morning in Recife and in Amsterdam before that, and an old man who stops walking stops. At the end of February they began to follow him. A pack of boys first, and then grown men behind the boys, and then whoever was on the street and liked the sport. They walked behind him and beside him and shouted at him all the way to the gate and all the way back. Thief. Fool. Usurer. Ox. Ass. Beast. You killed our Lord. You have no hope. Hell is waiting for you, old man, and all your people. One of them threw a fish head that struck him on the back of the neck. A sailor walked in front of him backward for a hundred paces with his breeches down. Women laughed in the doorways. The two Company men walked behind with the casks on their shoulders, and when the boys looked back at them for the next word they gave it, in a Dutch they had been taught for the purpose. On the third day Daniel went with him, and by the fifth Daniel was shaking. They had come as far as the brewer's horse mill, where the street opened, when Daniel stopped him by the sleeve. Uncle, let us go from here.

sections.heading: IV. The Elephant
sections.text: When he was a man of fifty, he said, still in Amsterdam, they brought an elephant to the city from the Indies, a cow elephant called Hansken, and showed her at the fair. He had gone to see her with his sons, who were boys. She could wave a flag and fire a pistol and beat a drum, and take a coin out of a man's pocket with her nose and give it to her keeper. They led her through the crowd at the fair, he said, from one booth to the next, through thousands of people. Boys pricked her with sticks. Men threw things to see her start. Somebody put a lit pipe to her ear. She did not start. She went where she was led, through all of it, with all of it falling on her from every side, and did what she had been taught to do. That was why they could lead her into a crowd. The Prince of Orange had sent for her, and a prince could have sat on her back. So, said Valverde. It is my part now to be the elephant. Most people are not good. They will shout. I will go where I am going. Behind them the brewer's horse went round and round inside the mill, blindfolded, turning the stone. The horse is good because somebody trained it, he said. The elephant also. But a man has to be trained by somebody too, a

sections.heading: V. The Stuivers
sections.text: His name was Domingo. He had been born in Angola and baptized at Luanda by a Portuguese priest, and sold to the Dutch, and carried to Recife, and from Recife to this island, where the Company owned him and rented him out by the day. He had not heard his own language spoken to him as to a man in eleven years. He told Valverde that, standing by the horse mill, and Valverde told him who had been paying the boys, and Domingo said he knew. The next morning the old man went out walking at the same hour, up the Heerestraat to the land gate and back. Two boys followed him, out of habit, and called him an ass, and then, because nobody took it up, stopped. A sailor said something. A woman in a doorway told the sailor to hold his tongue. By the end of March the old man walked alone. By April the boys walked with him, because he would tell them a story if they did, about Hillel, or about the elephant, or about Recife; and one of them, a cooper's boy named Jochem, could tell the whole of the Hillel story by Pentecost without a mistake, and did, to anyone who would stand for it. The other Company man, Francisco, began to come to the back room on the Brugh Straat on Friday evenings and stand in t

title: Ask On, My Son
logline: A tavern widow with an old grudge pays boys, sailors and Company slaves to follow a Jewish refugee from Recife up the Heerestraat.

verses.text: For with these animals does no man reach the untrodden country (Nirvana), where a tamed man goes on a tamed animal, viz. on his own well-tamed self.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk who had been an elephant trainer before he was ordained stands with other monks on the bank of the Aciravatī river, watching a trainer fail to teach an elephant a trick. He remarks that if the man pricked the elephant in a certain place it would learn quickly. The trainer overhears, does it, and the elephant submits. The other monks report it to the Buddha, who calls the monk in, asks whether it is true, and on hearing yes rebukes him: what has he to do with elephants or any tamed animal? No such vehicle carries a man to the place he has never been; only his own well-tamed self can. Many who heard the teaching were set on the path.
bg.history:
Wild horses on Nevada's public ranges were hunted from airplanes and trucks for pet-food plants until a Reno woman, Velma Johnston, known as Wild Horse Annie, followed a bleeding truckload to a slaughterhouse in 1950 and spent the rest of her life campaigning. A 1959 law banned hunting them with motor vehicles and aircraft, and the Wild and Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 made them "living symbols of the historic and pioneer spirit of the West" under federal protection. The Bureau of Land Management gathers horses off the ranges and offers them for adoption, each freeze-marked on the left side of the neck with its birth year and number; since about 2001 removals have outrun adoptions.

Sixmile Conservation Camp is fictional; its program is modeled on the real one at the Northern Nevada Correctional Center in Carson City, which began in October 2000 and since 2007 has trained only BLM wild horses and burros. Inmates, often with little or no experience of horses, give each animal about 120 days of training; the horses go out “green broke” through public competitive-bid adoptions several times a year, with bids starting at $150 and a catalog paragraph written by each trainer. Visitors may not wear blue denim. Royce's people are the Basques of northern Nevada, who came from the Spanish and French Pyrenees to herd sheep and settled around Winnemucca, Elko and Battle Mountain, which still have some of the highest shares of Basque ancestry in the country. The camp's hay is watered by wheel lines, rolling sprinkler pipe moved forward one set at a time.

sections.heading: I. Mister
sections.dateline: Sixmile Conservation Camp, near Carson City, Nevada · August 2014
sections.text: Odell Pruitt called everybody Mister. He had been calling everybody Mister since 1979, when he came into the Nevada State Prison at thirty-seven with a life sentence for killing a man in the parking lot of a Reno card room, and it had gotten him into fights the first ten years, because the men thought he was mocking them, and the officers thought he was mocking them, and some of the time he was. After that it stopped being mockery. It was just what he said. Mister Ochoa. Mister Bledsoe. Mister Officer Grant. By 2014 he was seventy-two years old, with a white beard trimmed close and reading glasses on a cord, and he had been moved down through the custody levels one at a time over thirty-five years until he arrived at Sixmile, a minimum camp in the sagebrush south of Carson City, where there was a chain-link fence you could have climbed in a minute and nobody did. On Tuesday nights after chow he held a reading group in the education trailer. It was not on any list of programs and it did not earn anybody any good time. There were eight or nine men in it, sometimes twelve, sometimes four. They read one book, the same book, over and over, a library copy of Epictetus with the spine held

sections.heading: II. The Round Pen
sections.text: The education trailer stood at the south end of the camp, and to get back to the units from it you walked along the fence of the horse program. The program had been running in Nevada since before Royce came in. The Bureau of Land Management gathered wild horses off the ranges every year, more than anybody wanted to adopt, and some of them came in trailers to the prisons, where the inmates gentled them and started them under saddle for about four months, and then the horses went through a public adoption a few times a year, a competitive bid, with an auctioneer, and families from Reno and Gardnerville and California bid on them and took them home. Each horse had a freeze mark on the left side of its neck, white hair in a row of angled symbols that told the year it was born and its number. Each one came off a herd management area with a name, Fish Creek, Little Owyhee, Triple B, the names of dry country. The men in the program got paid a little, worked outside all day, and came back to the unit smelling of horse, and there was a waiting list to get in. Royce was not on the list. He had put in for it when he came to Sixmile and been told no, on account of the colts in the trailer. He

sections.heading: III. Green Broke
sections.dateline: The round pen · the next evening
sections.text: The program supervisor was a civilian from Dayton named Hal Nygaard, who had trained horses all his life and believed in going slow. He went home at four. Danny waited until he was gone, and the officer at the barn was busy with a count sheet, and the other trainers had put their horses up. Then he went into the tack room and got a soft cotton rope. He had trouble getting the loop around the hind pastern. Humo kicked him once in the thigh, hard, and he limped for a week afterward. But he got it, and ran the rope up through a loop around the gray’s neck and pulled the foot up under the belly and tied it off, the way he had heard it, and then Humo was standing on three legs in the middle of the pen with his nostrils open and his whole body shaking. Danny picked up the saddle pad. The two men who saw it from the hay barn told it afterward, and so did Danny, much later. Humo fought. He hopped on three legs and threw himself sideways and went down in the dirt of the pen and lay there groaning and thrashing his head, and got up, and Danny kept on with the pad, slapping it on his back, his neck, under his belly, down his legs, over and over, the way he had heard it, while the dust came up

sections.heading: IV. Is It True
sections.text: It was Bledsoe who told Pruitt. He was not a talker either; he told it because it had been sitting on him all week. He told it before group, when it was just the two of them setting out the chairs, the whole thing, the fence and the rope and what the hay crew saw from the barn and the paragraph in the catalog, which one of the clerks had shown around. Pruitt listened with his reading glasses in his hand. Then he put them on and opened the book and waited for the others. When they were all there, nine of them, and Royce at the end of the table with his arms crossed, Pruitt did not open the book. He looked down the table. Mister Etcheverry. Royce looked at him. On Tuesday last, at the round pen, did you tell those men how to tie up that gray horse’s foot and sack him out until he quit? Nobody moved. Somebody’s chair creaked and stopped. Yes, Royce said. I did. It’s true. Pruitt nodded slowly, as if a man had told him the time. Mister Etcheverry, he said, what have you got to do with horses? He did not raise his voice. He never had to, in thirty-five years. He said it quietly and it went down the table like cold water. You are a man in blue in a camp in the desert with eight to twenty

sections.heading: V. The Adoption
sections.dateline: The horse pens · the second Saturday of October
sections.text: The adoption came on a cold bright Saturday with the first snow on the Carson Range. The public came in through a side gate at the south end of the camp, a hundred and fifty people in down vests and good boots, with horse trailers lined up along the road outside, and walked along the pens with their catalogs reading the paragraphs. Nobody in blue denim. No cell phones. No photographs. The trainers rode their horses around the arena one at a time while the auctioneer talked them up, and the bidding started at a hundred and fifty dollars. The hay crew was not allowed down there. Royce watched from the far edge of the alfalfa, beside the wheel line, a quarter mile off, where he could see the arena small and bright with the people around it like a ring of birds. When Danny rode Humo into the arena the gray went around once at a walk and once at a trot, head low, ears neither forward nor back, and stopped when Danny stopped him, and stood. A family from Minden bought him for four hundred and twenty-five dollars, a man and his wife and a girl of about eleven in a pink parka who had been standing at Humo’s pen all morning reading the paragraph out loud to her parents. Danny led the horse

sections.heading: VI. Wheel Lines
sections.dateline: The camp alfalfa · that fall and winter
sections.text: Some of the men in the room that night said afterward that something happened to them, sitting there, that had not happened in any program or chapel or court. Bledsoe said it was like hearing somebody say your name in a place where you didn’t know anybody knew it. A young man named Teo Maldonado, who had come to the group twice before and not liked it, came every Tuesday after that until he was paroled in 2016, and wrote Pruitt letters from Reno for years. They said things changed for them from that night. They did not say how. Royce did not come to group the next Tuesday. He came the one after, and sat in the same place, and when the book came to him he read his paragraph, and then he said, without being asked, I don’t know how to do it. And Pruitt said, No, Mister. Nobody does. You do it anyway. He did not go along the fence by the round pen anymore. He went back the long way after group, around by the kitchen, and he moved the wheel lines in the alfalfa in the mornings, twelve hundred feet of aluminum pipe on wheels taller than a man, that you uncoupled and rolled forward by a crank, one set at a time, to put the water on the next strip of the field. It was work you could not hu

title: Green Broke
logline: An old buckaroo doing time beside a prison mustang program tells a struggling young trainer how to make a gray horse quit.

verses.text: The elephant called Dhanapalaka, his temples running with sap, and difficult to hold, does not eat a morsel when bound; the elephant longs for the elephant grove.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich old Brahmin of Sāvatthī with four sons is widowed. Afraid he will remarry and the fortune will be divided, the sons wait on him, rub his hands and feet, and talk him into handing over everything he has. Each daughter-in-law in turn drives him from her door (“Don’t you know the way to your other sons’ houses?”), and the old man ends up begging with a bowl and a staff. Hearing that the Buddha greets strangers kindly, he goes to him, and the Buddha teaches him verses to recite when the Brahmins assemble with his sons among them; the verses praise the staff that keeps off bulls and dogs above ungrateful children. The law of the day is that a son who eats his parents’ wealth and will not support them is put to death. The sons fall at their father’s feet, he pleads for them, and they carry him home in a chair. Restored, he brings the Buddha a pair of cloths as a teacher’s due and gives him two of his four daily meals; the Buddha says he will go where he pleases, and goes to each son’s house in turn. At a feast the sons boast of how well they now care for their father, and the Buddha tells of the elephant Dhanapālaka, who, captured by a king, would not eat for longing for his blind mother in the forest. His hearers weep.
bg.history:
Ramallah, north of Jerusalem, was founded as a Christian town, and its Greek Orthodox Church of the Transfiguration dates from 1852. Ramallah merchants began emigrating to the United States in 1901, and by the 1950s about a quarter of its natives had left; the American Federation of Ramallah, Palestine was founded in Detroit in 1959 and still has local clubs from Jacksonville to San Jose. In Knoxville, as the historian Jack Neely has written, a few Christian families from Ramallah were living on Gay Street by 1927. The women of Ramallah once embroidered a palm-tree motif in cross-stitch on the backs of their dresses. Israel took Ramallah in the June 1967 war. Its census of the occupied territories that September left out at least 270,000 Palestinians who were abroad or had fled, and many were later refused the right to return to live, as Human Rights Watch has documented.

The Lawson McGhee Library on Church Avenue, founded in 1885, is the oldest continuously operating public library in Tennessee. For most of its history it served only white patrons; Black Knoxvillians used a separate Free Colored Library, opened in 1918 with Carnegie money, which closed in 1961. The Orthodox churches read the Old Testament in the Greek Septuagint, whose psalm numbers run one behind the Hebrew Bible's (its Psalm 136 is “By the rivers of Babylon”), and the Septuagint's Proverbs differs in places from the Hebrew text. The scripture here is from Lancelot Brenton's English translation, first published in 1844. In 2022 Orthodox Easter fell on April 24, a week after the Western date, and the date cookies of the feast, ma'amoul, are still pressed in carved wooden molds.

sections.heading: I. Four Envelopes
sections.text: Elias Musleh opened his first store on North Broadway in 1974, in a cinder-block building that had been a filling station, with a cooler of milk and a cooler of beer and a rack of bread and a hot plate behind the counter where his wife Samira made the pies she sold by the slice to the men from the cabinet shop next door. He was twenty-nine. He had been in Knoxville eight years. By 1990 he had four stores, one on Broadway and one on Chapman Highway and one on Clinton Highway and one out Magnolia Avenue past the old Sears, gas and groceries and cold beer and lottery tickets and a hot case with fried chicken and spinach pies, and a sign on every one in red letters that said MUSLEH MARKET, and four sons, Hanna and Issa and Fadi and Sami, who had done their homework on milk crates behind four different counters and grown up and married and gone into the stores themselves. He gave each of them a store on the day of his wedding. It was the way his own father had done in Ramallah with the olive terraces, one terrace to each son when he married, the way everybody did. He kept the house on the ridge in West Knoxville, and the money in the bank, and Samira. Samira died in January of 2021, at

sections.heading: II. The Doors
sections.dateline: Farragut, Powell, Halls · fall and winter, 2021
sections.text: He went to Hanna's first, because Hanna was the oldest. Hanna had a house in Farragut with a three-car garage and a pool with a cover on it for the winter, and his wife Rula gave Elias the guest room downstairs and put the oud in the closet. It was good for three weeks. Then it was the dishes, and his television too loud, and his cigarettes on the back deck. On a Saturday in November he came back from the Greek church, where he had stood through the liturgy as long as his knees would let him and then sat, and Rula was standing in the open door of the garage with her arms folded, and she said it before he was out of the car. Did you give Hanna a thousand dollars more than the others? A hundred? You gave every one of them the same. I saw the papers. So why is it always this house? Don't you know the way to Issa's? To Fadi's? You don't remember how to drive to Powell? Elias stood by the car. He said something to her in Arabic that his mother had said to people, a thing about God and her house, that he had never in his life said to a woman, and he got back in the car and drove to Powell. He was at Issa's until the middle of December. Then Dana said it, in a different way, with the chil

sections.heading: III. The Desk
sections.dateline: Lawson McGhee Library, Church Avenue · January 2022
sections.text: Her name was Avis Nance. She was sixty-six years old, and she had been a reference librarian on Church Avenue for thirty-eight years, and she had grown up in Burlington, on the east side, and when she was a little girl the library on Church Avenue had not been for her. There had been the other library then, the colored library, and then there had not been, and she had come downtown on the bus at nine years old with her library card in her hand to the big library, and the woman at the desk had looked at her for a long time, and given her the book. She had not been to church since her mother died. She said she had read too much. She had a short grey natural and reading glasses on a beaded chain and a face that, as the men said, did not frown. It was not that it smiled. It was that it was open, like a door that was not going to close on you. She looked up at him from the desk. Mr. Musleh, she said. He had not expected that. He stood there with the cane. You had the store on Broadway. I used to buy my milk at your store when I lived on Fourth and Gill. Twenty years. Your wife made the spinach pies. She took her glasses off and let them hang on the chain. Sit down. Sit down, Mr. Musleh.

sections.heading: IV. The Wedding
sections.dateline: A hotel ballroom on the river · February 19, 2022
sections.text: All that winter, everybody had been getting married. The weddings that had been put off in 2020 and put off again in 2021 were all happening at once, in the winter of 2022, as if the whole community had been holding its breath. The one in February, a few weeks before Lent, when the church would stop marrying anybody until Easter, was a granddaughter of his cousin Khalil, marrying a Ramallah boy from Detroit, and it was at the big hotel by the river downtown, and everybody was there. Everybody. The Ramallah families of Knoxville and the ones from Detroit and Chicago and Jacksonville, three hundred and fifty people at round tables, the old men nearest the dance floor, the women in their gold. His sons sat at a table near the front, all four of them, with their wives, in good suits, under a centerpiece of white roses. Rula had on the gold bracelets Samira had left her. Hanna had his reading glasses pushed up on his head, the way Elias wore his. Elias came in at ten o'clock. The doorman did not want to let him in, and then a cousin's boy recognized him and went white and let him in. He came in his overcoat and the trousers he had been wearing for a week, with his white beard and the al

sections.heading: V. The Card
sections.text: Hanna bathed him himself that night, in the big bathroom upstairs, on his knees by the tub, and washed his hair with the good shampoo, and trimmed his nails with the clippers from Rula's drawer, the way you do it for a child, and shaved him in the morning. Then he called his brothers and their wives and Rula into the kitchen and said, in Arabic and then in English so there could be no mistake, that their father would live a week in each of their houses, around and around, as long as he lived, with the best room and the first plate. Nobody said anything. Rula went upstairs and came down with clean sheets for the downstairs room, and made the bed, and took the oud out of the closet in its case and leaned it in the corner by the window where he could see it. He slept. He ate. He ate roast chicken with rice and pine nuts and Rula's lentil soup, and the color came back into him in two weeks and the cough went away and his knee was better. He looked at himself in the mirror in the downstairs bathroom with his beard trimmed short and white, and thought: I owe this to the woman at the desk. He had no money to buy her anything. Everything had been in the envelopes. So he went into the garag

sections.heading: VI. Red Eggs
sections.text: Easter came late that year for the Orthodox, a week after the American one, and the week before it Hanna came into his father's room and sat on the end of the bed. Yaba, Easter. Who should we have? Whose honor is it this year? You choose. The woman at the library is my friend, said Elias. I don't know anybody else. Then invite her. Her and her people. Whoever she wants. We'll set up in the yard. Avis Nance came at two o'clock on Easter afternoon, in a yellow dress and a hat, and she brought her people, which was not what Hanna had expected. She brought the men from the second floor. Eleven of them, then fourteen, as a second car came up the drive: the men who slept at the mission and spent their days on the benches by the windows, the one with the disability check, the one who had been in the Army with somebody in Detroit, the one with the dog. Some of them had borrowed shirts. Elias knew every one of them by name, and they knew him, and they called him Pops in front of his sons. The four sons had rented tables and white cloths and set them up on the lawn by the pool, under the willow oaks, with the cover off the pool now and the water blue. There was a lamb Fadi had been roasting

title: The Cane
logline: A widowed Ramallah grocer signs everything over to his four sons, and one by one their wives show him the door.

verses.text: If a man becomes fat and a great eater, if he is sleepy and rolls himself about, that fool, like a hog fed on wash, is born again and again.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala goes through a period of eating rice by the bucketful, with sauce and curry to match. One morning after breakfast he comes to the Buddha so heavy with sleep that he paces wearily and then sits down to one side. The Buddha asks whether he has come before he was rested; the king says he always suffers after a meal, and the Buddha answers that overeating always brings suffering, and speaks the verse of the fat man rolling in his sleep like a great hog fed on fodder. Then he teaches a second verse, on knowing the measure in food so that one ages slowly and guards one’s life, to a young Brahmin named Uttara, and tells him to recite it whenever the king sits down to eat. In time the king is content with a pint-pot of rice, grows lean and cheerful, and gives incomparable gifts for seven days. The commentary tells nearly the same episode under verse 204 (story 15.6).
bg.history:
The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy ran its commuter trains from the new Union Station, opened in 1925, west through a string of railroad suburbs toward Aurora, on the line that is now Metra’s BNSF Line. The same tracks carried livestock east from Iowa and Nebraska to the Union Stock Yards, where more meat was processed through the early 1920s than anywhere else on earth. Small stations were kept by an agent-operator who sold tickets, handled freight and express, and worked the telegraph; from the Civil War on, many American telegraphers were women. Oakmere, the Sandquists and the Dunnings are fictional. In 1926 the wire carried Gertrude Ederle’s Channel swim on August 6 and, on September 23, Gene Tunney’s ten-round decision over Jack Dempsey in the rain at Philadelphia.

Luigi (Alvise) Cornaro, a Paduan who claimed Venetian nobility, wore himself out with eating and drinking by about forty and, on his doctors’ advice, cut himself to about twelve ounces of food a day. His Discorsi della vita sobria, written from his eighties on, was a great success and was translated into English again and again for four centuries; the edition Mrs. Sandquist finds, The Art of Living Long, was published in Milwaukee by William F. Butler in 1903. Prohibition had made liquor the vice good Methodists did without; the table was another matter.

sections.heading: I. The Day Book
sections.dateline: Agent’s day book, Oakmere station, C.B.&Q. · January 1926
sections.text: Jan. 11, Monday. Cold. 4 above at 6:00. Lit the waiting-room stove 5:40. Hog extra east 7:38, forty-one cars, steaming like a laundry. No. 22 on time 7:52, took 63 commuters. Sold 9 monthly commutation books. Mr. H. Dunning, village president, came down at 7:30 and walked the platform the whole length three times and sat down on the bench by the baggage truck with his mouth open and missed the 7:52. Sent him in on the 8:20. He said, I don’t know what’s the matter with me, Mrs. Sandquist. I know what’s the matter with him. Ham, eggs, fried potatoes, buckwheat cakes, sausage, a bowl of oats with the top of the milk on it. His cook told my niece. Jan. 12. Same. Caught the 7:52 this time but it took the brakeman to boost him. Jan. 14. Mr. Dunning came into the office after the 7:52 had gone without him and asked could he sit a minute. I said sit. He sat in my chair by the key and his eyes went shut and his head went down on his chest and the sounder went on clacking and he did not hear it. I let him. At 8:05 he woke up and looked around like a man coming up out of a well. Did you come down before you were rested, Mr. Dunning? No, I slept eight hours. It’s after I eat. Every day of my l

sections.heading: II. The Blanks
sections.dateline: The same book · January and February
sections.text: Jan. 18. The Dunning boy, Walter, 13, has been coming in after school since Thanksgiving to learn the key. I let him sit at the dead one and practice. He is slow on his numbers and fast on his letters, which is backwards. Today I took down the book that was in lost-and-found when I came here, which nobody ever claimed and which I have read through four times: The Art of Living Long, by Louis Cornaro, a Venetian gentleman who ate himself nearly to death by forty and then stopped, and lived to be past a hundred. Printed in Milwaukee, 1903. Somebody left it on the 5:14. I copied a piece of it on a yellow message blank in my best hand, the way I would take down a telegram, and gave it to Walter. Every time your father sits down to eat, I said, you read him this. After the blessing. Before he takes a bite. Breakfast and supper and Sunday dinner. Every time. He won’t like it. He didn’t like the hogs either. In this manner, I accustomed myself to the habit of never fully satisfying my appetite, either with eating or drinking—always leaving the table well able to take more. In this I acted according to the proverb: “Not to satiate one’s self with food is the science of health.” — Louis Cor

sections.heading: III. Weights and Measures
sections.dateline: The same book · spring and summer
sections.text: Apr. 6. Mr. D. weighed himself on the baggage scale while the 7:52 was whistling for the crossing. 214. He was 241 at Christmas, he says. He wrote it on the wall by the scale in pencil, which I do not allow, and I let it stay. Apr. 20. Walter got his numbers. Sent 25 words a minute clean. May 4. The breakfast at the Dunnings’ is one bowl of oats, the boy says. One bowl and a cup of coffee, and the cook is put out and says she does not know what she is in that kitchen for. June 22. Hot. The Rebekahs’ picnic. Mr. D. stood on the platform an hour with me in the heat helping the old ladies off the 8:20 with their baskets, and laughed at something one of them said, a big laugh, and I could not remember ever hearing him laugh before. Aug. 6. Over the wire in the afternoon: the Ederle girl swam the English Channel, first woman ever, beat the men’s time. Mr. D. came off the 5:14 and I read it to him off the blank and he took off his hat and threw it up in the air on the platform, at his age, and it came down on the track, and Walter went down and got it. Aug. 27. 192 on the baggage scale. Cornaro says when he left the table he had to sing. Mr. D. has gone back into the choir at the Methodi

sections.heading: IV. Fight Night
sections.text: Sept. 23. Rain here and rain in Philadelphia. Dempsey and Tunney for the title. Half the men in the village have radios and the other half came down to the depot because the Western Union was carrying the rounds and I would read them out through the window. Forty-some men on the platform under umbrellas and in the waiting room. Somebody brought a washtub of sandwiches from the lodge hall, ham and cheese, and a dishpan of doughnuts. Mr. D. stood at the window with the others. Every round I read out, the tub went around. He took one sandwich at the first round and ate it slow. The tub came around nine more times and he let it go by nine times, and said no thank you nine times, and I counted, because I count everything, it is my job. Tunney took it on points, ten rounds. Dempsey’s eye shut. The men went home in the rain arguing. Mr. D. stayed and helped Walter carry the empty tub back up to the lodge hall, the two of them under one umbrella, and I heard them singing going up Burlington Avenue, something from the hymnal, the boy flat.

sections.heading: V. Christmas Week
sections.text: Dec. 24. 6:10 a.m. Mr. D. came down in the dark with the Methodist church’s big coffee urn on a coaster wagon, and Walter pulling, and three dozen doughnuts from Kuhn’s bakery in two boxes, and set up on a sawhorse table under the depot light. Every man who came for the 7:52 got a cup, and every man for the 8:20. The section men. The brakemen off the hog extra, who stood there steaming in the cold with their cups. A man off the freight who had been riding the rods since Ottumwa, and Mr. D. gave him three doughnuts and his own gloves. 186 on the scale. Dec. 25. Christmas. No commuters. He came down anyway and the urn went to the section gang and the switch tender and me, and a family going to Galesburg on No. 9 with four children asleep on the bench. Dec. 26, 27, 28. Every morning. Six o’clock. The urn, the wagon, the doughnuts. Dec. 29. Mrs. Dunning came down with him and poured. People are coming to the 7:52 who take the 8:20 as a rule, just to have the coffee and stand under the light with the village president in his old overcoat, which hangs on him now like a horse blanket. Dec. 30. 12 below. He brought a second urn. Dec. 31. Seventh day. At 8:25, when the 8:20 had gone, he cam

sections.heading: VI. A Man I Admire
sections.text: A Man I Admire. By Walter Dunning. The man I admire is my father, Mr. Harold Dunning, who is the president of the village, but that is not why. Last year he was sick every day after breakfast and went to sleep on the bench and the brakeman had to boost him up on the train. That is true. You can ask the brakeman. His name is Mr. Riordan. Mrs. Sandquist at the depot wrote down something from a book by a man from Venice for me to read to my father before every meal. I read it to him 900 times about. I counted the meals. At first he said every time, Thank you, Walter, in a voice. Then after a while he said it in his regular voice. Then in the summer he started saying it with me. He knows it by heart now and so does my mother and so does the cook, Hilda, though she says it does her no good, she is not the one. My father lost 55 pounds. He sings bass. On fight night he only ate one sandwich. At Christmas he gave coffee to everybody at the depot for seven days including a tramp who got his gloves. Mother says he is a different man but he says no, he is the same man, only less of him. The reason I admire him is it is hard to leave food on your plate when it is right there. I know because I

title: The Hog Extra
place: Oakmere (fictional), a Burlington-line suburb west of Chicago, Illinois
logline: Told in a depot agent's day book: a drowsy village president, a carload of hogs, and a boy with a yellow message blank at every meal.

verses.text: This mind of mine went formerly wandering about as it liked, as it listed, as it pleased; but I shall now hold it in thoroughly, as the rider who holds the hook holds in the furious elephant.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the novice Sāṇu has a voice so fine that the monks keep asking him to chant, and he never once pleads a sore heart or a tired body; every time, he gives the merit of it to his mother and father. His parents in this life do not know it, but his mother from his previous life, now a yakkhinī, a spirit, comes with the gods to listen and receives it, and the spirits honor her with the first seat for his sake. Grown to manhood, Sāṇu turns discontented and goes home alone, unkempt, meaning to give up the robe. His mother argues with him and fails, then sits him down and goes to wash rice for him. The yakkhinī seizes him; he falls foaming and twisting, the village gathers, and his mother laments that spirits are said not to touch those who keep the holy days. Through him the spirit answers: do no evil, openly or in secret, for there is no flying away from it. He wakes and asks why she weeps for a living man. She answers that people weep for one who, though living, has died again, and that she snatched him like goods out of a burning house and he wants to burn again. He gives up the plan, and she provides his robes for full ordination. The Buddha tells him to master his wandering mind as an elephant driver masters a rutting elephant with the hook. Sāṇu becomes a great teacher and lives to a hundred and twenty.
bg.history:
The Cane Ridge revival in Bourbon County, in August 1801, drew between ten and twenty-five thousand people to a Presbyterian sacramental meeting hosted by Barton Stone. Presbyterian and Methodist preachers spoke from the meetinghouse, a tent and stumps and logs at once; Black worshippers held their own preaching; and thousands fell in the “falling exercise,” some lying motionless for hours, while others were seized by “the jerks.” Children who had fallen and risen were allowed to exhort, sometimes held up by grown men: one boy of about twelve, at Indian Creek that June, exhorted from a log for an hour with a man at each arm and lifted a handkerchief and let it fall as a warning to sinners. By 1810 child exhortation had all but disappeared. In 1803 Stone and four other ministers left the Kentucky Synod, and in 1804 they agreed to take no name but Christians; in 1805 the revival preacher Richard McNemar joined the Shakers.

The Methodists turned the revival into a system. A promising convert could receive a permit to exhort from the quarterly meeting; if the meeting recommended him, the annual Western Conference could admit him “on trial” as a traveling preacher and send him to a circuit, on an allowance of eighty dollars a year for a single man, rarely paid in full, as Peter Cartwright remembered of his own start in 1802–1804. The camp meeting born at Cane Ridge spread across the country with them. The Combs family, Brother Tull and the Gaithers are invented; the boy’s descendants turn up two centuries later in Sinners Welcome.

sections.heading: I. The Log
sections.dateline: Cane Ridge, Bourbon County, Kentucky · August 1801
sections.text: Sandy Combs fell on the Saturday afternoon, in the woods below the meetinghouse. He was twelve. He had come over from Stoner Creek with his father and his stepmother in the wagon on Friday, with a sack of meal and a side of bacon and two quilts, and by Saturday noon there were more people in the woods at Cane Ridge than he had known there were in Kentucky. Wagons stood in the trees in every direction as far as you could see, and horses tied to every sapling, and fires smoking at every camp. There was preaching at the meetinghouse and preaching at the tent and preaching from wagon beds and stumps. A little way off the colored people had their own preaching. Under all of it was a noise like a river in flood, singing and praying and shouting and crying all at once, and the noise never stopped, not even in the night. He had been watching people fall since Friday. A man would be standing and singing and then go down in the leaves as if he had been shot, and lie there, and the people around him would kneel and pray over him, and after an hour or two, or sometimes a day, he would get up shouting. Sandy had not been afraid of it. He had been curious about it, the way he was curious about a

sections.heading: II. The Two Mothers
sections.text: His own mother was named Hannah, and she had burned to death when he was two. It was in the winter of 1791, in the first cabin his father put up on the creek, the year they came over the mountains. His father was off at the salt lick. The chimney was sticks and clay, the way they all were then, and it caught in the night, and the roof went in before anybody knew. Rachel Ferrell was sixteen and lived on the next place down. She saw the light and ran up the creek in her shift, and she went into that cabin through the fire and came out with the baby, and went back in for his mother and could not find her, and came out the second time with her hair burning. She put her hair out in the creek. Then she sat on the bank holding the boy against her until his father came home. Jesse Combs married her the next year. She raised the boy as her own, and they never had any of their own after, and Sandy called her Mama all his life. His mother Hannah was buried under a big sycamore by the creek with a fieldstone at her head. He did not remember her. He used to go and sit on the stone. After Cane Ridge, Brother Amos Tull took him up. Brother Tull was a Methodist local preacher, an old man with a fa

sections.heading: III. The Chair
sections.dateline: The Combs place on Stoner Creek · March 1807
sections.text: By the spring of 1807 Sandy Combs was eighteen years old and as tall as his father, and his voice had broken long ago, and something in him had broken with it. The meetings were not what they had been. Barton Stone and some of the other revival preachers had left the Presbyterians and called themselves only Christians, and a few had gone up into Ohio to the Shakers, who danced and did not marry. Nobody held up children on logs to exhort anymore. People said it had been a disorder. Sandy was too big to stand on the end of a bench and too young to be a preacher, and he went around with Brother Tull carrying logs and building fires and calling people in, and he found that he did not want to do it. He wanted other things. He did not always know what they were. A piece of land in the Green River country. A horse that could run at the Lexington races. A girl in Paris named Polly Ritchie, whose father kept a still. His own house, with a door that shut, and nobody standing on the end of a bench in it. The thoughts went every way at once, like cattle out of a broken lot, and he could not get them back in, and he quit trying. He did not tell Brother Tull. One morning in March, with his hair

sections.heading: IV. The Ring
sections.dateline: Brother Tull’s place on Hinkston Creek · August 1807
sections.text: Before he left for the conference, he went to see Brother Tull. The old man was in the lot behind his barn with the red bull. It was August and the bull was in a temper because of the Gaither cows in the next field. He was bellowing and throwing his head and pawing up the ground, and the lather stood on his neck. Brother Tull had a hickory staff in his hand, about six feet long, with an iron hook at the end of it, and the hook was through the brass ring in the bull’s nose. He was walking the bull around the lot, slowly, at the end of the staff, and every time the bull flung his head toward the fence the old man gave the staff a little turn, not much, and the bull’s head came back around. Sandy stood at the fence and watched. The bull was a ton of meat and Brother Tull was seventy-one years old and weighed about as much as a sack of meal. After a while Brother Tull walked the bull into his stall and shut it in and hung the staff on two pegs on the wall of the barn, and came over and leaned on the fence beside him. I heard about what happened at your mama’s, he said. Sandy said he expected the whole county had. Brother Tull looked out over the lot. You’ve had a mind that went whereve

sections.heading: V. The Staff
sections.text: He rode circuits for fifty-four years: across the Green River country, through Tennessee and southern Indiana and Illinois, and at the last in Missouri, where he settled in Boone County and preached until he could not get up on a horse. He was ordained deacon and then elder, and he read everything that came over the mountains, so that the young preachers called him the Library. He married once, late, and buried her. He held something like four thousand meetings in his life, by his own count, and at every one of them, as long as he could stand, he was the one who stood up at the beginning and called the people in. He never could make himself say it any other way. Come on in, sinners. Come on in. He died in 1882, at ninety-three, in a chair by a hearth in Columbia, Missouri. Rachel had been dead forty years by then. On the wall over the chair, on two pegs, hung a hickory staff about six feet long with an iron hook at the end of it, worn black and smooth at the place where his hand had been.

title: Out of the Fire
logline: A twelve-year-old who exhorted at Cane Ridge walks home at eighteen to quit, and his stepmother sits him in the good chair.

verses.text: Be not thoughtless, watch your thoughts! Draw yourself out of the evil way, like an elephant sunk in mud.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Baddheraka is an elephant belonging to the king of Kosala, mighty in his youth. Worn out by age, he wades into a great lake one day, sticks fast in the mire and cannot get out, and the people who see him marvel that so strong an elephant has grown so weak. The king orders his elephant-trainer to free him. The trainer appears at the lakeside dressed as if for battle and has the battle-drum beaten. The old elephant's pride is roused, and he rises, walks out of the lake and stands on dry land. When monks report it, the Buddha tells them that the elephant has only pulled himself out of ordinary mud, while they have flung themselves into the far deeper mire of the defilements, and he urges them to strive with all their might to get out. Hearing the verse, those monks reach awakening.
bg.history:
Circuses have wintered in Hugo, in the Choctaw Nation of southeastern Oklahoma, since the Al G. Kelly and Miller Brothers Circus moved there in 1941. As many as twenty shows have been based there at one time or another, and the town calls itself "Circus City, USA." Circus people lie buried in Showmen's Rest at Mount Olivet Cemetery. In circus language every elephant, male or female, is a "bull," and its keeper a bullman. A "mud show" was a circus that moved by wagon from town to town. Its wagons sank so often on wet lots that elephants were kept to pull them out. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers finished damming the Kiamichi River for Hugo Lake, seven miles east of town, in 1974. A year later, in July 1975, two elephants escaped from a circus's off-season camp near Hugo into the woods.

In August 1972 Idi Amin gave the Asians of Uganda ninety days to leave the country, and each could take only a small sum of money with them (expulsion of Asians from Uganda). Most went to Britain, and about a thousand came to the United States. In the mid-1970s Gujarati families from India and East Africa began buying run-down roadside motels, which were cheap during the slump that followed the oil embargo. Investing about $40,000 in a business could qualify an immigrant for permanent residence. Insurers would not cover the motels and banks would not lend on them, so families financed one another and did all the work themselves, and some competitors answered with "American Owned" banners. Within a generation about half of the motels in the United States were owned by Indian Americans, most of them Gujarati. In 1979 the second oil crisis brought gasoline lines back to American highways.

sections.heading: I. The Night Desk
sections.text: The Kiamichi Motor Court had twenty-two rooms in an L around a gravel lot on the east side of Hugo, a sign with a neon arrow that had stopped pointing in 1971, and an ice machine that worked when you kicked it. Navin Patel bought it in the fall of 1976 for forty-one thousand dollars, which was the money his wife's brothers in Leicester had raised, and a little more than the forty thousand the government in Washington wanted to see a man put into a business before it would let him stay. No company in Oklahoma would insure it. No bank in Choctaw County would lend on it. Navin's cousins in Durant and Idabel and Paris, Texas, had put in a thousand here and two thousand there, and he was paying them back a room-night at a time. He lived behind the office with his wife and their two daughters. His wife cleaned eleven rooms in the morning and Navin cleaned the other eleven. The girls stripped beds after school. And from eleven at night until seven in the morning, Navin's uncle sat at the front desk. Everyone called him Kaka, which only means uncle. He was seventy. For thirty-four years he had taught English and mathematics at a secondary school in Kampala, and in August of 1972, when the

sections.heading: II. The Bull
sections.text: Hugo was a circus town. Three or four shows wintered there, more some years, and from November to March the fields south and east of town were full of trucks with lettering on their sides, and tigers in steel cages in a tin barn, and camels grazing behind barbed wire along the farm roads like something out of the Bible. In March the shows went out on the road. The trucks pulled out one morning in a long line with their horns going, and the town was quiet again until Thanksgiving. Not everything went. At the Bradley Brothers quarters on the Kiamichi road, three miles east of the Kiamichi Motor Court, the old animals stayed behind, the ones who could no longer make the jumps. A lion with no teeth. A pony mare who was blind. And Rani. In a circus every elephant is a bull. Rani was a cow, a female Asian elephant, and the bull men called her the old bull, or Old Lady, or Mama, and she was sixty years old by the best guess anybody had, which made her older than most of them. She had come off a ship in New York before the Depression with a crate number stenciled on her flank. She had worked for six shows under four names. Bradley Brothers had painted RANI on the leather headpiece she wore

sections.heading: III. The Lake
sections.dateline: Hugo Lake · a Sunday in May
sections.text: It rained for five days that May. The Kiamichi came up, and the Corps of Engineers let water out of the dam, and the arms of the lake spread out over the bottomland and then drew back and left behind them a mile of grey mud as smooth as cake icing, with dead trees standing up out of it. On Saturday night a wind came up out of the southwest ahead of a line of storms, and somewhere in the night it took down a section of the old fence on the far side of the quarters. Dewey found the gap at five in the morning, and her tracks going through it, each one as big around as a washtub and full of rainwater. She had walked a mile and a half through the timber in the dark and come out on the west arm of the lake and gone down the bank into the water to drink, or to bathe, or for the reason old animals go off by themselves, which nobody ever knows. She had waded out thirty yards. And there, on the flat where the water had been ten feet deep the week before, the mud had taken her. She was down in it past her knees, and then past her belly, and when she tried to swing herself free she only went deeper. By the time Dewey limped out of the trees with the sheriff's deputy behind him, she was standin

sections.heading: IV. The Drum
sections.text: Ray Bradley, who owned the show, was in a motel room in Joplin, Missouri, between a matinee and an evening performance, when the sheriff got through to him on the telephone. He listened a long while without saying anything. Then he said, Put Dewey on. Somebody ran down to the bank and brought Dewey back up to the deputy's car, and he stood bent over with one hand on the roof and the radio handset to his ear. Dewey, said Ray Bradley, a long way off and full of static. You get her out of there. Dewey Haskins put the handset back. He stood for a moment by the car. Then he asked the deputy to drive him to the quarters, and they went off up the gravel road in a hurry, and the people on the bank looked at each other. He was gone an hour. When the deputy's car came back down through the timber, Dewey got out of it in the spec. He had kept it in a footlocker under his bed for nine years. A white silk turban with a glass jewel in front the size of a hen's egg and a plume of dyed ostrich feathers coming up out of it. A short jacket of purple satin crusted all over with gold braid and sequins, gone green at the edges. A red sash. Baggy white trousers tucked into red boots that curled up at th

sections.heading: V. The Other Mud
sections.dateline: The Kiamichi Motor Court · that night
sections.text: They went straight to the motel. It was not eleven yet and Kaka was still in the back, so they waited for him on the floor of the office on the bedspread from Room 14, in their muddy shoes, and when he came out in his cardigan and sat down behind the counter they all began to tell him at once. He let them. Dinesh held up his hands to show the rope burns. Raju told about the drum and the turban and how the mud had sounded, and Bharat told about the man on the bank, and Mahesh, who did not usually say much on Sundays, told about her ears. Kaka, you should have seen her ears. Like she heard her name. Kaka listened to all of it. When they ran out he sat for a while with his hands folded on the closed book. Out on the highway a truck went by, and the lights of the Starlite Motel came and went across the window. So, he said. The old bull got herself out of the mud. They waited. That was only mud. Lake mud. It comes off with a hose. He looked at them, one at a time, the way he had looked at boys across a classroom in Kampala for thirty-four years. And you boys. Every one of you has gone into a worse mud than that. Headfirst. Up to here. He put the edge of his hand against his own throat.

sections.heading: VI. Plates
sections.text: The gasoline ran short that summer, the way the truckers had said, and the highway went quiet, and the banks took back four motels between Durant and the Arkansas line. The Kiamichi Motor Court was not one of them. That was the summer the Desai brothers sat down together on the tailgate of a pickup behind the Antlers Motor Inn and settled their four hundred dollars in ten minutes. It was the summer Bharat drove to Dallas and told his father's lender the truth, and Mahesh signed up for a night course in Paris, Texas, and passed his engineering exam three years later, and the summer the beer stopped turning up in the ice room at the Kiamichi Motor Court and nobody ever said a word about it. On the first hot morning in June Raju walked across Highway 70 to the Starlite Motel with a box of his aunt's sweets from the kitchen, the ones she made for Diwali, and knocked on the office door, and the man who owned the Starlite opened it in his undershirt and stood there looking at him a long time. The sign stayed up until the next spring, when the wind took it. Kaka went on sitting at the front desk from eleven until seven. On Sunday nights the young men kept coming, more of them every year,

title: The Old Bull
logline: In a circus town in the Choctaw Nation, young Gujarati motel men watch an old elephant sink into the mud of Hugo Lake.

verses.text: If a man find a prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, he may walk with him, overcoming all dangers, happy, but considerate.
If a man find no prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, let him walk alone, like a king who has left his conquered country behind,—like an elephant in the forest.
It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.

bg.commentary: This commentary story continues the quarrel of the monks of Kosambī (told in this series as The Washing Cup). Having failed to reconcile them, the Buddha spends the rains alone in the Protected Forest, where a noble elephant, Pārileyyaka, serves him. Afterward the great lay followers Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, and five hundred monks who have been living elsewhere, ask Ānanda to bring them to the Teacher. Ānanda leaves the monks outside and goes in alone; the elephant charges him with a stick until the Buddha calls it off, then offers to carry his bowl and robe. Ānanda declines, and he does not set his things on the stone slab where the Teacher sits. When the monks come in, they pity the Buddha for having had no one to serve him. He answers that the elephant did everything, speaks the three verses, and the five hundred become arahats. Read the full commentary story. The words standing in for the verses are from Montaigne's essays "Of Solitude" and "Of Friendship," in Charles Cotton's translation as edited by W. C. Hazlitt. By 1571 Montaigne had withdrawn from public life to the tower of his château, and he began the Essays there.
bg.history:
After the Great Fire of 1910 burned about three million acres of Idaho and Montana, the Forest Service built fire lookouts on summits across the Northwest. The most common design, the L-4, was a gabled cab with heavy shutters, and more than a thousand were put up across the western states. The ones of the 1930s were made in Columbia Falls, Montana, and shipped in pieces small enough to pack in on animals. Inside stood the lookout's chief tool, the Osborne Fire Finder: a round, glass-topped table with a map under the glass and the 360 degrees etched in its rim. For lightning there was a stool standing on glass insulators.

In 1930 the Forest Service bought a ranch in the Ninemile valley northwest of Missoula and opened the Ninemile Remount Depot. For thirty-two years it bred mules to pack supplies to fire crews and backcountry lookouts, and at its height it kept over 1,500 animals and thirty-five packers. Pack strings still winter there.

sections.heading: I. The Seminar Room
sections.text: The trouble in the English department began with a saucer of pipe ash. Mr. Dace, who lectured on the modern poets and filled every room he lectured in, smoked through a seminar in the library's Seminar Room, under a card that said NO SMOKING BY ORDER OF THE LIBRARIAN, and left the saucer on the table when he went. Dr. Pell, who taught Old English and the history of the language and knew every rule of the library by heart, found it there in the morning. He asked Mr. Dace whether he had seen the card. Mr. Dace said he had not. Then it is nothing, said Dr. Pell, and Mr. Dace thought no more about it. But that week Dr. Pell said to his graduate students, as a joke, that the modern poets did not read. By March the department had two seminars where it had had one, the student paper had printed eleven letters, and the faculty wives sat at separate tables at the Faculty Club. Edmund Coyle had been chairman for twenty-one years. He had built the department out of three men and a borrowed classroom, and both of the quarrelers had been hired by him. He was the son of a smelterman from Butte. As a young man he had worked a fire guard's summer in the Coeur d'Alenes and come out of the Big Burn

sections.heading: II. Sadie
sections.dateline: Blue Point Lookout, Lolo National Forest · July to September
