sections.text: Blue Point was a fourteen-foot square of windows on top of a rock, an L-4 cab with a shingle roof and heavy shutters that propped out like awnings, built at Columbia Falls and carried up the mountain in pieces on mules. In the middle of the floor stood the Osborne firefinder, a round table two feet across with a map of the whole country under its glass and the 360 degrees cut into its rim, and a sighting ring that turned on it, so that a man who saw smoke could lay the hair of the sight across it and read the bearing to the ranger station down the telephone wire. Against the walls were a bed, a table, a wood stove and a stool with glass insulators on its four legs, for standing on in lightning. What happened up there was told afterward by Ole Brekke, a Ninemile packer who had never read a book in his life and did not care who knew it, and by a forestry student on the next lookout to the west, who watched Blue Point every day through his glasses and wrote it down in his log. Ole brought the first string up on the second of July: six mules with groceries, kerosene, the canvas water bags and the professor's books. Among them was a big brown molly named Sadie who had been at Ninemile s

sections.heading: III. Miss Varner
sections.dateline: The Blue Point trail · the last week of September
sections.text: By the time the fall rains came and the fire season ended, the whole university had heard that the chairman of English was living on top of a mountain with a mule. The president wanted him back for the fall quarter. Mr. Lyle Danner, the lumberman, who had paid for the new wing of the library, wrote to say the same, and so did Mrs. Hattie Burke of the Board of Education, who had sent seven sons through the university and was the most formidable woman in western Montana. And the students came back in September from their summers in the mines at Butte and the harvest in the Palouse and the sawmills and the fire crews, and went to the department office, and asked Miss Varner to take them up. They had not heard him lecture since spring. Edna Varner had been secretary of the English department for sixteen years. She typed his letters and his examinations and knew which drawer he kept his pipe cleaners in. She drove forty of them out to the trailhead on a Saturday in a borrowed school bus, and they climbed all morning, and at the saddle below the last pitch, where they could see the lookout, she stopped them. Let me see him first, she said. Three months of nobody, and then forty of you ov

sections.heading: IV. The Catwalk
sections.text: They came up and stood around the catwalk in their boots and their summer sunburns, looking at the mule, who looked at them. There was not room for all of them inside. A girl from Great Falls said what most of them were thinking. Professor, you must have had an awful summer. All alone up here, at your age. No one to cook. Nobody to talk to. Hauling your own water up that hill. Sadie hauled my water, Coyle said. Sadie did everything. He came out onto the catwalk and stood with his hands on the rail. Below them the whole country lay open, ridge behind ridge to the Bitterroots, blue and then bluer, with the first snow on the high ones and no smoke anywhere. Montaigne had one friend in his life, he said. When the man died he said the only reason he could ever give for loving him was, because it was he, because it was I. If you find a friend like that, keep him your whole life and be glad of him. If you don't, go by yourselves. You can do worse than by yourselves. Bias said the greatest part is the worse part, and he was a wise man, and he had sat on committees. Some of them laughed. Then he took the book out of his coat pocket and read them the place he had read most that summer. ‘Tis

sections.heading: V. The Hood
sections.dateline: Blue Point · the first of October
sections.text: Ole Brekke came up a week later with the string to close the lookout. He hauled down the stove and the bedding and nailed the shutters closed. Last of all he put the canvas hood over the firefinder, the way the manual said, and tied it, so the glass would not crack in the cold. When he came out the snow had started. Sadie was standing at the head of the trail by herself, already headed down, waiting for the others to fall in behind her.

title: The Firefinder
logline: After his department's feud over a saucer of pipe ash, an English professor spends the fire season on a Montana lookout with a mule.

verses.text: If an occasion arises, friends are pleasant; enjoyment is pleasant, whatever be the cause; a good work is pleasant in the hour of death; the giving up of all grief is pleasant.
Pleasant in the world is the state of a mother, pleasant the state of a father, pleasant the state of a Samana, pleasant the state of a Brahmana.
Pleasant is virtue lasting to old age, pleasant is a faith firmly rooted; pleasant is attainment of intelligence, pleasant is avoiding of sins.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the Buddha is living in a forest hut in the Himalaya country at a time when kings oppress the people they rule, and he asks himself whether sovereignty could be exercised without killing or conquest or sorrow, with justice. Māra, the tempter, overhears the thought and takes it for ambition. He urges the Buddha to rule: a man of his powers could turn the Himalaya to gold, and Māra will see to everything wealth can do. The Buddha answers that a mountain of gold twice over would not be enough for one person, tells Māra the two of them have nothing in common, and speaks these verses on what is truly pleasant. Many gods who were listening, the story adds, understood.
bg.history:
The Angel Island Immigration Station opened in 1910 to enforce the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which barred Chinese laborers and let in only a few exempt classes, among them merchants, students and teachers. Most others who came claimed to be the children of citizens, many of them as “paper sons,” and were questioned before a Board of Special Inquiry on the smallest details of a village and a family. By the mid-1920s the wait for a hearing ran two or three weeks, but a man on appeal could be held as long as two years. The Immigration Act of 1924 narrowed the exempt classes further. On December 7, 1925, in Jeu Jo Wan v. Nagle, the federal appeals court in San Francisco upheld the exclusion of a Chinese teacher who held the old certificate, ruling that the new act limited teachers to “professors of colleges, academies, seminaries, or universities.” Moy Sin-saang is invented; the ruling is not. California had been Gold Mountain in Cantonese since the Gold Rush.

The detained men’s own society, the Zizhihui or Self-governing Association (in the Toisan speech of most detainees, Gee Gee Wui), called itself in English the Angel Island Liberty Association. The historian Him Mark Lai dated it to 1922; the Angel Island foundation gives 1918. Lai’s essays describe its officers, chosen from the men held longest and “at times respected intellectuals,” its dues, books and classes for the children, and the coaching notes that Chinese kitchen workers smuggled to the officers’ table under the words ga choi. Former detainees also remembered the “dark room,” a linen closet where the association shut up boys who stole or fought. Lai records two dining-hall disturbances in 1925, one on June 30 that brought soldiers with fixed bayonets from Fort McDowell, and notes that the food was apparently not the cause. A week earlier, on June 23, British and French troops had fired on a demonstration in Canton, the Shameen Incident. The poems the detainees cut into the barracks walls can still be read there. The schoolmaster’s two passages are from James Legge’s translation of Mencius.

sections.heading: I. The Wooden House
sections.dateline: Angel Island, San Francisco Bay · June 1925
sections.text: The men called the place the wooden house. It stood on the north side of the island above a cove, a long barracks of fir boards with bars on the windows and a fence around the yard, and that summer about two hundred of them slept in one room of it on iron bunks hung three high. The country they had come to lay across the water. They had called it Gold Mountain since before they could walk. From the windows on the water side a piece of it could be seen, a long line of bare hills that were brown all day, and for a quarter of an hour before the evening fog came through they were the color the name said. Moy Sin-saang had the bottom bunk by the second post. He was forty-four years old, a schoolmaster from a village of the Moy name below Toisan city, and he had come in the middle of March on a teacher’s paper to take the evening classes at a school on Stockton Street. For forty years and more a teacher had been one of the few kinds of Chinese the law let in. The new law of the summer before used the word differently, and nobody at the station could tell him whether a man who taught children their first thousand characters over a dry-goods store still counted. His file had gone to Washin

sections.heading: II. The Visitor
sections.text: Now there is one who listens for a thought of that kind. The men of the wooden house told it this way afterward. He heard the schoolmaster asking whether a man might govern, and took it that the schoolmaster wished to. And he reckoned that a chairman has a great deal to see to, and that a man with a great deal to see to can be caught looking the other way. The door was locked from outside, as it was every night, and the watchman had his chair in the hall. Nobody heard the bolt. A man was sitting on the edge of the Sin-saang’s bunk. He wore a gray suit of American cut and a straw hat, like the interpreters who came over on the morning boat, and he had a gold chain across his vest and a good deal of gold in his mouth. He spoke low. Chin, in the bunk above, said afterward that he spoke pure Hoiping, the speech of Chin’s own market town. Wong, across the aisle, said no, Toisan city, anybody could hear it. Every man who was awake heard the talk of the next lane over from his own mother’s door. Sin-saang, he said, take the chair tomorrow. They will give it to you if you only look up when they look at you. Be the one the old book asks for. Keep this room with nobody in the closet and nobo

sections.heading: III. The Added Dish
sections.text: In the morning the room chose a Hoiping man named Fong, who had been a shipping clerk in Hong Kong and had some English, and he did well enough. The two boys came out of the closet in time for breakfast. Old Lew was landed in August, after seventeen months, and wept on the stair, and left the Sin-saang his blanket. The Sin-saang kept his board and his cup of water. He taught the character for a person to every new boy who came up from the boat. He wrote the letters. When the room looked at him, on the days when there was something to decide, he looked up and said what he thought and went back to what he was doing. Each evening he watched the hills go gold for their quarter hour, with the interest of a man looking into the window of a shop where he needs nothing, and then the fog took them. In December the judges in the city ruled on another schoolmaster’s paper, the same kind as his. Under the new law, they said, a teacher meant a professor of a college or an academy, a seminary or a university, and a certificate that said teacher and no more would not do. His own order came the week after. He would go back on the next boat. On his last evening the cook’s helper came out of the kit

title: The Added Dish
place: Angel Island, San Francisco Bay, California
logline: A schoolmaster detained on Angel Island is offered the chair of the men's own association by a visitor no bolt keeps out.

verses.text: The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.
Whomsoever this fierce thirst overcomes, full of poison, in this world, his sufferings increase like the abounding Birana grass.
He who overcomes this fierce thirst, difficult to be conquered in this world, sufferings fall off from him, like water-drops from a lotus leaf.

This salutary word I tell you, ‘Do ye, as many as are here assembled, dig up the root of thirst, as he who wants the sweet-scented Usira root must dig up the Birana grass, that Mara (the tempter) may not crush you again and again, as the stream crushes the reeds.’

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two brothers become monks in the time of an earlier Buddha, Kassapa. The elder, Sodhana, takes up meditation and reaches awakening. The younger, Kapila, takes up study, becomes famous and rich, and grows so proud that he calls right wrong and wrong right and mocks the other monks as “empty-fists.” His brother admonishes him and gives him up. When no one will answer him at the recitation of the monastic rule, Kapila declares there is no Dhamma and no discipline, and walks out. His mother and sister follow his example, and all three go to hell. In the same age five hundred bandits take the precepts from a forest monk and keep them even when they are killed. Ages later they are reborn on one day as the sons of five hundred fishermen, and on their first outing they net a golden fish with breath that fouls the whole monastery. The king brings it to the Buddha, who has the fish name its brother, its mother, its sister and its fate. The fish dies, the Buddha teaches on craving, and the fishermen’s sons become monks.
bg.history:
Puritan Massachusetts gave full church membership, with the right to take the Lord’s Supper and vote in church affairs, only to those who could give a public account of their conversion. The Half-Way Covenant, endorsed by a synod in 1662, let the baptized but unconverted children of members bring their own children to baptism. It set off a pamphlet war among the ministers and split congregations. In Boston, members who left First Church in 1667 founded the Third Church, and the two churches did not share communion for fourteen years. Ministers trained at Harvard College read the Scriptures in Latin, Greek and Hebrew, and towns paid them in money, provisions and firewood. In 1684 Increase Mather published An Essay for the Recording of Illustrious Providences, a collection of sea deliverances, apparitions and other wonders gathered from ministers and witnesses across New England.

Along the North Shore, fishing towns like Marblehead lived on cod. Small boats worked the near ledges and, farther off, the grounds toward the Isles of Shoals and Nova Scotia, and the catch was split, salted and dried on wooden flakes along the shore, then shipped by the quintal from Salem and Boston to Europe and the West Indies. Marblehead was never firmly under Puritan control, and when its church was formally gathered in 1684 it had only fifteen men and thirty-nine women in full membership. Gull Cove, Cranfield and every person in this story are invented.

sections.heading: I. Two Callings
sections.text: Hannah Golding brought her two sons over from Essex with her daughter Thankful at the breast, and buried her husband at sea the second week out. She settled at Ipswich and kept a little shop of pins and thread and Spanish salt, and she raised the boys hard, on the catechism and on cornmeal, because those were what there was. When they were grown, Samuel at twenty and Elnathan at seventeen, the two of them went together to old Mr. Pell, who had been their minister since the ship, and asked him what was required of a man. Mr. Pell had no teeth left and very little patience, and he answered them as if they had asked the way to Rowley. Two things. Learning, and godliness. A man may have the first without the second and be damned. A man may have the second without the first, and be saved, and know very little about it. Samuel said he would see to his soul. He was not quick at books and knew it. He took a grant of land up the Merrimack, at the edge of the settled country, where the woods came down to the river, and went up there with an axe and a Bible and a cow, and lived alone, and prayed. He did that for five years, and at the end of it something had been settled in him that never cam

sections.heading: II. Empty Hands
sections.text: The church at Cranfield called him at twenty-six, and in five years he had made it the most talked-of pulpit north of Boston. People rode in from three towns on a Sabbath to hear him. He preached two hours by the glass and turned the glass over and went on, and nobody slept. He had a voice like a bell and a face that warmed when he spoke of the mercy of God, and when he preached on the glory of Christ, old men wept who had not wept since England. The town raised his salary three times. They built him a house with a parlor and gave him a pew for his mother and sister at the front, under the pulpit, and every November the whole town turned out with ox-sleds to bring in the minister's wood, forty cords of it, more than any minister in the Bay was given. He began to notice how much he was given, and to want more, and to know that what he knew was the reason. And he began, slowly, then all at once, to find that the other ministers of the Bay did not know very much. At the meetings of the ministers he took the other side of every question, to see if he could carry it, and he could. When the synod was called on the baptism of the children of half-members, he spoke against it until it pass

sections.heading: III. Seven
sections.dateline: The woods above the Merrimack · October 1666
sections.text: Four years before Samuel died, seven men came to his door in the night. They were runaways, most of them, bound servants who had broken their indentures, and one was a sailor off a Bristol ship, and their captain was a big red-headed man named Harnett who had run from a farm at Andover. All that summer they had lived in the woods and come out at night to rob the farms along the river, cows and pigs and corn and once a whole cellar of cider, and in September they had broken into a house at Haverhill and taken the money out of a chest, and the man of the house had come at them with a fowling piece and been knocked down and lay a week before he could speak. Now the townsmen were out after them, forty men with guns and dogs, and the seven came through the dark with the dogs behind them and saw Samuel's light. They pushed in at the door. Samuel was sitting at the table. He did not get up. Hide us, said Harnett. For the love of God, Goodman, be our refuge. Samuel looked at them a long time. There was a great deal of mud on them, and blood on one. There is no refuge for you in this house, he said. There is no refuge for you anywhere but the commandments. Will you keep them? All of you? Ev

sections.heading: IV. The First Fare
sections.text: The seven grew up together on the rocks and in the boats. They learned to split and salt fish before they could write their names, and some of them never did learn that, and by twelve they were going out with their fathers to the ledges off Cape Ann, and by sixteen to the Isles of Shoals, and by eighteen down east to Cape Sable for the spring fare. Ben Tuck was the best of them in a boat and the first of them in everything else, and the other six followed him as if it had been settled before they were born, which in a sense it had. Gull Cove was not a godly place. It had a meetinghouse, and a minister, and a tithingman with a long staff to wake sleepers. But the men were at sea half the Sabbaths of the year and drunk a fair part of the rest, and when they were in church they sat in the back and smelled of fish. Not one fisherman in ten was in full communion. The ministers of the Bay spoke of Gull Cove as they spoke of the Isles of Shoals, with a sigh. In the summer of 1686, when the seven were twenty, Ebenezer Tuck gave them his old shallop, and they caulked her and rigged her and went out on their own for the first time. It was not a real fare. They had a seine, and they meant to

sections.heading: V. The Fish Speaks
sections.text: Mr. Amos Hollings was twenty-eight years old. His father had fished out of Marblehead and drowned off Cape Sable, and the church at Marblehead had paid for the boy to go to the college because he could read Latin at nine and there was nothing else to be done with him. He had been called to Gull Cove because no one else would come. He was a plain, quiet young man with chapped hands, who preached for one hour exactly, and who could be found most days in his garden behind the parsonage on his knees, digging quitch grass out of his bean rows with a knife. They carried the hogshead into the meetinghouse because there was nowhere else to put it, and set it down before the pulpit. Half the Cove crowded in after it, and stood in the pews and on the benches. Mr. Hollings looked into the water. The cod hung there, gold, turning slowly. Then it opened its mouth. Every person who was in the meetinghouse that morning said the same thing about it for the rest of their lives, and some of them lived to be very old. They were fishing people, who lived in the smell of fish and never noticed it. This they noticed. It was the smell of a sickroom where somebody has lain a long time dying, and of a priv

sections.heading: VI. Quitch Grass
sections.text: They buried the cod in the sand above the tide line beyond the point, deep, and the smell did not leave the meetinghouse for a month. They washed the floor with lye and whitewashed the walls and kept the doors open in the rain, and still on the Sabbath you could catch it, under the smell of wet wool, and people looked at each other. Mr. Hollings preached that Sabbath to the fullest meetinghouse Gull Cove had ever had. Men stood in the doorways. The seven sat together in the back, in their good shirts, all in a row. He did not preach on hell. Everyone had expected him to, and he did not. He preached on what the Scripture says a church must do with a scorner, which is to put him out, for the sake of the others and his own, and to have no more to do with him until he mends. Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease. — Proverbs 22:10 And then he talked about his bean rows. He said that every man in that meetinghouse knew quitch grass, because every man there had a wife with a garden. He said that you could cut it off at the top every morning of your life and it would be back by evening. He said that after a rain it came up twice as thick, a

title: The Yellow Cod
logline: Seven young fishermen born on one night haul in a golden cod whose breath fouls the whole meetinghouse.

verses.text: As a tree, even though it has been cut down, is firm so long as its root is safe, and grows again, thus, unless the feeders of thirst are destroyed, the pain (of life) will return again and again.
He whose thirst running towards pleasure is exceeding strong in the thirty-six channels, the waves will carry away that misguided man, viz. his desires which are set on passion.
The channels run everywhere, the creeper (of passion) stands sprouting; if you see the creeper springing up, cut its root by means of knowledge.
A creature’s pleasures are extravagant and luxurious; sunk in lust and looking for pleasure, men undergo (again and again) birth and decay.
Men, driven on by thirst, run about like a snared hare; held in fetters and bonds, they undergo pain for a long time, again and again.
Men, driven on by thirst, run about like a snared hare; let therefore the mendicant drive out thirst, by striving after passionlessness for himself.

bg.commentary: Walking into Rājagaha for alms, the Buddha saw a young sow wallowing in filth and smiled. Ānanda asked why. The sow, he said, had once been a hen that lived beside a hall and listened to a monk reciting; from the mere sound she was reborn a princess, Ubbarī. The princess saw a heap of maggots in a privy, held the sight in her mind, and reached the first absorption, and from that was reborn in a Brahmā heaven. Then she fell, to a rich household and then to this sty. Standing in the street he spoke six verses on craving: the cut tree that grows again from its root, the streams that run everywhere, the creeper, the hare in the snare. The sow went on through seven more births, in the Golden Land, at Benares, in a horse dealer’s house in one port and a mariner’s in another, in a noble house in the capital of Sri Lanka, and at last as Sumanā, a villager’s daughter whose village emptied out and who married the king’s minister. A monk at her door remarked to his companions what a wonder it was that a young sow should be the minister’s wife. She remembered everything, was shaken, got her husband’s leave, and went forth. She won the first fruit on hearing one discourse recited and arahatship, back in her home village after the war, on hearing another; and on the day she died she told nuns and monks all thirteen of her lives and urged them to keep at the work. Here is the full commentary story. In this retelling the one who sees and smiles is the sow, and the thirteen lives are one woman’s addresses.
bg.history:
Minnesota has crowned a state dairy princess, Princess Kay of the Milky Way, since 1954, chosen from among county princesses; several early ones came from Freeborn and Mower counties. The J. R. Watkins company of Winona sold liniment, vanilla, pepper and farm remedies door to door, was the largest direct-sales firm in the world in the 1940s, and went through bankruptcy and a sale in 1978. The Twins of 1965 took first place on July 1 and kept it, and their games went out over WCCO. A gilt is a young sow that has not yet farrowed, and the Chester White is an old American white breed. Tenant farmers in the Corn Belt customarily moved on the first of March. Creeping charlie, or ground ivy, roots at every joint of its stem, which is why pulling it does not work.

sections.text: Arnold Enger had the Watkins route in the south half of Freeborn County for thirty-one years. For the house he carried vanilla and black pepper and the red liniment. For the barn he carried stock dip and fly spray and a hog mineral, and so at every place he went to the barn as well as to the kitchen door. That summer he had a boy riding along to carry the case, a nephew of his wife’s named Dale, who was fourteen. On a morning in August they pulled into Tollef Sande’s yard north of Hayward and nobody came out. The Sandes had gone to a funeral in Blue Earth. Arnold walked back to the hog house to leave a pail of mineral on account. There was a radio going in there. Tollef kept one on a nail over the feed alley, tuned to WCCO, because he held that a gilt farrowed easier with a voice in the building. That was the summer the Twins were in first place, and no barn radio in southern Minnesota got shut off at night. sections.text: In the rooms they tell it that the gilt knew what Arnold knew and the rest besides. This is what there was to know. Glenna Hovey was born in her grandfather’s house in Hegre, a town of two hundred then, and the grandfather lost the house. Her folks rented forty acres next to Hegre Lutheran. From the time she was six the hens were her job, and the hens liked the south wall of the church, where the ground was warm. On Tuesdays and Thursdays the confirmation class recited with the windows open. She stood under the sill with a pan of oyster shell and the hens around her feet. She heard twenty voices say a thing together and then ask together, What does this mean? and then say what it meant. She could not have told you a word of it afterward. But the sound of it went into her, and they say it never came out. That life ended overnight, the way it does for a hen when the hawk comes. The landlord’s son came home from the service wanting the place, and the Hoveys were out by the first of March, which is the day tenants move in that country. verses.text: He who having got rid of the forest (of lust) (i.e. after having reached Nirvana) gives himself over to forest-life (i.e. to lust), and who, when removed from the forest (i.e. from lust), runs to the forest (i.e. to lust), look at that man! though free, he runs into bondage.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk who lives with the great ascetic Mahā Kassapa and has mastered the four meditative absorptions visits his uncle, a goldsmith, is taken with the gold ornaments in the house, and leaves the order. Too lazy to work, he is put out of the house, falls in with thieves and is caught. As he is led bound to the place of execution, beaten at every crossroads, Kassapa sees him, has his bonds loosened and tells him to take up his old meditation subject again. He regains the fourth absorption and sits among the raised weapons without fear, until the executioners, astonished, report him to the king, who sets him free. The Buddha then sends a radiant image of himself and speaks the verse, which plays on vana, both "forest" and "desire"; the man reaches the first stage of awakening where he sits, rises through the air to the Buddha, and becomes an arahant before the assembly.
bg.history:
In 1694 the mystic Johannes Kelpius brought a company of learned German Pietists to the Wissahickon Creek near Germantown to await the end of the world, a community remembered as the Society of the Woman in the Wilderness, after the twelfth chapter of Revelation. According to Julius Sachse's German Pietists of Provincial Pennsylvania (1895), their log tabernacle was forty feet square, set to the points of the compass, with a roof lantern where members watched the sky by night so that their lamps would be trimmed if the Bridegroom came. After Kelpius died in 1708 most of the brothers returned to the world, the watch was abandoned, and a few lived on as recluses along the creek. His Method of Prayer on inward, silent prayer was translated into English in 1761 and reprinted at Germantown in 1763. Brother Wendel, the widow Ott, Christoph Bender and the Kayser shop are invented. Germans had been coming since the Palatine emigration of 1709, and in greater numbers from 1717.

Under William Penn, Pennsylvania had the mildest criminal code in the colonies: property crimes were punished with restitution, and only murder carried death. That law expired with Penn in 1718, and under Governor William Keith the Assembly made a large number of offenses capital, as in England. Pardons still came: in 1725 a woman convicted of burglary in Pennsylvania was pardoned on condition that she leave the colony.

sections.heading: I. The Watch
sections.text: Christoph Bender came up the river in the fall of 1717 at thirteen years old, alone, off a ship from Rotterdam on which his father and mother and a sister had died between the Downs and the Delaware Capes. The ship's master sold the other orphans' time to farmers on the wharf. Nobody would buy Christoph's, because he had the flux, and an old man in a brown coat who had come down to the river to sell bark and roots paid his passage money out of a cloth bag and walked him to Germantown, six miles, holding him up by the back of his collar. The old man was Brother Wendel. He was one of the last of the learned men who had come over with the Magister in 1694 to wait in the forest for the end of the world. There had been forty of them then, and a log house on the ridge above the creek, forty feet square and set true to the compass, with a little room on the roof where one of them sat every night of the year with a brass telescope, watching the sky so that if the Bridegroom came at midnight their lamps would be found trimmed. The Magister had been dead nine years. Most of the forty had gone back into the world, to marry and to keep school and to plead in the courts and buy land, and the wa

sections.heading: II. Front Street
sections.text: His mother's brother was a goldsmith in Philadelphia. Christoph had not known it until a German from Front Street bought dried snakeroot from Brother Wendel at the market and asked whose boy that was, and heard the name Bender, and said Jacob Kayser had a sister who married a Bender in Kreuznach. In the summer of 1723 Brother Wendel sent Christoph into the town with a parcel of medicines for the goldsmith's wife, who had an ague, and told him to come back the same night. Jacob Kayser's shop was on Front Street above the High Street, in a brick house that faced the river, with a glass window of small square panes and a counter of walnut. Christoph stood at the counter with the parcel and waited, and while he waited he looked into the case. He had never seen gold close. There were shoe buckles in the case and knee buckles, and a pair of sleeve buttons with a lion stamped in each, and a row of mourning rings with a little skull enameled black on the bezel and a name and a date inside, ordered by the dozen for a funeral, and a gold chain for a watch laid out in a long curve on green baize. It went through him in waves from the knees up, and his teeth went with it, and the crowd saw it and laughed, and he thought he would be sick on his own coffin before they ever got him to the gallows. verses.text: Wise people do not call that a strong fetter which is made of iron, wood, or hemp; far stronger is the care for precious stones and rings, for sons and a wife.

That fetter wise people call strong which drags down, yields, but is difficult to undo; after having cut this at last, people leave the world, free from cares, and leaving desires and pleasures behind.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, thirty monks from the country come to see the Buddha, and the next morning, walking for alms, pass the king’s prison and see robbers and murderers bound in fetters, ropes and chains. That evening they ask whether any bond is stronger. These are nothing, the Buddha says, beside the longing for wealth, crops, sons and wives; and he tells of a poor man of long ago whose wife asked him to wait for one child and then another, until he rose in the night and left, talked his way past the city guards, and went up into the Himalaya.
bg.history:
Punjabi men, most of them Sikhs from the Doaba, were farming cotton in the Imperial Valley by the 1910s. California’s Alien Land Law barred them from owning farmland, so they held it through bankers, lawyers and, later, their American-born children; partners with nothing on paper sometimes ended in court or worse. Immigration law kept their wives in India, and several hundred married women of Mexican descent, founding the Punjabi-Mexican families of California. The Luce–Celler Act of 1946 at last let them become citizens, own land in their own names and send for relatives, a year before the Partition divided Punjab. The El Centro gurdwara opened in 1947 in a building that the town’s Japanese American Buddhists had been forced to sell after their wartime removal.

The two sloks are numbers 53 and 54 of the fifty-seven attributed to Guru Tegh Bahadur, which close every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition holds that he sent the first from his imprisonment in Delhi in 1675, and Macauliffe, whose 1909 translation is used here, follows the account that his young son Gobind Rai wrote the second in reply. Correhuela is field bindweed, whose roots run several yards down and which regrows from any piece left in the ground. Kehar Singh, his partner and everyone else in the story are invented.

They came from Niland and Calipatria and the ditch camps east of Holtville, and four came the whole way from Casa Grande in a Ford truck with a cracked block, and they parked along the side street by the hall the Japanese families had built for their Buddha. The Japanese families had been sent to the camps in the war and had been made to sell it. The Punjabi farmers of the valley had bought it, and for one year now it had been their own temple, the only one south of Stockton. They were old men, most of them. They had come to California before the first war, when a man from the Doaba could still get in, to pick and then to lease and then to grow cotton on land that the law said they could not own. So the land had gone into the names of bankers and lawyers, and later into the names of their own children as fast as the children were born. The law had also left them no way to bring a wife. The ones who married had married Mexican women from the cotton camps, and their sons were called Singh and served Mass. They had come for the birthday, and they had come to see Doña Cuca. A gray bus stood at the curb with the state’s name on it. Two deputies were bringing men out to it, eleven men on one long chain. Doña Cuca, eleven men could not have broken that chain. A mule could not. Is there anything in the world that holds a man harder than that? She was drying the big kettle. She set it down and went out the back door in the dark and came in again with something trailing from her fist. Give me your hand. She wound it four times around his wrist and tucked the end under. Break it. He turned his wrist and it parted. Some of the men laughed. Two fingers, she said. A child can do it. sections.heading: IV. The Row
sections.dateline: Doña Cuca’s eighty acres · Monday, first light
sections.text: Andrés did not sleep in the hall with the others. Some time before morning he drove out the Holtville road, and when the sky went gray he was standing at the end of her lettuce, and she was already in it, bent double over the short hoe, a quarter of the way down the first row. He did not have a hoe. He got down on his knees in the next row over. The lettuce was up four inches. Every few feet a string of correhuela had come out of the ground beside a plant and gone up it, around and around, always the same way, and laid its own leaves over the top. He took hold of the first one to pull. Don’t yank, she said, without straightening. You’ll bring the lettuce. So he found the end of it with his thick fingers and turned it back off the plant, one turn and then the next, the way it had come. It took a long time. When it was free the lettuce stood up by itself, a little crooked. He held the vine. It had one flower on it, white with a pink stripe, just coming open because the sun was on it now. He looked down the row. It ran a quarter of a mile to the ditch. Now the next one, said Doña Cuca.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Queen Khemā, wife of King Bimbisāra of Magadha, is so proud of her beauty that she will not go near the Buddha, because she has heard that he finds fault with beauty of form. The king has songs made in praise of his Bamboo Grove, which he had given to the Buddha, and when she hears them she asks what grove they are singing of; it is her own. When she goes, the Buddha makes a woman appear beside him, more beautiful than Khemā, fanning him with a palm-leaf fan, and Khemā cannot look away. The Buddha then ages the woman before her eyes to an old woman and at last to a heap of bones. Khemā sees that there is no core in the body, and the Buddha speaks a verse on the body as a sick, leaking thing that only fools desire, and then the verse of the spider and its web. She attains awakening. The Buddha tells the king she must now either go forth or pass away, and the king says, let her go forth. She became the nun the Buddha named foremost in wisdom. bg.history:
By the First World War about 12,000 Romanians lived in Cleveland, most of them peasants from Transylvania, then part of Austria-Hungary. The largest settlement was on the West Side, between West 45th and West 65th streets on either side of Detroit Avenue, near the factories and docks where the men worked; most of the early immigrants were young men who lived in boarding houses run by families from their home districts. In 1904 they founded St. Mary’s, the first Romanian Orthodox parish in America, and built its first church on Detroit Avenue. See Romanians in the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History and St. Mary’s Romanian Orthodox Church on Cleveland Historical.

Văratec, in Neamț County, was founded in 1785 and grew into a village of nuns living in small houses along lanes around the church; in 1909 it had 304 nuns and sisters, and it was long known for its embroidery and weaving. In Orthodox tradition, as in Catholic, a married person may enter monastic life only with the consent of the spouse.

sections.heading: I. The Photograph
sections.text: On Detroit Avenue, a few doors from the church, there was a photographer’s studio with a window full of brides, and in the middle of the window, for three years, hung the photograph of Ileana Bratu. She had come from Săliște, below the mountains in Transylvania, in the spring of 1907, to marry Ioan Bratu, who kept a boarding house for twenty-two men from Săliște and a grocery under it, at the corner of West Fifty-fourth Street. She was nineteen. She had brought with her one trunk, and in the trunk her mother’s best ie, the white blouse worked at the shoulders and cuffs in black and red, so close that the linen hardly showed, and the week after the wedding Ioan took her down to the studio in it and had her photographed, standing, with one hand on a carved chair and her hair down her back as a girl wears it, though she was a married woman. The photographer asked to keep a print for the window. Ioan, who was proud, said yes. The men in the boarding house called her Cosânzeana, after the princess in the stories, Ileana Cosânzeana, who is so beautiful you can look at the sun but not at her. They said it at first behind her back and then to her face, and she let them. The men who came ov

sections.heading: II. The Wood on the Rocky River
sections.dateline: West Fifty-fourth Street · spring and summer
sections.text: Ioan Bratu was not a priest’s son, but he had been raised to fear God and to give, and he did both. He had saved, and bought land, as men from Săliște did, and one of the pieces he had bought was eleven acres of beech and maple woods on the bluff over the Rocky River, west of the city, for which he had no use at all except that the beeches reminded him of home. In the summer of 1909 he had given Maica Agafia leave to live there. Some of the men from the boarding house went out on a Sunday and built her a hut of logs and boards under the trees, with a little porch and a shelf for an icon, and after that she lived in the woods like the old hermits in the mountains at home, and came into the city only for the dead. People began to go out to her. They went out Detroit Avenue on the streetcar and walked the last of it, women mostly, at first, and then some of the men, on Sunday afternoons, and sat on the ground in front of her porch, and she talked to them a little, not much. They came back quieter than they went. Ioan went every Sunday he could. Ileana would not. It grieved him. He did not know how to say so. He was a man who said things with money. On Saturday nights a pair of lăutari

sections.heading: III. The Girl with the Branch
sections.dateline: The bluff over the Rocky River · a Sunday in July
sections.text: She went the next day, in her good kerchief and the ie from the photograph, with two of the women from the boarding house. She told herself she was going to see the wood. It was everything in the song. The beeches went up gray and smooth and the light came down green through them, and there was a smell of leaf mold and of water, and the river was loud below the bluff. A spring came out of the bank. At the edge of the trees by the hut there was a linden in full flower, and the bees in it made a sound like a held note on the fiddle. Twenty or thirty people were sitting on the ground in front of the porch. Maica Agafia sat on the step in her black with her hands in her lap, talking to them in her small voice, and beside her, standing, a girl was fanning her with a branch of the linden to keep the flies off. Ileana stopped where she was. She had never seen the girl in the colony. She would have known. The girl was perhaps seventeen, in an ie like her own but finer, the work at the shoulders so close it looked like a single piece of red and black, and her hair was down her back. She was more beautiful than anyone Ileana had ever seen, or ever imagined, more beautiful than the photograph

sections.heading: IV. Ioan
sections.dateline: West Fifty-fourth Street · the following week
sections.text: She did not take off the kerchief. She did not go down to the studio and ask for the photograph, which hung in the window until the photographer took it down himself, in the fall, to make room. She cooked for twenty-two men and washed their shirts and swept, and did it all very well, and sat at night in the kitchen with her hands in her lap and the lamp out. She did not cry.
