sections.heading: V. Văratec
sections.text: She sailed from New York in October with a letter from Maica Agafia to the abbess, and her trunk, and in the trunk her mother’s ie, which she gave at Văratec to the sisters who did the embroidery, to unpick for the thread. Văratec was a village of nuns, three hundred of them, in little whitewashed houses along lanes under the hills, each with its garden. She was given a garden. In it there was a linden. She was tonsured as Monahia Agafia, at her own asking, after the old woman on the Rocky River. Visitors who came to Văratec in the years between the wars, when the convent was full of famous ladies from Bucharest going on retreat in good shoes, sometimes asked to be taken to the nun who had been in America, because they had heard she could answer anything. She could not answer everything. But she would let them sit on the bench under her linden and ask, and she would listen until they had heard their own question, and then say one thing. The ladies went home and quoted it at dinners, usually wrong. There is a story that one of them, a beautiful young woman with a famous name, asked her once whether it was true that she had been the most beautiful girl in Cleveland, America, and that

title: The Linden Branch
logline: The most beautiful bride on Cleveland's Romanian West Side crosses the street to avoid an old nun, until her husband hires fiddlers.

verses.text: Give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle, when thou goest to the other shore of existence; if thy mind is altogether free, thou wilt not again enter into birth and decay.
Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has cut all fetters, who never trembles, is independent and unshackled.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Uggasena, a rich man's son of Rājagaha, falls in love with an acrobat's daughter he sees dancing on top of a pole. He refuses food until he can have her, and her father agrees only if he will travel with the troupe. He drives their carts and hauls their gear, and his wife mocks him in songs to their baby son. Stung, he learns the art himself and comes home to perform on a pole sixty cubits high. At the height of his act the Buddha enters the city, and the whole crowd turns to look at him. The Buddha sends the Elder Moggallāna to invite Uggasena to go on. He turns fourteen somersaults, and the Buddha tells him to let go of past, future and present. Uggasena is freed where he stands, comes down unafraid and is ordained. When the monks doubt his claim that he felt no fear, the Buddha speaks the second verse. A past-life story tells of a young couple who fed an elder on their way to work at a shrine, and when he smiled, called him an actor.
bg.history:
By the middle of the eighteenth century Newport was one of the busiest ports in British America, with a population of 6,753 in 1755. Much of its wealth came from the triangle trade: molasses from the Caribbean was distilled into rum, the rum was shipped to West Africa, and it was traded there for captive people. In 1764 the town had twenty-two rum distilleries. Rhode Island's paper money, the "Old Tenor" bills, had lost so much value that when the colony converted them to lawful money in 1763 it took twenty-six and two-thirds Old Tenor shillings to make one (Rhode Island pound). The town's Colony House, built in 1739, stood at the head of the open ground where the Long Wharf ran out into the harbor.

Quakers had been welcome in Newport since 1658, and they rose high in its trade and government. Their Great Friends Meeting House, raised in 1699, is the oldest surviving house of worship in Rhode Island. Each year it hosted the New England Yearly Meeting, when Friends from all over the region crowded into the town. Recognized ministers, women as well as men, were called "public Friends." Many traveled in the ministry for months or years at a time, carrying a certificate from their monthly or quarterly meeting and relying on the hospitality of Friends along the way. Newport had no theatre of its own in these years. When a London company of players opened a playhouse on Easton's Point in 1761 in defiance of a town council vote, the colony soon answered with a law against stage plays that stopped performances for decades.

sections.heading: I. The Benches
sections.text: Once a year, or once in two years, a company of rope-dancers and tumblers came up the coast from the southern colonies and played a week at Newport, on the open ground below the Colony House at the head of the Long Wharf. Their master was a Frenchman out of London named Garnier, and they were eleven in all, with three wagons, a sea-chest of spangles and a great many ropes. They stretched the tight rope between two masts and the slack rope between two others, and they set up a spar of sixty feet in the middle of the ground and stayed it with lines to the corners like a ship's mast. People came in from Portsmouth and Middletown and over the ferry from Jamestown, and they stood on benches set on top of other benches and threw coppers and Spanish silver and the Colony's paper money, which was worth so little by then that a gentleman would throw it by the handful and think nothing of it. On the fourth day Garnier's daughter climbed the spar. She went up it hand over hand with her feet bare, turned over once in the air at the top, and came down standing on the cap of the mast, on a board no wider than a Bible, sixty feet over the cobbles. Then she danced there. She sang a French song and

sections.heading: II. The Wagon
sections.text: They played New York and Perth Amboy and Philadelphia, and went down through the Jerseys and Maryland to Annapolis and Williamsburg, and the next spring north again. They played courthouse greens and tavern yards and fairs, wherever the magistrates would let them, and left in the night wherever they would not. Edmund drove the lead wagon. Wherever they stopped he cut grass and carried water for the horses. Wherever they played he set up the masts and the scaffolds and stayed the spar, swept the ground, took the money at the rope, and when it was over he struck it all and loaded it again. He had never done a day's work in his life. His hands bled for a month and then were horn. In the spring at Annapolis Nan had a son. They named him Josiah, for Edmund's father, who did not answer the letter. Nan went back up on the rope three weeks after, and in the evenings she sat on the wagon step with the boy on her knee and bounced him and sang to him. She made the songs up as she went, in English and in French, to old tunes. Hush, my little carter's son,carter's son, carter's son,son of a hewer of wood and drawer of water,son of a know-nothing, hush. Edmund was greasing a wheel. He listened t

sections.heading: III. The Spar
sections.text: The war with France had been declared that spring, and every wharf in the town was fitting out a privateer. Edmund got a sixty-foot topmast out of a brig at the Long Wharf that would not be ready for sea for a month, and he had the crier go through the town and printed bills put up on the doors of the taverns: Seven Days Hence, on the Ground below the Colony House, Mr. EDMUND LISLE, Son of a Merchant of this Town, will Perform upon the Spar. His father tore the bill off the door of the distillery with his own hand. His mother read it at the window and sent him a cold chicken by Cudjo. It was the week of the Yearly Meeting, when the Friends of all New England came to Newport to sit together in the Great Meeting House, from Nantucket and Dartmouth and Lynn and Smithfield, and every Quaker house on the Point had six to a bed. So the town was full. On the seventh day the people built the benches up three and four high around the ground, and stood on them, and sat on the Colony House steps, and climbed the rigging of the ships at the Long Wharf to see. Among the Friends that week was an old woman from the mainland named Mercy Dunbar, a public Friend, which is to say a minister, who had

sections.heading: IV. The Invitation
sections.dateline: The Colony House ground · the same forenoon
sections.text: Mercy Dunbar stopped at the edge of the crowd and looked up at him a long while with her hand shading her eyes. Then she said something to Deborah Pell, and Deborah came forward through the benches, and the people let her by, and she went straight across the empty ground to the foot of the spar and stood there with her feet apart and put back her head and called up to him, in a voice that had called across a good deal of water. Look down here, Edmund Lisle! Thou that art so strong on the rope! Make a stage for the people! Make them laugh! Edmund looked down at her. Something came back into him all at once, warm, the way blood comes back into a hand. Even the Quakers want to see it, he thought. The old woman wants to see me do it. And he called down from the cap of the mast: Look up here, Friend! Thou that art so wise and strong! I'll make a stage for the people! I'll make them laugh! And he went up off the board into the air and turned fourteen times, over and over, so fast the spangles on the scarlet jacket made one ring of light around him, and came down standing on the cap of the mast with his arms out, and the benches came back to him with a roar that sent the gulls up off ever

sections.heading: V. The Ground
sections.text: Then he came down. He did not climb. He walked off the board onto the stays as if they were a staircase and came down the line to the ground, hand over hand and sometimes no hands at all, and stepped off onto the cobbles and went across to where the old woman stood and knelt down in front of her. Let me come with thee, he said. Let me be one of you. Mercy Dunbar put out her right hand and he took it. Come then, Friend, she said. This is the part that people would not agree about afterward and that the Friends never put in any minute. A good many people on the benches swore to it, and the sailor in the rigging of the snow swore to it, and Caleb Hart, who was not given to fancies, swore to it all his life: that when Edmund Lisle stood up from his knees he was not wearing the scarlet jacket or the white stockings or the spangles, but a plain coat of grey drugget and a broad hat, like any Friend from the Point. And that his hair, which had been as brown as a chestnut, was white, and his face was the face of a man of sixty, quiet and lined and very kind. And then they looked again and he was Edmund Lisle, twenty-four years old, in a scarlet jacket, holding an old woman's hand. And yet t

sections.heading: VI. The Smile
sections.text: The talk went all through the Quaker houses on the Point that week, and the young Friends kept it up longest. How could a man who had it in him to come to that in a single forenoon have run off down the coast after a rope-dancer's girl, and carried water for a Frenchman's horses for two years? And if he had been that kind of man, how had he come to it at all? Mercy Dunbar heard them at it one evening and asked what they were talking about, and they told her. It's the one thing, she said. Both of them. And she told them a story. When she was a girl of twenty, she said, Friends raised the Great Meeting House here on the Point, and Friends came from all over the colony with wagons of food to feed the men who were raising it. On the road from Portsmouth she was walking with an old public Friend from England who had come over in the ministry. A young man and his wife came up behind them with a cart full of bread and cheese and salt fish for the raising. The young woman saw the old Friend walking and said to her husband: Look, there's a minister going in, and we've a whole cart of victuals. Give him something. So the husband got down and filled the old man's hat with bread and cheese, an

title: Cloud of Witnesses
logline: A rum merchant's son runs off with a rope-dancer, learns her art, and comes home to climb a sixty-foot spar.

verses.text: If a man is tossed about by doubts, full of strong passions, and yearning only for what is delightful, his thirst will grow more and more, and he will indeed make his fetters strong.
If a man delights in quieting doubts, and, always reflecting, dwells on what is not delightful (the impurity of the body, &c.), he certainly will remove, nay, he will cut the fetter of Mara.

bg.commentary: In the commentary a young monk takes his ticket-meal to the assembly hall, finds no water there, and goes to a house for some. The young woman of the house tells him to come to her and nowhere else when he needs water. In time she gives him gruel as well, then a seat and a meal, and sits near him and says how lonely the house is. He grows discontented with the monk’s life and so sallow that visiting monks ask what is wrong; his teachers bring him to the Buddha, who rebukes him and then tells a story of the past. A brilliant young archer, married to his teacher’s daughter, kills fifty bandits with fifty arrows and pins their chief, but his wife, taken with the bandit at a glance, hands the bandit the sword. The bandit, reasoning that she would betray him as easily, strips her of her ornaments at a river and abandons her; the god Sakka, as a jackal who drops his meat to snatch at a fish and loses both, shames her. The Buddha identifies the monk as the archer, the woman as the wife and himself as the jackal, and speaks the two verses. Read the full commentary story; the tale within it is a version of the Jātaka of the Little Archer (no. 374). The old story lays the whole blame on the woman. The retelling keeps its events and its closing identification, and lets the teller have second thoughts.
bg.history:
The Klamath Project, begun in 1906, drained lakes and marshes on the Oregon–California line and irrigates some 200,000 acres from Upper Klamath Lake. Malin was settled on former lake bottom in September 1909 by sixty-five Bohemian families, who named it for a town near Kutná Hora; it is still known for horseradish. In the drought of 2021 the Bureau of Reclamation, bound to protect endangered sucker fish in the lake and salmon downstream, kept the project’s main canal closed for the season, and the 2022 allocation was again a small fraction of normal. Farms that had deep wells pumped them, the water table fell, and shallow household wells failed across the county: 117 were formally reported dry by late July 2021, with officials suspecting more than 300, and reports kept coming through the winter. Families hauled water in five-gallon jugs. The state paid for storage tanks and trucked water for nearly 300 homes, and well drillers had waiting lists of up to a year.

Klamath Falls has had a Latter-day Saint congregation since 1930 and a stake since 1953; the area belongs to the Oregon Eugene Mission. Missionaries, most of them eighteen to twenty, serve in pairs for eighteen months or two years under a mission president, are fed by local members, and do not enter a home where a lone woman is present without another adult. “Trunky” is their own word for a missionary whose mind has gone home ahead of him. The chapter the president declines to read, Alma 39, is a father’s rebuke to a son who left his mission to follow a woman named Isabel. The people in this story, the ward and the Havlik farm are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Dinner Calendar
sections.text: Elder Bowman was nineteen and came from a seed-potato farm outside Sugar City, Idaho. His brother had served in the same mission six years ahead of him, and had been the kind of missionary a ward remembers, so that when the younger one stood up to introduce himself in sacrament meeting an old sister in the second row said, quite loud, Oh, it’s the little Bowman. It stuck. He did not mind. He had been the little Bowman all his life. He had also shot a bow since he was six years old, and had twice been state champion in the 4-H barebow, and the fall he was fourteen he had put an arrow through a cow elk at forty yards across a draw, but he did not bring that up, because his brother had told him that nobody in the mission field wants to hear about your elk. He had been out nine months. His companion that transfer was Elder Pappas, from The Dalles, a calm, heavy-shouldered boy who wanted to be a diesel mechanic and read the scriptures the way he would read a service manual, slowly, looking for the torque specs. Their area was the whole south end of the county, down to the California line: Merrill, Malin, the farms along the Lost River, and the dry bed of what had been Tule Lake before t

sections.heading: II. Water
sections.dateline: The Havlik place · June and July
sections.text: Malin was settled in the fall of 1909 by sixty-five Bohemian families who came out from the Midwest to farm the lake bottom. They named it for a town at home, and they found horseradish growing wild there the size of a man’s arm and took it for a sign. A Havlik had been one of the sixty-five. The house was his, a tall plain farmhouse with a porch on two sides and a row of Lombardy poplars the wind had been working on for a hundred years. The woman who came around the corner of it, wiping her hands on her jeans, was perhaps twenty-seven. She had her hair tied up in a bandanna and dust to the elbows. She looked at the white shirts and the black name tags and the four blue jugs. You’re the ones on Dalton’s place, she said. I heard his well went. Pump house is around the side. The hydrant sticks, you have to lean on it. Her name was Tess. That was the first day, and all of it, except that when they had the jugs in the trunk she walked out to the car and said, When you need water again, come here. Don’t go anyplace else. I mean it. That well’s the one thing on this place that works. They needed water every second day. Four jugs, twenty gallons, was drinking and dishes and a spit bath, w

sections.heading: III. Yellow
sections.text: By the last week of July Elder Bowman was not eating what the calendar brought. He pushed Sister Dalton’s funeral potatoes around the plate and said they were good. He was awake at two and again at four. In the mornings he sat through his hour of study with the book open at the same page of Mosiah and his eyes on the wall above it, and on the days that were not water days he was short with people, and on the days that were he shaved twice. He had stopped fixing the wheel line. He had moved on to the conversation with his father, and the one with his brother. He had worked out that a man could be released honorably for a number of reasons, and that fifteen months was not so long to give back. Elder Okafor, the district leader, came down from Klamath Falls on the twenty-eighth to work a day’s exchange. He was from Houston and missed very little. He rode with Bowman through three appointments and a flat tire, and at four in the afternoon, parked outside the Malin post office, he turned around in the seat. Bowman. What is the matter with you? You’ve gone yellow. I mean it, look in the mirror, you’re the color of a legal pad. Elder Bowman looked at the dash for a while. I’m not happy ou

sections.heading: IV. The Mission Home
sections.text: President Taufa had taught wood and metal shop at a high school in West Valley City, Utah, for thirty-one years before he was called to Oregon. He was a broad grey man of sixty-two who was missing the first joint of his left ring finger, which he said was the only thing a table saw ever taught him that he had not already known. He had been born in Nukuʻalofa and brought to Salt Lake at nine. The elders said of him that he could sit through a whole interview and say eleven words, and you would walk out having confessed things you had not known you had done. He had the other three wait in the front room. Sister Taufa gave them orange juice. The door of the office was left open, as it always was. Elder Bowman. They tell me you want to go home. Is that true? Yes, President. The president nodded slowly. Your brother served here. People in Klamath say Bowman and it means something. You came out in the same church, with the same book, under the same call. You could have had them saying, the little one, he was the best we ever had. And you are going to let them say he went home in his tenth month, trunky. That is a serious thing you are doing to yourself. I want you to hear me say so. He l

sections.heading: V. The Archer
sections.text: There was a young man once, he said, in a country with tigers in it, who was called the Little Archer. He had gone to the far side of that country to learn from the best teacher there was, and he learned so well that the teacher gave him his own daughter to marry. So he took his wife and his bow and started home. At the mouth of a forest fifty bandits came out at them. The Little Archer had fifty arrows. He shot fifty times and fifty bandits lay down in the road. The fifty-first was their chief, and the quiver was empty. The archer threw down his bow and took hold of the chief with his hands and put him on his back in the dust and knelt on him, and called over his shoulder, Wife, bring me my sword. She came with it. And she looked down at the bandit lying there, with his hair in his eyes, and he looked up at her. It took as long as it takes to say it. She put the hilt of the sword into the bandit’s hand. The best shot in that whole country, said President Taufa. My father would stop there and look at us. Dead of one look. It wasn’t even his. The bandit took the woman and went on. But as he walked he thought, She did that to a husband she had known for years, for me, whom she has kn

sections.heading: VI. The Hydrant
sections.text: They were back by dark. The next water day was a Saturday. I’ll take the hydrant, Elder Bowman said in the car, and Elder Pappas looked at him sideways and handed over the jugs. It did stick. He leaned on it. From the pump house door a man could see the whole place, and for the first time since June he looked at it. He saw the wheel line, which he knew. He saw that the green pivot was the only green thing to the horizon, and that it was green on a power bill. The meter on the pole was spinning like a coin. He saw a real estate sign lying face down in the weeds by the gate, with the post already on it, not yet stood up. Through the front room window there was a hospital bed, stripped, with the rails still raised, and a walker folded against it. There was a pair of a big man’s irrigating boots on the porch by the door, set side by side, with six months of dust in them. He had walked past those boots eleven times. And he saw her come around the house with a feed bucket, when she did not know anybody was looking. She was not coming across the yard with two glasses. She was a tired woman of twenty-seven, with her mouth set and one hand in the small of her back, who had buried her father

title: The Near Bank
logline: In a drought summer, a young missionary whose well has gone dry fills his jugs at a lonely farm, and starts shaving twice.

verses.text: He who has reached the consummation, who does not tremble, who is without thirst and without sin, he has broken all the thorns of life: this will be his last body.

He who is without thirst and without affection, who understands the words and their interpretation, who knows the order of letters (those which are before and which are after), he has received his last body, he is called the great sage, the great man.

bg.commentary: In the commentary several senior monks reach the Jetavana monastery late at night and are given the room of Rāhula, the Buddha’s son, a novice who is said to be eight years old and already fully awakened. Seeing no other place, he lies down outside the door of the Buddha’s own chamber. Māra, the tempter, reasons that the son lies there “as though his finger hurt him,” and that to pinch the son is to pinch the father. He takes the form of a huge elephant, winds his trunk around the boy’s head and trumpets. From inside, the Buddha tells him that a hundred thousand like him could not frighten his son, and speaks these verses. Māra says, “The ascetic Gotama knows me,” and vanishes.
bg.history:
After students and young professionals failed to seize the Frankfurt guardhouse in April 1833 (the Frankfurter Wachensturm), a number of university-trained Germans left for America. One cluster bought farms in the Shiloh Valley east of Belleville, Illinois, where their neighbors named them the “Latin farmers” and the place the Latin Settlement. Many were freethinkers. In 1836 they began a German library society that grew into the Belleville Public Library, the oldest in the state. Others, the Giessen Emigration Society of 1834, settled across the Mississippi in Missouri. Shiloh itself takes its name from a Methodist meeting house raised after an 1807 camp meeting. The Lohrs and their guests are invented.

Their books are real. In the study scene of Goethe’s Faust, Part One (1808), Faust struggles to translate the Greek logos in the first line of John while the poodle he has brought home swells behind the stove “wie ein Elefant” and turns out to be Mephistopheles; the English here is Bayard Taylor’s (1871). Penelope’s speech on the gates of horn and ivory turns on a play between elephas, ivory, and elephairomai, to cheat, and between keras, horn, and kraino, to fulfil; the English is Butcher and Lang’s (1879). In Homer elephas means only ivory; the animal comes into Greek later. Horace’s ode Integer vitae was sung by German students everywhere in F. F. Flemming’s four-part setting of 1811. Its opening says that the man whole in life and clear of wrong needs no Moorish javelins or bow; the English stanza is John Conington’s (1863). Franz Passow’s Greek and German lexicon was the standard one of the 1830s.

sections.heading: I. The Lexicon
sections.dateline: Shiloh Valley, St. Clair County, Illinois · October 1838
sections.text: The Americans up at Shiloh called them the Latin farmers. They had come over in ’thirty-three and ’thirty-four, after the business at Frankfurt, doctors of law and of philosophy, a forester, two apothecaries, and they had bought prairie east of Belleville at a dollar and a quarter the acre and learned to plow it out of a book. It was said of them that they could curse an ox in Greek and that the ox was not improved by it. Heinrich Lohr had taught Greek to the two upper forms of a Gymnasium in Hesse for eleven years. Here he had eighty acres, a log house with a loft, a yoke of oxen named for the sons of Atreus, and a boy. His wife had died in their second August, of the fever the Americans called the ague and dosed with Sappington’s pills. The boy was called Rudolf and was eight years old. Lohr did not know how to teach a child anything except the way he had taught the upper forms, so that was how the boy had it. At eight Rudolf had his German letters and his Latin ones and his Greek, and he knew the order of each, which stood before and which after. He could go into the big Passow, a lexicon that weighed as much as a churn, and come out with any word in the time it took a grown man

sections.heading: II. The Guests
sections.text: Four of the old Giessen men were coming over from the Missouri side for the meeting of the Library Society, which the valley had founded two years before, and they were looked for on the Thursday by daylight. The ferry at St. Louis was held for wind. They came at midnight in a farm wagon, four gentlemen and one lantern, the oldest of them a former Hofrat who now raised hogs on the Femme Osage. They had to be fed, and when they had been fed they had to sing, since they had not all been in one room in four years. They sang Integer vitae in four parts as they had sung it as students, Horace’s ode to the man of clean life who needs no javelins. Then the Hofrat, who had the voice for it, read from the First Part of Faust, the scene in the study. The doctor has brought a black poodle home from his walk. He sits down to put the Gospel of John into German and cannot get past the first line, because he cannot decide what to do with the one word logos, and behind the stove the dog begins to grow. Behind the stove still banned,See it, an elephant, expand!It fills the space entire,Mist-like melting, ever faster. — Goethe, Faust, Part I (the Study) Schwillt es wie ein Elefant, the Hofrat said a

sections.heading: III. Behind the Stove
sections.text: The Americans tell this part with the Devil in it. The Germans, who had left the Devil in Hesse with the Grand Duke’s police, tell it with the thing out of the Hofrat’s book. They agree on what it did. It is said to have looked at the boy lying across the sill, and at the shut door behind him, and to have reasoned this way. The father is in there among his books. The son is out here, like a sore finger held away from the hand. Pinch the finger and the whole man will feel it. The stove had burned down to a red line at the door. Behind it something that was not smoke began to gather. It swelled as it had been made to swell in the reading, gray, with a hide like a wet road, until its back was among the rafters and the loft boards lifted and creaked. It had a head the size of the meal chest. From the head a long gray arm came down, feeling, and went once around the boy’s head where he lay, the way a man laps a rope around a post. Then it screamed. None of the four gentlemen in the loft had ever heard an elephant. They said afterward it was the cry the cranes make going over in November, if every crane in Illinois had been in the room. The boy opened his eyes. He looked at what had hold

title: Sawn Ivory
place: Shiloh Valley, St. Clair County, Illinois
logline: An eight-year-old who knows his Greek letters gives up his bed to four old scholars and sleeps across his father's doorsill.

verses.text: ‘I have conquered all, I know all, in all conditions of life I am free from taint; I have left all, and through the destruction of thirst I am free; having learnt myself, whom shall I teach?’

bg.commentary: In the commentary the Buddha, newly awakened, has spent seven weeks near the tree and sets out on foot for Benares, eighteen leagues off, to teach five former companions. On the road he meets Upaka, a follower of the Ājīvikas, a rival school of ascetics remembered for teaching that everything is settled by fate. Upaka admires his calm senses and clear complexion and asks in whose name he has gone forth, who his teacher is and whose doctrine he holds. The Buddha answers that he has no teacher, and speaks this verse. Upaka neither approves nor disapproves; in the older telling he says only, “It may be so, friend.” Shaking his head, he takes a side path and goes to the house of a hunter. Read the full commentary story. Later tradition has him marry the hunter’s daughter and, years afterward, come back.
bg.history:
On November 4, 1979, a group calling itself the Muslim Student Followers of the Imam’s Line seized the American embassy in Tehran and began the hostage crisis. Khatt, line, became the word for a person’s politics, and the revolution’s slogan was “Neither East nor West, Islamic Republic.” More than fifty thousand Iranians were then studying in the United States, many at small colleges. President Carter ordered them to report to immigration officers or face deportation, and on November 14 froze Iranian assets in American banks by Executive Order 12170, which cut many students off from money sent from home. A federal judge held the reporting order unconstitutional on December 11, and an appeals court reversed her on December 27 (Narenji v. Civiletti). In about two months 54,486 Iranians were interviewed; several hundred were eventually deported. The college, Kamran, Siavash and the Skaggs family are invented. U.S. Route 60, the old Midland Trail, follows the Kanawha River down to Charleston and runs on to Huntington.

Kamran’s religion is the ordinary practice of Twelver Shia Muslims, each of whom follows the rulings of a living senior jurist, a marja’; the practice is called taqlid. Opening the poems of Hafez at random for an omen is an old Iranian custom, kept especially on Yalda, the longest night of the year, with pomegranates. The poem is number XXXI in R. A. Nicholson’s Selected Poems from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz (1898), an early English selection of Rumi’s lyrics. It has long been sung as his, though scholars have not found it in the oldest manuscripts of his Divan, and it may be by a later hand.

sections.heading: I. Seven Weeks
sections.dateline: The upper Kanawha Valley, West Virginia · December 1979
sections.text: There were forty-one Iranians at the college that fall, most of them in engineering, and after the fourth of November there was no way for any of them to be only a student. The Americans wanted to know whose side they were on. Somebody hung a bedsheet from the third floor of the men’s dormitory with a thing about the Ayatollah painted on it, and in the cafeteria line a boy from Beckley asked Kamran every day, not unkindly, when he was going to let those people go. The Iranians wanted to know the same thing from one another, and were harder about it. Shahi, Tudeh, Mojahed, Hezbollahi. Khatt-e ki hasti, they said. Whose line are you. In Tehran the ones who had gone over the embassy wall called themselves the students who followed the Imam’s line, and since then the word was in everything. Kamran Yazdani kept his answer short. He was a junior in civil engineering, the son of a cloth merchant in the Yazd bazaar, and he believed more or less what his father believed. A man could no more work out the whole of religion for himself than do his own surgery, so he chose one learned man and followed him, and Kamran followed the same grand ayatollah his father did, whose book of rulings his mo

sections.heading: II. Whose Line
sections.text: Randy’s father’s place was up Peddler’s Run, four miles of dirt off the highway, and Randy had said to wait at the mouth of the run and he would come down with the truck when he was done feeding. Kamran stood by the mailboxes with his suitcase. It was a gray noon, two days past the longest night of the year, which he had kept alone with a pomegranate from the Kroger and his mother’s Hafez. The river was the color of a nickel. Coal trucks went by, and their wind moved his coat. A man was walking toward him down the shoulder from the direction of town, carrying a gym bag. He walked like someone with a long way to go who was not thinking about the way. When he was near enough Kamran saw who it was, and for a moment did not believe it, because of the face. Everybody Kamran knew that month had the same face. It was gray under the eyes from the news, and tight at the mouth from being asked. Siavash’s was clear. The skin was clear and the eyes were quiet. He looked like somebody who had slept and eaten and owed no one, in a month when no Iranian in America slept. Salaam, Kamran said. Don’t be tired. Your color has come back. You look well, brother, you look better than any of us. Where ar

sections.heading: III. Peddler’s Run
sections.text: Randy’s father ran coonhounds and a trapline, and had put in thirty years at the alloy plant between the two. There were hides drying on boards along the porch wall, and a buck from Thanksgiving week cut and wrapped in the freezer on the back porch, and four Walker hounds that came out from under the house and sang at the suitcase. Mr. Skaggs shook Kamran’s hand and asked was he the Iranian. Kamran said he was. Mr. Skaggs said well, he didn’t reckon Kamran had took anybody hostage personally, and to come in out of the cold, there were beans. A girl was splitting kindling by the smokehouse, Randy’s sister, home from nursing school. She did not look up yet. At the supper table Kamran opened his mouth twice to tell about the man on the highway, and could not find where it began. Later, in the room they gave him, he took his mother’s Hafez out of the suitcase and held it shut for some time with his finger along the edge of the pages. Then he put it back between the shirts without opening it. From the window he could see a little of the highway at the mouth of the run, where the lights of the trucks went by, heading down the valley.

title: Neither East nor West
logline: In the hostage-crisis winter, an Iranian student waiting by a West Virginia highway meets a countryman whose face has no worry in it.

verses.text: The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three raise four questions: which gift is best, which flavor, which delight, and why the destruction of craving is called supreme. For twelve years they ask one another across ten thousand worlds, then go to the Four Great Kings, who send them to Sakka, lord of the gods, who knows at once the answer to whatever a thousand beings have pondered. Sakka says only a Buddha can answer, and leads the whole throng by night to Jetavana, lighting up the grove. The Buddha answers: the gift, taste and delight of the Dhamma are best, and the end of craving ends all suffering. Sakka then asks that the merit of the teaching be shared with the gods, and the Buddha tells the monks that from then on the merit of every sermon, and even of words of thanksgiving, is to be given to all beings.
bg.history:
A streetcar line out to Reeds Lake opened in 1875 with horse cars, ran for years behind a steam engine the town called the dummy, and was electrified in the early 1890s. The railway company ran an amusement park at the lake, Ramona Park, with a theater pavilion, steamboats, and a figure-eight coaster from 1903, to fill the cars on summer evenings. East Grand Rapids incorporated as a village in 1891 and had 466 people in 1900 and 800 in 1910, a lake resort turning into a suburb along the line. The city across the river was the Furniture City, whose twice-yearly furniture market brought buyers from all over the country; Dutch and Polish immigrants were among the many who found work in its furniture factories, and its West Side was home to working-class immigrant families, the Polish parish of St. Adalbert among its churches. Grand Rapids gave up its streetcars in 1935. The Thursday Club, its members, Mr. Sackett and Mrs. Brink are invented.

The kindergarten movement, after Friedrich Froebel, reached Grand Rapids early: an 1891 county history records the Misses Bacon’s kindergarten training school, which ran for about twelve years before 1882, and a free kindergarten and creche opened in 1888 by a circle of the King’s Daughters, where working mothers left their babies and fetched them in the evening (Baxter’s history of Grand Rapids). Froebel’s first gift is a set of soft yarn balls on strings. “Good-Morning to All,” by the Louisville kindergarten teachers Mildred and Patty Hill, appeared in their Song Stories for the Kindergarten (1893); the words are quoted here from a later edition, where it is marked “To be sung standing.” Its tune is the one later sung as “Happy Birthday.” Bacon’s “Of Truth” opens his Essays (1625). Edwin Arnold’s The Light of Asia (1879) was read in parlors and women’s clubs across the country.

sections.heading: I. Minutes of the First Meeting
sections.dateline: East Grand Rapids, Michigan · Thursday, October 6, 1898
sections.text: The Thursday Club met at the residence of Mrs. Josiah Orcutt on the lake road at half past two o’clock, twenty-nine members present, the afternoon fair and the steamer still running. The constitution was read a second time and adopted. Article Three, limiting the membership to thirty-three, was debated and kept, on the ground stated by Mrs. Orcutt that thirty-three is the number of ladies who can be seated in one parlor if the piano bench is used. The village had already begun to call the club the Thirty-Three, and the club did not object. Mrs. Lyman Hale read a paper on Sir Edwin Arnold’s The Light of Asia, which she had borrowed from the Ladies’ Literary Club downtown and must return Saturday. The paper was much admired, especially the passage on the young prince seeing the old man by the road, which Mrs. Hale read twice. In the discussion Mrs. Orcutt observed that the club, and every club she had ever belonged to, talked a great deal and settled nothing. She moved that four questions be set for the season and answered by the annual meeting in May, so that the club might for once have something to show. The questions were proposed from the floor, amended, and adopted as follows:

sections.heading: II. Laid Over
sections.text: May 25, 1899. Annual meeting. The four questions, not having been settled, were laid over to the autumn. Mrs. Orcutt said it was no disgrace. The Greeks had not settled them either.Laid over. November 2, 1899. Each member reported the answers given at her own supper table. Mr. Orcutt: the best gift is a receipted bill. Mr. Van Ess: the best taste is beefsteak and the best pleasure is not being asked questions at supper. The secretary’s husband, Mr. Walter Pell, said he would think about it, and has said so since. The answers of the hired girls were also reported, and were on the whole better.Laid over. March 1900. The questions were written out and sent to the column of questions answered in the Herald. Reply pasted in below: The Herald does not undertake questions of opinion.Laid over. August 1901. Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Kuiper, summering at the Bay View assembly, put the four questions to the lecturer after his afternoon address. He answered for an hour and fifty minutes. On the steamer home the two members could not agree on what he had said, and in the end neither could tell the other.Laid over. January 1902. Mrs. Orcutt died on the ninth, at seventy-four. The club attended in a bo

sections.heading: III. Special Meeting
sections.text: A special meeting of the club was held jointly with the four trustees of the village, at the club’s request, since by this date the questions were no longer the club’s alone. The whole village had taken them up. The boys at the Ramona boat livery put them to strangers for a joke, and two of the strangers had come back the next Sunday to ask whether there was an answer yet. The schoolroom was full and people stood at the windows. Each trustee was asked in turn. Mr. Bostwick, who has the ice-houses on the west shore and knows the lake as well as any man living, said he did not know. Mr. Kellogg, who leads the band in the pavilion at Ramona and has played to more people than live in the county, said he did not know. Mr. Dykstra, who sells bedroom suites at the market to half the country, said he did not know, and that his grandmother in Zeeland would have known, but she was dead. Mr. Hunt, of the bank on Wealthy Street, said he did not know either. He moved that the questions be referred to Mr. Elias Sackett, division superintendent of the street railway, on the ground that Sackett knew everything. The motion was carried. Mr. Sackett was sent for at the car house and came in his shirt

sections.heading: IV. The Car
sections.dateline: Wealthy Street to the West Side · the same night
sections.text: Entered by the secretary at the request of the club, which wished an account in full and not in minutes. It was one of the open summer cars, with the benches straight across and no sides, and Mr. Sackett had every lamp in it lit. When it came round the loop at the lake it lit up the water as far as the steamer dock. Thirty-one of the thirty-three were aboard. The four trustees were aboard. Mr. Kellogg’s cornet player came with his cornet and did not play it. The livery boys rode on the step, and husbands, and the Van Ess boys, and people none of us knew who had stood at the schoolhouse windows, and Mr. Sackett rode on the front platform beside the motorman with his cap on. We went in along Wealthy Street at a quarter to ten. People came out on their porches as we passed, because no car runs that line lit up like that at night, and I suppose we looked like something going to a fire or a wedding. Some of them called out to ask where. Mrs. Hale called back, To get it answered, and they did not know what she meant, but two men left a porch and ran and caught the step. Down the hill into the city the stores were dark. On the bridge over the Grand River the lamps of the car lay in the wa

sections.heading: V. Good Morning to All
sections.text: One thing more happened that night, which the secretary did not see and had from Mr. Sackett. When the rest of us were back on the car he stayed on Mrs. Brink’s step. He said to her, If that is the best gift, you have been giving it over here twenty-two years, and the whole East Side, and me on my own car every morning, have never had any of it. The next time you give it, let us have a share. She said that every morning at nine her children stood up at their tables and sang, and she showed him the place in the book. Good-morning to you, Good-morning to you, Good-morning dear children, Good-morning to all. — Mildred J. Hill and Patty S. Hill, “Good-Morning to All,” Song Stories for the Kindergarten All is all, she said. I never thought to tell them so. From tomorrow I will. And when they say the blessing at noon I will tell them that one goes to everybody too, the cars and the bridge and your side of the river. Even the thank-you. Everything they say in that room. So the next morning Mr. Sackett issued an order, which is pasted in below, that every car on the Bridge Street line passing the kindergarten at nine o’clock on a school day should ring its gong twice. title: Laid Over
logline: For twelve years a suburban women's club carries four questions in its minute book, until a streetcar man knows whom to ask.

verses.text: Pleasures destroy the foolish, if they look not for the other shore; the foolish by his thirst for pleasures destroys himself, as if he were his own enemy.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a rich man of Sāvatthī called Aputtaka, “Childless,” dies without an heir, and King Pasenadi of Kosala spends seven days carrying his wealth to the palace. At noon the king comes to the Buddha and describes how the man lived: he drove off servants who brought him fine food, clothes and carriages with sticks and clods of earth, ate broken-rice porridge with sour gruel, wore hemp, rode a broken-down chariot and held a parasol of leaves over his head. The Buddha explains. In a past life the man told his wife to give alms to a silent solitary sage, and she gave the best food in the house; meeting the sage on the road, he looked in the bowl and regretted it, saying his servants should have had it. He also killed his brother's only son in the forest for his inheritance. The gift made him rich; the regret kept him from enjoying anything; the murder left him childless through seven lives and sent him to hell, where, his merit spent, he is again. When the king laments that the man never used his wealth or gave it to a teacher living nearby, the Buddha speaks this verse.
bg.history:
In the 1890s the coal under the mountains of eastern Kentucky was being bought up, often cheaply and before any railroad reached it. The most famous buyer, John C. C. Mayo, was a schoolteacher from Paintsville who began buying mineral rights with his teaching salary, formed a land company in 1888, and later devised the broad form deed, which severed what lay under the ground from the surface and let the mineral owner take it by almost any means. Timber came out first. Logs were hauled to the creeks and floated down the forks of the Kentucky River on the spring floods, the “log tide,” gathered into rafts at Beattyville and taken down to the sawmills at Frankfort, a trip of a week or more. In late summer families dug wild ginseng, “sang,” for export to China; in recent decades most of the country's wild ginseng exports have come from the southern Appalachian states, especially Kentucky. The rhododendron and mountain laurel thickets of those coves are so dense that they are called laurel hells, because it is nearly impossible to get through one.

When a person died with no heirs at all, the property passed to the state by escheat, an old common-law rule that once sent a dead tenant's land back to the Crown. Kentucky's statutes of the period provided for escheaters, appointed by the state Auditor, who sued in the name of the Commonwealth in the circuit court of the county where the property lay. Jehu Carnes is buried by an Old Regular Baptist preacher, who lines out the hymn the way that church still does, reading each line for the congregation to sing back. Bearpen Fork, its school and everyone on it are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Jars
sections.dateline: Bearpen Fork of the North Fork of the Kentucky River · August 1899
sections.text: Jehu Carnes was found dead on the fourth of July, sitting at his own table with his spoon in his hand and a bowl of mush in front of him gone hard as plaster. He was seventy-nine years old. He had lived alone at the head of Bearpen for fifteen years, since his wife died, and before that he had lived there with her and no children for twenty-seven. He had no brother living and no sister and no nephew and no niece, and when the circuit clerk went through the books at the county seat to see who his heirs might be, there was not one, not a cousin, not anybody, back to the Revolution. They buried him on the point above the house beside his wife. The preacher, an Old Regular Baptist from over on Carr Fork who had known him sixty years, stood at the head of the grave with his hat in his hand and lined out a hymn, and the few who came sang it back to him the long slow way, and afterward the preacher opened his Bible to the twelfth of Luke and read one verse and closed it again. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? — Luke 12:20 Nobody on Bearpen thought that was unkind. They knew what he

sections.heading: II. How He Lived
sections.text: Mr. Webb had been asking about him all week while the men dug, and everybody on the creek had something to tell. He had owned the best land on Bearpen, nine hundred acres of it, bottom and hillside and the high woods, and the biggest poplar timber anybody had ever seen. For forty years he had cut it and snaked it down to the creek with oxen, and every spring, when the snows melted and the log tide came, he had sent it down the North Fork in rafts, to Beattyville and on down the river to the sawmills at Frankfort, and come home with money. In the nineties a man from Pittsburgh had come through buying up the coal under people's land for next to nothing, and Jehu Carnes was the only one on the creek who made him pay ten times what the others got, and in gold. The tides had always come high for him. Other men's rafts broke up on the shoals and his came through. Other men's sons drowned breaking jams and his hired hands came home. Whatever he touched made money. He had never seemed to know what to do with it except dig a hole. He lived in the same two-room log house he had built in 1846. He wore tow linen, the coarse stuff spun from flax waste that people had stopped wearing after the w

sections.heading: III. Noon
sections.dateline: The Bearpen school · the dinner hour
sections.text: The Bearpen school was a log house with one door and one window and a stick-and-mud chimney, and a stove that smoked, and split-log benches with peg legs, and forty-three scholars in it from six years old to nineteen, sitting by size. The common school ran in the summer and fall in that country, from July until the roads got too bad to walk, and in the middle of the day the children took their dinner buckets out under the beech trees and ate cold cornbread and beans and played Antny-over across the roof. Miss Orpha Day had taught it for forty years. She was sixty years old and had never married, and she had been to every meeting on the creek in her life and never once gone up to be saved, which the preachers held against her and the mothers did not. She was a thin straight woman with grey hair pulled back hard and spectacles she had bought in Lexington the one time she went there. Everybody on Bearpen under the age of fifty had learned their letters from her, and some of their mothers had too. People went to her about things they did not take to the preacher or the doctor or the law. It was said on the creek that Miss Orpha knew things. Nobody knew how. She was sitting on the doors

sections.heading: IV. The Walking Man
sections.text: When Miss Orpha was a girl there was a man who walked the mountains. Everybody from the Big Sandy to the Cumberland knew him, and nobody knew where he came from. People called him Old Tagg. He did not preach and he did not peddle and he did not beg. He walked the ridges with a stick, winter and summer, in a long coat, and slept in barns and corn cribs where people let him, and if somebody set food in front of him he ate it and said Thank ye and walked on. Those were nearly the only words anybody ever heard him say. Children followed him a mile down the road just to be near him, and he let them. Dogs that bit everybody else lay down in the road when he passed. Old people said a house he had eaten in did well. Some said he had been a preacher once and lost his voice and found something better. Some said he was the Wandering Jew. Miss Orpha said, sitting on the sill, that she had seen him twice as a girl and had never in her life seen anybody look so much as if he had come to the end of something. In the fall of 1857 Old Tagg came up Bearpen and stopped at the Carnes place at dinnertime. Jehu was thirty-seven then and newly married to Ruth Fields from over on Rockhouse, who was a good

sections.heading: V. Sang
sections.dateline: The high woods above Bearpen · September 1859
sections.text: Jehu had a younger brother named Elisha who owned the other half of the Carnes land, the lower half, the wide bottom at the forks and the best of the poplar. In the spring of 1859 Elisha drowned on the North Fork breaking a log jam at the head of a tide, and his wife had died two winters before of the lung fever, and he left one child, a boy named Davy, six years old. The boy came to live with his uncle Jehu and aunt Ruth, and the circuit court made Jehu his guardian, and the land went into Jehu's keeping until the boy was grown. Miss Orpha knew Davy Carnes. It was her first school, the summer she was twenty, in a smaller house than this one, and he was the youngest scholar in it, a towheaded boy who could already say the alphabet backwards and was proud of it. She said he was a talker. He went everywhere holding his uncle's finger, because his uncle was the biggest thing he had left, and as they went he talked. That's my daddy's mule. That's my daddy's bottom. Them's my daddy's poplars, Uncle Jehu, ain't they. When I'm big I'm going to raft them to Frankfort. Jehu heard it every day. And he thought, Miss Orpha said: He talks like that now. When he's grown, what will there be left

sections.heading: VI. Where He Is
sections.text: Mr. Webb had not said a word. So that's your answer, Miss Orpha said. The dinner Ruth gave got him his money. What he said in the path kept him from ever touching it. Every time he looked at a biscuit he saw it throwed away. And the boy took his children from him, and his name, and that's why it's going to Frankfort with you in a wagon. It's not the first time, either. You go back in your books, Mr. Webb, you'll find more than one on these creeks died with jars in the ground and nobody to dig them. And now? Mr. Webb said, and did not know why he asked it. Miss Orpha took off her spectacles and wiped them on her apron. The good's all used up, she said. He used it up on gold. He never laid by any more. There's nothing holding him anywhere now. He's in the laurel, Mr. Webb. Further in than any man ever crawled. He's been in there since the fourth of July, and he can't find his way out, and nobody's hollering his name. Mr. Webb sat on the step for a long while. Under the beeches the children were playing Antny-over, throwing a yarn ball over the roof of the schoolhouse and yelling, and a boy of six or seven came running around the corner after it and stopped dead at the sight of the ma

sections.heading: VII. The Laurel
sections.text: In October a wagon came up Bearpen with an iron stove in it, and window glass, and a crate of new readers, and a slate for every child, and a bell for the roof. There was no note with it. Nobody on the creek had to ask who sent it. Some said Cyrus Webb had spent every cent of his fee on the Carnes estate to buy it, and some said more than that. But before that, in the last week of September, when the sang berries were red, he came back up the creek with four men and axes and asked Miss Orpha to show them the way. She took them up past the last cleared ground into the cove under the ridge. She had not been there in forty years. She went to it as straight as if she had been there the day before. The men cut into the laurel with their axes, and it was slow, the trunks twisted together like a rope and hard as iron, and they cut for most of a day, a tunnel a man could stand up in, with the cut laurel piled behind them. At the end of the afternoon one of the men stopped cutting and called back. He was lying where he had been thrown, very small, gone mostly back into the leaves after forty years, under the laurel, with one shoe still on. Miss Orpha knelt by him in the leaf mold. Mr. Webb

title: Laurel Hell
logline: The state's escheater digs up forty-one thousand dollars in fruit jars from a miser's cabin and asks the old schoolteacher why.

verses.text: The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by passion: therefore a gift bestowed on the passionless brings great reward.
The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by hatred: therefore a gift bestowed on those who do not hate brings great reward.
The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by vanity: therefore a gift bestowed on those who are free from vanity brings great reward.
The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by lust: therefore a gift bestowed on those who are free from lust brings great reward.

bg.commentary: In the commentary the Buddha has gone up to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to teach, seated on the god Sakka’s throne, the Yellowstone Rock. Two gods sit near him: Indaka at his right hand and Aṅkura at his left. As greater gods arrive, Aṅkura gives way to each until he is sitting twelve leagues off, while Indaka keeps his seat. In his human life Aṅkura had given alms for ten thousand years from a row of cooking-fires twelve leagues long; Indaka had once given a single spoonful of his own food to the elder Anuruddha. The Buddha asks Aṅkura why he sits so far away, and his voice is heard on earth. Aṅkura wonders that so small a gift outshines his “as the moon does the stars”; Indaka answers that he sowed a little seed in a good field. The Buddha tells Aṅkura that gifts should be given with discernment, and speaks the four verses.
bg.history:
News of gold on the Klondike reached Seattle in July 1897, and within months tens of thousands of people were trying to reach the Yukon. Most landed at Skagway or at Dyea and crossed the Coast Mountains. The Chilkoot Trail, thirty-three miles from Dyea to Lake Bennett, was an old trade route owned and closely guarded by the Chilkoot Tlingit, many of whom now worked it as packers at rates that reached a dollar a pound. Canadian authorities required each person to bring a year’s supply of food, so a stampeder had to relay close to a ton of goods over the pass, climbing it dozens of times. Sheep Camp, the last stop below the summit, held several thousand people that winter. More on the Klondike Gold Rush.

After days of heavy snow and a warm south wind, a series of avalanches struck the trail above Sheep Camp on Palm Sunday, April 3, 1898. Native packers had refused to go above Sheep Camp that weekend. The slides came as the story gives them; the last, near noon, buried a column of people coming down from the Scales along a rope. Some fifteen hundred stampeders dug for four days. The dead are usually put at sixty to sixty-five. Many lie in the Slide Cemetery at Dyea, which soldiers of the Fourteenth Infantry helped prepare. The White Pass railroad from Skagway reached Lake Bennett in 1899, and Dyea emptied; its site and the trail are now part of Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park. Mikkelsen and his kettles, Isaac, Rudd, the Garritys, the yellow rock and the Easter service are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Row of Fires
sections.dateline: Dyea to Lake Bennett · August 1897 to March 1898
sections.text: Anker Mikkelsen was a wholesale grocer of Tacoma, a Dane, fifty-six years old, a deacon of his Lutheran church and a careful man. In the eight weeks after the Portland came into Seattle with her ton of gold, he sold more beans, bacon, flour and evaporated potatoes than he had sold in the eight years before. The Canadians would let no man over the passes without a year’s provisions, the better part of a ton, and every clerk and streetcar conductor on Puget Sound was buying his ton. By the end of August Mikkelsen had forty thousand dollars he had not had in June. He could not sleep on it. He had looked at the men who bought. He had weighed out a year of beans for a consumptive bookkeeper, and for two boys from a hop farm who could not have been seventeen, and he had taken their money and wished them luck. He told his wife he was going north to give some of it back along the road it had come down. He did it the way he did everything, with a plan and a ledger. The trail from tidewater at Dyea to the head of Lake Bennett, where the boats were built, was thirty-three miles, which the old Hudson’s Bay men would have called twelve leagues, and it went over the Chilkoot Pass. Mikkelsen set

sections.heading: II. The Spoon
sections.text: It had snowed for five days. Then the wind went round to the south and blew warm, and the new snow on the mountain turned heavy and began to talk. Isaac was a Chilkoot man, from the people who had owned that trail before there was any Dyea. His grandfathers had carried eulachon grease over it to trade with the people of the interior, and had let nobody else use it, not even their own cousins the Chilkats. He was thirty or so. He packed for wages. In the bad autumn, when the trail was mud and the stampeders were frantic, the packers had got as much as a dollar the pound to the summit. Now that the tramways were running, it was down to a nickel. Isaac carried a hundred and forty pounds at a trip with a strap across his forehead, and he could tell you what that came to. He had brought one load up to the Scales that morning. It was his last. He sat on it to eat before he went down. He had a tin pail with what was left of his own dinner, beans cooked with a piece of salmon, and a spoon. He did not eat at Mikkelsen’s kettle, which was thirty yards off with fifty men around it, pushing. Nobody had told him he could not. He did not like the way they ate. Old Andrew Rudd came down off the G

sections.heading: III. Palm Sunday
sections.text: The first slide came down on the tents at the Scales at two in the morning and buried twenty men, and they were all dug out alive. That frightened the ones who were left. Toward ten o’clock a second buried three people lower down, who were got out, and a third killed three in their blankets on the Long Hill. Then a whole crew of tramway men, coming down to camp, were caught in the ravine above the Stone House, and not one of them walked out. A little before noon the people from the Scales started down together, some two hundred of them, in single file, holding to a rope, in snow so thick they could not see the man ahead. They were in the same ravine when the mountain let go. It made very little noise. It covered a third of them, some as deep as fifty feet. Somebody fired a rifle, and somebody else, and within the hour there were fifteen hundred men up from Sheep Camp with shovels. They had been climbing over each other for eight months. Now they dug in lines, and passed the snow back hand to hand, and did not speak. They dug for four days. A few came out breathing. The rest were laid on sleds and brought down to a tent at Sheep Camp, sixty of them and more, nobody ever knew the rig

sections.heading: IV. The Yellow Rock
sections.text: The girl was Nell Garrity. She was eleven. Her father had died at Sheep Camp of a fever in October, on his way to the Klondike. Her mother had turned his outfit into an eating tent with three plank tables, because the outfit was all they had and there was no money to go home on. Nell waited on the tables. She had carried beans and coffee to perhaps ten thousand men that winter. She was the one person at Sheep Camp, apart from Rudd, who was not going anywhere and did not want to. She had watched them all go by, and she had got so she could tell which ones would be back in a week selling their goods for the fare home. She did not think much of gold. She had seen what it looked like on people. Above the last tents of the camp there was a boulder the size of a cabin, with yellow lichen all down its south face. It was the one dry place to sit in that canyon, and Rudd sat there in the mornings with his face to the sun he could not see, and Nell sat with him when her mother could spare her. She told him who was going by. He told her other things. On Easter morning the snow had stopped at last. The dead were still in the long tent, waiting for the trail to be fit for the sleds, and the cam

sections.heading: V. One Kettle
sections.dateline: The Chilkoot Trail · April to June
sections.text: Mikkelsen walked back. It took him three days, over the summit from the Bennett side, against the whole stream of them going the other way. He came past his own kettles one at a time, Lindeman, Deep Lake, Happy Camp, the Crater, and at each he stopped and looked at the men around it. He had never done that. He saw the eyes over the rims of the bowls, fixed on the trail. He saw that he could have fed them until the Judgment and they would not have known they had eaten. He was not bitter. He told his wife afterward that it was like finding the error in a column that had refused to prove for eight months. The figure had been right. He had entered it on the wrong side of the book. At Sheep Camp he went to the widow’s tent and sat down across the plank from old Rudd, and asked if he might buy him his dinner, and Rudd said he might. They ate. Nell brought it. Mikkelsen watched how the old man took a thing that was given him. He took it whole. He did not look past it at anything else. He struck twelve of the kettles before May. The thirteenth he kept, at Sheep Camp, and he stood at it himself. He did not ladle with his eyes down. He looked at each man who came. He turned nobody away. But

sections.heading: VI. Good Ground
sections.text: The railroad went over the other pass, from Skagway, and was through to Bennett in the summer of 1899. After that nobody had any reason to climb the Chilkoot. Dyea had been a town of several thousand, with a long wharf run out over the tide flats. In a few years it had hardly anyone in it, and the hotels were being pulled down for the lumber. The dead of Palm Sunday who were not sent home were buried in a clearing in the spruce behind the town, in rows, and the soldiers of the Fourteenth helped make the ground ready. Every headboard there has the same date on it. Rudd is not among them. He died in his sleep at the widow Garrity’s in the fall of 1898, the week the mail contract went to the railroad, and was buried in the little yard at Sheep Camp. Nell and her mother went out on the last boat that year. She taught school in Ballard for thirty-eight years, and was known for being able to tell, in the first week, which of forty children could not be told anything yet, and for waiting. Anker Mikkelsen went back to Tacoma and his scales. He sold groceries until 1911. He gave away a great deal after that winter, though less of it in money, and he was never again heard to say how much. Wh

title: Thirteen Kettles
logline: A Tacoma grocer feeds the whole Klondike stampede from thirteen free soup kettles, and a packer gives a blind mail carrier one spoonful of beans.

verses.text: Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear, in the nose restraint is good, good is restraint in the tongue.
In the body restraint is good, good is restraint in speech, in thought restraint is good, good is restraint in all things. A Bhikshu, restrained in all things, is freed from all pain.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five monks have each taken one of the five sense doors to guard, and they fall to arguing over whose door is the hardest. They ask the Buddha. He will not set one above another: all the doors are hard, he says, and this is not the first time the five of them have failed at it. He then tells the birth story of the road to Takkasilā, in which five guards walking with a prince through a haunted forest are drawn off one at a time by a sight, a sound, a scent, a taste and a soft couch, and are eaten by the ogresses who laid them out; the prince walks on with an ogress at his heels, does not look at her, and is made king after the king who took her in is devoured with his household.
bg.history:
The American Miners’ Association, the first national miners’ union in the United States, was founded in January 1861 at West Belleville, Illinois, by British-born miners, some of them old Chartists. By 1863 it had lodges in the deep shafts around La Salle, opened in 1856 where the Illinois and Michigan Canal met the river, and it held its convention there that March, a month after the legislature passed the anti-strike statute the miners called the La Salle Black Laws. The union was gone by 1869. The verse stands on the title page of its 1864 constitution, reproduced in Edward Wieck’s The American Miners’ Association (1940); in the twentieth century it was set to music as “Step by Step.” Illinois passed no mine-safety law until the 1870s, and what protection the men had was the custom they carried from British pits.

Mines of the period were ventilated by a furnace that drew air through the workings, and the current was steered by wooden doors kept by boys called trappers, a job described in the article on child labor in British pits. The Davy lamp of 1815 enclosed its flame in wire gauze; in firedamp the flame lengthened and took a blue cap, and in black damp it sank and went out. The man who carried one through the pit before each shift was the fireman, later the fire boss. The Bluff shaft, the Gelli pit and everyone in them are invented.

sections.heading: I. Five Doors
sections.text: The Bluff shaft went down better than three hundred feet to a vein of coal three and a half feet thick, and there were five doors in it. A door in a coal pit keeps nobody out. It turns the air. A furnace burned day and night at the foot of the upcast and drew the foul air up that side of the shaft, and the good air fell down the other side to take its place. Left to itself the good air would have gone the forty yards across the pit bottom from the one to the other and never troubled the men at the coal half a mile in. So the short ways were shut with doors. The air came to a door, found it shut, and went the long way round, past every man lying on his side under the coal with his pick. It took his powder smoke with it, and the black damp that leaked out of the old workings, and carried them up and out. But the mules had to come through with the cars. So every door had a boy to pull it open for the trip and shut it after, and the company paid him fifty cents a day and called him a trapper. Tommy Bate, whose father was a Staffordshire man, had the first door, forty yards in from the pit eye. Dai Rees had the second, far down the main road, where nobody passed for an hour at a time. J

sections.heading: II. Evan Lamp
sections.dateline: The pit eye · Monday, before the shift
sections.text: Evan Pugh was the fireman. They called him Evan Lamp because there were three Evans at the Bluff and he was the one who carried the Davy. He came from Monmouthshire. He was near sixty, which is old for underground, and he had a blue line across the bridge of his nose where a cut had healed with the coal still in it. He went down alone at four every morning, two hours before the men. He carried the safety lamp with the wick pricked low, and he walked every road in the pit and went into every place where a man would work that day. He watched the flame. He laid his left hand flat to the roof and rapped beside it with a stick and listened. He smelled the air at the mouths of the old workings, and drew it in over his tongue, as the old firemen at home did, who said a man could taste black damp, sour, before it dimmed his light. He wet his cheek and turned it to feel which way the air was going. Where a place was fit he chalked the day of the month on the coal and E.P. under it, and no man at the Bluff put a pick to a face that did not show that morning’s chalk. Illinois had no law yet for the safety of coal pits. It was the custom, brought over with the men, and the lodge held to it. Th

sections.heading: III. The Gelli
sections.text: He had been fourteen, he said, and carried the fireman’s tools. The fireman was Lewis Probert, who had the first Davy lamp in that valley. The Gelli was a fiery pit and made gas at every fall. There were five doors between the Deep and the pit eye, and five boys on them, and every one of those boys Lewis Probert had told the same thing in the same three words. Keep your door. One morning Probert took him into the Deep and held up the lamp, and the flame put on a cap. It was a blue cap as long as a thumb, sitting on the yellow. She is in, Probert said. He stayed behind to hang sheets across the road and turn what air there was, and he gave the boy the lamp to carry out to the overman, so that the overman should see the cap with his own eyes and keep the men on top. He told him three things. Hold it level. Walk, because a Davy will pass its flame through the gauze if you run with it. And do not stop to look at her. She is very pretty, he said, and that is all she is. So the boy walked. The cap should have shrunk as he came out toward good air. It grew. He came to the fifth door and it was standing open with a sprag under it. The trapper had found a warm place off the road and was asl

sections.heading: IV. Chalk
sections.text: Nobody said anything. The cage was coming down again. They could hear the rope. I do not ask which of you has the worst door, Evan Lamp said. The air does not ask. It tries all five and goes by whichever one is open, and then it is no matter how well the other four were kept. A door is no use by itself. And every one of you has all five to mind, at whatever door you’re sat. Your eyes, your ears, your nose, your mouth, and the whole skin of you. When you have minded those, there is your tongue to keep still, and your wits to keep by you, and that last is the hardest, and it keeps the rest. He asked Tommy Bate whether his father had the Association’s book of laws in the house. Tommy said he had. It was on the shelf with the clock. Then you have seen what is printed on the front of it. Say it. Tommy knew it. He said it standing up, the way he had heard the men say it, and by the fifth line the other four were saying it with him. Step by step, the longest marchCan be won, can be won;Single stones will form an arch,One by one, one by one.And, by union, what we willCan be all accomplished still.Drops of water turn a mill,Singly none, singly none. — Constitution and Laws of the American M

title: Singly None
logline: Five boys who mind the air doors in an Illinois coal pit quarrel over whose door is hardest, and ask the old fireman.

verses.text: He who controls his hand, he who controls his feet, he who controls his speech, he who is well controlled, he who delights inwardly, who is collected, who is solitary and content, him they call Bhikshu.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, two young monks who were ordained together and go everywhere together bathe in the river Aciravatī and stand drying in the sun. Two geese fly over. One monk says he can put a stone through a goose’s eye, the near one and then the far; his friend says he cannot; the first pebble makes the bird turn its head and the second goes in at one eye and out at the other. Other monks bring the pair to the Buddha, who asks if it is true, and then tells them that householders long ago had scruples over far smaller things. His story is the birth story of the Kuru rule: a kingdom without rain borrows a neighbor king’s lucky black elephant, gets no rain, and sends to have the neighbor’s five precepts written on a gold plate; the king, his mother, his surveyor, his charioteer, his treasurer, his grain-measurer, his gatekeeper, a courtesan and others each protest that they cannot be sure they have kept them, on account of some trifle; the precepts are copied and kept, and the rain comes.
bg.history:
The Minidoka Project was one of the first works of the federal Reclamation Service. It was approved in 1904; Minidoka Dam on the Snake River was finished in 1906 and the north-side canal in 1907, and settlers took up farm units of eighty acres in what had been sagebrush. The lake behind the dam was set aside in 1909 as a bird reservation, now the Minidoka National Wildlife Refuge. Norland, its drugstore and its people are invented; Rupert, the project town nearby, is real.

The Boy Scouts of America was four years old in 1914. The sixth point of its Scout Law is quoted here as printed in the first Handbook (1911), which also required a First Class Scout to swim fifty yards. The year before, the Weeks–McLean Act had put migratory birds under federal protection for the first time, and on September 1, 1914, eleven days before this story, Martha, the last passenger pigeon, died in the Cincinnati Zoo. “Don’t Kill the Birds” is Lesson LV of the 1879 McGuffey’s Third Eclectic Reader. Darwin’s recollections, and his son’s account of the cross-beak, are in the first volume of the Life and Letters (1887).

sections.heading: I. The Bar
sections.dateline: Norland, Minidoka County, Idaho · Saturday, September 12, 1914
sections.text: Orrin Sayles and Walt Brandt had stood up together in May in the basement of the Methodist church, each with his right hand raised and three fingers straight, and said the Oath and the twelve points of the Law in front of Mr. Harbison and eleven other boys. They were thirteen. After that night you did not see the one without the other. On the second Saturday in September they walked the three miles down to the river to swim. A Scout had to swim fifty yards to make First Class, and below the old ferry the Snake had a slack place behind a gravel bar where a boy could pace it off. They swam it four times apiece. Then they lay on the bar to dry, with the stones warm under them, and talked about nothing, the way you can with one person. The desert came down to the water on both banks. Seven years before there had been nothing on the north side but sage and jackrabbits and wind. Then the government dam went in above, and the canal, and people came from Iowa and Nebraska and Utah and took eighty acres apiece, and now when you stood on the bluff you could see the exact line where the laterals stopped, green on this side of it and gray on that.
