Above the dam the lake was a bird reservation

sections.heading: II. The Prescription Case
sections.text: Lyle Harbison had come to the project in 1908 from a ditch farm in Colorado by way of a pharmacy course in Denver, and he kept the only drugstore in Norland. He was forty-four and unmarried. He had started the troop two years back because he was asked, and because nobody else would, and the Methodists lent the basement. On Saturdays the farm families were in town and the fountain was three deep. The five boys came in the alley door. Orrin had the goose rolled in his shirt. Mr. Harbison was behind the prescription case counting tablets onto a tile with a spatula, by fives. He looked up and saw who it was and what the shirt had in it. He looked down again and finished the count, funneled the tablets into a bottle, wrote the label, and pasted it on square. Then he wiped his hands and came around. He unrolled the shirt on the back counter. He turned the head with one finger, this way and that way. Orrin. Is this yours? Yes, sir. With a stone. Two. The first one was to make him turn his head. Mr. Harbison stood a while. Out front the fountain hissed and a child was asking for strawberry. “And do not seek to take the life which you can never give,” he said. I had that out of the Third Re

sections.heading: III. The Upper Ditch
sections.dateline: Colorado · about 1880, as he told it
sections.text: When he was a boy, Mr. Harbison said, there were two ditches out of the same river. His father farmed under the Upper. The one below was called the Fairview. They had the same river and near enough the same decree, and on the Upper the water got to the last man on the last lateral every August, dry years too, and on the Fairview it quit halfway down and the bottom forty farms burned up. The Fairview people studied on it and decided it was the horse. The Upper had a ditch rider named Dunham who rode a gelding black as stove polish, and it was said along the river that water followed that horse. So one July the Fairview board drove up and hired him off the Upper for the season. They paid forty dollars, in gold. Their own rider rode the black horse up and down the Fairview until September, and the bottom forty burned up the same as before. The next spring they came back with a tablet and a pencil. They said, Write down for us how you people run your ditch. Whatever the rule is, we will have it lettered on a board in gilt and hang it in our headgate house. The Upper people did not know they had a rule. So the Fairview men went around and asked them one at a time. The president of the d

sections.heading: IV. Two. One.
sections.text: Those were farmers, Mr. Harbison said. Nobody had sworn them to anything. And you stood up with your hand in the air. He looked at Orrin’s hands, which were hanging at his sides. I have watched you pitch. Those hands will do whatever you tell them, and that is not common. It is a thing to be careful with, the way I am careful with what is in the blue bottles. Your hands. Where your feet take you. And your mouth, Orrin. This didn’t start with a stone. It started with “Watch.” He went to the shelf over the desk where he kept the Pharmacopoeia and the Dispensatory, and brought down a thick book in a brown binding, the first of two. This man could throw. I know what is said about him on Sundays, and this is not that part. This is his son writing. He once killed a hare sitting in the flower-garden at Shrewsbury by throwing a marble at it, and, as a man, he once killed a cross-beak with a stone. He was so unhappy at having uselessly killed the cross-beak that he did not mention it for years, and then explained that he should never have thrown at it if he had not felt sure that his old skill had gone from him. — Francis Darwin, The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (1887), vol. I, ch. II

title: Skill and Sport
logline: A thirteen-year-old Idaho Scout with the best arm on the project tells his friend he can hit a flying goose in the eye.

verses.text: The Bhikshu who controls his mouth, who speaks wisely and calmly, who teaches the meaning and the law, his word is sweet.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, want a season away from the crowd and spend the three months of the rains with the monk Kokālika on one condition: that he tell nobody who they are. In return they teach him. As they leave he cannot hold it any longer and tells the village, calling the people cattle for not having known. The villagers run after the two with gifts; Kokālika follows, expecting the frugal elders to refuse and the gifts to fall to him. They refuse, and do not pass them on. When they return with a great following and the gifts are shared among everyone but him, he reviles them as greedy; they leave; the villagers drive him out. He goes to the Buddha and three times accuses the two, and three times is told, “Say not so.” As he leaves, boils the size of mustard seeds break out over his body and grow. His own former teacher, now a god, comes down to plead with him and is insulted in turn. He dies and falls into the Lotus hell. When the monks say that his tongue ruined him, the Buddha tells the birth story of the tortoise carried through the air on a stick by two geese.
bg.history:
Sharon Springs, fifty miles west of Albany, was a sulphur spa from the 1820s. When Saratoga’s hotels shut out Jews, German Jewish families came here instead; by the 1920s the guests were mostly Eastern European Jews, the white-columned sulphur temple and the Imperial Baths went up in 1927, and the Adler Hotel opened in 1929 with a hundred and fifty rooms and two kitchens. After the Second World War many of the summer people were Holocaust survivors, a good number of them Hasidic and Orthodox, taking the baths on doctors’ orders. Small self-catering boardinghouses like Koppel’s, called kokhaleyns, lined Main Street. The Imperial Baths closed in 2005.

The Rebbe of Hlinitz, his court on Hewes Street, and everyone on the street in Sharon Springs are invented. What is not invented is the teaching. The Talmud’s tractate Arakhin (here in the old spelling, Erchin) is the classic source for the laws of lashon hara, harmful speech, and tradition ties slander to afflictions of the skin, as with Miriam in the Book of Numbers. Belief in the return of souls, gilgul, runs through Kabbalah and Hasidic storytelling, and the Rebbe tells the tortoise’s fall in that key. Both passages are quoted from Hebraic Literature: Translations from the Talmud, Midrashim and Kabbala (1901).

sections.heading: I. The Back Room
sections.dateline: Sharon Springs, Schoharie County, New York · June 1954
sections.text: The whole village smelled of the water. It came out of the hill as white as skim milk and stinking of eggs, and people had been riding up from the city to sit in it for a hundred years: first the Vanderbilts, then the German Jews whom Saratoga would not have, then the Jews from Galicia and Hungary, and now, since the war, the ones who had come through the other thing with their joints and their skin and their nerves in such a state that a doctor on the Grand Concourse could only tell them to go and take the baths. They drank the water out of paper cups at the temple with the white columns. They lay in it in the tubs at the Imperial for twenty minutes by the attendant’s clock, and were wrapped in sheets and left to sweat. In the afternoons they sat in rocking chairs on the porches, porch below porch down the one steep street, and talked. Koppel Weingast had the porch halfway down. He had come from Galicia in 1922, a yeshiva boy with a good head and a quicker mouth, and had gone into boarders. Weingast’s was not the Adler, which had a hundred and fifty rooms. It was eleven rooms and two kitchens, one for meat and one for dairy, where the women cooked for their own, and a front parlor

sections.heading: II. Beheimes
sections.dateline: Main Street · the last week of Av
sections.text: They were going back to the Rebbe for Elul, as a hasid does. Koppel carried the valise up the hill himself. The three of them stopped at Mrs. Sobel’s for a glass of tea and a roll, and then the two went on to the corner of Route 20 to wait for the bus, and Koppel started home. It was three in the afternoon. The porches were full. He got as far as the middle of the street, where both sides could hear him. Beheimes! he said. Cattle. Cows in a field! Three months Reb Shaya and Reb Mottel of Hlinitz sat among you. The Rebbe’s right hand and the Rebbe’s left. In my back room, over my dairy kitchen. Pincus, one of them lay in the next tub to you at the Imperial, and you told him he was using too many towels. And you knew nothing. Nothing! And now they are standing at the corner for the Albany bus. The rocking stopped all the way down the hill. Why didn’t you tell us? said Mrs. Sobel from her doorway. Then everybody was moving. A honey cake came out of a kitchen still in its pan. Somebody had a bottle of slivovitz put by for a son’s engagement. A furrier from the Bronx, who was taking the cure for his hands, went up the stairs two at a time for a wool blanket still in its paper. The docto

sections.heading: III. Two Buses
sections.text: They kept their word the next summer, and they did not come alone. Two chartered buses stopped at the corner of Route 20, and sixty of the Rebbe’s hasidim got down from them in their long coats, gray men and boys, behind Reb Shaya and Reb Mottel. The street had been waiting since Shavuos. The hotel keepers had drawn lots for who would house whom, and none of them would take a dollar. The two asked for the back room at Weingast’s, and had it. Every day there was honor, and every day something came up the hill. A manufacturer in Gloversville sent five dozen pairs of lined gloves against the winter. The furrier sent to the city for knitted vests. The bath people sent books of tickets. There was medicine, and a case of wine. The hasidim who had come on the buses shared it all out among the sixty, a pair to each and a vest to each, down to the boys. To Koppel, who lived there, who was standing in his own parlor while they did it, nobody thought to hand anything. Reb Shaya and Reb Mottel did not hand him anything either. That night he was in his chair on the porch, and the next chair was not empty. Last year a honey cake was beneath them. This year they take with both hands. Gloves they

sections.heading: IV. Three Times
sections.text: He shut the house and took the bus to the city and went to the Rebbe. The Rebbe of Hlinitz had come out of the war with one lung and no one of his own, and he held his table on the parlor floor of a brownstone with the wall knocked through. He was not a man who spoke. People said that since 1945 he had used perhaps a hundred words a week, and most of those on children. The gabbai let Koppel in after the evening prayer. Koppel did not wait to be asked. Rebbe. Shaya and Mottel are takers. They are in the hands of their appetites, the both of them. Don’t say that, Koppel, the Rebbe said. Have trust in Shaya and Mottel. They are good. The Rebbe believes in them. I am the one who saw. With my eyes. A year they wouldn’t touch, and then with both hands. Don’t say that, Koppel. Have trust in Shaya and Mottel. They are good. They have things hidden inside them. They are not what the Rebbe thinks. They are bad men. Don’t say that, Koppel, the Rebbe said the third time, and the rest of it after, in the same voice, like a man holding a door for somebody who will not come through it. Koppel got up from the chair. A hasid leaves the Rebbe walking backward, with his face to him. Koppel turned aro

sections.heading: V. Reb Tuvia
sections.text: Koppel had had a teacher once, in Hlinitz. Reb Tuvia the dayan had taken him into his own house, an orphan of seven with a mouth on him, and taught him for nothing until he was seventeen. Reb Tuvia died in his bed in 1931, a very old man, and the whole town said the same thing at the grave: there went one who had finished, one of those who are not sent back. On the second night in the ward Koppel opened his eyes, and Reb Tuvia was standing at the foot of the bed. The man in the next bed, a Pole with his leg in traction, swore for the rest of his life that the old Jew stood a hand’s breadth above the linoleum. Koppel. It is a cruel thing you did. Make your peace with those two. Who are you? Tuvia. Your teacher. You? Koppel got up on one elbow. Nothing about him worked any more except the one thing. You were supposed to be finished. All Hlinitz said it. A soul that doesn’t have to come back. So what are you doing back? A fine tzaddik! You know what you’ll be? A ghost on a garbage dump, that’s what you’ll be. Reb Tuvia looked at him the way he had looked at him across the Gemara when he was seven. Let it be for you, Koppel, he said, according to your own mouth. Then there was only the

sections.heading: VI. The Third Meal
sections.text: On the Sabbath of Return, at the third meal, the light goes and nobody may kindle a lamp, and the hasidim sit on at the long table in the dark with a piece of challah and a piece of herring and sing without words. Between one tune and the next the talk that week was Koppel. His mouth buried him. Thirty years a decent Jew, and one summer. If he had only swallowed it. The Rebbe heard them. It was not the first time, he said, and because he so seldom said anything, sixty men stopped chewing. That soul fell by its mouth once before. There was a tortoise, he said, in a pond in the mountains. Two wild geese came down on that pond and stayed a season, and the three of them became friends. When the cold was coming the geese said, We winter in a cave of gold on a mountain far from here. It is a good place. Come with us. How does a tortoise come? We will carry you. If you can keep your mouth shut. I can keep it shut. So they found a stick, and the tortoise bit down on the middle of it, and the geese took the two ends in their beaks and went up. They flew over a village. The boys in the road looked up. Look! Two geese carrying a turtle on a stick! And the tortoise thought, You little nothings

title: Two Walls
logline: A boardinghouse keeper they call Koppel the Radio must keep one secret all summer: who the two quiet men in his back room are.

verses.text: He who dwells in the law, delights in the law, meditates on the law, follows the law, that Bhikshu will never fall away from the true law.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha announces that in four months he will pass into final nirvana (parinibbāna). Thousands of monks crowd around him, weeping and asking each other what they will do. One monk, Dhammārāma, keeps away from them and will not say why. The others report that he has no love for the Teacher. Summoned, Dhammārāma explains that he has not yet freed himself from desire and means to reach the goal while the Buddha is still alive, so he has gone off alone to reflect on and remember the teaching. The Buddha praises him: those who honor him with garlands and perfumes do not truly honor him, and those who practice the teaching do. At the end of the verse Dhammārāma becomes an arahant.
bg.history:
Across the Thames River from New London, Groton has been the Navy's submarine town since 1916, when the Naval Submarine Base New London became the first in the country. It calls itself the Home of the Submarine Force. Electric Boat builds submarines on the same shore. A sailor who completes the year-long qualification on a boat is designated "Qualified in Submarines" and wears the dolphins. Enlisted men have worn the silver pin since 1950. For a century the bars and tattoo shops along New London's waterfront served the men off the boats, and their shops were papered with flash, ready-made designs in black outline and a few colors, made for quick work on walk-in customers.

In 1961 New York City made it unlawful to tattoo a human being, citing a hepatitis outbreak that later critics said had nothing to do with tattooing. The ban held for thirty-six years. Tattooing went on behind drawn shades, and the city did not legalize it again until 1997 (the rise and fall of the ban). Apprenticeship is still the old way into the trade: years of sweeping, drawing and watching, then practice on fruit and on pig skin from the butcher, which comes closest to human skin for learning how deep the needle goes (how apprentices practice).

sections.heading: I. Fourth of July
sections.dateline: Bank Street, New London, Connecticut · March 2024
sections.text: Royal Tate had tattooed on Bank Street since 1973, in a long narrow room between a bar and a shop that sold used anchors, and in all that time he had never put up a sign with his name on it. The sign said TATTOO. The window said TATTOO. People knew. He had come to it sideways. He was a cook on submarines out of Groton in the sixties, a Black kid from Portsmouth, Virginia, who had gone into the Navy because his father had, and he had worn the silver dolphins and fed a hundred and twenty men in a galley the size of a closet. On leave in New York in 1965 he had gone looking for a tattoo and found that the city had outlawed them four years before. A man on a stoop sent him to a man in a back room on the Lower East Side, who did the work with the shades drawn, on a kitchen chair, and let Royal watch. Royal went back every leave for three years and swept the floor and watched. When he got out he knew how to build a coil machine from scratch and how to pull a line, and he knew that he would never do anything else. The walls of the shop were flash from floor to ceiling, sheets of it in dime-store frames gone yellow: swallows, anchors, daggers through roses, panthers, hula girls, the Rock o

sections.heading: II. The Line
sections.text: The shop filled up and stayed full. The apprentices and the two other artists came in on their days off and sat around his station. Old customers came in from Norwich and Mystic and Westerly with their sleeves rolled up to show him what he had done in 1979. Somebody put a vase of white roses on the counter by the register, and the next day there were three vases, and by May the counter was covered and the room smelled like a funeral parlor over the green soap. Men he had tattooed on the boats stood in the doorway and could not say anything and went next door to the bar. A woman from Groton brought a framed picture of her husband, dead twenty years, showing the eagle Royal had put on his back. Kevin, the senior apprentice, made a list of everyone who wanted to get one of Royal's own flash pieces from his hand before the Fourth, and the list went to four pages. Somebody started a hashtag. People slept in their cars on Bank Street to be first in line on Saturdays. What are we going to do, Kevin kept saying, at night, when they were cleaning the stations. What are we going to do after. Dominique Ruiz did not come in at all. She was twenty-six. She had grown up on Hempstead Street four

sections.heading: III. Four Blocks
sections.text: She came in on a Tuesday after closing, with her kit in one hand and a grocery bag in the other. The roses had been cleared off the counter that morning by the cleaning woman, who could no longer stand it. Kevin and Marisol and the two artists were still there, and they stopped talking when she came in. Royal was sitting in his own chair, the old red barber's chair at the first station, because he did not like the bed. He was thin now. His hands were the same. They tell me you quit on me, he said. Is it true? Yes, said Dom. Why? She put the grocery bag on the counter and did not take anything out of it. You said four months, she said. Everybody's in here getting your swallows. Everybody's crying. I can't do anything about the four months. And my line still shakes. You told me it shakes because I want it to be over, and because I'm thinking about who's going to see it. So I've been home pulling lines on grapefruit where nobody can see. I want to pull one straight before you go. While you can still look at it. Royal looked at her for a long time, the way he had looked at her sketchbook. Good, he said. Good. Then he turned the chair a little so he was facing the rest of them, Kevin an

sections.heading: IV. Dolphins
sections.dateline: The first station · the same night
sections.text: Royal rolled up his left sleeve. On the inside of his forearm, among fifty years of pieces he had put on himself, were the dolphins he had put on himself in 1967 in a bunk on the boat, with a sewing needle and a bottle of India ink, the night he qualified. They had been the first thing he ever tattooed. They had gone soft and green and blurred the way homemade work does, and nobody had ever touched them, because he had never let anybody else put a needle in him. Line them, he said. Just the line. Go over mine. Dom set up her station on the counter where the roses had been. She bagged the machine and the cord. She poured the black into a cap and wiped his arm down with green soap. He watched her do every bit of it as if she were being graded, which she was. Then she put her left hand flat on his arm to stretch the skin, the way he had shown her two years before with his hand over hers, and touched the needle down at the bow of the submarine where the dolphins' noses met. The machine ran. Nobody in the shop said anything. Kevin had come up behind the chair and stood with his arms folded, and then he unfolded them. She did not think about who was watching. She did not think about the

title: A Case of Grapefruit
logline: An old Bank Street tattooer has four months to live; his shop fills with roses, and his youngest apprentice stops coming in.

verses.text: Let him not despise what he has received, nor ever envy others: a mendicant who envies others does not obtain peace of mind.
A Bhikshu who, though he receives little, does not despise what he has received, even the gods will praise him, if his life is pure, and if he is not slothful.

bg.commentary: In the commentary a bhikkhu coming back from his almsround meets a friend who has gone over to Devadatta, the cousin who tried to take the Saṅgha from the Buddha and then split it. The friend asks whether he got anything to eat and says: here we receive rich offerings, stay with us a while. He stays several days. Reported and summoned, he answers that he does not share Devadatta’s views, and the Buddha replies that even so he roves about as though he held the views of everyone he meets. The Buddha then tells the birth story of the gentle state elephant Mahilāmukha, “Damsel-Face,” who overheard burglars talking by his stall night after night, took their talk for instruction and began killing his keepers, and who was cured when good men were set to talk of kindness within his hearing.
bg.history:
In the 1960s and early 1970s a handful of companies sold raw desert lots by the tens of thousands in New Mexico, Arizona and Florida to people in the Northeast and Midwest who had never seen them. The standard method was the free dinner: an invitation by mail, a meal at a hotel or restaurant, a color film of the good life in the sun, and a salesman at every table. The best known of these developments was Rio Rancho, whose developer, the Amrep Corporation, was later convicted of fraud. Congress had answered the trade in 1968 with the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act, which required a printed property report to be given to every buyer; salesmen learned to present it as a receipt. Ocotillo Mesa Estates, the Coachlight Inn, Thayer & Son and everyone in them are invented. Mr. Thayer’s story of 1925 remembers an earlier round of the same business, the Florida land boom, when Florida lots were sold sight unseen to northerners.

Brighton is an old suburb on the southeast edge of Rochester; Twelve Corners is its crossroads. Rochester was then a company town for Eastman Kodak, which since 1912 had paid its workers a yearly “wage dividend,” known locally as the Kodak bonus and paid in March. The city is also known for the lilacs of Highland Park, which bloom in the middle of May. The psalms are from the Psalter of the 1928 American Book of Common Prayer, which divides the hundred and fifty psalms over the mornings and evenings of a thirty-day month. Psalm 141 falls on the twenty-ninth evening and Psalm 37 on the seventh. The asterisk in each verse marks the pause for chanting.

sections.heading: I. The Plaza
sections.text: Russ Hoyt ate his lunch in the car that day because he had shown the Bonesteel house at eleven and was showing it again at one, and there was no sense driving back to the office in between. He parked in the plaza lot at Twelve Corners with the heater running and unfolded the waxed paper on his knee. Liverwurst on rye, an apple, two of Jean’s molasses cookies. He had sold houses for Thayer & Son for eight years, on a draw of a hundred and twenty-five dollars a week against commission. He had closed one sale since Thanksgiving. A bronze Toronado pulled in nose to nose with his Rambler and Gary Spangler got out of it in a camel coat. Gary had sat at the next desk for six of the eight years. In October Don Voss had walked out of Thayer’s and taken four of the seven salesmen with him, and Gary was one of the four. Voss had been the best producer the firm ever had. He had gone in to Mr. Thayer after Labor Day and said that Mr. Thayer was sixty-one and ought to keep the insurance side and the name on the window and let a younger man run the selling the way selling was run now. Mr. Thayer had said no. That was all anybody at the front of the office heard of it. Gary got in on the passenger

sections.heading: II. The Coachlight
sections.dateline: West Henrietta Road · Monday through Thursday
sections.text: The land was called Ocotillo Mesa Estates and it was in New Mexico. Voss had the franchise for it from Syracuse to Buffalo. The invitations went out by mail, engraved, to lists he bought: men between forty-five and sixty with the house paid for, and above all Kodak men, because the company paid its wage dividend in March and every man in the plant had known since Christmas about what his would be. There were twelve round tables in the banquet room of the Coachlight Inn, and at each one sat three couples and a closer. At Gary’s table there were three couples, Gary, and Russ. A Manhattan came first. Then the prime rib, an inch thick and hanging over the plate, with a baked potato in foil and sour cream in a paper cup, and afterward a parfait in a tall glass. Russ ate all of it. He had not had beef like that since his wedding. When the plates were cleared the lights went down for the film. It ran twenty-two minutes in color. A man in a yellow shirt drove a golf ball toward a mountain. A woman his age came up out of a swimming pool, laughing. There was a horse. Out the banquet room windows the snow was coming sideways off the lake across the parking lot, as it had been since the second

sections.heading: III. The Telephone
sections.dateline: Thayer & Son, Monroe Avenue · Friday morning
sections.text: Mrs. Bonesteel telephoned at half past nine. She was seventy-four and had been a widow since August. The couple who had seen the house twice had offered two thousand under what she asked, and she wanted to know from Russ whether she ought to wait for spring. He meant to tell her what he would have told her any other week. What he said, tilted back in his chair with the cord across his chest, was that he had another party very much interested in a house on Elmwood, and that these people would not wait on her, and what did she suppose Mr. Bonesteel would have wanted her to do? There was a silence on the line. Then she said in a smaller voice that she supposed she had better sign. He hung up pleased. A minute or so later he was less pleased, and could not have said why. There was no other party on Elmwood. Miss Fitch sat at the front desk, eleven feet off. She had kept the books and the telephone at Thayer’s for thirty-four years, and she heard everything said in that room whether she cared to or not. She had already taken one call that morning, from Mrs. Arthur Kimball, who wanted to ask in confidence whether Mr. Thayer had gone in with Mr. Voss on the New Mexico property, seeing tha

sections.heading: IV. Babyface
sections.text: Lyman Thayer was the Son on the window. He was a lay reader at his church and had read the lessons there for thirty years in a voice that never rose, and people who bought houses from him sometimes said afterward that they could not remember his having sold them anything. Each day at five, when the telephones stopped, he took a Prayer Book out of the top drawer and read the psalms for the evening at his desk. The book was open in front of him when Russ came in. Sit down, Russell. I am told you have been eating with Don Voss’s people. Is that so? Yes, sir. Four nights. Gary Spangler asked me. He’s a friend of mine. Russ had spent the afternoon getting it ready. I don’t hold with what they’re doing out there, Mr. Thayer. I never sold a lot. I never would. I ate the dinner. I will grant that you don’t hold with it. Mr. Thayer looked at him without any heat. But you go about, Russell, as though you held with whoever you happen to be sitting beside. Mrs. Kimball took it so last night. Mrs. Bonesteel would have taken it so this morning, if she had known who it was she was talking to. Russ had nothing ready for that. This is the twenty-ninth, Mr. Thayer said. These are the psalms for the

sections.heading: V. The Front
sections.text: On Saturday morning Russ drove to Antlers Drive with a gray pamphlet he had carried out of the Coachlight in his coat pocket, and sat in the Kimballs’ kitchen, and read them the page about water. There was no water. There was no power to the block the plat had shown them, or any date for it. Art Kimball’s check had gone to Syracuse in Friday’s mail. It took him until June, and a letter from Mr. Thayer’s lawyer, to get it back. On Monday Russ telephoned Mrs. Bonesteel before he took off his overshoes. He told her that there had not been any party on Elmwood. He told her the offer she had was a winter offer. If it were his mother’s house he would take the sign down and put it up again the second week of May, when the lilac hedge along her drive came out and did the selling for her. She said she was glad, because she had not slept. It put his commission off until summer, if it came to him at all. His desk had been moved over the weekend. Nobody mentioned it. It stood at the front now, at a right angle to Miss Fitch’s, near enough that their wastebaskets touched. At noon he unfolded the waxed paper on his blotter. Liverwurst on rye, an apple, two molasses cookies. Miss Fitch was on the

title: The Partition
logline: A house salesman on a thin winter draw lets an old friend seat him at a week of free prime rib dinners where desert lots are sold.

verses.text: He who never identifies himself with name and form, and does not grieve over what is no more, he indeed is called a Bhikshu.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin of Sāvatthī gives the first of his crop five times over: from the field, the threshing floor, the storehouse, the pot and the dish. He is called Pañcaggadāyaka, Giver of the Five First-Fruits. One day the Buddha stands at his door while he eats with his back to it. His wife, afraid he will give his dinner away, tries to hide the visitor and whispers to him to pass on; the Buddha shakes his head, she laughs aloud, a radiance falls into the house, and the Brahmin turns. He offers the half he has not eaten. The Buddha accepts it, saying that first, middle or last portion are all fit for one who lives on what others give, “like the petas,” the hungry dead. Asked what makes a bhikkhu, he speaks the verse on name-and-form, and husband and wife are both established in the path.
bg.history:
Punjabi men, most of them Sikhs, came to California's farm valleys from about 1907. Immigration law kept their families in India, and California law barred them from marrying white women, so several hundred married women of Mexican descent, often sisters marrying partners. Their households cooked chicken curry and roti beside beans and tortillas, spoke Spanish and English, and baptized their children Catholic. See Punjabi Mexican Americans and the University of California, Davis, archive on the hard years of 1923 to 1945. The nearest gurdwara was the one founded at Stockton in 1912, some five hundred miles north.

After United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind (1923) held Indians ineligible for citizenship, the California Alien Land Law barred them from owning or leasing farmland. They farmed on through verbal understandings with Anglo bankers, lawyers and farmers; a Holtville bank whose director held land for Punjabi clients was known as the “Hindu Bank.” In May 1933 an Imperial County grand jury brought a conspiracy case against four Punjabi farmers and their Anglo partners; the four were convicted, and three were sent to San Quentin before an appeals court ordered a new trial in 1934 that was never held. From 1933 on, most Punjabi farmers in the county registered as guardians of their American-born children and held the land in the children's names, as the historian Karen Leonard documented in “Punjabi Farmers and California's Alien Land Law”. The Luce–Celler Act of 1946 opened citizenship to them. The verses are from Shaikh Farid and Guru Teg Bahadur in the Sikh scripture; the Ninth Guru's sloks are read at the conclusion of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. Andrés, Lupe, Mr. Varney and the old man are invented.

sections.heading: I. Primicias
sections.dateline: East of Holtville, Imperial Valley · 1921 to 1933
sections.text: Inder Singh came down to the Valley in 1913 with a gang of men from Jullundur to pick cotton, and stayed to grow it. By 1921 he had cut his hair, leveled eighty acres under the East Highline Canal with four mules and a Fresno scraper, and married Guadalupe Robles of Sonora, whose older sister had married his partner the spring before. The Mexicans on the place called him Andrés. The Anglos in town called him Andy, and called him and every man like him a Hindu, though he was a Sikh and had told them so. He grew cotton for the bank. For the house he kept an acre along the head ditch in corn, melons, okra, chiles, and in winter the mustard greens of his own country, and it was that acre people talked about. When the first of anything came ripe in it, he picked it and carried it out to the road and gave it to whoever came along. When he loaded the wagon for town, the first crate went off the tailgate at the first tent he passed. When he brought home the hundred-pound sack of flour, the first scoop out of it went down to the pickers' camp in a lard pail before the sack was leaned in its corner. When Lupe cooked, the first ladle out of the pot went out the kitchen door. And when his plat

sections.heading: II. The Door
sections.dateline: The kitchen · a noon in late October 1933
sections.text: They were picking. He had been at the scale since before light, and at noon he came in and sat down at the table with his back to the door, the way he always sat, because the glare off the yard hurt his eyes. Lupe set the plate down: chicken curry the way he had taught her, beans, and four rotis off the comal, which she made of his flour and went on calling tortillas. The first of the garden had gone to the road in June. The first of the wagon had gone, and the first of the sack. The first of this pot had gone out to the weigh crew an hour ago, and the rest of the pot after it, because there were more of them than she had counted on. He looked around the kitchen for the fifth. The boy was at school. The yard, when he turned his head, had only chickens in it. He waited a little, and then he tore a roti and began. He had eaten half the plate when the old man came to the door. Everybody under the Highline knew him. He had come to California before any of them, and worked the railroad grades in the north, and somewhere along the way had let go of working for wages or for shares. He had no lease and no partner and no banker. He walked the canal banks from Calexico to Niland with a blank

sections.heading: III. The Second Half
sections.text: He carried the plate to the door and pushed the screen open with his foot. Baba ji. I gave the first of the garden and the first of the wagon and the first of the sack and the first of the pot, and then I looked for someone and saw no one, and I sat down. I have eaten half of this. My hand has been in it. It is all there is in the house. Will you take it from me? Any other holy man he had ever met would have looked at a half-eaten plate and remembered somewhere he had to be. The first of the pot is good, the old man said. The middle of the pot is good. What is left on the plate is good. He said the next thing in Spanish, so that she would have it too. I am like the dead, hija. I eat what was set out for somebody else. Lupe, who in a week would be laying bread and salt on a table for her mother and her two brothers, stopped laughing. He took the plate in both hands, and said over it a couplet of Farid's that every man from that country knew. Eat hard dry bread, and drink cold water;Farid, on seeing another's buttered bread let not thy heart long for it. — Farid, Slok XXIX Andrés stood in his own doorway and was gladder than the five gifts had ever made him. He had given the top of e

sections.heading: IV. In the Boy's Name
sections.text: The lawyer from Brawley had seen a good many of these men sign, that fall, and knew the look they wore doing it. Andrés signed as guardian of the estate of Jesús Inder Singh, a minor, the way a man signs for a crate at the depot that is addressed to somebody else. Then he asked the clerk where a person could get a cold drink. Once a year he put on a clean shirt and went before the judge with his accounts. He slept. He went on giving the five firsts, since there was no reason to stop, and Lupe went on telling him God asked for one. She cooked one roti over the count every noon from then on, and never mentioned it. The law changed in 1946, and in 1949 he raised his right hand in the same courthouse and came out a citizen. The lawyer, an old man himself by then, asked whether he wanted the eighty acres moved over into his own name at last. Jesús was twenty-three and running the place. Leave it, Andrés said. He had turned his chair around that October. For the rest of his life he ate his noon meal facing the door, with the glare in his eyes and the plate set a little toward the edge of the table.

title: In the Boy's Name
logline: A Punjabi cotton farmer who gives away the first of everything is halfway through his dinner when an old man comes to the door.

verses.text: The Bhikshu who acts with kindness, who is calm in the doctrine of Buddha, will reach the quiet place (Nirvana), cessation of natural desires, and happiness.
O Bhikshu, empty this boat! if emptied, it will go quickly; having cut off passion and hatred thou wilt go to Nirvana.
Cut off the five (senses), leave the five, rise above the five. A Bhikshu, who has escaped from the five fetters, he is called Oghatinna, `saved from the flood.'

Meditate, O Bhikshu, and be not heedless! Do not direct thy thought to what gives pleasure that thou mayest not for thy heedlessness have to swallow the iron ball (in hell), and that thou mayest not cry out when burning, `This is pain.'
Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.
A Bhikshu who has entered his empty house, and whose mind is tranquil, feels a more than human delight when he sees the law clearly.
As soon as he has considered the origin and destruction of the elements (khandha) of the body, he finds happiness and joy which belong to those who know the immortal (Nirvana).
And this is the beginning here for a wise Bhikshu: watchfulness over the senses, contentedness, restraint under the law; keep noble friends whose life is pure, and who are not slothful.
Let him live in charity, let him be perfect in his duties; then in the fulness of delight he will make an end of suffering.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa (“Soṇa of the costly earring”) lives in Avanti, far to the southwest, where monks are few. The elder Mahā Kaccāna twice refuses to ordain him, warning how hard it is to eat alone, sleep alone and stay celibate, and it takes three years to gather the ten monks his full ordination needs. He travels to the Buddha, shares his room, and at dawn intones the whole Chapter of the Eights; the Buddha's “Well done” is taken up by the gods, and the spirit in his mother's house, 120 leagues away, applauds. He then asks, for his teacher, that five monks may ordain in the border countries. His mother arranges to hear him preach, and when her maid comes three times to say that thieves are emptying her copper room, her silver room and her gold room, she will not leave the sermon. The thieves' leader, posted beside her to kill her, has everything put back; nine hundred thieves ask her pardon, are ordained in cloth dyed with red clay, and sit each under his own tree on a mountain, where the Buddha appears to them and speaks these nine verses. They cross the desert through the air to bow at his feet. Read the full commentary story. The poems Soṇa chants survive as the Aṭṭhakavagga of the Sutta Nipāta; the first of them, on desire, already tells the hearer to bale out the ship.
bg.history:
During the Vietnam War tens of thousands of American airmen were stationed at bases in Thailand such as Udorn and Takhli, and many came home with Thai wives. Those women, scattered among Air Force towns across the United States, were among the first Thai Americans, and in a number of places they pooled their money to buy a house and bring a monk to live in it. Holloman Air Force Base lies just outside Alamogordo, under the Sacramento Mountains; the village of La Luz is immediately north. The house-temple in the story, its monk, the Whitlocks and the crew from El Paso are invented.

Wat Thai of Los Angeles, in North Hollywood, began in a house in 1971; its Thai-style main hall was consecrated in 1982, and it is generally counted the first Thai temple in the United States. Luang Pu Kham, a monk of the Thai Forest Tradition, is invented. A boy can become a novice under a single monk, but full ordination, not given before the age of twenty, needs a chapter of ten monks, or five in outlying regions, an allowance the monastic code traces to Soṇa's errand, along with thick-soled sandals and frequent bathing. A spirit house for the guardian of the land, the phra phum, stands in the yard of most Thai homes; the commentary's first applauding gods are the bhummaṭṭhaka, the ones who live on the ground.

sections.heading: I. The Earring
sections.text: Kalaya Whitlock had come from Udon Thani in 1965 as the wife of an Air Force crew chief, with a baby not yet walking and two suitcases, and had buried the crew chief in 1975. By 1981 she owned the Siam Kitchen on White Sands Boulevard, the building it was in, and the two buildings beside it. She did not trust the bank with more than the mortgage. What she made she turned into gold, in chains, by weight, the way her mother had, and wore some of it and kept the rest at home. Her son was seventeen and was called Sonny by everyone, including her. He bussed tables, played second base badly for the Tigers, and wore in his left ear a gold stud his mother had given him when he was twelve, which got him into two fights a year. He was the only boy in Otero County who went to the temple without being driven. The temple was a three-bedroom house on a gravel street near the railroad, bought by eleven Thai wives who had put in forty dollars a month apiece. It had one monk. Ajahn Thongdee was past sixty and had been sent out from Bangkok, and it was said of him that he could take four words of the Buddha's and talk on them until the ice was gone from everybody's tea, and that when he was done you

sections.heading: II. Ten Monks
sections.text: A novice can be made by one monk. A monk cannot. By the rule as the Ajahn had always kept it, the full ordination wants ten, sitting together inside a marked boundary, and in 1981 there were not ten Thai monks between El Paso and Denver. So the novice Sōno swept the gravel, carried the bowl behind his teacher down a street where the only people who came out were the eleven wives, and learned. The Ajahn taught him the way he had been taught, by ear. He gave him the Chapter of the Eights, sixteen old poems out of the Sutta Nipāta, a line at a time, in Pāli, until the boy could chant all sixteen from the first word to the last without a book, and then he made him say what every line meant, in Thai and in English. It took most of three years. It was three years also before ten monks could be got into Otero County on one day, by car from Denver and Houston and by air from California, and Kalaya fed all ten. Sōno was twenty that spring. They ordained him in the back yard, inside eight stones. That summer the Ajahn sent him west. A very old monk from the forest monasteries of the northeast, Luang Pu Kham, whom the Ajahn had bowed to as a young man, was spending the rains at the Thai templ

sections.heading: III. Sadhu
sections.text: It is eight hundred miles, most of it desert. The old man received him as if he had come from across the street. He asked whether the road had been hard, whether he had eaten, how his teacher's knees were. Then, in front of forty monks who had been waiting weeks for ten minutes with him, he told the attendants to lay a second mat in his own room for the young monk from New Mexico. Sōno could not make himself go in. He walked up and down the temple yard under the big tiled roof most of the night, and went in at last and sat on the mat, and did not sleep much. Before light the old man was sitting up. Your teacher taught you something, he said. Let me hear it. So Sōno chanted the Chapter of the Eights, in that small room, to one listener, while the window went grey. All sixteen, from the poem on desire to the poem Sāriputta asks for at the end. He did not drop a syllable. When the last line had gone out of the room, the old man said: Sadhu. Sadhu, bhikkhu. Well said. You have it whole. The Thai people in Los Angeles tell the next part. They say that when Luang Pu Kham said sadhu that morning, something took it up outside. The spirit of the ground the temple stood on said it, and the o

sections.heading: IV. The Spirit House
sections.text: Kalaya's house stood at the east edge of town where the streets give out toward the mountains. In the corner of the yard, on a post, where the shadow of the roof never fell on it, was the spirit house: a little red-and-gold temple the size of a birdhouse, for the one the ground had belonged to before she bought it. Every morning she put out rice, a glass of water, and whatever was in flower. She was setting down the glass when somebody clapped. Two hands, close by, and a voice. Sadhu! Who is that? said Kalaya. It's me, sister. Who is me? The one who lives in your yard. She looked at the little house. Twenty years I bring you rice, she said, and you never clapped for me once. I am not clapping for you. Then for who? For your son. This morning in the old teacher's own room he chanted the Dhamma, and the old teacher said sadhu. Then all of us said it. I only said it last. Wait, said Kalaya. My son chanted to the teacher? The teacher did not chant to my son? Your son to the teacher. She stood in the yard with the rice spoon in her hand, and the gladness went through her from the feet up, five kinds of it, she said later, one after another. Then she thought: if he can chant it to that o

sections.heading: V. Copper, Silver, Gold
sections.dateline: Alamogordo · a Saturday night in August 1984
sections.text: The temple's front room held thirty people, so Kalaya rented the VFW hall. She hung it with marigolds. She borrowed an armchair from a furniture store and covered it with gold cloth for the preaching seat. She closed the restaurant and brought every person who worked for her except Teresa Montoya, who waited tables and was nineteen, and whom she left at the house. The house needed somebody. It had a block wall around it with bottle glass set in the top, an iron gate, bars on the windows, and two Dobermans on run wires. The driveway was tarred, soft by day and hard at night, so that anybody who crossed it in the afternoon left his shoe size. In the floor of the back bedroom, under a rug, was a safe set in a yard of concrete. All of this was known up and down Highway 54, and for two years a crew of nine men out of El Paso, who worked the base towns, had been driving past it slowly. Their trouble had never been the wall. It was that she was always home. That night they watched her car go. They dug under the wall on the arroyo side, where the caliche was rotten, and came up inside. What they did about the dogs is not told. The dogs were all right in the morning. The one who ran the cre

sections.heading: VI. Red Clay
sections.text: When Sōno came down from the chair, a big man got on his knees in front of Kalaya and put his forehead on the linoleum. Ma'am, I need you to pardon me. For what? I sat behind you all night with a gun. If you'd got up to go home I was going to kill you. All right, said Kalaya. I pardon you. The other eight came up one at a time and said what they had done, and she pardoned each of them in the same four words. Then Dub said: If you mean that, ask him if he'll take us. Whatever he is. We want to be it. She turned to her son and put her hands together, as a laywoman does to a monk. Venerable sir, these men liked the way I listened and the way you chanted. They want to go forth. Let them. There were not nine robes in New Mexico. They tore Kalaya's bedsheets to the measure, and Sōno dyed them in a washtub with red clay out of the arroyo behind the temple, and they dried on the chain-link the color of the hills. The Ajahn shaved nine heads on the carport and made nine novices. And when, that October, five monks could be got together in one back yard, he read them the old teacher's answer out of his own book, with his finger on the line, and ordained all nine. Sōno gave each man one thing

title: Red Clay
logline: A Thai restaurant owner in an Air Force town sits down to hear her son the monk chant, and nine burglars go to work on her house.

verses.text: As the Vassika plant sheds its withered flowers, men should shed passion and hatred, O ye Bhikshus!

bg.commentary: In the commentary, five hundred monks take a meditation subject from the Buddha and go to practice in the forest. They see jasmine flowers that opened that morning dropping from their stems by evening, and resolve to be released from lust, hatred and delusion before the flowers are released from theirs. The Buddha, sitting in his Perfumed Chamber at Jetavana, sends forth a radiant image of himself to them and speaks the verse, and all five hundred reach awakening.
bg.history:
The Hutterites are communal Anabaptists who trace their origin to Moravia in the 1520s and came to Dakota Territory from Russia between 1874 and 1877. They hold all property in common, eat together, attend a service every evening, and practice Gelassenheit, yieldedness or self-surrender. As German-speaking pacifists they were singled out during the First World War. In the summer and fall of 1918 colonies in the Dakotas and Montana had sheep and cattle seized and auctioned to buy Liberty Bonds, and drafted young men who refused uniforms were held in army camps and prisons. Four men from the Rockport colony, David, Joseph and Michael Hofer and Jacob Wipf, were court-martialed and held at Alcatraz, then moved to Fort Leavenworth, where Joseph died on November 29 and Michael on December 2, 1918; Joseph’s body was sent home dressed in the uniform he had refused. Nearly all the colonies moved to Canada in 1918 and the years after (Encyclopedia of the Great Plains). The colony in this story, its people and its flax field are invented.

The Martyrs Mirror (1660), Thieleman van Braght’s collection of accounts and letters of Anabaptist martyrs, is quoted here in Joseph F. Sohm’s English translation of 1886 (full text); it includes the burning of Leonhard Keyser at Schärding in 1527 and the letters of Matthias Servaes. Each flower of flax lasts only a day and is replaced by new ones each morning (National Park Service).

sections.heading: I. Five O’Clock
sections.dateline: A colony on the James River, South Dakota · Tuesday, July 16, 1918
sections.text: We are one people, so we tell it as one. The bell rang at five on its post by the kitchen, the way it had rung every morning since our grandfathers set the post in 1874, and we got up, a hundred and nineteen of us, and washed, and the men went out to the barns and the women to the kitchen and the children to wait for the children’s table. From the yard you could see the flax. It was the forty acres on the bench above the river, and that morning it was blue all the way to the cottonwoods. It is not a blue you see anywhere else. It is the color of a thing that is going to be gone by afternoon. Every flower on that field opens at sunup and by the middle of the day lets go of its five petals, and the next morning there are new ones, and nobody has ever seen one flower last two days. Vetter Paul did not come out to look at it. Vetter Paul was ninety-one and had been our preacher since before most of us were born, and since Easter he had lain in the small room at the end of the long house with the window toward the field, and his right hand did not work and his words came few. At Easter, when they carried him in to sit at the Lord’s Supper for what everyone thought was the last time, he

sections.heading: II. Nine O’Clock
sections.dateline: The flax bench · the same morning
sections.text: We were weeding the flax by hand that week because the wild mustard had come up in it, and it was the young men and the girls in a line across the field, bent, pulling. When you weed flax in bloom the flowers brush your face. It is like walking through the sky in your work clothes. Andreas was at the end of the line, next to the road. He pulled mustard as if every plant were a man on the bond committee. Basl Rebekka, who was the field boss for the girls and had a voice that could stop a runaway, watched him a while and then said, not loud, Before the blue is down, Andreas. It is nine o’clock, he said. I have till noon. Some laughed. It is a thing we do; we laugh at ourselves before anyone else can. But in the line, bent over, each of us knew what we were holding. For one it was the steers; she had raised a red one on a bottle and seen him go down the road on a rope. For one it was a word a storekeeper said to his wife at the counter. For one it was the boy in the guardhouse at Funston, whose one letter said he was well and was not allowed to say more, which was worse than anything it could have said. For one, and none of us said this aloud, it was the nice young woman in the bank w

sections.heading: III. Noon
sections.dateline: The eating house · the same day
sections.text: They came at dinner. Three automobiles and a stock truck from town, and a dozen men we knew by name, because we had sold them geese and bought their binder twine for forty years. Mr. Lindahl from the elevator was one. He did not get out of the car. They had come for the sheep, as they had said they would. Our steward, Vetter Michel, went out wiping his mouth and stood in front of them and said what he had said the week before, that we could not stop them and would not try, and that what they did they would answer for and not we. Somebody had painted the word on the side of the stock truck already, in yellow. One of the younger men threw a can of the same paint against the wall of the eating house, and it ran down the boards. Another of them, who was drunk at noon, which was the only thing about it that surprised us, spat on Vetter Michel’s beard. Vetter Michel stood there with it on him. That was when Andreas came round the corner of the wash house with a hay fork. We tell this part plainly because it happened. He did not raise it. He came round the corner with it in his two hands and stopped, and everything in the yard stopped, the men from town and our men and the women in the do

sections.heading: IV. Three O’Clock
sections.text: We went back to the field because the mustard was still in it. By three the blue was mostly down. The petals lay in the furrows between the rows like a blue sheet somebody had torn and dropped, and the flax stood above them green with its little bare stars, already making seed. Nobody spoke for a long time. Then the girls in the line began, very low, one of the old hymns, the long ones from the old country that take a quarter of an hour, and the young men took it up, and Andreas did not. He said, to nobody: It’s easy for him. He’s lying in bed. He doesn’t have to stand in the yard. Nobody answered that. It was what we all thought. An old man in a bed can say set it down. He has already set down everything; his hands can’t hold a spoon. We were young and strong and the town was taking us apart one animal at a time, and our brother was in the guardhouse at Funston, and the four Rockport boys were on their way to an island we had never seen. And it was coming on to evening, and the blue was down, and we were still holding it. Every one of us, the whole line. That was the first time in the summer that all of us knew it at once, standing in one row in one field. We said to each other, t

sections.heading: V. Six O’Clock
sections.text: This is the part that is told more than one way, so we tell it the way most of us saw it. The sun was low over the river and came across the field flat and yellow, and at the far end of the flax, where it runs out against the cottonwoods, Vetter Paul was standing. He was in his black coat, with his hat, the way he went to the Lord’s Supper. He was standing up straight, which he had not done since Easter. The light was behind him and also, some say, came from him; the girls at the near end of the line said the flax around his feet was blue again, a ring of it, as if it had opened for him late. He did not walk toward us. He stood, and he looked down the line at each of us, and then he raised his right hand, the one that did not work, and held it out flat and turned it over, the way you turn your hand over to let something drop out of it. Then he said, and we all heard it at our different distances the same, as if he were standing beside each one: the story of Leonhard Keyser, that we had all had from him as children. How Keyser was a priest who came over to our people, and they took him to burn in Bavaria in 1527. How on the cart he leaned down and pulled a flower from the edge of th

sections.heading: VI. Gebet
sections.text: At the evening service Vetter Michel prayed for the men from town, every one by name, Mr. Lindahl too, and that night for the first time that summer we could all say amen to it. Vetter Paul died in September, before the move. By then the elders had been north and bought land across the line, and that fall and the next spring we went, nearly all of us, the way our people have always gone when a country could not keep us: Moravia, Hungary, Russia, Dakota, Canada. We sold the forty acres on the bench for what we could get. In November the two Hofer brothers from Rockport died at Leavenworth, and one of them came home in the uniform he had refused to put on, and we sang for them on the way north. Samuel Kleinsasser came out of Funston thin as a lath in the spring of 1919 and found his brother waiting for him at the depot in Manitoba with a team. We are not saying we never hated again. We are people. But we knew after that what it was to set it down all at once, a whole field of us, and that it can be done in a day, and that it does not take a lifetime unless you let it. The new owner of the bench did not sow flax. He put it in wheat. But flax volunteers; the seed lies in the ground a l

title: Before the Blue Is Down
logline: The summer the town takes their cattle, a Hutterite colony tries each day to set down its hatred before the flax drops its petals.

verses.text: The Bhikshu whose body and tongue and mind are quieted, who is collected, and has rejected the baits of the world, he is called quiet.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Santakāya (“Calm in Body”) never makes an improper movement of hand or foot, never yawns and never stretches. It was said that he had been born of a lioness, and that a lioness who has found prey lies seven days in a cave on a bed of red and yellow mineral powder. If she finds on the seventh day that a movement of her tail, ears or feet has scattered the powder, she tells herself, “This does not become your birth or lineage,” and lies fasting seven days more. If the powder is undisturbed she comes out, yawns, stretches, surveys the four quarters, roars three times and goes hunting. The monks report the elder's composure to the Buddha, who says a monk should be like him, composed in action, speech and thought, and at the end of the verse the elder becomes an arahant.
bg.history:
In 1858, after California passed a series of laws against its Black residents, several hundred of them accepted an invitation from Governor James Douglas and sailed from San Francisco to Victoria. Beginning in 1859 a number of these families took up land on the north end of Salt Spring Island, the first place in the colony where settlers could pre-empt unsurveyed land. Many had been born enslaved; the best known of them, Sylvia Stark, was born in Clay County, Missouri, crossed the plains to California as a girl, and lived on the island until 1944. The Tollivers and Mr. Pryor are invented, but the island's first teacher was a Black graduate of Oberlin College, John Craven Jones, who taught for years without pay in a log schoolhouse at Central, built in 1861, that also served as the church. The BC Black History Awareness Society and the Salt Spring Island Archives have mapped the homesteads.

The winter of 1861–62 was cold enough to kill livestock across the island. Settlers' accounts are full of cougars, which they called panthers; the archives note that the teacher held school in two places so that children would not have to walk far through cougar country. Between 1867 and 1868 three Black settlers were killed near Vesuvius Bay, among them the Sunday school teacher William Robinson. An Indigenous man, Tshuanahusset, was hanged for Robinson's death on evidence that historians now doubt, and a number of families left the island afterward. Hawaiians who had worked for the Hudson's Bay Company, known as Kanakas, settled around the island's south end in the same decades. Charles Wesley's hymn was first published in 1742 and stood in Methodist hymnbooks throughout the nineteenth century.

sections.heading: I. The Winter
sections.dateline: Above Vesuvius Bay, Salt Spring Island · January 1862
sections.text: Keziah Tolliver was sifting the last of the meal when the panther came into the house. It was the winter the cold killed the stock. Ice stood in the passage between the island and Vancouver's Island, the boat from Victoria had not called at Vesuvius Bay in three weeks, and her husband was on the other side of that ice with the money for flour. She had a boy of six named Eli and a baby girl. The cow had died standing. They had a calf left in the lean-to, and in the dusk she heard the calf scream once, and then heard nothing at all. The door was a split-cedar door on leather hinges. It came in slowly, the way a door does when a dog noses it, and the thing that put its head around the edge was the color of a dead fern and as long as she was. She let the sieve go. It rang on the puncheons, and the meal went out across the floor in a pale skim. She sat down in it where she stood, with the baby in her lap and her back against the hearth stones, and she pulled the boy down against her side. Eli. Don't you move a finger. Don't move a foot. We are not people who run. The panther walked the room. It ate the venison off the table. It came across the floor and stood over them long enough that

sections.heading: II. What They Said
sections.text: After that winter the island said that Keziah Tolliver was a panther. They did not say it unkindly. A panther had walked up to a woman with a baby in her lap, they said, and seen its own cousin, and lain down. Old Kimo at the south end, a Kanaka who had packed for the Company for thirty years and fished now off Isabella Point, said he had known it the first time he saw her walk. And everybody on the island knew how it was with the she-panthers of the Divide, or said so. When one of them has made her kill, they said, she goes up into a cave under the high rocks, and the floor of that cave is laid a hand deep with the red dust of rotted cedar and the yellow dust of old maple leaves. She lies down on it and she lies seven days. On the seventh day she gets up and looks at her bed. If a twitch of her tail or her ear has scattered that dust, or a forefoot or a hind foot has, she tells herself, That does not suit what you were born, and she lies down again and goes hungry seven days more. If the dust is as she left it, she tells herself, That suits what you were born. She comes out of the cave, yawns, stretches, looks to the north and the east and the south and the west, screams three tim

sections.heading: III. The Bench
sections.dateline: The log schoolhouse at Central · spring 1873
sections.text: At seventeen Eli Tolliver was a long, spare young man who cleared land with his father and kept forty sheep. Nobody on the island had seen him do a needless thing with his hands. He did not drum on a table or pick at a cuff. On the school bench he sat with his palms on his knees and his feet side by side through a two-hour sermon, whenever a preacher rowed over from Nanaimo, and through the meetings afterward, where the men talked about roads and wharves and who would sit on the new council. He did not yawn. He did not put his legs out in front of him. He spoke when he was asked something, said the amount that answered it, and stopped. They were not easy years to sit still in. Three men of the settlement had been killed in their own cabins in '67 and '68, one of them the man who taught the Sunday school in that same room, and not everyone on the north end believed the right man had hanged for it. Families had sold out and gone to Victoria. The boys Eli's age had gone to the Nanaimo pits for wages. In the schoolhouse of an evening, when a limb came down outside, every head went around except one. That spring a panther began taking sheep along the lake. The men made up a purse of twe

sections.heading: IV. The Door
sections.text: Eli walked home behind his sisters without saying anything, which was usual. He had sat still eleven years because of where he came from. He had known that the way he knew his name. But standing in the schoolhouse door with his back to the room, hearing the hymn come two lines at a time, he had looked for the thing in him that did the keeping still, the hand on the scruff, and it was gone. He could not have said when it went. The stillness was there with nobody holding it. It was like the meal on the floor that morning when he was six, lying as it fell. His mother had supper on. She was past forty and still walked like something that had come down off the Divide. She looked at him once across the table and then looked again, longer, the way Mr. Pryor had once looked at her floor. Afterward he went and stood in the doorway. The light was going. He yawned, which his sisters had never seen and talked about for a week. He put both arms over his head and stretched until his knuckles touched the lintel. He looked north toward the bay, and east over the lake, and south to the Divide, and west where the sun was going down behind Vancouver's Island. Then he called the sheep, three times, th

title: Sifted Meal
logline: On Salt Spring Island they say a settler's son who never fidgets was born of a panther, and they have his mother's kitchen floor to prove it.

verses.text: Rouse thyself by thyself, examine thyself by thyself, thus self-protected and attentive wilt thou live happily, O Bhikshu!
For self is the lord of self, self is the refuge of self; therefore curb thyself as the merchant curbs a good horse.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk meets a poor hired laborer walking along in a ragged loincloth with a plow on his shoulder and asks why he does not go forth. The man asks who would ordain someone like him; the monk says he will, takes him to Jetavana, bathes him with his own hands, ordains him, and has him hang his loincloth and plow on the branch of a tree at the edge of the monastery grounds. He is named Naṅgalakula, “Plowman.” Living on the rich offerings given to the Buddha, he grows discontented and decides to go back to work for hire. But at the tree he scolds himself (“Shameless fellow!”) and returns, and he does this again each time the discontent comes back. When the monks ask where he keeps going, he says he is visiting his teacher. Soon he reaches arahantship and stops going, and when the monks tease him, he says that while he was bound to the world he went back and forth, and now he does not. They report this to the Buddha as a false claim; the Buddha says it is true, since his son has admonished himself and reached the goal. Read the full commentary story. A close twin of the story, about the monk Pilotika, is told in 10.10, The Sugar Sack.
bg.history:
Mount Angel Abbey was founded in 1882 by Benedictine monks from the Abbey of Engelberg in Switzerland. It stands on a butte about 485 feet high above the farm town of Mount Angel in the Willamette Valley, a hill that, as the Oregon Encyclopedia notes, Native people had long used as a place of prayer. Bavarian Catholic settlers followed the monks, and the monastery was rebuilt after a fire destroyed it in 1926. The surrounding country grew hops, berries, filberts and grain; by the early 1950s machines had replaced the big hop-picking crews. The Rule of St. Benedict requires that a newly received monk's own clothes be kept in the wardrobe, so that if he ever leaves he can be sent out in them; the passages here are from Leonard Doyle's 1948 translation.

In the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, the Soviet army returned to Budapest early on November 4, and the workers' district of Csepel was one of the last places to hold out, until November 11. About 200,000 Hungarians fled the country. Some 70,000 crossed into Austria over the small bridge at Andau, which James Michener made famous in The Bridge at Andau. Most of those admitted to the United States passed through Camp Kilmer in New Jersey between November 1956 and June 1957 before being resettled around the country.

sections.heading: I. The Road
sections.text: Ferenc Gál owned a scythe, a pair of work trousers gone white at the knees, one shirt, and a cardboard suitcase with a Red Cross label on it from a camp in New Jersey. He was thirty-three years old. He had been in America six years and nine months, and in that time he had picked strawberries and pole beans and filberts and Christmas trees, he had strung hop yards in the spring and fed vines into the picking machines in August, he had grubbed stumps and pulled mustard out of wheat and plowed for German farmers who did not want to plow on Saturday, and he had mowed ditch banks, which was what he was best at, and what he was doing on the afternoon Brother Meinrad saw him. The scythe was his own. He had bought the blade in Salem, from a hardware store that still carried them for the old Swiss, and made the snath himself out of ash, the way his grandfather had made them on the Great Plain east of the Tisza, with the two handles set to the length of his own arm. Everything else he had was borrowed or given or worn through. The shirt had been a good flannel shirt when a church in Portland gave it to him in 1957. Now it was more hole than shirt, and the holes had been mended with thread of

sections.heading: II. The Oak
sections.dateline: Mount Angel Abbey · August and September
sections.text: The abbey stood on top of the butte, four hundred feet above the town and the fields, the way abbeys stand on top of things in Switzerland, which was why the Swiss had put it there. The Indians had called the hill something else before the Swiss came. Brother Meinrad said the old people in town said it was a place where the tribes had come to pray, from as far as the Klamath country, and that the monks had not chosen it by accident, whatever they told you. There was a church with two towers, and the long brick monastery that had been built after the fire of 1926, and the seminary, and gardens, and a grove of fir, and, out at the edge where the drive came up from the road and the abbey's ground ended, a white oak older than any of it, low and wide, with its lower limbs out flat over the grass like arms. Brother Meinrad took him to the dairy barn first. He ran water into the steel sink where they washed the milk cans, hot, and had him take off the shirt and bend over, and he washed Ferenc's head with a bar of soap and his own old hands, and cut his hair short with the clippers he used on the calves when they had ringworm, and washed it again. Ferenc stood bent over the sink in the ba

sections.heading: III. Bread
sections.text: They rose at four-thirty for Vigils. They sang the Office seven times a day in Latin, the whole Psalter in a week, all hundred and fifty, the way the Rule said, and Brother Isidore stood in the back row of the choir with the lay brothers and did not know the Latin and learned it by sound, the way he had learned English by sound in the hop yards. He worked in the dairy with Brother Meinrad and in the orchard and in the woodlot. He ate in the refectory in silence while a monk read aloud from a pulpit, and the food was good. The food was very good. That was the thing he had not expected. The farmers in the valley gave the abbey everything. They brought eggs in flats and cream in cans and sides of beef at butchering, and in November, when they killed hogs, they brought sausages and smoked hams and blood pudding in such quantities that the cellarer stood in the kitchen door with his hands up. The women of Mount Angel brought kuchen and stollen and cookies in tins, and the hop growers brought money, and at Christmas a man who had made a fortune in prunes brought a crate of oranges from California for every monk in the house. They gave it because their grandparents had given it, and becau

sections.heading: IV. Szégyentelen
sections.dateline: The white oak · November 1963 to March 1964
sections.text: It was raining, the long fine Willamette rain that does not fall so much as stand in the air. The shirt was still on its limb. It had been out three months and it was black with wet and green along the seams with something growing, and the trousers under it hung straight down heavy with water, and above them in the crotch of the limb the blade of the scythe showed a line of orange rust along its back where the rain had run. He took the shirt down and held it. It smelled of oak and rain and under that, still, of the bunkhouse and the hop kilns and himself. He had meant to put it on. He had meant to put it on and take down the scythe and walk down the hill in the dark and be in Salem by morning and stand in line at the cannery. Instead he stood under the oak holding it, and he heard himself talking out loud, in Hungarian, the way he had talked to himself in the bunkhouses and the berry fields and on the marsh at Andau, because there was nobody else in America to talk to in it. Szégyentelen, he said. You shameless one. Look at you. Look at what you want. You want to put this back on. This. You want to go back down there and stand in the dark at five in the morning in front of the cont

sections.heading: V. The Hayfield
sections.text: After March he did not go anymore. He did not decide not to. It was only that the thing that had sent him went quiet one night in the wind under the oak and did not get up again. The hams were hams. The bell was the bell. When it rang he got up, and when he got up he was glad to be up, and when he sang he sang, and when he ate he ate, and when he milked he milked, and there did not seem to be anybody left over standing off to one side watching him do it and adding up whether it was worth it. He could not have explained it any better than that, and nobody asked him to. In June, when the grass on the hilltop meadows was up to a man's waist, Brother Meinrad's tractor broke a pitman arm on the mower and there was a week's wait for the part from Portland, and the hay could not wait a week. Brother Meinrad stood at the edge of the meadow behind the church and looked at it, and then looked at Brother Isidore. Brother Isidore walked out the drive to the oak. He did not take down the shirt. He did not look at it. He reached up and took the scythe out of the crotch of the limb, and walked back with it, and sat on an upturned bucket in the dairy barn for an hour with a whetstone and a hammer

sections.heading: VI. The Tools
sections.text: Father Placid was in his chair by the window with the Rule on his knees, closed. He did not need it open. He listened to the two novices without turning his head. They said that Brother Isidore had been going out to the oak by the road all winter, every week, sometimes twice, in the dark, and that he had told them he was going to see his teacher, and that now he said he did not need to go anymore because he was not in the world anymore. They said that he was a novice of nine months. They said that it was either a lie or pride, and that either way somebody should say something. When they were done Father Placid sat a while longer. Out the window, past the cloister garden, you could see the end of the drive and the white oak, and in the crotch of its lowest limb, if you knew where to look, a short dark curve that was the back of a scythe blade. He told you the truth, said Father Placid. The two novices waited. He had a teacher, said the old man. It is hanging on that tree. A shirt and a scythe. When he wanted to go back to the world, he went to his teacher, and his teacher showed him what the world was for him, and he scolded himself, and came home. Nobody else scolded him. Nobody el

title: The Scythe
logline: A Hungarian refugee mowing ditches for wages hangs his rags and his grandfather's scythe in an oak at the edge of a Benedictine abbey.

verses.text: The Bhikshu, full of delight, who is calm in the doctrine of Buddha will reach the quiet place (Nirvana), cessation of natural desires, and happiness.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the young Brahmin Vakkali is so taken with the Buddha’s physical beauty that he becomes a monk only to be able to look at him, and gives up study and meditation to do nothing else. The Buddha waits, then tells him: “What shall it profit you to look upon this body? Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.” Vakkali still cannot leave him, so at the start of the rains the Buddha sends him away. After three months apart, believing the Teacher will never speak to him again, Vakkali climbs Vulture’s Peak to throw himself off.
