The Buddha sends a radiant image of himself, speaks the verse, and stretches out his hand: “Come, Vakkali, do not fear, look upon the Realised One.” Vakkali springs into the air toward him, reaches awakening in flight, and comes down at the Teacher’s feet. He was later named foremost among those inclined to faith. Read the full commentary story, or the Vakkali Sutta (SN 22.87), where the Buddha tells him, “One who sees the teaching sees me.” The scripture quoted in the story is the Contemplation Sutra, one of the three Pure Land sutras that Shin Buddhists hold as their scripture. It tells how Queen Vaidehī, imprisoned by her son, prayed toward Vulture’s Peak, and how the Buddha came to her there.
bg.history:
After Pearl Harbor, the F.B.I. arrested Issei community leaders, Buddhist priests among them, and held them in Justice Department camps such as Fort Missoula in Montana. Under Executive Order 9066, some 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast were then removed from their homes. Many from Los Angeles County were held first at the Pomona Assembly Center on the county fairgrounds, and most of them were sent on to the Heart Mountain Relocation Center. The first inmates arrived there on August 12, 1942. The camp held 10,767 people at its peak in January 1943, which made it the third-largest town in Wyoming. Its barracks stood inside a barbed-wire fence with nine guard towers, on a sagebrush flat between Cody and Powell, with Heart Mountain about eight miles to the west. Winter lows reached about thirty below zero. Early in 1943 the government’s “loyalty questionnaire” divided the camp, and in 1944 the Heart Mountain Fair Play Committee organized a draft resistance that ended in the largest mass trial in Wyoming history.

About two-thirds of Heart Mountain’s people were Buddhist. In 1942 the camp’s eight priests, of several sects, formed the Heart Mountain Buddhist Federation, and services, Sunday school and O-Bon were held in a makeshift church. Hundreds of inmates left the camp on seasonal leave to work the sugar beet harvest in Wyoming and Montana, where farmers needed their labor and townspeople often met them with hostility. Inmates also went out in hiking parties to the mountain. The camp closed on November 10, 1945. Most of the barracks were sold and hauled away, and the site is now a National Historic Landmark with an interpretive center. Block 22, the Nakai and Hamada families and the stone garden are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Bucket
sections.dateline: Pomona Assembly Center, Los Angeles County Fairgrounds · May 1942
sections.text: Shigeru Nakai was nineteen, and until the second week of May he had been a sophomore at U.C.L.A. with a slide rule in a leather case and a plan to be an engineer. His father, a doctor on East First Street, had been taken by the F.B.I. on the night of December 7 with his medical bag still in his hand, and was in a camp in Montana, and wrote once a month on paper with holes cut in it. Shig had brought his mother and his little sister to the fairgrounds at Pomona on the bus, with the two suitcases each that they were allowed, and had stood in the line for typhoid shots and in the line for mattress ticking to stuff with straw, and on the third evening, sitting on the step of Barrack 14 in the heat with the asphalt still soft from the day, he saw the gardener. He was a man of about fifty, in a clean khaki shirt with the sleeves rolled, carrying a bucket of water down the row between the barracks. Somebody had planted a little pepper tree at the end of the row, a seedling a foot high in a coffee can, and the man knelt and gave it water a cupful at a time, watching it go into the dirt, and then stood up and went back for more. That was all he did. Shig watched him make the trip four times

sections.heading: II. The Stone Garden
sections.dateline: Heart Mountain, Wyoming · autumn 1942 to spring 1943
sections.text: The trains brought them to Wyoming in August, three days and nights with the blinds pulled down, and let them off on a sagebrush flat between Cody and Powell where hundreds of tar-paper barracks stood in rows inside a barbed-wire fence. West of the camp, eight miles off across the flat, the mountain stood up by itself out of the plain, grey limestone with a steep blunt head on it, and whichever way you turned in Heart Mountain you saw it. It was in the window of every barrack. It was at the end of every street. The Nakais were put in Block 22. Mr. Hamada and his wife were in Block 22 too, four barracks down, and Shig took that as a sign, though he did not believe in signs. The camp gave him a job on the staff of the high school, which would open in October in barracks with no desks, teaching algebra to boys only three years younger than himself at nineteen dollars a month. He went for two weeks and then stopped going. He had signed up for correspondence courses from a university extension office back East, and the books came in the mail, and he did not open them. His mother asked him what he did all day. He said he was studying. What he did all day was stand where he could see Mr.

sections.heading: III. Go Back
sections.text: In May the farmers around Powell came to the camp office looking for hands to thin sugar beets. They had been glad enough of the camp's labor at harvest the fall before, though in town the workers had not always been made welcome. Mr. Hamada signed up for the summer. He would be on a farm on the Shoshone flats below the mountain, he and five other men from the block, sleeping in a bunkhouse, hoeing beets from dawn to dark at a wage the farmer would set, until the season was over. Shig went to the camp office the same afternoon and asked to be put on the same crew. That evening Mr. Hamada came down the row to the Nakais' barrack and knocked on the door, which he had never done, and asked Mrs. Nakai's pardon, and asked if he could speak to her son outside. They stood on the step. The mountain was black against the last of the light. I went to the office, Mr. Hamada said. I told them to take you off the list. You're not coming. Hamada-san— Go back, he said. Go back inside to your mother. Stay here. And he went down the step and up the row in the dusk, and did not look around. The truck left for Powell on a Tuesday morning. Shig did not go to see it off. He lay on his cot with his face

sections.heading: IV. The Mountain
sections.text: By that summer the camp let the young people out in parties to hike to the mountain, with a pass from the office and a promise to be back before dark. The Boy Scouts went, and the Y.B.A., and boys from the high school in twos and threes with canteens and sandwiches from the mess hall. Shig got on the list for a Saturday with a group from Block 24 he did not know. He did not take a canteen. They left at four in the morning through the gate and walked west across the flat in the dark, eight miles through the sage, and the mountain grew in front of them as the light came until it filled the sky. The others stopped to rest on the lower slopes, in the timber, and ate their sandwiches. Shig went on alone. He climbed all morning. There was a trail of sorts and then there was not. He went up over loose rock and through stunted pines bent all one way by the wind, and then out onto the bare grey limestone of the summit, with the wind pushing at him, and walked to the edge of the north face, where the rock broke off and went straight down for a very long way. He could see everything from there. He could see the whole Big Horn Basin laid out yellow and green, and the river, and the checkerboar

sections.heading: V. Shinjin
sections.text: Mr. Hamada came back from the beets in September with his wages in an envelope and finished the stone garden by the mess hall before the snow. Shig helped him. He did not stand at the corner of the laundry anymore. He carried the stones, and set them where he was told, and when Mr. Hamada was not there he went on with it by himself and did not seem to notice the difference. He went back to teaching algebra. He opened the correspondence books. At the Buddhist church that winter, on a Sunday when the ministers asked Mr. Hamada to give the talk, he spoke about shinjin, the true entrusting, which is the heart of the Shin teaching and the hardest thing in it to explain. He did not explain it. He said there were people who studied it for fifty years and people who knew it in one afternoon, and that the second kind were rarer, and that he had known only one of them. He did not say who. Nobody in Block 22 needed him to. The camp closed in November 1945. Those who were left were given twenty-five dollars and a train ticket, and the barracks were sold off for lumber to homesteaders, and the wind came over the flat and filled in the streets with sage. title: Heart Mountain
logline: In a Wyoming incarceration camp, a Nisei college boy can do nothing but watch the Issei gardener who leads the Buddhist young people.

verses.text: He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a poor grass-carrier named Annabhāra gives his only meal to a solitary buddha and wishes never again to hear the word "there isn't." His rich employer, Sumana, tries to buy the merit of the gift. The solitary buddha compares merit to a lamp that lights a whole village without growing less, so Annabhāra gives it away freely and is made rich. Reborn as Anuruddha, the Buddha's cousin, he grows up so sheltered that when his mother sends him an empty covered bowl, the gods fill it with cakes. As a monk he becomes foremost in the divine eye. Seeing that his old friend Sumana has been reborn as a boy, he takes the child as his novice, and the boy becomes an arahat as his hair is cut. When Anuruddha falls ill, the seven-year-old flies to Lake Anotatta for water. The nāga king Paṇṇaka covers the lake with his hood and tells him to fetch water from the Ganges. The boy calls the gods of every heaven to witness, grows huge, treads on the nāga's hood, and fills his jar from the jets that spring up. The nāga pursues him, is told to beg the boy's pardon, and becomes his servant. Later, when monks tweak the novice's ears, the Buddha asks for water from Anotatta to bathe his feet. Of five hundred novices only the youngest goes, carrying a vast golden vessel and refusing the nāga's offer to carry it. The Buddha ordains him on the spot at the age of seven.
bg.history:
Lily Dale, on Upper Cassadaga Lake in Chautauqua County, was incorporated in 1879 as the Cassadaga Lake Free Association, a summer camp for Spiritualists and freethinkers. By the 1890s its season ran from mid-July to the end of August, with lectures and mediums in an open-sided Auditorium that seated about fifteen hundred, hotels, a library, and a Children's Lyceum that met each morning in Library Hall. The Lyceums followed the manual written by Andrew Jackson Davis in the 1860s, which sorted children into twelve groups named from the youngest up: Fountain, Stream, River, Lake, Sea, Ocean, Shore, Beacon, Banner, Star, Excelsior and Liberty, each with its own badge color. Women spoke from the platform on equal terms with men, and suffragists including Susan B. Anthony came to speak. In 1897 the Buddhist reformer Anagarika Dharmapala of Ceylon was among the season's speakers. The National Spiritualist Association, founded in 1893, has its headquarters there today.

Saratoga Springs, whose mineral springs the Mohawk had used long before European settlement, was by then the country's grandest spa, with its waters bottled and sold as cures for dyspepsia and much else. By the 1880s more than two hundred wells had been drilled around the town, most of them to extract carbonic acid gas for the soda fountains of the cities, and the pumping stopped the flow of many springs. In 1908 the state passed laws against the pumping, and the springs were taken into a state reservation, now Saratoga Spa State Park.

sections.heading: I. The Dinner Pail
sections.text: Annis Wheelock, before she was anybody, was the hired girl on Sumner Hale's farm on the ridge above the Cassadaga lakes. She was seventeen. She milked, churned, scrubbed, carried, and in haying time took the men their dinners in the field and then went back for her own, which was corn bread and a piece of salt pork in a tin pail with a cloth over it, set aside for her on the back of the stove. Sumner Hale was the richest man in the town of Pomfret. He gave a great deal away, at the church and on the roads, with his name on it, and he was proud of what he gave. One noon in July, coming back across the field for her pail, Annis met an old man on the road. He was a tin peddler by the look of his pack, but he had no tin in it, and he had a tin cup in his hand with nothing in it either. He did not ask for anything. When she said, Have you not had your dinner? he looked at her a long time and said, I expect to have it, daughter. Then wait, said Annis. She ran to the house. The cook had kept her pail. She ran back with it and gave him all of it, the corn bread and the pork. She remembered all her life what she was thinking while she ran. That when she had wanted to give anything, she had

sections.heading: II. The Season
sections.dateline: The Hale farm and the camp grounds · June–August 1897
sections.text: By the summer of 1897 Annis Wheelock was seventy-four, and her gift was the most famous in the camp at Cassadaga. She came every season for the June picnic and stayed until the grapes were picked. Old Sumner Hale was dead thirty years. That spring, sitting in her parlor in Buffalo with her eyes shut, she had looked for him, the way she sometimes looked for people, and found him. He was standing behind a small boy in a grape vineyard on the ridge above the lake, with his hand on the boy's head. The boy was his grandson, Hiram Hale's youngest, and his name was Sumner too. He would be seven in July. She wrote to Hiram Hale, whom she had known since he was a baby, and he wrote back that he would count it an honor to have her for the season. So she boarded that summer at the Hale farm and was driven down to the camp each morning in the Hales' democrat wagon, past the gate where the ticket man took a quarter from visitors and touched his hat to her. She sat on the platform of the Auditorium under the great roof on its posts, with the curtains drawn up and the lake shining beyond. She gave sittings in the parlor of the Grand Hotel. She heard Mrs. Twing and Mr. Hull, and the young man from

sections.heading: III. The Rock Spring
sections.text: The camp was empty by then. The hotels were shut, the boats pulled up, the Auditorium curtains let down and tied. The two of them had the grounds nearly to themselves. Annis kept her hours as she always had. She sat up half the night on the cottage porch, walking up and down it when her legs allowed, sitting for the spirits, and by the middle of September she had brought on the dyspepsia that came on her every fall. She went yellow and could not keep her supper. Sumner found her on the porch in the gray of the morning with her hand pressed under her ribs. What ails you, Mrs. Wheelock? My old trouble. Have you had it before? Many a time. What cures it? She smiled. Water from the Rock Spring at Saratoga, child. I drank it when I was a girl and it cured me, and nothing else ever has. Then I'll fetch you some. She looked at him. Saratoga was three hundred miles away across the state. Can you? Yes, ma'am. The spring belongs to a man named Asa Pennock now, she said. He knew me once. Tell him your errand, and ask him for a jar of water for medicine. Sumner took a quart Mason jar off the pantry shelf and went out of the cottage. That is all anyone on the grounds saw of it. The man who kept

sections.heading: IV. Mr. Pennock
sections.dateline: The camp ground, Lily Dale · the same day and the next
sections.text: Sumner was on the cottage porch by noon. He unscrewed the jar and put it in Mrs. Wheelock's hands. Drink it, ma'am. Asa Pennock was a day behind him. He took the morning train to Albany, then the New York Central west to Buffalo, and changed twice more. He got down at the Lily Dale station on the evening of the next day with his eyes red as sumac and his collar sprung, and walked into the closed camp ground asking at every cottage for Mrs. Wheelock. He had shut down his pumps and come straight on. In the train, he had told the conductor, he had decided he would either wring the boy's neck or carry him to Niagara and throw him over the Falls, he had not yet decided which. Annis had not drunk the water yet. She was sitting on the porch with the jar in her lap. Pennock stood at the foot of her steps and took off his hat, because he could not help it, he had known her when he was young. Mrs. Wheelock, he said, that boy of yours took my water without my leave. Don't drink it. Sumner, said Annis, is that so? No, ma'am, said the boy. Mr. Pennock gave it to me. He said so three times. Annis knew that the boy could not lie. So she unscrewed the jar and drank. It was cold and tasted of iron,

sections.heading: V. The Lyceum
sections.dateline: Library Hall and the Grand Hotel · opening week, July 1898
sections.text: The camp opened the next summer on the fifteenth of July. Annis came down to the Grand Hotel on the first afternoon, on the boy's arm, to pay her respects to Mrs. Electa Barnard. Mrs. Barnard was eighty-four, the oldest trance speaker in the movement and the one people came farthest to hear. She had been on the platform since the year after the rappings, in every hall from Boston to San Francisco. She was a small, wide old woman in black silk, almost blind, and off the platform she hardly spoke at all. On the platform, when the spirits had her, her voice filled the Auditorium to the back rows and out onto the lake. People said there was nothing she did not know. That afternoon she was sitting on the long veranda of the Grand Hotel in a wicker chair with her hands folded on her cane, and everyone who came in at the gate came up the steps to her. The mediums and lecturers and patrons on the veranda made a great deal of Annis, and then of the boy. Some of them had heard about the Rock Spring and did not believe it, and some had not heard. They patted his cropped head. A test medium from Cleveland took hold of his ear between two fingers and gave it a shake. Well, little medium, aren't

sections.heading: VI. The Platform
sections.text: On Sunday the Auditorium was full, fifteen hundred people on the benches and more standing on the grass beyond the posts with the curtains rolled up and the lake bright behind them. The band played. The speakers came up onto the platform and took their chairs, and the boy came up with them in a clean collar, with his red Fountain badge pinned to his jacket, and sat in a chair that was too big for him. His feet did not reach the floor. In Library Hall that week there was no other talk among the mediums. They had all seen the pitcher come in over the lake, or knew someone who had. A medium from Cleveland, the same one who had shaken the boy's ear on the veranda, said she had been in the work thirty-one years and had never seen a power like it. Nobody had. They were still saying it when Mrs. Barnard came in on her cane one morning to hear the Lyceum, and asked them what they were talking about, and they told her. She sat down. She was quiet a long time. Then she said that such a power was given to any child, any child at all, who came to it whole and gave it everything he had. That was all she said in her own voice.
