title: The Rock Spring
logline: An old clairvoyant takes a seven-year-old grape farmer's son to serve her, and sends him for water from a Saratoga spring a man has capped.

verses.text: Stop the stream valiantly, drive away the desires, O Brahmana! When you have understood the destruction of all that was made, you will understand that which was not made.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a brahmin named Pasādabahula, “Great Confidence,” hears the Buddha and from then on feeds sixteen monks at his house, greeting every one of them as an arahat, a fully awakened one. The monks who are not yet awakened think he believes there are arahats among them; the ones who are think he cannot tell; all of them grow uncomfortable and stop coming. The brahmin, grieved, goes to the Buddha, who tells the monks that the greeting is only an expression of confidence, in which no fault can be found, that the brahmin’s love for arahats is boundless, and that they should therefore cut off the stream of craving and settle for nothing less.
bg.history:
The New Haven Colony allowed only church members to hold civic rights. When the royal charter of 1662 folded it into Connecticut, which had no such rule, and as the churches debated the Half-Way Covenant of 1662, which let the children of baptized but unconverted parents be baptized in turn, the minister of Branford, Abraham Pierson, who disapproved of the covenant, led his people away. With settlers from Milford under Robert Treat, they founded Newark on the Passaic, carrying Branford’s church records with them. The Branford company arrived in 1667, the land was bought from the Hackensack that July for a list of goods that included guns, kettles, coats and ten pairs of breeches, and in the new town no one was to enjoy full citizenship, vote or hold office unless a member of a Congregational church (Newark Public Library).

Puritan churches admitted full members by a “relation,” a spoken account of the candidate’s experience of saving grace, which the church weighed by what it called the judgment of charity, since only God could see the heart. The Geneva Bible, the Bible of the Puritan migration, is quoted from the 1599 edition (text). Hopestill Ambler, Goodwife Bray, Sergeant Ruggles, the Lacey boy and the fire are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Relation
sections.dateline: Newark, East New Jersey · the Lord’s day, February 1667/8
sections.text: The relation of Hopestill Ambler, planter, made before the church at the noon exercise, he desiring to be received into full communion. Taken down as near his own words as the clerk could keep up, the room being cold and the ink thick. Brethren, I will be short, for I have tried this before and been long and it came to nothing. I was born in Norfolk and came over a child in the year 1638 with the company that sat down at Quinnipiac, and I have lived all my life since among the people of God, at New Haven and then at Branford, and now here. I have sat under the best preaching in the world. I have seen men and women stand where I stand now and tell how the Lord broke them and bound them up, and the tears ran down my face, and I went home and could find no such thing in myself. Not the breaking and not the binding. Thirty years. I have been a good neighbor, I hope, and paid my rates. I am not a saint. I never could say I was. But I will tell you what I can say, which is that I have loved the saints. I have loved them more than my meat. When I was a boy at New Haven and a member went by in the street, I would stand and look after him as you would look after a ship going out with all it

sections.heading: II. The Noon Table
sections.dateline: The house lot nearest the meeting-house · summer and autumn 1667
sections.text: The Lord gave me the lot nearest the meeting-house. I did not ask for it. It fell to me by the draw, and I took it for a sign of what I was to do, which was to feed people. Between the morning exercise and the afternoon, the families that live near go home to their dinners, but there are those whose lots lie out toward the great meadows and over the brook, and the young men who have no house yet, and they used to sit in the meeting-house and eat cold bread. So from the first Lord’s day in July I set my table for them. My wife and I fed sixteen. Pottage, and rye-and-Indian bread, and what fish the river gave, and in the fall venison the Indians sold us, and beer. Brethren, you know how I greeted them. Some of you were among the sixteen. I stood at my door and I said: Come in, saints. Sit down, saints. Saints, will you have more? I said it to every one. I said it to Sergeant Ruggles, who gave his relation at Branford in 1644 and has walked with God ever since, and I said it to the Lacey boy, who is eighteen and who I know for a fact went over to the Dutch at Bergen in August and came back merry. I said it to all of them alike. I could not see what the Lord sees and I did not try. Whe

sections.heading: III. Goodwife Bray
sections.dateline: Her house by the Watering Place · November 1667
sections.text: So I went to Goodwife Bray. You all know why. She is the oldest woman in this town, past seventy-nine. She was the midwife at Branford twenty years and at New Haven before that. There is hardly a soul here under thirty that she did not catch in her two hands, and she says she can tell a man’s whole disposition by the way he came. She does not speak in meeting, as women may not, and she does not need to. I told her the whole of it. She heard me through, shelling beans into her apron. Then she asked me why I said it. I said I did not know. I said, because I love them. Because it is the only thing in the world I want, and I want it so much I see it everywhere. She said, Go home and set the table. The next Lord’s day, between the exercises, she put on her hood and walked across the lot to the meeting-house, slow, on her stick, and went in where the sixteen were eating their cold bread, and stood in front of them. Some of you were there. I was not. This is what was told me, and if I have it wrong the brethren who were there will set me right. She said, Which of you will tell me why you have left Hopestill Ambler’s table for this? And the young men told her: he calls us saints, and we ar

sections.heading: IV. The Chimney
sections.text: Brethren, I would have stopped there and been content. But the Lord was not done, and this is the part I have never been able to say until now, and I am standing here to say it. On the eighth night of the eleventh month, the chimney took fire. It was clay and wattle, as most of ours are yet, built in haste last summer, and it went up in the night and took the thatch, and by the time we had the children out the whole house was burning. You came running, all of you, with buckets from the Watering Place. The sixteen came first. They were young and they ran. They threw water till their coats froze on them, and it did no good, and we stood in the snow and watched it go. Everything I had built with these hands since we came over the water from Branford. The second house in six months. I stood there, and Goodwife Bray came and stood by me, wrapped in a blanket somebody had put round her, and the light of my house was on her face. I said to her, That is twice. The Lord takes everything I make. She said, Hopestill. Did you think you made it? And she said the other scripture to me. Not loud. I do not think anybody heard it but me. For we knowe that if our earthly house of this tabernacle be

sections.heading: V. The Vote
sections.dateline: The clerk’s note · the same day
sections.text: The brethren being asked whether they were satisfied, Sergeant Ruggles rose and said he had heard many relations and few so short, and that the judgment of charity had never been easier to give, and he for one was satisfied. The rest held up their hands. Hopestill Ambler was received into full communion. When the vote was declared he said nothing, but sat down, and was seen to be laughing without noise. Noted also: that this winter, since November, nine of the young men who ate at Ambler’s table have come before the elders desiring to give their relations, of whom three have been heard and received, the Lacey boy among them. The others are in the way. Noted also, at Goodwife Bray’s request, though it is not the church’s business: that when the exercise was over and the people went out, Ambler stood at his new door in the snow, the pottage being hot, and called to the whole congregation coming down the steps, members and half-way and the children and the two Dutchmen who had come over from Bergen to hear the preaching, Come in, saints, and a great many more than sixteen went in, and the door was left open, and nobody went red.

title: Come In, Saints
logline: In a new Puritan town meant only for saints, a man who has never been sure he is one greets everyone at his table as one.

verses.text: If the Brahmana has reached the other shore in both laws (in restraint and contemplation), all bonds vanish from him who has obtained knowledge.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is a single paragraph. Thirty monks from a distant country come to see the Buddha and sit down. The elder Sāriputta sees that they are ready for the last step, goes to the Buddha and, without sitting down, asks a beginner’s question on their behalf: people are always speaking of “the two states”; what are they? The Buddha answers that they are calm and insight (samatha and vipassanā; in Tibetan, zhiné and lhakthong), and speaks the verse. At the end of it all thirty are arahats. Müller, following another reading, took the two for restraint and contemplation.
bg.history:
Camp Hale, in a high valley north of Leadville, was built in 1942 to train the ski troops of the 10th Mountain Division. From 1958 to 1964 the Central Intelligence Agency used a fenced corner of it to train some 250 to 300 Tibetan resistance fighters, in four contingents, the last of which arrived in October 1962. The program was secret; the cover story was atomic testing. The trainees, among them monks who had given back their vows to fight, called the camp Dumra, the Garden. Instructors went by first names and gave the Tibetans American ones, young English-speaking Tibetans interpreted, and by the instructors’ own account the longest part of the course was Morse code and radio procedure. On Saturday nights the trainees took over the kitchen. Lyle, Jampa, Gen-la and Classroom Three are invented, as are the fates given for them.

The earlier teams were parachuted into Tibet, and most of those men were killed or captured. After overflights stopped in 1960, graduates were sent overland or to the guerrilla base in Mustang, in Nepal, which held out until 1974. In 2010 a plaque was placed at Camp Hale, and in 2022 the valley became part of a national monument. The great monastery at Lithang, in Kham, was besieged in 1956 with bomber aircraft overhead; Tibetan accounts say it was bombed. The lines Gen-la chants are from the eighth chapter of Śāntideva’s Bodhicaryāvatāra, which Tibetan monks commonly learn by heart; the English is L. D. Barnett’s abridged version of 1909.

sections.heading: I. Two Things
sections.text: The Americans called the place the Ranch, and the Tibetans called it Dumra, the Garden. It was a fenced corner of an old Army camp at nine thousand two hundred feet, a few Quonset huts and four classrooms under the snow, with signs on the road that said explosive ordnance to keep the elk hunters out. The instructors went by first names only. Lyle taught code. He was thirty-eight, from Hastings, Nebraska, a Navy radioman in one war and an instructor at a Navy school after it, and his wife believed he was testing cold-weather equipment for the Army. He had Classroom Three, thirty men who had come in October. They had been flown in at night with the windows covered, and nobody had told them what country they were in. Most were Khampas, from the east of Tibet, horsemen and traders and a good many former monks, and none of them had ever seen a telegraph key. They had American names, because the Americans could not manage the others. In five months Lyle had to bring every one of them to twelve words a minute, sending and receiving, in five-letter groups off a one-time pad, on a set that ran from a hand-cranked generator. After that they would go home and be the only voice coming out of t

sections.heading: II. The Question
sections.text: By February Lyle knew the class was good. Jim knew something else about it, and it was Jim who told him, in his careful school English, on the path one night. These ones have stopped asking when they will go, Jim said. The other rooms ask every day. In October these ones quarrelled at volleyball, and Hank and Dale did not speak for a week. Now look at them. I think they are very near something. It only needs a push. Lyle said twelve words a minute was the only thing they needed to be near. Jim agreed that this was so. The last Saturday of the course, the sending test was over and all thirty had passed it. Lyle stayed behind after supper to box up the practice keys. The men came into Classroom Three anyway and sat down at their desks, all thirty, with Walt in the second row where he always sat. The stove ticked. Nobody had called a class. Jim came in last. He walked to the front, to his place by the desk, and he did not sit. He put his hands together and spoke to the second row in Tibetan. He spoke slowly and formally, and Lyle caught the one word he knew. What did you ask him? I said, Gen-la, people are always speaking of the two. What are the two? You know what the two are. Dit an

sections.heading: III. Loose Wrist
sections.text: Monday morning was the receiving test, and after it Lyle ran the class through one more hour of sending, for his own satisfaction. He had taught code for sixteen years. He knew the sound of a frightened hand, which clips the dits and leans on the dahs, and the sound of a hand that wants to be finished. He walked the rows with his eyes shut. He heard thirty keys that morning and there was no hurry in any of them and no drag, and when he opened his eyes every wrist in the room was lying loose on the desk as if it belonged to nobody. They left that week, at night, in a bus with the windows painted over. There was no more jumping by then. They were flown back across the Pacific and went in on foot, some over the passes into Tibet and most up to Mustang. Lyle was not told where any of them went, and over the years he learned the ends of only five. Two were killed inside Tibet before the summer was out. One did nineteen years in a Chinese prison and came out of it, a visitor said, the calmest man in Lhasa. One kept a tea stall in Pokhara. It was said that Gen-la carried the radio for his group and never the rifle, and that he sent for six years from a ridge above the Kali Gandaki, slowly

title: Dit and Dah
logline: A code instructor at a secret camp teaches thirty Tibetans that everything is made of two things, and hears them repeating it.

verses.text: He for whom there is neither this nor that shore, nor both, him, the fearless and unshackled, I call indeed a Brahmana.

bg.commentary: The commentary story is four sentences long. Māra, the tempter, puts on a disguise, comes to the Buddha at Jetavana and asks what this “far shore” is that people keep speaking of. The Buddha knows him at once and says, “Wicked One, what have you to do with the far shore? That may be gained only by those who have freed themselves from the passions.” He then speaks the verse, and many of those listening enter the stream.
bg.history:
By 1708 enslaved Africans and their descendants were the majority of South Carolina’s people. They raised cattle in open-range cowpens, burned tar and pitch, grew rice, and built and crewed the dugout cypress canoes that carried all of it to Charles Town; the College of Charleston’s Lowcountry Digital History Initiative describes that early world. Many came from Senegambia, where Islam was old and boys learned the Qur’an by writing it on washable boards. Lamin, the landing and everyone on it are invented. The Yamasee War of 1715 was real: it left St. Bartholomew’s Parish, the next one south of the Stono country, plundered and burned, and afterward most of the Yamasee withdrew to Spanish Florida.

The “far shore” was real too. In October 1687 eight men, two women and a small child reached St. Augustine from Carolina by boat, and the governor refused to give them back. In 1693 the Spanish crown ordered liberty for all such fugitives, “the men as well as the women,” on condition of Catholic baptism. For the next seventy years people went south by canoe through the creeks behind the Sea Islands, as the National Park Service recounts in its history of Africans in St. Augustine. One of them, a Mandinga man baptized Francisco Menéndez, became captain of the free Black militia and, in 1738, of Fort Mose, the first legally sanctioned free Black town in what is now the United States. Freedom there was conditional and often slow in coming. People went anyway.

sections.heading: I. The Log
sections.dateline: A landing on the Stono River, St. Paul’s Parish, Carolina · March 1719
sections.text: The Englishman who owned the landing had him in the plantation book as Boatswain, one Negro man, old, a canoe maker. His name was Lamin. He had been a boy on the Gambia, where a teacher made him write the Book on a wooden board in ink of pot-black, and wash the board, and write it again, until what had been on the board was in him where no water could get at it. He was taken at about twenty. That was forty years gone, with Barbados in between, and he still had most of it. At the landing he made canoes. A cypress came down in the back swamp, oxen dragged it to the bank, and Lamin did the rest with fire and an adze. He laid coals along the top of the log and let them eat down a hand’s depth, scraped out the char, and laid coals again. It took most of a month to get the inside of a tree out of it. When the walls were two fingers thick he filled the hull with water and dropped hot stones in and wedged the sides apart with sticks, a little wider each day. Then it was a boat. It went into the book, and it carried tar barrels and rice down to Charles Town on the tide. He liked to say there was no carpentry in it. I don’t make anything. I take out what isn’t canoe. Five times a day he went

sections.heading: II. The Asker
sections.text: The man came along the bank at the hour when Lamin had finished the sunset prayer and was rolling up the skin. He wore an osnaburg shirt torn at the shoulder, and he was mud to the thigh, and he said he had run from a place up Goose Creek nine days back and had eaten nothing in three. Lamin gave him what was in the pot, hominy and a piece of mullet. The man ate some of it. He sat on the cypress chips with his back to the new hull on its blocks, and he looked at the quarter: the six houses, the smoke, the path that went back toward the swamp. Father, he said, everywhere I go they are talking about the far shore. The far shore, the far shore. What is it they mean? Where does a man find this far shore? Lamin knew him then. It is told two ways how he knew. The plain way is that a man nine days in the marsh does not leave fish in the bowl, and he looks at a canoe before he looks at anything else on a landing, and this one had not looked at the canoe once. He was counting houses. There were men in the parish who paid for that kind of counting. The other way it is told, the dogs had not barked when he came, and the tide mud where he had walked held no track, and Lamin called him by a name

sections.heading: III. The Ebb
sections.text: What the asker had not counted lay in the cane behind the chip pile, flat on the ground, where it had been lying since before he came. There were eight grown people and a child, from three plantations, waiting for the dark of the moon and the ebb at midnight. A woman called Phibba had come from across the river with her girl of four. There were two brothers the English had named for Angola, and a cattle hunter from the cowpen at the head of the creek, and the rest. They had heard every word. Some of them had been sick with fear since sundown. They were afraid of the scout boats and of the open water at the sounds. They were afraid of the Spaniard and his water and his saints, and afraid most of all that the place was only a thing people said. One of the brothers had already whispered that he would go back before he was missed. All of them had carried the far shore in their minds as a bank so distant that the fear of the miles between had grown heavier than the thing they were leaving. Phibba told it years afterward in Augustine, where she was called by another name and sold oranges at the plaza gate. She said that between one breath and the next the river stopped having a wrong sid

title: Neither Bank
logline: A muddy stranger sits down by an old canoe maker's fire on the Stono and asks where a man might find the far shore.

verses.text: He who is thoughtful, blameless, settled, dutiful, without passions, and who has attained the highest end, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

bg.commentary: In the commentary a man who is a Brahmin by birth and lineage notices that the Buddha calls his own disciples Brahmins, and reasons that the title ought to be given to him as well. He goes and asks. The Buddha answers that he calls no one a Brahmin for birth or lineage, only the one who has reached the goal, and speaks the verse; the Brahmin is established in the first fruit of the path. Read the full commentary story. The nearest Jewish counterpart to a Brahmin by birth is the Kohen, the hereditary priest descended from Aaron, and Hillel’s saying in Pirkei Avot makes the same turn from sons to disciples. It is quoted from Charles Taylor’s Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1897), where it is numbered i. 13; most editions count it 1:12. The tractate is traditionally read a chapter a week on the Sabbaths between Passover and Shavuot, the weeks of the counting of the Omer.
bg.history:
New York’s Jews, about a hundred people at the turn of the eighteenth century, worshipped in rented rooms, first on Beaver Street and by 1700 on Mill Street, now South William Street. They did not build a synagogue of their own until 1730. The congregation became Shearith Israel, the oldest in the United States. Most of its early families were Portuguese and Spanish Jews, many only a generation or two out of the Iberian peninsula, with a growing number of Ashkenazim, and the Gotham Center describes the friction and the shared life between the two. Dona Branca, Daniel Cohen Faro, Hirsch and the children are invented.

Branca’s childhood is the world of crypto-Judaism. After the forced conversions of the 1490s, families in Portugal kept what they could of Jewish practice in secret for two centuries, without books or clergy, and it was very often the women who carried it. Around them Iberian society sorted people by the statutes of limpieza de sangre, purity of blood, which traced a “New Christian” ancestor back through the generations. In the priestly blessing, which Spanish and Portuguese congregations perform on the festivals, the Kohanim remove their shoes and the Levites wash their hands, and a Kohen who is on bad terms with the congregation is not supposed to go up.

sections.heading: I. The Basin
sections.dateline: Mill Street, New York · the weeks of the Omer, 1706
sections.text: Dona Branca Lopes lived in one room over a cooper’s shed at the low end of Mill Street, three doors from the house where the nation rented an upper floor for its synagogue. She was past seventy. She had been born at Trancoso in Portugal, in a house where her mother lit the Friday lamp inside a clay jar so that no light showed at the shutters. In that town there was no synagogue, no scroll, no reader and no priest, and a neighbor who saw clean linen on a Friday could send a family to the Holy Office. She had come out by Bayonne and Amsterdam. A nephew in the Curaçao trade brought her to New York, and the yellow fever of 1702 took him and left her. Now she taught the children of the nation their letters, for whatever the parents sent up the stair: a loaf, a string of candle ends, half a cord of wood in the fall. There were about a hundred Jews in the town that year, most of them Portuguese like herself, and a few Germans the Portuguese called tudescos. Her pupils were seven. The eldest was a girl of eleven, Sarah Nunes. The youngest was Leyb, five years old, whose father Hirsch was a tudesco from Fürth and made tallow candles in a shed behind the slip. Inside her door, on a stool, st

sections.heading: II. The Cohen
sections.text: Senhor Daniel Cohen Faro shipped flour and barrel staves to Curaçao and brought back cocoa. He had a brick house on Dock Street and a pew, such as it was, nearest the ark. He was a Cohen. His father had been one and his father’s father, and the two spread hands were cut on his grandfather’s stone at Ouderkerk. On the festivals he took off his shoes and went up before the ark with his prayer shawl over his head and blessed the congregation, and when a firstborn son was redeemed the five pieces of silver were laid in his palm. He was not a proud man about most things. About this he was careful, which he held to be different. He passed under her window every day on his way to the waterside, and every day he heard it. Now my priests may begin. One afternoon he climbed the stair and looked in at the door. He saw a bench of children. One was a girl, and one was the tudesco’s boy, whose feet did not reach the floor. He thought about it for a week, because he was a fair man. A widow may call children what she likes. But she was learned in her way, and the nation deferred to her on the fast days and on how a thing had been done in the old country. In six years she had never called him anyth

sections.heading: III. The Cup
sections.dateline: The eve of the Feast of Weeks, and the morning
sections.text: He counted the days with the rest of them each night after the evening prayer, the thirty-fourth, the fortieth, the forty-eighth. He did nothing. A man can turn a sentence over for two weeks and still call it thinking. On the forty-ninth day, before sunset, he walked down to the shed behind the slip. It stank of tallow. The boy Leyb was on the floor sorting wicks by length. Daniel put forty shillings on the bench in Spanish silver and said, in Portuguese, that he had weighed that cask in a wet week, and that a wet week adds nothing to tallow but does things to a man’s temper. Hirsch looked at the money for some time. He had been expecting the constable. He answered in a Portuguese that was mostly German. He said his beam scale had been his father’s and might be a little kind to the seller. Then he took down a pound of candles, weighed it where Daniel could see the pointer, and put it on top of the money. Neither of them touched either pile. After a while the boy got up off the floor and took his father’s hand and looked at the Cohen’s shoes. In the morning the upper room on Mill Street was hung with green boughs from the Bowery road, and the reader chanted the portion about the mou

title: The Widow's Priests
logline: A widow out of Portugal calls the children on her bench her priests, and the town's born priest climbs the stair to ask why.

verses.text: The sun is bright by day, the moon shines by night, the warrior is bright in his armour, the Brahmana is bright in his meditation; but Buddha, the Awakened, is bright with splendour day and night.

bg.commentary: In the commentary it is the evening of the great festival that closes the rains. King Pasenadi comes to the monastery in all his ornaments, the elder Kāḷudāyī sits at the edge of the assembly deep in meditation, his body the color of gold, and the sun is setting as the moon rises. The Buddha’s attendant Ānanda looks at each radiance in turn and tells his teacher that his alone satisfies. The Buddha answers that the sun shines by day, the moon by night, the king when he is adorned and the saint when he is absorbed, but that Buddhas shine by night and by day alike.
bg.history:
About five hundred colonists were at Jamestown in the autumn of 1609, and about sixty were alive the next spring. The winter is remembered as the Starving Time. The Powhatan chiefdom, on whose land the fort stood, kept the English penned inside it; they ate horses, dogs, rats and laundry starch, burned their own houses for firewood, and in at least one case ate the dead. On May 23, 1610, the survivors of the wrecked flagship Sea Venture arrived from Bermuda in two small ships they had built there. On June 7 the colony was abandoned, and within days it was turned back in the river by the arrival of Lord De La Warr with three ships. Alse Reeve, Kit Dawe and the shipwright Nicholas are invented.

The governor’s state is from William Strachey’s letter known as the True Reportory: the repaired church with its two bells, prayers at ten and four, the fifty halberdiers in “fair red cloaks,” the green velvet chair. Midsummer Day of 1610 did fall on a Sunday by the old calendar, with the moon close to full. The collect is the one the Prayer Book appoints for every evening of the year. What followed the relief was not gentle. That August De La Warr sent soldiers against the Paspahegh, whose town was burned and whose people, the children of their chief among them, were killed; by the next year the Paspahegh no longer appear in the record as a nation on their own ground.

sections.heading: I. The Winter
sections.text: Five hundred English were in the fort when the leaves came down, and sixty in May. The ground was Paspahegh ground and nobody had asked the Paspahegh for it. By November the great king Powhatan’s men had shut the English up inside their own palisade, and whoever went out past the blockhouse after roots, or after a shot at a deer, did not come in again. They ate the horses. They ate the dogs and the cats and then the rats, and the starch meant for ruffs, boiled to a paste, and the leather of their shoes. They ate worse than that, and it is set down in other places. They were afraid of the woods, so for firewood they pulled down the houses of the dead, and then the gates, and then the palisade itself, a post at a time. There was no minister. Master Hunt was two years in the ground and the man sent to follow him was cast away on the Bermudas and thought drowned. So the widow Alse Reeve did what there was to do. She had come in the August ships with a husband, a joiner, who died of the flux before the first frost. She was fifty or near it, a Wiltshire woman who could read, and she owned a Prayer Book that had lost its back board. When word came that someone in a cabin would not see mor

sections.heading: II. Midsummer Day
sections.text: Then in three weeks everything was altered. Sir Thomas Gates came up the river in two pinnaces built of Bermuda cedar, with near seven score castaways who had lived ten months on wild hogs and turtles and sea birds and were as fat and brown as farmers. They looked at the sixty and the sixty looked at them. Gates gave the place up and put everyone aboard, and they were a day down the river when my Lord De La Warr’s longboat met them, with three ships behind it and a year’s victual, and turned them round. His lordship had the fort scoured and the church mended. There were two bells again, and prayers at ten and at four, and on a Sunday he went to the sermon with the Council and the captains and fifty halberdiers in red cloaks, and sat in the quire in a chair of green velvet. Midsummer Day fell on his third Sunday. At evening, before the watch was set, he walked the round of the new bulwarks with his guard behind him. The widow was sitting on the well curb picking over ship’s pease in her apron, and Kit sat by her, because that was where he sat. He was a boy who looked at things. He looked up the river, where the sun was going down red into the trees of the far bank and the whole brea

sections.heading: III. The Flux
sections.text: The summer sickness came up with the heat, as it does on that river, and it went hardest with the new-come. The widow went back to sitting on floors. There were ministers now, and candles out of the store for the dying, and she said the collect all the same. On a night when she was at the far end of the fort, the shipwright Nicholas lay in his cabin with the flux and nobody by him. He told it afterward. He woke in the black of the night wanting water, and a cup was put to his mouth. When he had drunk he saw who held it. It was the ship’s boy who went about after the widow, sitting on the floor with his back to the bed frame, his lips moving over something he had by rote. The candle allowed for the cabin had burned out before midnight. Nicholas could see the boy’s face well enough, and the cup, and the grain of the wall post behind him. He was a man who had been looked at all his life for his own stillness, and he knew what he was seeing. He said nothing and shut his eyes. In the morning the boy was asleep where he sat, with the cup in his lap, and the light in the room was the ordinary kind, coming in under the door.

title: Light Enough
logline: A ship's boy who survived the Starving Time looks at the sunset, the moon, the governor's red cloaks, and the grey widow shelling pease.

verses.text: Because a man is rid of evil, therefore he is called Brahmana; because he walks quietly, therefore he is called Samana; because he has sent away his own impurities, therefore he is called Pravragita (Pabbagita, a pilgrim).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a brahmin who had gone forth as an ascetic under some other teacher heard that the Buddha called his own monks pabbajita, “those who have gone forth,” and reasoned that the name ought to fit him too, since he had also left home. He went to the Buddha and said so. The Buddha answered that nobody is called gone forth for leaving a house; a person is called gone forth because the stains have gone forth out of him, and spoke the verse, which explains each holy name by a pun on what has been put away. The brahmin reached the first stage of awakening as he listened.
bg.history:
The Separatists of Plymouth Colony had come out of the Church of England, out of Nottinghamshire to Amsterdam in 1608, then to Leiden, then over the sea in 1620. In the 1630s the great migration into Massachusetts Bay drove up the price of livestock, and William Bradford recorded kine selling at £20 to £28, a milch goat at £3 or £4, and female kids at 30 to 40 shillings. Planters who had stock went out to their outlying grants for meadow, the Duxbury people were dismissed to form their own church, and Bradford feared the scattering would “be the ruin of New England.” In 1640 cattle prices collapsed: a cow that had been worth £20 fell to £5. Bradford’s own account is in his history of Plimoth Plantation. Rowland Fenn’s Boston is the town of the Antinomian Controversy, after which Anne Hutchinson’s supporters were disarmed and many went to Aquidneck Island in 1638.

Bradford also describes the earthquake of about the first of June, 1638 (June 11 by the modern calendar): heard before it was felt, like distant thunder out of the north, shaking platters and dishes off the shelves while “the cheefe of this towne were mett together at one house” with friends who were removing, so that women outdoors had to catch hold of posts and pales, with a second, weaker shock about half an hour later. He noted that the summers for several years afterward were cold. The sermon the widow quotes was given at Plymouth in December 1621 by Robert Cushman, a layman and the colony’s agent, during his month-long visit on the Fortune; it was printed in London in 1622 without his name. The text here follows the Boston reprint of 1846, The Sin and Danger of Self-Love.

sections.heading: I. The Removals
sections.text: By the spring of 1638 the town was going over the water. Every week a cart went up the shore toward Duxbury with a bedstead roped on it legs up and a kettle wedged between the legs, and every week a shallop went off from the landing toward Greens Harbor with somebody's chests to the gunwales. Nobody was leaving the colony. They were only leaving the town. Kine sold at twenty pound in the Bay that year, some at twenty-eight, and a man with kine had to have meadow, and the meadow was across the bay. The houses they left stood with the doors pegged, and grass came up in the dooryards, and the street that had lived close under the fort hill for seventeen years was, as the old planters said to one another, very thin. The Widow Ware did not remove. She was sixty-eight. She had walked out of Nottinghamshire in 1608 with the others and lived fourteen years in Leiden, where she learned to sit with the sick, and had come over in the Anne in the summer of 1623 with her husband Thomas, a cooper, and two boys. Thomas died in the infectious fever of 1633, the year the great flies came up out of holes in the ground and made the woods ring. Both her sons had gone to Duxbury with their cattle and w

sections.heading: II. Platters and Dishes
sections.text: He came again on the first day of June with two more kids, because the Greens Harbor man’s brother wanted a pair, and after he had sold them he sat at her table in the afternoon with the door open for the warmth and went on with it. He had been going on with it since Candlemas. She sat by the door mending a shift and let him. Come out from among them, and separate yourselves, saith the Lord. It’s the whole ground your people stand on. And I’m the only one in this patent that’s done it. She bit the thread. The noise came before anything else. It came out of the north, low, a murmur like thunder a long way off over the woods, and they both looked toward the door to see the cloud, and there was no cloud. Then it was nearer and under them. The pewter on the shelf above the hearth began to talk, platter against platter, and walked, and three of them went off the edge one after another and rang on the hearthstones. The pail by the door slopped. The whole house leaned and came back like a ship. She was out of the door before he was off the bench. Outside the street was moving the way a blanket moves when somebody under it turns over. She took hold of the pales of her garden fence with bot

sections.heading: III. The Second Noise
sections.text: He sat on her chopping block among the bean poles with his back to the house. He was going to go home. He would go home and not come in again, and that would be one more place, and he caught himself putting it on the hand with the others. The second noise came then, out of the north the same way, but lower, and the ground went under him once like a horse shifting its feet, not so strong as the first. Up and down the street he heard the women cry out and run for their posts again. He did not take hold of anything. He sat on the block with his hands on his knees and let it come through him and go on south toward Manomet and the Cape, and he saw the thing. He could never afterward say it better than that. He had been looking out from it all his life, the way a man looks out from a window and never sees the glass, and now for the space of the shaking it was outside him and he was looking at it. It was small. It was the size of a sparrow. It had come out of the bishop’s church with him and out of his brother’s door and off the ship at Boston and down the path to the neck, and it was fed, and loud, and it was not Rowland Fenn. It was only a thing he had been carrying. He had five places

title: Hatched at Home
logline: In a Plymouth emptying out for cattle meadow, a goat-keeping Seeker tells an old Separatist widow that he alone has truly come out.

verses.text: No one should attack a Brahmana, but no Brahmana (if attacked) should let himself fly at his aggressor! Woe to him who strikes a Brahmana, more woe to him who flies at his aggressor!
It advantages a Brahmana not a little if he holds his mind back from the pleasures of life; when all wish to injure has vanished, pain will cease.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, people at Sāvatthī praised the elder Sāriputta, the Buddha’s chief disciple, for a patience nothing could break. A brahmin of wrong views set out to provoke him and struck him hard on the back as he went for alms. Sāriputta did not even turn around. The brahmin, stricken with remorse, fell at his feet, begged pardon and invited him to take his meals at his house, and Sāriputta accepted and handed him his bowl. A crowd gathered at the door with sticks and stones to kill the brahmin, and Sāriputta asked them whether the man had struck them or him, and sent them away. The monks grumbled that he went on eating with a man who struck people. The Buddha said that one who has destroyed anger does not strike back, and spoke the verses.
bg.history:
By the 1880s the Chicago and North Western carried commuters from a string of villages along the lake into its Wells Street station, rebuilt in 1881. On May 4, 1886, a bomb thrown at police breaking up a labor rally in the Haymarket killed seven officers and led to the trial of eight anarchists; seven were sentenced to death, and four were hanged on November 11, 1887. The same decade was the height of Robert Ingersoll’s fame as “the Great Agnostic,” a lecturer who had practiced law in Peoria.

Mr. Pryor’s nonresistance goes back to the New England Non-Resistance Society, formed at a peace convention in Boston in September 1838 that admitted women as equals; its Declaration of Sentiments was written by William Lloyd Garrison. Adin Ballou, a member, founded the Hopedale Community near Milford, Massachusetts, in 1842, a “Practical Christian” commune that failed after fourteen years and became the Draper brothers’ loom-parts town. Ballou’s Christian Non-Resistance (1846) was later admired by Tolstoy. The Declaration is quoted here from the text printed in William Lloyd Garrison: The Story of His Life Told by His Children, volume 2 (1885).

sections.heading: I. The Wager
sections.text: There were eleven of us that year who rode in to the city every morning in the smoking car of the 7:52, and if you had asked any of us what we thought about we would have said the price of coal, or the Board of Trade, or our wives, or the anarchists. That was the year of the anarchists. Since May every paper in Chicago had been full of the bomb in the Haymarket and the seven policemen, and in August the jury gave seven of the eight men the rope, and the whole North Shore said it was about time. Gates, who sold coal and feed by the depot, said he would pull the trap himself and not charge the county. We laughed at that. We were not cruel men. We were the kind of men who live eighteen miles out on the North Western so that our children will have elms. We talked about Elias Dunning too, the way you talk about the weather in another town. Dunning kept books for a wholesale grocer on Lake Street and rode the coach behind us, because he did not smoke, and in nine years not one of us had ever seen him put out. You could step on his foot in the aisle. You could spill your coffee down him at the Wells Street lunch counter. Young Hollis from the Board of Trade had once, for a joke, taken his

sections.heading: II. The Platform
sections.text: It was a fog morning off the lake, the kind where the engine comes up the track as a sound before it is a thing. We were standing in a bunch at the smoking-car end of the platform with our papers. Dunning was down by the coach steps with his umbrella and his dinner in a newspaper, reading the timetable on the board, which he must have known by heart. Thayer walked down the platform past us. He was not laughing. He came up behind Dunning in the fog and hit him between the shoulders with his fist, as hard as a big man can hit, so that it sounded on the boards, so that Dunning’s hat went off and his whole body went forward a step. Some of us shouted. Most of us didn’t do anything. Dunning did not turn around. He stood a moment where the blow had put him. Then he bent and picked up his hat, and set it on, and when the train came in out of the fog he climbed into the coach with his umbrella and his dinner, and sat down by a window on the far side, and we could see his hat through the glass, and it did not move, and it did not look back. Thayer stood on the platform with his hand still closed. The conductor called. He got on with us. He did not say a word to Rogers Park. He did not light

sections.heading: III. The Gate
sections.text: Ober’s wife was one of the people who sat in Mr. Pryor’s parlor on Sundays, so we knew the hour. Dunning went in at Thayer’s gate at a quarter to one. By two there were nine of us outside it. Nobody had said, Let’s. We would like that to be understood. Gates came by Ober’s house after church and said he thought he would walk down Ridge Avenue, and Ober got his hat. The village had been laying the new brick walk on the east side of Ridge since August, and there was a pile of paving brick at the corner where the workmen had left off, and a heap of broken ones beside it, and when we came to the gate most of us had a brickbat in our coat pocket or our hand, and I could not tell you which of us picked up the first one. Gates had his buggy whip. Young Hollis had a piece of lath. We were church members, all but two. We stood in the street in our Sunday coats in the thin October sun, and the leaves came down off Thayer’s elms, and we could smell the dinner through his windows, roast chicken and something with cloves, and we waited for the coward to come out of his door. He came out at half past two. Dunning was ahead of him on the walk. Thayer was carrying Dunning’s umbrella for him, the w

sections.heading: IV. The Parlor
sections.text: What happened next we have only from Mrs. Ober, and she says she has it right, and we have no reason to think she hasn’t. Mr. Pryor’s people met at four. There were seven that day, in the front parlor full of clocks, the old man’s own and other people’s, ticking on every wall and shelf, none of them together. The old man was seventy-four and had made loom parts in Massachusetts before the war. He sat by the stove with a clock in pieces on a tray on his knees, the way he always did, and he hardly ever spoke. The others read and talked. He fixed the clock. Everybody had heard about the gate by then. Miss Kittredge, who taught the fourth grade, said she had heard, too, that this was the second Sunday Mr. Dunning had eaten at that man’s table, and that he meant to go every week, and she did not think it right. It’s one thing to forgive him, she said. We all forgive him. It’s another thing to sit down to his chicken every Sunday as if nothing had happened. It tells him nothing happened. A man who will hit one person from behind will hit another. Next time it will be somebody who can’t bear it. It will be a woman, or a child. And it will be because Mr. Dunning let him think it was all ri

sections.heading: V. The Doorstop
sections.text: Royal Thayer gave up the smoking car. We missed him. He rode in the coach with Dunning every morning after that, for years, the two of them on the same seat, the big man and the small one, and on wet mornings it was always Thayer who carried the umbrella. He never told us what they talked about. He did not stop reading the Truth Seeker, and Dunning did not stop going to Mr. Pryor’s, and Mrs. Thayer said they argued at her table every Sunday for nine years and never once raised their voices, and that the chicken got cold. The morning they hanged the four men at the county jail, a year and a month after, the smoking car of the 7:52 was quiet. Somebody had the Inter Ocean and read out the times, and nobody said anything about pulling a trap. Gates looked out of the window the whole way to Wells Street. I don’t know what he was thinking. I know what I was. I have the brickbat still. It is half a paving brick, red, with a corner of the mortar left on, and it has held the parlor door open against the lake wind for thirty years. My wife likes it there. Every time I stoop to move it I feel in my hand exactly how heavy it is, which is about as heavy as a man’s fist, and I set it down again

title: Brickbats
logline: In the Haymarket year, the smoking-car regulars of a commuter train watch a freethinking lawyer test a quiet bookkeeper with his fist.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not offend by body, word, or thought, and is controlled on these three points.

bg.commentary: Mahā Pajāpatī Gotamī was the sister of the Buddha’s mother, Māyā, who died seven days after his birth; she nursed him and raised him, and later became the first woman ordained. In the commentary, the Buddha gave her the eight “heavy rules” privately before they were announced, and she accepted them, and that acceptance was her ordination; she had no preceptor or teacher but the Buddha himself. The women of her retinue, whose own ordination had come through her, began to say that she had no preceptor and had put on the yellow robe by herself, and they would no longer keep the observance days with her. The Buddha told them that he was her teacher and preceptor, and that one who does no wrong by body, speech or mind is not to be held in doubt, and spoke the verse. (In the Vinaya’s fuller account she asks three times, cuts her hair and walks barefoot to Vesālī, and says she accepts the eight rules as a young woman accepts a garland and sets it on her head.)
bg.history:
In 1816, the Year Without a Summer, the ash of the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora chilled the Northern Hemisphere. In northern New England hard frosts came through May; on June 6–8 snow fell across the region, with about a foot reported at Danville, in Caledonia County, and sheep and poultry died; frosts in July and late August killed most of the corn. The following winter Vermont families were reported living on such things as nettles, clover tops and hedgehogs (porcupines), and the state lost an estimated ten to fifteen thousand people to emigration westward in 1816 and 1817. Three years earlier, in 1813, the state had suffered a season of overlapping epidemics, pneumonia (“lung fever”), “spotted fever” and typhus among them; the Woodstock physician Joseph Gallup estimated some 6,400 deaths in its five worst months.

Physicians of the period were trained mostly by apprenticeship, “reading physic” for several years with an established doctor, their preceptor, sometimes adding a course of lectures such as those at Dartmouth’s medical school in Hanover. The Vermont Medical Society was chartered in 1813. No American medical school granted a degree to a woman until Elizabeth Blackwell’s in 1849. The Oath is quoted from Francis Adams’s translation in The Genuine Works of Hippocrates (1849); the passage omitted at the ellipsis is the oath’s promise not to cut for the stone.

sections.heading: I. Three Times
sections.dateline: From the daybook of Silas Whitcomb, physician · North Calder, Vermont · May 1816
sections.text: May 12. Hard frost in the night. Corn not in. Rode to Bemis, wife, intermittent fever, bark. To the Gray children at the Hollow, all four with the hooping cough, nothing to be done but sit. .75 May 13. Aunt Lydia came down the hill road on foot this forenoon and sat in my kitchen and asked me to take her to read physic. She is fifty-eight. I said it could not be done, there being no precedent, and that she knew more already than half the doctors in the county, which is true, and does not answer her. She went home. May 18. Freeze again, ice on the trough a finger thick. Sheep pens at Ladd’s. Patience Ladd delivered of a son, Lydia attending, sent for me only to sign the paper. Nothing for me to do there. Lydia asked again on the road home. I said no. I set down here, since a daybook is for what was owed and paid, what is owed. My mother Mercy Farrow died seven days after I was born. Her sister Lydia came over the hill the next morning with her own milk still in her, having lost a boy in March, and put me to the breast, and two years after married my father, and raised me. She taught me my letters from the almanac. She held the basin the first time I bled a man and did not spill it w

sections.heading: II. Snow in June
sections.text: June 6. Rain went to snow by morning. In June. June 7. Snow all day, driving. Near a foot at Danville they say. Ladd’s new-shorn sheep dead in the pasture, eleven of them, and I am told the same at every farm up the valley. The apple trees were in full flower. They stand in the snow white on white and the blossoms are brown by night. Rode to the Bemis place through drifts to the horse’s knees. Sally Bemis there before me. June 8. Snow squalls. At dusk Lydia at my door. She had walked the four miles down from the hill in it in her house shoes, having nothing else that would do, her skirts frozen to the knee and her feet blue. She had brought her own Denman on midwifery and the case-book she has kept since ’13 in a sack on her back. She did not ask again. She sat by my fire with her feet in a pail of water and the book in her lap and waited for me to say it. I said it. God help me, I made conditions first. I wrote them on the back of a bill of Ladd’s and read them to her, and I have pinned the leaf in here, so that it is in the book with the rest of what I owe. I take them. Lydia Whitcomb She heard them out. Then she said, When I was a girl in Rindge, when the apple trees came out in

sections.heading: III. Her Women
sections.text: July 6. Frost. Corn black in the low fields. Hannah Ladd, ague. Paid in rye, which nobody can spare. .50 July 10. Lydia to my house for her reading, Cullen Chap. IV. I asked after the women’s meeting, it being the full of the moon. She said they did not come. July 14. It is said at Bemis’s store, and it came round to me by three roads, that Lydia Whitcomb has no preceptor. That a woman cannot read physic with her own boy that she nursed. That it is a kindness and not a reading, that there was no examination and no paper and no fee, that she put the name on herself as you put on a bonnet. And the women she taught have taken it up, being made, they say, uneasy. If she had no teacher, who taught them? What are they, then? Sally Bemis would not have her at her lying-in on the 12th and sent eleven miles for Dr. Pratt, who came drunk. July 30. Folded in here, a letter left at my door, unsigned, but I know the hand, having seen it on every one of her cases in ’13. Doctor — We mean no disrespect to her or you. We followed her through that winter into every house and would again. But she has learnt us everything we know and now it is said she never learnt it of anybody but put it on herself

sections.heading: IV. The Full of the Moon
sections.text: Sept. 7. I went round to the five of them in the forenoon, house by house, and told each one I would be at Mrs. Whitcomb’s kitchen tonight at moonrise and wished she would come and hear me, and if after that she did not want to sit with her, I would say no more. Patience Ladd shut the door. The others said they would come. Four came, and then, late, Patience, with her shawl over her head as if it were raining. I did not sit down. I said: You say she has no preceptor. She has. I am her preceptor. I examined her, the evening of the eighth of June, in my kitchen, with her feet in a pail, and I examined her every week since, and I would put her up against any student in the Medical Society. She has no paper because there is no paper in this State for a woman. I set her conditions before ever I set them for you, and she took them first, and she keeps them better than I keep mine. If she has no teacher, then I have none, for she taught me to read. Hannah Ladd said, But she is your mother. I said, She is, and I had no other. Then I said: You ask who taught her. Ask instead what she has done. You were in the houses with her the winter of ’13. Did any one of you ever see her do a sick perso

sections.heading: V. In Another Hand
sections.text: The last pages of the book for that year are not in his hand. Feb. 2. S. W. down with the lung fever since the 28th. I keep his book till he is up, condition the sixth. Bled him myself, eight ounces, having nobody to ask leave of but him, and he gave it. Nettle broth. — Feb. 9. S. W. sitting up. Wants his book back. Not yet. Feb. 11. To Victory, Mrs. Hadlock, delivered of a daughter at four in the morning, Hannah Ladd with me and did the most of it. Nothing in their house but potatoes and the clover tops they dried in the fall. Took no fee, cond. the fourth. Mr. Hadlock would not have it so and paid a hedgehog, dressed, which we ate at Hannah’s on the way home, and it was good. Feb. 16. Patience Ladd came and asked would I take her niece to read with me, she being fifteen and willing. Read her the leaf. She took it in both hands. —

title: May Wreath
logline: In the year it snowed in June, a country doctor's daybook records how he took the aunt who raised him as his only pupil.

verses.text: After a man has once understood the law as taught by the Well-awakened (Buddha), let him worship it carefully, as the Brahmana worships the sacrificial fire.

bg.commentary: Sāriputta, the wisest of the Buddha's disciples, first heard the Dhamma from the elder Assaji, a quiet monk whose bearing on his alms round caught his eye. Assaji said he was new and could give only a little, and spoke four lines about causes and their ending; Sāriputta understood at once. From then on, wherever Assaji was staying, Sāriputta bowed in that direction and even lay down to sleep with his head toward it. Other monks decided he had gone back to worshipping the directions and reported him. When the Buddha asked, Sāriputta left the answer to the Buddha's own knowledge, and the Buddha explained that he was honoring the teacher through whom he had learned, as a Brahmin honors the sacred fire.
bg.history:
Takoma Park was laid out in 1883 as a commuter suburb on the B&O's Metropolitan Branch just outside Washington. In 1904 the Seventh-day Adventist Church bought land there along Carroll Avenue and moved its headquarters from Battle Creek, Michigan; the church's publishing house, college and the Washington Sanitarium followed. The sanitarium opened on June 13, 1907, on the bank of Sligo Creek, treating patients with water, air, massage and plain food. It trained nurses from the start, and a nurses' dormitory went up in 1909. Hot fomentations, salt glows and cold mitten frictions were the ordinary tools of Adventist hydrotherapy.

Ellen G. White's The Ministry of Healing (1905) was a "relief book": she gave up her royalties, the publishers printed it at cost, and church members sold it door to door to help pay the debts of the denomination's sanitariums. Canvassers' weekly results, by name, county, book, hours and orders, were printed in union papers such as the Columbia Union Visitor. The book appeared the same year Samuel Hopkins Adams's series "The Great American Fraud" in Collier's exposed patent medicines like Peruna, which was largely alcohol; the Pure Food and Drug Act followed in 1906. On the Eastern Shore, girls and women of Sadie's age spent the summer peeling tomatoes at piece rates in the canning houses, paid in tokens for each bucket.

sections.heading: I. The Lane
sections.text: Sadie Upton was seventeen the summer the canvasser came up the lane, and she had been skinning tomatoes since the first of the month in the top room of the canning house at Hobbs Landing, where the steam from the cookers came up through the floorboards and the girls stood in rubber aprons to the ankle. You filled a bucket and the runner took it, and the bucket came back to you with a tin check stamped with the packer's initials. At night she stood the checks on the kitchen windowsill in rows of ten, and on Saturdays she turned them into money, and most of the money went to Denton for her mother's medicine. Her mother took Peruna for catarrh and Lydia Pinkham's Compound for the rest, and since Sadie's father went over the side of a bugeye in the Choptank two winters back, she took a good deal of both. She slept afternoons on the lounge with her mouth open. She was yellow under the eyes and short with the little ones, and sweet as anything for an hour after supper, and then she slept again. The doctor from Denton came twice and left calomel and a bill. The cannery ran out of tomatoes early one evening, and Sadie was sitting on the back step with her feet in a pan of water when a man

sections.heading: II. The Reports
sections.dateline: The nurses' home, Takoma Park · autumn 1909
sections.text: The Columbia Union Visitor came to the reading room of the new nurses' home on Thursdays, eight pages, and Sadie read it from the back. On page seven, under the conference reports and above the notices for the camp meetings, were the Canvassers' Reports, set in small type in columns: the name of the canvasser, the county, the book, the days and hours, the orders taken, the value. She ran her finger down Chesapeake. Chesapeake, Week Ending October 1, 1909 J. W. Ashby, Talbot Co., Md.   MH   5   41   9   $13 50 East by south. Her father's compass was a brass box the size of a biscuit with a card in it marked in thirty-two points, and the glass had a crack across Nor'west that she had stopped seeing. On the inside of her trunk lid she had pinned a railroad map of Maryland and Delaware, and with a thread and a pin stuck through Takoma Park she could lay off the line to any county in the Chesapeake Conference. She set the compass on the floorboards, let the card settle, turned herself until she faced the point, and knelt. She did not pray to him. She was particular about that. She prayed for him, for his feet and his chest and the dogs at the gates, and then she gave thanks for the man,

sections.heading: III. A Letter
sections.dateline: Slipped under the office door · January 1910
sections.text: Dear Dr. Mortensen, We write this with great reluctance and only after prayer. We do not wish to make trouble for a sister. But we believe it is our duty, as it is written that we are our brother's keeper, and we have read what Sister White has written about the deceptions of the last days and the working of spirits, and we are afraid. Every Thursday Miss Upton consults a brass compass. She has a map in her trunk with a pin in it. She kneels to a different quarter of the heavens each week, sometimes east, sometimes south, once to the northeast. She turns her bed around to lie toward the same quarter. Before Christmas there was a week when she knelt to all the quarters one after another, turning on her knees in the dark, and did not speak when Miss Kinney asked her what she was doing. Miss Dorsett, whose brother is at the Foreign Mission Seminary, says the Mohammedans in Egypt bow toward Mecca five times a day. But their Mecca does not move. She is the best nurse among us and we love her. That is why we have written. Respectfully,Ethel KinneyMabel DorsettLottie Snyder

sections.heading: IV. The Oath
sections.dateline: The superintendent's office · the same week
sections.text: Dr. Hanne Mortensen was sixty-one. She had been born on a farm near Aalborg and brought to Wisconsin at six, and had gone to Ann Arbor for medicine when there were few enough women in the lecture room that the men counted them, and from there to Battle Creek, and from Battle Creek to Calcutta for seven years, and from Calcutta to this office with a window over the creek. She had a way of looking at a girl that the girls said was like being auscultated. She sent for all four of them after morning worship. The three who had signed stood by the bookcase. Sadie stood by the window with her hands folded on her apron bib. Miss Upton. These young women tell me you kneel to the points of the compass. Sadie looked at her a while. Doctor, she said, you know what I kneel to. Dr. Mortensen did not answer her. She held out her hand to Mabel Dorsett. Thursday's Visitor, please. Page seven. Read me the Chesapeake. Mabel read the names in the order they came. Bowen, Queen Anne's County. Lankford, Somerset. Then she stopped, and read the next one slower. J. W. Ashby. Frederick County. Which way is Frederick County, Miss Upton? Northwest by north, Doctor. I read the applications, Dr. Mortensen said

sections.heading: V. The Chart
sections.text: He came in on the afternoon train from Frederick with a canvasser's cough that had gone down into his chest a week before and stayed there. Somebody at the Frederick church had put him on the car. He walked from the Takoma station up the hill with his satchel, at the same pace, and fainted on the sanitarium steps. Ashby, J. W.   age 53   colporteur   adm. 4:40 p.m. Lobar pneumonia, right lower lobe. T. 104.2. P. 120. R. 36. Rusty sputum. Orders: hot fomentations to chest q. 2 hrs, 3 changes each, followed by cold mitten friction. Water freely. Night special: Miss Upton. He did not know her. She had been a girl on a step with her feet in a pan of water, and now she was a nurse in a cap with her sleeves rolled, and he was a man with a fever of a hundred and four who thought for an hour around midnight that he was back in Calvert County and the dog had his satchel. She did not tell him. She brought the fomentations down the hall folded against her own body, three changes, and laid them on his chest so hot that he said Oh, and then nothing, and she rubbed his arms with the cold mitten until the skin came up pink, and she counted his breaths with her watch. 11:00   Fom. to chest x 3. C.

title: The Compass Card
logline: A student nurse at an Adventist sanitarium kneels each week toward a different county, and her roommates fear she has taken up with spirits.

verses.text: A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana.

bg.commentary: A Brahmin with matted hair, born of a Brahmin family, noticed that the Buddha called his own monks "Brahmins," and came to ask that the Buddha call him one too, since he was one by birth. The Buddha answered that he did not call anyone a Brahmin for his matted hair, his clan or his birth, but only for the truth and the Dhamma in him, and spoke the verse. Many who heard it reached the first stage of awakening. The whole story is only a few lines long.
bg.history:
Parma, south of Cleveland, boomed after the Second World War into one of the largest suburbs in Ohio, home to General Motors and to large Ukrainian, Slovak, Polish and Hungarian Catholic communities; Cleveland television hosts made a running joke of its white socks and pink flamingos. In January 1977 the ABC miniseries Roots ran eight nights in a row and set off a wave of family-history research across the country. Scottish heritage societies, clan associations and amateur pipe bands grew with it. A Burns supper on or near January 25, Robert Burns's birthday, follows an old order: piping in, the Selkirk Grace, the haggis piped in and addressed, the Immortal Memory, the toasts. Since 1971 American haggis has been made without sheep's lung, which U.S. food rules forbid.

The Great Blizzard of 1978 struck the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes from January 25 to 27. Rain turned to heavy snow before dawn on the 26th, with winds strong enough to bring zero visibility all day. It was the worst blizzard in Ohio history: 51 people died, more than 5,000 National Guard troops were called out, and the whole Ohio Turnpike closed for the first time. The MacCrimmons were pipers for generations to the chiefs of Clan MacLeod, based at Borreraig near Dunvegan on Skye, where they kept a piping college. “MacCrimmon Will Never Return” is one of the best-known laments for the pipes.

sections.heading: I. Piping In
sections.text: There were fourteen of us that winter, if you count Murdo, and you had to count Murdo. Six pipers, four snares, two tenors, Danny Kovac on the bass, and Pipe Major Murdo MacAskill, who was seventy-one and had been born in a black house in Glendale on the Isle of Skye and had come to Cleveland by way of the Clydebank yards in 1949 and been a millwright at the GM plant on Chevrolet Boulevard until they gave him his pin. We practiced Tuesday nights in the basement of the Methodist church on Pearl Road with the Sunday-school chairs stacked against the wall. Most of us had never been to Scotland. Danny was Slovak. Lesia Hnatiuk was sixteen and Ukrainian Catholic, and practiced in her father's garage on Snow Road with the door up in all weathers because her mother would not have it in the house. The Szabo twins were Hungarian. Two of the snares were Methodists from Brook Park whose grandfather might have been Scotch, they said, or Welsh. We had learned the pipes from Murdo the way you learn anything from a man who does not talk much, by doing it wrong in front of him until he stopped wincing. Murdo called three people in his life a piper. One was a man named Angus Lamont who had taught h

sections.heading: II. Piping In of the Haggis
sections.text: The haggis came from a butcher on Lorain Avenue who made it for the Scottish societies every January, and it was American, which meant there were no lungs in it. You couldn't have sheep lung in food in this country since 1971. Murdo said every year that an American haggis was a haggis in the way a wax apple was an apple, and every year he addressed it anyway. Danny carried it in on a silver tray behind Lesia, who piped it in, and Murdo stood up at the head table with a knife from the Sokol kitchen and gave it the whole address in a voice we had never heard him use, the voice, Bev said afterward, of a man in a pulpit in Skye. When he came to the cutting he cut, and it steamed, and everybody clapped. Then he sat down and ate a little of it, and said it was very good, and it was not. Outside the rain had stopped sounding like rain.

sections.heading: III. The Immortal Memory
sections.text: Don gave the Immortal Memory. He had asked for it in November, and Murdo had said Fine, and Don had been working on it since Thanksgiving in his den on a yellow legal pad. It ran thirty-five minutes. It was about Burns, some of it. Mostly it was about Skye, which Don had never seen, and the MacCrimmons at Borreraig, and the clans, and the blood. Blood, he said, remembers. Some of us in this hall are here because we like the music. Some of us are here because we can't help it. Because the music's in us from three hundred years back. He looked at the head table when he said it. He finished with a verse from “Scots, Wha Hae,” and the Lakewood people stood up and cheered, and Danny's mother, who was from Bratislava, clapped politely, and Lesia looked at her plate. Murdo stood and raised his glass to the Immortal Memory with the rest of us. He did not say anything about the speech. He looked, we thought, tired. At a quarter to eleven somebody opened the side door to go out for a smoke and the door was pulled out of his hand.

sections.heading: IV. The Storm
sections.text: It came up out of the south and west, and by one o'clock the wind was over fifty, and some time before three the rain turned to snow, and the snow did not fall so much as go by. The windows of the Sokol hall went white and stayed white. You could not see the cars in the lot. You could not see the lot. The radio in the kitchen said to stay off the roads, and then that the Turnpike was closed, and then that the National Guard was being called out, and then the power went off for a long minute and came back with the lights a little browner than before. Eighty people at a Burns supper looked at each other in their kilts and good dresses and understood they would be sleeping on a gymnasium floor. We pushed the tables to the walls. The Sokol ladies made coffee in the big urns. Somebody found the gym mats and somebody found the flags from the Slovak national days and people slept under the flags. Murdo sat on a folding chair by the coffee with his pipes across his knees and his eyes shut. He was not asleep. Murdo never slept that we knew of. It was close to four o'clock when Don came and stood in front of him. He had been drinking a little, the toasts and then the bottle the Lakewood men

sections.heading: V. Toast to the Lassies
sections.text: At six the furnace quit. The Sokol custodian went down to the boiler room and came back up and said it was the flue, the snow had drifted over the vent on the lot side of the building and it was backing up and he had shut it off before it put us all to sleep for good. Nobody could open the lot-side door. The wind had packed it shut. It was Don who knew where the vent was. He had sold a softener to the Sokol in 1974 and been in that boiler room, and he knew how the pipe ran out through the block wall and where it came up on the outside, behind the dumpster, eighteen inches off the ground, under, by then, about six feet of snow. He went out the front door, which faced away from the wind, with a coal shovel from the boiler room and the custodian's flashlight, and went around the building on his hands and knees in the kilt. He was gone forty minutes. Bev stood at the front door with it open a crack the whole time. When he came back his beard was a solid block of ice and his knees were red and raw and he could not open his hands. But the custodian went down and lit the boiler and in a quarter of an hour the radiators began to knock. We sat Don down by the urn and Bev and Danny's mother

title: For A' That
logline: Snowed into a suburban Burns supper, a water-softener salesman with a new clan pedigree asks the old pipe major why he is not called a piper.

verses.text: What is the use of platted hair, O fool! what of the raiment of goat-skins? Within thee there is ravening, but the outside thou makest clean.

bg.commentary: A fraudulent Brahmin took a "bat vow" and hung upside down from a tree by the gate of Vesālī, demanding a hundred coins, a servant girl and other gifts, and threatening that if he fell the city would be destroyed. Afraid for their city, the people gave him everything. When monks later saw him strolling about and he told them he had got what he wanted, the Buddha said he had been a fraud in an earlier life too: an ascetic with matted hair and a deerskin who, after tasting monitor-lizard meat, tried to club the old lizard that came each evening from an ant-hill to sit near him. The wise lizard saw through the pretended sleep, escaped into the ant-hill, refused his offers of rice, salt, oil and pepper, and rebuked him with the verse. The ascetic was the same man; the lizard was the Buddha. Read the full commentary story. The lizard (godhā) is the Bengal monitor, which shelters in burrows and old termite mounds and is still eaten in parts of South Asia.
bg.history:
Ocean Grove was founded in 1869 by Methodist clergymen as a seaside camp-meeting ground. Families rented tents for the season, its Great Auditorium was finished in 1894, and until 1981 its laws barred horses, wagons and later cars from its streets on Sundays, with chains across the entrances. Its northern neighbor across Wesley Lake, Asbury Park, was laid out in 1871 by the brush manufacturer James A. Bradley as a dry Methodist resort and grew a boardwalk, pavilions and hotels. The Agassiz Association, founded in 1875, enrolled thousands of young naturalists in local chapters and for years used St. Nicholas magazine as its organ.

From the 1880s on, Muslim peddlers from villages in the Hooghly district of Bengal sold embroidered cotton (chikan) and other "Oriental" goods on the boardwalks of Atlantic City and Asbury Park, and spread through a network reaching New Orleans, Charleston and Chattanooga, a history recovered in Vivek Bald's Bengali Harlem. The fine shadow work of chikankari is stitched on the reverse of sheer cloth and seen through it from the front. Rabindranath Tagore's translation of Songs of Kabir, made with Evelyn Underhill, was published in New York by Macmillan in 1915; the Immigration Act of 1917, passed that February over President Wilson's veto, created the "Asiatic Barred Zone."

sections.heading: I. No. 41
sections.text: Minnie Lathrop was thirteen that summer and a corresponding member of the St. Nicholas Agassiz Association, Chapter 512, Newark, and she kept a Record. The Association asked its members to observe closely, to describe exactly, to set down only what they had seen with their own eyes, and to mark plainly whatever they had only been told. She had a green cloth notebook from the stationer's on Broad Street, and a pencil on a string, and by the middle of July she had forty species of the Grove in it, from the fiddler crabs on the Wesley Lake mud to the black skimmers that came over the surf at dusk dragging their lower bills along the water as if they were ruling lines. Her family had a tent on Pilgrim Pathway for the season, as they had every summer since she could remember, a striped canvas front with a wooden cottage built on behind it for the kitchen. Her father came down from his drugstore on Friday nights on the train. Her mother went to the Great Auditorium twice a day, and to the Young People's Meeting, and to the Holiness Meeting, and on Sundays the gates of the Grove were chained at both ends and no wheel turned on any street, and the only sound from morning service to supper

sections.heading: II. The Subscription
sections.dateline: Pinned to the willow · the third week of July
sections.text:
The vow, it turned out, could be satisfied. The manager had it written out. One hundred dollars in silver. A suit of clothes. A railroad ticket to Philadelphia. And a girl to sit by the Yogi with a fan through the heat of the day and bring him his rice, because a holy man under a vow could not lift his own hand to his mouth. Several of the Asbury Park hotel men, who did not want a dead Hindoo hanging in a tree across from their verandas in the height of the season, got up a paper. Minnie copied it into the Record, all of it, because the Association said to set down everything exactly. Copy of the subscription, as pinned. sections.heading: III. Mr. Gani
sections.text: Mr. Gani sold handkerchiefs. He walked the Asbury Park boardwalk end to end all day with a bundle in a white cloth on his shoulder, and when a lady stopped him he set the bundle down on the rail and undid the knot, and there were handkerchiefs and table runners and children's collars and a few long scarves, all of white cotton so fine you could read through it, all worked in white thread. He wore a little white cap and a long coat and spoke English slowly and well. He was from a district called Hooghly, on a river in Bengal, he said, and there were other men from his villages who sold the same work in Atlantic City and New Orleans and Charleston. His name was Abdul Gani Mondal. The ladies of the Grove called him the Hindoo, and he did not correct them, though Minnie found out from him later that he was a Mussulman and had been to the mosque in Calcutta, and that the Yogi's card was spelled wrong. Minnie had bought a handkerchief from him in June with her birthday quarter, and after that she stopped by him every afternoon she was let over the footbridge, because he knew the names of things. He knew the black skimmers. He had seen birds like them on the river at home. He knew what a

sections.heading: IV. No. 42
sections.dateline: Cookman Avenue · the second week of August
sections.text: No. 42. The same.
