Observed through the front window of a chop house on Cookman Avenue, about half past one, while waiting for Rafiq, who had gone in the side door to sell a table runner to the proprietor's wife. Hair cut short. Gray suit. Derby hat on the chair beside him. Right way up. Eating fried clams, a beefsteak, and a dish of stewed tomatoes. Two bottles of sarsaparilla. Has gained flesh. Identified by the ears (pierced) and a white mark of paint not quite washed out of the left eyebrow. Rafiq agrees. When Rafiq came out, the man in the gray suit came out behind him, picking his teeth, and saw Minnie on the curb with her notebook, and must have known her, because she had stood under the willow every day for three weeks. He looked at her a long moment. Then he winked, and tipped the derby, and said in a voice from somewhere around Paterson: Got everything I came for, sis. He walked off toward the depot swinging his arms. Minnie found that she was shaking, and could not have said if it was anger or something else. Rafiq spat in the gutter, very neatly, and then looked around to be sure his uncle had not seen.

sections.heading: V. No. 43
sections.text: They told Mr. Gani, both of them at once. He went on folding a table runner while they talked, in thirds and then in half, the way he always did, so the work was inside. He was like this before, too, he said when they were done. That kind does not change his ways from one life to another. In my district there was a fakir just the same. Maybe this one. Who knows. He set the runner on the pile. You want the story? Write it down, then. Write that you did not see it. Minnie opened the Record. Near a village outside Chinsurah, Mr. Gani said, there lived a fakir in a little hut at the edge of the rice, with long matted hair and a goatskin, and a family in the village fed him every day because he was holy. Behind his hut was an old white-ant hill, taller than a man, and in the ant-hill lived a gosaap, which is a great lizard as long as Rafiq, brown and slow, with a forked tongue and a tail like a whip. It was very old. In the evenings it came out of its hole and sat in the dust near the fakir's door, the way the old men of the village sat near a holy man in the evenings, because it believed he was one. Now some of the people of that district eat gosaap, said Mr. Gani, though his own peopl

sections.heading: VI. The New Books
sections.dateline: The public library, Asbury Park · November 1916
sections.text: Twenty years later Miss Minnie Lathrop, assistant librarian, unpacked a shipment of new books from Macmillan at the back table and wrote the accession numbers inside the covers. One was a thin blue book, Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, who had won the Nobel Prize three years before and whose picture had been in all the papers. She had the pen in her hand to number it. Instead she sat down on the high stool and read it through, while the radiator ticked and the November light went off the windows, and under the numeral LXVII she found it. I do not know what manner of God is mine. The Mullah cries aloud to Him: and why? Is your Lord deaf? The subtle anklets that ring on the feet of an insect when it moves are heard of Him. Tell your beads, paint your forehead with the mark of your God, and wear matted locks long and showy: but a deadly weapon is in your heart, and how shall you have God? — Songs of Kabir LXVII, tr. Rabindranath Tagore (1915) She did not know where Mr. Gani was. He had come back to the boardwalk two more summers and then not again. Rafiq had written her a postal card from New Orleans in 1903, in a good round hand, about a bird he had seen there. In

title: Shadow Work
place: Ocean Grove and Asbury Park, New Jersey
logline: A girl naturalist records a 'Hindoo fakir' hanging upside down at the Methodist camp-meeting gate, and a Bengali handkerchief peddler tells her about the lizard.

verses.text: The man who wears dirty raiments, who is emaciated and covered with veins, who lives alone in the forest, and meditates, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

bg.commentary: One night Sakka, king of the gods, comes with his retinue to sit before the Buddha on Vulture’s Peak and listen. The nun Kisā Gotamī, “Gotamī the thin,” the same woman who once carried her dead son from house to house in search of medicine, comes through the air to pay her respects, sees the king of the gods, and turns back. Sakka asks who she is. The Buddha answers that she is his daughter, foremost among the nuns who wear robes sewn from cast-off rags, and speaks the verse.
bg.history:
Providence was founded in 1636 by Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts Bay, and it filled up with other people the Bay had pushed out, among them supporters of the minister John Wheelwright in the Antinomian Controversy, whose petitioners were disarmed by order of the General Court in November 1637. Williams himself left the Baptist church he had helped to found and became a Seeker, one of those who held no church to be rightly gathered and met in silence to wait. Because the town kept no established church, it kept no churchyard either, and for its first sixty years families buried their dead in their own plots; the town did not vote to lay out the North Burial Ground until 1700. Some of the settlers at Pawtuxet, a few miles south, quarreled with their Providence neighbors over land and in 1642 put themselves under the government of Massachusetts, which kept its claim there for sixteen years (William Arnold).

Williams wrote A Key into the Language of America on his first voyage to England, to secure a charter for the colony, and his friend Gregory Dexter printed it in London in 1643. It is a phrasebook of the Narragansett language, with Williams’s observations of Narragansett life and a short poem at the end of each chapter that usually turns the comparison back against the English. In May 1647 the four towns met at Portsmouth under that charter and adopted a code of laws that listed witchcraft among its capital crimes; the same month, on May 26, Alse Young of Windsor was hanged at Hartford, the first recorded execution for witchcraft in the English colonies.

sections.heading: I. Informations
sections.dateline: Pawtuxet, under the government of the Massachusetts · 20 September 1647
sections.text: Informations taken before me, Nathaniel Harrowe, a magistrate of the Bay, at a house at Pawtuxet, concerning a woman of the plantation of Providence, Thomasine Ashby, widow, called the Lath, who is reported to go through the air. Ephraim Tull, aged fourteen or thereabout, saith: That on a night in August last he was at the falls of the Moshassuck with a lantern to take eels, and saw a woman come down the river in the air, at the height of the tallest pine, not swimming nor walking, but going as a heron goes, with her arms at her sides. That she had on a coat of many pieces and a man’s hat tied under her chin with a list of cloth. That she came down on the flat rock below the falls and sat. That he knew her for the Lath, who has a hut in the woods above the falls. That he was afraid and put out his lantern, and could not get home past her, and so sat in the dark until it was light, and she sat also, and did nothing in all that while, not so much as turn her head. That in the morning she said, Good morrow, Ephraim, the eels are under the bank, and went up into the woods on her feet. That the eels were under the bank. Joan Pratley, wife of Robert Pratley, aged about forty, saith: That

sections.heading: II. To Hannah
sections.text: My dear Hannah, I am well and the Pawtuxet business is near done. Arnold and his neighbors have had their say about the meadows and the Providence men have had theirs, and I have written it all down for the Court, which is what I was sent to do and the least of what has happened to me here, and that is why I am writing to you tonight and not tomorrow. On Monday the Pawtuxet men brought me three persons to swear to a woman of Providence who goes in the air. I enclose what they swore, in my own hand. You will see I did not sign it. You will have heard by now about the woman hanged at Hartford in May, and you know the Providence men put witchcraft among the felonies in their own new code at Portsmouth the same month, so there is no place left in this country for such a woman to go. The Pawtuxet men knew all that. They are no friends to Providence and they wanted me to carry her back to Boston on a horse, and I could have done it. A magistrate of the Bay is a great man at Pawtuxet, Hannah. I had not known how great until I saw how they looked at my cloak. Last night I went up to Providence to see the old man the witnesses named. It is five miles by the path. I took Tull the boy’s fathe

sections.heading: III. Endorsed
sections.dateline: On the back of the informations, in another hand
sections.text: Rec’d of my husband, the 27th of September. Not proceeded upon. Kept. H. H. The paper stayed in a Dorchester chest for a long time, folded in four, under a child’s linen cap with the strings cut off. Hannah Harrowe went out to meeting on the first Sabbath in October, and the women made room on the bench, and nobody said anything about it, and that was right. Of the four men of the trained band, one of them, a Watertown man named Tobias Kember, sold his lot within the year and went to Providence and was a Seeker there the rest of his life, and never would say why, except that he had stood in the dark one night holding a lantern and found he did not need it. In April, when the alewives came up the Moshassuck so thick that a boy could take them in his hands, Ephraim Tull went to the falls in the gray of the morning and found the Lath sitting on the flat rock below them, in a black broadcloth cloak gone green along the shoulders, with the silver clasp cut off and a patch of sacking let into the back where she had given the good cloth away to somebody. The fish went up past her in the white water, all silver, all one way. She did not look at them, and she did not look at him, and the he

title: Cast Clouts
logline: A Massachusetts magistrate sent to take depositions against a widow who flies writes home to his grieving wife instead.

verses.text: I do not call a man a Brahmana because of his origin or of his mother. He is indeed arrogant, and he is wealthy: but the poor, who is free from all attachments, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a brahmin notices that the Buddha calls his own disciples “brahmins.” He reasons that since he was born of a brahmin mother, the Buddha ought to call him one too, and goes to ask. The Buddha answers that he does not call a man a brahmin because of the womb he was born from; a man who clings to possessions is only a bhovādī, one who goes about saying “sir,” and only the one who has nothing and grasps at nothing does he call a brahmin. At the end of the teaching, the brahmin enters the stream. Here the title becomes hombre sincero, from the first line of Martí’s Versos sencillos, and the “sir” becomes señor. Read the full commentary story. The poet is José Martí (1853–1895), whose lines from Versos sencillos (1891) became the words of “Guantanamera”; his essay “Mi raza” appeared in New York in 1893. The verses are quoted here in the original Spanish, which is in the public domain; the English in the story paraphrases them.
bg.history:
In April 1980, after some ten thousand Cubans crowded into the Peruvian embassy in Havana seeking asylum, Fidel Castro opened the port of Mariel to anyone who wanted to leave. Between April 15 and October 31, the Mariel boatlift brought about 125,000 Cubans to Florida, along with some 25,000 Haitians. Exiles hired whatever boats they could, and the Coast Guard reported that Cuban officials forced overloaded boats to take on passengers, sometimes at gunpoint, while boaters waiting in Mariel paid five dollars for a ham sandwich. Many of the newcomers were younger, more working-class and darker-skinned than the exiles of the early 1960s, and some had come from prisons and mental hospitals. They were held at the Orange Bowl and in a tent city under I-95 at the foot of Little Havana, and the hardest to sponsor were sent to Fort Chaffee in Arkansas. Many of the earlier exiles belonged to families of the old Havana clubs, and in 1967 they founded the Big Five Club in Miami. In Cuba, children left at the Casa Cuna, the Havana foundling home, were given the surname Valdés, after Bishop Gerónimo Valdés, one of its early patrons.

Cándido’s trade was that of the lector, hired by cigar workers in Cuba from 1865 on to read newspapers and novels aloud while they rolled; the Montecristo brand took its name from the novel the rollers loved. Octavio fought at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961; the captured men of Brigade 2506 were released in December 1962 in exchange for some $53 million in food and medicine. On Calle Ocho, Máximo Gómez Park, known as Domino Park, has drawn Cuban men to its tables since the early 1970s.

sections.heading: I. The Palms
sections.text: On the wall of Octavio Iturralde’s office on the ninth floor of a bank on Brickell Avenue there was one photograph, and everybody who came into the office was told about it whether they asked or not. It showed a road of red earth running straight away from the camera for a kilometer between two rows of royal palms, a hundred and twenty palms on each side, white-trunked and smooth and as tall as a six-story building, and at the far end of the road, small and white, a house with a portico. That was the Central Santa Rosalía, in the province of Matanzas. His great-great-grandfather had planted the palms. There had been Iturraldes in Matanzas since before the English took Havana. The house was a school now, he had heard. The palms were still standing. Nobody had told him so but he knew it, because a royal palm does not fall down for a revolution. He was fifty-seven. He had left in 1960 with one suitcase, like everybody, and come back in April of 1961 with a rifle on the beach at Girón, like the best of them, and spent twenty months in Castro’s prisons, and come home to Miami on Christmas Eve of 1962, when the Brigade was ransomed for fifty-three million dollars in food and medicine. He

sections.heading: II. Mariel
sections.dateline: Mariel Harbor and the Florida Straits · May 1980
sections.text: In the first week of April a bus crashed through the gate of the Peruvian embassy in Havana, and Castro took away the guards, and in two days ten thousand people were packed onto the embassy grounds, in the trees, on the roof, on the walls, and the government called them trash. Then on the twentieth of April Castro said that anyone in Miami who wanted their relatives could come and get them at the port of Mariel. Miami went to sea. Men who had never been on a boat hired anything that floated, shrimpers and party boats and cabin cruisers and lobster boats from the Keys, and the captains charged a thousand dollars a head and more, and the boats went south across the Straits by the hundreds, and the first of them came back into Key West on the twenty-first with forty-eight people aboard. Octavio had a cousin in Havana, Lourdes, his mother’s sister’s daughter, and her husband and two boys. He hired a shrimp boat out of Stock Island with a captain named Earl who spoke no Spanish, and in the second week of May he went himself. They sat in Mariel harbor for nine days. There were a thousand boats at anchor, and the Cuban officials came out in launches and took the lists of names and went a

sections.heading: III. The Lector
sections.text: The old man’s name was Cándido Valdés. Octavio found that out in July, in the park, when he looked up from his tiles on a Saturday morning and saw him on the bench under the trees with the Diario Las Américas open across his knees, reading it out loud. He was reading the whole thing. The front page, the editorials, the box scores, the deaths. He read it the way he had read Monte Cristo on the boat, standing up inside his voice, every word given its weight, and the men at the tables nearest him had stopped playing to listen, and then the next tables had, and when he came to the end of an article somebody would say otra, another, and he would turn the page. It came out over the summer, the way things come out in a park. He was seventy-three. He had been a lector for forty-one years at a cigar factory in Havana, which was a job that only existed in Cuba and in Tampa: you sat on a platform at the front of the big rolling room, above three hundred men and women at their benches, and read aloud to them all day while they rolled, newspapers in the morning and novels in the afternoon, and they paid you themselves out of their wages, so you read what they voted for. Mostly they voted for Du

sections.heading: IV. The Question
sections.dateline: The third table · a Saturday in September
sections.text: It went on bothering Octavio all summer, and he could not have said why, and it bothered him more that he could not say why. He had pulled the man out of the sea. He had given him twenty dollars. His family had planted the palms in the song. If anybody under those trees was a sincere man from where the palm grows, it was an Iturralde of Matanzas. The old man knew the song as well as he did. He had heard him sing it. On a Saturday in September, when the heat had begun to go out of the mornings, Octavio finished his game and stood up and went over to the bench where Cándido Valdés sat with the paper folded on his knee and the coffee boy’s tray beside him, and sat down at the other end of it. Maestro. He used the word the rollers would have used. Can I ask you something? Ask. You call that boy hombre sincero. You call the Haitian with the cart hombre sincero. You call Tito hombre sincero, and Tito sleeps in the alley. And you call me señor. He heard his own voice and did not like how it sounded and went on anyway. My family has been in Cuba since before the English took Havana. My great-great-grandfather planted the palms in that song. I was born under them. I went back with a rifle.

sections.heading: V. The Poor of the Earth
sections.text: That’s the race, Cándido said. The only one. The generous and the disinterested. It isn’t born. Nobody is born into it. The boy with the coffee came over with nothing and sends his tips to his mother and keeps nothing. The Haitian gives me his mangoes. Tito has nothing left in this world to hold on to but his hands, and he gave me those, the day I came, to carry my suitcase. And me? You, the old man said, not unkindly, are holding on to a road with two hundred and forty palm trees on it, ninety miles away, that you will never walk on again. And a club for dancing. And a bank. And that word. With all that in your hands, what am I going to call you? You’re a señor. It’s not an insult. Señor is a fine word. It’s what you call a man by what he has. Octavio said nothing. You sing it every April, Cándido said. Hombre sincero, de donde crece la palma. Everybody stops there. Nobody reads the rest of the book. The man who wrote that song had nothing. Not a peso. He lived in a rented room in New York and wrote for the newspapers and gave everything he had to the war and went home to fight it and was shot off his horse five weeks after he landed. That’s who said hombre sincero. Listen to what

sections.heading: VI. The Soup
sections.text: Cándido Valdés read the newspaper under the trees on Calle Ocho for six more years, until his eyes went, and then for two more after that from memory, Martí and Dumas and the Gospel of Saint Luke, which he said was the best-written thing in Spanish, though it was not Spanish. When he died, in 1988, the men at the tables took up a collection and buried him at Woodlawn, on Eighth Street, up the road from the park, and the stone they bought says CÁNDIDO VALDÉS, LECTOR, and nothing else, because nobody knew the year he was born. But that was later. On a Saturday morning in the spring of 1981, a year after Mariel, Octavio came to the park with his newspaper under his arm and sat down at the third table, and the four of them turned the fifty-five tiles face down on the concrete and mixed them, which the Cubans call making the soup, all eight hands at once going round and round, the bone tiles clicking against each other with their black backs up, every one of them the same as every other from the back, so that you could not tell, until you drew it and turned it over in your hand, whether you were holding the double nine or the blank. Octavio drew his ten without looking at them and stood

title: Hombre Sincero
logline: A Bay of Pigs veteran from an old Matanzas family asks the Marielito lector in Domino Park why he calls everyone sincere but him.

verses.text: Give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle, when thou goest to the other shore of existence; if thy mind is altogether free, thou wilt not again enter into birth and decay.
Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has cut all fetters, who never trembles, is independent and unshackled.

bg.commentary: A rich man’s son, Uggasena, falls in love with an acrobat’s daughter he sees dancing on the top of a pole, and lies down to die unless he can have her. Her father will not sell her, but gives her to him if he will travel with the troupe. Uggasena drives the carts and fetches grass and water and sets up the apparatus, and when his wife sings to their baby about the son of a cart-driver and a know-nothing, he learns the acrobat’s art himself and comes home to perform on a sixty-cubit pole. At the height of his act the crowd turns to look at the Buddha entering the city. The Buddha sends Moggallāna to ask him to perform; Uggasena turns fourteen somersaults, hears the Buddha’s verse on the top of the pole, and is freed. He comes down, is ordained, and instantly takes on the look of an elder of sixty. When the monks doubt his claim that he felt no fear coming down, the Buddha confirms it with a second verse. Read the full commentary story (the same story is told at Dhp-a 24.6).
bg.history:
Union Village, founded in 1805 in Turtlecreek Township near Lebanon, was the first and largest community of the United Society of Believers in Christ’s Second Appearing, the Shakers, west of the Alleghenies. It had more than 600 members by 1818, and its families lived by farming, broom making, garden seeds, and medicinal herbs and extracts. The Shakers lived celibate, held goods in common, and worshiped in song and ordered dance; men and women converts left marriages behind when they joined. “Simple Gifts,” a dancing song generally attributed to Elder Joseph Brackett of the Maine Shakers, dates from 1848. In 1912 the remaining Shakers sold Union Village to the United Brethren in Christ, who opened a children’s home there in 1913; the grounds are now a retirement community.

In the 1840s American political parties raised tall campaign poles in town squares: Democrats raised hickory, for Andrew Jackson, “Old Hickory,” and Whigs raised ash, for Henry Clay’s Ashland (a Springfield, Illinois, marker records a 150-foot Democratic hickory pole there in 1844). In 1849 cholera killed roughly 6,000 people in Cincinnati, about one in twenty, and spread into the surrounding towns; Lebanon’s Western Star of July 27, 1849 reported deaths in Franklin and Waynesville while declaring Lebanon itself free of the disease. On July 3, 1849, President Zachary Taylor proclaimed the first Friday in August a national day of “Fasting, Humiliation, and Prayer” on account of the pestilence.

sections.heading: I. The Seats
sections.text: I was not born yet for any of the first part, so I give it the way my mother gave it to me, and the way the town gave it to me later, which was not the same way, and I have tried to put the two together where they meet. Varnell’s Olympic Circus came up the pike from Cincinnati every June with four wagons, eleven horses, a round top of canvas, and a family of tumblers out of Lancashire who had been in the country since 1830 and still said summat and nowt. They played Lebanon two days at the end of Broadway, past the Golden Lamb, and the farmers came in from Turtle Creek and Deerfield and Mason and set the seat planks so full that the boys built their own seats on top of them, a bench on a bench on a barrel, swaying, and watched from up there under the canvas with their heads nearly in the smoke of the lamps. My father, Asa Lindley, was up on one of those. He was twenty-two. His father had the dry-goods store on Broadway with the plate window and the bolts of Merrimack calico standing in it like organ pipes, and Asa clerked there and kept the ledger in a good round hand and was expected to have the store, and had never once in his life climbed anything higher than the ladder to the t

sections.heading: II. Hush
sections.text: They played Xenia and Springfield and Urbana and Bellefontaine, and went down through Dayton and Hamilton to the river, and over into Indiana at Madison and Kentucky at Maysville, and wintered in Cincinnati in a livery barn on Sycamore Street where Varnell kept the horses fat and the family thin. They played wherever a town would let them have a lot and a license, and left in the night where it would not. My father drove the property wagon. Wherever they stopped he watered eleven horses at whatever creek or town pump there was, and cut grass for them with a scythe if the farmer would let him, and he dug the holes and set the poles and stretched the canvas and drove the stakes, and when it was over he pulled the stakes and folded the canvas and loaded the poles and drove on. He had never done a day’s outdoor work in his life. His hands bled a month and then went to horn. The tumblers called him the Clerk. I was born in March of 1847 in the livery barn on Sycamore Street, in the harness room, with the horses talking the whole time through the wall. They called me William for my mother’s father, and the tumblers called me the Clerk’s Boy. My mother went back up the mast in April. In t

sections.heading: III. Handbill
sections.text: The cholera came up the river to Cincinnati again that summer, worse than in thirty-two, and the city buried more than a hundred some days in July, and anybody who could get out got out, up the pikes into the country, and some of them carried it with them. It was at Franklin and at Waynesville. In Lebanon the Western Star kept telling the town it was free of it, which meant everybody in town was afraid of it. The President had appointed the first Friday in August a day of fasting, humiliation and prayer across the whole country on account of the pestilence, and the churches on Broadway were getting ready. Varnell would not play the river towns that year. He brought the show up the pike to Lebanon at the end of July, and my father went to the printer at the Star office with three dollars and came out with this, which I have, which my mother kept in her trunk until she died and which is in front of me now with the folds worn through. The hickory pole stood at the crossing of Broadway and Main. The Democrats of the town had raised it for General Cass the summer before, a hundred and ten feet of shagbark hickory in two pieces, scarfed and banded with iron, out of the Little Miami botto

sections.heading: IV. The Hickory Pole
sections.text: The town had fasted on the Friday, or said it had, and on the Saturday it came to the square. They came in from all the townships, in spite of the cholera or because of it. They backed hay wagons into the square in a ring and set benches up in the wagon beds and chairs on the benches, and stood on the chairs, and sat on the roof of the market house and in the windows of the Golden Lamb and up in the elms. Somebody said three thousand. My mother sat in the bed of a hay wagon by the Star office with me on her knee. I was two years and five months. I believe I remember the elms, but I am not sure. My father went up the hickory pole at a quarter after three in a scarlet jacket all over spangles that had been Varnell’s, and white tights, and bare feet. He went up the way she had gone up the mast in 1846, hand over hand, and the square went quiet under him the way a church does. Above the iron bands he went slower. At the top he got his knee on the plate, then a foot, then the other foot, and he stood up a hundred and ten feet over Broadway and let go of the pole with both hands. He could see the whole county from there, he said afterward. The Miami bottoms and the hills toward Waynesvil

sections.heading: V. Day Book
sections.text: The Shakers kept a journal at every family, a line or two a day, weather and work and who came and who went. In 1912, when I went to the sale, a brother of the last few let me sit in the office and copy out what the Center Family book said for that August. I give it as it was written. Sat. 4th. Very warm. Eldress H., Brother Amos and four others to Lebanon with the extracts. Returned near dark, and brought with them a young man of the town, Asa Lindley, son of the merchant, who had been with a show. He wishes to try the life. His hair entirely white, though he gives his age as 25. Sun. 5th. Meeting. A.L. present on the brethren’s side. Was asked by some of the young brethren after meeting whether he was not afraid coming down off of the pole, it being above 100 feet. He says, Nay, he had no fear at all. Some of the young brethren think this is not the truth, seeing what has happened to his hair, and say that it is a show-man’s brag and he must labor to overcome it. Mon. 6th. Hot. Cutting oats. A.L. in the broom shop. Brother Seth spoke to Eldress H. about A.L. saying he had no fear, that he thought it a lie and not fit for a Believer. Tues. 7th. Eldress H. spoke in the evening meet

sections.heading: VI. The Sale
sections.text: My mother went back up the mast in September of 1849 and stayed up it nine more years, until her knees went, and she never sang that song to me again. She kept the spangled jacket in her trunk and wore it once more, to be buried in, at Cincinnati in 1866. I was on the road by then with the big shows, Spalding’s and afterward others, and I have been on it ever since, a leaper and then a rider and then thirty-one years an equestrian director, and I have seen every kind of turn there is and a good many people come down off a good many things. I never saw anybody else come down the way he did. I saw him once. I was fourteen, and the war had started, and I walked out from Lebanon along Turtle Creek without telling anybody and asked at the office for Brother Asa. They let me sit with him in the broom shop for an hour. He had a broom-corn vise and a winding wheel, and he wound brooms the whole time I was there and talked to me, and his hair was white, and he was the happiest man I have ever sat with in my life before or since, and I was very angry, and he let me be. When I got up to go he said, Will, does thy mother still sing? and I said not that song, and he said, That’s a shame. It was

title: Come Round Right
logline: A dry-goods merchant's son follows a circus girl onto the road, learns her art, and comes home to stand atop the town's hickory pole.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has cut the strap and the thong, the chain with all that pertains to it, who has burst the bar, and is awakened.

bg.commentary: Two brahmins, one with an ox called Little Tawny and the other with an ox called Big Tawny, argue over whose ox is the stronger. Tired of arguing, they load a cart with sand on the bank of the Aciravatī river and yoke the oxen to it. Some monks come down to bathe and watch: the brahmins whip the oxen, the cart does not stir an inch, and the straps and thongs break. The monks tell the Buddha, who says that anyone can cut those outward straps; a monk must cut the inner strap of anger and the thong of craving. Hearing the verse, the five hundred monks are freed.
bg.history:
Oakland County, north and west of Detroit, is dotted with hundreds of small glacial lakes, and after the Second World War the townships around them filled with subdivisions of commuters to the auto companies, many of them organized into lake and property-owner associations with private beaches. In 1986 Ford built two Broncos. The full-size Bronco, in its third generation (1980–1986) based on the F-150, came from the Michigan Truck Plant in Wayne, Michigan, and could be had with a 5.8-liter V-8. The compact Bronco II, derived from the Ranger pickup and built alongside it at the Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky, was sold from the 1984 model year; for 1986 it got a fuel-injected 2.9-liter V-6.

William James delivered his Talks to Teachers on Psychology to schoolteachers in Cambridge and elsewhere in the 1890s and published them in 1899 with three talks to students, among them “The Gospel of Relaxation.” There he argues that American “over-tension” is a habit, that feeling follows action as much as action follows feeling, and that a person who never gives up wholly to the chair they sit in cannot be at rest. The American Red Cross, which hired Wilbert E. Longfellow in 1914 to organize its volunteer life-saving corps and went on to build a national water-safety program, taught most of the country’s twentieth-century learn-to-swim classes, adults among them, through local volunteer instructors like Mrs. Wachowski.

sections.heading: I. Entry
sections.dateline: Lake Ellery, Commerce Township, Oakland County, Michigan · Monday, June 16, 1986, 6:48 a.m.
sections.text: Adult Beginners, Session One. Skill: enter the water safely and stand. There were eleven of us, and none of us could swim, and all of us lived within a mile of the water. That was the thing nobody on the lake knew, or if they knew they were nice about it. We had moved out from Royal Oak and Livonia and Redford and the east side, some of us in 1971 and some last fall, for the schools and for the lake, and we had docks, and pontoon boats some of us, and children who swam like otters, and for years we had sat on the end of the dock in a folding chair with our feet out of the water and said we did not care for it much. The Lake Ellery Property Owners Association put a notice in the spring newsletter, between the reminder about lawn fertilizer and the minutes of the April meeting, that Mrs. Wachowski would give a two-week course for adult beginners at the association beach, seven to eight in the morning, Red Cross method, free to members, and that the class would be confidential. Somebody on the board had underlined that word. Eleven of us called her. Two of us called her twice, to back out, and she said she would see us Monday. So that Monday we came down the path from Heron Point Driv

sections.heading: II. Bobbing
sections.text: Skill: hold the breath and put the face in the water. Come up. Do it again. Everybody on the lake knew about Gary and Dennis. They were both engineers at Ford, both in Truck Operations at Dearborn, both forty-four, both from Livonia, both on the association board, and they lived next door to each other on the point, and for two years they had been arguing about trucks. Gary had been on the full-size Bronco since 1979, the big one, built on the F-150 frame at the Michigan Truck Plant in Wayne, with the 351 V-8. Dennis had been on the Bronco II since before it had a name, the little one off the Ranger, built down at Louisville, with the new fuel-injected 2.9 V-6 that came in this year. Each of them drove the one he worked on. Both trucks were tan, two-tone, tan over darker tan, and they sat side by side in the two driveways on the point like a cow and her calf, and the children on the lake called them Big Tan and Little Tan, and so did everybody else eventually, and so, by the end, did Gary and Dennis. The argument had started at the Fourth of July picnic in 1984 over which one would pull a pontoon trailer up the launch, and it had gone on through two Christmases and an Easter brunch

sections.heading: III. Front Float
sections.text: Skill: take a breath, put the face in, let the legs come up. Five seconds. Recover to a stand. Mrs. Wachowski came down the path at seven exactly, as she always would, every morning of those two weeks, with a canvas bag over her shoulder and a whistle on a shoelace around her neck. She was sixty-eight. She had taught girls’ physical education at Pontiac Central for thirty-four years and given Red Cross swimming lessons every summer since 1946, at Elizabeth Lake and Cass Lake and Sylvan and the Pontiac Y, and she had taught, she said once, something over four thousand people to float, and she was proudest of the ones who were over forty. By then Gary and Dennis had both driven off to Dearborn, separately, and the beach was empty except for the trailer and the strap and the post lying on its side. She looked at all of it. She looked at us in our row holding the rope. She put her bag down on the lifeguard chair and took off her sandals and walked into the water in her suit to her waist, and stood in front of us. Well, she said. What happened here? So we told her. All of us at once, and then one at a time. Big Tan and Little Tan. The two straps. The hitch ball. The fence. Somebody star

sections.heading: IV. Back Float
sections.text: Skill: lie back on the water with the ears under. Arms out. Let it hold you. It took the whole hour, and we did not all get it that first day. But we will say what happened, because it is the reason we tell this. She took us one at a time, with her hand flat under the small of the back. Lie back. Ears in. Look at the sky. She said the same thing to every one of us, in the same voice, not loud. She said the water would hold us up if we would let it, and that the only thing in the lake that could sink us was the part of us that was holding on. She said a line from the book without looking at it, as if it were a line from a song she had sung so often it had worn smooth, that a person who never gives himself up wholly to the chair he sits in, but keeps his muscles half contracted for a rise, cannot be anything but anxious. Give yourself up to the chair, she said. This is the chair. And she took her hand away. Ray Fenner went first. He lay back stiff as a plank and sank and came up coughing and lay back again, and the second time something went out of his shoulders and he floated, sixty-one years old, with his eyes wide open, looking at the sky over Commerce Township, and he started to

title: Tow Strap
logline: Eleven grown suburbanites who never learned to swim stand in a lake and watch two Ford engineers settle whose Bronco is stronger.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, though he has committed no offence, endures reproach, bonds, and stripes, who has endurance for his force, and strength for his army.

bg.commentary: Dhanañjanī, a Brahmin's wife and a follower of the Buddha, cries out in praise of him whenever she sneezes or stumbles, and one day does it while serving a meal to Brahmins. Her furious husband goes to defeat the Buddha with a riddle (what must one kill to live at ease?) and is answered: anger, "a poisonous root, sweet at the beginning." He becomes a monk. His younger brother, the Insolent Bhāradvāja, comes to abuse the Buddha and is asked whether, when guests refuse the food he sets out, it is not still his own; so too the abuse the Buddha refuses. Two more brothers come to revile him and are won the same way, and when the monks marvel that he became their refuge without a word in reply, he speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story; the exchanges are in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 7.1, 7.2 and 7.4). The teacher reads from The Great Controversy by Ellen G. White, which quotes John Wesley's journal of his 1736 voyage to Georgia with a company of Moravians.
bg.history:
Tennessee law forbade ordinary work on Sunday, and in the late 1880s and 1890s it was turned against Seventh-day Adventists, who kept Saturday and worked on Sunday. Around the Adventist school at Graysville, in Rhea County, members were charged in 1894 and 1895 for such things as stripping fodder, carrying boards and helping dig a well. At Dayton in March 1895 Judge J. G. Parks said he doubted the justice of the law but enforced it; the defendants refused on conscience to pay even small fines and went to jail instead.

After a second round of convictions that summer, the county revived its chain gang, and in July 1895 Adventist prisoners were carried north in wagons to break rock for the approaches of a bridge near Spring City, later lodging in a barred log house near Graysville. Their guard agreed not to work them on Saturday, and not to count Saturdays against their sentences. Adventist papers such as the American Sentinel carried the story nationally, and many secular newspapers took the prisoners' side. Swafford, the Bratchers and the Tallent boy are invented.

sections.heading: I. Delphia
sections.dateline: The Bratcher place, Rhea County, Tennessee · June 1895
sections.text: I will tell my part first because it is the smallest and it is where it started. I sneeze in threes. I always have, from a girl. My mother said it was the pepper in our blood. And I am a stumbler. I catch my toe on nothing, on the edge of a rag rug, on the shadow of a door, and Absalom used to say I could fall down a well that was not there. And from the spring of 1893, when I first sat under Brother Swafford's reading in Ma Kelso's front room and came out of it knowing the seventh day, whenever I sneezed or tripped or coughed so it hurt, what came out of my mouth was Even so, come, Lord Jesus. I did not decide it. It came out of me the way the sneeze did. Absalom was a Methodist local preacher, and his father was, and his grandfather rode a circuit out of Knoxville when it was Indian country. All four of the Bratcher boys could preach, and three of them did. It was a preaching family, and they were known for it from Washington to Smith's Crossroads. I married into it at seventeen. Every quarter when the presiding elder came for quarterly meeting, the preachers ate at our house. It was the custom. I killed four hens and a rooster and made the dumplings and the stack cake the day be

sections.heading: II. Absalom
sections.dateline: The rock pile at the bridge approach, near Spring City · the next morning
sections.text: I am the oldest. I will try to say it straight. There had been Sabbath-keepers in the Cove for twenty years and nobody minded them much until they built their school at Graysville and got a store, and then somebody minded. A man swore out a warrant on Silas Swafford for plowing his bottom on a Sunday in April. There were others charged, for fodder pulling and for carrying boards and for helping dig a well. The judge fined them and said he did not much like the law himself but it was the law. Not one of them would pay a cent of it. Paying, they said, would be keeping Sunday. So they lay in the jail at Dayton. Then the court got the chain gang up again for them, that had not been used in years, and in July they hauled them up the valley in two wagons and set them to breaking rock for the approaches of a bridge. I had preached against them. I had preached against them by name. It was hot already at seven. There was a guard on a stump with a shotgun across his knees, a Tallent boy I had baptized. There were nine men in that line with hammers, and a pile of blue limestone higher than a barn, and a pile of broken rock beside it the size of a corncrib, and the sound of it. If you have not

sections.heading: III. Wash
sections.text: I was the lawyer of us. I had read law at Cleveland and I was acting for the state that term because the attorney general was down with his kidneys. It was my office indicted my own brother. I want that understood. I did it in the regular course. When I heard Ab had gone over to them I went up to the rock pile on a Sunday afternoon, when they were not working because the law would not let them, which is a joke I did not see at the time. They were sitting in the shade of the log house where the gang slept. I said what I came to say. I said it to Swafford. I will not write it all down. I called him an old fool and a Jew and a disturber of the peace of a Christian county and a stealer of wives and of brothers, and some other things, and I am a lawyer and know how to say a thing so it goes in. I went on a good while. The others got up and went inside. He did not. He sat on the step with his hands between his knees and heard every word as if I were reading him a deed. When I had run down he said, Wash, when the quarterly meeting comes to your house, does Lou set the table? I said what did that have to do with it. She kills her hens and makes her stack cake and sets it all out for them?

sections.heading: IV. Pretty and Clabber
sections.text: Our names are Sunderland and Thomas, but nobody has called us that since we were in dresses. I am Pretty and I taught singing school, the round notes and the shape notes both, and I am vain, I know it. My brother is Clabber because he was a sour baby and has been a sour man, and he runs the sorghum mill. He cannot write, so I am writing for both of us, and he says to put down that he does not agree with how I tell it. We went up together the second Sunday in September because there was nobody left to go. Our father was dead. Ab was keeping Saturday. Wash was keeping Saturday. Our mother had not left her bed in a week. Clabber said somebody had to whip that old man and he would hold my coat. I am not going to tell what we said because it was worse than Wash, and Clabber says that is the only part I have right. I will tell this. While I was saying it, Swafford was looking at me the way you look at a horse you are thinking of buying, all over, without any hurry. And when I was done he said, You've got a good voice, Sunderland. Your mother always said so. And he said to Clabber, How's the cane this year, Tom? And Clabber, who had come to whip him, told him how the cane was, for a quart

sections.heading: V. The Time Book
sections.dateline: The log house below Graysville · October 1895
sections.text: This last part is mine again, Delphia's, because I was there and none of them can tell it. By October there were four Bratchers on the county's books, Ab and Wash on the gang, Pretty and Clabber bound over, and the gang was moved down the valley to a log house a mile and a half from Graysville with bars on the windows and the front door left open at night, because where would they go. On the Sabbath we women carried dinner up. The Tallent boy ate with us. He had not been made to and he did it. After dinner the men sat on the floor of the big room, and it came up, the way it does when men are full, how it had been. One of the Graysville men said it was a wonderful thing. Four brothers, he said, and every one of them came up that road to curse him, and every one of them went home ours. And not one hard word back. Not a word in his own defense. He just stood there like a post and let them hang their coats on him. Brother Swafford was by the door with the light behind him. He said it was nothing to do with him. He said, I can't take credit for a thing I didn't do. I didn't do anything. Then he said if they wanted to hear about not answering back they ought to hear about it from Ab's si

title: Even So
logline: A preacher's wife cries out for the Second Coming every time she trips, so four preaching brothers climb to a chain gang to curse an old Sabbath-keeper.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who is free from anger, dutiful, virtuous, without appetite, who is subdued, and has received his last body.

bg.commentary: Sāriputta, the Buddha's chief disciple, comes on his alms round with five hundred monks to his mother's house in his home village. She, a Brahmin woman who never forgave him for leaving a great fortune, seats him and feeds him while abusing him as an "eater of leavings" who licks the backs of strangers' ladles, and abuses the monks for making her son their page-boy. He eats and goes back without a word. Rāhula, the young novice, reports it to the Buddha in a short exchange of questions and answers; when the monks marvel at Sāriputta's calm, the Buddha says that those whose taints are gone do not grow angry, and speaks the verse. Read the full commentary story, or about Sāriputta. The teacher's poem is by Zabel Yesayan (Essayan), born in Scutari (Üsküdar) in 1878, quoted in Zabelle C. Boyajian's translation from Armenian Legends and Poems (1916). The grandmother's proverb about monks is from the Armenian proverbs in the anthology Armenian Literature (1904).
bg.history:
Survivors of the Armenian genocide of 1915–1923, many of them from Kharpert (Harput) and the provinces of the east, built one of the largest Armenian communities in America in Watertown, a trolley suburb on the Charles just west of Cambridge, where many found work at the Hood Rubber Company. Factory workers began raising money door to door in 1926 for an Armenian Apostolic church on Mount Auburn Street. Services were first held in the new building in June 1933; the heating and the church hall were finished in 1934, and the parish had already taken over the Sahag Mesrob Armenian school.

In the Armenian Church's home blessing (Tnorhnek), given in the seasons after Christmas and Easter, a priest visits each household, blesses bread, water and salt set out on a tray, burns incense, prays for the family and leaves a wafer stamped with a cross. Armenian celibate priests, who may become vardapets and bishops, take a new name at ordination. The ladle in the story comes from a sermon of Mkrtich Khrimian ("Hayrik") after the Congress of Berlin in 1878: other nations took their share of the harissa pot with iron ladles, while the Armenian petition was a paper ladle that went soft in it. The Garabedians, Varjouhi and the priest are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Blessing
sections.dateline: Dexter Avenue, East Watertown, Massachusetts · the Tuesday after Easter, April 1934
sections.text: The tray was on the dining table under the good cloth: a glass of water, a saucer of salt, a slice of the Easter choreg. Hripsime Garabedian had set it out at six in the morning and then sat in the parlor in her black dress with her hands in her lap for five hours, and when the bell rang she let it ring twice before she got up. He was on the step in his black robe and his pointed hood, with the censer in his hand and the little case of wafers under his arm, and behind him on the walk were the four altar boys from the new church on Mount Auburn Street, and her grandson Arto was one of them, with his hair wet down. Her son kissed her hand. She let him. Come in, Father, she said. Sit. You must be tired. How many houses is it today? Twenty? Thirty? Sit down. He began the prayers standing. She did not sit down either. He lit the charcoal from the box of matches she handed him, and put the grains on it, and the smoke went up. Thirty houses. And in every one a cup of coffee and a piece of somebody's choreg and a spoon of somebody's harissa and a quarter in your hand at the door, and you say thank you, Digin, God bless your table, and you go next door and do it again. I have seen you. Mrs.

sections.heading: II. Questions and Answers
sections.dateline: The Sahag Mesrob school, the church hall on Mount Auburn Street · Saturday
sections.text: Arto brought Varjouhi a piece of his grandmother's choreg wrapped in wax paper, as he had been told to, and set it on her desk and asked her to eat. Her name was Mrs. Takouhi Kalfayan, but nobody under fifty in the parish called her anything but Varjouhi, which only means teacher. She had come from Van. She had taught the alphabet in that city in the year the city was besieged, and in Erivan the year after, to orphans, in a tent, and now she taught it on Saturday mornings in the new hall on Mount Auburn Street to the children of rubber workers from Hood's, who would rather have been playing ball. She was very small. She had a way of asking you something as if the answer had been yours from the beginning and she only wanted to hear you say it. She broke off a piece of the choreg and ate it and asked him questions the way they did in the old catechism, and he answered the way the catechism answers. Where were you on Tuesday? On the house blessings, Varjouhi. With Hayr Surp. To whose houses did you go? To the houses on Dexter Avenue. To my grandmother's. And what did your grandmother say to Hayr Surp? She said he was a beggar. She said he licks other women's ladles. What else? She sai

sections.heading: III. Incense
sections.dateline: The church hall · the same afternoon
sections.text: The story had gone through the parish by then. The hall had only opened that winter, and the heat had only just been put in, and the men who had carried the boxes of hymnals in from the truck were still sitting at the long tables in the afternoon with coffee, and the altar boys were stacking chairs, and the women were in the kitchen, and all of them were talking about it. It was a wonderful thing, the men said. You know her, Hripsime Garabedian. You know her tongue. She said it all, in front of the boys, in front of God and the censer. And he did not raise his eyes. Not one word, not to his own mother. A man of thirty, and a priest. He sat and ate his harissa. What other man in this parish could do that? Mardiros said he himself would have thrown the bowl. Hagop said his own mother would have thrown it first. Varjouhi was at the end of the table with her coat on, waiting for her ride. Somebody asked her what she thought. She said that she did not think it was so wonderful. She said that a man has to have something lit in him to catch fire when it is thrown, and that a man who has let all of that burn up already has nothing left in him for it to catch on. She said it is not that he

title: The Paper Ladle
logline: On his Easter house blessings a young celibate priest comes to his own mother's door, and she sets out harissa and every word she has saved.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle.

bg.commentary: This short commentary story is a second telling of the episode in 5.10, after the nun Uppalavaṇṇā has been assaulted. Some of the monks talk it over among themselves: the awakened are not dry trees or anthills, they say, but beings of flesh and blood, so surely they too still take pleasure in the senses. The Buddha answers that they do not. Pleasures do not cling to such a person, any more than water clings to a lotus leaf or a mustard seed stays on the point of an awl, and he speaks the verse. Here the nun is the same woman as in Honey on the Knife, ten years on, and, as there, the violation is secret filming rather than assault.
bg.history:
In 2018 hidden-camera crime, called molka in Korean, became the subject of the largest women's protests in South Korean history. Beginning in May, women gathered every few weeks near Hyehwa Station in Seoul, most of them dressed in red, under signs reading "My Life Is Not Your Porn." The August 4 rally, held in a heat wave, drew about 70,000 people; one sign read "Our Rage Is Hotter Than The Heat Wave." South Korean police recorded some 6,800 reports of spycam crimes that year.

Northern Virginia's Korean community is centered in Annandale, in Fairfax County. Gat, the Korean leaf mustard used for a pungent kimchi, is a form of brown mustard (Brassica juncea), whose small round seeds are the mustard seed of the kitchen. The cook's line is from the Sutra of Forty-two Sections, traditionally the first Buddhist sutra translated into Chinese, in D. T. Suzuki's English (1906). All the people in the story are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Red
sections.text: Lee Ha-eun watched the fourth rally on her phone in the kitchen of her apartment, with the sound low because her roommate was asleep. It was Saturday afternoon in Seoul and two in the morning in Fairfax. Seventy thousand women sat on the pavement outside Hyehwa Station in a heat wave, nearly all of them in red, holding signs. One of the signs said MY LIFE IS NOT YOUR PORN. Another said OUR RAGE IS HOTTER THAN THE HEAT WAVE. They were chanting about hidden cameras, in toilets and changing rooms and motel rooms, and about the police, who did not find the men who put them there. Ha-eun was twenty-six and in her second year of a social work degree at George Mason. She had a red T-shirt on. She had put it on when she got up to watch, without thinking, and then had thought about it. She was sixteen the fall her uncle died. In her mother's house the story was that Jang-ho samchon had been killed in an accident in the country, on a farm road in the rain, and that the nun from the Centreville temple had something to do with it, and that it was not to be talked about. Her mother had not set foot in a temple since. Ha-eun had found out the rest at nineteen, from a girl at a church retreat who

sections.heading: II. The Townhouse
sections.text: The townhouse was an end unit off Route 29, with a square of yard, a bus stop at the corner, and a candle in the front window that was not lit in the daytime. Two nuns lived there that year, Cheongryeon and a younger one who was at the temple. Cheongryeon opened the door herself. She was forty-six, in summer grays, with her head new-shaved and a gardening glove on one hand. She listened to Ha-eun say who she was, standing on the step with the two friends behind her and her face hot. Then she took off the glove and said come in, it's too hot out here. She made barley tea and set it on the low table and sat on a cushion. Ha-eun had written out what she wanted to say and did not look at the paper. She said she was sorry. For her uncle, for her family, for her mother, for the ten years nobody had said it. Thank you, Cheongryeon said. That's kind of you. It isn't yours. Grace had the recorder on. She asked whether Sunim had seen the rallies. Cheongryeon had. She said the young women in Seoul were right, and that the police there should listen to them, and the police here. Are you angry? Grace asked. Cheongryeon thought about it. I was, a little, for a day. At the deputy. He didn't know

sections.heading: III. The Argument
sections.text: They argued about it until one in the morning at Ha-eun's kitchen table, with the recorder off and a bag of shrimp chips going soft. Min said it was dissociation. She said it kindly. It was the textbook picture, she said: the flat calm, the street-you-used-to-live-on, the not being angry at a man who did that to you. People survived by stepping out of themselves, and some of them never stepped back in, and a temple was the perfect place to never step back in, because everybody would call it holiness. Grace said maybe it was the opposite, that she was performing it. That a nun had to be calm in front of the congregation the way a pastor's wife had to smile, and they had sat there and gotten the performance. Ha-eun's roommate's boyfriend, who had come out of the bedroom for water and stayed, said with respect he didn't buy any of it. She was a human being. She wasn't a stone Buddha in a garden. Human beings had bodies, they wanted things, they got angry, they liked things, and anybody who said they didn't was either lying or broken. Things come up, they don't stay, he said. Come on. Everything stays. Ha-eun didn't say anything. She was thinking about the candle in the window, and the

sections.heading: IV. The Needle
sections.text: The old cook from the Centreville temple was ninety that year and lived with her son's family in a split-level off Ravensworth Road. She had stopped cooking at the temple at eighty-five, when her knees went, and now she sat in a chair by the window of the family room with a sewing basket and a jade plant and mended everything the family owned whether it needed mending or not. Ha-eun's grandmother had known her in the old days. It took two phone calls to get invited. The cook was sewing a button onto her great-grandson's school shirt when Ha-eun came in. On the windowsill was a jar of small round brown seeds that her son had saved from the gat he grew along the fence, the bitter red-leafed mustard for kimchi, to plant again in the spring. Ha-eun told her everything. Min's word, and Grace's, and the boyfriend's. She said she did not know which of them was right and she did not know why it mattered to her so much, except that it did. The cook bit off the thread. She did not answer for so long that Ha-eun thought she had not heard. Then she unscrewed the jar and took out one seed between her thumb and finger, and held the needle up point first, and set the seed on the point. It sat the

title: The Seed on the Needle
logline: In the summer of the Seoul spycam protests, a young woman goes to apologize to the nun her uncle wronged ten years before.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, even here, knows the end of his suffering, has put down his burden, and is unshackled.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin's slave runs away, is ordained (this was before the Buddha made the rule against ordaining slaves) and becomes an arahant. One day the Brahmin sees him entering the city with the Buddha and seizes him by the robe in the gateway. The Buddha turns and asks what he means by it. This is my slave. His burden has fallen from him. The Brahmin understands at once that the man is an arahant, asks Is that so?, hears Yes, and is himself established in the first fruit of the path. Here the gateway is a canal lock, the ordination is four years on a swamp island, and the rule that came afterward is a Virginia law.
bg.history:
For more than two centuries the Great Dismal Swamp on the Virginia–North Carolina line sheltered maroons, people who had freed themselves and lived on its dry “islands.” After draining for rice failed, the swamp’s companies turned to cutting juniper (Atlantic white cedar) for shingles, working enslaved men hired from their owners by the year; the getters could earn money for shingles beyond their task, and maroons supplied them shingles in exchange for goods and cash, a trade Encyclopedia Virginia describes as an informal economy that let the swamp’s hidden residents live. The Dismal Swamp Canal, dug largely by enslaved laborers from 1793, opened its full twenty-two miles in 1805, at first to shallow flats and log rafts carrying shingles and staves.

Virginia’s manumission act of 1782 let an owner free a slave by will or by a deed proved in the county court, and required the freed person to carry an attested copy. On January 25, 1806, the Assembly passed a new act, in force from May 1, under which anyone freed afterward who stayed in the state more than twelve months could be seized and sold. Olaudah Equiano’s Interesting Narrative (London 1789; New York, W. Durell, 1791) prints in full the deed by which the Montserrat merchant Robert King freed him in 1766; the form the elder copies, and the two passages he reads, are Equiano’s words.

sections.heading: I. Ran Away
sections.dateline: Near the Great Bridge, Norfolk County, Virginia · January 1801
sections.text: TEN DOLLARS REWARD. RAN AWAY from the subscriber, or rather did not return to him at Christmas from his hire, a Negro man named JEM, about twenty-eight years of age, five feet nine or ten inches high, stout made, with a white scar across the back of his left hand got from a froe. He has been hired these three years past to the getting of shingles in the Dismal Swamp and is well acquainted therein. He is a professor of religion, a member of the Baptist society, sings well, and can say over a good deal from books though he cannot read. It is supposed he is lurking about the Swamp. Whoever takes up the said fellow and secures him so that I get him again shall have the above reward. EZEKIEL HODGES. Elder Ezekiel Hodges wrote it out three times at the kitchen table before he was satisfied, and each time he struck the words a member of the Baptist society and each time he wrote them in again. They were true. He had put Jem under the water of the Northwest River himself, in the spring of 1797, with the ice just off the banks, and Jem had come up out of it gasping and laughing with his arms thrown wide, and the people on the bank had sung him out. It did not seem to Hodges a thing a man ou

sections.heading: II. The Island
sections.text: There are places in the swamp where the ground lifts a few feet out of the black water and stays dry, and on them the old people built houses of juniper poles and reeds that nobody outside ever saw. Sib had lived on one of them since before the war with the King. Nobody knew whose she had been. Some said she had come in as a girl from the Company's plantation by Suffolk, in the time when they first set people to ditching for the gentlemen who meant to drain the whole Dismal and plant it in rice. Some said she had been born on the island. She was small and very dark and walked with a stick of gallberry, and when Jem came to her in the first week of January 1801, he came with everything he owned on his back. He had the froe and the maul. He had his blanket and his pot and a sack of meal, and the overwork money sewn into the waist of his breeches, nineteen dollars and some shillings, and a knife, and a pair of shoes he did not wear in the water. He had the whole of a list he had been keeping for nine years: every Christmas, every hire, every dollar the shingle men had paid to Hodges for the use of his arms. He could say it off the way he said off Vassa. He said it to Sib the first nig

sections.heading: III. The Lock
sections.text: The canal company had been digging its ditch through the east side of the swamp since 1793, with hired men and bought men up to their waists in the peat, and in 1805 they let the water through from end to end, twenty-two miles from the Pasquotank to the Elizabeth. It was too shallow yet for anything but flats and log rafts. But the flats came, loaded to the gunwales with shingles and staves, and at the Deep Creek end, where the water had to be let down to the river, the company built a lock of swamp timber with a keeper's house beside it. Sib had not come out of the swamp in eleven years. She came out that March because a getter named Moses, who had been taking the island's shingles for most of that time, had been sold away to Carolina over the winter, and the new man would not deal with anybody he had not seen. She sat in the bow of the flat with her stick across her knees. Jem poled. There were eleven thousand shingles in the flat and Moses's brother walking the towpath, to say the load was his. Ezekiel Hodges was at Deep Creek that morning to see about corn. He had not been looking for anything. He was standing on the walk across the lower gates with the keeper, talking about th

sections.heading: IV. These Presents
sections.dateline: Near the Great Bridge · March and April 1806
sections.text: That night he took the African's book down for the first time in five years and sat with it at the kitchen table after the house was asleep. He found the page Jem had said back to him, about the register office and the winged feet, and read it, and could not stay on it. He turned forward to the place he had always liked best, the conversion, where the man at sea in his trouble is shown the cross, and he read the sentence he had read aloud a dozen times in a voice he now could not stand to remember. I felt an astonishing change; the burden of sin, the gaping jaws of hell, and the fears of death, that weighed me down before, now lost their horror. — Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative, ch. X (1789) He sat with that until the candle guttered. A man could have that, the burden of sin lifted, and keep the other burden on another man's back, and call him by his Christian name at a baptizing. He had done it. He would have gone on doing it. What he could not get past was that the one he held had put down both, out there on a hummock among the bears and the reeds, the one the elder had laid on him and the one the elder had preached, and had come up into the lock with nothing on him a

title: These Presents
logline: A Baptist elder who preaches the falling burden grabs the shirt of the man who ran from him, in a new canal lock.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana whose knowledge is deep, who possesses wisdom, who knows the right way and the wrong, and has attained the highest end.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Sakka, lord of the gods, comes one night with his retinue to hear the Buddha speak. The nun Khemā sets out through the air to visit the Teacher, sees Sakka there, pays her respects without coming down, turns around and goes. Sakka asks who she was, and the Buddha answers: my daughter Khemā, of great wisdom, who knows well what is the path and what is not the path, and speaks the verse. Khemā had been the queen of King Bimbisāra, so proud of her beauty that she avoided the Buddha, and became the foremost of his nuns in wisdom. Here Sakka is a studio head, the “thousand eyes” are cameras, and the path that is not a path is a painted street.
bg.history:
After Pearl Harbor the Army hid the Lockheed plant in Burbank, where the P-38 Lightning was built, under a canopy of chicken wire, netting and painted canvas meant to look from the air like an ordinary California suburb, with artists and set designers from Disney, Paramount and 20th Century Fox helping. Trees were made of chicken feathers glued to wire and sprayed green and brown, the airfield and lots were painted to pass for alfalfa, and workers took in laundry at the “burlap bungalows” on their breaks. A longtime Lockheed man recalled, as LAist reports, that the only giveaway from the air was a railroad track that seemed to begin and end inside the canopy.

The Aircraft Warning Service put hundreds of thousands of civilian volunteers on observation posts who phoned “flash” reports of every plane they saw or heard to Army filter centers; in May 1944 the War Department announced its inactivation, effective May 29. Some 130 Women Airforce Service Pilots flew pursuit planes for the Air Transport Command, among them pilots of the 6th Ferrying Group at Long Beach, ferrying aircraft from the factories, as the WASP Museum recounts.

sections.heading: I. The Book
sections.dateline: Observation Post Item-41, Burbank, California · May 1944
sections.text: The post was a plywood shack on the roof of Inez Albright’s two-car garage, with a telephone, a stool, a pair of Navy binoculars, a chart of silhouettes tacked to the wall and a ledger that the Army called the post log and everyone on the block called the Book. You went up by a ladder from the alley. The Army had put it there in the winter of 1942, when nobody knew yet whether the Japanese would come over the San Gabriels some night, and it had been manned every hour since, in four-hour watches, by forty-one volunteers from the streets around, most of them women, most of them over fifty, two of them Boy Scouts. Mrs. Albright was chief observer because she had more hours than anybody and because she could tell a Vega from a Harvard by the sound before it cleared the roofs. She was sixty-four. In 1919 she had flown a Jenny upside down over the Pomona fair with her husband standing on the top wing, and later, after he was killed doing it at Bakersfield, she had taught flying for sixteen years at a dirt field out in the Valley until the war shut down private flying along the coast. Since then she had flown nothing. She wore her husband’s leather coat on the night watches and kept her F

sections.heading: II. The Visitor
sections.text: The visitor was Mr. Saxe. Everybody on the street knew the car, which was a Packard as long as a hearse with a driver who sat in it all night reading, and everybody knew who he was, because he ran a studio, one of the big ones over the hill. Mrs. Ochs said he had a thousand cameras. She meant it the way people meant it then, that he could see anything he wanted to see, anywhere in the world, and make you see it too. He had first come up the ladder in March, in a white suit, asking whether it was true that Inez Albright of the old Albright Flying Circus was on this roof. His studio had hired her in 1927 to fly through a barn for a picture about the war in France, and she had flown through the barn, and he had never forgotten it. After that he came every week or two, after dark, and sat on an apple box with his back against the shack while she watched the sky, and she talked to him in the plain pleasant way she talked to everybody, about the Jenny and the fairs and the wind off the Tehachapis, and about nothing, and he listened like a man drinking water. He told her one night that his own art department had designed half the canopy across the street. It’s good work, she said. Nobody

sections.heading: III. One, Bi-motor
sections.text: Danny Kowalski, fifteen, of the Scout troop at St. Finbar’s, had the early evening watch with Mrs. Albright that Thursday, because his mother worked swing at the plant and because he liked the binoculars. He was the one who wrote it in the Book. He kept the Book that summer, after it was over, in a drawer of his bureau, until the Army sent a man in a car to ask for it back, and he gave the man the Book but copied the page first, and kept the copy. There had been a postcard at noon, from Long Beach. Mrs. Albright had read it on the porch and said nothing about it, which was usual, but she had gone up the ladder half an hour before her watch, which was not. At six-thirty the Packard came up the street and stopped at the curb, and Mr. Saxe came up the ladder in his white suit with a paper sack of cherries from the market on Magnolia, and sat on his box with his back to the shack and offered the cherries round. The sky over Glendale was going rose and then red. Swallows were working the air over the canopy, coming down very low over the painted streets and the feather trees and the burlap roofs, and Danny would always remember that, that the birds were not fooled, that they went for th

sections.heading: IV. Secure the Telephone
sections.text: He did not come back. On the last night half the block climbed the ladder by turns to sit a while, and there were more people on the roof than the roof was built for, and nothing came over at all. At midnight Mrs. Albright made the last entry in her square hand and closed the Book and tied it with the string, and Danny copied the page into his school notebook before the man from the Army came for it in August. 2400Post Item-41 secured per orders. Manned 20,352 hours since Feb. 1, 1942. No enemy aircraft observed. All ours. — I.A. The canopy came down after the war, and the factory stood out in the sun again with its sawtooth roofs, and the men who took the netting off found swallows nesting in the feather trees. Mrs. Albright flew again in 1946, a rented Cub out of a field in Van Nuys, and in her eighties she was still telling people that you look for the track that doesn’t go anywhere. She kept the feather on the shelf over her kitchen sink until it was gray. Kay never flew over again that anybody saw. She did not need to. The old woman said she knew where she was.

title: The Feather Trees
logline: On a garage-roof plane-spotting post beside a factory disguised as a suburb, a studio head sits nights with an old barnstormer.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who keeps aloof both from laymen and from mendicants, who frequents no houses, and has but few desires.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the monk Tissa takes a meditation subject from the Buddha and settles for the rains in a rock cave, fed by a laywoman of the village. The deity who lives in the cave cannot bear to share it with so virtuous a man; she searches his whole life for a flaw and finds none, then seizes the laywoman’s youngest son and demands, in turn, that the woman get licorice, then resin powder, from the monk as medicine. The woman refuses to make him a physician, but agrees to sprinkle the water she bathed his feet in on the boy’s head. Then the deity stands at the cave mouth and calls Tissa great physician. He reviews his life, finds no speck on his conduct, feels great joy, restrains it, and becomes an arahant without lifting a foot; he tells the deity to leave. When the monks refuse to believe he was not angry, the Buddha speaks the verse. The thirty-two parts of the body he recites are the meditation subject.
bg.history:
Kentucky stayed in the Union and was exempt from the Emancipation Proclamation, so slavery there ended only when the Thirteenth Amendment took effect in December 1865. The limestone country along the Green River is riddled with caves and sinkholes; at nearby Mammoth Cave enslaved men mined saltpeter and, from 1838, enslaved guides such as Stephen Bishop and Mat and Nick Bransford explored and led tours, and Bransford descendants went on guiding into the 1930s.

Freed Black Kentuckians built their own churches quickly after the war. In 1869 delegates met at the First Baptist Church of Lexington to organize the Kentucky General Association of Colored Baptists; its constitution provided for messengers from the district associations into which local churches gathered. Joppa, Little Zion and their people are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Praying Man
sections.dateline: The bluffs above the Green River, Hart County, Kentucky · June 1884
sections.text: I will tell it the way it happened to me, because nobody else saw my side of it, and I am the one who did the wrong. I lived in the cave above Joppa with my three. You know the one if you are from there. It opens under a ledge in the bluff where the sinkhole woods come down to the river, low at the mouth so a grown person has to stoop, and then it stands up tall inside and goes back a long way, and there is water in it that you hear before you find. Cold all year. The same cold in August as in January, so that in summer the air comes out of the mouth like breath, and the boys from Joppa used to dare each other to stand in it. They did not come in. They said a woman lived in there. That was so. I came in the winter of the big snow, before the war, with Phebe who was eight and Lewis who was five and the baby I had not named yet, because you wait. We had come up out of Barren County four nights walking, and they were behind us with the dogs, and the river was too high and too cold, and the cave was there. I meant to stay one night. I am not going to tell you more about that winter than that we did not come out. You can understand it or not. After a while the cold did not trouble us, a

sections.heading: II. Looking Back Along Him
sections.dateline: Joppa and the bluff · June and July
sections.text: In the morning he went down to Joppa. I followed him. Nobody sees me if I don’t want them to. Joppa was eleven houses then, and a church of hewed logs that doubled for the school, and a store that belonged to a white man in Munfordville. He walked through it the way a man walks through a place where he means to ask for something, slow, and he stopped at nobody’s door, and at the last house before the woods Viney Hollins came out on her step with flour on her hands and looked at him and called him in. She knew who he was. Everybody in that country knew Brother Isom Gaines, though most had never laid eyes on him. He was the one Mother Easter Tolliver had raised up out of her church at Little Zion, who preached when they asked him and did not ask, and had no house, and ate what was put in front of him.
