Viney sat him at her table and gave him cornbread and buttermilk and a plate of greens. Then she brought her washpan, the tin one with the dent, because his feet were cut from the bluff, and knelt and washed them, and dried them on her apron. She asked him where he was staying. He said in the cave above. She asked him how long. He said Mother Easter had given him a word to carry, and he

sections.heading: III. The Boy
sections.dateline: Viney Hollins’s house · a Tuesday in July
sections.text: I am going to tell this part plainly and not make it any better than it was. Viney had four. The least one was Sam, five years old, with a head like a little brown egg and a way of following the preacher down to the gate every day and walking along beside him a piece, saying the parts over with him to show he knew them. The teeth. The skin. On a Tuesday in July, in the morning, while his mother was at the churn, I went into that child. I had been a mother. I want you to know I knew what I was doing. I took him by the throat from inside and closed it. He fell down on the floor of the kitchen and his heels went on the boards, and his eyes stood out of his head, and the froth came out of his mouth, and Viney left the churn and fell on her knees and took him up and screamed, What is this, what is this, Jesus, what is this, and I spoke to her out of the air of her own kitchen. I have got your boy, I said. I don’t want nothing for him. But that praying man that eats at your table carries a root. You go ask him for a piece of it, and boil it down in lard, and put it in the child’s nose, and I will turn him loose. That was the whole of my plan. If he gave it, he was a root doctor. Everybod

sections.heading: IV. Foot Water
sections.text: He came down the path at noon the way he always came, saying the parts, and Sam was not at the gate. Viney met him at the step with her face scrubbed and her eyes red and sat him down at the table and put the bread in front of him and the buttermilk, and while he ate she brought the dented washpan, and knelt, and washed his feet, the way she did every day, and dried them on her apron. Then she stood up with the pan in her two hands. Brother Isom, she said. Sam is sick. I want to put this water on my boy’s head. He looked at the pan. He looked at the child in the corner on the pallet with his throat working. If he had a thought about it, it did not get as far as his face. Put it, then, he said. She poured it on the boy’s head, all of it, and it ran down into his ears and his collar and the tick of the pallet, gray with the dust of my bluff, and I let him go. He sat up coughing and hollered for his mother, and she grabbed him to her wet and all and rocked him there on the floor, and the preacher finished his bread, and thanked her for it, and put his shoes back round his neck, and went out the gate. I was at my door before him.

sections.heading: V. Root Doctor
sections.dateline: The mouth of the cave · afternoon
sections.text: It had rained in the night and the fringe was coming off the ledge, a line of drops all across the mouth, and the flat rock inside it was dark with wet. He came up the last of the path saying the bones, the marrow, the kidneys, and stooped under the ledge, and I stood up in my own door and said it with all I had. Doctor! Root doctor! Don’t you come in here! He stopped where he was, on the flat rock, with the drops coming down all round him. Who is that? It’s me that lives here. And I watched him do what I had done. I watched him turn and look back along his own life, the whole length of it, from the river in 1866 to the rock he was standing on, looking for the day he doctored anybody. He took his time. He looked the way an honest man counts money that isn’t his. I never doctored nobody, he said. You never? Never. Then I will tell you. Tell me. Stand back from my door first. Now. Didn’t Viney Hollins this very day take the water she washed your feet in and pour it on her boy’s head, when he was took? She did. Well. Is that what you mean? That is what I mean. Then something happened in him that I had never seen happen in anybody, living or dead. I had gone over his life three times w

sections.heading: VI. Little Zion
sections.dateline: The district association, under the beeches · August 1884
sections.text: I have been other places since. But I went to the association first, in August, because I wanted to see what they would make of him. It met that year at Little Zion, in the grove, with tables of dinner under the trees and the preachers of eleven churches on the benches and the people standing all round, and Brother Isom came walking in on the third day out of the woods with his shoes round his neck. They asked him had he finished what he went to do. He said he had. Then they made him tell it, the cave and Viney and the foot water and the woman at the door, and he told it the way he told everything, without any shine on it. And she called you a root doctor, said one of the preachers, right to your face. And you were not angry. No. Not at all? No. The preachers looked at each other. They went to the front bench where Mother Easter Tolliver was sitting with her stick between her knees, ninety years old, so small her feet did not reach the ground, and the oldest of them bent down and said it to her low. Mother, that boy is telling a story. Any man would have got mad. Mother Easter did not look up at him. She was looking at Isom, across the grove, where he stood by himself at the edge o

title: Foot Water
place: Green River bluffs, Hart County, Kentucky
logline: The woman who has kept a Green River cave for thirty years tells how she tried to drive out the praying man who sat in her door.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who finds no fault with other beings, whether feeble or strong, and does not kill nor cause slaughter.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a monk takes a meditation subject from the Buddha into the forest and becomes an arahant. Walking back to tell the Teacher, he passes through a village where a wife has just quarreled with her husband and set out for her family’s house; she follows close behind the monk, who never once looks at her. The husband catches up, decides the monk has taken her, and beats him badly while she protests that the monk never looked at her or spoke. Back at the monastery, the monks who rub his weals ask whether he got angry. He says he did not, and they go to the Buddha to report that he is lying. The Buddha answers that those free of the pollutants have laid down the rod and feel no anger even toward those who strike them.
bg.hist_title: The Mennonites of the Skippack and Salford, 1777–1778
bg.history:
The Swiss and South German Mennonites who settled the Skippack, Salford and Franconia country north of Philadelphia had in 1725 adopted the Dutch Dordrecht Confession of 1632 as their own; its articles on revenge and on oaths bound them to refuse both the sword and the swearing of oaths. The Revolution tested both. Pennsylvania’s Test Act of June 1777 required an oath or affirmation of allegiance and stripped those who refused of many civil rights, and men who would not muster paid fines. The Franconia Conference divided in 1778 when the minister Christian Funk, who argued for paying the war tax, was put out of office. The quotation in the story is from the English translation of the Confession by Joseph F. Sohm, printed with the Martyrs Mirror in 1886. In Franconia practice, ministers were chosen by lot, with a slip of paper hidden in one of several hymnbooks.

In the fall of 1777 the British took Philadelphia, and Washington’s army spent the winter at Valley Forge. In January 1778 the Pennsylvania Supreme Executive Council made John Lacey a brigadier general of militia, and his men patrolled the country between the Delaware and the Schuylkill to keep farmers from carrying produce into the occupied city, where the British paid in hard money. On May 1, 1778, British troops surprised Lacey’s camp at the Battle of Crooked Billet. The Hunsbergers, Detweiler, the Schlossers and the egg wagon in the story are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Wall
sections.text: They have put you in the row by your father, Velte, and the clay is so wet it shines. I am standing outside the wall because I have stood outside it for fifty-two years and my legs do not know another place to stand. Your brother Abraham’s widow is inside, by the hole, with her hands in her apron. She saw me come up the lane. She knows what I have under my shawl. She is the only one living who does. Nobody in there will say anything over you that is about you. That is your people’s way, and it was my mother’s, and it was mine until I was nineteen and married Philip Schlosser at the Reformed church on the Skippack Road. A preacher read. They sang a long hymn out of the thick book, lined out, one line and then all of them after it. Then the men took up the shovels. The boards they let you down on were planed. That is the whole of it. You were seventy-three. I have things to say to you that I did not say on the road, because on the road you never once turned around.

sections.heading: II. The Road
sections.dateline: The Great Road below the Swamp · April 1778
sections.text: That spring the English had the city and our army was starving at the Valley Forge, twenty miles off, and the militia under General Lacey was riding the roads between the two rivers to stop farmers from carrying anything into Philadelphia, where the English paid in hard money. Philip was a sergeant in it. He was a smith by trade, and he shod the militia horses for nothing, and on his nights home he talked about the Mennists. Non-jurors, he called them, because they would not take the Test oath, and Tories, which they were not, and other things. Your people paid the fines for not mustering. Your people would not take Continental paper if they could help it. Most of them would not pay the war tax either, and up at Franconia there was trouble over Preacher Funk, who said they should. Philip had all this by heart. He said it at the table with his mouth full. On the fourteenth of April he came home and told me, as a good joke, that he and four men had stopped a wagon on the Salford road that morning going down to the city with butter and eggs, and the wagon belonged to an old Mennist widow, and they had made her stand and watch while they broke every egg in the road and tipped the butte

sections.heading: III. The Axe
sections.text: Philip came up behind us at the ford below the mill, riding one of the militia horses. He had his hickory stick, the one he carried for dogs, as thick as a woman’s wrist at the knob end and worn dark where his hand went. He did not say anything to me. He rode past me and pulled the horse across the road in front of you and got down. Where are you taking her. You looked at him. You did not look at me even then. I said, Philip, he never looked at me. He never said one word. I walked behind him on my own. Leave him be. So you took yourself off, he said, behind a Mennist. And then, and I have heard it every day since: Then he can have what you have coming. Velte, I have told this to nobody but Barbara and my own daughter, and now you. You took the axe off your shoulder. Philip stepped back, and I thought, God help us, now. And you bent and laid it down in the road. You did not drop it. You laid it down the way my mother laid a loaf on the board, with the bit turned toward the ditch and the helve along the wheel rut, where no hand could come at it quickly, not his, not yours. You put the bundle beside it. Then you stood up and let your hands hang. He beat you across the back and shoulde

sections.heading: IV. What Barbara Told Me
sections.dateline: Abraham Hunsberger’s kitchen, Lower Salford · that night
sections.text: Barbara told me the rest in 1811, at my mother’s burying, when I had come back for the first time and stood at this same wall. She came out to me through the gate. She said, You are the one from the ford, and I said I was, and she told it to me the way you would hand a woman back something she had dropped. You came in after dark. Abraham was at the table, and your brothers Jacob and Christian, and Barbara at the fire. You had been the whole winter in the Swamp, cutting cordwood for your aunt Anna, a widow on a timber lot past the Milford line with nobody to cut for her, and they had not seen you since the first snow. You set the axe in its corner. You said you would eat later. You said you had to go over to the old preacher’s in the morning and tell him something. Barbara saw the blood come through your shirt when you sat. She got the shirt off you, and it was stuck. She said the weals stood up on your back like the ribs in corduroy, so many that she started counting to keep her hands steady, and stopped at thirty because there was no more back to count on. She warmed goose grease in a saucer and put it on with two fingers while the boys held the candle. Who did this. You told them

sections.heading: V. The Loom
sections.dateline: The weaver’s house on the Indian Creek road · the next morning
sections.text: Barbara went with them, because she had the saucer of goose grease in her apron and meant to take it on to you after. So she heard it. Detweiler was past seventy. He had been a weaver all his life and a preacher since 1742, when the lot fell on him: the slip of paper in the hymnbook, the one with the verse on it, The lot is cast into the lap. He used to say the lot had made a mistake and been too proud to take it back. He was at his loom when they came in, throwing the shuttle, and he did not stop. Abraham told it. The smith, the ford, thirty weals and more. And then: He says he was not angry. We think he is lying. We have come to you because it is a lie in the face of the whole congregation, and we do not know what to do with a brother who lies about a thing like that. The old man threw the shuttle and beat the weft up with the batten and threw it back. Was it you, he said, who sent him to the Swamp? Or was it me? It was you. It was me. In November. He came here with his fists like this. He showed them, without letting go of the shuttle. He had been in the road when the militia took the Bergeys’ horses, and he wanted to hit somebody, and he was frightened of how much. So I gave hi

sections.heading: VI. The Stick
sections.text: Philip died in the fall of 1811 at the forge, of his heart, with the tongs in his hand. I buried him in the Reformed ground on the Skippack Road under a stone with his name on it and a willow, because that is what we do. The stick hung behind the forge door for thirty-three years. He never carried it again after that April. I do not say that means anything. He did not say. Some days I thought he was ashamed of it, and some days I thought he was keeping it the way a man keeps a gun he has used. When he died I took it into the house. My daughter wanted it for the fire. I said no. I have had it in the corner by my bed for seventeen years, and every winter I have asked myself why, and the answer I have come to is that I was waiting to give it back to somebody, and there was only ever one person it could go to. The men are filling you in now. Barbara is looking at me. She is near eighty and she still holds her apron the same way, as if there were a saucer in it. I am going to go in at the gate, Velte, the first time since I was nineteen. Nobody will stop me. Your people do not stop anybody; that was always the trouble with them, Philip said. I am going to walk up the row to the new clay

title: The Hickory Stick
logline: At a Mennonite burial in 1828, a smith's widow tells the dead man what she saw at a ford in the war spring of 1778.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who is tolerant with the intolerant, mild with fault-finders, and free from passion among the passionate.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a brahmin’s wife cooks for four venerable brahmins and sends her husband to the monastery to fetch them; he is given four seven-year-old novices who are already arahants, Saṁkicca, Paṇḍita, Sopāka and Revata. Furious, she sets them on low seats and sends him for elders. Sāriputta comes, sees the novices unfed, says they ought to be fed first, and leaves with his bowl; Mahā Moggallāna does the same. The husband then brings an old brahmin from another sect, who is Sakka, king of the gods, in disguise. He bows to the novices with the five limbs and sits on the ground beside them; the couple beat him and drag him out, but he is still sitting in the same place. When he makes himself known, they serve the meal, and the four novices leave through the gable, the front and back of the roof and the earth, while Sakka goes another way; the place is called the House with the Five Openings. The monks doubt that the novices felt no anger, and the Buddha answers with the verse.
bg.hist_title: A shraddha in the western suburbs, 1987
bg.history:
A shraddha is the Hindu rite for dead ancestors, held on the anniversary of a death by the lunar calendar and in the fortnight of the ancestors each year. In many families invited brahmins are fed as the ancestors’ guests, and rice balls (pinda) are set out for crows; a crow taking the offering is widely read as a sign that the ancestor is satisfied. A boy of a brahmin family becomes eligible to take part in rites after his upanayana, the sacred-thread ceremony, called munj in Marathi; the Laws of Manu set the brahmin boy’s initiation in the eighth year after conception, so a newly initiated boy is often seven. Manu’s chapters on the student and on the shraddha (II and III) supply the scripture of the story, in Georg Bühler’s translation for the Sacred Books of the East (1886), with its well-known lines on caste and on women that the teacher in the story has to read past.

Indian immigration to the United States grew quickly after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended national-origin quotas, and many of the engineers, doctors and scientists who came settled in suburbs such as Woodridge in DuPage County, near Argonne National Laboratory and the research corridor along the East-West Tollway. Through the 1970s and 1980s these families built their first temples in houses and in churches bought from shrinking congregations, and the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago, which had met in homes and rented halls in Downers Grove and Romeoville, opened its temple at Lemont in July 1986. The temple, the Joglekars, the boys and their teacher in the story are fictional.

sections.heading: I. Notice of Loss
sections.dateline: Prairie State Mutual, Downers Grove office · Monday, September 14, 1987
sections.text: Claim no. 87-DU-31906 · Policy HO-3 · Insured Shrikant V. and Vasanti S. Joglekar, 7 Juniper Court, Woodridge, IL · Taken by phone, B. Nowak. Date of loss Sat 9/12/87, approx. 2:30 p.m. Type Other. Description (insured’s words) “Five openings. One in the attic gable, one in the front of the roof, one in the back of the roof, one in the basement floor. The fifth one we cannot find.” No storm reported in DuPage on 9/12. No fire. No vehicle. No tree. Insured states no one was hurt. Insured asked twice whether the company would need to know who was in the house. Advised adjuster will call. Assigned D. Hajek, field. Note Tarp on roof per insured. Rain forecast Wed.

sections.heading: II. Recorded Statement
sections.dateline: Shrikant Joglekar, taken at the kitchen table · Tuesday, September 15
sections.text: Please state your name and occupation for the tape. Shrikant Vishnu Joglekar. I am a process engineer at Argonne. Not a scientist. I want that on the tape. I make the equipment do what the scientists drew. Tell me about Saturday, Mr. Joglekar. Take your time. Saturday was my father’s shraddha. The yearly rite for the dead. He died in Pune last September, on this tithi, this day of the moon, and we could not go. Two tickets were twenty-one hundred dollars and our daughter had just started high school. So this was the first year. My wife had cooked since Thursday. You have to feed Brahmins at a shraddha. The Brahmins eat and the fathers are fed. My mother always had four. My wife wanted four. Brahmins meaning priests. Meaning men of that caste who know the rites. In Pune you send a boy down the lane. Here there are perhaps eleven in the whole western suburbs, and in September every one of them is at a wedding in Schaumburg. So Saturday morning she sent me to the mandir. The temple. It is in the old Lutheran church on Seventy-Fifth Street, they bought it in 1984, you have seen it, there is still the cross-shaped window. I went to the office and said to the volunteer, Mr. Pandya, I nee

sections.heading: III. Dispatch Log
sections.dateline: Village of Woodridge Police · Saturday, September 12
sections.text: 14:22 911 call, 7 Juniper Ct. Female caller screaming, also second female voice (juvenile?) in background. Caller states “a man will not leave, we put him out and he is still sitting.” Caller asked if man is armed. Caller states no, he is old. Caller asked if anyone hurt. Caller states “we hit him, he is not hurt, he is waving his hands.” Unit 4 dispatched. 14:24 Same caller back on line. States “no assistance needed, we know who he is now.” Line disconnected. 14:31 Unit 4 on scene. Spoke w/ RP and husband at door. RP states misunderstanding w/ elderly family guest. Officer did not observe guest. Officer observed four male juveniles seated in living room, approx. 7 yrs, eating. No complaint. Unit 4 clear.

sections.heading: IV. Statement of the Insured
sections.dateline: Vasanti Joglekar, handwritten, eleven pages · Wednesday, September 16
sections.text: Mrs. Hajek, you asked me to write it because I could not say it into the machine. I will write all of it. My husband is a good man and he left out the part that is mine. My father-in-law, Appa, I lived with him for nineteen years in Pune before we came here. He taught me to drive a scooter. He ate my food every day for nineteen years and said every day, Salt is a little less, and every day the salt was correct. When he was dying they phoned us at three in the morning and the line was so bad I could hear the sea in it. We did not go. We had the money, really. We did not go because of tuition and because of the cost and because we told each other next year. So this was the first shraddha, and I thought, this one at least I will do correctly. The book says the fathers come and sit near the Brahmins when they are seated. Appa was going to come and sit in my living room. I wanted to give him the best chairs. Then my husband brought me four children. I was so angry I could feel it in my teeth. My mother used to say that kind of anger is like salt thrown on the coals, it spits, and I was spitting. I put the children on the garage stools. I did not give them water. A Brahmin must not take

sections.dateline: Kowalczyk Roofing & Siding, Lisle · Thursday, September 17

No footprints in insulation. Opening 2. Front slope, approx. 4 ft below ridge. Round, approx. 14″ dia. Shingles, felt and 1/2″ plywood cut clean, no splinter, no debris on roof or in attic below. Patch decking, felt, 1 bundle 3-tab, brown blend (match not guaranteed). Opening 3. Rear slope, same, approx. 14″. Same. Opening 4. Basement floor slab by furnace. Round, approx. 14″. sections.heading: VI. Letter
sections.dateline: Vasudha Phadke, graduate student, University of Chicago · Monday, September 21
sections.text: Dear Mrs. Hajek, Mr. Pandya at the temple gave me your number and said you would like a statement from the boys, since they were present. Their parents have asked me to answer for them, because I teach the Saturday class and they are seven. I am a graduate student, not a priest. I teach the boys their sandhya, their morning and evening prayers, how to say them and roughly what they mean. I can tell you what they told me and what happened at class. They came back to the hall at ten past four. Their names are Aniket, Mihir, Rohan and Sameer. Sameer had a Cubs cap. They were fed and happy and a little sleepy. They did not seem to think anything unusual had happened, except that the lady had given them the dining chairs after a while, and the kheer was very good, and an old man had bowed to them, which they found funny. The older boys in the class, who are twelve and thirteen, had heard by then from somebody’s mother about the stools, and the five hours, and the two priests walking out. They asked the little ones, Weren’t you mad at her? And all four said no. And the older boys came to me together and said, Vasudha-tai, they are lying. Anybody would be mad. Five hours on a garage stool
