title: Cause Undetermined
logline: An insurance claim file on four round holes in a Woodridge split-level, opened the day of a Marathi family's first shraddha.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana from whom anger and hatred, pride and envy have dropt like a mustard seed from the point of a needle.

bg.commentary: This is a sequel to Little Wayland (commentary 2.3). In the Dhammapada commentary, the elder Mahā Panthaka expels his younger brother Culla Panthaka from the monastery when, after four months, he still cannot learn a single verse. After Culla Panthaka’s sudden awakening, the monks gossip that even a fully awakened elder like Mahā Panthaka must sometimes feel anger. The Buddha corrects them: those who have destroyed the defilements have no anger, and Mahā Panthaka acted only because he put the meaning and the teaching before everything else.
bg.history:
Caddo Springs is fictional, set on the Tombigbee in the western Black Belt, named for its band of rich dark soil, where cotton plantations held the largest numbers of enslaved people. Demopolis and Linden, the real towns mentioned, are in Marengo County; Demopolis stands on the Tombigbee. Royce Pettaway, the veteran, fought at the Chosin Reservoir in Korea in the winter of 1950, two years after President Truman’s Executive Order 9981 ordered the desegregation of the armed forces, a change carried out largely during the Korean War.

The men of the grove go out each morning with tin pails and stand silent at back doors, as Buddhist monks go on the alms round; in 1950s Alabama the back door was also the door of segregation, where Black visitors were expected to call at white homes. The scripture Hattie Greer quotes at the stove is 1 Corinthians 13:4–5 in the King James Version: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind … is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.”

sections.heading: I. The Count
sections.dateline: The grove on the Tombigbee · August 1959
sections.text: By Monday the men in the grove had told it to each other so many times that it had worn smooth, like a step. They told it at the well in the morning, filling the buckets. They told it walking into Caddo Springs with their tin pails, two by two, along the sand road. They told it at night by the fire on the riverbank, where Brother Sutton was not, because Brother Sutton had walked up to Demopolis on Sunday to sit with a dying man and had not come back. They told it about Wayland. Put him out, said the man from Sumter County, whose name was Ike Walley, and who had sharecropped cotton for thirty years for a man who once docked him a week for a broken hoe handle. His own brother. Walked him out past the last row like you’d walk a dog off to shoot it. He wasn’t ugly about it, somebody said. That’s what I’m saying. That’s worse. The veteran, Royce Pettaway, who had been at the Chosin Reservoir and did not sleep, said nothing for a long time, and then said the thing they had all been coming around to. Doctor asked him how many. He said forty-nine. Little was standing at the well with a bucket in his hand, fifty feet off. Forty-nine. The white boy from Mobile, Dale, with the burn scars up b

sections.heading: II. The Back Doors
sections.text: It went into town with them. That was how things went in Caddo Springs; you could not set a word down on the sand road without it walking itself up to Depot Street by noon. Marcus Coleman, who was eleven and had seen the grove full of men and had not slept right since, told it in the barbershop on Depot Street on Tuesday, the part about the grove and the part about the gate, and when the barber asked him why Little had not been at the supper in the first place, he told that too. By Wednesday the women at Mount Pisgah knew it. By Wednesday night it had gone up the hill. Wayland walked his road every morning that week, the same as always, the road he had set for himself, which was the long one, out past the gin to the Negro quarter by the tracks and then up the back alley behind the big houses on the hill. He stood at back doors with his tin pail and his eyes on the ground and took what people gave, and said thank you either way, the way Brother Sutton had taught them. Some doors gave him the same as always. Some doors that had always given him something gave him nothing that week, and looked at him a while through the screen first, so that he would know it was not for lack of biscui

sections.heading: III. The Face
sections.text: Here is what Wayland knew, and did not say, because nobody asked him, and because a man who stands up to explain himself has already started to tell a story about himself, and he had come out to the grove to stop doing that. He knew he had watched his brother for four months with the lily verse. He had heard him at the well and in the outhouse and walking the sand road and in his sleep, saying the first two lines and losing the second two, every day, over and over, like a man bailing a boat with a sieve. He had watched it wear Little down. He had seen him stop eating. He had seen him sit at the back during Brother Sutton’s talks with his hands between his knees and his face shut, a boy who could name every bird on the river by the sound of its wings, being made to feel stupid every day by the one thing in the world he loved. Wayland knew, because he had been out to the grove three years and had watched men come and go, that a man can sit under the pecans until he dies and get nothing out of it but sore knees and shame, and that the shame is worse than the drinking it replaced. He had seen two men go back to the bottle from it. He did not intend to see his brother go. And he knew th

sections.heading: IV. The Needle
sections.text: Brother Sutton came back from Demopolis on Thursday night, and Friday morning he walked into town with his tin pail like any other man, and his road that day, for no reason anybody could see, took him up the alley to the Pruett kitchen. Hattie Greer was putting up pickles. It was the time of year for it. There were cucumbers soaking in a crock of brine on the floor, and quart jars in a row on the table, and a bowl of little yellow mustard seed, and dill, and garlic, and the whole kitchen smelled of vinegar coming to a boil. She had a needle stuck in the front of her apron, because she had been letting out the seam in Mrs. Pruett’s housedress between batches, and she was in no humor for anybody. She opened the screen for him. She would not have opened it for anybody else from the grove that week. She put a biscuit in his pail with more force than a biscuit needs. You come about Wayland, she said. I come for breakfast, said Sutton. But go ahead. She went ahead. She told him about carrying the two of them up the carriage house stairs in 1952 with paper tags pinned to their jackets. She told him about Little’s wandering sums and the old man setting the tablet down like it might break.

sections.heading: V. The Fire
sections.text: That night by the fire they started in on it again, because it had become the thing they did by the fire, the way some men whittle. Ike Walley said it. Dale said it. Mr. Teague said his piece about how it is still in there, even in the best one, and Royce Pettaway said forty-nine. Wayland was not there. He had walked out to the Mabry gate after supper to sit with the man from Linden, who had come back and was sleeping by the road, to tell him there was a place for him now. Brother Sutton came down from his cot and stood at the edge of the firelight with his hands in his pockets, and they did not hear him until he spoke. What are y’all sitting here talking about? They told him. It took a while, because they each told their part, and they had had a week to get good at it. He listened to the whole thing with his head a little to one side, the way he listened to everything, as if it were music from a long way off and he was trying to make out the tune. No, he said, when they were done. It was quiet enough to hear the river. That man doesn’t have it in him, Sutton said. Not mean, not proud, not jealous. Not the thing you saw on his face Saturday either, Dale. I saw his face too. I was l

sections.heading: VI. The Roll
sections.text: The reporter from Birmingham came down in the spring of 1983, twenty-four years later, because Marcus Coleman, who was a doctor himself by then, with his father’s practice on Hackberry Street, had told him the story of the full grove over a long lunch at a medical meeting, and the reporter had thought it would make a Sunday feature. He drove out to the Mabry place in a rented Chevrolet. Brother Sutton had been dead nine years and was buried at the edge of the pecans under a fieldstone with nothing on it. Little Reed talked to the men under the trees in the afternoons now, and there were seventy of them, and people came from as far as Atlanta to sit at the back. Little would not talk to the reporter about himself. He said he did not have anything to say about himself that the reporter would find interesting, and went down to the river. So the reporter talked to Wayland. Wayland was forty-four. He still kept the roll and set the roads, and he still walked the long one himself every morning with a tin pail, out past where the gin had been to the houses by the tracks and up the back alleys on the hill, where some of the back doors were opened now by the grandchildren of the people who

title: No Guile
logline: The week after the grove filled with Little, the whole county decides his older brother Wayland put him out from jealousy.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who utters true speech, instructive and free from harshness, so that he offend no one.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the elder Pilindavaccha greets everyone he meets, monks and laypeople alike, with vasala, the word for an outcaste: “Come, outcaste! Go, outcaste!” The monks complain to the Buddha, who calls him in and asks whether it is true. “Yes, venerable sir, it is true.” The Buddha tells the monks not to take offense. Vaccha has no hatred in him; he was born a brahmin in five hundred lives running, and the word is only the habit of all those lives. One who has rid himself of the defilements never uses words meant to wound. Then he speaks the verse, and many who hear it enter the stream. Other sources call Pilindavaccha the disciple most dear to the gods. Read the full commentary story, the same episode in the Udāna (3.6), or the entry on Pilindavaccha in the Dictionary of Pāli Proper Names.
bg.history:
The Thomas Fire of December 2017 destroyed more than a thousand structures in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, among them homes in the canyons along Highway 33 above Ojai. A year and more later, many owners were still living in trailers on their lots while they fought their insurers for the money to rebuild. On January 17, 2019, a winter storm pushed the Ventura River, which is dry most of the year, over its banks near its mouth and flooded an RV park beside the freeway. The Tuesday crew, its church, Dana Whitcomb and the Combs family are invented. Mr. Penrose comes from Fire Year; his cottage is in the Taormina community, built as a retirement colony for Theosophists beside Krotona, with French Norman cottages and gas lamps along its lanes. The Seabees’ home base was the Naval Construction Battalion Center at Port Hueneme.

Walt’s word comes a long way. The great revival at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in 1801, which drew close to ten thousand people, made the outdoor revival a fixture of American Protestant life, and the tent revival carried it into the twentieth century. In the 1930s the Dust Bowl and the Depression brought more than a million “Okie” migrants to California, most of them Baptist, with Methodist and Pentecostal minorities. Some found work in the oil fields; the Ventura Avenue field, in the hills along the river north of Ventura, was among the most productive in the country by the 1950s. Horatio Palmer’s Sunday-school hymn “Angry Words” appeared in 1867 and went into more than a hundred hymnals.

sections.heading: I. Sinner
sections.text: Walt Combs called everybody sinner. Morning, sinner, to the crew coming up the drive at seven with their coffee. Hand me that flat bar, sinner. Watch your feet there, sinner, that’s a nail. He said it to the driver from the lumberyard in Ventura and to the county inspector who came out to sign off on a set of steps. He said it to the young pastor. He said it to the pastor’s wife when she brought sandwiches up at noon in a cardboard flat: Thank you, sinner, these look good. He said it to his blue heeler, Buck, who rode to every job on the passenger side of the truck, and to his worm-drive saw when it bound in wet wood. He was eighty-four years old. He had been a finish carpenter in Ventura County since 1958, a good deal of the staircase between Ventura and Ojai was his, and you could not get a thumbnail into a single joint of it. The Tuesday crew had been going out from the little Presbyterian church off Highway 33 every week since the Thomas Fire. There were six of them that spring, all retired. They did the jobs too small for a contractor to drive out for and too odd for the insurance to pay for: a ramp, steps up to a trailer door, a fence to keep a neighbor’s horses off a lot whe

sections.heading: II. The Ramp
sections.text: The second week of March they built a ramp for Mr. Penrose. He lived in one of the little French-looking cottages at Taormina, beside the Theosophists’ grounds on the west side of town, where the roofs flared out at the eaves and there were gas lamps on posts along the lanes. He was eighty-eight. He had fallen in the autumn and come home from the hospital with a walker, and there were three brick steps up to his door that he could no longer manage. The cottage had not burned. He had spent the worst of the fire on a cot at the fairgrounds in Ventura, he told Linda, and come home before Christmas to find it standing, with ash on the windowsills and a dead hummingbird in the birdbath. He had wiped the windowsills and buried the hummingbird and gone on. Walt called him sinner from the first minute. Morning, sinner, when Mr. Penrose opened the door in a cardigan buttoned to the throat. Mind the cord, sinner. You want the rail on this side or that side, sinner? Good morning, Mr. Combs, said Mr. Penrose. That side, please. Gary winced every time. It took two Tuesdays to frame the ramp and deck it and set the rails, and Mr. Penrose sat in a chair in his doorway the whole time and watched t

sections.heading: III. The Complaint
sections.text: Dana Whitcomb’s letter came to the church office on a Monday in April. The young pastor printed it out and gave it to Joan, and Joan read it and put it in her shirt pocket behind the flashlight. Dana’s house had burned the first night the fire came over into the canyons, in December of 2017. She had been at work, managing a dental office in Ventura, and by the time she got to the roadblock on 33 they would not let her through, and by morning there was nothing up the canyon to go through to. She had lived in a trailer on the slab for sixteen months. Her insurance company had paid her for the contents and was still arguing with her about the house. Her husband had moved to Bakersfield in the fall. The crew had built her steps and a deck for the trailer and a shed and part of a fence, seven Tuesdays in all, and Walt had called her sinner on every one of them. I am grateful, she wrote. I want to be clear about that. I am not a member of your church and you came anyway, and I’ll never forget it. But I have been called a lot of things since the fire, by the insurance company and the county and people who think I should have taken the check and moved to Bakersfield too. I have tried to be

sections.heading: IV. Sinners Welcome
sections.dateline: The canyon above Meiners Oaks · May 2019
sections.text: Joan drove up to Dana’s on a Thursday by herself and sat on the new steps and told her. It did not take long. Dana listened with her arms folded and said she didn’t know. She said she would think about it. She said she had been raised Catholic in Oxnard and nobody had said the word sinner to her face since her First Confession, and she hadn’t liked it then either. The hills had come back green over the winter, as green as anybody could remember, and in April the wild mustard came up yellow across the whole burn, so thick on the slope behind Dana’s slab that you could not see the black on the oaks unless you went right up to them. The oaks were putting out leaves straight from their trunks, in tufts. By the middle of May the sun on the slab was something you had to get out of before noon. The crew came up the last Tuesday of the month to finish the fence, and Walt brought a shade. He had a barn on a lot behind his house in Oak View where he kept things, and in the barn, folded on a pallet under a tarp, was the last of his daddy’s tent. The rest of it had gone over lumber piles on job sites for sixty years and worn out a piece at a time. This was the last piece, about twenty feet by

title: Sinners Welcome
logline: On a church crew rebuilding after the Thomas Fire, an old carpenter calls everyone sinner, and a new volunteer starts keeping count.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who takes nothing in the world that is not given him, be it long or short, small or large, good or bad.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a Brahmin of Sāvatthī takes off his outer cloth so that it will not catch the smell of his body, lays it aside, and sits down facing his house. A monk who is an arahant passes, sees the cloth and no owner, and takes it for a cast-off rag of the kind monks made their robes from. The Brahmin runs up shouting that he is a thief; the monk asks if it is his and hands it back. When he tells the story at the monastery the other monks tease him: was it long or short, coarse or fine? He answers that he has no attachment to it either way, and they report him to the Buddha as a liar. The Buddha says he speaks the truth: those who are free of the pollutants do not take what belongs to others.
bg.history:
Twice a year through the middle of the nineteenth century the Métis of the Red River country, French- and Michif-speaking Catholic families of mixed Indigenous and European descent, gathered at Pembina, just south of the forty-ninth parallel, and went out onto the plains of what is now North Dakota after buffalo. The great hunt of 1840, described by Alexander Ross, counted 1,210 carts and 1,630 people and reached the Sheyenne River nine days out. The hunters elected captains, soldiers and guides; a flag raised in the morning meant march and lowered in the evening meant camp; the Red River carts, built without iron and never greased, were drawn up at night in a circle with the shafts outward. Women cut and dried the meat and made the pemmican.

The laws of the hunt in the story are those recorded for the hunt of 1840, ending with the one on theft: “even to the value of a sinew,” the offender was brought to the middle of the camp and the crier called out his or her name three times, adding the word “Thief.” Priests rode with some hunts and not others. The arrow sash, the ceinture fléchée, was finger-woven at L'Assomption in Lower Canada, sold through the fur companies, and worn over the blue capote. The autumn hunt of 1847 in the story, and everyone on it, are invented. Lemaître de Sacy's French Bible, made in the seventeenth century, was the most widely read French Catholic translation of the period.

sections.heading: I. Le Ramasseux
sections.dateline: Pembina to the Sheyenne River · September 1847
sections.text: Isidore was fifteen that fall and belonged to no cart. His mother had died the summer before, and his father he knew only as a name other people remembered. When the hunt went out from Pembina he went with it on foot, behind the last of two hundred carts, in the noise of their dry axles, which a person could hear for half a day's ride across the plain. A camp on the move sheds like a dog. Something fell off every cart every mile: a linchpin, a child's moccasin, an awl, a tin cup, a twist of tobacco, a strap. Isidore walked at the back and picked it all up. When the guide's flag came down in the evening and the carts drew into their circle with the shafts turned out, he went around the inside of it holding each thing over his head and calling À qui? À qui ça? until somebody put out a hand. What nobody claimed by dark he used, or gave to whoever was nearest. His capote had been three men's before it was his. So they called him le Ramasseux, the one who picks up. He ate at any fire that had room. He cut meat for any woman who handed him a knife. He was not sad, which bothered some people, and he never seemed to be holding anything, which they did not notice until later. No priest rode

sections.heading: II. The Sash
sections.dateline: Camp on the Sheyenne · the day after the first run
sections.text: They ran buffalo nine days out, and the next morning the whole camp was meat. The women had it cut thin as cloth and hung on the racks, with slow fires under, and the smoke and the smell of fat lay over the carts and got into everything. Narcisse Laframboise was twenty, from White Horse Plain, and owned the best sash on the hunt. It was an Assomption sash, wool, fine as a woman's hair ribbon, red with the arrow pattern down it in blue and white and yellow, and he had been two winters paying for it. He would not have it in that smoke, and he would not have it on him while he worked and take the smell of his own sweat. He carried it fifty steps outside the circle to the creek and hung it on a buffaloberry bush in the clean wind. Then he went and sat behind his cart, facing his tent, to scrape a hide. Isidore came along the creek with two kettles. He saw a sash on a bush. He looked up the bank and down it and across the water and saw no one. Another boy would have thought, that is too good to be lost. It did not come into Isidore's head. He had picked up a silver thimble and a broken trace in the same morning, once, and held them up exactly alike. The thing was there and its person wa

sections.heading: III. Long or Short
sections.dateline: The same evening, at the fires
sections.text: Isidore told it himself, at the first fire he sat down to, the way he would have told that he had found a cup. The boys his own age had it off him in a minute. So, Ramasseux. This sash you took. Was it a long one or a short one? Was it fine or coarse? Did it have arrows on it? What color? Come on, you had it in your two hands. I don't know, Isidore said. Red. Never mind if it was long or short. I thought it was left. They howled. There was not a child on the hunt who could not have told you that sash to the thread: the length, twice around Narcisse and down to his knee, the fringe, the blue next to the white. But the older boys did not laugh, and two of the soldiers, who had been listening, did not either. He's lying, one of them said. Nobody alive takes that sash off a bush and doesn't look at it. He looked. He wanted it, he took it, and he gave it back because he was caught. That was another matter. That was the law, and the middle of the camp, and a name called three times. They got up and went to the captains' fire, and took the boy with them, and Narcisse came, and half the camp behind. The captains listened and then sent for old Josephte. She said the prayers, evenings and Su

title: A Sinew's Worth
logline: On a Métis buffalo hunt where theft of even a sinew is cried in camp, an orphan boy takes a fine sash off a bush.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who fosters no desires for this world or for the next, has no inclinations, and is unshackled.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Elder Sāriputta spends the rains retreat at a monastery with five hundred monks, and the lay people there promise him all the requisites. When the season ends, not everything has come. As he leaves to see the Buddha, he asks the monks to send on whatever is brought for the young monks and novices, or else to send him word. The monks decide that craving must still be alive in him. The Buddha tells them it is not so: Sāriputta was thinking only that the givers should not lose the merit of their gift, and that the young ones should not lose what was rightly theirs. Read the full commentary story, or about Sāriputta, the disciple who looked after the newly ordained. The commentary tells the same story next of Moggallāna; in this series that is Field Tickets.
bg.history:
From the 1910s the Santa Fe and other railroads recruited Mexican men to build and maintain their lines in Kansas, many from Michoacán, Jalisco and Guanajuato, housing them in converted boxcars or shacks beside the tracks. Colonies grew up at the division points, and at Newton the Santa Fe housed Mexican families along West First Street from about 1911, in the neighborhood people called the Ranchito. Harvey County was also the heart of Kansas Mennonite country; Russian Mennonites settled there in the 1870s with the Santa Fe's help and brought hard winter wheat with them. In 1931 Kansas grew the largest wheat crop in its history, 251 million bushels, and the farm price fell to about 33 cents a bushel.

Between 1929 and 1939, most likely somewhere between half a million and a million people of Mexican descent, forty to sixty percent of them American citizens, left or were pushed out of the United States in what is called the Mexican Repatriation, through deportation, relief cuts, pressure from employers and local officials, and cheap train fares to the border; 1931 was the peak year. Many Mexican readers in the United States followed the San Antonio daily La Prensa. Amado Nervo (1870–1919), one of the best-known Mexican poets of his time, wrote “En paz” in 1915. Parcels went by the Railway Express Agency, the express company sixty-nine railroads took over in 1929.

sections.heading: I. The Crossing
sections.dateline: Kesler siding, Harvey County, Kansas · July 1931
sections.text: The Kesler section was eight miles of the Santa Fe main line west of Newton, double track on crushed rock across wheat country so flat that a man tamping ties at one end of it could see the water tank at the other end, wavering. Don Feliciano Arreola had been its foreman since 1919. He had a gang of eleven men, a motor car that started on the third pull, a tool house, and four old boxcars set off at the end of the siding on short rails of their own, with stovepipes through their roofs and little windows the men had cut with a keyhole saw and hung with flour-sack curtains. The married men lived in three of them with their wives and children. The fourth was the bunk car, where the single men slept, and the boys. There were five boys that summer. Beto Ochoa was sixteen, and his father Tomás worked on the gang. Nacho Galván was seventeen. Rafa Lomelí said he was sixteen and was fifteen. The two Dávalos cousins, Chuy and Lalo, had come up from Laredo in April with a paper from a labor agent and nothing else. Don Feliciano had put all five in the bunk car with Chencho Bañuelos, who was fifty and snored and had carried a rifle for Obregón, because the boys were a little afraid of Chencho

sections.heading: II. Night School
sections.text: Amparo Ledesma came out from Newton on Tuesday and Thursday nights in her brother's Ford. She was twenty-three. She had been born in a section house at Emporia and finished the high school there and two years at the Teachers College before the money ran out, and now she dressed chickens on the line at the Fred Harvey plant on East First Street, eight hours a day, and twice a week she drove eight miles to sit at a plank table in the Kesler tool house under a hanging lantern with any man who wanted his letters. She did it for nothing. She was small and plain and said very little, and the men, who were twice her age and some of them three times, called her Señorita and stood up when she came in. Don Feliciano came every time. He could read printed Spanish slowly with his finger and he could not write at all. For eighteen years he had signed the Santa Fe's time book with a mark. He sat at the end of the bench with his dinner pail on his knees, both hands around it, as if somebody might need it handed to them. By October he could write FELICIANO in capitals that leaned on one another, and then ARREOLA, which was harder, and he practiced on the backs of the forms the roadmaster sent out.

sections.heading: III. The Address
sections.text: On his last Sunday he rode into Newton and walked out to the Ledesma house at the edge of the Ranchito to give back the pencil and the tablet. The Señorita would not take them. Her mother put him at the kitchen table and put coffee in his hand, because he would not ask for it, and he sat there two hours with his hat on his knee. Nobody remembered afterward what was said. Her mother said only that it was quiet, and that when he left he bowed to the girl as if she were the priest. On Monday morning, the last day of the Kesler section, he called Chencho and the boys to the motor car before the whistle. He gave Chencho a page from the tablet. On it, in the leaning capitals, was his sister's name and the name of her street in Tangancícuaro, Michoacán, the first thing he had ever written that was not his own name. When the señora Voth brings the other two, he said, take them. Give one to Nacho. Chuy is going with the Emporia extra gang, so send his on to him there, by the express. And if she does not bring them, write and tell me. Chencho folded the page in four and put it in his hatband. Rafa asked if Don Feliciano wanted his own comforter back, for the train, because the trains to El P

sections.heading: IV. What the Señorita Said
sections.text: Seven men came to the night class that Thursday, under the Halstead foreman now, and they were early, and they talked while they waited. Eighteen years, Chencho said, and what does he take home? A cardboard suitcase. And still. Send me word about the blankets. What does he want, that I mail him two comforters to Michoacán so he can sell them in the plaza? He was always careful with things, said Amador Rentería. A man doesn't change at the end, said his brother Lino. Even a good man. At the very end there is still a little something he wants. The boys said nothing. Rafa sat on his hands. Tomás Ochoa looked at the floor. The Señorita came in with the cold, unwound her scarf, and stood a moment at the end of the plank table looking at them, and they all stood up. What are you talking about? Chencho told her. He was a soldier and he told it straight, and he was a little ashamed by the end of it. No, she said. He doesn't want anything. He was thinking about two people. The señora said she would make five. She wrote it down. It is hers to give, and if nobody is at the crossing to take it, or nobody tells her, she loses the giving of it. He did not want her to lose that. And the boys were

title: The Comforters
logline: A Mexican section foreman on the Santa Fe leaves for Michoacán before the Mennonite women's promised comforters reach his boys.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has no interests, and when he has understood (the truth), does not say How, how? and who has reached the depth of the Immortal.

bg.commentary: This commentary story is told twice, word for word, first of Sāriputta and then of his friend the Elder Mahā Moggallāna. After a rains retreat with five hundred monks, Moggallāna leaves before the promised requisites have all arrived, and asks that whatever comes for the young monks and novices be sent on, or that he be told. The monks take it as a sign of craving. The Buddha says Moggallāna has none: he was only thinking that the donors should not lose their merit and the young monks should not lose their rightful gain. Moggallāna was the disciple foremost in psychic power, remembered for seeing what others could not and going where they could not follow. Read the full commentary story, or about Mahā Moggallāna. Its twin in this series is The Comforters.
bg.history:
The first scientific description of a Badlands fossil, a jaw from a rhinoceros-like beast brought out by a fur trader, was published in 1846. After that came a long line of collectors: Joseph Leidy described the finds, F. V. Hayden and Yale's O. C. Marsh worked the beds with army escorts, and from the 1870s the Geological Survey, Yale, Princeton, the American Museum, the Carnegie Museum, the University of Nebraska and the South Dakota School of Mines all sent parties, many of them made up of students (National Park Service history). Princeton's summer expeditions, from 1877, chose their students by examination, and in 1890 brought a Menodus skull, one of the titanotheres, out of the Badlands. The land between the White and Cheyenne rivers was opened to settlers in 1890, and ranchers ran cattle along Sage Creek under the long escarpment called the Wall, now in Badlands National Park. Parties outfitted in Rapid City, the nearest railroad town.

The rocks hold the mammals of a lost world: titanotheres with forked horns on the nose, three-toed horses, land tortoises, and so many sheep-sized oreodonts, then called Oreodon, that geologists named the layers in order the Titanotherium beds, the Oreodon beds and the Protoceras beds. The quarrel between Marsh and E. D. Cope over credit for discoveries, the Bone Wars, ended only with their deaths in 1897 and 1899. James Hutton, whose Theory of the Earth argued for the immense age of the earth, found what he took for conclusive proof in the tilted rocks he saw from a boat at Siccar Point in 1788.

sections.heading: I. Sage Creek
sections.dateline: The White River Badlands, South Dakota · June and July 1902
sections.text: Wakeman College sent a party into the Badlands in any summer the trustees could be talked into it, and in 1902 there were five students, a cook, a wagon and team hired from a livery in Rapid City, and Joel Kolb. Kolb was sixty-one. He had driven a wagon for the Yale parties in the seventies, when the Sioux still held the country and the soldiers rode along, and he had collected since for whoever would pay him, and for eleven years now that had been Wakeman, which paid him little and on time. He was big and slow and the color of the clay, and he talked less than the mules. What he could do was find. In the mornings he walked out alone into the breaks with a canvas bag and a pick and a canteen, and at noon he came back and said there was a turtle on the second bench below the knob with the cap rock on it, and there was a turtle. The boys tried following him and lost him in a quarter of an hour. Ernie Hoag, who was sixteen and from the college's preparatory department and had come along to wash the pans, said he had watched Kolb walk round behind one butte at noon and come out on the far side of the next before Ernie had counted twenty, and that was a quarter mile of ground. Will Dunn

sections.heading: II. The Skull
sections.text: In August Kolb found the titanothere. It lay in the lowest beds below a slump, a skull longer than a man's arm with the two blunt horns on the nose, and it took him and Otto Brase nine days to get it out. They trenched round it, hardened the bone with shellac, and wrapped it in strips of gunny sack dipped in plaster of Paris, and when they had turned it over and jacketed the underside it weighed something over eight hundred pounds. It went into the college's wagon with Kolb's own boxes, and filled it. The boys' crates went up the creek to the Bastians' barn to wait for haying. There were forty-one. Ernie had three, and one of them held a whole turtle, shell and all, that he had found by himself on his own ground and ticketed in his own hand, E. Hoag, No. 112, the first thing he had ever found in his life that nobody had found before him. A letter came out from the store at the White River crossing with the Bastians' mail. It was from Professor Dalgleish. The trustees met the second week in September, and he wanted the skull in the building before they did, and he wanted Kolb. The boys would finish out the month under Dunning and come home by the railroad. On the morning he left, Ko

sections.heading: III. The Bone Room
sections.text: The boys came home on the twenty-ninth. The skull was already in the basement under the main hall, which everybody called the bone room, on a bench by the north windows, and Kolb was taking the jacket off it a little at a time with a chisel and a dental pick. The forty-one crates had not come. Every afternoon at four Kolb put down the pick and walked to the depot and asked the agent whether there was anything from Rapid City. He had written twice to Sage Creek. The boys saw him go and saw him come back, and on the first Saturday in October, with Kolb gone down the hill again, they talked about it over the sorting trays. Every day, said Dunning. Every day at four. He wrote Bastian twice. He's afraid they'll come in when he isn't there. So would I be, said Frank Ostrom. That's not it. You heard about Cope and Marsh. Thirty years in this business, a man learns what a bone is worth. I'll bet you he wants to be the one who unpacks them. You know who writes the cards. We wrote the tickets, said Otto. In the field. Wait till they're in the cases. A man doesn't change at the end of his life. Even a good one. There's always something he still wants. Ernie Hoag said nothing. He was washing a

title: Field Tickets
logline: A college's old bone collector, who seems to see into the ground, leaves the Badlands before a ranch wagon brings in the students' crates.

verses.text: In a hamlet or in a forest, in the deep water or on the dry land, wherever venerable persons (Arhanta) dwell, that place is delightful.
Him I call indeed a Brahmana who in this world is above good and evil, above the bondage of both, free from grief from sin, and from impurity.

bg.commentary: Revata was the youngest brother of Sāriputta. With all their siblings gone into the order, their mother married him off at seven to keep him at home. At the wedding, hearing the bride blessed with the long life of her 120-year-old grandmother, he saw what age would do and slipped away from the wedding carriage on the pretext of relieving himself, three times and then a fourth. Thirty forest monks ordained him once they understood that his brother was Sāriputta, whom they knew by his monk's name rather than his birth name Upatissa. Revata became an arahat in an acacia forest. When the Buddha came to see him by the short and haunted road, with five hundred monks fed along the way by the merit of the Elder Sīvali, Revata made lodgings for them all by psychic power. Two old monks who grumbled were made to forget their oil, water pot and sandals, went back, and found only thorns, with their things hanging in an acacia. The laywoman Visākhā heard both reports and asked the Buddha, who spoke verse 98; he then told Sīvali's past lives (the honeycomb given for nothing, the siege in which he shut the lesser gates), and spoke verse 412. Read the full commentary story, or about Khadiravaniya Revata, Revata Khadiravaniya, “Revata of the acacia forest.”ldquo;Revata of the acacia forest.Revata Khadiravaniya, “Revata of the acacia forest.”rdquo; The same story is told in this series as Uña de Gato.
bg.hist_title: The Southern Tier and the hills, 1949–1950
bg.history:
Carpatho-Rusyns, from the northern slopes of the Carpathians in what are now Slovakia, Poland and Ukraine, came to America in great numbers before the First World War; by 1920 about 13 percent of all Rusyn Americans lived in New York State, and many worked in mills, mines and factories. In Endicott and Johnson City the Endicott Johnson shoe company employed about 20,000 people under George F. Johnson's “Square Deal,” commemorated on arches over the road, and gave land for churches, including the lots for Endicott's Russian Orthodox parish of Sts. Peter and Paul, organized in 1914. Rusyn weddings kept the old capping of the bride: before the bride's dance her veil was taken off and replaced with the married woman's kerchief or cap.

After the Second World War the Displaced Persons Act of 1948 admitted nearly 400,000 refugees from the camps of Europe by 1952, among them Orthodox clergy and monks who had fled west ahead of the Soviet armies. The hawthorn, also called thornapple and whitethorn, is quick to take over abandoned pasture. The Monastery of the Dormition, Thornapple Hill and the people of the story are invented. Athanasius's Life of Antony, the founding book of Christian monasticism, is quoted from H. Ellershaw's translation in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (1892).

sections.heading: I. The Capping
sections.text: Anna Hrinko had given six children to the Endicott Johnson Corporation's town, and five of them had gone to God. That was how she said it at the counter of her grocery on the North Side, slicing kolbasa for the wives of cutters and lasters: Five to God. She did not say it gladly. Her husband had died in the tannery in 1941 and left her the store, the house behind it, a share in the Rusyn burial society, and money in the First National Bank that she did not speak of. Petro, the oldest, had gone first, in 1938, to the Russian monastery in the hills above the Mohawk, and now he was Father Sergius and wrote her twice a year in a hand she did not recognize. The three girls had followed him into the convents one after another, Mary and Olga and Justina, and then John, and then Steve. Every one of them had stood in her kitchen with a cardboard suitcase and said the same thing in the same quiet voice, as if Petro had taught it to them. Michael was the last. He was seventeen and worked summers at E-J sorting heels, and he was the only one of her children who still came to the store after Mass and ate pirohy standing up at the counter and laughed with the customers. Anna looked at him and sa

sections.heading: II. Father Sergius's Brother
sections.dateline: The monastery above the Stony Kill, Herkimer County · June 1949
sections.text: There were thirty monks then at the Monastery of the Dormition. Half of them had come over in the last two years under the Displaced Persons Act, old men who had walked out of the Carpathians ahead of the Red Army and lived four years in camps in Bavaria, and they sat on the bench by the bakery in the sun with their hands on their knees and did not say much in any language. The rest were Americans, sons of miners and shoemakers and steelworkers, who had come up the hill one at a time with cardboard suitcases. Michael came up the hill at seven in the morning in his wedding suit, which was grey with road dust to the knees, with the carnation brown and the knot of his tie pulled down. Brother Nikolai, who kept the gate, looked at the suit and at the carnation and asked him whether he was lost. I want to be a monk. In that suit, you don't look like anybody we would know what to do with. Who sent you? I'm Petro Hrinko's brother. The youngest. Nikolai went and asked. He came back with two of the old monks, and none of them knew any Petro Hrinko. There's no Hrinko here, said Father Pimen. He's here. Tall. He has a scar on his chin from a sled. You call him Father Sergius. The monks looked

sections.heading: III. Thornapple Hill
sections.text: He lived that summer in the milk house, which still had its roof, and cut his way into the thornapple a few yards a day with the bucksaw, and stacked the cut wood for winter, and prayed. A farmer down the hill named Rhinehart brought him milk in exchange for help at haying and decided after a month that the boy was harmless. The thorns went through his shoes and his cassock and the backs of his hands, and the cuts healed and he got new ones, and by August he had stopped noticing them. What else happened to him on that hill nobody could tell. The old monks who heard about it afterward said that before the Dormition fast was out he had come to the end of what they had taught him, and gone on past it, which they said happened sometimes to the young ones, very seldom, and could not be explained, and should not be talked about too much. Rhinehart said only that the boy had got very quiet, and that his own dog, who bit everybody, would lie down across the boy's feet. He stayed through the winter. Nobody came up the hill but Rhinehart.

sections.heading: IV. The Hill Road
sections.text: In the summer of 1950 Father Sergius asked again to go to his brother, and this time Vladyka Anatoly said, Yes. We'll all go. All was a great many. The Archbishop was eighty, and wherever he went the monks went with him, and wherever the monks went that summer the pilgrims went too, out of every Russian and Rusyn parish from Endicott to Utica: the old women in black who came on foot as far as they could, the shoemakers' families in borrowed cars, a bus from Binghamton and a bus from Johnson City. By the time they gathered at the monastery gate there were five hundred of them, counting the children, and two trucks of camp beds and kettles borrowed from parish halls. At the bottom of the monastery hill, where the road split, Father Sergius stopped the Archbishop's car and asked which way. Vladyka, there are two roads. One goes round by the valley, through Cooperstown and Oneonta and every town on the river. It's long, nearly twice as far, but there are people all along it. The other goes straight over the hills by the old turnpike, ninety miles. There's nothing on it. No gas, no towns. The farmers say it's a bad road, and the old women from the Lemko villages say worse than that. The

sections.heading: V. The Thorns
sections.text: They came up the last mile in the evening, in a line of headlights, expecting a milk house in a thicket and planning to sleep in the buses. What the pilgrims found, they told for the rest of their lives on the North Side, and some of them are telling it still. There was a church at the top of the hill, a little one, of new logs, with a blue dome over it and a cross on the dome that caught the last of the light. There were cells down both sides of the pasture, enough for every monk, with a bench outside every door, and long walks mown green between the thornapples, which stood along them like an orchard, and there was a guest house and a kitchen and a well with a roof over it, and room in the barn, which no longer seemed to have fallen in, for every pilgrim and every child. There was a cell at the top of the hill under an old pear tree with a carpet on its floor and an icon corner already lit, and Brother Michael was standing at the door of it in a cassock that fit him now, waiting for the Archbishop. Father Sergius got down from the car and stood looking at his brother, and then went and put his arms around him, and neither of them said anything that anyone could hear. How it had b

sections.heading: VI. Pani Vasko's Table
sections.text: Paraska Vasko kept a boardinghouse for Endicott Johnson men on the North Side, three doors from the house Anna Hrinko had bought for a bride and groom who never lived in it, and for thirty years every monk and priest and pilgrim who came through the Southern Tier had eaten at her table. She could not read Russian or English very well, and she had buried a husband and two sons, and she was the cleverest woman on the North Side, which everyone knew and nobody said in front of her. In October Father Pimen and Father Iov came down to Endicott to collect for the monastery roof, and on their first morning they washed their faces and said, Let's go to Pani Vasko's and have some soup, and they went. She sat them down with borshch and bread and asked them, as she asked everybody that fall, whether they had been with Vladyka to Thornapple Hill. We were. They say it's beautiful there. Beautiful? said Father Iov, and showed her the scabs on his wrists. A pasture full of thorns. An old milk house. A place for crazy people. For hermits. That afternoon two of the young monks, Brother Nikolai and Brother Vasyl, came to the door on the same business, and she sat them down at the same table and aske

sections.heading: VII. The Honey
sections.text: Brother Simeon's mother was there too, Mrs. Barna from Squires Avenue, and over the tea somebody asked her, because everyone in the parish had heard about the farm wives on the turnpike, whether Simeon had always been like that. Always, said Mrs. Barna. From before he was born. I carried him ten months, and three days he lay crossways, and the midwife went home and said I would die. Then he came, and since then he never once wanted for anything. Why should that be? The monks looked at the Archbishop, and the old man put down his glass and told them a story from the Lemko hills, the way the old people told it. In a village there was a poor man who went one morning to pay his rent to the steward, and on the way, in a lime tree by the road, he found a wild comb of honey. He cut it down, bees and all, and carried it on its branch, meaning to give it to the steward instead of the rent. In the town a servant from the castle stopped him. The count was giving a feast for the bishop the next day, and there was every kind of food, and honey cooked in everything, but no fresh comb, and the count had sent his men out of every gate of the town with money to find some. What do you want for it? t

title: Thornapple Hill
logline: The last Rusyn son left at home slips away from his own wedding car toward the monastery where his brother has a new name.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who is bright like the moon, pure, serene, undisturbed, and in whom all gaiety is extinct.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, a frontier forester shows a merchant a stand of red sandalwood, and when a shrine is raised over the relics of the earlier Buddha Kassapa he sets a moon-shaped disk of sandalwood inside it. Reborn in a rich Brahmin family at Rājagaha, he has a light like the moon shining from his navel and is named Candābha, “Moonlight.” Brahmins carry him from town to town in a carriage and charge people a hundred or a thousand coins to stroke his body for luck. At Sāvatthī they quarrel with the Buddha's lay followers and bring the boy to the monastery to see whose power is greater, and in the Buddha's presence the light goes out three times; the boy, “like a crow in a basket of charcoal,” asks for the charm that does it, is told it can only be taught to one who has gone forth, ordains, and is given the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body as “a preliminary.” He becomes an arahant within days and tells the Brahmins to go, since he will never return. The monks think he is lying; the Buddha says he speaks the truth.
bg.history:
The 1950s Texas drought ran from about 1949 to 1957, and by its end 244 of the state's 254 counties had been declared federal drought disaster areas. Ranchers fed prickly pear to their cattle, burning off the spines with kerosene pear burners. In the hills west of Austin, cedar choppers, Scotch-Irish families who had come by way of Appalachia and the Ozarks, cut Ashe juniper for fence posts and burned it for charcoal; their best years were the 1940s and 1950s, before chainsaws and steel posts put most of them out of work around 1960.

The postwar healing revival began in 1946 and peaked in 1956, when 49 evangelists were holding major campaigns. In small towns the undertaker often ran the only ambulance, in a combination car that served as hearse or ambulance as needed, a practice that lasted in the United States until the late 1970s. The drought broke in the spring of 1957, with rains that brought deadly floods.

sections.heading: I. Red Cedar
sections.text: Mr. J. W. Stucky bought cedar posts for a yard in San Antonio, and he was known from the Pedernales to the San Saba as the man who never forgot a name. Before he went up any creek he would stop at the last store and get the names: who lived up there, and his wife's name, and the names of the children in order, and which one had been sick. Then he would drive his buggy up to the door and call the woman by her name, and ask after each child by its own name, and leave a bolt of calico and a sack of candy and a pocketknife for the man of the house, as if he were somebody's uncle come home. The women thought he must be some kin they had forgotten. By the time the man came in from the brakes Mr. Stucky had eaten supper and was sitting on the gallery like he owned it. That was how he came to know Isom Pace, who chopped cedar on the breaks above the Llano and burned what was left for charcoal. After supper Mr. Stucky asked him, the way he asked every man, whether he had seen anything up in the brakes worth looking at. Nothing much, Isom said. Some big old cedars in a draw up there. The heart of them is red. How many? A good many. Mr. Stucky went up the draw with him in the morning, and the

sections.heading: II. The Light
sections.text: His grandson Delmer was born in a cedar camp on the Pedernales in the spring of 1942, and he had a light in him. It came from his navel, round and pale as the moon, about the size of a saucer, and in the dark it shone through his shirt and lit the side of whatever he was next to. His mother said the first night she could have read the Bible by it. The old people in the camp said it was because of the cedar moon. Isom had been dead ten years by then, but they remembered the gable. His uncle Arlis was a preacher by then, Pentecostal, with a tent. Arlis believed the light came from God. That was the first thing to understand about him. He believed it the way he believed the sun came up, and he also saw, being a man who had been poor all his life, what a light like that would do in a tent. When Delmer was nine his mother let him go on the road with his uncle for the summer, and after that he did not come home except at Christmas. They had a used Army tent that held three hundred, a generator, two hundred folding chairs and a truckload of sawdust, and a man named Fentress who had sold cemetery lots in Fort Worth and who handled the money in a King Edward cigar box. Arlis preached for an

sections.heading: III. Ransom
sections.text: In the middle of August they came to Ransom, the county seat, on the river, and pitched the tent on the old camp-meeting ground east of town, between the square and the cemetery, next to the tabernacle with the gray wooden moon in its gable. Nobody had held a meeting under the tabernacle since the war. On the Saturday morning, early, the whole town came down the road past the tent, walking and in pickups, in their good clothes, with flowers in coffee cans and cakes under dish towels and casseroles wrapped in newspaper to keep them hot. Arlis stood at the front of the tent and asked them where they were going. To Mr. Hext's, a woman said. For Mrs. Tolliver. Mrs. Tolliver had taught the third grade in Ransom for forty-one years and had died on Thursday, and she was laid out at Hext Furniture and Funeral, up the hill from the tabernacle, and the visitation was all day. Come in here first, Arlis said. There is a boy in this tent with a light in his body that God put there. Whoever touches it, the Lord will remember. You never saw anything like it. A rancher named Corley Wade, who had sold the last of his cows in July, laughed, not unkindly. Preacher, Mr. Hext has laid out every soul in

sections.heading: IV. The Charm
sections.dateline: Hext Furniture and Funeral · August to October
sections.text: Wiley Hext was seventy-four. He had come to Ransom in 1909 to sell furniture, and in those days the furniture man also sold the coffins, and somebody had to lay the dead out in them, so he had learned that too. He ran the only ambulance in the county, a black Cadillac combination car that was a hearse by day and turned into an ambulance when the phone rang at night, with a cot in the back and a red light he clamped to the roof. He was a Church of Christ man, and a widower, and he did not talk much. When they came up the hill he was in the front parlor in his shirtsleeves, combing Mrs. Tolliver's white hair with a pocket comb and laying each curl where she had worn it. Arlis brought the boy in at the door, and the light went out. It went out between one step and the next. In the dim parlor, among the sprays of gladiolas, the boy stood there in his white shirt, and there was nothing in it but a boy. Somebody said afterward that he looked like a crow in a coal scuttle. Arlis took him back out on the porch, and in the shade of the porch the light came up again in his shirt, round and pale, plain as ever. They brought him back in to Mr. Hext, and it went out. The third time, Delmer went

sections.heading: V. The Bench
sections.text: Arlis came again in November, and this time Fentress was driving. The drought had not broken, and the meetings had been thin all fall; people who had sold their cattle had no dollars left to put in a cigar box. They found the boy on the courthouse square in a pair of Mr. Hext's old khakis with the cuffs turned up, waiting with the Cadillac outside the drugstore while the old man got his prescription. Well? Arlis said. Have you got it? Delmer looked at his uncle, and at Fentress behind the wheel, and at the tent folded in the truck bed with the generator. Y'all go on, he said. I'm not coming. I'm not ever going back out there. Arlis argued with him and then prayed with him right there on the sidewalk, with his hand on the boy's head, and the boy let him. Then the truck went off down the San Saba road. Fentress lifted two fingers off the wheel as they passed the bench. The old men on the bench under the pecan by the courthouse door had heard every word. They played dominoes there every morning there was no rain, which that year was every morning, and they knew the boy, the way they knew everybody who had come to town since 1910. title: The Cedar Moon
logline: In the seventh year of the Texas drought, a healing-tent preacher charges a dollar to touch the moon-colored light in his nephew's body.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has traversed this miry road, the impassable world and its vanity, who has gone through, and reached the other shore, is thoughtful, guileless, free from doubts, free from attachment, and content.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Suppavāsā of the Koliya clan carries a child for seven years and then labors for seven days because the child lies awry. She bears the pain by holding three thoughts, of the Buddha, of his followers, and of the peace where such pain is not, and she sends her husband to greet the Buddha in her name. He says, "May Suppavāsā be healthy; in health and happiness may she bring forth a healthy son," and at that moment she does. She feeds the Buddha and his monks for seven days, and from the day of his birth the child strains their drinking water. He grows up to become a monk and a saint. When the monks marvel at how much he suffered in the womb, the Buddha says he is free of all of it now, and speaks the verse.
bg.hist_title: From California to San Juan Island, 1858–1859
bg.history:
California entered the Union as a free state, but an 1852 law let people who had been brought there enslaved before statehood be seized and returned, and Black Californians could not testify against whites in court. In 1858, the year of the Archy Lee case, the legislature took up a bill to bar Black immigration altogether. That April the Black community of San Francisco sent a Pioneer Committee of thirty-five north on the steamer Commodore to Victoria, in the British Colony of Vancouver Island, where Governor James Douglas, himself of mixed Caribbean ancestry, had let it be known they would be welcome. They landed on April 25, and several hundred people followed that year, among them Mifflin Gibbs. The Legislative Assembly of British Columbia tells the story here.

San Juan Island lies seven miles across Haro Strait from Victoria, in waters fished by Coast Salish peoples. The treaty of 1846 left it unclear which country owned it. In December 1853 the Hudson's Bay Company landed sheep and a crew of European, Hawaiian and Native men there and founded Belle Vue Sheep Farm; by 1859 some 4,500 sheep grazed at stations across the island. On June 15, 1859, an American settler shot a Company pig, and by August 461 American soldiers with fourteen cannon faced five British warships in what is called the Pig War. No one was hurt. General Winfield Scott arrived in October and arranged a joint military occupation, which lasted until an arbitration under the German emperor awarded the islands to the United States in 1872. Both camps are now San Juan Island National Historical Park. The Tollivers, Keoni, Mrs. Oakes and Lot Pembroke are invented, and no Black family is recorded on the Company farm. The Pilgrim's Progress (1678; second part 1684) was among the most widely owned books in English-speaking Protestant homes of the time; the text here follows George Offor's edition of the 1850s.

sections.heading: I. The Carrying
sections.dateline: Howard County, Missouri, and Marysville, California · 1852–1858
sections.text: Lavinia Tolliver was carrying when her husband bought her. That was in Howard County, Missouri, in the spring of 1852. Amos Tolliver had been two years in the California diggings with the man who owned him. He came home with his own price paid and nine hundred dollars over in a belt, and he laid the nine hundred down for his wife. The paper was signed on a Tuesday. She was some four months along, and that night she told Amos the child had waited to have a free mother, and it could wait a little longer and have free ground. People have told it since as though she were boasting. She said afterward that she only knew it, the way you know rain is coming. They went out from Independence with a train in May. It was the cholera year on the Platte, with graves at every camp, and she walked most of the way behind the wagon because the jolting was worse than walking. Her time came due on the Humboldt and went by. The child moved in her, strong, and stayed where it was. They stopped at Marysville. Amos shod mules and Viney washed for miners. California was called free soil. That same spring its legislature had made a law under which a colored person brought in before statehood could be claime

sections.heading: II. Seven Days
sections.text: Victoria that year was tents and mud and men going to the Fraser for gold. Viney carried through a seventh winter there. Seven miles over the strait lay an island that the Queen and the United States both claimed, with little on it but the Hudson's Bay Company's sheep. In the spring of 1859 Amos hired on with the Company farm there. He was given a cabin with half a roof at a sheep station above the bay, among Kanaka shepherds from the Sandwich Islands and their wives. The Lummi and Songhees people had fished the reefs off that shore longer than anybody could say. Neither country had asked them. In June an American settler shot a Company pig in his potatoes. By August there were American soldiers dug in on the south end with cannon, and five British warships lay in the bay with their ports open. Amos went for his wife in October all the same, because she sent for him to. A Company sloop put them off at low water, and she went over the side and waded up onto the stones. She stood there a minute with her skirt dripping. She looked at the flag on the hill and then at the flags on the ships. Neither one has got it yet, she said. This will do, she said, and the first pain took her before

sections.heading: III. The Chair
sections.dateline: Yates Street, Victoria · the seventh day
sections.text: Lot Pembroke kept a barber's chair on Yates Street. He had been a ship's cook for thirty years, out of Newport first and then New Bedford, and a Quaker woman had taught him his letters when he was a boy. He owned a razor case, a Bible and a Bunyan. He read from the Bunyan to whoever was under the lather, and on Thursday nights he led a class of colored people in the room behind the shop. The Tollivers had sat in that class for a year. He seldom said ten words together that were his own. It should have been one day by canoe. Keoni and his brother paddled, and fog held them overnight on a rock in the middle of the strait. Amos came into the shop at noon on the seventh day, wet to the knees. Mr. Pembroke was shaving the mate of a lumber brig. Viney Tolliver greets you, Amos said. He had meant to stop there, as he had been told. Seven days she's been at it, he said. Mr. Pembroke lifted the razor off the mate's throat and held it in the air. He looked at the clock on his wall, which said a quarter past twelve. Let Lavinia Tolliver be well, he said. Let her be well, and bring a well son. Then he finished the mate's left cheek. He told Amos to eat something and go home. Amos was back the

sections.heading: IV. The Dipper
sections.text: Viney was on her feet in three days. She sent word by the Company sloop that Mr. Pembroke and the whole class were to come up, and she would feed them a week. Fourteen came. They slept on fir boughs in the cabin and under the sloop's sail, and for seven days she fed them mutton, clams, potatoes, bread out of the Dutch oven, and salmon bought off the canoes at a bit apiece. That same week the general the President had sent came to terms with the governor, and most of the soldiers and all but one of the ships went away. Everybody who was there told the next part the same way. The child was three weeks old, and he looked three weeks old. On the first day of the feast he got down off the bed. He took the tin dipper from its nail, went to the bucket, and strained creek water through a cloth to get the fir needles out. Then he carried it round to the company in both hands, beginning with Mr. Pembroke. He did that all seven days and never spoke. Mr. Pembroke took the dipper from him each time and said thank you, as he would to a grown man, and made no other remark. When the sloop had gone the child lay down again and was a baby for the usual time. Mrs. Oakes said he had had seven years to

sections.heading: V. Halfway In
sections.text: The two countries kept a camp apiece on the island for twelve years and never fired a shot. In 1872 the Emperor of Germany, who had been asked to judge, gave the island to the United States. The marines went home, and most of the Kanaka families crossed to the British side, where they could hold land. The Tollivers stayed. There had been a war by then, and the ground was not what it had been in 1852. Tarry was twenty. He had signed his share of the homestead over to his sisters and he owned a boat. He carried people and freight across the line to Victoria and back for what they could pay, and Sundays he spoke a little at the schoolhouse. Nobody on the south end had seen him hurried, or put out, or wanting anything that was not already in his hand. Mr. Pembroke was past eighty. He came up that August for the last time, to a meeting on the prairie above the bay, and after the dinner the old hands sat in the lee of the wagons and got to talking about Tarry, who was down at the water. Think of it, Mrs. Oakes said. Seven years shut up in the dark. Over the Platte in the cholera, and six years in California, and then seven days crosswise in the rain with the guns run out.
