title: Seven Winters
logline: A freedwoman carries her child from Missouri through California for seven years, waiting for ground she is willing to have him born on.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who in this world, leaving all desires, travels about without a home, and in whom all concupiscence is extinct.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, Sundarasamudda (“Ocean of Beauty”) is the son of a very rich house in Sāvatthī who wins his parents’ leave to become a monk and goes off to Rājagaha. His mother, weeping on a festival day, promises a courtesan the whole household if she can bring him back. The woman takes a house on his alms street and feeds him, first at the door, then on the veranda, then (with the help of some bribed boys) indoors, then on the top floor of a seven-storied mansion, where she tries every art on him. The Buddha, far away, smiles, tells Ānanda who will win, and sends a radiant image of himself with the verse; the monk becomes an arahant and leaves through the roof peak. The Buddha then tells how the same monk was once a wind-deer lured into a palace by honeyed grass.
bg.history:
The Ephrata Cloister was founded in 1732 on Cocalico Creek in Lancaster County by Conrad Beissel, who appears here only as “the Superintendent.” Its celibate brothers and sisters wore white habits, slept on narrow benches with wooden blocks for pillows, kept a midnight watch, ate one sparing meal a day, ran a paper mill and a press, and sang hymns in four and more parts to Beissel’s own system of harmony. The community’s chronicle, the Chronicon Ephratense (1786; quoted from J. Max Hark’s 1889 translation), records that before opening the singing school Beissel judged fruit, milk and meat injurious to the voice, and that the Brethren insisted he keep a sentence saying the same of the love of women. The hymnal that carried that preface was printed at Ephrata in 1747. Brother Simeon, his rag round and his private rule are invented.

Vater Lorenz is invented too, but hermits like him were real. In 1694 about forty German Pietists under Johannes Kelpius settled on the ridge above Wissahickon Creek near Germantown to await the millennium; after Kelpius died, a few stayed on as solitaries into the 1740s and were visited for counsel. Christoph Saur printed Luther’s Bible at Germantown in 1743, the first Bible in a European language printed in America. Many German immigrants of those years came as redemptioners, sold into terms of service to pay their passage.

sections.heading: I. The Outer Ring
sections.dateline: Germantown and the Ridge, Pennsylvania · summer 1744
sections.text: Heinrich Schönsee tanned leather on the Wingohocking and owned shares in three ships, and it was said in Germantown that he could have bought the Main Street from the market square to Chestnut Hill and had money over. He had one child, a son, Matthias, who was nineteen and could sing. The tanyard and the ships were to be his. One First-day after dinner Matthias saw people going out along the road toward the Ridge, a good many of them, with loaves under their arms and candles in their hands. He asked where they were going. To hear the old man, they said. I will go too. The old man was called Vater Lorenz. He had come over fifty years before with the forty brethren who built their cabins in the woods above the Wissahickon to wait for the Lord, who was to come that same year. The Lord had not come that year. The master of the forty had died young, and the rest had married or wandered off, and the cabins had fallen in. Lorenz had stayed. He had a hut and a spring and a patch of beans. On First-days he sat on a stump before the door and talked a little, and whoever had walked out sat on the ground. A boy named Christel, from the paper mill down the creek, carried his water. Matthias sat

sections.heading: II. The Fair
sections.text: The November fair came on in Philadelphia, and the young men of Germantown rode down to it past the Schönsee house. The mother stood at the window. There went the Kepler boy, who had learned his letters on the same bench as Matthias, in a blue coat with silver buttons. There went young Dietz in a chaise with a wife beside him and a drummer walking ahead. She sat down on the window seat and wept, and her husband came and stood by her and wept as well. That is past our son’s getting now, she said. A woman came to the house that same hour with lace to sell. She was Anna Barbara Kuntz, called Bärbel, twenty-four years old. She had come over from the Palatinate at fourteen and been sold off the ship for her passage, seven years to a tavern on Water Street. When the seven years were out she had nothing but what she had learned there, and she had taken rooms in the part of the city they called Helltown, where a clever woman who was good company could keep herself. She saw the mother’s face. Mother, why do you weep? I keep thinking of my son. Where is he? Gone among the brethren. Would it not be right to bring him home? It would. He does not wish it. He has left the Ridge now and gone out

sections.heading: III. The Tenor
sections.text: On the Cocalico they had named him Brother Simeon. He wore the white habit with the hood and went barefoot until the ground froze. He slept on a bench the width of his shoulders with a block of wood under his head, and rose at midnight, and ate one meal a day. None of it was hard for him. The hard thing, and the thing he loved, was the singing school. The Superintendent had made a music of his own for them, in four parts and five and six, the women above and the brothers below, and he kept the school himself, four hours at a stretch, ending at midnight. They sang with the mouth hardly open and the breath held back, so that the sound came from nowhere a visitor could point to. People of quality drove out from Lancaster to hear it and went home quiet. Matthias had the high part among the brothers. It was the one true note he owned, and it sat at the very top of what he could reach. The Brethren wrote the rule of that school down afterward in their chronicle. …he declared all fruit, milk, meat, to be viands injurious to the voice. …godly virtue must be at the source of our whole walk, because by it you obtain favor with the spirit of singing, which is the Holy Spirit. — Chronicon Ephr

sections.heading: IV. Queen Street
sections.text: Bärbel took note of the street he came in by. She hired the tallest house on it, two floors of brick and two garrets one above the other under a steep German roof with a knob at the peak. She baked on Fifth-day night so that the house smelled of it on Sixth-day morning. The first weeks she gave him rags, good ones, a torn linen sheet, and cold water in a cup, and stood back from the door with her eyes down. He blessed the house and went on. Then there was a small loaf in the sack among the rags, still warm. He found it on the road home. Bread was what he ate; it would have been waste to throw it in the ditch. It was white bread, and there was butter worked into it. The next week there was another. In May she said, Brother, sit down right here on the bench and eat it while it is hot. She put out her hands for his sack, and he gave it to her. She brought milk in a cup. There is no better door on your whole road than this one, she said, and it was so. He sat on her bench in the sun every Sixth-day of that month. There were boys on Queen Street. She gave them honey cakes and told them, When the brother comes, you come too, and run up and down before the bench and kick up the dust. If I

sections.heading: V. The Top of the House
sections.dateline: Lancaster and the Ridge · a Sixth-day in July
sections.text: They say there are forty ways, and that she knew them. She yawned and stretched. She bent to the floor for something that had not fallen. She looked ashamed and rubbed one bare foot upon the other. She scratched on the boards with a stick. She spoke loud, as though the street could hear, and then low, as though no one must. She ate a pear and held it out to him. She sang a little, and wept a little, and laughed at herself for weeping. She took off her cap and put it on again. She loosened what was laced and laced it. Then she stood in front of him with her hair down and said it to him as a rhyme, the way a girl says a counting game. My feet are washed, my shoes are red. You are young, and you are mine. I am young, and I am yours. We will both turn holy when we are old and go to God on two sticks. Brother Simeon sat with his hands on his knees. What have I done, he thought. I never looked where I was walking. He was shaken through. And he did not get up. At that same hour, sixty miles east, Vater Lorenz was sitting on his stump on the Ridge with his dinner of bread on his knee, and he smiled. Christel had never seen him do it over nothing. Father, what are you smiling at? In Lancast

sections.heading: VI. Honey
sections.dateline: The Ridge · that evening, and the First-day after
sections.text: Before the old man had finished his bread, Matthias was kneeling in the bean patch in front of him in the white habit, with his hood back. He looked at the old man from his cap to his cracked shoes, the whole body of him, the way a man looks at the house he was born in. Then he put his forehead to the ground. Christel dropped the water bucket and had to go back down for more. On First-day the people who walked out had the story already, from a carter. They sat on the ground and talked it over among themselves. For the sake of his tongue, they said. Bread with butter in it. He was that near lost, and the old man held him up. Vater Lorenz heard them. It is not the first time I have seen that one caught by the tongue, he said. Nor the first time I spoke for him. And he told them a thing from before he crossed the water, when he was a page of fourteen at the court of a small count on the Lahn. The count had a pleasure garden and a gardener named Sander. A roe deer began coming into the garden, a wild one out of the hill forest, the kind that is gone at the sight of a man. Sander let it go and did not frighten it. One day the count asked him, Have you seen anything strange in the garden

title: Honeyed Grass
logline: A rich tanner's son sings the high part at the Ephrata Cloister; his mother pays a woman from Philadelphia to bake him home.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, leaving all longings, travels about without a home, and in whom all covetousness is extinct.

bg.commentary: The commentary's story of Jaṭila ("Matted Hair") is one of its longest. A rich man's daughter, kept at the top of a seven-story palace, bears a son to a sorcerer who flies in at her window, and sets the baby adrift on the Ganges in a new pot. Two women bathing claim the pot and its contents, and the king divides them. The woman who gets the child means him for the Elder Mahā Kaccāna, who sees that the boy must first be rich and leaves him with a merchant in distant Takkasilā. The boy sells twelve years of unsold stock in one day, marries the merchant's daughter, and steps into his new house as a mountain of gold eighty cubits high breaks out of the ground behind it. Years later, wanting to go forth, he sends men out with a gold brick, whip and cord to learn whether anyone is as rich; they find Meṇḍaka with his golden rams and Jotika, whose gate-sweeper is given a priceless blanket to wipe her feet. He tests his three sons with a spade at the mountain, and only the youngest can dig. The reason lies in a former life, when he told a monk collecting for a shrine to "throw your Teacher into the water," repented, and made three jars of golden flowers with only his youngest son to help. He becomes a monk; his sons feed the Buddha and the monks for half a month; the monks doubt that he feels no longing for the gold or his sons, and the Buddha answers them. Read the full commentary story. The long past-life histories of Jotika, which the commentary tells along the way, are kept here only as rumors heard at his gate, and the former-life quarrel is moved into Matt's own married years. On the elder who places the boy, see Mahā Kaccāna.
bg.hist_title: The trail and a Maine town, 1979 to 2025
bg.history:
The Appalachian Trail runs almost 2,200 miles from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Katahdin in Maine, marked the whole way by white paint blazes two inches wide and six inches tall. Each year a few thousand people set out to walk all of it. They take trail names, write in the notebooks ("registers") kept at the shelters, which in Maine are called lean-tos, and are fed along the way by strangers. Dogs may walk nearly all of the trail, but they are barred from Great Smoky Mountains National Park and from Baxter State Park, where the trail ends; the park boundary is just north of Abol Bridge, at the far side of the Hundred-Mile Wilderness. Hikers cross the Kennebec River by a canoe ferry.

Starbird Falls and its people are invented. The Swift River in Oxford County is real, and people do pan placer gold from it at Coos Canyon in Byron. The ice storm of January 1998 coated much of Maine, Oxford County included, in freezing rain in the second week of the month, and left more than half a million people in the state without power, some for two weeks or longer; stores sold out of kerosene heaters, lightbulbs and generators. Maine towns still govern themselves by annual town meeting, usually in March, voting one by one on the numbered articles of a warrant, each of which begins "To see if the Town will."

sections.heading: I. The Cooler
sections.dateline: South Fork of the Shenandoah, Virginia · July 1979
sections.text: There was a hotel upriver, seven stories, and the man who owned it kept his daughter on the top floor with one maid to watch her. That was the summer people had started jumping off ridges under nylon kites. One evening a man came in at her window. The maid said afterward that he had no kite. He flew, she said, the way you would walk across a room. In July the daughter had a boy. She sent the maid out for a new Coleman cooler, the green steel kind. She laid the baby in it on a folded towel, propped the lid with a wooden spoon, and put daisies and black-eyed Susans on top. Carry this down and set it in the river, she said. If anybody asks, it's a picnic I'm sending to the church. The maid did as she was told. Nobody asked. Six miles down, below a low-water bridge, two women were bathing. One was Opal Shifflett, who was sixty. The other was Dreama Good, who was not much younger. They saw a new cooler coming down the current with flowers on it. That cooler's mine! Dreama called. Then whatever's in it is mine, said Opal. They waded out and brought it in to the gravel and lifted the lid. For a minute neither of them said a word. Then they both spoke at once, and they kept at it for six w

sections.heading: II. The Store
sections.text: Starbird Falls is eleven miles down the road from where the trail crosses, in Oxford County, on the Swift River. People there have panned gold out of the Swift for a hundred and fifty years, a few flakes to the pan, and have always wondered where it washed down from. Orrin Thurlow kept the store by the bridge. He let hikers sleep in his barn and held their mail, and he had known Footnote for ten years. He'll walk, later on, Footnote told him. Right now he's two. Keep him a while. Orrin was a widower with a daughter, Lila, who lived winters with his sister in Rumford. He gave the boy the room over the store and brought him up as his own. Orrin was a good man and a poor storekeeper. He bought whatever a salesman showed him and sold perhaps half. He had taken over the place in 1986, and by the end of 1997 he had twelve years of goods on the shelves, in the back room and in the cellar. There were lamp chimneys and wicks. There were kerosene cans, stovepipe elbows, candles by the gross, rock salt and wool socks. He had flashlight batteries in sizes nobody used. He had a carton of cumin that no one in Oxford County had ever asked for. On the seventh of January, 1998, a Wednesday, Orrin h

sections.heading: III. The Brick, the Whip and the Cord
sections.text: They had three boys, Wade, Curtis and Ben. Matt ran the store after Orrin. He paid for the school roof, the new plow truck and three parts in four of the town budget. He took what he needed from the hill with a spade and did not think about it much. Every September Gone came down the road with her people. He fed them in the yard and stood a while afterward watching them go back up toward the crossing. Lila died in the winter of 2021. By the next fall the boys were men, or near it, and he knew what he wanted. But he had got it into his head that a man could not walk off from the biggest pile there was. The biggest pile had duties. If there were another like it somewhere, the town would let him go. So he made a brick, a buggy whip and a length of cord, all three of gold. He gave them to Dunc Coolidge and Leroy Poulin, who clerked for him. Drive around the country, he said. Act like you're after nothing in particular. See if anybody has what we have. They drove a long way. In the Texas Panhandle a rancher named Ramsey found them leaning on his fence. What are you boys after? Nothing in particular, said Dunc. Ramsey looked at the whip. Nobody carries a gold buggy whip after nothing in

sections.heading: IV. Article 31
sections.dateline: Town meeting, the Grange hall · March 2025
sections.text: Town meeting is the first Saturday in March. The warrant that year had thirty-three articles. They voted the plow contract and the salt shed and argued forty minutes over a culvert. Then Mrs. Arsenault, the moderator, read the next one in the same voice. Article 31. To see if the Town will give Matthew Shifflett leave to go. It was quiet enough to hear the furnace. Go where? said the first selectman. Up the trail, Matt said. He stood, with his cap in his hands. Behind the dog. For good. And who pays for the school? The hill stays where it is. My boys stay with it. I can't carry it and I'm not asking to. He told them about Ramsey's eight acres and about the woman at the gatehouse drying her feet. I thought we had the only one. There's more of it around than I knew. I thought you ought to hear that before you voted. An old man in the back said he had known Matt since he came up the road on a hiker's pack, and he had always figured somebody would come back for him. A woman said her mother had bought the pepper. They voted by show of hands. Mrs. Arsenault did not need to count. The ayes have it, she said. Go where you're inclined, Matt. Article 32.

sections.heading: V. The Spade
sections.dateline: Behind the house · the next morning
sections.text: He took the three of them up behind the house after breakfast. He had a spade with him that he had made years before from the hill itself. Wade. Cut me a piece out of it. Wade was twenty-three and strong. He set his boot on the spade and drove it. It rang as if he had hit ledge, and the shock went up both his arms. There was no mark on the hill. Matt took the spade and gave it to Curtis. Curtis picked a different place and swung with his whole back. It rang the same. Then he gave it to Ben, who was nineteen. Ben pushed it in with one foot. It went in to the step, as it would go into a potato hill in June, and he turned up a spadeful of gold as loose as loam. That'll do, Ben. Wade and Curtis stood looking at the place. This didn't come up for you two, Matt said. He said it gently. It came up for me and for Ben. You'll have to go shares with him. He'll do right by you. Wade started to ask why, and then he remembered why. Curtis had remembered already.

sections.heading: VI. The North Wall
sections.text: Footnote had died in 2012, on the trail, in his sleep, at eighty-one. Two years later Gone's people were building a lean-to in his name on the brook above the crossing. They had the floor laid, the roof on and three walls up. Then the money ran out, and the north side stood open to the weather. One of them was a carpenter called Plumb. He came down to Starbird Falls to go door to door. The north wall's open on Footnote's lean-to, he told people. We're short for the logs. People gave him what they had. Then he climbed the rise to the house in front of the hill, reasoning as anybody would have. Matt and Lila were in the middle of a fight. It was about nothing, the kind you have in a house with too much in it. Matt came to the door with his face still hot. The north wall's open on the lean-to, Plumb said. I figured you of all people would want to know. Go throw your dog in the river, Matt said. Plumb stood where he was. Behind Matt, Lila had stopped with a dish towel in her hand. Matt Shifflett. If you're that mad at me, say it to me. Holler at me if you want. What did that dog ever do? She was walking before you were born. She'll be walking when every one of us is gone. It went out o

sections.heading: VII. The Barn
sections.text: He left in April with a pack Ben had weighed at twenty-two pounds. He rode a bus to Georgia and found her on Springer Mountain with eleven others. She smelled his hands. It is in the registers that whatever was left in him went out of him somewhere in the first week, on a wet day, going up Blood Mountain. By Virginia his hair had matted the way it had in the basin, and the trail called him Mats. They went around the Smokies by the road, since dogs are not let through the park. They crossed the Shenandoah on a highway bridge in June. He looked down at the water once and went on. In September they came down the road into Starbird Falls. The registers say five hundred. It was nearer sixty at any one time, with more arriving behind. They stopped at the door of the house under the hill. Wade came out, then Curtis, then Ben. For half a month the three of them fed Gone's people. They set planks on sawhorses in the yard. There were baked beans, biscuits, corn, chowder and blueberry pie. Wade ran the grill and Curtis drove to Rumford for more of everything. Their father ate at the planks with the rest. He slept in Orrin's old barn with the rest too, and Ben brought him his plate the same as

sections.heading: VIII. The Line
sections.text: They went north in the morning. The three sons stood at the door. Ben lifted one hand, and his father lifted one, and that was all of it. It is eighteen days from there to Abol Bridge, across the Kennebec in the ferryman's canoe and through the Hundred-Mile Wilderness. Past the bridge the trail goes into Baxter State Park and up Katahdin to the end, and at the park line there is a sign. No dogs. She did what she had done every October since anyone had kept count. She sat down at the sign. The company went by her one at a time. Some put a hand on her head and some could not look at her. Howdy went by last and told her she was going to make it. Then they were all in the trees, climbing toward the thing they had walked two thousand miles for. Mats had the book now, in its bread bag. He took off his pack and sat down next to her at the line. They stayed there until the last voice was gone up the mountain. Then she stood and shook herself and turned around. There would be late ones south of them, still coming, with the snow not far off. He followed her. The white mark on her chest was turned away from him now, but there was one on every tree.

title: The Dog's Book
logline: A foundling floated down the Shenandoah in a cooler grows rich in a Maine trail town and asks town meeting for leave to follow a dog.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, leaving all longings, travels about without a home, and in whom all covetousness is extinct.

bg.commentary: The commentary hangs two stories on this one verse. The first is Jaṭila’s, and this is the second. The rich man Jotika (“the radiant one”) lives in a jeweled palace that the god Sakka raised for him, with seven walls and a yakkha at each gate. His wife was brought to him from Uttarakuru, the northern continent where nothing is owned, with one pot of rice that never runs out and three crystals that cook it, and the household lives by the light of gems and has never seen a lamp. When King Bimbisāra comes to see the palace, the little prince Ajātasattu walks beside him holding his finger and decides that when he is king this householder will not keep it. Years later Ajātasattu, with Devadatta’s help, has his father killed. He marches on the palace, takes his own reflection in the walls for a defending army, and is routed by the yakkha of the first gate. He flees to the monastery, where Jotika is spending the Observance Day listening to the Buddha. Jotika tells him that a thousand kings could not take a thread from him against his will, and offers the twenty rings on his ten fingers. The king leaps eighteen cubits and then eighty and cannot pull one off. Jotika straightens his fingers and they fall into the king’s robe. Then, shaken by what he has seen, he asks the king’s leave to go forth. He becomes an arahat, his wealth vanishes, and the gods take his wife back to Uttarakuru. When the monks doubt that he feels no longing, the Buddha answers with the verse. Read the full commentary story. The palace and the king’s first visit are told inside the story before it. On the king, see Ajātasattu, and on the wife’s country, Uttarakuru.
bg.hist_title: Lake Tahoe and the white disk, 1968 to 2025
bg.history:
Lake Tahoe lies across the California and Nevada line at more than six thousand feet, with seventy-two miles of shoreline, about a third of it in Nevada. The hotel-casinos stand at the south end, in Stateline, and the east shore above them has long been a place of large private estates behind walls. The Sayers, the Regent, Mr. Bright and his house are invented.

The disk is real. A Secchi disk, named for the Italian astronomer who devised it in 1865, is a plain white plate lowered on a line; the depth at which it can no longer be seen is the measure of the water’s clarity. The University of California, Davis has taken that measurement at Lake Tahoe since 1968, with a ten-inch disk, from a research boat, at a long-term station and a mid-lake station, some twenty to thirty times a year. The average for 1967 to 1971 was 97.4 feet, which is still the restoration target. The 2024 average was 62.3 feet. Peg Ostrander and her crew are invented, as are the strips over the depth sounder. The words on them are from Thoreau’s essay “Walking,” printed in the Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, a month after he died, in which he derives “sauntering” from sans terre, without land or a home.

sections.heading: I. The Stone Light
sections.dateline: East shore of Lake Tahoe, Nevada · 1998
sections.text: There was a house on the Nevada side with no lamp in it. It belonged to a man named Bright. The night he was born, in Carson City, every ring and watch and belt buckle in town gave off light, and the rifles in the sheriff’s rack shone so that the deputy on duty read his paper by them. People said that was where the name came from, though it had been his father’s name too. When he was of an age to marry, a crew came to clear a lot for him above the public beach. A carpenter none of them knew walked onto the site and asked what they were doing. Then he told them to go home. He won’t live in anything you can build. By morning the house stood there, seven stories of it, with seven walls around it and a gate in each wall. Nobody on the east shore has ever claimed the work. The walls and floors were of stone so clear and so polished that they gave back the lake. There were stones in the ceilings that gave light, and the household ate and read by them. His wife came from the north. She never said how far, and it was understood to be past where there are roads or fences. She brought with her a quart pot of rice and three stones the size of goose eggs. A pan set on those stones got hot, and

sections.heading: II. The First Gate
sections.text: In March of 2025 A.J. Sayer and a lawyer named Devlin had the old man found unfit to manage his affairs. They put him in a locked unit in Carson City, and A.J. signed for who went in to him and what went in with them. Bim Sayer died there in June. He weighed a hundred and nine pounds. One nurse said he had stopped eating. Another said, once, and afterward would not say it again, that the trays had stopped coming. By August the Regent was A.J.’s, and he remembered the breakfast. He came up the shore road on a Tuesday morning with eleven black Suburbans. He had forty men. Some were lawyers and some were the kind the casino kept for other work, and those were armed. He had a locksmith. He had a paper Devlin had drawn up, which did not need to be good. The outer wall of Bright’s place ran along the highway for a quarter mile. A.J. came around the last curve and saw eleven black cars and forty men coming at him out of the stone. He put his foot on the brake. He’s got his own, he said. He knew. He’s got as many as we have. The column sat on the shoulder with the engines running, facing itself. Then the woman at the first gate came out. Her name was Mrs. Coley. She had swept that gatehous

sections.heading: III. Twenty Rings
sections.text: There was one thing out there, and it was the university’s boat. The university has kept a record of how clear the lake is since 1968. Every couple of weeks, the year round, the boat goes out to the same two stations. Somebody lowers a white disk the size of a dinner plate on a marked line and watches it down. The depth where you lose it gets written in the log. Then you bring it up until you have it again, and that gets written, and the number halfway between is the reading. In the first years it averaged ninety-seven feet. In 2024 it was sixty-two. For thirty-six of those years the hand on the line had been Peg Ostrander’s. She was a field technician, sixty-three years old. She had outlasted three directors, and she answered most questions with the number. Bright had been riding along on reading days for eleven years. He had come the first time to ask whether the lake was getting brighter or darker, and she had handed him the logbook. After that he drove around to Tahoe City on those mornings, straight from breakfast, paid for the diesel and sat on the stern locker. While the disk was down Peg would say a sentence or two to whoever was aboard. It was mostly about not wanting the

sections.heading: IV. Sixty-One
sections.text: He did not go back up the shore road. He walked off the dock at Tahoe City that afternoon in what he had on. The lake has seventy-two miles of shore, and he slept on some part of it, a different part most nights, and ate what he was handed. On reading days he was at the dock before the crew. On the second trip Peg gave him the line. Don’t help it, she said. That was all the instruction there was. Everybody helps it at first. You know about where it went last time, and you see it a foot longer than it can be seen. On the nineteenth of September he let the disk down over the shaded side. He watched it go from white to a greenish white, and then to something he was not sure of, and then he was sure it was gone, and he said so. He brought it up until it was there again. Sixty-one, he said. He had not wanted it to be anything. When he raised his head the east shore had changed. Where the wall had been there was granite and manzanita and a stand of Jeffrey pine, with the highway in plain sight behind. A.J. had been up there twice that month with the locksmith and been turned back at the first gate. The third time there was no gate. They stood on bare rock with Devlin’s paper. A.J. still

title: The White Disk
logline: A casino heir brings forty men to take a lakeshore house that has no lamps, and finds its owner out watching a disk sink.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, after leaving all bondage to men, has risen above all bondage to the gods, and is free from all and every bondage.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, an acrobat who performs from place to place hears the Buddha teach, goes forth as a monk, and soon becomes an arahat. One day, walking into the village for alms with the whole community of monks behind the Buddha, the monks see another acrobat going through the same act he used to do, and ask him whether he still longs for that life. He says he does not. The monks go to the Buddha and accuse him of speaking falsely. The Buddha answers that his son has passed beyond all bonds, and speaks the verse, which in the Pāli speaks of a human yoke, a divine yoke, and freedom from every yoke. The commentary tells the same story again word for word for the next verse (418), where the Buddha says instead that the monk has left behind both delight and discontent. The series met an earlier acrobat, Uggasena, in Cloud of Witnesses.
bg.history:
Between about 1904 and the early 1910s some thousands of Molokans and related Spiritual Christians left Transcaucasia, many from the Kars region, and settled on the east side of Los Angeles. Most of the Los Angeles families were Pryguny, or "Jumpers," whose worship includes leaping when the Holy Spirit is felt to descend. Refusal of military service was one of their chief reasons for leaving Russia, and during the First World War dozens of Molokan men in the United States went to jail for defying the draft. They kept no icons and no priests, chose elders to lead their meetings (sobranie), sang psalms in long unwritten melodies, and ate no pork. The first neighborhood was "the Flats," on the low ground along the east bank of the Los Angeles River below Boyle Heights. The men worked in lumber yards and mills, and in the Depression many took up city rubbish routes. Their elders worried that the picture shows were pulling their children away, and many families moved out toward Karakala and East Los Angeles in the 1920s and '30s.

Hollywood's stunt trade grew out of rodeo and the circus. Cowboys like Yakima Canutt did falls and horse work in westerns, while acrobats and high divers took the falls from roofs and towers in comedies and thrillers. On the carnival lots and at county fairs, the "free act" that drew crowds onto the midway was often a high act, such as a high dive into a tank or a sway pole, a tall flexible pole that the performer bent far out over the crowd from a small platform at the top. One of the best known, Arzeno Selden, "the Stratosphere Man," built himself a sway pole 175 feet tall and toured carnivals and fairs with it until a fall in Florida ended his life in 1951.

sections.heading: I. The Lot
sections.text: Vasily Novikoff was the boy who climbed things. He came over from the Kars country in his mother's arms in 1908, when he was two, and by the time he was nine he had been to the top of everything in the Flats that would hold a boy. He went up the lumber stacks at the yard on Alameda Street where his father drove a team, and walked the ridge of the planing-mill roof with his arms out. He went up the telephone poles on Utah Street by the spikes and sat on the crossbar with his feet hanging and watched the river. The year he was eleven he went up the water tank by the railroad tracks and stood on the rim of it in the wind, and a railroad bull pulled him down by the ankle, and he went before the juvenile court with a great many other Russian boys that year and stood there with his cap in his hands while the judge talked to his father through a girl from the Bethlehem Institutions who could interpret. His father was Pavel Novikoff, a big, quiet man who had driven freight wagons over the mountain roads between Kars and Erzurum, and who in Los Angeles drove a lumber dray for four dollars a day and came home too tired to eat. His mother was Avdotya. She baked bread on Saturdays for the whol

sections.heading: II. The Pictures
sections.text: Garnier taught him for five years. He taught him the ladder and the plate and the handstand on the plate, and the slide for life down the long wire to the ground, and he taught him the sway. That was the whole of it, the old man said. A pole will carry you if you let it. You lean, it comes with you. You go out to the end and it bends and slows, and at the very end of the arc there is a moment when it has stopped going out and has not yet started back, and in that moment you weigh nothing at all. Nobody in the crowd can see it. Only the one at the top knows it is there. That's what they pay you for, Garnier said, and they don't even know they're paying for it. They played county fairs from Phoenix to Klamath Falls, Fresno and Salinas and Tulare and Yakima, and the free act was the thing that brought the crowd onto the lot. When the old man's hands began to shake, Vasya took the pole himself. The bills said BILL NOVAK, THE HUMAN COMET, and he went up it every night in white tights with a spangled sash around his waist, and the people backed away screaming under him the way they had for Garnier. In the winter of 1926 Garnier died in his bed in a rooming house in Riverside, and left Va

sections.heading: III. Come Down
sections.text: His mother died in March of 1935, in her bed on Utah Street, of the dropsy, with the neighbor women around her. This time the telegram came in time. He drove in from Culver City in the Packard in a camel-hair coat, and parked it in the street in front of the house, where the little boys stood around it and would not touch it. They had laid her out in the front room in her white kerchief, and all that night the singers sat with her and sang. Vasya did not go in. He stood outside the door in the dark yard with his hat in his hands, a clean-shaven man in a good coat among men with beards, and the brothers who came and went nodded to him and did not say anything. Through the door he could hear the old men leading and the others coming in behind them, the long notes going up and holding and coming down, and after midnight he heard old Lukyan Ivanovich lead a psalm he remembered from the bench when he was five years old, and the whole room took it up. Душа наша избавилась, как птица, из сети ловящих: сеть расторгнута, и мы избавились. Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped. — Psalm 124:7 (Synodal 123:7; King James Version) L

sections.heading: IV. The Top of the Swing
sections.text: The young men of the sobranie watched him. Most of them had been to the picture shows on Brooklyn Avenue on Saturday nights against their fathers' wishes, and some of them had seen him fall off a roof in a black coat with his arms out and had not known it was him. They asked him about the stars, at first, the cowboys and the comedians. He said they were men like other men. They asked him what the pole was like, up there at the top. He said it was very high. What they watched most was what he did when the Spirit came. Everybody knew that the Spirit came on the meeting in its own time, and when it came the people rose, and the old men went up in their little jumps, and the women, and sometimes a young man would go up so high and so long, his hands in the air, that the elders would stop singing to watch him. The young men waited for Vasily Novikoff to do it. A man who could stand on one foot at the top of a ninety-foot pole in a wind would jump in the Spirit, surely, so that the whole Flats would hear about it. And he did not. When the hall rose and the boards began to shake, Vasya rose too, and lifted his hands, and went up a little on his toes, the way old Lukyan did, and that was a

sections.heading: V. The Free Act
sections.dateline: Mission Road · a Sunday in October 1937
sections.text: That fall the Agafonoffs, out in Karakala, had a new son, and on the third Sunday of October the whole sobranie walked out from Clarence Street after morning meeting to bless him and to eat at their table. They went the way they always went, in a long slow file up the hill and along the streets, the old men in front, the women behind with their kerchiefs bright in the sun, the young men straggling at the back. Lukyan Ivanovich walked at the head of them with his eucalyptus stick, and the singers sang as they walked, so that people came out on their porches along the way to see the Russians go by. On a vacant lot off Mission Road a carnival had come in. It had a Ferris wheel and a merry-go-round and a cookhouse that smelled of onions and hot grease, and a banner over the gate that said BIG SUNSET SHOWS, and in the middle of the lot it had a pole. It was taller than Garnier's had been, a hundred and ten feet at least, painted silver and red in a spiral, and stayed with wires halfway up. A boy in white tights was at the top of it, and the band was playing, and the crowd under him was the crowd of every Sunday on the east side, Mexican families in their good clothes, Jewish boys from B

sections.heading: VI. The Yoke
sections.text: On Monday, after the trucks were in, the three young men went to see Lukyan Ivanovich. Old Ivan Stepanovich Popoff went with them, because the young men had told him, and he agreed it was a serious thing. A lie spoken among the brothers was a sin, and a man who had come back from the picture shows had to be watched more carefully than other men. That was only right. The old man was sitting in his yard behind the house on an upturned crate, in the last of the light, with a set of harness across his knees. It had belonged to the gray horse he drove for twenty years on Alameda Street, and the horse was long dead and he had no wagon, but every so often he took the harness down from its nail and oiled it. He did not look up. He went on working the oil into the leather with his thumb while they told him. Mitya did most of the talking. He told about the carnival and the pole and the boy on top, and what they had asked and what Vasya had answered. He said no, said Mitya. He said it to our faces. He did that for fourteen years, Lukyan Ivanovich. He was famous. A man doesn't do a thing like that for fourteen years and then stop wanting it. He said what isn't so. He should be spoken to, said

title: The Sway Pole
logline: A Molokan boy from the Flats runs off to sway atop a carnival pole, then comes home in a Packard for his mother's funeral.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has left what gives pleasure and what gives pain, who is cold, and free from all germs (of renewed life), the hero who has conquered all the worlds.

bg.commentary: The commentary says only that "the story is the same as the foregoing." An acrobat who performed from place to place heard the Buddha teach, went forth and became an arahat. One day, walking into the village for alms with the whole community behind the Buddha, the monks saw an acrobat going through the same act he used to do, and asked him whether he had no longing for that life. He said no. The monks told the Buddha that he had said what was not true, and the Buddha answered that his son had abandoned both delight and discontent, and spoke the verse. The same story stands behind verse 417, told in The Sway Pole, and the acrobat Uggasena of Cloud of Witnesses began the line of rope-dancers that ends here.
bg.history:
The Great Friends Meeting House on Farewell Street, built in 1699, is the oldest surviving house of worship in Rhode Island. The New England Yearly Meeting worshipped there until 1905, and since 1971 it has belonged to the Newport Historical Society, which keeps it as a museum. Early Friends were often buried without any stone, or under very plain ones. The small meeting in this story, its yearly hour in the old house, the stone shop and the Garniers are invented. Jo's career follows the shape of many circus lives of her generation: the fair "free acts" that kept family high acts on the road dwindled, and performers went to the one-ring Big Apple Circus, which played its tent in Lincoln Center's Damrosch Park from 1981, and to the large Canadian touring shows.

George Fox, the first leader of the Quakers, wrote to Elizabeth Claypole, Oliver Cromwell's daughter, when she lay ill and "much troubled in mind" in 1658, the year of her death. The letter is printed in his Journal, and Friends still quote its opening; later in the letter Fox writes that when a person goes astray "the mind flies up in the air." In the Pāli of verse 418 the word Müller renders "cold" means cooled, as a fire is cooled, or a fever.

sections.heading: I. The Last Garnier
sections.text: Jo Garnier was born in a trailer behind the grandstand of the Ionia Free Fair in Michigan in July of 1966, between the two shows her father did each night on the sway pole. Her people had been on the rope in this country since before the Revolution, and her father liked to say so to the fair boards, and to add that one of them, back at the start, had danced on a ship's mast at Newport in Rhode Island and then run off and married a Quaker, and that the family had never got over it. He said it as a joke. It was the only story about the family that everyone in it knew. She was on the wire at six and on the pole at sixteen, when her father's back went. She worked the fairs with the family until there were no more fairs that hired a free act, and then she went to New York and flew for the one-ring circus in the tent at Lincoln Center, and then for the big Canadian shows, in Las Vegas and on tour, for fifteen years. She was a flyer and then a catcher and then, when her knees began to go, she went back to what she had started on and did a slack-wire act thirty feet up, alone, in a white leotard, that the papers in Montreal called the stillest thing in the show. In Phoenix in 2005 a riggin

sections.heading: II. Washington Square
sections.dateline: Newport · a First Day in August 2024
sections.text: Once a year, in August, the historical society let the meeting hold worship in the old house on Farewell Street, the great meetinghouse of 1699 where the Friends of all New England had gathered every summer for two hundred years. The meeting walked there together from the Point, the eleven of them who were left and a few summer attenders, the long way, through town, because Walt liked to go by the water. He went in front with his cane. Jo walked at the back with Abby Sherman, who was twenty-four and home from graduate school, and Abby's friend Dana, a counselor from Providence who had been attending since the spring. Washington Square was full of the Sunday crowd off the cruise ship, and in the middle of it, in front of the Colony House, a troupe of street acrobats from Montreal had strung a slack wire between two steel tripods and set up a speaker. A boy was walking the wire in sneakers, and then a girl went up after him in a white leotard and stood on it with no hands, and lay down on it on her back, and stood up again, and rocked it, side to side, slowly, in the long swings that make the crowd under a wire draw in its breath. The tourists had their phones up. A man in a captain'

sections.heading: III. The Old House
sections.dateline: The Great Friends Meeting House · the same forenoon
sections.text: Walt did not say anything to them on the street. He went up the steps and in, and sat down on the front of the old benches facing the room, where the ministers had sat in the old days, because his knees would not take the gallery stairs, and the others sat down where they liked in the wide plain room under the beams, and the door was shut, and it was quiet. It was quiet a long time. The traffic went by outside on Farewell Street. The benches were the same benches. Jo sat by a window with her hands open on her knees, and if anything was going on in her it did not show. Abby looked at her and then at the floor. Dana looked at the clock. Toward the end of the hour Walt stood up. He stood with both hands on the head of his cane, and the old benches creaked all through the house as people leaned to listen, the way they say those benches always creaked when somebody rose who did not rise often. Friends, he said. I was told this morning that one of us said what isn't so. I was told she must want a thing she gave up. Or she must hate it, and won't say. I don't believe it's either. I've sat next to her thirteen years. She's put down the wanting, and she's put down the not wanting, both, and

sections.heading: IV. Plain Stone
sections.dateline: The stone shop on Spring Street · October 2024
sections.text: In September the meeting took up a question that had been before it, off and on, for nine years. In the old Friends' burying ground across town, where the early Friends had been put in the ground with no stones over them at all, the book kept by the recorder showed two who had lain side by side since 1819 with nothing to mark them: Edmund Lisle, who had been a public Friend and traveled in the ministry as far as Georgia, and Ann his wife. A descendant in Ohio had written offering to pay for a stone. Friends do not hurry. But in the fall they united on it, a small plain stone, no taller than the grass would let it be, with the two names and the years and nothing else, and they asked Jo to cut it. She did it in the back of the shop on a Tuesday, from a piece of Pennsylvania slate as dark as a mussel shell. She laid out the letters in pencil on the polished face, plain Roman capitals an inch high, and then she stood at the stone with the mallet and the chisel and cut them, all day, one stroke and then the next, the chips coming off in little gray flakes, and the light from the alley window going slowly across the floor. The other carvers went home at five. She finished at a quarter to

title: Plain Stone
logline: Walking with her Quaker meeting through Washington Square, a gravestone letterer who once worked the high wire passes beneath a street troupe's slack wire.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who knows the destruction and the return of beings everywhere, who is free from bondage, welfaring (Sugata), and awakened (Buddha).
Him I call indeed a Brahmana whose path the gods do not know, nor spirits (Gandharvas), nor men, whose passions are extinct, and who is an Arhat (venerable).

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the brahmin Vaṅgīsa can tell where any dead man has been reborn by rapping on his skull, and other brahmins dress him in two red robes and tour him from town to town for fees. At Sāvatthi they quarrel with the Buddha’s followers over whose teacher is greater, and everyone goes to the monastery to find out. The Buddha sets out five skulls, of men reborn in hell, as an animal, as a human, among the gods, and of an arahant. Vaṅgīsa reads the first four, and the Buddha applauds each answer, but the fifth defeats him. Wanting the “spell,” he goes forth, is given the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body, keeps telling his old companions to wait a little, and soon becomes an arahant. When he tells them it is now impossible for him to go, the monks think he is lying, and the Buddha answers that his son now knows all about the passing away and rebirth of beings. Vaṅgīsa became the order’s great improviser of verse.
bg.history:
Chögyam Trungpa, a Tibetan teacher trained in the Kagyu and Nyingma lineages, settled in Boulder in the early 1970s, founded the umbrella organization Vajradhatu in 1973, and in 1974 founded the Naropa Institute, whose first summer session drew more than 2,000 people. That summer Allen Ginsberg, Anne Waldman, Diane di Prima and John Cage were asked to found a poetics program, which Ginsberg and Waldman named the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics, and Ram Dass taught a course on the Bhagavad Gita to more than a thousand students. Trungpa was a gifted and influential teacher who also drank heavily, often kept students waiting for hours, and was later the subject of serious accounts of sexual relationships with students and abuses of power, including the 1975 seminary incident involving the poet W. S. Merwin.

The Evans-Wentz edition of the Bardo Thödol, translated by Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup and published in 1927 as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, was widely read in the American counterculture; it describes the dull lights of the six realms that draw the dead toward rebirth and the Clear Light that frees them. A kapala is a cup made from the crown of a human skull, used in Tibetan Vajrayana ritual, and Chöd, the “cutting” practice associated with the eleventh-century yogini Machig Labdrön, is traditionally done in graveyards and charnel grounds with a hand drum and a thighbone trumpet, the practitioner offering his or her own body in visualization. The verses of Vaṅgīsa and the commentator’s story of his skull-tapping appear in C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s 1913 translation of the Theragatha, Psalms of the Brethren.

sections.heading: I. The Professor’s Desk
sections.text: Thayer Vance was nine the first time he did it. His grandfather had taught anatomy at the Harvard Medical School for thirty-one years, and on the desk in his study, between the inkstand and a tin of horehound drops, he kept a skull that had come out of the teaching collection when the collection was replaced. It had a brass hinge in the crown so the top lifted off like a lid, and a number inked over the left eye. The boy was not supposed to touch it. He was alone in the study one wet afternoon in March, waiting to be driven to the dentist, and he flicked it on the forehead with the nail of his middle finger, the way his mother tested a melon. The sound was small and dry. Behind the sound, though not in the room, a light came up. It was dull and bluish, the blue of skim milk in a glass, and it lasted as long as the sound lasted and went out. He did it again. Blue again. He told nobody. Over the next nine years he tapped every skull he could get his hands on, which was not many: two in the biology laboratory at Milton, one in a junk shop on Charles Street that wanted thirty dollars for it, and on a family trip to Rome, while his sisters were looking the other way, a whole wall of the

sections.heading: II. The Crate
sections.text: Gil Ostrow and Danny Kehoe had been to Kathmandu twice and come back the second time with a Volkswagen bus that had been green once and a tea crate that had been shipped by sea to Oakland, full of what Gil called Himalayan ritual art. There were brass bells and dorjes, a thanka with water damage, a dozen prayer wheels for the tourists, three thighbone trumpets wrapped in newspaper from Asan Tole, and at the bottom, packed in rice straw, eleven skull cups. The Tibetans called them kapala. Some were mounted in silver with a silver lid. Some were bare bone, the crown of a head sawn off clean at the brow and polished inside by a hundred years of use. Gil sold the bells and the wheels from a card table outside a head shop on Thirteenth Street. He had not sold a single skull. Thayer met them at a party in a rented house on College Avenue, where somebody had filled one of the bare kapalas with Red Zinger tea and was passing it around as a joke. When it came to Thayer he did not drink. He tapped the rim with his fingernail, and a dull white light came up behind the music and the talk and went out, and he said, before he could stop himself, Oh, this one went up. sections.heading: III. Sunday
sections.text: Boulder that summer was full past bursting. More than two thousand people had come for the institute, and they slept in vans along the creek and on the floors of rented houses and in tents up Sunshine Canyon. They filled the auditorium at Boulder High, and on the nights the Rinpoche spoke he was often an hour late and sometimes two, and taught in a suit with a glass beside him that everybody could see was not water, and said things that made the room laugh and then go so quiet you could hear the wiring in the lights. More than a thousand had signed up to hear Ram Dass on the Bhagavad Gita. The two crowds looked at each other across the parking lots. The Rinpoche’s older students had cut their hair and wore jackets, and said sitting, and Ram Dass’s people still said far out, and the town said hippies about both. On Sunday morning the Hill was quiet. Gil had the card table out early for the church crowd. A few doors up, four people came out of a house carrying things: a tall woman with a box of incense from the head shop, a man in a Vietnam field jacket with a coffee can full of marigolds from somebody’s yard, a heavyset nurse with a bag of oranges, and a skinny girl with nothing. sections.heading: IV. Five Skulls
sections.text: Her name was Dolkar. She was about fifty. She had been born in Nangchen, in Kham, and given at nine to a hermitage of women who practiced the cutting, which meant that they went at night to the places where the dead were laid out for the vultures, and beat the big hand drum and blew the thighbone trumpet, and offered their own bodies, in the mind, piece by piece, to anything that was hungry. In 1959 she had walked out over the passes with two other nuns, one of whom lived. She had broken stones for road crews in Sikkim for seven years and cooked for a Denver geologist and his wife in Kathmandu for five more, and when they came home they brought her with them. She did not go to the Rinpoche’s talks. He is a great lama, she said, when the house asked her. I am a cook. The twelve students paid her and were a little afraid of her. The kitchen was at the back of the house, with a window that looked west at the first Flatiron. When the four came in with Thayer and the two dealers, there were five clean white dish towels already folded in a row on the oilcloth. The nurse said afterward that Ama-la had folded them at six, before anybody had heard of Thayer Vance. Dolkar looked at Thayer’s

sections.heading: V. The Things Before
sections.dateline: The back porch · July and August
sections.text: There was a board on the back porch, sanded smooth, with a folded blanket at one end. It had been there since spring, the nurse said, and nobody in the house had known what it was for. Dolkar taught him the refuge in Tibetan, syllable by syllable, at the kitchen table, until he could say it without looking at her mouth, and then she showed him how to go down on the board, knees and hands and forehead, and slide forward full length with the arms out, and come back up, and say it, and go down again. She gave him a string of a hundred and eight bone beads to count on. When he asked how many, she said a hundred thousand. He laughed. She did not. There was one other thing. In the morning, she said, before you bow, knock on your own head. She showed him, on her own gray hair, with a fingernail, two taps, like a person at a door. Then say what is in it. He knocked on his own head on the porch at five the next morning with the magpies going in the yard, and listened, and no light came up. Nothing at all. He tried again. It frightened him so badly that he went into the kitchen, where she was already lighting the stove, and told her it didn’t work on him. Say what is in it, she said. Brains.

sections.heading: VI. Impossible
sections.dateline: Mapleton Avenue · the end of August
sections.text: The summer session ended. The vans along the creek pulled out one by one for California. Gil packed the bus for Santa Fe, where the man on Canyon Road wanted more white skulls for the winter trade, and pulled up in front of the house on Mapleton and leaned on the horn. Thayer came down the walk with the two robes folded over his arm. Well? said Gil. You get it? Gil, I can’t go now. It’s impossible for me to go. You get it or not? It isn’t a thing you get. He put the robes through the window onto the seat. Sell the white ones for what they’re worth. Sell the smoke ones too. They’re all the same now. They were always the same. Gil looked at him for a long time through his sunglasses. Then he said the old woman had got her hooks in him, the way they always did, and he put the bus in gear. Danny sat in the passenger seat with the robes on his lap and did not say anything, and looked back once. In the kitchen that night the man in the field jacket was angry. His name was Walt Garza, and he had been sitting with Dolkar for two years, and he said it in front of everybody. The kid’s lying to somebody. Either he told those two he’d come back with the goods, and he’s stiffing them, or he’s s

title: The Fifth Skull
logline: In Naropa's first summer, a Harvard dropout who can tap a Tibetan skull cup and tell where its owner went is put to the test by a cook.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who calls nothing his own, whether it be before, behind, or between, who is poor, and free from the love of the world.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the merchant Visākha hears the Buddha teach and attains the third path, non-return. That day he walks past his wife Dhammadinnā at the window without his usual smile, eats in silence, and then tells her that all the wealth in the house is hers. She asks what he will do; he says he is finished with worldly affairs. "Who will accept the saliva you have rejected?" she answers, and asks to go forth herself. He escorts her to the nuns with rich offerings. She goes to live in the country and soon reaches full awakening, then returns to Rājagaha. Visākha, not daring to ask whether she has come back discontented, questions her on the paths; she answers each, until his last question, when she tells him he has gone too far and should ask the Buddha. The Buddha says her answers were well said, that he would have answered the same, and speaks the verse. Their conversation is preserved as the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, which ends with Visākha asking what lies on the other side of unbinding.
bg.history:
Seattle's Chinese community is older than the city's fire of 1889 and survived its expulsion of Chinese residents in 1886. The neighborhood around King and Jackson Streets was cut through by Interstate 5 in the 1960s and crowded by the Kingdome from 1976 until its demolition in 2000; Hing Hay Park, with a pavilion built in Taipei, opened on King Street in 1975, and a new Chinatown Gate was dedicated at the foot of King Street in 2008. Cantonese dim sum houses and small storefront temples are part of its life. The Diamond Sutra, the Perfection of Wisdom text whose Dunhuang copy of 868 is broadly considered the oldest dated printed book, is read and lectured on in Chinese Buddhist temples everywhere; its ninth chapter takes up the four fruits of the path, and its eighteenth says that past, present and future thought cannot be grasped. Shifu's story of Deshan and the old woman with the rice cakes is a classic of Chan: the word for her refreshments, dianxin, Cantonese dim sum, can be read as "touching" or "dotting" the heart-mind.

Full ordination for women died out in the Theravāda countries in the Middle Ages, but the Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇī lineage continues in East Asian Buddhism, and women from many countries, including the United States, travel to Taiwan for ordination programs lasting six to eight weeks. A Chinese Buddhist who leaves home (chujia, Cantonese chut ga) shaves the head, receives a Dharma name and the novice precepts, and later the full precepts; laypeople greet monastics with three full bows. The women's monastery, the temple on Jackson Street and the Lucky Pearl are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Window
sections.text: For thirty years Leung Wai-man came back from the produce market at ten minutes to seven, walking up King Street from the alley behind the restaurant with a box of gai lan on his shoulder, and for thirty years Chan Mei-ling was at the window. It was the upstairs window, the one over the red sign. Lucky Pearl Seafood and Dim Sum had the ground floor and the kitchen in back, and above it were three rooms where they had lived since 1988, when they bought the building with a loan from the bank on Jackson Street and money from four of his cousins and every dollar she had saved working the cart at a dim sum house in Vancouver. She stood at the window at ten minutes to seven every morning in her housecoat with a cup of hot water with lemon in it, and he came up the street with the box, and when he got under the sign he looked up and smiled, and lifted two fingers off the box and wiggled them at her, which was a thing he had done since the first week, and which their son Kevin, when he was little, thought was the funniest thing in the world. Wai-man was sixty-three. He had come from Hong Kong in 1975, a dim sum cook since he was fourteen, with burn scars on both forearms from the steamers

sections.heading: II. Take It
sections.text: Staff meal at the Lucky Pearl was at three-thirty, in the dead hour between lunch and dinner, at the big round table in the back with the lazy Susan. The cooks and the waiters and the dishwashers ate, and Wai-man and Mei-ling ate with them, and every day for thirty years Wai-man had served her first. He would turn the lazy Susan and pick out the best piece of steamed fish, the cheek, with his own chopsticks and put it in her bowl, and say Sik faan, eat, and only then would anybody else start. That Monday he sat down and ate his rice. He ate the gai lan and the tofu and he did not touch the fish or the soy-sauce chicken or the pork. He did not turn the lazy Susan. He did not say sik faan. He ate slowly, with great attention, as if rice were something he had just heard about and wanted to understand, and when his bowl was empty he set his chopsticks across it and sat there, and the whole table went quiet around him and nobody looked at Mei-ling. He’s angry, she thought. Something I did. Something with the money. That night after closing, when the cooks had gone and the chairs were up on the tables and the only light in the dining room was the red glow from the sign coming in through

sections.heading: III. Leaving Home
sections.text: Wai-man drove her up himself, in the van, which was now Ah Fong’s van and which Ah Fong lent them for the day. In the back were the offerings: two fifty-pound sacks of jasmine rice, a case of peanut oil, a case of soy sauce, ten pounds of dried shiitake, a box of the good oolong, a check, and a suitcase with almost nothing in it. The women’s monastery was two hours north and east, past the tulip fields and the dairies and up a gravel road into the foothills, on a hundred acres of second-growth fir that a retired couple from Bellevue had given to the Dharma in the 1990s. There were nine nuns there and an abbess from Malaysia, a long wooden hall, a kitchen, a meditation hall with a woodstove, cabins in the trees, and a bell. Wai-man carried the rice in from the van on his shoulder, one sack at a time, the way he had carried the gai lan up King Street, and set it down in the kitchen, and bowed to the abbess three times, forehead to the floor, and drove back to Seattle alone in the long July light. They shaved her head the next week. She had worn her hair to her shoulders since 1975. An old nun from Penang did it with clippers and then a razor, in the yard, while the others chanted, an

sections.heading: IV. The Steamer
sections.text: She asked to stay in the country. The abbess had meant to send her down to the temple in Seattle after her novice year, to help in the city where they needed a nun who spoke Cantonese, but Fa Yu asked to stay, and stayed. She wanted, she said, to be quiet for a while. She had not been quiet since she was eleven years old. She did not know how to be quiet. She sat in the meditation hall at four-thirty in the morning with the woodstove ticking and her legs on fire and her mind running the front of the Lucky Pearl, table nine wants more tea, table four has been waiting for the lo mai gai, the fish man is short again, Kevin hasn’t called. It went on like that for months. The abbess told her not to fight it. The abbess told her to watch it the way you would watch a busy dining room from the kitchen door, everybody coming and going, and none of it, the abbess said, is yours. They put her in the kitchen, naturally, because she was a restaurant woman. She cooked for ten. She made the vegetarian dim sum for the festival days, mushroom and bamboo shoot in a rice-flour wrapper, chive dumplings, turnip cake, because Wai-man had taught her the pleats in 1981 and she had never told anybody she k

sections.heading: V. Questions
sections.dateline: The temple on Jackson Street · October 2019
sections.text: In the fall of 2019 she asked the abbess to send her down to Seattle after all. The abbess asked why, now, when she had asked to stay. Fa Yu said that the old women who came up on the bus could not come up anymore, a lot of them, their knees, their sons wouldn’t drive them, and that there were people on King Street who had eaten at her tables for thirty years and would listen to the Dharma from her who would never listen to it from a stranger. She said there was nothing left for her to do in the country. The abbess looked at her a long time and said yes. Wai-man heard on a Thursday that she had come back and was staying in the room behind the shrine at the temple on Jackson Street. He had been living in a rented room on Maynard Avenue for a year and a half, cooking in the temple kitchen every day but Monday, keeping the eight precepts, sitting with Shifu in the evenings. He had not seen her since July of 2018. He did not know why she had come back. He thought, Maybe it was too hard. Maybe she misses the restaurant. Maybe she wants to come home. And he thought that he could not ask her that. It would be a terrible thing to ask a nun. He went on Friday afternoon. She was sitting on a

sections.heading: VI. Well Said
sections.text: He bowed to her three times again, and got up, and went down the hall to Shifu’s room, where the old man was sitting at a card table eating oranges, and sat down, and told him all of it. The questions, the answers, every one, as near as he could remember them. Then the last question, and what she said. Shifu peeled an orange in one long piece and laid the peel on the table in a spiral. What she told you is well said, he said. Every word. If you had asked me, I would have told you the same, and not so well. He put a section of orange in his mouth and ate it. That one is my daughter in the Dharma, Mr. Leung. She went to the country a restaurant woman and came back the old lady at the tea stall. Deshan would have gone hungry all the way home. Then he took down the sutra from the shelf behind him, the old English one with the cracked binding that he read on Wednesday nights, and opened it near the middle, and read to him, slowly, in English, the way he did, as if he were reading the words for the first time. And why? Because, O Subhûti, a past thought is not perceived, a future thought is not perceived, and the present thought is not perceived. — Diamond Sutra 18 She has nothing behind

title: Thirteen Pleats
logline: A Chinatown dim sum cook comes home from a Diamond Sutra talk, walks past his wife at the window, and hands her everything.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, King Pasenadi and the citizens of Sāvatthī take turns feasting the Buddha and his monks, each trying to outgive the other. After six rounds the king lies down in despair, and Queen Mallikā devises the Gifts beyond Compare: a pavilion of sāla wood, golden boats of perfume, noble girls to fan the monks, and five hundred elephants each holding a white parasol over a monk. One monk is left without an elephant, and only rogue elephants remain. The queen has a young rogue stood beside the Elder Aṅgulimāla, once a murderer who wore a garland of his victims’ fingers; the animal tucks its tail, drops its ears, closes its eyes and stands motionless. The king then gives away everything in the hall. When Aṅgulimāla tells the monks he felt no fear, they accuse him of lying, and the Buddha answers, “My son Aṅgulimāla has no fear.” Read the full commentary story, or about Aṅgulimāla and King Pasenadi.
