bg.history:
Western Missouri came out of the Civil War emptied and burned. In August 1863 General Order No. 11 expelled most rural families from Cass, Jackson and Bates counties, and for years afterward returning families found little standing on their farms but chimneys. The Pacific Railroad reached Pleasant Hill, on Big Creek, in 1865. Missouri’s constitution of that year kept former Confederates and their sympathizers from voting, holding office, practicing law, teaching or preaching unless they swore a sweeping test oath. The Supreme Court struck down the oath for clergy in Cummings v. Missouri (1867), but the voting ban stood until 1870, and it kept the war’s two sides apart in every county seat.

The German Baptist Brethren, called Dunkers or Dunkards (see Schwarzenau Brethren), began in Germany in 1708 and came to Pennsylvania in the 1720s. They dressed plainly, refused oaths and lawsuits, and would not bear arms. Many older members in the 1860s still read Luther’s German Bible. The Pryces, Mr. Reese, the Big Creek congregation and the dinners are fictional.

sections.heading: I. The Colonel’s Dinner
sections.text: There were fifty Dunkard brethren on Big Creek that August, counting old Elder Ebersole and his own few. The rest had come into Cass County on the cars to Pleasant Hill and then on foot, from Illinois and Iowa and the new settlements in Kansas, to hold a council and to raise a second meetinghouse, the first one having grown too small. They wore the plain coat with the standing collar and the broad black hat, and beards with no mustache. They would not swear an oath or go to law or carry a gun, and during the war both armies had shot some of them for it. Mallie Pryce watched them go by on the Pleasant Hill road from her own front gallery, two and two, carrying their tools. Her husband watched too. Abner Pryce had been a colonel of the state militia and was now the largest dealer in horses and mules between the Osage and the Kansas line. Four years before, he had ridden into the Dunkards’ yard with forty men and a rope to take the worst bushwhacker in western Missouri, the one they called Beads, who wore dead men’s fingers on a string around his neck. He had found an old man mending harness and a young one splitting kindling, and he had ridden out again without either. He did not tal

sections.heading: II. The Town’s Dinner
sections.text: Nobody in Cass County agreed about the war. The Colonel’s party had won it and held the courthouse, and under the new constitution a man could not vote or hold any office until he swore he had never once fed or pitied a rebel, and most of the families who had come back to their chimneys could not swear that, or would not. They traded at the same stores as the Colonel’s people and did not speak to them. And each side wanted the Dunkards at its table, the way two brothers who have quarreled will each want the preacher to come home with him after church. On Tuesday morning Mr. Tolliver Reese, who kept the dry goods store on the square and had spent the war years in Texas, walked out to Big Creek and asked the Elder if the brethren would take dinner with the town. They set the tables in the square under the locusts. There were eleven hams and every hen in Harrisonville that had quit laying, and pies down the middle of the boards the whole length. The Colonel went, because it would have looked small not to, and Mallie went with him and counted the hams. She had stood in that square on a court day two summers before. She had been coming out of Reese’s with a card of buttons when a boy sh

sections.heading: III. Mallie’s Plan
sections.text: She let him lie an hour. Then she went up with the lamp. Abner. What ails you? You know what. I don’t. So he told her, to the wall. He had fed them three times and been bettered three times. He had put down the rebellion in this county and he could not put down a dry goods merchant with a ham. If he could not give those people more than Tolliver Reese could, he did not know what he was for. Mallie had trimmed bonnets in a shop in Lexington before he married her, and the town had never let her forget it. She had learned in that shop that people do not remember what was on the hat. They remember that nobody else had one. Did you ever hear of a colonel whipped by a county seat? she said. Turn over and listen. You can’t beat them at victuals. Every woman in Harrisonville can cook. So don’t cook against them. He turned over. Have Lon build a pavilion in the walnut grove. Make it round and open at the sides, out of that new walnut plank from the steam mill, and big enough for fifty to sit. Send to Kansas City on the cars for fifty white umbrellas, the kind that screw to a buggy seat. Borrow every buggy from here to the state line. Put one of your horses to each buggy, and in each one set

sections.heading: IV. Forty-Nine Horses
sections.dateline: The Pryce place · the next week
sections.text: It took six days. The walnut came from the mill still wet, purple-brown and smelling sour, and Lon and four men framed the pavilion in a ring among the trees. The umbrellas came down from Kansas City in two crates, white cotton on steel ribs. Buggies came from Pleasant Hill and Peculiar and from over the line at Paola, some with their owners’ daughters still in them. The lemons came in a barrel, each one wrapped in paper. Mallie went down into the icehouse herself with a lantern and scraped back the sawdust and counted the blocks left from January, and there were enough. The girls slept four to a bed in the Pryces’ house, and it sounded like a henhouse until midnight. On the Friday evening the Colonel came in from the lots with his hat in his hand. Mallie. I’m a horse short. You have two hundred head out there. I have forty-nine broke to harness. I sent that string to the railroad graders in July. The rest are mules that never had a collar on and the ones in the back lot, and you know what’s in the back lot. Let those see a man on foot and they come on like a March wind. She did know. And she knew which one he was not naming. There was a bay stud colt back there, three years old. H

sections.heading: V. The Fiftieth Buggy
sections.dateline: Big Creek meetinghouse · Saturday, first light
sections.text: Forty-nine buggies stood in the meetinghouse lane before sunup with their umbrellas furled, and forty-nine girls in their summer muslins sat holding the lines and not talking much, now that it had come to it. The brethren came out from morning prayer and stopped at the sight. Elder, said the brother from Illinois, this is show. This is the very thing we left the world to be shut of. It’s his show, said the Elder. It needn’t be ours. Get up in it, Daniel, and hurt nobody’s feelings. And he climbed into the first buggy himself, an old man of sixty-eight, and thanked the child who was driving it. The fiftieth buggy stood at the end of the line with its shafts on the ground. Then the colt came up the lane. Lon had him on two ropes with a man on each, and a third man walked well behind with a whip, and they had tied a coat over the animal’s head. He came sideways, in jumps. The horses nearest him began to back in their breeching, and a girl cried out. Mallie had driven out in the Colonel’s own rig. She got down and went to where Gabriel Mantooth was standing at the tail of the line. He was the last, as he was the last at every table. Mr. Mantooth, there is a buggy for you and no driver.

sections.heading: VI. The Grove
sections.text: The brethren sat in a ring in the walnut pavilion with the copper boilers shining down the middle like ten small suns. The ice had been cut from the Pryces’ pond in January and kept under sawdust, and it knocked against the copper. Girls crushed mint in their hands and dropped it in. They went around with dippers and with palm-leaf fans. The old men from Iowa sat very straight and were fanned, and bore it. All of Harrisonville had followed the buggies out and stood among the trees. They looked at the ice and at the walnut. They looked at forty-nine horses on a picket line, and at one bay colt standing loose beside the pavilion with his eyes half shut. Nobody had tied him, and he did not offer to go. The town knew when it was beaten. Mr. Reese said so to the Colonel, in so many words, and the Colonel, who had gone to bed over a ham, found it did not taste the way he had expected. He stood up at the end of the meal. Elder Ebersole. Whatever is under this roof is yours and your people’s. The boilers, the benches, the umbrellas, whatever is good in it and whatever isn’t. The roof too, and the posts. He stopped and looked out at the colt. And that horse, if any man of yours will have hi

sections.heading: VII. Walnut
sections.text: The brethren went home on the cars the next week with the meetinghouse roofed. Each man from Illinois and Iowa and Kansas carried a white cotton umbrella under his arm, which caused some talk in the congregations there. The copper boilers went to the sisters on Big Creek for apple butter. The pavilion came down a board at a time. Lon drew the nails himself and would not let his men split a plank. It was good walnut, and by the first frost it had dried to the color of a saddle. That fall anybody on the Harrisonville road could see a bay horse coming along in the shafts of a borrowed wagon with a load of walnut plank, and a young man with no mustache walking at his head. The young man held no line and carried no whip. They went north a long day’s haul to a place near the ford on the Little Blue, where a widow and four children had come back in September to a chimney and a cellar hole. The walnut went up around the chimney. It took three weeks. The horse stood in the yard the whole of every day without a halter while the walls rose. Children climbed his legs. A dog slept under him. The hammering started each morning and stopped each night, and the widow came out with water for the man

title: The Fiftieth Buggy
logline: A militia colonel and a county seat compete to feed fifty Dunkards, until his wife orders fifty buggies and comes up one horse short.

verses.text: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who knows his former abodes, who sees heaven and hell, has reached the end of births, is perfect in knowledge, a sage, and whose perfections are all perfect.

bg.commentary: In the commentary, the Buddha falls ill with a disorder of the humors and sends his attendant, the elder Upavāṇa, to the brahmin Devahita for hot water. Devahita is overjoyed to be asked. He gives hot water and a jar of molasses and has one of his men carry the water on a shoulder pole. The elder bathes the Buddha in the hot water and gives him the molasses mixed in water to drink, and the illness passes. Devahita then comes to the Buddha with a question in verse: to whom should one give, so that the gift bears great fruit? The Buddha answers that gifts to one who is truly a brahmin, the sage who knows his former lives, sees heaven and hell and has come to the end of birth, bear the greatest fruit, and Devahita takes refuge and becomes a lay disciple.
bg.history:
In mid-February 2021 a run of winter storms, the worst of them named Uri, drove arctic air deep into Texas. Demand for power broke records while frozen gas supplies and unwinterized plants failed, and in the early hours of February 15 the state’s grid operator began cutting power to keep the whole system from collapsing. More than 4.5 million homes and businesses lost power, some for days, in temperatures that reached −2 °F at Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport on February 16, the coldest in North Texas in seventy-two years. Pipes burst across the state and many people faced hypothermia in their own homes; the state later put the death toll at 246. See the 2021 Texas power crisis. Gas appliances with a standing pilot, which need no electricity, were for many families the only heat or hot water left.

The Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt now has many parishes in American cities and suburbs, including in Dallas–Fort Worth. Its hymns, sung to hand cymbals and triangle, were handed down orally for centuries, and the parish cantor, the mu’allim or “teacher,” taught them to the deacons by ear. Most cantors of the older generation were blind, since the blind were thought to have the finer ear; the most famous modern cantor, Mikhail Girgis El Batanouny (1873–1957), helped preserve the chants. Psalm 14 in the Greek numbering (15 in the Hebrew) is among the psalms of the First Hour of the Agpeya, the Coptic book of hours prayed each morning. The Mo’alem, Dr. Nabil, Bishoy, Bà Sáu and the church off Pipeline Road are invented.

sections.heading: I. The Ear
sections.text: The Mo’alem Fahmy Wassef had been blind since he was three years old, from a sickness of the eyes in a village above Asyut, and he had been a cantor since he was eleven, because in those days that was what a blind boy in a Coptic family became if God had given him an ear. He had sung in the churches of Shubra for forty years and in Texas for twenty-two. He was eighty-four. He lived alone in a second-floor apartment in a complex behind a tire shop on Pipeline Road, four minutes on foot from the church, which he had chosen for that reason over his son’s spare room in Keller, and he walked to every service with one hand on the rail of the outside stair and the other on the shoulder of whatever boy had been sent for him. He could tell the cars in the church parking lot by their engines. He could tell the boys by their breathing before they opened their mouths. People said, and it was the kind of thing people say, that he could tell you which deacon in the choir had not prayed that morning, and that when he sang the Midnight Praise in the month of Kiahk he heard another choir behind his own and slowed down so as not to get ahead of it. He did not say anything about that. He did not say

sections.heading: II. The Freeze
sections.text: It began to snow on the Sunday, which was Valentine’s Day, and it went on snowing. By evening the highways were glass. In the night it got colder than anybody in North Texas had felt in seventy years, and in the small hours of Monday morning the lights went out in the apartment complex behind the tire shop and in half the houses in Euless and Bedford and Hurst, and they did not come back. The grid was failing. The gas lines that fed the power plants were freezing at the wellheads, and the plants were tripping off one after another, and the people who ran the grid were cutting power to whole towns at a time to keep the rest of it from going down. On Tuesday morning the thermometer at the airport stood at two below zero. Bishoy’s parents’ house had a tankless water heater and an electric range and a heat pump and nothing worked. They sat in the living room in their coats around a fire in a fireplace that had never been used, burning the slats of a broken bed frame, and his mother called everybody in the church directory one after another to see who was alive. The Mo’alem did not answer his phone on Monday. His son in Keller could not get his car out of the driveway. On Tuesday mornin

sections.heading: III. The Pilot Light
sections.text: Dr. Nabil Habashy was seventy-one years old and the most important man in the parish, after the priests, and some said before them. He had come to Texas in 1979 with a doctorate in geology from Cairo University and a job with an oil company in Houston, and he had made his money in the 2000s in the Barnett Shale, the great field of gas that lay under Fort Worth and the towns around it, so that in a sense the gas that heated half of the Metroplex had passed under his hands before it got to them. He knew the Coptic liturgy by heart in Coptic and could explain the Greek of it to the priests. He chaired the building committee for the new church, the real one with a dome, that was going to be built on the land the parish had bought off Highway 10, and the fund stood that winter at four million dollars, and a great deal of that was his. He was a proud man, and a correct one, and people were a little afraid of him. He lived in the same brick ranch house in Bedford that he had bought in 1986, which had a gas range and a gas furnace with an electric blower that did not work and a gas water heater in the hall closet that was older than his grandson. It had a standing pilot, a small blue flame

sections.heading: IV. The Basin
sections.text: The woman in the apartment below the Mo’alem’s was Vietnamese, a grandmother whom everybody in the complex called Bà Sáu, and she had been looking after him since the lights went out, bringing up rice soup heated on a little butane camp stove she had bought for hurricanes in Houston twenty years ago. She had a statue of the white-robed Quan Âm on the shelf over her television, with an orange and a cup of tea in front of it, and the Mo’alem had told Bishoy once that her stair was the only one in the complex that did not ring when you climbed it, because she swept it. When she heard the boys on the stair she came up with the stove under her arm and set it on the Mo’alem’s kitchen counter and lit it, and put the stockpot on it to keep the water hot, and went back down again without having said a word in any language they shared. Bishoy had never bathed anybody. He had seen his mother do it for his grandmother before she died. He found the plastic dishpan under the sink and filled it with the water from Dr. Nabil’s heater, cut with a little from the thermos so it would not scald, and knelt on the floor of the bedroom, and took the Mo’alem’s feet out from under the blankets one after th

sections.heading: V. The Question
sections.text: Dr. Nabil came to the apartment on the Saturday after the thaw, in the afternoon, when the Saturday class was over and the Mo’alem had been walked home. He brought nothing. He had thought for a long time about what to bring and had decided that the Mo’alem would only give it to a boy. He climbed the stair slowly with his hand on the rail, and it rang under his feet. The Mo’alem knew him before he knocked. They sat in the two chairs by the window. The room was warm again and smelled of Bà Sáu’s rice soup and of the radiator. Nabil asked about his health, and was told, and asked about his stomach, and was told it was a stomach again, thanks be to God and to Dr. Nabil’s water heater, and they were quiet a while. Then Nabil said that he had a question he had been carrying around for a year and had not been able to put down. It was about the building fund. He had given, he said, a great deal of money to the new church, and he would give more. He had given to the monasteries in Egypt, to the bishop’s charities, to the orphans in Upper Egypt, to the family of every man in the parish who lost his job in the oil bust, and he did not say any of this as a boast, he said it as an accountant wo

sections.heading: VI. The Back Row
sections.text: The building committee met the following week, on Zoom, and Dr. Nabil Habashy proposed that a part of the fund, a large part, be set aside before anything was poured for the dome, for the parishioners who had come out of the freeze with burst pipes and no insurance, and for the apartment complex behind the tire shop on Pipeline Road, where the water had come through three ceilings, and for whatever else the Mo’alem might point at, though the Mo’alem had not pointed at anything and would not. There was an argument. He won it. He was used to winning arguments, and this time he did not enjoy it, and he noticed that. Then he went to Abouna and asked to be made a member of the Saturday class. Abouna thought he was joking. The Saturday class was for boys. Dr. Nabil was the chairman of the building committee and the oldest deacon in the parish by rank and knew more Coptic than the priest did. Dr. Nabil said that was true, and that he knew the words to every hymn in the book, and that he had not learned one of them properly since he was twelve years old, and that he would like to learn them now from the Mo’alem, the old way, by ear, one line at a time, before one of them died, and he did n

title: Black Honey
logline: In the Texas freeze, a blind Coptic cantor sends a boy across the ice to ask the parish's proudest man for hot water.
